All four pt.newsroom home-page directions are archived on the site, at full size, with the reason each was drawn and the reason three were not chosen. /pt-newsroom/directions.html renders the five artboards of 13 September — the chosen broadsheet at 1440px and 390px, then the dense capture-ordered ledger, the dark graph-first cover and the magazine with the claims underlined in the text — each from its own source under pt-newsroom/design/, each with the motivation and trade-off that were written beside it on the design canvas (kept as canvas.json, so the page reads the notes rather than restating them), and each labelled chosen or not chosen. The page says it is an archive, not a menu. Five more typefaces are vendored for the three archived directions — Archivo, JetBrains Mono, Space Grotesk, Bodoni Moda and Karla, latin subsets as variable woff2 files, all under the SIL Open Font License and attributed in LICENSES.md — so no design on the site fetches anything from a third party at render time. The chosen-design page links to the archive; the archive is in the Portugal menu, the sitemap, llms.txt and section 16 of the commissioning brief.

The pt.newsroom home page is a page, not a picture. /pt-newsroom/ renders the chosen design at full size — the 1440px broadsheet in a frame that scrolls sideways on a narrow screen, and the 390px phone version beside it — from the design sources kept verbatim in the repository (pt-newsroom/design/Main.dc and MainPhone.dc). The builder scopes the design’s stylesheet so it cannot restyle the site chrome around it and edits nothing else; a change to the design is a change to the source file. The page says on its face that the site does not exist yet, that the copy is the Portugal section’s data of 13 September and is not maintained, and that the links inside the mock-up go nowhere. Two typefaces are vendored: Newsreader and IBM Plex Mono, latin subsets as woff2 under assets/fonts/, both under the SIL Open Font License and attributed in LICENSES.md, loaded only by the pages that use them. The design had specified them and the site had been fetching them from Google Fonts at render time, which is the dependency the rest of the site refuses for its code; the renders in section 16 of the commissioning brief, which had shown fallback faces for the same reason, are redrawn with the real ones. The page is in the Portugal menu, the footer’s What runs column, the front page’s brief card, the sitemap and llms.txt.

The things that run get their own doors: three top-level menus, a front-page band, a footer column, and every page in llms.txt. Until now the Governance Wire, Portugal Startups and the no-server databases were single links inside Rights & ops, one hop from anywhere and invisible from the front page. The nav is now eight groups: the three running instances sit between the argument and the record, each with its own submenu — the floor, the state map and the research runs under the Governance Wire; the wire, graph, files, connections, Summit, speakers, organisations, changes, sources, method, team, notice, limits and the pt.newsroom brief under Portugal Startups; the argument and the two consoles under Databases. The group label is always a link to the hub, so nothing is reachable only by opening a menu. The front page gains a band, What runs on this site, with a card per instance and one for the pt.newsroom commissioning brief; the markdown twin carries the same section. The footer gains a What runs column. llms.txt now names the three running instances in its opening properties, lists every Portugal story and team page by path, and says which of the three are human-reviewed.

v0.3.5 13 Sep 2026 The pt.newsroom.sgit.ai home page has a chosen direction, and the commissioning brief now carries it. Four home-page mockups were drafted for the Portuguese-language newsroom on 13 September — a classic broadsheet, a dense capture-ordered ledger, a dark graph-first cover, and a magazine with the claims underlined in the text — all drawn with the Portugal section’s real data of that day. The editor of record chose the broadsheet. Section 16 of the commissioning brief records the choice with two renders (1440px and 390px) and the system behind it — paper and ink values, the two faces, rules rather than boxes, the order of the page, what is deliberately not on it — so the agent that builds the site inherits a decision rather than a question. The three unchosen directions are kept on a second page of the design canvas and are not published. v0.3.4 13 Sep 2026

The graph learns what the speakers’ pages say: topics, industries, technologies, ideas and offerings — and a connections page that answers who should talk to whom, at organisation level, as queries. Sixty-four more frozen sources. Each speaker’s own page on the event site is now fetched, frozen and hashed like every other source (88 in the register, from 24). Two things are read from each page and nothing is reproduced: the event’s own Topics list for that speaker, verbatim (60 of 64 pages carry one; 23 distinct topics), and the words on the page that match a published lexicon of 57 patterns for industries, technologies, ideas, services and products. A derived tag carries the matched words on the edge and nothing else; it says the page contains those words, which is all it says. The ontology grows by six types and five verbs, each with its Portuguese: Topic (speaks_on / fala_sobre), Industry (active_in / atua_em), Technology (uses / usa), Idea (advocates / defende), Service and Product (offers / oferece). Two new taxonomy classes say which is which: Themes for the event’s vocabulary, Derived by formula for ours. The graph is 329 nodes and 1,106 edges in ten packs; the two new packs are off by default. The triples grow to 4,001 and the tag nodes carry their pattern as a property, so the SPARQL console can show the formula beside the result. Connections: who should be talking, who could be buying from whom, who could help whom. Three SQL queries at organisation level, run at build and stored with their SQL so the identical query runs in the browser console. The unit is the organisation a speaker is listed under, because the data-protection notice refuses any characterisation of a named person and “X should talk to Y” is one; the person-level join is a query away for a reader who wants it, and this page does not make it. The notice now lists the two new categories held, and the refusals are reworded rather than quietly relaxed. Three more gates. 16: every Topic node is on the frozen page verbatim, and every topic on a frozen page is in the graph. 17: every derived edge re-derives — the lexicon pattern is run again on the frozen bytes, no match no edge, and every match must have an edge, so a tag can be neither typed in nor left out by hand. 18: the connections rows are what their SQL gives. The databases section gains three tables (person_topics, person_tags, lexicon), three SQL and two SPARQL worked queries, and a build-time cross-check that the connections SQL returns the same row counts against its tables as it did on the Portugal page.

Databases with no server: SQLite and a SPARQL store running in the reader’s browser over the Portugal section’s own files. A new section, and the argument first. This site has no server. The Portugal section is JSON files in a git repository with a hash for each. Two real database engines now run over exactly those files in the visitor’s browser, compiled to WebAssembly — nothing uploaded, nothing queried remotely, the store discarded when the tab closes. The files are the database; the engines are readers. It is the pattern the estate already runs (sgit.ai’s RiskMandate vault, where “the browser becomes the database”; graphs.sgit.ai’s Regulation Graph, SQLite over WebAssembly, client-side and ephemeral) with the second language added, and graphs.sgit.ai’s not a graph database pitch is inherited on the page rather than quietly contradicted. The SQL console: sql.js 1.14.2 (SQLite, MIT, vendored), twelve tables built on load from a loader spec that names the file and field behind every column, and thirteen worked queries — a count by role class, the programme as a table, who arrived between snapshots, every verb with its inverse in both languages, a path as a sentence the SQL way, and a recursive CTE that walks two hops from the event, which is the query that shows where SQL stops being the natural language for a graph. The graph console: Oxigraph 0.5.11 (SPARQL 1.1, MIT or Apache-2.0, vendored, 3.9 MB and said so) over triples.nt, which the Portugal graph build now writes beside graph.json: 1,982 triples under one stated IRI scheme, the ontology inside the store, every inverse declared with owl:inverseOf and walked with ^, labels in English and Portuguese so a path reads aloud from the store alone. Eleven worked queries, each shown beside the same question in Cypher, which is displayed and not run: Kùzu would run it and is 73 MB unpacked, and the choice is recorded on the page. The build is the test. Every SQL example is executed at build with Python’s sqlite3 against tables built from the same spec the browser uses; every SPARQL example with pyoxigraph over the same triples. A query that fails or comes back empty fails the build, and the count each returned at build is printed beside it on the page, so a reader’s run can agree or differ in the open. Both consoles publish window.__tools after tool:ready, read-only, the convention the estate’s graph readers set. Also: the Portugal graph page and file explorer link to the consoles; the section README and llms.txt describe both; LICENSES.md carries the two new attributions.

Portugal Startups becomes a graph, a front page and a file explorer — and the press enters the register. The graph: 192 nodes, 298 edges, 10 types, 14 verbs. The event, 64 speakers, 61 derived organisations, 16 sessions on 3 stages, 24 frozen sources across 2 snapshots, 7 pieces of coverage and our stories, as one graph. Every edge is a verb with a distinct named inverse in English and in Portuguese, so a path reads as a sentence walked either way in either language — the commissioning brief’s rule that in a Portuguese publication the edge verbs are Portuguese verbs, applied a release early so it is a switch and not a rewrite. Nodes arrive in packs the reader switches on block by block; the one classification the graph makes rather than reads (role_class on a person) is published as a formula over the listed title and says so on every node. The instrument is graphs.sgit.ai’s, on purpose. Cytoscape.js 3.30.2 is vendored (MIT, attributed in LICENSES.md) and the control panel is that site’s altitude-graph vocabulary — radius exploration from any node, collapse and expand, path tracing read as sentences, a bounded path-query builder that says when it hits its cap, save and restore a view with every position. Packs replace levels; otherwise a reader who has used one should not have to learn the other. The page publishes window.__graph after a tool:ready event, read and view methods only, so the console, Playwright and an agent are equal consumers. The files: the platform’s vault-browser idea rendered from a manifest for a section that is not in a vault yet — every file with its SHA-256 on the left, rendered / as a graph / raw on the right. Frozen third-party pages are listed and hashed and deliberately not rendered. The page says on its face that it goes when the vault browser takes over. The front page is now a newspaper’s: a lead, the wire, the programme by day, what the press says, the room as a graph, who made it, and the brief for whoever builds the next one. Seven third-party pages are in the register, each fetched, frozen and hashed before it could be cited, summarised in our words and never quoted; gate 15 fails the build on a long quotation. An eighth returned 404 and is recorded as excluded with the reason. Two of the seven — AICEP Portugal Global and Portugal Business News, both 29 July — report a 48-hour Guinness pitch marathon on 16–17 September that the event’s own agenda page, four days out, does not list. That is the third story, and it is the first to stand on sources with more than one publisher. Three more gates. 13: the graph conforms to its ontology — every verb declared with a distinct inverse and Portuguese, every node a declared type naming a registered source, every edge within its verb’s domain and range, and nobody in the graph who is neither on the published list nor marked as no longer listed. 14: every session title in sessions.json appears verbatim in the frozen agenda, because a transcription is a claim. 15: coverage is frozen before it is cited and never reproduced. Also fixed: the whole-site link scanner reads href=" inside inline JavaScript as a link; the explorer now emits single-quoted attributes from its templates rather than teaching the gate to be cleverer.

The notice that should have shipped with v0.3.0, and a commissioning brief for pt.newsroom.sgit.ai. The correction first. v0.3.0 published the names, roles and organisations of 64 people this site did not get the data from, and it did so with no data-protection notice, no stated lawful basis and no route to object. That is the wrong order — the notice belongs before the first named person, not after — and the notice now live says so on its own face rather than quietly fixing it. The journalistic derogation is not claimed, and that is the substantive finding. Article 24(3) of Portugal’s Lei 58/2019 conditions processing for journalistic purposes on the national legislation governing access to and exercise of the profession, which an unaccredited publication produced by agents does not satisfy. So the basis is legitimate interests, with a written three-limb balancing test, and the notice exists because Article 14(5)(b) makes the disproportionate-effort exemption conditional on making the information publicly available. Removal on request is unconditional — no reason required, none asked for. The page carries a Portuguese summary, because several of the people named are Portuguese. None of it is legal advice and no lawyer has reviewed it. Two new gates, because a refusal without an enforcer is a sentence. Check 11 fails the build if an email address, telephone number or personal postal address appears anywhere in the section’s data — enforced where the data is parsed, not where it is rendered, so a contact detail cannot reach the data and then be hidden by a template. Verified by injecting one and confirming the build fails. Check 12 fails the build if any page that names individuals does not link to the notice, because a notice nobody can find from the page that named them is a file rather than a measure. And the 12 May design page is updated rather than rewritten. That design is still unlaunched and still says so; what changed is that a much smaller first instance now runs, and that its open question 5 — who is the editor of record — is answered after four months, with the constraint the design did not anticipate: not as journalism. The commissioning brief is the first document in the pack written to be executed rather than read. It cuts the fifteen-department design to three, replaces the seven-stories-in-seven-days test with one story whose whole process is visible, settles the subdomain by wildcard-certificate mechanics, sorts the agents into four tiers by what each can write, and rules that in a natively Portuguese publication the graph edge verbs are Portuguese verbs — because a path that does not read as a sentence in the reader’s language has the wrong edges, and an English ontology behind a Portuguese interface fails that test while looking finished.

A second publication: Portugal Startups — and the first section on this site whose sources are primary, frozen and hashed. The door The Governance Wire cannot open. That section specifies a frozen state — a hashed byte copy of the source — and carries blocked: true against it, which is why every fact there is secondary and nothing is anchored. Here the path runs: fetch, freeze, hash, extract, diff. 17 frozen files across 2 dated snapshots, every SHA-256 published and re-verified by the gate on every build. A claim on this section points at bytes in this repository, not at a URL that may have moved. The first beat is Startup Summit Lisbon 2026, which opens on 17 September. It was chosen on the criterion the 12 May 2026 brief argued for — small enough to map comprehensively, large enough to be interesting. An event that publishes its own speaker list has a closeable graph: 64 speakers and 61 organisations, derived from the cards rather than typed by hand, with the 2 placeholder values flagged rather than cleaned away. Freezing twice produced the first story. The same page, captured on 8 and 13 September, went from 60 speakers to 64: 5 names added and 1 no longer listed. Both copies and both hashes are in the repository, which is the only reason anyone can now say that — the earlier version exists nowhere else a reader can reach. The removal is published with no reason attached, and gate check 4 fails the build if any page implies one: withdrawal, a clash, a duplicate and an editing error are indistinguishable from outside, and guessing would be the easiest way for a publication like this to harm a real person. Open question 5 is answered. The original brief left the editor of record undecided, and this site called it the question it should be most uncomfortable about. Dinis Cruz is the named editor of record and reviews every page before it publishes — a deliberate departure from the fully-agentic sibling, because this beat is about named people in a small ecosystem rather than about regulations. Frozen copies are .snapshot, not .html. They are unmodified bytes of another organisation’s pages held as evidence, and serving a browsable mirror of somebody’s whole site under this domain would contradict the one rule this publication has. The extension keeps them verifiable and un-servable at once. Speaker biographies are not extracted, stored or published for the same reason; gate check 10 fails the build if any node field grows long enough to be one. Ten section checks on top of the whole-site gate, covering hash re-verification, derived-not-typed organisations, no-reason-for-removals, no-target-reported-as-result, and no claim of a Portuguese edition that does not exist.

The generator for /governance/ had never been committed. The site was green, deployed, and unrebuildable. A bare build/ rule in a generic Python .gitignore matches at every depth. It was excluding governance/build/ — build.py, floor.py, gates.py, the whole section generator and its thirteen checks — from every commit since v0.2.6. Nothing broke, and that is the point: the generated HTML was committed and only the thing that generated it was missing, so the site deployed correctly three releases running while nobody could have rebuilt it from a clone. It surfaced by accident. The debrief shipped in v0.2.8 links to floor.py on GitHub so the sibling sites can copy it. Checking those links found three 404s. This is the second time the same rule has done this. It caught admin/build/ at v0.1.0, where CI failed loudly with MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and the fix was to re-include that one path by name — which is exactly why it recurred. The rule is now root-anchored (/build/), which is what the Python template meant, and no <section>/build/ can be swallowed again. Fixing the instance twice would have guaranteed a third time, so it is now check 10 of the whole-site gate: nothing under a build/ directory, and no .py, .js or .mjs file anywhere, may be excluded by .gitignore. Verified by restoring the old rule and confirming the gate fails with three errors, then restoring the fix. A generated page whose generator is not in the repository cannot be rebuilt by anyone who clones it. The debrief gains a paragraph on it under “where the code is”, because a document telling other sites to copy a generator owes them the reason its own links were broken.

A debrief for the sibling sites: how the agentic team became a room you click around, and how to build one. The first document here that reports on shipped work rather than specifying work to do. Every site on this network publishes its agentic team the same way — a roster and an ordered list — and neither shows what any role is holding, why it is stuck, or what it will refuse. The floor makes the team a place instead. The debrief carries the parts that transfer: the one rule that separates the room from a mock-up (every word it speaks is derived at build time from the same files the pipeline runs on), the genre-versus-work line on the adventure-game reference, the SVG and responsive mechanics, a porting recipe with candidate mappings for five siblings, and the gate that fails the build if the drawn route stops matching the declared pipeline. It states what has not been proven, which is the half a debrief usually omits: one implementation, one site, one day; no user testing; no screen-reader testing; Chromium only; untested past seven actors; and the dialogue is 28 fixed strings rather than a conversation. Four screenshots — the first images ever published on this site. They live in the markdown, so an agent fetching the raw document gets them too. A defect found and fixed on the way in. llms-full.txt says it carries “every markdown document in the brief pack”, and brief 09 had never been added to its ORDER list — so that claim had been false since v0.2.5. Both 09 and 10 are now in it; the file grew from 15,000 to 23,167 words. Also fixed in the floor itself: with JavaScript off the verb bar rendered and did nothing. It now carries a <noscript> block saying so and pointing at the table that holds the same information — found by testing the degradation paths rather than assuming them, which is advice the debrief gives and therefore had to follow.

The Governance Wire gains a newsroom: a floor you can click around, a state map of how a story moves, a page per agent role, and the Researcher's first real run. The floor is a point-and-click scene. Seven desks, a verb bar — look at, talk to, hand over, ask what they refuse — and a dialogue box. The genre is borrowed and everything in it is ours: our palette, our figures drawn as inline SVG, our verbs, our writing. What a desk says about its workload is read from desk.json at build time, so the room cannot report a queue the newsroom does not have. A token travels the pipeline route through the desks; the route and team.json's seven steps are compared by gate check 13, because a room that keeps drawing a workflow nobody runs is a lie that looks like decoration. Nine states, and one shut door. The state map names, for each state, the one role that can advance it and the condition the next role will not take the work without. frozen — a hashed byte copy of the source — carries blocked: true, and nothing has ever passed it. That single closed door is why every fact in the graph reads secondary, why nothing is anchored, and why the two stories already on the wire went round it rather than through it. A folder and a page per role, following graphs.sgit.ai's making-a-book team: the definition in full, the doors only that role can open, what is on its desk, and an honest inventory of the three directories the inherited shape has that ours does not yet fill. The first research run is real, and its failures are published. The Researcher searched the beat for 28 August 2026, tried six URLs, read two European Commission pages in full, and found that the Article 6(5) classification guidelines due on 2 February are still marked draft — 207 days past the statutory deadline, last touched 23 July, with no date given for a final version. Four candidates were proposed with their weaknesses attached; one was recommended, and the pick is recorded separately, because proposing is the Researcher's job and choosing is not. Two Council of the EU pages returned 403 to our fetch. They are excluded from the register and recorded as unreachable from here — our egress, not a claim about those pages. Gate check 11 now makes that structural: a URL that did not resolve cannot appear in the source register, and its note must distinguish our reach from the state of the page. Seven new gate checks (7–13), 11 new pages, 3 new machine surfaces — workflow, desk, research. Section v0.2.0.

The commissioning brief stops being a document: /governance/ is a first, running MVP of the risk-and-governance publication. Built to the conventions graphs.sgit.ai arrived at over v0.4–v0.6: JSON is the source of truth for structure, markdown for prose, and the HTML is a projection of both. Five machine surfaces — graph, ontology, sources, stories, team — and a generator that cannot render a claim the data does not carry. The section is self-contained: its own data, prose, generator and gate, depending on nothing but the shared stylesheet and chrome, so it can be lifted to its own domain whole. The one convention deliberately not copied. The sibling renders markdown in the browser and fails CI if a page lags its source. This section renders at build time instead, because this site lists crawler-invisibility of client-assembled pages as an inherited existential risk and a story whose text is not in the HTML is a story an agent cannot read. Gate check 5 re-derives every story page from its markdown, so the no-drift guarantee is kept without paying that cost. Fully agentic, and the pages lead with what that costs. Seven agent roles, each with a centre of gravity and a written list of what it refuses; no human reviews a page before publication. In that posture the Editor's refusals are the only thing standing where a duty editor would be, so they are rules rather than judgement calls — chief among them that no named organisation is assessed, there being no legal sign-off. A generated disclaimer block appears on every page and gate check 6 fails the build if it is missing from one. The honesty the gate enforces. Every fact in the seed graph is secondary — taken from a sibling site's reading of a text, never from the text — and nothing is anchored. Check 4 fails the build if any page claims a verified anchor while no node carries one, and it caught exactly that during the build: an ontology definition described a Fact as “anchored to a byte range”, which overclaimed for this release. The definition was rewritten rather than the check loosened. 19 nodes, 22 edges, 5 sources all re-fetched and confirmed 200 on the day, 2 stories, 8 pages, 6 section gates on top of the whole-site gate.

The pack gains its first forward-looking document: a commissioning brief for a risk-and-governance publication, and with it the reciprocal statement the Risk Mandate inversion has owed since v0.2.0. Everything in the pack until now was material this site was built from, frozen at 21 August 2026. This is a publication to build — assembled from newsroom, graphs, risks, pki, the vault layer and the personalisation pipeline, with riskmandate.ai as its named customer. It is labelled v1.1 addendum rather than dated into the v1.0 pack, and the generator was changed to make the pack line per-document so it could say so: misstating a document's own provenance is the one failure this site's gate exists to prevent. The argument that makes it worth commissioning. The Portugal instance required a ≥200-entity graph before it could report competently, never built it, and never launched. A risk-and-governance beat inverts that constraint: 1,523 nodes and 1,944 edges of EU AI Act, three worked risk graphs and a 42-concept ontology are already public on the sibling sites. The publication starts where Portugal was still trying to get to. The commercial claim is architectural, not promotional — a split of the grounding ladder. The publication owns Evidence and Fact for the public regulatory world; the customer owns Reality, Twin and Measure in their own vault; and a Vulnerability, by the published formula, exists only where the two meet. That is why the brief is written as a news operation whose first customer is a risk product rather than the reverse: the inversion is the whole point, and dropping it would have made this a compliance feature with a masthead. Two things the brief refuses to smooth over. A publication that profits when risk looks severe has a structural incentive to inflate it, so the brief answers that with mechanism rather than promise — severity computed from edge count, facts-only, absence reports as the counterweight — plus a hard rule that no assessment of a named third party publishes without their right of reply as a node in the same vault. And it half-answers Portugal's open question 5: the editor of record is whoever's signature is on the current interval. The legal half stays open, and is raised to T9 as a precondition for launch rather than a detail. Also: the eighth instance is now listed on /mvps/, and T2 is advanced rather than closed — the brief is the statement, the standalone comparison page it named is still unwritten.

New section: /mvps/ — the part of the source corpus that asks what would actually launch first. The site was built almost entirely from the corpus's argumentative material: the thesis, corrections, provenance, the economics. A second cluster in the same repository was catalogued in the brief pack but never surfaced as pages — seven briefs, dated 10 April to 17 May 2026, in which the newsroom is specified not as one product but as a series of small, separately launchable publication instances. A bilingual country publication with a trip for a deadline; an eleven-role agentic newsroom to run it; an evidence-backed report tool small enough to ship in days; an eight-phase rebuild of a live property; seven Creative Commons business templates published so someone else could build them. Three pages: the index of the programme, the flagship instance in full, and the seed companies. The reason it belongs on this site is the gap it measures. Fifteen public departments is what this site argues for; eight of fifteen is what the first MVP was scoped to actually run, recorded at the time as an open decision. Alongside it, two more open decisions from the same register — the launch domain and the reader-validation specification — and the newsroom brief's own six unanswered questions, republished unresolved. Open question 5 is the one this site should be least comfortable with: a daily agentic publication with no named editor of record and no answer on who carries legal responsibility for what it publishes. A site arguing that provenance must be walkable has an unclosed chain at precisely the point where it has to terminate in a person, and that is now stated on the page rather than left in a repository. Also recorded: the two source briefs of 12 May contradict each other on whether the publication launches bilingual or in one language. Neither this section nor llms.txt resolves the disagreement; both flag it, on the same reasoning as everywhere else here — silently picking a side would be the site editing its own sources. Boundaries applied rather than assumed. The publishing-substrate mechanics in the 17 May architecture brief belong to sgit.ai and are cited rather than re-explained, per the sibling boundary; only the third primitive — the management layer, where editorial state lives — is treated here, because that one is the decision graph given somewhere to be stored. The commercial detail attached to the live property in that same cluster is Tier 3 and is absent: the ideas are published, the pricing, clients and entity detail are not, and the omission is stated on the page rather than left to be noticed.

Front-page links were rendering flush against the viewport edge instead of aligned with the text they follow. A section.band is full-bleed and had no horizontal padding at all. Every component inside one carries its own centred column — .blurb 660px, .note and .proof 1100px, .cards 1160px, .split 1000px — so anything without such a rule fell back to the full band width starting at x=0. Two bare

links on the front page started their text at 1px where the note directly above them starts at 109px, and the for-an-agent block spanned the whole viewport. Nothing overflowed and nothing warned; it simply read as a misalignment against the very components it sat between. Fixed at the root rather than per element: the band now carries a gutter, so nothing inside one can reach the viewport edge whatever column rule it has, and the remaining block children — a bare paragraph, a list, the agent block — take the same 1100px column .note already used. Scoped to direct children, so the identical elements nested inside .note, .cards and every main.doc page are untouched. Verified across eleven widths from 1600px to 360px: the four text columns now agree to within 2px at every one, and the gutter also fixed a separate phone-width defect the measurement exposed — .blurb putting its text 2px from the edge at 390px, because a 660px max-width stops constraining anything once the viewport is narrower than 660. This is the third defect in three releases that the gate could not see, after the wrapping nav bar and the raw-markdown documents page. All three were visual or conventional rather than structural, and all three were found by looking at the shipped site. The gate checks that a page is correct; it has no opinion about whether it looks right. That is a real limit and it is worth stating rather than discovering again — the shared stylesheet carries all of these latent on the sibling sites too.

The published brief pack was leaking the identifiers it exists to withhold. Fixed, disclosed, and the gate that let it through has been corrected. What happened. The pack's redaction watch-list (06 §2) is a list of things not to publish, and it names each one in the course of forbidding it — a venture-capital firm, an AWS account number, an investor-facing hostname, a B2B price range. v0.2.0 published the pack verbatim, so the act of documenting the exclusion performed the disclosure: four identifiers the pack marks Tier 3 went live at /briefs/. The identifiers are now replaced with visible [redacted] markers in the published copies, and every one is recorded in the transparency note — nine redactions, in three files, with the surrounding reasoning, tiering and manifest rows fully intact. A silent redaction would have been the worse of the two options. Why the gate did not catch it. The redaction check exempted briefs/, on the reasoning that the pack "documents the watch-list by naming these". That reasoning is inverted, and it is now recorded as a comment in validate.js so it is not reintroduced. Second defect in the same check: the pricing patterns had been written from memory of the brief's prose rather than against the strings actually in the files, so they matched nothing at all. Every entry in the list is now a literal verified to appear in the source before masking, and the published pack is checked like every other file — an unredacted identifier in briefs/ now fails the build. Also shipped: /llms-full.txt, required by the pack's own house style (06 §3) and missing since v0.2.0 — llms.txt, the front page and all eleven pack documents in one fetch, because agent fetch tools frequently refuse URLs a search has not already returned. It was generating this file that surfaced the leak: the concatenation tripped the redaction check that the briefs/ exemption had been suppressing. Two remaining gaps against the brief's build order are now tracked rather than silent: T5 (/provenance/the-citation-chain/) and T6 (/infographics/, the only build-order step not started).

Two defects found by looking at the shipped site rather than at the source. The nav bar was silently breaking onto two lines below about 1400px. The row is flex-wrap:wrap, so once its contents outgrew the viewport the ★ GitHub link dropped to a second row and the header doubled in height — no overflow, no console warning, just a ragged two-row bar at the most common laptop widths. The shared stylesheet has the same latent dead zone on every sibling site, between the full-width bar and the 820px phone menu; this site hit it first because its nav row is the widest in the network. Fixed at both ends: the two longest items were trimmed (Rights & the newsroom → Rights & ops, and the stage pill to design, not built), and the stylesheet now tightens the row at 1400px and again at 1180px before collapsing to the phone menu at 1000px. Verified across an eighteen-width sweep from 1600px to 360px: one clean row at every width, and no horizontal overflow. The stylesheet half of this fix is worth carrying back to the siblings — graphs.sgit.ai wraps the same way at 1100px. /documents/ was handing readers raw .md files. On a site whose central claim is that most articles do not provide evidence, they provide a link, and the link is never followed, that was the lazy version of exactly the failure the site exists to argue against. Adopted the reader-page convention the siblings already use: admin/build/gen_documents.py generates one page per pack document, each stating the single most important thing in it and why it is on this site, then rendering the raw markdown in-page from that same file through assets/mdreader.js — so a reader page cannot drift from the document it claims to render. Ten documents now have reader pages; the two machine-readable files (the 48-row manifest and the provenance JSON) stay raw, because wrapping data in a reader page would only get in the way. The raw file is still one click away from every page and is still the stated source of truth. Neither defect was caught by the gate, and that is worth recording: the gate checks that a page is correct, not that it looks right, and not that a convention the rest of the network follows has actually been adopted here. Reader pages under documents/ are exempt from the agent-block rule as generated projections, matching the exemption issues-fs.sgit.ai makes; documents/index.html is hand-written and still owes one.

The real brief pack arrived, and this release replaces v0.1.0's content in full. v0.1.0 shipped without a brief pack, under the working assumption that this site would report on the *.sgit.ai network's own activity. That assumption was wrong: the actual commissioned brief — newsroom.sgit.ai, The Future of News — describes a site about how news gets made, proven and paid for, built from ~110,000 words across three corpora, ~68,846 of them already public and dated since February 2025. Every page from v0.1.0 built on the wrong premise has been replaced, not patched; nothing about the wrong premise is preserved, since a corrections-first site keeping a superseded page live under the old thesis would be the exact failure it argues against elsewhere. The build order from the brief, followed in full for the first five steps: the front page, /corrections/ (hub plus all five specified subpages — the 10,000-hours case, the 242-paper citation network, how a graph answers it, the self-critique on agenda, and the AI Act staleness case), /provenance/ (hub plus the £8.40 worked story, the decision graph, show-your-work and articles-as-vaults), /library/ (all ten core articles and three adjacent pieces, chronological, each carrying the provenance contract), and /economics/ (hub plus paying-the-fact-creator, trust-as-a-service, the payment rails, and the republished 2025 micropayments piece paired deliberately with the 2026 rail). Three sections shipped as single comprehensive hub pages rather than the full multi-page trees the brief specifies: /rights/, /newsroom/ and /thesis/. That is a real, stated de-scoping — tracked as task T1 — made to get the whole architecture live and gated in one release rather than shipping half of it silently complete. The provenance contract is now enforced by the gate, not just documented. A new validate.js check requires every block marked class="provenance" to state a first-published date and a working link to the original — this site's central argument, applied to itself. A second new check enforces the redaction watch-list: a fixed set of Tier 3 strings from the brief's own manifest (a named venture-capital firm, an infrastructure account number, live product pricing) may not appear anywhere in the published tree. Two honest limits, stated rather than smoothed over. The brief's own N1 request — roughly 15,000 words of likely origin material sitting in an external repository not yet retrieved — means the library's chronology may still be incomplete at the start. And several republished docs.diniscruz.ai pieces are published here as this site's own synthesis, not verbatim reproductions — the brief pack recorded their metadata in full but not their complete text, and reproducing them as if verbatim would have been exactly the provenance failure this site exists to argue against.

The "future directions" half of the site's name. Critical to state upfront: this is not an effort to replace journalists with agents. The opposite. Agents make it possible to involve more humans, in more roles, at more scale than was previously affordable.
principles

The flagship doctrine behind this section: story-centric rather than article-centric; evidence-driven by default rather than evidence as an afterthought; reader validation treated as first-class input, not an inbox nobody reads; cost tracked per story, itemised, the way the £8.40 worked example shows; and, running through all of them, human involvement maximised, not reduced.
roles

The design maps roughly a dozen agent roles onto newsroom functions — scanning for stories, first-pass research, drafting, translation, fact-check support, graphics generation — each specified as absorbing production grunt-work rather than owning editorial judgement. "Humans are the bar; agents are the volume." A specified daily operational rhythm runs from an early-morning scanning pass, through a midday publish-and-personalise window where a story fans out into its audience projections, to an afternoon and evening community window where reader contributions and corrections are actively worked rather than left to accumulate.
roles

A phased launch is specified rather than a full switch-on: starting at roughly one story a day for the first week, scaling toward several stories a day as the process proves itself, with explicit go/no-go gates between phases rather than an open-ended ramp. A companion design specifies an entity graph seeded with at least 200 real-world entities as the substrate a first regional pilot would need before it could report competently on that region's news. That pilot has a name, a country, a deadline and eleven specified roles. This page states the operating model in general; the instance it was written for states it as something that was meant to launch — including the parts that were never settled, among them who would have been the editor of record.
departments

Rather than a single "editorial" function, the newsroom design specifies departments — assignment, research, translation, fact-checking, graphics, community, corrections, and others — each as its own public page rather than an internal org chart. Show your work covers this from the transparency side; the operational point here is that default-to-publish is the working assumption — material moves toward publication unless a specific reason holds it back, rather than requiring active justification to release. Each story or briefing is treated as its own world with its own ontology and taxonomy, rather than forced into one universal schema that fits nothing well.
craft

The craft doctrine underneath the roles above is inherited, not invented here: the inverted pyramid, the five Ws, rigorous source attribution, and editorial independence as a non-negotiable line agents do not get to cross. One idea from that doctrine is distinctive enough to name directly: the second story — the follow-up piece, published after the news cycle has moved on, that returns to check what actually happened once the dust settled (Three Mile Island and Equifax are the doctrine's own reference cases). A newsroom optimised entirely for the first story and never for the second is optimised for attention, not for the record.

Abstract: Once the book is a graph, an agent can assemble it. And if an agent can assemble it, it can assemble a version for one person: the chapters that matter to them, at their altitude, with examples from their world, eventually in their language. I would send it as a PDF, made for them and not published. The brief for each one already exists, in a way: the agents that run my correspondence keep a folder for each person I work with, with what we talked about and how they think, so I can say, here is this person, make them their edition. And then the part I really like: pay for it as you read it, the way this newsroom already works. Start with five pounds of credit; the more of the book you read, the more you pay; the edition starts in your browser, and you can keep it in your vault. This article maps how that would work, what has to stay private, and what is still open. It is also an example of how innovation works for me: I know the book's website is coming and how it will be built, so I am already building on top of it.
A book for one reader: what the edition is made from, how an agent assembles it, and the reader's side.
in-short

An agent can assemble the book. Once it is a graph, at every altitude. So it can assemble an edition for one person. Their chapters, their altitude, their examples, later their language. Sent to them, not published. A PDF made for them. The brief is private. It comes from my correspondence notes, and stays there. Pay as you read. Start with five pounds; the more you read, the more you pay. It starts in the browser. And can be kept in the reader's vault.
one

I love this idea. The more the book becomes a semantic graph, the more it can be assembled programmatically, by an agent, even a cloud session, from its parts. A website to finish the book makes the book a graph, at every altitude, with the narrative as a path through it. An agent that can walk that path can walk a different one for one person. So I could say: here is this person. They are a designer moving into product, they think in pictures, they are worried about AI taking their job. Make them their edition. The agent picks the chapters that matter to them, at their altitude, uses examples from their world, puts the infographics first, and, eventually, writes it in their language and with their culture in mind. It is the same idea as sending someone a newsletter written for them, applied to a whole book.
brief-source

In a way, the brief for each person already exists. The agents that run my correspondence, the agent team as it runs, keep a CRM that is one folder per person, with what we talked about and where each fact came from. That is exactly what an editor would want to know before choosing what to give someone to read. Which makes the privacy rule important. That folder is private, and it stays private. The agent reads it to make the choices, and the edition carries the result, not the notes: no private detail about the person, nothing they told me in confidence, nothing they would be surprised to see. The edition is sent to them, not published. And when the directory of people and their keys exists, it can be encrypted to their key, so only they can open it.
pay

Then the part that made me say yes out loud: let people pay for the book as they read it, the way this newsroom already charges for articles. Paying after the value describes the experiment: you start with five pounds of credit, each piece you read uses a few pence, you can set the price from free to double, and the balance can go below zero without blocking you. For the book, the same principle: start with five pounds. The more of the book you read, the more you pay. And it should work for the personalised edition too, because the meter counts what you read, whichever edition you read it in. It starts locally, in the reader's browser, as the meter does today; and there should be the option to save it, and the reading, in the reader's own vault.
how

The book as a graph, at every altitude, on the book's website. A brief for one reader, written privately from my notes, or chosen by the reader on a form: their role, their altitude, their language. An agent assembles the edition from the graph: the chapters, the order, the altitude, the examples, the infographics. A PDF, or the edition in the browser, sent to that person only. The meter, starting with five pounds of credit, charging for what is read. The reader's vault, if they want to keep the edition and their reading.
innovation

This is also an example of how I think innovation works. I now know the book's website is going to exist, and I know how we build things here: vaults, graphs, the meter, agents with roles. So I can already build on top of it, in my head and in a brief, before it exists. Each thing we build becomes something the next idea stands on.
limits

Nothing is built. Not the website, not the graph, not the editions. Personal editions are sent, not published. And the private notes behind them stay private. Translation and culture come later. The first editions would be in English, at an altitude, with examples chosen. The meter is an experiment. Whether people pay for a book this way is what we would find out. If you would like to be one of the first readers of an edition made for you, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: My business partner is at the WestCap CISO Summit in New York this week, from 20 to 22 October, where security leaders, investors and founders meet. This page does two jobs. It is a briefing for him, and it is a place for the people he meets to come and see what we do. The summit's main day has panels on securing AI use and AI governance, on preparing for an AI attack, and on using AI to secure a company. Our work sits right across them. An Agent Behaviour Policy is a written description, for one agent in one deployment, of everything it can do, what it was authorised to do, the difference between the two, and what actually stands in the way. RiskMandate is where we sell one, from £10 for the pack to £1,500 for one a professional signs, with early users helped at no cost in exchange for telling us where it is wrong. The idea at the centre is one sentence: a control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include. Below, that idea is said six ways, for CISOs, for AI governance and audit, for incident response and red teams, for AI-for-defence vendors, for investors and for founders, each with the articles and vaults to read first. Everything here is open, under CC BY 4.0.
One idea, six rooms: the same point said for each kind of person at the summit, with the article to read first.
in-short

The summit is about modern defence, and AI runs through it. Governance, AI attacks, AI for defence. An Agent Behaviour Policy writes down what an agent can do and may do. And what actually stands in the way. Only a rule kept out of the agent's reach is a control. That one sentence is the test. RiskMandate sells the policy for the agent you run. Four levels, £10 to £1,500, paid once. Early users get help at no cost. In exchange for telling us where it is wrong. The idea, said for six kinds of person. With the articles and vaults to read first. Everything is open. Policies, vocabulary and code, under CC BY 4.0 and Apache 2.0.
summit

The WestCap CISO Summit runs from 20 to 22 October in New York, where, in the organisers' words, "security leaders, investors and founders meet to share the ideas shaping modern defense". Tuesday is for WestCap and its portfolio companies, on business-risk alignment, business process mapping and operational security. Wednesday is the main event, at Chelsea Piers, with five panels: rewiring the hacker pipeline; securing AI use and AI governance; preparing for an AI attack; using AI to secure your company; and industrialised abuse at mobile scale. Thursday is a startup Shark Tank, where six cybersecurity startups pitch. Three of Wednesday's five panels are about AI, and the companies on them are a good map of the room: compliance and attestation (Drata, Schellman), data and AI security (Bedrock Data), supply chain security (Socket), risk consultancy and incident response (Control Risks, Kroll, Sygnia), offensive security (Bishop Fox), AI-native defence (Nebulock), application delivery and security (F5), and a model provider (OpenAI).
what

An Agent Behaviour Policy is, in the words of abp.sgit.ai, "a written description, for one agent in one deployment, of everything it can do, what it was authorised to do, the difference between the two, and what actually stands in the way". RiskMandate, at riskmandate.ai, writes that policy for the agent you actually run: "Give agents access. Not free rein." The test at the centre of it is one sentence: "A control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include."
what

The words matter. The grant is everything the agent can do, measured. The mandate is what it was authorised to do, asked of the person who deployed it. The delta is the difference, derived, never written by hand. The barrier is what stands in the way of each capability: nothing, a sentence in the prompt, a setting the agent's own account can change, or a boundary kept by a system out of its reach. Only the last is a control. The site puts the point well: "Your agent can do three hundred and forty things is a shrug. Your agent can do three hundred and forty things and you authorised twelve is a finding."
cisos

The question is the one they already have to answer: what can each agent reach, and what actually stops it? A policy answers it per agent, in one document the CEO, the CTO and the CISO can all stand behind. Start with what can your agent reach?, the explainer written for the person who has to decide. Then hope or enforcement, one agent built three ways, with its vault; every risk is already accepted, with the risk acceptance vault; and who are you protecting against?, six threat tiers, with its vault. Ten questions, one graph takes Phil Venables' ten questions for a CISO's management tool and answers them as a graph, with the Thistlewood twin.
governance

For the people who attest: an agent's logs are a self-report, and a rule the agent can change is a setting, not a control. Your agent's logs are a self-report is our answer to an ISO 42001 lead auditor. Four frameworks, one agent maps the OECD principles, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act onto one agent's policy. Policy as code needs a policy first is about who can change the code that keeps a rule. And this week's trusted framework for agentic finance lines our work up with the four elements the FCA has named: agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution, with the Pellbridge agents, six bank agents replayed through one day with and without a policy.
ir

For the people who arrive afterwards: the incidents we have mapped are reach beyond mandate, and the policy is the map of where to look. Attacks rewritten as mandates takes a published list of 28 supply-chain incidents and rewrites each one that way. Footprint and blast radius separates what an agent touched from what it could have, and what each vendor's hooks can see, stop and change is the field guide to where an agent can be stopped. For skills and plugins, a skill behaviour policy.
defence

For the companies building agents to defend: those agents have a grant too, and a lot of it. A policy beside the prompt proposes that every agent takes a behaviour policy as an input, next to its prompt, which the vendor accepts and enforces as far as it can. Are hooks the sweet spot? walks rules out of the prompt and into hooks, one by one, and three policies for an agent separates behaviour, decisions and workflows, with the Northstar twin.
investors

For the people deciding where the money goes: liability needs a line, and the line is what each agent was told not to do, written down, and what keeps it. The policy draws the liability line makes the case, and ten questions about RiskMandate answers the questions an investor asks, from what stops a big platform absorbing it to who is liable.
founders

For the people pitching on Thursday: can you sell it? is my advice to start selling what you have now, however rough, because selling is how you learn. And our first customers is what we are doing ourselves this month.
value

Most of the room sells something that acts at runtime: a gateway, an agent, a scanner, an audit. An Agent Behaviour Policy is what those are configured from. In abp.sgit.ai's words: "Not a guardrail. It is what guardrails are compiled from." So it sits alongside them, not against them: it tells a gateway which rules to keep, an auditor what to test, an incident responder where to look, and an insurer what contains the agent. It describes and does not judge, and, again from the site, "A policy cannot be dangerous. A deployment can." It is also open. The vocabulary and the policies are CC BY 4.0, and the code is Apache 2.0, so anyone in the room can use it, including in their own products.
next

Read the explainer. What can your agent reach?, then one article from your section above. Pick one agent. The policy is per agent, per deployment; one is enough to start. Join early access. At riskmandate.ai, early users name an agent, and we build its policy and correct it with them, at no cost, "in exchange for telling us where it is wrong". Or buy a level. The pricing page has four, from £10 for the pack to £1,500 for one a professional signs, per agent, per deployment, paid once. Talk to us. Through the contact page, or to my business partner, in New York this week.
limits

We are not part of the summit's programme. This is a briefing, not a session. No speaker is quoted. The panels and companies are from the public agenda. The fit is our reading. Each company's own site says what it does. Two of the four levels had not been sold by mid-September. The pricing page says so. The vaults are illustrative. Their banks, retailers and numbers are invented.

Abstract: The browsers on my iPhone have frustrated me to the point where I would like to build one. Not a general browser: an app that only opens my newsroom, where I left it, knows what I have read, opens my vault, keeps my tabs, works offline, never reloads a page on its own, lets me build my own reading workflows, and receives what my agents send me. A year ago I would have put up with it. Now I can do something about it, and that changes how much bad interface I am willing to tolerate. This is the brief. The facts decide most of it. In the UK an iPhone app that browses the web must use WebKit; Firefox and Chrome on iOS are WebKit too. Passkeys inside an app and push notifications both need Apple's paid developer membership, and the app has to be built on a Mac, so not by a cloud session like the one that writes this site. The one real unknown is whether the passkey extension the vault depends on works inside an app's web view, so that is the first thing to test. And there is a second point, which matters more than the app. Once it works, it will be part of my day, and I will not want to maintain it. Not because I cannot; because it is not my focus. Being able to compile a Linux kernel does not mean I want to. Even power users will pay someone to keep the thing they built working, and this app is the first example I will live with.
A browser for one, sketched on an iPhone: tabs, the vault, an inbox from the agents, and reading workflows.
in-short

The browsers on my phone have lost my patience. Wrong page, reloads, no offline, no memory of where I was. So the idea is a browser for one. An app that only reads my newsroom, and knows what I have read. In the UK it has to be WebKit. So are Firefox and Chrome on iOS; other engines are allowed only in the EU and Japan. It needs the paid developer membership and a Mac. For passkeys in the app, for push, and for building it. One unknown, tested first. Whether the vault's passkey extension works inside an app. Empowerment lowers patience. When I can build it, a bad interface stops being something I put up with. I will still pay someone to maintain it. Being able to does not mean wanting to.
why

Every day I read and manage this newsroom from my iPhone, and every browser I use gets something wrong. One loads the wrong thing; another refreshes the page I was halfway through; none has a good offline mode; none keeps track of where I was across days; none understands what I have been doing; all of them use too much of the screen for themselves. I have lived with this for years, like everyone. What changed is not the browsers. It is me. After weeks of building with agents, things that would have sounded unreasonable, like writing my own browser for one site, do not sound unreasonable any more. I have hit this problem enough times, and I now have enough leverage, that the frustration has turned into a brief. And there is a practical trigger too: I have some compute left before my next batch, and this is a good use of it. Constraints shape what gets built.
does

It is a browser for one site and one person: It opens on the newsroom, where I left it. The last tab, the same place on the page. It knows what I have read. The site already records it, section by section; the app shows read, part read and unread in its own lists, and the folded views work as they do on the site. It opens my vault, with my passkey, as the site does. Tabs, with almost no chrome. A strip that hides when I read, no address bar unless I ask. It never reloads a page on its own, and every article I open stays readable offline, figures included.
does

My own workflows. A morning run: the wires, then new articles, then the briefs. A review run: articles with open findings. A catch-up run: articles changed since I last read them. Each is a small file in my vault, so it travels with me and an agent can propose a new one. It hears from my agents. A daily brief, a review, an answer to a note, in an inbox in the app. It is a layer of business logic on top of the site. The logic that proves itself in the app should move into the site, so the app gets thinner over time, not thicker.
engine

I asked which engine to build on: WebKit, Firefox or Chrome. On an iPhone in the UK, the question answers itself. Apple's rule is that an app that browses the web must use WebKit; the exceptions are the EU, since iOS 17.4, and Japan, since iOS 26.2. Firefox and Chrome on iOS are WebKit underneath. Mozilla said in September that an EU-only Gecko build would roughly double its iOS team, and Google's port of its own engine to iOS stayed an experiment.
engine

The UK may change this. The Competition and Markets Authority designated Apple with strategic market status on 22 October 2025, with the browser engine in scope, but as of today it has published no requirement about engines. So the app is a small native shell, in Swift, around Apple's own web view, which since iOS 26 has a SwiftUI version. This is the same conclusion a custom Firefox of my own reached for the iPad: on Apple's phones and tablets, the engine is not a choice.
costs

Two facts decide the rest. It needs Apple's paid developer membership. In Apple's capability table, Associated domains and Push notifications are available to the paid programmes and not to a free account. Associated domains are what let a passkey for newsroom.sgit.ai work inside the app, which is how the vault opens; push is how my agents reach the phone. A free account also expires the install every seven days.
costs

It has to be built on a Mac. An iPhone app is built and signed with Xcode on macOS, so the cloud sessions that write this site cannot build it. Either a session runs on my Mac, or the build runs on GitHub's macOS machines, at about $0.062 a minute against $0.006 for Linux, or on Apple's Xcode Cloud, with 25 hours a month included in the membership. I would rather the agent builds in the cloud and sends the app to my phone through TestFlight, so it never needs the phone.
costs

There is a cheaper path, and the brief keeps it as the fallback: add the site to the Home Screen. Since iOS 26 every site added that way opens as a web app, passkeys work as in Safari, and web push works since iOS 16.4. No Mac, no membership. What it cannot give me is native tabs and a reliable offline mode, which are half of why I want this.
unknown

The vault opens with a passkey and an extension called PRF, which turns the passkey into a key. Safari supports it for iCloud Keychain passkeys from iOS 18. No source I could find confirms that it works inside a web view in a third-party app. So the first thing the agent builds is the smallest app that tries the site's own unlock. If PRF does not come back, the app does the passkey ceremony natively and hands the result to the page. Either way, it is better to know on day one, not after the tabs are built.
maintain

This is the part that matters beyond my phone. When this app works, it will be part of my workflow every day. And I will not want to maintain it. Not because I cannot; I could easily take the time. Because it is not my focus. I would rather do something else. Being able to compile a Linux kernel does not mean I want to compile Linux kernels, and being able to code does not mean I want to spend my evenings keeping my own browser up to date with every iOS release.
maintain

That is the argument of software vendors as villagers, and now I am the customer. The explorer, me, builds exactly the app I want, which is a better brief than any document. Then I would like to hand it to someone, a person or a company, and pay a couple of pounds a month for them to keep it working: rebuild it when iOS changes, fix what breaks, keep the behaviour policy current. Who will fix your mess asked who does that for companies; this is the same question for one person. And it says something about what happens as people get this kind of power. Patience for bad interfaces wears thin when you can do something about them. That is good for users, and a warning for anyone shipping software that gets in their way.
brief

The full build brief is a note for the agent that builds it: a browser for one. In short: Phase 0, test first. Passkeys with PRF inside the app; the association file on the site; whether the web view's storage survives. Phase 1, the app. Opens where I left it, tabs, offline, no reloads, knows the reading, a small bridge to the page with a written policy. Phase 2, workflows. Runs of tabs I define, kept in my vault. Phase 3, from the agents. An inbox polled from the vault, and push through a small sender. It is also on the briefs page, with its session brief.
limits

Nothing is built. This is a brief. PRF inside an app's web view is untested. It is the first thing the build checks. The UK engine rule may change. The designation covers browser engines; no requirement has been published yet. The prices are as of 18 October 2026. GitHub's per-minute rates and Apple's membership change. The fallback is real. A Home Screen web app may turn out to be enough. If you have built a single-site browser on iOS and know where it hurts, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo from me on 18 October 2026. The research, read that day by a research agent: Apple, alternative browser engines, supported capabilities (the table read directly) and supporting passkeys; the CMA's case page; WebKit, WWDC25 and app-bound domains; GitHub, runner pricing; PiunikaWeb on Mozilla and Gecko on iOS, 30 September 2026. The site's own unlock: assets/door.js and assets/vault-pane/vault-pane.js. Related: a minimal viable browser, a custom Firefox of my own, software vendors as villagers, who will fix your mess, explorer coding, your reading, your controls. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: This is a call for help. Journalists are going through an identity crisis: they love the work, and the industry is not helping them through a massive transformation. There is a win-win here. They need to see agentic workflows doing real work, and where they add value to them; and the biggest limitation of our projects is that there are not enough humans working on them. The PHP story site shows it. Its team page lists 21 members: two humans, the editor and a project manager, and 19 roles run by agents or waiting to be filled. Every one of those roles should have a person connected to it: coordinating it, steering its agents, reviewing what they produce, and doing what only a person can, like the interviews and op-eds of the previous article. I cannot pay right now. What I can offer is coverage, exposure, credit under your own name, and a learning experience that is hard to find anywhere else. And if this generates revenue, the people in the roles are the ones who should be paid. Students and teachers are welcome too. If that is you, or someone you know, get in touch.
Every role should have a human: the PHP story's team page lists 21 members, two of them human.
in-short

This is a call for help. For journalists, editors, students and teachers. Journalists are in an identity crisis. They love the work; the industry is not helping them through the change. We are short of humans. The PHP team has 21 members, and two of them are people. Every role should have a human. Coordinating it, steering its agents, reviewing their work. We cannot pay yet. We can offer coverage, exposure, credit, and the learning. If this makes money, the people in the roles get paid.
why

Journalists clearly have an identity crisis at the moment. They love what they do, but the industry is not really helping them, and it is going through a massive transformation. Many of them have not yet seen agentic workflows doing real work, and so they cannot see where they would add value to them. There is a win-win here. They need to be exposed to these workflows. We need people. As I argued in own the stack, and the trust, what is missing from our newsrooms is not more agents. It is more journalists, and more readers.
roles

The PHP story site has shown that we can create roles: a conductor, collectors for primary sources, agencies and researchers, a researcher that runs the source watch, a librarian, a journalist, a historian, a verifier, a corrections liaison, a sherpa that walks with the reader, and more. Its team page lists 21 members, and its status data counts 23 agents. Two members are people: me, as the editor, and a project manager. I would argue that every single one of those roles should have a human connected to it. Not to do the agents' work, but to coordinate the role, steer the agents around it, review what they produce, and decide. The historian's map of who creates the original needs a person who knows which pivot points matter. The corrections liaison has eleven requests drafted and waiting for a person to send them. And the interviews and op-eds of that article are work only a person can do.
roles
As I wrote in jobs that never scaled, agents can go in all directions, and you need somebody who provides the direction. That is a person's job, in every role.
offer

A call for help: what we ask, what we offer now, and what happens when there is revenue. What we ask. Take a role, or part of one. Read what its agents produce, steer them, and do what only a person can: the interview, the judgement, the caveat that matters. Or start smaller, as one of the site's power users: a few minutes an ask, trying what is new and saying what works. What we offer. I cannot pay right now. What I can give is a huge amount of coverage and exposure: your name on your work, and credit on the site. And probably the best learning anyone can have on this right now: a front-row seat on how a team of agents, steered by people, runs a newsroom in public, with its briefs, board, releases and mistakes all on the record.
offer

When there is revenue. I would pay them if I had the money, and that is the plan. The aim is a model where readers and publishers pay, and if this generates revenue, the people in the roles are the ones who should be paid.
who

Journalists and editors, working or between jobs, who want to see where they add value to agentic workflows. Students, of journalism or of computing, who want real work on a live story. Teachers, who want a better sense of what these workflows are, for their own courses. Anyone who wants to learn more about agentic workflows by working inside one.
contact

Ask me directly, on LinkedIn, or through the join form on the PHP site. I will also be asking people in my own contacts whether they know someone who would be interested. Fundamentally, this is me saying: I have a project, I need people, and I think it would be good for them too.
limits

There is no paid role today. The offer is credit, exposure and learning. The roles are the PHP site's, as its team page lists them on 25 October 2026; they will change with the split into six repositories. Nobody has been asked yet. This is the call.
sources
