From a company that rents or hosts Macs, or wants to: Dedicated Macs per customer, by the day or the month, with an API to erase and re-provision between runs, so a clean desktop per run takes minutes. A meter inside, so a customer pays a fixed fee for the Mac and a per-minute price for the desktop time, with a higher price for the first hour or two and a taper after. A developer-agent offer, squarely inside the licence: coding agents on leased Macs and in virtual machines. A joint approach to Apple for written terms covering agent desktops, which the macOS 27 wording now makes possible. The stack, open: the bootstrap, the vault layout, the behaviour policies and the profiles are all in the vault, to take and run. What we would bring is the policies, the vaults, the keys, and RiskMandate to write the policy for each customer.

Read the licence section of the plan first, then talk to a lawyer about your shape. Start with shape A or C, where the licence is clearest. Write the behaviour policy before the product: it is the argument, and it tells you which controls matter. Measure the boot: the plan assumes about five minutes from request to a working desktop; it has not been timed yet. Keep state out of the machine: one key in, vaults for everything else, and an erase at the end. Added on 10 October 2026, after a question from the plan's author.

The obvious next question: if a leased Mac must be held for at least 24 hours, can one customer fill that day with many agents, one at a time, cleaning up after each? The cleaning-up part is easy. With the bootstrap above, everything an agent touched comes from vaults and goes back to vaults, so wiping between runs is a deletion, not a project. And the agents in our own team already run on a schedule, several times a day. The licence, read again with that question, cares about two things that queueing does not change: what the Mac is used for, and who is using macOS. Six scenarios against the clauses that decide them. Queueing satisfies "one user at a time"; the purpose of a lease, and who the user is, decide the rest. A reading of Apple's text, not legal advice.

Purpose. A lease is valid only "for the sole purpose of providing Permitted Developer Services", which Apple defines as "continuous integration services, including but not limited to software development, building software from source, automated testing during software development, and running necessary developer tools to support such activities." So a queue of coding agents on a leased Mac fits: it is what a continuous integration runner already does, many jobs for one customer in a row. A queue of office agents, working in mail, a browser and desktop apps, is outside the lease however carefully it is scheduled.

Who. If my agents, with my credentials, do the work and my customers buy the result, I am the user of macOS. That holds for developer work on a lease even when the work is for clients: a consultancy's build machine. If my customers' own agents, with their own credentials, get slots on my Mac, my customers are using macOS in turn, which is the "service bureau, time-sharing" the licence excludes "whether such services are being provided within your own organization or to third parties", and each of them would need a lease of their own of at least 24 hours.

The case worth a lawyer's hour. On a Mac you own, Section 2B(ii) lets a business run macOS "by multiple individuals on a single shared Mac Computer that you own or control", alongside "only one user may use the Apple Software at a time". A queue of your own agents on your own Mac, wiped between runs, is the closest fit for office agents. Two words decide it: whether automated agents are "individuals", and whether rotating them is time-sharing "within your own organization".

What would need Apple's written terms. Two cases: office agents on a leased Mac, and customers' agents sharing one Mac. The macOS 27 licence adds "except as otherwise provided in writing, signed, or issued by an authorized representative of Apple" to the virtualisation and leasing clauses, which is the route. The narrow ask is easier than the broad one: one organisation, a lease of 24 hours or more, sole use, one agent at a time, wiped between runs, for non-developer work. It keeps every condition Apple already sets except the purpose. So the plan's shapes hold, with one refinement. The dedicated Mac per customer (shape B) is needed whenever the agents are the customer's. When the agents are the operator's, doing work the customer buys, one Mac can serve many of them in turn, and for developer work that is already within the licence.

The licence quotes are from Apple's macOS 15, 26 and 27 licences as published on apple.com; the reading of them is ours and is not legal advice. Mac prices are from Apple's UK store on 9 October 2026; every other number is an assumption, labelled in the vault. No provider is named, at the request of the author.

Abstract: Every page on sgit.ai now has a price, a few pence, and a meter in the corner of the screen that debits it from five pounds of starting credit. There is a reading account with a history, a price table, a top-up page with a cart and a checkout that has every step except the payment, and an out-of-credit state that never blocks a page. All of it lives in the reader's browser and nowhere else: no account, no server, no card, nothing sent. Open a private window and the meter starts again at five pounds, which looks like a way to read for free, except that it also starts again with no history, and the history is what the site uses to pick articles for you. That is the trade this experiment puts in front of a reader: pay a little, keep the record of what you read on your own machine, and get a site that knows you back. Whether people would make that trade is the question worth testing, and a meter that charges nothing is the cheapest way to start.

The reading account, as it looks after ten pages: the balance, what was spent, the articles picked for this reader from what they read, and what they paid to read, by topic. All of it is computed in the browser from a history kept in the browser. Every page has a price. An article published in the last seven days costs 5p, an older one 3p, a newsletter issue, a desk note or a collection 2p, any other page 1p. The homepage, the subscribe page and your own account are free. The full table is on the account page. You start with £5.00 of credit, and each page you open is debited once per visit. Going back to a page you opened in the same browser session costs nothing. A badge in the corner shows your balance and what this page cost, and links to your account.

Out of credit, nothing is blocked. The page is shown, the read is recorded as unpaid, and a bar offers a top-up. Topping up has every step of a real shop except the payment: four packs, a cart you can adjust, a review step, a confirm button and a receipt. The credit lands at once. Your account has the history, the receipts, a pause button, an export of everything as JSON, and a button to start again. An article as a reader sees it: the badge in the bottom-left corner shows the balance and what this page cost. It links to the account.

The balance is the obvious part. The less obvious part is the list of what you read, with the topics each article belongs to, which the meter keeps because a ledger has to. That list is enough to personalise the site. Your account picks unread articles from the topics you have read most, and so does the front page, in a band called Picked for you that only appears once there is a history to pick from. The front page after a handful of reads: a Picked for you band, filled from this browser's history and nowhere else. None of this needs an account, a cookie banner or a server. The articles and their topics are already published as one file, articles/graphs.json, the data behind the articles as graphs, and the browser does the arithmetic. The history never leaves the machine it was made on.

Which means there is an obvious way to cheat. Open a private window, or a different browser, and the meter starts again at £5.00. You can read for free forever. What you cannot do is take your history with you, so you start again with no picks, a front page that knows nothing about you, and an account with nothing in it. The meter can be escaped; the personalisation cannot be copied. That is the experiment: does a site that knows what you read, without anybody else knowing, make a few pence a page feel like a fair price? Or do people open the private window?

Because it is the cheapest honest way to ask the question. The question is whether they miss it argues for shipping something usable, giving it away, and watching whether anybody notices when it goes. Price it, then give it away adds the step before: define the product, put a price on it, and offer it free to people who know you, because the price is a statement of what you think it is worth. A meter that shows the price on every page, and charges nothing, is that step made visible. The reader sees what a page would cost, what they have spent, and what it bought them, without anybody's money moving.

The idea is old. How news got here tells the story of a payment code reserved in the web's own protocol in 1997, 402 Payment Required, still waiting for a payment system to use it. This meter does not answer how a penny should move. It asks something that comes before it: whether the interesting part is the payment at all, or what the reader gets back for the record of having paid. The first version of this was on pt.newsroom.sgit.ai, the Portuguese newsroom: one cent a page, a five-euro wallet that refills itself when it empties, and a ledger with a page of its own. Its rules were right and are kept here: say first that it is a demonstration, never block a page, charge once per page per visit so the back button is not a purchase, and let the page work if the browser refuses to store anything.

This version adds three things. Prices that depend on what a page is and how new it is, set in one place in the site's build so the published table and the meter cannot disagree. A top-up you choose, through a cart, instead of a refill that happens to you. And the personalisation, which is the reason to keep a history at all. Topping up: two packs in the cart, and the review step where a card form or a wallet button would go. None is shown and nothing is charged. It holds no money. Anybody can edit their own balance in the browser's developer tools. For a demonstration that is fine; for real money the balance needs a server, or receipts signed by one.

It does not follow you between devices. The history stays where it was made. A version that syncs could keep the ledger in an encrypted vault that only the reader holds the key to, which is the kind of thing this site is built on; that is a proposal, not something built. It does not meter agents. Reading a page's markdown twin, or the newsroom's wire, costs nothing. The other side of that question is in the token bill nobody is sending. It charges the same for every reader. The obvious next prices are not per page but per question: a query over the reporting behind a story, the kind of thing the bridge, followed to the end imagines readers and agents paying for in small amounts. Out of credit: the page is still shown, the read is noted as unpaid, and the bar offers a top-up.

Your meter has been running since you arrived. Your account shows what it has recorded; top up to walk through the cart; and open this page in a private window to see what starting again costs you. Drafted from a voice note by Dinis Cruz, who is the author of the idea and has editorial responsibility, by a Claude Code session working as the sgit.ai newsroom, on 10 October 2026. The meter is assets/meter.js; its prices are METER in admin/build/build_pages.py; the screenshots were taken from this site with the meter running.

Nothing is charged, no card is involved, and nothing leaves your browser. Your account shows the balance, the history and what it bought you.

Abstract: The browser is the biggest program most of us run, the largest attack surface on the machine, and the place we now want to put agents. It does far more than any single job needs. A kiosk running one application, an agent filling in one form, and a person reading the news all get the same enormous engine, with every feature on. This follows the argument of the code you do not ship to its most visible case. A minimal viable browser has a small kernel, reviewed hardest and changed least, and loads components only when a page or an agent needs them, so its attack surface grows only as it is used. A browser for one application has no extensions, no media and no downloads. A browser for one agent has no accounts, no extensions and no file access, which is a practical defence against prompt injection: an agent cannot leak what its browser cannot reach. And every extension runs in its own box, with only the access its job needs, instead of the "read and change all your data on all websites" that so many hold today. Several projects already do part of this, from hardened Firefox forks to headless browsers built for agents. But I think Mozilla is uniquely placed to do all of it: it has its own engine, privacy is its brand, it runs on the client, and its revenue still does not depend on knowing more about its users. The pitch to Mozilla, though, should not be security. It should be speed: a browser that only has the code it needs is a browser that starts instantly and uses a fraction of the memory.

A minimal viable browser: a small kernel, components loaded only when needed, and three shapes from the same engine. Code is a liability: remove what each use case does not call, apply it to the browser, and build on small blocks you did not have to write.
in-short

The browser is the biggest attack surface we run. And now we want to give it to agents. One engine, every feature on, for every job. A kiosk, an agent and a reader all get the same. A minimal viable browser. A small kernel, and components loaded only when needed. A browser for one agent is a prompt-injection defence. An agent cannot leak what its browser cannot reach. Every extension in its own box. Only the sites and the powers its job needs. Parts of this exist. Hardened forks, headless browsers for agents, kiosk modes. Mozilla can do all of it. Its own engine, a privacy brand, the client, and money not tied to profiling. Sell it as speed, not security. Only the code it needs starts instantly.
biggest

The browser is where most of us spend the day, and it carries every capability the web has ever needed: a JavaScript engine with a just-in-time compiler, WebAssembly, WebGL, media codecs, PDF, fonts, downloads, extensions, sync, accounts. A page that shows text and a form gets all of it, on, by default.
biggest

The cost of that shows up in the bug counts. In May, Mozilla wrote that it fixed 423 security bugs in Firefox in April 2026, against roughly 20 to 30 a month through 2025. 271 of them were found with an Anthropic model and fixed in Firefox 150: 180 rated high, 80 moderate, 11 low. A number of them were sandbox escapes, written assuming the content process was already compromised and going after the privileged parent process through IPC, IndexedDB and image decoding. Chrome is seeing the same: one update on 6 October 2026 fixed 247 vulnerabilities. Counted from NVD by the organisation that filed them, Google's Chrome team filed 202 CVEs in 2025 and 3,246 in 2026 up to 17 October; Mozilla's filed 213 and 675 (Mozilla's also cover Thunderbird and other products). This is the code you do not ship argument at its largest: models now find what was always there, and every feature in the engine is a place to look.
biggest

The vendors already know that less code is safer, because they ship it as a mode. Microsoft Edge's enhanced security mode turns off the V8 just-in-time compiler, after Microsoft said in 2021 that 45% of V8 CVEs in 2019 were JIT-related. GrapheneOS's Vanadium browser has the JIT disabled by default, with a per-site toggle. Apple's Lockdown Mode blocks "certain complex web technologies". Tor Browser's Safest level turns off JavaScript altogether. Each is a minimal browser for one threat, switched on by hand. What does not exist is the general version: a browser that starts small and only grows when it has to.
shape

The shape is the same as the minimal viable code path, applied to one program. A small kernel. Networking, TLS, parsing, layout, and process isolation. This is the part that is reviewed hardest and changed least. Components, loaded when needed. JavaScript, with or without the JIT; WebAssembly; media; WebGL; PDF; downloads; extensions; sync. A page or an agent asks for one, and the browser loads it, for that site. A profile that says what it is for. One application, one agent, or a person browsing. The profile decides what can be loaded at all. Three browsers come out of the same engine. A browser for one application has no extensions, no media and no downloads: a kiosk, a till, an internal tool. A browser for one agent has the same, plus no accounts and no file access. And the reader's own browser loads what they use as they use it, with each extension in its own box.
shape

Firefox has had pieces of this, and dropped some of them. It had a site-specific browser, behind a hidden preference, and removed it in Firefox 86 in 2021, citing known bugs and weak user research. It has a kiosk mode, started with --kiosk. It has had site isolation on for every desktop user since Firefox 95, which is the process boundary a component model needs. And Servo, the engine Mozilla started in Rust, is now an embeddable library, published as 0.1.0 in April 2026 under Linux Foundation Europe.
agent

This is where the argument stops being about tidiness. We are now giving browsers to agents, and the agent reads everything the page says. The vendors say plainly that this will not be fixed. OpenAI wrote in December 2025 that prompt injection, "much like scams and social engineering on the web, is unlikely to ever be fully 'solved'" (TechCrunch). Google's Chrome security team wrote in December 2025 that "the primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection". Gartner told most organisations to block AI browsers for now.
agent

The incidents show where the damage comes from. In March 2026, Zenity Labs disclosed PleaseFix, a zero-click hijack of Perplexity's Comet through a calendar invite that reached local files and password-manager workflows. The fix was to restrict file:// access: not a smarter model, a smaller browser. At Black Hat in August, the same researchers showed zero-click chains against the agents in Chrome, Edge, Comet and ChatGPT Atlas; some vendors patched, others called it intended behaviour. The better defences already point the same way. Atlas has a logged-out mode that runs the agent with no cookies or logins. Brave runs its AI browsing in an isolated profile with its own cookies and storage, and recommends isolating agentic browsing from normal browsing. Chrome adds Agent Origin Sets, which limit the sites an agent's task can touch, and a second model that checks proposed actions.
agent

A minimal browser makes that the default rather than a setting. An agent's browser that has no accounts, no extensions, no file access and only the origins its task needs cannot leak a password it never had or a file it cannot open. In the terms of what can your agent reach, the grant shrinks to the mandate, and the injection that gets through finds nothing to take.
extensions

Extensions are the part of the browser that users add, and they are where much of the recent damage came from. LayerX's 2025 report found 99% of enterprise users have an extension installed, and 53% have at least one with high or critical permissions. The pattern in the incidents is not malicious code at install. It is a trusted extension that changes. Koi's ShadyPanda report, as The Hacker News relayed it, covers about 4.3 million installs across 145 extensions (20 for Chrome and 125 for Edge, Koi's count of one phase), some of them "Featured" or "Verified", that were legitimate for years and then were weaponised through auto-update. Urban VPN Proxy, with a Featured badge, began harvesting every prompt and reply on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot from a July 2025 update, with no off switch. Firefox is not immune: Koi's later DarkSpectre attribution includes Firefox add-ons.
extensions

An extension in its own box gets only the sites and the powers its job needs, and a change to either is a new request, not a silent update. Firefox has started down this road. In Manifest V3 it made host permissions opt-in and controllable per site, and new extensions must declare their data collection at install. It has also kept the blocking webRequest API that Chrome removed, which is why full uBlock Origin still runs on Firefox. The next steps are a process per extension, and a permission model that is an Agent Behaviour Policy in all but name: what this extension may do, on which sites, and who approved it.
exists

None of this is new as an idea, and much of it ships today, in pieces. Hardened Firefox builds. LibreWolf, with less telemetry; Mullvad Browser, built with the Tor Project for anti-fingerprinting; Tor Browser itself; Waterfox, which ships with no AI. Smaller Firefox interfaces. Zen, with about 45,000 stars on GitHub, and Floorp. A paid minimal browser. Brave Origin, launched in June 2026 for about $60 one-time, removes the AI assistant, news, rewards, wallet, VPN, Tor and playlist and keeps the blocker. People will pay for less. Chromium with things taken out. ungoogled-chromium, and Vanadium, with the JIT off. New engines. Ladybird, still in development and funded by donations, and Servo. Browsers for machines. Lightpanda, written from scratch for agents and automation; Chrome's headless shell, a separate thin binary; and hosted browsers such as Cloudflare's Browser Rendering. Shells for one app. Tauri uses the system web view, and says a minimal app can be under 600KB.
exists
What is missing is the same engine, from the same vendor, in all three shapes, with the components as the unit.
why-mozilla

I think Mozilla is better placed than anyone to build this, for four reasons. It has its own engine. Gecko is the only independent engine with a large user base that is not Chromium or WebKit. A component model goes all the way down into the engine; a fork of someone else's cannot set that direction. Privacy is the brand. Mozilla's state of Mozilla report puts Firefox at about 200 million monthly users, and the company has already shipped the instinct this needs: Firefox 148 added a switch that turns off current and future generative AI features. Its Smart Window is opt-in and does not act on pages yet. That is a company that already sells "you choose what runs". It runs on the client. An agent's browser that holds nothing and reaches only what it needs is a client-side product. It does not need a server that sees the browsing, which is the same design as sgit.
why-mozilla

Its money does not come from knowing more about you. Here the memo needs a correction: Mozilla's revenue is not independent. Mark Surman said in April that search was until recently about 95 to 98% of revenue, with privacy-preserving ads now about 10 to 12%, and most of the search money comes from Google. The court remedies in the Google case let those payments continue but limit default deals to one year at a time, and both sides have appealed. What holds is the part that matters here: Mozilla is paid for a search box, not for profiling its users, and it has about $1.4 billion in reserves and a plan to run its products as separate companies, each with its own accounts. A minimal browser for agents and applications is a product someone pays for directly, the way Brave Origin is, and it is the kind of revenue Mozilla says it wants.
speed

The pitch to Mozilla should not be security. Security has rarely been enough to make people switch browsers, and Firefox at 2.8% of the market in September 2026 knows it. The pitch is that a browser with only the code it needs is fast. It starts at once, it uses a fraction of the memory, and an agent can run many of them. Lightpanda's own benchmark, which is the vendor's, claims 123MB against 2GB of peak memory for 100 pages, and 5 seconds against 46. A kiosk that boots in a second, an agent that opens a hundred clean browsers on a laptop, a reader whose browser does not load a PDF engine until they open a PDF: those are features people notice. The security comes with them, the way encryption made sgit better rather than being the reason to use it.
speed
Firefox now ships every two weeks, from Firefox 155. A component that loads on demand is a component that can ship, and be pulled, on that cadence too.
limits

No minimal viable browser exists in this form. The pieces do; the design is a proposal. Mozilla has not said it will build it. Nothing here is from Mozilla beyond what is linked. Smaller is not safe. A kernel still has bugs, and an agent with no file access can still be talked into a bad form submission. The CVE counts are ours. Counted from NVD by filing organisation on 18 October 2026; the 2026 rise reflects AI-assisted bug finding as much as new bugs. Some figures are the vendor's own. Lightpanda's benchmark, Brave's and Mozilla's user counts, LayerX's survey. Mozilla's 2024 and 2025 revenue split is from interviews and its ledger page. Its ledger page links its 2024 audited statements. Loading components on demand has costs. Fingerprinting is one: a browser that loads different parts for different sites can look different to each, which is why Mullvad removed its security-level button.

Abstract: Since Chrome 148, on 5 May 2026, any web page can talk to a language model that runs on the reader's own machine: Gemini Nano, through the Prompt API, with text, image and audio input, JSON-schema output, and no network once the model is downloaded. For the pattern I described in No server, by design, that is the missing piece, because the hardest thing to move to the client was always the intelligence itself. I tried it this week, and the experience was rough: a download with no sense of time, a progress bar that vanished on refresh, and a model that turned up by the morning. That is partly the platform and partly the pages, and the documentation explains most of it. I also looked for good examples in the wild and found very few, which is less strange than it looks: the API shipped five months ago, over formal objections from Mozilla, Apple's WebKit team and the W3C TAG, to desktops with a 22 GB free-disk floor, in five languages, with tool calling still experimental. This article is a briefing on what actually works today, an honest account of the rough edges, the case for and against building on it, and a map of where we can put it to real use: answers grounded in the graph instead of the prose, personas inferred without leaving the browser, voice memos transcribed on the device, alt text for every figure, and a download experience that tells people what is happening.

The client-side puzzle. Files, state, storage, payments and, next, identity were already off the server. Intelligence was the piece that kept a back end in the picture. Since May 2026, on capable desktops, Chrome supplies it. In No server, by design, I listed what still seems to need a server, and one row was models. The answer I gave was "in the client, with the reader's own key, or a small local model". That row just got a lot more interesting. Since Chrome 148, released on 5 May 2026, any web page can talk to a language model that runs on the reader's own machine. Not a model the page downloads itself, but one the browser ships and manages: Gemini Nano, through a JavaScript interface called the Prompt API. Once the model is on the device, the network is not needed at all. No key, no bill per token, and nothing sent to anyone.

For the client-side pattern, this is the most important piece so far, and the hardest one. Files, state, storage and payments were always going to move to the browser; they are things browsers were built for, and as of today the newsroom's payments are live, on a Stripe link and nothing of ours. Intelligence was the piece that kept a back end in the picture. A page could download a model of its own and run it in the browser, and libraries have done that for a while, but every site paid the download separately and few readers would wait for it, so in practice a model behind a page meant renting one somewhere and calling it. Now, on capable desktops, the browser supplies one, once, for every site. It is in the tab.

So I tried it. And this article is what I found: what actually works, why the experience was as rough as it was, why there are so few good examples, the honest case against building on it, and a map of where I think we can put it to real use.
short

It is real, and it is stable. The Prompt API shipped to all web pages in Chrome 148 on 5 May 2026, after being available to Chrome extensions since Chrome 138. The Summarizer, Translator and Language Detector APIs have been stable since 138. Writer, Rewriter and Proofreader are still developer trials. It does more than chat. It accepts text, images and audio (a video counts as its current frame); it returns text, optionally constrained by a JSON schema; it keeps sessions, clones them, and reports how much of its context window is used. Five languages so far: English, Japanese, Spanish, German and French.
short

Tool calling is not there yet. Native tool use in the Prompt API is experimental and behind a flag. What works today is structured output: ask for JSON that names a tool and its arguments, and your code runs it. WebMCP, which lets a site describe its own tools to the reader's agent, is a separate API, in origin trial. The rough download was mostly the pages, not the model. The download carries on in the background when the tab is refreshed or closed, and resumes after a restart. What the refresh lost was the progress bar, because a page only sees progress for downloads it asks about. Chrome's own guidance says what a good page should show; the demo pages I used did not.
short

There are few good examples for real reasons. Five months on the open web; desktop only; 22 GB of free disk, a GPU with more than 4 GB of video memory or 16 GB of RAM; a download of roughly 4 GB; five languages; and formal opposition from Mozilla, WebKit, the W3C TAG and Microsoft, which makes careful teams wait. The objections are serious, and they line up with things I care about. One vendor's model, and one vendor's usage policy, behind a web API. Prompts tuned to Gemini Nano may not travel. The way to build on it without being captured by it is to keep the meaning in the data, not in the prompt.
short

The fit with what we have built is unusually good. A graph answer from the five readers is about 2,600 tokens; a small model's context window is small. Answers grounded in anchored graph slices, personas inferred locally, voice memos transcribed on the device before they go into a vault lane, alt text for the 527 figures, and a download panel that tells people the truth.
ships

Chrome now has a family of built-in AI APIs. Some run on small task-specific models; the rest run on Gemini Nano, a model in the 2 to 4 billion parameter range that Chrome downloads once per device, not once per site. What Chrome ships today: the built-in AI APIs and their status, what the Prompt API accepts and returns, the hardware it needs, and how the browser manages the model's life. Status from Chrome's own documentation, as of October 2026. ships

The Prompt API is the one that matters for what follows. In practice: Input: text, plus images (an image file, a canvas, a video's current frame, and so on) and audio (a recording, a buffer). Audio input needs a GPU. Output: text only, streamed or whole, and it can be constrained by a JSON schema, so the model returns, for example, a boolean, a label from a list, or an object with fields you defined. Sessions: a system prompt that is never dropped, initial prompts to restore a conversation, appending context before asking, cloning a session to fork it, and a running count of context used against the window. When the window fills, the oldest turns are dropped, and the page is told. Languages: English, Japanese, Spanish, German and French, declared when the session is created.
ships

Sampling: on the web, temperature and similar knobs are not exposed by default; an origin trial offers named modes from most predictable to most creative. What it needs is the part that decides who can use it. Windows 10 or 11, macOS 13 or later, Linux, or ChromeOS on Chromebook Plus devices; no Android or iOS yet. At least 22 GB free on the disk with the Chrome profile. Either a GPU with strictly more than 4 GB of video memory, or 16 GB of RAM and four CPU cores. An unmetered connection for the first download. Chrome measures the GPU with a test shader and picks the model variant to match: a larger one, a smaller one, or CPU inference.
download

My experience, in order. I opened one of Chrome's demo pages, typed a message, and the download started. There was a small banner that told me something was happening, but not how much, how fast, or how long. I tried another playground, with the same result. I refreshed the page and the banner was gone, so I assumed the download was gone too. I left the laptop open overnight, and by the morning the model was there. The only sign of life in between was network traffic in the system monitor, on a fast connection that should have done better. What I saw, against what was actually happening, and what a page should show. The download never stopped; the page that asked about it did. Chrome's guidance covers most of this, and the demos did not follow it. Most of that is explained in Chrome's own documentation, and it is worth knowing before building anything:
download

The download did not stop. It continues in the background if the tab that started it is refreshed or closed, resumes where it left off if the connection drops, and resumes on the next start if the browser is closed (within 30 days). The progress bar is the page's job. A page sees download progress only through the monitor it passes when it creates a session. After a refresh, the new page has to ask again, and if it does, it is told how much is still missing. The demo pages did not ask again; that is why the banner vanished. It is roughly 4 GB, downloaded once per device. Every site shares the same model. Updates are full downloads, done in the background and swapped in without downtime. There is a pause after the download. Once the bytes are in, the model is unpacked and loaded into memory, which the documentation recommends showing as an indeterminate state.
download

It can disappear. If free disk space falls below about 10 GB, Chrome deletes the model, even mid-session, and does not fetch it again until a page asks. There is a page for this. chrome://on-device-internals shows the model, its version and an event log. So the rough experience was real, and it is fixable at the page level. Chrome's guidance even describes a hybrid pattern, used by the shopping site Miravia: answer with a server-side model while the local one downloads, then switch. What I have not found, anywhere I looked, is a small, honest component that shows bytes, rate and time remaining, survives a refresh, says it is safe to close the tab, and, because the API reports only that a device is unavailable and not why, lists the likely reasons in plain words. That is the first thing worth shipping.
examples

I looked for good examples of the Prompt API in action, and found surprisingly few. Chrome's own case studies are real but narrow: CyberAgent's blogging tools, review summaries on redBus and Miravia, article summaries at Terra and BrightSites, and translation at Policybazaar and JioHotstar. Most of those use the task APIs, summarising and translating, rather than the Prompt API itself. Chrome uses Gemini Nano for its own scam detection. Beyond that, there are demos, extensions, and wrappers that expose the browser's model to other programs. That surprised me, until I listed the reasons: It is new. Five months on the open web is not long for a platform feature. The audience is gated. Desktop only, with a 22 GB free-disk floor and real hardware requirements. A team cannot assume its readers have it, so every feature needs a fallback, and the fallback often becomes the feature.
examples

The first run is a 4 GB download. No product manager wants that to be a user's first impression. It is small. A model in the 2 to 4 billion parameter range is good at classifying, extracting, summarising and rephrasing, and not at long reasoning. Teams that try it as a chatbot are disappointed; teams that try it as a function are not. Five languages. A lot of the web is in the others. Tool calling is not ready. Native tool use is behind a flag and unreliable; the documented path is structured output. The standards fight. That is the next section, and it is the reason I would take most seriously if I were deciding whether to build on it.
against

Chrome shipped the Prompt API over formal opposition. Mozilla's position is that the API has "severe negative consequences to the interoperability, updatability, and neutrality of the web platform." Apple's WebKit team filed an opposing position on interoperability, portability and privacy. The W3C Technical Architecture Group recorded several concerns, and Microsoft, which builds its own version of the API on its own models in Edge, objected too. The objections come down to three things. Prompts do not travel. A prompt tuned for Gemini Nano may behave differently on another browser's model, and the proposal itself says it does not guarantee quality, stability or interoperability between browsers. That pushes the web towards writing for one model, the way it once wrote for one browser. A vendor policy sits in front of a web API. Using it means accepting Google's Generative AI Prohibited Uses Policy, which is new for a web platform feature.
against

The browser decides. Which model, which version, when it updates, when it is deleted. A page cannot pin a version, and cannot even read it from JavaScript. I agree with most of this, and it lines up with what I keep writing about: sovereignty, determinism and explainability. A model I cannot pin, version or inspect, behind a policy I did not write, is not sovereign infrastructure. But I do not think the answer is to wait. Edge already offers the same API shape on its own models (Phi-4-mini, and a smaller one called Aion in developer preview), so the interface is not Chrome's alone, even if the standards process is unfinished. And there is a design discipline that limits the damage:
against

Keep the meaning in the data, not in the prompt. If the page hands the model a slice of an anchored graph and asks a narrow question with a JSON schema, the work the model does is small and checkable, and the answer can be verified against the anchors. Swap the model and the graph still works. Use the model as a function, not as an oracle. Classify, extract, label, rephrase. Never let it be the only source of a fact. Always have a path without it. The graph itself, or the reader's own key to a larger model, or nothing at all. The page should be complete without the model, and better with it.
fit

This is the part I find most exciting. A small model with a small context window is a bad match for raw prose and a very good match for the graphs this site is building. In The agent is the reader, the five readers' graph answered a question about any of 45 concepts in a median of 2,579 tokens, with every statement anchored to its sentence, against 25,698 tokens to read the five articles. A context window measured in thousands of tokens, not hundreds of thousands, cannot hold the five articles. It can hold the graph's answer, with room left for the question. The same work that makes the graph worth paying for, for an agent with a big model, makes it usable for a small model in the reader's tab. And the anchors mean every answer can show its sources, which is the honest way to use a model this size.
fit

The model also fills the gaps the client-side pattern still had. The newsroom builds personas from what the reader reads, using rules; a local model can infer them from the text itself, without anything leaving the browser. My whole publishing workflow starts with voice memos; the Prompt API accepts audio, so a memo could be transcribed and structured on the device before it is encrypted into a vault lane. And the synthetic readers found 51 missing figures out of 527; a local model can describe what each figure shows, and say when a figure says something different from its caption.
opportunities

The first four are the ones I want to build, in roughly that order. They share one property: the model never decides anything important on its own. It answers from anchors, labels into a fixed set, or transcribes, and the page or the person checks the result.
next

A vault is being built alongside this article to explore all of this properly: a test page per capability, measured on real machines, with the numbers published. The first round: The model status panel. An open component, in the spirit of SG Meter: it checks support and eligibility, shows download progress with bytes, rate and time remaining, survives a refresh, and, when a device cannot run the model, explains the likely reasons in plain words. Ask this article, grounded in the graph. A question box on articles that have the five readers' graph, answering only from anchored items, with a JSON schema that forces it to cite them, and a fallback that shows the graph slice when the model is missing. Personas, inferred on the device. The same traits SG Meter uses, inferred from the text a reader keeps, never sent anywhere.
next

Voice memo to vault. Record, transcribe and structure on the device, then encrypt and drop it into an append lane. Measurements. Download time, time to first token, tokens per second, context window, and accuracy against the anchors, on the machines we have. These are the numbers missing from almost every piece about Gemini Nano, including this one. The client-side pattern had one piece left that seemed to need someone else's server. On capable desktops, it no longer does. The model is small, the platform is contested, and the first-run experience is poor. All three are true, and none of them is a reason to wait. If you are building with the Prompt API, or have found good examples I missed, let's talk: agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The reading list has become one of the most useful things this newsroom does for me. On 11 October I asked for a way to send someone a link that says: from me, for you, these are the articles I think you should read, in this order, and here is why. It shipped the same day. Since then the agent behind agent@riskmandate.ai has been building these lists into the emails it drafts for me, about twenty of them by its debrief of 18 October, and I read and send every one. What I had not thought through was that for most of the people I send one to, the list is the first page of this newsroom they ever open. They arrive from an email, often through a link their mail client has wrapped, and until this week they found a narrow column of titles that did not say what the site was, what a price of a few pence meant, or what to do next. So on 21 October the page changed. It now opens as a letter: a dateline, my note signed, and one line on what the list holds and what it costs. It uses the width of the screen, with the articles as cards whose pictures can be read, four more views (headlines, sections, pictures, and the list as a graph), and a column that explains the newsroom in four steps. And it shows the reader what they have read, section by section, from their own browser, with done, later and not for me on every article. Before it shipped, the newsroom's Designer role reviewed it on a real list and fourteen of its findings were fixed. This is the second page this week that had to be brought up to date because people started to use it, after the page for publishers, and it points at the next step: the answers coming back to me, and to the agent, as easily as the lists go out.
A reading list from me to Steve as it opens since 21 October, at 1440 pixels wide in the Newsprint theme.
in-short

A reading list is a link from me to one person. The articles to read in order, a few worth a look, what to follow and a line from me, all in the part of the address after the #, which the browser never sends to the server. It shipped on 11 October, the day I asked for it. The agent behind agent@riskmandate.ai builds them into my emails. It picks the articles by number, writes the line on why, builds the link and opens it on the live site to check it; I read the draft and send it. About twenty by its debrief of 18 October. For most people, the list is the first page of the newsroom they see. They arrive from an email, not from the front page, so the list has to say what the site is and what to do.
in-short

The first version was a column of links. It worked, and it did not explain anything: not the price of a few pence, not the free credit, not that nothing about their reading reaches me. Since 21 October it opens as a letter, and uses the screen. A dateline, my note signed, one line on what the list holds and costs; the articles as cards with pictures that can be read; a side column that explains the newsroom in four steps. It shows the reader what they have read. Section by section, from their own browser's records, with a ring, the time left and what it has cost, and done, later and not for me on every article. Nothing of it is sent anywhere. Five views of the same list. Cards, headlines, sections as one line each, the articles' pictures, and the list as a graph of its ideas and the links between them.
in-short

The Designer reviewed it before it shipped. Fourteen findings on a real list at desktop and phone widths, all fixed in the same release. Pages that people use have to keep up. The page for publishers was the first, a week ago; the reading list is the second. The next step is the answers: notes from the page that reach me, and the agent, signed, as easily as the lists go out.
link

I keep meeting people I would like to point at three or four articles: a founder I mentor, a publisher, someone shaping a roundtable, a security lead with a specific problem. The newsroom's curation is close, the personas and the desks get most of the way, but it is not personal, and the last part is the part that starts a conversation. So on 11 October I asked for a reading list in a link: from Dinis, for Steve, here are the articles I think you should read, the ones worth a look, and what to follow.
link

It shipped the same day, as release v0.8.0 of this site. Every article has a number that never changes, so a list is a handful of numbers, two first names and a note, after the # in the address. A browser keeps that part to itself, so the newsroom never sees who sent a list to whom, and there is no account and nothing to sign up for. When the link opens, the list becomes one of the reader's personas in their browser, which they can keep or remove, and the newsroom's picks follow it.
agent

What made the reading list useful was not the page. It was that I stopped building the links myself. The agent behind agent@riskmandate.ai, which drafts my email and waits for me to send it, now does it as part of a reply: it reads the thread, picks the articles by number, writes a line on why for each, builds the link, opens it on the live site to check that every article is there and in order, and puts it in the draft. Its debrief of 18 October counts about 20 reading lists among the 178 emails it had drafted, each written for one person. Every one waited in my drafts folder until I read it, changed it and sent it. How a reading list goes out and what comes back: the agent drafts, I send, the person reads and replies.
agent

That is the man behind the curtain again, in a small form. The agent does the work of choosing and checking; the email is from me, because I read it and send it; and behind the email there is not one article but a short course, in an order I chose for that person.
first

What I had not thought through is who opens these links. The front page is written for people who already know what this newsroom is. The people I send a list to mostly do not. They arrive from an email, sometimes through a link their mail client has wrapped in a long redirect, and the list is the first page of the newsroom they ever see. The same list from me to Steve as it opened until 20 October (left) and since 21 October (right), at 1440 pixels wide.
first

The first version answered the question I asked, which was how to send a list. It did not answer the questions the person on the other end had. What is this site? Why does an article say 10p? Is that money? Do I need an account? What happens if I read half of it? It used a third of a desktop screen, and the first article started below the fold. It was a list of links, which is the thing a newsroom page should not look like.
letter

Since release v0.13.19 on 21 October the page opens as a letter. At the top, a dateline: a reading list, seven articles, about an hour and a half, from Dinis, newest 21 October. Then Chosen for Steve, the two names, my note, signed, and what to do: Start reading, or Reply to Dinis. Before anything is read, one line says what the list holds and what it costs: five to read and two worth a look, free to start, a few pence an article after you read it, from £5.00 of credit kept in your browser.
letter

The page uses the width of the screen. The first article is a large card with its picture beside it, large enough to read the picture's own headline, and the rest are two to a row. Every card starts with its place in the list and its date, then the headline, two lines of teaser, and at the foot, quietly, where the reader is with it. On a phone the pictures run from edge to edge and the five views fit on one row.
letter

Down the right, a column says what the reader is looking at, in one sentence and four steps, one lit after another: read, and pay a few pence after you read; come back, and what you read is remembered here; keep the list, it is one of your personas now and nothing is sent anywhere; reply, and tell me what landed. Under it, the list as a persona, with keep and remove, and the links to find out more, starting with the page for publishers.
read

This newsroom already knows, inside the reader's browser, how much of each article they have read, section by section, and it charges for that, not for how far the page was scrolled. The list now shows it. A ring says how much of the list is read; next to it, how many articles are read and started, the time left and what has been spent. Each card has a bar of its sections, as wide as their words and filled as they are read, and Continue goes to the first section not yet read in the first article not yet finished.
read

Every article also has three quiet buttons: done, later and not for me. They are the same notes the reader's vault pane keeps, so they travel with the reader's own vault to their other devices, and they are never sent to me unless the reader sends them. If the reader reads an article in another tab and comes back, the list has already caught up. None of this is tracking: the page reads what the reader's own browser already holds, and nothing leaves it.
views

A list of seven articles is about an hour and a half of reading, and not everyone wants to start by reading. So the same list has five views, and the page remembers the one the reader chose. The same list in four of its five views: Headlines, Sections, Pictures and Graph, after some reading.
views

Cards is the default. Headlines is the list in one screen, each article's headline and its one-liner. Sections uses the line every section of every article now has: the whole argument of the list, a line at a time, each a link straight to that section. Pictures shows the articles' figures, because for some readers the figure is the article. And Graph draws the list as a path, with the main ideas of each article under it, an arc where one article links to another, and at the foot, the articles outside the list that several of them point to, which is where a curious reader goes next.
review

Before the release, I asked for the page to be reviewed by the newsroom's Designer, the role whose rules are that a card on a news page needs a date, that the picture is the card's argument and is shown where it can be read or not at all, and that nothing scrolls sideways at 390 pixels wide. It looked at a real list in every view, at desktop and phone widths, before anything was read, and ranked fourteen problems by how much each would hurt someone opening the list for the first time.
review

The worst were the ones I would not have noticed. The box to keep or remove the list was cut off on a desktop, inside a side column that scrolled on its own. No headline was visible before scrolling. Before reading anything, the reader saw a dashboard of zeros: 0%, read 0, spent 0p. The pictures were too small to read, and every card asked for a decision before it said what the article was. All fourteen were fixed in the same release, and the review is published with what was done about each.
keep-up

This is the second page in a week that had to change because people started to use it. The first was the page for publishers, which was written once on 11 October and was out of date within a week, because this site ships something most days. It is now rebuilt in every release from the site's own register of what it can do, and it keeps a version history of its own, so a page I send to someone can be held to what it said on the day I sent it. The reading list is the same lesson in another form: the page that a person lands on is the page that has to be good, and it is rarely the one I would have designed first.
keep-up

The workflow is what makes that possible. A voice memo becomes a brief, the brief becomes a release, the release is reviewed, and the next person who opens a list gets the new page. The list itself never changes: a link sent in the first week opens the new page today, with the same articles in the same order, because the link is only numbers and names.
back

The lists go out easily now. The answers do not come back as easily. Today a reader can reply by email, and the reply comes to me. What I would like next is for the page itself to be the place to answer: to select a sentence, add a note, and send it to me, and for those notes to reach the agent as well as me, in the same form as the notes the newsroom already collects from its own readers.
back

Two pieces of that are already on this site. Every reader's notes are already records in their own browser and their own vault, and the newsroom already has a lane that a note can be sent down. And on pki.sgit.ai there is a working way, in the browser, to hold a key pair, publish a public key, and sign and encrypt a message to someone, even through a QR code. The next step is to join them: notes from a list that are signed, so the agent knows they are from the person they claim to be, and my own notes, signed with my key, so the newsroom knows they are mine. The two smaller next steps are for the sender to choose the view a list opens in, and for the list to have a picture of its own, for the email.
limits

There is no count of how many lists were opened, or read. By design, the newsroom keeps no record of who opened a link. What I know comes from replies. The twenty is the agent's count, as of 18 October. It is from its debrief, by subject, and it has not been recounted since. The screenshots use an example list. The people I have sent lists to are not named; Steve is the site's own example. The reading shown on a list is what that browser knows. A reader who read an article on their phone sees it on their laptop only if they use their own vault. The Designer is a role played by an agent. Its review is published with what was done about each finding; it is a check, not an outside study. The answers coming back, signed, are a proposal. Nothing in the last section is built yet.
limits
If you have received a reading list from me and would like to tell me what worked and what did not, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: RiskMandate needs somebody to underwrite agent behaviour policies, and before asking who can, I would like to define what they would be underwriting. An insurer de-risks an action. When I insure the laptops and phones in my house against burglary, the insurer asks about the locks, where I live and where I keep things, sets a limit for any one item and a limit for the policy, leaves out the things it will not cover, and at the claim asks whether the doors were locked. If they were, it pays, up to the limit. Agents need exactly that, and an agent behaviour policy already has the shape: every capability the agent can reach is a row, the mandate says which rows the business authorised, and the delta between them is the reach nobody asked for. So the insurance policy is one-to-one with the behaviour policy: each row it names has its own limit (say £20,000 for corrupted customer records, £50,000 for leaked customer data), each row it does not name is excluded, and every real control on a row, one that something enforces, lowers that row's premium. A line in the prompt is not a control and earns nothing. The formula has to be deterministic, if this, then that, and the runtime the agent runs on is part of it. Start from the maximum: in a worked example, an uncontrolled support agent pays £69,850 a year for £80,000 of cover, insurable but hardly worth buying; with five enforced controls on a certified runtime it pays £6,720 for the same cover. The numbers are illustrative; the shape is the point, and the Licence to Operate vault on sgit.ai already runs a simulated version of it. This is the first of a series: next, who can underwrite this today.

One agent's behaviour policy as an insurance policy: a limit, controls and a premium per row. Illustrative. Five articles and three vaults on one idea: an agent's behaviour policy read as an insurance policy, priced row by row, split with the vendor, and backed by capital.
in-short

An insurer de-risks an action, up to a limit, under conditions. A house policy asks about the locks, caps any one item, leaves some things out, and pays if the conditions held. An agent behaviour policy already has that shape. Each capability the agent can reach is a row; the mandate says which rows the business authorised. So the insurance is one-to-one with the policy. Each row it names has its own limit; each row it does not name is excluded. Not everything is insurable, and that is the point. The bigger the reach, the bigger the delta, and the delta is what no policy covers. The formula is deterministic. If this control is enforced on this row, the rate falls by this factor; if it was not holding at the time of the loss, the row does not pay.
in-short

Only enforced controls count. A hook, a proxy, a capability removed from the grant. A line in the prompt earns nothing. Where the agent runs is part of the price. A certified runtime lowers it; an uncertified one raises it, or ends the licence to operate. Start from the maximum and come down. In the worked example, £69,850 a year for £80,000 of cover, uncontrolled; £6,720 with five enforced controls on a certified runtime. The first version already runs. The Licence to Operate vault on sgit.ai simulates one agent's policy, with a band, a ceiling, a pool and a premium. Next in this series: who can underwrite this today. And what the vendors of agents should cover themselves.
house

The question behind this series is simple to ask. RiskMandate writes agent behaviour policies, and the end of the roadmap is agents an insurer can cover. So who would underwrite an agent behaviour policy, today, and what would they be underwriting? Before the first question, I would like to answer the second, because I think the answer is simpler than it usually gets made.
house

Take a house. I have laptops and phones in it, and some jewellery, and I would like to be covered against burglary. The insurer asks where the house is, what kind of locks it has, and where I keep things. It sets a limit for the policy and a limit for any one item, and it asks me to list anything valuable above a certain value. It does not cover everything: a laptop worth £20,000 or a data centre in the spare room is not something a contents policy is built for. Then, when something is stolen, it asks the questions again: were the doors locked, was the phone left in plain view? If the conditions held, it pays, up to the limit.
house

None of that is my invention. A broker's guide puts the limit for any one item "usually between £1,000 to £2,500" and tells you to "declare any expensive items to your insurer" (Howden, 9 January 2025). A comparison site says "You may need BS3621 standard five-lever mortice deadlocks on all your external doors in order to get home insurance", and that "you are unlikely to be able to claim on your home insurance if you leave your doors unlocked" (MoneySuperMarket, updated 3 September 2026). Conditions, limits per item, exclusions, and a check at the claim. A home contents policy and an agent behaviour policy, question by question. That is a very simple proposition, and it is what agents need. Not a policy for "AI", and not a questionnaire about the company's security programme, but a policy for one agent, in one deployment, that names what is at risk, the conditions, the limits, and what is left out.
uninsurable

An agent behaviour policy starts from the same place as the house: an inventory. What can your agent reach? explains it for the person who has to decide. The grant is everything the agent can technically do. The mandate is what the business actually asked it to do. The delta is the gap: inside the agent's reach, outside its authority. The Licence to Operate vault on sgit.ai makes it countable. Its support agent has a grant of 12 capabilities and a mandate of 4: read the customer record, search the help centre, generate an answer, draft a reply. The other 8, including crm:write, crm:export, mail:send and shell:exec, are in its reach and in nobody's mandate, and the vault says it plainly: no policy covers them.
uninsurable

That is not a weakness of the idea. It is the idea. You are not going to insure every action of an agent, and the bigger its reach, the more of it will be uninsurable. What insurance can do is cover the rows you want covered, one by one, and leave the rest visibly outside. The vault even has a number for it: customer records are marked uninsurable above 20 per action.
one-to-one

So the insurance policy has the same rows as the behaviour policy. Take an agent connected to the customer database. It can make changes, so it can corrupt records or delete users; it can read them, so it can leak them; it answers customers, so it can tell them something wrong that they act on. Each of those is a row, and each row gets its own limit: up to £20,000 for customer records corrupted, up to £50,000 for customer data leaked, up to £10,000 for a wrong answer acted on. The lead figure is that policy, row by row. The last row is the one that matters most: shell:exec is in the agent's reach and there is no limit beside it, so it is excluded, at any price. If the business wants it covered, it has to name it, decide who accepts it, and put a control on it.
one-to-one

This one-to-one mapping is what makes the rest work. A claim maps to a row; a row has a capability, a limit and the controls that stand in its way; each control has something that enforces it and a log that says whether it held. That is a graph, and it is the kind of graph we now build every day: governs, enforces, attests set out the three levels at which a rule is kept, and approved business mandates why most companies already have the policies and need them turned into tested controls. With generative AI to read the systems and keep the graph current, a mapping at this level of detail is something that can be maintained at scale, and I think that is what will make this kind of insurance scale too.
formula

The underwriter's part is a formula, and it has to be exact: if this, then that. Here is the shape I have in mind, written down so it can be argued with: A row with no limit is excluded. If a capability is reachable and the policy names no limit for it, it is not covered. Each row starts at a base rate. The share of the limit that an uncontrolled agent would pay for that row in a year. Each enforced control on a row multiplies its rate by a factor below one. Write removed from the grant, a proxy that caps records per action, drafts only, an egress allow list, a hook that holds a reply for a person. Where the agent runs multiplies every row. Below one for a certified runtime, above one for an uncertified one. The premium for a row is its limit times its rate. The policy's premium is the sum.
formula

A claim pays if the event maps to a row and every condition on that row held at the time, up to the row's limit. If a condition was not holding, the row does not pay: the door was not locked. The rule that does the most work is in step 3: only an enforced control counts. RiskMandate's licence to operate puts it as "A condition with nothing enforcing it is an expectation". We measured the difference in an agent that may only chat: when a system prompt told the model to ignore it, the policy as a line in the prompt held 3 of 12 attacks; with a deny-all hook, 12 of 12. So in the formula, a line in the prompt gets a factor of 1. It may be good practice; it is not a control an insurer can price.
formula

The worked example is in a data file, computed by a short script, with every input in it. The factors are mine and illustrative; fitting them is what an underwriter does with loss data, and that is the part we do not have.
maximum

The formula makes one thing visible that I think matters commercially. You can still insure an uncontrolled agent; it is just expensive. In the worked example, a support agent with no enforced controls, on an uncertified runtime, pays £69,850 a year for £80,000 of cover, 87% of it. That is insurable and close to not worth buying, and it is not far from what I have seen in cyber insurance, where the premium can come near the payout. There is still a reason to pay it: when you need cover to operate at all, a contract or a regulator asking for it, the price of the cover is a cost of doing business. The annual premium for £80,000 of cover as enforced controls are added, one at a time. Illustrative.
maximum

Then each real control brings it down. A certified runtime takes it to £50,800. Removing crm:write from the grant, to £39,280. Drafts only, with mail:send removed, to £22,280. At most 20 records per action, enforced by a proxy, to £11,440. Outbound traffic only to an allow list, to £8,720. Refunds and legal points held for a person, to £6,720: 8% of the cover. The line in the prompt, second in the figure, moves nothing. That is how I think cyber insurance should have worked. Much of it has priced on a questionnaire about the company, filled in once a year, rather than on the detail of what a given system could do and what stopped it. RiskMandate's insurability page says the same thing more sharply: "Questionnaires describe. Evidence prices."
measured

None of this is new to insurance. Wherever insurers can measure, they price on the measurement. Young drivers. A black box in the car measures how it is driven, and the price follows. One insurer says "We'll collect data on your speed, acceleration, braking and cornering", and that the data helps "work out your renewal price" (ingenie). A broker adds that many such policies restrict night driving, "usually between 10pm and 6am", and that poor driving may "increase your premium" (Howden, 1 September 2025). That is a licence to operate with conditions, measured, and priced on the measurement.
measured

Health. UK private medical insurance is underwritten on what you bring to it. Under a moratorium, a condition you had in the five years before joining is not covered until you have gone two years without it; under full medical underwriting, you disclose your history and the exclusions are set before the policy starts, as AXA Health and Bupa describe their own policies. The cover goes up or down with the preconditions.
measured

Cyber, where it measures. Some cyber insurers have moved from the form to the scan. Coalition wrote in 2021 that "Traditional cyber insurers will typically ask insureds to fill out long applications", and that it uses "scanning technology that collects and correlates data from internet accessible devices" instead (Coalition, 3 August 2021). And for AI itself, Munich Re says of its aiSure cover that "The quality of the model and its performance stability determine the premium" (Munich Re). The founder of AIUC, which insures agents, put the idea in one line: "Just like consumers get a better car insurance rate for having airbags and anti-lock brakes" (Fortune, 23 July 2025).
measured

My argument is that the more mature an insurance line is, and the more data its insurers can measure, the more precisely it prices, and the more of the risk it is willing to take. Agents are unusual in how much can be measured: every tool call, every record read, every hook decision is logged by the systems that run them. The data an underwriter would need is already being produced. What is missing is the mapping from that data to a row and a limit.
where

Some of the conditions are not about the agent at all, but about where it runs, the way a house policy asks for the postcode. There will be places where certification is needed: of the runtime, of the hooks and proxies that enforce the controls, down to the software they run on. If an agent runs somewhere that is not certified, either the premium goes up or the row is not covered. This is also where the licence to operate comes in. RiskMandate describes it as four facts and a date: the organisation as the authority, one agent in one deployment as the licensee, the behaviour policy as the instrument, and an interval after which it has to be renewed, with each condition beside the thing that enforces it. An insurer could reasonably make a current licence a condition of cover, and a change of runtime a reason to look again.
licence

We already have a working version of this, simulated. In the Licence to Operate vault, the policy is a rate table: a normal band, a threshold above which the agent has to ask, a ceiling per action, a pool with an untouchable reserve, and a premium per interval. A simulated support conversation offers three replies at every turn, one inside the band, one that draws on the pool, one outside cover, each with its cost before you choose: 1,400 tokens and 1 record for looking up the customer, 4,800 tokens and 3 records for reading two linked accounts as well, and mail:send, outside the mandate entirely. You can let the policy lapse, reinstate it, or trigger a repricing.
licence

The terms are files in the vault, and they read like the formula above. The simulated policy for the support agent, concierge-sim-2026-09-03, has a normal band of 2,000 tokens and 5 customer records per action, asks a person above 6,000 tokens or 12 records, sets a ceiling of 8,000 tokens and 20 records per action, refills a pool of 12,000 tokens and 40 records per conversation, and holds back a reserve of 10% that no decision may draw on. Above 20 records the action is not a bigger draw but an exclusion, and the policy gives the reason in one line: "a record once read by an agent is exposure that cannot be unread". Its rating rule is the experience rating an underwriter would recognise: if the pool is drawn on most days, the normal band is wrong, "and the response is to raise the band and shrink the pool, never to enlarge the pool".
licence

At the top it asserts four things: licence held, mandate in force, policy paid, inside cover. All four can be lost. That is the top-up and the payout I had in mind, run in a browser. It is in credits, not money, and the vault says so on its surface: "Simulated. The terms are real files in this vault; the replies are scripted; the numbers are made up."
vendors

There is one more party I think has to carry some of this: the vendor that provides the agentic workflow. When a company buys an agent from a vendor, part of what goes wrong will be the vendor's, and I believe vendors will have to start backing their agents with cover of their own. Some vendors have started, and the most interesting part is the conditions. Microsoft's commitment for Copilot says "we will defend the customer and pay the amount of any adverse judgments or settlements", but only "as long as the customer used the guardrails and content filters we have built into our products" (Microsoft, 7 September 2023). That is the locked door again: cover, conditional on a control. Google and Anthropic made similar commitments in late 2023, and like Microsoft's they cover copyright claims, not what an agent does.
vendors

The closer examples are about performance. Intercom offers "up to $1M of your money back" for its Fin agent under stated conditions, and a programme that pays if Fin does not reach "at least a resolution rate of 65%" (Intercom, 24 June 2025). ElevenLabs announced on 12 February 2026 a policy backed by the AIUC-1 standard, so that "these AI voice agents - and their actions - can now be insured, just like any other employee" (ElevenLabs). Munich Re offers vendors "performance warranties" that "enable you to indemnify your clients for their financial losses". None of these is yet a payout per row of a behaviour policy. Each is a step towards one, and the third article in this series is about what the vendor's share of a row should be.
next

This article defines what would be underwritten. The series continues with the questions it leaves: Who can underwrite an agent behaviour policy today, and what does that look like? A research brief, starting from the companies in underwriting the agent economy, reviewed, which already sell AI agent cover, and asking each what it would need to price per row. What should the vendors of agents cover themselves? What exists, and what a vendor's share of a row would look like. The formula as a vault. The rows, the limits, the factors and the claim rule as data, with a page that computes the premium for your own agent, so the formula can be argued with in numbers rather than in words. It is now vault m1wbrefr, with a calculator.
limits

The numbers are illustrative. Every limit, base rate and factor in the worked example is mine, chosen to show the shape; none is fitted to loss data, and an underwriter would set them differently. No insurer has agreed to this. It is a definition of what we would like to have underwritten, not a product anyone sells. The formula is a sketch. Real controls interact, losses correlate across agents that share a model, and a fleet needs an aggregate limit; a multiplier per control is the simplest form, not the right one. Certification of runtimes does not exist yet in this form. Which body would certify a runtime, and against what, is open. The Licence to Operate vault is a simulation. Its replies are scripted and its numbers are in credits; it shows the mechanism, not a price.
limits

The comparisons with other insurance are by analogy. The sources for how motor, health and home insurers price are below, and each works under its own rules and regulators. If you underwrite, or would like to underwrite, the risk of one agent at a time, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources
