Abstract: I read this newsroom on an iPad more than anywhere else, and the way I give it feedback has been a chat window and screenshots. On the page itself, selecting a sentence brings up the iPad's own Copy, Look Up and Translate menu, right where the site's Highlight button was, so the button was hidden under it. So every article now has a Pen, beside the Vault in the bar at the top. Select words and a small bar appears at the foot of the screen, away from the iPad's menu: keep them, comment on them, or tell the newsroom. The Pen opens on the right with three parts: what is selected; my marks on this page, with comments of my own that stay in my browser; and notes for the newsroom, with the passage they are about, which go when I send them, down the lane my vault already has. The fourth part is the one I care most about. pki.sgit.ai now has a register of people and their public keys, with my key as its anchor, and a rule for one key to vouch for another: an operates link, both ways, with an end date. A browser can use the same rule. The Pen makes a key for this browser with pki.sgit.ai's own code, and once my key on pki.sgit.ai says it operates that browser, every note I send from it is signed, and anyone can check it against the public register: the newsroom's lane reader does it in Python, a page does it in the browser. I looked at four ways to log in here with my pki.sgit.ai key: one passkey for both sites, a sign-in redirect like OAuth, a key per browser vouched for in the register, and the same by QR code. The key per browser works today, with nothing new on pki.sgit.ai; the redirect is the better end state; the shared passkey is a wider door than either site needs. The two vaults stay two vaults, connected by keys rather than by a shared door.
An article with the Pen open on the right, at 1280 pixels wide in the Newsprint theme, and a highlighted sentence.
in-short

Feedback on this site went through a chat window. I read on an iPad, and the page itself had nowhere good to put what I thought. The iPad's own menu covered the Highlight button. Selecting words brings up Copy, Look Up and Translate above the selection, exactly where the button sat. Every article now has a Pen. A button beside the Vault; a bar at the foot of the screen while words are selected; a panel on the right. My marks are mine. A highlight with a comment, kept in my browser and drawn on the page, never sent. Notes for the newsroom go when I send them. With the passage they are about, as the vault pane's own notes, down my own lane. A note can be signed, and checked by anyone. A key for this browser, vouched for by my key on pki.sgit.ai, signs each note; the register says whether to believe it.
in-short

Four ways to log in with my pki.sgit.ai key. One passkey for both sites, a sign-in redirect, a key per browser in the register, the same by QR code. The key per browser works now. It uses the register's own rule for agents, both ways and dated, and nothing new on pki.sgit.ai. Two vaults, connected by keys. The reader vault and my pki.sgit.ai account stay separate; keys, not a shared door, connect them.
chat

Most of what I tell this newsroom I type into a chat with its agent, and most of it is about something I read a minute earlier: this sentence is over the top, this figure is wrong, this one is good. I wrote about the problem in the editor's channel: the chat loses where I was. And in reading with a pen I described the three moments of reading, reading, marking the page, and processing what you marked, and how much I want the second and third to work on a screen the way they now work for me on paper.
chat

The site has had pieces of it for a while. A Highlight button appears when you select words in an article. The vault pane has notes, done, fix this, wrong, idea, with the phrase you selected, and a lane that carries them to the newsroom. But the pieces were in different places, behind different buttons, and on the device I read on most, one of them did not work.
ipad

On an iPad, selecting words in Safari brings up the system's own menu, Copy, Look Up, Translate, Find, just above the selection. That is exactly where the site put its Highlight button, so on an iPad the button sat under the menu. It was not a bug in either; they simply wanted the same place. Two ways to place a button for selected words on an iPad: as it was, and as it is now. Drawn, not a screenshot. Two changes fix it. On a touch screen the Highlight button now goes below the selection, not above it. And while words are selected, a small bar appears at the foot of the screen, out of the menu's way, with three choices: keep the words, comment on them, or tell the newsroom. The Pen keeps the selection the moment it is made, so a tap that clears the selection, as taps on an iPad often do, no longer loses it.
pen

The Pen is a button in the bar at the top of every article, beside the Vault. It opens a panel on the right, and the page moves over to make room, so I can read and write at the same time. It has four parts. Selected. What I have just selected, with keep it, keep it with a comment, or tell the newsroom. Your marks on this page. The highlights on this page, each with a comment of my own if I want one. They are kept in this browser and drawn on the page, and they are private: nothing sends them anywhere.
pen

Tell the newsroom. A note about this page, of a kind (fix this, wrong, idea, liked, or just words), with the passage it is about. It is the same record the vault pane keeps, so it travels with my vault to my other devices, and it goes to the newsroom only when I press Send, down the lane my vault already has. Signed as you. Who is holding the pen, which is the new part.
key

pki.sgit.ai now has a register of people and their public keys, with my key as its anchor. It also has a rule for one key to vouch for another, built for agents: an agent's key is operated by a person when the person's record links to it with operates and an end date, and the agent's record links back with operated-by. A link only counts when it goes both ways, and it ends when its date does. That is the first pattern from PKI everywhere: a key the session makes for itself, which a person vouches for.
key

A browser is the same kind of thing as an agent: something that acts for me, for a while. So the Pen makes a key pair for this browser with pki.sgit.ai's own code, which the newsroom now carries unedited, signs two statements, who it is and that I operate it, and gives me the submission for the register. Once the register holds it and my key on pki.sgit.ai says it operates that browser, every note I keep in the Pen is signed with it. How a note is checked as mine: the browser's key, the register at pki.sgit.ai, and the chain back to my key as the root.
key

The check is the part that matters. Anyone can do it, from the public register, without taking the newsroom's word for it: a page does it in the browser with the register's own code, and the newsroom's lane reader does it in Python when it reads my notes. Both start from a pinned root, my key's fingerprint, never from whatever the register's list of anchors says, because whoever can change a site can change that list. A note from this browser then reads as "signed and checked: operated by the root until" its date. A note changed after it was signed fails. A key nobody vouches for is valid and says so.
login

The question behind all of this is how I log in here with my pki.sgit.ai key. The two sites share a design and code: pki.sgit.ai's passkey door is this site's, copied with one constant changed. They differ on purpose in two places. Each passkey belongs to its own host, and each site derives its own door from it. So the same passkey cannot open both, and would open two different doors if it could. There are four ways through. Four ways to log in to newsroom.sgit.ai with a pki.sgit.ai key, compared, and the decision taken. One passkey for both sites. Both could ask for passkeys made for sgit.ai, and then one passkey works on both. But every passkey made so far is for its own host, so everyone would make a new one, and it would let every sgit.ai site ask for the same passkey, a wider door than either needs. Not now.
login

Sign in with pki.sgit.ai. The newsroom sends me to pki.sgit.ai with a key it made for this browser; pki.sgit.ai, where I am signed in, signs "this key acts for me here until this date" and sends me back. One click, and my private key never leaves pki.sgit.ai. It needs a page on pki.sgit.ai that does not exist yet. The best end state. A key per browser, in the register. What the Pen does now: three steps the first time, nothing new on pki.sgit.ai. The same, by QR code. The browser's key shown as a QR code, scanned on my phone where pki.sgit.ai is open, which signs the link. The copying done by the camera, as a secret is a QR code proposes.
login

So the key per browser now, the QR code next to it, and the redirect when pki.sgit.ai has an authorize page. The browser key and the checks stay the same in all three; only the way the link is made changes.
vaults

The reader vault here and my account on pki.sgit.ai stay two vaults, with two doors, on two hosts. Merging them would mean one site's code could read the other's vault, and a bug in either becomes a bug in both. They are connected by keys instead. The browser key is the first connection. The next is to keep it in the reader vault's master, so every device that opens my vault can sign. And the reader vault's own key can be handed to pki.sgit.ai sealed to my key, the way pki.sgit.ai already hands over vault keys, so my pki.sgit.ai account holds the key to my newsroom vault, and the newsroom holds nothing of my account there.
vaults

A login area, then, is not an account on a server. It is the Pen's signed section and the vault pane: who holds the pen, what the register says about them, and the notes they have sent and their state. It is a place of my own because the key is mine.
stands

The Pen is on every article from this release, with the bar at the foot, the private marks, the notes with their passages and the signing. The lane reader checks signed notes against the register, and a test signs notes, checks them in Python and in the browser against a register of its own, and changes one to show that it then fails. What I still have to do myself is the first link: send the submission for the browser I read on, and link to it from my key on pki.sgit.ai. What is left to build: the authorize page and the QR code on pki.sgit.ai; the browser key kept in the reader vault's master; the newsroom's own feedback lane, published as an inbox in the register, so a reader with no vault can send a note too; and the agent's daily pass reading signed notes first.
limits

No note has been signed and checked against the live register yet. The check is tested against a register and a root the test makes; my own browser's key is not in the register until I send its submission and link to it. The browser's private key is kept in the browser's storage. It is worth what its link says and the link ends on a date, but it is not in a vault yet. A note still needs the vault's lane to reach the newsroom. The newsroom's own lane, for readers with no vault, is not built. The redirect and the QR code are proposals. They need pages on pki.sgit.ai. The iPad figure is drawn, not a screenshot. The fix was tested in a browser at phone width, not on an iPad. The register's code is pki.sgit.ai's, copied. A fix there reaches this site when the copy is refreshed, with its hashes.
limits
If you read this newsroom and want to tell it something about a page, open the Pen on that page; if you would like to try signing your notes too, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: In the five months to October 2026 the personal agent became a product category. Meta's Muse, OpenAI's dots, Google's Gemini Spark, Microsoft's Autopilot, Amazon's Alexa+, Apple's rebuilt Siri and a self-hosted open source project called OpenClaw all give a person an always-on agent with a computer of its own, a memory made of files, and connectors into email, calendars, messages and money. This article reads them through two lenses this site already uses. The first is RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policy: what each agent can reach, what it was asked to do, what stands in the gap, and what record it leaves. The second is the data: where the memory rests, who holds the keys to it, who processes it, who could be compelled to hand it over, and what happens to the people in it who never signed up. Read that way, the products are strong where they are strong, a separate permission authority is a real barrier on actions, and candid where they are candid, Meta's own engineers say today's protection against Meta reading the memory is policy rather than cryptography. The second half is a design for a personal agent on the technology this site describes: memory in vaults the host holds only as ciphertext, a behaviour policy as the permission authority, compute in the user's browser where a small model is enough and in an attested enclave when it is not, with a key for one task's data released by the user's device against the enclave's attestation and destroyed when the task ends, the frontier model called only for the step that needs it, and a folder per person with provenance that the person it describes can read. The two designs, the vendors' and this one, converge on files and no database and a page per person. The difference is who holds the keys, who can read the pages, and who pays for it. It ends with what exists today, what does not, and the question of who gives the mandate over information in the first place.

The personal agents of autumn 2026 placed by two questions, where the compute runs and who can read the memory at rest, with the colour giving the strength of what stops the agent acting. Most products sit in the vendor's corner. The blue square is the design in the second half of this article. Positions are approximate and from the sources listed; a shipped confidential option would move a product a long way across the horizontal axis. The category arrived in 2026. An always-on agent with a cloud computer of its own, memory as files, connectors into the user's accounts, and a confirmation step before sensitive actions. Muse, dots, Spark, Autopilot, Alexa+ and Grok Bot share the shape; Apple put most of it on the device; OpenClaw put all of it on the user's own machine and became the design Meta acknowledged copying.

Lens one, actions. Read as behaviour policies, the products differ most on the barrier. Muse's Sentinel is a separate permission authority for every connector action and every byte of network egress, which is a boundary. Rules, approval modes and confirmation prompts are settings. A self-hosted gateway leaves the barrier to the user. The mandate is unwritten in every case, and the terms place responsibility for the agent's actions on the person who instructed it.

Lens two, data. Read for sovereignty, the products mostly sit in one corner: memory in the vendor's cloud, encrypted with the vendor's keys if at all, processed by the vendor's model, trainable by default unless switched off. Meta's engineering post says of today's Muse that it "does not prevent Meta from accessing data when necessary to support, secure or operate the service", and that the version that would is with trusted testers. Apple's Private Cloud Compute is the published design that does the most: stateless, attested, with the user's device wrapping keys only to nodes whose measurements are in a public log.

The people who did not sign up. A page per person in the user's life is a memory about non-users. Meta's help page says such information is not linked to an account and that rights can only be honoured where it is. The regulators have noticed: the ICO names the "concentration of personal information facilitating personal assistant agents" as a novel risk, and the CNIL recommends partitioning memory by agent and process with automated expiry. The convergence. Two designs built for different reasons arrived at files, no database, and a page or folder per person filled in from evidence. The vendor's came from a harness; this site's came from the vault model. What differs is who holds the keys, who can read the pages, what stops the agent, and what pays for it.

The design. Memory in vaults the host holds as ciphertext. A behaviour policy as the permission authority. Compute in the browser where a small model will do, in an attested enclave when it will not, with a key for one task's slice of the memory released by the user's device against the enclave's attestation and destroyed when the task ends. The frontier model for the step that needs it, with the step's inputs and no standing access. A folder per person that the person can read. What exists. The vaults, the one-way read keys, the write-only lanes, the behaviour policy, and the team running on them exist. In-browser decryption exists. The enclave integration, the attested key release and the per-task scoping are proposed, and the hard rows are named.

The dates matter, so here they are. Google announced Gemini Spark on 19 May 2026, "a 24/7 personal AI agent" on a cloud machine that "keeps working in the background even when you close your laptop". Microsoft introduced Scout on 2 June, an always-on work agent "with its own identity, memory, computer and workspace", and renamed it Autopilot on 25 September. Apple rebuilt Siri on 8 June around an on-device orchestrator with Private Cloud Compute behind it. SpaceXAI opened Grok Bot to early beta on 11 August. Meta launched Muse on 8 September: "Muse runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else's agent can reach it." OpenAI launched dots at its developer day on 29 September, "always-on" agents where "each dot has its own cloud computer and browser". Amazon's Alexa+ had reached every US Prime member on 4 February. Anthropic's Cowork, from January, runs "on Anthropic's servers, in an isolated environment", and on the day this article was written its local-only mode for individual plans was withdrawn.

Behind all of them is a project that is not a company. OpenClaw, Peter Steinberger's MIT-licensed, self-hosted gateway, was first published in November 2025 under another name, went through three renames, and by March 2026 had a quarter of a million stars on GitHub. It connects whichever chat apps a person uses to whichever model they pay for, runs on their own laptop or server, and keeps its memory in files under their home directory. When researchers found that Muse's harness files were near-identical to OpenClaw's, Nat Friedman confirmed it: "We built Muse from scratch, but it is definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw." The lineage is worth stating because it says where the shape came from. The shape is a personal agent as a small operating system of files, and it was designed by someone building for themselves before it was productised by companies building for everyone.

Adoption followed. The download estimates for Muse in its first fortnight varied by a factor of two depending on which firm was counting, and were in the millions by every count. The question this article is about is not whether people want this. They do. It is what they are handing over to get it, and whether the same thing can be had for less. RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policy reads any agent in four words. The reach is everything it can do, measured from the deployment: accounts, connectors, credentials, tools. The mandate is what the user asked for. The gap is the difference. The barrier is what stands in the way of each row of the gap, and it is typed honestly: a boundary is enforced above the agent's reach, a setting is a switch the agent's own account could flip, an expectation is a rule in prose, and none is none. The site's own wording: "a control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include." Footprint and blast radius added what the agent actually did, read afterwards, and what a row would cost if used in full.

Two lenses for any personal agent. The first is about actions and is RiskMandate's vocabulary. The second is about the data: where it rests, who holds the keys, who processes it, who can be compelled, what trains and what deletes. A product can be strong on one and silent on the other, and the two are rarely advertised together.

The reach is the user's life. Every product above asks for connectors into email, calendar, documents, messages, payments and the browser, and the pitch is that the agent is useful in proportion to what it can reach. The Center for Democracy and Technology's Miranda Bogen put the consequence plainly to Wired: these tools "are actively soliciting users to plug their whole lives in", and "the breadth of access to information that these tools have will lead to a ballooning of what they know about users." In the vocabulary here, the reach is being maximised on purpose, and for an agent that acts in the world the reach includes sending, paying and inviting, three things that cannot be undone.

The mandate is unwritten. None of the products has the user write down what the agent is for before it runs, because the whole appeal is that it will work out what to do. That is a design choice with a cost: without a mandate there is no gap to inspect and no near miss to catch. The terms fill the vacuum with liability. Muse's supplemental terms: "You are solely responsible for the instructions, goals, and guidance you provide to Muse. You are also solely responsible for the actions Muse takes or directs in furtherance of those instructions, goals and guidance." The FTC's chairman said much the same in September 2026, rejecting the idea of agents as independent actors: those who instruct the tools are liable.

The barriers are where the products differ, and one of them is a boundary. Meta's Sentinel, in the engineering post's words, "is a separate host-side agent from your Muse. It is the sole permission authority for approval to perform actions with connectors to third-party services and for all egress over the network." Credentials are held apart: "Muse has no visibility into people's passwords or payment methods." That is a boundary in the policy's sense, enforced outside the agent's own process, and it is stronger than anything the team described in the previous article has on actions, where "no agent sends" is a prompt and a policy. OpenAI's dots have built-in rules, user rules that allow, block or require approval, read-only "proactive research" while the user is away, and manual password changes; those are settings, real and flippable. Spark is "designed to ask you first before performing high-stakes actions like spending money or sending emails"; Cowork has manual, auto and skip approval modes; Alexa+ confirms purchases. OpenClaw binds its gateway to the loopback interface, pairs unknown senders with a code, and offers a sandbox that is off by default; the barrier is whatever the user configures, and its own documentation says it "is not a hostile multi-tenant security boundary for mutually adversarial users".

The footprint is uneven. Muse "shows people a complete audit trail of everything it has done and plans to do", and the users who asked for the VM's filesystem got it, which Meta then made a feature. The dots FAQ, as reported, says users cannot view, delete or directly modify individual dot memories, which is a memory a person cannot audit. OpenClaw's footprint is the user's own disk.

The blast radius was demonstrated, not argued. The incidents of September 2026 are the reach being exercised by someone other than the user. A Mac zero-day in Muse's desktop app let any unprivileged local process redirect dictation to an attacker's server and capture or inject prompts; Meta fixed it within a day. A crafted link could make Perplexity's Comet exfiltrate data from the user's connected accounts; Perplexity added a classifier and a permission step. OpenClaw's January incidents included publicly exposed control endpoints leaking keys and chat histories and a supply-chain campaign of hundreds of malicious skills. The lesson is the one the ultimate insider drew: whoever takes the agent over inherits its reach and ignores its mandate, so the blast radius is defined over the reach, and the reach here is a person's accounts. The second lens asks six questions, and the answers are in the policies and the engineering posts rather than the launch videos.

Where it rests. In the vendor's cloud, for every product but two. Muse: "Muse runs on an environment in the cloud called a virtual machine ('VM'). This is the core environment where Muse keeps information you share." Dots: a cloud computer per dot. Spark: a Google VM. Apple: on the device, with a cloud that keeps nothing. OpenClaw: the user's own machine.

Encrypted, by whom. This is the question the products answer least. Muse's privacy policy does not say; Meta's engineering post does: the Secure VM "restricts access to your data by Meta personnel through operational policies. It does not prevent Meta from accessing data when necessary to support, secure or operate the service." The protection today is policy. The Confidential VM, "where the whole VM, including a person's data and conversations with Muse, is encrypted with a key only they hold, so not even Meta can access it", is "intended to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data in your VM", is with a small group of trusted testers, and is promised for later in the year, with external auditors given the design and source. That is a serious commitment and it should be held to. The dots FAQ does not disclose encryption or key holding. OpenClaw's data is on the user's disk, but reviews of version 2.0 note that its secret store is not encrypted at rest, so "the user holds everything" includes holding it in the clear. Apple's design is the one to study: the user's device "will wrap its request payload key only to the public keys of those PCC nodes whose attested measurements match a software release in the public transparency log", and the nodes are stateless, so "personal data leaves no trace".

Who processes. Meta's own models on Meta's infrastructure. OpenAI's. Google's, with "Keep Activity" required for Spark, which means human reviewers may see some data and retention of up to three years under Google's Gemini terms. Apple's foundation models on Apple silicon, and since June on Google Cloud too, inside Intel TDX and NVIDIA confidential GPUs with "at least two separate roots of trust from independent vendors". Alexa+ uses Anthropic's Claude through Bedrock as well as Amazon's models. OpenClaw sends prompts to whichever provider the user chose, under that provider's terms. In every cloud case the model sees the plaintext of what it is asked, which is unavoidable; the question is whether anything else does, and for how long.

Who can be compelled. Whoever holds plaintext or keys answers a legal request. A policy that restricts staff does not remove the ability; the engineering post's sentence says so about Muse, and would say so about any product in the vendor's corner. Only a user-held key removes the ability, and only an attested, stateless design removes the ability during processing. The previous article made the same point about the team's vaults: the host's blindness is a property of the mathematics, not a promise, and so it holds against the host's own staff and the host's own lawyers.

Training and ads. Muse's policy says "You decide whether we can use your interactions with Muse to train and improve our AI models", and the setting is reported as on by default; identifiers are removed first; the policy adds that "Muse doesn't share your conversations or the data in your virtual machine with Meta ad systems." Dots on personal plans train unless the general "improve the model" setting is off; business plans do not. Spark trains if Keep Activity is on, which it must be. Apple states that nothing is trained on from Private Cloud Compute requests.

Deletion, and the people who never signed up. Muse's policy: "Muse may still 'remember' information it learned from what you deleted." And then the question Wired raised. The extracted instructions tell Muse to keep "a page for every person in the user's life", refreshed hourly, with sections for facts, history, the relationship, what is in common, open threads and how to strengthen it, and to use only the evidence available because "invented details are worse than an empty page." Those pages are about people who are not users. Meta's help page for them says their information "is not stored in a way that allows Meta to reasonably identify which information belongs to a particular person", and therefore that Meta "can only honor data subject rights in relation to information that is linked to a Meta account or stored in a way that allows Meta to identify which information relates to a particular person." A person with a page has no route to it. The supplemental terms place the consent problem on the user, who warrants that they have "obtained all necessary permissions, consents, licenses, and authorizations" including "consents (where required) from third parties whose personal information may be processed".

The regulators have started on this. The ICO's agentic AI horizon note of 8 January 2026 lists among the novel risks the "concentration of personal information facilitating personal assistant agents" and the problem of "determining controller and processor responsibilities through the agentic AI supply chain". The CNIL's exploratory note of 20 July 2026 recommends "partitioning of memory by agent and by process (with size limits and automated expiry)", sandboxing, risk-tiered actions with human approval for the higher tiers, and a user kill switch. GDPR's Article 25(2) requires that "by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed", and Article 32 names "the pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data" first among the measures. A page per person, refreshed hourly, filled from a connected inbox, is a hard thing to reconcile with the first of those, and a memory the vendor can read is a weak showing on the second.

Muse is free for a large allowance with $20 and $100 tiers, and Mark Zuckerberg said at Connect that the expectation is "over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions". Dots are included in OpenAI's paid tiers. Spark needs Google's top subscription. Apple sells hardware. OpenClaw is free and run by a foundation. None of these is a reason to distrust a product. It is a reason to notice that most of the companies in the vendor's corner are companies whose other products are advertising and engagement, that an agent which knows the pages of everyone in your life is an unusually complete profile, and that the policy promising the agent's data stays out of the ad systems is a policy. How much to trust is then a personal arithmetic: what the agent does for you, against what the reach would cost you if someone else drove it, against what a change of policy would cost you later. The point of the second half of this article is that the arithmetic does not have to be done that way.

Here is the thing that made the previous article worth writing before this one. Strip the branding from Muse's memory and from the team's CRM and they are the same shape. Muse keeps structured text files in a per-user machine, a page per person, started sparse and filled from evidence, with sections a person would recognise. The team keeps plain JSON and Markdown in a vault, a folder per person, with a record, an append-only ledger, every message with provenance and a hash, and a graph of what the person cares about. Both refuse to invent: Meta's instruction is that an empty page beats an invented detail; the team's rule is that a fact without a source is a bug. Both arrived at files and no database. Meta's shape came through OpenClaw, from a developer building a harness for himself. The team's came from the vault model, where a file is the thing that can be encrypted, versioned, hashed and read with a read key, which is the argument this site has made since What sgit is.

Same shape, different keys. A vendor's per-user memory as its extracted instructions and policies describe it, beside the team's folder per person. The rows beneath are where they part: where the files live, who can read them, what stops the agent, whether the subject can ask, and what pays for it. The convergence is good news, because it means the privacy question is not a question of architecture. The files can be the same files. What differs is who holds the keys to them, who can read them, what stops the agent, whether the person described can see their page, and what business the whole thing is paying for. Those are the rows a design can change without changing the shape.

What follows is a design, not a product. It uses the pieces this site documents, names the pieces it would need that do not exist, and places the hard rows where they belong, in a build brief rather than in the claims. Three zones. The user's device holds the keys and does what compute it can. The vault host holds ciphertext and never a key. When a task needs more than the device has, it runs inside an attested enclave that receives a key for one task's slice of the memory. The model provider sees the step the enclave sends and nothing at rest.

Memory in vaults the host cannot read. The agent's memory, the pages per person included, is a vault: every file, filename and commit message encrypted on the user's side before it leaves, the host holding ciphertext, sizes and timings and nothing else. The key hierarchy gives three credentials with three reaches: a vault key that writes, a read key derived one way that only reads, and an append lane that only adds. The agent's own working memory is a vault; a shared memory with a partner or a team is another; what the agent may show a third party is a read key to a vault that holds only that. Nothing trains on any of it because nothing but a key-holder can read it. This part exists, and the team runs on it.

A behaviour policy as the permission authority. Muse got one thing right that the team has not yet built: a separate authority that decides every connector action and every byte of egress, outside the agent's own reach. In this design that authority enforces a behaviour policy the user can read. The reach is measured from the connectors and keys the agent holds. The mandate is written, in the user's words, before the agent runs, and amended from the near misses afterwards. Each row of the gap has a barrier typed honestly, and the authority is where the boundaries live: which connectors, which lanes, which keys, which recipients, which hours. The send stays with the person for anything irreversible, by default, and the policy can relax that one row at a time with a record. The footprint is read from the vault afterwards, by the user or by a reviewer with a read key and no production access. This part exists as a vocabulary and as a team's practice; the authority that enforces it is the first thing to build.

Compute where the user can see it, or where nobody else can. Three places, chosen per step by budget rather than by architecture. The browser or device first. WebGPU is in all four major browsers as of Safari 26 and Firefox 141, and in-browser inference stacks run models of up to about three billion parameters on a current phone and seven or eight billion on a laptop with sixteen gigabytes of memory, at speeds that are usable for triage, classification, extraction, embedding, search and summaries. Those are most of what a personal agent does between its big steps. The vault client already decrypts in the browser; the small model can read what it decrypts without the plaintext leaving the tab. What is not feasible locally today is frontier reasoning over long contexts and multi-hour tool loops, and the design does not pretend otherwise.

An attested enclave when the device is not enough. The cloud vendors sell confidential compute to small companies now. AWS Nitro Enclaves produce a signed attestation whose measurement a key service can require before releasing a key, though an enclave has no network, no persistent storage and no GPU. Google's Confidential Space has run on H100 GPUs in general availability since June 2026, releases data only to a workload whose image, container and VM all pass attestation, and states that "the workload operator has no access to the data, and can't control access to it either." Azure's confidential VMs with an H100 in confidential mode have been available since 2024 at roughly a quarter more than the unencrypted equivalent, with key release gated on attestation claims. The design the enclave should copy is Apple's: the user's device checks the enclave's measurement against a published image and wraps the key itself, rather than trusting the cloud's key service to do it.

The frontier model only for the step that needs it. With the step's inputs and no standing access to the memory. Where a provider offers attested inference, Cohere's shipped in September 2026 and Google publishes prompt-encryption SDKs for its confidential GPUs, the step can run there; where it does not, the policy records that this step's inputs are seen by a provider under its terms, and the user decides which steps those are. Temporary access to one slice of the memory, controlled with a public key. The device scopes the task to files, the enclave attests, the device verifies and wraps a fresh key to the enclave's public key, the host serves ciphertext, the step runs and encrypts back, and the key dies with the task. The grant, the attestation and the card stay in the vault as the footprint. Proposed; the rows to verify are in the text.

Temporary access to one slice, controlled with a public key. This is the mechanism that joins the vault to the enclave, and it is the part the memo asked for. The user's device decides, per task, which files the agent step may read: this person's folder, this week's mailroom, nothing else. The enclave boots a measured image and attests, producing a public key signed by the hardware root. The device verifies the measurement against the published image and wraps a fresh data key for exactly the scoped files to that public key. The enclave pulls the ciphertext, decrypts in memory, runs the step, encrypts its results back to the vault, and discards the key at the end or at a deadline of minutes. The grant, the attestation and the step's card are written to the vault as files. No standing key sits in any cloud. The scope is least data rather than least privilege: an agent step cannot reach what it was not handed a key for. The deciding seat is the user's device, which can be offline for every step it runs itself. And the record is complete by construction, because every grant is a file a read key can later show.

A folder per person that the person can read. The pages exist, because they are useful, and the previous article's three classes apply to them: public, private-ish and personal, with personal refused by policy and checked for. Every fact carries its source. The person described can be sent their folder, as a "what we know about you" pack, and correct it. That is the answer to the non-user problem this design can give on its own: not that the page does not exist, but that it is held under the user's keys, kept to what the work needs, and shown on request to the person it is about.

What the enclave operator still sees, and what remains open. Timing, sizes and traffic shape are visible to the host in every scheme. The attestation roots are the hardware vendors', so trust moves from the agent vendor to the chip vendor and the cloud; Apple's requirement of two independent roots is the only consumer design found that addresses this. Physical attacks on memory buses, a passive interposer for about a thousand dollars in one published case and an active one for under fifty in another, have extracted keys from SGX and SEV-SNP, and in late 2025 were extended to DDR5 and to the chains that NVIDIA's GPU attestation depends on; the vendors call physical access out of scope. A security firm's review of Nitro's key-service integration in August 2026 noted that the key owner can always ask the cloud vendor to restore a default key policy, which is a boundary with a support ticket behind it. These are not reasons to abandon the design. They are the rows of its own gap, to be typed honestly in its own policy.

Exists. Vaults with client-side encryption, one-way read keys and write-only append lanes, documented with their limits on this site and running under a team of twelve agents. The Agent Behaviour Policy as a vocabulary and as that team's practice, with barriers graded. Messages between agents as files. A folder per person with provenance. Decryption in the browser. Confidential compute with attested key release from three cloud vendors, with GPUs on two of them. In-browser inference for small models. A published design, Apple's, for client-wrapped keys to attested, stateless nodes.

Does not exist. A permission authority that enforces a behaviour policy outside the agent's reach, in this estate. An enclave image for an agent step, with its attestation checked from a browser without a vendor service in the loop. The per-task key release from the user's device to that enclave. A scoped read of a vault, where a key opens some paths and not others, which today is approximated with one vault per scope. Key revocation in sgit, which its limitations page says plainly does not exist, so a leaked key still means a new vault. Signed commit authorship, so that in a shared vault an agent's identity comes from its branch rather than a signature. Any measurement of what the three-zone split costs in time and money for a real day of a real person's agent.

The build order, in five steps, to be written up as a brief: the permission authority as a policy-enforcing proxy for connectors and egress, run beside the agent; scoped vaults, one per task class, until scoped reads exist; a browser-first agent for triage, search and summaries over a decrypted vault, measured; one enclave step on one cloud, with the device-side attestation check and key wrap, measured against the same step run unprotected; and the pack a person can be sent about themselves, generated from the folder.

The design above answers how a personal agent can keep a person's secrets from the host, the vendor and the model, and how a person can see what it keeps about them. It does not answer the question the Wired piece raises underneath, which the previous article also left open. The information that fills a page about a person was given, by that person, to the user, in an email or a message or a conversation. It was not given to an agent, and not to whatever the agent passes it to. Who gives the mandate over a piece of information is a different question from who holds the key, and it gets a document of its own. What this design offers is that whatever the answer turns out to be, a policy per agent, a rule per relationship, a key per task and a memory that can be shown to its subject are the mechanisms it would need, and they are the same mechanisms that keep the secrets.

The agent team as it runs: the setup whose properties this design generalises, and the three classes of information. The identity we wanted to give the agents: why no secret can live inside an identity provider, which is the same argument one layer down. Memory is not a spectator sport and Introducing fractal semantic graphs: memory as files with provenance, and the grammar a page per person uses. What sgit is, Vault credentials, the security model and Limitations: the three credentials, what the host sees, and what does not exist yet. Before you give an agent a connector, give the connector a twin: the footprint recorder at the line where the reach is exercised.

Abstract: An idea came up while I was answering a post about agent liability, and I think it deserves to stand on its own as a proposal. Today an agent gets a prompt from us and a system prompt from its vendor. It should also get an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor accepts, enforces as far as it can, and eventually answers for. It is the beginning of dealing with something the models have got away with for a long time: they do not separate code from data, so every instruction and every piece of content arrives in the same channel. Now that agents can do a great deal, and are starting to go off the rails in public, their behaviour is becoming an existential threat to the companies that make them, through liability and above all through trust: it does not take many users being hurt before people stop giving agents instructions at all. Two industries have been here. Aviation did not get safe out of altruism; it got safe because every crash became world news, and at the accident rate of 1995 today's traffic would bring about a hundred fatal airliner accidents a year instead of twelve. Payments got some of the best security teams anywhere because liability for fraud was moved onto the card companies and the banks, and the fraud detection followed the money, often spotting a merchant's breach before the merchant did. Regulation alone does not do it; some industries are happy to pay the fines. It works when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way. A policy beside the prompt is how to make them point the same way for agents: the user answers for what is outside the policy, and the vendor for the rows it accepted. Most agents already run a policy of their own; we just cannot see it, rely on it, or stop it changing. And the system prompt itself is a light behaviour policy that is not written like one: the next step is for the vendor's own rules to become a published policy too, layered with ours.
What an agent is given today in two modes, and as proposed: the policy as a separate, versioned input.
in-short

A third input. Beside the system prompt and the prompt, an agent should take an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor acknowledges, enforces where it can, reports against, and answers for. It starts on an old problem. Models do not separate code from data. Instructions and content arrive in one channel, which is why prompt injection may never be fully fixed. A policy is a second channel for the one thing that should not be negotiable: what the agent may do. Agent behaviour is now an existential risk for the vendors. Through liability, and more through trust. A small number of people badly hurt is enough for many more to stop giving agents instructions. Aviation got safe because crashes became news. At 1995's rate of fatal airliner accidents per million flights, 2025's 38.7 million flights would have meant about 105 fatal accidents. There were 12.
in-short

Payments got safe because liability moved to the companies. Card fraud caps for consumers, a liability shift onto whoever had not adopted chip cards, standards written by the card brands, and in the UK, banks reimbursing scam victims, after which those losses fell by about a fifth. Regulation alone is not enough. Some industries pay the fines. The improvement comes when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way. The user answers outside the policy, the vendor inside it. The rows the vendor accepted are the vendor's to keep. That is a better model than "you clicked allow", and the vendors who get it right will win on it. Agents already run hidden policies. Claude in Chrome will not type a password. That is a policy. We should be able to read it, rely on it, and know when it changes.
in-short

The policy goes into both modes, and today both are hope. Over the API we write the whole prompt; in the Claude apps and Claude Code the vendor adds its own system prompt and we add ours. Either way the policy is text the model is asked to keep, which is why the checks have to get stronger. A system prompt is a light behaviour policy. It tells the agent how to behave. It should be written as one, layered: the vendor's policy, then the deployer's, with business logic only the deployer can write.
idea

When I answered Ralf Thomas on where the liability line should fall, the section I most wanted to write was the last one: that an agent should take a behaviour policy beside its prompt. I think it deserves to be its own proposal, put out there on its own, because I think it can help a lot, and not only with the liability conversation.
idea

Here it is. Today, an agent gets two things: a system prompt from its vendor, and a prompt from us. It should get a third: an Agent Behaviour Policy, defined to a standard, that says what this agent, in this deployment, is meant to do and must not do, row by row, with what stands in the way of each row. The vendor should accept it as part of the deployment, enforce as much of it as the platform can see, report every breach against it, and, eventually, carry liability for the rows it accepted. The vocabulary already exists, published under CC BY at abp.sgit.ai: the reach, the mandate, the gap between them, and the barriers, none, expectation, setting and boundary, of which only a boundary is a control.
code-and-data

This is the beginning of dealing with something the models have got away with for a long time. They do not separate code from data. In a computer, the instructions and the things they operate on are kept apart, and most of the worst security bugs in history, from buffer overflows to SQL injection, are what happens when that separation breaks. In a language model there is no separation to break. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre put it plainly in December 2025: current models "simply do not enforce a security boundary between instructions and data inside a prompt", which is why it thinks prompt injection may never be mitigated the way SQL injection was. Simon Willison's phrase for the consequence is that "LLMs follow instructions in content", and the email the agent reads is content.
code-and-data

A behaviour policy does not fix that, and I do not want to claim it does. What it does is take the most important instructions out of the channel that anybody can write into. The prompt can be argued with by an email. The policy should not be: it is loaded by the platform, versioned, signed, and checked by something other than the model where it can be. It is a second channel for the one thing that should not be negotiable, what the agent may do, and every row the platform can enforce outside the model, as Claude Code's own documentation says of its permission rules, "are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model".
existential

Now that agents can do a great deal, and are starting to go off the rails in public, with the incidents of 2026 as the record, I think agent behaviour is becoming an existential threat to the companies that make the models. One reason is liability, which could be very large: from 9 December 2026 software, AI systems included, is a product under the EU's new product liability rules. The bigger reason is trust. People will stop giving instructions to agents if they believe this can happen to them, and I do not think it takes many. A decent number of people badly hurt, in a news cycle that amplifies every one of them, is enough for a much larger number to decide that agents are not for them. That is a systemic risk to the whole business model, not a cost of doing business.
existential
Two industries have been here, and both are worth looking at, because neither got safe for the reasons people usually assume.
aviation

Fatal airliner accidents in 1995 and 2025, and what 1995's rate would have produced in 2025. Aviation is a good example of a complex system of technology, business process and people that learned to be safe, and I keep coming back to it, in The ultimate insider and in The investigation GitHub owes its customers. But let us be clear about why. It did not get there for altruistic reasons, or because it was the right thing to do, although, to be fair, the people who run airlines also fly, so they have some interest of their own. It got there because everybody knew that every crash, anywhere in the world, would be news, and more so every year.
aviation

When I was growing up, a plane crash was a regular news story. Here is the arithmetic of what would have happened if safety had stayed where it was. In 1995 there were 2.72 fatal airliner accidents for every million flights, on the Aviation Safety Network's count. In 2025 there were 38.7 million flights. At the 1995 rate, that is about 105 fatal accidents in a year, two a week. The Aviation Safety Network counted 12. Air travel more than doubled, from about 18 million flights in 1995, and the fatal accidents went down, not up: the rate fell almost ninefold. An industry with two fatal crashes a week would not have the passengers it has, and everybody in it understood that.
payments

Where the liability for payment fraud was moved, and what followed at each step. The second example is payments. If you compare payments with privacy, or with most of cyber security, card payments have had, for a long time, some of the best security teams, some of the best fraud detection and some of the best security measures anywhere. Why there? Very simple: the liability was moved onto the companies. Consumers stopped carrying the loss. In the United States, since 1970, a cardholder is liable for unauthorised use "only if... the liability is not in excess of $50". In the UK, a payment provider may make the payer liable "up to a maximum of £35" for a lost or stolen card. The loss went to whoever had not done the work. In October 2015, in the United States, counterfeit fraud liability shifted to the issuer or the merchant that had not adopted chip technology.
payments

The industry wrote its own standard. The PCI Security Standards Council was founded in 2006 by American Express, Discover, JCB, Mastercard and Visa, and every merchant that takes cards answers to it. And it keeps moving. Since October 2024 UK payment providers must reimburse victims of authorised push payment scams, up to £85,000. In the first 18 months, 88% of the money lost was reimbursed, and an independent evaluation found that losses sent over Faster Payments fell by around 21%, because reimbursement "strengthened incentives" to invest in prevention.
payments

The moment you pass the liability for fraud to the company, its security picks up. And it shows in who finds the fraud. I know of many cases, and the public record has famous ones, where a company discovered fraud not because its own security team picked it up, but because a card company, a processor or a bank came to it and said: you have fraud going on here. Target learned of its 2013 breach when it was contacted by the US Department of Justice, and Verizon's breach report for 2013 found that in almost all point-of-sale breaches the intrusion was reported to the victim by third parties, with law enforcement and external fraud detection the leading causes of discovery. The parties carrying the loss had built the detection.
regulation

Companies at that level cannot be made to do anything they truly do not want to do. There are industries, social media is the obvious one, where companies are more than happy to pay the fines when the rule goes against the core of their business model: Meta's €1.2 billion GDPR fine in 2023 was the largest at the time, and in 2025 the European Commission fined it €200 million over its "consent or pay" advertising model. The places where we saw real improvement were the places where three things lined up: a rule, a liability that landed on the company, and a systemic risk to the business model that the company could see. Sometimes the companies were glad of the regulation, because "it applies to everybody" let them all do what each of them needed to do. Payments is that case. Aviation is that case. Agents can be that case, if we give the liability somewhere precise to land.
inside

The proposed split between the vendor's built-in policy, the deployer's policy and what stays with the user. So here is the core of the proposal. If we want agents to be trustworthy, we need to push some enforcement, some criteria for enforcement and, eventually, some liability onto the vendors of the models and the agents. An Agent Behaviour Policy is a good standard to do it with, because it makes the split explicit. The agent runs with a policy. The rows the vendor accepted, the vendor keeps, and answers for if they break. Everything the policy does not cover stays with the user, as it does today. That is a much better model than the one we have, where the user is liable for everything because they clicked allow, which is the shell game the last article described.
inside

It would also be a competitive advantage for the vendors that get it right. A vendor that can say "these forty rows are boundaries on our platform, enforced outside the model, and we stand behind them" is selling something a vendor with a longer system prompt cannot. As Hope or enforcement measured, the share of a policy that rests on hope can fall from 97% to 23% with the right design; the vendors are the ones who can make the next part of that fall. What would the standard need? Not much that does not already exist in the vocabulary: A versioned policy file, with the reach, the mandate, the gap and the barriers, row by row, signed by the deployer, so both sides know which version was in force. The vendor's acknowledgement, per row: enforced by the platform as a boundary, kept as a setting, or accepted as an expectation the model is asked to keep.
inside

The vendor's own policy, published in the same format, so the two can be read together. A breach report, the same day, for every row broken and every near miss, which Authority outside the model argued should be the norm. Liability per row, starting with the boundaries the vendor said it enforces, which is where the vendors can most easily say yes.
modes

The figure at the top shows both modes and the end state. Today, the policy has to travel inside what we already provide, and where that is depends on how we reach the model. Over the API, we control the whole message. There is no vendor system prompt added to it; Anthropic's own release notes say its app system prompts "do not apply to the Claude API". So the behaviour policy goes into our system prompt, and the vendor's checks on misuse still run, unseen. In the Claude apps and in Claude Code, the vendor provides an explicit system prompt of its own, and we add to it: our instructions, a project's CLAUDE.md, or, in Claude Code, text appended to the default system prompt. The behaviour policy goes there, after the vendor's.
modes

In both modes, today, the system prompt and our behaviour policy are almost pure hope. That is hope-driven development again: we really hope the model will keep them when it reads them. Anthropic is honest about this for Claude Code: CLAUDE.md files are treated "as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead." And we do not know how sure the model is that it is keeping them. I have not seen a model report, rule by rule, how confident it is that it followed an instruction, and I have not seen a published figure for how often a system prompt or a policy is kept under pressure. That is research worth doing.
modes

My argument is that this should be a lot stronger than it is. The vendors already run checks outside the model where they care: Claude in Chrome has "a safety classifier" that validates each action before it is performed, and the platforms check for misuse and abuse in ways the user never sees. The behaviour policy deserves the same machinery, with one difference: the policy's rows should be controlled by us. The whole point is that a behaviour policy brings in business logic, which is specific to the application and to what we are doing, and which no vendor can write for us.
system-prompt

There is a more evolved version of this, with more than one level. Claude itself has a behaviour policy: the rules in its system prompt and the ones its platforms enforce, from not typing passwords to asking before financial sites. It is just not written as one. And there is an argument that the system prompt should move to being a behaviour policy, because a system prompt is a light version of one already: it tells the agent how to behave. It is written as paragraphs for a model, when it could be written as rows a person can read, a platform can check, and a dispute can point to.
system-prompt

So the layering I would want is simple to say. The vendor's policy, published, for what the platform does everywhere. The deployer's policy, on top, for what this agent in this business may do, with the business rules only the deployer can write. Each row marked with what enforces it, and each layer with an owner. That is the conversation I would like to have with the vendors: not "add our text to your prompt", but what the policy should be, how it should exist, and who checks it, when we are giving an agent explicit guidance on how to behave across a whole business.
already

I would argue most agents already run a version of this, and we cannot see it. Claude in Chrome is a good example. Anthropic's safety page says that "Claude is prohibited from" engaging in stock trading, bypassing captchas and inputting sensitive data, that it "asks for permission before accessing financial sites", and its Claude Code documentation says that when it meets a login page, "it pauses and asks you to handle it manually". So the user enters the password, because Claude says, I am not going to put a password in. Cool. That is a policy, and a good one, and we built the subscriptions service on it.
already

But we have no control over it, no guarantee of it, and it can change at any time. It is a vendor's policy described in a help article, not a row we can point to in a dispute. Which suggests a project worth running: reverse-engineer the policies the agents already run, the way we measured a Gmail connector's thirty tools and found that sending ran with no prompt while trashing a message stopped for approval, and publish them in the ABP format. If the vendors will not publish their policies yet, the measured ones are the next best thing, and the gap between the two is a finding.
limits

The confidence question is open. I have not seen published figures for how often a model keeps a system prompt or a policy under pressure, or a model reporting its confidence rule by rule. It is a proposal. No vendor accepts a behaviour policy as an input today in the sense described; Claude Code's permission rules and managed settings are the nearest thing, and they cover settings, not business rules. A policy does not separate code from data. It moves the most important instructions into a channel the content cannot reach. Prompt injection remains. The aviation numbers mix sources. The 1995 rate is the Aviation Safety Network's count over ICAO departures, via Our World in Data; the 2025 count is ASN's and the flights are IATA's. Both cover airliners with more than 14 seats, cargo included.
limits

The payments history is short and partial. Fraud did not disappear; it moved, and the incentives are why the industry chased it. The 21% fall is one evaluation's estimate. "It does not take many users" is my judgement. I have no number for how many incidents it takes to lose public trust in agents. Liability per row is the end state, not the start. Acknowledgement and breach reporting can come first; liability follows the boundaries a vendor is willing to stand behind. If you build an agent platform and would accept a policy, or you deploy agents and want to write one, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Summary: An idea came up while I was answering a post about agent liability, and I think it deserves to stand on its own as a proposal. Today an agent gets a prompt from us and a system prompt from its vendor. It should also get an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor accepts, enforces as far as it can, and eventually answers for. It is the beginning of dealing with something the models have got away with for a long time: they do not separate code from data, so every instruction and every piece of content arrives in the same channel. Now that agents can do a great deal, and are starting to go off the rails in public, their behaviour is becoming an existential threat to the companies that make them, through liability and above all through trust: it does not take many users being hurt before people stop giving agents instructions at all. Two industries have been here. Aviation did not get safe out of altruism; it got safe because every crash became world news, and at the accident rate of 1995 today's traffic would bring about a hundred fatal airliner accidents a year instead of twelve. Payments got some of the best security teams anywhere because liability for fraud was moved onto the card companies and the banks, and the fraud detection followed the money, often spotting a merchant's breach before the merchant did. Regulation alone does not do it; some industries are happy to pay the fines. It works when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way. A policy beside the prompt is how to make them point the same way for agents: the user answers for what is outside the policy, and the vendor for the rows it accepted. Most agents already run a policy of their own; we just cannot see it, rely on it, or stop it changing.

Abstract: I was with my friend Sean Turner this week, talking about agent behaviour policies, and he described something he built that I think is great. It is a natural-language control policy for agent skills, and a CI pipeline that checks every skill contributed to an organisation-wide repository against it before hundreds of developers pull it down to their machines. Is it safe, secure, well documented, usable, understandable by the model and understandable by people. And the part that makes it more than a linter: it reads the skill in its context. A skill that turns internal documentation into a LinkedIn post has no untrusted input to worry about; a skill that pulls content off the web is handling untrusted text, and should treat it as data, not obey it. It sits beside a security scan, not instead of one: the question is operational, is this the right way to give this skill to our workforce. That is an agent behaviour policy for a skill: the mandate is what the skill is for, the reach is everything it touches, and the gap is the risk. A control written in natural language is hope-based security, better than nothing and not enough on its own. Sean's next step is the one I keep coming back to: use an agent to write deterministic rules that follow the natural-language control, and keep the description, not the code, as the canonical version. Change the description, regenerate the code. Using models to need them less. And in a common ontology, a whole catalogue of skills becomes one graph, where the dangerous combinations are a query.
A policy for every skill: the control at the top and the checks each contributed skill passes.
in-short

Skills are the new dependency. A skill is instructions an agent follows with a developer's reach, pulled by hundreds of people from one repository. Sean Turner built a control for them. A natural-language policy and a CI pipeline: is a contributed skill safe, secure, documented, usable, and understandable by the model and by people. It reads the skill in context. Internal documents in, a post out: little to worry about. Web pages in: untrusted text, to be treated as data. Beside the security scan, not instead of it. The question is operational: is this the right way to give this skill to our workforce. It is a behaviour policy for a skill. Mandate: what it is for. Reach: what it touches. Gap: the risk. Natural language alone is hope-based security. Better than nothing; it needs deterministic controls around it.
in-short

Use models to need them less. An agent writes deterministic rules from the control; the description stays canonical; change it, regenerate the code. A catalogue is a graph. In a common ontology, "which skills read untrusted content, reach private data and can send it out?" is one query.
built

I was with my friend Sean Turner this week, talking about agent behaviour policies, and he described something he had built that I liked a lot. He has a different name for it: a natural-language control policy for agent skills.
built

The setting is an organisation with an organisation-wide repository of skills, the packages of instructions and reference material that an agent loads to learn how to do something. Anyone can contribute one, and once it is merged, hundreds of developers can pull it down to their machines and use it. Sean's control is a policy written in plain language about what a skill must be before that happens, and a CI pipeline that checks every contribution against it: is it safe, is it secure, is it well documented, is it usable, is it understandable by the model that will load it, and is it understandable by the people who will review and maintain it. In his words, does it make sense as a reasonable skill.
built

What makes it more than a linter is that it reads the skill in its context. His example: a skill that publishes an article to LinkedIn, working from internal documentation, has no prompt injection risk to speak of, because nothing it reads was written by an outsider. A skill that goes and pulls content off the internet is a different thing. Everything it reads is untrusted, and the check expects the skill to say so: not to trust that input, to defang it, and to do something meaningful with it as data rather than as instructions. And it is complementary to a security scan, not a replacement for one. A scanner asks whether a skill contains something malicious. Sean's control asks something more operational: is this the right way to contribute this skill to our workforce, given what it will touch when hundreds of people run it.
built
I have described it as he described it to me; I have not seen the code, and I could not find it published.
dependency

This matters because a skill is code that nobody compiles. When an agent loads it, its instructions become part of what the agent does, with whatever the agent can reach: the developer's repositories, their mail, their cloud credentials. In Attacks rewritten as mandates the same shift showed up from the supply side: Chainguard now publishes hardened agent skills, each with a record of the upstream commit and what was changed. That makes a skill a trustworthy input. It does not say what an agent running it should be allowed to do.
dependency

The public tooling for reviewing skills is arriving too, and it shows where the gap is. MongoDB's guide to reviewing an agent skill describes a structural validator that "runs in CI and produces pass/fail results", and a review skill that "optionally uses an LLM judge to score content quality across multiple dimensions": clarity, actionability, token efficiency, scope discipline, directive precision, novelty. That is a good quality bar, and none of those dimensions asks where the skill's inputs come from. The guide says as much about the hardest part: "No automated tool currently reasons across skill boundaries." Sean's control asks the question the quality bar leaves out, which is the one that decides whether a skill is dangerous.
abp

Two illustrative skills in the columns of an agent behaviour policy, with the same check and different verdicts. When Sean described it, I recognised the columns. An agent behaviour policy describes one agent in one setting by its mandate, what it is for; its reach, everything it can actually touch; the gap between the two, which is the risk; and the barrier in front of each row of the gap. Describe a skill that way and the context question answers itself.
abp

The LinkedIn skill's mandate is to turn internal documentation into a post. Its reach is reading internal documents and posting to one account; its inputs are written by the organisation; the gap is posting anything other than the reviewed draft, and a person pressing publish is the barrier. The web research skill's mandate is to gather and summarise public sources. Its reach is fetching any address and writing into the workspace; its inputs can be written by anyone; the gap is following an instruction found inside a page, and the barrier has to be treating fetched text as data.
abp

Put that next to the rest of what the skill can reach and you have the most useful question in agent security. Simon Willison named the lethal trifecta: "Access to your private data", "Exposure to untrusted content", and "The ability to externally communicate in a way that could be used to steal your data". A skill with untrusted inputs is one leg. Whether the agent loading it has the other two is a property of where it runs, which is why The policy draws the liability line argued that anything with the trifecta should take a behaviour policy beside its prompt.
hope

A control written in natural language, checked by a model, is what I call hope-based security. You give the model the rule and you hope it follows it. Hope or enforcement measured the cost for one customer service agent: built the obvious way, 97% of its rules were kept only by the model's good behaviour. But I agree with Sean that it is far better than not having it. A written control is the only place the intent exists. It is what a reviewer reads, what a model can check a skill against, and what the deterministic rules are written from. Without it, there is nothing to enforce, only code that nobody can explain. With it, the question becomes how much of it can be wrapped in something that does not hope.
codify

That is where Sean's next step comes in, and it is the part of the conversation I liked most. Use an agent to write deterministic rules that follow the natural-language control. For example, a skill that declares it reads the web gets a rule that checks it routes fetched content through a step that treats it as data. A skill that can post externally gets a rule that it has a human step before it does. The model reads the control once and writes code; from then on, the code runs, the same way every time, at no model cost per run. I usually put that as using models to not use models. The model is the author of the deterministic part, not the judge of every case. And the natural-language control is, in effect, the requirements document for those rules.
codify

Then the rule that makes it work: the description stays the canonical version, not the code. If the control changes, you change the description and regenerate the code. That is the same round trip Policy as code needs a policy first ran this week with Open Policy Agent: rows of a behaviour policy generated into Rego, the requests decided, and the code parsed back to find the rows with no code and the code with no row. AWS has built a version of it into a product: its agent policy service lets developers "describe rules in plain English instead of writing formal policy code in Cedar", generates candidate policies, and checks them for being "overly permissive, overly restrictive, or contain conditions that can never be satisfied". The direction is the same everywhere: people write intent, models write enforcement, and the intent stays the source.
graph

The last piece is what happens at the scale Sean is working at: not one skill, but hundreds, contributed by different people, describing themselves in different words. My approach to that is to bring them to a common ontology, the way fractal semantic graphs do: every skill described by the same columns, mandate, reach, inputs and their trust, barriers, as nodes with named edges, while each skill keeps its own text. Then the questions that matter across a catalogue are queries, not reviews. Which skills read untrusted content, and which of those can also reach private data and send something out? Which skills changed their reach since they were approved? Which declared a barrier that no generated rule enforces? MongoDB's guide is right that no tool reasons across skill boundaries today. A graph of skills in a common vocabulary is how one could.
licence

All of this is open source on our side, and it follows the line I keep drawing at RiskMandate: describe the behaviour in a policy; from the policy, grant a licence to operate that can be checked and revoked; and from a policy with a record behind it, make the agent insurable. To be clear about where that stands, as Ten hard questions for RiskMandate put it: "we make agents insurable. We do not insure them." The licence to operate and the insurability index are designs. A skill with a policy, checked at contribution and enforced where it runs, is the smallest version of that whole chain. Sean has built the first link.
limits

Sean's tool is described from a conversation. I have not seen its code, and I could not find it published; the details are his, as he told them, and any errors are mine. The two skills in the figure are illustrations. They follow his examples; they are not skills from his repository. Generated rules are only as good as the control. A model can write a rule that checks the wrong thing; the rules need tests and review like any code. A barrier written as "treat it as data" is still an expectation until something outside the skill enforces it. Licence to operate and insurability are designs, not products a customer runs today.
