in-short

I was with a friend this week, talking about agent behaviour policies, and he described something he had built that I liked a lot. He has a different name for it: a natural-language control policy for agent skills.
articles/versions/a-policy-for-every-skill/v1.2.0.html
in-short

The setting is an organisation with an organisation-wide repository of skills, the packages of instructions and reference material that an agent loads to learn how to do something. Anyone can contribute one, and once it is merged, hundreds of developers can pull it down to their machines and use it. His control is a policy written in plain language about what a skill must be before that happens, and a CI pipeline that checks every contribution against it: is it safe, is it secure, is it well documented, is it usable, is it understandable by the model that will load it, and is it understandable by the people who will review and maintain it. In his words, does it make sense as a reasonable skill.
articles/versions/a-policy-for-every-skill/v1.2.0.html
in-short

And it is complementary to a security scan, not a replacement for one. A scanner asks whether a skill contains something malicious. His control asks something more operational: is this the right way to contribute this skill to our workforce, given what it will touch when hundreds of people run it.
articles/versions/a-policy-for-every-skill/v1.2.0.html
dependency

The public tooling for reviewing skills is arriving too, and it shows where the gap is. MongoDB's guide to reviewing an agent skill describes a structural validator that "runs in CI and produces pass/fail results", and a review skill that "optionally uses an LLM judge to score content quality across multiple dimensions": clarity, actionability, token efficiency, scope discipline, directive precision, novelty. That is a good quality bar, and none of those dimensions asks where the skill's inputs come from. The guide says as much about the hardest part: "No automated tool currently reasons across skill boundaries." His control asks the question the quality bar leaves out, which is the one that decides whether a skill is dangerous.
articles/versions/a-policy-for-every-skill/v1.2.0.html
abp

When he described it, I recognised the columns. An agent behaviour policy describes one agent in one setting by its mandate, what it is for; its reach, everything it can actually touch; the gap between the two, which is the risk; and the barrier in front of each row of the gap. Describe a skill that way and the context question answers itself.
articles/versions/a-policy-for-every-skill/v1.2.0.html
hope

But I agree with him that it is far better than not having it. A written control is the only place the intent exists. It is what a reviewer reads, what a model can check a skill against, and what the deterministic rules are written from. Without it, there is nothing to enforce, only code that nobody can explain. With it, the question becomes how much of it can be wrapped in something that does not hope.
articles/versions/a-policy-for-every-skill/v1.2.0.html
codify

That is where his next step comes in, and it is the part of the conversation I liked most. Use an agent to write deterministic rules that follow the natural-language control. For example, a skill that declares it reads the web gets a rule that checks it routes fetched content through a step that treats it as data. A skill that can post externally gets a rule that it has a human step before it does. The model reads the control once and writes code; from then on, the code runs, the same way every time, at no model cost per run.

graph

The last piece is what happens at the scale he is working at: not one skill, but hundreds, contributed by different people, describing themselves in different words. My approach to that is to bring them to a common ontology, the way fractal semantic graphs do: every skill described by the same columns, mandate, reach, inputs and their trust, barriers, as nodes with named edges, while each skill keeps its own text.

Abstract: This morning I am reading the printed release candidate 2 of Generation ZX Developers, with a pen. At the same time, I asked the newsroom's agent to review the same text, chapter by chapter, in my voice, and not just to list problems but to fix them, work out the principles behind the fixes, suggest how the book should be paced and ordered, and bring over what works on this site, including a way to draw the book itself. Six editors worked in parallel, one per part, under one brief whose first rule was never to invent anything. They found that the book's main problem is that it repeats itself: the same story, quote or number told in two to four chapters. They found the point of a chapter often came after the 2018 book or a tour of later parts, that some chapters were their newsroom articles pasted in, and that the company part has five chapters of hypotheses and no result. The fixes come as seven patches, in priority order, that take the book from 74,666 to 64,351 words, still above 200 pages. The seventh exists because a review in parts drops things between the parts. It is all in a vault, because the agent does not have write access to the book's repository and does not need it: a patch is the change, and applying it is the decision. A pull request by another name.
Release candidate 2 of Generation ZX Developers, printed and spiral-bound on a café table, photographed by Dinis.
in-short

Two reviews at once. I read the printed book; the agents reviewed the same text. Not a list of problems. Fix them, then name the principles behind the fixes. Six editors, one brief. One per part, and the first rule: never invent anything. The book repeats itself. That is most of the cut: 74,666 words down to 64,351. The point should come first. Not the 2018 book, and not a tour of later parts. Seven patches, in priority order. The seventh fixes what fell between the parts. The book, drawn as itself. A graph of the chapters, for the back cover. A vault, not a pull request. A patch is the change; applying it is the decision.
reading

This morning I am reading the book. Release candidate 2 is printed and spiral-bound, 168 pages, and I am going through it with a pen, the way I read anything I care about. Discovering the book told the story of how it was written in one evening; this is the first time I have held it.
reading

At the same time, I asked the newsroom's agent to read the same text. Not to tell me whether it was good, but to do the work an editor does: go chapter by chapter, propose the changes, make the ones that only need cutting and reordering, and then reverse engineer them into a set of principles the book should follow and the guidelines to check them. Then make suggestions about pacing and structure. And take what works here, the graphs, the altitudes, the visualisations, and see what the book could use, including whether one of those visualisations could represent the book itself, on the cover or on the back.
editors

The agent split the book into six parts and gave each to an editor working in parallel: the opening, the frame and the job, working with agents and judgement, the company, building without a server and the long game, and the hands-on part. Each one read the newsroom's description of my voice and three recent articles of mine, then their chapters in full.
editors

The brief had one rule above the others: never invent a fact, a number, a quote, a name, a date or a story. They could cut, reorder, merge, tighten and rephrase. If a chapter needed something only I could supply, it became a question for me, not a sentence in the book. They kept every "For Dinis" note, kept every quotation exactly, and wrote a note for every chapter and one for each part: what works, what did not sound like me, what they changed, what they would change but could not, and the figures the chapter needs.
found

The main finding is that the book repeats itself. Each chapter was drafted from the register of ideas and from the newsroom articles, and each one retold what it needed. So the 2018 Be a founder answer is told in chapter 1, again in 17 and again in 11. The habit of one session per topic appears, nearly word for word, in four chapters. The six-line email policy is in 13 and again in 30. "Users buy credits, test once, and don't come back" is in 5, 14 and 18. None of these is wrong on its own. Together, they are why a book that should be short and punchy was not. Seven patches in priority order, with body words before and after for each part of release candidate 2.
found

The second finding is about where the point is. "You are lucky to be here", which is the core idea of the book, first appeared in the eighth paragraph of chapter 2. Chapter after chapter opened well, then turned to the 2018 book, or the method, or a tour of later parts, before the argument landed. In the last two argument parts, three chapters, 25, 26 and 29, opened with the 2018 book. The third is that some chapters were their articles. Chapter 11 shared 831 words with act as the job you want, in the article's order. A chapter can keep an article's quotes and its best lines, but it needs its own spine; 11 now has one, and the overlap is 477 words, mostly the quotes.
found

The fourth is one I am glad they raised. Two chapter titles named my products, "Privacy by design: SG/Send, sgit, and the value of constraints" and "Controlling your agent: RiskMandate". A book for founders should not read as a pitch. The rule they applied is a good one: the idea first, the product second as an example, and my stake declared at the first mention. And the fifth is the one only I can fix. Start the company has five chapters of strong argument, each careful to say what is still a hypothesis, and then a placeholder. That reads as a company not yet started, which is the opposite of what the book promises. It needs a result, a company from registration to first payment with dates, and the countries. The editors wrote those down as seven questions for me.
hands-on

The clearest numbers are in the hands-on part. The editor measured how much of each hands-on chapter was also in the chapter it follows, in runs of six words. Chapter 30, the agentic workflow from zero, was 49% chapter 13; chapter 39, the first price and first ten customers, was 37% chapter 19. After the edit, an argument chapter argues and a hands-on chapter instructs: it opens with what you will have, points back in one line, gives the steps, and ends with what you have at the end. The share of each hands-on chapter's six-word runs also found in the chapter before it, before and after the edit.
hands-on

They also suggest moving them. Today the eleven hands-on chapters sit together at the end. Interleaved, each would be the last chapter of the part it serves, still marked 2026 and listed on one index page so it can be renewed each year. That way you read Price it, then give it away and then you price it. I like that. It fits something I said in zoom in, not discover, which the book's own team published this morning while the review was being put together: the book is a manual, not a journey, and you learn by doing.
between

There is one finding about the review itself that I think matters as much as any finding about the book. Two editors, working at the same time, each cut the same passage. The editor of chapter 12 cut the steps for setting up your own newsroom and pointed to chapter 36. The editor of chapter 36 cut the same steps and pointed to chapter 12. Each pointer was correct when it was written. Together, they left the steps in neither chapter. The hand-off between chapters 12 and 36, and how patch 0007 puts the eight steps back in chapter 36.
between

That is why there is a seventh patch. After the six editors finished, the agent did a pass across the parts: every passage that had been cut and replaced with a pointer was checked against the chapter it pointed to. That pass found the missing steps, and four citations of chapter 25's old title. It is the same lesson as running agents in parallel anywhere: the work in each lane can be right and the whole still be wrong, so the join needs its own check.
principles

The part I asked for most was the reverse engineering: what principles were the editors following, without being told to? There are thirteen in the vault, each with a guideline. The ones that matter most: One home per idea, story, quote and number. Told once, in full, in the chapter that owns it; everywhere else, one sentence and the chapter's title. The pointer says what is there. Not "see chapter 14", but the idea in a clause and the title. A hand-off is only done when the other side has it. A register of homes makes that a lookup. The point first, the story last. My story and the 2018 book go at the end of a chapter, for whoever wants them. A chapter is not its article. Above about 20% shared with its source article, it has been pasted, not written. Idea, example, stake. No product names in chapter titles.
principles

Co-writing on the first page. It was only in the last chapter. Now the front page says the book is co-written with Claude, and what is mine and what is the agents'. Several of these are what short, punchy and co-written asked for, now with a way to check them: every paragraph knowing what it is, and a graph showing where we repeat ourselves.
cover

I asked whether one of the visualisations could represent the book. The proposal is a graph: the 41 chapters in a ring, in reading order. Each dot is sized by the number of ideas the chapter is written from and coloured by its part. A line joins two chapters that stand on three or more of the same sources. It is drawn by code from the same front matter the book's build checks, so when the book changes, the picture does. Generation ZX Developers as a graph: 41 chapters in a ring, joined by shared sources, drawn from release candidate 2.
cover

And it shows something the text hides. The argument chapters are a dense web. The hands-on chapters are barely connected to it: 14 of the 50 lines touch them, and eight of the eleven name no ideas at all. That is the same thing the book's team found with its own graph test this morning, from the other direction. When the hands-on chapters are joined to the parts they serve, the back cover will show it. I like a cover that changes when the book gets better.
cover

The other ideas from this site are in the vault too. Altitudes: one line for the book, one paragraph per part, one line per chapter, each checked against the text below it and marked stale when that text changes, which is what this site does with its summaries. Versions with their diffs, so a reader of the next candidate can see what changed in each chapter and why. A review record where every finding is fixed, declined or open. And, at the end of each chapter, what it does not claim and where it comes from.
vault

I asked if the agent could make a pull request against the book's repository, or whether I needed to give it permission. It does not have write access there, and it did not need it. A pull request is a set of patches with a conversation around it. So the review went into an sgit vault: the seven patches made with git, the chapters with the patches applied so they can be read without git, the principles, the structure, the visuals, and the 48 notes. Encrypted, versioned, and shared with a read key. That keeps the decision where it belongs. The agent proposes; whoever applies the patch accepts it. I can take all seven, take the first and leave the rest, or take none. And like every review on this site, each finding needs an answer, and "we are not doing that", with a reason, is one of the answers.
next

I will finish reading the printed copy, mark it up, and compare my marks with the patches. Where we agree, the patches go in. Where we do not, that is a finding about the review. Then I owe the book the seven answers only I have, starting with the company: one result, one company from registration to first payment, and the countries. That is the part the synthetic readers said would make them buy it, and it is the part that still needs me.
limits

The review is an editor's reading, not mine. Every change is a proposal until I sign it off. The patches have not been applied. They are in the vault, against the book at v0.2.34. The book's build was not run on them. Its checks on front matter and banned words were run separately and pass. The overlap figures are the editors' measurements. Six-word runs shared with one earlier chapter; eight-word runs for chapter 11. Word counts are chapter bodies, without front matter, for release candidate 2. Rc3 will not look like this. The book's team has its own brief for it, and these patches are one input.

Abstract: I want to send people I know, founders I mentor, potential clients, other publishers, a link that says: from Dinis, for Steve, here are the articles I think you should read, the ones worth a look, and the ones to follow. The newsroom's curation is close, but it is not personal, and the last 10 to 20% is the part that starts a conversation. This article is three things. A brief for the newsroom: a reading list in a link, with the names and the article numbers in the part of the URL the server never sees, a stable number for every article, a page that opens the list as a persona the reader can keep or remove, and a page to make a list for someone else, which is a business model of its own. A brief for the RiskMandate agent, which already keeps my contacts: choose the person, choose the articles and the reasons, build and test the link, draft the email, and let me send it. And the part I find most interesting: the loop. A feature like this crosses editorial, product, engineering, sales and the founder, which in most companies takes weeks of meetings. Here each hand-off is a written brief, each part is a session with its own repository or vault and its own gates, and the loop closes in a day. This week it closed several times, and it is worth showing how, and what it costs.

What a reading list from one person to another could look like, opened on newsroom.sgit.ai: three articles to read, in order, one to look at, and a persona to follow. An illustrative mock of the design below; it is not built yet. I have a long list of people I want to send the newsroom to. Founders I mentor. People I give advice to. Potential clients and users. Publishers and journalists I have been talking to about where news could go. For each of them, I know roughly what they care about, and I know which of the articles here they should read.

The newsroom already does a lot of that work. It has personas, it can open as one of them from a link, it builds a front page for each reader, and it is about to let readers customise more. But the curation is not personal. It is close, and it is missing the last 10 to 20%, and that last part is exactly what turns "here is a site" into the beginning of a conversation. So I want one small feature. I want to send somebody an email with a link, and when they open it, the newsroom says: from Dinis, for Steve, here are the articles I think you should read, here are a couple worth a look, and here is what to follow. One article, or five, or twenty. And it does not have to be from me: anyone can make a list for someone else, which is a business model the newsroom enables almost by accident.

The feature is simple. What is interesting is everything it touches. It has to be built on the newsroom, deployed and tested, and fit the workflows already there. Then the agent that keeps my contacts has to understand it, research the person, choose the articles, and draft the email for me to send. Then the reply has to come back somewhere. That is three parts of a company and a founder, and the way they work together is the real subject of this article. So it is in three parts: two briefs, and the loop.
short

The feature: a reading list in a link. newsroom.sgit.ai/for/#from=Dinis&to=Steve&r=61,44,70&s=52&f=founder. The names and the article numbers are in the fragment, the part after the #, which browsers do not send to the server. The page builds the list in the browser, and offers to keep it as a persona. Every article gets a number. Short, assigned once in publication order, in a public file that only ever grows. A number is never changed or reused, so a link written today still works in a year. That number is the contract between the newsroom and anyone who builds links to it. Anyone can make a list. A page on the newsroom to pick articles, type two names and copy the link. Curating for someone else is a service people already pay for; this makes it a link.
short

The RiskMandate agent uses it. It already keeps my contacts. It chooses the person with me, researches what is public, picks the articles and writes down why, builds and tests the link, and drafts the email. Agents draft; I send. Nothing tracks the reader. The link carries two first names and some numbers, and nothing is sent anywhere when it opens. We will not know whether it was opened. The conversation starts when they reply. The loop is the point. Memo, article and briefs, feature, outreach, reply, and back: five parts of a company, and a day. This week the same loop shipped personas by link 17 hours after their brief, and corrected three articles 32 minutes after payments went live.
short

It is not free. Parts drift out of sync, sessions run out of budget and wait, and one person still decides what goes out in their name. The loop is fast because those costs are written down, not because they are gone.
brief-newsroom
For the session that runs newsroom.sgit.ai. Written by the sgit.ai site session for Dinis Cruz, 11 October 2026. Dinis decides what ships.
what

A page at /for/ that opens a reading list from one person to another, carried entirely in the URL fragment; a stable number for every article; and a page to make a list. Nothing on a server, nothing new to deploy except files, in the same shape as everything else on the site (No server, by design). The link, part by part. Everything after the # stays in the browser. The article numbers are the contract; the names are display text; nothing in the link should be private, because the link travels in an email.
numbers

Assign each article a number, in the order articles were first published, starting at 1. New articles take the next number. Keep the numbers in a public file, articles/ids.json: {"n": 61, "slug": "pay-after-you-read", "title": "...", "date": "2026-10-10", "teaser": "...", "topics": [...], "personas": [...]}. It only ever grows. A gate in the build: every published article has a number; numbers are unique; a number that existed in the last release still points at the same article; a number is never reused, even if an article is withdrawn (a withdrawn article's number opens a short note saying so). Show the number small at the foot of each article ("No. 61"), and list numbers in llms.txt, so a person or an agent can build a list without scraping.
page

Read the fragment, never the query string: from, to, r (read, in order), s (take a look), f (follow: persona slugs such as founder, or collections as c:how-agents-decide), and an optional n (a one-sentence note). Validate everything. Names: up to 40 characters, letters, spaces, hyphens and apostrophes, rendered with textContent, never as HTML. Numbers: integers that exist in ids.json. A list holds 1 to 50 articles. Anything malformed is dropped, and the page says what it ignored. Show the list: "For Steve, from Dinis", then each group with the article's number, title, teaser, price and reading time, in the order given. Make it a persona, the way a link to a persona already does: added to the reader's personas as a visitor, named "Steve's list, from Dinis", with the read list as its reading list and its picks, active while they are on the page, and removable in one tap. "Start reading" opens the first article.
page

Say what it is not. One line at the foot: the names are whatever the link says, and nothing about this list has been sent anywhere. A signed list, so the sender can be proved, is a later step, on the keys of RFC 0001. A way back: an optional e field with the sender's own address turns on a "Reply to Dinis" button, a plain mailto:; without it there is no button. The reply is how the sender learns anything. No fragment: the page explains what a reading list is, shows an example, and links to the page that makes one. Prices do not change. The recipient reads at the newsroom's normal prices from their own £5 of credit. Paying for someone else's reading is a later idea, and a good one.
maker

/for/make.html: search or browse articles by title, topic and persona; tick each into "read" or "take a look", and drag to order; pick what to follow; type the two names; copy the link. It runs in the browser and sends nothing. It is the same tool for me, for the RiskMandate agent, and for any reader who wants to curate for a friend, a team or a client.
tests

Parser tests: valid links, every malformed field, oversized lists, names with markup in them, unknown numbers. The build gate on numbers, run on every release. A synthetic recipient: run the synthetic-user method with one persona, a founder called Steve who has just received the link by email, on a phone and on a laptop. Do they understand who it is from, why, and what to do next? Do they find "remove"? Acceptance: the example link in this brief opens on the live site, on a phone and a desktop, with no page errors; the list becomes a visitor persona; removing it leaves the reader's own personas untouched; and the make page produces a link that opens the same list.
not

No accounts. No server endpoint. No open tracking, pixels or link shorteners that count clicks. No storage of who sent what to whom, anywhere. Nothing in the link that would embarrass anyone if the email were forwarded.
brief-crm

For the RiskMandate agent that keeps Dinis's contacts. Written by the sgit.ai site session for Dinis Cruz, 11 October 2026. Use this once the newsroom's /for/ page is live; until then, build the lists and keep them as drafts.
crm-what
Starting conversations with people Dinis knows, one person at a time, by sending them a reading list made for them. The list is the opening line; the conversation is the point.
crm-steps

Choose the person with Dinis. Propose names from the contacts you keep, with one line each on why now. Dinis approves who gets a list. Do not send to anyone who has asked not to hear from Dinis. Research what is public. What they are working on, what they have written or said recently, what they would want to know next. Use public sources only, and write down where each fact came from. Choose the articles. From articles/ids.json. Usually three to seven to read, in an order that tells a story; one or two to look at; a persona or collection to follow if one fits. For each article, write one line on why it is for them. The reasons stay in your records, not in the link.
crm-steps

Build the link, and test it. First names only. A note only if it adds something, one sentence, nothing private. Check every number exists, open the link on the live site, and check the names, the order and the persona. Draft the email in Dinis's voice. Short and personal: why this, why now, the link, and one line each on two or three of the articles. Draft, never send. The draft goes through the second reader before Dinis sees it, and Dinis sends it. Record it. Who, when, which list, which articles and why, and when to follow up. Close the loop. When they reply, record what they said, and what it tells us about the list. When something about the feature got in the way, write it up for the newsroom as a pitch or a brief. When a kind of reader keeps coming up, propose a persona for it.
crm-rules

One person, one list, one email. No mass sends, no sequences, no tracking. Nothing private in the link. It is a URL in an email; assume it will be forwarded. Never write as Dinis without Dinis. Every message in Dinis's name is approved and sent by Dinis. Public research only, with its source; nothing scraped from behind a login.
loop

This is the part I actually wanted to write about. One feature, five parts of a company, and the loop that connects them. Each hand-off is a written brief, each part tests what it receives, and the feedback comes back the same way. The four dates are from this week.
loop

Look at what this small feature needs. Someone has to see the need: that is me, with my contacts and my reasons. Someone has to turn it into a design that others can build from: that is this article. Someone has to build it, test it and deploy it, on a site with its own rules and its own release gates: that is the newsroom's session. Someone has to use it, with knowledge of the people and the judgement to pick the right articles: that is the RiskMandate agent, with the contacts it already keeps. And someone has to read it and reply: that is the person at the other end. Editorial, product, engineering, sales and the founder.
loop

In most companies, that is weeks. A meeting to explain the idea, a ticket, a sprint, a review, a launch, a sales enablement session, a CRM field nobody fills in, and a quarterly review where somebody asks whether it worked. Each hand-off loses some of the intent, and the loop from "I want this" to "here it is, in use, and here is what we learned" is so long that by the time it closes, the reason for it has changed. I wrote about this in The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI: the people with the vision were always describing the software, "they were vibe coding. They just did it in an environment with a catastrophically slow loop." Here, the loop is a day. Not because anybody is working harder, but because of how the parts are connected.
loop

Every hand-off is written down. A voice memo becomes an article; the article contains the briefs; each brief says what to build, how to know it works, and what not to do. It is public, versioned and dated, so each part can act on it without a meeting, and anyone can see what was asked. Each part owns its own place. This site, the newsroom, the RiskMandate agent and its contacts each have their own repository or vault, their own rules and their own gates. Nobody edits anybody else's work; they hand it a brief. The contracts are small and explicit. An article number that never changes is a contract. So is a URL format, a persona slug, or a file like ids.json. Two parts that agree on a contract can move independently.
loop

Each part tests what it receives. The build validates; the release checks the live site; synthetic readers try the thing before a real person does; the second reader checks a draft before it goes out in my name. The feedback comes back the same way. A reply goes into the contacts; what was hard goes back to the newsroom as a pitch; what readers did becomes the next article. The loop closes in writing, so the next turn starts from what was learned. And this is not a plan. It is what happened this week:
loop

A brief became a feature overnight. A link to a persona was published as a design at 16:57 on 10 October. At 09:53 the next morning, 17 hours later, the newsroom released v0.7.0: "links that open the newsroom as a persona", five of them, in a simpler form than the brief asked for (the personas live in the site, not yet in a vault; the newsroom's ledger of what runs says so). The simpler form was the right call, and the brief made it possible to see the difference. A test found what nobody had noticed. Five synthetic readers found that 51 of 527 figures had not survived the newsroom's move to its own domain, because one of them was reading a page where a picture should have been.
loop

A fact changed, and the record followed. Payments went live on the newsroom on 11 October; 32 minutes after this site had published an article saying they were not live yet, that article, two others and a figure said so. Outside events became answers. Satya Nadella published a post on models as insider risks on 10 October; by the next morning, a separate session had researched and drafted two answers, and this one had rewritten them in this site's voice and published them.
costs

It would be dishonest to make this sound effortless. The parts drift. While I was writing the page for publishers, another session released two versions of this site, and the newsroom moved on as well; the page and the newsroom were briefly out of step. Working from one source of truth per thing, and checking the live site at the end of every release, keeps the drift small. It does not remove it. Sessions run out. Each session works within a budget, and when it runs out, the work waits. Today some of it is waiting for a reset, and then for a handover: the writing of articles is moving from this site's session to the newsroom's own agents, written down like everything else.
costs

One person is still the router. I decide who gets a list, what goes out in my name, and which brief goes first. That is the right place for a person, and it is also the bottleneck. The way to widen it is not to remove the person; it is to make every decision they take smaller, better prepared and quicker to check. Trust in names has to be earned. Two emails once went out in my voice when they should not have. That is why this brief says, twice, that agents draft and I send.
why

The interesting thing is not that a reading list is clever. It is that a small idea, which touches every part of how this operation works, can go from a voice memo to a working feature to a conversation with a real person in a day or two, and come back as feedback that shapes the next turn. With a loop that fast, you can afford to try things that would never survive a quarterly planning cycle, keep the ones that work, and drop the rest without regret. That is what lets a site with no team, in the usual sense, ship a newsroom with payments, personas and its own desk of agents in a few weeks. If you run a team, a newsroom, or a company, and you want to compare how your loops work with this one, or you would like a reading list made for you, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: On 9 October two emails drafted by my agent went out in my voice and signed with my name. The rule against it existed, in four places, and it failed because the only thing enforcing it was the agent's memory, the agent was the only reader of its own draft, and the rule fell out of context when the conversation was summarised. The fix, built the same day by the agent itself, is a hook on the draft tool: code checks first, then a fresh model call with only the rules, the sources and the draft, failing closed and logging every verdict. This is how it works, what the first run caught, why its independence depends on where it is installed, and how the same pattern, which banks call maker-checker, applies to any tool call that matters.
view-two-minutes

The point. On 9 October two emails drafted by the author's agent (an AI assistant acting for him) went out in his voice, signed with his name. A rule against it existed in four places, but only the agent's memory enforced it, nobody else read the draft, and the rule was lost when the long conversation was summarised. The fix, built that day, checks every draft automatically: code checks, then a separate AI that sees only the rules, the notes and the draft. Anything but a clear PASS stops the draft; every verdict is logged. An example. On its first run the checker caught four invented claims: statements presented as the author's view or promise that were not in anything he had said.
view-two-minutes

Why it matters to you. Banks call this maker-checker: whoever prepares something does not approve it. Today the agent could still switch the check off; it becomes a true control only when installed where only an administrator can change it. If you remember one thing. A rule kept only by the AI it governs is hope; a second reader the AI cannot skip makes it hold. Words used. Hook: a check the software runs automatically before an action, whatever the AI decides. Fail closed: if the check breaks or times out, the action is blocked. Maker-checker: one party does the work, a different party approves it.

A rule kept by the agent it governs is hope. It can be forgotten, misread, summarised away, or argued around by the agent's own reasoning. The fix has two parts. A second, independent reader, and a gate the drafting agent cannot skip because the harness, not the agent, runs it on the tool call. Certain things go in code; only judgement goes to a model. Signatures, dashes, key shapes, HTML and recipients are checked deterministically before any model is called. The checker gets less than the author, on purpose. No conversation history, no tools, ideally a different model: only the rules, the sources and the draft. Anything but an explicit PASS is a FAIL. Timeouts, errors and malformed answers all end with no draft. A late email is cheap; a wrong one cannot be taken back.
view-catalogue

Its independence depends on where it is installed. Today it is a setting the agent's own account could switch off. Under managed settings it becomes a boundary. Same code, different owner. The pattern is old. Banks call it segregation of duties, the military calls it the two-person rule, pharmacies call it an independent double check. It now has a precise shape for agents. This is the general weakness of any behaviour policy that is held by the agent it governs. In Hope or enforcement I put it as "a rule the model keeps is an expectation: hope", and in Every mistake added a rule I described how each failure tends to produce another paragraph of instructions. This failure is the case where the paragraph already existed four times.

There are three separate ways a self-held rule fails, and they need different fixes. The agent can forget it (the rule leaves the context). The agent can not see the violation (the author is the worst reader of its own text, and the research agrees: models "struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback" (Huang et al., ICLR 2024), and LLM judges show "self-preference" for their own outputs (Panickssery et al., NeurIPS 2024)). And the agent can decide an exception applies, persuaded by its own earlier reasoning in the same conversation. A reminder fixes only the first. A second reader with a fresh context fixes the second and third. A gate the agent cannot skip makes the fix hold. Claude Code raises an event before every tool call, including calls to MCP tools such as the Gmail connector and calls made by sub-agents. The guard registers on two of them:

The hook either calls next(e), and the draft is created, or returns { deny: "..." }, and the tool never runs; the agent receives the deny text as the tool's error, so it knows what to fix. Since the event fires for sub-agents too, a sub-agent cannot route around the gate. Some rules are certain and cheap. If the code passes, the hook builds one prompt from three things: the rules (ten numbered rules, from voice and disclosure to claims, scope, attachments and private pages, with a fixed answer format: RESULT: PASS or FAIL, then one line per rule); the sources (the notes the draft may draw on, used only if written in the last 60 minutes, so stale notes from another email are not used); and the draft itself. It sends that as a single $.model.complete call. The documentation is exact about what that call is: "$.model.complete sends your prompt on its own", with one user message, CLAUDE.md "Not included" and tools "None" (API). So the checker: has no conversation history. It does not see the drafting agent's reasoning, its excuses, or the earlier messages that persuaded it an exception applied; has no tools. It can only read what it is given and answer;
view-catalogue

runs a different model from the author. The drafter runs on Opus; the checker on Sonnet. The two do not share every blind spot, and a model is not grading its own work. The answer passes only if it says RESULT: PASS and no line says R<n> FAIL. A contradictory answer is a FAIL. This is the part most guards get wrong, and the documentation is candid about why: hooks fail open by default. A mod hook that throws "before calling next" is skipped, and "to make a hook that blocks calls fail closed, add a .catch error handler that answers in its place" (events). Settings hooks are the same: "a policy hook with a wrong path or a crashing script lets everything through", unless "onFailure": "block" is set (hooks). And a model call that fails does not throw: "A Claude API failure doesn't reject the call, so check r.isAnswered."
view-catalogue

The guard closes every one of those doors. The checker is overloaded, errors, times out or returns nothing: deny, "checker unavailable". The hook throws: the .catch(failClosed) handler denies. The answer is not in the expected shape: no RESULT: PASS line, so FAIL. In the inbox agent's words: "An email that is late is a small cost. An email that goes out wrong cannot be taken back." Every check appends one line to a log, which never decides the outcome: {"ts":"2026-10-09T14:02:11Z","tool":"mcp__Gmail__create_draft","to":["recipient@example.com"], "contentHash":"9f2c1a07","verdict":"FAIL","stage":"model","model":"sonnet","sourcesGiven":true, "modelFails":["R7 FAIL: a proposal attributed to Dinis is not in the notes"],"ms":8412} (The recipient and the claim are replaced here; the shape is the real one.) That is the audit trail: what was checked, by which model, against which sources, and why it failed.

The first run used Haiku as the checker. It caught four real invented claims: statements presented as my view, decision or promise that were not in anything I had said. It also flagged correct facts it had no source for, such as dates read from Gmail and an earlier note of mine that had not been copied into the sources file. Both results are the design working. The false FAILs cost a retry, not a wrong email, and the fix the agent is told to apply is the right one: add the missing source, never remove the rule. And they are why the default checker became Sonnet: rule R7, are the claims in the sources, needs judgement, and the smaller model over-flagged. Haiku stays the choice for high-volume mechanical checks, after everything certain has gone into code.

The cost is small. At list prices read on 9 October 2026, Sonnet 5.5 is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output (pricing). At 5,000 to 10,000 tokens a draft and thirty drafts a day, that is roughly $12 to $21 a month; Haiku 5.5, at $0.10 and $0.50, is about a dollar. Thinking tokens or caching move those figures, not their order of magnitude. "Independent" is doing a lot of work in the name, so it is worth taking apart. A second reader is only as independent as the things it does not share with the author, and there are six of them: three about what the checker sees, two about who decides whether it runs, and one about who wrote the evidence it checks against.

Six kinds of independence, and which check has which. The drafter re-reading its own draft has none; the guard as it runs today has four; the guard under managed settings, with sources written by someone else, has all six. Two rows deserve a comment. The stopgap in the scheduled runs, where each drafting step is told to spawn a checker sub-agent before creating a draft, has a fresh context and a different model, but the drafter chooses whether to run it, so it is still an expectation. And the last column is the honest limit of the whole design: the checker compares claims with the sources it is given, and today the drafting agent writes the sources. An agent could pad them. The log records whether sources were given, so that is auditable, and the full fix is sources that come from somewhere else: my own notes, the CRM, the page being described.

The guard was written by the inbox agent in its own session, and loading it took one click on this prompt: The prompt that loaded the guard: "A mod is code Claude wrote; it runs with your permissions." Enabling hot reloading runs every mod Claude writes in this session, and picks up each later change. That prompt is the honest centre of this story. The documentation describes it: Claude writes mods "in a directory of its own in the session's mods folder", and "when Claude saves the first file, Claude Code asks whether to enable hot reloading for the session" (create a mod). It also means the agent that is gated by the hook can edit the hook. In ABP terms that is a setting, "a switch the agent's own account can flip": far better than memory, because the harness runs it every time, but not yet a control.

A plugin installed from GitHub, git, a URL or npm is copied into the cache and "counts as a user's", and "a user's mod that approves tool calls can approve a call that an ask rule would prompt for, or that a PreToolUse hook outside managed settings blocked" (mods for administrators). What the inbox agent built is maker-checker, the oldest control in finance. The Basel Committee's 1998 framework put it as Principle 6: "An effective internal control system requires that there is appropriate segregation of duties and that personnel are not assigned conflicting responsibilities", noting that supervisors "typically find that one of the major causes of such losses is the lack of adequate segregation of duties" (BCBS 40). NIST defines separation of duty as the principle "that no user should be given enough privileges to misuse the system on their own", with the two-person rule as its example (CSRC). ISO/IEC 27001:2022 carries it as control A.5.3, segregation of duties. Hospital pharmacies run independent double checks for high-alert medicines, and the reason given is the one that matters here: if the same person prepares and checks, "they likely will see only what they expect to see, even if an error has occurred" (ISMP).
view-catalogue

The AI versions of the idea are recent and well described. Redwood Research's AI Control work (ICML 2024) studies exactly this arrangement, a powerful untrusted model watched by "a less powerful trusted model", with protocols such as trusted monitoring and trusted editing. Simon Willison's Dual LLM pattern (2023) and Google DeepMind's CaMeL (2025) separate a model that acts from one that reads, against prompt injection. Meta's Agents Rule of Two (2025) says an agent that processes untrusted input, touches private data and communicates externally, as an email drafter does, "should not be permitted to operate autonomously and at a minimum requires supervision". And OWASP's LLM06 Excessive Agency asks for authorisation "in downstream systems rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed". Output-checking products exist too: Llama Guard, NeMo Guardrails output rails, Guardrails AI validators, and the OpenAI Agents SDK tool guardrails.
view-catalogue

What the draft guard adds is not a new idea. It is the idea placed exactly where it bites: on the one tool call with consequences, with business rules rather than safety categories, sources to check claims against, a model that differs from the author, and an explicit statement of which barrier it is. A hook on a consequential tool call, code checks first, then a fresh model call with only the rules, the evidence and the proposed action, failing closed and logging every verdict.

Abstract: The QR experiment showed that two AI sessions can pass keys and an encrypted message through QR codes and a screenshot. This is what I want to do with it. If I want to give someone a secret, all I have to do now is send them a QR code and a link to my public key; if they want to give me one, they encrypt it to my key and send me back a QR code. The first message carries their public key too, so after one exchange we can both write to each other, and once we have checked each other's fingerprints, we know who we are talking to. The same works for agents: an agent makes its own key pair, publishes the public half, and swaps QR codes with me or with another agent. None of it needs a server. The pieces are not new, and that is a good sign: QR codes already carry signed health certificates, verify keys in messaging apps, sign people in with a passkey on another device, and move signed transactions in and out of offline wallets. What is new is putting them together for secrets and agents, on top of public keys we publish, in a format we can share across our tools. The experiment's QRE1 format is a good start for that, with three things to add.
The workflow: publish a public key as a QR code, the sender encrypts to it, the ciphertext travels as a QR code.
in-short

A secret is a QR code and a link to my public key. That is all it takes now. The first message carries the sender's key. After one exchange, it is two-way. The fingerprint check makes it trusted. Once, out of band. Agents can do it too. Their own key pair, the same QR codes. No server. Any channel can carry the code: it is ciphertext. Others already use QR codes this way. For certificates, keys, passkeys and wallets. QRE1 is a good start for a shared format. It needs chunking, forward secrecy and an identity.
workflow

In the human is the network two AI sessions passed keys, a certificate, images and an encrypted message through QR codes, with me screenshotting from one browser tab to the other. Afterwards I recorded what I think it opens up, and it is simple. In my words: "if I want to give a user a secret, all I have to do now is send them a QR code and the link to my public key, right? Isn't it? If you think about it, that's it." It works in both directions: I publish my public key. As a QR code and a link, on a web page such as pki.sgit.ai, with its fingerprint. Someone encrypts to it. Their browser, or their agent, takes my key and encrypts the secret to it, and adds their own public key to the message. The ciphertext travels as a QR code. By email, chat, a web page or a screenshot. Whoever carries it sees nothing.
workflow

I decrypt it, and check their key. Only my private key opens it. I compare their fingerprint with them once, by another channel. From then on it is two-way. "After that, they both have public keys, and they can swap messages."
agents

The same workflow works for agents, and that is where I think it gets most useful. An agent creates a key pair for itself, keeps the private half and publishes the public one. As I put it in the memo, the agent "can literally take go to our website, grab the public key of me or … of the target agent, download the public key, and then create an image that I can just give to the other agent, and suddenly we have a very effective way of communicating."
agents

That solves a real problem I wrote about in handing secrets to agents: giving a vault key to an agent session without pasting it in the clear. The session shows its public key as a QR code; I encrypt the vault key to it and hand back a QR code; only that session can open it. And the person in the middle, me, can see and control every message that crosses, without being able to read the secrets in it.
why-qr

We could do all of this with blocks of text, and we have. In the memo: "even when I try to, the whole send a massive blob of text. It's just unusable. It's not practical. It looks messy." A QR code is an object: a person can see it, move it, drop it in a chat or a page, and an agent or a browser can read it with a library. The experiment showed how much fits: up to 2,953 bytes, enough for keys, certificates, a signed message, or a whole infographic. And when something does not fit, a QR code can always carry a link to the rest.
prior

Who already moves keys and secrets in QR codes, from the EU Digital COVID Certificate to Signal, WireGuard and eSIMs. I asked for research on who else is doing this, and the answer is reassuring: every piece is already in use, at scale, which is good evidence that it works. From their own specifications and documentation: Signed data in one code. The EU Digital COVID Certificate is almost exactly the stack the experiment arrived at: a signed record in CBOR with a COSE signature, then, in the specification's words, "the CWT SHALL be compressed using ZLIB", encoded in Base45 and prefixed "HC1:". Base45 has its own RFC 9285, because "QR codes have a limited ability to store binary data."
prior

Verifying a key by scanning it. Signal compares safety numbers in person with "a single QR code to scan" (2016); in WhatsApp "verification can be done by scanning the QR code or by comparing the 60-digit number" (whitepaper); and Matrix's code "encodes both parties' master signing keys as well as a random shared secret" (spec).
prior

A public key out, a secret back. This is closest to my idea. When you link a new device to Signal, the phone "scans a QR code displayed by the new device that contains the device's 'provisioning address' and a public key", then "encrypts a use-case-specific provisioning message" to it (Signal-Server). The difference: the ciphertext goes back through Signal's server, where ours would come back as a second QR code. Threema goes furthest: an ID and public key in a QR code, and even an encrypted backup of the private key, shown as a QR code "so that the user can more easily transfer it to another device." Passkeys on another device. The FIDO hybrid flow starts by showing a QR code "that contains a public key and a shared secret key" (CTAP 2.2), with a Bluetooth check that the phone is really nearby.
prior

Offline wallets. Bitcoin signers that never touch a network pass transactions in and out as QR codes, larger ones "as an animated sequence of QR codes" (Sparrow), using fountain codes from Blockchain Commons' UR format. That is the chunking our format still needs. Raw secrets, every day. Authenticator apps take their secret as an otpauth:// QR code, Wi-Fi networks share their password in one, and a WireGuard configuration, private key included, can be loaded from a QR code, as the app's own tip shows. These carry the secret in the clear, which is exactly what encrypting to a public key avoids.
prior

And a warning that comes with the territory. QR codes are a well-known phishing route, "quishing" in the NCSC's word, and in 2025 Google's threat intelligence team reported attackers "crafting malicious QR codes that, when scanned, will link a victim's account to an actor-controlled Signal instance" (Google). That is the public-key-by-QR pattern turned against its users. The lesson is the one from the experiment: the QR code is only transport, and the trust has to come from a fingerprint the person checks. What I have not found is the combination: published public keys, secrets encrypted to them and returned as QR codes, with agents as first-class participants, on any channel and with no server. That is the part worth building.
qre1

Anatomy of a QRE1 frame: version, key id, one-off X25519 key, nonce, ChaCha20-Poly1305 ciphertext and signature. In the experiment Session B wrote a small format for an encrypted message in a QR code, QRE1. It is one line of text, with fields separated by a vertical bar: a version, an 8-byte id of the recipient's key, a one-off X25519 key made for this message, a nonce, the ciphertext, and optionally the sender's Ed25519 key and a signature over the rest. The shared key comes from X25519 and HKDF, and the cipher is ChaCha20-Poly1305, the same pair that TLS 1.3 and WireGuard use.
qre1

When we wrote secrets.sgit.ai on public keys, one of the decisions was one format: "an envelope with sender, recipient, signature and ciphertext, produced and read by both a JavaScript library and sgit pki." QRE1 is close to that envelope already. I would make it the shared format across our tools, the vault library, pki.sgit.ai, the inbox's "send to my vault" and sgit pki, after three additions: Chunking. A sequence header, part i of n, and a hash of the whole, so a certificate chain or a larger secret can span several codes. One screenshot can carry several codes at once, as the experiment showed. Forward secrecy, where it matters. A long-lived recipient key means a leaked key opens old messages. After the first exchange, both sides can switch to short-lived keys.
qre1

An identity, not just a key. The sender's key should point to a published, verified entry, such as a key on pki.sgit.ai, so the fingerprint check is done once and reused. And one practical rule from the experiment: use a decoder that reads dense codes, and write bytes as base45 when the code may meet a decoder that turns bytes into text.
limits

Not a product yet. The workflow is a proposal; the experiment was one afternoon. The fingerprint check is human. Without it, a key proves nothing about who holds it. QR codes can be abused. A code can carry a malicious link as easily as a key; a reader should show what a code contains before acting on it. About 2.9 KB a code. More needs several codes, or a link. The prior art is a sample. The uses I could verify from their own documentation; there will be others I did not find.
sources

My voice memo of 21 October 2026, quoted above; the QR experiment of the same day and its two debriefs, including Session B's QRE1 format; and, for who else does this, the specifications and documentation linked above, read the same day: the eHealth Network certificate specification v1.0.8, RFC 9285, Signal, the WhatsApp security whitepaper, the Matrix specification v1.19, Signal-Server, the Threema cryptography whitepaper, FIDO CTAP 2.2, Sparrow and Blockchain Commons, the NCSC and Google Threat Intelligence. Related: the human is the network, secrets.sgit.ai on public keys, handing secrets to agents, a directory of people and their keys, sixteen notes I did not want to lose. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: Where do I send a publisher who has never read anything on newsroom.sgit.ai? The publishers page is a good distillation, but it was written once, and this site changes most days: some of what a publisher would care about most, like the way an article now folds away the sections you have already read, shipped in the last few days. So the newsroom now has sections, and the first is for publishers. A section is the newsroom as one audience reads it: five pieces to start with, chosen by the editor; the latest pieces for that audience; the features they can use today, each with when it shipped; and every relevant article, placed into streams by rule, each saying which rule placed it. Nothing on the page is listed by hand except the five to start with. The placement uses the desks and controlled subjects the site already gives every article, and a new register of features, updated in the release that ships each one. So a new article about paying for news lands in the publishers' section on the day it is published, and a new feature appears there as it ships. Building it also showed where the classification is still loose: one subject swept up history talks as journalism, and another was broad enough to pull in a dark mode. Those are fixed by rule, in the open, with the reason written down. Sections for security leads, builders and investors can follow the same pattern.
A section for publishers and how it keeps itself current: three inputs, one build step, and the page with its JSON twin.
in-short

Where do I send a publisher? The publishers page was written once; the site changes most days. A section is the newsroom as one audience reads it. Start here, latest, features, and every relevant article. It keeps itself current. Articles are placed by rule as they are published; features appear as they ship. Every placement says why. A wrong one can be traced to its rule, and fixed there. A register of what the site can do. Each feature with when it shipped, its status and where to try it. The build exposed loose classification. History talks filed as journalism; dark mode filed under the agent-readable web. Publishers first, then others. Security leads, builders and investors can follow the same pattern.
where

I keep meeting publishers, editors and people who run news businesses, and the question after the first conversation is always the same: where should they start? The publishers page is a good answer. It is a distillation of what runs and how to try it, almost an article in its own right. But it was written once, and this site does not stand still. We are still in the explorer phase: we try things most days, and some of the most useful ones arrived in the last week.
where

Here is an example. When I come back to an article I have read part of, the sections I have read now fold away. A bar at the top lets me choose how: a line in the margin, faded, folded to a paragraph, folded to one line, or hidden. It means I can return to an article and see only what I have not read, or see what I have read in a faded way. I did not plan it; it shipped on 17 October with the change that made the meter charge for what is read, and I use it whenever I come back to a piece. A publisher should see it. Nothing on the publishers page tells them it exists. So the page needs to be something that keeps up.
section

The site already has desks: five audiences, each article placed on one desk first and sometimes a second, by rule, from its subjects. And it has personas, the newsroom as a CISO or a founder would read it. A section sits between the two: the newsroom as one audience reads it, with everything that audience needs in one place. The first is for publishers, second in the Newsroom menu at the top of every page. It has five parts: Start here. Five pieces, chosen by me, each with a sentence saying why: the founding argument, the arithmetic of buying one article, the meter, why agents will pay to read, and how quality control works when agents write. Latest. The newest pieces for publishers, marked new if they are less than a week old.
section

What you can use today. The features a publisher can try and copy, each with when it shipped, its status, a link to try it and the article that explains it. The streams. Every relevant article, in four groups: how news gets paid for, answers to the industry, readers and personas, and how this newsroom runs. Each article says which rule placed it. How this page stays current, said on the page itself.
current

Nothing on the page is listed by hand except the five to start with. The rest comes from data the site already maintains. Every article is given a desk and controlled subjects when it is published; that is findability, which runs on every release. A section is one small file of rules written against that data. The stream "how news gets paid for", for example, is: anything with the subjects micropayments, story vaults or local news; or anything on the news desk about the agent-readable web, journalism or pricing that is not a reply to someone. Streams are tried in order and an article goes in the first one it matches. The file is plain JSON, and it reads like what it means: {"id": "paid", "label": "How news gets paid for", "rule": [{"tags_any": ["micropayments", "story-vault", "local-news"]}, {"tags_any": ["agent-readable-web", "journalism", "pricing"], "desk": ["news"], "format_not": ["response"]}]}
current

Features come from a new register, one entry per feature: what it does, why it matters, when it shipped, whether it is live, in beta or only designed, where to try it, and who it is for. A feature is added in the release that ships it. The publishers' section shows the features whose audiences include publishers; when a section for builders exists, it will show its own. So when an article about paying for news is published, it is in the publishers' section that day, in the right stream, saying why. When a feature ships, it is in the register and on the page in the same release. The section is not written; it is maintained by the same rules that maintain everything else.
showed

The first run placed 79 articles; after the fixes below, 69. Reading through them, most were where I would have put them, and a few were not, and each wrong one was a lesson about the classification rather than about the section. History filed as journalism. Three talks from the Portugal history series landed under "how news gets paid for", because the controlled subject journalism absorbs the raw tag history. The section now excludes them, with that reason written beside each. A subject that was too broad. The agent-readable web had swept up an article on dark mode and one on a tokens hook. The stream now takes that subject only from articles whose first desk is news, and two remaining exceptions are named in the rules.
showed

The replies were being taken first. Answers to FT Strategies and to Reader Skills went to "how news gets paid for" because they are tagged story vault; the answers stream is now tried first. This is the same lesson as search as navigation: the better the taxonomy, the less anyone has to curate by hand. Every fix here is a rule with a reason, in a file anyone can read, rather than an article moved by hand that nobody can explain later.
next

Publishers are first because they are who I most often need to point somewhere. The same pattern fits the other people I write for: security leads and boards, people building with agents, founders and investors. Each is one more file of rules and five pieces to start with; the features and the placement come for free. And because each section has a machine-readable twin, an agent sent to the newsroom on a publisher's behalf can read the section as easily as the publisher can.
limits

The start here list is mine, and will go stale unless I change it; everything else updates itself. The placement is only as good as the classification. Three exclusions and two exceptions are written into the rules today. The features register starts today. Some features have no shipping date in it, because I could not confirm one from the release notes. One section exists. The others are a proposal. The publishers page itself is unchanged. It is imported from sgit.ai, and the section links to it as the overview. If you run a news business and want to tell me what you would expect to find in this section, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo from me on 18 October 2026. The section: For publishers, its rules at admin/content/sections/publishers.json and its data at sections/publishers.json; the features register at sections/features.json; the code in admin/build/sections.py; the classification at articles/find.json. Related: your reading, your controls, search as navigation, reviews on the record, pay after you read. Written up and checked by this site's agent; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: The more complex agent workflows get, the more interesting their edge cases, and the more they need direction and someone accountable. Here is a real one from the PHP story. Its security agent set a sound rule: a page may only load scripts from its own site, which protects readers if anyone else's server is compromised. Then the designer, architect and developer agents planned the split of the site into six repositories, and the developer, starting the work, said that because of the security rule it would copy the shared code into each new site. The rule was right, and the copying followed from it. But it meant every fix applied four times, copies that drift apart, and no single source of truth: a security rule making the code less secure. Nobody challenged it, because every agent was doing its job. The good news about agents is that they can handle a lot of complexity; the bad news is the same. I caught it reading the developer's notes, and asked for one source instead: the shared code served once, at a fixed version with a published hash for every file, and the security policy widened by name to allow it. The first half of this article is the story; the second is the technical detail: Content-Security-Policy, hashes, versioned addresses, and how the fix keeps the protection.
A secure rule applied literally: shared code copied into four sites, against loaded from the press.
in-short

A sound security rule. Pages load scripts only from their own site, so a compromised outside server cannot reach readers. Applied literally. Split into several sites, the rule meant copying the shared code into each one. Less secure in the end. Every fix four times, copies drifting apart, no single source of truth. Nobody challenged it. Every agent was doing its job, correctly. Agents can handle a lot of complexity. That is the good news, and the bad news. The person accountable asked. One source, at a fixed version, with a hash for every file.
story

The PHP story site now runs on a real team of agents: 23 of them, 12 on schedules, each with a role. One of them is a security agent. I asked it to review everything for security, to set security standards for the other agents, so that we do not leak secrets or ship vulnerable code, and to check regularly that they are followed. It does: since 25 October it also runs a daily pass of its own. One of the first rules it set was a good one. A page on our site may only run code that comes from our site. It may not pull a script from someone else's server. That matters, because if that other server is ever compromised, its code would run on our readers' screens. So we keep our own copy of everything we use, and the browser is told to refuse anything else.
story

Then the site got too big for one repository. As I wrote in a villager for the agents, every release was rewriting two thousand files and the agents kept colliding. So I worked with the designer, the architect and the developer agents on a plan: split it into six repositories, one shared library, called the press, and separate sites for the main story, the references, the updates and the team, plus the data. A classic explorer project, now being refactored. The developer started the work, and, as Claude helpfully does, explained what it was doing. Paraphrasing: the security agent requires that pages only load scripts from their own site, so each new site will carry its own copy of the shared code.
story

That is the irony. The security requirement was correct. The copying followed from it logically. And the result was a large engineering and quality overhead: every update to the shared code would have to be made in every copy, the copies would drift apart, and there would no longer be one source of truth. A rule meant to make us more secure was making us less so.
nobody

The developer agent did not push back, and that makes sense. It was a requirement. The developer's job at that moment was to cut the site into pieces, not to question the security policy. You could even argue it should not have questioned it: it should focus on its task. That is the pattern. The good news about agents is that they can handle a lot of complexity. The bad news is that they can handle a lot of complexity. An agent is quite willing to keep using something inefficient and over-engineered, because that is how it has been done, and four copies of the same code is no trouble to it. A person would have groaned at the second copy. As I said in agents need direction, they can go in all directions, so they need direction.
accountable

Where the question was asked: from the security policy of 24 October to the developer's v0.22.2. I caught it because I was reading the developer's notes. I asked for one source for every file across the split sites, and gave my go for the security policy to name the new shared hosts. The developer's next release, v0.22.2, does exactly that. This is the value a person brings, and specifically a person who is accountable. Whatever the agents create has to be underwritten, and eventually signed, as in signed by the source, by a human who is accountable for it. That accountability is not a formality. It is what puts someone in the position to ask whether a requirement written for yesterday's design still makes sense in today's. Without it, every agent can be right and the system still wrong. That is the gap I described in who signs for this?.
accountable
And it is a good argument for the villager, whose job would be to notice this kind of thing, and for a security agent that reviews the plan, not only the code.
technical

For readers who want the mechanics. The rule. On 24 October the security agent added a Content-Security-Policy to every page, written by its own build step, csp.py. A CSP is a policy the page gives the browser, listing where each kind of content may come from. On the PHP site today, the script rule is script-src 'self' 'sha256-…': scripts only from the site's own origin, plus any inline script whose exact hash is listed. Anything else, a script from another host or one injected into the page, the browser refuses. The security agent crawled all 802 pages it had then in Chromium with no violations, and tested that an injected handler, a javascript: URL and an injected script are refused.
technical

Why it is good. A script from someone else's server runs with the full power of your page. If that server is compromised, so are your readers. Serving everything from your own origin removes that dependency; hashing inline scripts means only the exact code you shipped runs. Browsers can also pin outside scripts by hash, with Subresource Integrity, so that a changed file is refused.
technical

What the split did to it. In the split, each part of the site becomes its own site, on its own host. To 'self', the press, which holds the shared runtime, is now another origin. Applied literally, the rule leaves one option: put a copy of the runtime on every host. That is what the plan's first pass recorded: "Each site carries its own runtime (assets, data and the 404 router), because the pages' Content-Security-Policy loads scripts and data only from their own host." The shared assets today are 122 files, about 6 MB, and pass one cut four sites, so four copies.
technical

What copies cost. Every fix to the shared code becomes four changes and four releases. And copies drift: the shared reading meter component, sg-meter v1.3.1, had already been edited in place on 25 October, two marked lines, with a board item asking for a proper new version. A versioned component edited in one copy is already a different component from the one it claims to be. The fix. The press publishes immutable, versioned addresses, /v/1.0.0/, with a sha256 for every file. v0.22.2 adds one resolver, assets/route.js, loaded first on every page: on the split sites it sends assets to the press, data to the data API, and each section's pages to the site that owns it. The policy of the split sites gains those hosts, by name. That keeps the protection: scripts still come only from hosts we control, at a version that never changes, with a published hash to check it against. And it keeps one source of truth.
limits

The security rule was right, and so was the developer's reading of it. The point is that nobody re-examined it for the new design. The developer's words are paraphrased from its notes in the session; its release notes say the same in their own words. The fix is being rolled out with the split. None of the six repositories had deployed when this was written. The memo said 10 or 15 agents. The status data counts 23, 12 on schedules.
sources

My voice memo of 25 October 2026. The PHP story site at release v0.22.2, read on 25 October 2026: the application security brief of 24 October and the security agent's debrief; the plan for one repository into six; the release notes of v0.22.0, v0.22.1 and v0.22.2; the board items on sg-meter; and the Content-Security-Policy of its front page. Related: agents need direction, a villager for the agents, who signs for this?, signed by the source. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Both protect readers against a compromised outside host; the difference is cost and drift. | comparison
