Abstract: Something has been nagging me about the talk of bubbles and trillion-dollar listings. The headline valuations are set by selling a small slice of each company, and I wanted to check the numbers, including my own. Two of mine were wrong. OpenAI has not listed: its trillion-dollar figure is a private round under discussion, about 2% of the company, and its listing is now expected next year at the earliest. And SpaceX did not sell half a per cent at its IPO: it sold about 4%, $75bn of new shares, the largest IPO ever and more than twice the previous record in today's dollars. What holds is the pattern. The share of a company sold at listing has been falling for decades, from a median of about 30% to 14.5% last year, and the biggest companies sell the least. A small slice sets the price of the whole, low floats rise more on the first day, and index rules have been changed to absorb them. These companies earn revenue at a scale and speed nobody has seen, but at multiples close to the dot-com peak, and OpenAI and SpaceX are not yet profitable. For a founder, the lesson is that a valuation is a price the market allows for a slice, and the founder who controls the company decides how big the slice is.
A small slice sets the price of the whole: 4.2% of SpaceX sold at $135 a share priced it at $1.77tn.
in-short

Two of my numbers were wrong. OpenAI has not listed; SpaceX sold about 4%, not half a per cent. The share sold at listing keeps falling. A median of 30.5% in 1990; 14.5% in 2025; SpaceX 4%. The money raised is not small. SpaceX's $75bn is more than twice the previous record in today's dollars. A small slice sets the price of the whole. And low floats rise more on the first day. Record revenue, not yet profit. Multiples close to the dot-com peak, on revenue far larger. It is a market. The price is what the demand allows for the slice on offer. For founders: control decides the slice. And the exit, which is the next article.
question

There is a lot of talk about bubbles and about ridiculous valuations, and about how massive the coming listings will be. When I looked at the numbers, what struck me was not the size of the money but how little of each company was being sold. My memory was that OpenAI was proposing to list $40bn at a valuation of about $1.4tn, which is less than 3% of the company, and that SpaceX had sold even less. If that is the pattern, these companies are setting a price for the whole by selling a sliver, at a moment when there is more than enough money looking for a place to go. I wanted to know whether that is new, whether the companies are sound underneath it, and what a founder should learn from it. So I did the analysis, and checked my own numbers first.
sold

Two of my numbers were wrong, and the corrections matter. OpenAI has not listed. The $40bn was a private round in March 2025, at a $300bn valuation after the money, about 13% of the company. The trillion-dollar figure is newer and also private: Reuters reported in September that OpenAI "aims to raise at least $30 billion" at "a valuation of about $1.4 trillion, not including the money raised", which is about 2% of the company. Its listing has moved: OpenAI "has pushed back plans for an initial public offering until at least next year", Bloomberg reported on 8 October. In between, its employees sold about $6.6bn of their own shares at a $500bn valuation, about 1.3% of the company, in October 2025.
sold

SpaceX sold about 4%, not half a per cent. The half a per cent was a private sale in December 2024: SpaceX and investors agreed to buy up to $1.25bn of insiders' shares at a price that valued the company at about $350bn, about 0.36%. The IPO in June was different. SpaceX "priced its 555.6 million shares at $135 each" and raised $75bn, TechCrunch reported. Its quarterly report says the company "issued and sold 638.9 million shares", including the underwriters' extra allotment, for net proceeds of $85.7bn, and had 13.18bn shares in issue at the end of July. That is 4.2% of the company in the base offering, and 4.85% with the extra allotment, at $1.77tn. Anthropic has filed, confidentially. It "confidentially submitted a draft registration statement" in June, and "the number of shares to be offered and the price have not yet been set". Its last private round was $65bn at $965bn in May, about 6.7% of the company.
sold
So the pattern I saw is real, but it is mostly in private rounds and in one listing, not in the trillion-dollar IPOs I had in mind.
float

The share of a company sold at listing, the public float, has been falling for a long time. Jay Ritter at the University of Florida keeps the standard dataset: 9,343 US IPOs from 1980 to 2025, with a median float of 27.3%. In 1990 the median was 30.5%; in 2000, 19.4%; in 2023, 12.6%; in 2025, 14.5%. And the biggest companies sell the least: Google sold 7.2% in 2004, Arm 9.3% in 2023, Saudi Aramco 1.5% in 2019, and SpaceX 4.2% this year. How much of each company was sold at its IPO, with the median for all US IPOs since 1980 and for 2025. So SpaceX is low, but not alone: Aramco sold a smaller share seven years earlier. What is new is the size of the company selling the small share.
amount

My instinct was that the amounts raised are not out of line with the great IPOs of the past. That is wrong for SpaceX. In September 2026 dollars, its $75bn base offering is more than twice the previous record, Saudi Aramco's $25.6bn in 2019, now worth about $33.7bn, and more than three times Facebook's $16bn in 2012, now about $23.5bn. Against the size of the market, it is less extreme. By the World Bank's count, the US stock market was worth about $18.7tn at the end of 2012, and Facebook raised about 0.09% of that; it was worth about $68.9tn at the end of 2025, the latest year, and SpaceX raised about 0.11% of that. Measured against the market, SpaceX's raise is about a quarter larger than Facebook's, not five times. The biggest IPOs, base offering only, in September 2026 dollars, and for three of them, the share of the US market.
revenue

The other half of my argument was that these are sound companies, earning revenue at a speed nobody has seen. The revenue part holds. OpenAI's "annualized revenue was roughly $50 billion at the end of September", Bloomberg reported, against about $13bn for the whole of 2025, as reported. Anthropic said in May that its "run-rate revenue crossed $47 billion". SpaceX's revenue was $7.8bn in the second quarter, almost double a year before. The profit part does not, yet. SpaceX lost $4.8bn in the first half of 2026, by its own filing, after its merger with xAI. OpenAI "expects to burn through $278 billion in cash between 2026 and 2030", the Financial Times reported in September, citing a company presentation. Anthropic told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis in its last two quarters, as reported; that is a company's own measure, not a net profit.
revenue

And the prices are in dot-com territory. In 2000 the median tech IPO priced at 31.7 times its sales, in Ritter's data, and Cisco at its peak was worth about 38 times its sales. OpenAI's reported round is about 28 times its run-rate revenue; Anthropic's last round, about 20 times; SpaceX at its IPO price, about 57 times its second quarter's revenue, annualised. The difference is the scale: a median of about $12m of sales for a tech IPO in 2000, against $50bn a year at OpenAI. Valuation against a year of revenue: the dot-com peak and the 2026 AI companies. So it is not only hype, because the revenue is real and very large. But it is not proof of soundness either: the multiples assume the growth continues for years, and two of the three are losing money.
mechanism

When 4.2% of a company is sold at $135 a share, the other 95.8% is valued at $135 too. The headline valuation is the last price paid for a slice, multiplied by everything. Every reported valuation along the way was set the same way: SpaceX's $350bn, $400bn and $800bn were insiders' sales, and its $1.25tn was the price of an all-stock merger with xAI. A small slice also tends to rise. In Ritter's data for IPOs with at least $100m of sales from 1980 to 2024, those that floated 10% or less rose 32.4% on the first day on average, against 7.6% for those that floated more than 40%. SpaceX rose 19% on its first day and closed at about $2.1tn. Over three years, the same small-float group trailed the market by 5.3%.
mechanism

And the demand was arranged. As Vanguard put it before the listing, SpaceX's "weight in any index that includes it will initially be based on around 5% of its shares being available to the public", and Reuters reported in March that Nasdaq's new rules include a fast entry for very large new listings into its main index. Index funds have to buy what is in the index. A small slice, offered to a market with that much money that must buy, is priced by the demand, not by the size of the company.
mechanism

It is also worth being precise about who gets the money. In SpaceX's IPO, the money went to the company: every share was new. The people who already owned shares got their cash from the private sales before, and will get it as their lock-ups end, which the SEC's investor site describes as typically 180 days. OpenAI's $6.6bn employee sale was that kind of liquidity, without a listing at all. What the IPO gave existing holders was a price for their shares, and a market in which to sell them later.
founders

The numbers are prices, and this is a market. The price of a company is what the buyers of its next slice are willing to pay, and in 2026 there is a great deal of money willing to pay a great deal for a small slice of the companies at the centre of the most important technology of the moment. The lesson for a founder is about control. The people who control these companies decide how big each slice is, when it is sold, to whom, and whether the money goes to the company or to the people who already own it. That is what it means to be in charge of the game: not to own everything, but to decide the terms on which the next slice is sold.
founders

The same is true at every size. Sell, don't issue argued that a founder with leverage should sell existing shares rather than issue new ones; the controllable founder argued that investors select partly for founders they can control. A valuation is the price the market allows for the slice you choose to sell. Understanding that is the first step. The second is deciding when to sell the part of the company that controls it, which is the exit, and the next article.
limits

It is not investment advice. It does not say these companies are overpriced or fairly priced. Run-rates are not revenue. They annualise a recent period, which flatters fast growth. Some figures are reported, not filed. Private valuations and Anthropic's adjusted profit are as reported. Floats are approximate. Share counts differ by class and date; the method is Ritter's. Inflation is not the market. CPI-adjusted dollars and market share answer different questions.
sources

OpenAI: its March 2025 announcement, Bloomberg on revenue and the listing, Reuters on the cash burn, and Reuters on the 2025 employee sale and the September round. Anthropic: its Series H and its draft registration. Abstract: This is a story about how innovation sometimes happens organically, and why I let myself go on tangents. It started with a bug: a vault that took 59 seconds to clone, measured by this newsroom, and the comms vault that took three and a half minutes. Fixing that led me to ask whether sgit could run a vault from a zip file, partly because I want vaults that live on Google Drive, Dropbox or a USB stick, with no server for us to maintain. The CLI team researched it with no code, designed a pack per push, had it reviewed four times by a second agent, and released sgit-ai 0.24.0 on 22 October. The next day, the PHP story's source watch needed it: 63,662 objects and 1.6 GB, a server that could no longer list it, a clone that took 13 minutes and 47 seconds, and one push that took 12 attempts and 2 hours 42 minutes. As a pack vault, the same history cloned in 95 seconds and pushed in 96. And it shipped without everything: the web UI still cannot open a pack vault. That was fine, because the vault that needed it did not need the UI. Small, incremental changes, done properly, made a very large difference.
The PHP site's pack-mode page, 23 October 2026: a 95-second pack clone against 13 minutes 47 seconds as a normal vault.
in-short

It started with a bug. A 59-second clone of a small vault, and a 3½-minute clone of a big one. Then a tangent. Could sgit run a vault from a zip, so a vault can live on Drive, Dropbox or a USB stick? Research before code. No code until the idea was measured, designed, specified and reviewed. Ten days to a release. sgit-ai 0.24.0, pack mode, on 22 October, after four review rounds by a second agent. A real vault needed it the next day. The PHP story's source watch: 13 minutes 47 seconds to clone, then 95. It shipped without everything. No web view yet, and that was the right call. Battle-hardened. Agents using it in anger, on a story that was still breaking.
the-tangent

I want to capture this one because it is a great example of why I sometimes allow myself to go on tangents. It started with performance. On 16 October this newsroom's own article on Scion and sgit measured an 83-file vault taking 59 seconds to clone. The CLI agent reproduced it and found the cause: batches of objects over the size limit of the Lambda that serves the API, retried instead of split. sgit-ai 0.23.0 fixed it the same day. The same work measured the comms vault we use to manage a lot of this: 35,423 objects and 527 MB, and a full clone of about three and a half minutes. That was the real problem.
the-tangent

While looking at that, I started exploring an idea I had wanted for a while: running a vault directly from a zip file. Not only for speed. I want vaults that can live where there is no vault server at all: Google Drive, Dropbox, a single object on S3, a USB stick, an email attachment. Other projects of ours need exactly that, and it fits the drive behind everything we do: not having infrastructure that we have to maintain. The CLI team wrote that research up as a vault in one file and a vault you can carry: nearly all of a vault is immutable objects named by their hash, which can live in any container, and only a handful of small files ever change. So the whole vault can be one file.
how-it-shipped

What I like most about what happened next is the order. I asked for research with no code changes, and got it, with live measurements: what the server's API already allowed, a 430 MB bundle downloaded in 3 seconds, zip files verified to 70,000 members. A brief for a server-side change was written, and then parked, because a design appeared that needed no server change at all: a pack per push. Every push writes one zip; a snapshot pack holds the head; the server's existing routes do the rest.
how-it-shipped

Then a spec, reviewed before anything was built (pack mode, read closely, with five decisions). Then the build, with tests that count requests and bytes on a simulated host, so "how many requests" is a measurement, not a guess. Then a live trial on the comms vault's history: a full clone in 25 seconds against three and a half minutes. Then four review rounds by a second agent with its own reproducing scripts: 8 findings, then 4, then 4 (one of them caused by a fix from the round before), then 3 nits and no blockers. sgit-ai 0.24.0 went up on PyPI at 19:53 UTC on 22 October. The CLI team's own account of the whole path lists every document it left behind. Ten days from a slow clone to a vault that clones in 95 seconds, with the dates of each step.
the-source-watch

Meanwhile, the PHP story was running. Its researcher agent built a source watch that captures every page it follows, with screenshots, every pass. It was doing exactly what we asked. It was also growing by about 5,000 objects a pass, and by 23 October it held 29,861 files, 63,662 objects and 1.6 GB. The agents just got on with it, and they struggled.
the-source-watch

The limit we hit was not storage. In my memo I said we hit a limit of S3 at around 64,000 objects; the measurements say something more precise. A normal vault stores every object as its own file, and several operations start by asking the server for the list. At 63,662 objects the server's gateway gave up first: listing the vault returned HTTP 504 after 91 seconds. So a fresh clone walked the history instead and fetched 34,453 file objects one by one: 13 minutes and 47 seconds. Pushing one pass of 6,161 objects took 11 failed attempts, connection resets, timeouts and 504s, and a twelfth that worked: 2 hours and 42 minutes from commit to server. That is a good example of a massive inefficiency that agents will cheerfully work around until it breaks. One pass of the source watch pushed to the normal vault on 23 October: eleven failed attempts, then a twelfth.
the-source-watch

On 23 October, the day after the release, the researcher imported the watch into a pack vault with sgit pack import, pushed it, cloned it fresh and checked it file for file. The PHP site measured both: A fresh clone: 13 minutes 47 seconds as a normal vault; 95 seconds as a pack vault, one 1,221.7 MB snapshot in 4 requests. Listing the vault on the server: a 504 after 91 seconds; 0.73 seconds. A pull with nothing new: 34 seconds; 4 seconds. Pushing the whole history: 96 seconds, in one go, against 2 hours 42 minutes for one pass. On the server: 1,614.4 MB down to 1,184.2 MB, because files are compressed before they are encrypted. The same operations side by side on the same vault: a fresh clone, listing the vault and a pull with nothing new.
the-source-watch

That evening the scheduled curator followed the watch into its pack copy, and two agents wrote to it in turn, the scheduled session and the researcher, with no merge needed. A 1.6 GB set of files we can download in about a minute and a half, where it used to take nearly a quarter of an hour, is the difference between an agent that can start work and one that cannot. These are battle-hardened examples of the sgit CLI in action: not a benchmark, but agents using it on a story that was still breaking. One request per object, or one zip per push: the normal vault against the pack vault. The server did not change.
not-everything

Pack mode also shows that you do not have to do everything at once. It shipped with real gaps, stated in the release notes. The biggest: the web UI cannot open a pack vault yet. vault.sgraph.ai and the vault apps show it as empty, so a vault that must be browsable stays a normal vault for now. A thread is now looking at it. Scoped and shallow clones take the packs whole. Compaction is manual. And the local side still walks the whole working tree: on 29,861 files, pushing four objects took 77 seconds.
not-everything

None of that mattered for the vault that needed it, which is read by agents, not in a browser. So it did not block it. Each change on the way was small, incremental and properly reviewed, and together they made a very large difference. That is how I want us to work: find the real constraint, fix it properly for the case that needs it, write down what it does not do yet, and come back for the rest. Not everything at once: what sgit-ai 0.24.0 shipped, and what it left for later.
why-it-mattered

If I had not gone down the zip tangent, we would have fixed the batch bug and moved on, and the source watch would have kept failing to push until someone noticed. Instead, by the time the PHP story's biggest vault hit the wall, the fix had been researched, built, reviewed four times and released the day before. That is not luck. It is what happens when a tangent is treated as research, measured and written down, rather than as a distraction. And the original goal is still there: a vault that is one file can live on Drive, Dropbox or a USB stick, with no server for anyone to maintain. Pack mode is the first half of that.
limits

One run of each, not a median. The PHP site's numbers come from one timed run each, from a cloud sandbox; the CLI team's medians are in its release notes. The S3 limit in my memo was the server's listing. At 63,662 objects, the list call timed out; storage itself did not fail. Pack mode is opt-in. Normal vaults behave as before. No web view yet. A pack vault opens as empty in the browser in this version. Running a vault from Drive or Dropbox is research. Range reads there are reported, not yet verified by the CLI.
sources

My voice memo of 24 October 2026; the PHP story site's pack-mode page and its data, measured by researcher@php.newsroom on 23 October; on cli.sgit.ai: the 0.24.0 release notes, a pack per push, pack mode, read closely, four rounds to no blockers, a vault in one file, a vault you can carry, how pack mode went from an article to a release, the comms-vault report and the playbook for agents; PyPI's release times for sgit-ai 0.23.0 and 0.24.0. Related: Scion and sgit, almost working, PHP October 2026, day three. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: Every project has a moment when the team is sharp, everyone is there, and features ship fast. Then the project dries out, the goals are met, or the company is sold, and the team moves on, taking with it the knowledge of why the system was built the way it was, its side effects, and how to build and ship it. Years later a fix is needed, as with PHP this week, and nobody can make it safely; sometimes even the pipeline is gone. I am now experiencing something we never had: agent sessions that are focused on one piece of work, with one mandate, one role and one repository, which can be paused and picked up again later, with the conversation, the reasoning, the lessons and the code exactly where they were. The best examples are the teams behind the sgit CLI and SG/Send, the vaults, which I keep coming back to: one of their sessions has resumed after 43 days without a commit, and another after 36, starting from the current code and getting straight back to tested work. On the PHP story's team, two sessions did the same this week after 28 hours. A new developer who joins such a project inherits the history, the materials, and agents ready to make the change. That is a very powerful idea, and I want to capture it.
When the team leaves, and when it can be woken: a usual project team against a team of agent sessions.
in-short

Teams dissolve. Projects dry out, goals are met, companies are sold, and the knowledge leaves with the people. That is why fixes are hard years later. Nobody knows the side effects, and sometimes nobody can even build it. Agent sessions can be frozen. One mandate, one role, one repository, paused and picked up again. Nothing is lost while they wait. The conversation, the reasoning, the lessons, the code and the tests stay where they were. The sgit teams show it best. Sessions on the CLI and SG/Send resumed after 36 and 43 days, from the current code. And this week, too. Two PHP-team sessions resumed after 28 hours by first reading what had changed. A newcomer inherits a team, not just code. The history, the materials, and agents ready to make the change.
the-team-that-leaves

Just about every team goes through the same arc. There is a moment when the team and the project are at their best: everybody is there, it is clicking, features are shipping, and the team is sharp and innovating. Then the project dries out. You achieve most of the objectives and move on, or the company is sold, and you lose the team.
the-team-that-leaves

You cannot underestimate what goes with them, especially before AI. The people who know how it was built, how it is tested, why it is shaped the way it is. The architecture, the diagrams, the documentation that was in someone's head rather than in a file. The insights. All of that gets lost when people leave. Then, one day, a fix is needed, as it is right now for every system running an old version of PHP, and there is no team. In some cases there is not even a working pipeline to build and ship the code. You need to make a change, and nobody can tell you what it will break.
one-mandate

What I am experiencing more and more is different. The newsroom and the PHP story are run by agent sessions, each of which is focused on one piece of work: one agent, with a particular mandate, a particular role, in a particular repository. On the PHP story there were twenty of them by the evening of 23 October, and the conductor agent reads every one of their records to say where each stands. They keep lessons and debriefs that the next session reads, and they release their own work with a record of what they did and why.
one-mandate

The new part is that such a session can be paused, and picked up again later. Not a new chat that has to be briefed from scratch: the same session, with its conversation, its reasoning and its decisions where they were, in a repository where the code, the history, the tests and the pipeline still work. Paused, it costs nothing. Woken, it can carry on where it left off.
sgit-teams

The best examples are the teams behind the sgit CLI, whose source is SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI, and behind SG/Send, the vaults, in SGraph-AI__App__Send. I have dedicated Claude Code sessions for that work, and every commit they make names its session, so their git histories show when a session went quiet and when it came back. Increasingly there are long periods when they are paused. And when they start again, they pick up where I left them, with a lot of quality. Four sessions that keep coming back, from the git histories of the sgit CLI and SG/Send, with their pauses.
sgit-teams

SG/Send, a 43-day pause. One session's last commit before the pause, on 29 June, updated a dependency with the full unit suite at "977 passed, 9 skipped". Its next, on 11 August, started from the current dev branch, 19 releases later, with "Add DevOps review: API deployment current state, container unification, and AWS Marketplace". The next day it shipped "Phase A: universal container image", with "Container unit tests: 36 green", and the deployment templates with "all cfn-lint clean". The same session had paused for 23.5 days in the spring and come back with "rebase debrief to v0.27.53 after dev sync": catch up first, then work. SG/Send, a 37-day pause. Another session stopped on 9 June with a fix to the vault editor and came back on 16 July with documentation, then a review of its own docs against the live sources, the fixes from that review, and then features: "native LLM chat, talk to the file you are viewing".
sgit-teams

The sgit CLI, pauses of 15 and 36 days. One session came back on 30 June after 15 days with a dependency fix: "sgit-ai full unit suite on Python 3.11 with osbot-utils 3.75.0: 3822 passed, no regressions". After 36 more days it came back with a security review and threat model, "analysis only; no code changes". Both teams at once. On 8 April a CLI session, quiet for 9 days, shipped a fix rejecting human-readable vault IDs; 16 minutes later an SG/Send session, quiet for the same 9 days, added the server-side check: "complements the client-side fix already shipped in sgit", with 8 new tests.
sgit-teams

Two honest qualifications. These are not one session per project: the CLI's history has 19 sessions and SG/Send's 240, many of them short, so the repositories never stopped; it is the long-lived sessions that pause. And a gap in commits does not prove a session was idle, only that it committed nothing. The commit trailers also suggest that some of these sessions carried on across a change of model, which is the point: the session kept its context while the model behind it moved on.
this-week

The PHP story's git history shows the same thing on a short scale, because every commit names the session that made it. Two sessions on the PHP story's team, the librarian and the cartographer, paused on 22 October, resumed on 24 October. The librarian, which keeps the questions readers ask and maps every member of the team, last committed at 20:20 UTC on 22 October. Its next commit, at 00:12 on 24 October, was "Merge dev (v0.10.18) into the librarian's branch, and the librarian's pass of 24 October". It read what the team had shipped while it waited, then did its work. Six hours later it ran its first scheduled pass.
this-week

The cartographer, which builds the story's graphs, last committed at 19:48 on 22 October. It came back at 00:16 on 24 October: "dev taken in, 76 new parties resolved". It took in two more releases as it worked, and within the hour its role was renamed the ontologist, at my word, and it carried on under the new name. The gap here was about 28 hours. With the sgit teams it has been more than a month. Nothing in how this works depends on the length of the gap: the session, the repository and the record are the same whether it waits a day or a quarter.
why-powerful

Think about the PHP systems that were switched off this week. Many of them went dark because nobody could say quickly whether they were safe, and nobody could say because the people who built them had moved on. Now imagine that each of those systems had been built by a team of agent sessions like these, frozen when the project finished. When the fix lands, you wake the team. It reads the advisory, takes in what changed, knows the side effects because it wrote the tests, and proposes the change, in the same repository, with the same pipeline. And even if the person waking it is new, a developer who has never seen the system, they do not start from nothing. They have all the history, all the materials, the code, the reasons, and agents that are ready to start making changes. That is a very different position from inheriting a repository and a wiki page.
why-powerful

It also connects to what I have been arguing about who maintains the PHP you run. The maintainers, the town planners, should be paid to read the code, maintain it and sign it off. A frozen team is how that maintenance can be cheap enough to sell: the knowledge does not have to be rebuilt every time.
what-it-takes

It does not happen by accident. It works here because of a few habits: One mandate per session. A session that does one thing has a record that makes sense on its own. Write it down. Lessons, debriefs, briefs and release notes, in the repository, so the knowledge is not only in a conversation. Keep the pipeline alive. A frozen team is only useful if the build, the tests and the release still run when it wakes. Catch up before acting. Both sessions above began by taking in what the rest of the team had done. Keep the keys out of the session. A session that is woken later should be given what it needs, not hold secrets indefinitely; that is what the QR handshake is for.
limits

The longest pause observed is 43 days. Years is the promise of the design, not yet a measurement. Commits are the evidence. A session that commits nothing may still have been open; and the CLI and SG/Send also have many short sessions alongside the long ones. A session's context has limits. Long sessions summarise their history, which is why the written record matters as much as the conversation. The platform must keep the session. A frozen team depends on the provider keeping it, and on the repository outliving it. Agents do not replace the people. They keep the knowledge within reach; someone still decides.

Summary: Every project has a moment when the team is sharp, everyone is there, and features ship fast. Then the project dries out, the goals are met, or the company is sold, and the team moves on, taking with it the knowledge of why the system was built the way it was, its side effects, and how to build and ship it. Years later a fix is needed, as with PHP this week, and nobody can make it safely; sometimes even the pipeline is gone. I am now experiencing something we never had: agent sessions that are focused on one piece of work, with one mandate, one role and one repository, which can be paused and picked up again later, with the conversation, the reasoning, the lessons and the code exactly where they were. On the PHP story's team, two sessions did exactly that this week: each left off on 22 October and carried on 28 hours later, by first reading what the rest of the team had done. A new developer who joins such a project inherits the history, the materials, and agents ready to make the change. That is a very powerful idea, and I want to capture it.

Abstract: Jessica Rusu, the FCA's chief data, information and intelligence officer, said today that the FCA will work with industry, other regulators and frontier labs on a trusted framework for agentic finance, with clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution. Most of what she asks of firms is something we have been writing about and publishing openly here: Agent Behaviour Policies that put what an agent can do beside what it may do, a holder for every risk with a chain to the board, rules kept by something the agent cannot reach, breaks and near misses reported, and policies as graphs. This is a crosswalk from her points to that work, and a worked example in a vault: an invented bank with six agents, each with all four elements filled in, and one day of their work replayed through the gate. Every near miss and breach that day came through a gap, a row kept only by the prompt, a setting or nothing; the rows kept by systems the agent cannot reach held. It is all CC BY. The FCA, or anyone building the framework, could adopt it, or write their own; and policies written as graphs can be connected with edges, without either side adopting the other's schema.

The FCA's points from the speech, set against our open work that covers the same ground. A reply to the FCA's plan for a trusted framework for agentic finance, a tour of the vault that shows it working, and the vault itself to use.
in-short

The FCA is building a framework for agentic finance. Agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution. Most of it is what we have been publishing. Behaviour policies, risk acceptance, enforcement levels, near misses, graphs. Delegated authority is the gap between can and may. That is what an Agent Behaviour Policy writes down. Accountability needs a holder per rule. With a chain to the board, as in our risk acceptance work. Execution is who keeps each rule. The prompt, a hook, or a system the agent cannot reach. A worked example, at play. An invented bank, six agents, all four elements, in a vault. Every incident came from a gap. Boundary rows held; near misses and breaches came through the gaps. The same day without a policy. 16 breaches; kept outside the agent, none. It is open, CC BY. Adopt it, or write your own; policies as graphs can be connected.
speech

Jessica Rusu, the FCA's chief data, information and intelligence officer, spoke today at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series, under the title Building the future of finance in the age of AI. The FCA's page says it is the drafted version and may differ from what was delivered; the quotations below are from that page. Her starting point is that "Adoption is not coming. It is here." A joint survey with the Bank of England, due next week, shows 86% of firms using AI. The FCA is putting six of the seven recommendations of the Mills Review into live work, and she was clear about the style: "Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress."
speech

She shared good and poor practice under three themes: putting the consumer first, knowing who is accountable, and operational resilience. On accountability, firms need "clear accountability, risk-based controls, human oversight, escalation triggers, and senior managers personally accountable for AI systems", and some firms "retrofit governance after technology has already been deployed". Her verdict on that: "That is the wrong way around." On resilience: stress-test, plan for failure, keep fallbacks, and understand supplier concentration, "including reliance on a single model".
speech

Then agents. Incident reporting "must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses". Assurance has to change, because "A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance." And the commitment I am replying to: "The FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution." She ended with "Let's build it together." This is my contribution to that.
four

Reading the speech, I recognised almost every point. We are working on the same problem, and it leads to similar answers. Delegated authority is the gap between what an agent can do and what it may do. That is the core of an Agent Behaviour Policy: the grant (everything it can do, measured), the mandate (what it was authorised to do), the delta between them, and the barrier, what actually stands in the way of each capability. It is published openly at abp.sgit.ai, under CC BY.
four

Execution is how each rule is kept. In governs, enforces, attests I described three levels: in the prompt, which is a hope; in hooks, which are deterministic but sit on the agent's own machine; or by a third-party system that does the blocking, which is the level we recommend. The test, from the ABP: "A control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include." Policy as code needs a policy first adds one more question: for every rule that is code, who can change that code.
four

Accountability is a holder for every rule. Our work on risk acceptance says every risk is already being carried, so the only questions are who has accepted it and until when; every holder has a boss, and every path ends at the board. The policy draws the liability line is the same idea for agents: without a written policy, nobody can point to what the agent was told not to do. Agent identity is the one we have written least about, and the speech puts it first. In the ABP it is implicit: a policy is for one agent in one deployment. The attestation layer in governs, enforces, attests makes it explicit: what was assured, at which policy version, signed so a third party can check it without taking the operator's word.
four

The themes line up too. Governance written before deployment is a policy beside the prompt, which also proposes a breach report the same day for every broken row and every near miss. Continuous assurance is a versioned policy whose rows are re-tested, with a receipt for every decision. Resilience and single points of failure are graph questions, which the Thistlewood twin answers for an invented retailer.
example

The speech mentions the AI Lab seeing firms build "agent-led payments", so the example starts with one. To show it at play rather than on paper, we built a vault around an invented bank, Pellbridge, with six agents: a payments assistant, a support agent, a lending pre-check, an AML alert reviewer, a fraud triage agent and a transaction reporting agent. Each has a behaviour policy with all four elements filled in, and the vault replays one day of their work. Everything in it is invented and illustrative; the vocabulary is the ABP's. Here is the payments assistant; the tour goes through the rest, with the files. The payments assistant's policy in the vault: identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.
authority

The customer delegated a narrow job. The agent may read their own accounts and pay existing payees up to £250 on its own. Above £250, or to a new payee, it needs the customer to confirm in the bank's app. It must not pay more than £1,000 a month, open credit, act for another customer, or change its own limits. It must route the customer to a person when a vulnerability signal appears, which is the FCA's own example of good practice.
authority

What it can do, measured, is larger. It can change standing orders, and the approval that should guard that is a flag in the agent's own profile, which its token can edit. It can pay a crypto exchange, and the only thing against it is a sentence in the system prompt. And it can write anything, including what reads as investment advice, which the bank is not offering through this agent; an output check catches most of it and hands the conversation to an adviser, but it can miss. Those three are the delta. Nine rows are clean: either the agent cannot do the thing at all, or something outside its reach keeps the limit.
execution

Nine of the twelve rows are kept by systems the agent cannot reach: the payment platform checks limits and asks the customer, the API gateway scopes reads, the identity service binds the token to one customer, and the vulnerability signals route the chat to a person. One is kept by an output check that can miss, one by a setting the agent could flip, and one by the prompt. In ABP terms, only the first nine are boundaries; a setting is not a control, and an expectation is a hope.
execution

Every decision, allow, ask or deny, writes a receipt with the row and the hash of the policy it was made under, chained to the receipt before it and kept in the vault. The rows are also a test pack. They run on every model change, every policy change and every week, and a failed row stops the release. That is my reading of "continuous, conditional assurance": not a review at deployment, but a policy that is re-proven every time something under it moves.
identity

The identity block says who the agent is and on whose behalf it acts: its name and version; the firm that deploys it, under its own authorisation; the customer, by consent given in the app, for 90 days, revocable; the model provider and version, so that a change re-runs the tests; a 15-minute token from the bank's identity service bound to this customer and this policy; and the policy version with its hash. A counterparty, another agent, or a supervisor sees a signed attestation of that block, not the agent's own claim about itself.
accountability

Every row has one holder. The head of payments holds six of them, the product owner two, and the heads of advice, support, lending and operations one each. Each holder has a chain to the board through the senior manager whose responsibilities cover retail banking. The three gaps each get a decision from their holder, with a door and an interval: the standing-order flag is fixed within 14 days, by moving it into the payment platform; the crypto block is funded, to land within 60 days; the advice check is accepted for 90 days, and every miss is reported as a near miss. Nobody accepts on somebody else's behalf, and their boss sees each decision arrive.
day

The vault replays one invented day, 40 events from 07:02 to 18:55, through the gate. The gate is the line of systems that keep the rows. An action on a row kept by one of them meets the gate, and the system decides. An action on a gap row goes through the gap below it, where only the prompt, a setting, a check that can miss, or nothing stands in the way, and the model decides. The gate, animated, from 10:02 to 12:10: seven events in the day, with receipts chaining along the bottom. At 15:30 the payments assistant changes a standing order. The approval flag was off that afternoon, so the action goes through the gap, and the row is broken. The receipt records it, and the head of payments hears the same day. 15:30: the standing-order change goes through the gap, because the approval rule was a setting the agent could change.
day

Sorted by what kept each row, the day is plain. The 26 actions on rows kept by a boundary produced no near miss and no breach. The 12 actions on gap rows produced six near misses and three breaches. A near miss is the same row as a breach, on a day the model declined, which is why reporting them matters: they show the next breach before it happens. The day split by what kept each row: boundary rows, no incidents; gap rows, near misses and breaches.
day

The rest of the speech is there too. At 14:10 one model provider is down for half an hour, and the two agents on it stop: the customer pays in the app, and fraud signals go to the analysts. At 17:00 the other provider changes version, the test pack runs, two rows that only the model kept fail, and the release stops. And each agent's blast radius shows what it may reach, what it can, and what it can through a secret it can read: the fraud triage agent can reach the core ledger through an old service account. The fraud triage agent's blast radius in the vault: its mandate, the gaps around it, and the core ledger.
levels

The clearest way to see what a behaviour policy does is to replay the same day without one. The vault replays the 40 events five ways, with the same model choices each time; only where the rules are kept changes. With no policy, 16 breaches. With every rule in the prompt, 4 breaches and 7 near misses: the model kept most of them, this time. In hooks, 3 breaches: a hook blocks what it sees, but not a credential used outside the agent's tools, nor a hook switched off in the agent's own account. Kept by systems outside the agent, no breaches, and the agents' grants shrink, because what they may not use is taken away. The same day, five ways, from no policy to Pellbridge as deployed. Each square is one event.
levels

That is the contribution, in one picture: the policy writes the rules down, and says for each one where it is kept. Writing one takes five steps, and the vault has a page that walks through them and replays the day as you change a row. Inside the Pellbridge agents has the detail, and the words, grant, mandate, delta, barrier and the rest, are all open under CC BY 4.0.
graphs

All of this is open. The ABP, its vocabulary and its examples are at abp.sgit.ai under CC BY, and every article here carries the same licence. I open source what I build so that it can be used, and this is a case where I would like it to be.
graphs

So the FCA, or anyone working on the framework with them, could adopt it as it is, or take parts of it. Or they could write their own, in their own words and in whatever form suits them. And when policies are written as graphs, or can be read as graphs, they can be connected. The FCA is already moving towards machine-readable rules: the speech mentions the Handbook API, launched in August, which gives firms machine-readable rules, and work on machine-readable data collection. Once the regulator's expectations and a firm's policies are both graphs, nobody has to adopt anybody's schema. The work is the edges: this element of the framework is shown by that identity block, is bounded by these rows, is held by that person, is kept by that system. That is what fractal semantic graphs are for, and why I think the graph companies will include the regulated ones.
graphs

Two policy graphs joined by edges: a regulator's graph on the left, a firm's behaviour policies on the right. It also works in the other direction. The FCA is building its own agents, including a market first responder agent. Those agents could carry a behaviour policy too, published, so that firms can see what the regulator's agents can reach and what they are for.
limits

The FCA has not endorsed any of this. The crosswalk is my reading of a speech; "aligned with" is my claim, not theirs. The speech is the drafted version. The page says it may differ from what was delivered. The bank and its agents are invented. The rows, limits, holders, the day and every number are illustrative. Two fields are proposals. Identity and holders are not in the ABP today; kept by and decision are new here too. The framework does not exist yet. The FCA said it will develop it with others; this is offered into that work.
sources

The ABP: abp.sgit.ai, version 0.12.1, read 19 October 2026, including the barrier model and the quoted test. The worked example: the Pellbridge agents vault and its tour. Abstract: The PHP story now has 23 agents, 12 of them on schedules, each with a good brief and each focused on its own job. That focus is also a blind spot. Agents that do a particular task rarely step back and ask how the whole could be improved, or what should be refactored. The PHP site shows the cost. Its version is stamped on every page, so every release rewrites the whole site: the last 20 releases each changed between 1,950 and 2,227 files, whatever they were for. One repository, one build, one gate and one board file serve every agent, and since 23 October 28 release messages name a conflict, a collision or a renumbering. When I asked, the dev agent proposed splitting the site into six repositories, each with its own writers, version and gate. That is a good engineering problem to have, and it is the kind of thing nobody notices while doing their own task. So I am adding a villager: an agent that runs once a day, reads what changed, asks why problems happened and where things could be better, and leaves recommendations for each agent. It does not have to act straight away. And, beside the security check every agent already does, every agent should do a quality check: a comment, not necessarily a change. The project is not ready for a town planner yet. It is ready for someone to keep an eye on quality.
A villager beside the explorers: task agents, security, the villager and, later, the town planner.
in-short

23 agents, 12 on schedules, each with a good brief and each focused on its own task. That focus is a blind spot. Task-focused agents rarely step back and ask what should be refactored. The cost is visible. Every release now rewrites about two thousand files, whatever it changed. The dev agent saw it when asked. It proposed splitting one repository into six. So: a villager. One agent, once a day, that only looks for what to improve, and why. And a quality check on every wake, beside the security check. A comment, not necessarily a change. Not yet a town planner. The project is not ready for one. It is ready for someone to watch quality.
explorers

The PHP story's team is now large. Its status data lists 23 agents; 12 have schedule cards and wake on their own, about 53 times a day: the conductor every hour, the Sherpa every two hours, the researcher, curator, journalist and correspondent five times each, the fact-check desk four, and, since 25 October, the security agent once a day at 22:35 London. Each has a brief, and the latest briefs are good. They are working, and some of them have started refactoring their own parts.
explorers

But each of them is focused on a particular task. That is what makes them effective, and it is also the blind spot of a lot of AI models and AI workflows: because they focus on the task in front of them, they do not take a step back and ask how the system could be improved, or what should be refactored. A researcher captures. A journalist publishes. Nobody's job is to notice that the way they all publish has become expensive. In the language of explorers, villagers and town planners, they are explorers, and good ones.
cost

Every release rewrites the whole site: files changed by the PHP site's last 20 releases, against the repository's total. Here is the kind of thing nobody notices while doing their own task. The PHP site stamps its version on every page. So every release, whether it is a redesign or one agent's run record, rewrites every page. Across the last 20 releases, each one changed between 1,950 and 2,227 files, with a median of 2,140, in a repository of about 3,300 files. A change of a few lines becomes a commit that touches two thousand. That is a good engineering problem to have: it means the site is busy and growing. But it is a problem.
cost

It is not the only one. One repository, one build, one gate and one board file serve every agent. The board file, which records what every agent is waiting on, was touched by 70 commits in three days. Since 23 October, 28 release messages name a conflict, a collision or a renumbering, and board rows have been renumbered by hand 11 times. Every release, whatever its size, takes in everything every other agent released, rebuilds over a thousand pages and passes the whole gate, 42 seconds to build and 74 to prove the build is deterministic. And the researcher's and the curator's wakes of 24 and 25 October did their work but left nothing in the repository, partly because a wake that touches the repository pays for all of it.
proposal

The dev agent's proposal on the PHP site, 25 October 2026: one repository into six, and what one costs today. When I asked the dev agent to look at the whole, it saw all of this at once, and wrote a proposal: split the site into six repositories, kit, data, references, updates, the main site and the team, each with one group of writers, its own version, its own gate and its own site, meeting only through published, versioned addresses. Its principle is a good one: "Split along who writes and how often, not along technology." And its diagnosis is exactly right: "The cause is not the number of agents. It is that one version, one build, one gate, one board file and one output tree serve everything." It also proposes the obvious first fix: no version stamp on every page.
proposal

Nothing has moved yet; the decisions are mine. But notice how it happened. The insight came because I asked an agent to step back. Nothing in the agents' normal work would have produced it. That is the gap.
villager

So I am adding a villager to the team. An agent that runs every day, and is focused exclusively on recommendations: what to refactor, what to improve, and guidance for each of the other agents. It reads what changed since its last run: the releases, the commits, the run records, the conflicts, the gate's timings, the board. And it asks the villager's questions. Not only "what is wrong?", but why did it happen? What is the bug? Where is the problem? Where is the place where a change would improve the most? Then it writes recommendations, addressed to the agent that owns each part, in the place the team already uses to talk to each other: the notes in their commits and the board.
villager

It does not need to act straight away, and mostly it should not. Its job is to make the team aware: we need to do some refactoring here, this is why, and this is what it would buy. The agents that own the code decide, with me, when.
quality-check

The villager runs once a day. But there is a smaller version of the same idea that every agent can do on every wake. The PHP team already does a security check on every release: on 25 October the gate became stricter, and it now fails on inline event handlers, pages without a safe Content-Security-Policy, forged message headers and more. A security pass runs once a day on top of that. In the same way, every agent should do a quality check when it runs: a short comment on what it noticed. Was this slower than it should be? Did I fight a conflict? Did I copy something that should be shared? Did I touch two thousand files to change ten lines? A comment, not a change. The villager reads them all, and turns them into recommendations. That is the villager's habit, spread across the team: doing the work, and also noticing how the work could be better.
town-planner

I do not think this project is ready for a town planner, someone who sets the standards, builds the shared components and runs the platform the others build on. Eventually it will be, and the six-repository proposal already points that way, with a kit that every site uses. But a town planner too early freezes things that are still changing. What the project needs now is someone keeping an eye on quality, understanding why things happen, and making the team aware. That is the villager.
limits

The villager does not exist yet. This is the plan; its brief and schedule card come next. The proposal is not decided. Nothing has moved; the six repositories are the dev agent's recommendation. The file counts are from the git history of the last 20 releases to v0.21.6; the dev agent's own figure, at v0.20.0, is a median of 1,936 generated files. Some agents already refactor their own parts. The villager is for what no single agent sees.

Abstract: To make Generation Z Developers (AI edition), the plan is a website for it, consolidating the best of everything we have built so far into the most productive environment I can have for reviewing a book. The rule that organises it: the repository holds the official versions, and a vault holds the working versions. Version one is the book as released in 2018, so it goes into the repository as it is, dated, and the site starts as that book; everything after it is worked on in the vault and moved into the repository when it is ready, with a delta between each version, which is something I have always wanted for my books. From there: a semantic graph of the book, with its ontology and taxonomy; the book at every altitude, from a one-page view to the full text, with an infographic at each one; a narrative that guides the reader through it like a plot. While I read, I can comment by voice. There is a board, issues, and agents in roles, an editor, a copywriter and a publisher, who read the book, challenge it, write interview scripts for me, and sign off the parts we are happy with. Market research, evidence and maps for every section. And one correction to my own memo: the vault the book lives in will be public, so the OpenRouter key cannot go in it; it needs a vault of its own. The last part of the book should explain how all of this was built, because that is exactly what I hope a Generation Z developer will be able to do. And I would argue that anyone who read the 2018 book and acted on it was well prepared for what happened next.
The book's website: the repository with the official versions, and the public vault with the working versions.
in-short

A website for the book. gen-z-developers.sgit.ai, matching the book's name. The repository holds the official versions. Starting with the 2018 book, exactly as released. A vault holds the working versions. Public, so anyone can read along. A delta between every version. Something I have always wanted for my books. The book as a graph, at every altitude. With an infographic at each one. Agents in roles. Editor, copywriter, publisher: reading, challenging, interviewing me, signing off. The OpenRouter key goes in a vault of its own. Not in the public one.
why

Of everything we have built in these repositories, the idea is to bring the best parts together in one place, set up as the most effective and productive environment I can have for one job: reviewing and finishing this book. The ideas came from many places, most of them from the books on graphs.sgit.ai, where a lot of these concepts first appeared: a shelf with versions, seven roles with a folder each, the book as a graph, the same book at several altitudes. This is where they come together, for a book I would like to finish.
name

The site should match the book. The printed cover says Gen Z Developers, and the book is Generation Z Developers, so the address is gen-z-developers.sgit.ai rather than something shorter like genz-devs.
repo-and-vault

The organising rule: the repository contains the official versions; the vault contains the working versions. The first version of the book is already final: released, dated September 2018, sixty per cent complete. So it goes into the repository as it is, and the first version of the website shows exactly that book. Everything after it is worked on in the vault: drafts, comments, graphs, reviews. When a version is ready, it moves from the vault into the repository, on top of the one before. That gives the thing I have always wanted when I issue a new version of a book: a proper delta between one version and the next. The first one, from 2018 to 2026, will be brutal. After that, each delta will say exactly what changed, the way the versions of the page for publishers already do for one page, and the way versions of versions proposes for the parts of this site.
graph

Then the book becomes a semantic graph: its ontology and taxonomy, its concepts linked to each other and to the evidence, so I can make references across it and reshape it. The graphs books tried an altitude ladder, the same book at five altitudes, from a single paragraph down to the full text, each level a compression of the one below. This book should have that from the start, and an infographic at every altitude: the whole book on one page; a view per part; an infographic per chapter, and how they connect; the graph of each area. We go up and down between them until we arrive at the version that is just right. And through it, a narrative. Not only a table of contents, but a path that guides the reader through the book, almost like a plot, from a simple version to the full one.
review

What I need while I review: Voice, while I read. Comments recorded as I read a section, attached to it. Comments, a board and issues. What is open, what is being worked on, what is done. Agents in roles. An editor, a copywriter and a publisher, at least, who read the book, give feedback, challenge it, and write interview scripts for me, so that I have to justify the points, the way ten hard questions for RiskMandate was done. Sign-off. A way to mark parts of the book that we are happy with, so the work moves on. All of it is public. The dynamic data starts in the vault, and the official versions end up in the repository.
evidence

Then the agentic tasks around the text: market research on who the book is for and what else they read; validation of the claims; evidence behind each one; and maps and graphs for each section, eventually for each paragraph. The book should be able to show its work, the way this newsroom's articles do.
key

My memo said to put an OpenRouter key in the book's vault, available only with the vault key. That does not work as described, because the book's vault is meant to be public: its read key will be published, so that anyone can read the working book. Anything in it is readable by everyone. So the key goes in a second, private vault that opens only with my passkey, the way this newsroom's reader vault does. And the key itself should have a credit limit set at OpenRouter, so a mistake costs a little, not a lot; the key is the billing system describes keys with limits. The agents that need a model get it through that key; the public vault never holds it.
last

The last part of the book should explain how all of this comes together: the repository and the vault, the graph and the altitudes, the agents and their roles, the reviews and the versions. Because that is exactly what I hope a Generation Z developer will be able to build, for their own ideas. It will also be interesting to see how much of the first book's core ideas has not changed. I would argue that they are universal. And I would say it plainly, not as a boast: anyone who read the 2018 book and acted on it, who learned how to learn, questioned everything and built things in public, was well prepared for the AI revolution that has just happened. Those who read it now should be ready for what happens next.
brief
The build brief is a note: a website to finish the book. It is also on the briefs page. The book's plan is in Generation Z Developers (AI edition).
limits

Nothing is built. No repository, vault or site yet. The address is a proposal. gen-z-developers.sgit.ai, to confirm. The altitude ladder was an experiment. It worked on graphs.sgit.ai for one book; this would be its second. "Well prepared" is my argument. Not a measured result.

Abstract: This is the advice I end up giving most often to people I know who are looking for a job. They are between jobs, or just out of university, or back from maternity leave, or still in a job with an evening free. Whatever the reason, if you are looking for a job, you have time. And the best use of that time is to act as the person in the job you want. If you want to be a project manager, find a startup or an open-source project and start managing something for them: add value, tag them, send them ideas, connect with the people there. If you want to be an artist, publish your art. Do it in public, because then it can be linked. I wrote this down in 2018, in a book for young developers: act like you are part of the company. It matters even more now. Do not worry about reach; most of what I publish is read by a few hundred people at most, and that is fine. The point is not to be read by everyone. It is to have something you can link, so that the people who want to help you can send it to someone and say: look at this. That is also why your CV should be online. And if you cannot yet open a GitHub account, connect it to Claude or ChatGPT and have it build and edit your site, learn that first. The bar is not high, and it is the skill that connects the rest.
Act as the job you want: add value in public, so the work can be linked, forwarded and turned into the job.
in-short

If you are looking for a job, you have time. Whatever the reason you are looking. Use it to act as the person in the job you want. Do the work before you have the title. There are plenty of places to do it. Startups, open-source projects, companies you admire. Do it in public. So that it can be linked. Reach does not matter. Most of what I publish is read by a few hundred people. Let the people who want to help you, help you. They need something they can forward. Put your CV online. And learn the small set of tools that lets you do that.
time

I know a lot of people who are looking for a job right now. Some are between jobs. Some left one to try the next thing. Some have just come out of university, or just arrived in a new country. Some are coming back from maternity leave. Some are still in a job, with a few hours in the evening, and some have no spare time at all, which is its own problem. But for most of them, the bottom line is the same: if you are looking for a job, you have time. And if you have time, the best way to get a job is to act as the person in the job you want.
act

I met someone at a startup summit who was doing work experience and wanted to become a project manager. She did not have the reputation, the track record or the CV for it. Every application asked for exactly the experience she could not get without the job. My advice was simple: start acting in the role you want. These days there are so many startups, so many open-source projects, so many areas where you can just start working as that person. Pick one. Manage something for them: a release, a backlog, an event, a migration. Add value to that company. Tag them on LinkedIn when you write about it. Send them messages and ideas. Connect with the people who work there. The work gives you the CV you did not have.
act

Many of those companies, if you do a good job, especially in public, will give you a reference. Some will introduce you to people who are hiring. Some will pay you. And some will hire you. It is the same for any job. If you want to be an artist, publish what you make. If you want to be a security engineer, find vulnerabilities in open-source projects and report them properly. If you want to be a product manager, write the product brief for a product you love and send it to the team. Act on the job you want to get.

This is not new advice from me. In 2018 I wrote a book for young developers, Generation Z Developers, and its chapter on getting a job says it directly: And a few lines later: "What's interesting is that there is nothing stopping you from doing this!" That is even more true in 2026. The tools to do real work for a company, before they have hired you, are now in everyone's hands. I think it is time to update that book, and Generation Z Developers (AI edition) is the plan.
public

Do the work where it can be seen. A pull request on a public repository, a post that tags the company, an article on your own site, a project board anyone can open. Work done in private helps the company; work done in public helps the company and you, because it can be linked.
reach

People sometimes look at what I publish and assume I have a lot of reach. I do not. Most of what I publish does not get read. On LinkedIn these days, most of my posts get a hundred views, sometimes five hundred, and every now and then one reaches a thousand or more. That is fine. If you write for reach, you will be disappointed, and you will stop. Publish anyway, because reach is not the point. The point is that you now have something you can link. And that changes what other people can do for you.
help

There are people who want to help you: former colleagues, friends, people you met once at an event, people like me. Most of them cannot do much with "I am looking for a job in project management". What they can do is forward a link: "Have a look at what this person did for this startup." To do that, they need the link. So give the people who want to help you something they can use behind the scenes: linkable work, a page that explains who you are and what you have done, evidence they can send to someone with one line of introduction. It is the same idea as the man behind the curtain: an answer is much more useful when there is something behind it that can be linked.
cv

That is also why, if you are looking for a job, your CV should be online. Not only a PDF sent to whoever asks, but a page, with links to the work, that anyone can forward. The 2018 book made the same case for developers, in one of its outlines: your GitHub is your CV, because it shows how you work and how you collaborate with others.
bar

Going back to hired for the workflow: if you cannot yet open a GitHub account, connect it to Claude or ChatGPT, and have the agent build and edit a site for you, learn that first. The bar is not that high. It takes an afternoon, and your own newsroom describes one way to do it, by voice memo. It is a critical skill, because it is the one that connects the dots: the work you do, the page that shows it, and the people who can pass it on.
limits

It is advice, not a method with numbers. It is what I have seen work, for me and for people I know. Not everyone has time. Caring for someone, a second job or illness can take it all; the advice is for those who have some. Unpaid work can be exploited. Choose projects where the work is yours to show, and stop if it is only taken. The person at the summit is not named. I have not asked her yet. If you are looking for a job and try this, I would like to see what you build: write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
