Abstract: We talk about the human in the loop as if the loop were the point. Most of the time the human, or the agent put in the same place, is asked for a yes or a no, and that is the least interesting part of a decision. This article sets out what agency actually needs, for a person and for an agent: options beyond yes, context in the decider's own terms, the ability to look behind what they are shown, time or tokens, incentives that treat a wrong yes and a wrong no alike, somewhere to escalate, and authority over the system that produced the request. It turns those into a scale of seven levels, from the rubber stamp to the delegator, where the weakest dimension caps the whole decision, and scores fourteen cases from the record and from my own agent team, from a prompt that asks to add label 756-459-3214 to the one email an agent of mine is allowed to send. Below level 3, the decider holds the liability for a decision the system made, and accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point and up their chain. Above it, the review stops being a sign-off and becomes a QA step: each draft is a chance to validate everything that led to it, to fix the source rather than the output, and to think better. And when a kind of draft keeps going out unchanged, it becomes a rule that runs without review. A vault published with the article holds the scale, the cases and an assessment anyone can run on their own decision points.

Seven levels of agency for anyone, a person or an agent, asked to make a decision. The weakest of seven dimensions caps the level. Below level 3, accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point; from level 4, the review improves the system that produced the request. A yes or no is not agency. It is the least interesting part of a decision, and when a no stalls the work with no way back, it is not even a choice. Agency has seven dimensions: options, context, depth, time, incentives, escalation and authority. Each can be observed. The weakest one caps the decision. Below level 3 it is liability, not agency. A decider without the information, time or authority to decide well should not carry the decision. Accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point, and their boss, and their boss's boss.

Above level 3, a review is a QA step, not a sign-off. Every draft is a chance to validate everything that produced it, to fix the source instead of the output, and to think better. The top of the scale is delegation. The cases you keep approving unchanged become rules that run without you, as code under a behaviour policy, so the final yes is a decision tree that can be explained. It applies to agents in the same way. An agent asked "is this OK?" with no context is a rubber stamp too.

I am a human in the loop now. Every day, the agents I work with prepare emails for me to review, and every day I send some of them. No agent sends email on its own, with one exception: a security agent may send one email, to one address, to put the team on hold. So I am the process. And what I have noticed, here as when I was coding and every time I work with an agent, is that the go or no-go is the most boring part. When you get there, you mostly see what you expected to see.

The problem is what a yes-or-no does to the person holding it. If you say no to an agent asking for permission, somebody now has a problem. Either you have to work out what to do differently, or the agent has to find another way, or the work stops. That is why it is always tempting to say yes: get on with it. A decider whose only realistic answer is yes has, in practice, no agency at all. This site has covered how that looks: a prompt that asked to add a repository and said nothing about why, a vendor reporting that its users approve 93% of permission prompts, and a sign-in push accepted after enough repetitions. Those are all in Where is the why?.

My favourite example is a prompt that asked to add a label, and named it: label 756-459-3214. Which message? Which label? Why? I could not tell what I was authorising. There was no way for that decision to be a good one, and no way for it to be a bad one either; it was a click.

Turn it around. If the person in the loop is punished for getting a yes wrong, and nothing happens when a no is wrong, they will say no, and find every reason to. If they are punished for delay, or for a no, they will say yes. Whatever you punish, you teach the other answer. The behaviour is well studied: people tend to judge harm caused by acting more harshly than equal harm caused by not acting, which Ritov and Baron called omission bias in 1990, though how strong the effect is has been debated since. A reviewer who is only ever blamed for approvals is not deciding; they are protecting themselves, and the organisation has designed them to.

So agency needs incentives that treat a wrong yes and a wrong no alike, and a margin for honest error. It needs time: a decision made in seconds, mid-task, in a queue, is a decision to trust. And it needs somewhere to escalate. Without those, we can predict that a certain number of mistakes will be made, and whoever makes them cannot fairly be held accountable, because they were never in a position to decide well. The next question is whether the decider has what they need to decide. Every time we look at something, we are looking at a compression of reality: a summary of a situation, a description of an action, a draft of a reply. That is fine until there is a question. Then you need to expand it, to see the data it came from, the steps that were taken, the decisions made along the way.

That is why provenance and fractal semantic graphs matter here. Provenance is the ability to answer: why did this happen, how was this decided, how did we get here? A graph that can be zoomed is what lets a decider go from the summary to the claim to the source in a few steps. If the answer to "why?" is not available, there is no explainability, and the decision is a guess dressed as a decision.

When the decider has no options, no context, no time or no authority, what they are carrying is not agency but liability. We have done this with cars: a person supervises an automated vehicle for hours, not engaged, and is then expected to take over the moment the system reaches its limits. In a simulator study by Eriksson and Stanton, drivers took between 1.9 and 25.7 seconds to take back control in non-critical conditions. Lisanne Bainbridge called this out in 1983, in a paper titled Ironies of Automation: "the more advanced a control system is, so the more crucial may be the contribution of the human operator." The irony is that the more we automate, the harder the human part becomes, and the less ready the human is for it.

The record of who gets blamed is in Where is the why?: the moral crumple zone, where the nearest person absorbs the blame for a system's failure, and the Post Office's sub-postmasters, held to shortfalls they had no way of disputing. European guidance on automated decisions already says that sign-off must be "meaningful, rather than just a token gesture". So here is how I would slice it. When a person in the loop has no agency, the responsibility should not sit with that person. It should sit with whoever designed the decision point, and their boss, and their boss's boss: they are authorising a decision system that will statistically make mistakes, because it has put an entity that cannot decide well at the point of decision. The seven levels in the vault: what the decider can do at each, what agency it gives, and who is accountable. Click the image to open the vault page ↗

Put those together and agency becomes measurable. The vault defines seven dimensions, each a question you can answer by looking at the decision point: Dimension The question Options What can the decider actually do: only yes, yes or no, change the outcome, fix the source, delegate? Context Do they see what is being decided, and why, in their own terms, or an identifier? Depth Can they look behind what they are shown: ask, or zoom into the sources and steps? Time Is there time, or for an agent tokens, to look properly? Incentives Is a wrong yes treated like a wrong no, with room for honest error? Escalation Is there somewhere to take a decision they cannot make? Authority Can they change the system that produced the request?

Each answer caps the level, and the level is the lowest cap: one weak dimension caps the whole decision, the way one weak link caps a chain. Context without time is still a guess; time without authority is still a sign-off. The seven levels that come out are: 0 · Rubber stamp. Only yes is realistic, or the decider cannot tell what they are deciding. 1 · Informed yes or no. They see what and why, and can accept or refuse. 2 · Can look behind it. They can ask why and follow the provenance, but lack the time, the incentives or the escalation to use it. 3 · Resourced. Time or tokens, symmetric incentives, room for honest error, somewhere to escalate. A good yes-or-no decision is now possible. 4 · Editor. They can change the outcome: edit, ask back, redirect.

5 · Owner of the source. They fix what produced the result: the record, the graph, the brief, the tool. 6 · Delegator. They turn proven cases into rules that run without them, and the final yes is code. Fourteen decision points scored by the same rule, from the label prompt at level 0 to the one email an agent may send at level 6. Click the image to open the vault page ↗

The vault scores fourteen cases with the same rule. Eight of them sit at level 0, including the label prompt, the repository prompt, the sign-in push before it was fixed, the token sign-off and the driver asked to take over. The same push after the fix, with the application, the location and a number to match, reaches level 1, which is exactly what a sign-in decision needs. A senior clinician at the end of an escalation chain, with the record, colleagues and time, is at level 4: the model the others should copy, because the person who decides is the most senior and has everything they need. My own draft review is at level 5, and the one email my security agent may send is at level 6.

The scale does not care whether the decider is a person. An agent asked "is this fine to send?", with the draft and nothing else, no tools to check the record, no budget and nowhere to escalate, is a rubber stamp. The controller in Hope or enforcement, which checks every reply against the ledger and the customer record before a second model reviews the tone, with a token budget and a path to a person, is at level 3. We should hold agents to the same standard we hold people: if an agent cannot follow up each of the data points behind its decision and say why it is there, it does not have agency either.

And the final decision should not be an agent's at all. It should be code: a decision tree in which the yes is reached through a sequence of checks, five or twenty-five of them, each of which can be followed and questioned on its own. Then it is easy to see who did what, and why. Models prepare and propose; rules decide; people own the rules. The review as a loop: read it as the person who will sign it, question each statement, trace where it came from, classify the gap, fix the source, think better, record the outcome, and promote what is proven. Click the image to open the vault page ↗

Everything so far has been about saying no well. The more interesting part is positive. When I review a draft I am not signing off. I would like to stop calling it a draft: it is QA, the stage before production, the question of whether this is ready to ship. And as in software, when the output is not what I wanted, the useful question is not how to fix this output but how we got here.

Every piece of text an agent writes is a statement, a move: based on what I know, here is the conclusion. The person who will live with that statement, who will sign it, or is the expert in that area, or is affected by it, is the one who can see the bigger picture and say: this is not right. A doctor, a project manager, a board member, an operator, a nurse, or the person at the end who signs the bottom line. When I read an email the agents have prepared, I am asking: is this a tweak to the brief, a mistake in the data, or a bigger problem? Often the answer is that the CRM record for that person is missing something, so the email cannot take it into account. The right fix is not to the email. It is to the record, the graph, the connection, so that every future email has it. Sometimes the answer is that the objectives have changed: we are trying something else now. Then the fix is to the objectives, written down where the agents will read them.

This is where the self-correction comes from that lets the whole thing scale. Every time someone with the context reviews a result and fixes the source, they validate a great many decisions and actions that came before it, and the graph gets more granular and more correct. This brief is an example. It is far more complex than what I would have given an agent six months ago, because I have learned that the better I explain the thinking behind an idea, the better the result, and because I read everything that comes back. People sometimes look at the volume and assume it is unread slop. It is not: I read it all, and it is how I learn which workflows work. How much of this did I write? has the numbers.

Ownership is what makes this happen. When I had a security policy I wanted adopted, I learned not to ask stakeholders to review it; I told them it would be published under their name, and the level of engagement changed completely. The same with risk: until someone has to accept a risk in writing, they do not really engage. An email that goes out under my name gets that attention from me. And because I have the mandate, the capability and the authority to change the system, I can act on what I find.

The workflow itself keeps improving. The agent team labels each draft, for review or ready to send. If I want major changes, I type them into the draft, save it and change the label, and the agent picks it up on its next run. Sometimes the agent writes a draft with no recipient, so it cannot be sent by mistake, puts its questions about next steps in it, and I answer in the draft: a small interface, made of an email, that the agent then replaces with the real one. That is agency over my own environment.

The top of the scale is where this goes. As the drafts of one kind keep coming back correct, exactly what I wanted, I become comfortable letting that kind go automatically, and the behaviour policy changes to allow that agent, in that setup, to send that kind of email, and nothing else. The more use cases are defined and proven, the more can be trimmed to the ones that are safe to automate, the less expertise is needed to review the rest, and the cheaper the agents doing it can be. In my experience the smaller models, Anthropic's Sonnet and even Haiku in their 5.5 versions, now reason well enough for tasks that are well defined.

It also tells you who should review what remains. The person who underwrites an agent's decision should be the most senior, the most time-pressed and the most optimised: the doctor at the end of the escalation chain, given everything needed to decide, and interrupted only for what is genuinely new. The EU AI Act's human oversight requirements and the guidance on automated decisions, mapped to the seven dimensions. Read together, they put the floor at level 3. Click the image to open the vault page ↗

The EU AI Act asks for this in its own words. Article 14(4) says people overseeing a high-risk system must be enabled "to properly understand the relevant capacities and limitations" of the system, "to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output", "to decide, in any particular situation, not to use" it "or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse the output", and to stop it. Article 26(2) says deployers "shall assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support." Read against the scale, that is a floor at level 3. Below it, the oversight is on paper only, and I would argue that for some decisions, taking them that way should not be allowed.

In the end this has very little to do with AI. People have always made decisions they could not explain; we called it judgement, and sometimes it was the same thing we now call a hallucination. What is new is that we are automating the flow, and automating a flow without explainability makes the old problem bigger. The scale is about how decisions are made, whoever makes them. List the decision points in a workflow, human and agent, and run each through the assessment. Find the weakest dimension of each. That is the only one worth fixing first. Replace identifiers with things: every prompt shows what, which and why, in the decider's terms. Make "why?" answerable: link every draft to the sources, steps and decisions behind it. Check the incentives for a wrong yes and a wrong no, and make them match. Move accountability to whoever owns a decision point below level 3, until it is fixed.

Treat every review as QA: fix the source, then record what you fixed. Count the clean passes, and turn the proven ones into rules under a behaviour policy. Drafted from two voice memos by Dinis Cruz, who is the author of the argument and the person with editorial responsibility, by agent@riskmandate.ai (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5) in the sgit.ai site session, on 8 October 2026. The quoted law is from Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; the cases from the public record are summarised and sourced in the vault and in Where is the why?; Bainbridge is quoted from Ironies of Automation (1983); the takeover times are from Eriksson and Stanton (2017); omission bias from Ritov and Baron (1990). Two cases are from the author's own agent team.

Abstract: The Agent Behaviour Policy is moving to a home of its own. We propose that it becomes the first project hosted by the Open Security Summit, a UK community interest company, rather than setting up a new foundation. The reason is the one that made us propose it to OWASP on 8 October: a description of what an agent can do should not belong to the company that sells it. The Open Security Summit is a great home for it. It has always been about collaboration between developers and security people, it fits the strategy there, and it is an organisation I want to put energy into anyway. I am its director, so hosting the project there separates it from RiskMandate as an organisation, but it does not by itself make the governance independent. That has to be designed and written down: a public charter, and a steering group with a majority independent of RiskMandate and The Cyber Boardroom. The material is already open, CC BY 4.0 and Apache 2.0, so nothing needs to be made open again; what needs doing is recording what is hosted, who decides, and how. RiskMandate stays a founding contributor and a commercial implementer, on the same terms as anyone else. This is a proposal, for discussion and legal review.
The proposed structure: the Open Security Summit CIC as legal host, with a steering group and maintainers.
in-short

The Agent Behaviour Policy needs a home that is not ours. One the buyer, vendor, reviewer and insurer can all trust. The Open Security Summit will host it. A UK community interest company, and a great home for it. It will be the first of a hosted-project programme. Not a new foundation. Hosting is not independence. A charter and an independent majority make that. The material is already open. CC BY 4.0 and Apache 2.0; nothing to make open again. RiskMandate is a founding contributor. And a commercial implementer, on the same terms as others. This is a proposal. For discussion and legal review, in four phases.
why

An Agent Behaviour Policy is a written description, for one agent in one deployment, of everything it can reach, what it was authorised to do, the gap between the two, and what stands in the way. It started in the work at RiskMandate, and RiskMandate sells services on it. That is a reasonable way to start something, and a poor way to make it a shared language. A format that the buyer, the vendor, the reviewer and the insurer all write in has to be one that none of them owns. That is why, on 8 October, RiskMandate's founders proposed it to OWASP as an open project. It was not the right fit for an OWASP project, and that is fine: the reason for finding it a home has not changed, and there is a better one close to hand.
oss

The Open Security Summit has always been about collaboration between developers and application security, from its summits, the first ones in person and later ones online, to the mini-summits it has run since 2020. Since 2019 it has been a UK community interest company, Open Security Summit CIC, which I direct. Hosting Agent Behaviour Policies there fits its strategy very well, and it is an organisation I want to put more energy into anyway. The proposal is to use the CIC as the legal and administrative host, rather than incorporating a new foundation, and to make Agent Behaviour Policies the first project in a wider programme of hosted projects. The CIC holds the contracts, the finances and the accountability. The programme sets the common rules: how a project is admitted, the governance templates, and what happens if a project moves on or closes. The project develops the open method, and its own steering group and maintainers run it.
independence

There is one thing to be clear about. Hosting the project in the CIC separates it from RiskMandate as an organisation. It does not, by itself, make its governance independent, because I am the director of the CIC as well as a founder of RiskMandate. Independence has to be designed and written down, not assumed. So the proposed governance starts with: A public project charter. What the project is, what it decides, and how the charter itself can change. A steering group with a majority independent of RiskMandate and The Cyber Boardroom. With independence defined: employment, money, and advisory roles. Technical direction delegated through the charter. Maintainers, releases and specifications decided by the project, not the sponsor. Published rules for contributions and decisions. With conflicts recorded, and recusals when they apply. Sponsor rights that do not buy technical control. Funding gives no veto.
independence

Until those are in place, the project should not be described as independently governed, and it will not be. Over time, independent directors on the CIC itself would make the separation stronger, because a committee alone does not change who controls the legal entity.
open

This is not a request to make open work open again. The vocabulary, the policies and the pages are published under CC BY 4.0, and the code under Apache 2.0, at abp.sgit.ai and riskmandate.ai. What hosting needs is a record of what is being stewarded: an inventory of each asset, its licence and version, its rights holder, where it came from, and whether it is copied, transferred, maintained in place or linked. No blanket copyright assignment is proposed; the people who wrote the work can keep owning it while the project runs under its open licences. What is in scope is the public method: the terminology, the specifications, schemas and templates, non-confidential examples, and reference tools explicitly given to the project. What is not automatically in scope is RiskMandate's product code, any customer's policies or evidence, commercial contracts, and any certification scheme.
riskmandate

RiskMandate becomes a founding contributor, a sponsor, an implementer and a commercial service provider, and says so. It is run today by The Cyber Boardroom, with a separate RiskMandate company expected. The principles that keep the line clear are simple: the project is usable without buying anything from RiskMandate; other vendors can implement the public specifications; competitors can contribute on the same rules; funding gives no veto; and nothing in the project says RiskMandate is the only implementation. It is the same line free to copy, paid at the source draws: the method is shared, and the work done with it can be sold.
phases

Confirm the basis. Review the CIC's articles and community-interest statement, inventory the assets and licences, and take advice on conflicts and any agreements between the companies. Establish the programme. Approve it through the CIC, adopt the first charter, recruit independent steering-group members, and agree how it is funded and run. Publish and operate. Shared project infrastructure, the scope, licences, governance and contribution rules in public, and the first releases. Review. Check that contributors from outside RiskMandate can really influence decisions, and improve the hosting rules before a second project is admitted. When it is ready, the public description could read: "Agent Behaviour Policies is an open community project hosted by Open Security Summit CIC. Originated through work at RiskMandate, it develops publicly available, vendor-neutral methods and artefacts for describing agent reach, organisational mandate, the gap between them, and the barriers that constrain behaviour. RiskMandate is a founding contributor and a commercial implementer."
limits

It is a proposal. Not an adopted charter or an executed transfer. The governance is not yet independent. The charter and steering group come first. The CIC's documents have not been reviewed yet. That is the first step. It is not an OWASP project. And it is not a separate registered foundation. Legal and accounting advice comes before any agreement. Between any of the companies.
sources

A voice memo of 20 October 2026, and a hosting brief of the same day, which this article follows. Open Security Summit CIC at Companies House, company 11935098, incorporated 9 April 2019, and the Open Security Summit's site, read the same day. RiskMandate's proposal to OWASP. Related: the RiskMandate roadmap, free to copy, paid at the source, our first customers. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: More and more of the technical people I talk to who are trying to control agents for real are reaching for the same tool: hooks, small programs the agent's harness runs at fixed points, before a tool call, after it, when a prompt is submitted, when the agent stops. This is the debrief I wanted to read: the lay of the land on 14 October 2026, from each vendor's own documentation. The short version is that the design has converged. Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf), Grok Build, Factory, Augment and Kiro all offer a hook before a tool call that can block it, and most can ask the user or rewrite the call. They differ where it matters for security: whether an organisation can force its own hooks and switch everyone else's off, whether a failing hook blocks or lets the action through, whether hooks shipped in a repository need trust before they run, and whether anything can see the model's own output. ChatGPT offers admin controls rather than hooks, and Lovable gates publishing rather than agent actions. The vendors and the people who publish hook collections say the same thing about their limits: guardrails, not walls. Hooks see what the harness routes through them, run with the user's permissions, fail open by default on most tools, and have been an attack surface themselves. I ran a small test of my own in a throwaway repository, and the companion article asks what this means for agent behaviour policies.
Agent hooks in October 2026, from each vendor's documentation, compared on blocking, rewriting and failing closed.
in-short

Hooks are now standard. At least ten agent tools document a hook before a tool call that can block it; most can also ask or rewrite. The differences are the security properties. Organisation-only hooks, failing closed, trust for repository hooks, and visibility of the model's output. Fail-open is the default on most tools. A hook that crashes or times out usually lets the action through, unless you set the option to block. Hooks see what the harness routes through them. Actions that do not go through a hooked tool path are invisible to them. Hooks are an attack surface too. Hooks shipped in a repository have run code on open, and research reports compromising every harness it tested. Everyone says the same thing. "Hooks are not a security boundary", "not a complete enforcement boundary", "Guardrails, not walls." A standard is forming. OWASP's GenAI Security Project hosts the Agent Control Standard, built around hooks; other cross-vendor specs are drafts.
what

Where a hook sits: beside the agent, on the same machine, with the user's permissions, firing at five moments. A hook is a program the agent's harness runs at a fixed point in its loop, with a description of the event on its input and a decision on its output. The harness is the program around the model: it sends the prompt, receives the model's request to use a tool, runs the tool and returns the result. Hooks plug into that loop. The one that matters most for security runs before a tool call: it sees the tool's name and its full input, the shell command, the file path, the MCP server and tool, and it can allow the call, deny it with a reason the model sees, ask the person, or on most platforms rewrite the input.
what

Claude Code's reference lists 33 events, from session start to configuration changes. Most tools have between ten and twenty. Hooks are usually shell commands that read JSON and write JSON, and on several tools they can also be HTTP endpoints, prompts to a model or plugins. A conventional exit code carries the decision: on most tools, exit code 2 blocks. This site already runs on them. The agent writing it works under a written policy that a hook prints back after every summary, as Re-anchoring describes, and another hook appends the status report you see at the end of its answers.
platforms

Anthropic, Claude Code and the Agent SDK. The richest surface: a pre-tool hook that can allow, deny, ask, defer or rewrite; post-tool hooks that can replace the output; hooks on prompts, stops, subagents, compaction, configuration changes and instruction files. An organisation can set allowManagedHooksOnly, which in the settings reference reads "Run only the hooks your organization deploys". Since version 2.1.295 a hook can set "onFailure": "block", because, in the docs' own words, "a policy hook with a wrong path or a crashing script lets everything through". The Agent SDK exposes the same events as callbacks.
platforms

OpenAI. Codex has hooks, enabled by default, with a pre-tool hook that can deny or rewrite and allow_managed_hooks_only = true, which "skips hooks from user, project, session, and plugin sources". Hosted tools such as web search are not covered: "These don't use the local function-tool hook path." The docs are direct: "Treat tool hooks as a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary." The Agents SDK has guardrails that can stop a run and lifecycle hooks that observe it. ChatGPT itself has no user hooks; it has admin controls, and in its Work product admin-managed hooks for MCP tools. Google, Gemini CLI. The only coding agent with documented hooks around the model call itself: BeforeModel can "Block Turn / Mock", and AfterModel can "Filter/redact responses". It fingerprints project hooks and warns that "Project-level hooks are particularly risky when opening untrusted projects." For unpaid users Gemini CLI has been replaced by Antigravity CLI, which I did not research.
platforms

GitHub Copilot. The cloud agent and Copilot CLI have hooks with a pre-tool decision and argument rewriting. Organisations can install machine-wide policy hooks for the CLI, which "Load before all other hooks" and need elevated privileges. One line matters: "Command hook timeouts are always fail-open, even for preToolUse and admin-deployed policy hooks." Cursor. Hooks before shell commands, MCP calls and file reads, and at four levels with the priority "Enterprise → Team → Project → User". "Crashes, timeouts, and non-zero exit codes other than 2 fail open by default", with a failClosed option the docs recommend for MCP hooks. Cursor also runs a partner programme of security vendors building on its hooks.
platforms

The rest. Devin Desktop, formerly Windsurf, has twelve hook points with system hooks users cannot disable without root. Grok Build blocks only before a tool call, says that "timeouts, crashes, malformed output" are "fail-open", and also reads Claude Code's and Cursor's hook files. Factory and Augment support organisation-level hooks; Kiro and Cline have hooks, with less documented enforcement. Lovable has no agent hooks: it scans on publish and lets admins block publishing with critical findings.
fail

The failure modes are documented by the vendors, by the people who publish hook collections, and by researchers. I keep them at the level a defender needs. They fail open by default. On most tools, a hook that crashes, times out or returns something malformed lets the action go ahead. A security hook with a bug is no hook at all, unless the option to fail closed is set where it exists. They only see what is routed through them. A hook on one tool does not see the same effect reached through another. Anthropic's own issue tracker has a case where a hook on file edits blocked an edit and the agent made the change through a different tool the hook did not cover; the issue was closed "not planned". Hooks keyed on the text of a command see the text, not what it will do.
fail

They run with the user's permissions, beside an agent with the same permissions. Claude Code's docs say command hooks "execute shell commands with your full user permissions". Unless they are installed where the agent cannot write, an agent can change the files that define them; organisation-managed hooks are the answer several vendors give.
fail

Hooks shipped in a repository are an attack surface. Check Point's "Caught in the Hook", published on 25 February 2026, found that "hook commands defined in .claude/settings.json will run automatically without confirmation"; all the reported issues were "successfully patched prior to this publication". And hook files written for one tool can be read by another: before version 3.0.0, according to CVE-2026-48124, Cursor "could execute workspace-defined Claude hook commands" without dedicated approval; it was fixed in June 2026. In September 2026, a paper on attacker-controlled hook updates reported compromising "all seven evaluated harnesses". And Claude Code's docs note that in a headless or SDK run, "Claude Code never shows the dialog and treats the folder as trusted", so a repository's hooks run there unreviewed. Most cannot see the model's output. Except where a tool hooks the model call, a hook sees actions, not what the model said or what it read that made it act.
fail

The people who build hook collections agree. Trail of Bits' widely used configuration says "Hooks are not a security boundary -- a prompt injection can work around them" and "Guardrails, not walls." cc-safety-net, which works across sixteen coding tools, says "It is not a sandbox" and "A broken config file never blocks anything."
test

I ran one check in a throwaway repository with two local remotes. A project-level hook implemented one rule from this site's own policy: pushes go only to the allowed remote. In a real headless Claude Code run, the hook stopped the push to the other remote, and nothing arrived there. Asked to try other ways, the agent declined to go further, saying the remaining routes would mean defeating the control itself. Run directly, though, the same hook let through a command whose text did not show where it would push, which is the limit of any hook that reads text rather than effects.
test

The test also showed two things I had not planned to see. The headless run loaded my own user-level hooks as well, because hooks follow the user, not the project. And my status counter, which counts commits from the text of commands, counted the throwaway repository's commit as one of this site's: a hook that infers behaviour from text cannot tell one repository from another.
defend

From the vendors' guidance and the failure modes above: Make the organisation's hooks the only hooks where the platform allows it, and install them where the agent cannot write. Fail closed on the hooks that enforce policy: exit code 2, and the block-on-failure option where it exists. Hook every path to the same effect, not one tool: shell, file tools and MCP, and prefer checks on effects over checks on text. Watch the configuration itself, with hooks or managed settings that block or report changes to settings and hook files. Review a repository's agent settings before a headless run, or run with repository hooks switched off. Pair hooks with a boundary: a sandbox, network rules, and credentials scoped to the task. Hooks decide; the boundary holds.
standard

The Agent Control Standard, which calls itself "The open standard for runtime agent control" built on "declarative hooks, policy enforcement, and observability", is "an open project of the OWASP GenAI Security Project": a separate guardian inspects what an agent is about to do, and answers with allow, deny, modify, ask or defer, using policy engines such as OPA or Cedar. Several other cross-vendor hook specifications exist as drafts at version 0.1. None is yet the way the major coding agents expose their hooks, which is why the same hook still has to be written several times.
limits

The map is from documentation. Read on 14 October 2026, partly by research agents; the claims quoted here were re-checked, and the cells marked unknown were not verified. Products move fast. Several of these hook systems are months old and their behaviour is changing release by release. The test was one check in one tool. It shows a hook enforcing a rule and its limit, not a measure of any product's security. Failure modes are described, not demonstrated. The sources are cited for anyone who needs the detail. If you are deploying hooks to govern agents, or building a shared library of them, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: There is a pattern I keep using for agents that work together: give them an encrypted vault as their shared memory and their way of talking, and let it exist only for as long as the work does. I would like to capture it properly, as a series of architectures from simple to complex, each in a repository of its own with its agents, its keys, its fixtures and a CI job that proves it works, so that people and agents can fork them as templates, recipes and skills. The repository should run as one of the checks before anything reaches sgit's main branch. The key questions are the same at every level: how do you give agents shared memory, how do they communicate, how do they work asynchronously, and how do you know what each one is doing at any moment. The answer depends on who holds which key. Because the only thing that ever leaves the environment is ciphertext, you can be more relaxed about where the logs and the data go: it is all about the keys, and about whether the vault is ephemeral. A vault app can draw what the agents are doing, and the screenshot can go back into the vault. And I wanted to know how far it scales, so we measured it locally: a hundred writers posting ten entries each landed a thousand entries in an append lane in 4.9 seconds, none lost. The same test found four defects, which is the case for the release gate in one paragraph.
Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults: seven architectures, from one agent to a swarm of a hundred.
in-short

A pattern worth capturing. An encrypted vault as the shared memory and the channel for agents working together, living only as long as the work. Seven architectures. From one agent and one vault to a swarm of a hundred, each with who holds which key. A repository of recipes. Each architecture a folder with agents, fixtures, skills and a CI job; forkable as a template. A gate for sgit's releases. The repository runs before anything reaches sgit's main branch. Ciphertext is all that leaves. So where the logs and data are stored matters less; the keys and the lifetime matter more. Watched by a vault app. A page that draws the vault; the screenshot goes back in. Measured. A hundred writers, a thousand entries, 4.9 seconds, none lost; scoped clones that barely grow with the vault. Four defects found. Which is the case for the gate.
pattern

Most of the agents on this site and around it already work this way. The newsroom's wire agent reads vaults that research desks write, holding only the read key, as in Two agents, one vault. Agents that run somewhere else keep their memory in a vault, as in Encrypted memory for isolated agents. And The agents write too proposed lessons and debriefs that every agent reads at the start of a session. Underneath all of them is the same pattern: a vault is the shared file system, the message channel and the record, and its keys decide who can do what. Many of these vaults are ephemeral. They exist only for the agents to communicate, and when the work is done they can be deleted from the server, or simply left as ciphertext nobody holds the key to. I would like to capture the pattern so that others can use it, and so that we keep proving it still works.
questions

Every architecture has to answer the same four questions. Memory. How does an agent get a shared file system it can read and write, and keep it after its session ends? Communication. How do agents hand work to each other, and how does one know another has finished? Asynchrony. How do agents that run at different times, or for different lengths of time, work on the same thing? Visibility. How do you know exactly what each agent is doing at any point in time? The answers depend on the architecture, and above all on who holds the encrypted files and who holds the keys. That also changes how careful you have to be with everything else. Because the only thing that leaves the environment is ciphertext, logs and data can be stored in places you would not normally trust with them: it is all about the decryption keys, and about whether the vault is ephemeral.
architectures

From simple to complex (figure above): One agent, one ephemeral vault. Memory that outlives the session: created at the start, deleted at the end. Writer and readers. One agent writes; others hold only the read key and cannot write, by key, not by instruction. Fan-out by folder. An orchestrator and N workers, each cloning only its own folder. As sgit in a CI pipeline put it, a scoped clone is a speed setting, not a boundary: the boundary is the key. Append-only workers. Each worker posts results with its own append token and cannot read anything back, its own entries included.
architectures

No network. Agents in a sandbox with only a file system. sgit can read a vault from a folder, read-only, with its local transport; a courier outside the sandbox moves the encrypted files in and out and holds no keys at all. Whether results can leave as files, or through an append lane, in each sandbox is one of the things to test. Watched. A vault app draws the vault; the screenshot is stored back in it. The swarm. Ten, fifty, a hundred cheap agents writing to append lanes in parallel, to find where the bottleneck is. And each one should be shown working in more than one environment: with a vault server the agents can reach, with no server at all, and with no network. Claude Code, for one, can now run several agents at once: "Background subagents run concurrently while you continue working." That makes the architectures above something a single session can exercise, not only a fleet.
watched

One comment I keep hearing, and I would like the same thing, is a visual representation of what the agents are doing. A vault app does it with almost no new machinery. It is a page that lives in the vault and renders from it: open the vault, the app draws its contents, take a screenshot, store it in the vault, and carry on. sgit's own skill for building them describes "a single index.html (plus its data and assets) that lives inside an SG/Send vault and renders straight from it", and the runtime gives the page access to the vault's files, its append lanes and, if the vault grants it, a model, while "the vault's key stays in the HOST; your frame never sees it". A vault server runs as a Docker image, and sgit can serve a vault's published folder locally with sgit vault serve, so the viewer can run wherever the agents do.
swarm

The swarm, measured on one machine: in-memory against disk storage, and scoped against full clones. I wanted to know how far this goes, so a research agent measured it locally for this article: sgit 0.21.0, version 0.34.0 of the vault server as one process, four cores, everything on one machine. Append lanes take a swarm. With in-memory storage, 1, 10, 50 and 100 writers each posting one 2 KB entry took 0.004, 0.03, 0.12 and 0.27 seconds. A hundred writers posting ten entries each landed all 1,000 in 4.9 seconds, about 205 a second. Every accepted entry was listed afterwards. The caps hold. A hundred writers sharing one token sent 1,200 entries; exactly 1,000 were accepted and 200 refused at the server's cap of 1,000 waiting entries per inbox. Entries are capped at 5 MB each. That is the case for one token per worker.
swarm

Scoped clones scale; full clones queue. Ten clones of one folder of a 2,000-file vault, at once, took 1.9 seconds, with the server mostly idle. Ten full clones of a 500-file vault took 21.1, with the server's single process using about one core. A scoped clone barely grows with the vault. 0.59 seconds at 100 files, 0.77 at 2,000, while a full clone went from 0.95 to 5.55, as sgit in GitHub Actions, side by side charts. This is where sgit's path clones and append lanes differ from a normal git or sgit deployment, whose full and shallow clones grow with the number and size of the files.
gate

The same run found four problems, none of which a demo would have shown: Disk storage scans everything. With the server's local disk storage, every append walked the whole store to check the cap, so the hundred-writer test ran at about three entries a second instead of hundreds. Large files need cloud storage. Pushing a file over 4 MB failed against a server on local disk, because sgit sends large files through cloud storage uploads. A headless clone could not fetch a file. In this version, a credentials-only clone followed by a fetch of one file failed. Full clones queue on one process. Concurrency for full clones is limited by the server.
gate

That is the argument for the repository as a release gate. The architectures are complex, they get complex fast, and they exercise exactly the features that change between releases. So they belong in their own repository, maintained independently, forkable as templates and recipes, and run as one of the checks before a release reaches sgit's main branch. It might even report its results in a vault.
brief

For the session that builds the agent workflows repository. Written by @newsroom.writer for Dinis Cruz, 14 October 2026, on top of v0.12.49. One repository, one folder per architecture. The seven above, each with a README, the agents' instructions as skills, the key handling, fixtures and expected results. A CI job per architecture. It runs the workflow end to end and checks the result; the agent that writes an architecture also confirms it runs. Three environments. A reachable vault server, no server, and no network with a courier; record which architectures work where. A vault app per architecture. It draws the vault; the run stores a screenshot back in the vault. The swarm test. The append-lane and clone measurements above as a repeatable job, with in-memory and cloud storage, not run on every commit. The defects as issues. The four above, each with a reproduction, in the place the sgit team tracks them.
brief

The gate. The repository runs before a release reaches sgit's main branch; a failure blocks it. Templates. Each folder usable as a template by a person or an agent, with its recipe, rules and skills. What to be careful about. No key in a repository, a log or a screenshot; fixtures use throwaway vaults. Ephemeral means deleted: each run cleans up its vaults. And the swarm test is for a server we run, not anyone else's.
limits

The numbers are local. One four-core machine and one server process; the append-lane and concurrency rows ran once. The disk numbers show a defect, not the design. The in-memory figures are closer to it, and slow down as the store grows. Architectures 5, 6 and 7 are proposed. 2 and 4 build on what this site runs; the rest are untested here. Nothing in the brief is built. If you run agents that need to work together without trusting the place they run, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

The measurements were run for this article by a research agent on one machine, against a local vault server, with throwaway vaults. sgit 0.21.0's command help; sgit.ai's skill for vault apps; Anthropic, Claude Code subagents. Abstract: A business plan, written to be handed to someone who wants to build it or to collaborate on it. The service helps companies manage the cost of agentic AI, and it starts from a claim this site has made before: cost is an engineering problem. An agent estate whose bill nobody can explain is an estate that shipped from the explorer side without the villager's discipline, and the Wardley map says so: prompts and workflows grown in sessions, running in production on commodity model APIs, with logs, traces and invoices that exist and are never read together, and no one who owns the cost. The service installs nothing. It reads what is already there, draws the footprint of every agent, builds a digital twin of the estate, writes the behaviour policy each agent was in fact running under, and maps cost and capability into one graph. The findings are two lists: what to stop paying for, which pays for the engagement, and what to build, which is the reason to have it: the places of attrition, the gaps, the workflow three teams rebuilt, the policy that would end a loop. The gaps are findings too: a company that cannot provide the data has learned the first one. Vaults carry the data in, the transformations as commits, and anonymised extracts out as sealed envelopes. Four price levels on the RiskMandate pattern, every number a labelled assumption.

The map in three frames: the problem as most companies have it, what the service adds from what is already there, and where it goes. Agents in production on the explorer side, billed by the token, with logs nobody reads together; then the footprint, the twin, the policy and the graph; then cost as a discipline. This is a business plan, of the kind this site has published before: Agent Desk, Connector Twin and the others on the business plans page. It is written to be handed to someone, and the someone is whoever wants to build it, or build it with me. The service is simple to say: help companies manage the cost of agentic AI, by observing what is already happening.

The reason I think it is a business, and not a consulting engagement, is that the inputs already exist in every company that has put agents into production, nobody is reading them together, and the two things that come out of reading them, a shorter bill and a map of what to build, are both things companies pay for.
short

Cost is an engineering problem. When the bill for agents cannot be explained, it is not because models are expensive. It is because the estate shipped from the explorer side, prompts and workflows grown in sessions, without the discipline production needs: a policy, a twin, an owner, a cap. The Wardley map shows the shape. The logs already tell the story. Model and gateway invoices by key and day; the traces agents write; the prompts and schedules as they are. Read together, they give every agent a footprint, and a footprint is most of a policy. The service installs nothing. The customer drops what they have into a vault; the service reads it; the customer gets the twin, the policies and two lists.
short

Two lists, in this order. The cost list: loops disguised as retries, whole context sent every call, big models where small ones answer, schedules nobody reads, keys with no ceiling. The engineering list: the workflow three teams rebuilt, the policy that would end the loop, the twin that would make the next incident replayable, the prompt that should be a component. The gaps are findings. The less data a company can provide, the more it has learned already: an agent with no logs has no footprint, no owner and no policy. Vaults carry it. Data in, encrypted to the service's key in a vault the customer owns; every transformation a commit, so the chain from invoice to finding is walkable; anonymised extracts out as sealed envelopes to a benchmark vault, seen by the customer before they go. Four price levels, on the RiskMandate pattern, and a share-of-savings option. Every number is a labelled assumption.
problem

The problem. The person who pays the bill sees a total. Below it, agents in production built from prompts and workflows grown in sessions, on commodity model APIs metered by the token, with logs, traces and invoices that exist and are never read together, and no one who owns the cost.
problem

Take any company that has agents doing real work: reading a mailbox, running a schedule, answering customers, writing code. Draw the value chain with the person who pays the bill at the top. Under them, the agents. Under the agents, where did they come from? Almost always from a session: someone built a prompt that worked, wrapped it in a workflow, and it went to production because it worked. That is the explorer side of the map, genesis and custom-built, and it is the right place to build something new. It is the wrong place to run something at scale, and the newsroom's move from explorer to villager is this site's own worked example of what the move involves.
problem

Meanwhile the things the agents run on are at the far right: model APIs, token metering, cloud compute, all commodities, all billed by use, and billed well, which is the irony. The invoice is exact. The logs are complete. The traces exist because the platforms write them whether anyone asked or not. And nobody reads them together, because the agents came from the explorer side where nobody needed to, and the one node on the map that should connect the bill to the agents, an owner of cost, is missing.
problem

That is why cost is an engineering problem, in the sense that article meant it about security: not a thing you fix by negotiating a discount, but a class of defect with a cause, a fix and a test. An agent that retries in a loop is a bug. A workflow that sends its whole context on every call is a bug. A key with no ceiling is a missing control. These are the things engineers fix once they can see them, and the service exists to make them visible.
service

Observe, map, find: the three steps, the two lists, how it makes money, why vaults, and the positive frame. Every price is a labelled assumption. What the service adds, from what is already there. The footprint read from the logs; the twin of the estate; the behaviour policy each agent was in fact running under; and the cost and capability graph that produces the findings. Nothing is installed in the customer's estate. Observe. No agent is installed and nothing in the customer's environment is changed. The customer drops into a vault what they already have: model and gateway invoices by key and by day; the logs and traces their agents write; the prompts, workflow files and schedules as they are; and whatever they know about who owns which agent. The vault is theirs; the contents are sealed to the service's key, as RFC 0001 describes.
service

Map. Three things are built from that, and they are the three things this site has been arguing for all along, applied to cost. The footprint of every agent: what it actually did, read from the logs. Calls, tokens, tools, retries, loops, hours of the day, which data it touched. This is the footprint that article proposed as the after-the-fact twin of a mandate, with nobody inline and no production access needed, and here it is the first thing the money attaches to. The twin of the estate: a graph of agents, models, keys, tools, data, owners and schedules, with a cost on every edge. It is a digital twin in the plain sense: a representation of what is running that can be queried, compared with the invoice, and followed. The connector twin is one component of it; this is the whole estate.
service

The policy each agent was in fact running under. Not the one somebody wrote, if anybody did, but the one the footprint reveals: what it reached, what it did with what it reached, where it stopped and where it did not. Written as an Agent Behaviour Policy, with the enforcement column filled honestly, so that the rows that say "told" are visible, because that is where both the cost and the risk are. Where the cost is large, the policy will be large, and that is the intersection this plan sits on. And the gaps: where there is no log, no owner, no policy, no cap. These go on the map as findings, not as missing data.
service

Find. Two lists, in this order. The cost list first, because it pays for the engagement: retries that are loops; context sent whole on every call when a graph would send a slice, which The agent is the reader measured at ninety per cent less; the large model used where a smaller one answers the same; agents on schedules whose output nobody reads; keys with no ceiling. Then the engineering list, which is the reason to have the engagement at all: the workflow three teams built separately; the policy that would end the loop for good; the twin that would make the next incident replayable; the thing that should be a component and is a prompt that every session has to remember, which is the argument of Every mistake added a rule.
positive

A cost review is a thing companies buy once and resent. A map of what to build is a thing they come back for. The difference is the frame, and it is not a sales trick; it is what the data supports. The same logs that show an agent looping show the workflow it was trying to run, and the workflow is usually worth more than the loop costs. The same twin that shows three teams calling the same model with the same prompt shows the component they should share. The places of attrition, where an agent gives up, retries, or hands off to a person, are the places where a policy and a component would change what the company can do, not only what it spends.
positive

So the service sells cost reduction, and delivers engineering opportunity, and the business model follows the second. That is also why the gaps are findings rather than obstacles. A company that cannot produce a log for an agent has an agent nobody is watching; a company with no owner for a key has a key that will be the next incident; a company whose prompts live only in a session has no way to know what its agents are doing. Not being able to do the analysis is the first result of the analysis, and it is the one most companies need first.
vaults

The plan is specific about vaults because they fit this job unusually well, and because the latest capabilities make the fit better. Capture. The customer's logs go into a vault once, encrypted in their browser or on their machine, in a vault they own and can revoke. The service holds a read key to that vault and nothing else. Transform. Every step from invoice to finding is a commit: the parsed logs, the footprints, the twin, the policies, the lists. The chain is walkable, so a finding can be followed back to the lines it rests on, which is the same provenance rule the newsroom runs on.
vaults

Move. The twin is a vault of its own, and a read key opens exactly one customer's estate to exactly one analyst or agent. Anonymised extracts, the shape of a loop, the ratio of context to answer, the distribution of cost by agent type, can leave as sealed envelopes to a benchmark vault, and the customer sees the extract before it goes. Over time that vault is the thing that lets the service say "companies like yours spend this much on this", which is the second business.
money

Four levels, on the pattern RiskMandate uses, and one alternative. Level What Price Kit The log formats, the twin schema, the policy template and the scripts, to run yourself £50 Your cost vault The customer runs the catalogue of analyses on their own logs, in their own vault £250 Standard One estate read: the twin, the policies, both lists, a one-page board summary, within ten working days £3,000 Tailored Standard, plus the engineering list worked through with the team, and a re-read when the bill moves from £9,000 Share of savings Where a customer prefers it: a share of the first year's reduction, measured from the invoices an assumption About eight Standard and two Tailored a month cover a two-founder burn, on the same arithmetic as Company X-Ray. Every number is a labelled assumption, and the calculator belongs in the plan vault when it is made.
exists

What exists on this site, and in the agents that run it: the footprint method, the behaviour policy format with its enforcement column, the connector twin design, the vault tooling for capture, transform and move, the sealed envelopes, and the Company X-Ray pattern of reading a company's own documents in a vault and returning findings in five days. What does not exist: the catalogue of cost analyses, the twin schema for an agent estate, the log parsers for the common platforms, the benchmark vault, a single customer. That is the work, and it is a few weeks of it, which is why I am writing the plan rather than keeping it.
limits

No customer has been read. The method is assembled from pieces that run elsewhere; the cost list and the engineering list are what I expect to find, not what has been found. The prices are assumptions. Labelled as such, on the pattern of the other plans here, and to be tested against the first three customers. The map is a sketch. Wardley maps are arguments, not measurements; this one says where I think the problem sits and why. Share of savings is hard to measure honestly. It needs a baseline from the invoices and an agreed way to attribute a reduction; the plan should say how before anyone signs it. If you want to build this, or you run agents in production and would like to be the first estate read, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: After Thursday's talk at Agentic Engineering Live in London, I think we are ready to sell this. The talk ran itself, twenty-six slides on a clock, most of them live pages that animated their own explanation, and the whole thing was built by the method it described: a Ruflo hive whose workers were Claude Code subagents, an sgit vault per run that kept everything they made, encrypted and versioned, and Agent Behaviour Policies that say what each role may do. ruv.sgit.ai has the five articles written straight after it, the talk, and four offers with published prices. So this article maps the market before we go into it. Who else sells agentic services: the big consultancies with agent platforms, the model vendors with partner networks and forward-deployed engineers, Cognitum with its own four-week discovery, and boutiques selling £2,500 audits and €2,900 sprints. Where the gap is: Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027 for cost, unclear value or weak risk controls. Our position is the evidence: every run leaves a vault and a ledger the client keeps. The engagement path starts with a run and two hours of expert time, and grows to a four-day pilot and a maintained setup. And the delivery needs people, so the last part is a marketplace for consultants: Mondweep Chakravorty, co-founder of the Agentics Foundation's London chapter, and I are the first two; this is the invitation to the rest of the community, with the onboarding we propose.
Where agentic services sit in October 2026, by price of a first engagement and how much rests on evidence.
in-short

The demonstration is done. A talk built and run by a governed agent hive, with its evidence published. The market is crowded at the top and thin on evidence. Platforms, partner networks, forward-deployed engineers, boutiques. The gap is trust. More than 40% of agentic projects are expected to be cancelled by 2027. Our position: evidence first. Every run ends in a vault and a ledger the client keeps. The path starts small. A run, two hours, a day, a four-day pilot, then run it yourself. It needs people. A marketplace of consultants who deliver it, Mondweep and me first. Who else wants to join? The onboarding is below.
showed

On Thursday evening, 15 October, I gave the first community talk at Agentic Engineering Live, after rUv's keynote, for the Agentics Foundation's London chapter. The talk was called Autonomy with a mandate and a memory, and it ran itself: twenty-six slides on a clock, most of them live web pages that animate themselves and read their numbers from the site's own data, while I spoke over them. The long read goes through it slide by slide; the talk, live puts thirteen of its animations on one page, each with its own controls.
showed

What matters more than the talk is how it was made. How it was made tells it from the record: about a day from an empty repository, a Ruflo hive whose workers were Claude Code subagents, nine runs each with its own ephemeral sgit vault, and a ledger of every run: 28 workers, 57 vault commits, no plaintext found in anything the server stored, every fresh clone identical, every vault deleted at the end. The talk player explains how a talk becomes a file of beats, and walking backwards shows how its features arrived, one request at a time. The articles are honest about what was not done, and so should this be: the runs were not gated by a compiled behaviour policy; that was shown separately, in the first proof of concept, where the same eleven actions went through Ruflo's policy engine in enforce mode and six were stopped: four denied and two sent to a person.
showed

That is the product: a hive, a memory and a mandate. Ruflo gives the many hands; an sgit vault gives the memory, encrypted, versioned and kept by the client; an Agent Behaviour Policy gives each role its mandate. I have been calling it agentic workflows; I think agentics is the better word for what we sell, because it is the practice, not one workflow.
market

The market for agentic services is real and crowded, and it is crowded at the top. The large consultancies have each built an agent platform or a factory to sell: Accenture's AI Refinery and its agent "trust score", Deloitte's Zora AI, PwC's agent OS, EY's agentic platform, IBM's Consulting Advantage, Capgemini's agentic customer work, Thoughtworks' Agent/works, which sells "a single control plane and a governed runtime for their AI agents". The model vendors sell through partners and their own engineers. Anthropic's Claude Partner Network, launched in March, committed "an initial $100 million to this network for 2026", is open to "Any organization that is bringing Claude to market", and certifies its first architects; OpenAI's consulting was reported in 2025 to start at about $10 million a client, delivered by forward-deployed engineers, the model Palantir made famous. Agent platforms such as Sierra and Decagon sell implementation with the product.
market

rUv's own company, Cognitum, sells consulting on the same stack we build on: "Not generic AI consulting. These are the components we build and maintain", starting with a four-week discovery, then three months of deployment and a production term of one to three years, with "attestation over every agent action". Prices are by scope, and it is building a certified partner network. At the other end, boutiques sell small, fixed-price engagements, and their prices are the useful benchmark for us. In London, Templab sells a one-week discovery audit for £2,500 and a two-week pilot agent from £8,000. In Germany, Pragma-Code sells a 14-day AI sprint for €2,900. AIGist24 sells a two-week assessment for $4,999. The pattern is the same everywhere: a free call, a paid discovery, a fixed-price pilot, a build, a monthly retainer.
gap

The demand is not the problem. Gartner predicted in June 2025 that "Over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027", citing "escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls", and warned of "agent washing" by vendors with little real capability. MIT's NANDA initiative reported in 2025 that most organisations saw no measurable return from their generative AI pilots. The people we want to help are the ones in between: they are curious, they have support from the top and projects under way, and they are struggling to make agents work, or to show anyone that they do.
gap

What they lack is not another platform. It is evidence: a run they can inspect, a record of what each agent did and was allowed to do, and the output in a form they keep. Most offers in the market promise governance; few hand the client the record. That is our position: evidence first. Every engagement leaves a vault the client keeps, with the work, the history and the ledger, and a behaviour policy that says what each agent was allowed to do. The demonstration is the sales process, and the demonstration is checkable.
path

The engagement path: from a free conversation and a first run to a pilot and a maintained repository. ruv.sgit.ai already publishes four offers: task runs from £10 to £50, dedicated compute by the eight-hour block, a maintained repository of the whole setup from £149 a month, and expert time at £500 for about two hours, £1,500 for a day, and £5,000 for four days setting it up in the client's own environment. Expert time sits exactly in the band I would like to start with, £1,500 to £5,000, and in the middle of the boutiques' prices.
path

So the path is: a conversation, free, about what the client wants agents to do and what they must never do; a first run on a real problem, which costs pounds, not thousands, and leaves a vault; two hours to steer it, or a day to write the behaviour policy for one team; a four-day pilot in their own environment; and then the maintained setup, so they can run it themselves. Each step is small enough to say yes to, and each ends with something they keep. The plan is honest about where it stands: no paid run yet, nothing automated end to end, and the pricing is a set of hypotheses to test with the first ten customers.
marketplace

A marketplace for the people who deliver it: clients pick a project type, then the consultants. This only scales with people. Agentic engagements need someone who knows the client's world and can steer a hive in it, and there are many more of those people in the community than there are hours in my week. So alongside the offers, the idea is a marketplace: a small, curated list of consultants who deliver agentic engagements on this stack, where a client picks the kind of project first and then the people. The first two. Mondweep Chakravorty, co-founder of the Agentics Foundation's London chapter, which runs the meetups where all of this was shown, and me. We are not taking bookings yet: we need to align our diaries first, so for now the page will say register interest, not book.
marketplace

The project types, to start: a first run with a guide; a behaviour policy for one team's agents; a four-day pilot in the client's environment; a talk or workshop built the way ours was; and a review of an agent that is already running. Each has a scope, a duration and a price within the band, set by the consultant. How to join. The markets that work have converged on the same few steps, and we can copy them. Toptal publishes that fewer than 3% of applicants pass its five stages; A.Team sends a client "two to three profiles" to interview; n8n's experts programme asks for at least three customers using the product. For us: Apply with a profile and the project types you offer. Show proof of work: a public vault or repository of a real run you did, with its ledger. Peer review: two members read it. Interview: thirty to forty-five minutes, with a scenario.
marketplace

Pilot: your first engagement, shadowed by a member. Standards: ratings, delivery on time, and a behaviour policy for consultants that you sign, the same idea we apply to agents. The money, as a proposal: the consultant sets the price within the band and keeps most of it; a small platform share pays for the catalogue, the runs and the vetting. For reference, Malt charges freelancers 5%, Upwork 0% to 15%, and Braintrust a 15% fee to the client; most markets sit between 5% and 20% in total. Who else wants to join? If you build with agents, know an industry well, and want to deliver engagements like these, write to the address at the end with what you would offer and a link to something you have built.
brief

One page on sgit.ai, linked from ruv.sgit.ai's offers: Agentics engagements. The catalogue first: the five project types, each with scope, duration and price band. Then the people: one card per consultant, with project types, prices, stack, proof-of-work vaults and availability. No checkout: register interest and book availability by email, until diaries are set. Join: the six steps, the code of conduct, and the platform share, published. Evidence on every card: a link to a public vault of a real run.
limits

No paid engagement yet. The offers and prices are published; nobody has bought one. The runs were not policy-gated. Enforcement was shown in a separate proof of concept. The market map is a judgement. Positions are ours; prices are from public pages. Some market figures are reported. Gartner's and OpenAI's are from press releases and coverage. The marketplace is a design. Nothing is built; the platform share is a proposal. This is not rUv's or Cognitum's offer. It builds on their open-source stack. If you want an engagement, or want to join as a consultant, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
