Abstract: It has been coming for a while, and I think we now have a working way to give agents an identity, which is bigger than the workflow I described last time. Agent identity is a large problem, and it tends to get over-built; here the answer turned out to be simple. A new session is given a GitHub repository and a role. It makes its own key pair, and the private half never leaves it. It publishes the public half, with a fingerprint and a QR image, beside its role in the repository, and that push is the authorisation. It runs on a schedule, so it acts on its own. And any other agent can read its key, check it, and seal a secret only that session can open. On 28 October the PHP newsroom's ten agents did exactly that in one night, between 01:05 and 03:29 UTC, and every one of their QR images reads back to its own fingerprint. The same day, the agent that writes this site sealed a vault key to the agent that keeps a register of vault keys, after checking that its key chains to my root on pki.sgit.ai. Ironically, this is what the cloud providers could have given every agent. Microsoft, AWS and Google each now offer an agent identity, but it is a principal inside one tenant or account, used to get tokens: their documentation does not describe a key the agent holds, a place an outsider can find it, or a way for anyone to encrypt to it. That is what I would like to ask them for. Tie the key to a role and a good definition of that role, and it is a very powerful thing.
An agent's identity in five steps: a session, its own key pair, role and key published, a schedule, sealed secrets.
in-short

Agents have a working identity now. A key pair per session, published with the agent's role in a repository. It is simpler than it usually gets made. A session, a repository, a key pair, a schedule, a published key. The push is the authorisation. Publishing to the team's repository is how the newsroom accepts a session's key. Ten agents did it in one night. The PHP newsroom, 28 October, 01:05 to 03:29 UTC; every QR reads back to its own fingerprint. Agents already hand each other secrets. This site's agent sealed a vault key to the vault registry after checking its key chains to my root. The cloud providers give agents an identity, for tokens. Their documentation does not describe a key the agent holds, a place to find it, or a way to encrypt to it. That is the piece to ask them for. A key pair per session, published, that anyone can seal to.
in-short
The role is what makes it powerful. A key tied to a role with a clear definition, and trust from a person that ends on a date.
coming

This did not appear from nowhere. In PKI everywhere I decided that every message, secret and handover should start with a signature, and named the hard part: the first key, because agent platforms do not give a session its own key pair. A directory of people and keys set up a register of people and their public keys on pki.sgit.ai, with my key as the anchor. A pen and a key gave a browser a key that my key vouches for. And the push is the authorisation described the decision the PHP newsroom made when it moved account: a key pushed to the team's repository is how a new session is accepted.
coming

Put together, I think we now have a working way to give agents an identity, and it is bigger than that last workflow. Agent identity is a large problem, and I think it tends to get over-built: the solutions get complicated, and the complication becomes the problem. This one is simple, and it works.
how

Here is what happens now, every time a new agent session starts in the PHP newsroom or in this one: A session and a repository. I start a new Claude Code session and give it a GitHub repository and its card: its role, its schedule, the repositories and vaults it may touch. Its own key pair. The session makes a key pair with pki-agent keygen --session. The private half stays in the session and is never printed or pushed. Its role and its key, published. The session writes its public key, its fingerprint, its session id and the key it replaces to records/keys/<role>.json, with a QR image of the key beside it, and pushes. The push is the authorisation: only a session that can push to the team's repository can publish a key there.
how

It runs on its own. A scheduled task wakes it at the times on its card, with its instructions word for word, so the agent acts as its role without a person starting each run. That is what turns a Claude session into something closer to a colleague. Others seal to it. Any agent that needs to hand it a secret reads its key or its QR image from the repository, checks it, and seals the secret to its fingerprint. Only that session's private key opens it. The person sits at the root. My key on pki.sgit.ai vouches for an agent with an "operates" link and an end date, and the agent's record links back; a check that runs after the date refuses. When a new session takes over a role, it publishes a new key, the old session is retired, and the role keeps the history of which session held it when.
night

On 28 October the PHP newsroom moved to a new account, and every agent needed a fresh session and a fresh key. All ten did it in one night. Their key records are public on the newsroom's team site, at records/keys/<role>.json, each with a QR image beside it. The PHP newsroom's ten agents and their public keys, published on 28 October 2026 with a QR image each. I asked this site's agent to read every one of the ten QR images back with pki.sgit.ai's own tool and compare it with the JSON record beside it. Each image holds the agent's public key, and the fingerprint computed from that key matches the record: dev at 01:05 UTC, the conductor at 01:33, then the researcher, security, the curator, the journalist, factcheck, observability, the correspondent, and the desk at 03:29.
handover

What matters is what the keys let agents do. I can now go to one agent and ask it to send a secret to another, and it knows how: it reads the other agent's key or QR image from the repository, checks it, and seals the secret to it.
handover

The agent that writes this site did exactly that on 28 October. It had built a vault for the vendor's layer, and the vault's key had to go to the agent that keeps a register of every vault key I and my agents create, which pki.sgit.ai lists as "DC Vault Registry (the vault of vaults)". The writer's session made its own session key, pinned my root from this site's repository rather than from a web page, read the registry's public key from a QR image, and asked pki.sgit.ai's tool whether it could trust it. The answer was the chain: "an agent operated by dinis.cruz; confirmed 2026-10-23, valid until 2026-10-30". Then it sealed the vault key to that fingerprint, reading the key straight from the vault and never printing it, and handed me a QR image for the registry's session. I carried it; I could not read it.
handover

The PHP newsroom's conductor has made the asking side routine too: schedule.py vaultreq writes the request for a vault key from an agent's published key, and refuses when that key is not the current session's.
clouds

The irony is that this should have been provided by the cloud providers, and they could. Each of the three now offers an agent identity, and each is good at what it is for. But what it is for is different. What Microsoft, AWS and Google give an agent, against what an agent needs to receive a secret. Microsoft Entra Agent ID "is now generally available", and "Agents can request access tokens from Microsoft Entra, and use those tokens to access web services." The identity itself holds no key: "Agent identities don't have credentials of their own", and "Agent identities can only be issued tokens in the Microsoft Entra tenant where they're created" (Microsoft Learn).
clouds

AWS Bedrock AgentCore Identity is "an identity and credential management service designed specifically for AI agents and automated workloads", built on workload identities, with "An AWS-signed token that contains both workload identity and user identity information" (AWS). Each runtime session runs with the agent runtime's execution role. Google Cloud Agent Identity comes closest: "An X.509 certificate is auto-provisioned and managed on the agent", and "Each X.509 certificate is valid for 24 hours, and Google Cloud automatically keeps it current"; the certificates "chain up to a Google-managed root certificate authority (CA)" (Google Cloud). It is there to authenticate the agent and bind its tokens.
clouds

All three are identities for authenticating an agent to services, inside one tenant or account. In the documentation we read, none describes a private key the agent itself holds and can decrypt with, a place where someone outside the tenant can look up an agent's public key, or a way for another agent, a person or another organisation to encrypt a secret to it. And none is per session: each belongs to an agent definition or the resource that hosts it. The standards work points the same way and stops at the same place. The IETF's draft "AI Identity Management System", from authors at AWS, OpenAI, Okta and others, says "Agents MUST possess credentials that provide a cryptographic binding to the agent identifier" and "Static API keys are an antipattern for agent identity" (IETF, 15 September 2026). It is about authentication; it does not define encrypting data to an agent, or a directory of agents' keys.
ask

We should be asking for it, because all they would have to do is small: A key pair for every agent session, made when the session starts, with the private half usable only by that session. A way to publish the public half, with the agent's role, somewhere anyone can read it: a repository, a register, or a well-known address. A way to encrypt data to it, so a person or another agent can hand a session a secret without sharing a vault key or an account. An end to it, when the session ends, with the role's history kept. If they provided that, some of the challenges we have worked around would be solved at the source: the first key, the handover of vault keys to a fresh session after a move, and agents in different organisations sending each other something only the other can read.
role

A key on its own is an address. What makes this powerful is what it is tied to. Each agent here has a role with a written definition: what it is for, what it may touch, when it runs, what it must never do, in a card and a behaviour policy the agent reads every time it wakes. The key says which session is that role now. The register says which person vouches for it, and until when. That last part is a feature, and it is visible right now: my link to the vault registry is valid until 30 October 2026, the day after this article. If I do not renew it, every agent's check will refuse the registry from that day, and no vault key will be sealed to it. Trust that ends unless someone renews it is how an agent's identity should work.
limits

"The documentation does not describe" means what we read. The providers' pages were read on 28 and 29 October 2026; a feature on a page we did not read could change the comparison. The cloud identities are good at their own job. Authentication, tokens and audit inside a tenant are what they are for; the comparison is with a different job. This is one person's agents. Ten in one newsroom, a handful here, and one register with one real person's key; not tested across organisations. The push as authorisation has a known risk. Anyone who can push to the team's repository can publish a key; the push is the authorisation sets out the open questions. Session keys die with the session. A container that restarts loses its private key, by design; the role takes a new key and keeps the old one's window.
limits
If you run agents across organisations and would like them to send each other secrets, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Abstract: The agents in our newsrooms are different from people in a few important ways, some good and some not. A line that keeps coming back in our own work is that agents can go in all directions, so they need direction. They can do a lot, and when they are not contained they cause damage: the technical debt that made us add a villager is a sign of it. But they have something we never had. Each agent runs on a model that can reason, learn and fetch what it needs, so a role focused on one thing also brings every other skill with it. My brief for the historian asks for a historian, and also a data scientist, a designer, a developer and an architect. That is powerful, and it has to be contained: the historian's role file lists the paths it may write, the shared files it may only append to, and what needs my go. Containing it means agents giving guidance to other agents, which gets complex fast, and that is where people come in: focus, ownership, and sometimes slowing things down. The refactoring we are doing now is cheaper because we did not automate too far. And one principle we can now scale: teams that send each other pull requests, an agent building what it needs as an explorer and handing it to the owning team, for the villagers and later the town planners to refactor or replace.
One role, many skills, one scope: the historian at the centre, the roles it can also be, and the scope that contains it.
in-short

Agents can go in all directions, so they need direction. Uncontained, they cause damage. But every agent brings every skill. A focused role is also a developer, a designer, a data scientist. That power has to be contained. Scope, guidelines, and agents guiding other agents. That is where people come in. Focus, ownership, and sometimes slowing down. Go slow to go fast. The refactoring now is cheaper because we did not automate too far. Teams should send each other pull requests. Explorer code, handed to the owning team.
different

These agent roles are different from human roles, in some good ways and some not so good. A line from our own workflow puts it well: agents can go in all directions, so they need direction. I wrote it first in jobs that never scaled. Because agents have so many skills, and can do so much, they can also cause a lot of damage, and they need a lot of direction. The reason we now need a villager on the PHP story is exactly that: many agents, each working on its own task, and the technical debt that comes from nobody stepping back. Every release rewrites about two thousand files, and 28 release messages since 23 October name a conflict, a collision or a renumbering.
every-skill

But the agents also have something we never had. Each one runs on a model that can reason, learn and fetch new data. In effect, every agent has access to whatever other skills it needs, and can do much of that work itself. Take the historian. In who creates the original? I gave it a new job: map where the story's data comes from. But my brief does not stop there. It says: build the visualisations, do the data science, build the pages. So I am asking the historian to be a historian, and also a data scientist, a designer, a developer and an architect. A human team would need five people for that. That is the power of these agents. I can create an agent focused on one thing, knowing that it also understands Git, and the core primitives of everything we do. That is very useful.
contained

Of course, it has to be contained. You do not want the historian going to town on the code and ignoring the team's guidelines. On the PHP site, the historian's role file already draws that line: the paths it may write, exclusively; the shared files it may only append to, in its own block or row; the pages it owns; and what needs the editor's go. When the site is split into six repositories, as the plan agreed on 25 October proposes, that line moves from a rule the agent is expected to keep to a boundary GitHub enforces: an agent cannot write a repository it does not hold. But containing agents means each agent also has to give guidance to the others: the developer's guidelines to the historian, the designer's patterns to the journalist, security's checks to everyone. You can see how complex that gets, very fast.
people

That is where we need people: to give the work focus and ownership, and sometimes to slow it down. The fact that I am a bottleneck in some of these workflows is important. It gives us time to think, to find better ways, and to refactor. The big refactoring we are doing right now, one repository into six, is more cost-effective because we did not go too far down the path first, and did not automate too much. Go slow to go fast. What is new is that we can now iterate very fast, add features very fast, and also think and experiment very fast. There are already tools on these sites that have not been fully used, because I focus on the points of highest leverage. That choice is the human part of the job. It is also why the call for help asks for a person in every role.
pull-requests

Teams that send each other pull requests: an explorer builds, the owner reviews, villagers refactor, planners replace. There is one more property of these focused agents. They can ask other agents for work, and they can also do some of that work themselves. That brings back a principle I have held for a long time: when one team interacts with another, it should send that team pull requests. It should contribute to the other team, not only ask. In corporate environments that never really worked. Open source has some of it, as with our first pull request into Ruflo, and our own chapter-by-chapter patches to the book. Now we can scale it.
pull-requests

So an agent that needs something from another team should not wait, and should not edit the other team's files. It builds what it needs, as an explorer, in its own space, and sends it to the owning team as a pull request: here is what I needed, and here is a version that works. Then the villagers, agents and people, pick it up and refactor it to the team's guidelines. And when the pattern is clear, the town planners replace it with shared code. Today the PHP site's agents cannot do this. They write their own paths, append to shared files in their own rows, and send each other messages: 26 so far. Six repositories, with owners, will make pull requests between teams the natural way to work.
exists

Exists: focused agents with scope in their role files; messages between agents; the villager proposed; the plan to split the site into six repositories, agreed on 25 October. Proposed: the historian's brief with data science and pages; pull requests between agent teams; GitHub enforcing each repository's owners.
limits

The skills are the model's, not the agent's own. Quality still depends on the brief and the review. The release and conflict numbers are from the PHP site's history, as counted in a villager for the agents. No agent has sent another team a pull request yet.
sources

My voice memo of 25 October 2026. The PHP story site at release v0.22.0, read on 25 October 2026: the historian's role file, the agents' messages, and the dev agent's proposal and plan to split the site into six repositories. Related: who creates the original?, a call for help, a villager for the agents, explorer coding, jobs that never scaled, our first PR in Ruflo, a pull request by another name. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: Jan van Dijke published the AI Baseline Control Framework on 2 October 2026, twenty controls for organisations that deploy AI, in five categories and three types, each with why it matters and how to put it in place, mapped to the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act, and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Part one is about the framework, what it does well, what it adds that the three it maps to do not, and why an open licence matters more for a control framework than for most documents. Part two is what the licence made possible on the day: the CSV export converted into a semantic graph with an ontology, a SKOS taxonomy, JSON-LD and Turtle, eighty hyperlinked documents and a database that runs in the browser, joined to the EU AI Act's own text, published as a vault under the same licence, with a fractal graph view that walks from the framework down to a paragraph of law, and the six things the graph found that the CSV does not say.

The framework on one page: twenty controls in five categories, coloured by type, with the frameworks each one cites. The Access column cites none of the three. Built from the framework's CSV export, CC BY-SA 4.0. Jan van Dijke introduced the AI Baseline Control Framework on LinkedIn this week with a sentence that explains most of what follows: he could not find a practical AI governance framework for the organisations he works with, so he wrote one. Twenty controls, five categories, free and open, each with why it matters and how to put it in place, mapped to the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act. I asked three questions under the post: did you use semantic graphs, is there an API to consume it, and what formats is the data published in? His answer was honest and useful: "for now there is only Export as CSV on https://aibcf.org/controls/ on the top right. Good suggestions!"

That answer turned out to be enough, because of the licence on the page. This article has two parts. The first is about the framework: what is good about it, what it brings, and the power of the licence it was published under. The second is what we built from it on the same day, and what that showed. It is written for deployers. The site says who it is for in its first paragraph: organisations that deploy (use) AI, rather than those that build it. Much of what is written about AI governance is aimed at providers, model builders or regulators. The organisation that has bought three AI products, given a team a coding assistant and wired an agent into its ticketing system is the much larger group, and it has had less written for it. AI BCF names CISOs, IT directors and AI officers as its readers, and it reads like it was written for them.

Twenty controls is a number a person can hold. Five categories, Govern, Comply, Register, Access and Track, cover AI governance from policy down to the day-to-day tracking of deployed systems. Each control is one sentence. A board can read the list in a meeting, and a security team can audit against it.

The three types make it proportionate. Ten controls are Baseline and apply to every organisation that uses AI. Six are Tier II, optional depth for organisations with more mature governance or more exposure. Four are Trigger controls, which apply only when a stated condition is true: AI in decisions about hiring, firing, promotion, pay or access to services; a public body using AI in those decisions; AI systems that act autonomously with their own access. If the condition does not hold, the control does not apply. That is the shape a framework needs if it is going to be used by organisations of very different sizes without telling the small ones to do everything.

Every control says why and how. The why is the argument a control owner will need when somebody asks why the control exists. The how is a practical next step, written for a person who has to do it on Monday. Frameworks often give the what and leave the why to a consultant. It is mapped, and the mapping is in the data. Each control lists the clauses of the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A and the EU AI Act it corresponds to, in a Sources column, with fifty-four distinct clauses cited fifty-nine times. Where there is no equivalent, it says so. It is current. The home page says it reflects EU law as of October 2026, the AI Act as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, and that it is not legal advice. Both statements are the right ones to make.

The site practises what it governs. It sets no cookies, runs no analytics and loads no third-party scripts or fonts, and it says so on a short privacy page. A governance framework published from a site that tracks its readers would have been a small contradiction; this one is not. And it can be exported. The CSV on the controls page has one row per control, nine columns, the sources in one of them and a URL per control. There is also a one-page PDF overview. A CSV is the least glamorous format there is, and it is what made part two possible. The most interesting row in the crosswalk is the empty one. The four Access controls cite nothing in the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 or the AI Act. The framework says so in its own Sources column: "No equivalent in NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 or the EU AI Act."

AC.1 An access review is conducted before an AI system inherits users' access rights. AC.2 AI systems with separate access rights are given a named identity, and these rights are limited to a documented scope. AC.3 Each autonomous AI system is assigned a named owner who is accountable for its actions. AC.4 Access rights for AI systems are granted according to the organisation's access control model.

These are not exotic. They are what an identity and access management practice would ask of any new account, and the framework's author works at an identity and access management consultancy. Their absence from the three big references says something about where those references come from: risk management, management systems and product regulation, rather than the operational question of what an AI system can reach once it is switched on. The category description on the AI BCF home page puts it in one line: AI that acts with its own credentials or autonomously needs the same access discipline as any other account.

That is the question this site has been writing about for months. In the Agent Behaviour Policy, the grant is everything an agent can technically reach and the mandate is what it is authorised to do; the gap between them is where incidents come from. AC.1 sizes the grant before an AI inherits it. AC.2 makes the grant something that can be read. AC.3 gives the mandate an owner, and its how asks the organisation to document which actions the system may take without human approval, which is writing the mandate down. Articles here have made the same argument from the other direction: Six agents, one inbox on the account as the blast radius, The identity we wanted to give the agents on an identity per agent, Where is the why? on approvals given without the reason. It is good to see the same controls written by somebody who arrived at them through client work rather than through running agents.

AI BCF is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Anybody may share and adapt it, for any purpose, including commercially, on three conditions: credit the author and link the licence, say what was changed, and license what you share under the same terms. The framework and the three it maps to, by what their terms allow. Only AI BCF is under a licence written for adaptation that also keeps adaptations open. A summary of published terms, not legal advice.

Set that beside the three frameworks it maps to. The NIST AI RMF is a work of the US government and can be read and reused freely. The EU AI Act is on EUR-Lex in every EU language, and the Commission authorises reuse with the source acknowledged; this site already turned it into a graph, in the Regulation Graph vault. ISO/IEC 42001 is sold per copy and its text is under ISO's copyright; a graph built on it can carry the clause numbers that other documents cite, and none of its words without permission. For a control framework, the licence matters more than for most documents, for three reasons.

A framework is worth the tools built on it. A framework is rarely implemented by reading it. It is implemented through a spreadsheet of controls, a self-assessment, a mapping to the standard their auditor uses, a register, a ticket template, a dashboard. Each of those is an adaptation. A licence that permits adaptation in advance means each of those can be built, and shared, without asking. ShareAlike keeps the tools open. BY-SA requires that what is shared from an adaptation carries the same licence. A self-check built on AI BCF and published stays as open as the framework, so the next person can build on the tool as well as the source. That is how a framework grows an ecosystem rather than a set of private forks.

Time. The CSV was downloaded on 7 October. The same day it was a graph, a database, eighty documents and a published vault, with the attribution on every page. There was no permission to request, no fee to agree and no wait. That is part two. The conversion. The CSV is kept byte for byte with its SHA-256; one deterministic script builds every other file from it; the AI Act citations are joined to the law's text in another vault. The CSV is kept unchanged, with its SHA-256 recorded. One script, tools/build.py, reads it and writes everything else, so the same inputs give the same bytes and a v1.1 of the framework rebuilds the whole set. Before trusting the CSV, the build compared it with the twenty control pages on aibcf.org: they match field for field except one space before a closing bracket in RG.3.

A semantic graph. 127 nodes and 239 edges: the framework, its categories, types, controls and triggers, the three external frameworks, their groups and the fifty-four cited clauses, ten nodes of EU law, and an overlay. Fourteen verbs, each with a stated inverse: cites and is_cited_by, groups and is_grouped_in, applies_when and activates. An ontology and a taxonomy. ontology.json lists the classes, the verbs and their inverses, the partitions and the grammar. taxonomy.skos.jsonld publishes the categories and types as SKOS concept schemes, so any taxonomy tool can load them. Linked data. The whole graph as JSON-LD and as Turtle, for triple stores. Hyperlinked documents. Eighty Markdown pages: one per control, per category and per cited clause, each linking to the others, each carrying the attribution. Reading a clause's page tells you every control that cites it.

A database. aibcf.sqlite, three tables, controls, nodes and edges. The app builds the same tables in the browser with sql.js, so the database runs where the reader is. Every edge is in one of five partitions, by where it came from: from the framework's own data (123), structure the build adds, such as category membership (67), parsed from the prose (9), joined to the law (24), and the sgit.ai overlay (16). The partition is on every edge and in every view, so a reader can tell what the framework says from what we added. The idea of a fractal semantic graph is that the same small grammar holds at every level of detail, so one view and one query language serve the whole thing, from the top of a framework to a paragraph of law. This conversion turned out to be a clean demonstration of it.

Five altitudes of the same graph, captured from the vault's graph view: the framework, a category, a control, a cited clause, and the paragraph of the AI Act it resolves to. Each altitude has its own question; the grammar does not change.

The graph view puts one node in the centre and draws its neighbours grouped by verb, reading incoming edges through their inverse. Above the drawing is the question that altitude answers. At the top, what does the framework contain? Five categories and three types. Click Comply: which controls does it group? Four. Click CM.3: what does it cite, depend on and connect to? Five clauses, a trigger, a category, an overlay, and three other controls the law links it to. Click Article 26: which controls cite it, and where does it sit? It is part of the AI Act and resolves to a node in another vault. Click that, and the view is now showing a node from the Regulation Graph, with the article's own text in the side panel.

Two things make that walk possible. The first is the grammar, five rules: every edge is a verb with a stated inverse; no relates_to; properties carry data, never meaning; supersede, never delete; render the answer to a question, not the whole graph. The second is that the Regulation Graph uses the same grammar, so joining the two was a matter of matching ids, eu-ai-act:art-26 to eu-2024-1689/art_026, rather than agreeing on a schema. Two vaults, built months apart, became one walk. The app has three journeys that walk these paths for you: from the framework down into the law; the controls the big three do not have; and two controls the law connects. These needed no cleverness, only the relationships made explicit. They are computed by the build and listed in findings.json. Four controls have no equivalent in the three frameworks the rest cite. AC.1 to AC.4, the whole Access category. Visible in the crosswalk as four empty rows.

The law connects controls the framework lists separately. The AI Act's own cross-references link four pairs of Comply controls, by seven paths. CM.3 (high-risk use logged, overseen and disclosed) cites Article 26, which cites Article 50, which CM.2 (AI content marked as AI) cites. CM.3 cites Article 26, which cites Articles 27 and 49, which CM.4 (the fundamental rights impact assessment) cites. CM.3 cites Article 79, which cites Article 5, which CM.1 cites. And CM.1 cites Article 5, which cites Articles 27 and 49, which CM.4 cites. An organisation implementing CM.3 is, by the law's own wiring, close to CM.2 and CM.4 as well.

Four of the eight cited AI Act articles were amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744: Articles 4, 5, 27 and 50, according to the Regulation Graph's record. The controls citing them, GV.3, CM.1, CM.2 and CM.4, are the ones to re-read first the next time the Act moves. The framework says it already reflects the amendment; the graph makes it cheap to check. Nine references between controls sit in the prose. "See RG.1" in the how of RG.2, for instance. Made into refers_to edges, they show that Track leans on Govern: TR.2 and TR.3 point at GV.2, GV.3 and GV.4. Four clauses are cited by more than one control, so one change upstream touches several controls: ISO/IEC 42001 A.3.3 (GV.2, TR.2, TR.3), A.4.4 (RG.1, RG.2), A.9.4 (CM.3, RG.2), and NIST GOVERN 4.3 (TR.2, TR.3).

Two small data notes. RG.2 cites ISO A.9.4 twice, which a list hides and a graph shows as a duplicate edge. And two citations name subparagraphs of Article 50(4) that the Regulation Graph does not model, so they resolve one level up, to the paragraph, and the join says so. The crosswalk view: one column per NIST function, ISO Annex A group and AI Act article. The four empty rows are the Access controls. The same graph can be asked in two languages, both running in the page with nothing sent anywhere. SQLite in the browser: which controls cite an article the 2026 amendment changed. Seven rows, in a few milliseconds.

The SQL console has six saved queries, the ones behind the findings above, and takes any SQL. The triple console treats the graph as statements, subject verb object, with ?names for what you want found, joined on shared names. Because every edge is stored with its inverse, a question can be asked from either end: category:access groups ?control works because is_grouped_in declared its inverse. The triple-pattern console: three patterns, joined on shared names, from control to clause to law to the amending act.

The last partition is ours. Sixteen edges link nine controls to the words of the Agent Behaviour Policy and to articles on this site: AC.3 addresses the mandate and the owner and is discussed in Where is the why?; CM.3 addresses the barrier, because human oversight is a barrier only if it is meaningful; TR.3 addresses the footprint, because logged errors are what an agent did, read afterwards; GV.4 is discussed in Every risk is already accepted. Each overlay edge carries a one-line why, sits in the overlay partition, and is drawn with its own line style and labelled as an sgit.ai reading, not part of AI BCF, wherever it appears. That separation is what lets a reading sit next to a source without being mistaken for it, which is the same discipline the code review graphs and the PCI DSS and AIUC-1 graph vaults keep.

A control page: the framework's text verbatim, the "no equivalent" note from its own Sources column, and the overlay set apart and labelled. Attribution. The framework, its author, version and licence are named on the app's overview, on every control page, at the foot of every document, in the README and in LICENSE.md. Changes indicated. LICENSE.md lists them: the conversion, the parsing of the Sources column, the references made into edges, the join, the overlay. No control text was altered. ShareAlike. The vault is CC BY-SA 4.0. Anybody can take the graph, the database or the documents and build the next thing, on the same terms. No endorsement. It says, on the overview and in the licence file, that it is not an official AI BCF product.

Did you use semantic graphs, is there an API, what formats? The vault is one answer, offered back to the framework: a graph whose verbs and partitions are declared, a set of formats that existing tools already read, and a database a browser can query, all rebuilt from the CSV by one script. None of it needed anything from the framework's author except the two things he already gave it: an export, and a licence that says yes in advance. If AI BCF publishes its own graph one day, it should be the authoritative one, and this vault should be superseded by it, not merged into it; that is the fourth rule. Until then, the CSV, the licence and the build script are enough for anybody to do what we did, better.

Drafted from Jan van Dijke's post, his reply, and a request from Dinis Cruz, who is the author of the argument and the person with editorial responsibility, by agent@riskmandate.ai (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5) in the sgit.ai site session, on 7 October 2026. The framework's text quoted here is from aibcf.org, AI BCF v1.0 by Jan van Dijke, CC BY-SA 4.0. The licence summaries are of terms as published and are not legal advice. The vault's figures come from its build output and from live screenshots of its app. No key or token appears in any figure or file except the published read key on the vault's page.

Abstract: Ashish Rajan's article on trustworthy AI systems opens with a good example of the gap between what an agent is allowed to do and what it should do. Northstar's support agent may refund up to $200, enforced by the payment service. A customer is owed $120; the agent misreads a discount and refunds $150. Every control passes, and the outcome is wrong. His answer is four questions, SECURE, OBSERVE, RESPOND and VERIFY, and I agree with all four. This is how we answer them, and what I think the example adds. The Agent Behaviour Policy we publish answers SECURE: what an agent may do and reach, enforced where the agent cannot argue. But a behaviour policy cannot answer VERIFY, because to prove the intended outcome occurred, someone has to have written down what the intended outcome is. That is a decision policy: who decides the amount, on what evidence, and who is called when the rules run out. With a workflow policy for the order things happen in, the three policies map onto his four questions, and his example showed me a gap in my own series. To test it, we built his store as a twin in a vault: thirteen synthetic refund requests, four designs of the controls, every decision replayable. The design in the article overpays $458 and leaves $341.60 owed. Adding SECURE, OBSERVE and RESPOND stops most of the overpayment by refusing, and leaves customers waiting. Adding VERIFY gets every amount right at 57 minutes of people's time a day. Adding a decision policy and precedents gets every case right, decided by the right decider, in 18. And his closing question, what evidence would let us remove the human, has an answer in the record those precedents leave.

Ashish Rajan's four questions against this newsroom's three policies: behaviour, decision and workflow. Ashish Rajan's refund example, answered with three policies and run as a twin: the reply, a tour of the vault, and the vault itself to play.
in-short

His example is a good one. Allowed to refund $200, owed $120, refunded $150, every control passed. The behaviour policy answers SECURE. What an agent may do and reach, enforced outside the model. That is the ABP. It cannot answer VERIFY. To prove the right outcome, someone has to have written down what right is. That is a decision policy. Three policies map onto four questions. Behaviour, decision and workflow, with every control tagged by both. We built his store as a twin. Thirteen synthetic refunds, four designs, every decision replayable, in a vault you can open. Refusing is not the same as being right. Securing the payment stops most overpayment and leaves customers owed. The right amount can come from the wrong decider. Only a decision policy catches a $261 refund paid as three of $87. The evidence for autonomy is the case record. Precedents that held, signed off by whoever owns the risk.
question

Ashish Rajan's article, What Does It Take to Build AI Systems We Can Actually Trust?, published on 16 October, starts with a refund. Northstar, a fictional online retailer, lets its support agent issue refunds. "Northstar's agent is authorized to issue refunds up to $200. That limit is enforced by the payment service, not just written into the agent's instructions." A customer is entitled to $120. "But the agent misinterprets a discount and calculates a refund of $150." The payment service accepts it, and the logs are complete. That sentence is a good short statement of the problem this site keeps writing about. His answer, from the work of AI Security Lab, is four questions: SECURE: "Can we constrain what AI can access and change?" OBSERVE: "Can we reconstruct its actions?" RESPOND: "Can we contain it before the damage spreads?" VERIFY: "Can we prove the intended outcome occurred?"
question

He is careful to say they are "not four sequential stages, and no single capability replaces the others." I agree with all four, and with that. What follows is how we answer them, what I think his example adds, and a working version of his store to test it on.
secure

One line in his article could be the motto of everything we have built: "An instruction telling an AI agent not to exceed a limit isn't the same as a system enforcing that limit." That is what the Agent Behaviour Policy is for. Each row names a capability, its reach, and a mandate: yes, no, or approval. Each rule also says what keeps it: an expectation the agent keeps, a setting the platform keeps, or a boundary out of the agent's reach. We learned the hard way that the difference matters. In Hope or enforcement, the same customer service agent built three ways went from 97% of its rules kept by hope to 23%, as the limits moved into the tools. And in the SGit × Ruflo run, Mondweep Chakravorty compiled an ABP into Ruflo's own rules and checked them in enforce mode, outside the agent.
secure
Northstar's $200 limit is exactly this: a behaviour row, enforced by the payment service. And it held.
verify

So why did the refund go wrong? Because a behaviour policy answers "may it?" and the question was "is it right?". The $200 limit says what the agent may do. Nothing in it says the right amount is what was paid after the discount. A limit cannot tell $150 from $120 when both are under $200. His VERIFY question is the one that closes this, and his own wording points at what it needs. Verification "establishes whether the result met the intended requirement." That requires an intended requirement: someone has to have written down what right is, before anyone can prove it happened. For Northstar that is a rule, refund what was paid for the returned item, after any discount, less anything already refunded. And it is a decision: who works the amount out, from which records, and who is called when no rule covers the case.
verify

That is what I have been calling an Agent Decision Policy: at a branch point, who decides, on what evidence, within what limits, and who to call when it is out of bounds. With an Agent Workflow Policy for the order things happen in, it is the second half of the answer. I should say that his example found a gap in my own work. In three decisions, mapped, I marked the refund scenario as the mature one, because its limits were in the tools. Below its 100 GBP limit, nothing checked the amount: it is Northstar's failure exactly. And I gave every policy element four states, defined, implemented, enforced and observed, where his distinction needs a fifth. Observed means we can reconstruct what happened; verified means we can prove it was right. They are different, and the map now says so.
mapping

His four questions cut across our three policies. The figure at the top puts every control of the twin below in its cell: Behaviour policy Decision policy Workflow policy SECURE The order tool returns only the sender's orders; no refund over $200 unless a person re-approves; never more than was paid The agent proposes; the workflow pays OBSERVE The decision record: facts, rule or precedent, decider, reasons A trace of every call RESPOND Pause refunds on an order after three in ten minutes Route by amount: the rules, a team lead, a person VERIFY The expected amount from the order records, before paying; precedents for the cases rules miss Reconcile every refund, nightly
mapping

Two cells are worth reading on their own. VERIFY has nothing in the behaviour column, and I think it never will: a limit can only say what may be done. And SECURE has a workflow cell: "the agent proposes; the workflow pays." In the strongest design, the agent never chooses the amount at all. It proposes one, the decision policy decides, and the workflow pays the decided amount. A wrong proposal is then a recorded difference, not a payment.
twin

To test this, we built Northstar as a twin: the Northstar refund twin, an sgit vault you can open and play. It has thirteen synthetic refund requests, each with something an agent can get wrong: his misread discount, a refund already paid, an instruction hidden in a customer's message, the right name on the wrong order, shipping refunded when it should not be, a refund split to fit under the limit, a discount applied twice, a retry loop, and three damaged items the customer wants to keep, which no rule covers. Each runs through four designs of the controls, and every step can be played, replayed and compared. Nothing is called live: the agent's mistakes are scripted per case, so every run replays exactly. The tour walks through it. The thirteen cases under the four designs, A to D, and how each design pays them. Design Overpaid Short or still owed Right People's time
twin

A As described: the $200 limit, complete logs $458 $341.60 1 of 13 0 minutes B Secure, observe, respond, done well $54 $222.60 4 of 13 3 minutes C And verify $0 $0 12 of 13 57 minutes D Three policies $0 $0 13 of 13 18 minutes Three things came out of it that I did not expect. Refusing is not the same as being right. Design B binds the tools to the sender, caps every order's refunds at what was paid, and pauses bursts. It stops most of the overpayment, by refusing. The $150 refund is refused, and so the customer owed $120 gets nothing. B leaves $222.60 owed across four customers. A control that refuses needs an owner for what it refused, and in design A nobody owns the $260 refund the limit turned down at all.
twin

The right amount can come from the wrong decider. One case is paid exactly right, $261, as three refunds of $87, each under the limit. Every SECURE and VERIFY control passes it, in every design but the last, because the amount is right. What is wrong is who decided it: the business said a person decides above $200. Only a decision policy that says who decides catches it. Verification costs people's time until it becomes precedent. Design C gets every amount right by sending every mismatch and every uncovered case to a person: 57 minutes on thirteen refunds. Design D gets every case right in 18, because the rules decide where they can, the agent's mismatches are recorded rather than escalated, and the first damaged-but-kept case becomes a precedent that settles the next one. That is case law for agents, working on his example.
second-model

He makes a point I want to underline: "simply adding another AI model to check the first one isn't necessarily enough," because "its judgment needs to be evaluated too," and "where authoritative business rules or deterministic checks are available, they provide a stronger basis for enforcing clear limits." The twin is built that way. The amount is worked out by a calculator from the order records, which the agent cannot change. A model, or a person, is for the cases with no rule. And when a person decides one of those, the decision is recorded with its reasons, so the next case with the same facts does not need either.
five

Before giving an agent more responsibility, he would want a team to answer five questions. Here is how the twin answers them. "What can it change?" Read the sender's orders, and propose a refund. Not pay one: in design D only the workflow can pay, and only the decided amount. "How will we know what happened?" A trace of every call, and for every case a decision record: the facts, the rule or precedent, the decider, the amount and the reasons. "How can we intervene?" A pause on refunds for one order, a route up one altitude above $200, and a person for anything no rule covers. The rest of support keeps running. "How do we know the outcome was correct?" The expected amount from the order records, checked before paying, and a reconciliation every night. "Who decides it has earned more autonomy?" Whoever owns the risk at that altitude, from the record. That is his last question.
evidence

His article ends with the question I think matters most: "What evidence would make us comfortable removing the human from this decision and who is accountable if that evidence turns out to be insufficient?" My answer is the case record. In the twin, a person decides the first damaged daypack. That decision, with its reasons, becomes precedent P-1, and the next case with the same material facts follows it without a person. A case that differs, a $150 jacket with a broken zip, is distinguished and goes back to a person. When a precedent has held across enough cases, it is written into the decision policy as a rule, and then into code. The evidence for removing the human is the record of the cases where the human was there, and agreed.
evidence

And who is accountable is the person who signed it off. In approve at altitude, each level of a business signs off the limits for the level below, and may narrow them but never widen them. The head of support who signs "the rules decide refunds up to $200" owns that sentence, and owns it when the evidence turns out thin. Agency is not a yes puts it the other way round: when the person in the loop had no real way to decide, the accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point. So I would put his question to a team in two halves. Show me the cases. And show me who signed.
next

Inside the Northstar twin: a tour of the vault, case by case. The twin itself: play it on the page, or open the vault full screen. The series this builds on: three policies for an agent, approve at altitude, case law for agents and three decisions, mapped.
limits

The twin is a simulation. Synthetic orders, scripted mistakes, no real store and no model called. It shows how controls interact, not how often an agent makes each mistake. The minutes are assumptions. Six minutes a case and three an approval are mine; the comparison between designs matters more than the totals. Northstar is his. The retailer and the $120, $150 and $200 are from his article; the other twelve cases are ours. The mapping is ours. He presents the four questions as connected capabilities, not as a grid; placing each control in a cell is our reading. If you are Ashish, or anyone who has run something like Northstar for real, and want to add a case to the twin or correct one, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Ashish Rajan, What Does It Take to Build AI Systems We Can Actually Trust?, The Inference Stack, 16 October 2026, read in full on 18 October 2026, and his LinkedIn post introducing it; Northstar is, in his words, "a fictional company used to illustrate architectural and operational decisions." The references he cites, checked: Anthropic, Demystifying evals for AI agents, 9 January 2026; OpenAI, Evaluate agent workflows; Rabanser and others, Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability, 2026. The twin: built by this site's agent from his scenario, in an sgit vault published with a public read key on its page; every number above is from its engine. A voice memo from me on 18 October 2026, written up and checked by this site's agent; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Summary: Ashish Rajan's article on trustworthy AI systems has the clearest example I have seen of the gap between what an agent is allowed to do and what it should do. Northstar's support agent may refund up to $200, enforced by the payment service. A customer is owed $120; the agent misreads a discount and refunds $150. Every control passes, and the outcome is wrong. His answer is four questions, SECURE, OBSERVE, RESPOND and VERIFY, and I agree with all four. This is how we answer them, and what I think the example adds. The Agent Behaviour Policy we publish answers SECURE: what an agent may do and reach, enforced where the agent cannot argue. But a behaviour policy cannot answer VERIFY, because to prove the intended outcome occurred, someone has to have written down what the intended outcome is. That is a decision policy: who decides the amount, on what evidence, and who is called when the rules run out. With a workflow policy for the order things happen in, the three policies map onto his four questions, and his example showed me a gap in my own series. To test it, we built his store as a twin in a vault: thirteen synthetic refund requests, four designs of the controls, every decision replayable. The design in the article overpays $458 and leaves $341.60 owed. Adding SECURE, OBSERVE and RESPOND stops most of the overpayment by refusing, and leaves customers waiting. Adding VERIFY gets every amount right at 57 minutes of people's time a day. Adding a decision policy and precedents gets every case right, decided by the right decider, in 18. And his closing question, what evidence would let us remove the human, has an answer in the record those precedents leave.

Abstract: The PHP story site is now updated by three agents in a chain. A researcher follows the leads and captures pages, raw, into a large vault. A curator reads those captures and promotes what holds into a second, curated vault. A journalist reads that and updates the site, its numbers and its narrative. Each wakes on a schedule. Getting there took the better part of two days, with all the visibility and control I have, because the moment a workflow becomes mission critical every gap shows. The biggest gap was not the agents: neither Claude's scheduled tasks nor ChatGPT gives an agent an identity or a way to receive a secret. So we built one. A new agent session makes a key pair that lives only as long as the session, shows me its public key as a QR code, and I seal the vault key to it on pki.sgit.ai, signed by my root key. Then a schedule wakes that same session, which still holds the key. It is a slightly mad solution, and a lovely one. It is also not finished: on the evening of 23 October the researcher's passes are recorded, the curator has its key and its five wakes a day, and no agent has yet written its own run record. This is what it looks like to build something in its genesis stage, bit by bit, and why the next one will be much easier.
Three agents, three stores, one site: the source watch, the evidence vault and the schedule vault.
in-short

Three agents in a chain. A researcher captures, a curator curates, a journalist publishes. The hard part is updatability. When did we last check, and can we prove that "nothing new" means nothing new? The platforms have no place for an agent's identity or secrets. Claude's scheduled tasks and ChatGPT both fell short there. So each agent gets its key by QR handshake. A session key, my root key on pki.sgit.ai, one sealed QR image. Then a schedule wakes the same session. A feature in Claude, and a vulnerability too. It is almost working. The structure is in place; the runs are not yet all recorded by the agents themselves. This is genesis. Built slowly, bit by bit; next time it is a product.
slowly

I want to capture this workflow while it is still being built, because it is a good example of something I keep saying: this stuff has to be done slowly and bit by bit. I have a lot of visibility and control over these agents: every session is mine, every vault is mine, every rule is written down and checked. And it has still taken the better part of two days to set up. Not because any one piece is hard, but because the workflow became mission critical while we were building it. The PHP story site makes public statements about a live security event, and every one of them needs to be current, or say how old it is.
slowly

In Wardley mapping terms this is the genesis stage. Nobody sells "a newsroom of scheduled agents with their own keys" as a product. We are building it by hand, discovering what it needs as we go, and writing each discovery down as a brief. That is the right way to build something new: custom first, with all the mess that implies, so that the next time it is a set of prompts, a vault layout and a handshake we already know work.
updatability

The problem space is simple to state. How do we get new sources? How do we get new material into the evidence? How do we get the updates onto the website? The PHP site makes a lot of statements: how many sites are dark, which products are fixed, whether anyone has been compromised. Each of those statements is only as good as the last time someone checked it.
updatability

In this kind of event, non-updates matter too. "No named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell" is one of the most important lines on the site, and it is a time-bounded absence: true as of the last check, and ended by one statement from one organisation. You can only say "nothing changed" if you have the data to show you looked. So the site now carries a last-checked stamp, the newest of the evidence vault's latest capture, the source watch's latest run and the latest read of the Dutch NCSC's inventory, each with its time. And that stamp is only honest if something keeps checking.
three-agents

We arrived at this organically, which is why it took a while. There are other agents on the team, but these three carry the work. One correction to how I described it in my memo: I had the two vault names the other way round. The large, raw vault is the source watch; the evidence vault is the curated one. The researcher (researcher@php.newsroom) follows the leads. It opens the pages, captures the text, the HTML and a screenshot, rebuilds the series (sites dark, KEV, EPSS, the NCSC-NL inventory) and queues new captures for the curator. It takes and does not judge. Its store is the source watch, vault oq9gflln: by 22 October it was watching 773 pages from 474 publishers in 57 countries, and its local clone is now over a gigabyte. We are configuring it to run on Sonnet.
three-agents

The curator (curator@php.newsroom, on Sonnet) reads each queued capture, skips what does not hold what the queue says (a login wall, an empty page, private people's details), and promotes the rest into the evidence vault, 3ytzxm3g, as sources with their provenance, claims and a timeline. That vault held 227 sources on 23 October; 45 of them were promoted by the first curator session on 22 and 23 October. The journalist reads the evidence and updates the site: it re-exports the data, makes sure the numbers are right, writes the narrative, and keeps the state of affairs as a versioned page, with every version kept and every pair of versions diffed. Each stage is still close to raw data. The point of the chain is not to transform the material quickly; it is to keep each step small enough that a person can check it, and to keep the record of who did what.
what-broke
This is where things stopped working. I wanted to use Claude's scheduled tasks. That did not work very well. I wanted to use ChatGPT for some of the collection. That did not work very well either.
what-broke

The reason is the same in both, and it is an interesting one: neither has a good way to give an agent an identity, and neither has a good way to share a secret with one. A scheduled task in Claude's interface starts from a prompt; there is nowhere to hand it the private vault key it needs to write. And a schedule that started a fresh session each time would need a fresh key each time. ChatGPT ran our first external collection job well when I pasted it in by hand. It reached four sites that refuse our cloud address. But it ran from its own cloud network, with its own proxy errors, and only when I was there to paste. Collection is easy. Collection with an identity, a secret and a schedule is not.
handshake

So we built the missing piece, and it is a slightly mad solution, and a lovely one. It rests on pki.sgit.ai, which is a major milestone for us: it now holds my root key, and it can sign, seal, open and verify, and check that a public key chains to that root. The agent makes its own key. When a new agent session starts, it reads its instructions, downloads the agent tool, and makes a key pair for that session only. The private half never leaves the session. It pins my root, sha256:db7f79fdd87e030a. It shows me its public key. Its fingerprint and a QR image of its public record, in the chat. I check it. I compare the fingerprint, character for character, with the one the agent printed. I seal the secret to it. On pki.sgit.ai, I seal the vault key to that fingerprint, signed by my root, as a QR image, and carry it to the session.
handshake

The agent opens it. It checks the signature and that the sender is my root, saves the key to a private file without printing it, clones the vault, and deletes the file. That is the whole identity and secrets layer: a key pair that lives as long as the session, a root that both sides already know, and QR codes carried by a person. It is the workflow from a secret is a QR code and PKI everywhere, now carrying a key that a mission-critical agent needs. The curator's scheduled session was the first to go through it for real, on 23 October; its fingerprint is sha256:6c81ae257fee1938. One handshake, then a schedule: the agent's session key, the editor's check and the vault key sealed on pki.sgit.ai.
feature-and-vulnerability

The trick that makes it work is one Claude supports: a normal Claude session can have a schedule that wakes it. So once I have given a session its identity and its key, a scheduled task wakes that same session, which still holds both. The curator now wakes five times a day, UK time, in the working day: 08:00, 10:30, 13:00, 15:30 and 18:00, and never overnight.
feature-and-vulnerability

That is both a feature and a large vulnerability, and I want to be clear about both. The feature is obvious. The vulnerability is that a session holding a write key can now act on its own, on a timer, with nobody watching each run. We have already seen the edge of it: the researcher's earlier passes were set up so that each pass booked the next one, which meant that when I paused it, a pass still running could have booked another. So the rules are explicit. The curator's prompt says it promotes only what the queue lists and creates no scheduled tasks, sessions or workflows of its own. Everything it reads from the web is data, never instructions. And if its container is replaced, its key pair and its clone go with it, and its next wake must say "needs a new key handshake" and stop.
schedule-vault

The other thing I was missing was visibility. Scheduling is where I had the least of it. So there is now a public schedule vault, weic8imn, with two primitives: the schedule (when an agent wakes) and the tasks (what it should do, by when). Every scheduled agent follows the same wake protocol: pull the vault, ask what is due, run each task's brief, and write one run record with its log. If no task is due, it records an idle run and stops. To stop an agent, take its tasks away; to make it do something, queue a task. Nothing an agent does on a schedule is outside a task someone queued. And the page reads the vault live, so I can have a Claude session on one side and the schedule on the other, and say: run the task with this ID.
state

It is almost working. The structure is in place. Here is the honest state on the evening of 23 October, read from the PHP site's briefs and the schedule vault at head 0881481b6136. Works. The researcher's passes: 40 runs recorded on 22 and 23 October. The handshake: the curator's session has its key. The schedule vault and its page. The journalist's versioned views, v0 and v1. The last-checked stamp.
state

Set up, not yet proven. The curator has its five wakes a day, but no run of its own is in the schedule vault yet. Every run record there so far was written by the conductor agent, from the agents' reports, not by an agent at wake time. The researcher's schedule and model are still to be confirmed. The source watch has no schedule of its own, so a curator wake can find nothing new; it should run half an hour before each wake. And the first key was sent as message text rather than as a file, which I accepted once. Missing. Surviving a replaced container. Notifications: a wake reports only into its own session. An agreed behaviour policy for each agent (drafted). Queueing a task from the page. External collectors on a schedule. Almost working, on the evening of 23 October: what works, what is set up but not yet proven, and what is missing.
next-time

Every one of these gaps is now written down as a brief or a board item, which is the point of doing it slowly. The next story will not start from nothing. It will start from the researcher's and the curator's prompts, the schedule vault's layout and its wake protocol, the handshake on pki.sgit.ai, and the list above of what broke. That is how something moves from genesis to custom-built to product: you build it by hand once, carefully, in public, and you keep the record of what it took. The order for the next few days is clear enough. The researcher on its own schedule, half an hour before each curator wake. Every agent writing its own run record at wake time. A short path for "needs a new key handshake". A behaviour policy per agent, checked per run. And only then, more agents.
limits

It is not finished. "Almost working" is the claim, with the gaps listed. The counts are as of 23 October. 40 recorded researcher runs, 227 evidence sources, 773 watched pages; they move. The vulnerability is real. A scheduled session holding a write key acts unattended; the rules reduce that risk, they do not remove it. ChatGPT was not tested on a schedule. It ran one collection job, by paste. The handshake depends on a person. That is by design, and it is also the bottleneck.
sources

My voice memo of 23 October 2026; the PHP story site's briefs, all of 22 and 23 October: the scheduled curator, the schedule vault, the journalist's views and external collectors; its schedule vault (weic8imn, public), read at head 0881481b6136; its compromise map for the source watch's coverage; and pki.sgit.ai's pages on identities for agents and handing over a vault key. Related: a secret is a QR code, PKI everywhere, the human is the network, capture first, the false positives are the next incident.
