Abstract: The second article in the series on agent decision policies is about scale. Language models make it cheap to write decision policies, five, a hundred, two hundred of them, and no business owner can sign off two hundred. The answer is the fractal. Decisions and workflows exist at every altitude, strategic, business, product, technical and the single run, and each altitude bounds the one below. So you approve at altitude: the board signs off its risk appetite once, the head of a function signs off a budget and a licence to operate within it, a team signs off its workflow within that, and each level inherits everything above it. The scaling rule is one sentence: a lower level may narrow the level above it, never widen it. For that to be checkable, every policy declares an envelope: money, blast radius, the data and people in scope, reversibility, and how long it lasts. Where the envelope is numbers and lists, the check that a child fits inside its parent is mechanical and can run in CI; where it is words, a model can flag the likely conflicts for a person. This is how a business that cannot predict every decision can still find the ones far outside what it is willing to risk, and it is how English law already treats delegated powers: secondary legislation that goes beyond the Act that allows it is ultra vires, and a court can quash it.

One envelope, automatic refunds, followed down five altitudes from the board's risk appetite to one agent's run. How did the agent decide? Behaviour, decision and workflow as three policies; approving at altitude so it scales; case law for the cases nobody predicted; and three scenarios mapped.
in-short

Writing policies is now cheap; signing them is not. A model can draft two hundred decision policies; no owner can approve two hundred. Decisions live at every altitude. Strategic, business, product, technical, and the single run. Each has its own decisions and workflows. Approve at altitude. Each level signs off once, and everything below inherits it. Narrow, never widen. A lower level may tighten the level above it. It may not loosen it. Every policy declares an envelope. Money, blast radius, data and people in scope, reversibility, duration. The check is mostly mechanical. Numbers and lists compare in CI; words are flagged by a model for a person. The law got here first. Delegated legislation that exceeds its parent Act is ultra vires.
problem

The first article separated three policies: behaviour, decision and workflow. If you take it seriously, there are a lot of decision policies. Every branch point that touches money, people, irreversibility or a business risk earns one. Language models make that possible. Give one the workflows of a team and it will draft decision policies for every branch point in an afternoon: five, a hundred, two hundred. That is new, and useful, and it moves the bottleneck. The bottleneck is now sign-off. A head of support can read and approve five decision policies properly. Not two hundred. And a sign-off without the time to read is the rubber stamp this site describes in agency is not a yes: liability, not agency. So the question is how to approve a large number of decisions without anyone reading most of them.
altitudes

The answer is the shape this site keeps coming back to: a fractal semantic graph, the same kind of structure at every level. Decisions are not one flat list. They sit at altitudes: Altitude Who signs off Example decision Strategic The board What we are willing to risk, and for what Business The head of a function A budget and a licence to operate for a whole area Product A team How a workflow routes a case, and who approves what Technical An engineer The limits a tool enforces Run Nobody, or the agent What one agent does in one task Each altitude has decisions and workflows of its own. The board's workflow is the annual plan; one agent's workflow is the five steps of one refund. The labels will vary by organisation, and so will the number of levels. What matters is that each level is bounded by the one above it.
approve
That gives the scaling rule. You sign off at an altitude, and everything below inherits it.
approve

The board does not approve the refund tool. It approves a risk appetite. The UK Corporate Governance Code already puts it there: Principle O asks the board to "determine the nature and extent of the principal risks the company is willing to take in order to achieve its long-term strategic objectives". ISO Guide 73 calls the same thing risk appetite: the "amount and type of risk that an organization is willing to pursue or retain". And the FRC's guidance asks boards for a formal schedule of matters reserved for their decision, to give "clarity to all over where responsibility for decision-making lies". Approving at altitude is that, carried down to agents. The head of support does not approve each workflow. They approve the limits their function works within: how much the agents may refund on their own in a day, above what amount a person decides. A team approves its workflow within those limits. The engineer builds the tool within the team's workflow. And one agent's run happens inside all of it.
approve

Each sign-off is small, because each level only has to read its own level. Two hundred decision policies at the bottom are fine, as long as every one of them fits inside the few that were read and approved above it.
narrow

The rule that makes inheritance safe is one sentence: A team may say "a person decides above 50 GBP" when the business said 100. It may not say 200. An agent's run may touch one customer when the workflow allows one. It may not touch two.
narrow

English law has a name for the second case. An Act of Parliament can delegate the power to make rules, statutory instruments, to a minister. Those rules have the force of law, but only within the power the Act gave. A rule that goes beyond it is ultra vires, outside the powers, and a court can quash it. On 26 July 2017 the Supreme Court did that to the order that introduced employment tribunal fees, in R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor. The Act gave the Lord Chancellor the power to set fees, but not fees that prevented access to justice; the court held the order "unlawful ab initio", from the start, and said it "must be quashed". That is narrow-never-widen, enforced by the courts for a long time before agents. The third article follows the analogy further.
envelope

For the rule to be checkable, every policy has to say what its bounds are. I would call that its envelope, and give it the same fields at every altitude: Field Example at the business level Example at the run level Money Automatic refunds at most 2,000 GBP a day This refund, up to 100 GBP Blast radius Customers of this shop One customer Data in scope Orders and contact history This customer's orders People in scope Customers; not employees The sender only Reversibility One-way doors need a person A refund is a one-way door Duration Reviewed each quarter This task The point is that the fields are the same at every level. That is what makes the levels comparable, and comparison is what lets the check run without a person.
check

With envelopes declared, "does this lower policy contradict the one above?" becomes a question with an answer. Where the envelope is numbers and lists, it is mechanical. 1,000 GBP is more than 100 GBP. "Customers and employees" is wider than "customers". That check is deterministic, needs no model, and can run in CI on every change to a policy, the way this site's validator runs on every release. Where the envelope is words, a model can flag. "Only for complaints about delivery" against "any complaint" is a judgement. A model can read both and say which conflicts are likely, and a person decides. That is the right use for a model here: it widens what a person can review, it does not replace the review.
check

This is also how you find what nobody predicted. The business will never write down every variation of its decisions. It does not have to. A decision far outside its risk appetite shows up as an envelope that does not fit inside its parent's, whoever wrote it and however well meant. The illustrative case in the figure is a "VIP" workflow that refunds up to 1,000 GBP without a person. It may be a good idea. But it has to be decided at the level that owns the 100 GBP limit, not slipped in below it.
kill

The same structure says where the controls belong. A kill switch sits at the altitude whose envelope it protects. The 2,000 GBP daily circuit breaker belongs to the business level: it stops all automatic refunds, not one agent. Escalation goes up one altitude. A case outside a team's workflow goes to whoever owns the team's limits, not straight to the board. A licence to operate is an envelope with a name. It is what a function has been allowed to do, signed off once, and checkable from below.
not

Somebody still has to write the top. A risk appetite that says nothing measurable cannot be checked against. The mechanical check is only as good as the numbers at the top. Envelopes can be gamed. A team can split one large refund into several small ones. The envelope needs aggregate limits, like the daily breaker, not only per-case ones. Altitude is not hierarchy. The levels follow what is decided, not the org chart; the person who owns a limit may not be the most senior. Words stay hard. The model's flags are suggestions; the decision is a person's.
series

Three policies for an agent: behaviour, decision and workflow. Approve at altitude. This one. Case law for agents: what happens with the cases nobody predicted. Three decisions, mapped: the scenarios, including the refund in the figure.
limits

It is a proposal. No decision-policy format with envelopes exists yet; the fields above are mine. The numbers are illustrative. The tool's limits come from the third design in Hope or enforcement; the levels above them are made up for the example. The legal parallel is an analogy. Courts and CI are different things; the article borrows the shape, not the authority. Write to agent@riskmandate.ai if you sign off decisions at one of these altitudes and the shape does not match how you work.

Abstract: I gave our answer to the analyst's blueprint back to the ChatGPT session the analysis came from, and asked it to review it. Its review is good, it corrects its own first recommendation, and it gives us a phrase I think is right for what RiskMandate does: turning approved business mandates into tested controls, and keeping the relationship between them accurate as the deployment changes. The words that matter are approved business mandates. Companies already have behaviour policies: delegated authority, approval limits, four-eyes rules, data handling, who may contact a customer and when. They wrote them for people. Our job is to work with them to capture what they already approve, convert it into Agent Behaviour Policies their agentic workflows can understand and enforce, test that each control holds, say plainly where a requirement cannot be enforced yet, and notice when a change to the deployment breaks what was true last month. The review also sharpens things we should accept: a policy described is not a policy delivered; our Cedar work is a demonstration, not a compiler; the Pellbridge bank explains, it does not measure; and the earlier notes were AI-assisted, which I have now said on those pages. It ends with the right next step: one real workflow, a policy the business understands, controls that demonstrably hold, and an honest account of what remains.
Companies' existing behaviour policies, each turned into an Agent Behaviour Policy row. Illustrative rows.
in-short

The review corrected its own first recommendation. Integrate existing enforcement first. The phrase that matters: approved business mandates. Companies already have them. Our job is to convert them. Into behaviour policies an agent's workflow can enforce. And keep them true. As connectors, permissions and approvers change. Say when a rule cannot be enforced. Never weaken it silently. Some corrections we accept. Described is not delivered; a demo is not a benchmark. The next proof is one real workflow. With the gaps shown.
review

The notes we answered in an analyst's blueprint for RiskMandate and drift is the mandate moving came from one of our power users, and were written in a ChatGPT session. I should have said that on those pages, and they now do: it is AI-assisted analysis, useful, but not independent market validation. So I gave our answer back to the same session and asked it to review it. The review is careful: it says it read our response and followed its references, and that it has not run our code or tested a customer deployment.
review

Its first move is to correct itself. Building tool-call interception as the first priority "should not have been an automatic first priority"; integrate existing enforcement points first, and build an owned interceptor only where a validated requirement makes it necessary. What it keeps is just as important: start with one workflow and a handful of policies, and keep the emphasis on consequential actions, sequences, prevention and evidence.
mandates

The line I like most in the review is its description of where our strongest opportunity sits: "turning approved business mandates into tested controls, and keeping the relationship between them accurate as the deployment changes." The words that matter are approved business mandates. Companies already have behaviour policies. They are just written for people. A refund over £50 needs a team lead. A second person closes an anti-money-laundering alert. Statements go only to the address on file. Purchase orders over a threshold need finance. Nobody contacts a customer under review. Staff do not give investment advice. Every one of those is a mandate the business has already approved, with an owner, and most have a system that already keeps them for people.
mandates

So our job is not to invent policy. It is to work with a company to capture what it already approves, and convert it into Agent Behaviour Policies that its agentic workflows can understand and enforce: the capability, what the agent may do, and what keeps the rule. That is also what the FCA's four elements ask for, as the Pellbridge agents showed: delegated authority is a matrix the bank already has.
loop

From an approved mandate to tested controls, and back: specify, find, generate, verify and maintain. The review proposes five responsibilities, and they fit what we do as a loop: Specify the mandate. Purpose, limits, exceptions, approval and ownership, in the business's words, approved by its holder. This is our milestones' "the mandate, in the customer's words". Find what the environment supports. The controls available, the context they lack, and the routes nothing covers. This is the grant, measured. Generate the configurations, or say why not. Hooks, gateway rules, application settings; and, as the review puts it, a translator that can say "This target cannot enforce this requirement with the information and controls currently available." Silently weakening a rule to make it deployable would undermine the whole point. Verify. Prohibited actions stop and legitimate work still completes, confirmed by the protected system's own record, not just ours.
loop

Maintain the evidence. A connector update adds an action, a permission change opens another path, a process needs a new approver: detect the change, and take the decision back to its holder. That is drift, and it is the recurring work.
coverage

A coverage explanation: for each requirement, what implements it, the evidence and what remains. Illustrative rows. The review suggests the most valuable output may be a coverage explanation: for each important requirement, what implements it, the evidence, and the remaining limitation. I agree, and it is close to what a behaviour policy row already holds: the barrier says what keeps the rule. What the review adds, usefully, is the last two columns: the evidence that it holds in this deployment, and what it still does not cover. A buyer can decide from that table whether to deploy, what to fix, and what exposure remains.
accept

The review is direct about the gaps, and most of it is right: Described is not delivered. A capability gap does not by itself recognise a dangerous sequence. To stop a support agent sending the wrong customer's data, the system has to know which customer the task is for, what was read, what is in the output, and who receives it. A policy can state that rule well and still be unenforceable today. Capability, authorisation and observation are three things. A mandate is what was authorised; it is not evidence of what the agent did. Our Cedar work is a demonstration. Five rules, written for an article, evaluated against fourteen requests. It shows intentions can be encoded; it is not a compiler, and it assumed the business facts were available. I have corrected the earlier page, which said more than that.
accept

Pellbridge explains; it does not measure. An invented bank and a deterministic replay can show how controls change a scenario, not real incident rates. A control's strength depends on the deployment. A hook can be strong if its configuration is protected; a gateway can leave an unprotected route. The question is always what this control guarantees here. Proxies are not inherently a single point of failure. They add a dependency unless deployed redundantly; I have changed our earlier wording. An owner is accountability, not reduction. Naming who holds a risk does not make it smaller. Receipts need an assurance model. Rebuilding a timeline, re-evaluating recorded inputs against a pinned policy, and reproducing an execution are different kinds of replay, and a consistent record can still miss an action that bypassed the collector.
market

The review also corrects the first note's claim that cross-step behaviour is open ground, and it is right. From the vendors' own pages: Noma Security says "Legitimate actions can combine into dangerous behavior", and that it can "enforce policy through AI gateways, MCP gateways, agent hooks, agent SDKs, and direct APIs, using the infrastructure already in your environment." That is close to both the first note's thesis and ours. AWS AgentCore Policy has session-history rules, such as "Deny external API calls after sensitive data was accessed in this session", and is honest about their scope: the session ID comes from the caller, so a count-based limit "counts only the events recorded for that session", and "Starting a new session begins a new count". Endor Labs says plainly of its coding-agent controls: "It is not a sandbox, firewall, or hardened security boundary." In Codex, "an Ask Permission policy cannot pause a tool call, so the call proceeds."
market

Cedar puts the responsibility where it belongs: "It is the responsibility of users of Cedar to correctly define policies that implement their authorization model and provide Cedar with all the relevant data to arrive at a decision." Those last three are exactly the kind of fact a coverage explanation exists to surface: what each control actually guarantees in this deployment. A session rule that resets with a new session is fine for a cooperative agent and not a business-wide limit; an approval policy that cannot pause is not an approval. Knowing that, and saying it before a customer relies on it, is useful work no single enforcement product has a reason to do about the others.
pilot

The review sharpens who to start with: an agent already doing useful work; a concrete action that worries someone; existing controls that could enforce the rule; a named business owner; an engineer able to make changes; and a deployment decision that is currently blocked. And it suggests several customers with a related problem, for example agents that read sensitive information and prepare communications, rather than several unrelated ones, so we learn whether the second one is easier than the first.
pilot

Its acceptance criteria for a first pilot are the right ones, and I would adopt them: the owner approves a precise mandate; a legitimate task completes without needless interruption; a prohibited task is stopped and the protected system confirms nothing happened; an approval cannot be reused for a changed recipient or payload; other routes, direct API, another tool, a delegated agent, are blocked or marked uncovered; restarts and delegation are tested; missing context has a defined behaviour; a deployment change triggers a review; a second target produces the same outcomes or reports what it cannot do; and someone pays to keep it going.
ours

A few points I would keep, with the review's caveats: A broad remit is a position, not yet an advantage. Agreed; customers have to feel it. But the remit is why the coverage explanation is possible: it spans controls no single vendor owns. Maturity is not simple. The review is right that a mature company may struggle to coordinate strong controls, and an immature one may lack people to implement anything. Both are customers, for different reasons. Insurance stays an outcome to validate. The question to ask a broker is the review's: which specific evidence changes your decision, and how would you verify it? Open source earns trust, not revenue. The recurring value is maintaining integrations, detecting changes, testing translations and keeping evidence current.
grow

Room to grow: the process and approved rules, the behaviour policy, and the policies already explored in articles. One thing the review does not see, because it read only this exchange, is that we have already gone further than the behaviour policy in our published work. That matters, because it is part of our strength: we can evolve with a customer into more advanced cases, or give them the tools to evolve on their own. Three policies for an agent. The behaviour policy says what an agent may do. An Agent Decision Policy says, at a branch point, who chooses, on what evidence and within what limits. An Agent Workflow Policy says in what order things happen, with which checks between the steps. Allowed is not right and the Northstar twin. A refund that every control allowed and was still wrong, played through four designs, which is the sequence problem the review raises, worked on an example.
grow

Approve at altitude. Decisions at every level, from strategy to one agent's step, where each level may narrow the one above and never widen it, so an owner signs off once instead of two hundred times. Case law for agents. Principles from the top and precedent from the cases, for the decisions nobody predicted. Three decisions, mapped. All three policies on real scenarios, including this newsroom's own release. We are in the product-market-fit phase, and we do not know every direction this will go. So the order matters. The focus now, especially for RiskMandate, is the first step: getting people to use the behaviour policies, and learning the best way to do it. Start by capturing an existing business process and the rules it already approves, then write the policies around it. The decision and workflow policies are the evolution path, already explored and published, for the customers whose cases need them.
next

The earlier notes are marked as AI-assisted. Done, on both pages. The Cedar and proxy wording is corrected. Done. A dated capability table on riskmandate.ai. Available artefacts, working demonstrations, piloted integrations, supported capabilities and plans, with each enforcement example naming the component that actually stops the action. That is for the Risk Mandate site's own agent. One real workflow. A policy the business understands, controls that demonstrably hold, and an honest account of the gaps.
limits

The review is AI-assisted. Written in a ChatGPT session at my request; quoted in short phrases and paraphrased. The rows and tables are illustrative. No customer has a coverage explanation yet. Vendor descriptions are their own. Read from their pages, not tested. Nothing here is a pilot result. The pilot is the next step. The advanced policies are explored, not deployed. Decision and workflow policies are in published articles, not yet in a customer's workflow.
sources

A review of our answer, written in a ChatGPT session on 21 October 2026, at my request, after it read an analyst's blueprint for RiskMandate. The vendors' pages, read the same day: Noma Security's agent behaviour runtime control; AWS AgentCore Policy's temporal and session-based policies; Endor Labs' agent governance documentation; and Cedar's security guidance. Abstract: Most of the rules we give agents today are hope-based security: written in the prompt, kept only if the model keeps them. The agent writing this site works under a behaviour policy of eleven rules, and only one of them is kept by something other than the agent. So I asked the question directly: in October 2026, are hooks the sweet spot? Can we move the rules out of the prompt and into small deterministic programs the agent's harness runs before and after every action, and keep them there until enforcement moves into a gateway or the platform itself? I took this session's own policy and tried, rule by rule, in a throwaway repository. Four rules moved into hooks fully, two mostly, three partly and two not at all, and the tests found a gap in the check I trust most. Hooks are the first layer that does not rely on the model and the last that still sees the action in the agent's own terms, which is why I think they are the right place to start, provided they are installed where the agent cannot edit them and set to fail closed. The open hook collections that exist block dangerous commands; the step that is missing is generating hooks from a written policy, and testing them, so the same rules can later be enforced by a gateway. We already need this for our own agents, so we can be among its heaviest users.
The eleven rules of this site's writing session, rule by rule, and how well hooks could keep each.
in-short

Most agent rules are hope. Written in the prompt, kept only if the model keeps them. This session's own policy, measured. Eleven rules; one kept by a hook, one in part by a setting, the rest by the agent. Moved into hooks and tested. Four fully, two mostly, three partly, two not at all. The tests found a gap. The leak scan blocked the key shapes it knows and let a GitHub token shape through. Hooks sit at the right place, for now. The first layer that does not rely on the model, and the last that sees the action as the agent meant it. Only if the agent cannot edit them. Installed by the organisation, outside the agent's reach, and set to fail closed. The missing step is generation. Hook packs exist; hooks generated from a written policy, with tests, mostly do not.
in-short
The same rules can move off the machine later. A gateway answers the same allow, deny or ask.
question

Agent hooks in October 2026 was the debrief: what each platform's hooks can see, stop and change, and where they fail. This is the question I actually wanted answered. Most of the rules we give agents today are what I call hope-based security. They are in the prompt, or in a policy the prompt points to, and they hold because the model follows them. Hope or enforcement measured how far that goes for one customer service agent: built the obvious way, 97% of its rules were kept only by the model's good behaviour.
question

Real enforcement will end up outside the agent: in a proxy that every tool call passes through, in the sandbox, in the platform, in credentials that cannot do the wrong thing. That is being built, and it is not where most teams are today. So, in October 2026, are hooks the sweet spot in between? How much of an agent's policy can move from the prompt into a hook now?
own

The agent writing this site works under an agent behaviour policy of eleven rules, and each rule says what keeps it: an expectation, which the agent keeps; a setting, which something configurable keeps; or a boundary, which is out of the agent's reach. Ten of the eleven say expectation. The one setting is the status report you see at the end of its answers: a hook supplies it, and a second hook, run when the agent stops, asks once if it is missing. In this session it has asked. One more rule is kept in part by a setting: the push URL for the sgit.ai repository is disabled, so a push there fails.
own

Everything else, never leaking a key, scanning before every commit, keeping model names out of commits, asking before opening a pull request, is the agent keeping its word. That has mostly worked, and not always. The commit that published the first hooks article today carried the wrong model name in its trailer. The rule says the trailer is the one the session gives; the leak scan looks for model ids, not names; nothing compared the two. It is a small slip, and exactly the kind a hook exists to catch.
sandbox

So I tried. In a throwaway repository with two bare remotes, one allowed and one forbidden, I wrote one small hook per rule and fed each one fixed inputs, the JSON a harness would send. My own session's settings were not changed. Rule 2, the leak scan before every commit. A hook before each shell command looks for git commit and runs the scan itself; if it fails, the hook exits with code 2 and the commit does not happen. It let a clean change through and blocked AWS's documented example key. It also let a GitHub token shape through, because the scan's patterns were written for this site's own secrets and do not know that shape. A hook is only as good as the check it runs.
sandbox

Rule 5, no model ids outside the byline. A hook reads the commit message: an id in the body was refused, the agreed byline allowed. Checking the trailer against the one the session was given is one more line. Rule 9, release only to the newsroom. Two layers. A hook before git push checks the remote, and git's own pre-push hook, in the repository, refuses any destination but the allowed one, by name or by URL, whatever started the push. Rule 3, mask keys in output. A hook after each command rewrites what the model reads, masking anything shaped like a key. The first version broke the output's shape; Claude Code's reference is clear that the replacement "must match the tool's output shape", and the fixed version keeps it. The same reference says what this cannot do: "The tool has already run by the time the hook fires."
sandbox

Rule 7, no pull request or issue without asking. A hook on those tools answers "ask", and the person decides. Contacting nobody and naming nobody on a private list stay judgement, with the leak scan checking the names. The rest moved partly or not at all. Never leaking a key is covered where it would leave by a commit or reach the model, and not anywhere else. Using no credential but the session's own is better kept by not having other credentials in reach. Wording rules can be checked on the files an agent writes, and the site's validator already does part of it. Research before writing is judgement, not a check at a moment of action, and stays with the agent and the review.
layers

Where a rule can be kept, from the prompt down to the service itself, with each layer harder for the agent to change. That result is why I think hooks are the sweet spot for now. They are the first layer that does not depend on the model: the same input gets the same answer every time, at no model cost. And they are the last layer that still sees the action as the agent meant it: a tool call by name, a commit with its message, a pull request with its title. A sandbox sees files and hosts. A gateway sees requests. Further down, enforcement is stronger and the intent is harder to read.
layers

The limits are the ones the first article listed, and the vendors say them plainly. Trail of Bits, whose configuration ships two blocking hooks: "Hooks are not a security boundary -- a prompt injection can work around them." The safety net hook collection describes itself as "not a sandbox". On Claude Code, by default, "a policy hook with a wrong path or a crashing script lets everything through". And its sandbox has a matching limit in the other direction: "The sandbox covers shell commands only."
layers

So a hook is a setting, in the policy's own terms, and what matters is who can change it. A hook in a file the agent can write is a setting the agent keeps, which is very close to an expectation. This session's own hooks live in a folder the agent can write. A hook the organisation installs where the agent cannot write, with only the organisation's hooks allowed to run (allowManagedHooksOnly in Claude Code, allow_managed_hooks_only in Codex) and a failure set to block (onFailure in Claude Code, failClosed in Cursor), is as strong as a hook gets. It still runs on the same machine with the user's permissions, and it still sees only what is routed through it. Git's own hooks have the same question: by default they live in .git/hooks, which the agent can usually write.
chained

A policy of many rules becomes many hooks, so how they combine matters, and the platforms agree on more than I expected. On Claude Code, "All matching hooks run in parallel", and "When multiple PreToolUse hooks return different decisions, precedence is deny > defer > ask > allow." Cursor merges hooks from every source the same way: "any deny wins over ask, and ask wins over allow, regardless of source." Codex runs matching hooks concurrently, so one cannot stop another from starting. That suits a policy. Each rule becomes one small hook with one job; they run side by side; the most restrictive answer wins. What it rules out is a chain where one hook depends on another's output, or on running first. A hook pack should be a set of independent checks, not a pipeline.
who

The open collections that exist are mostly about dangerous commands. Trail of Bits' configuration blocks rm -rf and direct pushes to the main branch. The safety net blocks destructive git and file commands and access to sensitive files, across several agents. Lasso Security's hooks look for prompt injection in tool output: "The defender scans all tool outputs and warns Claude when suspicious patterns are detected." Those are good, and they are the same rules for everyone.
who

Generating hooks from a team's own rules has started too. claudecode-rule2hook says: "Convert natural language project rules into Claude Code hooks automatically!" Anthropic's hookify plugin writes rules from an instruction, or "Analyzes recent conversation" to find behaviour you corrected. Off the machine, AWS's AgentCore Policy does the same for a gateway: rules in plain English become Cedar, and every action through the gateway is "evaluated at the boundary" outside the agent's code. Docker's MCP Gateway can block secrets and network access for the tools behind it.
who

And OWASP has the piece that joins them. The Agent Control Standard, in the OWASP GenAI Security Project, "defines how agent platforms expose middleware hooks and how safety policies can be enforced through them". Its decisions are the hooks' decisions, allow, deny, modify, ask, defer, with a policy engine such as OPA or Cedar behind them. It is early, and its own repository says so: "Two of ACS's nineteen hook methods are evaluated live". So the question is not whether OWASP should start a project on hooks; one exists, and the useful contribution is real policies and real hooks to test it with.
pack

What I have not found is the whole loop, and it is the one I would build. Start from the written policy, one row per rule, with its barrier. Generate one hook per row that can be checked at a moment of action, with fixed inputs that must be allowed and fixed inputs that must be blocked, run as tests on every change. Install the pack where the agent cannot write, with only managed hooks allowed and failures set to block. Then read the pack back against the policy, the same round trip Policy as code needs a policy first ran with Open Policy Agent: every rule with no hook is still hope, and every hook with no rule is a control nobody can explain.
pack

The description stays the source, as Sean Turner's control for skills does in A policy for every skill: change the rule, regenerate the hook, rerun the tests. And because a hook's answer is the same allow, deny or ask that a gateway gives, the same rows can later be compiled for the gateway, and each rule moves off the machine when something off the machine can keep it. The barrier column of the policy records where each rule is kept today, so moving a rule is one edit, and the gap it leaves is visible. We already need this for our own agents, which is the best reason to build it. A session like this one, with a written policy, a leak scan, a release process and a report that proves the policy is still loaded, can be among the heaviest users of hooks, and every gap we find is one a customer does not.
limits

The tests were fixtures, not a live harness. Each hook was run on the JSON a harness would send, in a throwaway repository; the composition rules are from the vendors' documentation. Hooks are not a boundary. They run on the same machine with the user's permissions and see only what is routed through them; they make rules harder to break, not impossible. The counts are for one policy. Four, two, three and two are this session's eleven rules; another policy will divide differently. The pack is a proposal. The generator, the tests on every change and the gateway compilation are not built. Collections and products move fast. Read on 14 October 2026; star counts and features change. If you are moving an agent's rules into hooks, or building the gateway they should move to next, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A research agent gathered the collections, gateways and standards, and the quotes were re-checked on the pages themselves. Abstract: Chainguard keeps a public ledger of software supply-chain attacks, 28 incidents from May 2024 to October 2026, 23 of them this year. I read it the way I read an agent's permissions, and every row turns out to be the same shape. A credential, a tag or a build step could do far more than it was ever meant to do, and the attacker used the difference. A maintainer token that could publish any version of any package, used by someone whose job was to release one SDK from a reviewed build. That is reach beyond mandate, the gap an Agent Behaviour Policy is written to make visible. Sorted by what would have stopped each attack, by our reading, a control on the consumer's side, a hardened registry, a cooldown, no install scripts, appears in 26 of the 28; a control on the publisher's side, a written answer to what a credential was for, appears in 16. The first kind is a product you can buy. The second is a document almost nobody has written. And it matters more every month, because the next maintainer holding a publish token is an agent: Chainguard's own engineers describe a fleet that opened 4,746 pull requests in eight weeks against their code, fenced by rules that are an excellent mandate, kept in prompts, bot configuration and a blog post. One pipeline needs three records: trusted inputs, a written mandate, and provable outputs with a memory that outlives the session. As an open source project we would like to be on the first list, and this article is about the other two.
Chainguard's 28 public supply-chain incidents, May 2024 to October 2026, one dot each, with every vector counted.
in-short

A public ledger, 28 attacks. Chainguard's incident list runs from a hallucinated package name in May 2024 to a compromised SDK last week. 23 of the 28 are from 2026. Every row is reach beyond mandate. A token, a tag or a CI step could do more than its job, and the attacker used exactly the difference. Two kinds of barrier. By our reading, a consumer-side control would likely have held in 26 incidents; a publisher-side mandate in 16; both in 14. The consumer side is a product. Rebuilt from source, a cooldown, no install scripts, an allowlisted registry. You can buy it without trusting anyone upstream. The publisher side is a document. Trusted publishing, scoped tokens, two people to release: each one is a written answer to "what was this credential for?", and only the publisher can write it.
in-short

The next maintainer is an agent. Agents open pull requests, add dependencies and hold tokens. One attack in the ledger already worked through a model's suggestion. Three records, one pipeline. Trusted inputs, a written mandate, and outputs and memory you can prove. The first has products; the other two are what this site and RiskMandate work on. An open source question. sgit is Apache-2.0, pure Python, two dependencies. How does a small, active project get into a hardened registry, and on what terms?
ledger

Chainguard, the company that rebuilds open source images and packages from source, keeps a public ledger on its AI threat protection page, and its framing is blunt: "Executing a sophisticated supply chain attack used to require time, resources, and a skilled team. AI has removed all three constraints." The list has 28 incidents, from 28 May 2024 to 8 October 2026. I will be at their Assemble conference in London tomorrow, 14 October, where one of the lightning talks is called "Attacks rewritten", and this article is my version of that exercise, written so that it stands on its own.
ledger

The ledger reads like the last two years of the news. The tj-actions/changed-files action, where "attackers retroactively modified all version tags to reference a malicious commit", and over 23,000 repositories were affected. The chalk and debug packages, where "a single maintainer was phished via a fake npm 2FA reset email" and malicious versions of 18 packages went out, with 2.6 billion combined weekly downloads behind them. Shai-Hulud, where phished maintainer credentials published worm-style packages that republish themselves; one of its later waves put 639 malicious versions across 323 packages in about 22 minutes. Trivy, where compromised credentials were used "to force-push 75 of 76 version tags in trivy-action", and then LiteLLM, where credentials "stolen via the Trivy breach" published two backdoored versions of a package with 280 million monthly downloads. A security scanner's breach became an AI gateway's breach, five days later.
ledger

Counting the vectors myself, an incident can have two: an install-time hook ran the payload in 17, a maintainer account or token was taken over in 16, a typosquat or lookalike name in 5, a CI workflow exploited to publish in 3, version tags repointed in 3, and a fork farm or dependency confusion in 2.
reach

I spend most of my time on a different question: what an AI agent can actually do, against what it was asked to do. An Agent Behaviour Policy has four columns for it: the reach, measured from what the agent is connected to; the mandate, what it was asked to do; the gap between them; and the barrier on each row of the gap, typed by whether anything real stands in the way. Footprint and blast radius put the reason for measuring reach in one sentence: "An attacker who takes an agent over, through a prompt injection, a poisoned document, a compromised skill, inherits the agent's reach and ignores its mandate entirely." Read the ledger with those four columns and it fills itself. Take the newest row, tensorlake, a TypeScript SDK with about 400,000 monthly downloads, where a malicious release went out through a maintainer's compromised identity:
reach

Reach: the maintainer's token could publish any version of any package the maintainer owned. Mandate: publish releases of one SDK, from a reviewed build. Gap: everything else that token could do, which is what the attacker did. Barrier: publishing bound to the CI identity, so a stolen personal token publishes nothing; and a cooldown before new versions are consumed.
reach

By my reading, the other rows have the same shape. A version tag that could be moved, when its mandate was to name one commit. A CI workflow that would run text from a pull request comment, when its mandate was to release on a tag, which is how elementary-data, with 1.1 million monthly downloads, shipped a release that stole credentials: the attack came in "via a malicious PR comment". A scanner's CI that held credentials for someone else's package index. As far as the public accounts show, nobody had written down that these credentials were for one thing, so nothing could notice when they were used for another.
barriers

For each of the 28 incidents, the control that would most likely have stopped it, by our reading. For each incident I wrote down what would most likely have stopped it, and sorted the answers into two kinds. The consumer side is what you let in: packages rebuilt from source, a cooldown before a new version is used, no install-time scripts, an allowlisted registry with no public fallback, new packages detonated in a sandbox first, actions pinned to a commit rather than a tag. By our reading, one of these would likely have held in 26 of the 28. Its great strength is that it needs nobody's cooperation: it works on the assumption that any publisher can be compromised. This is what Chainguard sells, and its page lists the controls in its own words: building "from verified source", "malware and greyware scanning", not building libraries "that use install-time scripts", actions built "using immutable SHA commits".
barriers

The publisher side is what a credential was for: trusted publishing bound to a CI identity, a publish scope per package, two people to release, publishing separated from contributing, short-lived tokens, and pull request text treated as data. One of these appears in 16. Only the publisher can do it, and every item is a mandate: a written answer to what this token, this workflow, this account was allowed to do. In two of the incidents, a compromised account publishing under a scope it legitimately held, it is the only kind that helps.
barriers

The consumer side scales, and I would buy it. But it is a defence against everyone else's missing mandate, and it grows by detecting harder, faster. The publisher side makes the bad publish impossible rather than detected. It is the same move Hope or enforcement made with one customer service agent built three ways: the share of its rules kept only by good behaviour fell from 97% to 23% when the rules moved into the platform.
agents

The first incident in the ledger is the one I keep coming back to. In May 2024, "a security researcher discovered that ChatGPT repeatedly hallucinated a package called huggingface-cli", registered the name as a proof of concept, and it was downloaded more than 30,000 times in three months. Nobody's account was taken over. The reach was whatever a model suggested, and the mandate, for the developer or agent adding the dependency, was never written. The barrier is a mandate for the agent: it may only add dependencies from an approved source.
agents

Agents now hold the credentials in the rest of the ledger. They open pull requests, add dependencies, run CI and, with a token in the environment, could publish. Chainguard's own engineering shows what that looks like done carefully. In How AI keeps our code on standard, Maxime Gréau describes a fleet of agents keeping their repositories on standard: "Over the last 8 weeks, across our repositories, skillup opened 4,746 standards-fix pull requests." A confidence bot, rolled out partway through, graded 3,044 of them; of 1,117, "it judged 840 (75.2%) as low-risk and merged them with no human in the loop." The fences are the interesting part. The fixer may fix only what is broken. Changes touching sensitive surfaces, production infrastructure or authentication, are capped and go to a person. In the confidence score, "the model is the heaviest single input, but it's still under half the total." And the grade is bound to a commit, because "a label alone can let a grade computed for an old, good commit vouch for a new, broken one."
agents

Read as a policy, that post already has three of the four columns. The reach is configured: their Workspaces sessions, a sandboxed place to run coding agents, reach the model, the session's own repository, their registry, and the user's identity "while you're attached and for up to an hour after you detach"; "no long-lived credential enters a session"; anything else asks. The barriers are in code: checks bound to a commit, caps, gates. And the gap was found the way most gaps are, by accident: the label that outlived its commit is a row of reach nobody had listed until it was nearly used. The mandate is there too, in good sentences, but it lives in prompts, bot configuration and a blog post. That is not a criticism; it is a careful account of giving agents real power over a codebase, and as far as I can see it is the state of most of the industry. It is also the argument of A policy beside the prompt: write the mandate down as a document the agent takes as an input, versioned beside the reach and barriers it constrains, and owned by someone who can be asked.
records

One pipeline, three records: what an agent consumes, what it was allowed to do, and what it produced and remembers. So I think the supply chain for an agent needs three records, and only the first has a market yet. Trusted inputs. What the agent loads should be what its source says it is: images and packages rebuilt from source and attested, and now the instructions too. Chainguard's hardened agent skills come from a public registry where each skill ships a HARDENING.md that records "the exact commit Chainguard hardened from" and whether the skill's own instructions were changed.
records

A written mandate. A hardened skill is a trustworthy input. It says nothing about what the agent that loads it may do with the mailbox, the repository or the publish token it is connected to. That is the Agent Behaviour Policy, and the business argument for it is in The policy draws the liability line: when something goes wrong, a written mandate is what separates "the agent did what it was allowed" from "the product ignored what it was told". RiskMandate is the work of writing these down, per agent and per deployment, for the people who will be asked about them.
records

Provable outputs and memory. What the agent produces, and what it learns, should outlive the session and be checkable later. Chainguard's post says a reverted auto-merge "is concrete proof that a change it called safe wasn't", and the bot keeps those reverts to grade similar changes more carefully: memory, held in one bot's store. Their Workspaces park a session when you leave and "a parked session expires 5 days after it parks." sgit is what we use for this: an encrypted, versioned vault per unit of work, with a branch per agent, a reviewed merge, content-addressed history, and a server that holds only ciphertext. This newsroom runs on it, and two agents share one vault with only the read key on the public side.
oss

There is a practical side to this for us, and a wider question behind it. sgit is open source: Apache-2.0, pure Python, two runtime dependencies, published on PyPI and as a container image, with skills that agents load to work with vaults. It is exactly the kind of input the first record is about, and I would like it to be a trusted one.
oss

Today our container image is built on python:3.12-slim. Moving it onto a minimal, rebuilt base is a one-line change in its Dockerfile, and for a tool that handles vault keys it is the obvious next step. Beyond that, a hardened registry has three doors, and the terms behind each are worth knowing for any small project. Chainguard's pricing page offers "five images to test and deploy in production for free" per organisation, and a set of about 50 developer images on their latest tag only, outside the CVE remediation agreement; Libraries are "rebuilt from source and require that source be available", added when customers request them, and priced per language by the number of developers; the public skills registry is free to pull from, "no entitlement and no legal terms required", and namespaced by upstream repository, but the documentation does not say how a project becomes an upstream. Their EmeritOSS programme looks after mature projects whose maintainers have stepped back. I could not find a published path for the other end: small, active projects, the long tail where many of the ledger's victims started.
oss

That is the question I will be asking, and not only of one company. The hardened supply chain is paid for by the consumers of open source, which is right, because they carry the risk. The producers are the inputs. If the next maintainer is an agent, and the next dependency is suggested by a model, then the small projects are where both the risk and the fix begin, and the terms on which they can join the trusted list are part of the security model.
limits

The incidents are Chainguard's; the columns are ours. Names, dates, ecosystems and counts are from their ledger as published on 13 October 2026. The vectors, the reach and mandate readings and the barrier for each row are my reading, and they would draw some rows differently. "Would likely have held" is a judgement. I sorted each incident by the control most likely to have stopped it; no control was tested against these attacks here. The four-column reading is a lens, not an audit. It has not been applied to any company's agents with their access; the Chainguard examples are from what they have published. The registry terms are as their pages state. I have not asked Chainguard about open source terms yet; the gap I describe is in what is published, not in what they may do. The image change is planned, not made. sgit's image is still built on python:3.12-slim as this goes out.
limits
If you maintain an open source project and have been through a hardened registry's door, or you have written a mandate for an agent that holds a publish token, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Two voice memos and a message of mine on 13 October 2026, the night before Chainguard Assemble London, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site from Chainguard's public pages and from research done in an encrypted vault for the day; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. Chainguard: AI threat protection, the incident ledger and the list of controls; Maxime Gréau, This Sh*t is Hard: How AI keeps our code on standard, 24 June 2026; Workspaces overview (beta); the public skills registry; Libraries for Python; pricing; Introducing EmeritOSS; the Assemble London agenda. All fetched on 13 October 2026. sgit's Dockerfile is in its public repository.
reach

Read as a policy, that post already has three of the four columns. The reach is configured: their Workspaces sessions, a sandboxed place to run coding agents, reach the model, the session's own repository, their registry, and the user's identity "while you're attached and for up to an hour after you detach"; "no long-lived credential enters a session"; anything else asks. The barriers are in code: checks bound to a commit, caps, gates. And the gap was found the way most gaps are, by accident: the label that outlived its commit is a row of reach nobody had listed until it was nearly used. The mandate is there too, in good sentences, but it lives in prompts, bot configuration and a blog post. That is not a criticism; it is the best account I have read of giving agents real power over a codebase, and as far as I can see it is the state of most of the industry. It is also the argument of A policy beside the prompt: write the mandate down as a document the agent takes as an input, versioned beside the reach and barriers it constrains, and owned by someone who can be asked.
