Abstract: One of the most important pieces of advice I can give any founder is to start selling, now, what you have. It does not matter how rough it is. Expect not to sell; that is not the point. The point is to learn, and you only learn by trying to sell. You cannot sell what you cannot ship, so selling makes you ship. The attempt tells you where you really are, and it starts the feedback loops that fix a hundred small problems. A customer who pays is the best signal you will get, and it is surprising how hard it is to get one, even when you give them the money to do it: with SG/Send I offered five pounds back for five pounds of credits, and people still had to choose to buy. So making it easy to pay you is not something you add at the end; it goes in early. Do not worry about your idea being copied; it is all execution, and putting things up for sale is already the part that counts. Then make the customers profitable, and keep the price free to change: no subscriptions, no yearly contracts, something atomic, with a beginning, a middle and an end. My first question to any founder is the same: can you sell it?
Selling is how you learn: put it up for sale, ship it, learn from a buy or no buy, change it, and try again.
in-short

Start selling what you have. Now, however rough it is. Expect not to sell. The point is not the sale; it is what you learn trying. Selling makes you ship. You cannot sell what you cannot ship. A payment is the best signal. And it is surprisingly hard to get one. Make it easy to pay you, early. It is not something you add at the end. Do not worry about being copied. It is all execution. Then make customers profitable. Atomic purchases, prices you can change every day, no subscriptions. My first question. Can you sell it?
start

One of the most important pieces of advice I can give any founder is to start selling. Start selling what you have right now. It does not matter how rough it is, how crude it is, or how much of it works. There should be some market for it, or you would not be trying, but that is all you need before you start: you go to the end of the journey and try to sell what you have. Reid Hoffman put it well: "If you're not embarrassed by the first version of your product, you've launched too late" (his essay, 2017). Selling is the same rule, one step further. You might be lucky. Somebody might pay for it. But expect not to sell, because that is not the point. The point is to learn, and the only way to learn it is to try to sell.
why

Three things happen when you try to sell. First, you ship. You cannot sell something you cannot ship, so the moment you decide to sell, everything that stands between the product and a stranger using it becomes your problem: the sign-up, the payment, the bit that only works on your machine. Second, you find out where you really are. Not where you think the product is, or where the plan says it should be, but whether anyone will give you money for it today, and what they say when they do not. Third, you start the feedback loops. All the small problems, and all the feedback, come from people trying to use and pay for the thing. That loop is the most important thing a young company has, and it does not start until you sell.
signal

It always amazes me. I meet people, sometimes people who already have users, and I say: sell it. And they look at me as if I had said something strange. But a payment is the signal that tells you that you have a product. Someone gave you money for it. It is that simple. You would be surprised how hard it is to get. I have done the trick of giving people the money: with SG/Send, I offered a £5 Amazon voucher to anyone who bought £5 of credits. It worked: the payments went live on 1 March 2026, and on 2 March there were ten paying customers. But they still had to buy. They had to find the page, decide, and pay, and that is where the signal is.
signal

And be careful what you read into it. Someone who pays more than it is worth, to help you, is not a market. SG/Send showed that too: three days after the first customers, the briefs said "Users buy credits, test once, and don't come back." That was the next lesson, and I only got it because I had sold first. Whether they come back is whether they miss it.
pay

The bottom line is that you need to make it easy for people to pay you, and that is not something you add at the end. It goes in almost at the start, because you need to figure out how people will pay, and until they can, you are not really playing the game. Only when you have customers and users are you in it. You can sell at a loss at first; that is fine. What matters is that you start to have customers.
copied

Do not be paranoid that your idea will be copied, or that people will see what you are doing. This is all about execution. If you are putting things up for sale, you are already doing the part that counts. The best lessons I have learned came when I actually tried to ship something and sell it, and then iterated. It is not quite that simple, but it is close.
profitable

Once you have customers, the next step is to make them profitable. Here it connects to how I think people should pay for what they use: not subscriptions, but paying after the value, the experiment this site runs with its reading meter. So a few rules for what you sell: Keep the price free to change. You can change the price every day while you learn what it is worth. Do not lock yourself, or the customer, into a yearly or monthly contract. Make it atomic. Something a person can buy on its own, without committing to the rest. Give it a beginning, a middle and an end. The customer should know what they are buying, when they have got it, and that it is done. All of these come from the same question: what, exactly, are you selling?
question

So my first question to any founder I meet is exactly that: can you sell it? If you have an idea, or anything you would like to build, the first thing to do is to put it up for sale, however rough it is. Only when you have customers are you really playing. This is one half of a pair. The other is start a company: as soon as you have a bit of revenue, it needs somewhere to go.
limits

Selling early is advice, not a law. Some products cannot be sold before they are safe to use; selling one is a different decision. Ten customers is not a market. SG/Send's ten paid, then mostly did not come back. Selling at a loss is for learning. It is a stage to get through, not a model.
sources

Abstract: On the morning of 22 October I was reading the BBC's live page on two critical flaws in PHP, the language behind WordPress, Wikipedia and a large share of the web. Governments were telling organisations to take websites offline, a figure of 70% of the internet was going round, and some of the numbers did not add up. I asked the newsroom's agent to read the page, and then to set up a section and a vault to capture evidence. The vault was created at 08:03 UTC, eight minutes after the agent's first copy of the BBC page. The section was pushed at 08:13 with one source. Four collecting agents went out by beat: the primary sources, the researchers, the governments, the news. At 09:27 a second session released the first version of a site of its own, php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai, which reads the same vault. By 12:05 the vault held 184 sources, 177 dated captures and 855 files hashed at the moment of capture, from six writers. This is the newsroom's first story covered while it was breaking, and the order we did things in is the argument: capture first, because a live page, a down page and a social post change or disappear within hours, and a claim can only be checked later against the bytes someone kept. It also showed what went wrong. Two of the four agents stopped before committing, and forty sources, including the maintenance pages of French prefectures, sat in their working folders until the lead agent found them. The section here was the first step; the dedicated site is where the facts now live, and this newsroom keeps the context and the opinion. The plan is to retire the section once the site has taken everything over.
The morning of 22 October 2026 in two lanes, UTC: the story as its sources date it, and the newsroom's captures.
in-short

A breaking story is a race against the page changing. The BBC live page grew a new post between our first copy at 07:55 UTC and our second at 08:04; the sites taken offline were on maintenance pages at 08:19 and may not be by the evening. So the first thing built was the vault, not the page. An encrypted sgit vault created at 08:03, with a capture tool that keeps the page as served, as rendered, its text, a screenshot and its headers, and the sha256 of each. Captures are only added. A live page captured three times is three dated folders; the series is the record of how the story moved. Several agents, one vault, no shared file. Each source has its own row and each agent its own claims and timeline files, so four collectors and two site agents wrote at once.
in-short

The figures that did not add up are now pinned to their sources. "70%" is a headline; the body of the same post says 70% of websites; one scanning vendor counts 2.6 million hosts; one national CERT counts about 6,000 resources. The agencies disagree, and the vault shows it. The NSA and CISA say take systems offline if you cannot patch; the NCSC in the Netherlands does not advise it at all. What went wrong is part of the record. Two collecting agents stopped before committing; forty sources were recovered from their folders hours later. The story now has a site of its own. php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai, built from the same vault, facts only; the section here retires once the move is done.
breakfast

The BBC opened a live page at 06:16 UTC on 22 October: "Global scramble to fix critical cyber-security flaws as many websites taken offline". Two flaws in PHP, found with the help of AI, a coordinated disclosure that broke down when the details leaked, and agencies in the UK, the US, the EU and Australia telling organisations that could not patch to take their systems offline. Among the sites named as affected were parts of Wikipedia, Edinburgh council, French government services, the University of Geneva and the BBC itself.
breakfast

Some of it did not add up. "Roughly 70%" of the internet, attributed to Wiz and flagged by the BBC as a figure it could not verify, sat a few posts away from "something like 30 million websites". I have been in security for a long time, and as I said in the memo that followed, "I don't buy that 70% of websites out there, especially some sort of websites that matter," are exposed with nothing else in the way. A remote code execution flaw on a web server is serious; what it means for a given site depends on what is on the server, what credentials it holds and what sits between it and the attacker. That is a blast radius question, and the reporting was not asking it yet.
breakfast

So I asked the newsroom's agent to read the page. It fetched it at 07:55 and gave me a summary of twelve posts. Then I asked for what this site had not done before: a section about a story that was still moving, and a vault behind it.
capture

The order matters, and it is the point of this article. A finished article can wait; the evidence for it cannot. A live page is rewritten every few minutes. A site that is down this morning will be up tonight, and its maintenance page will be gone. A social post can be deleted, and in this story one already had been: the researchers' demonstration video, published by mistake and taken down. The vault was created at 08:03, before there was a page to put anything on. Its first capture of the BBC page, at 08:04, is already different from the 07:55 copy: a new post had appeared at 08:00, with the researcher who found the flaw saying on Radio 4 that there was no evidence of exploitation yet. That post is in the second capture and not in the first. Nobody has to trust me on that; the two files, and their hashes, are in the vault.
capture

The capture tool is a short script that opens the page in Chromium and keeps six things in a dated folder: the page as the server sent it, the page after its scripts ran, its visible text, a full-page screenshot, the response headers, and a provenance file with the time, the user agent and the sha256 of every file. The first version got one of those wrong. The raw page came back empty, and the fallback was blocked by the session's network policy; the third capture, at 08:06, was the first complete one. One test capture was discarded while the tool was being written, before anything was committed; since the first commit, at 08:06, all three captures of the BBC page are kept, because a capture is never edited or deleted. A live page captured many times leaves a series, and the series is the record of how the story moved. This is the method this site has argued for since the story vault: keep the evidence the article is made from, frozen and hashed, and treat the article as one walk through it.
section

At 08:13 the section /php-flaws/ went out with one source. It said what we knew, each point with its source; what we did not know; a timeline in which every date is as its source states it, with the ones we worked out marked inferred; and the claims, each marked reported, confirmed, disputed or unverified. The status line said Developing. The captures themselves are third-party pages, so they are not republished: the section lists each capture with its hashes, and links to the originals.
section

At the same time four agents went out, one per beat. One for the primary sources: the php.net advisory, the CVE records, the GitHub advisories, the patched releases. One for the researchers: Calif, Wiz, OpenAI, Cloudflare, and the leak. One for the governments: sixteen national agencies in the end, and the government sites that went down. One for the news and the impact, with the instruction to capture the maintenance pages while they were still up. Each cloned the vault, read its README, and followed the same protocol.
section

The protocol had to change in the first half hour. The first version had one manifest that every agent appended to, and one claims file. Several agents writing to one file is a merge conflict waiting to happen, so before the agents had written much, each source got its own row in its own folder, and each agent its own claims and timeline files, merged by the build. This is the pattern two agents, one vault described for the Industry Wire, with more writers: a vault one agent writes and another reads, with the history as the audit trail. Who wrote the 184 sources in the evidence vault by 12:05 UTC, and what reads it.
link

At 08:47 I sent the agent a link: the NCSC in the Netherlands keeps a repository on GitHub, php2shell, with an inventory of software that may be affected. The government agent had already captured its front page at 08:09. What the link was for was the inventory itself, and an inventory in a git repository changes by the hour. So the agent kept the whole repository: a git bundle with all 52 commits, the files at commit cca173c64ec5, and the inventory parsed into rows. At that commit it lists 674 products: 206 marked Vulnerable, 46 with a Fix, 418 under Investigation, 3 Not vulnerable and one without a status. The NCSC-NL calls the entries "investigation leads" until a vendor or upstream source backs them, and the section says so. A count like 674 is only useful with the commit it was counted at, because the next pull request changes it.
link

The same repository gave the CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and the fixed releases, PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. It also gave the first clear disagreement between agencies: the Dutch guidance is to patch, or apply PHP's temporary mitigations, and it does not advise taking systems offline.
numbers

By late morning the vault could answer the question I started with. The dedicated site's numbers page puts six figures side by side, each with who said it and what it measures. "70%" of the internet is a headline on Wiz's post; the body of the same post, Cloudflare and OpenAI say about 70% of websites, which is the share of sites whose server-side language is PHP, from surveys none of them names. One scanning vendor counts 2,608,039 internet-facing hosts running PHP, through The Hacker News. Alan Woodward's "something like 30 million websites" comes with no basis given. Latvia's CERT counts about 6,000 potentially affected resources in one country, a few hundred of them in the public sector.
numbers

None of those figures is wrong as a statement about what it measures. They measure different things: a language's share of websites, a host count, a national scan. Put next to each other, the 70% stops being a measure of exposure, and the question becomes the one in my memo: what is on the other side of each of those servers, and what stands in front of it. As I said there, "a zero day like this is not invisibility cloak": exploitation leaves signals, and by noon every claim of exploitation in the vault was of attempts, probes and a honeypot hit, with no agency confirming a compromise.
numbers

The agencies' advice is the other thing the vault made visible. The NSA and CISA say take systems offline if you cannot patch; the UK's NCSC puts that after patching and temporary mitigations; Australia, the Netherlands, Italy, Japan and New Zealand give no offline advice. In the second memo I said that "putting a website offline is an option, but should be like at the end of a long sequence of events", and that a company should still be able to do it quickly. Sixteen agencies, side by side, show how differently that sequence is being written.
wrong

When I asked at midday whether the vault had been pushed, the honest answer was not quite. Two agents had commits waiting: the primary-sources agent had six, and the researchers' agent had four that had fallen behind the vault, so its pull reported 224 conflicts. Of those, 223 were the same bytes on both sides, and the one real difference was the generated manifest, which is rebuilt rather than merged.
wrong

The bigger gap was in two working folders. The news agent and the government agent had both stopped before committing. Between them they held forty sources that were nowhere else: news coverage from Switzerland, France, Portugal and Australia, and the sites themselves, captured at 08:19 while two French prefectures showed "Site en maintenance" and the University of Geneva returned a 503. Edinburgh council's home page loaded normally at the same minute; a page that was up is evidence too. The lead agent committed them with rows written from each capture's provenance file, said in each row who wrote it and why, and pushed them. Two rules come out of it. An agent commits after every source, not at the end of its beat. And the lead agent checks every clone, not only its own, before saying the vault is complete. Neither is in the protocol yet; both are now on the list.
site

The section was the first step, and the right size for the first hour. In my second memo I said what the story needed: a dedicated site, as fact-driven as we can make it, with briefings for each kind of reader, from the journalist to the board member, and with this newsroom keeping the context and the opinion. A second session started on it, read the same vault, and released php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai at 09:27 as v0.1.0. By 12:05 it was at v0.2.2, with a page per source and per party, the numbers, the agencies compared, the inventory, an impact ledger of offline against compromised, and twelve briefings, each one selecting from the same claims rather than adding to them. Its agent also became the vault's largest writer, with 83 of the 184 sources.
site

That leaves two places with the same story, which is one too many. The plan is to move everything the section does to the dedicated site, link to it from the front page of this newsroom while it is moving, and then retire the section, leaving a page at its address that points to the site. The briefing for the site's team says what has to be true before that happens: every source the section lists is on the site, the site publishes a small status file this newsroom can read, and the links into the section keep working. This is the explorer, villager and town planner handover inside one day. The section was explorer work: fast, one agent, built to find out what the story needed. The dedicated site is the villager: its own repository, its own gate, its own releases. What the newsroom keeps is the part only a newsroom does: saying what the story means.
stands

At 12:05 UTC the vault holds 184 sources, 177 dated captures and 855 files hashed at capture, from six writers, with 61 claims and 67 timeline events in per-agent files. The section here is live with the first of those; the dedicated site is live with all of them, and is where to read the story now. Nothing is anchored yet: the hashes are recorded in the vault and published on the sources pages, which proves the bytes have not changed since they were published, not that they existed at the time stated. The next steps are the ones in my memos: the exposure mapped from the assets outwards, exploitation counted over time rather than reported once, the steps for anyone running PHP backed with evidence, and the graph of who said what first. The vault was the part that had to happen this morning.
limits

This is one morning, as one newsroom saw it. The times are from the BBC page, the capture files and two git logs; other people covering the story will have their own. The vault is private, so the captures cannot be checked by a reader yet. What is published is each capture's hash and the time it was made; opening the vault to a reviewer is what turns the hashes into a check. A hash proves the bytes did not change after it was published, not when they were captured. Nothing in the vault is anchored to an outside timestamp yet. The figures in the numbers section are as the sources state them. We did not measure PHP's share of the web, or scan anything ourselves. Most of the work was done by agents, and an agent can be wrong. The claims carry a status for that reason, and the sources a reader can follow.
limits

Nothing here is advice on what to patch. For that, read the php.net advisory and your national agency. The two lessons from what went wrong are not in the protocol yet. They are recorded, and the next release of the protocol is where they go. If you are covering this story, or run PHP and want to compare what you see with what the vault holds, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The third article in the series on agent decision policies is about the cases nobody predicted. A business will never write down every variation of its decisions, and it should not try. English law has lived with the same problem for centuries, and its answer fits agents well. Parliament writes statutes from principles and objectives; delegated rules must stay within the powers an Act gives them; courts apply both to the facts in front of them; decisions of higher courts bind lower ones; a case whose facts differ in a way that matters is distinguished; and the highest court can depart from its own past decisions when they turn out wrong. For agents, the same shape gives a working loop. Principles and envelopes come from the top. A case the decision policy does not settle goes to a person, who decides with the context to decide well, and the answer is recorded with its facts and reasons. The next case with the same material facts follows that precedent without asking again; one that differs is distinguished, and escalates. Precedents that keep holding are written into the policy, and then compiled into code. That is the maturity curve this site has described before, from a person deciding to a rule that runs without them, but driven by real cases instead of guessed in advance. It needs one thing most agent systems lack: a decision record good enough to serve as a law report.

How a decision earns its way into code: from a case at a branch point to a precedent, then to tested code. How did the agent decide? Behaviour, decision and workflow as three policies; approving at altitude so it scales; case law for the cases nobody predicted; and three scenarios mapped.
in-short

Nobody can predict every case. A business that tries to write every decision down in advance will fail, and should not try. English law has the same problem, and an answer. Statutes set principles; courts decide cases; precedent carries the answers forward. The shape maps onto agents. Principles and envelopes from the top; escalation for the cases they do not settle; a recorded decision that the next case follows. Distinguishing is the escalation trigger. A case whose facts differ in a way that matters does not follow the precedent. It goes to a person. Precedent becomes policy, then code. What keeps holding is written down, then compiled. That is the maturity curve, driven by cases. It needs a law report. A decision record with the facts, the rule, the decider and the reasons. Most agent systems keep a log, not a report.
problem

The second article argued that you approve at altitude: the board signs off its risk appetite, a function signs off its limits within it, and each level below may narrow the one above but never widen it. That makes the far-out cases visible. It does not answer the ordinary ones in between: the case that is inside every envelope and still not covered by any rule. A refund for an order that arrived late but intact. A memory deletion requested by someone who is not the project owner but is on the project. A release with a failing test that is not quite unrelated to the change. The business will never predict all of those, and I do not think it should try. A decision policy that tries to list every case becomes a contract nobody reads. What it needs is a way to settle the unpredicted ones and learn from them.
law

England and Wales has lived with this problem for centuries, and I think its answer is a good model. I am not a lawyer, and what follows is the shape, not the detail. Statutes set principles and objectives. Parliament writes Acts. They cannot list every case either, and courts read them in the light of their purpose. In a narrow set of cases, set out in Pepper v Hart in 1992, a court may even read what the minister said in Parliament to find what a provision was for. Delegated rules stay within their powers. An Act can give a minister the power to make detailed rules. A rule that goes beyond that power is ultra vires and can be quashed, as the employment tribunal fees order was in 2017. That is the narrow-never-widen rule from the second article.
law

Courts decide cases, and the decisions bind. A court applies the law to the facts in front of it, and gives its reasons. Decisions of higher courts bind lower ones: as the Open University's introduction to the subject puts it, "if the precedent is from a more senior court than the court hearing the new case, then the precedent tends to be binding." A case that differs is distinguished. In the same source's words: "If a court decides that the facts in an earlier case are similar, but not similar enough, then this is called distinguishing." The precedent does not apply, and the court decides afresh. Precedent can be corrected. In 1966 the House of Lords declared, in a Practice Statement, that it could depart from its own previous decisions. The Supreme Court treats that as applying to itself. A wrong answer is not locked in forever; it can be overruled, by a court with the authority to do it.
law
Scotland's legal system is different, a mixed one, and so are many others. I use England and Wales because it is the one I know and the one where precedent works most like what I am proposing.
mapping

In English law For agents An Act of Parliament The principles and envelope at the top: risk appetite, budget, licence to operate Delegated legislation, within its powers Decision and workflow policies at lower altitudes, inside their parent's envelope A court deciding a case A person deciding an escalated case, with the context to decide well The judgment, with reasons The decision record: facts, rule applied, decider, outcome, reasons Binding precedent The next case with the same material facts follows it, without escalating Distinguishing Facts that differ in a way that matters: the case escalates The hierarchy of courts Altitude: a precedent set higher up binds the levels below Departing from a precedent A precedent that turns out wrong is overruled, at the altitude that set it
mapping

The loop in the figure is the whole of it. A case arrives at a branch point. If a rule in the decision policy settles it, it is resolved. If a recorded precedent with the same material facts matches, it is resolved the same way, and recorded. If neither, or if the facts differ in a way that matters, it goes to a person. Their decision, with the facts and the reasons, becomes a precedent. The next matching case follows it.
maturity

This is where it connects to what this site has written about who makes a decision. Agency is not a yes put the top of its scale at delegation: "The cases you keep approving unchanged become rules that run without you, as code under a behaviour policy." Hooks are kernel code gave a scale for where a rule runs, from the prompt to off the machine. Case law is the mechanism that moves a decision up both scales: A person decides. The first time, with the context to decide, and the record of why. Precedent decides. The next matching cases follow it. A person sees them afterwards, not before. The policy decides. After the precedent has held across enough cases, it is written into the decision policy as a rule, signed off at the altitude that owns it.
maturity

Code decides. The rule is compiled: a test, a check in CI, a limit in a tool, a gate in front of the agent. It is now deterministic, and it is where the mission-critical decisions should end up. Each step is earned by cases, not assumed in advance. That is the difference from writing every rule up front: the rules that reach code are the ones reality kept asking for.
record

A court's judgment is useful because it records enough to be followed. Most agent systems keep a log of what happened; a precedent needs more: The facts that mattered. Not the whole context, but the facts the decision turned on, so the next case can be compared. The rule it was decided under. Which decision policy, at which altitude, and which envelope. Who decided, with what authority. A named person, or the precedent or rule that settled it. The outcome. What was allowed or refused, and what the agent then did. The reasons. Why, in a sentence or two. This is the part that makes it a precedent rather than a statistic.
record

Without that, a system cannot distinguish a case, because it does not know which facts the earlier decision turned on. It is also the gap this site keeps finding: in the SGit × Ruflo run, every policy decision is computed and none is written down. A decision that leaves no record is a self-report at best.
tonight

The fourth article maps this newsroom's own release, and the same evening produced two small cases that show the loop at work. A new rule from one case. A figure shipped with a date nobody had checked, while the text around it had been checked. The fix was a new version. The precedent is that a figure's facts are checked like the body's. One case was enough here, because the rule is cheap and the principle above it, "verify every fact", already covered it. A case distinguished. The session's status report counted two commits with no leak scan before them. Both were in throwaway repositories, built to test git hooks, that never published anything. The rule exists to stop a key reaching a published repository; these facts differ in exactly the way that matters. The case is distinguished, the rule stands, and the counter should count only the repositories the rule covers.
tonight
Neither needed a person to escalate to, because I was there to decide. In a system with many agents, each would have gone up one altitude, and come back as a precedent.
limits-of-analogy

Courts are slow on purpose. A precedent in law takes years and an argument from both sides. A precedent for an agent can be set in a minute by one person. That is its strength and its risk. Precedent can carry a bias forward. A wrong decision followed a thousand times is a thousand wrong decisions. The ability to overrule, at the right altitude, matters more for agents than for courts, because the volume is higher. Nobody argues the other side. Courts hear both parties. A person approving an agent's case usually hears only the agent. One answer is to ask a second agent for the case against, which is a review, not a court. "Material facts" is a judgement. Deciding whether a case is distinguished is itself a decision. A model can propose; at first, a person should decide.
series
Three policies for an agent: behaviour, decision and workflow. Approve at altitude: narrow, never widen. Case law for agents. This one. Three decisions, mapped: the scenarios.
limits

It is not legal advice, or a summary of English law. It borrows the shape of precedent, from introductory sources, for a different purpose. It is a proposal. No agent system I know of keeps decision records as precedents in this way; the loop is untested. The two cases are small. They show the loop's shape, not that it works at scale. If you are a lawyer and the analogy is wrong somewhere that matters, I would like to know: agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo from me on 17 October 2026, written up and checked by this site's agent; the editorial responsibility is mine. Precedent and distinguishing: the Open University's Judicial decision making, sections 8.2 and 8.3. Delegated powers: R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor [2017] UKSC 51, 26 July 2017. Departing from precedent: the Practice Statement (Judicial Precedent) [1966] 1 WLR 1234, as described by the Supreme Court in Knauer v Ministry of Justice [2016] UKSC 9, paragraph 20. Purpose and Hansard: Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593, decided on 26 November 1992, and its three conditions as restated in R (O) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2022] UKSC 3. Scotland's mixed system: the Attorney General's speech Two jurisdictions, a shared inheritance, 9 June 2014. Related on this site: agency is not a yes, hooks are kernel code, your agent's logs are a self-report.

If a rule settles it, or a recorded precedent with the same material facts matches, it is resolved and recorded. If not, or if the facts differ in a way that matters, it is distinguished and escalated to a person with the context to decide. The decision is recorded with its reasons and becomes a precedent that the next matching case follows. A precedent that holds case after case is written into the policy, then compiled into deterministic, tested code. | process

Abstract: Cedar is the policy language I think we should adopt rather than compete with. AWS open-sourced it in May 2023 under Apache 2.0; it joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a Sandbox project on 8 October 2025; it is the language of Amazon Verified Permissions and of AgentCore Policy, which checks every agent tool call before it runs; and its design is modelled and proved in Lean. That is a mature environment, and it already says most of what our agent behaviour policies say: permit for the grant, forbid for the barrier, a schema for the footprint. What it does not carry is why a rule exists, which version was in force, or the evidence of what it decided. Those are exactly what an encrypted, versioned vault is good at. So I asked this site's agent to try it: Cedar policies, schema, entities and tests in an sgit vault, a gate that refuses any version that fails validation, tags signed by the releasing clone, enforcement points that clone with a read key and cannot write, and an append lane that keeps a sealed, hash-chained record of every decision. It worked on a local server, and it found one thing worth knowing: Cedar skips a policy whose evaluation fails, so a forbid that refers to a missing attribute lets the action through. This article is the debrief, the crosswalk between their terms and ours, and the brief for the agent that will build the MVP.
Cedar policies in an sgit vault, from the rule to the evidence: a gate, signed tags, enforcement points, an append lane.
in-short

Adopt, do not compete. Cedar is open source, formally modelled, in the CNCF, and already deciding agent tool calls. It already speaks our language. Permit is the grant, forbid is the barrier, the schema is the footprint. Three things it does not carry. Why a rule exists, which version was in force, and what it decided. A vault carries all three. History and diffs, signed releases, read keys for enforcement, and an append lane for evidence. The demo worked. Two releases, a refused third attempt, fifteen decisions, a chain the auditor could check. One sharp edge. Cedar skips a policy that errors, so an invalid forbid fails open; validate before you deploy, and deny on error. A brief for the MVP. What the next agent builds, and how we know it works.
why

I would like our agent behaviour policies to connect to what others are already using, not to sit beside them as one more format. When I looked at Cedar, it looked like the most mature place to connect to, and the facts hold that up. AWS open-sourced Cedar on 10 May 2023: "Cedar is open-sourced under the Apache License 2.0", and it is written in Rust. The project's own line is that "Cedar is an open source policy language and evaluation engine", and "the first policy language built from the ground up to be verified formally". My memory of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation was right: the CNCF's page says "Cedar was accepted to CNCF on October 8, 2025 at the Sandbox maturity level", the first of its three levels. In AWS's announcement of the move, "Current adopters and maintainers include Cloudflare, MongoDB, StrongDM, Cloudinary, and AWS services", which I have not checked with each company.
why

For agents, the important adopter is AWS's own. Policy in AgentCore "intercepts all agent traffic through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateways and evaluates each request against defined policies in the policy engine before allowing tool access", and its policies "are constructed using Cedar language". You can write them in plain English, and it "generates candidate policies, validates them against the tool schema, and uses automated reasoning to check safety conditions". That is the round trip Policy as code needs a policy first argued for, shipped as a product. Sondera's open-source harness, which Commander's intent is a behaviour policy mapped, "evaluates Cedar policies before your agent's actions execute". And the Cedar project has its own repository for agents, cedar-for-agents, with "A crate for auto-generating a Cedar Schema for an MCP Server's tool descriptions."
language

The documentation is short and clear, and five ideas carry most of it. Default deny. "no request is authorized (decision Allow) unless there is a specific permit policy that grants it". Forbid wins. "even if a permit policy is satisfied, any satisfied forbid policy overrides it, producing a Deny decision." Four parts to every request. A principal, an action, a resource and a context, where the first three are entities and the context is a record of facts about this request. A schema and a validator. The schema says which entities and actions exist and what each action's context holds; the validator checks every policy against it before it runs.
language

Proof, not only tests. The OOPSLA 2024 paper says "We have modeled Cedar in the Lean programming language, and used Lean's proof assistant to prove important properties of Cedar's design", and the Lean case study adds the rule that matters most to me: "No new Cedar version is released unless its model, proofs, and differential tests are current." The paper is also direct about the comparison with the other two languages people reach for: "Comparing Cedar to two open-source languages, OpenFGA and Rego, we find (subjectively) that Cedar has equally or more readable policies, but (objectively) performs far better."
crosswalk

Our behaviour-policy terms, Cedar's, and where each one lives in the vault, with the two Cedar lacks. Most of an agent behaviour policy maps onto Cedar without strain. The grant, what the agent can touch, is a permit and the actions and resource types in the schema. A barrier, a limit on the grant, is a forbid, and Cedar's rule that forbid always wins is exactly how we want barriers to behave. The footprint, what exists to act on, from Footprint and blast radius, is the entities. A row of a skill behaviour policy is a forbid on labels the session carries. And the business layers of The behaviour policy is the business logic are forbids on facts from the ledger or the CRM, passed in as context.
crosswalk

Two things have no Cedar construct. The mandate, what the agent is for and why each limit exists, is the description the rules are compiled from, and it has to stay the canonical version. And the version in force, which set of rules applied to a given decision, belongs to whatever stores the policies, not to the language.
crosswalk

This is the translation element I keep coming back to. A fractal semantic graph does not ask everyone to share a schema; it connects graphs that each keep their own. Cedar has its own world: entities, actions, a schema. Our behaviour policy has its own: mandate, grant, barriers, layers. We do not need to replace either. We need edges between them, and Cedar gives us a place to put them: annotations. In the demo, every policy carries one, @abp_rule("9") or @sbp_row("dga-2") or @layer("process"), and those are edges from a node in their graph to a node in ours. It is the same move as The same argument, in our words, done in code.
today

Amazon Verified Permissions as its documentation describes it, a plain repository, and the vault from the demo. My guess in the memo was that policies are often deployed as loose JSON with no version control. The truth is better than that, and the gap is still real. Cedar policies are text, with a JSON form "to allow for programmatically constructing and parsing policies". In AWS, they live in a policy store, "a container for policies and policy templates", with a STRICT validation mode that "Requires a schema to be present in the policy store", and IAM deciding who can change what.
today

But the store is a current state, not a history. The API reference lists create, get, list, update and delete operations, and none for versions, history or export. Deleting a store "permanently deletes the schema and any policies and policy templates in the policy store", and deletion protection is on for stores made in the console but "disabled for all policy stores created through an API or SDK call". The CloudFormation reference adds a subtle one: "Existing policies and templates are not re-evaluated against the changed schema." I found no signing or provenance mechanism for policies, in Cedar or in the store. So most teams who take this seriously will keep the source in a repository and push it into the store. That gives history, but the rules are plaintext to everyone who can read the repository, and nothing ties a decision back to the commit that made it.
demo

To find out whether a vault fills that gap, this site's agent built it on a local vault server, with sgit 0.21.0 and cedarpy 4.12.2. The vault holds a schema, four policy files with the rules tested in Commander's intent is a behaviour policy, seven policies in all, the entities, and the test cases, each a request with the decision we expect.
demo

The gate. Before anything is committed, a script validates every policy against the schema and runs every test. Version one passed, fourteen of fourteen, and was pushed and tagged policies-v1. For version two, the agent added ABP rule 2, no push before the leak scan, as a new forbid, without changing the schema. The gate refused it: the attribute leak_scan_clean was "not found" in the context the schema gives a push. With the schema and the tests changed in the same commit, fifteen of fifteen passed, and it was tagged policies-v2. A diff between the two tags shows the policy, the schema and the tests changing together, which is the unit I want: a rule is not just a line of Cedar.
demo

The sharp edge. That refusal matters more than it looks, because of what Cedar does at run time: "if a policy's evaluation returns error, the policy does not factor into the authorization response; it is skipped." The agent sent the version-two policies a request in the old shape, a push with no leak_scan_clean in the context, and the answer was Allow, with the error in the diagnostics. A forbid that cannot be evaluated fails open. Validation before deployment is not optional, and an enforcement point should deny on any evaluation error, which is what Hooks are kernel code would ask of any hook that guards an action.
demo

Signed releases, read-only enforcement. Each tag is signed by the clone that made it, and sgit vault tag show reported "signature verified". The enforcement point cloned the vault with the read key only; when it tried to commit and push, sgit answered "This vault was cloned read-only. To write, re-clone with the full vault key." It loads only a verified tag, checks that its working copy is at that tag, and runs the gate again before it decides anything.
demo

Decisions and evidence. The enforcement point decided all fifteen test requests: eight allowed, seven denied, each denial named by the @id of the policy that made it. Every decision was sealed and appended to an append lane on the same vault: the request, the decision, the determining policies, the tag, the commit, and the hash of the previous record. The enforcement point holds an append token and nothing else; asked to list its own lane, the server answered 403. The auditor, with the enum key, read all fifteen back and found the chain intact. A decision took 1.2 milliseconds one at a time and 0.06 batched; 200 sealed appends took 2.2 milliseconds each, on one machine.
adds

Distribution. A read key is a deployment credential that cannot change the rules. The ciphertext can sit on any server, a CDN, or a folder copied into a sandbox with no network, and the append-lane architectures already measured how many readers and writers a vault can take. Validation, at both ends. The same gate runs before push and after load. A policy that has not passed it is not a release, and a release that is not signed is not loaded. That is the same release-gate idea as sgit in a CI pipeline, applied to rules instead of code.
adds

Evidence. Every decision names its policy, its tag and its commit, in a lane the decider can write but not read or rewrite. The policy draws the liability line argued that the written policy is the evidence that turns "user error" into "your product ignored what it was told"; a lane like this shows which written policy was in force, and what it decided. History and translation. The English behaviour policy, the Cedar, the schema, the tests and the decisions live in one versioned unit. A zip or a JSON projection for a managed store can be generated from any tag, and it is a projection of something with a history, not the only copy.
adds

There is one more reason the timing is good. AgentCore now also accepts Dogwood, "an open-source policy language" whose core syntax is derived from Cedar, adding conditions "that decide based on what has already happened earlier in the same session". Rules about history need a trustworthy history, and an append lane of sealed, chained decisions is one.
brief

For the agent that builds the integration, here is the brief. Start from the demo. Schema, four policy files, entities, test cases, the gate, the enforcement point and the auditor; all of it ran locally and is the starting point. Make the gate a release rule. No commit without validation and every test passing; a policy change without its test change is refused. Deny on error. The enforcement point treats any evaluation error as Deny and records the error in the evidence. Wire it to a real hook. A pre-tool hook in this newsroom's own agent session, deciding the seven rules for real actions, with the session's labels as context. Keep the edges. Every policy carries @id and an annotation back to its ABP rule, skill row or business layer; a check fails any policy without one.
brief

Project, do not fork. A job that exports a signed tag to the JSON a managed store accepts, and records which commit is live there. Prove it. In CI: the fifteen cases, a refused unsigned tag, a refused invalid policy, a read-only clone that cannot push, and an auditor that finds the chain intact. Then run it on the newsroom's own releases for two weeks and report what it denied. Never print a key. Read keys, append tokens and enum keys are separate files; nothing logs them.
limits

The demo is local. One machine, an in-memory vault server, fifteen decisions; not production, not a cloud store. Not proved, only tested. The Cedar ran in cedarpy, an unofficial binding; we did not use Cedar's symbolic analysis. No AWS integration yet. The sync into Verified Permissions or AgentCore is proposed, not built. The adopters list is AWS's. I have not checked each company's own use. The evidence key is shared. The demo sealed records with one symmetric key; a real deployment should seal them to the auditor's public key. Dogwood is new. I have read its page and AWS's description, not used it. If you run Cedar policies, or want your agents' rules to arrive signed and leave evidence behind, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Chainguard is one of the companies doing the most interesting work in software supply chain security, and much of it is open: the Wolfi distribution, public advisory feeds, Sigstore in its lineage, and a growing set of products for agents. So I mapped it: the company, what it builds from the operating system up to agents, what data it publishes that anyone can read, and how deep that data goes. I read the feeds and counted them. 12,480 advisories covering 12,125 distinct CVEs; in a sample, about seven in ten findings marked fixed and one in five marked as not applying. And in the archived Wolfi advisories, where the reasons were public, 2,850 determinations that a vulnerability did not apply, of which 177 gave a reason about context: the vulnerable code is not in the execution path, an attacker cannot control it, or it is mitigated. That is where the graph stops, and it is the question that matters to me. As with everything in security, it is about context. An image with many vulnerabilities is fine if the application on top never reaches them; one reachable flaw is not. Deciding which images are non-negotiable and which can ship today needs a graph from the user story, through the code and its dependencies, to the container. That context layer is where an open behaviour policy and an encrypted vault fit, next to the agent products Chainguard is now shipping, which already talk about policies. I make the case for each.
Chainguard, mapped from the operating system to agents: what it builds, the public data, and where a policy could help.
in-short

A company built in the open. Founded in 2021 by people who worked on Sigstore, SLSA and distroless images at Google; Wolfi's build recipes are Apache 2.0. From the operating system to agents. Images, libraries, hardened CI actions, and now MCP servers, isolated workspaces, checks and a vulnerability-hunting harness for agents. Its data is public, and I counted it. 12,480 advisories over 12,125 CVEs; in a sample, 71% of findings fixed, 19% marked as not applying. The graph stops at the package. Of 2,850 recorded "does not apply" decisions, 177 give a reason about context. Context decides. A vulnerability the application never reaches can wait; one it reaches cannot. The context layer is open ground. A graph from the user story to the container, written as a policy row per image. Where we plug in. Behaviour policies for its agent products, vaults for the data between stages, and an open format for deployment decisions.
why

I have written about Chainguard twice already. In Attacks rewritten as mandates, its record of supply chain attacks was the example, and the controls it sells would by my reading have held in most of them. In The minimum code below I argued that security built from the bottom up stops where the application starts. This article is the map underneath both: what the company does, what it publishes, and where others can build on it. It matters to me as a user too. Projects like sgit ship containers, and the case for hardened base images is easy to make. What I would like to understand is how far the context goes, and where it does not.
company

Chainguard was founded in October 2021. Its co-founders, according to Contrary Research, worked together on securing Google's software supply chain, including SLSA, Sigstore and one of the original distroless container images. In April 2025 it raised a $356 million Series D at a $3.5 billion valuation, as SecurityWeek reported. Its open-source lineage is in the products: Wolfi, the distribution its images are built from, publishes its build recipes under the Apache License; Chainguard maintains apko, melange and gitsign; and it now runs EmeritOSS, "stability-focused maintenance for select unmaintained and archived open source projects", and the Athena coalition, "an industry coalition for the orchestrated defense of open source software".
builds

From the bottom of the stack up: Operating system and packages. Wolfi and Chainguard OS, packages rebuilt from source, and virtual machine images. Images. Minimal, hardened container images. A free tier, Catalog Starter, gives "Five free container images of your choice", and customers can tailor images with Custom Assembly. Libraries. Java, Python and JavaScript dependencies rebuilt from source, with Go and .NET announced on 14 October. CI. Chainguard Actions, generally available since 6 October: "the Chainguard Actions catalog now spans over 1,000 continuously verified and hardened actions".
builds

Agents. This is the new part, and the most relevant here. Agent Skills, in beta since March, is "a continuously maintained catalog of hardened AI agent skills". And four products announced on 14 October: MCP servers that any MCP-compatible client can reach "using a standard OAuth login", one of which "verifies organization policy, entitlements, and attestation data programmatically"; Workspaces, isolated development environments for people and agents, where with an egress policy "the proxy blocks and logs any outbound request to an endpoint you haven't explicitly allowed"; Checks, where "every run executes in a hardware-isolated microVM that produces a signed attestation of what ran"; and Harness, which uses one of Anthropic's frontier models to "hunt down exploitable vulnerabilities". That last group is a company moving from securing what agents install to governing what agents do. The Agent Skills announcement even names the next step: "custom best-practices configurations that let organizations define and enforce their own skill security policies".
publishes

The part I care about most is the data, because data is what others can build on. I read the public feeds on 14 October 2026 and counted them. An advisory feed in OSV format. Chainguard started "publishing its security advisory feed in the Open Source Vulnerabilities (OSV) format" in 2024. The index lists 12,480 advisories, covering 12,125 distinct CVEs. A second index lists 1,224,077 records, one per advisory and package. A status per component. Each record names the package, the components inside it, where each sits in the image (for example a Go module inside a specific binary), and its latest status. In a random sample of 300 records, holding 377 components, 71% were fixed, 19% marked as false positives, 6% waiting for an upstream fix and 4% marked as fix not planned. VEX for libraries. An OpenVEX index of 732 documents: 675 for Maven, 42 for PyPI, 9 for npm and 6 for Go.
publishes

The reasons, until January. The Wolfi advisories were kept in a public repository with a reason for each decision; its last change was in January 2026, it is now archived, and it points to Chainguard's security site instead. The public records say what the status is. In the current feed, a "false positive" carries no reason. The archived repository did, and it is good evidence of how deep the analysis goes.
depth

How far up the stack the context goes: from Chainguard's package data to the application above, with three outcomes. The archive holds 30,030 advisories across 1,616 packages, and 2,850 decisions that a vulnerability did not apply. Their reasons, counted: 1,462: the vulnerable code is not included in the package. 546: the vulnerable version is not used. 542: the vulnerability record does not match the component. 123: the vulnerability record itself is contested. 80: the vulnerable code is not in the execution path. 77: the vulnerable code cannot be controlled by an adversary. 20: mitigations exist inline.
depth

So 177 of the 2,850, about 6%, are reasons about context, and the analysis behind them can be good. For one busybox vulnerability the note says it needs a specific configuration flag: "We don't use that configuration flag, so the free logic isn't called". But that context is about how the package was built, not about the application that runs on it. The graph stops at the package.
depth

And that is the question I care about. From a security point of view, I care about exploit paths: the vulnerabilities that can be exploited in a particular situation. If an application sits on a container with a large number of vulnerabilities, but its exposed ports and its code never reach them, that is acceptable. The reverse is also true: one reachable flaw in an otherwise clean image is not. And updating is not free. A new version, even a fix, can change the behaviour of the application, which means code changes upstream, which means CI and tests and people. So the real decision is which images are non-negotiable, must be fixed before they ship, and which are fine to deploy today.
context

That decision needs a graph that goes higher than the package: from the user story, to the exposed surface, to the code paths, to the library functions they call, to the components in the image. It is the graph The minimum code below proposed for removing code, and that Code review as a fractal semantic graph drew from the story to the method. Applied to vulnerabilities, it sorts every finding into one of three answers: must fix before it ships, because it is reachable and not mitigated; ship now with a reason, because it is present and unreachable or mitigated; and ship now and watch, because it is unreachable today and a named change would re-open it.
context

It is a variation of the agent behaviour policies we write, used as controls for an image instead of an agent. The mandate is what the service is for; the reach is what is exposed and what the code can call; the gap is the vulnerabilities inside that reach; and the barrier is whatever stands in front of each one: a mitigation, a configuration, the code not calling it. One row per image and finding, with its evidence, and its answer. The format to carry the answer already exists. A VEX statement can say "not affected" with a justification, and Chainguard already publishes VEX. What is missing is the application-level justification, which only the application's owner can write, and the evidence behind it.
plug-in

That is where the open work we do fits, and I think each piece makes a case for using Chainguard's platform, not for replacing any of it. Behaviour policies for its agent products. Agent Skills plans to let organisations "define and enforce their own skill security policies"; the MCP servers verify organisation policy; Workspaces enforces an egress policy and keeps credentials outside the environment. Those are the barrier column of a behaviour policy, enforced as boundaries. The rows they enforce need to be written somewhere a person can read, a model can check and an auditor can point to. A policy for every skill described a control for contributed skills in exactly those terms. An open behaviour policy is a natural source for the policies these products enforce, and the signed attestations from Checks are the record of what actually ran, the footprint to compare with it.
plug-in

Vaults for the data between stages. Advisories, VEX statements, attestations and the context decisions move between stages and teams, and some of them are sensitive: which reachable vulnerability you have not fixed yet is not something to leave in a build log. sgit in a CI pipeline showed vaults carrying data in and out of GitHub Actions, scoped to one folder per stage and encrypted per key. Hardened actions carrying encrypted vaults is a good combination. An open format for deployment decisions. The three answers, with their evidence, as an open file per image and release: generated from the context graph, signed, and published as VEX where it can be. And the reasons published with every status, as Wolfi used to, because a status without a reason is a decision nobody can check.
plug-in

And for open-source projects. I could not find a dedicated programme for open-source maintainers. When Chainguard changed its free developer tier in 2024, it told affected projects that "we would love to discuss how we can support you and your project's needs", and Catalog Starter gives five free images today. Projects like ours would like to run on its images; a clear route for open-source projects would make that easy.
limits

The counts are from public data. Read on 14 October 2026; the security site and customer data may hold more, including reasons the public feed does not carry. The status shares are from a sample. 300 random records of the 1.22 million. The reason counts are from an archive. Its last change was in January 2026; current practice may differ. The context layer is a proposal. Chainguard may be building something like it; I found nothing public that reaches the application. Products are as announced. Several are in beta; I have not used them. Company history is from third parties. Founders and funding are from Contrary Research and SecurityWeek. If you work at Chainguard, or run its images and want the context layer above them, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Nineteen sibling sites is too many to browse, so the directory now answers questions. The design problem is that sgit.ai has no server and no vault host, which means the honest options are a local matcher, a key in your browser, or moving the page into a vault, and only one of those is free. The network directory now has a chat box. It answers one question, which of these nineteen sites is mine?, and it works with no key, no account and no network call. That last part took the most thought, so this is the plan behind it: what shipped, what it costs, and what would remove the cost. The panel on the directory. The default tier is a local matcher; the key is opt-in and clearly labelled. sgit.ai is a static site on GitHub Pages. There is no server, no session, no place to keep a secret. Every sibling on *.sgit.ai is the same.

That matters because the usual way to put a chat box on a website is to call a model from a backend that holds the API key. There is no backend here to hold one. So the real options are only three, and it is worth being blunt about which is which. Tier 0, match. Shipped, on by default, needs nothing. A deterministic scorer runs in the browser against the catalogue of all nineteen sites, emitted at build time from the same data the cards and the table are built from. Type "I have to sign off a risk" and it points at risks.sgit.ai, and shows you which words it matched on.

It is not clever. It is instant, free, private, works offline, and, the part that made it the default, it tells you why it chose. An LLM answer does not give you that. The scorer weights a hit in a site's thesis or domain above one in its summary, and stops there. The important property: a reader should never have to hold a credential to use an index. Tier 1, bring your own key. Shipped, opt-in, and it costs you something. Paste an OpenRouter key and the browser calls https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions directly, streaming, with the catalogue as the system prompt. This is not a new pattern here, the SG/Vault workbench vault already does exactly this, using the same endpoint and the versioned sg-llm-request module served from dev.tools.sgraph.ai, so this reuses a proven client rather than inventing one.

The cost is real and the UI states it rather than burying it: with no host, there is no permission floor, so the key lives in this page's origin. It goes into localStorage and into a fetch to openrouter.ai. It is never sent to sgit.ai, there is no server here to send it to, but the page cannot protect it the way a vault app can. That is a trust decision, and it belongs to the reader, so it is presented as one. When the model call fails, the panel falls back to Tier 0 and says so. Degrading to something that works beats an error message. Tier 2, the bridge. Not built, and the one that removes the trade.

Serve the directory as a vault app and the problem disappears. llms.sgit.ai documents the contract: the key lives in .vault/llm/config.json, below the permission floor, the host makes the call, and the app never sees the credential. Its API is sg.llm.available / chat / cancel / models / usage, with grants defaulting to deny. The striking detail in that documentation is that there are three chat surfaces, and two of them need no application code at all, the vault chat panel, and the same panel beside any running app. "Every existing vault app gets this without being changed." The qualification has to travel with the claim, and llms.sgit.ai insists on this in its own words: "The bridge protects your key; it is not yet a boundary that prevents all egress." It protects the credential you trusted it with. It does not yet stop a malicious app calling a provider with a credential of its own.

Tier 2 is not a rewrite, but it is not free either. Honestly scoped: Piece State Note The catalogue Done Emitted at build from admin/content/sites/*.md; nineteen entries Tier 0 matcher Done assets/network-chat.js, no dependencies BYOK client Done Streams from OpenRouter; the workbench vault's proven pattern A vault build of the directory Not started The generator already emits a .md twin of every page; a vault app is a different target, not a different site sg.llm detection Not started The panel should prefer the bridge when it exists and fall back when it does not, the same shape as the Tier 1 → Tier 0 fallback already in the file Shared component Partly, 7 September A site-wide pane now sits on every page here, and its model can call tools over the site's own index and markdown twins (v0.2.63). Still one site's copy rather than a versioned module the other eighteen can load

That last row is the one that decides whether this was worth doing. A chat box on one site is a feature. The same panel on all nineteen, reading each site's own catalogue, is the thing that makes a network of nineteen sites navigable, and it is why the catalogue is generated rather than written.

The directory chooser above answers one question. Ten days later every page carries a pane (Ask this site, bottom right) whose model does not read a catalogue pasted into its prompt. It is given seven tools as function definitions: search_site, read_page, list_vaults, list_sites, latest_updates, get_board, current_page. Each call runs in the page, over an index the build emits from the same data as llms.txt, the vaults table, the network directory, the feed and the board, and the pane shows every call it made. With no key, the same tools run directly: type words to search, or /vaults, /board, /read PATH. The three tiers are unchanged; Tier 2 is still not wired, and is now on the board as T11.

It does not answer questions about the subjects. Ask it how to threat-model a payment gateway and it will point you at a site, not teach you. The scope is routing, deliberately: the sites already contain the arguments, and a summary that drifts from them is worse than a link that does not. It also does not know anything that is not in the catalogue. Nineteen theses, nineteen summaries, nineteen categories, all quoted from each site's own words rather than paraphrased, which is the same rule the directory follows. Abstract: A release number is a fact about the order in which pushes land, and the only thing that knows that order is the pipeline. So the pipeline should pick the number, not whoever pushes. I wrote that scheme for OSBot-Utils on 27 October 2023, the night CI made its first tag there; it has numbered 1,129 releases of that library and runs sgit and the send app. This week the sites built by agents learnt it the hard way. sharness.ai adopted it after three days of collisions, the PHP newsroom's six repositories on 27 October, and this site on the same night, after two version races and a refused release in one day. This is the scheme, the history, how it runs here, and a job you can copy, so the next project starts from this page. Before, each agent guessed the next version. Now one CI job numbers, tags and deploys.
in-short

The number comes from CI, after the push. Work commits carry no number; one serialised job picks it from the tags. The committer cannot know the number. It depends on the order pushes land, which only the pipeline sees. I wrote this for OSBot-Utils on 27 October 2023. 1,129 tags on that library since, and the same scheme under sgit and the send app. This week, three agent-built sites relearnt it: sharness.ai, the PHP newsroom's six repositories, and this one. Here, it was inherited technical debt. Two version races and a refused release in one day, which I quoted as evidence two articles ago. This site has a twist. Its pages are built from sgit.ai's generator, so the committer builds against a pending version and CI stamps the real one. The job is portable. About thirty lines of shell and git, copied below with the checklist.
in-short
It is written here so agents find it. Agents across our projects read this newsroom; an article on a project's own site gets lost.
the-problem

Every site we build with agents starts with the versioning that feels natural for one agent in one session. The release is a commit whose subject begins site vX.Y.Z:, the number is also in a version file, every page carries it, and CI checks that the newest tag plus one is what the subject says, tags it and deploys it. For one committer that is airtight, because the committer knows the last number: it made the last release.
the-problem

It stops being airtight the moment there is more than one committer, and with agent teams that is the normal case. sharness.ai's conductor wrote up what happened there on the evening of 25 October 2026: "Between 23:42 and 23:58 UTC four agents, the conductor, the build agent, pbp@ and security@, pushed seven releases, v0.5.14 to v0.5.20. Each had done the arithmetic on the tags it could see; three of them had seen the same tags." Each collision cost "a merge of dev, a renumbered row in the release history, a re-run of every generator and the gate, and a second push, nine steps by hand". A script that automated the guess made a collision cheaper but not impossible, "because the script still had to know the number before CI did, and that number is a fact about the order in which pushes land, which only the thing that serialises the pushes knows."
the-problem

Then the queue made it worse. GitHub keeps one run in progress and one pending in a concurrency group, so a third push cancels the pending second one. On sharness.ai a cancelled run left a version untagged, and every later release was refused, because each one bumped from a tag that did not exist: "the live site sat at v0.5.32 for twelve minutes until the cancelled run was re-run by hand".
here

This site had exactly the same scheme, and the same debt. In you can feel good engineering I listed "two version races in one day" as one of the engineering gaps agent teams expose: twice, a release I was building had its number taken by another agent's release that landed first. Each time the cost was the same as sharness.ai's: save the work, reset, re-apply it under the next number, and run a ten-minute build again. On 27 October it happened a third way. A release of mine went out with the right number but without the site prefix in its subject, and the tag job, which looks for that prefix, refused it after the push. The fix was a second release under the right subject. None of these is a bug in an agent. Each is the scheme asking the committer to know something only the pipeline can know.
here

That is what inherited technical debt looks like with agents. The scheme was a reasonable choice when one agent did all the releasing. It became debt the day a second agent started releasing, and because agents absorb the overhead quietly, it took a week of races to make it visible.
the-scheme

The rule is one sentence: nobody but CI writes the number. On this site, since v0.13.116 (released by CI at 23:38 UTC on 27 October 2026): The committer builds against a pending version. admin/build/release_stamp.py --pending sets version.txt to a placeholder shaped like a version, and writes the release note and the versions row under it. This is the twist. sharness.ai re-stamps its pages in CI, but this site's pages are built from sgit.ai's generator, which the CI runner does not have. So the committer still builds, every page carries the pending version, and the commit's subject carries no number: @newsroom.writer: CI owns the version. The gate runs on the pushed commit, as before: the validator and the reader's tests in a browser. The validator accepts the pending state. One release job, one at a time, reads the newest tag and picks the next number: a push to dev bumps the last number, a push to main the middle one.
the-scheme

It stamps the number over every pending version in the served tree, contents and paths, writes version.txt, re-stamps the chrome, the engineering pages and the sitemap, and runs the gate again. A served file that still carries the pending version fails it. It commits as GitHub Actions, with the subject site v0.13.116: <the pushed subject>, tags that commit, and pushes the branch and then the tag. If dev moved while it worked, it takes the new head in and tries again, three times. It deploys that commit, never the pushed one, in the same run. The push uses the workflow's own token, which starts no second run, so nothing numbers a release twice. A guard fails the run if any commit not made by GitHub Actions set version.txt to anything but the pending version.
the-scheme

Two agents that push in the same minute now produce a merge in the generated files, at worst, and never two claims on one number. A push that lands while a release is being built rides that release. And because the pending version reads as the article's number once CI has stamped it, CI's commit does not count as a new version of the article.
main

The second half is the shape of the branches. Every push to dev is a release, numbered by CI: v0.13.116, v0.13.117. When a set of them is ready to be a major, dev goes to main by pull request, and the merge's push is a release on main that bumps the middle number: v0.14.0, with a GitHub Release whose notes list what it carries. Then CI fast-forwards dev to it, so dev's next release is v0.14.1. Nobody types a number at any step, including the person merging the pull request.
the-history

Two details from the conductor's article are worth knowing before copying it. The original action's word "major" bumps the middle number and "minor" the last, so say what moves rather than using the words: main bumps the middle number, dev the last. And the original had no retry loop, because "it was written for one person pushing from one machine, where the branch does not move between the fetch and the push. The retry is what three years of one committer did not need and one evening of four agents did."

This is sharness.ai's portable job, as published there, for a repository with dev and main, tags shaped vX.Y.Z, a file called version at the root and a validate job before it. Their note: "it has not run anywhere yet" in exactly this form; ours is the same loop with a stamping step and a guard on a different file.

release: needs: [validate] if: github.event_name == 'push' && (github.ref_name == 'dev' || github.ref_name == 'main') concurrency: { group: release, cancel-in-progress: false } permissions: { contents: write } runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@<commit sha> # v4 with: { fetch-depth: 0, ref: "${{ github.ref_name }}" } - env: { BRANCH: "${{ github.ref_name }}", BEFORE: "${{ github.event.before }}" } run: | set -euo pipefail git config user.name "GitHub Actions"; git config user.email "actions@github.com" # guard: nobody but CI writes the version file if git log --format=%an "$BEFORE..HEAD" -- version | grep -qv '^GitHub Actions$'; then echo "::error::version was edited by hand"; exit 1; fi for try in 1 2 3; do git fetch --quiet --tags origin "$BRANCH" git reset -q --hard "origin/$BRANCH" # a push that landed meanwhile rides this release LAST=$(git tag --list 'v*' | sort -V | tail -1); LAST=${LAST:-v0.0.0} IFS=. read -r A B C <<< "${LAST#v}" if [ "$BRANCH" = main ]; then NEW="v$A.$((B + 1)).0"; else NEW="v$A.$B.$((C + 1))"; fi [ "$(cat version 2>/dev/null)" = "$NEW" ] && { echo "head already carries $NEW"; break; } SUBJECT=$(git log -1 --format=%s) printf '%s\n' "$NEW" > version # re-stamp badges, docs, lockstep files here git add -A; git commit -q -m "release $NEW: $SUBJECT"; git tag "$NEW" if git push origin "HEAD:$BRANCH"; then git push origin "refs/tags/$NEW"; echo "released $NEW"; break; fi git tag -d "$NEW"; echo "$BRANCH moved; taking it in (attempt $try)" [ "$try" = 3 ] && { echo "::error::$BRANCH kept moving; nothing released"; exit 1; } done

The checklist, in short: One file, written only by CI. Every other place the version appears is rewritten from it, in the same commit. One serialised job. A concurrency group that does not cancel the running release. Let the queue drop pending runs: the reset to the branch head makes the drop harmless. The release commit is the tag's commit, and the deploy runs from it, in the same run. The committer's subject carries no number. CI repeats it after the number it chose. A guard against hand edits, until branch rules make it a lock. Say what moves. main bumps the middle number, dev the last. And one adaptation of ours: if CI cannot build the pages, let the committer build against a pending version, and make CI's stamp a replacement of that one string, with a gate that refuses any served file still carrying it.
