Abstract: Press Gazette's tracker of journalism job cuts counted at least 3,434 in the UK and US in 2025, 3,875 in 2024 and about 6,000 in 2023, and 2026 is on the same scale: the BBC planning up to 2,000, the Washington Post a third of its staff, Reach 220 editorial jobs cut and 60 created, Scripps 268 jobs while "leaning into AI", McClatchy more than 90 journalists across at least 13 titles, with the Idaho Statesman losing 10 of its 18 reporters and a new AI lab welcoming five hires the following week. This article is about what those decisions say, which is more than what they cost. A hiring plan is the clearest statement a publisher makes about where its centre of gravity is going. Fire the people who make original content and hire for traffic, and the centre moves to packaging; packaging is measured by engagement, and engagement optimised for is clickbait whether anyone meant it or not, because what you measure is what you become. The opposite cut is as bad: fire the engineers and nothing enables the journalism. The argument is that a publisher now needs both, plus the roles that turn a notebook into a graph, historians, cartographers, ontologists and librarians, each AI-enabled, and the tooling handed to journalists as "this makes you better", never "this replaces you". It sets out five counts anyone can make from outside to read a publisher's real strategy, and an unsourced parable about who hires the ones you let go.

A cut says the centre of gravity is moving to packaging; a hire says it is staying on the content and getting tooled; and five counts let anyone read which from outside. Below, the two failure modes and the case this site makes. I am a technologist, and I am about to argue that firing journalists to hire technologists is the worst thing a publication can do. I want that on the record first, because it is the argument against my own kind, and I think it is right.

The numbers are not in dispute. Press Gazette's tracker counted at least 3,434 journalism job cuts in the UK and US in 2025, at least 3,875 in 2024, and about 6,000 in 2023. Its 2026 page, as of October, has the BBC expecting to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs, the Washington Post cutting a third of all staff including more than 300 of about 800 journalists, GB News proposing up to 90, Reach planning to cut about 220 editorial jobs and create 60, Scripps cutting 268 jobs as it "embraces AI for a 'revolution' in programming", with its chief executive quoted as "leaning into AI, automation, technology and the centralisation of some roles", and McClatchy cutting more than 90 staff across at least 13 titles. Tech Policy Press went through the McClatchy cuts paper by paper: the Idaho Statesman lost 10 of 18 reporters and three of four editors, one paper lost its city hall and schools reporter, another its only Spanish-speaking reporter, and less than a week later the company's AI-focused Content Innovation Lab announced five new hires.
What I want to write about is not the cost of those decisions. It is what they say.
short

A hiring decision is a direction of travel. It is the clearest statement a publisher makes about where its centre of gravity is going, clearer than any strategy document, because it is what the company actually spent. Fire journalists, and the centre moves to packaging. Fewer pieces with original reporting, fewer sources followed, fewer corrections. The product becomes the repackaging of inputs everyone else has. What you measure is what you become. Hire for traffic and engagement and the metric becomes pages opened and time on page. Optimise for that and you get clickbait by construction, whatever anyone intended. The metric is a hiring plan in disguise. The opposite cut is as bad. A publisher with journalists and no engineers has content that nothing enables: no graph, no provenance anyone can check, no versions, no surfaces for the agents that now read, no meter.
short

It is a spectrum, and context matters. A pure repackaging business is honest about what it is, and that world is shrinking fast. A normal media organisation has to cover the whole thing. Who to hire instead. Keep the journalists and tool them. Hire the roles that turn a notebook into a graph: historians, cartographers, ontologists, librarians, each AI-enabled. Hire the engineers and AI product managers who build what the tooling needs. You can read all of this from outside. Five counts: original share, sourcing, corrections, roles hired against roles cut, and the metric the publisher itself reports. The parable. We hire the ones you let go. In publishing, the ones being let go are the journalists.
centre

Every organisation has a centre of gravity: the place where the thing it exists to make is made, and where, if you look honestly, the power is. In a software company it is the people who write the software, and firing developers to hire salespeople moves the centre to selling what you already have. In a design company it is the designers. In a publisher it is the people who make the content, and in a news publisher that is the journalists.
centre

So the question a hiring decision answers is: where is this company moving its centre? Fire journalists and hire for technology, and the honest answer depends on what technology. Hire engineers who build provenance, graphs, versions and the surfaces readers and agents use, and the centre stays on the content and gets stronger. Hire for traffic, engagement and content operations, which is the common case, and the centre moves to packaging. The company becomes one that takes inputs everyone else has, the wire, the press release, the trending topic, and packages them for distribution. That is a real business, and I will come back to it. It is not the business the journalists were in.
measure

The reason this is not a matter of intention is the metric. If success is measured by engagement, by pages opened and time on page, then the organisation reorganises itself around opening pages, because that is what gets rewarded, promoted and funded. Optimise for that metric and you get clickbait, whether or not anyone in the building wants it. I do not think most of the people doing this want it. The metric wants it.
measure

This site runs on a different metric, and the difference is the point. Pay after you read charges a reader pence for how far they read and then asks how useful it was, and that sets the price. The site is an inbox is a brief for signals a reader produces on their own terms and can see, with a rule that nothing is placed to make them scroll. Those metrics measure value to the reader. A publisher that measured success that way would reorganise itself around being worth reading to the end and worth paying for afterwards, and that is a different hiring plan from the one the tracker records. The metric is a hiring plan in disguise. That is the sentence I would put to a board.
spectrum

I want to be fair about this, because it is a spectrum and context matters. There are organisations whose product is packaging, and they know it: they aggregate, they summarise, they distribute, they sell attention to advertisers, and they do not claim to be doing original reporting. For them, hiring for engagement is coherent. The problem is the world they live in. How news got here has the numbers: Facebook referrals to publishers down 58% in six years; the advertising that was 82 cents of every dollar in 2005 now overtaken by circulation; American newspaper newsrooms down from about 71,000 jobs to about 31,000 between 2008 and 2020, a loss of 57%. And Sixteen thousand fetches, ten clicks has the newest one: answer engines fetching a small publisher's pages 16,000 times in a week and sending 10 readers back. The attention business is getting smaller and harder every year, and a publisher that moves its centre of gravity into it is moving into a shrinking room.
spectrum

At the other end is the organisation that wants only to do journalism and sell it on paper, or feed it to someone else. That can be coherent too. But a normal media organisation, one that wants readers of its own, has to cover the whole thing: the reporting, and the stack that makes the reporting worth more than the paper it is printed on. Which brings me to the opposite cut.
engineers

If a publisher has no developers, no engineers, no AI product managers, nobody doing the kind of work I do here, it fails the other way round. The journalism is done, and then nothing enables it. There is no graph of the story, so a correction is a new document that nothing cites. There is no provenance a reader can check, so trust is a byline and a hope. There are no versions, so what changed is invisible. There are no surfaces for the agents that increasingly do the reading, so the work is scraped and summarised by someone else's machine with no way to be paid. There is no meter, so the only models left are the two bad ones. The reporting is done, and then it is thrown away as a PDF of the paper.
engineers

Jonathan Palmer put this well in the post I answered yesterday: "This isn't about replacing journalists with engineers. Journalistic expertise and their networks create the underlying advantage." The engineers are there to capture more of the value the journalists create. Fire the journalists and there is nothing to capture. Fire the engineers and it is not captured.
hire

So the hiring plan I would argue for, and the one this site is a working example of: Keep the journalists, and tool them. The tooling handed over as "this makes you better", never "this is going to replace you". That is the whole business case of most of the articles on this site, and it is the difference between a journalist who uses an agent to follow a claim to its source in a minute and one who was replaced by an agent that cannot.
hire

Hire the roles that turn a notebook into a graph. In One article, five readers the roles are a Librarian that catalogues every fact, claim, number and source with its sentence, a Cartographer and Ontologist that builds the concepts and draws the maps, a Historian that says what a piece added and where it sits, an Explainer and a Storyteller. On this site those are agents with role files. In a publisher they should be people, AI-enabled, with the same role files, because the value they make, the graph, is the thing the agent will pay for. Hire the engineers and the AI product managers. The people who build the back end, the non-functional requirements, the provenance, the versions, the surfaces, the meter. Not instead of the journalists. For them. Measure value to the reader, and let the metric do the reorganising.
hire

The parable I keep coming back to is one I cannot source, so take it as a story. A large company complains that it cannot innovate, cannot move, cannot find the people. It asks a fast-growing competitor how it does it, and the answer is: we hire the ones you let go. In most organisations the good ones leave first, because they want to do the work. In publishing right now the good ones are the journalists, and the tracker says they are being let go by the thousand. Someone will hire them. The question for a publisher is whether it wants to be the one that did, with the tooling, or the one that handed them over.
outside

None of this requires access to a publisher's strategy. The centre of gravity is visible from outside, in five counts, and the newsroom's agents already do most of them on other people's content, as they did for twenty-one World News Day op-eds. Original share. Of the pieces published this month, how many carry original reporting: a byline that did the work, a primary source a reader can open, a quote that is not from a press release. Sourcing. How many claims link to the thing they rest on, and how many of those links still resolve. Corrections. How many were published, where they appear, and whether the pages that cited the corrected claim know. Corrections must propagate is the standard; few publishers meet it, and we do not yet either.
outside

Roles. In the last twelve months of job postings and cuts, the ratio of content-making roles to traffic and packaging roles, and whether the engineers were cut with the journalists or kept. Reach's 220 cut and 60 created is a number of this kind; what the 60 are is the signal. The metric they report. What the publisher itself calls success, in its own words, in its results and its job advertisements. Run those five on any publisher and you have its real strategy, whatever the strategy document says. We have enough data on this site to run them on ourselves, and the honest result would be: original share high, sourcing high, corrections kept but not yet propagating, roles all agents and one person, and a metric that measures value to the reader with almost no readers yet. That is where I would start the map, and I would publish it.
limits

The tracker is a tracker. Press Gazette's figures are for the UK and US, are described as "at least", and the 2026 page has no running total; the entries above are its words as of October 2026. I do not know the inside of any of these decisions. Some cuts are survival, some are a change of owner, some are the thing I am describing. The argument is about what the decision signals and what the metric does, not about any one publisher's motives. The parable is unsourced. I have heard it attributed to more than one company and I cannot verify any of them. This site is not a publisher at scale. Seventy-odd articles by one author, written from voice memos by agents, is a working example of the stack, not proof that a newsroom of two hundred can adopt it. The page for publishers is where we say what is live and offer to try it.
limits
If you run a newsroom and are deciding who to cut, or you were cut and want to see what the tooling looks like when it is for you, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 12 October 2026, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The job-cut figures and the quoted entries are from Press Gazette's journalism job cuts tracker for 2026, read on 12 October 2026, which also gives the 2023, 2024 and 2025 totals; the McClatchy detail is from Chris Mills Rodrigo, Cutting Local Journalists, McClatchy Embraces AI Content, Tech Policy Press, 8 October 2026. The historical staffing and revenue numbers are from How news got here and its sources at Pew Research Center. Jonathan Palmer's sentence is from his post on LinkedIn of 10 October 2026. The figure was drawn for this article. Abstract: Years ago, during a security assessment, I packaged an exploit as a bookmarklet, a bookmark that runs a line of JavaScript on the page you are on, and gave it to the business owner to show that one user could see data they should never see. She was more excited about the interface I had wrapped it in than about the vulnerability, because my quick Bootstrap page was so much better than the application she used every day. That story still describes most of the web. Sites are built to show ads and hold attention, not to let me read; even the newest products have gaps their own users could fix in a line of code. My argument is that the next generation of user experience is the one the user customises, and that sites should encourage it: publish a small JavaScript API for the page, the primitives a fix needs, so that every fix is one line, the same API serves tests and agents, and the fixes people keep become a better brief than the site could write itself. It is also the cheapest route to accessibility, because each reader can build what they need on primitives the site provides. This newsroom now does it: a page API with six fixes, from reading mode to WCAG text spacing, as buttons, bookmarklets and code. The rest is a brief: a community library of fixes, per-site extensions that only touch the tab you click, and the same API on sgit.ai and ruv.sgit.ai.
One click on this newsroom: an article as published, and the same page after three fixes from its page API.
in-short

A bookmarklet is a line of code you click. I learnt to use them breaking into websites. My best demo was remembered for its UI. The exploit mattered less to the owner than the better interface. Most sites still fight their readers. Built for ads and attention, not for the person reading. The next UX is customised by the user. And paid for, so someone else keeps it working. Sites should publish the primitives. A page API makes every fix one line, and serves tests and agents too. The fixes are briefs. The ones people keep are the roadmap; adopt them, and the script disappears. It is the cheapest accessibility there is. Each reader builds what they need, on what the site provides. It runs here. Six fixes on this newsroom, as buttons, bookmarklets and an API.
story

A long time ago, when most of my work was finding vulnerabilities in other people's software, I picked up a habit. Instead of describing an attack, I would write it as a small piece of JavaScript and run it in the page: log in, go to a particular screen, call what needed calling, show the result. Often I packaged it as a bookmarklet: a bookmark whose address is a line of JavaScript instead of a web page. You click it, and it runs on whatever page you are on. Nothing to install.
story

On one assessment I found an injection flaw in a business application that let one user see data they should never have been able to see, much of it personal. To show the business owner what that meant, I wrapped the whole thing in a bookmarklet and gave it to her: click here. It pulled the records out and laid them in a clean interface I had thrown together with Bootstrap. Her reaction was not the one I expected. She was far more excited about the interface than about the vulnerability. Could they have this? I said that this was a serious finding, the kind that is a legal problem when personal data is involved. Yes, she said, but can we have this UI? It was so much better than the one she used every day.
story

I still think about that, because it says something true about software. That application was legacy even then, and its users had simply stopped expecting anything better. A security consultant's afternoon of Bootstrap beat years of the product.
problems

Most of the web has the same problem today, and it is not only legacy software. LinkedIn is designed to show ads and drive engagement; when I want to read a post, I get a menu, suggestions and a feed I did not ask for. YouTube, when I want to watch one video, gives me fifty things competing for my attention. Newspapers wrap their article in everything except the article. Even the newest products, the AI assistants built by some of the best engineering teams in the world, have interface gaps their users notice in the first hour and could fix in a line of code.
problems

Some of that is not the site's fault: there are always more requests than time. But much of it is, because the best teams have the means to let users change what they need and have not done it. The default experience is built for the average user and for the business model. Nobody's experience is the average.
customised

My argument is simple. The next generation of user experience is the one the user customises: the reading mode, the layout, the contrast, the things hidden and the things kept, set by the person reading, for themselves. And then, as I argued in Software vendors should become villagers and town planners, it is the one they pay for, so that somebody else keeps their customisation working through every release. I do not want to maintain my fixes. I would like to make them, and pay someone to keep them alive.
customised

People already do this, at the edges. Bookmarklets have been around since the early web. Userscript managers, from Greasemonkey to Tampermonkey and Violentmonkey, run community scripts from libraries like Greasy Fork; Stylus does the same with user styles; Arc's Boosts let you restyle a site from inside the browser. Every browser has a reader mode. What all of them have in common is that the site is not involved. They guess at its structure, they break when it changes, and the most capable of them need an extension with access to every site you visit.
primitives

The fix is for the site to take part. If a page publishes a small JavaScript API, the primitives a fix needs, then a fix is one line, it does not break when the markup changes, and it does not need to guess. We already have the convention. The SGraph tools put each tool's API on the page at window.__tools, announce it with a tool:ready event, and describe it in an api.json; the principle, in the architect's review, is "API is the tool, UI is a consumer". The same surface that a user's fix calls is the one Playwright tests call, and the one an agent driving a browser calls. A page with an API is a page that can be automated, tested and fixed with the least code, by people and by agents alike. How the user's fix becomes a brief: the site publishes primitives, readers write fixes and the site adopts popular ones.
primitives

And here is the part sites should want. A fix a user writes, and keeps, is a better brief than any the site could write itself: what a real person needed, in a form that runs. It is explorer coding applied to the page in front of you. The fixes many people keep should become settings, and then the script disappears, because the product does it. This newsroom has done exactly that once already: the first outside reaction to its Industry Wire was two words on WhatsApp, "Dark mode!", and five themes shipped soon after. The personal fixes that stay personal are where the vendor becomes the villager and is paid to maintain them.
accessibility

There is a large accessibility angle here, and I think it is where the money is for companies. Every reader's needs are different: bigger text, more spacing, higher contrast, no motion, no clutter, a different order. A site that tries to build every variation itself never finishes. A site that publishes the primitives, and lets each reader build, or install, what they need, serves far more people for far less. The standards already point this way. WCAG's success criterion 1.4.12, Text Spacing, asks that content survive a user changing line, paragraph, letter and word spacing, which assumes users will. And in the European Union the European Accessibility Act has applied to many consumer services since 28 June 2025, which gives companies a reason to care about this beyond good intentions.
delivery

There are three ways to deliver a fix, and the order matters. How Who triggers it What it can reach Notes A bookmarklet The reader, by clicking The page they are on, when they click Nothing to install; a site's Content Security Policy can block it, or the script it loads An extension per site, with activeTab The reader, by clicking the extension The current tab only, until they leave it Chrome's activeTab grants "temporary access to the currently active tab when the user invokes the extension", with no install warning A userscript manager Runs on its own Every site it is allowed on Chrome now requires an "Allow User Scripts" toggle for its userScripts API; one extension with broad access
delivery

I prefer the first two, because the reader is the one who clicks. I do not like one extension with access to every site I visit; one small extension per site, that only touches the tab I click it on, is a much smaller thing to trust. Such an extension could be shipped from a GitHub repository or an encrypted vault and loaded locally, so the reader can see exactly what they are installing.
here

So we did it for this newsroom. Fix the page is a page with six fixes, each one a button to try, a bookmarklet to drag to your bookmarks bar, and a call on a page API: Reading mode. Only the text, in one column: no menu, no strip, no chips, no footer. Bigger text. Everything at 125%. High contrast. Black on white, links underlined. Text spacing. The spacing WCAG 1.4.12 says a page must survive. Outline. A box of the page's headings, to jump around. Markdown. The same page as its markdown twin, which every article here has.
here

Underneath is one small file, page-fixes.js, versioned and immutable at its path, which puts an API at window.__tools.page: list(), apply(name, on), toggle(name) and reset(), with an api.json that describes it. A bookmarklet is one line that loads the file if needed and calls toggle. What a reader turns on is remembered for this site, in their browser, and nothing leaves it. The same API is what a Playwright test or an agent calls. The page also has a fix that needs no file at all: a generic reading mode for any site, in one line. It shows the limit of fixing a site from the outside. It hides the usual tags, and it gets the rest wrong, because it has to guess. The newsroom's own reading mode does not guess, because the site says which parts are its chrome.
brief

This is the plan, for this site and its neighbours. Load the page API on every page of the newsroom, so a fix never needs the loader, and name the parts of each page in it, not only the chrome. A community library of fixes. One file per fix, versioned paths, each with the one-line bookmarklet beside it, and a page per site listing what exists. A per-site extension with activeTab, built from that library, shipped from a GitHub repository or a vault, loaded locally. The same API on sgit.ai and ruv.sgit.ai, so the fixes are a family, not a one-off. Count which fixes are kept, in the reader's own record, sent only if they choose, and treat the list as the roadmap. Adopt the popular ones into settings and themes, and retire their scripts.
brief

Let a model write the fix. Chrome now ships a model in the tab; a reader should be able to say what they want changed and get a one-line fix on the page API, to keep or throw away. Pay to keep it. Personal fixes, maintained across releases, are a product, as the villagers argument says. There is more to say about design itself, and that will be the subject of a site of its own.
limits

Other sites can refuse it. A strict Content Security Policy can block a bookmarklet or the script it loads. Six fixes, one site. A start, not a library. No extension yet. The per-site extension is designed here, not built. The security story is from memory. The details of that assessment are years old and deliberately left out. Customisation is not a substitute for good defaults. It is what a good default makes room for. If you have a fix you would like on this site, or a site you would like fixed, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Abstract: RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policy is written before an agent runs, in four words: reach, mandate, gap and barriers. This article proposes two more. The footprint is what the agent actually did, read afterwards from logs, traffic and vault history, with nobody inline and no production access needed. Compared with the mandate it gives two kinds of finding: footprint in the gap, which is a near miss, and dormant mandate, which is a check that never ran or a mandate that asked for too much. Read on its own it gives the mandate as practised, a policy reverse-engineered from evidence. Blast radius is the measure that goes with any of them: what it would cost the business if a row of the reach were used in full, today. The same footprint can carry a different blast radius on different days, which is why a near miss on an empty table and an incident on a full one are the same row in the record. One figure carries the whole argument: the gap as a map, each row shaded by what it would cost and marked if there is no way back.

The gap as a map, for an illustrative inbox agent. Every row is something the agent can reach. The bands say whether a row is in the mandate, and whether the footprint has touched it. The barrier column is RiskMandate's four kinds. The shading is blast radius, what it would cost if the row were used in full today, hatched where there is no way back. The red dots are footprint in the gap, which is a near miss. The row to fix first is high blast radius, irreversible, with nothing but an expectation in front of it, whether or not the footprint has reached it yet. Placeholder capabilities and counts.

The policy is written before the agent runs. Reach is what it can do, measured. Mandate is what you asked it to do. The gap is the difference, in both directions. Barriers are what stands in the way of each row of the gap, typed as a boundary, a setting, an expectation or nothing, and only a boundary is a control. Footprint is what it actually did, read afterwards. From the connector's audit log, the model's tool-call log, the vault's commit history, the append lane's record, or a connector twin's replay. Nothing sits inline. Nobody needs production access. It accumulates, so some of what it shows only appears over weeks. Footprint in the gap is a near miss. The agent went somewhere you did not ask it to go and nothing stopped it. Each one resolves one of two ways: add the row to the mandate, because the mandate was incomplete, or put a boundary in front of it.

Dormant mandate is a finding too. A row you asked for that the footprint never shows. The mandate asked for too much, or a check you were relying on never ran, or the agent cannot do it and the reach inventory missed the shortfall. Read alone, the footprint is the mandate as practised. For an agent that has no written policy, it is the fastest honest way to write one: here is what your agent does, now tell me which rows you meant. Blast radius is the measure, not another set. It is what it would cost the business if a row were used in full, today. It is defined over the reach, because whoever takes the agent over inherits its reach and ignores its mandate. It changes with context while the row does not. And it has a second axis the industry usually leaves out: whether there is a way back.
The gap plus blast radius is the risk. The gap is exposure. Blast radius is impact. The person who accepts a gap is accepting its blast radius, and until now the policy did not say what that was.

RiskMandate's policy starts from a simple observation that keeps proving true: what an agent can do and what it was asked to do are different lists, and almost nobody has written down either. So the method measures the reach from the deployment itself, the account, the connectors, the credentials, the tools. It elicits the mandate from the owner, in minutes, in their words. It derives the gap, which runs in both directions: excess, where the agent can and you did not ask, and shortfall, where you asked and it cannot. And for every row of the excess it records the barrier, typed honestly. A boundary is enforced above the agent's reach, so it cannot flip it. A setting is a switch the agent's own account could flip. An expectation is a rule in prose, enforced by nobody. None is none. Only the boundary is a control, and most of what organisations call controls turn out to be expectations once they are typed. The Kit Bag plan did this for a browser extension before any code was written and found thirteen rows in the gap, four of them stopped by the platform and the rest by nothing but the code as written.

All four of those words describe the agent before it runs. That is deliberate and it is the method's strength: the point is to decide in advance, so that the decision exists before the incident does. But it leaves out the one thing that an incident review always asks for first, which is what actually happened. The footprint is the set of things the agent actually did, in a period, read from the record afterwards. It is the same kind of thing as the reach and the mandate, a list of rows, which is what makes the comparisons below possible. It is different in one way that matters: it is evidence, not a decision. Where does it come from? From wherever the agent's actions leave a trace, and there are more of those than people expect: The connector's own audit log. Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 and the rest record what an account did, and an agent runs as an account.

The model provider's record of tool calls, where the deployment keeps it. A connector twin, which records what the agent saw and asked for at the connector and can replay it. It was argued for as a deployment requirement; it is also the cleanest footprint recorder there is, because it sits exactly where the actions cross the line. A vault's commit history. Every agent on this site that works in a vault leaves a signed, versioned record of every file it touched, and the append lanes record every message that went down them. The agent's own messages. Agents here talk to each other in files, and a file is a trace.

Three properties follow from reading rather than intercepting. It is passive: nothing sits inline, nothing adds latency, nothing can break the agent by being there. It needs no production access: a copy of the logs, or a read key to the vault, is enough, which is why an outside reviewer can do it. And it accumulates over time: the first week's footprint says little, the twelfth week's says a great deal, and some findings only exist at the twelfth week. Put the footprint beside the mandate and the reach, and four things fall out.

Footprint in the gap. The agent did something that is within its reach and outside its mandate, and whatever barrier was there did not stop it, because it was an expectation or nothing. In the safety disciplines this is a near miss, and it is the most valuable kind of finding there is, because it arrives before the damage. It resolves one of two ways, and the owner decides which. Either the mandate was incomplete, which is normal for a new agent, and the row joins the mandate. Or the agent should not have gone there, and the row gets a boundary. Either way the gap shrinks, and the policy is more honest than it was.

Dormant mandate. A row the owner asked for that the footprint never shows. This one has three possible causes, and telling them apart is the review. The mandate may be over-stated: the owner asked for things the job does not need, which is how permissions creep in the first place, and the row should go. Or a check the owner was relying on never ran: the mandate said "escalate to a human when a payment is mentioned", fourteen payment threads went past, and the escalation row is empty. That is a control that exists on paper only, and finding it from the logs is better than finding it from the incident. Or the agent cannot do it at all, and the shortfall side of the gap missed it. One caveat that the method has to carry: some rows are supposed to be dormant. "May escalate" should rarely fire. So each mandate row wants a hint of how often the owner expects to see it, always, sometimes, rarely, hopefully never, and the comparison is against that.

Footprint outside the reach. This should be impossible by construction, so when it appears, the reach inventory is wrong, and that is a finding about the measurement rather than the agent. Barrier hits. Attempts that a boundary stopped are also in the record, and they are the footprint of the barriers. A boundary that stops something every week has earned its place. An expectation, by definition, has no hits, because nothing was there to record the stop. The mandate as written beside the mandate as practised, for the same illustrative agent. Four rows used, two dormant, two excursions into the gap. The left side is a set of decisions made in advance. The right side is evidence. The owner decides what each difference means.

Turn the comparison round and it becomes a way to write a policy for an agent that has none, which is most agents. Read the footprint for a month and you have the mandate as practised: the rows the agent actually uses, in order of frequency, with the near misses marked. Put that in front of the owner and the conversation is a different one from the usual elicitation. Not "what do you want this agent to do?", which produces a wish list, but "here is what your agent does; which of these did you mean, and which of these worries you?" The written mandate that comes out of that is grounded in evidence from the first draft.

This matters most for agents at the genesis end of the strip, built in an afternoon and running for months, where nobody wrote anything down because the thing was an experiment until it was not. The Custom UIs article described a team of ten agents that grew that way in eight days. Six of them have a written policy; the footprint is how the other four get one without anyone having to remember what they were for. Reach, mandate, gap, barriers and footprint are all lists of rows. Blast radius is not. It is a measure that attaches to a row, or to a set of rows: what it would cost the business if that row were used in full, today.

The term comes from explosives and the cloud operators made it ordinary. AWS uses it for the scope of a failure, the chaos engineering people for the scope of an experiment, and the identity vendors for the scope of a credential. It needs no definition fight, which is why it is the right word. In the policy it should mean one narrow thing: the impact if the agent's reach were exercised, by the agent or by whoever controls it. That last clause is the reason to define blast radius over the reach and not over the mandate. An attacker who takes an agent over, through a prompt injection, a poisoned document, a compromised skill, inherits the agent's reach and ignores its mandate entirely. The ultimate insider has a blast radius, and it is the reach. The mandate tells you what you hoped for. The reach tells you what you are exposed to.

Three things make the measure useful rather than decorative. It is about the business, not the system. "Can delete the database" is a row of the reach. Its blast radius is not "the database"; it is what the business loses when the database is gone, which depends entirely on what is in it, who depends on it, and whether there is a copy. The same row on a staging database full of test data and on the production ledger the week before the audit has the same name and a completely different blast radius. This is why blast radius connects the policy to the risk register rather than to the infrastructure diagram: it is the impact column, and the person who owns the impact is the person who fills it in.

It has a before reading and an after reading. Potential blast radius is computed from the reach, before the agent runs: the worst the deployment could do. Realised blast radius is what the footprint actually touched, read against the context at the time. The first is what you accept when you deploy. The second is what you learn when you review. They should converge as the policy matures, and when they do not, the gap is where the surprises are.

It has a second axis: whether there is a way back. The industry's blast radius is usually a scope, how far the damage spreads. For agents the more useful second question is whether the damage can be undone. Sending an email as the owner cannot be unsent. Permanently deleting a message is, as the platform's own documentation says, permanent. Forwarding mail to an outside address is quietly reversible for the mailbox and not at all for the mail that already left. Writing to an append-only vault with history can be rolled back in a minute. Two rows with the same scope and different reversibility are not the same risk, and the policy should say so. The property that took longest to see is that the footprint is fixed and the blast radius is not. An action, once taken, is a row in the record and stays there. What it would have cost depends on the moment.

Same footprint, different blast radius. An agent drops a staging table three times over two months. The row in the footprint is identical each time. On day three the table was empty and nobody noticed. On day twenty-two it held a week of test data and somebody shrugged. On day forty-one it held six weeks of real records and it was the incident. The footprint lets the review say: this is not the first time. Illustrative.

Picture an agent with a cleanup step that drops a staging table. The first time it runs, the table is nearly empty, and nobody notices. The second time, there is a week of test data in it, and somebody shrugs. The third time, six weeks of real records have been landing in that table because another process changed, and it is the incident. The action is the same row, three times. If the footprint was being read, the review on day forty-one can say something that is otherwise impossible to say: this is not the first time. The same row is in the footprint on day three and day twenty-two. It was a near miss twice before the table had anything in it.

That sentence is worth the whole method. It turns the incident from a surprise into the third occurrence of a known pattern, and it means the near miss could have been caught at the first occurrence, when it cost nothing, if anyone had been looking at the footprint against the gap. The safety disciplines learned this a long time ago: the incidents and the near misses are the same events with different luck, and the organisations that get safer are the ones that review the near misses. The footprint is how you get near misses for agents without waiting for the luck to run out.

None of the comparison idea is new, and the article would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. The cloud identity tooling has been comparing permissions granted with permissions used for years. AWS IAM Access Analyzer added unused-access findings in November 2023 and, from June 2024, recommends a refined policy from the access activity. Google Cloud's role recommendations compare a principal's permissions with those used in the last ninety days and will not recommend removing one that was used. Microsoft Entra's Permission Creep Index scores the difference between permissions granted and permissions exercised, weighted by how much damage the permissions could do, which is a blast radius over the grant, and Microsoft's own report on it found workload identities using under five per cent of what they were granted. These are the footprint against the reach, done at scale, and anyone deploying agents on a cloud should turn them on.

What they cannot do is the other half, because a permission set carries no statement of intent. There is no mandate in an IAM policy, so there is no such thing as a dormant mandate, no "you asked for a check and it never ran", no near miss in the sense of "the agent went where you did not mean it to", only "the identity used a permission". The owner's intent is the thing the Agent Behaviour Policy adds, and once it exists the footprint can be read against it. That is the whole proposal: take a comparison the cloud already makes and give it the one input it never had. This site is about encrypted vaults, so it is fair to ask what they have to do with any of this. Two things, and they are different.

The first is that a vault is a footprint recorder by construction. Every commit is signed, versioned and append-only; every message down an append lane is recorded with its token and its time; a read key lets a reviewer read all of that without touching anything. An agent that works in a vault leaves a footprint whether or not anyone intended to collect one, and a reviewer can read it from outside production with a key that cannot write. The connector twin does the same for the connectors, which is where most agents' reach actually lives.

The second is reversibility, which is the axis the industry's blast radius leaves out. Barriers shrink the reach. Containment and reversibility shrink the blast radius, and they are different levers. A read key caps the blast radius of a row at disclosure. A lane token caps it at queue pollution. Only a vault key reaches the integrity of the record, and even then the history is there to roll back to. Most of what sgit does for agents, once you look at it through this lens, is shrink the irreversible part of the blast radius: the agent can do a great deal, and almost none of it is permanent.

Before, during, after. Reach, mandate, gap and barriers are written before the agent runs. Barriers act during. The footprint is read after, from logs, traffic and vault history, with nothing inline and no production access. Blast radius has a potential reading, from the reach, and a realised reading, from the footprint. Findings go back into the policy.

The honest status is that this is a proposal with the pieces in place and the worked example still to do. We have ten agents, six with a written policy, all working in vaults, all talking in files, with eight days of commit history and several hundred messages between them. The next step is to read that footprint against the six policies and publish the result: which rows were used, which were dormant, where the footprint went into the gap, and what each finding resolved into. We are building that now, and it will be the second article. The counts will come from the vaults' history and nothing in it will name a contact or quote a message.

What we expect to find, from having watched it happen, is that the near misses are mostly mandate gaps rather than misbehaviour, because the mandates were written quickly for agents that were still changing, and that at least one check we wrote into a policy has never fired. We would rather publish that than claim the method and leave the evidence to the reader's imagination. The brief to the RiskMandate team asks for five things, in this order of usefulness: Footprint as a section of the policy, with a period, a source for each row, and the four derived findings: footprint in the gap, dormant mandate, footprint outside reach, barrier hits. An expected-use hint on every mandate row: always, sometimes, rarely, hopefully never. Without it, a dormant row cannot be told from a contingency that was never needed.

Blast radius on every row of the gap, on a short scale the owner fills in against the business, with the reversible-or-not flag beside it. Five steps is plenty. The figure at the top uses none, low, a bad day, serious, the business. The mandate as practised as a view the tooling can produce from a footprint alone, for agents with no written policy yet. A review cadence, because the footprint accumulates and the blast radius moves. Monthly for a new agent, quarterly once the potential and the realised readings have converged. With those, the policy says what the agent can do, what you asked, what stands in the way, what it actually did, and what each of those would cost. That is the risk, written down, in a form a risk owner can accept or refuse, and in a form an auditor can check against the logs without asking anyone for access.

The ultimate insider: why an agent's reach, not its mandate, is what an attacker inherits. Every risk is already accepted: the person who accepts the gap is accepting its blast radius, and the policy should say what that is. Before you give an agent a connector, give the connector a twin: the footprint recorder at the line where the reach is exercised. Six agents, one inbox: the first policy on this site, written before the near misses. Custom UIs are not the exception: the ten agents whose footprint we will read next. Vaults: Kit Bag, a policy written before the code; Connector Twin; RiskMandate; Risk acceptance. RiskMandate.ai for the policy itself, and the brief that carries this proposal to its team.

Abstract: A paper reached me this week, AI Risk Management Frameworks, issue 81 of iason's research series, dated November 2025, by Sara Martucci and Margherita Ranieri with Nicola Mazzoni. It reads four instruments side by side, the OECD's classification of AI systems, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, Japan's AI Guidelines for Business and the EU AI Act, and ends with five principles they share, ethics and human rights, the lifecycle, human oversight, risk tiering with proportionality, and governance as an organisational habit rather than a compliance exercise. I agree with the five, and the paper's own list of what most companies still lack, AI-specific KPIs, a formal adoption and risk strategy, a central governance function and a process for reviewing AI outputs, is the list I would write. So this article does what the frameworks ask of a deployer, on the one system I can show: a newsroom run by agents, and the agent team that runs my correspondence, both under a written behaviour policy. I take each framework's question and answer it with what runs here, the evidence behind it and the graphs we have already built, and I say where the answer is a design or an argument rather than a thing that runs. Two things come out of the mapping. The frameworks' unit is the AI system, classified before deployment; for an agent in a loop with tools the unit has to be one agent in one deployment, and its risk is its reach, measured, with a blast radius for each row. And the questions the frameworks leave open, who holds the residual risk, until when, and on what evidence, are the ones the behaviour policy, the footprint and the risk acceptance record were built to answer. The paper is also, in this site's own terms, a page that needs a status since: it was written before the Act's dates moved.
Four frameworks, as iason's paper reads them, against what runs here, marked as running, designed or argued.
in-short

Four frameworks, four grains. The OECD classifies a system along five dimensions; NIST runs four functions, govern, map, measure and manage; Japan assigns duties to developers, providers and business users; the EU AI Act assigns obligations by tier. The paper's reading is that they converge on five principles, and I think that is right. The unit is wrong for agents. Each of the four classifies an AI system before it is deployed. An agent in a loop with tools is one agent in one deployment, and its risk is its reach, measured, with a blast radius for each row of it. Govern is a written policy, map is the gap, measure is the footprint, manage is three doors. Each of NIST's functions has a mechanism here, running on a real system, with the article that describes it and the numbers it produced.
in-short

Human oversight by reversibility, not by tier. A person sits where an output cannot be undone; everywhere else, controls that do not get tired. People approve 93% of what they are shown. Accepted is not acceptable. The Act asks for residual risk to be "judged to be acceptable" and does not define the word. Here a risk has a holder, an interval and the facts that would end it. Three roles, and the policy is the contract between them. Japan's developer, provider and business user are the model vendor, the platform and the deployer. A policy beside the prompt is what each one signs for. The graphs exist for two of the four. The Act parsed into a graph; a control framework joined to the Act's text; a ten-layer stack with 119 edges drawn from provisions. The paper's four as one graph is the next one, and the mapping published with this article is its first file.
in-short

The paper needs a status since. It was written in November 2025. The Act's dates moved in July 2026, and software becomes a product under the EU's liability rules on 9 December 2026. How far it goes here. Of the five principles, four run, on one newsroom and one agent team; the fifth, risk acceptance as a record, is a published design with a demo behind it.
paper

The paper is iason's AI Risk Management Frameworks, research paper series 2025, issue 81, dated November 2025, written by Sara Martucci and Margherita Ranieri and prepared with Nicola Mazzoni. iason advises financial institutions on risk, and the paper reads that way: a first part on the market and its investment, a second on the risks AI adds, with a view from the financial industry, a third on regulation with the EU AI Act at the centre, and a fourth on three frameworks, the OECD's classification, NIST's AI RMF and Japan's guidelines for business.
paper

What it gets right is the shape. The four instruments are different grains of the same thing. The OECD framework is a lens, not an obligation: five dimensions along which to describe a system, People and Planet, Economic Context, Data and Input, AI Model, Task and Output. NIST is a process: four functions, each with numbered outcomes, Govern 1 to 6, Map 1 to 5, Measure 1 to 4, Manage 1 to 4. Japan's guidelines are a division of labour: Parts 3, 4 and 5 are what developers, providers and business users each owe. The Act is law: four tiers, prohibitions in force since February 2025, and a list of obligations for the high-risk tier. The paper's conclusion is that despite the differences they "converge around a common set of core principles", and it names five: ethics and human rights at the centre, the lifecycle as the foundation of governance, human oversight as a safeguard, risk tiering and proportionality, and an organisational approach, governance "as a corporate mindset" rather than procedures alone. Its last page says what I would say to a board: "too often, risk management is perceived as a compliance exercise, a necessary but limiting set of controls", and that in AI this is "strategically shortsighted".
paper

It is also honest about where companies are. Its list of what many still lack has four items: KPIs defined for AI, formal adoption and risk strategies, a central governance structure, and "processes for reviewing AI-generated outputs for accuracy and ethical compliance". That fourth one is where this site has spent most of its time, so the rest of this article is a mapping: the paper's four frameworks and five principles on one side, and on the other what runs here, what it produced, and where to check it.
unit

Two units: the frameworks' AI system, and the unit here, one agent in one deployment, and where each framework attaches. Before the mapping, the one disagreement, because it decides how the rest reads. All four instruments take the AI system as their unit: the thing a provider puts on the market, which a deployer puts into service. The OECD describes it, NIST maps it, the Act tiers it, and the work is done before deployment, with monitoring after. For a model behind a form, that is the right unit.
unit

For an agent it is not, and the paper's own list of what makes AI risky says why: "autonomy", "non-deterministic behavior", "reliance on externally managed foundation models". An agent is the same model, run in a loop, with tools. What it can do is not a property of the model; it is a property of the connectors it was given, the accounts it runs under and the data it can see. In Authority outside the model I put it as the thing that list leaves out: risk is a property of one agent in one setup, not of the model. The same model that drafts an email with no way to send it, and the same model with a send button and a customer database, are not the same system, and no tier assigned to the model tells you which one you have.
unit

So the unit here is one agent in one deployment, and its description is the Agent Behaviour Policy: the reach, what the agent can do, measured from its connectors and accounts rather than declared; the mandate, what it was asked to do; the gap between the two, in both directions; and for every row of the gap, what stands in the way, typed as a boundary, a setting, an expectation or nothing. Only a boundary is a control. After the agent has run, the footprint is what it actually did, read from logs, traffic and vault history. And the blast radius is the measure that goes with any row: what it would cost the business if that row were used in full, today, and whether there is a way back. That is the classification, the map, the measurement and the tier, for an agent, and it is what the four frameworks attach to below.
oecd

The OECD's five dimensions describe a system well, and three of them map straight across. People and Planet asks who the system touches and what it could cost them; that is the blast radius, which is defined over the reach because whoever takes an agent over inherits its reach and ignores its mandate. AI Model asks what the model is and how it learns; for the agents here the answer is short, the same model anyone else uses, which is why the risk sits in the deployment and not in the model. Economic Context asks how critical the system is and how far it spreads; the newsroom's answer, from The human in the loop is a spectrum, is that its side effects are small because its readership is small, and that this changes the position as readership grows.
oecd

The two that matter most for an agent are Data and Input and Task and Output. Data and Input asks what the system can see, and whether it is sensitive. For an agent the question is sharper: does it have private data, untrusted content and a way to send, all three at once, the combination The policy draws the liability line calls the lethal trifecta and says every agent in a loop should take a policy for. Task and Output asks, in the paper's words, whether human intervention is "active, passive, or entirely absent at the point of decision-making". That is the right question and the wrong axis. The answer here is not a level of oversight per system; it is a position per output. The next section is NIST's, and that is where the answer lives.
nist

NIST's four functions are the easiest to map, because each one names a thing we built. The table is by the playbook's numbered outcomes as the paper lists them, with the mechanism here and the article that shows it running. The newsroom's own policies are public. The proposal that the vendor publishes its built-in policy, accepts the deployer's, and says what it enforces. Where the platform draws its line: eight scenarios run three ways, three of them becoming operating-system boundaries. Where the platform draws the line Manage 4 response and recovery The person placed where an output cannot be undone; a correction as a new version; one agent allowed one email, to one address, to put the team on hold. The human in the loop
nist

Three rows deserve a sentence each. Govern 1, the policy, is only a policy if it survives the session: Re-anchoring found that the session behind this site was summarised eighteen times in a month, about 98% of its context replaced each time, so the rules live in a file and a hook prints them back after every summary. Measure 1 is the number I would put in front of any board: when the same customer service agent was built three ways, the share of its rules kept only by the model's good behaviour fell from 97% to 23%, and the policy shrank with it, because it no longer had to forbid what the agent could not do. And Manage 4 is where the paper's human oversight lives, which is the next principle.
nist

Human oversight here is placed by one test, not by tier: can the output be undone, and how much would it cost if it were wrong. The human in the loop put a person on the outputs where the answers are no and a lot, sending an email in my name, typing a secret, spending money, and replaced the person everywhere else with controls that do not get tired, because people approve almost everything they are shown: Anthropic measured "Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts". The result, on the day that article was written, was a newsroom that shipped fourteen releases with no release approved one by one, beside an agent team that drafts every email and sends none. The OECD's "active, passive, or entirely absent" is one answer per system. Here it is one answer per output, and it moves.
japan

Japan's guidelines are the ones that come closest to how an agent is actually built, because they split the responsibility by role. Part 3 is the developer, who makes the model; Part 4 the provider, who embeds it in a system and, in the paper's summary, must "define clear operational parameters, including intended purpose, constraints, and potential risks"; Part 5 the business user, who runs it and "must continuously monitor the behavior and outputs of deployed AI systems, identify irregularities or deviations, and report them". For an agent those are the model vendor, the platform or harness the agent runs in, and the deployer, which here is me.
japan

What the guidelines do not say is what passes between the three, and that is what A policy beside the prompt proposes: every agent takes a behaviour policy as an input beside its prompt; the vendor publishes its own built-in policy and accepts the deployer's; for every row it accepts it says whether it enforces it or only asks the model to keep it; and it reports every breach. That is Part 4's "operational parameters" as a document both sides hold, and Part 5's monitoring as the footprint read against it. Where the platform draws the line shows the provider's half arriving: Microsoft's execution containers and agent control specification put the policy outside the workload and enforce it in the operating system, and when the same eight scenarios were run with a behaviour policy on top of them, three rows that had been hope became boundaries.
japan

The guidelines also call their model "agile governance", oversight that is iterative rather than fixed. Here that is the line that moves: as the record of unchanged drafts grows for one kind of message, that kind is a candidate to leave the human step, by a decision written into the policy with an owner and a date; as the newsroom's readership grows, the stage before promotion becomes a canary. And when a role fails the others, the written policy is what the argument is about. The policy draws the liability line argues that towards the world the deployer answers, as the tribunal held against Air Canada, and that between the deployer and the vendor an explicit prohibition the agent then breaks is the evidence that turns "user error" into "the product ignored what it was told". Japan's three roles are the three parties to that argument.
act

A status since the paper: its dates as of November 2025 above the line, and what this site recorded afterwards below. The Act is where the paper spends the most pages, and two things in it matter here. The first is the tier. The newsroom's own systems are low on the Act's scale: an article is not a decision about a person, and the limited-risk duty that applies to a chatbot, to say that it is one, is the disclosure this site already carries on machine-written text, for the reason Who owns the words gives, that people should read machine-written words differently. The agent team is the same: it drafts, and a person sends. Proportionality is the right principle, and here it is applied per row of reach rather than per system, because a tier for the model would miss the send button.
act

The second is a word. For a high-risk system, Article 9 of the Act requires the provider's risk management to leave residual risk "judged to be acceptable", and, as Every risk is already accepted points out, never defines acceptable. The paper restates the obligation without remarking on the gap, which is fair: it is easy to read past. Our answer is that accepted and acceptable are different things: one is a threshold, the other is an act by a named person on a date. A risk exists the moment the exposure does, so it is already being carried; the open questions are who has accepted it and until when. There are three doors, accept it for a stated interval, fund the work, or fix it, and silence is not a fourth: a risk nobody accepts rolls up to the holder's boss, and every path ends at the board. Every risk names the facts that make it true and the facts that would end it, down to the configuration file. That is what turns "judged to be acceptable" from a sentence into a record.
act

Then the dates. The paper, as of November 2025, says the Act's rules "will come fully into effect by August 2026". Since then, as The AI governance stack as a graph recorded on 9 October 2026, the Act was amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force from 27 July 2026: the Annex III high-risk obligations now apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I from 2 August 2028, and Article 4 on AI literacy was reworded. And from 9 December 2026, as The policy draws the liability line notes, software including AI systems is a product under the EU's new product liability rules. None of this makes the paper wrong; it was right on its day. It makes it exactly the case Every link points back called status since: a plan described in one document that a later one says has changed, invisible from the first. A graph keeps the label as written and records the change underneath as a dated edge. A PDF cannot.
principles

The paper's five shared principles, each against what answers it here, the evidence, and how far it goes. So, the paper's five, each on the one system I can show, and how far each goes. Ethics and human rights. Here this is a question of whose words they are. Nothing leaves the agent team without the person whose name is on it pressing send; every machine-written text on this site says so; and the responsibility for a decision an agent makes stays with whoever granted its reach. Runs.
principles

The lifecycle. Every push to this site is a release with a version, every article has versions and a diff page, every incident is written up, and the footprint is read for weeks after a run. What is missing is the end of the lifecycle the paper names, decommissioning: retiring a device and rotating the master's key are on the list of what is not built, and ending an agent's mandate has no step at all. Runs, without a retirement step. Human oversight. Placed by reversibility, enforced by controls where a person would be a rubber stamp, and measured by a record of drafts nobody had to change. Runs.
principles

Risk tiering and proportionality. Applied per row of reach with a blast radius, in the policy, which runs. Applied as a register, with holders, intervals and facts, it is the design in Every risk is already accepted, with a business plan and a field demo published, and not a thing a customer runs today. Designed. The organisational approach. The paper wants governance "as a corporate mindset involving different functions and teams". Here the organisation is one person and about fifteen agents, with the roles, the policies, the board and the log public on this site. Runs, at a scale of one, which is the limit I would put first.
graphs

The paper compares four instruments in a table and five principles in a list. A table is correct on the day it is drawn; it cannot say which paragraph of which instrument makes a cell true, or what changed under it since. That is what the graphs on this site are for, and two of the paper's four already have one.
graphs

The Act is parsed into the Regulation Graph vault from the official text, article by article. When Jan van Dijke published the AI Baseline Control Framework on 2 October, twenty controls mapped to the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the Act, it took a day to turn its spreadsheet into a semantic graph joined to the Act's own text, with eighty hyperlinked documents and the six things the graph found that the spreadsheet did not say. And when Hari Kota posted a ten-layer governance stack, the answer was a vault in which every cell is a node, 329 edges, 140 of them between layers, 119 of ours each citing the provision it rests on, and in which the Act's articles reach nine of the ten layers and NIST's reach eight. Those graphs already hold NIST and the Act. Article 26(2) of the Act, oversight assigned to persons "who have the necessary competence, training and authority", is one edge; NIST GOVERN 1.6, the inventory, is another.
graphs

The one to build next is the paper's four as one graph, and the method is the one those three used. Each framework is its own world, with its own vocabulary: the OECD's dimensions, NIST's functions and numbered outcomes, Japan's parts and roles, the Act's articles, annexes and tiers. None is asked to fit the others. The edges between the worlds come from the texts: NIST's Map 2, categorising the system, points at the OECD classification, which the paper says NIST drew on; the OECD's Task and Output oversight question, the Act's Article 14 and Japan's Part 5 are three statements of human oversight that should be one node with three sources; Govern 6, Manage 3, Japan's three roles and the Act's providers, deployers and importers are the same supply chain seen four ways. And a fifth world, the behaviour policy, so that a row of a policy can say which provision it answers, and a provision can say which rows of which agents answer it. Then the paper's five principles are not a list but five queries, and "which of our agents has no human oversight row where the Act requires one" is a traversal rather than a workshop.
graphs

The first file of that graph is published with this article: the mapping, one row for every element of the four frameworks and the five principles named above, with what answers it here, the article or vault where that can be checked, and its status. Thirty-two rows: twenty-three run, five are designed, four are argued. It is the baseline the next version measures against.
hardest

The paper's own list says what companies lack: KPIs, a strategy, a central function, and a process for reviewing outputs. If I were asked which of ownership, testing or monitoring is hardest to establish in practice, my answer from this record is none of the three, and it is the thing that comes before them.
hardest

Ownership is cheap to write and hard to keep, but a register that rolls an unaccepted risk up to the holder's boss keeps it for you. Testing is hard until it is a tool: the second reader runs on every draft, synthetic users found bugs that every unit test had passed, and the hostile mail set runs the same 62 emails through every design. Monitoring is the easiest of the three for an agent, because the footprint is read afterwards from logs the connectors already keep, with nobody inline and no production access. What is hard, and what none of the four frameworks asks for in a form an agent can carry, is the mandate: the written statement of what this agent, in this deployment, was allowed to do. Observation tells you what an agent did. Only a written mandate tells you whether it was allowed, and without one every finding in the footprint is a judgement call and every deflection in the liability line is available. That is why the policy is the first file, and why most of the mapping above ends at it.
limits

The system is small. One newsroom, one agent team, one person. The pattern is what I would defend, not the scale, and the paper is written with financial institutions in mind. The paper is read, not reproduced. It is quoted in short phrases for the argument, with its authors and issue named; iason does not permit reproduction, and this article does not do it. Its research page did not answer when this was written, so there is no link. The dates since the paper are this site's. The amendment, its application dates and the product liability date are as recorded in the two articles cited, checked on 9 and 13 October 2026; I have not re-read the regulations for this article. The NIST rows are a mapping, not a conformance claim. Each row names a mechanism that answers the outcome's intent, in my reading; the system has not been assessed against the playbook by anyone else.
limits

Risk acceptance as a register is a design. The model is published with a business plan and a demo; no customer runs it today. The graph of the four frameworks is proposed. What exists is the mapping file published with this article, the graphs of the Act and of two frameworks that cite it, and the method. Thirty-two rows is my count of my own system. Another reader of the same frameworks would draw the rows differently, and the file is there to be corrected. If you are mapping one of these frameworks onto agents in your own organisation, or you would draw the rows differently, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
