Abstract: I would like readers of this newsroom to be able to talk to it with a capable model, for free, without us paying for their questions and without us ever holding their key. The newsroom already answers questions from its own passages, with Chrome's built-in model or the reader's own OpenRouter key, and OpenRouter's free models stop at 50 requests a day until you buy credits. So we looked at every free inference offer we could find, as it stands on 18 October 2026, for material that is not private. Two things decide whether a provider works for this. Can anyone start free without a card? And can a web page call it directly, so the key goes from the reader's browser to the provider and nowhere else? We read each provider's pricing, limits and terms, and tested every API from the newsroom's own address. Four pass both tests: Groq, Google's Gemini API through AI Studio, Mistral's free mode, and OpenRouter's free models, which also offer a sign-in flow so the reader never copies a key. Cohere's trial and Pollinations pass too, with smaller limits. Cloudflare Workers AI has the most generous free allowance and does not train on what you send, but a page cannot call it, so it needs a small server the reader can deploy. NVIDIA's catalogue is strong and free, but it fails both tests that matter here, and its terms say trial use only. And a lot changed in 2026: GitHub Models was retired, Hugging Face stopped giving free accounts credits, and Cerebras and SambaNova now need a card. This is the map, what is possible, what is not, and what we will build.
Every free inference offer we checked on 18 October 2026, placed by two questions.
in-short

The goal. A reader talks to the newsroom with a capable model, free, on their own key, which we never hold. Two tests decide it. Free without a card, and callable from a web page directly. Four pass both. Groq, Gemini through AI Studio, Mistral's free mode, OpenRouter's free models. Two more, smaller. Cohere's trial, and Pollinations, which answered without any key. Cloudflare is the most generous, and needs a server. A page cannot call it; a Worker the reader deploys can. NVIDIA fails both tests that matter. A strong free catalogue, but no browser access, a phone check, and trial-only terms. 2026 took a lot away. GitHub Models retired; Hugging Face credits gone; Cerebras and SambaNova need a card. Free means they may learn from it. Fine for what this newsroom publishes; never for anything private.
want

The newsroom can already answer a question. The search page finds the passages that match, and a model answers from them alone, citing each one, with the passages shown beside the answer. There are two engines today. Chrome's built-in model runs on the reader's own machine with no key and sends nothing anywhere, but only in browsers that have it. Otherwise the reader pastes their own OpenRouter key, which stays in their browser and goes only to OpenRouter. The idea is not new here: a chat box on a site with no server set out the trade, and the key is the billing system showed a whole product built on the user's own key. The gap is the first step. OpenRouter's free models allow 50 requests a day until you have bought at least $10 of credit. Someone who just wants to try it should not need a card.
want

So the question for this research: as of October 2026, where can a member of the public sign up, get a key, and call a frontier or near-frontier model for free, from a web page, with the key going from their browser to the provider and nowhere else? The material is this newsroom's published articles, so privacy is not the concern. We assume the provider may keep and learn from what is sent, and we say where it does.
method

Two research agents read each provider's own pricing, rate-limit, model and terms pages on 18 October 2026, and called the live model lists where they could. Where a fact came only from a third party, it is marked as reported. Then we tested the one thing documentation rarely says: whether a web page can call the API at all. A browser will only send a request with a key to another site if that site answers a preflight check saying it allows it, the rule called CORS. We sent that preflight to every provider's chat endpoint, from the newsroom's own address, https://newsroom.sgit.ai, and recorded the answer. A provider that does not answer it cannot be called from a page, whatever its docs say.
method

One caution about names. Many of the model names below, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Qwen 3.8, Kimi K2.5 and others, are newer than what the agent that wrote this was trained on. They are given exactly as the providers' live pages and model lists show them.
changed

GitHub Models was retired on 30 July 2026. The playground, catalogue and inference API are gone, for everyone. It had been the easiest free option for anyone with a GitHub account. Hugging Face free accounts no longer get monthly credits for Inference Providers. Its pricing page lists "None" for free users, who can buy credits; we did not find the date of the change. Cerebras now needs a verified payment method. New accounts get $5 of credit, which expires 30 days after it is granted; the earlier free tier with no card is gone. SambaNova needs a card and bought credits before the first request, from about 14 August 2026, as reported; its rate-limit docs still describe a free tier. OpenRouter's free list changed. Today's free models are NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 family, Google's Gemma 4 and some smaller ones; the free DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi and gpt-oss variants are not on it.
changed

Google changed Gemini keys. From 28 May 2026, new AI Studio keys are "auth keys", and the API rejects requests from unrestricted standard keys. Mistral renamed its free tier. La Plateforme is now Mistral AI Studio, and the Experiment plan is now Free mode.
works

Free, with no card. Limits are per model and shown in the console; the published table gives openai/gpt-oss-120b 30 requests a minute, 1,000 a day and 200,000 tokens a day, though the page does not say which plan that table is for. Models include openai/gpt-oss-120b, openai/gpt-oss-20b, qwen/qwen3.8-27b and llama-3.3-70b-versatile. It is OpenAI-compatible at https://api.groq.com/openai/v1. Requests are not retained by default; Groq may log them for up to 30 days to troubleshoot or investigate abuse. The browser test allows any page. It is fast, and gpt-oss-120b is a capable open model. For a reader trying it, this is the simplest start. Free with a Google account, from 18, with no card. Free models include gemini-3.8-flash, gemini-3.6-flash and gemini-3.5-flash-lite, and Gemma 4; Gemini 4 and the Pro previews are not free. Limits are no longer published and are shown only inside AI Studio. There is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, under /v1beta/openai/ on generativelanguage.googleapis.com. The browser test allows the newsroom's address.
works

Two things to say plainly. On the free tier, Google uses what you send "to provide, improve, and develop Google products and services and machine learning technologies", and "human reviewers may read, annotate, and process your API input and output". And the terms carve out the UK, the EEA and Switzerland, where the paid data terms apply to all use, and where apps offered to users must use paid services. A reader in London using their own free key for their own questions is a different case from an app offering Gemini to everyone, and our guidance would need to say so.
works

New accounts start in free mode, "with no credit card required". Limits are shown in the admin console; the docs do not publish them. Which models are free is not stated; the current API includes mistral-medium-latest, mistral-small-latest and mistral-large-4. It is OpenAI-style at https://api.mistral.ai/v1. Requests may be used to improve the models unless you switch off "Anonymous improvement data" in the admin privacy settings. The browser test allows any page. Free with an account, from 18. Free models allow 20 requests a minute and 50 a day, or 1,000 a day once you have bought at least $10 of credit at some point. The free list on 18 October had 19 entries, including nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free, nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free, google/gemma-4-31b-it:free, and openrouter/free, which picks a free model for you. Whether a free model's provider keeps or learns from your words depends on the model, and OpenRouter has a separate privacy setting for free models. The browser test allows any page.
works

OpenRouter has one thing the others lack: a proper sign-in for apps. The page sends the reader to OpenRouter, they approve, and the page receives a key of their own, through OAuth with PKCE. The reader never copies or pastes a key, and can revoke it at OpenRouter. The newsroom already uses OpenRouter, so this is the shortest step. Cohere's trial key. Free on registration: 1,000 calls a month, chat at 20 a minute, with the Command A family. Its own API, not OpenAI's shape. The browser test allows any page. Pollinations. In our test, a chat request with no key at all was answered. Its docs say keys are expected, so we would treat keyless use as tolerated, not promised. It also has a "Sign in with Pollinations" flow, OAuth with PKCE, where the reader approves an app and it receives a key with its own budget. The browser test allows any page.
catch

Cloudflare Workers AI. The most generous free allowance we found: 10,000 "neurons" a day on a free Cloudflare account, which by its own rates is very roughly 100,000 to 300,000 tokens of gpt-oss-120b a day. Free models include @cf/moonshotai/kimi-k2.5, @cf/openai/gpt-oss-120b, @cf/zai-org/glm-4.7-flash and Llama 4 Scout. And "Cloudflare does not use Customer Content processed by Workers AI to train AI models." The catch: its REST API refused the browser preflight, so a page cannot call it. A Worker can, and a reader can deploy one into their own free account; then nobody else sees their key.
catch

Alibaba Model Studio, international. About a million free tokens per model, for 90 days, for first activations from 8 September 2026, on models including qwen3.8-max and deepseek-v4.1-flash, and the browser test allows the newsroom's address. It says it "will never use your data for model training". The catches: account details must be completed, and the "Free Quota Only" switch is now off by default, so a reader must turn it on or be billed once the free quota runs out. Z.ai. glm-4.7-flash and glm-4.5-flash are priced free, and are reported to allow one request at a time. The API does not answer the browser preflight, so it needs a server in between. Fireworks and DeepInfra answer the browser preflight, but offer only small starter credits: Fireworks $1, after which the account is suspended without a payment method.
not

NVIDIA, build.nvidia.com. You can sign up free, with no card, though many reports say a phone number is needed for the key. The live catalogue is strong: moonshotai/kimi-k2.6, z-ai/glm-5.3, deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash, the Nemotron 3 family, 81 models in all. But it fails the browser test: no CORS header. Its trial terms say access is "for limited trial purposes only and without use of the API Service or Generated Content in production", and that NVIDIA collects "User Content and Generated Content to improve NVIDIA products and services, including AI models". It is a good place for a developer to try models from a script. It is not something to offer readers from a page. SambaNova. No browser access, and a card and bought credits before the first request. Cerebras. A card, and $5 that lasts 30 days. Together. A $5 minimum purchase. Hugging Face Inference Providers. No free credits for free accounts. GitHub Models. Retired.
table

Provider Free, no card From the page Learns from it Groq Yes Yes Not kept by default Gemini, AI Studio Yes Yes Yes, human review; not in UK, EEA Mistral free mode Yes Yes Yes, opt-out OpenRouter free Yes, 50 a day Yes Depends on model Cohere trial Yes, 1,000 a month Yes Opt-out Pollinations Yes, even keyless Yes Not found Alibaba Model Studio Yes, 90 days Yes No Cloudflare Workers AI Yes No, needs a Worker No Z.ai Yes No Not found NVIDIA Yes, phone No Yes Cerebras, SambaNova No, card Cerebras yes Together, Hugging Face No Yes GitHub Models Retired "From the page" is our preflight test on 18 October 2026, from https://newsroom.sgit.ai. "Learns from it" is each provider's terms for free use, in short; the sections above quote them.
key

medium The design is bring your own key, and the newsroom never holds it. Where it is kept. In this browser's storage for the session, or for longer if the reader asks, or in the reader's own vault, so it follows them across devices. The vault pane already keeps a reader's account that way. Where it goes. From the reader's browser to the provider, with the question and the passages, and nowhere else. The page shows what it sent and which model answered, as the search page does today.
key

What protects it. A key in a page can be read by any script on that page, so the page that holds it must load nothing it does not control. Google's own docs say "never expose keys client-side in production"; that advice is for a developer shipping their key inside an app to everyone. Here it is the reader's key, in the reader's browser, used by the reader. Even so, the safest keys are the ones a sign-in issues, scoped to this use and revocable, and the ones with a spending limit of zero because they are free.
agents

I asked whether an agent could do the sign-up for a reader. I think it should not, for three reasons. Most sign-ups now ask for a phone number or a captcha, on purpose. OpenRouter's terms forbid "multiple accounts as a single user, for purposes of bypassing or circumventing use limits", and an agent creating accounts at scale is the obvious way to do that. And NVIDIA's forum moderators already report ten to twenty automated rate-limit requests a day written by AI agents; providers are watching for exactly this. What an agent can do well is guide: open the right page, explain each step and each setting, point at the privacy switch, check that the key works, and store it where the reader chooses. The account, and the agreement to its terms, stay the reader's. The sign-in flows from OpenRouter and Pollinations are the cleanest version: the reader approves once, and nothing is copied.
possible

Possible today, from a page, for free: A capable open model answering from the newsroom's passages: gpt-oss-120b or Qwen 3.8 on Groq, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Mistral Medium, or Nemotron 3 Ultra on OpenRouter. A sign-in instead of a pasted key, with OpenRouter or Pollinations. A key kept by the reader, in their browser or their vault, that we never see. Possible, with a server the reader runs: Cloudflare's larger free allowance and models such as Kimi K2.5, through a Worker in the reader's own account. Not possible, as far as we found: A free, keyless, dependable frontier model for everyone. Pollinations comes closest, and says it is not guaranteed. Calling NVIDIA, SambaNova or Z.ai from a page. Promising any of these limits for long. In 2026, four free offers we would have recommended at the start of the year disappeared or gained a card: GitHub Models, Hugging Face's credits, Cerebras and SambaNova.
possible
Anything private. On the free tiers, assume your words may be kept, learned from and, on Gemini, read.
plan

Later, and in this order: Add Groq, Gemini and Mistral beside OpenRouter on the search page, each with a short guide: where to sign up, which setting to check, which model to choose, and what the provider does with your words. Use OpenRouter's sign-in instead of a pasted key. Let the key live in the reader's vault, as well as in this browser. Publish a Worker a reader can deploy for Cloudflare, with the steps. Recheck this map every quarter, because it will change.
limits

A snapshot. Everything here is as of 18 October 2026, and free tiers change often. Limits move. Several providers show limits only inside their consoles; we report what is published. Third-party facts are marked. Phone checks at NVIDIA, SambaNova's date and Z.ai's concurrency are reported, not confirmed. The browser test is one test. A preflight from our address; a provider can change its headers at any time. Not legal advice. The UK, EEA and Swiss carve-outs in Gemini's terms are summarised, not interpreted. If you know a free offer we missed, or one that has changed, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

So we looked at every free inference offer we could find, as it stands on 18 October 2026, for material that is not private. Two things decide whether a provider works for this. Abstract: I think we have hit on a commercial model almost by accident. This newsroom, and the book's website, already charge per use: every reader starts with £5 of credit, and each page draws a few pence from it. Now apply that to our behaviour policies and hooks. They are open, CC BY 4.0 and Apache 2.0, and anyone may copy them. But a hook is code: Claude Code's own documentation says a plugin "can execute arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges". Taking one from a website you do not know is like downloading software from unknown sources, and a company will not do it. So the official website, with its brand, its authority, its usability and its trust, is where people will come, even for something free to copy, and it can charge per use there: a customer with £50 of credit might pay £1 for the page with a hook on it. To earn that, it cannot be us saying "trust us". The policies we publish, the hooks above all, should be reviewed and audited by others, with the scanners and services that now exist for skills and plugins, and signed with our keys. The price is something to discover.
Free to copy, paid at the source: the policy and its hook are open; the official site adds provenance and a signature.
in-short

We already charge per use. Every page on this newsroom draws a few pence from prepaid credit. Our policies and hooks are open. Anyone may copy them, fork them, run them. But a hook is code. It runs on your machine, with your permissions. So the source matters. A company will not run code from a website it does not know. The official site can charge per use, even for open content. £1 a page from £50 of credit, say. To earn it, others must review it. Scanners, audits, and a signature from our keys. The price is to discover. High or low, it is what customers are happy to pay.
meter

This is already running. On this newsroom every reader starts with £5 of credit, and each page they read draws from it: 10p for a new article read to the end, 5p for an older one, less for other pages, and in proportion to how far you read. You can set the price of a page from free to double, or refuse it, and the balance can go below zero; when you want to, you top up with a £5 payment link, which has been live since 11 October. The book's website runs the same meter. I wrote about why in paying after the value: you pay for what you have already read, not for what you hope to read. What I had not seen until now is how far that goes. It is a way to earn from the traffic to a website, whatever the website holds, and it works even when what it holds is free to copy.
open

Everything we publish about Agent Behaviour Policies is open: the vocabulary and the policies under CC BY 4.0, the code under Apache 2.0. Anyone can take a policy or a hook and use it. The fork next door argued that this is what protects our customers: if we stop delivering, someone else can carry on. But think about what a policy is for. Some of our policies are code. The hook in a leak without breaking the policy runs on every tool call an agent makes. Claude Code's own documentation is plain about what that means: "A Claude Code plugin you install can execute arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges", and hooks "are shell commands that run with your full user permissions". It also says "A marketplace's name tells you who publishes the catalog, not what each plugin in it does."
open

So a copy of our hook on a website you do not know is like downloading software from an unknown source. It might be the same text. It might not. From a company's point of view, that is not a risk worth taking for something that sits in the path of every action its agents take. They will come to the official site: the one with the brand, the authority, the current version, and the trust.
charge

That is where the model is. Even when someone uses the content under its open licence, even when all they are doing is using the website to find the policy or the hook they need, the use can be metered, and charged per use. The price can be quite different from a news article. A customer who starts with £50 of credit might pay £1 for the page with a reviewed hook on it, and draw the credit down as they use the site. Or it might be much less. That is the question to discover with our first customers: what they are willing to pay, and what they are happy with.
charge

It does not conflict with hooks are kernel code, which said nobody should pay to run a hook. Running it stays free, and so does copying it. What is metered is the visit to the source: the page where you get the current, reviewed, signed version, with its record. People already pay for this in software. Red Hat says "A Red Hat subscription allows customers to download Red Hat tested and certified enterprise software", and its products "are backed by a dedicated Product Security team". Docker runs a Verified Publisher programme, "a paid subscription program that provides high-quality images from commercial publishers verified by Docker". The reason is the same one: Sonatype reports that "Throughout 2025, Sonatype identified more than 454,600 new malicious packages".
review

The official site only deserves that trust if it is not just us saying "trust us". So the policies we publish, and the hooks above all, should be reviewed and audited by others, and the record published next to them. There is now a whole set of services for this, built for agent skills and plugins, and we should use them, paid or free: Cisco's Skill Scanner, open source, a "Security Scanner for Agent Skills", which says of itself that it "provides best-effort detection, not comprehensive or complete coverage". Snyk's Agent Scan, formerly Invariant's mcp-scan, which scans "agent components on your machine for prompt injections and vulnerabilities". NVIDIA's SkillSpector, a "Security scanner for AI agent skills", which we used in a skill behaviour policy; and NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails and garak, its guardrails toolkit and its "LLM vulnerability scanner". Socket, whose audits now appear on the skills.sh registry, and Anthropic's community plugin marketplace, where every plugin has "passed automated security scanning".
review

No scanner is enough on its own. When we ran NVIDIA's scanner over a skill that reads your chat history, searches HackerNews and sends a report to Slack, it said "SAFE", and the skill had the whole lethal trifecta, honestly described. A scanner and a policy answer different questions. So the record should hold both: what the scanners found, and what a person who reviewed it, by name, signed off.
signed

The last piece is the one that turns the brand into something a machine can verify. Every policy and hook we publish should be signed with our keys, as PKI everywhere argued for everything we send, and the keys should be in a register anyone can check. The software world has the tools: Sigstore, where signing events are "recorded in a tamper-resistant public log", and SLSA, where a package at level 1 "has provenance showing how it was built". Then a copy found anywhere can be checked against the source, and the source is where the review, the signature and the current version live.
limits

The prices are not set. £1 a page is an example; the right price is to discover. No policy is audited yet. The reviews and signatures are what we will do next. Scanners miss things. Cisco's says so itself; ours rated a risky skill safe. Copying stays free. The licences do not change. The second meter is the book's site. Both are ours, and small.
sources

A voice memo of 20 October 2026. Claude Code's plugin security page. Cisco's Skill Scanner, Snyk's Agent Scan, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, NeMo Guardrails and garak, and Anthropic's community plugins. Red Hat's subscription FAQ, Docker's Verified Publisher programme, and Sonatype's 2026 report on open source malware. Sigstore and SLSA. Related: paying after the value, the fork next door, hooks are kernel code, a skill behaviour policy, PKI everywhere, our first customers. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: I was with someone today who runs their customer relationships in a spreadsheet, a customised one, and runs them well. The jump from that to what our agents do, one folder per person in an encrypted vault with a record, an append-only ledger, every message word for word and a summary the agent rebuilds, is too high to make in one step, and it does not need to be made in one step. Almost all of it can be done with what a Google Workspace account and a Claude seat already give you. This is the walkthrough. The row becomes a folder in Google Drive with four plain documents and one the agent writes; Claude's app, connected to Drive and Gmail, works inside the folder under a behaviour policy that is the instructions of one Project, and the three rules that matter carry straight over from ours: draft and never send, append and never rewrite, stay in the folder. Then the migration from the sheet, five exercises from a question to a campaign so that the habit forms, what the agent will get wrong at first, and when the folders are worth moving into a vault. It is written so that an agent can send it, with the person's own names filled in, to anyone who asks.

The row becomes a folder with four documents and one the agent writes; the agent is a Claude Project whose instructions are the policy; the five exercises below the line are the first week. Today I sat with someone who runs their relationships in a spreadsheet. A good one, shaped over years to how they work, and it does what a spreadsheet does well: one row per person, a stage, a date, a next step, and a notes column that holds whatever fits. What it cannot hold is what happened: the emails, word for word, the call last Tuesday, what was promised, what they care about and what we have that meets it. That lives in Gmail, in a notebook, and in the person's head, and only one person can read it in context.

What our agents run is described in The agent team as it runs: one folder per person in a vault, with a record, a ledger that is only ever added to, every message with its provenance, the notes from each call, a graph of interests, and a summary generated from the files beneath it. The jump from the spreadsheet to that is too high to make in one step. The good news is that almost all of it can be done, today, with a Google Workspace account and a Claude seat, and that the behaviour policies we wrote for our agents apply without change, because they are about what an agent may do with your mail and your files, and that is the same in anyone's environment.

This is the walkthrough. Assume a Workspace account, which gives Gmail, Drive, Docs and Sheets, and a Claude account on a Team or Pro plan that is the only account with access to that Workspace. No developer, no vault, no new tool until the last section.
short

The row becomes a folder. One Google Drive folder per person, with four documents you keep and one the agent writes: the record, the ledger, the messages, the notes, and the summary. The agent is a Project in the Claude app, connected to Drive and Gmail, whose instructions are the behaviour policy. Six lines, and three of them are ours: draft and never send; append and never rewrite; stay in the folder. The migration is one afternoon. Export the sheet, make the folders, let the agent fill each record from the mail it can read, correct it once. From then on nothing is retyped. Five exercises make the habit: ask, prepare, draft, debrief, campaign. Each is one message to the agent and each is safe, because the policy makes it safe. It will get things wrong at first, in two predictable ways, and the fix for both is a line in the policy, which is how ours grew.
short

The vault is the later step, for when the folder has to be shared with another agent, kept where the operator cannot read it, or carried between tools. By then the files are already in the right shape.
why

The difference is not the tool. It is what counts as the record. In a spreadsheet the record is the row, and the row is a summary you typed. In a folder the record is everything that happened, kept as it happened, and the summary is derived from it. That reversal is what gives an agent something to work with, and it is what Memory is not a spectator sport means by memory being many memories rather than one: a contact in the CRM has a world of its own, and the folder is that world.
why

Concretely, a folder can hold what a cell cannot: every message with the person, word for word, with the date and where it came from; a timeline that is only ever added to, so a correction is a new line and the history stays; the notes from a call, in the person's folder, the same evening; and a summary that is rebuilt from the files beneath it, so it cannot drift from them. And it can be read, all of it, by a second reader before you ask a question. That second reader is the agent.
folder

Make a folder in Drive called Contacts. Inside it, one folder per person, named with the person's name. Inside each, five documents, with these names so that the agent and you mean the same thing: Record, a Google Doc. Role, company, how you met, stage, priority, the next step and its date, and what they care about, as a short list. Every fact in it says where it came from, in brackets: "(email, 3 Oct)". This is the row, promoted. Ledger, a Google Sheet. One line per event: the date, in or out, the channel (email, call, meeting, note), and one sentence. It is only ever added to. A correction is a new line that says "correction to 3 Oct:". Tasks are lines too, and the latest line about a task wins.
folder

Messages, a Google Doc. Every email and note exchanged with the person, pasted word for word, newest at the bottom, each with a heading of the date, the direction and the channel. The agent can read your Gmail, so it can do this for you; the point of keeping a copy in the folder is that the folder is complete on its own. Notes, a Google Doc. Calls and meetings, dated. Including what you said into your phone in the car afterwards; VoiceDebrief turns that into text in your browser, and the text goes here. Summary, a Google Doc. Written by the agent from the four above, rewritten whenever you ask, and never edited by hand. If it is wrong, the fix goes in the record or the ledger, and the summary is regenerated. That rule is what keeps it honest.
folder

That is the whole structure. It is the same structure as ours, minus the hashes and the graph, which come with the vault. A person with no interest in software can keep it, and a person who leaves can hand it over.
agent

In the Claude app, connect Google Drive and Gmail from the connectors settings; on a Team plan an admin enables them first, then you sign in with your Google account. Drive gives the agent search and reading of your Docs and Sheets; Gmail gives it reading, searching and drafting. Whether the agent can also write files into Drive from a conversation depends on your plan and settings, and the walkthrough works either way: where it cannot, it gives you the text and you paste it into the document, which takes ten seconds and keeps you in the loop. Then make one Project, called Contacts, and put the behaviour policy in its instructions. This is the part that carries over from ours unchanged, because the policy is the business logic and the first layers of it are the same for everyone: You work for me. Every email you write is a draft that I read and send. You never send.
agent

You read the Contacts folder in my Drive and my Gmail. You write only into a person's folder in Contacts, and only into their Ledger, Messages, Notes and Summary. You never change the Record without showing me the change first. You add to the Ledger and the Messages. You never rewrite or delete a line. A correction is a new line. Every fact you put in a Record or a Summary names where it came from. If a person has no folder, you ask before making one. If a request would reach outside the folder, you ask. At the end of every task you say, in one line, what you read and what you wrote.
agent

Six lines. The ones we learned the hard way are the first three, and Six agents, one inbox has the honest table of which rules the tools enforce and which are only told. In the Claude app today, "draft, never send" is enforced as far as Gmail drafting goes, and the rest is told, which is why line 6 exists: the one-line report is the twin that lets you check. One more setting worth making, from the same article: if the agent has its own Google account rather than yours, give it its own account on your Workspace and restrict what that account can do. That is the control that covers mail, files and connectors at once. For a first week, your own account with the policy above is fine; for a second agent, or a second person, buy the seat.
migration

One afternoon, in four steps. Export the sheet as CSV and drop it in the Contacts folder. Tell the agent: "Here is my contacts sheet. For each row, tell me the folder you would make and the Record you would write. Do not make anything yet." Read the list. This is where the stages and the priorities get agreed between you. Make the folders. If the agent can create files in your Drive, let it make the folders and the five documents, from a template folder you made once. If it cannot, make the template, and copy it per person; twenty people is twenty minutes.
migration

Fill the records from the mail. Per person: "Read everything in my Gmail with Jordan Example from the last year. Write the Record and the first Ledger lines from it, each fact with its source, and paste the key emails into Messages." Read the Record. Correct it once, in the document. This is the only retyping you will ever do. Generate the summaries. "For every folder in Contacts, write the Summary from the Record, the Ledger and the Notes." Read three of them. Where one is wrong, fix the source document, not the summary, and ask for it again. From then on, the rule is that nothing is retyped. An email arrives: the agent adds the Ledger line and pastes it into Messages. A call happens: the voice note goes into Notes, and the agent updates the next step. The sheet is closed, and the Summary is what you open.
exercises

Each of these is one message in the Contacts Project. Do them in order over the first week; each one uses the folder in a way the one before did not. Ask. "Who have I not spoken to in more than a month, grouped by stage, with the last Ledger line for each?" The agent reads every Ledger. You get the list a spreadsheet filter would give you, with the context a filter cannot. Prepare. "I am meeting Jordan on Thursday. Brief me from the folder: what we last agreed, the last three emails, what we promised and have not done, and what they care about that we have something for." Two minutes of reading replaces twenty of searching Gmail.
exercises

Draft. "Draft my follow-up to Jordan after Thursday, in my voice, from Notes. Do not send. Add a Ledger line that says a draft exists." You open the draft in Gmail, change two words, send it, and tell the agent "sent", which becomes the next Ledger line. Debrief. After the call, speak for two minutes into your phone. "Here is my voice note after the Jordan meeting. Put the notes in their Notes document, update the next step in the Record and show me the change, add the Ledger line, and regenerate the Summary." This is the one that changes the habit, because the record is now kept at the moment the thing happens.
exercises

Campaign. "Find everyone in Contacts whose Record says they care about X. Show me the list with the reason for each. Then draft one note to each, personalised from their Record and their last exchange, and do not send any." The list first, then the drafts, then you send the ones you want. Our agents run outreach this way, and the article Custom UIs are not the exception describes the eight days it took to get there with vaults; with folders it is one message. If all five work, the person has what our agents have, short of the vault. If one does not, the reason is almost always in the next section.
wrong

Two things, both predictable, both fixed by a line in the policy, which is exactly how ours grew: Every mistake added a rule argues that the better fix is a component, and in the Claude app the component you have is the Project's instructions. It will put a fact in the Record without a source, or infer a stage from tone. The fix is to make line 4 stricter: "A fact with no source goes in Notes marked as your inference, never in the Record." Then it does. It will rewrite the Summary in a way that drops something you cared about. The fix is not to edit the Summary. It is to put the thing in the Record, where it is a fact with a source, and regenerate. The Summary is a view; the Record is the truth.
wrong
And one thing that is not a mistake: it will sometimes ask when you did not expect it to, because line 5 says to. That is the policy working.
vault

Three signals say it is time, and until one appears, the folders are enough. A second agent needs to read them, or a second person's agent: the inbox reader, the one that drafts the newsletter, a colleague's assistant. A Drive folder can be shared, but a vault can be shared by a read key to exactly one person's folder, which Drive cannot do cleanly. The files should not be readable by the operator. A Drive folder is readable by Google and by anyone with admin rights on the Workspace. A vault is ciphertext to everyone but the key holders, which is the point of where the vault keys live. The record has to carry between tools. When the folder is also read by a script, a site, or an agent that does not use Drive, plain files in a vault with hashes and a ledger are the format everything else can read.
vault

The reason to start with folders is that the shape is the same. A record, a ledger, the messages, the notes, a generated summary: when the day comes, the move is a copy, and the policy does not change at all.
send

This article is written to be sent. When someone asks how we run our contacts, the RiskMandate agent should send it with four substitutions: the person's own name for the examples, their Workspace and Claude plan for the setup paragraph, the names of three real contacts for exercises 2 to 4, and the topic they actually sell for exercise 5. Nothing else needs to change, and the policy must not.
limits

The Claude app's connectors move. What Drive and Gmail let the agent do, and whether it can write files into Drive, is as of October 2026 and varies by plan and settings. The walkthrough works with reading and drafting alone. Most of the policy is told, not enforced, in the app as in ours. The one-line report at the end of each task is how you check, and the seat per agent is the control that makes the rest settings. One afternoon is for twenty to fifty contacts. Hundreds is the same method in batches, and the point at which the vault signals start to appear. If you run your relationships in a spreadsheet and want the personalised version of this, or you have done the migration and want to compare, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 12 October 2026, recorded during a conversation with someone who runs their relationships in a customised spreadsheet; they are not named and no detail of their business is here. Written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The folder structure is the one our agents run, from The agent team as it runs, with the hashes and the graph left for the vault step; the policy lines and the enforcement caveats are from Six agents, one inbox and The behaviour policy is the business logic; the Claude app's Google connectors are described from their settings and help pages as of October 2026. The figure was drawn for this article; the person in it is fictional. Abstract: SG/Send started because sending a file was harder than it should be, and because I wanted to build a service where the server holds nothing: the best way to protect an asset is not to have one. Eight months later it has become sgit, encrypted version control with Git's model, and the vaults that this site runs on. The whole journey is in public repositories, so this time I asked this site's agent to check my memory against the record: 4,476 commits on the SG/Send app on 246 of its first 249 days, 1,620 on the sgit command line, 739 release tags, 1,389 brief files and 268 debriefs. The record changes the order I remembered. The vault and the data room were named in February, before folders, zips and Git; the first feature a paying user asked for went from proposal to production in 22 minutes; the move to Git's model took about two weeks of briefs and a simulation that found 14 gaps before any code was written. It also shows the pace: fast from February to May, a turn to focus in June, two long pauses on the command line, and a burst in October. And it shows the lesson: by 5 March the briefs already said "Users buy credits, test once, and don't come back." The technology worked. The use case was not there yet.
Eight months of SG/Send and sgit, week by week, from 8 February to 14 October 2026, with milestones marked.
in-short

A service where the server holds nothing. Encrypted on the client; the key never sent. Live in five days. First commit on 8 February, send.sgraph.ai live on 13 February. Users, payments, a 22-minute feature. Stripe on 1 March, ten paying customers on 2 March, folders as zips that evening. The ideas came first. The vault and the data room were named in February, before the features that made them. Copy Git. About two weeks of briefs, a simulation, and the name sgit by 16 March. The vault grew into apps. Previews, Markdown, HTML, and sandboxed vault apps by May. The pace is in the data. Commits on 246 of 249 days on the app; bursts and pauses on the command line. The market said: not yet. "Users buy credits, test once, and don't come back."
start

SG/Send began with a problem I had every week: sending a file, or a folder, to someone, securely, without either of us installing anything. I was deep in Lambda development at the time, so I built a service. And it was the first time I deliberately used my security background to shape a product from the start. The best way to protect an asset is not to have the asset. If people were going to use it, the last thing I wanted was to hold their data. The first commit was on 8 February 2026, and the same day a specification went in that set the rule everything since has followed: "files are encrypted on the client before upload, and the decryption key is never sent to the server." The spec was blunt about why: "This single architectural decision eliminates ~90% of the security risk surface." No server, by design is where that idea ended up.
live

On 12 February the team's historian recorded "a working MVP user site with end-to-end zero-knowledge encrypted file transfer, deployed to AWS Lambda", and on 13 February send.sgraph.ai went live. The historian's status report put it simply: "The project moved from 'infrastructure sprint' (v0.1.4 brief, 10 Feb) to 'live with real users' (13 Feb) in 3 days." The way of working was written down the same day: voice memos become briefs, "briefs flow down, debriefs flow up, and a clear folder structure makes everything findable." By 14 February there were explorers and villagers, the people who discover and the people who harden, with a note that "We are NOT creating the Town Planners team yet." That structure, and the 3,025 markdown files it produced this year, is how a lot of this got built so quickly.
users

Then I took it to market, end to end, which is where I learnt Stripe, pricing and everything else a real product needs. By the time I built the newsroom, I already knew how to do all of it: a good example of how exploring something early pays off later, in a way nobody plans. The pricing brief of 28 February set £5 for 500 file credits and named the real question: "will they buy more?" The Stripe checkout went live on 1 March. On 2 March, the briefs record, "SG/Send had its first 10 paying customers", recruited with a simple offer: buy credits for £5 and I would send a £5 Amazon voucher. "Several declined the Amazon voucher."
users

The first feature request came the same day: a user wanted to send a folder, not a file. At 20:26 the architect's proposal for folder upload as a client-side zip was committed; at 20:48 the implementation; at 22:15 a viewer for the zip on the download page. The debrief the next day: "First feature request (folder upload) shipped in 90 minutes." The viewer also came from a real problem: a week earlier, a recipient could not open a Markdown file inside a zip on a phone. "The recipient literally could not read the file they were sent."
data-room

On 3 March, while emailing material to investors, I realised something, and the brief records it: "we already built the data room." Folder upload, the zip viewer and the file previews, together, were a data room. The daily brief that day added the next step: "The vault is the persistent, editable evolution." This is where my memory and the record part ways, in an instructive direction. I remembered the data room and the vault as things the zip led to. The record shows I had named both earlier: the data room as an investor and product idea between 17 and 21 February, and "a personal data vault", with its own interface, on 22 February. The ideas came first. The features caught up with them, and when they did, I recognised what I had built.
git

The order I remembered, and the order the record shows: the memo's sequence beside the dated steps. A vault you can only replace whole is not much of a vault. Two sessions saving at once lost data; there was no history and no way to merge. The architecture brief of 4 March is the turning point, and it is short on hesitation: "stop inventing solutions to these problems. Git already solved all of them. Copy Git." The model was Git's, commits, trees, blobs, refs and branches, with encryption on top, and a server that is "a dumb key-value blob store" while "All intelligence lives in the client."
git

I remembered this as a week of briefs. The record says about two weeks: some 48 brief files on vaults, Git and the command line between 3 and 18 March. The most interesting of them is a case study of designing without code, using the model as a simulator of software that did not exist yet: "The process produced 6 revisions of a simulation document, found 14 architectural gaps, resolved 13 of them". The decision that makes the whole thing work came on 3 and 17 March: file names and ids that are encrypted but deterministic, derived from the read key, so that a server that knows nothing can still serve the right object to someone who holds the key, and "Knowing the read_key does not let you compute the write_key".
git

The name followed. The briefing for the sgit.ai domain called it "Git with integrated trust", and said the s "can stand for signed, secure, or sgraph". The sgit command arrived on 16 March as an alias of the command line, which had started on 3 March as sg-send-cli; on 20 March the package was renamed sgit-ai and published to PyPI. On 4 March the command line had already cloned a vault from the terminal. What sgit is describes what it became.
vault

Once sgit existed, the vault became its interface, and then much more than a better zip. It rendered Markdown, then images inside the Markdown, then CSV tables, audio and video, and by 30 March HTML. Claude learnt to create vaults through skills, from late March. And when HTML pages started to work well, the next question was obvious: why show the vault around the page at all? On 2 May the architecture brief for sandboxed apps put the security model in two lines: "The iframe cannot load anything, cannot access anything, cannot reach the network. It can run JavaScript." And: "The iframe is user-mode. The runtime is kernel-mode." By 8 May a vault whose app.json asks for it opens full screen as an app. That is what the vaults on this site, and on sgit.ai, are today.
pace

sgit's unit tests from 237 on 5 March to 4,232 on 14 October, and its releases to PyPI per month. The repositories show the speed, and its shape. The SG/Send app has 4,476 commits on 246 of its first 249 days, and 739 release tags from v0.1.0 to v0.34.0: 196 tags in February, 253 in March, then fewer each month, and five in September. The busiest weeks were in March, at 427 and 439 commits.
pace

The sgit command line has 1,620 commits, and its own rhythm: a fast start in March, its biggest week in early May at 337 commits, then two long pauses, 36 days from the end of June to early August and 28 days from late August to late September, and then a burst in October, when versions 0.17 to 0.21 shipped in eight days. It went to PyPI 20 times as sg-send-cli in March, and 89 times as sgit-ai since. Its unit tests grew from 237 on 5 March to 4,232 on 14 October.
pace

The data also shows who wrote what. Of the 1,671 commits under my name on the app, 1,298 are merges of the agents' branches, and most of the rest are brief files. The agents wrote the code; I wrote the briefs, read the debriefs, and merged. The agents' own share of the app's commits rose from 38% in February to over 85% from September. The agent team as it runs describes that team.
market

The technology worked. The use case did not land, and the briefs said so early. On 5 March: "We have paying customers but not enough usage. Users buy credits, test once, and don't come back. Credits sit unused." In April the plan was a different experiment, £5 of model credits in each user's vault, with the same test: "If users spend their £5, enjoy the experience, and then buy more credits, we have a business." On 19 June the strategy brief set the priority as "reaching profitability, the first batch of users using the product regularly", and from then on the briefs turn towards risk acceptance and RiskMandate. Nobody ran out of credits and came back for more, and nobody came back asking for the next feature. That silence was a signal in itself.
market

It was a platform without a workflow that needed it. The difference now is that I have the workflows: the newsroom, RiskMandate and the vaults themselves need exactly the features SG/Send built, which is why they are getting used. Explorers find things early; the use case decides when they matter. That is the next article: what SG/Send could be now, with the same technology and a real need.
limits

My memory was wrong in places. The order, the length of the Git work, and nine months, which is eight. Usage is described, not counted. The briefs say credits sat unused; I did not find usage figures. "30 paying customers" appears only in an investor one-pager, and the team's librarian could not verify it; ten is the recorded number. The iframe inspiration is my recollection. The sandbox briefs do not cite the chat apps. Commit counts include automation. Release tags and some commits are made by CI. If you are building something that works and nobody is using yet, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Abstract: How do you fund a startup? My answer starts with what a startup needs most, which is time. A startup is like a work of art: it is all-consuming, you have to love it and lose yourself in it, and making money should be a side effect of being good at it, not the reason. So the question is how to find as much time as you can while earning a living. The best alignment is to make money around the area you want to go into, and the best start is your own revenue stream: make the work you already do more effective, or sell to people you already know, because if you are not solving a real problem you are chasing shadows. You have more time than you think: stop watching streaming. In a weird way, the best place to start a company is while you are employed, because the constraint makes you focus, and if you are good, many employers would rather have you part time than lose you. I did exactly that. It is still a gamble. I paid off all my debt, started my GenAI startup and went back into debt, and I am using the money from an exit to pay myself instead of taking an executive role. Debt is paying someone to buy your time. What you do not want is regret.
Where a founder's time comes from: time you have, time inside the job, time you negotiate and time you buy.
in-short

A startup needs time first. Money is a means to buy it. It is a work of art. All-consuming; money should be the side effect, not the motive. Start with your own revenue stream. Make the work you already do better, and sell to people you know. You have more time than you think. Stop watching streaming. The best place to start is in a job. The constraint makes you focus. Ask for part time. A good employer would rather have half of you than none. It is a gamble, and debt is buying time. I went back into debt to do this. Avoid regret. There has never been a better time to start.
time

How do you fund a startup? It is a personal question, and the answer depends on a lot of circumstances; I have lived through several of them. But I think it starts with this: the most important thing a startup needs is time. And you have to accept that it will become an obsession. The way I look at it, a founder is like a creator, an artist. It has to be all-consuming. You have to be passionate about it, lose yourself in it, love it. That is why, in my book, making money from it should never be your motivation. Making money should be a side effect of being successful at it, which is why I think so much about how you structure it, how you map it with open source, and how you make the most of your ideas. I guess my roots in music connect there.
time
So the question is not where the money comes from. It is how you find as much time as you can, while, in most cases, still earning a living. I have always seen money as a means to an end.
revenue

The best alignment is when you start to make money around the area you want to go into. You are always learning, and you are using the technology you are excited about to make the money. That is why I think being profitable, working inside something you already work on, is always the best model. You already have a revenue stream, and you start by making it more effective. Even if that is all you achieve, it is already a major success: you increased your revenue, you enjoy what you do more, and you became much more productive.
revenue

So that is what I always recommend first. Do not go looking for companies. Look at what you are already doing, or what people you know are doing, and sell it to them. If you are not solving a real problem, you are going to chase shadows. That can work, but it is much more difficult. And sell it early: can you sell it?
more-time

If you are good enough to be thinking of creating a startup, you are probably already successful at something, or you have few expenses, and you have this drive to create. If you have no time at all, you cannot do this. But most of us have more than we think. Do not watch streaming. There is always time in your life; the question is how you use it.
job

In a weird way, the best place to start a company is while you are already employed. You have an income, so you have time. And the constraint on your time is actually good: it makes you focus on what matters, and ship it. The way to do it safely is to work in the open from the start, tell your managers, keep it on separate machines, and never compete with your employer. That is the subject of open source what you build.
part-time

Many companies, depending on your role, will be more than happy to reduce your time. I literally did that. I was working at a company and said: I would like to build things. I am happy here, but we have run out of things for me to build. So instead of leaving, I would like to go part time, fewer days a week, and do another gig. They were fine with it, because I gave them a good solution. So go to your boss and say: I would like to explore this, it is something I need to do. Assuming they are happy with you, most would much rather have you half the time than not at all, because replacing you is a nightmare. And if you are not in that position, maybe you should leave anyway: time is too short, and you should be somewhere that matches your skills.
gamble

Ultimately it is a gamble. You will move out of your comfort zone, and you might get into debt. I did. Ironically, I had finally paid off all my debt and got back into the black, and then I started my GenAI startup and went straight back into debt. It does not matter. Debt is a means to an end: you are paying somebody to buy your time, and if you succeed, you clear it.
gamble

I was also fortunate to have had an exit from a company I worked for. I could have used that money for other things. I have been using it to pay myself, so that I do not have to take a CISO role or an executive role, and can do what I have wanted to do. That is why I am so happy. It is a choice, and a risk I am taking, but it comes from that urge to create, which is what I feel I am: a creator. Investment is a different decision, and it should come later, when you are profitable and know what you are building; sell, don't issue is how I think that deal should look.
regret

What you do not want is regret: to look back and say, if only I had tried. As I say in the book, this is a unique time to be alive, and there has never been a better time to create a company. That does not make it easy. There is a lot of competition, because the pool of people who can do it is now much wider. But if you are the expert in your problem, you have the advantage.
limits

This is my path, not a plan for everyone. Debt and an exit are personal circumstances. Part time depends on your role and employer. It worked for me because I offered a good solution. Debt is a real risk. It buys time only if you can carry it. This is not financial advice.
sources

Time you buy: savings, an exit, debt, which is paying someone to buy your time. Investment comes later, when the company is profitable. | concept
