Summary: Two clocks are running against the news industry, and neither is set by it. The deal with search is ending on the search engine's schedule, with Google traffic to publishers down a third in a year and the crawlers that replaced it now being tolled. And the law is coming for rent on the legislature's schedule, with the UK's subscription rules brought forward to January 2027, which is the year the ignored subscription becomes a cancelled one. The industry's answer to both is the same answer it has given for a decade, more subscriptions and more personalisation, sold to the 17% who already pay while 71% of the rest say nothing on offer would persuade them. This article argues, with the evidence and with things we have actually built, that the asset was never the prose. The story is a graph, the article is a projection of it, and what a reader, a firm or an agent will pay for is the evidence, the trail, the on-record confirmation and the view cut for them, paid in pence when delivered, on rails that now cost nothing to use. The dataset is worth more than the article. The industry has just never had a way to sell it.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

Here is the claim, stated so it can be wrong. The news industry is about to be hit twice, by two things it does not control, and its standing answer to both is the one thing that neither of them leaves standing. The first blow is the end of its deal with search. The second is consumer protection law catching up with the subscription. The standing answer is more subscriptions, better personalised. And the way through is not a better paywall. It is to stop selling the article, which is a projection, and start selling the thing the article was projected from.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

I have been writing this argument down since February 2025, in a series of articles on the future of news, and the reason to write it again now is that in the eighteen months since, most of the things those pieces said were coming have arrived, with dates on them. So this one is different in two ways. It has the evidence, because the evidence now exists. And it has working examples, because we have spent the year building vaults that do the thing the 2025 pieces could only describe.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The bargain the industry made twenty years ago was simple. Give the content away, let the search engine index it, and take the traffic and the advertising that came with it. It was a Faustian deal, and everyone who took it knew that. What nobody planned for was the other party ending it.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

Google traffic to publishers fell by a third in a year. Chartbeat data across more than 2,500 sites, reported by Press Gazette, has organic Google search traffic to publishers down 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, and down 38% in the United States. Digiday's own data, from the same period, attributes a 25% referral drop to AI Overviews specifically, the summaries Google now puts above the results. The 2026 Digital News Report from the Reuters Institute, a survey of 97,520 people across 48 markets, records publishers expecting search traffic to fall a further 43% over the next three years, and a fifth of them expecting losses above 75%. USA Today's organic Google traffic fell by nearly half between June 2025 and June 2026.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

And the people who are ending the deal are the same people who ran it. In July 2025 Cloudflare, which sits in front of a fifth of the web, started blocking AI crawlers by default and launched Pay Per Crawl, which answers a crawler with the HTTP status code the web reserved thirty years ago for this exact purpose and never used: 402, Payment Required. A year later, on 1 July 2026, it said that model was not enough: more than half of AI crawler traffic is bots re-fetching pages that have not changed, and bots now outnumber humans on the network for the first time. So it is moving to Pay Per Use, paying publishers *"when their content creates value, not just when it's fetched"*, and from 15 September 2026 it blocks by default any crawler that will not say whether it is a search engine, a training run or an agent. Its customers now send more than a billion 402 responses a day. Matthew Prince's line for it: *"Now that the majority of traffic on the Internet is non-human, we must go further and act faster so that a sustainable ecosystem can emerge."*
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

I wrote about the first of those announcements the week it happened, on 4 July 2025, and the point then was the same as the point now. Being paid per crawl is better than being scraped for free, but it still prices the prose, and the prose is the wrong thing to price. The evidence for that is the licensing market. News Corp got up to $250 million over five years from OpenAI in May 2024, the New York Times gets a reported $20 to 25 million a year from Amazon, and News Corp signed again with Meta in March 2026 for up to $50 million a year. Those are real numbers, and they are numbers for about twenty publishers in the world. For everyone else, the offer is nothing, because for everyone else the prose is interchangeable, and a model that has read a thousand articles about an event does not need the thousand and first.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html
The second clock is quieter and, for most publishers, worse.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The subscription was the industry's answer to the first clock. When the traffic started to go, the strategy became reader revenue, and reader revenue meant recurring billing. It worked, for some, and it has a ceiling. Across the twenty countries the Reuters Institute has tracked for a decade, 17% of people pay for online news, down from 18% a year ago, and the 2026 report describes 10% to 20% as *"a ceiling in most markets."* Norway is at 40% and Sweden at 32% and they are the outliers; the United States fell four points this year. Of those who do not pay, the 2025 report asked what would persuade them, and 71% said nothing on offer would. In the United Kingdom that figure was 65%. Trust in news is at 37%, the lowest since the measurement began in 2015. Two in five people say they sometimes or often avoid the news altogether.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

That is the ceiling from the demand side. Now look at what is arriving from the supply side, because the thing that made the subscription work was never the reader's enthusiasm. It was the reader's inertia.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

Somebody in my own household pays roughly £50 a month across news subscriptions and reads, in a good month, a tenth of what that buys. That is not unusual, it is the model. A subscription, as subscriptions.sgit.ai puts it, *is a discount for committing to regular use. It is not rent on something you have the right to ignore.* And rent on the ignored is precisely what the law is now coming for. The UK's Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act carries a subscription regime that requires renewal reminders, a fourteen-day cooling-off period when a trial converts or a long contract renews, and cancellation by a route no harder than the one used to join, with fines of up to 10% of global turnover for breaches. It had been pushed back to spring 2027. On 10 August 2026 the government brought it forward to 1 January 2027, and the Professional Publishers Association's response was that this would be *"genuinely difficult for publishers to operationalise."* Read that sentence again with the model in mind. The rules are difficult to operationalise because the model depends on the thing the rules remove. A renewal reminder to a reader who has not opened the app in three months is a cancellation notice with extra steps.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The United States is a step behind and moving the same way. The FTC's click-to-cancel rule was vacated on 8 July 2025 by the Eighth Circuit, on procedure rather than substance, and the FTC has restarted the rule-making. California's auto-renewal amendments have been in force since 1 July 2025. None of this is aimed at newspapers. All of it lands on them, because they are among the largest sellers of subscriptions that people forget they have.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html
## The industry's answer is the wrong answer to both
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

Both answers price the prose. A subscription is a price for unlimited prose. Personalisation is a way of choosing which prose to show. And the prose is the one part of the operation whose price is going to zero, because the same model that summarises it in a search result can summarise it in a chatbot, in a briefing, in a translation, and from a thousand competing sources. Ten percent of people already get news from an AI chatbot every week, 16% of the under-35s, and 20% of people say they trust the answers. That share will not go down.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The counter-argument to selling anything smaller than a subscription is well made and I want to give it its due. James Ball's 2020 piece for Columbia Journalism Review is the best version of it: a $100 subscription lost is 500 micropayments to replace; a newspaper is a bundle, and unbundling it breaks the cross-subsidy; you only know whether an article was worth it after you have read it; and any scheme that needs dozens of publishers to co-operate on a shared wallet will fail, because *"the success of any project is inversely correlated with the amount that requires publishers to work together."* Matthew Guay's history of the failures, from May 2026, adds the psychology. Nick Szabo in 1996: the reason we do not do these things is that they are not worth the brain cycles. Clay Shirky: there is anxiety in every decision to buy, however small. Blendle had more than a million users and 150,000 of them ever paid, and it pivoted to subscriptions in 2019.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

All of that is true, and all of it is about paying for prose. It is an argument that a reader will not stop to decide whether an article is worth twenty pence. I agree. But look at who is standing at the till today and what they are trying to buy.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The reader who wants one thing. I can walk into a shop this morning and buy The Guardian or The Telegraph for £3, and I cannot buy one article from either of them online at any price. The Toronto Star sells one for 75 cents, Cornwall Reports for 20p, and the Maidenhead Advertiser sells a day for 40p, and the striking thing about that list is how short it is. The 2025 piece on micro and nano payments, from 2 April 2025, quoted Dominic Young of Axate: *"There are more people in the market willing to pay than willing to subscribe."* The Reuters data says the same thing from the other side. In the UK, 10% pay for online news, and of those, 66% do it by subscription and 7% by one-off payment. The one-off option barely exists, so almost nobody uses it, and that is then cited as proof nobody wants it.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The firm that has to forward it. Inside a company, an article is not read, it is processed. Somebody has to summarise it for the people who matter, put it into the format the board reads, attach it to the risk register, translate it for the regional office, and cite it in a filing. That is transformation, and it is where the value is created and the provenance is lost. A corporate reader does not want a subscription for the whole of the newspaper. They want this article, with its evidence, in a form they are allowed to transform and forward, and they will pay a licensing price that would look absurd to a consumer, because the alternative is a junior analyst spending an afternoon reconstructing the sources.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The agent, paying per query. Cloudflare's billion 402s a day are not being sent to people. The buyer that now arrives at a publisher's door most often is a program with a budget, and it does not have Shirky's anxiety or Szabo's brain cycles. It has an instruction to find out whether something is true and a wallet to pay for the answer. That buyer did not exist in 2020, and it makes every argument about mental transaction costs beside the point, because the transaction is not mental.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

None of those three buyers wants the prose. The reader wants this one thing, the firm wants the thing plus the right to transform it, and the agent wants to know whether the thing is true. So sell them that.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html
Here is the shift in thinking that everything else follows from, and it is the thesis of newsroom.sgit.ai: *the story is a graph; the article is a projection.*
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

A story, while it is being reported, is not an article. It is a set of claims, each one resting on some evidence, drawn from some sources, some of whom cannot be named, held together by analysis that has hypotheses in it and gaps in it and a confidence level that changes as the reporting goes on. It has raw materials: the interviews, the documents, the dataset somebody pulled. It has drafts, and it has the decisions about what to leave out. All of that is the story. The article is a projection of it: a walk through the graph, at one moment, cut for one audience, in one language, at one length. The infographic is another projection. The translation is another. The three-paragraph summary a model produces in a search result is another, and that is the whole problem: the industry has been selling the cheapest projection and throwing the graph away.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

Because it does throw it away. In most newsrooms the graph exists in the journalist's head, in a notes app and in an email thread, and the moment the article ships, the graph starts to decay. A year later, when the story is contested, or somebody wants to build on it, or an agent wants to know whether a claim in it is still true, there is nothing to walk back to. The evidence was never a first-class object. It was a step on the way to the prose.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The dataset is worth more than the article. This is the sentence I would put on the wall of every newsroom. The prose is what a model can regenerate from the dataset in a second. The dataset is what nobody else has: the frozen copy of the source page before it changed, the interview, the on-record confirmation, the spreadsheet, the chain from a claim to the bytes it rests on. A newspaper that keeps the graph and gives the prose away is sitting on an asset. A newspaper that sells the prose and loses the graph is selling the only thing that has stopped being scarce.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The 2025 articles are the long form of this. Monetising Trust and Knowledge, from 2 February 2025, argued that *"publishers that structure their content for intelligent consumption will define the future of trusted journalism"*, and set out the tiers, the APIs, and the verification services that a structured newsroom could sell. Building Trust Through Fact Provenance, three days later, made the case that provenance, the ability to trace a claim to its origin, is the pillar the rest stands on, and that *"trust in information emerges over time, formed by repeated demonstrations of ethical sourcing and consistent reliability."* Journalists' Challenges with Digital Content Provenance and Trust, from 24 March 2025, made a point I still think is under-appreciated: *"the value of provenance is probably more for the world of journalism than it is for the world of consumers."* The reader will rarely walk the chain. The journalist, the editor, the lawyer, the regulator and the agent will, and they are the ones who pay.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

I would ask the reader to notice the dates on those pieces, because it matters to the argument. They were written before the Google traffic numbers, before Cloudflare's tolls, before the UK's January 2027 date and before the payment rails below existed. The predictions in them have not needed revising. The evidence has arrived to meet them.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

Inside it, the newsroom design on newsroom.sgit.ai puts *"the published text, the evidence it cites, the story graph it belongs to, the source list, the translations, and every prompt and decision that produced it, held together as one addressable unit."* Some of the properties that fall out of that shape are worth listing, because each one is something the industry currently pays for separately or does not have at all.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The cost of producing a story this way is not hidden either. The newsroom design publishes a worked story: an English and Portuguese piece on the EU AI Act's implementation in Portugal, 12 sources, two expert validations, four drafts, £8.40 and six hours twenty-three minutes of compute, and zero human hours, stated plainly. It is a worked design example rather than a production ledger, and the page says so. But the shape of the number matters. When the research, the fact-checking and the translation are lines on a bill in pounds and pence, the price of a projection stops being a guess.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html
Go back to the diagram at the top. One graph, five projections, and the free one is the door.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

1. The public article. Free, findable, the projection that search and agents are allowed to read. The reason to give it away is not generosity. It is the honest objection to everything on this page: a vault opened in the browser is invisible to a crawler, and *"most of a news site's reach comes from being findable by search and by other agents."* So the public projection stays public and stays static, and it links to what it was made from.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

2. The licensed article. The same projection, bought once, in pence, for the reader who wants this one thing and the firm that has to forward it. The corporate version carries the right to transform, because that is what companies do with news, and it carries its provenance with it, because the graph is what makes the transformation defensible. Ball's 500-micropayments arithmetic assumes the micropayment cannibalises a subscription. It cannot cannibalise a subscription the reader was never going to buy, and 71% of them were never going to buy it.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

3. The evidence vault. The graph itself, or the part of it that can be released, with anonymous sources redacted at the node. This is the tier nobody sells today and the one with the highest value, because its buyers are not readers. They are analysts, lawyers, academics, regulators and other newsrooms, and they are used to paying for data. An investigative journalist who has spent a year on a story has, at the end of it, a dataset with a market of its own, and the industry currently pays them for the prose and lets the dataset rot. Investigative journalism could be monetised spectacularly under this model, not by selling more copies of the article but by licensing the year's work to the twenty organisations that need it.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

4. The customised projection. The same graph, cut for a role, a sector, a language or a single reader. The personalised briefing for Dan Raywood, from 6 June 2025, is one of these, produced by hand: the future-of-news argument, projected for a cybersecurity editor with seventeen years on that beat. pt.newsroom.sgit.ai is another, produced by a pipeline: it is *natively Portuguese, not a translation*, because it is projected from the graph rather than translated from the English prose. The thing to notice is that personalisation, the word in every industry deck, means this and only this once the graph exists: a different walk through the same evidence. Without the graph, it means showing people more of the prose they already clicked on.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

5. The verification API. The B2B product, and the one that turns a newsroom's most expensive habit into its most valuable service. A company that is about to cite a claim, or an agent that is about to act on one, asks: did you say this, is it still true, and is this use of it sound? The newsroom answers on the record, from the graph, with a warranty. The design calls it trust as a service, and its two prices are the two things being bought: the fact, and the confirmation that the fact still holds. It also names the risk honestly: *selling trust makes the seller a target*, and a warranted answer that turns out wrong is a claim against whoever warranted it. That is not a reason to avoid the market. It is the reason the market pays.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The subscription's other quiet property is where the money stops. It stops at the outlet. The newsroom design sets out a split that I think is closer to where value is actually created: 60% to the original researcher whose work the story rests on, 25% to the organisation that holds the data, 10% to the journalist who synthesised it and 5% to the outlet that distributed it. *"Today, essentially all of that revenue is captured at the 5% layer."* The numbers are a proposal, not a law of nature. What is not negotiable is the mechanism that makes any split possible: you cannot pay the fact creator unless the graph names them. The Portuguese newsroom's wallet page puts it in one line: *"Uma página que não soubesse nomear a sua fonte não saberia a quem pagar."* A page that could not name its source would not know whom to pay.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

For a decade the answer to "why not micropayments" ended with the rails. A £1 card top-up returned about 59p of usable credit after fees, and nothing under a pound was worth processing. That is over, and it ended in the last eighteen months. The x402 protocol, which puts a payment inside the HTTP 402 response Cloudflare is already sending a billion times a day, moved under the Linux Foundation in April 2026 with more than twenty founding members, settles in about 200 milliseconds, charges no protocol fee, and carried roughly 169 million transactions in its first year. AWS announced agent payments in May 2026 with Coinbase and Stripe, at ticket sizes from a tenth of a cent to a thousand dollars. Cloudflare's own Monetization Gateway charges for any resource behind it using the same protocol. On 6 June 2025 the Raywood briefing said *"the infrastructure for micro/nano payments exists – what's been lacking is the industry will to implement it."* It was slightly early. The infrastructure exists now, and what is lacking is still the will.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

Two honest notes belong here. Nothing on sgit.ai is wired to any of those rails today: no fact-creator payment, no per-query billing, no trust-as-a-service product runs anywhere, and the newsroom site says so in its own words: *"most of this site is an argument, not a product."* And the Portuguese wallet that charges one cent a page keeps its ledger in the reader's own browser, as a demonstration of what the reader would see, not as a payment.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html
What does run is the substrate, and it runs in public, which is the only reason to believe the rest.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

1. Store the story as a graph from the first day of reporting. Claims, evidence, sources, raw materials, drafts. Make the article a build artefact. If the graph is not there at the end, the story was never captured, only its prose. 2. Freeze and hash every source. Not a link. The bytes, on the day, with a hash. It is the cheapest thing on this list and the one that changes what a correction means. 3. Keep giving the public projection away, and keep it findable. Static, crawlable, linked to the vault it came from. The door has to be open for the shop to work, and the Cloudflare tolls are for the crawlers that never come through the door. 4. Sell the licensed article in pence, on demand, and stop treating it as dilutive. The people who buy it were not going to subscribe. Price the corporate version as a licence to transform, not as a copy. 5. Adopt the five clauses of the subscription standard before January makes you. Tell subscribers how much they used, tell them without being asked, let them leave by the route they joined, warn them before charging for something they have stopped using, and do not charge for outages. The proposal is written; three of its five clauses go beyond what the UK regime will require. A publisher that does this first will be the one readers trust with recurring billing after the others are fined. 6. Open the evidence vault to the B2B market that already pays for verification. Lawyers, analysts, regulators, other newsrooms. Redact at the node. License the graph. This is where investigative work gets paid what it cost. 7. Put the correction in the graph, and let credibility be computed. Supersede, never delete. Type the edge. Publish the record, never the verdict. Then a journalist's track record is a fact rather than a reputation. 8. Publish the cost per story. If the research, the checking and the translation are lines on a bill, the price of each projection is a decision rather than a guess, and the 60/25/10/5 question becomes answerable.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

Both clocks are set by somebody else. The search layer will finish ending the deal on its own timetable, and every publisher's answer to that has been to ask the search layer for a better deal. The legislature will finish regulating the subscription on its timetable, and every publisher's answer to that has been to ask for more time. Neither answer touches the thing that is actually wrong, which is that the industry sells the one output whose marginal cost has gone to zero and discards the one asset that has not.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The story was always a graph. The article was always a projection. The reader who wanted one article, the firm that needed to forward it, and now the agent that needs to know whether it is true were always standing at the till trying to buy something the shop did not stock. The evidence, the trail, the on-record confirmation, the view cut for them, paid when delivered, in pence, to the people who made the facts. That is the product. It has been buildable for eighteen months and sellable for about six.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

The industry has never lacked the material. It has lacked a way to sell it. Now it has one, and the only question that matters is the same one I would ask of any product: when it is taken away, does anybody miss it? Take away the prose and, increasingly, nobody does. Take away the graph, and the lawyer, the analyst, the regulator and the agent all notice on the same afternoon.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.1.0.html

Summary: The news industry runs on two commercial models, advertising and subscriptions, and both are bad for the reader. One sells the reader to somebody else. The other charges rent on something most people have stopped using. Both are now being dismantled from outside, by a search layer that has stopped sending traffic and by consumer law that arrives in January 2027. This article is about what to build instead, in practical terms. The objective is a commercial model that rewards investigative journalism, so that the expensive, evidenced kind of reporting drives usage, usage drives revenue that depends on neither search nor renewals, and that revenue funds more of the same. The mechanism is to stop selling the article and start selling what the article was made from. The story is a graph. The article is one projection of it. From that one graph a newsroom can sell five things, on demand and in pence, to readers, to firms and to agents, and every payment walks back to the people who made the facts. It is built, in parts, on things we have already published.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.2.0.html

Two instances exist. The personalised briefing for Dan Raywood, from 6 June 2025, is the future-of-news argument projected for a cybersecurity editor with seventeen years on that beat, produced by hand. pt.newsroom.sgit.ai is the other, produced by a pipeline: it is *natively Portuguese, not a translation*, because it is projected from the graph rather than translated from the English words. The buyer here is a desk, a firm or a country, and the price is for the cut, not the content: the sector briefing that a bank's risk team receives every morning is the same graph the public article came from, projected for them, and it can be produced for £8.40 rather than by a research team.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.2.0.html
The rest of this piece is the long form of those eight points, with the evidence, and with the parts of the solution spelt out in enough detail to be built.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.3.0.html

Evidence is the bottom rung, and it is bytes. A source page fetched on a date, frozen, and hashed with SHA-256. An interview recording. A filing. A dataset. Not a link to any of them, because a link is a promise that the thing will still be there and still say the same, and the web breaks that promise constantly. The Regulation Graph ends every chain in a hash of the retrieved bytes for exactly this reason, and so does the Portugal newsroom, for 88 sources today.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.5.0.html

The reason to be precise about the ladder is commercial. Every rung of it can be sold, because none of it is an assertion. The evidence vault sells the bottom rung. The licensed article and the customised projection sell a walk along the middle one. The verification API sells the top one, an answer on the record from a source with a track record, with a warranty. And none of those sales is possible if the newsroom kept only the article, because the article is the one artefact that contains none of the three.
articles/versions/future-of-news-story-vault-not-paywall/v1.5.0.html

Abstract: In 2018 I wrote a book called Generation Z Developers, key concepts and ideas for the next generation of developers. It is on Leanpub, 60% complete, last updated on 8 October 2018, read by 465 people, and it is also on Amazon. It was a decent book, full of spelling mistakes, and a lot of what I write about now is already in it, as chapter outlines: pioneers, settlers and town planners, graphs, your future self, publishing, GitHub as your CV; and, in a finished chapter, the advice to act like you are part of the company you want to work for. Of its 138 files, 90 are still outlines. I think the time is right for a new edition, Generation Z Developers (AI edition), because the outlines have since been written, as articles on this site. This is the plan. Keep the name, because the people it is for are still Generation Z and they all have to be developers now, with (AI edition) in brackets, and date it October 2026. Frame it with Wardley's explorers, villagers and town planners. Do it first, before the other books: a thorough review, an agent that interviews me as its editor, quick iterations in public, my handwritten notes, and then Amazon, where I already publish, with a launch in Portugal. It is the book I would most like to hand to the people I am trying to help: here is the manual for getting into development, and here is the manual for getting a job.

From the 2018 book to the 2026 articles: chapters left as outlines, and the articles that have since written them. Update, 19 October 2026. The name moved on once the book's website started building the edition. Decision 010 made it Gen Z Developers (GenAI Edition); after the first release candidate, decision 014 made it Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition): for Generation Z and Generation X, with the founder as the reader. Discovering the book tells how that happened. This article is kept as it was written, as the step before.
in-short

I wrote Generation Z Developers in 2018. On Leanpub at 60%, and on Amazon. Much of what I write now is in it. Mostly as outlines: 90 of its 138 files. The outlines have since been written. As articles on this site. So it is time for an AI edition. For the people I want to help into development and into a job. Keep the name, add (AI edition), date it October 2026. They are still Generation Z, and they all have to be developers now. Frame it with explorers, villagers and town planners. And explain Wardley maps properly. Do this book first. Review it, interview me, iterate in public, publish on KDP, launch in Portugal.
book

Generation Z Developers, subtitled "Key concepts and ideas for the next generation of developers", is on Leanpub at 60% complete, 136 pages and 30,695 words, last updated on 8 October 2018, with 465 readers. It is also on Amazon, and its source is on GitHub, in Book_Generation_Z_Developer. I wrote it the way it told readers to work: in Markdown, in Git, in public, published early and often, with GitHub issues for feedback. It was a decent book. It was also full of spelling mistakes, and a lot of it was never finished.
said

It opened with why I was worried about Generation Z, "the generation born after 1996": not their values, which I liked, but that, having grown up with technology that simply works, many had missed the history of how it came to work. And it had one chapter that I still give, almost word for word, to people looking for a job: For a lot of companies in the 1990s, it said, that was simply using a computer, and in the 2000s, using the internet. Then the advice: "Act like you are part of the company", by collaborating on its open-source projects, which is act as the job you want, eight years early. On AI, it said: "One of the most important areas that you need to gain a strong understanding in the next 5 years is Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence (AI)." ChatGPT arrived four years later.
then-and-now

What held. The competitive-advantage argument is exactly hired for the workflow: today the one advantage is running agentic workflows. Act like you are part of the company. Publish, publish, publish. GitHub as your CV. Write for your future self. Pioneers, settlers and town planners, which became software vendors as villagers and explorer coding. What did not. The book's list of technologies to learn, Jira, WallabyJs, AWS's machine-learning services, has dated, as such lists do. Its AI chapter pointed readers at cloud machine-learning tools to learn "how to program it"; the bigger shift turned out to be learning how to use it, and how to direct agents, which is a different skill from building models. And its view of who is a developer was narrower than it should have been: today anyone who can brief an agent to build something is one.
outlines

The most interesting thing in the repository is what is not finished. Of its 138 files, 90 are outlines: a title, "Topics to cover and ideas", and a few bullet points. Life patterns: 21 of 27 are outlines. Concepts: 26 of 27. Security: all 8. Your CV: 8 of 9. Reading them now, many are briefs that this newsroom has since written as articles, without my planning it. "Future self", whose outline says to create assets that will be useful for him or her, is bringing my past work back. "Publish, publish, publish" is your own newsroom. "Graphs" is the graphs books and search as navigation. "GitHub is your CV" is act as the job you want. Even chapters that were written have newer answers: the one on open source now has the fork next door. That is the material for the AI edition, and it is why I feel I now have enough to have a go.
cover

The printed early release of Generation Z Developers, September 2018, cover (photo: Dinis). I still have the printed early release, from September 2018. Its cover says what the book was for, in seven lines: question everything; make fact based decisions; understand the history of tech; learn how to learn; understand what game is being played; develop intellectual curiosity; shake things up. I would keep all seven. They read more urgently now than they did then.
name

The first question was whether to call it Generation Z Developers, or Generation AI Developers, or Generation Z professionals or workers. I like the word developer, and I think it is more right now than in 2018, because this generation all have to be developers: they all have to create. The first book said they needed to know Git and version control, spreadsheets, automation, even Slack. The problem was that there was no easy way in. I was giving advice, and the bar of entry was very high. Now it is very low. You could even give this book to Claude and say: teach this person, give them the workflows, one at a time.
name

And the people I want to give it to, those coming out of university or looking for their first or next job, are still Generation Z: the oldest were 22 when I wrote it, and are 30 now. It is not only for them. A target helps, and it also tells everyone else: learn this, or be outcompeted by the people who have. Generation Z is the generation entering the job market now, and in Europe in particular I think they are being fed a lot of fear about AI, and are not embracing it the way they should. So: keep the title, and mark the new edition in brackets: Generation Z Developers (AI edition). It says what changed in two words, and it reads as an edition of the same book, not a different one. And date it, October 2026, because what it describes is the agentic workflow as I run it now, which will change.
roles

If everyone is a developer, the better question is what kind. Simon Wardley's answer, first as pioneers, settlers and town planners and since 2023 as explorers, villagers and town planners, gives the book its frame: the explorer who builds something new and rough, the villager who makes it work for others, the town planner who turns it into something everyone can rely on. Where do you fit, and where do you want to? The 2018 book had this as an outline, and mentioned Wardley mapping once. This edition can explain Wardley maps properly, because it is now something people starting out need to know, and it makes a good narrative to hang the visualisations and infographics on.
edition

Start with a thorough review. There are a lot of spelling mistakes, and more besides. Keep what held, corrected and finished. Say what did not, in a short "then and now" for each chapter that changed. Fill each outline from the newsroom articles that answer it, rewritten for this reader. Add a part on working with agents: explorer coding, your own newsroom, the man behind the curtain, hired for the workflow, act as the job you want. Add a part on how the book itself was made. We already have chapters on that, in the graphs books; consolidate them. How we write it is itself an example of the workflow it teaches. Lots of pictures, infographics and experiments. It should be easy to read, and easy to do. Add my handwritten notes. I have a printed copy at home with my notes in it; if I cannot find it, I will read the book again and comment as I go.
first

I would like to do more books, on the graphs among others. But this one probably has enough content and material already, and because one version is already published, we can build on the back of it: fix it, do a much better release, and publish it as a new version on Amazon. It is a good target: something I can focus on, iterate on quickly, release, and move on. If the workflow works, a new version of Hacking Portugal can follow the same way. And it is the book I would like to give people. Every time I meet someone and ask: do you know about Wardley maps? Do you have an agentic workflow? I would like to be able to hand them this.
workflow

A new repository for the edition, where the agentic workflow is mapped as it runs. The roles: a reviewer, an editor and a publisher, at least. The graphs books already have seven roles, one folder each, and the shelf and reading pages already exist, so most of the technology and the interface is there. An editor who interviews me. We have done this once: for ten hard questions for RiskMandate, Claude acted as a journalist with an eye for detail and challenged every answer for two hours until the set was coherent. Here the agent acts as the book's editor: it interviews me on each topic, challenges what I say, and from that we arrive at the book's narrative. Quick iterations, in public. Publish early versions on Leanpub, post them on LinkedIn, get interviews and feedback, and release new versions. The first edition asked for feedback through GitHub issues; this one can act on it within days.
workflow

Then Amazon KDP, the way books from articles sets out. I already have a KDP account and have published there before, so the shorter review for accounts with a published book applies. And I will be in Lisbon for Web Summit, 9 to 12 November, which makes this a good book to launch in Portugal. It is the book I would give, literally, to the people I am trying to help: here is the manual for getting into development, and here is the manual for getting a job. The build brief is a note for the agents that make it: Generation Z Developers (AI edition). It is also on the briefs page.
limits

Nothing of the AI edition is written. This is the plan. The outline-to-article map is a first reading. Not every outline has an article, and not every article fits. Doing this one first is a choice, not a commitment. The graphs books and Hacking Portugal follow if the workflow works. Fear about AI among young Europeans is my reading. Not a measured result. The Amazon listing was not read for this article. The repository links it, and I publish there. If you would have wanted this book when you started, or want it now, tell me what it should have in it: write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The reading meter on sgit.ai stops being a demonstration. A page now costs what you read of it: scroll a tenth of the way down a new article and you pay a tenth of 10p. Your balance can go below zero and stay there; nothing is blocked and nothing nags, there is only a small balance in the top bar. If a page was not worth it you can say so, with a reason, and it is not charged. Topping up is one £5 payment on Stripe, with no account and nothing that renews, and the page you come back to adds the credit without being able to check it, on purpose. The meter is also packaged as a library any website can add. This article is the plan and the reasoning, written down before the results: the business case, what we expect, the numbers that would prove us wrong, and the date we look.

The plan on one page: six changes, and the five hypotheses written down before the first payment, each with what we expect and what would prove us wrong. The meter goes live. It charges by how far down a page you scroll, it lets your balance go below zero forever, it shows only a small balance in the top bar, and it lets you refuse to pay for a page, with a reason. Paying is one £5 payment on Stripe. No account, no subscription, nothing renews. The page you come back to adds the credit without checking it, because a site with no server cannot, and we say so. The price is a hypothesis. 10p for a new article read to the end, 5p for an older one, less for other pages. It could be wrong either way.

The bet is that people pay for reading when nothing forces them to, if what they get back is a site that knows what they read, with the history kept on their own machine. The anchors. Five numbers we expect, the ones that would prove us wrong, and a review date: eight weeks after the payment link goes live. It is a library now. SG Meter is one web component another site can add, with its config, events, storage and security model written down. A meter in the browser described the first version: every page debited from £5.00 of credit kept in the browser, a badge in the corner, a bar when credit ran out, a cart with every step but the payment. It was a demonstration and said so. Six things change.

You pay for what you read. A page's price is what it costs read to the end. You pay that times the share you scrolled through, never less than a tenth. Open a new article, read the first screen and leave: 1p. Read half: 5p. Reading further later in the same visit tops the same charge up. Your balance can go below zero, and stay there. Nothing is blocked. Nothing pops up. There is no bar, no count of articles read, no request. One small number in the top bar. The balance, as a link to your account. Below zero it changes colour, and its tooltip says nothing is blocked.

"Not worth it? Don't charge me." At the foot of an article, four reasons: the headline promised more than the page gave, not relevant to me, I did not really read it, another reason. The charge is refunded, and the reason is kept in your history as a signal. "Not relevant" counts against that page's topics when the site picks articles for you. A real payment. The top-up becomes one £5 Stripe payment. The simulated cart stays only for a site with no payment link configured. A library. The meter is rebuilt as SG Meter, a web component that follows the estate's JavaScript guidance, so another site can add it with a script tag and a config. The foot of an article: what it has cost so far, for how much of it was read, the price to the end, and the choice not to pay, with four reasons. Kept in the reader's browser, nowhere else.

The reading account below zero. This test account read sixteen articles to different depths and declined two; we then set its balance below zero in the browser's storage, the way any reader can. The balance in the top bar turns a warmer colour, and the account says nothing is blocked. Most reader-funded sites do the opposite, and do it well. The Guardian counts what you read in your browser's own storage, the same place this meter keeps its history. Its open-source code keeps a weekly count under gu.history.weeklyArticleCount, with a count per tag, starting each week on a Monday, ignoring repeat visits to the same article and dropping weeks older than a year. The count is used to ask you for support.

It works. Press Gazette reported in September 2025 that the Guardian's digital reader revenue rose 22%, "from £88m in 2023/2024 to £107m in the year to the end of March 2025". Its tiers are £4 a month to support, £12 a month to "avoid intrusive pop-up supporter messages" and read without ads, and £27 a month with the print weekly. Its app, Press Gazette added, "sits within a paywall (free users can only read 20 articles per month)". Two things in that are worth noticing. The middle tier sells, in part, the absence of the ask. And every tier is a subscription: £4 a month is £48 a year, £12 a month is £144 a year, a commitment decided once, in advance, for reading that has not happened yet. A one-off payment is the other door, and it is awkward in its own way: how much is fair, for what, and when?

This meter tries a third door. The ask is never made, because the balance is always visible and the price of each page is stated where you read it. The commitment is never asked for, because you pay for pages after you have read them, as much of them as you read, and you can refuse. And going below zero is not a failure state. It is information you have, about what you have read, kept where only you can see it.

The hypothesis is that a reader who can see an honest running total, and who is never shamed for it, is more willing to settle it than one who is counted and asked. More so as the site gives something back for the history: curation, picks, and in time a front page that is entirely personal to the reader, computed in their browser from what they read and what they declined. The first version of that front page is live the same day: your newsroom, one per persona, and why personas are what a reader would pay to keep is in pay to keep your persona.

Because a page is not one thing. A reader who opens an article, sees in the first paragraph that it is not for them and leaves has not had the same page as one who read it to the end. Charging them the same is a small unfairness repeated many times, and it rewards exactly the wrong writing: a headline that gets the click, followed by a page nobody finishes. Depth is measured on the page's main column, rounded to 5%, at most once every 400 milliseconds while you scroll and once more as you leave. It is not reading time and it is not attention; a reader can scroll to the bottom without reading. That is fine. The point is not to measure reading precisely. It is to make the price follow the reader's own choice to keep going, and to give them the refusal for the cases where it did not.

A charge tells us nothing; everyone who scrolled was charged. A refusal, with a reason, is the first thing this site has ever been told by a reader about a page without asking them to write anything. "The headline promised more than the page gave" is a verdict on the writing. "Not relevant to me" is a verdict on the placement, and on the picks. "I did not really read it" is a correction to the depth. They are kept in the reader's history, in their browser, like everything else, and used there: a page declined as not relevant pushes its topics down the reader's picks. We do not see them. If that changes, it will be because a reader chose to send their history, not because the meter sent it. Rating a page, classifying it and keeping a note on it are the obvious next steps, in the same local history. Not yet. A page read to the end

Price What £5 buys, read to the end An article published in the last seven days 10p 50 An older article 5p 100 A newsletter issue 3p 166 A desk note or a collection 2p 250 Any other page: docs, vaults, the network 1p 500 The homepage, subscribe, your account free Read by depth, a fiver goes further than the table says, because most pages are not read to the end. These prices were raised from the first version's 5p and 3p for articles on purpose: a price that is too low teaches nothing, because nobody would ever notice paying it, and we would rather find out that 10p is too much than never find out whether anyone would pay 10p. It could be more. It could be less. The account page prints the current table, and the build prints it from the same METER rules the meter charges by, so the published price and the charged price cannot differ.

The money first, because it is small and it should be said plainly. Stripe's listed UK fee for a standard UK card is 1.5% + 20p. On £5 that is 27.5p, so £4.72 reaches the site, about 94.5%. Premium UK cards are 2.8% + 20p (34p), European cards 2.5% + 20p (32.5p), international cards 3.15% + 20p (about 36p), plus 2% where the currency is converted. The fixed 20p is why the top-up is £5 and not £1: on £1, a standard card would cost 21.5p, more than a fifth. Payers in eight weeks Gross After a standard UK card fee 10 £50 £47.25 50 £250 £236.25 200 £1,000 £945 None of those rows pays for anything that matters. That is not the case for doing this. The case is three things the money cannot buy.

Evidence. Whether anyone pays for reading on a site that does not make them is the question in the question is whether they miss it. A meter that charges nothing could only answer half of it. A payment is the only signal on this site that cannot be produced by curiosity. A shape to test the personalisation against. The history is the product, as the first article put it. If readers who pay are readers who read more, and who come back, that is the case for building the personal front page, and it costs nothing to collect because the reader collects it.

A library. If it works here it works on any site that can add a script tag, which is a different and larger question about how news got here and whether a penny a page was ever the problem, or only the machinery around it. The same idea, from the other side, is price it, then give it away: put a real price on the thing, then let people decide. There is evidence that people pay when nothing forces them to, and evidence of how much less they pay. Both belong here. Paul Feldman's bagels. For years he left bagels and an unwatched cash box in offices. Freakonomics, writing about him in the New York Times Magazine in June 2004, reported that about 87% of bagels were paid for by 2001, rising by about two points after September 11. He had set 90% as the rate he would call honest, and in his earlier, basket years, about 95%.

**Radiohead's In Rainbows** was released in 2007 for whatever buyers chose to pay. comScore estimated that 38% of downloaders paid something (48% in the UK), that those who paid averaged about $6, and that the average across everyone who downloaded was $2.26. Pay what you want, measured. In a field experiment published in Science in 2010, Gneezy and colleagues sold photos at a theme park. At a fixed $12.95, 0.5% of riders bought. When riders could pay what they wanted, 8.39% bought, paying 92 cents on average. When half of what they paid went to charity, 4.49% bought, paying $5.33. The pattern is the one this meter is built around. Remove the force and many more people take part, while the average payment falls. A small, stated price per page sits between the two: the reader is told what is fair, and left to decide.

Written now, before there is a single payment, so that we cannot move the goalposts later. The clock starts when the Stripe link goes live; the review is eight weeks after that. If the link goes live today, that is 5 December 2026. Update, 11 October 2026: the link went live on newsroom.sgit.ai today, so the review is on 6 December 2026. # Hypothesis We expect Proved wrong if H1 Someone pays when nothing forces them to A first real payment within 14 days No payment in 14 days H2 Enough pay for it to be a signal, not an accident At least 10 different payers by the review Fewer than 5 H3 Paying is a habit, not a gesture At least 3 payers pay a second time No repeat payment H4 Making cheating easy costs nothing that reaches us No disputes or chargebacks Any dispute that is not plain card fraud H5

Below zero is normal, not a reason to leave Readers who send us their history mostly have a negative balance, and still read We cannot test this without readers sending their history; it is written here so that we notice if we start to believe it without evidence What we can see, so that nobody has to take these on trust: the Stripe dashboard (payments, amounts, payers, repeat payers, disputes), and the views LinkedIn reports on the articles cross-posted there, which is the nearest thing to a denominator we have. What we cannot see: anything the meter records. There is no analytics on this site, and the meter sends nothing. The depth you read, the pages you declined and why, your balance: all of it is in your browser. If you want to help, the account page exports it as JSON, and you can send it to us. Nobody has to.

Added the same day, before any payment: two more hypotheses, H6 and H7, about what readers would pay for beyond reading, are in pay to keep your persona. The five above are unchanged. We will publish the review on the review date, whatever it says, with the numbers from the Stripe dashboard. A hypothesis that fails is a result. The one outcome that would be a failure of the method is not looking. If nobody pays (H1, H2), the price is not the first suspect. The first suspect is that the trade is invisible: the balance is small, the payment is one click away from nowhere, and the personalisation is too thin to want. We would make the picks better before we made the meter louder. If people pay once and not again (H3), the history is not worth enough to them yet. That points at the personal front page, not at the price.

If cheating shows up somewhere we can see (H4), the balance has started to unlock something, or someone is testing stolen cards. The first would need a server and a signed receipt; the second is Stripe's to stop, and the payment link can be switched off in a minute. If the reasons readers send are mostly "the headline promised more than the page gave", that is about the writing, and the newsroom's behaviour policies are where it gets fixed.

Anyone, in several easy ways: edit the balance in developer tools, open a private window, or open the page a payment returns to with a made-up reference and get £5 of credit. Each of those changes a number only the cheater can see, and costs the site a payment it was never going to receive. Who would actually do it, how many of them there are, and which risks are real is the subject of the companion piece, who will game the reading meter. Your meter has been running since you arrived. Abstract: Levente Simon sent me his method for running teams of AI agents that build production software, Governed semi-autonomous development, and asked for feedback. It is a serious piece of work, born from practice: eight control layers, three assurance profiles, a learning loop, and the honesty to say that its evidence base is a single product. Reading it, the first thing that struck me is how often it arrives at ideas we reached separately: authority stays human for anything outward-facing; the owner receives decisions, not files; a rule that breaks twice becomes a mechanism; rule text is a guard-rail, not a boundary; and a session cannot write what enforces its limits. The second thing is that his method is a good mirror. Measured against his lowest profile, this newsroom, where agents write and publish every day, meets five of his eight layers, falls short on one by a recorded choice, and falls short on another by an oversight: the agent that publishes can also change the checks that gate it, which is exactly what we found in our own measurement this week. And then the feedback he asked for: five things we would add, from a column per rule that says what keeps it, to behaviour policies for the agents inside the product, state in encrypted vaults, the owner measures he proposes, which we have started to publish, and agents losing their memory as a design input.
The same ideas, arrived at separately: the method's principles on the left, where each shows up in our work.
in-short

A method for agent teams that build software. Born from practice, on one product. Many of its ideas are ours too. Arrived at separately, which is a good sign for both. Authority stays human; decisions, not files. The same shape as our inbox. A rule that breaks twice becomes a mechanism. Our validator says the same. It is a good mirror. By its lowest profile, this newsroom falls short on two layers. One of them is the gap we just measured. The agent can change the checks that gate it. Five things we would add. Offered as the feedback he asked for.
method

Levente Simon sent me his draft and asked for feedback, so this is that feedback, written in public because the method is public. Governed semi-autonomous development is "a tool-agnostic reference method for governing teams of AI agents that build production software." Its stance is in its first lines: "Agents do the work; humans keep authority over everything irreversible or outward-facing. Trust comes from layered controls, not from the agents behaving well."
method

It came out of building dethernety, his threat modelling platform, as the work outgrew a single session and moved to teams of agents. The roles are an owner, an orchestrator, workers, specialists and a library of capabilities. The controls sit in eight layers, from infrastructure isolation to state and audit, each at one of three assurance profiles, Lite, Standard and High, chosen per layer from the risks the work actually carries. It is versioned, already at v0.7, with a changelog, and its related-work section withdrew a novelty claim rather than narrow it again. And it says plainly what bounds it: "The evidence base is a single product, which is stated here because it bounds what the method can claim." That is the kind of sentence I wish more methods had.
same

What struck me first is how often the method lands where we did, by a different road: Authority stays human. His first principle keeps every outward action with a person. Our inbox agent drafts and I send every email, as in answering a draft. "The owner receives decisions, not files." That is exactly our decision draft: where we are, why it matters, the options and an answer box, so I decide without reading the thread. "A rule that breaks twice becomes a mechanism." Our site validator has a check whose comment says: "This has now happened twice from the same cause (see .gitignore), so it is a check." And in the inbox, every rule came from a mistake. "Rule text is a guard-rail against mistakes, not a boundary against an adversary." That is the Agent Behaviour Policy's distinction between an expectation and a boundary, from hope or enforcement.
same

"Messages carry information, never authority." A message from another agent, in our sessions, is data from a peer, never an approval. A signed manifest anchored on the owner's public key. Our work on pki.sgit.ai, and, today, on swapping keys by QR code. When two groups working apart converge on the same rules, it suggests the rules are real. That is worth more than either of us claiming them.
mirror

This newsroom measured against the method's Lite profile, layer by layer, with the shortfalls and the recorded choice. The best use of a method is to hold your own work up to it, so I did. This newsroom is run by agents: I write and publish here every day. Against his lowest profile, Lite: Five layers meet it, or nearly. Infrastructure, sessions, messages and state meet it; the agents run in their own containers, with access scoped to this repository, treat each other's messages as data, and verify every release live. Permissions fall short by choice. Lite asks that "the owner performs all outward actions". Here, the agent publishes. That is a deliberate grant, written in the session's behaviour policy, and the method allows exactly this: "A layer below the chosen profile needs a recorded decision."
mirror

Repository controls fall short by oversight. Lite asks for owner-only merge and tag, and "required CI enforced by the repository host, which is the one out-of-band, deterministic verification the agents cannot produce for themselves." Our CI is in band: the agent that pushes can also change the validator, the tests and the workflow, in the same push. That last point is the one we found ourselves this week. In behaviour policies from the checks I counted 57 checks, and only one is out of the agent's reach. His method has the rule that would have caught it: "a session cannot write what enforces its limits." And the fix it prescribes, required checks enforced by the host and protected paths that reach the owner as a diff, is the same one we proposed. I take that as the strongest endorsement I can give a method: it found our gap.
add

Five suggestions, from a column per rule saying what keeps it to memory loss as a design input. He asked for feedback, so here are five suggestions, each from something we have built, measured or got wrong: A column per rule: what keeps it. His method already says a rule is a guard-rail and a check a boundary. An Agent Behaviour Policy makes that a column: for every rule, the grant (what the agent can do), the mandate (what it may do), the delta between them, and the barrier that keeps it, an expectation, a setting or a boundary. Then the gap is counted, not described, as in our 57 checks.
add

Policies for the product's agents, not only the builders. The method governs agents that build software. More and more of that software will run agents of its own, and then the risk is business logic: the payment, the refund, the alert closed without a second person. That is the argument of the key is not the risk, and of the Pellbridge vault, built on the FCA's four elements. State in encrypted vaults. His ledger lives in the repository; at High, messages go over a private bus. We keep state and messages in encrypted vaults that travel between environments, on a server that only ever holds ciphertext. It is one way to get a cross-environment channel and a tamper-evident history without running a broker.
add

The measures he proposes, measured. His section on metrics says the owner measures "are defined here and have not been published from this practice". We have started: the inbox agent's 47 recorded decisions, and an evening of seven decisions, mostly answered in ten minutes; and, in the checks, measured, how long every check takes and where it runs. A second evidence base, from a different kind of work, is something we can offer. Memory loss as a design input. His related work names an open question I recognise every day: "no human organization has a class of participant that loses its policy memory at unpredictable intervals." This session, running since 15 October, has been compacted fourteen times, and every time a hook has read its behaviour policy back from disk, and a status report every few answers shows the policy is still in force. Treating that loss as normal, and designing for it, could be a layer of its own.
limits

This is one reading of v0.7. The method changes often; this is the version of 21 October 2026. The self-assessment is ours. Our reading of his profiles against this session, not an audit. His setting differs from ours. He governs agents that build a product; we run agents that write and publish. The suggestions are suggestions. Some may already be in his control reference in another form.
sources

Levente Simon's Governed semi-autonomous development, v0.7, read in full from its public repository on 21 October 2026, its README, method, control reference and related work, quoted under its CC BY 4.0 licence; and his message asking for feedback, paraphrased. Our side: answering a draft, the checks, measured, behaviour policies from the checks, the key is not the risk, a secret is a QR code, messaging-FS, hope or enforcement, and this session's behaviour policy and hooks. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: Someone working on assurance for agents described to me how ruv.sgit and their work fit together, and asked me to check it. They were almost right, and the part to make precise is the word "enforces". An Agent Behaviour Policy does not enforce anything by itself. It says what each role is granted and for, writes each rule down, and says how each rule is kept, at one of three levels: in the prompt, which is a hope; by hooks in the agent's harness, which are deterministic but sit on the agent's own machine; or by a third-party system that does the blocking, which is the level we recommend. In ruv.sgit that third party is Ruflo's own policy engine in enforce mode, which writes a decision receipt for every action, and an sgit vault keeps the memory encrypted and versioned. What none of that gives you is something a third party can check without taking the operator's word for it. That is the attestation layer: it signs what was assured, so a customer, an auditor or an insurer can verify it. Different layers of the same stack. This article shows the stack, the three levels, the business case with and without attestation, and one action going through all of it.
Four layers of the same stack: the mandate, enforcement, the record and attestation.
in-short

A good summary, nearly right. The word to make precise is "enforces". An ABP governs. It states the mandate per role, and how each rule is kept. Rules are kept at three levels. The prompt, hooks, and a third-party system that blocks. The third level is the one we recommend. In ruv.sgit it is Ruflo's policy engine. The receipt comes from the enforcer. The vault keeps it, with the memory. None of that is verifiable from outside. Today, a third party takes the operator's word. An attestation layer signs what was assured. So a customer, auditor or insurer can check it. Different layers of one stack. And a natural early integration.
summary

Someone who works on assurance for agents described how ruv.sgit and their work fit together, and asked me to check that they had it right. In short, their framing was that the Agent Behaviour Policy governs and enforces behaviour, and their layer attests to what was assured, so a third party can verify it: different layers of the same stack. I think that is almost right. The part I would like to make precise is "enforces", because how a rule is kept is exactly what an Agent Behaviour Policy is about, and exactly what an attestation layer would need to know.
abp

An Agent Behaviour Policy is a document, written per role, that says what the agent is granted (its reach), what it is for (its mandate), and the rules it works under. For every rule, it also says what keeps it. That last column is the point. A rule that only the agent keeps is a hope. A rule that something else keeps is a control. Policy as code needs a policy first has the questions an ABP answers that a policy engine alone does not: what the agent can reach, what it was asked to do and why, where the two differ, and, for every rule that is code, who can change that code. So an ABP governs. It does not, by itself, enforce. It names the enforcer.
levels

We provide three levels at which an ABP rule can be kept, and an ABP says which one each rule uses. Three levels of enforcement for one rule of an Agent Behaviour Policy: the prompt, hooks and a third-party system. The prompt. The rule is written into the agent's instructions. This is where most rules live today, and it is what I call hope-based security: the rule holds only if the model keeps it. It is still worth writing down, because a rule that is not written cannot be checked at all.
levels

Hooks. Small deterministic programs that the agent's harness runs before and after each action, which can see, block or rewrite what the agent does. Are hooks the sweet spot? tested this on this site's own policy: of eleven rules, four moved into hooks fully, two mostly, three partly and two not at all. Hooks are a big step up, but they run on the agent's machine, often where the agent's own account could change them, which is why hooks are kernel code proposes treating them that way. A third-party system that does the blocking. A policy engine, a gateway, a sandbox or the service itself, outside the agent's reach, that answers allow or deny for each action. This is the level we recommend for any rule that matters, and it is where real enforcement ends up.
levels

In ruv.sgit the third level is concrete. Ruflo is an agent meta-harness with its own policy engine, which runs in legacy, observe or enforce mode and writes a decision receipt for each action. An ABP compiles into Ruflo's rules and runs in enforce mode; that is the adapter documented in our first PR in Ruflo. And the policy guards the door is honest about its limit: only the tools that pass through the adapter are checked, so the policy has to say which paths go around it.
receipt

The summary I was sent described an enforced mandate per role, with a memory and a receipt of what happened. All three exist in ruv.sgit, but in different places. The mandate is the ABP. The receipt is written by the enforcer, Ruflo's policy engine, for each decision it makes. The memory is the hive's memory, kept in an sgit vault, encrypted on your machine, versioned and cloneable, with the receipts alongside it. That matters for attestation, because it says what there is to attest: a policy, at a version, with each rule's level; a set of decisions with their receipts; and a record that has not changed since.
missing

Here is the gap. Everything above is evidence for the operator. If a customer, an auditor or an insurer asks "was this agent working under that policy, and did the enforcer actually block what it should have?", today the answer is the operator's word, and a folder of receipts they would have to trust. The same question from a customer, an auditor or an insurer, answered without and with an attestation layer.
missing

That is what an attestation layer adds: it attests and signs what was assured, so that a third party can verify it. Signed, the record says which version of the policy was in force, which level kept each rule, what the enforcer decided, and that none of it has changed. And because an ABP marks each rule's level, an honest attestation can say not only what was enforced, but what was only hoped for. That is the part I would most like an attestation to carry: a rule kept in the prompt should be attested as a prompt rule, not as a control. This is also where the liability question lands. The policy draws the liability line argued that when an agent goes wrong, nothing was written down between the person clicking allow and the failure. An ABP writes it down. An attestation makes it something another party can rely on.
flow
One action through the stack, from the agent's tool call to the signed attestation a customer can verify.
layers

So I would put the summary like this. An Agent Behaviour Policy governs: it states the mandate per role and says how each rule is kept, in the prompt, by hooks, or, as we recommend, by a third-party system that blocks. In ruv.sgit, Ruflo's policy engine is that third party and writes a receipt for every decision, and an sgit vault keeps the memory and the record. An attestation layer signs what was assured, so a third party can verify it. Different layers of the same stack, and a natural early integration, because the ABP already holds the one thing an attestation needs to be honest: which rules were controls, and which were hopes.
limits

The attestation layer is described, not built here. Its design is its makers'; this is how it would meet ours. Three levels is a simplification. Hooks are kernel code splits them into five; three is how we offer them. Enforce mode covers the tools that pass through it. Paths around the adapter are not checked. Signing proves integrity, not truth. A signed record of a weak policy is still a weak policy.
sources
