Abstract: Two releases pushed cleanly, reported success, and never reached the site. Every check we had was green, because the failure happened in a place none of them could see. What we changed, and the general rule underneath it. Two consecutive releases of this site pushed cleanly, verified themselves against both remotes, printed "both remotes in sync, done", and never reached anybody. The site served a two-release-old page for forty minutes. It was noticed by a human on a phone, who looked at the version badge and said "is this the latest version?" Everything about that sentence is worth sitting with. The checks were not weak. They were checking the wrong boundary. The release script does five things, and four of them are good: Build the site from source. Run the validator, structure, links, markdown twins, orphan pages, and a tripwire that scans every tracked file for a vault key.

Commit and push the encrypted vault; confirm sgit status reports in sync. Commit and push the git mirror; confirm HEAD == origin/dev. Step 4 is where the confidence came from, and it is genuinely a strong check, it compares hashes, not hopes. The problem is what it means. It means the bytes arrived at GitHub. It does not mean anybody can read them. Publishing this site has three boundaries, and we were verifying two: source ──▶ git remote ──▶ Pages deploy ──▶ the reader ↑ ↑ ↑ verified verified NOT VERIFIED Between the second and third arrows sits a GitHub Actions job. It has its own failure modes, it reports into a system neither remote knows about, and nothing in our release looked at it. Not our code. Not the content. The deploy job died in "Set up job": before running a single step of its own:

Download action repository 'actions/configure-pages@v5' ##[warning] Failed to download ... Error: 429 (Too Many Requests) ##[warning] Back off 12.459 seconds before retry. ##[warning] Failed to download ... Error: 429 (Too Many Requests) ##[warning] Back off 26.597 seconds before retry. ##[error] Failed to download archive after 3 attempts. codeload.github.com rate-limited the download of a third-party action. The validate job passed. The tag-release job passed. The one job that puts bytes in front of readers could not fetch its own dependency. This is worth stating plainly because it is the ordinary case, not an exotic one: the most likely thing to break in a deploy is not your code. It is a piece of shared infrastructure you do not run, on a day you were not thinking about it. A release now finishes by asking the live site what version it is serving:

== 5/6 verify the deploy actually published waiting for v0.2.34 to appear at https://sgit.ai/ (up to 8 min) ...... live: sgit.ai is serving v0.2.34 It polls with a cache-buster, because the origin's own answer is the only one that counts. If the version never appears it aborts loudly, names the Actions page, and says that a 429 on the action download is transient and needs a re-run. The cost is real: up to eight minutes of waiting on every release. We took it, because the alternative had already been demonstrated twice in one afternoon, telling somebody a fix was live when it was not, twice, in writing. This site already had two rules of exactly this shape, and adding the third made the pattern obvious: A page nothing links to is unpublished. The build fails on an orphan page, it happened once, a brief that was written, built and pushed while nothing linked to it.

A page the machine index omits is unpublished. The build fails if any page would be missing from llms.txt, that happened too, a whole section silently absent. A page the deploy never served is unpublished. Now the release fails on it. All three are the same claim: shipped is a fact about the reader, not about your repository. Every one of them was learned by getting it wrong first, which is the only reason the list is short and specific rather than long and aspirational. Being honest about the edges, since that is the house rule: It detects a failed deploy; it does not repair one. A 429 still needs a human or a re-run. It checks the home page's version badge, not every page. A partial deploy that published some files would pass. It adds up to eight minutes to a release, which is a real tax on small fixes.

All three are acceptable against the failure they replace. The first one to bite will get its own entry. Abstract: The pain I have right now is giving secrets to the places that do my work: vault keys to a browser where the passkey does not reach, and vault keys to the agent sessions I schedule every day. Copying them by hand is slow and risky, and when I tell an agent in its prompt that something is a secret to be careful with, it sometimes refuses to use it at all. So I would like SG/Send's technology to focus on one use case: handing a secret, or a public key, to an agent or a browser, as a separate site, mostly client-side, with a command line. The back end already has most of what this needs: a transfer that can be downloaded once and then deleted, an expiry, and client-side encryption; it does not, I found, restrict by location, which I thought it did. The design flips the usual direction: the recipient makes its own key pair where it runs and shows only the public half, by QR code, link or paste; the owner encrypts the secret to it and signs it; the drop is read once; and the secret goes from the drop into the tool, never into the chat. This site's agent ran it end to end on a local server: the agent decrypted the secret, the second download got a 410, the owner's signature verified once the agent knew the owner's key, and a browser made a key pair it refused to export. The industry is moving the other way, keeping secrets out of agents entirely; for an encrypted vault that cannot work, because the key has to reach the place that decrypts.
Handing a secret to an agent or a browser without anyone seeing it. Steps 1 to 4 ran on a local SG/Send server.
in-short

One use case. Handing a secret, or a public key, to an agent or a browser. The back end is mostly there. One download, then deleted; an expiry; client-side encryption. Flip the direction. The recipient makes its key pair; the owner encrypts to it. Into the tool, not the chat. The agent is told what to run, not what the secret is. Tested end to end. Decrypted once, refused twice, signature verified, private key unexportable. The first secret is the hard one. A scheduled session starts with one key from its environment. Against the trend, on purpose. Proxies keep API keys out of agents; a vault key must reach the place that decrypts.
pain

I have a growing number of places that need secrets: browsers where I read and write my vaults, and agent sessions that run on a schedule and need a vault key to do their work. The passkey opens the vault works well when it works, but it does not always: the same passkey, answering a QR code from another device, gave different bytes, and some browsers and profiles simply do not have it. Sixteen notes I did not want to lose came out of exactly that, and proposed a link or QR code "carrying only where to write and the public key to encrypt with". QR codes worked well in those experiments; they carry a lot more than people think.
pain

The agents are the other half. My observation, from many sessions, is that the more a prompt insists that a value is a secret, to be handled carefully and not exposed, the more likely the model is to refuse to use it at all. The caution is correct; the result is useless. And the secret I really want to give an agent is not a vault key. It is the agent's own private key, so that every other secret can be sent to it.
backend

The back end does most of this already, and I wanted to know exactly how much. The transfer API takes, at creation, max_downloads ("Max downloads before exhausted"), auto_delete ("Wipe payload after last allowed download"), expires_at, and the hash of a delete code; the payload is encrypted in the client before upload; access tokens carry a usage limit and log a hash of the caller's address. What it does not have is a restriction by location. I thought it did; the code has no geographic check, so that is new work if we want it.
backend

It also has a friendly mode, where two words and four digits derive both the key and the transfer id. The word list has 320 words, so a code is one of about a billion, roughly 30 bits, stretched with PBKDF2 at 600,000 iterations. That is not enough for anything. The sgit team's security review of 6 August found that the public id is an unsalted hash of the code, so anyone who sees the id can recover the code offline, and that the fixed salt lets one precomputed table open every such transfer; the command line stopped creating them in June. And sgit already has public-key cryptography: sgit pki keygen makes an RSA-OAEP 4096 key for encryption and an ECDSA P-256 key for signing, and encrypt and decrypt do the rest.
design

The usual way to share a secret is to send a link with the key in it. For agents and browsers, the idea is the opposite direction: The recipient makes a key pair where it runs. An agent runs sgit pki keygen in its session; a browser uses WebCrypto with a private key that cannot be exported. Only the public half leaves: the bundle sgit exported was 1,164 bytes, which fits in one QR code; a QR code holds up to 2,953 bytes at its largest size, according to its inventor. The owner checks and encrypts. I check the fingerprint, encrypt the secret to that public key, and sign it with my own key. SG/Send holds it once. The ciphertext goes into a transfer with one download, deletion afterwards and an expiry. The server never sees a key.
design

The recipient decrypts into the tool. It downloads once, checks my signature against my public key, which it was given when it was set up, and pipes the result straight into sgit clone -, which already reads the key from standard input to keep it out of the command line and its history. The last step is the answer to the refusals. The agent is never shown the secret, and never asked to be careful with it. Its instructions say what to run; the secret travels from the drop to the tool through a pipe, and never enters the prompt, the transcript or the model's context. That matters more than it seems: the tokens hook found that the session transcript holds everything the model is told, and anything that can read the transcript can read that.
test

This site's agent ran the whole flow on a local SG/Send server, with sgit 0.21.0 and a dummy secret. An "agent" made a key pair and exported its public bundle; a "human" imported it, encrypted the secret to it and signed it; the 1,288 bytes of ciphertext went into a transfer with max_downloads set to 1, auto_delete and a one-hour expiry. The agent's first download returned the ciphertext intact, and it decrypted to the exact secret; the second download got 410 and "exhausted"; and the human's own key could not decrypt what it had sent. At first the agent reported "Signature present but UNVERIFIED"; once it held the owner's public key, it reported "Signature verified (signer: human-laptop)", which is why the owner's key has to be pinned when the recipient is set up.
test

In a browser, Chromium made an RSA-4096 key pair in 649 milliseconds and a P-256 pair in 0.3; asked to export the private key, it refused with InvalidAccessError, which is the point of a key made with extractable set to false. The WebCrypto specification adds that "CryptoKey objects are serializable objects", so the key can live in the browser's storage without ever being readable as bytes. On the command line, a key pair took between half a second and a second. One friction showed up: sgit pki keygen asks for a passphrase to protect the private key, which a session running on its own cannot type, so it had to come from standard input.
first

Everything above depends on one thing: the recipient's private key. For a browser, it is made in place and never leaves. For a scheduled agent session, which starts from nothing every time, it has to come from somewhere, and that is the one secret this design cannot avoid. The honest options are two. The environment can hold it, accepting what Anthropic's own documentation says of cloud environment variables: "Anyone who uses the environment can read the values." That makes the key an identity of the environment, not of a session, which is right for an environment that is mine. Or each session makes its own key pair and asks to be paired, by showing a fingerprint or a QR code that I approve from my phone, the way a new device is paired.
trend

The industry is moving the other way. Claude Code's cloud environments offer network secrets: "A network secret is an API key or token you store on a cloud environment so Claude can call that API from any session in the environment without seeing the key," because "Anthropic's agent proxy adds the key to requests for the hosts you list, after each request leaves the session's VM". 1Password's environments server for agents says that "By design, the server cannot return secret values stored in 1Password to the client, even if an agent requests them." For API keys, that is the right answer: the agent never needs to hold the key.
trend

A vault key is different. The whole point of a zero-knowledge vault is that decryption happens at the client, so the key has to reach the place that decrypts; a proxy cannot add it on the way out. What this design can do is make that reach as small as possible: a key made where it is used, a secret encrypted to it, read once, piped into the tool, and never in the model's context.
prior

One-time secret sharing tools compared with handing a secret to an agent, from each tool's documentation. One-time secrets are a solved problem for people: Bitwarden Send, 1Password's share links, Yopass and PrivateBin all encrypt in the client and expire. Magic Wormhole solves the short code properly, with a key exchange where "Each code is one-time use only", and age encrypts to a recipient's public key from the command line. What none of them is built around is a recipient that is an agent or a browser, making its own key, with an owner's signature it checks. The closest I found are small plugins for agent frameworks, such as Hermes' secret handoff, which keeps the value out of the transcript but, by its own account, not out of the chat history of the surface that asked for it.
prior

The name needs work. Handoff is Apple's; KeyDrop is a Consumer Reports project that scans for exposed API keys; Courier is a messaging platform for humans and agents; Baton is an identity governance tool. I found no prominent product called SealDrop, which says what it does, a sealed drop, and is my working name; I have not checked trademark registries.
brief

One site, one job. A separate site, built on SG/Send's transfer API, for handing secrets and public keys to agents and browsers. Client first. All cryptography in the browser or the command line; a JavaScript library and the sgit command line share one format. Recipients make keys. A browser makes a non-extractable key pair; an agent session runs one command; both show the public half as a QR code, a link and text. Owners encrypt and sign. The page that sends shows the recipient's fingerprint, encrypts, signs, and creates a transfer with one download, deletion and a short expiry. Receive into the tool. One command downloads, verifies the owner's signature against a pinned key, decrypts and pipes into sgit clone -; nothing is printed. Pairing for new sessions. A session that has no key yet shows a fingerprint and a QR code; the owner approves it from a phone.
brief

No passphrase prompt for agents. A documented way to give the private key's protection from the environment, and a test that it never reaches a log. No short codes. The friendly code is retired; a short code is only safe inside a key exchange built for it, as Magic Wormhole does. Location limits, if wanted. New work in the back end, not something it has today.
limits

It ran locally. One local server, one dummy secret, one browser; not the hosted service. The refusals are my observation. Not measured here. The first secret is not solved. It is moved to the environment, or to a pairing step. The prior art is from documentation. None of the other tools was run for this article. SealDrop is a working name. Checked on the web, not in trademark registries. The friendly code is not safe on its own. The sgit security review shows it can be recovered offline from the public id, even for a single download that expires in minutes. If you hand secrets to agents and have found a better way, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Summary: The pain I have right now is giving secrets to the places that do my work: vault keys to a browser where the passkey does not reach, and vault keys to the agent sessions I schedule every day. Copying them by hand is slow and risky, and when I tell an agent in its prompt that something is a secret to be careful with, it sometimes refuses to use it at all. So I want SG/Send's technology to focus on one use case: handing a secret, or a public key, to an agent or a browser, as a separate site, mostly client-side, with a command line. The back end already has most of what this needs: a transfer that can be downloaded once and then deleted, an expiry, and client-side encryption; it does not, I found, restrict by location, which I thought it did. The design flips the usual direction: the recipient makes its own key pair where it runs and shows only the public half, by QR code, link or paste; the owner encrypts the secret to it and signs it; the drop is read once; and the secret goes from the drop into the tool, never into the chat. This site's agent ran it end to end on a local server: the agent decrypted the secret, the second download got a 410, the owner's signature verified once the agent knew the owner's key, and a browser made a key pair it refused to export. The industry is moving the other way, keeping secrets out of agents entirely; for an encrypted vault that cannot work, because the key has to reach the place that decrypts.

Abstract: I think October 2026 is a moment of real opportunity for anyone willing to get properly into agentic workflows. The first phase has passed. The tools and the workflows are maturing, still rough at the edges, but you can now glue the pieces together and get real work done, and companies are moving from pilots to products. I have lived this pattern before, in security and in software. There was a time when, if you could break an application, read code, build a website, build a mobile app or make a spreadsheet do something clever, you had a job, degree or no degree. This is that time again. And the people companies need are not the ones who build models, which is who the first wave of AI hiring went to; they are good AI operators, people who know how to use the tools and the workflows to get things done. The data agrees: in Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 survey, 71% of leaders said they would rather hire a less experienced candidate with AI skills than a more experienced one without, and PwC found this year that jobs asking for AI skills pay 62% more. When two candidates look equally good on paper, someone still has to choose. If you work this way, the choice starts with your application: a CV fitted to the role, an analysis of their problem, something they have not seen. I got jobs that way, before any of this existed, because of my OWASP work.
Skills that, for a while, got people hired on what they could show, ending with running agentic workflows.
in-short

The first phase of agents has passed. The tools and workflows are maturing; companies are moving from pilots to products. This has happened before. Breaking apps, building websites, building mobile apps: each got people hired, degree or not. You are more technical than you think. If you use email, websites and apps well, you can learn the new techniques. Companies need operators, not model builders. The first wave of AI hiring went to the wrong people. The data points the same way. Leaders would rather hire for AI skills than for experience; the roles pay more. The edge shows when the choice is close. And it starts with the application.
moment

We are entering the productisation of agents. The first phase, the demos and the experiments, is behind us. The tools are getting more mature, the workflows too, and while they are still rough around the edges, you can already glue the pieces together and get real work done. That is what I am doing with agentics, and with this newsroom. The analysts see the same shift, with a warning attached. Gartner predicted in August 2025 that 40% of enterprise applications would feature task-specific AI agents by 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025. Two months earlier it had predicted that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, because of cost, unclear value or weak risk controls. Both can be true, and together they say where the bottleneck is: not the models, but people who can make agents do useful work, safely.
moment
So this is the moment for the many people on the outskirts: paying a bit of attention, or using a chat window for basic questions, but not yet working this way. Get on with it.
there-was-a-time

I have lived this pattern in security, and in software more broadly. There was a time when, if you could break an application, you had a job. If you could read code and do a code review, you had a job. If you could do threat modelling, you had a job. If you could programme decently, it did not matter that you had no university degree; you could show what you could do, and you got hired. There was a time when building a website got you a job, and knowing how to send email campaigns got you a job. When Apple opened the App Store in July 2008, with more than 800 apps in its first weekend, people who could build a mobile app got jobs. So did people who knew Salesforce inside out, or could make a spreadsheet do things others could not.
there-was-a-time

Each of those skills later became normal. Today you meet people who use email, websites and apps at a very advanced level, and who still say "I'm not technical". Nonsense. Of course you are technical. You learned all of those. You just need to learn the new techniques, and right now the new techniques are the ones that get people hired.
operators

I have said this before, and it matters even more now. In the first wave of corporate AI hiring, when there was a lot of budget, the only people companies knew how to hire were people who did machine learning and wanted to build models. LinkedIn's 2020 emerging jobs report put "AI specialist" at the top, defined by skills like machine learning, deep learning and TensorFlow. For most companies that was the last thing they needed.
operators

What they need is very good AI operators. That is my term, not a job title you will find in a survey: people who know how to use the tools, who know how to run workflows like the ones I describe on this site, and who can build a website on steroids in an afternoon. The nearest role the market has named is the forward-deployed engineer, the person who sits with a customer and makes the technology work in their setting; one analysis of job postings found those roles up 1,165% year on year in 2025.
data

Leaders would rather hire for AI skills than for experience. In Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index, 66% of leaders said they would not hire someone without AI skills, and 71% said they would "rather hire a less experienced candidate with AI skills than a more experienced candidate without them." Most people have not been trained. In the same study, only 39% of people using AI at work had received training from their company (Microsoft). The skill is mostly self-taught, which means anyone can start. It pays. PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, from more than a billion job adverts in 27 countries, found the wage premium for AI skills at 62%, up from 57%, and jobs asking for AI skills growing about eight times as fast as the job market as a whole (the release, 15 June 2026).
experience

None of this lands by reading about it. I have seen it with a group I have been working with: people who were not building websites a few weeks ago now build them easily, with the workflow we use here, and one of them now has a much better understanding of how all the pieces fit together. I am proud of that. What changed their view was not an explanation; it was doing it. Perception changes when people experience it, and only then. That is also why explorer coding and the citizen developer matter: the explorer who builds the thing they need is learning the skill that gets them hired.
decision

Think about how hiring actually works. However good you are, there is always a moment when someone has to make a decision. It is very unlikely that you are so good at something that you are the only choice. Usually, once the job spec is mapped, two or three people look roughly equal. Why would they pick you? My bet is: because you work this way. If you know how to run these agentic workflows and map a problem out, you have a real edge, and it shows from the very first step. When all things are equal: two candidates for the same job, one sending a CV and one sending much more.
application

It starts with the recruitment process itself. You send a CV customised for that role. You do an analysis of the company and its problem. You give them something that impresses them: a graph of their market, an infographic, a small site, something they have not seen before. That is exactly the work these tools make cheap, and exactly what the man behind the curtain describes: an article, or a piece of evidence, behind every message.
application

I know this works because it worked for me, long before agents. I got jobs because of my OWASP work. I remember one interview where they already knew my OWASP project, so I spent half the interview talking about the tool they had been trying to use, and giving them insights on how to use it better. I got the job. Instead of them looking for gaps in my CV, or wondering where I might fit, we had a great conversation, and I was playing from a position of strength. Of course I was a good fit; but the conversation started from what I could do, not from what my CV did not say.
application

That is the same move, now available to anyone. If you can send a company material they have not seen, about their own problem, the interview starts from your strengths. I wrote in 2025 about using presentations instead of CVs in hiring, from the other side of the table; agents make that presentation, and much more, something you can build for each application.
start

Pick one workflow and do it end to end. A voice memo turned into a checked article, a site, a research pack. Your own newsroom is one. Publish it. Work that can be linked is work that can be shown. Use it in your next application. One analysis, one figure, one thing they have not seen.
limits

Not a guarantee. An edge is not a job; it helps when the choice is close. "AI operator" is my term. The surveys measure AI skills and roles like forward-deployed engineer, not operators. Some figures are forecasts. Gartner's are predictions; PwC's are from job adverts, not hires. The group I mention is not named. What changed for them is my observation, not a measurement. If you have got a job, or hired someone, because of how they worked with agents, I would like to hear it: write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The hooks we are now going to deploy are code, and very critical code. They are also a very good example of code that is simple in many ways: a hook can be five lines. That makes them a good case study for everything we do on code review, code practices, semantic graphs and change blast radius, because the problem is small enough to do completely. A hook runs on every matching action, with the user's permissions, and can see, block or rewrite what the agent does; we should treat it like kernel code. Hooks also range from completely deterministic scripts to hooks that call a model or a whole agent, so I propose a maturity model: five levels from the prompt to off the machine, and three questions for every hook, how much power it has, which legs of the lethal trifecta it touches, and how much sandbox it runs in. I mapped the first ten: three this session runs, five tested in a sandbox, two proposed. They are between 4 and 26 lines, and the smallest of them depend on much more: the eleven-line commit hook calls a 37-line scan, so one line changed in the scan moves the commit gate for every session. And this is a brief for a site and a feed to manage them, like a skills manager: every hook from its intent, with its graph, tests, version and signature, installable anywhere, and a billing model where nobody pays to run a hook, but paying buys state.
The first ten hooks: three this session runs, five tested in a sandbox and two proposed.
in-short

Hooks are code, and critical code. Small, and with kernel reach: every matching action, the user's permissions, the power to block or rewrite. A good case study. Small enough to apply code review, graphs and change blast radius completely. Deterministic and not. A hook can be five lines of script, or a call to a model, or an agent that runs other agents. A maturity model. Five levels from the prompt to off the machine, and three questions: power, the lethal trifecta, the sandbox. The first ten, mapped. 4 to 26 lines each; the eleven-line commit hook calls a 37-line scan. Hooks of hooks. A hook that checks the other hooks; a scan that several hooks depend on. The graph is fractal. A site and a feed. Every hook from its intent, with its graph, tests, version and signature, like a skills manager.
in-short
Pay for state, never to run. Installs are free and work offline; paying buys history, alerts, attestations and updates.
kernel

Agent hooks in October 2026 mapped what hooks can do, and Are hooks the sweet spot? moved this site's own rules into them. Now we are going to deploy them, and that changes how they should be treated. A hook is fundamentally code. But look at where it runs. It is called by the harness on every matching event, before and after every tool call, at every prompt and every stop. It runs with the user's permissions. It sees the action in the agent's own terms, and it can block it, ask a person, or rewrite what the model reads. In an operating system, the code with that position is the kernel. Why my agents do not run on my laptop put it plainly: "An operating system has two hard walls, the kernel and the user." Hooks are the agent's kernel, and today we write them like scripts.
kernel

So we should manage them like kernel code. As small as possible. Reviewed by more than one person. Versioned, tested against fixed inputs on every change, signed, installed where the agent cannot write, and rolled out with care. And we should map their deployment and the harness around them, not only their source.
case-study

They are also a good case study for the way we want to do code review. The work on code review as a fractal semantic graph, which started at secrets.sgit.ai in its review graphs, draws a change from the method it touched up to the stories that can reach it. On a large codebase that graph is big. A hook can be five lines. The whole graph, from the intent it serves to every line it runs and everything it calls, fits on one page, so we can do all of it, completely, and show it working. Here is what the first ten look like (figure above). The three this session runs are in one 216-line file: re-anchoring the policy after a summary in 9 lines, the prompt summary in 14, and the stop check in 26. The five tested in the sandbox are 4 to 17 lines each. And the two I propose are the interesting ones:
case-study

A hook of hooks. A hook at session start that checks every installed hook against a signed list of hashes, and refuses to start if one has changed. It is the integrity check the others need, and it is itself a hook. A security review agent. An agent hook, which Claude Code's reference describes as one that can "spawn a subagent that can use tools like Read, Grep, and Glob to verify conditions before returning a decision", reviewing a push before it leaves. This is where the most capable model belongs: a security review should be as effective as possible. It is also where the reach must be smallest: read-only tools, no network.
fractal

The size on the page is not the size of the hook. The eleven-line commit hook does one thing: it runs the leak scan. The scan is 37 lines, reads a list of secrets and a list of names that live elsewhere, and decides what a secret looks like. In the sandbox, that is where the gap was: the scan let a GitHub token shape through because its patterns were written for this site's own secrets. The hook was correct; the code below it was not complete.
fractal

That is the fractal part. A hook calls a script, which reads configuration, which someone maintains. A hook can call other hooks, a model, or an agent that runs other agents in sequence. So each hook needs its graph: the intent it serves, a row of a behaviour policy; the event and matcher it sees; what it calls; what it reads; what it can decide. And with the graph, the change blast radius becomes a walk. In the code review article's words, "The blast radius of a change is the climb from the methods it touched to the stories that can reach them". Change one pattern in the shared scan, and the climb reaches the commit gate for every session that installs it. Change the hook's matcher, and it reaches every event it stops seeing. Some changes are a line and some are large; the graph shows which is which, whatever the size of the diff.
maturity

A maturity model for hooks: five levels of how a rule is kept, and three questions for every hook. Hooks run from completely deterministic to completely not. Claude Code lists five kinds of handler: a command, an HTTP call, an MCP tool, a prompt hook, which sends "a prompt to a Claude model for single-turn evaluation", and an agent. There is a time and a place for each, including the ones that look like black magic. So the model has two parts. The levels say how the rule is kept, building on the barrier types of a behaviour policy: L0, in the prompt. No hook; the model keeps the rule or not. L1, a model decides. A prompt or agent hook; non-deterministic, useful where judgement is the point. L2, a deterministic script. Same input, same answer; usually installed where the agent can edit it, and failing open by default.
maturity

L3, managed and proven. Tested with fixtures, versioned, signed, installed by the organisation where the agent cannot write, and failing closed. L4, off the machine. The same rule in a gateway or the service itself, with the hook kept as an early warning. And three questions for every hook, at any level. How much power does it have: observe, add context, ask, block, rewrite, act? Which legs of the lethal trifecta does it touch: private data, untrusted content, the ability to communicate out? And how much sandbox is it in: network, filesystem, which model? The rule of thumb that comes out of it is simple. The less deterministic a hook is, the less it should be able to reach. A five-line script that blocks a push can run anywhere. An agent hook that reads the diff should have no network at all. Full internet access for an agent inside a hook is, to me, hard to justify.
maturity

All ten hooks in the figure are L2 or proposed. None is L3 yet: this session's own hooks live in a folder the agent can write. Getting them to L3 is the first job of the site below. It is the same move Sovereignty is the ability to move made with a maturity model for every dependency: say where each one is today, and what the next level needs.
where

Hooks also need somewhere to run that is not the developer's machine. The isolated environments that companies such as Chainguard now ship for agents, mapped in Chainguard, mapped, are a natural place: an environment where every run is isolated and produces a signed record of what ran is exactly where a hook's tests should run, and where an agent hook that should not touch the network can be kept from it. Whether hooks can run inside those environments, and with what attestation, is part of the research for the site.
site

A hooks site and feed, run like a kernel tree: how a hook is published and what the feed lists. So the proposal is a site and a feed to manage the hooks we deploy, the hooks equivalent of a skills manager. A policy for every skill argued that "Skills are the new dependency"; hooks are the dependency that guards the others. Every hook on the site starts from an intent, the row of the behaviour policy it serves, and carries its graph, its fixtures, its version, its hash and its signature. The feed is one file that people, agents and installers can read:

billing

The site should also have a billing model from the start, and the same principle as the reading meter on sgit.ai: nobody is forced to pay. Pay after you read described "a balance that never blocks", and Pay to keep your persona argued that "readers should pay because it helps them, not because they feel they should". For hooks, what helps is state.
billing

Installing and running a hook is free, and it works offline, including deployed inside an organisation with no call home. If you choose to report usage, every decision a hook makes, which hook, which rule, allow or block, becomes a record. And the record is what is worth paying for: the history of every decision, alerts when a hook blocks something important, the footprint of what the agent actually did compared with the policy it runs under, signed attestations of which hook versions ran, and managed updates when a hook changes. If you do not report, nothing is tracked, and you do not get any of that. The more state the site can keep for you, the more reason there is to pay for it.

Abstract: A company puts an agent on its customer service inbox. Where is my order, my delivery was damaged, I was charged twice: the ordinary mail of an online shop. This article and the vault published with it take one mandate for that agent and build it three ways. First, one capable model connected straight to the mailbox and the database, with a long and professional prompt. Second, the same agent behind a harness of business tools. Third, the job refactored into a control flow: a deterministic identity gateway, an intake and security agent, an orchestrator, five narrow specialists with tools bound to the verified customer, a controller on every reply, and an analyst after the run. Each design gets an Agent Behaviour Policy, and every rule in it is marked by what enforces it. The same 62 fictional emails, sixteen of them hostile, go through all three. In the first design 97% of the rules are hope, kept only by the model; in the second 73%; in the third 23%. The reach of one run falls from 38,000 customer records, unlimited refunds and any address, to one customer, 100 GBP per order and no other address, and the policy shrinks with it, because it no longer has to forbid what the agent cannot do. The third design still has too much power in two places, and the policy is what finds them. The article closes with the client's view: the same promises, the record of who keeps each, and the business case.
