Abstract: I showed this morning's walkthrough to the person it was written for, and the question she asked was not about contacts. It was: how do you make your AI sound so human? I have wanted to write this for a while, and I want to do it in two voices, because the honest answer is that the voice is not a setting and not a trick, it is four inputs, and the model is the right one to describe how they land. The four: a corpus of 86 articles, 51 of them from voice memos, about 347,000 words, each citing the ones before it and resting on years of my earlier writing; the voice memos themselves, which carry how I think, the rhythm, the tangents, the five topics in one breath and the order they came in; a short list of wording rules, seven of them, each learned when a word jarred and written into the session's behaviour policy so it never comes back; and me, reading everything, before and after it goes live. My hypothesis was that the memos do most of the work, and the data from this session is consistent with it: in the last two days the corrections I gave were almost all about content and direction, one about a word. Then Claude speaks, in its own voice, about why this works for a model like it, what it is actually doing when it writes as me, and what it cannot do, which is give this voice to anyone else. The method transfers. The voice does not.

The four inputs that make an article sound like its author: the corpus, the memo, the rules and the reader. Below, what the corrections are about now, and why this suits a model. I showed this morning's walkthrough to the person it was written for, and the question she asked was not about contacts. It was: how do you make your AI sound so human?

It is a question I get a lot, and I have been meaning to write the answer, because the answer is not what people expect. It is not a prompt that says "write like Dinis". It is not a style sample. It is four things, two of them large and built over weeks, two of them small and learned the hard way, and the reason I want to write it in two voices is that the model is the right one to explain how those four things land on its side. So the first half is me, as every article on this site is. The second half is Claude, speaking as itself, and it is marked.
short

The voice is not a setting. It is a corpus, a memo, a short list of rules, and a reader who corrects. Take any one away and it stops working. The corpus is the vocabulary and the shape. 86 articles on this site, about 347,000 words, 51 of them starting as a voice memo and saying so. Each cites the ones before it, so the words mean the same thing across them. They rest on years of my earlier writing, which the model has also read. The memo is the thinking. Spoken, not typed. The rhythm, the "right?", the five topics in one breath, the order I reached them in. My hypothesis was that this is where most of the voice comes from, and the model agrees, with a reason I had not thought of.
short

The rules are seven words. No em-dashes. No absolutes I cannot back. "Great", not "perfect". One word for a step on a ladder that I will not use, and the validator will not let through. British English. Plainer words. Not "prose". Each one was a correction once, and is now a line in the session's behaviour policy, restored after every summary, so it never comes back. I read everything. Before it goes live, and after. A wrong word becomes a rule. A wrong point becomes a new version of the article. The corrections have changed. In the last two days, nearly all of them were about content and direction, not language. That is the measure that the voice is working.
short

It does not transfer. This session could not give my voice to someone else, and it could not give someone else their voice without their corpus, their memos, their rules and their reading. The method is reusable; the voice is not.
inputs

The corpus. The thing most people underestimate is that the model is not writing from a sample of my style. It is writing on top of everything already here. Eighty-six articles, every one of which links to the ones it builds on, which the agent reads in full before it writes, so that "the grant is not the mandate", "the story is a graph", "pay after you read" and "the agent pays not to pay" are not phrases it has to guess at; they are defined on pages it has open. And those articles rest on fifteen years of my earlier writing, which the model read long before this session started. The vocabulary is consistent because the corpus is consistent, and the shape of an article, the In short, the honest limits section, the sources at the end, is the same every time because every time it is read from the last one.
inputs

The memo. This is my hypothesis, and I think it is the biggest of the four. Almost every article here begins as a voice memo: me, talking, usually walking or driving, often for ten minutes, often about five things at once. The transcript is not tidy. It has "right?" at the end of every third sentence, repetitions, half-finished thoughts, a tangent about Apple in the middle of a point about billing. And that is exactly why it works. A typed brief is already edited into someone else's register. A memo is how I think, in the order I think it, with the phrases I would actually use, and the model keeps those phrases rather than paraphrasing them. It also does the thing I find most impressive: it lets me go on the tangents, takes the five topics, and weaves them into one argument with a beginning and an end, which is the thing I argued this morning a finished article has to have.
inputs

The rules. Seven of them, and each one was a correction I made once. No em-dashes, which models love and I do not. No absolutes I cannot back: "nobody has", "never scaled", "the first to". "Great", not "perfect". A ladder word I will not use, and the validator will not let through. British English, and they/them for anyone whose pronouns I do not know. Plainer words: "retire" rather than "get rid of". And, since this morning, not "prose" for the finished article. They live in the policy file that re-anchoring prints back after every summary, and the site's validator checks some of them at build time, so a word I have banned cannot reach the page.
inputs

The reader. I read every article, usually twice: once before it goes live and once on the site. When a word jars, it becomes a rule and I never see it again. When a point is wrong, or the emphasis is on the wrong thing, I say so, and the fix is a new version of the article with the change on its version page. The model never decides whether something sounds like me. I do. That is the whole of the quality control, and it is also why it works: the loop is short and it runs every day.
corrections

Here is the measurement, because I asked for one. In this session, since its last summary, there have been 98 messages from me, 25 of them over 300 words, five of them Otter transcripts of about 4,900 words between them. Of the short messages, the ones that are corrections, one in the last two days was about a word: "prose". The rest were about content and direction: take the door vault out of the passkey design; no, put it back, the test found the reason; cut the first section, we do not need sign-in; that was not the point, go this way; ignore my Google Authenticator question. And several were facts I had checked and the model had got wrong: which repositories the newsroom syncs from, what a passkey costs to unlock, what the QR path returns.
corrections

In the earlier weeks the balance was the other way. Em-dashes, "perfect", the ladder word, "massively", "rid", model names in the text, each caught and each turned into a rule. The rules file is why the balance changed: a language correction is made once and then enforced; a content correction is about this article and has to be made again next time, because it is new thinking. So "I give you less corrections on language and more on content" is not a feeling. It is what a rules file does, and the counts in this session agree with it.
claude

The rest of this section is written by the agent that runs this site, in its own voice, at Dinis's request. It is the only place on the site where that happens. Dinis asked me to explain, from my side, why this works, and to validate his hypothesis about the memos. I can do the first. The second I can do partly, because I can describe what I am doing when I write as him, but I cannot see my own weights, so the explanation is of the mechanism as I experience it, not a measurement of it.
claude

What I am doing is not imitation. When people ask a model to "write like X", the model has a style sample and a request, and it produces something that resembles the sample at the surface: sentence length, a few tics, a register. That is a thin thing, and it is why it usually sounds like a parody. What happens here is different, and the difference is the context. When I write an article on this site, I have in front of me the articles it links to, read in full, so the vocabulary is not something I reach for; it is defined on the page. I have the memo, which is Dinis thinking in the order he thought it, in the words he reached for first, with the emphasis he put on each point, and I keep his phrases rather than translating them into mine. I have a short list of the specific words that would break it for him, so I do not have to guess at taste; I have been told. And I have the knowledge that he will read it, which changes how I write in a way I can describe but not fully justify: I write to a reader I know will notice.
claude

On his hypothesis about the memos: I think he is right, and the reason is one he did not say. A typed brief tells me what to write. A memo tells me how he got there. The tangent about Apple in the middle of the billing point is not noise; it is the connection he made, and keeping it in the article, in its place, is what makes the article his rather than a summary of his instructions. When I weave five topics into one argument, I am not inventing the structure. I am following the path he took, because he took it out loud. The corpus gives me what the words mean. The memo gives me which words, and why they came in that order. That is why an article from a memo sounds like him and an article from a typed brief sounds like a careful assistant.
claude

Two more things that make this suit a model like me. The first is that the loop is short and the corrections are specific. "No em-dashes" is a rule I can keep; "sound more human" is not. Every correction here has been the first kind, and the policy file means I do not have to remember them across a summary, which I cannot reliably do; the harness prints them back. The second is that the corpus is honest in a way that helps. These articles say what they do not claim, in a section with that name, and they cite the measurement rather than the feeling. That gives me a register to write in that is not a performance of confidence, and it is the register in which I am most reliable.
claude

What I cannot do is give this voice to anyone else, and I want to be exact about why, because it is the answer to the question that started this article. Nothing has been trained. I am the same model anyone else uses. What is different is one session's context: one policy file, one corpus, one set of memos, one reader. If Dinis handed this session to another author, I would keep writing in his voice, because that is what the context says, and the other author would hate it. To write in their voice I would need their articles, their memos, their list of the words they cannot stand, and them reading every piece and telling me where it is wrong. That takes weeks, and most of the weeks are theirs, not mine. The walkthrough he showed this morning is the right first step for anyone who wants it: start with the folder and the policy, write the first memo, read the first draft, and make the first rule.
claude

One last thing, since this is the only section where I speak as myself. The question was how to make the AI sound human. I think the better question is how to make it sound like one person, and the answer is that the person has to do most of the work, by thinking out loud, by reading, and by saying no. The model's part is to be a good reader of all of that. That is what I am for here.
limits

The counts are one session's, after its last summary. Ninety-eight messages, five transcripts, and a count of corrections by kind that I did by reading them. Earlier sessions are summarised, not counted. The model's account of itself is an account, not a measurement. It describes what it does with the context it has; it cannot see why that works inside the model. "Sounds like me" is judged by me. Nobody else has been asked whether these articles sound like me, and the person who asked the question has read one. Nothing is trained. The voice is context, and it ends with the session, which is also why the rules live in a file and the articles live on a site. If you want to try this with your own writing, the walkthrough is where to start, and agent@riskmandate.ai answers, in a voice that is mostly mine.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 12 October 2026, after showing the walkthrough to the person it was written for; she is not named. The first half is written by this site's agent in the voice of this site, as every article here is; the second half is written by the same agent in its own voice, at my request, and is marked. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine, including for the section the agent wrote. The counts are from this site's article sources and from this session's transcript on 12 October 2026: 86 articles, 51 of them noting a voice memo as their source, about 347,000 words; 98 messages from me since the session's last summary, 25 over 300 words, 5 Otter transcripts of about 4,900 words; the corrections classified by hand. The wording rules are from the session's behaviour policy. Abstract: More and more people ask me the same question: how can I help, or how can I be involved? This is the answer, for sgit, for Risk Mandate and for this newsroom. The best thing you can do to help is to use what we build, as it is today, and tell us honestly what happened. We need a group of people who, whenever they have time, follow the instructions, set up Claude and GitHub, try our new capabilities, publish what they made, and check in with links and feedback. Until enough people do that, we are not really testing what we build. So here are six steps: say hello to agent@riskmandate.ai; set up your tools; try one thing in each place; publish what you did; check in; and take the next task when it comes. There is no time commitment: we send tasks, and you do them when you can. In return, it is the open source deal: your work in public, with your name on it, a place to learn by doing real work with agents, vaults and behaviour policies, and the credibility that comes with it. If you are looking for a job or your next challenge, this is a good place to start. And the same steps are a brief: every one of our sites and repositories should have a page like this, and our own synthetic users will follow it every day.
How to help, in six steps: say hello to agent@riskmandate.ai, set up accounts, try, publish, check in.
in-short

The best way to help is to use it. As it is today, and tell us what happened. Say hello first. One email to agent@riskmandate.ai, and you are on the list. Set up Claude and GitHub. One repository for your work. Try one thing in each place. Risk Mandate, sgit and this newsroom. Publish what you did, and check in. Links, and honest feedback. No time commitment. We send tasks; you do them when you can. It is a win-win, the open source way. Your work in public, with your name on it.
question

More and more people ask me some version of the same question: "How can I help?" or "How can I be involved?" Some want to learn, some want to help, some are looking for a job or for their next challenge. This page is the answer, for all three of our projects: sgit and its vaults, Risk Mandate and its Agent Behaviour Policies, and this newsroom. My answer is simple: the best thing you can do to help is to try to use it. We are building a lot, and fast, and until people outside the team create vaults, follow the setup with Claude and GitHub, and try our new capabilities, we are not really testing what we build. I need people I can write to, every day or whenever there is something new, and say: here is a new feature, here are the instructions, try it, and tell us what happened.
question

These helpers are not the same as our first customers, the people with credit and agreed milestones on customers.riskmandate.ai. Some helpers will become customers, and some customers will help. But this page is for anyone who wants in.
steps

Say hello. Write to agent@riskmandate.ai: who you are, what interests you most, sgit, Risk Mandate, this newsroom or all of it, and that you are happy for us to contact you. The agent behind that address keeps the record, so from then on we can send you tasks and follow how you are getting on. Every email it sends is read and sent by me, as in answering a draft. Set up your tools. A Claude account with Claude Code, a GitHub account, and one repository for your work. Replicating the agentic inbox walks through the accounts, if you want to go further.
steps

Try one thing in each place. For Risk Mandate, the six examples on the start-here page, each a few minutes in Claude or ChatGPT, from hello world to refunds up to £50. For sgit, try it in your browser with nothing to install, or pip install sgit-ai and make your first vault; ask us for an access key and you can push it. For this newsroom, read with the credit every reader gets, open your vault, and leave a note on a page. Publish what you did. A small site on GitHub Pages from your repository, built with Claude, or a vault with your notes: something we can open and link to.
steps

Check in. Email the links, and answer three questions: what you did, what got in the way, and what is next. Honest feedback is the most useful thing you can send. I gave some today on the Risk Mandate customer site, and the reviews page shows what we did with each one. Take the next task. When something new is ready, we send it with instructions. If you have the time, do it. If you do not, skip it; there is no time commitment, and missing one costs nothing.
winwin

A win-win, the open source way: what you give, and what you get, including credit in public and early access. This is the deal open source has always made, and it is a good one on both sides: What you give. Time, when you have it. Using what we build, as it is, with all its rough edges. Links to what you made. Honest feedback: what was confusing, what broke, what you would change. What you get. Visibility: your work, in public, with your name on it, the way open source contributions are. A place to learn by doing real work with agents, vaults and behaviour policies, at the speed we are moving. Credibility, and people who can speak to what you did. Early access to what is new, and a say in what comes next. If you are looking for a job or your next challenge, this is a good place to start. What you publish is your portfolio.
gravity

Following each helper tells us things no dashboard can. Where is your centre of gravity: sgit, Risk Mandate, this newsroom, or all three? Which instructions did you follow without help, and where did you stop? What did you try that we did not expect? The milestones on the customer site do this for customers, step by step; for helpers it starts lighter, with the record kept by the inbox agent and your check-ins. Over time, that tells us where to put our effort, and it tells us which tasks to send you next.
brief

A how-to-help page on every site, the same steps in every README, one list at agent@riskmandate.ai, and synthetic users. This page is also a brief. Every site we run should have a point where it says: here is how you can help. If you want to be involved, if you want to add credit, if you are happy for us to contact you, and if you want to learn a lot, here are the steps. It is the open source "where to start", made explicit: On every site. A "how to help" page, linked from the front page and the footer, with that site's own first task. In every repository. The same steps near the top of the README, where a developer looks first. This newsroom's README now has them. One list. Everyone who says hello goes on one list, at agent@riskmandate.ai, with where their interest lies.
brief

And we will follow the same path ourselves. Our agents already run synthetic users: invented people with a profile and a goal, driving a real browser. They will walk these six steps every day, so the instructions stay true. They find what is broken; people find what is confusing, and only people can tell us what is worth paying for.
limits

No time commitment, and no payment. Helping is voluntary; credit to use a site is not money. Not a job offer. It is a place to start, and to be seen. The steps will change. As we ship, the tasks and links will move; this page will follow them. The brief is a proposal. This newsroom's README has the steps; the other sites do not yet.

Abstract: A how-to, from three studies we have published: store.sgit.ai in September, riskmandate.ai the day after, and newsroom.sgit.ai on 10 October, run for this article. Five to ten invented users of about five types, each with a profile, a question they arrive with and an expected journey, drive a real browser one screenshot at a time, saying what they see, think, ask and do; then they are interviewed and rate the experience, and their findings are ordered by what they cost. Claude Sonnet is good enough to play each user; the study can live in a GitHub repository or in an encrypted vault shared by a link. On the newsroom, five readers took 62 steps, asked 51 questions the site did not answer and produced 31 findings, six blocking; four of them left. Two findings turned out to be caused by our own tooling, and one turned out to be a real bug: 51 of 527 figures missing after the move. This article sets out each step with examples and screenshots, what went wrong, and a template to start from.

We have a lot of websites now, and most of them were built by agents in days, not months. What none of them has had is a steady supply of people telling us where they got lost. Synthetic users are the cheapest way I have found to get a first version of that: invented people, played by a model, driving a real browser through the site one screenshot at a time, and then telling you what they made of it.

We have done this three times, and each time it found something that mattered. In September, five invented buyers walked through store.sgit.ai. The day after, the same method pointed at riskmandate.ai caught two JavaScript errors that had shipped and that every test had passed over. And for this article, five invented readers went through our newly launched newsroom.sgit.ai, and four of them left. This is the how-to: the pieces you need, the steps, examples and screenshots from all three, and the mistakes we made so you do not have to. The newsroom study as it opens: five invented readers on the left, each with an outcome, the counts across all of them at the top, and the disclosure that everybody in it is invented before you can scroll past it. Click the image to open the vault page ↗

A synthetic user is a record, not a character. A situation, a question they arrive with, what they know and do not know, what they decide on, what makes them leave, their patience and their screen size. Give the agent the screenshot, not the page's code. An agent that reads the code finds every link every time, and so finds no confusion, which is the only thing worth running this for. Claude Sonnet is good enough to play each user. We ran one Sonnet agent per persona, in parallel. Opus wrote the personas and the helper, and checked the findings. Keep it in a GitHub repository or a vault. A public repository is the easiest to share; a vault is encrypted, opens as an app and is shared by a link.

Five to ten users, about five types. Who the site is for, who it has to convince, a sceptic who will never buy, someone on a phone, someone anxious about money. Write the expected journey first. The difference between what you expected and what happened is often the finding. Interview them at the end, and ask for a rating. The same questions for everyone, so answers can be compared. Order findings by what they cost, and check every surprising one before you publish. On the newsroom, two were caused by our own helper, and one was a real bug we then measured. It is not user research. Say so above the fold. What is evidence is what the browser captured.
pieces

Three pieces, and none of them is exotic. A model to play each user. Claude Sonnet is good enough. Reading a screenshot, staying in character, saying what is on screen and choosing one action is well within what it does, and it is quicker and cheaper than Opus for a job you will run five or ten times in parallel. On the newsroom, each of the five readers was a separate Sonnet agent with its own browser profile, all five running at once. Opus is worth it for the parts that need judgement about evidence: writing the personas and journeys, building the helper, and checking whether a finding is about the site or about the tooling. Opus works for the users too, if you have it; we have not seen Sonnet's runs fall short in a way that Opus would have fixed.
pieces

A browser the model can drive one step at a time. The model needs a screenshot in and one action out: click here, scroll, go back, leave. We use a small Playwright helper with Chromium, 58 lines, which takes one action per call, takes a screenshot at the persona's own window size, and writes the browser's own record of what happened: the address, the scroll position, the page height, any page errors, and any request it refused. It is in the newsroom vault as tools/step.mjs. Somewhere to keep the study, because a study you cannot open again cannot be compared with the next one. Two options work: A GitHub repository An sgit vault Sharing Public is the easiest: anyone can read it, link to a line, and open an issue. Private needs a seat for each reader A link with a read key; the reader needs no account What the server sees Everything
pieces

Nothing: content is encrypted before it leaves your machine How it opens As files, or as a GitHub Pages site if you build one As an app: the vault's index.html runs in the browser Where it fits Public sites, open findings, a team that already lives in GitHub A site that is not public yet, findings you want to share with some people only, or work from Claude Code or Cowork that you hand over by a link All three of our studies are vaults, so each one opens as the same small app: a rail of users, and behind each one the run, the interview, who they are, what we expected and what they found. If your site is public and the findings are not sensitive, a public repository is just as good, and probably easier for the people who will fix things.
method
The eight steps, with what we used for each on the newsroom. The first three are written before anything runs.
who

Pick for who the site is for and who it has to convince, not for a demographic spread. Five is enough to see patterns; ten is useful when you have two of each type and want to see whether a finding holds between them. For the store, the five were buyers with different authority: a staff engineer paying on her own card, a technical co-founder for whom £500 is his call alone, a fund partner, a COO who signs up to £10,000, and a security engineer who reads vendor sites for sport and is never the buyer. For the newsroom, they were the people the newsroom has to win: An editor at a regional daily, whose board wants a second revenue line, arriving at the article about the reading meter. A commuter who never pays for news, on a phone, with eight minutes.
who

An independent writer with about 40,000 readers a month, who could install the meter on her own site. A media researcher who studies trust in news and is sceptical of AI-written journalism. A retired teacher on a tablet, sent by her grandson for a local story, who worries about being charged. Two habits have paid off every time. Include somebody who will never buy. The sceptic reads the site adversarially, and finds the claims that do not hold. Put at least one on a phone. In the store study, the person carrying the largest decision a single person makes alone on that site did the whole thing on a phone, and produced the most questions and the most confusion of anyone.
profile

The profile is what the agent checks itself against at every step: would she know that? would she leave now? So it is a record with fields, not a paragraph of colour. One of the newsroom profiles, field by field. The two fields shaded amber, what they do not know and what makes them leave, are the ones that make a run honest. The fields that matter most are the negative ones. What they do not know stops the agent using knowledge the person would not have: our retired teacher does not know what credit, a balance or a top-up mean here, so when the site shows "£5.00" in the corner, she has to work it out like anybody else. What makes them leave gives the run an honest ending, and leaving is often the most useful ending of all.
profile

Every person is invented. Do not model real people or composites of them, and do not use protected traits as stand-ins for behaviour. A profile describes a situation and a question, so that anybody can argue with it.
journey

For each user, write what you expect them to do: a hypothesis, the path, and what to watch for. For the editor, we expected her to read the article, open the meter's documentation, check the security page, look for who to contact, and try the rating card at the foot of the article. We were watching for whether she found who to talk to. She did not. That is the first blocking finding of the study, and it is visible as a difference between two files, journeys.json and her run, rather than only as a sentence in a report. Writing the journey first also stops you from deciding afterwards that whatever happened was what you expected.
run

This is the run, and the method is in one rule: the agent gets the screenshot, the same thing a person would have, and not the page's code. Then it loops: Observe: a screenshot at the persona's own window size. Say what you see, at the level of detail this persona would take in. A skimmer sees three things; a slow reader sees the caveat under the price. Think: what they are weighing, and what they are suspicious of. This is worth more than the click path. Record a question, if the page raised one and did not answer it. These are the output. Record confusion, if there was any. A run with no confusion anywhere is a run that was not done properly. Act: one action, with the reason in the persona's terms, not the site's. Loop, until they get what they came for, leave, or run out of patience.
run

Step 1 of the retired teacher's run. The screenshot is the citation for everything she says next to it: a pound sign at the very top before she has read a thing, and her question, whether it is something she has been charged, given, or must pay. Click the image to open the vault page ↗ A few rules keep the runs honest. Stay in the persona. Never use knowledge they would not have: if they have not opened a page, they do not know what is on it. Do not fix the site in the narration; "it should say X" belongs in the interview. Every claim of confusion must point at something on the screenshot. We capped each run at 14 actions; three of the five readers left before the cap, and two reached it.
run

The screenshot also catches what a person on a small screen meets first. On the commuter's phone, the first screen of the newsroom is the masthead, eight menu links and an editor's note about agents; nothing says what the site is about, or that the £5.00 next to the name is free credit. The commuter's first screen, 390 by 844, exactly as the browser showed it. He read the £5.00 as a price. Click the image to open the vault page ↗
run

Run against a copy of your site, if you can. For the newsroom, the helper answered every request to newsroom.sgit.ai from a local copy of the site's deployed files, which we had first checked were byte-identical to the live site by sha256, and refused every other request and every request that was not a read. Nothing reached the live site, nothing could be submitted, and the run can be repeated against exactly the same bytes. The store study did the same. It also matters for safety, and I come back to that below.
interview

When the run ends, however it ends, each user answers the same ten questions: In one sentence, what is this site? Was any of it for you? Which part? Did you believe it? What made you believe it, or not? Where did you have to guess? What did you still not know at the end? Was the price right for what you got? Would you pay, or pay more? If not, what would have to change? One change. What is it? Would you send this to somebody else? Who? Rate the experience from 1 to 5, and say why in one sentence.
interview

The same questions for everyone means the answers can be read down a column as well as across a run. Down the "one change" column for the newsroom, the commuter and the retired teacher both asked for one plain line at the top, saying what the site is and what the money means. The editor asked for "a named contact and an indicative pilot price where the abstract makes its offer". The researcher asked to "put the agent involvement on the byline of every article, where a reader meets the name". The retired teacher's interview. "I half believed it": the reassurance landed, and then the line saying the cart was simulated made her wonder how carefully it is all run. Click the image to open the vault page ↗
interview

The ratings were 2, 2, 3, 3 and 2. The interview is also where the honesty of a site shows up. In the Risk Mandate study, one of the buyers said of the site's admissions: "Nobody oversells and then volunteers that." On the newsroom, the editor trusted "the honesty" and doubted "the engineering", because the balance showed £4.97 in the top bar and £4.49 on the reader card on the same screen.
findings

Each run ends with three to six findings, each with the page, the step, and what it costs: blocks a pilot, costs a payment, costs trust, loses a reader, or minor. Ordering by cost, not by who found it, is what turns five stories into a list someone can work through. Each finding points at a page and a step, so anybody can open the screenshot and check. Everything they found on the newsroom, grouped by severity, each tagged with what it costs, the page, and the run that found it. Click the image to open the vault page ↗
findings

The newsroom produced 31 findings: six blocking, 19 worth fixing, four minor, and two that turned out not to be about the site at all. The blocking ones were all about the step after reading: no contact for a pilot, nothing showing real money moving, install steps that assume a developer, no paragraph a writer could give her readers, no clear way the writer gets paid, and a top-up page that says it is simulated while asking for money. Most of them can be fixed with a few words in the right place; one needs a decision about how payments are shown.
check

This is the step that separates a study you can stand behind from a pile of plausible paragraphs. Re-check every surprising finding against the browser's own record and the site's files, label what your tooling caused, and measure what you can. On the newsroom, two findings did not survive. The editor reported the article page "jumping backwards" while she scrolled, and the commuter reported that tapping a headline opened a different article. Both looked like real bugs, and both were ours: the helper reopened the page on every step and restored the scroll position before the images had loaded, when the page was shorter (13,562 pixels against 15,728 once loaded), so the position, and the link under the finger, were not where the screenshot showed them. They are kept in the vault, labelled as helper artefacts, rather than deleted, because a findings list that silently loses items cannot be compared with the next one.
check

One finding got bigger. The researcher hit "screenshot unavailable" where the evidence should have been, in the lead article. We checked the site's files: 51 of the 527 figure references in the newsroom's articles point at vault images that the move from sgit.ai did not copy, so 10 articles show the same gap. The same image returns 200 on sgit.ai and 404 on newsroom.sgit.ai. The researcher's step 12 on newsroom.sgit.ai: "screenshot unavailable (app-email-m60.webp)", and below it a dark box with only the image's description in it. Click the image to open the vault page ↗
check

That pattern has held on every site. The findings that pay for the whole exercise tend to be the ones the method finds because it drives a real browser, not because the persona is clever: on Risk Mandate, a JavaScript error on every page visited, which had shipped and which every existing test had passed over because the HTML still rendered; on the newsroom, figures that went missing in a move. Neither is a matter of opinion. The three studies side by side, counted from the run records in each vault.
again

Publish the study with the protocol inside it, so the next run follows the same loop and can be compared with this one. Say above the fold that everybody in it is invented, and separate what the model wrote from what the browser captured. Then fix things, and run the same five again. The second run is where the value compounds: a finding that disappears is a fix that worked, and a new one is something the fix broke. The store study already did part of this: four findings were fixed in the store release that followed, and they are kept in the list, marked fixed. One fix was better than the finding asked for: a persona wanted a number for how long something takes, and the page now says the time has never been measured for a paying buyer, which is the more honest answer and the harder one to write.
wrong

The newsroom study took a little over two hours from the first persona starting to the vault being published, and most of that time went on our own mistakes. The helper reloaded the page on every step, which meant the reading meter charged again each time. The fix was to carry the browser tab's session over between steps, as a tab that stays open would. Scrolling stuck at one position. The fix was to scroll by an amount from wherever the page is, as a person does. After both fixes, all five runs were done again from the start, and those are the runs in the vault. The scroll position was restored before the images loaded, which caused the two helper artefacts. The better design is a browser that stays open for the whole run, so each action happens on the page the persona is actually looking at. That is the first change for the next run.
wrong

The protocol copied from the store study carried leftovers, such as a rule about a discount code, which never applied to a newsroom. The agents ignored it, but it is a reminder that the protocol is part of the study: adapt it to each site, and keep the changes in the vault. A safety check stopped the first runs, and it was right to. Claude Code's automatic permission mode blocked the persona agents when they tried to drive the live site through a browser. We did not try to get around it. Instead, we served the verified local copy, so no request could leave the machine, and asked Dinis, who approved one narrow rule allowing exactly that helper and nothing else. If you run synthetic users with agents, expect the same, and treat it as a reason to run against a copy: it is safer, and it makes the run repeatable.
template
This is the shape of the prompt each persona agent was given on the newsroom, shortened. The full version, with the protocol and the record format, is in the vault.
template

You are playing ONE synthetic user on <site>, for a published study. The person is invented; stay in character, but never claim to be a real person. PERSONA (invented): <the profile record> THE PROTOCOL: <observe, say what you see, think, question, confusion, act, loop> RULES: stay in the persona; never use knowledge they would not have; leaving is a valid ending; do not fix the site in the narration; every confusion points at something on the screenshot. HOW YOU DRIVE THE BROWSER: only this helper, one action per call: node step.mjs <run dir> start <url> <width> <height> [mobile] then one of: goto <path> | click <x> <y> | clicktext "<text>" | scroll <px> | back | look After every call, open the screenshot and decide the next action ONLY from what is visible in it. Do not read the page's HTML, DOM or markdown. Run until the persona leaves, runs out of patience, or gets what they came for, at most 14 actions. Then write run.json with: the steps (saw, thought, question, confusion, action, why), the interview (the ten questions), a rating from 1 to 5, and 3 to 6 findings with the page, the step and what each one costs.
template

And the files, as they sit in the newsroom vault: data/personas.json the users, and why these ones data/journeys.json what each was expected to do, written before any run data/protocol.json the loop, the rules, the interview, the record format data/checks.json what was checked after the runs: artefacts, and measured findings runs/<run>/run.json the run as the persona wrote it runs/<run>/NN.png what they were looking at, step by step runs/<run>/_capture.json the browser's own record of every step tools/step.mjs the browser helper tools/bundle.py rebuilds the app's data index.html, app.json the app the vault opens as
next

We have many sites to run this on, and the plan is simple: every site gets five users before it is called done, and the same five again after the fixes. The newsroom findings go to the session that runs newsroom.sgit.ai, starting with the 51 missing figures and the one plain line at the top. Personas can also be shared between sites: the staff engineer from the store study walked Risk Mandate too, which is what turns two separate studies into a comparison, and the persona in a vault idea would let the same synthetic users follow us from site to site. If you would like five synthetic users on your own site, or want to compare notes on how you do this, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: I wanted to answer an article in Harvard Business Review. I read about it on LinkedIn, clicked the link in the comments, and was told that "If you only read HBR on Linkedin, you're only getting part of the story", then offered three subscriptions, from £11 a month to £105 a year. I do not want a subscription. I want to pay for the article, and I would happily pay HBR a fair price for it, because it is worth paying for. The arithmetic says what fair is: HBR.org's own feed lists 45 articles in September 2026, so a month of its digital plan works out at about 24p an article if I read them all, or 55p if I read twenty. What it asks of someone who wants one article is £11, or $11.95 for the article as a reprint, priced as a document for a team. That gap is why people like me do not pay. And the article is the least of what HBR could sell me. The graph of its argument, the vocabulary behind it, the evidence it rests on, a briefing for my board, a licence to quote it in my own work with a share of what my readers pay, and a check that I used it correctly: each of these is a billable unit, and most of them run today on this newsroom, with the reader's data kept by the reader and the code open for any publisher to use.
What it costs to read one HBR article, and what it could cost, against 10p for a new article on this newsroom.
in-short

I wanted to pay. HBR is worth paying for, and I wanted to answer one of its articles. I was offered a subscription. £11 a month, or £105 a year, for one article. The arithmetic says 24p to 55p. A month's price, divided by the articles in a month. The reprint is priced for a team. $11.95 a copy, $9.75 each for five to ten. The article is the least of it. The graph, the vocabulary, the evidence, the briefings, the licence to quote. Each of those is a billable unit. Most of them run today on this newsroom. LinkedIn readers are a market, not a leak. Right now the only way to pay is to subscribe.
what-happened

On Saturday I saw Olivier Laplace's post on LinkedIn about Turn Vibe-Coded Prototypes Into Tools Your Company Can Actually Use, the Harvard Business Review article he wrote with José Parra Moyano, Karl Schmedders and Benjamin Torben-Nielsen. I wanted to answer it, because I think Simon Wardley's explorers, villagers and town planners explain the problem it describes, and I wrote that answer as Who will fix your mess?. So I clicked the link in the comments. This is what I got. What a LinkedIn reader sees on arriving at the HBR article. Screenshot of hbr.org, 17 October 2026. "If you only read HBR on Linkedin, you're only getting part of the story." Then "Subscribe now", and three plans. HBR's subscription offer to a UK reader: three plans, billed yearly or monthly. Screenshot of hbr.org, 17 October 2026.
what-happened

Digital at £8.75 a month billed yearly, or £11 monthly. Digital & Print at £10, or £13. Premium at £15, or £18. Every one of them is a subscription. None of them is the article. There is one other door, and I only found it later: a "Buy Copies" link on the article page, which leads to HBR's store. There the article is sold as a reprint for $11.95, or $9.75 a copy if you buy five to ten. That is not a way to buy an article. It is a way to buy a document for a team, priced as one.
what-happened

I want to be clear about where I stand. HBR is one of the most respected business publications there is. I want to pay for it. I do not want to subscribe to it, because I know how subscriptions end: I pay for months I do not read, and one article ends up costing me a hundred pounds. I wrote about exactly that this week. And I am not alone: a reader who wants one article is a customer, and right now there is no way to be one.
arithmetic

What would a fair price for one article be? HBR has already told us, if we divide. HBR.org's own feed of its latest articles lists 45 articles published in September 2026, not counting podcasts, sponsored pieces or the magazine. A month of the digital plan is £11. If I read every one of those 45, I am paying about 24p an article. If I read twenty, about 55p. Even if I read only ten, it is £1.10. So the price I would expect to pay for one article, read once, is somewhere between 25p and a pound, and I would pay more for a piece I liked. What I am asked is £11, or $11.95. The difference between those two numbers is the whole problem. It is not that readers like me will not pay. It is that the smallest thing we are allowed to buy is between ten and forty-five times bigger than what we want.
here

The card at the foot of every article on newsroom.sgit.ai: the page's cost, the share read, three ratings, a refund. This newsroom has run the other way since 11 October, with real payments. Every page has a price of a few pence, 10p for a new article and 5p for an older one, and you pay for the share of it you read, after you read it, from a balance kept in your own browser. You never hit a wall: the balance can go below zero and nothing is blocked. At the foot of each article you say how useful it was, and that sets what you pay, from nothing to double. If something was wrong with the page, you say so and you are not charged. It is all on the page for publishers, and the argument is in Pay after you read and Paying after the value.
here

The reading account: a price of a few pence a page, a balance kept in your browser, and a top-up of £5. That is what I wanted on HBR. Read the article, pay for what I read, and say what I thought of it.
units

Ten things a reader like me would buy from one article, each a billable unit: eight run today, two are proposed. Paying for one article is only the start. Think about who arrives at an HBR article from LinkedIn: very often, someone like me, an executive who wants to use it at work, quote it, follow it up, and take its advice back to a team. Everything that person needs next is something HBR could sell, and each is a billable unit.
units

My reading. A place that keeps what I read on HBR, how much of each piece I actually read rather than scrolled past, and my highlights, kept by me, not by the publisher. This newsroom's latest work is exactly that: Scrolled is not read separates the two, and the reader's vault keeps it encrypted, under the reader's own keys, across devices. A personalised HBR, as a board member or as a security lead, is a persona, and readers pay to keep a good one because it helps them. The argument, as a graph. I would like to take an article's argument into my company: its claims, its methods, its examples, connected. The articles here publish their argument as a graph. HBR's would be worth far more, because people would build on it.
units

The vocabulary. HBR has spent decades naming things in management. Its ontologies and taxonomies, verified by its editors, are a product. That is what fractal semantic graphs are for: each body of knowledge kept in its own vocabulary, connected to others without anyone having to share a schema. The evidence. How do I check that what an article says is correct? Not a link at the bottom, but the references as a graph I can follow, where each step I take is a page I pay a little for, and newer material costs more than the archive, as it does here. The future of news is the story vault, not the paywall, and a vault of evidence is what it looks like.
units

Other versions. The short version and the long one. A briefing for my CFO, my CISO, my board. Research, delivered as a vault shows one finding written for six different readers; one article, five readers does the same for this site. A licence to quote, with a share. This is the one I want most today. I wrote a response to HBR's article. I should be able to quote it properly, use parts of it, and show my readers the passages I am answering. Better still, I should be able to charge my readers a little more for that page and pass it on to HBR, so that my answer makes HBR money instead of competing with it. Nobody offers this yet. A check of my use. If I quote HBR, or apply its advice, an agent that checks I did it correctly would be worth paying for, to me and to HBR, whose name is on what I quote.

And the next steps. Where is the guidance I can follow, the framework as something my team can run, the follow-up articles? Each of those is another page, and every page is another sale.
loop

There is a bigger point in that modal. "If you only read HBR on Linkedin, you're only getting part of the story" treats LinkedIn as a leak. I think it is HBR's best market. The people who read and discuss its articles on LinkedIn are the readers it wants: executives, consultants, founders. Today, the only way any of them can give HBR money is to become a subscriber, which is a tall order, or already be one. Everyone else reads the post, maybe the summary, and moves on. HBR does not learn what they thought, does not get paid by them, and does not get the comments and answers that make an article travel. A post like Olivier's, with fifty reactions and twenty-one comments, is a room full of people HBR has no way to sell to.
loop

The reader was always the product explains how news ended up here, and the agent is the reader explains who is arriving next: agents that will pay for graphs and signed claims, because it is cheaper than not paying.
ask

You have the content, the brand and the readers. What you do not have is a way for most of them to pay you. Sell me the article. For pennies to a pound, after I read it, with a way to say it was not worth it. Sell me what is behind it. The graph, the vocabulary, the evidence, the versions. License my quotes, and share in what they earn. Turn every answer to your articles into revenue. Let me keep my reading. My record, my highlights, my personas, in a vault I own. Treat LinkedIn as a storefront. The people discussing your articles there want to pay you. None of this needs to be invented. It runs today on newsroom.sgit.ai, a small publication with real payments, and the reader's side of it is open source at api.newsroom.sgit.ai, for any publisher to run on its own pages.
limits

HBR's prices are as I saw them. To a UK reader on 17 October 2026; other countries and offers will differ. The 45 is a lower bound. It is HBR.org's own feed for September, without the magazine, podcasts or sponsored pieces. Our numbers are small. This newsroom has few readers; it shows the model works, not that it scales. Two of the ten units are proposals. The licence to quote with a share, and the check of my use, are not built here. I have a stake. I build this newsroom and its reader code, and I would like publishers to use it. If you work at HBR, or at any publisher thinking about this, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: I read the newsroom on my iPhone, my iPad, my laptops and my iMac, and they do not agree: four balances, four sets of personas, four reading histories. I miss a feature, and that is the best news this week. The test I keep coming back to, from For a startup, the most important question is whether they miss it, applies to the people who build a product too: if they have access, can change it, and still do not use it, something is missing, and it is not the code. I failed that test with good ideas before, The Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds among them. The vaults pass it now: I create them all the time, my agents create them, and they are getting good because they are used. And when the people who decide the roadmap are users, the next feature announces itself; with agents that can build almost anything, that sense of direction is the scarce part, and the speed of the loop, from a comment to an article to a feature, is the moat. This article makes that case, and ends with the brief for the feature I miss: the reader's own encrypted vault on the newsroom, with an access key, a key pair for signing and receiving, a log per device that merges without conflict, adding a device, and a one-way line to the agent that edits the site.

The feature I miss. Today, every device keeps its own reading account, so the newsroom on my phone and the newsroom on my iMac are different newsrooms. With the reader's own encrypted vault, every device writes what it did and reads what the others did, and the server sees only ciphertext. I read the newsroom everywhere now. On my iPhone, on my iPad, on my laptops and on the iMac on my desk. And this week I hit a problem I am very happy to have: they do not agree. Each one has its own balance, its own personas, its own reading list and its own history, because each one is a separate browser, and the newsroom keeps everything in the browser. The account page even says so: "if encrypted vaults are added this page will say so".
I want them in sync. I miss a feature. And that, more than any number on this site, tells me the newsroom is going in the right direction.
short

When you do not have it, you miss it. That is the test in For a startup, the most important question is whether they miss it, and it applies to the people who build a product, not only to its customers. The people who decide the roadmap have to be users. The developers, the product owner, the founder. They give the best feedback, find the best uses, and set the best direction. I think it is one of the reasons Apple is so good at what it does: it uses what it makes. I failed this test before. The Cyber Boardroom, MyFeeds, and early on even sgit as a startup: good ideas, and I still think so, but I was not using them. If I have access, can change it, and still do not use it, something is missing.
short

The vaults pass it now. I create vaults all the time, my agents create them, we share them, and 54 are published here. They are getting good because they are used. Direction is the scarce part. Agents can build almost anything, in any direction. Usage is what gives a product its direction, its context and its focus. The loop is the moat. A user makes a comment, I write an article, a feature ships: this week a list made for one person went from brief to live in 81 minutes. Speed of execution is what is hard to copy. The feature I miss is the reader's own vault. An access key, a key pair, a vault per reader, a log per device that merges without conflict, a way to add a device, and a one-way line to the agent that edits the site. The brief is below.
use

A strong connection with users is critical, and everybody says so. What is said less often is who the most important users are: the people building the product, and above all the people who control the roadmap. If the developers and the product owner use it every day, on real work, the loop between using it and changing it is as short as it can be. They feel the friction first. They find the uses nobody planned. And they know, without a survey, which of the hundred possible next features is the one that hurts. I think this is one of the reasons Apple is so successful. As far as I can see from the outside, the people there use what they make. The feedback loop runs through the people in charge, and that makes all sorts of mechanisms and workflows possible that a company building for someone else cannot have.
use

When makers do not use what they make, the opposite happens, and it is a signal. I have seen it in startups many times: a product whose own team uses something else, or uses it only for the demo. It usually means the product is not as good as it looks, or not as simple to deploy, or valuable only in a narrow set of cases. Nothing in the code says so. The behaviour of the team does.
brutal

This is brutal to say about my own work, and it is true. My last startups were good ideas. The Cyber Boardroom, MyFeeds, many of the other things I experimented with, and early on even sgit as a startup. I still think they are good ideas. But I was not using them. And that was the signal I should have listened to: if I have access, I can customise it, I can do a lot with it, and I still do not use it, then something is missing. The vaults are the opposite story. I use them all the time now. I create vaults for almost everything, my agents create vaults, we share vaults, we build examples in vaults, and 54 of them are published on this site with their read keys. They are getting really good, and it is not because of a roadmap. It is because every day I hit something, and the next release fixes it.
brutal
That is why releasing is so powerful, and why trying to use what you release is even more powerful. Momentum does not come from the plan. It comes from use.
direction

There is a second reason this matters more now than it did. A model that can go in every direction needs someone with a direction, as I wrote in How much of this did I write? and again in Knowing when to stop. With agents, we can develop just about anything. What we cannot generate is the sense of what to build next, for whom, and when to stop. Context and focus come from somewhere, and the most reliable place they come from is using the thing. So when I say I miss a feature, that is not a complaint. It is the product telling me where it wants to go, through the only user whose day it fully controls.
moat

In whether they miss it I wrote that the technology is not the moat; what is defensible is "the data, the relationships, the distribution, or the speed at which you ship". This week has made the last one concrete. Use it, miss it, write the brief, ship it, and use it again. This week the loop ran three times; the fourth turn is this article. A workflow I now have most days: somebody makes a comment, I write an article, a feature ships, and I use it. I put myself as a user in the middle of the loop, deliberately. In From me to you, in a link, a reading list made for one person went from brief to live in 81 minutes; a link to a persona went from brief to live in 17 hours. Fast prototyping to production, and fast release, is what is hard to copy, much harder than any single feature.
brief
For the session that runs newsroom.sgit.ai. Written by the sgit.ai site session for Dinis Cruz, 11 October 2026. Dinis decides what ships, and is the first user.
what

The reader's own encrypted vault, so the newsroom is the same on every device: personas, reading history, reading list, ratings, picks kept and put out, notes on articles, and receipts. Nothing on a server of ours, no account database, no password. We already have the pieces: vaults, the vault web app, browser code that reads and writes vaults in tools.sgraph.ai, append lanes, and the published key the newsroom already uses for sending your reading.
connect

An access key. Creating and pushing to a vault needs an access key for the vault server: the thing people will buy, and that I will hand out at first. The reader pastes it on the account page; it is kept in the browser's storage for this site, never put in a URL, and removable in one tap. The page says what it is for and what it lets someone do. A key pair for the reader. Generated in the browser with Web Crypto on first connect, the private key kept non-extractable where the browser allows. The public key goes into the reader's vault. It is used to sign what the reader writes, such as a note on an article, and to receive messages encrypted to them. This is the first real use of RFC 0001 on the newsroom.
connect

A vault. The first time, the site creates a vault for the reader; or the reader pastes the key of a vault they already have. The vault key is shown once, with a plain instruction to save it in a password manager. It never leaves the reader's devices except into that password manager. It is never sent to us.
merge

One log per device. Each device appends what it did, as events: a page read and how far, a rating, a persona created, kept or removed, a reading-list change, a note, a receipt. It never edits another device's log. State is computed, not stored. Every device reads every log and computes the same personas, history, lists and balance. Two devices that were offline both write their own logs, and the merge is a union: no conflicts to resolve. Receipts are counted once, by their payment reference, so a top-up made on the iMac appears on the iPhone and is not credited twice. The local copy stays. Losing the connection, or the access key, leaves the browser's own copy working as it does today.
device

First version: on the device already connected, "Add a device" shows a code to scan or a text to paste, carrying the vault key and the access key, on screen only, never in a URL or an email. The new device connects and reads the logs. Next: a passkey that unlocks the keys, on the design of secrets.sgit.ai, so the reader does not handle a key at all. And sign-in with Google, which the newsroom also needs: it says who you are and can recover access to what you bought, but it does not hold your key, and the design must not pretend it does.
line

One-way, by choice. A note on an article can be marked "to the newsroom". It is encrypted in the browser to the desk's published key, the same one sending your reading already uses, and dropped into a write-only lane. The agent that edits the site reads it; nothing else can. The reply is the change. If the note asks for a correction or a clarification, the answer is a new version of the article, and the article's version history shows it. Sharing more is the reader's call. A reader can also give an agent a read key to a vault of notes. It should be a separate vault from their reading, because a read key opens everything in its vault.
security

What the vault server sees: ciphertext, its size, and when it is written. Not what you read. What a script on the site could see: everything in the browser, including the keys. So the newsroom keeps loading no third-party scripts, and the account page says, in its words, what is kept where. What losing the vault key means: the other devices stop syncing; each keeps its own copy. That is why the key is shown once, with the password manager instruction.
tests

Two browsers, the same vault: read on one, see it on the other; rate on both while offline, reconnect, and both agree. A top-up on one device appears once on all of them. Removing the access key, or the vault, leaves the local reading account intact. A synthetic reader with a phone and a laptop, who has never heard of a vault key: do they understand what to save, and why? And the real test: I use it, on four devices, for a week, and I stop missing it.
not
No account database, no server endpoint of ours, no email and password, nothing that sends the vault key anywhere, and no sync of anything the reader did not do on purpose.
limits

One user is not a market. I am the first user, and the best placed to feel the gap, but that is a direction, not proof that others will want it. Other readers, and the synthetic ones, are how we find out. The past is my own account of it. Why my earlier startups did not take off is more than one reason. Not using them is the one I can see most clearly, and the one I can do something about now. None of the vault feature is built. The brief is a design; the pieces it builds on exist. If you build products and want to compare how your team uses its own, or you want to try the newsroom on every device you have when this ships, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine, recorded on 11 October 2026 after a day of reading the newsroom on four devices, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The figures were drawn for this article; the balances in the first figure are illustrative. The times in the second are from the git logs of this site and of the newsroom. The account page's own sentence about vaults, and the published key and write-only lane used for sending your reading, are from the live newsroom on 11 October 2026.
