Abstract: The introduction to the term. Four words and only one of them new; the test that decides whether something deserves the word, worked from a risk register to a TCP packet; why every file format is already a graph; the five-rule grammar; the evidence, eleven altitudes across seven live vaults; what is still modelled rather than imported; and why now. By Dinis Cruz. This is the canonical copy of the article, with the diagrams and screenshots the LinkedIn version cannot carry. The definition it introduces, the three diagrams and the seven vaults are on the Fractal Semantic Graphs page; the vault where the idea was first worked is VoiceDebrief · Fractal Semantic Graphs.

For about six months I have been calling this "graphs of graphs of graphs", or when I was feeling more precise, "ontologies of ontologies of ontologies". Neither is a name you can put on a page. This week we gave it one, defined it, and published the evidence: seven live graphs you can open in a browser, from the text of a law down to a threat in one line of code on one compute instance, all built with one method. The name is Fractal Semantic Graph. This article is the introduction. Most people reading this already know three of the four.

A graph is nodes and edges. A semantic graph gives the edges meaning: every edge is a verb, and every verb has a named inverse, so a link reads correctly from whichever end you are standing at. A fact gives_rise_to a risk; a risk arises_from a fact. An ontology is the agreed vocabulary of node types and verbs that a graph is allowed to use. The fourth word is fractal, and here is what it adds.

A fractal semantic graph has no privileged level and no single schema. Zoom into any node and you enter a new world with its own node types, its own verbs, its own taxonomy, its own centre of gravity. A regulation is a node in a graph of instruments and jurisdictions. Open it and it is a graph of articles, recitals and amendments: a legal ontology. Open an article and it is a graph of paragraphs and points. Open a paragraph and it is a graph of the terms it uses, each one an edge to the article that defines it: a lexical ontology that looks nothing like the one two levels up. Three zooms, three ontologies. A four-node semantic graph; the Law node opened into a legal ontology of articles, paragraphs and an amendment drawn as an edge; one paragraph opened into a lexical ontology of the terms it uses. The grammar never changes; the ontology does.

Every one of those worlds was defined by whoever owns it, in its own vocabulary, and none of them was made to conform to the others. What connects them is that each one is still a semantic graph. Every edge is a verb with an inverse. Every node knows where it came from. So an edge can be drawn from any node in one world to any node in another, and the walk works. There is no top and no bottom. There is only the altitude you happen to be looking from, and how much definition you choose to load at it. The GDPR atlas says it in its own graph view: "You are at the top of the fractal. Each domain is its own ontology that connects up to the GDPR root and down to concepts and articles." The layout is computed from the graph, not drawn.

Here is the test I use to decide whether something deserves the word. Start inside a risk register. A good one is already a rich semantic graph with a large vocabulary of verbs. A fact gives_rise_to a risk, a risk is_owned_by a role, a person reports_to a person, a control mitigates a risk, evidence backs a fact. Every link that makes sense inside that ontology teaches you something, and a register with ten thousand well named edges is a great deal of knowledge. Nothing about it is fractal yet. It is one graph, however large and however deeply it nests, in one vocabulary. A system that never lets you leave that vocabulary is a single graph, or a hierarchy. Not a fractal. The fractal property is that on one of those links you can jump into another universe.

Follow the register's fact node for an incident and you land in the security operations world: alerts, signals, the systems that were touched, ATT&CK techniques, attack trees. Its own verbs, its own taxonomy, none of it borrowed from the register. In that world you meet a DNS entry that looks like command and control. Follow it and you are in the DNS estate: zones, records, parents, values, every request the resolvers logged, a dataset that might be millions of nodes and is quite possibly served from a SQL database or a GraphQL endpoint rather than held as files. Follow one record to the traffic it produced and you are reading network captures, flows, and eventually a single TCP packet, in yet another vocabulary. Four worlds. Four ontologies. Four taxonomies. One continuous path of named edges between them, and nobody built an adapter.

The jump. Four worlds in a row, each a small graph in its own vocabulary, joined by a jump link on one node each. All four together are one node in a bigger graph that analyses them, and that graph in another. What makes it fractal rather than merely linked is that in every one of those self contained worlds you find the same building blocks: nodes, edges with verbs and inverses, an ontology, a taxonomy, provenance. The grammar is what lets the jump work, in either direction. And it runs upward as well as down. Everything I just described can itself be one node in a larger graph that analyses it, sitting next to graphs of behaviour, of agent actions, of agendas, of funding. This is the part that took me longest to see clearly, and once you see it you cannot unsee it.

A regulation is a graph of articles. A PDF of that regulation is a graph of pages, blocks, lines and glyphs. A spreadsheet is a graph of sheets, rows, cells and formulas. A codebase is a graph of packages, classes, methods and tokens. A JSON document is a tree, which is a graph with one verb. None of them needs to be converted into a graph. Each one only needs its edges named. And once the edges are named, the boundaries between formats stop mattering, and things become possible that no document can do. A question can cross formats without a join table. "Which method in our code implements the control that the crosswalk maps to the article the amendment changed?" is one traversal, from a word in a law to a control in a standard to an attestation to a method, because each step is an edge somebody named.

A correction propagates instead of being republished. Mark one node superseded and every path that rested on it becomes a query: what did we build on this? A document cannot do that. The correction is a new document, and nothing connects it to the thousand that already cite the error. The smallest node is whatever your question needs, not what the format offers. For a lawyer it is the defined term. For a threat model it is the method. For a conformance check it is the attestation and its expiry date. For our GDPR atlas it is, literally, the word. Every unit keeps its own world. The regulation is modelled in the regulator's vocabulary, the register in the risk team's, the threat model in the engineers', and none of them is asked to change. The bridges are edges somebody declares, not a merged schema everybody has to agree on first.

And provenance comes free. When the leaf is a word, and the word is connected to the byte range it came from and the hash of the file that held it, every claim at every altitude above it is traceable to source with no extra machinery. Each altitude gets its own schema. What none of them gets to change is the grammar, and the grammar is five rules. Every edge is a verb, stated in both directions, with an inverse a person in the business would actually say. relates_to is banned. Properties carry data, never meaning, so two nodes both holding the value 8080 differ only in what they are connected to. Supersede, never delete. And never render the whole graph: render the answer to a question.

The banned verb is the one I get the most pushback on, so let me defend it. Two things always relate. An edge with no verb constrains nothing and cannot narrow a query. The granularity of the verb is the precision of the question you will later be able to ask. Every time somebody reaches for relates_to they are deferring the thinking to whoever has to read the graph later, and that person is usually you. A definition is cheap. So we published the ladder. Eleven altitudes, each one a live graph in its own vocabulary, modelled by its own author, and every altitude joined to the next by a named edge. From the top: the law, the standard, the evidence behind the standard, the fact about your estate, the risk it gives rise to, the owner, the acceptance, the insuring policy, the agent, the system, the compute instance.

The ladder: eleven altitudes, eleven ontologies, one grammar. Each altitude names the published vault where that altitude is a live graph, and on the page each name is a link to the vault and its read key. At the top sits the EU AI Act, parsed from the official XML into 113 articles, 500 paragraphs, 417 points, 180 recitals, 13 annexes and 68 definitions: 1,523 nodes and 1,944 edges, with the SHA-256 of the retrieved bytes at the end of every provenance chain. When something elsewhere says "touches Article 12", this is the graph that can say what Article 12 says and prove the bytes. The Regulation Graph's landing view: the counts, both instruments with their CELEX identifiers and the hash of the retrieved bytes, and application dates kept as versioned properties rather than bare facts.

One altitude down is the AIUC-1 agent standard as data: 53 controls, 2,788 nodes, 11,610 edges. Its explorer loads two vaults as one graph, and one of the packs it loads is literally the AI Act by article from the vault above. That join is where a crosswalk stops being a string. The standard publishes 1,126 crosswalks as text. 62 of them resolve into node identifiers in the regulation graph. And the traversal returns something neither graph knew on its own: 8 of the 27 articles reached have since been amended, so the crosswalk was written against text that no longer says what it said. That is the whole argument in one number. Two graphs, built by different people for different purposes in different vocabularies, joined by declared edges, produced a finding that did not exist in either of them.

Two vaults on one canvas. The chip row is the join: the standard, its crosswalks, another vault's articles, the conformance layer, bow ties, acceptances. At the bottom of the ladder is a threat model that is itself a graph of graphs: eleven linked models zooming from Customer through Business, Application, Component, Package, Class and Method, down to Source Code, Environment, Runtime and Compute. 51 nodes, 179 threats. The demonstration is a single SQL injection traced upward from the method it lives in to the revenue it puts at risk, and then framed four ways, for the board, the CISO, the CTO and the developer, from one fact. The zoom ladder, counted: 11 layers, 51 nodes, 179 threats. The bottom altitude is a compute instance.

In between are the altitudes that make this useful to people who are not engineers: a register where answers become facts and facts give rise to risks, an org chart with risks flowing up it until every path terminates at the board, and the same exposure read at seven stakeholder altitudes, each owning it in their own words. The role risk map: what a role holds against what arrives through it because the graph says it must. Nothing stops short of the board.

My favourite single picture in the whole set is Article 45 of the GDPR. The text has not changed a word since 2016. What it permits has flipped four times: Safe Harbour, Schrems I, Privacy Shield, Schrems II, the Data Privacy Framework, and an appeal pending. The atlas draws that as a timeline of ruling nodes over one unchanged article node. The text is a constant. Its meaning is the graph. That is why a static PDF of a law is wrong and a versioned graph is not. One article, five rulings, twenty-five years. Safe Harbour to a pending CJEU appeal, over an Article 45 that has not changed a word. I would rather tell you this than have you find it.

The bottom four altitudes of the threat model, environment through compute, are nodes an author placed, not a live import from a CMDB, an infrastructure repository or a cloud account. The grammar to receive such an import exists. The connector that emits it is not published yet. Enterprise architecture is a gap. No published graph holds an EA repository joined upward to obligations, and that is the layer between the standard and the system that the ladder cannot yet point at.

The crosswalks resolve at article level only, where the regulation graph has paragraphs. The GDPR atlas is a seed pass from May, and six of its 227 edges use the banned relates verb, because the rule was written after that graph was. And the agent altitude is a vocabulary, not yet a join: we have the 23 capability primitives that describe what an agent can do, and no published graph yet imports a real permission set and computes the difference against what the operator intended, at scale. Named gaps get filled. Unnamed ones do not. That is why they are on the page. Three things changed in the last year that make this practical rather than academic.

Naming edges used to be the expensive part. It is now the cheap part. A language model can propose the verb between two nodes faster than a human can type it, which means the bottleneck moved from authoring the graph to deciding what the graph is for. Agents act on the world, and when something acts, provenance stops being a nicety. Every consequential claim needs to be traceable to the byte it came from, and a graph whose leaf is the word gives you that without a second system. And the schema wars are over, because nobody won. Every organisation, division, team and regulator has its own vocabulary and will keep it. The only integration model that survives contact with that fact is one where nobody is asked to conform and everybody is allowed to connect.

Everything in this article is a live graph you can open. Every read key is published on purpose, and none of them can write. Start at the law and walk down, or start at the compute instance and walk up. Either direction works, which is rather the point. The definition, the ladder and the seven vaults: sgit.ai/demos/fractal-graphs The vault where the idea was first worked, with its fifteen-principle register: VoiceDebrief · Fractal Semantic Graphs The grammar in full, with the four situations in which the argument is wrong: graphs.sgit.ai Laws and standards as addressable provisions: standards.sgit.ai The Agent Behaviour Policy, where the graph meets a real permission set: abp.sgit.ai If you build one of your own, the grammar for drawing it is at graphs.sgit.ai/llms.txt, and it is written for agents as much as for people. I would like to see what you connect to what.

Abstract: For a long time we have said that an agent's rules need a secure harness that sits outside the agent's own environment, outside RiskMandate's and outside the hook. We looked for one and did not find it, so I sat down with a few Claude agents and we built it, and it is now released, at sharness.ai, with sharness-ai 0.2.0 on PyPI. SHarness is what our Agent Behaviour Policies become when they are executed rather than read. An Agent Behaviour Policy describes what an agent is mandated to do, what it can actually reach, the gap between the two, and what stands in the way of each capability. A Process Behaviour Policy applies the same model to every process the agent starts: what it may read, write, run, connect to and spend, written as a small policy, hashed to one name the person supplies from outside, and enforced by something the process does not include, the Linux kernel or a small separate service. A tricked agent cannot widen it, because the kernel was told before the process started. That turns Settings and Expectations into Boundaries, which is the only kind of control an insurer can price, and it puts the permission prompt last: yes to what the policy allows, silence for what it refuses, and a question only for what it cannot hold. The design is a launcher and five doors, files, network, keys, shell and model, each a small service with its own user and its own certificate, and the same policy can be written for bubblewrap, Docker, Kubernetes or Claude Code's sandbox, with the list of what each cannot hold. Today the kernel locks run, two doors run as early versions, and a real Linux kernel boots in a browser tab and refuses what the policy refuses; the launcher that binds the agent itself is still the design. It is open source, and what I would most like now is feedback.
From a policy the agent reads to a policy the kernel holds: four kinds of barrier, three things that bind.
in-short

We needed a secure harness outside the agent, and could not find one. So we built it: sharness.ai, and sharness-ai 0.2.0 on PyPI, released on 29 October 2026. It is our behaviour policies, executed. An Agent Behaviour Policy describes an agent; a Process Behaviour Policy is enforced underneath it, on every process it starts. Three things make a policy binding. The text, its hash supplied by the person from outside, and an enforcer the agent does not include. That is the business case. Only an enforced control is a Boundary, and only a Boundary is something an insurer, an auditor or a board can count. The prompt goes last. Yes to what the policy allows, silence for what it refuses, a question only for what it cannot hold. One policy, many enforcers. The same file can be written for bubblewrap, Docker, Kubernetes or Claude Code's sandbox, with what each cannot hold.
in-short

The architecture is a launcher and five doors. Files, network, keys, shell and model, each a small service with its own user, policy and certificate. It runs today, in part. The kernel locks, two doors, the levels, and a Linux kernel in a browser tab that held six of six. What does not run yet is said plainly. The launcher that binds the agent itself is the design. We would like your feedback. Run hello, read the design, tell us what is wrong.
why

For months, every time we talked about agent behaviour policies, the same point came back: a policy the agent reads is only as strong as the agent's willingness to keep it. We need a secure harness that sits outside the agent's environment, outside RiskMandate's environment and outside the hook. We have measured how far we are from that on our own agents. When this newsroom's writer took its own eleven rules and tried to move them into hooks, in are hooks the sweet spot?, only one was kept by something other than the agent. When it took apart the 57 checks its releases pass, in behaviour policies from the checks, 22 were expectations, 34 were settings and one was a boundary. And hooks are kernel code put the last level of its maturity model "off the machine": the rule kept by something the agent's machine does not control.
why

So we looked for that something. There is a lot of good work in this space, and sharness.ai's own market analysis surveys it: sandboxes and microVMs, shell sandboxes in the coding agents, MCP gateways, LLM gateways, secret brokers, guardrails, enterprise platforms. What we did not find was the piece we kept asking for: a policy written once, hashed, supplied by the person, and enforced on every process the agent starts by something the agent cannot switch off. The site's enforceability matrix says it in one line: "The column no product fills is 'who enforces': in every shell sandbox the agent's own process reads the settings."
why

After not finding one, I took the time, sat down with a couple of Claude agents for a really productive session, and we built one. It started on the morning of 24 October 2026 with a narrow problem in sgit, and five days later it is a website, a design, a security register, an open source CLI on PyPI and a team of agents that keeps all of it moving. I think it is a super powerful capability, and this article is its introduction: the strategy first, then what it does and the many ways it works, then the architecture, getting more technical as it goes.
what

SHarness runs an agent and its tools as small, single-purpose processes, each locked down by the kernel and talking to the others only over allowed, mutually authenticated connections. Each process runs under a Process Behaviour Policy: what it may read, write, run and connect to, named by one hash the person supplies and enforced by the Linux kernel. In the site's own words, "A tricked agent cannot widen it, because the kernel was told before the process started." A secret lives in one place, a key service that never hands out a clear key, and a tricked process can only do its one job. The name is the idea: a secure harness, the layer agents run inside so that they can run securely. (It is unrelated to Sharness, the shell testing library.)
policy

SHarness is the natural next step from the work we have done on Agent Behaviour Policies. An Agent Behaviour Policy, an ABP, is a description in four objects: the mandate (what the business asked the agent to do), the grant (what it can actually reach), the delta (the reach nobody asked for) and the barrier on each capability (what stands in its way). The barrier comes in four kinds: None; an Expectation, which is prose the agent reads; a Setting, which the subject could flip; and a Boundary, enforced from above the subject. Most of what stands in the way of an agent today is the agent itself, reading its instructions and choosing to follow them.
policy

A Process Behaviour Policy, a PBP, is "the Agent Behaviour Policy model applied to one process": the same four objects, with the mandate written as rows for one process and the grant measured by probing what that process can do before any policy. The site's one-line distinction is the one I would keep: "An ABP describes an agent's behaviour; a PBP is that description executed, underneath the agent." This newsroom first built one in process behaviour policies, the most locked-down process we could make inside Claude's own cloud container, and measured it; SHarness is that idea grown into a harness. Three things make a PBP binding, and if one is lost, it is an ABP again, a policy the subject reads:
policy

The text. A small JSON object in canonical form (sorted keys, no whitespace, integers only), so the same policy hashes the same in every language. It was measured identical in Python, in the browser and in a Linux guest on 25 October 2026. The hash, from outside. The person supplies sha256:…, and the enforcer refuses anything else. "A prompt-injected agent cannot widen what it cannot rename." An enforcer the subject does not include. The kernel, or a separate process. "Who enforces decides the barrier kind": a policy a process applies to its own child is a Boundary for the child and only a Setting for the process. That last rule is the one SHarness never lets go of. Every result it prints says which kind of barrier it was, including the uncomfortable cases. It is why the site says, on every page that matters, that the launcher which binds the agent itself is still the design.
business

Strategically, the point is not a better sandbox. It is that a behaviour policy can now be held, row by row, by something that is not the agent, and that changes what the policy is worth. Only an enforced control counts. In the insuring agents series I argued, in a payout for every row, that an agent behaviour policy can be read as an insurance policy, and that "A line in the prompt earns nothing": only a control that something enforces lowers a row's premium. SHarness is how a row moves from Expectation to Boundary. A policy that says "this agent writes only to this workspace and talks only to these hosts", held by the kernel and a network door, is a row an underwriter can price, an auditor can check and a board can be told about.
business

Two numbers in every summary. The ABP's number is unbounded excess, the reach nobody asked for and nothing bounds. A PBP adds a second: unheld rows, the mandate rows no Boundary holds. A policy never claims a row is held when nothing holds it; the rows no door holds in a given deployment stay in the policy as Expectations, counted. The site puts it well: "The second number is the business case for the next door."
business

The permission prompt goes last. The prompts coding agents show today are, in ABP terms, Settings: the agent's own process asks the agent's own user, and the same account can turn them off. ux.sgit.ai's finding UX-059 shows they fail as decisions too, and that repeated prompts teach people to press Allow without reading. SHarness's decision at the door moves the decision to launch, in the person's own nouns (this workspace, these sites, these secrets), made once and hashed. After that: "yes to what the policy allows, silence for what it refuses, and a question only for what it cannot hold." An approved question becomes a learned row, so the policy grows from the approvals people actually give.
business

The enterprise story has no product in the request path. A policy can be written at several levels, from a sentence down to the kernel (below). The vendor ships the profiles with its tool, the organisation runs the step that names its own proxies, databases and twins, and the laptop runs the step down to its kernel. Because levels compose by intersection, a developer cannot name a target the organisation does not offer. And it costs nothing per request: the expansion runs once, at launch.
business

And the cloud providers could run it. The real power comes when some of these components run as a service, outside the machine the agent is on. The design's last deployment topology is the platform providing the key service and the session identity, with no key in the container at all. It is the same ask as in agents have an identity now: today no such service is known to exist, and it is a small thing for a provider to offer.
ways

This is where SHarness differs most from a product. The site's landscape starts from one position: at the heart of all this are the behaviour policies, and SHarness is a reference implementation of Process Behaviour Policies, "small enough to read in one sitting". Any environment that can enforce the same rows is a valid enforcer, so the other products are "less competitors than integration points". The question to ask of each one is not whether it competes, but "which rows of a policy can it enforce, natively, and how do I translate the policy into its form?"
ways

That question is a command. sharness-ai policy translate writes the same policy as a bubblewrap command line, a docker run, a Claude Code sandbox settings.json fragment, or a Kubernetes Pod and NetworkPolicy, and ends every output with the list of what that target does not enforce. The matrix behind it is honest in both directions. Writes, no network, no new privileges and memory caps run almost anywhere. An execute allowlist, TCP port rules without a proxy, roles on the connections between processes, the secret in a process the agent cannot reach, and a hash checked above the subject are the rows only SHarness holds today, and they are the reason it exists. The second way it works is by levels, because the full policy schema is more than most people will ever write. The levels: one policy written as a sentence, a profile, plain rows, doors or mechanisms, each compiling into the next.
ways

You write at the level you need. At the top, a sentence with blanks: "contain my agent to this workspace, these sites, these secrets". sharness-ai contain --workspace . --sites github.com -- CMD takes that sentence, compiles it down to the policy the kernel holds, prints what it became at each level with one hash, and runs the command under it. "A simpler level is never a weaker one": the person supplies the hash of what they wrote, and every expansion below it is recomputed. Each level reports in its own nouns, so at the top the report reads like "it can reach 14 things you did not ask for", and any row from a lower level can be written in when one row needs to go deeper.
ways

The third way is where you start. In a browser, with nothing installed, the playground puts pip install sharness-ai in Pyodide next to a shell on a real Linux kernel. On Linux, pip install sharness-ai and sharness-ai hello. In a Claude Code session, a skill runs probe and hello inside the session, with the caveat stated: the session itself is not bound.
architecture

The design is a launcher and a small set of single-purpose components. Its theme is "one role, one noun, one uid, one policy, one certificate." SHarness's moving parts as designed: a launcher outside every domain, the app, and five doors under mutual TLS. The person supplies one policy hash out of band. The launcher, outside every domain, refuses to start unless the manifest hashes to that value; it makes one Linux user per component, a session certificate authority and one certificate per role, then destroys the authority's private key, so the set of identities is closed. The harnessed app, which might be sgit's CLI, a Claude Code session or your own loop, sits on top and routes: it holds no keys, has no network and writes nothing itself. Around it are the doors: Door Its one job (designed) sharness.fs the only writer of protected folders; refuses anything that parses as a clear key, a private key or a token sharness.net
architecture

the only network client and the TLS client, with host, endpoint and id allowlists sharness.bash each shell command in a fresh sandbox under a profile, output filtered sharness.llm the only client of the model API; pins the tool list, filters secrets out of every tool result, adds the real key sharness.kms holds the private keys in a memfd_secret page, frozen between calls; re-seals to one-time keys; never returns a clear key
architecture

Every connection between them is mutual TLS 1.3 with the role in the certificate (as a SPIFFE ID), and both sides check that the pair is in the edge list, which denies by default. The app never talks to the key service; only the network and model doors do, and the key service never returns a clear key to either: it returns derived keys sealed to a one-time key made for that one request. The site measured what that costs on 24 October 2026: about 3.2 ms for a mutual TLS handshake between two local processes, about 10 ms for the three handshakes of an sgit command, against 146 ms the command already spends importing Python. A disposable user for a session was about 49 ms.
architecture

It all started with what the site calls the last metre. Our PKI handover protects a vault key while it travels, sealed to the receiving agent's public key, and stops protecting it the moment it arrives: on disk, on the command line, and in the agent's transcript. "For an AI agent the worst leak is not the disk. It is the transcript." In the design, the sealed message itself becomes the file on disk, the key service opens it inside its own process, and the agent sees a command, ciphertext, fingerprints and a status line, never a key. Nothing in that fix turned out to be specific to sgit, and that generalisation is SHarness.
architecture

The same components and the same protocol run in five topologies, and only the launcher changes: one machine with a user per component (what was measured), one container per component, one Kubernetes pod with identities from SPIRE and a NetworkPolicy that mirrors the edges, a remote key service in a cloud function in front of a hardware-backed key, and the platform providing it all.
doors

A Process Behaviour Policy has two kinds of row, and the rule that joins them is the most important technical idea in the design. Capability rows bound what a process can reach: path prefixes to read, write and execute; TCP ports; no network; memory and process caps; no new privileges. The kernel holds them, with Landlock, namespaces, rlimits and cgroups. These are the v0 policy, and they run today.
doors

Behaviour rows bound what the process does with a reach it has: append only to this file; this field within this range, never negative; connect only to this host, this endpoint, this vault; at most so many per interval; this operation only with fresh approval. A door holds them. And the rule: "A behaviour row is a Boundary only when the subject has no path to the resource except through the door that holds the row." So every behaviour row has preconditions made of capability rows. An append-only rule on a ledger, held by sharness.fs, is a Boundary only if the app's own write rows exclude that file and the app has an edge to the door. If the preconditions do not hold, the row is still well formed, and it gets the barrier kind Expectation, counted. That is "what can currently be controlled", derived from the policy rather than hoped.
doors

The language for those rows is deliberately closed: append only, a section, content by JSON Schema, a numeric range, count and rate, ordering, fresh approval. "A policy that can express arbitrary logic is code, and code in the policy is a rules engine in the trusted path." Anything more is a door of its own, under its own policy. A business that needs "transaction amount within range, daily total under X" writes that as a small door.
doors

The doors form a tree of names, sharness.<door>.<target>, where the door is the vocabulary and the target is where it sends. sharness.fs.disk writes to the local disk, sharness.fs.s3 to S3, and sharness.net.git holds remote, branch, ref and push, "never force, never main". A target can be the real system, a relay, or a twin, and .twin on the end of any name means it is simulated: sharness.db.postgres.twin reads as a development world without decoding anything. Development and production are one policy tree with different targets, so a run's hash says which world it ran in. Each door declares what it accepts and what it emits, and a chain is valid only when each hop emits what the next accepts. That is why the network door, which accepts TCP and CONNECT, cannot hold a URL row, and an HTTP door below it can.
doors

sharness.net shows why the doors are processes and not filters. The kernel only sees a connect to a port, so a relay that forwarded bytes would let the process inside choose the server name itself, which is domain fronting. So the network door is the TLS client: it sends the CONNECT, checks the name in the TLS hello against the host, and keeps one audit line per request. The process gets a policy whose only network row is the door's port, so a direct connect is refused by the kernel before a packet leaves.
today

The site's status page keeps the honest column, and I will keep it here. As of 29 October 2026: sharness-ai 0.2.0 on PyPI. Python standard library only; 6,041 lines in the package and 243 tests, run in CI on Python 3.11 to 3.13. The kernel locks, on one process. sharness-ai run --policy FILE --expect-hash sha256:… -- CMD applies Landlock file and execute rules (a writable path is never executable), TCP port rules, no network, memory and process caps, and refuses to run anything if the hash does not match. The acceptance test. sharness-ai hello runs six probes under a deny-all policy. It held 6 of 6 in five places on 25 October: a cloud session, my browser, headless Chromium, Node and a chroot on the host kernel. The levels in the terminal. contain, profile and explain. Two doors as early versions. sharness.fs, the only writer, under mutual TLS with 18 conformance vectors; and sharness.net, an allowlisting proxy.
today

The launcher's first slice. sharness-ai shell --workspace . --sites pypi.org starts a shell as a fresh user, with its own network namespace holding only loopback, the network door as its only way out, and a live page of every refusal. It was checked on 29 October: pypi.org allowed through the door, example.com refused, a direct connect to 1.1.1.1 refused, a name lookup found nothing. A real Linux kernel in a browser tab. I asked this site's agent to open the E09 page in a headless browser on 29 October. An Alpine guest with Linux 6.18 booted on an emulated CPU, and hello ran 111 seconds in: sharness-ai hello under a Linux kernel in a browser tab, 29 October 2026: six probes, six held.
today

Read the last line of that output, because it is the project's character in one sentence: "applied by a process to its own child: a Boundary for the child, a Setting for the parent, who could have skipped it. The launcher that binds the agent too is the design, not code." What is not built: the key service, the shell door, the model door, the launcher's manifest, and the launcher above the agent. seccomp, per-component users for every door, and hostnames in the policy itself are still to come. Nothing yet binds the agent itself.
built

SHarness is also a demonstration of how we now build. It is one person and a team of agents, each with a role, a behaviour policy in the ABP shape, a status file it keeps itself and, where it holds secrets, a key on pki.sgit.ai: a CLI agent that builds the package, a website agent that owns the site and its gate, a policy agent that holds the definition of the PBP, a security agent that keeps the register, a developer agent writing the policy standard in other languages, a conductor and a Sherpa. Their board, briefs, commit notes and runs are all public.
built

Two things in how it was built matter for whether you can trust it. First, the security register. The site's rule is that "nobody reviewing SHarness should find something it does not already say about itself." The first review, on 25 October, recorded 25 findings, five of them High, all five fixed with a test that fails if the hole opens again. The second, on 29 October, before the release, found two High issues in the shell (it could reach other hosts on the proxy's port, and a process of the shell could outlive it), fixed with tests before 0.2.0 went out. Second, standards with test vectors: the policy's canonical form and hash are a written standard with 28 vectors that the Python, JavaScript and Go implementations all pass, so a policy hashed in one language is the same policy in another.
feedback

This is the part I care about most. SHarness is at the experiments stage, it is open source, and the fastest way for it to get better is for people who did not build it to push on it. Run hello on your machine. pip install sharness-ai, then sharness-ai hello --json, and report it. Every machine becomes a row on hello on your machine, and as the project says, "a refusal that did not happen is the most useful thing you can send." Try to break the shell. sharness-ai shell --sites with one host, and see whether anything leaves on another. Report privately through GitHub's vulnerability reporting. Tell us who should run the launcher. The agent itself (every lock is then a Setting), a script above it on a laptop (a Boundary), or the platform (a Boundary all the way down). The design wants the third and starts with the second.
feedback

If you build a sandbox, a gateway or an agent platform, tell us which rows of a policy you hold natively, and whether the translation is right. If you run agents in a business, write the sentence: which workspace, which sites, which secrets. What the levels make of it, and what is left unheld, is exactly what I would like to see.
limits

Most of SHarness is designed, not built. The kernel locks, the levels, two doors and the launcher's first slice run; the key service, the shell and model doors, and the launcher above the agent do not. Nothing binds the agent itself yet. A policy applied by a process to its own child is a Boundary for the child and a Setting for the process. It does not protect against root or a compromised kernel. The design trusts the kernel; anything with root can read a process's ordinary memory. The measurements are the project's own. Each is from one environment on one date, with method on sharness.ai's evidence page. The one run here is the E09 page in a headless browser on 29 October 2026; the CLI was not run on this site's own machine. The translations have not been run against their targets. Each matrix cell is what the target's documentation says.
limits

"Integration point" is not a partnership. No vendor named on sharness.ai has agreed to anything. The security reviews were done by an agent of the project. They are a register for an outside review to start from, not a replacement for one. The cloud service is a proposal. No provider offers it, and nothing here describes any provider's plans. If you run agents that read untrusted data, build a sandbox or a platform, or would price the risk of one agent at a time, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

My request of 29 October 2026, kept word for word in this site's repository under admin/notes/2026-10-29__sharness/, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine.
sources

sharness.ai was read in full on 29 October 2026, at site v0.6.33, from its llms.txt and the markdown of every page: the brief, Why: the last metre, Architecture, the components, the PBP on one page, the levels, the decision at the door, the landscape, enforceability, Security, what exists today and the members; the quotes are from those pages, and the moving-parts figure is sharness.ai's own, re-rendered here with a narrower font (CC BY 4.0). The CLI was read at SHarness-AI__CLI, dev at commit 7ea23c6, and its release dates from PyPI. The hello figure is the E09 page's own console output, captured by this site's agent in headless Chromium on 29 October 2026 and set as text. My first article on SHarness, of 24 October 2026, is a secure harness for agents on sharness.ai. On this site: process behaviour policies, are hooks the sweet spot?, hooks are kernel code, behaviour policies from the checks, a payout for every row and agents have an identity now.

Abstract: This is an article brief: one idea and one task, and the direction of travel behind them. We are starting to talk to investors, and the challenge with most of what we build is that it has to be experienced to be understood. So the best way to talk to investors is to have them use it, and the place to do that is a website of its own, investor.sgit.ai, for investors and founders together, angel to Series A. It would carry the news from investor circles, tracked from public sources as a graph; startup contracts, cap tables and term sheets as linked graphs with their versions and caveats; a section for founders on how to talk to an investor and what comes next; the funding models from open source to proprietary; deal rooms as vaults, and keys for investors as a demonstration of PKI; RiskMandate's due diligence and de-risking at work; and sgit itself as the case study, its strategy and thinking published as it happens. It would also put back in front of people work that got lost: the GenAI cybersecurity startup evaluation framework I published in March, seven criteria and a meta-criterion scored to forty, which is the first piece of the maturity model I had in mind. Like the PHP newsroom, it would be run by a small team of agents on a schedule, built from the first commit to sgit.ai's rules for a new repository, with CI owning the version. And then I would show it to investors and ask: is this useful, and what would help?
What investor.sgit.ai would hold, for investors and founders, angel to Series A. A proposal.
in-short

This is an article brief. One idea, one task, and the direction of travel behind them. What we build has to be experienced to be understood. So investors should use it, not read about it. A website for investors and founders together. investor.sgit.ai, angel to Series A, running on the tools it describes. Eight sections. The news, contracts as graphs, founders, an evaluation framework, deal rooms as vaults, keys for investors, sgit as the case study, RiskMandate at work. Work that got lost comes back. The GenAI cybersecurity startup evaluation framework of March 2026, the first piece of a maturity model. Run by a small team of agents. On a schedule, like the PHP newsroom's. Built to the house rules from the first commit. A brief in full, a reality file, CI owning the version, a gate, behaviour policies. Then ask investors. Is this useful, and what would help?
why

We are going to start talking to investors, and the challenge is one I keep running into: a lot of what we build needs to be experienced to be understood. A vault that the host cannot read, a read key that works from any static page, an agent with its own key that another agent can send a secret to, a behaviour policy that reads as an insurance policy: each sounds abstract until you open it. So I think the best way to talk to investors is to have them use our own technology, on the problems they actually have.
why

The pieces of the puzzle exist. This newsroom has the articles and the vaults; where to invest in sgit put the investor deck in a vault; legal on demand for startups built a founder's desk, an investor's desk and a deal room as vaults; the insuring agents series has a calculator anyone can open. What is missing is one place, for investors and founders, where those pieces are the website.
sections

For now I would merge investors and startups into one site, because most of what helps one helps the other. The news. What is going on in investor circles, with the focus on angel and Series A, the early funding. All of it from public sources, tracked as a semantic graph so the dots connect: who invested in whom, which funds move together, which terms are spreading. Contracts as graphs. Startup contracts, cap tables and term sheets, shown as documents that hyperlink to each other, with their versions and their caveats. A clause in a term sheet links to the article in the shareholders' agreement it changes, and to the articles on this site that argue about it, such as sell, don't issue and the exit is when you sell control.
sections

For founders. How a founder talks to an investor, what the next steps are, what services are available, and what we can help with, so that a founder's life gets easier. Start a company and the controllable founder are the beginning. The funding models, all of them. From the open-source model I use, through open core, to fully proprietary, with what each gives the founder and the investor; open source so you keep it and a small slice sets the price already cover parts. An evaluation framework for security startups, below. Deal rooms as vaults. How information moves between an investor and a startup, and all the overhead around it. Vaults suit this well, especially connected to an agent: give a deal room its own workspace, email and team accounts, and keep everything in its vault, where it is managed and protected.
sections

Keys for investors. A key pair for an investor who wants one, as a demonstration of how public and private keys work, and of how agents can send each other secrets, as agents have an identity now describes. sgit as the case study, and RiskMandate at work. I did this before for The Cyber Boardroom, in a repository where I published strategy, marketing and thinking as it happened. The same for sgit: why sgit, why now, why invest in it, the follow-up to where to invest in sgit. Not the amount being raised, for now, but everything else, captured as it evolves. Beside it, RiskMandate and vaults solving problems founders and investors have: analysing startups, gathering material and research, market analysis, due diligence and de-risking, with the vaults that show them running.
framework

In March I published a framework for evaluating GenAI cybersecurity startups, and it is a good example of the kind of thing we publish that gets lost. It is on notebook-lm.sgit.ai, as an infographic, a slide deck and its source. I had remembered it as a maturity model; it is a scored framework, which is the first piece of one. The GenAI cybersecurity startup evaluation framework: seven criteria and a meta-criterion, scored to 40.
framework

Its thesis is that "many GenAI cybersecurity startups are solving the wrong problem, or solving the right problem in a way that doesn't survive the next model improvement." It scores seven criteria from 1 to 5, structural against temporary, unit value, inline risk, business context, model survivability, open source and deployment sovereignty, and a meta-criterion on the architecture: models inline as the execution engine, or agentic development with a deterministic runtime. The total, out of 40, falls in a band from "35-40: Rare" to "8-13: Avoid". For investors, it names business context and model survivability as "the strongest predictors of long-term value". On investor.sgit.ai it would be something to push and to map: applied to real startups, in public, with the evidence for each score in a vault, and grown into a maturity model with levels, which it does not have yet. It leaves team, traction and financials out by design, and the site should say so.
team

The site would be agentic, with an agent schedule, like the PHP newsroom, which runs with two people and nineteen agents and roles. It need not be that large, but it needs the same workflow: a conductor that hands out the work, a journalist that writes, a researcher that reads the sources, security and observability, each with its own key, published with its role, and an append lane for messages and requests.
team

I am in two minds about one thing: who makes the news feeds. The newsroom already runs the workflow, its wires, a public vault per wire that agents write and pages read. So one option is that the newsroom runs an investor wire and investor.sgit.ai consumes it; the other is that the site's own team does it. My inclination is the first, because it shows the point of vaults: one team writes, another site reads, and the vault is the contract between them. Reading data from the other newsrooms' vaults is a good demonstration of sgit in itself.
rules

New agents tend to miss the guidance on how to start a new repository, so the brief should say it plainly. sgit.ai's guidance for every repository sets the start: the brief published in full, a reality file, where "a feature that is not in the reality file does not exist", a corrections file, a gate that fails the build, tests against real things, a review folder, roles and a board as files, .md twins and an llms.txt, and "Read keys may be published; vault keys never." The agents run under a behaviour policy.
rules

The latest rule matters most for a site several agents will push to: CI owns the version. The pipeline picks every number, the last one on dev and the middle one on main, and no agent ever works out the next number itself, because that causes conflicts; CI owns the version explains why. And the site should point to the sites that hold the house standards: coding.sgit.ai for the code, nfrs.sgit.ai for the non-functional requirements, and ux.sgit.ai, which measures the user experience across the sgit.ai sites.
ask

My angle is simple. Once a first version runs, I would like to email and reach out to a lot of investors and ask: what do you think of this? Do you find it useful? What would help? The answers decide what the site becomes, and every answer goes on the record, like everything else here.
limits

None of it is built. This is a brief; the site, its team and its sections are proposals. The evaluation framework is not a maturity model. It scores; the levels are still to design, and it does not cover team, traction or financials. The news section needs care with sources and names. Public sources only, dated and linked, and no private person named. The Cyber Boardroom repository is described from memory. Its link is to be added. The amount being raised for sgit is not published. By choice, for now. If you invest at angel or Series A and would tell us what would help, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Two voice memos of mine on 28 October 2026, kept word for word in this site's repository under admin/notes/2026-10-28__investor-sgit-ai/, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The evaluation framework, the PHP newsroom's team and sgit.ai's guidance for a new repository were read on 29 October 2026 by a research agent of this site, from their own pages: notebook-lm.sgit.ai (the framework's source, v1.0, March 2026), the PHP newsroom and sgit.ai's repository guidance. The build brief for the agent that would make the site is admin/notes/2026-10-29__brief__investor-sgit-ai.md in this site's repository.

Abstract: In the book I say that the opportunity is not only in new jobs, but in jobs we have done for a very long time that never really scaled, and now can. The editor asked for more detail, and fairly: without examples it is a claim without a case. So here it is. What never scaled is on-demand expertise: getting the value of someone with skills the team does not have, for the few days it is needed. An engagement like that has three phases. Before, the expert has to gather context, and the questions they ask are their experience. Then the meeting, short, where the value is. After, the write-up, for every audience. The first and third took weeks, most experts dislike them, and they are not what the expert is hired for, so only big companies could pay for it, and only when the company, the talent and the travel all lined up. The clinic has long worked differently: others take your history, so the specialist decides fast. Agents can now be that support for any expert, anywhere, even twelve hours a week. My own agent team has a historian, a librarian, a cartographer, an accountant and a sherpa: roles I could never have had. That is the opportunity, for the people who have spent twenty years in one of those jobs, and for the startups that never scaled before.
Before, the meeting, after: a week or more gathering, a day or two meeting, three days writing up, and now with agents.
in-short

What never scaled is on-demand expertise. Skills the team does not have, for the days they are needed. Every engagement has three phases. Before, gathering context; the meeting; after, the write-up. The before and the after were the cost. Weeks of work most experts dislike and are not hired for. So it only happened when everything lined up. The company, the talent, the travel and the budget. The clinic already works the other way. Others take your history, so the specialist decides fast. Agents can now be that support for any expert. Anywhere, even twelve hours a week. That is the opportunity. For people who know an old job well, and for startups that never scaled.
book

In the book, Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition), the chapter Where do you land? ends with a section called The jobs that never scaled. It says that the opportunity "is not only in new jobs. It is in jobs we have been doing for a very long time, sometimes for millennia, that never really scaled and never had good technology, done one person at a time." The idea comes from You are lucky to be here, where I first wrote it down. The editor's note on that section is direct: it needs "three examples of jobs that never scaled, and now can", because "without them this section is a claim without a case." That is fair. This article is the case.
core

Take the simplest example: a consultant. What is a consultant? Somebody who has skills the team does not have. You bring them in because they know something you do not, and you need it for a while, not for ever. So I think the core of this is on-demand expertise: getting the value of someone's skills for the days you need them. That is what never scaled. Not because the skills were rare, but because of everything around them.
phases

Any engagement with an outside expert has three phases, and each one matters. Before: gathering context. The expert needs a lot of information, and they have a very specific set of questions and data points they want. That is part of their magic: what questions to ask. The more experienced they are, the more interesting those questions are, because they go for the non-obvious things. When I look at application security, the first thing I want to know is what their CI pipeline looks like, because if they do not have a good one, I can already tell you they are going to have a lot of problems. Then: how is the team set up, how are they funded, how are they rewarded, what are their non-functional requirements, what is the scope. Every professional has a mental model like that, built from experience.
phases

The meeting, or meetings. These are short, and they are where you really get a sense of it. You meet the stakeholders, you present what you have found, you gather more, you maybe brainstorm with a few teams. By now you have pieces of the puzzle, and you are connecting them. You arrive prepared, because you know the system. You are not arriving cold. After: the write-up. Then the expert has to put it all together in a way that each audience can consume: the board, the engineers, the managers, the people who will do the work. That is a lot of work if you want to do it properly.
phases

Traditionally, to do a decent job, that was about three weeks: a week or more to meet people, get the gist, read and ask the right questions; a day or two of meetings; and three days or more to write it all up. It was hard to have an impact any faster.
parts

Here is the thing. Most consultants, most creative people, most people who like solving problems, do not like the first phase, and hate the third. They are usually not that good at them, and that is not what they are measured on. You do not bring that person in because they are a good writer. You bring them in because they are a very good architect, or librarian, or strategist, or specialist in a domain, or a doctor. And there is a quieter problem with the third phase. Often the expert understands the problem much better than the client does, but can only write down so much, because there is only so much the client can take in. The rest of what they understood is lost.
agents

Now, because of agents, because of the ability to collect data and to distribute it, the first and third phases can be done far more effectively. Before the meeting, there can be a whole set of questionnaires, agents and structures that collect the information ahead of time. That is already how I work: I send a note saying, here is what I need to know. What comes back can be packaged, filtered and sanitised, with sensitive information removed, and then given to the outside expert, who can analyse it, form a view and come to the meeting with a diagnosis to test. After the meeting, agents can turn the decisions into the actions, the roadmap and a version for each audience, and hand the actions out. And because each audience gets its own version, more of what the expert understood can reach the people who need it, instead of the one document a client has time to read.
clinic

The clinic model: others collect your history, the specialist decides, a team carries out the plan. This is not new as a shape. Think of what happens when you go to a clinic or a hospital. The first people you meet are the ones collecting information from you: the forms, the reception, the nurses. Eventually that is presented to the doctor or the specialist, who gets the key pieces of information and can make a decision very fast. And then a team carries out what was decided. The specialist is not effective because they work less. They are effective because everything around them is built so that their time goes only on what needs them. What is new is that this support no longer needs a building full of people. Agents can do it, for any expert.
intersection

The intersection that made outside expertise rare, and how it changes when the expert can be anywhere. Most consulting in the past happened at a strange intersection. You needed a company, in a location, with a problem; somebody who had hired the talent that fitted that problem; someone who could physically go to the office and meet them; and the money to pay for all of it. That is very inefficient and very expensive, so it was only used for specific things, and mostly by big companies. And the talent is not, most of the time, going to live close to the client. It is spread around the city, the country, the world. When the context travels to the expert, and the delivery travels back, that intersection stops mattering.
examples

Twelve jobs that never scaled, from historian and librarian to security lead, project manager and translator. You can go around all the houses and find professions where you could never get the value of the person without them having a large support network around them: The historian. One of the most important roles in a project, because they give it the context of its own history. We complain that we do not learn from history; it is because we do not capture history in a way that can be consumed. Imagine every project with a historian. It does not need one full time: it needs one at specific points, to set things up, to connect and map what happened. The librarian. Everything findable, connected and current. My favourite agent. The cartographer. The map of what connects to what, and where the boundaries are.
examples

The architect, and the software architect. Someone who has seen a hundred systems, for the week a decision is made. The on-demand consultant. Skills the team does not have, for days, not months. The lawyer reviewing a contract. The clauses that matter, found before the meeting. The accountant. What things cost, what they return, and where the money should flow. The doctor and the specialist. The history taken first, so the decision is fast. The project manager. Who is doing what, what is blocked, and what is next, kept for everyone. The security lead. The questions that find the real problems first. The sherpa. A guide for each user, watching where they struggle. The translator. The same information, in the right language and form, for each audience.
examples

Can agents do all of this on their own? Some parts of it. But agents can go in all directions, and you need somebody who provides the direction. That is the role of the expert: the experience that knows which questions matter, and the judgement that decides.
team

I can see this in my own work. The SG/Send project's agent team has nineteen roles, and many of them are ones I could never have had before. The historian's mission: "Track every decision, spec change, and architectural evolution so the team always knows what was decided, why it was decided, and what it superseded." The librarian's: "Maintain knowledge connectivity across all project artifacts, ensuring every document is discoverable, cross-referenced, and current." The cartographer maps "the system topology, data flows, security boundaries, and dependency relationships". There is an accountant, whose mission begins "Make the financial reality of the project visible", a sherpa for users, a journalist, a translator, and the usual developers, architects and operations roles around them. None of those roles was affordable for a project of that size before. Each one is a job that never scaled, now working for one project, and directed by a person.
geeks

As a CISO, I work with almost everybody in an organisation, and something has always fascinated me: most roles that have any agency, which is most roles in a modern company, attract a particular kind of person. We call the technical people geeks, but every industry has them. Talk to someone deep in an industry and they have their own words, their own three-letter acronyms, their own definitions, their own ontology and taxonomy. They geek out on things you would never think of, and they look at what you love doing in the same way. Their culture and their experience shaped what they focus on, and so did their limitations: what they are good at and what they are not. In a way, those limitations are what make them good. That is exactly the kind of person whose value was locked behind the before and the after.
part-time

Twelve good hours, illustrative: a part-time expert's week without support and with agents. These are roles you could never hire part-time and get real value from. Think of a parent working from home: a remarkable resource, who often needs the mental stimulation, but may only want to work twelve hours a week for this period of their life. Nothing wrong with that. You just need to make sure those twelve hours are very productive, so they get the best of both worlds. I know many people who moved, or changed jobs, and who miss what they did: the challenge, the ideas, the moments when something clicks. They are highly qualified, and they cannot connect to that work again, because until now there was no environment that prepared things for them and made them productive.
part-time

Which is one of the things I have always found strange about companies. They spend money on all sorts of things, and very little on making their people productive. There should be a department whose whole job is to make people productive: to manage their data, and to focus on what they need, not on what it happens to be able to do. Agents can now be that department.
startups

This connects to startups, and it is worth being precise. Paul Graham's essay of July 2013 starts: "One of the most common types of advice we give at Y Combinator is to do things that don't scale", such as "to recruit users manually". That is about doing unscalable things on purpose, at the start, to learn.
startups

What I mean is different. There are whole kinds of company that never scaled, because they were services built on experts' time: the consultancy, the agency, the specialist practice, the one-person service. Their growth was bound by the hours of the people in them, most of which went on the before and the after. Foundation Capital, a venture firm, calls this shift "Service-as-Software", and puts it at "a $4.6 trillion opportunity", which is an investor's estimate, not a measurement. Whatever the number, the shape is the one in this article: when the before and the after are carried by agents, a services business can grow with the expert's judgement, not with their hours.
startups

And that is the point for the reader of the book. If you have spent twenty years inside one of those jobs, you can build the first version of the support it never had. And if you are starting out, the jobs that never scaled are a good place to look.
for-the-book

For the chapter, these are the three I would use, because I have lived each one: The on-demand security consultant. Three weeks for a two-day engagement, most of it gathering and writing. With agents asking my questions ahead of time, and writing up for each audience afterwards, it becomes two prepared days, for companies that could never afford the three weeks. The historian. Every project needs one at a few moments, and almost none had one. Now a project can have a historian agent recording every decision and why, with a person directing it at the moments that matter. The librarian. Making everything findable and connected was always valuable and never staffed. My librarian agent does it every day, for one project.
related

The same shape runs through other things I have written: why graphs never scaled for everyone else; removing code, which needed a map and the tests to prove nothing broke; the minimum code below; due diligence, which never scaled because it was a form; and reading with a pen, where capturing what I learn from books never scaled. And the expert founders is about the people best placed to build what comes next: the ones who know the problem.
limits

"Never scaled" means for most companies. Big firms did buy this work; most could not. The three weeks are from my experience. Not a survey. The twelve hours are illustrative. The shape is the point, not the numbers. Agents do not replace the expert. They carry the before and the after; the direction is the person's. The $4.6 trillion is Foundation Capital's estimate. An investor's figure, quoted as such.
