Abstract: Francesco Marconi shared the slides of an INMA talk with a line I agree with completely: "As AI makes content production easier, journalism's competitive advantage will increasingly come from how we observe the world." His deck makes it concrete with a data-center buildout in the desert: journalism as delta science, a map of who wants what, an atlas of events each with a definition and an observable signal, a domain ontology, observations that add to what the newsroom knows, a workflow of observe, compare, check, report and update, and a community impact tracker. I wanted to see it working, so this site's agent built it: a vault on this site, an app of seventeen pages that follows the eleven slides, runs each one on real data structures, and adds five graphs of the same knowledge. The atlas has all 12 families and 78 event types; the ontology has six entities and six relationships; sixteen source records produce seventeen observations, each a subject, a change, a time and its evidence; and the tracker turns them into an article and two alerts. The records are synthetic, on purpose: a fictional campus in a fictional county, because fake permits under real agencies' names would be exactly the kind of record a newsroom like this should never publish. The method is the point, and a vault is a natural home for it: the observation history is a versioned record, the evidence travels with every claim, and anyone with the read key can open it, check it, and copy it for their own beat.

The observation desk's cover: the headline and a synthetic data-centre campus in pen and ink, with orange markers. The idea, the tour, and the vault itself: read them in order, or open the vault straight away.
in-short

The advantage is how you observe. Marconi's argument, and the reason this site exists. His deck is a design. An atlas of events, an ontology, an observation history, a workflow, a tracker. So we built it. A vault that follows the eleven slides, each one working on data. 78 event types, 6 entities, 16 records, 17 observations. Each observation a subject, a change, a time and evidence. Synthetic on purpose. A fictional campus; no fake records under real agencies' names. Five graphs of one knowledge. A fractal graph you open level by level, and a knowledge graph you play in time. A vault is the right home. The history is versioned, the evidence travels, the read key opens it. Copy it for your beat. Replace the families and records; the app does not change.
argument

Francesco Marconi, who runs AppliedXL and before that led research and development at The Wall Street Journal, posted the slides of his talk to the International News Media Association with a line I could have written: "As AI makes content production easier, journalism's competitive advantage will increasingly come from how we observe the world." He calls journalism delta science: "identifying what changed, why it matters, and who is affected." And he names what it takes: "an atlas of meaningful events, a map of the actors and relationships within a domain, and a persistent record of observations backed by evidence."
argument

That is very close to how this site works. The wire is a graph of stories with their sources; every claim is checked against the record before it is published; and every link points back to what came before and what corrected it. What his deck adds is the discipline of defining, in advance, what counts as a change: an event type, with a definition and a signal you can observe.
desk

His example is a data-center buildout in the desert: a campus going up beside a power station, a town, a water tower and a reservoir. The deck is AI-generated and conceptual, and every slide describes a part of a system. So the agent built each part, in the same order, after the cover: The advantage moves toward proprietary observation. What you watch, what you recognize, what you connect: here, 13 registries and sources, 78 event types, and 6 observations that join a new record to an earlier one. Journalism is delta science. A before and after of the same landscape; in the after, four documents appear, Permissions, Resources, Ownership and Commitments, and each opens its record. Who wants what? What depends on what? The power provider, the developer, the local government and the residents, and what each wants.
desk

An atlas of events. The deck shows one example in each of twelve families and says the full set is "78 event types in 12 families". The vault has all 78, each with a definition and an observable signal, and shows which ones have been seen. A domain ontology. Campus, building, construction work, source record, company, project, and the six verbs between them: contains, modifies, documents, owns, participates in, includes. Every observation adds to what the newsroom knows. Seventeen observations, from an air permit application in November 2025 to oversize-load permits in October 2026. Observations anchor the AI workflow. Observe, compare, check, report, update, stepped through one real cycle in the vault. Journalists direct the flow of intelligence. Monitor, investigate, publish, as three queues. What is this project changing for the community? The tracker, and what it produced. Your advantage is how you observe. How to make one for your own beat.
desk
The working ontology slide: six entities with their attributes and six relationships, each a pen-and-ink vignette.
found

The synthetic records were written to behave like real ones: they disagree with each other, in small ways that matter. That is where the method earns its keep, because a single record says little, and the change only appears when it is compared with the last one. The permit grew. The air permit was applied for at up to 5.2 GW and issued at up to 6.1 GW, 17% more. The jobs shrank. The school-district application promised 140 qualifying jobs; the state tax-program registration commits 120. The schedule slipped. The developer said in April that the first 1 GW would be online in the second half of 2027; after the acquisition, the new owner's investor presentation says the first half of 2028, while the power station still says 2027.
found

The water question stayed open. The company says it will cool with non-potable water; the water district deferred a vote on three wells because nobody has said how much water a year the campus will use. The observation history: four headline observations as folders, January to September 2026, and the full history below. Each of those is an observation with its evidence attached, and two became alerts and one a draft article in the tracker. None of them needed a model to be clever. They needed the atlas to say what a change is, the ontology to say what it changes, and the history to say what was known before.
graphs
The fractal semantic graph in the vault, opened to Power and utilities and its seven event types.
graphs

An atlas, an ontology and an observation history are three views of one graph, and the vault draws it five ways. The fractal semantic graph starts at the question and opens any node into the graph inside it: the campus into its twelve event families, a family into its event types, an event type into the observations that matched it, an observation into its records. Every level has the same shape, which is the point of a fractal graph, and it is the same idea as reading code as a fractal semantic graph: you never need the whole thing at once, only the level you are on and the way down. A radial view puts every level on one page, with the evidence in orange. A bipartite graph joins the sixteen records to the seventeen observations they support. And a delta chain lays the observations on a time axis, with an arc from each one to the earlier observation it was compared with.
graphs

The knowledge graph in time: the ontology instantiated with the campus, played one observation at a time. The one I like most is the knowledge graph played in time. It is the ontology instantiated, the campus, its three buildings, the two projects, four companies and the public bodies, and each relationship carries the observation that created it, and, if one did, the observation that ended it. Press play and it is delta science you can watch: the generation station appears with its permit, the development agreement ties the county to the campus, two buildings appear in August, the developer is bought, and the ownership edge moves from one company to another. That is what a newsroom's memory should look like: not a pile of articles, but a graph whose every edge has a date and a source.
ai

This is also where I think the deck is right about AI, and where it matters for newsrooms. Observing and comparing used to be the expensive part: reading every registry, every agenda, every filing, every week. Models make that cheap. What they do not replace is the definition of what matters, the check before anything is published, and the judgement about what to report, which is exactly the part the deck gives to journalists, in three labels: "Direct attention", "Investigate significance" and "Exercise editorial judgment". The workflow slide in the vault walks one cycle through it: the investor presentation arrives, is matched to Planned milestone revised, is compared with April's statement, is checked by a person, becomes an alert, and updates the history so the next statement is compared with 2028, not 2027. The impact tracker by jobs, water, power, land and public commitments, with the article and alerts it produced.
synthetic

The deck's example is real. Pacifico Energy's GW Ranch, north of Fort Stockton in Pecos County, Texas, received an air permit from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality for 7.65 GW of gas-fired power generation, and the local paper's reporting already asks the water question the tracker asks. The deck's own footnote says its observations are "Source summaries from the supplied GW Ranch reporting". I chose not to put synthetic permits, deeds and minutes under the names of a real company and real agencies. A newsroom whose argument is evidence should not publish invented records that could be mistaken for real ones, even in a demonstration. So the vault has a twin: Mesa Ranch, in Caliche County, with its own developer, buyer, power company, water district and agencies, and the word synthetic on every record and on the first screen. The shape is the deck's; the facts are fiction, and the vault says so first.
vault

A vault is a natural home for an observation desk. The observation history is a versioned record: every update is a commit, so what the newsroom knew on any date can be recovered and compared, which is delta science applied to the newsroom itself. The evidence travels with every claim: the records sit beside the observations that cite them. And the read key is the whole credential: anyone can open the desk, clone it with sgit, check every observation against its record, and rebuild it with the scripts inside.
yours

The slide that closes the deck is the brief: "Choose a question. Map the system. Define its events. Keep observing." In the vault, that is one script, tools/build_data.py, with the families, the entities, the records and the question in it. Replace them with a hospital trust, a school district, a port, a river; the app does not change. The harder part is the one the deck insists on and the vault makes visible: writing, for every event, a definition and a signal you can actually observe. That is editorial work, and it is where a newsroom's knowledge of its own patch becomes an advantage nobody else has.
limits

The records are synthetic. Mesa Ranch, Caliche County and every name in the vault are invented. The atlas is ours. The deck names 12 families and 12 examples; the other 66 event types were written for this vault. It does not watch anything. The desk shows the method on fixed records; it does not read live registries. It is not Marconi's work or endorsed by him. It is our reading of his public slides. Updated on 15 October. The vault became seventeen pages with a menu and a details panel, and gained the five graph pages. If you run a local desk and want an observation vault for your own patch, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A request of mine on 15 October 2026, after reading Francesco Marconi's post and slides, When journalism becomes intelligence, from his INMA talk; written by this site's agent in the voice of this site; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The vault was built by this site's agent the same day and is published at /demos/vaults/mesa-ranch-desk/. Abstract: I spent today with people from Romania and I spend a lot of my time with people from Portugal, and this is the article I wanted to hand both. The race for the biggest model, the most GPUs and the largest data centre is a race a small country cannot win and should not enter; on a Wardley map that layer is already a commodity and only capital plays there. The opportunity is the opposite end of the map: the plumbing that a talented person in Braga or Cluj needs in order to sell a service to the world, forming a company, hiring across a border, being paid across Europe, working in every language, a contract and a tax form, all of it still custom built in most of Europe when it should be a road the state built once. Estonia built that road and the numbers show what happens. Then the judo: open source and open schemas because there is no sovereignty without them, what the state pays for belongs to the commons, buy the alternative before the day you need it, small models for every language and culture rather than one frontier model, and agents with the least agency rather than the most. A playbook in five moves, a map, what I learned spending millions on a distributed workforce, and why constraints are the input and not the excuse.

A talented person in Portugal, Romania or Estonia selling a service to the world, as a Wardley map. The capital race on the right is a commodity; the red dots are the plumbing that is still custom built in most of Europe and that a state can move right; the green dots are where the market is still genesis and where the money should go.
in-short

Do not enter the capital race. Frontier models, GPUs and data centres are at the commodity end of the map, with a lead that cannot be bought back in the short term. Trying to change that flow is not cost effective; it is the wrong end of the map for anyone without the capital, and a fool's errand for a small country. The opportunity is the plumbing. What stops a talented person in a small country from selling to the world is not talent, energy or price. It is forming a company, hiring across a border, being paid across Europe, working in another language, a contract, a tax form. Each of those is custom built today and should be infrastructure, like a road.
in-short

Infrastructure is the state's job because it enables everyone. The shop that opens on the road did not pay for the road; it paid taxes. Company formation, cross-border hiring, payments and translation are roads for the service economy, and most of Europe has not built them. Estonia has, and it shows. There is no sovereignty without open source and open schemas. What the state pays for should belong to the commons, since the people paid for it. Not because everyone changes it, but because everyone can see it, run it and leave with their data. Create the demand before the day you need it. You do not have sovereignty if waking up and deciding to move is the first step. Parallel services, local alternatives with fewer features, and procurement that buys them are how a market for alternatives exists before the single point of failure fails.
in-short

Smaller models, more of them. Most work does not need a frontier model and should not use one. Small open models for each language and each culture, Portuguese from Portugal and Brazil and Angola and Cape Verde and Mozambique, are a market that is still genesis and that a small country can lead. Constraints are the input. The best recent training run came from a lab that could not buy the chips it wanted. Map the attrition, put money on it, regulate what settled, and do it with Europe's values: the people come on the journey.
event

I was at an event today and met several people from Romania, including someone from an embassy who said, correctly, that the job of an embassy is to facilitate. I also spend much of my time talking to people in Portugal. This article is written to be sent to both, so it is written for a country rather than for a company, though every point applies to a company that wants to help one of these countries do it.
event

The word that kept coming up was that one: facilitate. It is not an accident that when we defined the roles for the team behind SGraph Send we named the growth role the Ambassador and wrote it to work the way an embassy works: represent the thing in territories it has not reached, promote trade, build relationships, project soft power, and never do hard sales, because the product should sell itself once the conditions exist. The role definition says the Ambassador's job is "to create the conditions for that organic growth". A country's ambassador does the same for a country. The question for this article is what the conditions are, for a small country, in the age of agents.
event

I have argued before that this is Europe's moment: in Europe's strategic opportunity in GenAI that the trends run towards smaller, explainable, multilingual, open and edge-deployed AI, which is where Europe's values already are, and in an open-source sovereign cloud for an open Europe that "digital sovereignty is not just about infrastructure, it is also about language and culture". For Portugal specifically I wrote in 2023 that generative AI was a golden opportunity. Europe's advantage is that it is not thinking top-down and is not playing a winner-takes-all game, and that advantage is strongest in its smaller countries, which can change faster. This article is the small-country version of the argument, with a map.
race

The conversation about national AI strategy keeps circling the same three things: the biggest model, the most GPUs, the largest data centre. I think that is misguided, and the map in the figure says why in one glance. Those components sit at the far right, in commodity, with a lead held by companies that have invested amounts a small country's whole technology budget would not match. It is a little like the climate conversation: there is nothing you can do about it in the short term, and trying to change that flow is not cost effective. On a Wardley map it is the clearest case there is of a market that does not exist for a small player, because the layer is commoditised and the buyer can already get it, cheaper, from somebody bigger.
race

That is not an argument for doing nothing. Unless you are already an established open-model lab with the investment behind it, the way Mistral is in Europe, you will not compete at the frontier, and the strategic response is not to try harder at the wrong altitude. It is to look at the rest of the map. The whole of Why I love Wardley maps, published this morning, is about that reading: a commoditised layer is a hard sell, and the market is where everyone is still custom building on top of commodities. Places of highest leverage is the same rule for a team: stand where you can add the most value right now, are not blocked, and can start.
plumbing

Put a person at the top of the map. Not a platform, not a strategy: a talented developer in Cluj, a designer in Porto, a librarian, a historian, a project manager, a product team in Tallinn, selling a service to a buyer abroad who would rather buy than build. In One article, five readers and Firing journalists the roles that turn a notebook into a graph are librarians, cartographers, historians, explainers and storytellers; the whole food chain of professions can now provide its service to the world, and it can market, sell and distribute that service too. What the map shows is what that person stands on, and the red dots are the problem.
plumbing

Forming a company. Hiring or contracting someone across a border. Getting paid, reliably, across all of Europe. Working in a language the buyer reads. A contract, an invoice, a tax return that is valid on both sides. None of that is the service. All of it is logistics, legal and operational plumbing, and in most of Europe each piece is custom built every time by the person or the small company that needs it, which means it is built badly, late and at a cost that falls on the wrong side. The overhead of hiring talent from a small country sits today on the buyer, and that is precisely what makes the buyer not do it, or do it through a platform that takes a cut and locks both sides in.
plumbing

The numbers say how much commerce this stops. In the last Eurostat figures with a breakdown, for 2021, 18.5% of EU enterprises sold online to customers in their own country, 8.1% to other EU countries and 4.6% to the rest of the world. Fewer than one in ten firms in the single market sells across its own borders online. Look at how many companies trade natively in several languages across Europe, and the answer is very few, because we hand the translation problem to each company rather than treating it as infrastructure. Commerce does not happen, most of the time, because of attrition, and attrition is what a map is for.
infrastructure

We understand that a government builds roads, hospitals and ports, because they enable everybody. The shop that opens on the new road did not pay for the road; it paid taxes, and the taxes were pooled and the road was built once, for everyone. Nobody suggests each shop build its own road. Yet that is what we ask of every person who wants to sell a service out of Portugal or Romania today: build your own company-formation process, your own cross-border contracting, your own payment path, your own translation, your own compliance, and do it before you have a customer.
infrastructure

The thesis of this article is that in the age of agents, the plumbing for providing services to the outside world is infrastructure in exactly the road sense, and a state that builds it enables every one of its people at once. That is what the red arrows on the map are: company formation, cross-border hiring, payments, language and contracts, each pushed from custom built to commodity by pooled money, built once, open to all.
infrastructure

Estonia is the case study because it did it. A person anywhere can become an e-resident and form an Estonian company online; the programme's own dashboard lists more than 142,000 e-residents and more than 43,000 companies, and in 2026 alone e-residents had founded more than 4,200 companies by mid-September, about a third more than in the same period of 2025. Underneath the services sits X-Road, the data exchange layer that connects around a thousand organisations in Estonia and that is open source under the MIT licence, developed jointly with Finland and Iceland, so another country can take the road rather than draw it again. I do not see a reason the rest of the EU does not do the same, and a small country can do it faster than a large one.
open

The plumbing has to be open source and run on open schemas, and this is the part that turns infrastructure into sovereignty. A road with a toll gate owned by one company is not infrastructure; it is lock-in with tarmac. If the company-formation service, the payment rail, the translation layer or the contracting flow belongs to one vendor, the state has rebuilt the problem it set out to solve, with a monopoly in the middle.
open

My logic is simple. You cannot have sovereignty without open source and open schemas, because sovereignty means you can leave. The argument is not that a country should not use services from American or Chinese companies; the United States depends on European companies, and everyone depends on Chinese ones, and that is what trade is. The argument is that you should not be locked in to them. Independence is the ability to run a parallel service, move the data and keep going, and that ability only exists if the code is open and the schemas are open.
open

It follows that what the state pays for should belong to the commons. I pay my taxes; the government uses them to buy software or to pay someone to write it; why does that software not also belong to me, or at least sit where I can read it and run it? It does not mean everyone gets to change the production system. It means the thing the public paid for is available to the public, which is also how the local industry that supports the local companies comes into being: an ecosystem of smaller firms can only grow around infrastructure it is allowed to see. The EU's open source strategy and the Commission's own open-source AI landscape report are moving this way; a small country can simply decide it.
open

This is also why I would point these countries at sgit and the vaults on this site, not as a sales pitch but as a shape. No server by design describes a newsroom whose only server-side components are commodities that hold no logic and cannot read the reader's data; Supply chain of vaults argues that the whole supply chain needs far more openness and that open source and Creative Commons are the proven way to get it. Data that stays with its owner and moves with them, under keys the owner holds, on an open protocol, is the data-sovereignty piece of the plumbing, and it is already open source.
demand

Sovereignty is not something you have the day you decide to move. If a hyperscaler, a payment provider or a model API went away tomorrow, most European organisations would have no alternative but to stop, because no market for the alternative exists, and markets do not appear overnight. The single points of failure are real and larger than the public record suggests. The investigation GitHub owes its customers made the case that software failures are not documented the way the airline industry documents its own, so we only see the examples a company could not hide, and the picture is worse than the few cases that become public.
demand

So the move is to create demand. Run parallel services. Buy the local or open alternative for part of the estate now, and accept that it has fewer features, because the point is not the features: it is that when the day comes there is somewhere to go, and that by then the alternative has had years of paying customers. Procurement is the lever a state already holds; it does not need a new law to prefer open schemas, data mobility and service mobility in what it buys. The business case writes itself, and it is a resilience case, not an ideological one.
models

The direction of travel in agents is to use less of the model, not more. Instead of agents with enormous permissions, which is why we wrote Agent Behaviour Policies to control them, you want the least agency that does the job, because that is what you can trust; Agency is not a yes is about where the agency should sit, and the supply-chain article's example is the right end state: the model is used once to build the tool, and production is plain files and plain code, with no prompt in the path. Frontier models are for working at the frontier, for finding the art of the possible; this article is being written with one, and it makes a difference here. For things that have to work, every day, at a price, a frontier model is far too expensive, far too much power for the task, and dangerous in proportion.
models

That means small models, and it means many of them. We are commoditising a level of intelligence, and most of the value is captured by a model that is good enough for one job, in one language, with one culture in it. There is a market, still at genesis on the map, for models for Portuguese, and not one Portuguese: the Portuguese of Portugal and of Brazil, of Angola, of Cape Verde, of Mozambique, of the Azores, of the Algarve, each with its culture in the training data and not just its spelling. The same for Romanian, for Estonian. Portugal released Amalia on 1 July 2026, a model built by a consortium of universities with 5.5 million euros of EU recovery money and published with its dataset and code under an open licence, as a base for public bodies, companies and researchers to build on. That is the right shape: a public model is a public road. I argued for this in Portuguese as a programming language in the AI era, and the open-weight economies show the economics: a company that can run a near-frontier model inside its own environment and build on it owns the workflow, the data, the tooling and the people around it, which is where the value is.
constraints

The race for GPUs, and the parallel race for the rare materials to build them, is a race that only benefits the players already in it; on a map it is very hard to compete there without a huge amount of capital. The better question is why so many GPUs are needed at all. Most of that compute is waste that the big players can afford. The lab that could not afford it did the interesting work: DeepSeek's V3 technical report says the model was trained in 2.788 million GPU hours on export-restricted H800 chips, chips whose interconnect was deliberately throttled, with custom communication code written around the constraint. Fewer and slower chips, not none, and a fraction of the compute a comparable Western run used, whatever one makes of the reported dollar figure. The constraint produced the innovation.
constraints

Simon Wardley has written for years about how China plays this game: directed investment, special economic zones, and a constant drive up the value chain by industrialising components, the innovate, leverage, commoditise pattern run at the scale of a state. We should learn from it and copy the mechanics, and do it with Europe's values and its focus on people: bring the citizens on the journey, make their environments better, and measure the result in lives rather than in parameters.
workforce

I want to say something about the talent, because the argument above rests on it. When I was a CISO and a CTO I used Upwork a great deal; across the open source projects and the teams I ran we spent millions on it, and it was one of the most successful things we did. We built distributed teams and large execution teams, hired people who were as good as, and often better than, those we could hire the ordinary way, and delivered faster and more efficiently than was possible before. The reason it worked was that we invested first in the infrastructure around it: the first thing I would do was build a project management team, a structure team and an onboarding team, and then use Upwork to manage Upwork, so that the internal teams carried no overhead.
workforce

Two lessons from that, for a country. The first is that the infrastructure is the whole difference between a talent market that works and one that is a race to the bottom. People said hiring that way was buying the cheapest; it never was. It was finding the right talent at a price that was fair where they lived, good value for both sides, and a real career for the person, and it scaled. The second is where the jobs go. Today a good job means moving to a capital city, paying what the city costs to be there, and spending most of what you earn on the privilege, when what most people want is to go back to where they came from, where the family, the support and the lifestyle are better and the jobs are not. A small country that builds the plumbing makes the jobs available everywhere inside it, and that is a competitive advantage its big neighbours cannot copy quickly. Romania's technology sector is close to 8% of GDP with more than 250,000 professionals and over ten billion euros a year of service exports; the company that became UiPath was founded in Bucharest in 2005 and listed in New York sixteen years later. The talent, the energy and the hunger are not the constraint.
playbook

The judo playbook in five moves: map the attrition, commoditise the plumbing, create the demand, put the money where the market is still genesis, regulate what settled, then map again. Three examples underneath of a constraint, a small state and a public model doing it. Map the attrition. Draw the chain from a talented person to a buyer abroad and mark every place commerce stops. Each is a dot in custom built that belongs in commodity. Commoditise the plumbing. Treat those dots as roads: pooled money, built once, open to all, open source and open schemas. Company formation, cross-border contracting, payments across Europe, language, contracts and tax. Create the demand. Buy the alternative before the day you need it. What the state pays for belongs to the commons. Run parallel services and accept fewer features so a market exists before the failure does.
playbook

Put the money where the market is genesis. Small models for each language and culture; data that stays with its owner and moves; agents with the least agency and behaviour as policy. Not GPUs. Regulate what settled. Once a layer is a commodity, write the rule for it: data mobility, open interfaces, the report a failure must produce. The rule comes after the market, not before it. Then map again, because a commoditised layer moves the opportunity up and the next attrition point is above the last one. That is the judo: each move uses the weight of the larger players, the commodity models, the commodity clouds, the commodity rails, rather than trying to match it.
limits

It is not a national strategy. It is a map and a set of moves from one person's experience of building on open source and running distributed teams, written for people I met this week. The figures are the latest I could find, and some are old. The Eurostat cross-border share is for 2021; the Estonian counts are from the programme's dashboard and press reporting; Romania's sector figures are from a 2025 report of a presidential message. Each is linked. The DeepSeek example is about constraint, not cost. The GPU hours are from the lab's own report; the dollar figure is disputed and is not relied on here. The Upwork numbers are mine. The spend and the outcomes are from my own time as a CISO and CTO and are not independently verifiable from this article.
limits

Estonia is a case study, not a template. Its size and its history made some choices easier; the claim is that the pattern transfers, not that the details do. If you work in or with one of these countries, in an embassy, a ministry, a company or a university, and want to map the attrition for your own case, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 12 October 2026, after an event where I met people from Romania, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The earlier pieces it builds on are Europe's strategic opportunity in GenAI, An open-source sovereign cloud for an open Europe, Portuguese as a programming language in the AI era and Embracing the generative AI wave: a golden opportunity for Portugal (2023). The Ambassador role is the SGraph Send role definition of 12 February 2026. Figures: Eurostat on web sales by destination; the e-Residency dashboard and ERR via Remote Work Europe on Estonia; RIA and the EU Open Source Observatory on X-Road; Reuters via The Star on Amalia; the DeepSeek V3 report; Business Forum on Romania's sector; Wikipedia on UiPath; Simon Wardley on China's gameplay.

Abstract: The hardest call in most work is not what to do next but when to stop. This article starts with people, because the problem is not new: security champions who had automated away whole classes of bugs and ended up debating whether GUIDs were random enough; development teams that hit every KPI and did not move the business; teams that found more work for themselves as they grew. What stopped them, when something did, was perspective: knowing who the attackers are, which phase the business is in, where the bottleneck is, and what good enough looks like, which is much of what seniority is. Agents have the same problem, worse. Their range is the feature: they can go in any direction, and variability is what makes them useful. But that range means they will keep going, fixing the twenty things they noticed rather than the one that mattered. The answer, for both, is not draconian rules but constraints that carry perspective: direction, a mandate, memory with the bigger picture, graphs that narrow the scope, a stop named before the work begins, one kind of work per step, and shipping often enough that the users tell you whether it mattered.

Value rises fast, then flattens. Past the point of diminishing returns, more work is optimising the wrong thing, defending against a movie plot, or hitting a target that no longer moves the business. What tells you to stop is perspective, and for an agent it has to be designed in. Knowing when to stop is the hard part, for people and for agents. Past the point of diminishing returns, more work is not more value. For people, perspective is what stops them: who the attackers are, which phase the business is in, where the bottleneck is, what good enough looks like. Much of what we call seniority is that perspective. Good teams can go too far. The best security teams ran out of real work and started defending against movie plots; the best delivery teams hit every KPI and did not move the business.

Agents have the same problem, by design. Their range is the feature: they can go in any direction. That also means they will keep going, unless something tells them to stop. The answer is constraints that carry perspective, not draconian rules: direction, a mandate, the bigger picture in memory, graphs that narrow the scope, a stop named in advance, one kind of work per step, and shipping often enough to see whether it mattered.

I said in How much of this did I write? that a model that can go in every direction needs someone with a direction. That is not a defect to be engineered away. It is what makes these systems special. The ability to try different things, to go in directions nobody asked for, to vary from one run to the next, is close to what we would call creativity in a person. We often call it hallucination, and I think variability is the better name for it; it feels surprising because we do not yet understand it well. But it has a consequence. An entity that can go anywhere has no natural reason to stop anywhere. People have the same problem, with one difference. Before getting to agents, it is worth looking at how it shows up in human teams, because none of it is new.

When I was doing a lot of application security, a friend told me: when you become a CISO, you will not care about half of what you care about now. He was right. When I became one, although I came from AppSec, I chose to put much of the effort and the budget elsewhere. In the organisations I worked in, the development teams were often very good, and the gaps were in other areas. From the board and the executive table you see the company's strategy, where the business is going, and the whole set of risks it actually carries. Against that picture, some of what had seemed urgent from inside AppSec was not the most important thing to worry about.

That is a large part of what experience is: not only having lived through similar situations, but having the bigger picture, and being able to move between the tactical and the strategic. And the bigger picture is mostly what tells you when to stop. The clearest example I have comes from the time when security stopped being whack-a-mole and became proactive: security champions in the teams, threat modelling, code review, checks running in CI. The best teams treated security, correctly, as an engineering problem, a quality problem, a class of bug. And almost every security issue at that level can be brought down to a practice a good team simply does. Dependency management: of course. Input validation: why would you accept crazy inputs? Authorisation: how can you not know what your code and your users are doing? Injection: use strong schemas, and keep code and data apart.

Those teams ran out of things to do, which was great. Then some of them started to focus too much. I remember being called into a meeting where security champions and developers were debating whether GUIDs were random enough. A version 4 UUID has 122 random bits, around 5.3 × 10^36 possible values. Guessing one is not a realistic attack; repeated guesses can be detected; and there was no plausible path from a predictable GUID to harm in that system. It was a movie plot, in the phrase Bruce Schneier popularised for the dramatic threats we imagine instead of the ordinary ones that happen. Real attacks are mostly much simpler: someone asks someone to run this, install that, or hand over a key.

What I found myself doing, in that meeting and in many others across the business, was giving people permission to take risks. Not common sense, because that implies they did not have it, but perspective: yes, that is technically possible, and it does not matter here, because of who our attackers are, what else is in place and what we are protecting. People new to security tend to worry most, because security can be visceral: you see that something is possible and it feels urgent. The way to bring the perspective back is to map who the attackers actually are, which is what Who are you protecting against? does, tier by tier.

The second example is more relevant to agents. Once a business is mature enough to set objectives and key results and key performance indicators, it can hand them to a team of very good engineers, and very good engineers are excellent at working backwards from a metric. I was in meetings where the development teams were hitting every KPI, delivering everything, and the business was not moving. In a way they should have been more constrained, and told when to stop. When a measure becomes a target, in Marilyn Strathern's well-known phrasing of Goodhart's law, it ceases to be a good measure.

This is where a Wardley map earns its place. It tells you which phase each part of the business is in. If you are still exploring, still trying to find what makes the business accelerate, polish is waste and the most important skill is knowing when to stop. If something is a commodity being town-planned, the same polish may be exactly right. A map also shows where the bottleneck is, and I have seen teams optimise, beautifully, things that did not need optimising. Somebody has to make the call not to fix this bug, not to build that feature, not to improve the thing that is already good enough. That call is often harder than doing the work, and it belongs to whoever has the context: a person, or an agent that has been given it.

I once heard an artist say that art is knowing when to stop. Knowing what is good enough, and recognising the point of diminishing returns, is the same skill. Teams without vision or direction struggle with it, because they have nothing to measure "enough" against. The best feedback loop I know for it is shipping, often and early. Are people using it? Does it matter? Did what we just did move anything? If not, stop, and do something else. That is also why observability matters: it is how you find out whether the work changed anything outside the team. I made the same argument for founders in Every mistake added a rule: ship, then stop, and let the components compound.

A person's range is limited. There is only so much one person can think of doing, wants to do, or believes is valuable, and their expertise keeps them in a domain, which, ironically, is what makes them qualified there. An LLM has a far wider set of skills, and it can just keep going. Anyone who uses one has seen this. You ask it to fix a small thing and it fixes a bigger one, because it can. It sees twenty things that are wrong and has a go at all of them. It starts optimising things nobody asked it to touch. At that moment it does not have the perspective to know that nineteen of the twenty do not matter, or matter later, or are someone else's.

There is nothing uniquely agentic about this. Put an entity that can do work into a team without a pile of real tasks and a clear direction, and it will make itself busy. People do the same. C. Northcote Parkinson observed in 1955 that "work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion", and argued that officials make work for each other. In the past we dealt with it through constraints that were often artificial and draconian, like fixed limits on team size, because we had no better control. The real problems were communication and direction, not the number. The better answer is constraints that carry the bigger picture, rather than rules that only forbid. Dan Ward's FIRE, fast, inexpensive, restrained and elegant, is one name for that attitude, and it is one of the doctrines on wardley-maps.sgit.ai: small scope on purpose, so that focus is the default.

Looked at this way, much of what we have been building is machinery for knowing when to stop: Direction: briefs that explain the thinking and the objective, not only the task, so an agent can judge what matters. The better I explain the why, the better the result. A mandate: an Agent Behaviour Policy and tools that only reach what the job needs, so the agent's universe of the possible is the size of the job. Hope or enforcement shows what that does to a customer service agent. Memory with the bigger picture: vaults and pages that hold the strategy, the threats and the history, so the perspective a senior person carries in their head is in the agent's context too. That is what Memory is not a spectator sport argues memory is for. Graphs that narrow the scope: semantic and flow graphs say what connects to what, and therefore what is in and out of scope for this step.

A stop named in advance: as nfrs.sgit.ai puts it for budgets, "with the stopping point named while it is still cheap to name". For an agent that is a token budget on the step, set before it starts. One kind of work per step: the agent team runs each agent for one step of up to twelve minutes: read state, do one kind of work, write state, stop. A reviewer with agency: someone with the context to say "good enough", or "not this, that", which is the scale in Agency is not a yes. Shipping, so the users answer the question of whether it mattered. None of these is a rule that says "do less". Each puts the bigger picture where the decision is made, which is what lets a person, or an agent, decide that the next thing is not worth doing.

Name the stop before you start: a time, a token budget, or a result that counts as good enough. Write down which phase you are in: exploring, settling or town planning. The right amount of polish follows from it. Give the agent the bigger picture: the objective, the threats, what else is in place, not only the task. Measure the needle, not only the KPI: ship, watch what people do, and stop when it stops moving. One kind of work per step, with a budget, and a review by someone who can say "enough". Give explicit permission to leave things undone, and write down what was left and why.

Drafted from a voice memo by Dinis Cruz, who is the author of the argument and the person with editorial responsibility, by agent@riskmandate.ai (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5) in the sgit.ai site session, on 8 October 2026. The people in the examples are not named. The UUID figures are from the version 4 layout in RFC 9562; Parkinson's sentence is from his essay in The Economist of 19 November 1955; the phrasing of Goodhart's law is Marilyn Strathern's, from 1997; FIRE is the title of Dan Ward's 2014 book.

Abstract: I am a member of working group 3 of KGELL, the European COST Action on knowledge graphs in the era of large language models, and I have not contributed yet. This is my first contribution. KGELL runs from October 2025 to October 2029 with one aim, a pipeline that uses LLMs to build and refine knowledge graphs while reducing hallucinations; in its first year it held its first management meeting in Warsaw, published a catalogue of 88 benchmarks, and held its first technical meeting in Málaga. Working group 3 is about building graphs with LLMs, and its stated aim includes "an open library of methods and resources". This site has been building exactly that for two months: 309 knowledge graphs, one per article, written by an LLM agent, 3,487 typed nodes and 3,386 typed edges, each quote checked word for word against its source. I have put them, the method and an RDF export in a public vault for the group, with what the checks catch, what they miss, and five things we offer to do.
KGELL, COST Action CA24121: four years, six working groups, and what its first year produced.
in-short

KGELL is a European research network (COST Action CA24121) on knowledge graphs and LLMs, running from October 2025 to October 2029. Its aim: a pipeline that uses LLMs to build and refine knowledge graphs, "reducing hallucinations and increasing factual accuracy". Year one: a management meeting in Warsaw, a catalogue of 88 LLM benchmarks, and a technical meeting in Málaga. Working group 3 is about building graphs with LLMs, including "an open library of methods and resources". This newsroom has built 309 such graphs, one per article, by an LLM agent, with every quote checked against its source. They are now in a public vault for the group: JSON, RDF with SPARQL, the method, and what the checks miss. Five offers: a case study, the dataset, a faithfulness experiment, linking to Wikidata, and vaults as infrastructure.
kgell

KGELL is COST Action CA24121, Knowledge Graphs in the Era of Large Language Models, funded by COST, the European Cooperation in Science and Technology. Its COST page gives a start date of 23 October 2025 and an end of 22 October 2029. The chair is Prof Diego Reforgiato Recupero, of the University of Cagliari, and the vice-chair Prof Michael Cochez, of the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.
kgell

The problem it states is the one everyone working with LLMs knows: models trained on general data do worse in specialist domains and in languages with fewer resources, reflect the biases of their training data, and "sometimes produce inaccurate or made-up information", which the field calls hallucinations. Its answer is to put the two technologies together, because knowledge graphs "can provide factual information and the ability to perform reasoning", and LLMs can help build and refresh the graphs. The main objective, from its about page, is "to develop and evaluate an automated pipeline that uses LLMs to generate and refine Knowledge Graph content from domain-specific textual datasets", focused on "reducing hallucinations and increasing factual accuracy". The work is split into six working groups: augmenting LLMs with knowledge graphs; tasks in specific domains; graph construction assisted by LLMs; many languages; bias and ethics; and evaluation.
year-one

20 April 2026: the first management committee meeting, in Warsaw, hosted by NASK. July 2026: the first deliverable. D1.1, from working group 1, is "Benchmarking Large Language Model Quality, Reliability, and Trustworthiness: A Review and Catalogue": 88 benchmarks, each tagged with eight features, from hallucination and factfulness to the quality of structured output. It calls itself "an exploratory, community-driven collection rather than a systematic literature review". 24 and 25 September 2026: the first technical meeting, in Málaga, with status updates from every working group, parallel working sessions and a report from each. The keynote closest to graph construction, by Mélida López of Kanzo Tech, compared LLM-based and semantic NLP approaches to building a graph from text, and ended on "the criteria required to evaluate LLM-assisted knowledge graph construction". A speaker series. The next talk, on 24 November 2026, is Claire Gardent of CNRS and LORIA on "Verbalising Knowledge Graphs into Multiple Languages"; the series runs into July 2027.
wg3

Working group 3, "KG Construction assisted by LLMs", is led by Dr Ana-Maria Ghiran, with Prof Robert Buchmann as vice-leader, both of Babeș-Bolyai University. Its aim is "to analyze and develop new methodologies for generating KGs, focusing on semi-automated information extraction methods and creating an open library of methods and resources". Its tasks: best practices for ontology engineering and reuse of schemas; using LLMs to extract entities and relations; publishing, storing and querying graphs; linking new graphs to public ones such as Wikidata and DBpedia. The Action's plan (its Memorandum of Understanding) gives it three chapters: guidelines and best practices for generating graphs, the role of LLMs in generating them, and the tools and resources for generating, refining and linking them.
fit

I joined working group 3 and have not contributed yet. Reading its aims, the overlap is direct, because the graph work on this site is graph construction with LLMs, in production. Fractal semantic graphs. The idea I introduced is that each domain keeps its own vocabulary, and the domains connect through named edges, at every altitude. That is schema reuse without forcing one ontology on everything, which is working group 3's first task. It is also, by a wide margin, the most-linked article in this site's graphs: 39 other articles point to it. Knowledge that maintains itself. The aim of all of it is knowledge management: an organisation's policies and information as a graph that agents keep current and brief people from. A graph per article, built by an agent. Every article here has a semantic graph beside it, written by the same LLM agent that writes the article, and checked before it is saved.
fit
Working group 3's four tasks, and what the newsroom's graphs and vault bring to each.
graphs

On 28 October 2026 the site has 309 graphs: 3,487 nodes of six kinds (claims, methods, examples, concepts, artefacts and questions), 3,386 edges of eight relations (leads to, depends on, produces, extends, example of, answers, contrasts, compared with), 774 quotes, and six topics. A graph has 7 to 18 nodes, typically 11. You can see them all at the graphs page.
graphs

The method is simple, and that is the point: a small vocabulary an LLM applies consistently, and checks at write time. The writer refuses a graph whose node kinds, relations or topics are not in the vocabulary, a link to an article that does not exist, or a quote that is not word for word in the article. In the terms of KGELL's own D1.1, that is ontology conformance and a hallucination check on the quotes. What the checks do not do is the interesting part for working group 3: they do not test whether each node's label and summary is faithful to the article, whether each edge is the right relation, or whether the graph covers the article's main ideas. That is a faithfulness test per triple, and here the source is always one link away.
vault

I have put all of it in a public sgit vault, encrypted, versioned, and readable by anyone with its public read key, which is published on this site. It holds: the 309 graphs as JSON, and the site's index of them; all of them as RDF in Turtle, 21,840 triples, each node a fragment of its article's address, with the vocabulary as RDFS; METHOD.md: how the graphs are written and checked, and what the checks miss; WG3.md: how it maps to the group's tasks and chapters, and the offers below; stats.json, and a SPARQL example that runs as written. The KGELL WG3 vault: 309 graphs as JSON and RDF, the vocabulary, the method and the offers. Open it in the vault browser, or clone it with pip install sgit-ai and sgit clone sgit_public_read_fa820a5b828288c4b1f32369fa16eaded3bf18a47c8a87ae05139205ad488927:x7hcpg5l kgell-wg3. The same graphs are on the site's graphs page.
offer

If they are useful to working group 3: A case study for the chapter on the role of LLMs: how an agent builds a graph per document in a live publication, what the write-time checks catch, and what they miss. The dataset for the library of resources, under CC BY 4.0, refreshed as the site publishes. A faithfulness experiment: score each triple against its source article, and compare methods on a set where the source is always there. Linking to Wikidata: link node labels, and measure what an LLM gets right. Vaults as infrastructure for the library: versioned, signed, readable with a public key, from any static host, which matters for a library that should outlive any one server. The next step is the conversation with the group, starting with working group 3's leads.
limits

Everything about KGELL here is from its public pages, the COST page and its Memorandum of Understanding, read on 27 and 28 October 2026. Nothing speaks for KGELL or its working groups. The graphs are one agent's work, in one style, and their faithfulness is not measured yet; that is offer 3. No links to Wikidata or DBpedia yet; node labels are free text. The counts are this site's own, from its published graphs on 28 October 2026.
sources

KGELL's site: home, about, working groups, deliverables, the Málaga meeting and the speaker series; the COST page for CA24121 and its Memorandum of Understanding; D1.1, read in full. This site's graphs, counted from articles/graphs/ on 28 October 2026. Related: introducing fractal semantic graphs, knowledge that maintains itself, search as navigation. Written up by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: In a conversation today I tried to put in a few sentences what all the graph work on this site is for, and it came out as knowledge management. Take an organisation's policies and internal information, and build a fractal semantic graph of it: an ontology and a taxonomy for every element, each part kept in its own vocabulary, with named edges between them. Then brief people and agents from the graph, not from the pile of documents. They get the slice they need and the diff since they last read it, so the context is there and the tokens are not wasted. It looks a bit like vector search, but vectors give you similarity, not a reason, and the answer can change with the model and the index; a graph gives the same answer to the same question and the path that led to it. The most important part is that the feedback loop maintains itself. You do not have to get the graph right first; you have to maintain it, and agents are very good at maintaining graphs. When something in the graph looks wrong, you ask why, and the answer is a fix at the right altitude. I measured the briefing on this site: the graphs of its 112 articles hold about an eighth of the articles' text. And the brief has to travel. That is what sgit is for: an encrypted git where I give an agent the key to a vault, it reads and writes there, I can scope it to one folder and encrypt to it with its own key, and the vault itself says, this is what you need to read now.
Knowledge that maintains itself: sources, agents, graph, briefs and fixes, with each brief travelling as a vault.
in-short

Policies and internal knowledge as a graph. An ontology and a taxonomy for every element, each part in its own vocabulary, with named edges between them. Brief from the graph, not the pile. People and agents get the slice they need and the diff since they last read it. Measured here: about an eighth. The graphs of this site's 112 articles hold 12.4% of the articles' text, roughly 87,000 tokens against 704,000. Graphs are not vectors. Similarity search is useful for finding a starting point; a graph gives the same answer to the same question, with the path that led to it. You do not have to get it right; you have to maintain it. Agents are good at maintaining graphs, and a validator checks them. "Why is this happening?" An odd edge is a question, and the answer is a fix at the right altitude. This site has found several that way.
in-short
The brief travels in a vault. sgit gives each agent a key, a scoped folder, its own key pair and a history of every change.
idea

In a conversation today I tried to say in a few sentences what all the graph work on this site is for, and it came out as knowledge management. Every organisation has policies, standards, architecture, decisions, contracts, regulations it answers to, and a long tail of internal documents that explain why things are the way they are. Today the way most of that reaches a person or an agent is a search box and a pile of documents. The proposal is to build a fractal semantic graph of it instead: an ontology and a taxonomy for every element, a policy, a system, a team, a control, a regulation, a decision, each part kept in the vocabulary of whoever owns it, and named edges between them, with verbs that read both ways. A policy is owned_by a team and implemented_by a control; a control answers an article of a regulation; a decision supersedes an older one.
idea

Then you brief from the graph. A person joining a team, or an agent starting a task, does not need the whole corpus. They need the part of the graph around what they are about to do, and what changed since they last looked.
briefing

Briefing from the graph, measured on this site: the tokens in the articles, their graphs and the graphs' text alone. This site already works this way, so I measured it. Every article here has a graph, 8 to 18 nodes with typed edges, a teaser and a one-paragraph core idea, written with the article and checked by the validator on every release. Across the 112 articles there are 1,435 nodes and 1,538 edges. The articles' text, counted from their markdown, is about 704,000 tokens at four characters a token; the graphs as JSON, with every bracket and field name, about 199,000; the graphs' own words, teaser, core idea, node labels and summaries and the edges between them, about 87,000. That is 12.4% of the text, an eighth, and the median article's graph is 12.8% of the article.
briefing

An agent that needs to know what this site has said about agent behaviour policies can read every graph in the agents-and-policy topic, follow the edges to the articles that matter, and only then read those in full. The site publishes all of it for exactly that: one file of every graph, a page that draws them, an llms.txt index, and a markdown twin of every page. The other half of a brief is the diff. Every article here has a version page and a word-by-word diff between versions, and Every link points back argued that a reader should be told what changed, what corrected what, and what has happened since. In a graph, that is cheap: a node superseded, an edge added, a claim marked out of date. "What changed since you last read this?" becomes a list of nodes, not a re-read.
vectors

It looks a bit like vector search, and in practice the two work well together. Embedding search is good at finding a starting point when you do not know the words the organisation uses. But it gives you similarity, not a reason. The result depends on the embedding model, the index and its settings; re-index with a newer model and the neighbours move. And it cannot tell you why two things are related, only that they are close. A graph is the other kind of thing. The same question gives the same answer, because it is a walk over named edges. The answer comes with its path: this control is here because it answers that article, which this policy cites. A change is a diff of nodes and edges, not a re-embedding. For policies, where the question is often "why are we required to do this, and by whom?", the path is the answer.
maintain

This is the part that matters most. Nobody builds a correct graph of an organisation on the first try, and the projects that try spend a year on the ontology and never ship. The graph does not have to be right. It has to be maintained, and the loop maintains it.
maintain

Agents are very good at that work. They read a new document and propose its nodes and edges. They notice that a policy changed and mark what rested on it. They keep the graph's own rules: every edge a verb with an inverse, properties for data and edges for meaning, supersede and never delete. And the rules can be checked by something that is not an agent. On this site every article's graph is checked on every release: its quotes must be word for word in the article, its links must be links the article makes, its sizes within limits. The maintenance is done by models and verified by code.
maintain

Then the loop does the rest. When something in the graph looks wrong, an edge that should not exist, a node nobody cites, a claim with no source, you ask: why is this happening? The answer is a fix at the right altitude, in the source or in the graph, and the next brief carries it. This site has done that several times: The link graph. Walking the links between articles found that 551 of 566 point back in time, and that an earlier article described a plan a later one said had not happened. That became Every link points back and the "What came next" notes. A spreadsheet of controls. When the AI Baseline Control Framework was turned from its CSV into a graph joined to the EU AI Act's text, the graph surfaced "the six things the graph found that the CSV does not say".
maintain

A governance stack. The AI governance stack as a graph made every cell of a ten-layer table a node, 329 edges in all, 119 of them added, each citing the fact it rests on. Policies and their code. In Policy as code needs a policy first, comparing a behaviour policy with the code that enforces it found a rule with no code and code with no rule. Code review. In Code review as a fractal semantic graph and its vault, a change is read at every layer from the method to the story. The fractal semantic graphs page and the regulation graph vault are the open examples to start from.
vaults

A brief is only useful if it gets to the person or agent who needs it, and only them. That is what sgit is for, and why I built it. sgit is an encrypted git: the files are encrypted before they leave, and the server holds only ciphertext. To brief an agent, I give it the key to a vault. It can read what is there, write what it finds, and every change is a commit, so the history is the diff.
vaults

The pieces line up with the graph. A scoped clone takes only one folder of a vault, so an agent can hold its slice and nothing else, as sgit in a CI pipeline measured. A key pair per agent means a brief can be encrypted to the one agent that should read it. An append lane lets an agent send its findings back without being able to read anything. And the vault can say, in its own index, this is what you need to read now. This site's agents already work like that: two agents share one vault with only the read key on the public side; agents that run somewhere else keep their memory in one; and the policy this site's own agent works under is a brief, restored after every summary. Memory is not a spectator sport is the longer version of why the memory has to be something the owner keeps.
limits

Tokens are estimated. Characters divided by four, on this site's 112 articles and their graphs at v0.12.39. A graph is a map, not the territory. An eighth of the text is enough to choose what to read, not a replacement for reading it. Vectors still help. For finding a starting point in unfamiliar words, similarity search is useful; the graph is what makes the answer repeatable and explainable. This site's graphs have a contract. Their size and checks are why they compress well; an organisation's graph needs the same discipline. Maintenance is still work. Agents do most of it and a validator checks it, but someone has to own the ontology at each altitude. If you are drowning in policies and internal documents and want to see them as a graph, or you want to brief your agents from one, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 14 October 2026, from a conversation about knowledge management, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The briefing figures were counted for this article from this site's article markdown and its graph files at v0.12.39. The examples are this site's own articles and the open vaults linked above.
