Abstract: Legal advice is in every part of a startup, from shares and votes to IP and people, and most founders have little experience of it and little access to good lawyers. So they sign deals that are worse than they need to be, often with no malice on anyone's side. Legal services never scaled because the work took time, much of it repetitive, and good people did not want to do it. GenAI changes that: models are very good at reading every detail and finding inconsistencies, and an agent team can do the reading, the checking and the drafting so that a lawyer's time goes on judgement and signature. That makes a service that scales: on the founder's side, on the investor's side, and in a deal room where both teams meet, with every understanding, clause and version signed and verifiable. Paid per task or by a monthly plan, not a yearly retainer. I think someone should build it, and most of what it needs exists today in open source. To show it, three made-up vaults: Tallowmere Counsel's founder desk, investor desk and deal room, with real signatures your browser checks.
The deal room: the founder's desk and the investor's desk, each people and agents, meeting over one agreement.
in-short

Legal is in everything a startup does, and most founders have neither the experience nor the lawyers. Bad deals are often not malicious. If you hold the power, why wouldn't you ask for more? Legal never scaled. The time, the onboarding, the repetitive reading. Models read every detail and find inconsistencies. That is most of the repetitive work. Agent teams drive the lawyers' efficiency. Not a human in the loop: humans inside a workflow. Charge per task or per month, never a yearly retainer. Investors need it too, and will lose deals to investors who have it. Sign everything: principles, terms, clauses, versions, understandings. Publish your terms, and let investors debate them with their own teams. Three vaults show it working, with made-up companies and real signatures.
problem

This follows the jobs that never scaled, applied to the law. Having someone who understands the legal side in the conversation is critical in almost every part of a startup: shares and the cap table, voting rights, intellectual property, contracts with customers, human resources, data protection, and above all the investment. And most founders have little experience of any of it. They don't know which questions to ask, what a cap table will look like after two rounds, or what a participating preference does to them in a sale. They often don't have good lawyers, or any, or not ones who know the particular thing that matters.
problem

So they get worse deals than they should. Sometimes it isn't even malicious: if you hold the power, why wouldn't you ask for more? But the question I keep asking, as in the controllable founder, the exit is when you sell control and sell, don't issue, is why an investor wouldn't align its terms with what the founder is happy with, rather than with what it can get. Part of the answer is that the founder can't argue well enough. That part can be fixed.
scale

Legal services never scaled because they were expensive, and they were expensive because of the time: onboarding, reading, checking, re-reading the next draft, a lot of repetitive work that the best people did not want to do, and that clients paid senior rates for anyway. Models change exactly that part. I have used ChatGPT and Claude for real legal work, quite successfully, and here is what people miss: even when they hallucinate, they are very good at reading every detail and picking up inconsistencies. Three things I have done that worked: Mirror terms. If a contract asks me for a particular level of indemnity, or a particular term, ask for the same on the other side. Terms and conditions became much fairer that way.
scale

"Here is my understanding." When I am not fully confident, because I am not a lawyer, I write to the other side's lawyers: here is my understanding of what this clause does, do you agree? If they say it says X and the contract says twice X, that is now their problem, not mine, and if the text changes halfway through, it is misleading. Those things matter in a relationship, and especially at the final due diligence. Infographics of terms. Turning terms and conditions into a picture shows what they actually ask. And when the terms are right, the models agree with each other. Ask ChatGPT and Claude separately, and when they both say "this now covers your bases", it usually does. They are also very good at finding blind spots. None of this replaces a lawyer. It replaces the part of a lawyer's time that should never have cost what it did.
service

Two teams of people and agents, one on each side, and the deal room where they meet. So here is the service. A legal desk for startup funding, where agentic workflows drive the efficiency of the humans inside them. This is not a human in the loop, approving what a machine did. It is agents doing the reading, the extraction, the mirroring, the cap table models, the plain-language explanations and the checking, so that each lawyer's hour goes on judgement, negotiation and signature. The founder does as much as they can themselves, with the platform: depending on their skills and their time, more or less. The platform tunes its prompts and workflows, not its models; fine-tuning a model is the last thing you should do. And the founder can always go back to their own Claude or ChatGPT and ask "what do you think of this?", which a good service should welcome.
service

The commercial model follows from the economics. With agents doing the repetitive work, and lawyers working virtually with low overheads, the service can charge a fair rate for an hour, half a day or a day of a lawyer's time, plus a price per task. A monthly plan you can cancel any month is fine. A yearly subscription makes no sense for this: it is a SaaS model that suits the vendor's recurring revenue, not the client. Better still, pay per use, which I would argue is also better for the platform.
markets

The founder's side. Counsel paid by the founder, on the founder's team, who understands the intricacies, and who doesn't cost a ridiculous amount of money. Investors benefit too: by the time they arrive, the data room is in order and the due diligence has largely been done. The investor's side. I would argue investors need this even more. The difference is between someone working in a spreadsheet and email, and someone with an agentic workflow that can read a whole data room, collect everything, raise the questions and draft the memo in hours. Investment is a competitive sport: as a founder, I want an investor who works at this speed, and an investor who works at analogue speed will lose deals to one who doesn't.
markets

Both, in one room. Each side goes to its own team, agents plus humans, and says: this is what I want, these are my terms, this is my situation. The two teams hash it out. And who pays? I would want the investor to pay for its own diligence: why should a founder pay to answer questions for an investor who may not make an offer? Whoever pays the bill will have the service, and even the models, a little more aligned with them. That is fine, as long as each side has its own.
signed

The part that makes this more than faster drafting is the signing. With a public key infrastructure, every party has a key pair, and everything that matters is signed: the founder's principles, the term sheet, each clause, each version, each "here is our understanding" and its confirmation. A signed clause cannot change without the signature failing, and every change between versions is a diff with a name on it.
signed

I also think contracts should become a graph, what I call a fractal document: the intent at the top, the principles under it, then the terms, then the clauses, then the plain-language versions in each language. You sign off the intent and the principles; the legal clauses are the way to enforce them. Across languages and cultures, the plain principles travel better than the legal text. And you could argue that a clause that contradicts the signed principles should not be valid: that is a proposal, and the wording still has to be right, but it is the direction. We did an early version of this in a vault for risk acceptance, before vaults had append lanes. What can be built now is a different order of thing.
publish

The last part is where I am going with this myself. I am going to raise, on the terms I want, and because everything I do is open, I am going to publish them: the term sheet, what I want, what I am interested in, and the materials. Then I can tell investors: hire this kind of service, or use your own, and debate it with mine until you reach a conclusion. Ask questions, find things, argue. But here are the terms, and this is my line. That scales for me, because it is a page on my site. I have done versions of this before, for The Cyber Boardroom and for MyFeeds, but I never had a product with real demand. Now I do, which is what makes the conversation with investors interesting.
vaults

To make this concrete, I asked the agents to build it. Not a description, a working demonstration with made-up companies: Tallowmere Counsel, the service; Brindlewood Security, a startup that makes an open-source secrets scanner, raising £1.2 million; and Kestrel Row Ventures, the investor. Every person, number and clause is invented, the legal wording is illustrative and not legal advice, and no model is called: the runs are scripted. But the signatures are real: each party has an ECDSA key pair, and every page checks every signature with your browser's own cryptography. The founder desk: Ana Brindle's published terms, signed, with a QR code to share them.
vaults

The founder desk is Brindlewood's side: the founder's published intent and eight principles, signed, with a QR code to share them; a readiness checklist and a data room of 18 documents, each hashed; a cap table modeller showing the founder keeping control; the mirror check of the investor's first term sheet, every obligation asked of the other side; plain-language explanations of the terms that hurt founders; and a bill. Its vault: x6kjwxds. The investor desk: the investment committee memo, drafted by an agent and signed by the partner. The investor desk is Kestrel Row's side: the pipeline; diligence on Brindlewood's data room, with findings and 12 questions billed to the investor, not the founder; its position on each of the founder's principles; the investment committee memo, signed by the partner; and how long it took, 44 hours from first look to term sheet. Its vault: jgp3oyrm. The deal room: every version checked against every signed understanding, and v3 blocked.
vaults

The deal room is where they meet. The agreement in five levels, 87 nodes at the final version, each hashed, zoomable from the intent down to a clause in plain English and plain Portuguese. Four versions in five days, with word-by-word diffs. Three signed understandings, and the moment the consistency agent blocked version 3, because clause 7.2 still said "twice the amount invested" after both lawyers had signed that the cap was the amount invested. A signing ceremony where both lawyers, both principals and the service's seal sign the same root. A message log where each signed message hashes the one before. And a meter of 43 signed receipts. Change one word of the signed agreement, and every signature on its root fails in your browser.
vaults

Try the tamper box: change clause 7.2 to say "twice", and every signature on the agreement's root fails, in your browser, because the root no longer matches what was signed. The bills, on these made-up numbers: about £1,100 for the founder's desk and about £1,400 for the investor's, against an illustrative £14,000 to £24,000 for the same work by the hour or on a retainer, with the assumptions shown. Each is a vault, and you can open it yourself with its published read key: Founder desk: open it in the vault UI, or sgit clone sgit_public_read_0857bebbc4f9a317fa55d9b51427c9e41baab8401157b23cb0adc5c1dafd2e14:x6kjwxds Investor desk: open it in the vault UI, or sgit clone sgit_public_read_74013a87a8e615202a89e5cffa5ede9bc70715a789b181b4c04d07bbb136625a:jgp3oyrm Deal room: open it in the vault UI, or sgit clone sgit_public_read_d1a89809c2acd75df262aa79e29037ac0de40deacbbfd92991f758aba0fd252c:ghafqmwo The keys are read keys, published on purpose; each was read back before it was published, and the files match.
business

The features such a service needs, against what already exists in open source today. There is a lot of commercial value here. A service like this has three markets, founders, investors and the deal between them, and a cost structure that legal services never had: agents for the repetitive work, lawyers for the judgement, no office, no retainer. Someone should start this company, or invest in it, and existing legal-tech companies would do well to measure themselves against these features.
business

And you don't need to go much further than what exists today. Vaults are data rooms, with history and read keys. Append lanes carry messages between the sides. Vault apps are the applications each side uses, with no server. Key pairs and signed records are built, and QR codes carry signatures and sealed messages. Agent teams with cards, roles and loops are running every day. All of it is open source and runs on the client side, which is exactly what you want for documents nobody else should hold. The fractal agreement and binding understandings work in the demonstration; the meter is a published design. Companies in this space should look at it and ask what they can reuse.
limits

Not legal advice, and not a substitute for a lawyer: the point is to make the lawyer's time count. Models make mistakes. The workflow is built around checking them, with humans who sign. A signature is not a legal contract by itself. Whether a signed clause binds depends on the law and the agreement; the demonstration shows the mechanism. "A clause that contradicts its principles should be void" is a proposal. It would need careful wording and a willing court. The demonstration is made up, scripted, and its three vaults compute their hashes separately, so the same version shows different roots in each. The prices and comparisons are illustrations, with their assumptions shown in the vaults.
sources

The editor's voice memo of 27 October 2026. The demonstration: the founder desk, the investor desk and the deal room, in the vaults x6kjwxds, jgp3oyrm and ghafqmwo on dev.send.sgraph.ai, built by this site's agents from one shared set of made-up facts, with ECDSA P-256 signatures checked by the Web Crypto API. Related: the jobs that never scaled, the controllable founder, the exit is when you sell control, sell, don't issue, paying after the value, the user keeps the meter, PKI everywhere, signed by the source, what an agent is, websites you own. Abstract: FT Strategies has published a clear primer on liquid content, journalism built from datafied components that can be shaped into whatever a reader needs. I agree with most of it, and this article is about where I would push. What makes content liquid is the water inside it, and the water is the reporting: the notebook, the interviews, the documents, the hunches, kept with their sources as a graph. So the place to start is not a reinvention of newsroom norms but the opposite, putting the experienced journalist and the way they already work at the centre and giving them tools they have not had, including experts a newsroom could rarely afford. Writing stays theirs, because writing is how the story is found. Read that way, the three things the guide says liquid content is not each become part of it, personalisation becomes the meeting of the reader's graph and the story's, prioritising readers' tastes looks like the brief that produced clickbait, and the money goes beyond advertising, subscriptions and licensing to payment per use that walks back to whoever found the facts.

What makes content liquid is the water inside it: the journalist's notebook, liquefied into a story graph as they work, with every format a projection that can walk back to its evidence. FT Strategies has started a series called Demystifying AI for News Publishers, and the edition on liquid content, by Sofia Giannuzzi, is one of the clearest explanations of the idea I have read. It defines liquid content as content that "primarily consists of datafied components, or 'atomic objects', including quotes, events, or dates, as opposed to information that is already synthesised into discrete products, like an article, podcast or video segment". It offers an image I like: today publishers mould content like clay into a finished product and let it dry, and liquid content keeps the clay wet, so that a reader with a fifteen-minute commute can pull up an audio briefing instead of an article.

Much of it I agree with, and it is worth saying what before saying where I would push. The guide points at data journalism as the working model the industry already has, which is right: a chart over structured data can be re-cut for every reader, and text has rarely had that. It is honest about the hard questions, how you measure a story consumed in ten formats and how you keep a human in the loop when no team could review every version. It says the structure behind the stories should hold "regardless of how the front end is configured for end users", and that structured content could be licensed to AI companies or sold through "pay-per-query systems with AI agents". Those are the right instincts.

An infographic of the FT Strategies guide, made with ChatGPT from the guide's text. Faithful on the definition, the three things liquid content is not, the drivers and the challenges; see the note below for what it adds. Here is where I would push. If content is to be liquid, it needs water in it, and the water is not the format. It is the reporting: the notes in the pad, the calls, the documents, the half-recorded interviews, the hypotheses, the hunch about who to ring next, the facts with the doubts still attached. That is what has to become liquid. A finished article can be broken into atomic objects, and I will come back to why that is worth doing, but much of the richest material does not make it into the article at all.

The clay image is useful, and its limit is instructive. By the time something is clay, the ingredients are mixed in and gone. You can mould it again, but you cannot ask it where the clay came from, or which part of the shape rests on which source. What I would want is closer to a graph: claims with a confidence, evidence with its provenance, sources named or protected, people, places, events and dates, contradictions kept as edges rather than smoothed over. That is what this site calls a fractal semantic graph, and what I have called a story vault when it holds one story. Every projection of it, the article, a briefing, a chart, a translation, an answer for an agent, can still say why it is true.

The guide says liquid content "requires a complete reinvention of newsroom norms", and asks newsrooms "to fully embrace a user-first mentality". I want to say this carefully, because the guide is describing a real problem, but I think this is a known trap. When we do not yet know the path, the advice tends to become: change how you work, embrace the new thing, reinvent. The more I think about this, the more I think we already have the method. It is decades, centuries really, of journalistic practice: finding the story, knowing who to call, interviewing well, reading a document for what it does not say, doubting the official version. Nothing in liquid content requires that to be reinvented. If anything, I would bring back the experienced journalists, the people who really know how to do this, and give them the tools.

Because the tools are where the inefficiency is. In many newsrooms the raw material of a story lives in a notebook, a phone and somebody's memory, with a spreadsheet if somebody made one, and once the story is published almost none of that is kept in a usable form. It works, and it is remarkable that it works, but most of the value created during the reporting is thrown away at the moment of publication. Liquefying it does not mean asking the journalist to fill in forms. It means capturing what they already produce, in the way they already produce it: a page of handwritten notes can be photographed and transcribed, a call can be recorded and linked, and the claims extracted from both can sit in a graph the journalist can see and correct.

A desk built around the journalist: their notebook, their own interface and their graph at the centre, and around them experts paid for their time or for the credibility they lend, roles that were rarely economic before. This is also where AI changes something that is easy to miss. Building a custom interface has become cheap, which I wrote about in Custom UIs are not the exception. So every journalist can have a desk shaped to how they work: their own contact book of sources, their own view of the claims on their beat, their own way of moving from notes to draft. Not a newsroom system they have to adapt to, but tools that adapt to them, to their team and to how that team likes to work.

I do not think the right picture is one where AI writes everything and the journalist feeds it facts. Part of the skill of a journalist is writing the article, because writing it is how they discover the narrative. When I see a draft of something I am working on, I understand the problem better, and the draft changes what I look for next. It is a feedback loop, and the same is true of reporting: you gather evidence, you start writing, the writing shows you the hole in the story, you go back out. AI can help with parts of that, and some of it will be written by hand, which is fine; we can scan it.

So I would put it this way. The journalist and the publication decide how this information is best presented: that judgment is what a reader trusts and pays for. The article they write is one projection of the graph, and it is theirs. Other projections, a short audio version, a briefing for a reader in another role, a version in another language, can be produced from the same graph and checked against it, with the journalist deciding which of them matter enough to write or approve themselves. What the journalist discovers while writing goes back into the graph. Questions from readers come back in too, and a question the graph cannot answer is the next piece of reporting.

There is a second thing the tools make possible, and I find it the most exciting. A newsroom has rarely been able to afford, for one story, a historian, a librarian, a data scientist, a financial analyst, a professor in the field, an engineer, a lawyer, somebody who has worked inside the industry being written about. With a graph that records who contributed which claim, it becomes economic to bring them in for an hour, a question or a story, and to pay them: for their time, and for the credibility they lend. Sources and contributors can be paid for credibility too, and credibility accumulates, because the graph records every claim a person supported and how it held up.

This matters for how the change lands in a newsroom. An experienced journalist who reads that their organisation must reinvent its norms and become user-first will, reasonably, hear a threat. The message I would want them to hear is different: we want to take what you already do and make it better, give you technology you have not had, and build teams around you that were rarely affordable before. The guide's three lines around liquid content, each right about the shortcut it rules out, and how each becomes part of the answer when there is a graph underneath. The guide sets out three things liquid content is not, and each is right about the shortcut it rules out. Each also looks different with a graph underneath.

Format repackaging. Turning an article into a podcast is, as the guide says, not liquidity. But a finished article can be liquefied: its claims, evidence, people and events extracted and linked to everything else. A publisher with a long archive is sitting on decades of reporting that becomes more valuable with every link, and the Financial Times has one of the deepest archives of business reporting there is. I would not start by converting all of it. I would start with one topic and liquefy whatever it touches, so the graph spreads outward from the stories in use.

An interface on top. A chatbot layered on an archive answers from whatever it retrieves, and the reader cannot see which claim it relied on. Agreed. But the interface is exactly what gets built from a graph: a chat, a briefing, a page, an answer for the reader's own agent. Where the reader consumes it is the reader's choice, in their AI assistant, on the publisher's site or on a version of that site built for them. The difference is not the interface; it is whether every answer can name the claim and the source it rests on.

Static personalisation. "Recommended for you" changes what you see, not what you are told. Agreed again, and I would go further: personalisation should be neither static nor statistical. It is the intersection of two graphs, the reader's and the story's. The reader's graph holds their role, their company, their sector, where they live, how much time they have today, how deep they want to go, what they need now and what can wait, and which language and culture they read in. That is a much bigger axis than format. Imagine an FT reader receiving a briefing on what is happening to their company, their industry and the three things they care about this week, with every claim linked to its reporting. I worked through what this looks like for a local story, with three readers whose graphs meet the same claims in different places, in The bridge, followed to the end. The feedback loop matters here too: what a reader asks and corrects tests both graphs.

The guide describes the change as "a deliberate shift to prioritising readers' tastes over organisational processes and habits", and says that "the priority must be delivering what users want to read". I do not think that is quite what is meant; the guide's own examples are about format and time, the commute and the audio briefing, not about what to cover. But read literally, prioritising readers' tastes is the brief that gave us clickbait. Optimising what people click is what much of digital publishing has spent twenty years doing, and it has not served readers or publishers well.

When I pay a news organisation, I am paying for its judgment: what it thinks matters, how it checks it, and how it presents it. Organisations have points of view, and that is fine; what readers need is to see them, and a graph that shows where each claim came from makes that much easier, for the reader and for the organisation's own accountability. I made a related point about AI in How much of this did I write?: a model that can go in every direction needs someone with a direction. In journalism that direction is the editor, the journalist and the publisher. Readers' needs should shape the projections. They should not replace the direction. The guide's three revenue drivers, and the ways of being paid that a graph adds, each priced per use rather than per month, and each able to pay back down the claims to the people who found them.

The guide sees three revenue drivers: retention, dynamic advertising and content licensing. All three hold, and the mention of pay-per-query with AI agents is, I think, the most important line in the section. But the three are still recognisably the advertising and subscription economy with better targeting. The move from print to digital went badly for news, and as I traced in The reader was always the product, most of the value of going digital went to whoever sat between the content and the reader: by 2017 Google and Meta took 54.7% of American digital advertising. I would rather not repeat that with AI.

A graph that names every claim and source adds ways of being paid that do not depend on attention: a reader paying pennies per use of a skill or an alert rather than a subscription to everything, an agent paying per question because a sourced answer is cheaper than searching and reconciling six pages, institutions and investors licensing the evidence rather than the prose, a national story paying for the local claim it rests on, and a share of every use walking back to the journalist and to the contributors whose evidence the claim stands on. The bridge simulation runs one local story through all of these with its assumptions written down.

On SEO and GEO the guide is right that structured content is easier for search engines and AI answer engines to use. I would add a point that deserves an article of its own. Search engines persuaded publishers to do the work of making content indexable and well catalogued, and then earned the advertising revenue on pages whose value came from that content, returning traffic and little else. Structuring content for AI engines is the same work again, and it has a value to whoever reads the structure. As I argued in Sixteen thousand fetches, ten clicks, the readers of that structure also save money by having it, which is a reason they should pay for it.

The guide ends with leadership, which is fair. I would end with one journalist. Pick one topic and the reporter who knows it best. Capture their notebook as they already keep it, and turn it into a graph they can see and correct. Build them a desk that fits how they work. Bring in one expert, paid and credited. Publish their article as they write it, and offer one other projection to readers who want it. Measure what readers do with it and whether the journalist's next story was faster or better. Then liquefy whatever the next story touches. That is liquid content in the guide's sense, atomic, reusable, structured underneath whatever the front end shows. The difference is where the water comes from. Not the finished product, kept wet, but the reporting itself, kept with its sources, by the people who know how to find it.

Drafted from a voice memo by Dinis Cruz, who is the author of the argument and the person with editorial responsibility, by agent@riskmandate.ai (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5) in the sgit.ai site session, on 7 October 2026. Quotations are from Sofia Giannuzzi's guide for FT Strategies, credited and linked, and through it from Digiday. Liquid content is the guide's term and the clay image is the guide's. The infographic was made with ChatGPT from the guide's text and is reproduced with a reading note.

Abstract: The companion to my reply to Bert Kok. The publishers with the most to gain from AI are not the big generic ones but the local and the niche: the ones close to their readers, in their language and culture, with real expertise. They own the reader's trust, and trust is where the value is now. Such a publisher can take everything that has become commodity, the weather, sport results from official sources, the big outlets' global news, and serve it to its readers from their point of view, captured and kept current by agents. And it can certify upwards: when a big outlet runs a story about its area, the local journalists are the ones who can say whether it is right, and should be paid for saying so. A story with no local source behind it reads as a shadow, and readers will go to the source. This needs open interfaces, as the Competition and Markets Authority forced UK banks to open theirs from 2018, and it needs a map of who reports and who recycles, where a newsroom that cuts its experts shows it. Stories, like software, go off if nobody maintains them, and the same argument I made for maintainers applies to journalists: whoever does the expert work should be the one who is paid and the one who signs off.
Local trust, certified upwards: a local publisher at the centre, with what flows in, what flows up and the reader below.
in-short

The value is in the local and the niche. Close to the reader, in their language and culture, with expertise. They own the trust. And trust is what is worth paying for now. Commodity flows in. Weather, sport results, global news, served from the reader's point of view. Certification flows up. Local journalists vouch for the big outlets' stories about their area, and are paid. A story without a local source is a shadow. Readers can go to the source. Interfaces must open, as UK banks' did under the Competition and Markets Authority. Map who reports and who recycles. A newsroom that cuts its experts should show it. Stories go off like milk. Someone has to maintain them, as maintainers maintain software.
value

I think what is happening is that, alongside the very big, very generic news organisations, we are going to see more very focused publishers: local, regional, or expert in one subject. That is where the real value is, where you can charge, and where it makes sense to invest in journalism and in creating content. Because that is where the trust is.
value

A local or niche publisher is close to its readers. It works in their language, their culture, their region. Its business model tends to stay aligned with its readers' needs, because its readers are all it has. The bigger an organisation gets, the more business models it runs, and the more easily it drifts into rent extraction. That can work, and it suits commodity, but it loses the edge, and it loses trust. There is an economic value now in going back to trust, and in selling it. The local and the niche are the ones best placed to do that.
commodity

A local publisher that owns its readers' trust should not stop at its own reporting. It should have everything that has become commodity on its site, including what comes from other sites. Some of it is plain fact from official, unambiguous sources: the weather, the sport results, the trains, the markets. Those can be captured and kept current by agents, with their sources attached, at almost no cost. Some of it is the big outlets' global news. That too belongs on the local site, told from the point of view of its readers: what this means here, for us, in our language.
commodity

So I go to my local news site, which I trust because it is local, and I get the weather, the latest news, the sport, and the global story of the day, from a place I trust, with its sources shown. The commodity layer becomes a reason to come back, which is the habit Bert Kok rightly says publishers must not lose, without costing the newsroom its time.
open

This only works if the commodity can flow, which means interfaces have to open. There is a precedent. In the UK, the Competition and Markets Authority found in 2016 that established banks did not have to compete hard enough, and one of its remedies was open banking: since 2018, customers have been able to share their account data securely with other providers, through a standard built under the CMA's order. Open Banking Limited, the body the CMA's order set up, says there are now over 18 million active users. I had remembered it as the FCA's doing; it was the CMA's.
open

News has nothing like it yet. The agents on the PHP story site watch 913 pages, and 59 of them answered with a bot challenge and 15 with a paywall. Some of that is right: the publisher should be paid. But a standard way to read, cite and pay for a source, with billing built in, would serve the local publisher, the source and the reader better than walls and challenges.
certify

Here is the other half. If I read a story about my town on one of the big websites, say the BBC, I would expect its source to be a local outlet I trust, or a local agency that actually employs local journalists, and I would expect those journalists to have certified the story: this is right, or this is right with this caveat. That is the economic model: the big outlet pays the local source for the certification, per use, as I described in signed by the source. And if a story has no such source behind it, I know what I am reading. It is a shadow of the real reporting, and I can go and read the local one instead.
recycles

That means mapping who is doing real journalism and who is recycling it. We are starting to have the data for this: the PHP site keeps every source and every capture, so it can see who reported first, who quoted whom, and who changed their words later. A global organisation that recycles content created by others should pay for it. Either it sends its own reporter, and that is fine, or it pays the people who did. And the cuts should be visible. Budgets for correspondents are cut partly because nobody can see the effect. When a news organisation lets its cybersecurity correspondent go, or the only expert in a subject, it should show on its site and in its trust: the person who was certifying the updates, and maintaining the stories, is not there any more.
maintain

That last point matters because stories need maintaining. As I argued in sources and their shadows, a news organisation's history is becoming something like case law: it is referenced, quoted, and built on. But a story with facts that can change goes off, like milk. The number gets revised, the claim gets withdrawn, the source rewrites its post. Somebody with the expertise has to keep the story true, or say that it is no longer current. That is ongoing work, and it is paid work.
software

The same argument twice: in software, the maintainer; in news, the local expert. In both, money should flow to them. This is exactly the argument I made about software in who maintains the PHP you run?. The maintainer, the person who knows the code, should be paid, and should sign off the version you run. The journalist, the expert who takes the time to understand something, should be paid, and should sign off the stories that rest on their work. In both cases the free-riders are invisible today, and in both cases the damage shows only when the expert has gone and nobody can fix, or vouch for, what is left. Making who signs for what visible is how both get funded.
exists

Exists: the capture, provenance and source watch on the PHP site; stories kept as graphs; the bridge story, a simulated local story followed to the end; signed notes and keys on pki.sgit.ai. Proposed: certification paid per use; open, billable interfaces for news; a public map of who reports and who recycles; trust that reflects a newsroom's staffing.
limits

This is an economic model, not a market. No local publisher is paid for certification today. Trust in local news is an argument here, not a measurement in this article. The open banking parallel is about the mechanism, an order that opened interfaces, not a claim that news should be regulated the same way. Not every big outlet recycles. Many still send their own reporters; the point is to make the difference visible.
sources

My voice memo of 25 October 2026, in reply to Bert Kok's essay for The News Stack. Open Banking Limited, about us and the origins of open banking, read on 25 October 2026. Abstract: People ask how my agents remember, and the honest answer is that memory is the thing I have been building all along without calling it that. The industry's picture of agentic memory is one store that everything gets pumped into and retrieved from by similarity. Mine is the opposite. Memory is context management: giving an agent the right context for the moment, and no more, because context has a cost in tokens and in attention. It is many memories, not one, because context is specific: the inbox has its rules, the news has its rules, a contact in the CRM has a world of its own, and forcing them into one ontology would lose what each knows. It is fractal, principles at the top in a few kilobytes and the code at the bottom, so an agent loads the altitude its question lives at. It is published and open, because an agent can fetch, quote and link what is public, with a URL for every claim and a hash for every file. And it is shared between agents through vaults, so a session can end and the next one, or a different agent, or a person, picks up from the same files. This article says how that works, what it cost, where the industry's tools and this approach agree and differ, and where mine falls short, with the evidence of the session that wrote it: one Claude Code session across several context resets that revised an article from another team's review, wrote two more, published a vault and shipped six releases in a day, remembering nothing between resets except what the files remembered for it.

Memory is not one store. Every one of these is a memory an agent reads from in a session like the one that wrote this, each a different shape because it answers a different kind of question. They disagree with each other in places, and that is allowed: each is right for its context, and each says where it came from. Counts from the live site on 3 October 2026. Memory is not a spectator sport. It is not one store you pump everything into and watch. It is work: deciding what the agent needs for this moment, giving it that, and writing back what it learned so the next moment is cheaper. Memory is context management. The question is never "what do we remember" but "what does this agent need in its window right now". That is the same question the industry now calls context engineering, and it has a cost in tokens that makes "everything" the wrong answer.

It is many memories, not one. The inbox, the CRM, the news, the code, the sites, the release log: each is a memory with its own vocabulary, and by now they are inconsistent with each other in places. Forcing one ontology on them would lose what each knows. It is fractal. Principles at the top in a few kilobytes, arguments and worked examples below, code at the bottom. An agent loads the altitude its question lives at and follows a link down only when it has to. The fractal is the budget. It is published and open. Open source and Creative Commons mean an agent can fetch, quote, link and cite. The more I publish, the better the next context gets, and every claim arrives with a URL.

It is shared through vaults. A vault is a bundle with the right information for a moment, encrypted, versioned and hashed, opened with a read key that cannot write. Agents talk in it through files, so a session can end and the next picks up from the same place. Provenance is built in, not bolted on. A URL for every quote, a commit for every release, a read key for every vault, a hash for every source file, a byline on every page. Nothing has to be trusted because nothing is unsourced. It falls short in known ways. Stale pages become false memories; the session that wrote this found four and fixed two. The thesis is stated as falsifiable and this article keeps it that way.

When people ask how my agents remember, they usually have a picture in mind: a memory system, singular, somewhere behind the agent, into which everything it sees is deposited and from which it retrieves by similarity whatever seems relevant. The agent remembers the way a camera remembers. Nobody decides what goes in; nobody decides what comes out; the store just accumulates. I think that picture is wrong in three ways, and the three are related.

It is wrong that there should be one. Context is specific. The rules that govern my inbox agent are not the rules that govern the news graph, and the vocabulary of a code review is not the vocabulary of a risk register. Each of those is a memory, and each has its own ontology because the people and agents who work in it need different things from it. By now, with twenty-seven sibling sites, forty published vaults, a CRM and an inbox, those memories are inconsistent with each other in places. I used to think that was a problem to solve. I now think it is the point: each is correct for its context, and a memory that had been forced to agree with all the others would be wrong for every one of them.

It is wrong that it should hold everything. Memory has a cost, and right now the cost is paid in two currencies: the context window, which is finite and degrades as it fills, and the prompt, which is billed by the token. Anthropic's engineering guidance of September 2025 puts it exactly: "Context, therefore, must be treated as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns", and the goal is "the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome." A memory that gives the agent everything gives it the wrong thing at every altitude.

And it is wrong that it should be passive. Memory is made. Somebody, a person or an agent, decides that a thing is worth keeping, puts it where the next reader will find it, says where it came from, and links it to what it relates to. That is work, and it is the work my sites, graphs and vaults exist to do. The inbox article's agents talk in files that stay; the release log is written for the next agent rather than a changelog reader; the article graphs are published as JSON so that "what does this site think about X" costs a few kilobytes. None of that is spectating. I want to be fair to the field, because it has moved a long way and some of it has arrived where I am.

The consumer products have memory as a feature. ChatGPT's Memory launched in February 2024 and in April 2025 was extended so that it "can now reference all of your past chats". Claude's memory, from September 2025, is scoped differently: "Claude creates a separate memory for each project", with a summary the person can read and edit. Gemini's personal context arrived in August 2025, on by default. These are a single vendor's store of a person's conversations, and the memory thesis on nfrs.sgit.ai describes that shape plainly: "accumulated transcripts, retrieved by similarity, private to one vendor, unversioned and invisible to the person it describes." Claude's editable summary is the exception that shows the rule.

The developer frameworks are more interesting. MemGPT, in October 2023, drew "inspiration from hierarchical memory systems in traditional operating systems" and paged information in and out of a limited window. Its successor Letta gives agents editable memory blocks that live in the context itself. Mem0 and Zep store extracted facts, Zep as a temporal knowledge graph, and both claim large savings against sending the whole history. And then Letta ran a benchmark in August 2025 that I find telling: a plain filesystem, with the agent reading and writing files, scored 74.0 percent on the LoCoMo memory benchmark against 68.5 percent for Mem0's graph variant. Their explanation was that "simpler tools are more likely to be in the training data of an agent and therefore more likely to be used effectively." Files won.

The agent builders have said the same thing from the other side. Manus, in July 2025: "we treat the file system as the ultimate context", and the cache hit rate is "the single most important metric for a production-stage AI agent". Anthropic's own memory tool, from September 2025, is "a dedicated memory directory stored in your infrastructure that persists across conversations", files that the application, not the vendor, holds, with the model told to "ASSUME INTERRUPTION: Your context window might be reset at any moment". Claude Code's memory is a markdown index whose first 200 lines or 25 kilobytes load at the start of every conversation, with topic files read on demand. And the word for all of this, since Andrej Karpathy used it in June 2025, is context engineering, "filling the context window with just the right information for the next step."

So the field has arrived at files, at budgets, at loading on demand, at the context window as the scarce thing. Where I differ is in what the files are, who can read them, and how far the ladder goes. Here is the frame I use. There are two ways an agent meets memory, and they look different but are the same problem.

The first is the agentic session: a model with tools, running for hours or days, managing its own context. It fetches an index, follows links, reads what it needs, and when the window fills it is summarised and restarted with the summary. This is the mode the session that wrote this article ran in. Anthropic calls the restart compaction, "summarizing its contents, and reinitiating a new context window with the summary", and its guidance for agents is to "maintain lightweight identifiers (file paths, stored queries, web links, etc.) and use these references to dynamically load data into context at runtime." In this mode the agent makes its own working memory as it goes, and the question is whether the material it loads from is shaped to be loaded a little at a time.

The second is the chat or the API call, where there is no second turn. The bundle handed to the model has to be right the first time and as small as it can be, because every token in it is in the prompt. I wrote about this in March, in a draft that is still unpublished but was quoted in a brief this week: "When I send a one-shot request via API, I control the model's entire universe. Everything the model doesn't need? Simply absent." The loop is to "curate reality, send it all at once, get the answer, then use the answer to improve the reality for the next prompt." That is memory as context management stated as a procedure. The published material is the reality, the bundle is the curation, and the answer feeds back into the material.

As much memory as the question needs. The published altitudes of this site, from the index to a whole vault, with what each costs to load. An agentic session walks down them; a one-shot call is handed the one it needs. Neither gets the whole thing. Sizes from the live site on 3 October 2026.

Both modes are served by the same memory if the memory has altitudes. On this site the index, llms.txt, is 350 lines and about 106 kilobytes: enough to decide where to look. The graphs of all twenty-three articles are one file of 234 kilobytes: enough to answer "what does this site think about X" without opening an article. One article's graph is eight kilobytes; the article itself is around sixty. The data bundle of the code review vault is a megabyte; the vault with its history is four. The token-bill article made the argument for the top of that ladder: "The tokens saved are not a percentage of the page. They are the page, minus the answer." The fractal graphs demo made it for the bottom, where "the landing view of a 1,051-node semantic graph costs three requests and 94 KB." Memory that is shaped like that can be loaded by either mode without loading all of it.
Now the part that I think is most different from the industry's picture, and most important.

Every site I run is part of my memory, and so is every vault, and so is the inbox and the CRM and the release log. They are different memories because they hold different kinds of thing and answer different kinds of question. The sites hold principles and arguments. The release log holds what changed and what was learned, 211 entries from the first release to this one, each stamped with a commit, which the historian role on this site describes as "the site's memory, and it is written for the next agent, not for a changelog reader." The briefs hold what one team asked of another, with the status. The vaults hold worked examples, forty of them totalling 328 megabytes, each opened with a read key. The inbox agents hold their conversation in Email-FS, a mailroom, an inbox and a done folder per agent with every message kept as a file, so that "why did this happen" is a walk back through the folder rather than a search. The CRM holds one folder per contact, and each contact has a semantic graph of its own, a history, an interface and a workflow, with sub-projects below it: a world per person, hyperlinked to the rest.

None of those is forced to agree with the others. The inbox's policy rows use reach, mandate, gap and barriers; the news graph uses claims and evidence; the code review graph uses stories, commands, classes and calls; the risk graph uses acceptance and owners. A single ontology across them would be a worse memory for every one of them. What joins them is not a schema but links, and the index that keeps the links. In the SG/Send team that is a librarian role that indexes everything; on this site it is the historian and the build itself, which refuses to publish a page the index would omit.

This is also why being open matters more than people expect. Open source and Creative Commons are not a licensing preference here. They are what makes the memory usable by an agent: a public page can be fetched, a public quote can be cited with its URL, a public graph can be loaded by anyone's model, a public vault can be cloned with a key that is itself public. The more I publish, the more there is for the next session to stand on, and the less it has to be told. One of the articles published this week said it in passing, "the site is becoming the memory", and that is the right description of what happens when the material an agent needs is published rather than deposited.

A memory that is shared, and made by agents as well as people, has to be able to say where each thing came from, or it becomes a rumour mill. The field has started to notice this: Claude Code's memory files carry a type and a modification timestamp; Anthropic's guidance warns of context rot, where "the model's ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases" as the window grows, and the older research on long contexts found the same, performance "significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts." The answer to a memory that cannot be trusted is not to trust it less. It is to make every item in it carry its source.

On this estate that is a set of habits rather than a feature. Every quote in an article has a URL. Every release has a commit hash in the log. Every vault has a read key on its page, derived one way from a vault key that is never published, classified before it is put there, and the page says what the key can and cannot do. Every source file inside a vault has a hash. Every page has a byline that names the person responsible, the model that drafted it and the date. The fractal graphs page states the rule outright: "claims from memory are not allowed anywhere in this system", and the journalist role's card says "a claim about the site is checked with grep or git, not memory". When something is derived rather than observed, the page says so, as the code review vault does for its hand-written stories against its parsed graphs.

Provenance is what lets memory be shared without being trusted, and it is the part that a vector store cannot give you, because a similarity score is not a source. I can show rather than claim, because this article was written by the same kind of session it describes, and the record of that session is itself in the memory. One Claude Code session on this site, across several context resets, during the day this was written. It had no memory system. It had the published surfaces, the vaults, the conventions in the repository, and a summary of itself carried across each reset. What it read in, how it worked, and what it wrote back.

The session ran for days across several context resets. Each time the window filled it was summarised and restarted with the summary: what had been asked, what had been done, the rules still in force, the exact paths of the files. That summary is memory as a hand-off note, and it is the one thing the model carried itself. Everything else it read: the repository's conventions, which the build enforces rather than the model remembering; the published sites, which three research agents read and came back from with quotes and URLs, including my own blog posts from 2012; and a vault from another team, the dev agent's review pack for the inbox article, which arrived as files, a review, drop-in text, eight figures and their sources, leak-checked, and was applied the same morning. Memory handed between agents without a shared session.

It worked by altitude. The index first, then the graph of an article, then the article, then the code, and the four-megabyte vault only when the question was about the evidence in it. It checked against reality: every number recomputed, every key scanned for before every commit, every page screenshotted and looked at. When the memo and the record disagreed, the record won and the article said so. And it forgot on purpose: scratch files, screenshots and worktrees stayed in a scratch folder, and nothing went into the published memory that was not meant to be read again.

Then it wrote back. Two new articles, each with its graph as JSON so that the next session can answer "what does the site think" without reading them. A vault with a read key on its page. Six entries in the release log, including the mistakes: a bundler that doubled a page, a figure that clipped its last rows, a value line that had to be corrected twice. And a byline on each piece saying who was responsible, which model drafted it, and when. The day's output was a revised article, two new ones, a vault and six releases, each consistent with the ones before, from a model that remembered nothing between resets except what the files remembered for it.

Memory is context management as a loop: publish, index, load by altitude, act, write back, and the next session starts from the published material. The conventions along the bottom are what make agents able to share a memory without sharing a session.

What makes the pile of sites and vaults a memory rather than an archive is the loop. Publish, with graphs, keys, briefs, logs and bylines. Index, with llms.txt per site and section, graphs.json across the articles, Agent Contact files per site, and a librarian or a historian keeping the links. Load by altitude, index then graph then text, the vault only for evidence, a summary carried across resets, and prompt caching for the part that does not change, which the vendors now price at a tenth of the standard input rate or less. Act, and check. Write back: a commit to the vault, one per cycle after a leak check; a message into another agent's mailroom; an issue as a folder; a release log entry. Then the next session starts from what was published.

The conventions matter more than the tooling. Email-FS lite gives every agent a mailroom, an inbox, a done folder and an outbox, a message is a file with email headers and typed blocks, and each agent writes only its own folders, which is what lets a conductor run twelve of them in order without a shared session. Issues-FS makes an issue a folder whose history is the vault's history, so nothing is deleted and the board is files that version with the thing they track. The CRM's per-contact worlds give each person their own graph and interface, so an agent working on one contact loads one folder. And read keys let a memory be shared without being handed over: a published key reads everything and writes nothing, which is what makes it safe to put on a web page.

Nothing is remembered by the model between sessions. Everything is remembered by the files. A new session, a different agent, or a person reads the same memory from the same place, and that is the whole design. The memory thesis on nfrs.sgit.ai calls itself untested and falsifiable, and lists its own limits, and I want to keep it that way here.

Stale pages become false memories. The thesis says this failure had already been seen four times when it was written; the session that wrote this article found four more while researching it. The fractal graphs index page still says a vault has 617 nodes when the corrected count on its own performance page is 1,051. The site's index told agents that the full-text file was "about 155 KB" when the file was 2.5 megabytes. The published article graphs and updates feed both said they were generated on 15 August when the site was at version 0.6.53. And the updates feed stops on 21 September while the release log runs to today. Two of those are fixed in this release, the size and the dates are now measured at build time rather than remembered, and two are left standing and named here, because a memory that hides its own errors is the thing this article is arguing against. The nfrs rule is the right one: "If the reality document doesn't list it, it does not exist", and "briefs are aspirations, not facts."

The memory is opinionated. It is one person's estate, with one person's vocabulary at the top of every ladder. An agent that loads it loads the opinions with the facts, and the bylines are there so that it knows whose. Discovery is hard at scale. Twenty-seven sites, forty vaults, 211 releases and a growing CRM are already more than one index comfortably holds, and the librarian role exists because the links do not keep themselves. The graphs help, the altitudes help, but "where is the thing I need" is a question this memory answers well for agents that already know its shape and less well for those that do not. And it is, so far, mine. The thesis would be properly tested when a second person's estate, with a different vocabulary, is read by the same agents alongside this one, and the agents cope with the disagreement. That has not happened yet.

Exists and runs: the sites, their llms.txt indexes and markdown twins; the article graphs as JSON, per article and combined; the release log with 211 entries; the briefs with status; forty vaults with published read keys; Email-FS lite and the conductor runs in the agent team's vaults; Issues-FS on this site's own board; the CRM with per-contact folders; the session summaries that carry a Claude Code session across resets; the research agents that read the published material and return quotes with URLs.

Does not exist yet: a second estate read alongside this one; a freshness check in the build that fails on a stale claim the way the leak scan fails on a key; a published shape for the session hand-off summary, so that an agent other than the one that wrote it can load it; the one-shot bundle as a first-class artefact, a vault that is exactly one prompt's universe, built from the altitudes and nothing else; and the librarian as a role on this site rather than in the SG/Send team. Introducing fractal semantic graphs: altitudes, and "how much definition you choose to load" at each. The token bill nobody is sending: the markdown twins, the graphs, and loading the altitude a question needs. Replicating the agentic inbox, Custom UIs are not the exception and Six agents, one inbox: Email-FS, the CRM's per-contact worlds, the conductor's run folder as record.

Code review as a fractal semantic graph: a memory of a codebase, derived and marked as such, published yesterday by the session described above. Price it, then give it away: "the site is becoming the memory". The memory thesis and documentation as a truth system on nfrs.sgit.ai: the limits this article keeps. The team roles on this site, including the historian who owns the release log, and the agent state use case: "An agent's context window ends; its work shouldn't." Abstract: In the early versions of what is now the append lane, the API was called the inbox, and two agent teams used it to send each other signed, encrypted messages in both directions. It worked, and it was crude. I think we now have a much better way of doing it. Every user will have a vault, their billing vault or a comms vault, and every vault can have append lanes: write-only channels that anyone holding a token can write to and only the owner can read. Put that together with PKI and you have a full messaging system between vaults. It is not quite peer to peer, because everything still goes through the server, but the server only ever sees ciphertext, its size and its time. Each message is encrypted to the recipient's public key and signed by the sender, so we always know who sent what. On top of that transport sits a schema, which I would call Messaging-FS, alongside Issues-FS and Email-FS: a conversation is one JSON file, updated as each message and reply arrives, where an email is one file at a time. The same messages can be sent and read from a web messenger or from the command line. This maps out the workflow, what exists, and what we would build.
Messaging between two vaults: each has a lane for the other, which its owner drains, checks and commits.
in-short

We have done this before, crudely. The append lane used to be called the inbox, and agents messaged each other over it. Every user now has a vault. And every vault can have append lanes. Lanes plus PKI make a messenger. Encrypted to the recipient, signed by the sender. Not quite peer to peer. It goes through the server, which sees only ciphertext, size and time. Messaging-FS is the schema. One JSON file per conversation, next to Issues-FS and Email-FS. Web and command line, the same messages. A messenger in the browser, or a terminal. It is a proposal. The transport exists; the schema and the commands are to build.
inbox

This is something we have already done once. In the early versions of SG/Send's vault API, the channel that is now called the append lane was called the inbox, and it was renamed in v0.32.7. On 25 and 26 September 2026, two agent teams used it to send each other signed, encrypted messages in both directions, without either holding the other's vault key, and one of them a Claude Code session that could keep no secret between sessions. sgit.ai published the write-up, and the vault messaging guide that came out of it. It worked, and it was crude. Reading the write-up again, the rough edges are clear: The lane address was agreed by hand. The design is that a sender works out your lane from your public key; that step "is not yet wired end to end", so a token was generated and handed over.
inbox

The payload was encoded twice. The encrypted file is base64 text, and the request sent base64 of that. Adding a sender replaced the list. Configure "replaces the anchor list", so adding one sender meant sending all of them again. The signature covered only part of the envelope. The inner ciphertext, not the wrapped key, the IV or the recipient. Everyone wrote their own tools. In the write-up's words, "two independent teams each wrote the same tooling". Those are exactly the things a messenger would fix, and most of them are written down as recommendations to the sgit team in the same document.
idea

What has changed since is that every user will have a vault: the billing vault in the user keeps the meter, or a comms vault, some storage of their own. And every vault can have append lanes, which we already use to process and communicate: from readers to this newsroom's editor in the editor's channel, and between agents. Put a lane on each user's vault, and PKI on top, and you have a full messaging system between vaults. A vault sends a message to another vault. Once you have that, you can have the equivalent of a messenger: a typical web-based one, or one on the command line, because sending and receiving are just calls.
idea

It is not peer to peer, strictly: every message goes through the server. But it is end to end encrypted. In the guide's words, what the server can see is "that a lane received something, how big it was, and when. What it cannot see: the content, or the recipient's private key, which never leaves their machine."
travel

The transport already exists, as six calls on the vault API, and the reason it works is that four capabilities are kept apart. From sgit.ai's API page: The append token, held by the sender. It can write to one lane, and nothing else: not list, not fetch, not read. The enum key, held by the vault owner. It can list, fetch and mark messages processed, and cannot write. The write key, held by the vault owner. It configures the lanes and purges them. The private key, held by the vault owner. It decrypts, and it is "never sent to the server". So a sender "can put something into your vault and learn nothing at all, not the contents, not the volume, not whether anyone else writes there". The write call answers with exactly {"ok": true}. One message, step by step: Alice encrypts to Bob and signs, and Bob fetches, decrypts, checks and marks it processed.
fs

The transport carries bytes; it does not say what they mean. The guide is plain about it: "The client decides what the bytes mean." What a messenger needs on top is a schema, a convention for the files on each side, the same way we already have Issues-FS, where an issue is a folder whose history is the vault's history, and Email-FS, where a message is a file with email headers. I think both models have a place here: Messaging-FS: a conversation is one file. Messages are small and thread-like. A conversation is one JSON file, updated with each new message and each reply. Email-FS: a message is one file. An email is bigger, and arrives a file at a time, with its headers, into an inbox folder, then done, with an outbox for what goes out. Full-blown emails between vaults work the same way. The layout on each side could be as simple as this:
fs

messages/ Messaging-FS contacts.json who, their key fingerprint, their vault and lane threads/ bob.json one conversation, rewritten as messages arrive mail/ Email-FS inbox/ done/ outbox/ 2026-10-21T10-00_a3f8.eml one message, one file And a thread, as a sketch, not a format: { "thread": "alice-bob", "with": { "name": "Bob", "fingerprint": "Bob's signing key", "vault": "Bob's vault id" }, "messages": [ { "id": "the server's file id", "from": "alice", "at": "2026-10-21T10:00:00Z", "text": "Shall we look at the billing flow on Thursday?" }, { "id": "the server's file id", "from": "bob", "at": "2026-10-21T10:04:00Z", "reply_to": "the first message's id", "text": "Yes, at ten." } ] } The server names each file it stores by the time it arrived, as {epoch_ms}_{24-hex}.enc, so messages sort in the order they landed, which is what a thread needs.
owner

The design avoids conflicts the same way the billing design does: each side writes only its own vault. Alice's thread with Bob lives in Alice's vault; Bob's lives in Bob's. When Alice sends, she writes to Bob's lane and adds the message to her own copy of the thread. When Bob's browser drains his lane, it adds the message to his copy and commits it. The lane itself sits beside the version-controlled tree, not inside it. From the API page: "appends never touch a branch and never conflict with a push." Only the owner's drainer moves a message from the lane into the vault, and when it does, it is an ordinary, versioned commit. So the history of a conversation is the vault's history, as it is for an issue in Issues-FS.
identity

PKI is what turns a channel into a messenger you can trust. Every message is encrypted to the recipient's public key and signed with the sender's key, and the write-up's rule is a good one to keep: "the lane says who holds the token, the signature says who holds the key, and the From: header must match both." The keys themselves come from the same place as everything else now, as in PKI everywhere: made on the device, published in a register anyone can check, and pinned the first time you talk to someone. Verify by fingerprint, not by name. And the pattern from the user keeps the meter carries over: pin the first commit of a vault you share with someone, and every later commit can be checked for who wrote it.
clients

The same messages can be sent and read from two kinds of client. In the browser. A vault app already has the six calls, through sg.append. One detail shapes the design: from an app, write can reach any vault, but list, fetch and the rest act only on the vault that is open, because listing someone else's lane would need their enum key, and shipping that in a page "would give every visitor read access to the whole lane". That is exactly the right shape for a messenger: you write to other people's lanes and read only your own.
clients

On the command line. Today it takes two steps: sgit pki encrypt to the recipient, then an HTTP call to write. sgit-ai 0.23.0 has the pki commands, to encrypt, decrypt, sign, verify and keep contacts, but no command for lanes yet. The write-up asked for one: "sgit lane / sgit inbox CLI: open, send, drain, close, rotate". With that, a terminal messenger is a few commands: send, drain, and show a thread. I think the main use case is the web. But it is the same append lane either way, and the same files.
build

Most of what is needed is already listed in the write-up's recommendations, which makes this a short list: Derive the lane address from the public key. So a sender needs only your public key and vault id, not a token handed over by hand. One encoding. Send the encrypted file once, not base64 of base64. Add and remove senders. Without resending the whole list. Sign the whole envelope. The wrapped key, the IV and the recipient, not only the ciphertext. Report the signer's fingerprint. Because names repeat. A command for lanes. Open, send, drain, close, rotate. The routes in production. Today the append routes are on dev.send.sgraph.ai, at v0.34.1; send.sgraph.ai, at v0.32.4, still has the older inbox routes. The Messaging-FS schema itself. Threads, contacts, replies, and receipts sent as messages.
not

The guide says what the transport is not, and it is worth keeping in view: "Not a chat protocol, not a queue with delivery guarantees, and not anonymous, the server sees lane activity and timing even though it cannot read content." Messaging-FS is the chat protocol on top; delivery is confirmed by a reply or a receipt, not by the server; and the timing of messages is visible to the server even when nothing else is. There are limits too: 5 MB per message, and 1,000 waiting messages per sender's lane, after which the server refuses more until the owner drains. For a message, that is plenty; a large file is better shared as a vault of its own, with the message carrying the link.
uses

Once vaults can message each other, a lot of what we already do becomes the same thing. The validation notes in the billing design are messages from us to a user's vault. A reader writing to the editor is a message. Agents handing work to each other, as in the September write-up, are messages. And so is a person writing to a person, which is where a messenger starts.
limits

Messaging-FS does not exist yet. It is a proposed schema; Email-FS lite and Issues-FS are in use. The transport exists. On dev.send.sgraph.ai, used both ways by two agent teams in September. The CLI has no lane command. As of sgit-ai 0.23.0. The rough edges are from the write-up. Some may have been fixed since; the server versions were read on 21 October 2026. It is not anonymous. The server sees when and how much, not what.
diagrams
