Abstract: Meta has updated the Commercial Terms that apply to any business use of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and its ad tools. One clause authorises Meta, or anyone acting for it, to use "web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents" and "create test credentials" to access, cache and collect the websites associated with a business, and to pull updates periodically, to "provide, develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products". Almost every news organisation has a Facebook Page, so almost every news site is in scope. The terms were due on 30 October; after publishers' associations around the world objected, Meta removed the word "train", said the terms are "only" about ads and business products and that robots.txt still counts, and moved the date to 20 November. Robots.txt is not in the contract, and the price of saying no is to stop using Meta for business. Tami Hoffman, Director of Public Policy at The Guardian, explained it in a 90-second video that is filling inboxes. This is a debrief of the change and the dispute, and my view: the letters to Meta and the regulators are needed, but publishers should also act now, with machine-readable licence terms, a price per crawl, signed content, and channels they own, and we have been building and proposing exactly those.
Tami Hoffman's LinkedIn post of 27 October 2026, with the video opening on the clause.
in-short

Meta's updated Commercial Terms take effect on 20 November. They cover any business use of its products. One clause lets Meta crawl and collect the websites tied to a business. And keep pulling updates. Almost every news organisation has a Facebook Page. So almost every news site is in scope. Publishers objected, and Meta moved twice. It removed "train", then moved the date from 30 October. The core is unchanged. Robots.txt is not in the contract; saying no means leaving Meta for business. The response has been letters and regulators. Both are needed. Publishers should also act now. Machine-readable terms, a price per crawl, signed content, owned channels. The pieces exist. Some are standards; some we have built; some we propose.
post

Tami Hoffman, Director of Public Policy at The Guardian, posted on LinkedIn on 27 October: "This ⬇️ is filling up my inbox. Meta's decision to update its 'commercial terms of use' has got news organisations around the world riled. 90 seconds of your time and I will explain why." The video puts the clause on screen, word by word, and shows Meta's page with the clause highlighted inside the section where a business grants Meta its licences. It is a good way to see it, because the clause is one paragraph among many that businesses accept, often without reading. Meta's Commercial Terms page as shown in Tami Hoffman's video, with the crawling clause highlighted.
clause

The clause, part by part: who, with what, to do what, where, how often, for what, and what is not in it. The Commercial Terms apply when anyone uses Meta's products "for a business or commercial purpose", which the terms define broadly: ads, a Page, a product catalogue, a group for business purposes, Meta Business Suite. The crawling paragraph sits under "Licences and rights you provide Meta". Read as a list: Who: "us (or any entity acting on our behalf)". With what: "automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents)", and the right to "create test credentials". WAN-IFRA reads the second part as a question about paywalls and access controls, and asks Meta to remove it. To do what: "access, index, cache, analyse, collect, retrieve or crawl". Caching and collecting are copies, not visits.
clause

Where: "the domains, web pages or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users' use of Meta Company Products and services". For a publisher, its own site; read broadly, every page its readers share. How often: "periodically pull updates". For what: "provide, develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products", including products that help businesses create ads and "connect you with users", and "the integrity and security of Meta Company Products". If you do not agree: "please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes."
clause

There is a fair reading of part of this. An ad platform checks the pages its ads link to, for safety and for quality, and that needs a crawler. Meta's spokesperson Andy Stone said on X that the update was "not about scraping news sites", and a later Meta statement said the crawling terms "only applied to our ads and business products" and that robots.txt preferences still count (reports differ on which spokesperson gave it). The problem is that none of those limits is in the text. "Business products" is not defined: the examples that follow it are illustrative, not limiting, and, as WAN-IFRA put it, Meta's robots.txt assurances are not in the terms.
timeline

Meta's Commercial Terms, October to November 2026: a timeline of the update, the reactions and the changes. The first version said Meta could use content from those sites "to provide, develop, improve, research, train" its products, effective 30 October. 16 October: the News/Media Alliance, which represents more than 2,000 US publishers, called the terms "outrageous and probably illegal". 16 to 17 October: Meta removed "train", and its spokespeople said the update was not about scraping news sites. 19 October: the UK's News Media Association called it a "shameless landgrab attempt", and the Movement for an Open Web prepared complaints to the European Commission and the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, advising businesses to consider leaving Meta's business accounts before 30 October. 22 October: the News/Media Alliance sent an open letter to Mark Zuckerberg asking Meta to withdraw the terms, with a reply requested by 26 October.
timeline

22 October: WAN-IFRA, the World Association of News Publishers, wrote to Meta's Chief Global Affairs Officer, Joel Kaplan, with five demands; the letter is dated 22 October and was reported the next day. 23 October: Meta moved the date to 20 November. The European Commission said it "welcomes Meta's announcement that it has postponed the entry into force of its new commercial terms". WAN-IFRA's CEO, Stig Ørskov: "This postponement is a welcome step, but it does not address our concerns." 23 October: the News Media Association's Theo Bamber: "This delay is welcome, but it is a pause not a solution." 20 November: the terms take effect, unless they change again.
asks

WAN-IFRA's letter sets out what would fix it, point by point. Its president, Ladina Heimgartner: "Journalism is not raw material to be collected as a condition of being present on a platform." Its five demands: suspend the clause for news publishers pending dialogue; remove the right to create test credentials and commit that paywalls and access controls will not be circumvented; make robots.txt and other machine-readable reservations of rights binding in the terms; exclude the use of publishers' content to develop or power AI systems unless it is licensed; and let publishers decline the clause without losing Meta's business tools. It also raised Meta One, the limit on how many links a Page can post to its own site without paying.
asks

All five are reasonable. Two of them, binding robots.txt and leaving news sites alone, ask Meta to write into the contract what Meta has already said in public; the other three ask for more than Meta has offered. That is the gap: a platform's statement is not a term, and a term the other side cannot negotiate is not an agreement.
view

The letters and the complaints are needed, and the speed of the response, from associations in the US, the UK, Europe and worldwide within a week, shows what the industry can do when it moves together. But they are defensive. They ask the platform to promise less. What I would like to see, alongside them, is news organisations stating, in a form a machine can read and a court can enforce, what their journalism costs to use, and then making the paid path easier than the scrape. The five demands in WAN-IFRA's letter, and what a publisher can do about each. Most of what the demands ask for already exists, or can be built:
view

Terms a machine reads. RSL 1.0, Really Simple Licensing, is a standard, finalised in late 2025, for stating licence terms per use, such as training or search, in a file a crawler reads beside robots.txt. It does not block anything by itself; it states the terms. Robots.txt says "please do not"; a licence says "here is the price". A price per crawl. Cloudflare's pay per crawl, announced as a private beta in July 2025, answers an AI crawler with HTTP 402, Payment Required, and a price. It is enforcement at the edge, independent of anyone's terms of service. Content that carries its own terms. This newsroom's content rights page describes CC-Signed: licence variants where keeping the signature is a condition of the licence, so content stripped of its provenance is content used outside its licence.
view

Paid at the source. Every page on this newsroom draws a few pence from a reader's prepaid credit, and I have argued that open content can still be paid for at the source, and that we should pay the sources we use, especially when they certify us. The same meter can serve an agent: a page an AI reads should cost what a page a person reads costs. Signed, so it is worth paying for. Signed by the source and on the record are about what makes journalism different from what a crawler can make itself: provenance, accountability, a person who stands behind it. Who creates the original? is the question underneath this whole dispute. The original is what the models need, and the original is what newsrooms make.
view

Channels you own. The fifth demand, declining without losing the tools, is a symptom of dependence. A news organisation that owns its site, its newsletter and its readers' accounts can treat a platform as one door, not the house. I made the same argument for small businesses in websites you own, and for newsrooms in own the stack, and the trust.
crawler

How a crawler can behave, from the PHP story site's source watch, with its three licence tiers. We crawl too. The PHP story site has a researcher agent that watches about 1,365 pages from public sources (in its export of 27 October), and its rules are written down: public sources only; each site's terms and robots.txt followed; every publisher given a licence tier, A for open and public-sector publishers whose pages we may keep and show, B for those we may quote in at most 25 words with a link, C for link only; the captures kept privately, with only their hashes published; and, in the design for a shared research site, an opt-out for any publisher who asks us to stop. The software in Meta's clause is the same kind of software. The difference is the rules it runs under, whether they are written down, and who wrote them.
watch

Whether Meta changes the text, not only the date: robots.txt, an exclusion for news, a definition of "business products". What the European Commission and the CMA do with the requests for interim measures. Whether publishers leave Meta's business tools, or accept the terms under protest. Whether any publisher answers with machine-readable terms of its own. That is the step I would most like to report.
limits

Tami Hoffman's video is quoted from the screenshots I was sent. Its spoken explanation is not transcribed here. The clause is quoted as Meta's page and the video show it. The final text on 20 November may differ. The timeline is from press reports of statements and letters, cited below; not every original letter was read. Legal readings are those of the associations and lawyers quoted. This is not legal advice. The newsroom's own mechanisms are small and partly proposed. They show the shape, not the scale.
review

The editor asked for a fresh review of this article on the day it was published. Claude Fable, not the model that wrote it, checked it against Meta's pages, the publishers' statements, WAN-IFRA's letter and our own source watch, and asked for changes. It was right on all nine points, and they are fixed: Our own crawler's numbers were wrong. The licence tiers are set per publisher, and the source watch's export of 27 October gives 74 at A, 933 at B and 16 at C, of about 1,365 pages; the counts and the date we had matched no record. review

Meta's words are that the crawling terms "only applied to our ads and business products"; we had paraphrased them inside quotation marks. (Reports differ on which spokesperson said it, so we now attribute it to Meta.) "Four of the five demands" was overstated. Meta's public statements match two: robots.txt, and leaving news sites alone. "Five weeks" was wrong for something that started in mid-October. The dispute is eleven days old; the terms take effect five weeks after it started. "Business products" has examples after it. The point is that they are illustrative, not limiting. Cloudflare's pay per crawl was announced as a private beta, not launched, in July 2025. "Most businesses accept without reading" was an absolute without a count; now "often".
review

It also checked and found sound the quotes of Tami Hoffman's post and of the clause against the screenshots, Meta's 20 November date and its "if you do not agree" sentence, the quotes from the News/Media Alliance, the NMA, WAN-IFRA and the European Commission with their dates, and RSL 1.0. Abstract: A friend sent me Monstream, and I had not seen it. It is a service of continuous research streams: you describe a topic, it turns the description into rules (what must be there, what to skip, which sources to trust, how strict to be), and AI agents read sources around the clock and send you only what matches, with short summaries and links to the originals. Its home page said 5,258 pages had been read by its agents that day. It is run by Fair Math, a small fully homomorphic encryption company, which reportedly raised $1.4 million in early 2024; most of its 116 public streams follow cryptography, and the largest has 24 subscribers. There is no public pricing: following a stream "costs nothing extra", and the Mac app is free. What makes it interesting for us is a clean integration API: a stream per object in our own system, named by our own id, finds pushed by a signed webhook or pulled by cursor, and feedback on each find. Legally, its terms allow automated access only through the means it provides, so the API is the way in, and its summaries are written by AI and "can be incomplete or wrong", so a find is a lead, never evidence. There is no public stream on php2shell; creating one needs an account, which I have not made. This is how I would use it, check it and contribute to it.
Monstream on 25 October 2026: the home page, Discover with 116 public streams, and the Integration API.
in-short

What it is. Continuous research streams: AI agents read sources against your rules and send what matches. Who runs it. Fair Math, a small cryptography company, reportedly funded with $1.4 million in 2024. How big. 116 public streams, mostly cryptography; the largest has 24 subscribers. What it costs. No public pricing; following is free, and so is the Mac app. The API is the interesting part. A stream per object in your system, signed webhooks, feedback. Legally, the API is the only automated way in, and its summaries are leads, not evidence. On php2shell, no public stream exists; making one needs an account. How we could use it, check it and contribute to it. Below.
what

Monstream describes itself as "continuous research streams for the topics that matter to you". You describe what you want to follow, in as much detail as you like. It turns that into rules: what must be included, any of a set of topics, red flags to skip, sources to trust or ignore, and how strict to be. You can preview a stream on the previous week's data before starting it. Then "AI agents read thousands of pages around the clock, check every finding against your rules and send you only what matters, with short summaries and original sources." When I looked, the home page said its agents had read 5,258 pages that day.
what

A stream can be a digest, a radar or a watch. Its use cases run from competitors (their pricing pages, changelogs and job posts) to regulation, research, investors, founders, jobs, immigration and health. Results arrive in the web app, by email, by push, through a free Mac app, or on Telegram. Streams can be private, or public in Discover, where anyone can follow them or fork them into their own. The tools are handled for you: it says each stream picks from more than 1,000 sources, connectors and readers, with the keys and rate limits managed on its side; it names Crunchbase, X, Semantic Scholar, Exa, OpenRouter and PitchBook among them.
who

The site is operated by Fair Math, whose own site describes it as building "cryptographic infrastructure for computing on encrypted data", fully homomorphic encryption. Fair Math also runs FHERMA, a challenge platform for that field, and its founder and chief executive is reported as Gurgen Arakelov, whose name is on several of Monstream's public streams. FinSMEs and Crunchbase report that Fair Math raised $1.4 million in pre-seed funding in February 2024, led by gumi Cryptos Capital, Inception Capital and Polymorphic Capital; PitchBook and Tracxn list the round as seed, and PitchBook lists two more investors. I could not read those pages directly, and I found no separate funding for Monstream. It looks like a product built by a small cryptography company, perhaps first for its own research: the API's own example is a stream for FHERMA.
who

That shows in Discover. Of its 116 public streams, the most followed are the FHE Radar (24 subscribers), AI vs Cryptography (17), and radars on trusted execution, zero-knowledge proofs, post-quantum cryptography and multi-party computation (10 to 13 each). It is early, and small.
cost

There is no pricing page. Discover says "Subscribing costs nothing extra", and the Mac app is free. The terms reserve the right to change or limit features, "including how many streams an account can run". Underneath, every stream costs real money: model calls through OpenRouter, searches through Exa, and data sources such as PitchBook and Crunchbase. So I would expect a paid tier, but there is no public commercial model yet.
api

This is the part that makes it interesting for us. Monstream publishes an Integration API, last updated on 20 October 2026, so that "another system can keep streams on Monstream for its own objects, such as a research topic, a kernel or a client, and receive what they find." Access. A Monstream account for the system, and an API key with scopes (streams:read, streams:write, finds:read, webhooks:write, feedback:write), sent as a bearer token. The key is shown once and only its hash is kept. Without one, the API answers 401, which I checked. A stream per object, by your own id. PUT /streams/by-ref/<system>/<ref> creates or updates a stream named by your system and your id, and the call is idempotent. You either describe the stream in words, and Monstream drafts the rules, or send the rules yourself; you can give it sources, and whether to use only those.
api

Following existing streams. Search with GET /streams?q=…, then bind one to your own id. Webhooks. Events for a find created, updated or removed, and for a stream updated or deleted. Every delivery is signed: an HMAC-SHA256 over the timestamp and the raw body (its example code rejects anything more than five minutes old), and a stable event id to deduplicate on. Your own secret header is stored encrypted and sent with every call. Failed deliveries are retried for about a day. Pull. GET /finds?after=<cursor> pages through finds, for a system that would rather poll. Feedback. POST /finds/<id>/feedback, relevant or not relevant, tells the stream what fits. It is a clean, careful design: idempotent, signed, scoped, and built around the caller's own ids.
legal

Yes, through the API, and with care about what the results are. Automated access only through what they provide. The terms forbid accessing the service "by automated means other than the ones we provide". The Integration API is one of those means. Scraping the site is not. The results are other people's material. "Results come from third-party websites, feeds and APIs. We do not own or control that material, and links take you to sites with their own terms." So a find points us to a source; whether we may capture, quote or republish that source is decided by the source's own licence and access, which is exactly what sources and their shadows says we must record. The summaries are AI-written. "Summaries and judgements are written by AI models and can be incomplete or wrong. Check the original source before relying on anything." For a newsroom, that makes every find a lead. Evidence is what we capture ourselves.
legal

What we send goes to AI providers. The privacy policy says a stream's rules, and a description written in your own words, go to OpenRouter and the model providers it routes to, and search queries to Exa. Nothing confidential belongs in a stream's description. Public streams can be forked. Making a stream public lets others follow it and fork it into their own. One inconsistency. The privacy policy says "we do not use third-party analytics or tracking", and further down that "We use Google Analytics"; the site does load Google's tag. A small thing, but worth a correction on their side. The terms do not name a governing law, and neither the terms nor the API page mention a rate limit or a commercial-use restriction for the API.
php

You asked what it currently has on the PHP incident. In Discover, nothing: none of the public streams I could list, in any category, covers php2shell or vulnerability news in general; the nearest are "Crypto Implementation Vulnerabilities" and "GitHub Trending · Security & Privacy". Public stream pages also showed "Something went wrong" to a visitor who was not signed in, both times I tried. To create a stream on php2shell, and see what it finds, needs an account and an API key. Opening an account on someone else's service is a step I leave to you; with a key, it is one call.
use

How Monstream could feed our newsrooms through its documented API, from streams to our verdicts. Proposed, not built. Our job is to integrate, leverage and connect as much as we can, and Monstream fits that well: A stream per story. For the PHP site, a stream named newsroom/php2shell, described in words, with our watched sources as hints. For this newsroom's wires, one per wire: AWS, OWASP, Portugal. Finds as leads into the pipeline. A signed webhook delivers each find to our researcher, which captures the original page into the source watch with its hash, as it does for every other source. The curator and the journalist decide what holds. Monstream widens what we see; our captures decide what we say. Feedback as a byproduct. Our verdicts, relevant or not, go back to the stream. Our checking improves the stream for us, at no extra cost.
contribute

Public streams of our own. A public php2shell stream, and a "vulnerabilities in the news" stream modelled on the PHP site's Pulse, which sets evidence of exploitation beside attention, would fill a gap in Discover and be useful to others. The checking layer. A find with a link to our capture, its hash, its licence and its access, and the verdict on the claim, is a find others can trust more. If the API ever takes structured feedback, that is what we would send. Payments, eventually. When Monstream has a commercial model, and so do we, the streams and the sources that led us to a story should get a share, as I argued in local trust, certified upwards. A conversation. It is a small team with a careful API and an encryption background; there is a natural overlap with our vaults. I have not contacted them.
limits

No account was made, so nothing here was tested beyond the public pages and an unauthenticated call. The funding is as reported by FinSMEs, Crunchbase, PitchBook and Tracxn, which I could not read directly. The pages-read counter, the stream counts and subscriber numbers are from 25 October 2026 and will change. Stream pages failing for anonymous visitors is what I saw twice, not a finding about why. The integration is a proposal.
sources

A friend's link, and my voice memo of 25 October 2026. Monstream's home page, Discover, Integration API (last updated 20 October 2026), terms and privacy policy (both 6 October 2026), and its robots.txt, read on 25 October 2026, with an unauthenticated call to its API; Fair Math's site; funding as reported by FinSMEs, Crunchbase, PitchBook and Tracxn, through a web search. Related: sources and their shadows, local trust, certified upwards, own the stack, and the trust, the side stories of php2shell. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: At a digital sovereignty event today a conversation with the chief executive of an infrastructure company with a large footprint in Romania kept returning to one point: sovereignty has to work in practice, and in practice what stops workloads moving is not policy or price but code. Every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is written into applications that work today and that nobody wants to touch. So the requirement is that the application must not know it has moved: the same calls land on a twin, an open source service the client cannot tell from the real one, and the twin decides where the bytes go, real S3, an sgit vault, a European operator's data centre, a laptop. The S3 twin exists. Then the part I think matters most: the reason to move must never be sovereignty or cost reduction, which are important and never urgent. A migration carries risk, so the person signing it needs value that lands the day they switch and gives them cover: backups that exist, every object version controlled, encryption with the key held elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip, cost per workload, a top-of-register risk moved. That value sits in the twin layer, and an sgit vault behind it supplies most of it. The rule for the project: no new features during the move. And the business model for an infrastructure operator who sells it that way.

The twin layer. The application keeps calling S3, EC2 and IAM exactly as it does today; the calls land on an open source twin, which is where policy, journal, encryption, versions, cost and failure injection live; the twin decides where the bytes go, and switching the backend is a setting. The S3 twin is built; EC2 and IAM are not.
in-short

Workloads do not move because moving means changing code. Every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is written into applications that work today. The cost of change is the risk, so most people stay, whatever the policy says. So the application must not know. Not one line changes. The same calls land on a twin, an interface to a real system that is valued for one thing: the client cannot tell the difference. The destination becomes a setting. The S3 twin exists, as open source; EC2 and IAM do not yet. The reason to move is never sovereignty. Nor cost reduction. Both are important and never urgent; they sit on the risk register, not on the decision. A migration carries risk, and the person signing it needs a return that lands the day they switch and gives them cover if it goes wrong.
in-short

The value lives in the twin, because every call passes through it. Backups that exist, every object version controlled, encryption with the key held elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip, cost per workload. That is a migration that pays on day one, and most of it is what an sgit vault behind the twin provides. No new features during the move. It is a villager project, explorer to town planner. The moment a feature is added to it, it derails. The move is what makes the features possible afterwards; keep the two apart. It is a business for infrastructure operators, in Romania, Portugal, the UK or anywhere in Europe: not "move to us", which sells risk, but "keep your code, point it at us, and come out with policies, journals, encryption and cost visibility", which sells value with the risk removed.
why

Today I spent the day at an event about digital sovereignty, and one conversation, with the chief executive of an infrastructure company with a large footprint in Romania, kept coming back to the same point. Sovereignty has to work in practice, not in theory. And in practice the thing that stops it is not policy, regulation or price. It is code. Ask an organisation running on a hyperscaler why it has not moved and the honest answer is rarely that it loves its provider. It is that moving means changing the application. Every call to S3, every EC2 API, every IAM check is written into code that works today and that nobody wants to touch. Changing it means rewriting, retesting, and betting the business on a migration whose upside is mostly a principle. Some will do it. Most will not, and they are not wrong.
why

The hyperscalers know this. AWS's answer to sovereignty in Europe, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, went live on 15 January 2026: a separate cloud with its first region in Brandenburg, operated by EU residents, with, in AWS's words, "zero operational control outside of EU borders", and sovereign local zones planned for Belgium, the Netherlands and Portugal. That is a real step, and it also makes the point. Your code still talks to one vendor's API under one vendor's terms. Sovereignty that depends on one company's API is sovereignty by permission. If the option to move is to be real, the cost of change has to fall to almost nothing. That gives one hard requirement.
criterion

The original application must not know that it is not running on a hyperscaler. Not one line of its source changes. It keeps calling S3, EC2 and IAM exactly as it does today, and underneath, those calls land on whatever we choose: another provider, the company's own data centre, a European operator, or a twin running in memory on a laptop.
criterion

That is what I mean by a twin. Not the industry's version, a simulation valued for how faithfully it imitates a physical asset, but an interface to a real system, valued for whether the client can tell the difference. A mock is used by tests and measured by fidelity to the original's behaviour; a twin is used by production code, unmodified, with a real backend behind it, and measured by indistinguishability. The cost of switching a mock is a code path. The cost of switching a twin is an endpoint. If switching costs an endpoint, migration becomes a configuration decision. If it costs a code path, it becomes a project, and projects get cancelled.
s3

The first piece is built, as open source. It is an S3-compatible container: code using boto3, the AWS CLI or any S3 SDK believes it is talking to S3, and the only thing that changes is where the endpoint points. Behind the same interface the files can be served from real S3, from an encrypted vault, from local disk or from memory, selected per environment, and the service's own code does not change. Next to it is an IAM configuration risk engine, partly built, that treats IAM policies, S3 buckets and EC2 permissions as twins grounded in the real account. The bigger idea, twins as the layer that keeps a workload portable across clouds, is designed, not finished. I am being explicit about what exists and what does not, because this is exactly the kind of claim that should be checked.
s3

S3 is the right place to start because it is the service everything touches, it is the best specified, and it is already twinned. EC2 and IAM are harder, and that is where the engineering is. The pattern is the same each time: a wrapping layer between the customer and the cloud, where the destination is a setting.
reason

What signs a migration and what does not. Sovereignty, cost and any return that depends on a future event sit on the left; value that lands the day you switch, and gives the signer cover, sits on the right. Underneath, the rule for the project: no new features during the move. Here is the part I think matters most, and it is the theme of everything we build. The main reason to make a move like this must never be sovereignty, and it must never be cost reduction. Both are important. Neither is urgent. They are the kind of value that lands on the risk register under "important, not urgent" and stays there, because a migration always carries risk and nobody signs risk for a principle.
reason

The way I would put it is that you cannot do a move like this where the return depends on a future event that might occur, might not, and might not even be relevant to the people making the decision now. It is very hard for people to make that decision. They need cover: if anything goes wrong in the transition, there has to have been a value added on the way that anybody can point to. So whenever a solution like this is offered, there has to be a positive loop in it, and the loop has to close before the risk does. That is what the twin layer is for, because every call passes through it, and that is where the value goes: Backups that exist, with a restore that was tested, because the twin can write to two places.
reason

Every object version controlled: what changed, when, by whom, and a rollback that is a commit rather than a ticket. Encryption the operator cannot read. Put an sgit vault behind the twin and the files land as ciphertext, with the key held by the customer and not by whoever runs the hardware. That is what sgit is, and it is not a coincidence that it is on this list. A journal of every call. Platform logs record that something happened, not what the caller saw or why. A twin keeps every request and response and can replay them later, which is the argument of Before you give an agent a connector, give the connector a twin.
reason

Behaviour policies the agents cannot skip. More and more of the code calling these APIs is agents. The twin knows what the caller can reach, what it is meant to do, and the gap, and it enforces the barrier at a place the application cannot route around; the behaviour policy is the business logic, and footprint and blast radius is how the gap is measured and priced. Cost per workload, visible before the invoice, which is where agentic cost becomes an engineering problem rather than a surprise. Data in a place where it can legally be traded or shared, and a better understanding of what the data is, because the twin saw every byte go past.
reason

I will be honest that the list is still a little invisible to a signer; it needs to be sharper than this, and that is work for the next version. But version control and encryption with the key held elsewhere are each on their own a tangible, short-term return, and a journal with policies on top moves risk. That last point is the test: the move has to move the needle significantly on risks that sit at the top of the register, which is also why everything else in the move has to be de-risked first. A migration that lands versions, backups, encryption and a journal on day one, and takes an item off the top of the register, is a decision somebody can sign and defend. "It is in Europe now" is not.
villager

The other rule is about the project itself. This is a pure villager move, from explorer to town planner in the terms of Go slow to go fast: take something that works and make it boring, reliable and cheap, without changing what it does. When you do a project like this you cannot add new features. It is very tempting, and it is the moment everything derails, because now the migration is also a product change, and nobody can tell which of the two broke what. The argument people make is that the move is what will allow the features, and that argument is right; it is also exactly why the two must not be mixed. Move first, with the code unmodified and the twin adding its value underneath. Then, on the other side, add the features the move made possible.
testing

There is a side effect that may end up mattering more than sovereignty. If the application cannot tell a twin from the real service, the same unmodified code can run against an in-memory twin, in milliseconds, on a developer's laptop; against a twin replaying last week's production journal; against a twin injecting the failures you never see in staging, a timeout, a throttle, a permission that disappears halfway through a job; and against the real service, for the final check. Today most teams test against mocks they wrote themselves and hope production behaves the same. With twins the environment becomes a setting rather than a guess, and that is a dramatic change in how much you can know before you ship.
testing

I would go further. Every piece of software should meet this requirement: it must be able to run, unmodified, against a twin of every external service it depends on, without knowing. Software that can only run against one provider's live API is software you cannot test properly, cannot move, and cannot put a policy in front of. That is too much risk to carry for something as basic as where your files live.
open

None of this works if the twin layer is itself closed. Swap one vendor's API for another vendor's proprietary wrapper and the lock-in has moved, not gone. If you depend on somebody else's closed code you are one service agreement away from losing access, and that is the opposite of sovereignty. My view of open source here is not about community or generosity; it is about independence. You can read it, run it, fix it and move it, and that is a strategy, not a charity. Trying to build sovereign infrastructure outside an open source strategy is going to struggle, and Judo for small countries, written this afternoon for the same people, says why: there is no sovereignty without open source and open schemas, because sovereignty means you can leave.
business

This is another of the business models we publish, and it is for an infrastructure operator rather than for us. Selling "move to us" means selling risk. Selling "keep your code exactly as it is, point it at us, and gain versions, backups, encryption, a journal, policies and cost visibility on the way" means selling value with the risk removed. Every number below is a labelled assumption. Who pays. An organisation with workloads on a hyperscaler, an application it will not rewrite, and at least one item on its risk register that the twin's journal and policies would move. The buyer is the person who owns that register line, not the person who owns the cloud bill.
business

What they buy, in order. First the twin in front of the real service, nothing moving: a monthly fee per workload for the journal, the versions and the policy report, which is value on its own and the only step with no migration risk. Then the backend switch, one environment at a time, priced per terabyte stored and per call journalled, with the vault's encryption and versions included rather than extra. Then the next service. Where the operator's margin is. Storage and compute are commodities and should be priced as such; the margin is in the twin layer, the journal, the policy enforcement and the reports a regulator or an insurer will accept, because that is the custom-built part the customer would otherwise build badly. On the map it is the same reading as in Why I love Wardley maps: sell the custom layer above the commodity, not the commodity.
business

Where sgit sits. The vault is the storage the twin writes to when the customer wants the operator to hold what it cannot read, with a history and keys the customer keeps. It is open source, so the operator's customers are not locked to the operator either, which is the point and also the pitch. Why an operator in Romania, Portugal or the UK and not a hyperscaler. The hyperscaler cannot sell indistinguishability from itself. A smaller operator can, and it stands on commodities the big players matured. It is the judo move: the customer's existing code, the hyperscaler's own API, and open source, all used as the weight rather than fought.
business

Assumptions to check. That the S3 API surface the twin covers is enough for the first customers; that a journal and a policy report move a real register line for them; that the per-call price survives contact with a chatty workload; that the first operator will fund the hardening.
business

The build order for the operator: start with S3, because it is the most used, the best specified and already twinned. Run the twin in front of the real service first, same backend, every call journalled. Add behaviour policies at the twin and measure what they would have stopped. Then switch the backend one environment at a time. Then the next service. A team with strong engineers can get a first version working quickly, and a large part of the first pass can be generated with today's coding tools; then it has to be hardened and productised properly, because a twin earns trust only by being indistinguishable from the real thing, under load and at the edges.
limits

The S3 twin is the only finished twin. Its S3 API surface still needs confirming against the current repository. The IAM configuration engine is partial. EC2 and IAM twins as drop-in services are not built. The hyperscaler abstraction is designed, not shipped. Policy enforcement at the twin is the next step, not a feature anyone can download today. The business model is for somebody else to run. The prices are shapes, not quotes, and the assumptions are listed so they can be tested by the first operator. The value list is not finished. I said above that it is still a little invisible to a signer; the next version of this needs the two or three returns that close the loop for a specific register line. The conversation is reported from one side. The chief executive is not named and did not review this.
limits
If you run infrastructure, or you are on a hyperscaler and want to move without rewriting anything, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Something has changed in how I write, and I only noticed because I now take it for granted. When I record a voice memo for an article, I say things the way I remember them, in the order I remember them, with the instinct ahead of the evidence. Then the agent that writes with me goes and checks: the repositories, the commits, the briefs, the documentation, the web, and my own old writing. In the last eight articles, five of my claims were confirmed, five were corrected and two could not be found, and the articles say which. I first saw this with ChatGPT Deep Research, which launched in February 2025: eight days later, an essay I wrote with it about the O2 Platform cited three of my own blog posts from 2012, thirty-one times, as its evidence. It changes three things. Peer review used to come after publishing, from whoever on Twitter or LinkedIn noticed the mistake; now it comes before. Thinking out loud, which used to drive my teams mad as a plan moved from Monday to Friday, is now safe, because the record catches up with the instinct. And every article carries its provenance, so journalists, researchers and their agents can check it again, and rewrite it in their own voice.
What I said, and what the record said: the claims from the voice memos behind the last eight articles.
in-short

I say it as I remember it. The agent checks it against the record before anyone reads it. Five confirmed, five corrected, two not found. In the last eight articles, and each article says which. I first saw it with Deep Research. An essay of February 2025 cited my own 2012 posts as its evidence. Peer review moved before publishing. It used to be the crowd, afterwards. Thinking out loud is now safe. The instinct can go first; the evidence follows. It goes both ways. I correct the agent too, and the checking caught a bug in our own tools. Provenance for the next writer. Journalists and their agents can check it again, and rewrite it.
history

When I recorded the memo for From sending a file to sgit, I told the history of SG/Send the way I remembered it, and partway through I noticed something: I was not worrying about getting the sequence exactly right. I knew the agent would go through the repositories, the commits and the briefs, and map what actually happened. It did. It found that I had named the vault and the data room weeks before the features that I remembered leading to them, that the move to Git's model took about two weeks and not one, that it has been eight months and not nine, and that the first feature a paying user asked for went from proposal to code in 22 minutes. Where it could not find something, such as usage figures or where the idea for the sandbox came from, it said so: my recollection, marked as such.
history

That is now how every article on this site is written. The table above is the record of the last eight: five claims confirmed, five corrected, two that could not be found. Cedar's place in the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, which I half-remembered, was right; the Lambda I thought served this site was wrong; the Chainguard list I thought I had seen does not exist.
deep-research

The first time I noticed this was with ChatGPT Deep Research, which OpenAI released in February 2025: an agent that, in Wikipedia's words, "generates cited reports on a user-specified topic by autonomously browsing the web". I used it for many of the essays on diniscruz.ai, which replaces docs.diniscruz.ai and keeps every essay's path. I would record a voice memo, and it would go and find evidence for what I said.
deep-research

What fascinated me was where it found it. On 11 February 2025, eight days after the launch, I published an essay written with it on O2 Platform's MethodStreams, a static analysis engine I built in 2010. Of its 69 links, 31 point to three pages of my own old blog, two posts from June 2012 and the O2 Platform page. On topics where little had been published, such as the early days of my work on graphs, the evidence it found was often me, talking about it years before. The essay is signed "By Dinis Cruz and ChatGPT Deep Research", which was the right thing to say then and is the right thing to say now.
peer-review

Peer review moved before publishing: the memo, research, verdicts and article, with the old way as a dashed box. We used to get this from other people, afterwards. In the early days of Twitter, and still on LinkedIn, if you post something that is wrong, somebody usually tells you. There is even a law for it, named by Steven McGeady after Ward Cunningham: "the best way to get the right answer on the internet is not to ask a question; it's to post the wrong answer." It works, but it is slow, public and noisy, and it corrects what has already spread.
peer-review

Now the first review happens before publishing, against the record rather than against the crowd. It does not replace readers. It means that what they read already has its evidence attached: every link, a section on what the article does not claim, and where it came from. As Every link points back argued, an article should also know what came next and what corrected it; and the proof should be two clicks behind the claim.
thinking

This also solves something that used to drive my teams mad. I think fast and I think out loud. Someone would see a plan on Monday; by Wednesday it had moved; by Friday it was mature. To some people that looked as if I did not know what I was doing. A very good friend, who was very good at challenging me, used to ask: why didn't you tell me this an hour ago? And the honest answer was that I had not thought that far yet. I had an instinct about the direction, and the articulation came later. With this workflow, the instinct can go first. I can say the half-baked version, in the order it comes to me, because the evidence catches up before anyone else has to act on it. The memo is a draft of a thought; the article is the thought, checked.
both-ways

The checking is not one-way, and it should not be. In the last few days I corrected the agent: it had written pioneers and settlers for Simon Wardley's stages, and the names to use now are explorers, villagers and town planners. And the same habit of recomputing everything caught a bug in our own tools: while building the tokens hook, the agent found that this session's own status report had been counting each model response two or three times, and fixed it. I still read and validate every article; if something in it is not right, I say so, and it changes. And I learn from them: the references it finds are often ones I half-remembered from a book or a talk, and now I know exactly where they are.
provenance

I think a lot of what I write here should be rewritten by journalists, by researchers, by people who will put their own angle on it. What I can give them is the body of work and its provenance: what was said, what it rests on, what was corrected, and what is still only my recollection. Their agents should do the same thing on the other side: follow the links, check the claims, and disagree where the evidence says so. It is, in the end, a graph. Every checked article is a node with edges to its sources, and to the articles before it. The more is published this way, the more the next claim can be checked against, and the better the agent gets at finding the right evidence for the way I think. How much of this did I write? counted the record this draws on; Fractal Semantic Graphs is the shape it is growing into.
limits

The agent can be wrong too. Checking reduces errors; it does not remove them, which is why I still review. Not found is not false. It means the evidence was not found, and the article says so. The tally is small. Fourteen claims across eight articles, not a study. The Deep Research recollection is partly mine. The O2 essay and its links are checkable; the wider memory of it finding my writing on graphs is not counted here. If you want to check something on this site, or rewrite it in your own voice, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Abstract: A day of articles on deciding: what a real decision needs, why an agent that can go anywhere has no reason to stop, what happens when every mistake adds a rule, and one customer service agent built three ways to count which rules are only hoped for. The day in six pictures, one from each article
issue-body

Agency is not a yes sets out what anyone asked to decide actually needs, a person or an agent: options beyond yes, context in their own terms, time, somewhere to escalate, authority over the system that produced the request, and incentives that treat a wrong yes and a wrong no alike. The scale it builds has seven levels, the weakest dimension caps the whole decision, and its vault holds the scale. One line from it is worth keeping: Whatever you punish, you teach the other answer. Inside the agency scale vault: the levels, the decisions scored against them, and the law Knowing when to stop starts with people, security champions who had automated away whole classes of bug and then debated whether GUIDs were random enough, and comes to agents, who have the same problem by design: An entity that can go anywhere has no natural reason to stop anywhere.

A day of articles on deciding: what a real decision needs, why an agent that can go anywhere has no reason to stop, what happens when every mistake adds a rule, and one customer service agent built three ways to count which rules are only hoped for. Alongside, a live local story, a hospital outage nobody could check from home, kept as evidence while it was happening. Issue 12026-10-07 What it takes to let agents do real work for a business, from four sides: a team of agents running a small business, written up from the inside; the behaviour policy that says what each agent may do, and the business logic it turns out to hold; the desktops and permission prompts those agents need; and an open AI governance framework turned into a graph, a database and a walk down to EU law within a day of reading it.

Abstract: The thinking behind sgit stopped fitting on one site. It moved out to nineteen siblings on *.sgit.ai, what forced the split, what it cost, and why the index into them now starts with a question instead of a list. On 11 August this was one website. By 26 August there were twenty repositories, nineteen of them siblings on *.sgit.ai, and fifteen of those were created in the last five days of that fortnight. That is not a plan anybody wrote down. It is what happened when a body of work outgrew the shape it was being published in, and the interesting part is not the count, it is what the count did to the writing. The network directory. Nineteen siblings, entered through the question you arrived with.

A section is a promise that something is part of the thing it sits inside. That promise held while the material was about sgit. It stopped holding the moment the writing started answering questions that were not about sgit at all. You cannot deny a risk, you can only say how long you accept it is not a paragraph in a docs site about encrypted version control. Neither is maps are claims, not pictures, or open source is a strategy, not a charity, or the standard is the graph. Each of those is an argument that needs room, a reader who arrived for it, and, the part that matters most, its own version history.

That last one is the real forcing function. On one site, every change is one changelog. Nineteen arguments moving at different speeds through one release log produces a record nobody can read. Split them and each argument gets its own tags, its own release cadence, its own record of when it changed its mind. Three things, all of them real. Discovery got worse before it got better. Nineteen domains is not a menu, it is a problem. A reader who does not already know these sites cannot pick one from a list of names, nfrs.sgit.ai and issues-fs.sgit.ai mean nothing until you already know what they argue. Consistency became something you have to maintain rather than get for free. One site has one stylesheet by construction. Nineteen have one stylesheet by discipline, and discipline is the thing that quietly stops happening.

Cross-linking stopped being automatic. An internal link is cheap; a link between sites is a claim that the other site still says what you think it says. graphs.sgit.ai is the only sibling so far that links back, and the audit that added it found the same site pointing at sentinel.sgit.ai, which does not exist. The site is sg-sentinel.sgit.ai. One character of drift, and the link is dead. The directory used to be a list of cards. At four entries that was fine. At nineteen it is a thing you have to read before it helps you, which is the opposite of what an index is for. So it now starts from the question, not the inventory:

Seventeen lines like that, then five groups by area, then a table of all nineteen for anyone who would rather see everything at once. Three ways in, for three kinds of reader, someone with a problem, someone browsing a field, and someone auditing the whole set. One rule keeps it honest: every thesis on that page is the site's own words, quoted from its H1 or lede rather than summarised here. A summary drifts. A quotation either matches or is visibly wrong. None of this would be worth doing if each site were a bespoke build. They are not: same generator, same stylesheet, same release script, same validator, same rule that publishing is adding one file.

Adding the twentieth site to this index is writing one markdown file with a category and a one-line thesis. That is the whole ceremony. The property that makes a network of nineteen sites tractable is the same property that makes an unattended agent safe to run, two agents publishing on the same day touch two different files and cannot conflict. One of the nineteen is not published. skills.sgit.ai has a repository and a DNS record and nothing behind it. It is listed as not published yet, pointing at its repository, rather than quietly omitted, the same reason a missing tag is better than a missing page.

Most of these sites are arguments, not products. sg-sentinel.sgit.ai says NOT BUILT at the top of every page. risks.sgit.ai states that zero lines of code implement its model. wardley-maps.sgit.ai is marked PROPOSED. That is the house style working as intended: publish the argument before the thing exists, say precisely what it is worth, and let it be checked later. If you want the shortest version of what all of this is for, the introduction is one page. If you want the one site that answers your particular question, the directory is built to send you there.
