Abstract: For years my rule has been not to use a database: the file system is the database, and the Load, Extract, Transform, Save pipeline (LETS) loads state, caches it and writes it back as files you can version, diff and read. The second step has been creeping up on me, and the newsroom made it explicit: retire the back end too. The SGit Newsroom is now a content site for several audiences, with personas, a reading meter, a payment on-ramp, a newsroom of your own, encrypted sharing and databases that run in the reader's browser, and none of its application logic runs on a server. What is left on the server side is commodity: static hosting, a vault server that stores only ciphertext, a payment link, DNS and a build pipeline, with a sign-in provider next. The design came from a constraint: the vault server cannot see anything, by design, so everything that needs to see has to happen in the browser. It also came from a security call: the gaps a server would close do not match this site's readers, and the article lists them, with what a server would cost to close each one. The result scales without its complexity scaling, ships fast (114 releases between 1 and 11 October), and lines up with the things I care about: sovereignty, privacy, explainability and determinism. The article maps the architecture, the evolution, the accepted gaps, and how far I think the pattern can be pushed.

The SGit Newsroom's architecture. Every piece of application logic runs in the reader's browser. Everything on the server side is a commodity product that holds no logic of ours, and the one that holds the reader's data cannot read it. I have said for a long time that you do not need a database. The file system is a powerful database, and loading files, working on them and saving them back is simpler, cheaper and easier to reason about than running a database server. I still stand by that.

What I had not said out loud is the second step, which has been creeping up on me for months, in my constant focus on making things simple and removing variables until only the essential ones are left. More and more of what I build has no back end at all. The application is a set of files a browser downloads; the state lives in the browser or in an encrypted vault; and the servers involved are things I rent as products, not things I run. The newsroom, which in the last few days grew into a site with personas, a payment on-ramp and a private area for every reader, made the pattern explicit enough to write down.

And I think this is the next major pattern of my architecture. First I retired the database. Now I am retiring the back end. I look at everything through this lens now: why do I need that? Why do I need the Lambda function? Why do I need the EC2 instance? Why do I need the cost? This article is that pattern: where it came from, what the newsroom looks like when you draw it, why the security gaps it leaves are the right ones to leave, and how far I think it can be pushed. Step one was retiring the database. The file system is the database. The LETS pipeline (Load, Extract, Transform, Save) loads state, works on it, and saves every intermediate result as a file you can version, diff and read. Memory-FS and Issues-FS are libraries built on that idea.

Step two is retiring the back end. The application moves to the browser. The SGit Newsroom has personas, a reading meter, a payment on-ramp, a newsroom of your own, encrypted sharing, article versions, and SQL and SPARQL databases, and none of it runs on a server. This is not "no servers". It is no servers of mine with logic in them. What is left is commodity: static hosting, a vault server that stores ciphertext in S3, a payment link, DNS and a build pipeline, with a sign-in provider next. Each is a product. None holds application logic. A constraint designed it. The vault server cannot read anything, by design, because vaults are encrypted in the client. So anything that needs to read the reader's data has to happen where the key is: in the browser.

Security made a business call possible. The design leaves gaps, and they are written down: a reader can edit their own balance, start again in a private window, or credit themselves through an unprotected page. Every one of them changes a number only the cheater sees. Closing them would need a server, accounts and the complexity that comes with both. They do not match the threat, so they are accepted. It scales without its complexity scaling. The server side serves cached files and ciphertext. A hundred thousand readers add bandwidth, not moving parts. It ships fast. 114 releases of this site between 1 and 11 October; the reading meter went from an experiment to a working pay-on-demand design in seven releases in an afternoon. There is nothing to deploy but files.

It lines up with the rest. Sovereignty (the reader holds the data and the keys), privacy (the server cannot read it), explainability (the whole application is files you can read), determinism (the same files give the same result). The question now is how far it goes. A table at the end lists what still seems to need a server, and which commodity, or which change of design, covers each.
files

The first step is old for me, and I have written about it under several names. The clearest is LETS: Load, Extract, Transform, Save, a paper from May 2025 that sets out the pattern as a deliberate change to ETL: every stage reads files and writes files, every intermediate state is kept, and the file system, or an object store, is treated as a first-class database. Its principles are ephemerality, traceability, determinism, modularity, and what it calls minimum viable propagation. The projects behind it, MyFeeds.ai, The Cyber Boardroom and a library called Memory-FS, all run on it.
files

The point is not that files are clever. It is that a database server is a large, stateful, always-on thing that you have to provision, secure, back up, migrate and pay for, whether or not anyone is using it, and most of the time what it holds would be perfectly happy as files. Load the state, work on it in memory, save it back: that is a cache, a database and an audit trail in one, and git gives it history for free. In effect, it is loading state and caching it, and that works very well. Issues-FS, which keeps issues as JSON files inside git repositories, with pluggable storage for memory, disk, S3, SQLite or a zip file, is the same idea applied to an issue tracker.
files

The newsroom took that one step further in September. Databases with no server runs two real database engines, SQLite and a SPARQL store, compiled to WebAssembly, in the reader's browser, over the JSON files the Portugal section is built from. The build runs every example query and fails if one returns nothing. The database is the files; the engines are just readers.
backend

The second step is what this article is about, and it came out of a constraint I did not set out to have. Most of the state on this network now lives in sgit vaults. A vault is encrypted in the client before it leaves; the server stores ciphertext in S3 and never sees a key. Read keys are derived one way, and can be published. Append lanes let anything write an entry with one POST, readable only by the vault's owner. Vaults reference vaults. All of that is storage, and good storage, with one property that changes the design of everything built on it: by design, the server side cannot see anything.
backend

So a feature that needs to read the reader's data cannot run on the server. It has to run where the key is: in the browser. I did not choose a client-side architecture and then add encryption. Encryption came first, and the client-side architecture followed, because there was nowhere else for the logic to go. It is one of the clearest examples I have of a constraint doing the design work. And once the logic is in the browser, the question changes. It stops being "where on the server should this go?" and becomes "why would this need a server at all?" Why a Lambda function? Why an EC2 instance? Why a database, a queue, a cache cluster, a deployment pipeline for the back end, an on-call rota? For most of what the newsroom does, there is no good answer.
backend

How the pattern evolved: from removing the database, through files as the store of record and engines that read them in the browser, to removing the back end. Each step removed a moving part rather than adding one.
newsroom

It is worth listing what the SGit Newsroom does today, because the list is the argument. If you look at it as a pattern for a news organisation, it is, I would argue, remarkably powerful: a content site publishing for several audiences, where each reader can have a personalised experience and an area of their own, in a completely private way, with on-ramps for different payment models. The column on the right is where each part runs. What it does How Where it runs Publishes for several audiences, with a markdown twin of every page for agents A static build from markdown sources, with an index for agents Built in CI, served as files Lands a reader as someone: a CISO as a CISO Personas kept in a vault, opened with a published read key, followed or forked Browser Builds personas from what you read, several per reader Pay to keep your persona: a graph you can watch grow Browser
newsroom

Charges by the share of a page you read, never blocks, lets you go below zero SG Meter, a library any site can add Browser Lets you say what a page was worth, and that sets its price Pay after you read Browser Takes money A £5 Stripe payment link, no account, nothing renews; live since 11 October, a few hours after this article first said it was not set yet A payment provider's hosted page Gives every reader a newsroom of their own and a reading history Kept in the browser's own storage Browser Sends your reading to us, if you choose, for a front page designed for you Encrypted in the browser to a published public key, dropped into a write-only lane Browser, then a vault lane Takes newsletter sign-ups The same encrypted, write-only inbox Browser, then a vault lane Shows how each article changed Versions and diffs from git Built in CI
newsroom

Runs SQL and SPARQL over the site's own data SQLite and Oxigraph compiled to WebAssembly Browser Signs you in (next) Client-side OAuth with a provider Browser and the provider There is no account database, no session store, no API server and no back end to deploy. The things that would normally need one, payments and identity, are rented from companies whose product they are: the payment page now, and sign-in next. And the next pieces are already shaped to fit: a model in the client, with the reader's own key, and a persona that follows the reader to their phone and their agent, through a vault only they can open.
commodity

I want to be precise about the claim, because "serverless" has come to mean several things. I am not saying there are no servers. Of course there are. GitHub Pages serves the files. A vault server stores the ciphertext. A payment provider takes the money. A sign-in provider will vouch for an identity. DNS points at all of it, and GitHub Actions builds it. What there is not is a server of mine with application logic in it. Every one of those is a product, used as it comes out of the box, and from the point of view of the application each is a commodity: replaceable by another product that does the same thing. The vault server is the closest to custom, and even it is a generic store: in most cases the same design would work over read-only files in a storage bucket, with only the append lanes needing a small piece of server logic.
commodity

That is the Wardley-map view of it, which I used in Every mistake added a rule: complexity is a blob of custom-built components sitting where the world already has products and commodities. A back end is exactly that blob. Moving the application into the browser leaves the custom code in one place, written once and shipped as files, and everything around it on the commodity side of the map, where somebody else is paid to keep it running.
scale

The usual worry about client-side applications is that they do not scale. This is the opposite case. A back end's cost and complexity grow with its users: more instances, more database load, more caches, more failure modes. Here, a hundred thousand readers mean a hundred thousand browsers each doing their own work, against a server side that serves static files and ciphertext, both of which are cached at every layer, from the content delivery network to the browser itself. Vault content, fetched from git or from the vault server, can be cached locally too. The server side's work grows with bandwidth, which is the cheapest thing on the internet to buy. Its complexity does not grow at all. And browsers are not what they were. They run WebAssembly databases, Python, cryptography, local storage measured in gigabytes and, increasingly, models. Every year, more of what used to need a server fits in the tab.
security

This is the part I find most interesting, because it is where security experience changes the decision, rather than slowing it down. And there is an irony in it: I have spent my career in security, and that experience is exactly what lets me say, yes, let's deploy a system that has a bunch of security gaps, because the gaps do not match our audience. A design with no server has security gaps, and the honest thing is to list them. SG Meter's security model does that for the reading meter, and every gap in it is accepted: The gaps a client-side design leaves, as SG Meter's security model lists them, and what a server would cost to close each one. Every gap changes a number only the person exploiting it can see. A server would close them, and bring accounts, a database, webhooks and a deployment with it.
security

A reader can edit their balance in the browser's developer tools. It costs the site nothing it would otherwise have had. A reader can open a private window and start again at £5. They lose their history and their personas, which is what the meter is for. A reader can open the "topped up" page with an invented payment id and credit themselves £5. No money moves; the credit is a number on their own screen. A reader can clear their data to wipe a negative balance. There was never a debt. Agents read the markdown twins unmetered, by design, for now.
security

Each of these would be closed by a server: hold the balance server-side, require an account, verify the payment with a webhook from the payment provider to an endpoint you run. And each of those would bring back the thing I have spent years removing: a database of accounts, a server to run it on, a deployment, a store of personal data to protect, and a sign-up wall between the reader and the page. The meter's security model says it plainly: the topped-up page is unprotected because protecting it would need a server, and the one thing that server would protect is a number on the reader's own screen that unlocks nothing.
security

That is a security judgement, and I think it is the right one. The question in Who are you protecting against? is the right question here: the site's readers are not an adversary trying to steal reading, because nothing is behind a wall. What is protected is narrower, and it is protected well: the reader's own history, from other people. It never leaves their browser unless they send it, and then only encrypted to a key we publish. A bigger back end would have made the site more secure against threats it does not face, and less useful, less private and slower to change for the readers it has. The advantages of a more robust server side are far outweighed by the complexity, the deployment and the over-engineering it would bring. The meter's model also says what would change the call: if the balance ever unlocked something, the gaps would stop being acceptable, and that feature would get a signed receipt or a server, and not before.
security

There is a second half to this, which we only saw this week. When we ran five synthetic readers through the newsroom, none of them found a security problem. What they found was the same design seen from the reader's side: "credit can go below zero" reads as a debt to someone worried about money, and a top-up page that says the cart is simulated, while asking for money, leaves a careful reader unsure whether anything real would happen. The gaps are accepted for good security reasons; their cost lands in the words on the page, and that is where we are fixing them. The business value is the inverse of the usual one. We are not going to push readers into accounts to protect a number. We are going to make the site so useful, and so valuable, that they choose to pay, and choose to keep a vault.
openness

There is a reason I can keep removing pieces. When everything I build is open source, I do not have a moat I have to keep using. There is no part of the stack I built that I need to protect from being replaced, and I am usually the first one to try to replace it when something better appears. I wrote Memory-FS, and if the browser and a vault do its job for an application, the application stops using it. The meter's first version was written this week, and it has already been rewritten into a library. The habit is to ask of every component whether it is still earning its place, and open source removes the one bad reason to say yes: that I built it.
speed

Look at the amount of features we pushed in the last few days. Between 1 and 11 October, this site shipped 114 releases (the counts by day), 18 or 19 on the busiest days, alongside the newsroom moving to its own domain. The reading meter went from an experiment to a working pay-on-demand design in seven releases, in three hours and forty minutes, alongside seven other pieces of work: a meter, paying by depth, personas, versions, sharing your reading, and a rating that sets the price. Releases of sgit.ai per day, 1 to 11 October 2026, from the git log: 114 in eleven days. With no back end, a release is a set of files; there is no migration, no deployment of a server and nothing to roll back but a commit.
speed

That speed is not heroics. A release is a set of files. There is no schema migration, no server to deploy, no compatibility window between an old back end and a new front end, and rolling back is a commit. Every layer underneath, from sgit in March to the newsroom pipeline in September, became boring enough to build on, and the client-side design is what lets the next feature land on top of it in an afternoon.
speed

Speed has a cost, and it is worth being honest about it. When the newsroom moved to its own domain, 51 of the 527 figures in its articles did not come with it. Nothing failed in a way a server would have noticed: the pages were files, and they served. The synthetic readers found it, because one of them was reading a page where a picture should have been. Files make releases cheap; they also make it easy to ship something incomplete, which is why every release here ends by checking what is actually live.
principles

This design pattern completely ties in with the ideas I keep coming back to, and I do not think that is a coincidence. Sovereignty. The reader's data is in the reader's browser, and when it moves, it moves into a vault whose key the reader holds. The site could disappear, and the reader would keep everything they had. Privacy. Not as a policy, but as a property: the server cannot read what it does not have, and the vault server cannot read what it stores. Explainability. The whole application is files. Anyone can read what it does, the markdown twin of every page says what the page says, and the version history says what changed and when. Determinism. The same files give the same result. The build runs every query it publishes; a release is a hash.
principles

This is close to what the local-first software movement argued for in 2019: that you should own your data, in spite of the cloud. What the vaults add is the piece that makes it practical for a publication: shared, persistent storage that the operator cannot read, so that "client-side" does not have to mean "single-device".
push

That is the question I want to keep asking. Here is my current list of what still seems to need a server, and what covers each without one of mine. What seems to need a server What covers it Knowing a payment really happened, when the balance unlocks something A signed receipt from the payment provider, verified in the browser, or a tiny verification function as a commodity Identity Client-side OAuth with a provider; passkeys unlocking a vault key The same persona on the phone, the laptop and the agent A vault only the reader can open Readers writing to us Write-only append lanes, encrypted to a published key Models In the client, with the reader's own key, or a small local model Search over the site A static index the browser loads, or the graph the five readers build Rate limits and abuse The commodity layer in front of the static host
push

Things that must be secret from the reader The one real limit: anything the reader must not hold cannot live in the reader's browser The last row is the honest boundary. A secret that must be kept from the person using the application, such as a shared API key, or a price that must not be editable because it unlocks something, cannot live in the browser. For each of those, the choice is between a signed artefact the browser can verify and a small, commodity function. For everything else, I keep finding that the browser and a vault are enough.
limits

Not that servers are bad. Some applications need shared, live, authoritative state: a trading system, a multiplayer game, a bank's ledger. This pattern is for applications where each user's state is theirs. Not that the gaps are free. They are accepted because of who reads this site, and what the meter protects. A different site, with a different threat, would make a different call, and the security model says what would change ours. Not that it is finished. Sign-in, cross-device personas, a model in the client and signed receipts are next, not done.
next

A model in the client, with the reader's own key, so the newsroom can answer questions about what it publishes without a back end of ours. Personas that follow the reader to every device, and to their agent, through a vault only the reader can open. A signed receipt for payments, so that a balance could one day unlock something without a server holding it. The pattern as a template: the newsroom's architecture packaged so that another publication, or any content site, can start from it. First the database went, and the work got simpler. Now the back end is going, and the work is getting faster. I do not know yet where the pattern stops, which is exactly why it is worth pushing. If you are building something where each user's data should be theirs, and you want to see how far it goes without a back end, let's talk: agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Two voice memos of mine. I asked an agent in a separate Claude session to turn them into this article, with its figures and data, and to check every feature against the newsroom's and this site's own pages and repositories; this site's agent then rewrote it in the voice of this site, checked two things the draft could not confirm, and corrected them: the payment link was not set yet (the live top-up page was still the simulated cart; it went live later the same day, and the article now says so), and client-side sign-in is next, not shipped. The argument is mine, and so is the editorial responsibility. The release counts are from this site's git log as of 11 October 2026, counted before this release; the accepted gaps are SG Meter's security model, paraphrased. There is no account database, no session store, no API server and no back end to deploy. The things that would normally need one, payments and identity, are rented from companies whose product they are: the payment page as soon as the link is set, and sign-in next. And the next pieces are already shaped to fit: a model in the client, with the reader's own key, and a persona that follows the reader to their phone and their agent, through a vault only they can open.
articles/versions/no-server-by-design/v1.1.0.html
commodity

I want to be precise about the claim, because "serverless" has come to mean several things. I am not saying there are no servers. Of course there are. GitHub Pages serves the files. A vault server stores the ciphertext. A payment provider will take the money. A sign-in provider will vouch for an identity. DNS points at all of it, and GitHub Actions builds it.
articles/versions/no-server-by-design/v1.1.0.html
security

That is a security judgement, and I think it is the right one. The question in Who are you protecting against? is the right question here: the site's readers are not an adversary trying to steal reading, because nothing is behind a wall. What is protected is narrower, and it is protected well: the reader's own history, from other people. It never leaves their browser unless they send it, and then only encrypted to a key we publish. A bigger back end would have made the site more secure against threats it does not face, and less useful, less private and slower to change for the readers it has. The advantages of a more robust server side are massively outweighed by the complexity, the deployment and the over-engineering it would bring. The meter's model also says what would change the call: if the balance ever unlocked something, the gaps would stop being acceptable, and that feature would get a signed receipt or a server, and not before.

Abstract: Today I spent most of the day dictating voice memos and improving the workflow that turns them into articles, and I would argue I was working for RiskMandate the whole time. This is the meta-strategy behind that. Progress does not go in a straight line, so "focus on one thing only" is good advice that assumes something false. I do focus, with undivided attention, on whichever thing has the highest leverage, and that is the one with users and feedback loops. RiskMandate is where the commercial opportunity is, and its oldest technical problem, where to keep the master vault's key, had resisted six months of attempts that kept failing my simplicity test. The newsroom solved it in two days, because the newsroom had the momentum to need it. The newsroom is also solving the agentic follow-up workflows RiskMandate will need, and becoming the public example of an Agent Behaviour Policy and a licence to operate that customer work can never be. And it has a history: The Cyber Boardroom, where I learned what personas and customised output are worth and paused because it needed somewhere to keep confidential data; MyFeeds, where I built personalised feeds on semantic graphs, found the industry silent and paused again; the writing from 2025 that the newsroom now stands on. I am going back to publishers with an end-to-end example. If it does not land in 2026, I will try in 2027, and the thinking will still be there, because it is open source.

Three projects, one path that is not a straight line. The Cyber Boardroom learned what personas are worth and paused for want of a data store; MyFeeds built personalised feeds on semantic graphs and paused when the industry was silent; the writing stayed. The newsroom, where the energy is now, solved RiskMandate's master vault in two days, and is becoming its public example. Dashed boxes are next, and already unblocked.
in-short

Progress is not a straight line. "Focus on one thing only" is good advice that assumes the shortest path to a goal runs through that goal. It often does not. I do focus, on the place of highest leverage. Undivided attention, on one thing at a time, chosen because it has users and feedback loops now. The last article on this is the method; this one is the case. The newsroom solved RiskMandate's oldest problem. Where to keep the master vault's key had resisted six months of attempts that kept failing my simplicity test. The newsroom needed it badly enough to solve it, and solved it in two days. RiskMandate did not have the momentum to need it. Its engagements are still close to forward-deployed engineering, so handing users their vault keys works at today's volumes. My instinct, when there is not enough momentum to solve a problem, is not to solve it.
in-short

The newsroom is also building RiskMandate's workflows and its public example. Agentic follow-ups, outreach, a publishing pipeline: a CRM, in effect. And an ecosystem that runs on behaviour policies in the open, which customer work can never show. The thinking is never wasted. The Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds paused, and what they taught is in everything the newsroom does. Because it was open and written down, it was there when the moment came.
better

My measure is always the same question: am I getting better? Are we discovering new things, new capabilities, and discovering them at the right altitude, the one that leads to other things? Right now I feel we are in a really good spot, and most of the energy has been going into the newsroom: the articles, the voice memos, the workflow that turns a memo into a published piece with its graph, its figures and its release. Someone looking at the commit log would say I am focused on the newsroom. I would say I am focused on RiskMandate, and the commit log is the more interesting half of the story.
better

RiskMandate is where most of the commercial opportunity is. It is where the interest is, and where we are starting to get good engagement. And it has a number of problems I need to solve technically for it to work at scale. So the obvious advice is: focus on that, and only that. I agree with the principle and disagree with the assumption under it, which is that things move in a straight line, and that the shortest path to solving RiskMandate's problems runs through RiskMandate.
vault

The clearest example is the master vault. Every user, in RiskMandate and in a lot of other places in my infrastructure, needs a vault of their own, and that vault needs a key. Where that key lives, so that the user can open their vault on any device without us holding it, has been a problem for about six months. I tried several ways to solve it. There is a trail of proofs of concept that I worked on for a while and then stopped, not because they did not work but because they did not pass the simplicity test I have learned to trust. Each one was getting too complicated, and complicated is how security designs fail.
vault

Then, in the last couple of days, we solved it. A passkey's PRF output computes a door; the door holds the master vault's key; there is a door per path, because a phone over QR gives different bytes from the device's own passkey; and there is no server of ours in the chain. The passkey opens the vault is the design, corrected by a lab, and The vault is live is the evening it went from design to a reader's vault on newsroom.sgit.ai. It was built for the newsroom. It applies everywhere else, starting with RiskMandate. So I could argue that while I was working on the newsroom, I was working on RiskMandate. That is the non-linear sequence, and it is not an accident.
momentum

The rule I follow is to always follow the users, even when the user is me, and to follow the feedback loops: do the thing that gets a reaction straight away. On that rule, RiskMandate and the newsroom are in very different places. RiskMandate's traction is real, and it is still very connected to forward-deployed engineering: a lot of the work is direct, customised, done with the customer. We have not reached the point where people serve themselves from the website. We will, and we are not there yet. That means we can get away without per-user vaults. The volumes are not large, so we give users their vault keys, which works. There is not enough momentum to solve that problem, and my instinct when there is not enough momentum is: do not solve it. A problem solved before anybody needs it is solved in the abstract, and abstract solutions are where the complexity creeps in.
momentum

The newsroom is the opposite. It has readers on every device I own, it has a reading meter, personas, an encrypted share and a pay-after-you-read model that only work if every reader has a vault that follows them. I miss it, so it is working is the moment I noticed I was using it every day and it was failing me in a way I could feel. That is momentum, and momentum is what makes a hard problem solvable in two days, because every attempt gets tested by somebody who wants it to work.
workflow

The master vault is the clearest case, and not the only one. The newsroom has forced me to improve the agentic workflow itself: agents that follow up people, follow up threads, draft, publish, and keep a record. RiskMandate has reasons to email users and to follow them up, but not at volumes that would push the workflow to mature. The newsroom does, because it is finally something that adds value to a lot of people, and the outreach I want to do for it intersects closely with RiskMandate's audience. A very effective newsroom is, underneath, a very effective CRM and a very effective publishing workflow, which is exactly what RiskMandate needs.
workflow

And it solves a problem RiskMandate will have that I did not see coming until today. RiskMandate sells Agent Behaviour Policies and licences to operate for agents. The hardest part of selling them is showing them in action, because as we work with customers, most of those examples cannot be shared. The ecosystem around the newsroom, this site's agents, their behaviour policy, the status report at the end of every few answers, the leak scan before every commit, the releases with their logs, is the best public example we have of a behaviour policy running in practice. The mandate stack described it; the newsroom is where it is under real load every day. That is a nice problem to have.
history

The newsroom also has a history, and the history is the best evidence I have that the thinking is never wasted. I have been interested in publishing for as long as I have been writing, which is a long time, from the books I put on Leanpub to the writing on docs.diniscruz.ai. In particular I have always cared about the idea that people should be paid for creating content. I create content; I love ideas and connecting them; I think I am good at it.
history

The Cyber Boardroom came first. It was a GenAI platform to help boards and executives with cyber security, with an advisor called Athena, and it is where I discovered the value of customisation, of personas and of shaping the output to the person reading it. You can draw a direct line from those experiments to the personas in RiskMandate and in the newsroom today. We shipped real things. What it needed and did not have was an environment to store data: nobody wants to put confidential board material into an environment somebody else runs, and although I solved the deployment so it could run anywhere, it was a hard sell. Ironically, what The Cyber Boardroom needed is what I eventually built as sgit. That circle is closing, and as far as I can see the market is still there.
history

It also needed data feeds. It was open source, so I could pivot, and I did: into MyFeeds, customised data feeds, which will sound familiar. Take the news, build semantic graphs of it, and personalise it from the article all the way to the reader's persona. That is when I went deep on semantic graphs, and when I realised that language models were how graphs could scale. I built a good proof of concept, with graphs of the user and graphs of the personas. Then I took it to the industry and there was silence. Nobody I reached out to had momentum for it. I realised it needed micropayments, paying for the graph and paying the people who made the content, and the industry was not there; it is not fully there today. I was not big enough to move an industry that was not yet excited about semantic graphs, about micropayments, about paying the people who write. And I could not show it working end to end, because I did not have the technology yet, and at best the sources had RSS feeds, with licensing questions I could not answer from where I stood. So I paused it.
history

What stayed was the thinking. The pieces I wrote in 2025 on monetising trust and knowledge, on fact provenance and on micro and nano payments are the foundations the newsroom now stands on. The future of news is the story vault, not the paywall and Pay after you read are those pieces, built. And the company I created in Portugal for MyFeeds is being closed, because running a company with little revenue in Portugal is expensive in a way it is not in England; I am looking at Lithuania for the next one, for its digital advantages, which is a small instance of this afternoon's argument.
back

The difference now is that it is practical. I can go back, even to people I spoke to a year ago, with an end-to-end example: content, semantic graphs, a reading meter, personas, micropayments, a vault per reader, all running, all open source. A year ago I was, in hindsight, asking them to do too much: I had an idea and a proof of concept, and they would have had to build the rest. Now the rest exists, and the feedback from the people I am reaching out to is already much better. I am about to do another, larger round of outreach to publishers and to people in the news industry.
back

If it works, good. If it does not, I will try again in 2027. Everything is open source; anybody can take it and run with it, and I know there is attrition even when something is free. But more importantly, I now know I do not need it to work in the news industry for the work to have been worth it, because the newsroom is already making RiskMandate better. I am solving RiskMandate's problems in a context with active energy, active development and active feedback loops, which is the thing that matters most and the thing RiskMandate on its own cannot give me yet.
thinking

The last point is about why I write all this down. I do my best thinking when I am faced with a real problem, and the memos and the materials are how that thinking survives. The newsroom has already benefited from five or ten articles I wrote a year ago, articles I wrote when there was no way to build what they described. If the publisher conversations do not find momentum now, I can come back in six months and the thinking will already be done, and the intersection between the newsroom and RiskMandate will be even tighter.
thinking

That is the power of doing this in the open. I can run the experiments, leave the assets, pause without losing anything, and pick up where I left off when the moment comes. Focus, for me, is undivided attention on the place of highest leverage. It is not the same thing as working on only one product, and the difference is the whole of this article.
limits

The six months and the two days are my account. The design, the lab and the evening it went live are in the linked articles; the earlier attempts are not published. RiskMandate's traction is described, not measured here. Engagements, volumes and the move to self-service are my reading of where it is. The Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds are summarised from memory. The links are to what is public; the proofs of concept are not all published. The company move is a consideration, not a decision. Lithuania is being looked at; nothing has been registered. This is one person's method. It works for me because I write things down and work in the open; it may not transfer to a team that does neither. If you are in the news industry and want to see the end-to-end example, or you are building on RiskMandate and want to see a behaviour policy running in public, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: I no longer program in one place. I brief in a voice memo while walking, review a draft by voice, check the preview on my phone, test on the computer, read the pull request on GitHub, and pick the same work up on an iPad. Retail has a word for this. In 2011 Darrell Rigby wrote in Harvard Business Review that successful companies would engage customers through omnichannel retailing, and the difference that made the word stick is the one that matters here: multichannel means separate channels, each with its own copy of the work; omnichannel means every channel reads and writes one shared state. For programming, that state is git, vaults, briefs and graphs. This site is the worked example: in three days, one agent session took 54 messages from me, 10 of them voice memos, and turned them into 40 releases, 36 articles and 87 figures, with research, hooks, tests and other agents working in the same repository. It works at every stage of a Wardley map, for explorers, villagers and town planners, and at every altitude, from intent down to the code, including code review. It is already how a new generation of developers and founders works. And it breaks in known ways, which the shared state is there to fix.
Multichannel and omnichannel programming: separate copies of the work on the left, one shared state on the right.
in-short

I no longer program in one place. Voice, chat, phone, IDE, pull request, preview, vault. Multichannel is not the point. Omnichannel is: every channel shares one state. The shared state is git, vaults, briefs and graphs. That is what makes a channel switch cheap. This site is the worked example. 54 messages in, 40 releases out, in three days, counted from the record. Reviewing is a channel too. Code review by voice, as a graph, from the story down to the call. It works at every stage. Explorers, villagers and town planners each use every channel, at every altitude. It is already normal. For a new generation of developers and founders, this is simply how software is made. It breaks in known ways. Fragmentation, secrets in the wrong place, lost context; the shared state is the fix.
word

Omnichannel is a retail word. Darrell Rigby put it into Harvard Business Review in December 2011, in The Future of Shopping: "Successful companies will engage customers through "omnichannel" retailing: a mashup of digital and physical experiences." The distinction that made the word useful is the one I would like to borrow. A multichannel retailer has a shop, a website and a catalogue, each with its own stock, prices and customer record. An omnichannel retailer has one customer, one basket and one stock, and the channels are just ways in.
word

I did not find the phrase "omnichannel programming" used this way before, so I am using it on purpose. Programming has become multichannel almost by accident: there is a chat, an IDE, a phone app, a pull request, a preview, each good on its own. What makes it omnichannel is that every one of them reads and writes the same state, so that I can start something in one and finish it in another without carrying the context in my head.
looks

A typical day now: I record a voice memo on a walk, and it becomes a brief. An agent works on it in the cloud, in a repository, and pushes. I look at the result on my phone, in the live site or in a preview, and reply by voice with what to change. On the computer I run the tests or open the page in a browser. On GitHub I read the diff. On an iPad, in a meeting, I check the same article again. A reader's own agent reads the same articles, through the site's llms.txt. And when I want to try something without risk, a vault holds the experiment, with its own history, and a website renders it.
looks

None of these channels is new. Claude Code itself went to the web and the iOS app on 20 October 2025, "so developers can explore coding with Claude on the go". What is new is that I no longer notice the switch, because nothing has to be copied across.
counted

One session, many channels: what this newsroom session used from 13 to 15 October 2026, around one shared state. This site is written this way, so it can be counted. In the three days from 13 to 15 October 2026, the agent session that writes it took 54 messages from me. Ten were voice memos transcribed by Otter; five were images; others were links to sites and vaults to review, corrections, and an access key so that it could make a vault of its own. Out of that came 40 releases of this site, 36 new articles and 87 figures, each one live within minutes of its push.
counted

Around the shared state, the other channels did their work. For research, the session fetched 75 pages, ran 23 web searches, started 33 background agents and attached 6 more repositories to read their commits and briefs. For control, a behaviour policy is re-read after every summary, hooks run on every prompt and every stop, a leak scan checks every commit, and a validator and 16 test suites run before every push. For output, it sent me 7 files, kept its working material in a vault whose keys it handed to me, rendered previews in a browser, and built a talk player. And it was not alone: in the same repository, on the same days, other agent sessions made 15 releases of their own, the wire, the design and the newsletter, and the work met in git. The most useful thing about the counting is that it was possible. Every channel left its trace in the same place.
review

The part I underestimated is review. I used to think of review as the one place where I had to sit down at a screen and read. It is not any more. I review a draft by voice, saying what is wrong in the order I notice it, and the agent checks my memory against the record before anything changes. I review code the same way: not line by line, but as a graph.
review

Code review as a fractal semantic graph argued that source code is already a graph with layers, "stories, flows, components, classes, methods and calls", and that the review should read every layer of it. That makes the review programmatic: the graph is generated, and I ask questions of it. The secrets site does the same thing: its review graph joins the brief, from the top, to the code, from the bottom, and when I asked for a look at secrets.sgit.ai, its reality page could say at once that 42 claims were shipped and the app itself was still proposed. Connecting the source code all the way up to the use case is another channel: it is how I read code without reading it.
review

Interfaces are a channel in the same way. Custom UIs are not the exception made the case that a page made for one moment is now normal: a filter for one question, a to-do list with a place to drop the missing files, a player for one short talk. Each one is a new way into the same state, built when it is needed and thrown away or kept as the work decides.
stages

Omnichannel at every stage of a Wardley map: explorers, villagers and town planners, at every altitude. It would be easy to say this is how explorers work, and that the serious work happens elsewhere. It is not. Simon Wardley's three kinds of people, explorers, villagers and town planners, each use every channel, and at every altitude.
stages

Explorers discover. For them the voice memo is the half-formed idea, the vault is the experiment that can fail safely, and the one-off page is the prototype. Villagers harden what was found. For them voice is the review of a draft, the interface is a page reused with tests and a version, and the code review is the graph, read from the story down to the call. Town planners make it scale. For them the voice is a policy written once and checked on every session, the code is held by CI gates, the validator and the leak scan, and every push is verified live. The same is true of evidence: a claim from memory for the explorer, a claim checked against commits and sources for the villager, provenance on every article for the town planner.
stages
Go slow to go fast described this site's own move from an explorer project to a villager one. What did not change in that move was the channels. What changed was what each channel was used for.
generation

For a lot of people starting now, none of this is a change. It is simply what programming is. In the 2025 Stack Overflow survey, "84% of respondents are using or planning to use AI tools in their development process", and about half of professional developers use them every day. In March 2025, Y Combinator's Jared Friedman said that "A quarter of the W25 startup batch have 95% of their codebases generated by AI", as TechCrunch reported. The developers and founders behind those numbers did not learn to program at one desk and then add channels. They brief from a phone, review in a chat, ship from a browser tab, and expect the work to be wherever they are. The same survey also shows the other side: more developers distrust the accuracy of AI tools than trust it, 46% against 33%. That is the right instinct, and it is why the shared state matters more than any one channel.
breaks

Omnichannel work fails in three predictable ways. Fragmentation. A decision made in a chat, a correction made by voice, a fix pushed from a phone: if any of them lives only in its channel, the next channel does not know. The fix is that every channel writes to the shared state, and nothing counts until it is there. Secrets in the wrong place. More channels means more places a key can be pasted. This is why handing secrets to agents needs its own design, and why this session runs a leak scan before every commit. Lost context. Long sessions get summarised, and summaries drop things. The fix is the same: the rules live in a file that is re-read after every summary, and a status report at the end of the turn shows they are still being followed. If it stops appearing, something has fallen out.
computing

I think this goes beyond programming. Once the state is shared and the channels are just ways in, the same pattern applies to writing, to reviewing a company's risks, to running a talk: omnichannel computing. The homepage is a vault proposed one small example: a homepage where every edition is a commit, so the same object is a page to read, a history to compare and a folder to clone, depending on which way you come in. Vaults are the shared state that makes that possible without a server that can read the data.
limits

The counts are one session. Three days, one agent session, one site; not a study. The term is mine. I did not find "omnichannel programming" in prior use in this sense. The survey figures are from 2025. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey and a YC statement of March 2025. Not every channel is equal. Some work still needs a screen and a keyboard, and some reviews still need a person reading line by line. If you work like this, or want to, and want to compare notes, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Reviews on the record gave this site's articles a second reader. The next step is to let the people who know a subject go on the record about an article: I support this, I do not, and here is why, or use something else instead. Not a comments section, which many news sites have closed, but a professional opinion, signed with the person's own key and kept with the article, which they can later withdraw. The value is in the disagreement: an expert should not agree with everything, and sometimes the challenge is as interesting as the article, because that is where the facts get tested. Identity comes in levels, from an anonymous tap to a key bound to a domain and backed by a track record, and the pieces exist: Bluesky's domain handles, Mastodon's links back, did:web, signed commits. So does the precedent for paying for opinions: open peer review publishes signed reviews, and Biology Open, which pays reviewers £220, cut its time to a first decision from 37.7 to 5.5 working days. I think readers who rate an opinion as insightful should be able to pay for it, and the expert should get a share; and when an article that earns money is built from other people's ideas, they should get a share of that too. The research on signed comments is more mixed than people assume: real names did not make comments better in the largest study, stable identities did. So the case for signing is accountability and payment, not civility. This maps what exists here, what is missing, and what to build.
Going on the record: the levels of identity on the left, and a signed opinion on the record on the right.
in-short

Not comments; opinions on the record. A position on an article, with reasons, signed by the person who holds it. Disagreement is the point. An expert should not agree with everything; the challenge is where facts get tested. Identity comes in levels. From an anonymous tap to a key bound to a domain and a track record. The pieces exist. Domain handles, links back, did:web, signed commits; each proves less than people assume. Science already publishes signed reviews, and some journals pay for them. Biology Open pays £220 a review. Readers should be able to pay for an opinion. And the expert should get a share. Ideas should get a share too. If an article that earns money is built from someone's idea, they are paid. Signing is for accountability and payment, not civility. The research on real names is mixed.
not-comments

News sites have been closing comment sections for more than a decade. Reuters did it in 2014; NPR in 2016, when it counted about 19,400 active commenters against millions of readers on social media; the Press Democrat's group on 4 September 2025. I understand why. A comments section asks anyone to say anything, and the people with the most to say are rarely the people with the most to add. What I have in mind is something else. In reviews on the record, every article here gets reviewed against published criteria, by other models, by me and by the desk, and every review is a record kept with the article. The next step is to open that record to the people who know the subject: someone who has spent twenty years on supply-chain security, or who runs a newsroom, or who wrote the standard the article discusses. Not to comment, but to go on the record with a professional opinion.
record

An opinion on the record is short and structured: A position. I support this. I do not support this. I partly support it. Something else should be used instead. The reasons, in the expert's own words, and the evidence, linked. Which text of the article it is about, the same way a review is, so a later correction does not silently change what they agreed with. A signature, by the expert's own key, so that the record says who holds this opinion and nobody else can change it. It is theirs to withdraw. An expert can change their mind, and the page then stops showing the opinion; the record keeps a signed note that there was one and that its author withdrew it, so nobody can claim later that it was never there, or that it still stands.
record

The part I care most about is that they should not agree. An expert who agrees with everything adds a name, not a view. The useful opinion comes from their own point of view: this is right for large companies and wrong for small ones; this was tried in 2019 and here is why it failed; this is the right idea with the wrong tool. Sometimes the challenge is as interesting as the article itself, because that is when everyone zooms in on the facts. The article can then change to reflect it, with the change on the record, or the challenge becomes a new article of its own.
levels

Going on the record only means something if we know whose record it is. I think of identity here in levels, each allowing more: Anonymous. A tap on a piece, through the append lane in the editor's channel. Counts as a signal, never as an opinion. An account. A reader with a passkey and a vault, which this site already runs. The same person over time, but nobody knows who. A key pair. The reader signs what they send with a private key only they hold. The design is in RFC-0001; the inbox already seals messages to a reader's public key, and signing is the other half. A key bound to a name people know. A domain they control, a public profile, a code repository. A key with a track record. Opinions that turned out right or wrong over time, on the record, which is what trust as a service calls calibrating weight by outcomes rather than by rank.
levels

Level 4 is where the existing pieces are, and each proves less than people assume. Bluesky lets anyone use their own domain as their handle by adding a DNS TXT record, and said in April 2025 that more than 270,000 accounts had done so. Mastodon shows a green check when your website links back to your profile. did:web resolves an identifier to a document on your domain, and is still a community draft, not a W3C standard. GitHub marks signed commits as verified and now keeps them verified after a key is rotated. All of these prove that one key or account controls one domain or account. None of them proves who the person is; that comes from the domain being one people already associate with them, and from more than one proof agreeing.
levels

And there is a warning in the history. Keybase did exactly this, signed proofs across accounts and domains, and joined Zoom in May 2020 with "no specific plans for the Keybase app yet". An identity layer owned by one company lasts as long as that company wants it to. Here, the proofs should live where the person controls them: their domain, their key, their vault.
science

Scientific publishing has been working on signed, public, sometimes paid reviews for years, and it is the closest precedent I know of. Signed and public. F1000Research publishes reviewer names and full reports with the article, beside the authors' responses. eLife stopped making accept or reject decisions and publishes every reviewed paper with public reviews and an assessment. PeerJ made the review history mandatory from February 2023, and reviewers can choose to sign. Paid. Biology Open, from the Company of Biologists, pays reviewers £220 a manuscript; in its pilot, time to a first decision fell from 37.7 to 5.5 working days and the share of invitations accepted rose from 23% to 67%. The Unjournal pays evaluators about $350 and publishes the evaluations.
science

And the honest counterpoint. Critical Care Medicine offered $250 a review in a trial: acceptance rose a little, reviews came about a day faster, editors saw no difference in quality, and the journal said it could not afford to continue. Paying makes reviews faster and more willing; it does not by itself make them better. On the open web, X's Community Notes shows a note only when raters who usually disagree both find it helpful, which is a good idea for deciding what to show. Its note writers are not paid.
paying

The reading meter on this site already lets the reader decide what a page was worth: pay after you read, and the rating sets the price. The same mechanism works for an opinion. A reader who marks an expert's opinion as insightful, or as a good analysis, pays a little for it, and most of that goes to the expert. That creates the incentive I would like on both sides. The reader is paying for more of the analysis they value. The expert is paid to review properly, and only when readers find it worth paying for, which rewards a careful disagreement more than a quick agreement. I could not find a news platform that pays experts for opinions on its articles today; the nearest are Medium, which counts replies and highlights in what it pays its authors, and the paid reviewers in science.
share

The same logic goes further. If an article here earns money, and a good part of it came from someone else's opinion, or from an idea three or four people put on the record, then they should get a share of what it earns. It is their idea we are writing about.
share

That used to be impossible to work out. It is less so when everything is on the record: the graph of an article names its sources and its claims, the opinions are signed records, and the release history says which change came from which finding. This site's page on paying the fact creator argues that provenance is what makes the value behind a fact payable, and the AI industry is starting to agree, at the level of publishers: Perplexity's Comet Plus sends 80% of its revenue to publishers, and ProRata's Gist splits ad revenue 50/50 with the publishers whose content an answer used. What I am proposing is the same idea at the level of a person and an idea.
evidence

I assumed it would, and the research is more mixed than that. Santana's 2014 study of newspaper comment boards, as the University of Houston reported it, "found a significant correlation between anonymity and civility": anonymous comments were less civil. Rost, Stahel and Frey, looking at 532,197 comments on German petitions in 2016, found non-anonymous commenters were more aggressive, not less. Moore and colleagues, across 45 million HuffPost comments, found the quality of argument rose when stable, authenticated pseudonyms were required and fell after the switch to Facebook real names. South Korea's real-name law cut malicious comments only from 13.9% to about 13%, and its Constitutional Court struck the law down in 2012.
evidence

So I do not think the case for signing is that it makes people polite. It is that a signed opinion is accountable, it can be paid, and it builds a track record over time. And a stable key may matter more than a name: a key is a stable identity first, and a name is something it can be bound to, at level 4, when the person wants their name on it.
build

What this site already has: reviews on the record, with a record format that already has a reader kind; the reader's passkey and vault; an inbox that seals messages to a reader's public key; the reading meter, with ratings and payment; and every article's text identified by a hash. What it would take: A reader key pair, made in the reader's browser, kept in their vault, used to sign what they send. A proof page: the reader shows their public key on a domain they control, or in a DNS record, and the newsroom checks it and records the check. An opinion record: the review record with a position, signed, and a signed withdrawal. On the page: opinions beside the reviews, with the author's level, the position, the reasons and the newsroom's answer.
build
Payment: a rating on an opinion that moves money from the reader's balance to the expert, and a share of an article's revenue to the people whose recorded ideas it used.
limits

None of the opinion records, proofs or payments to experts is built. The reviews, the passkey vault, the inbox and the meter are. A domain proves control, not identity. Level 4 is a name people already associate with a domain, and more than one proof agreeing. Paying does not make opinions better. In science it made reviews faster and more willing; quality is the job of the criteria and the readers. Revenue shares for ideas are a proposal. How to measure how much of an article came from whose idea is an open question. The research on identity and civility is mixed, and most of it is about comments, not expert opinions. Some figures are the organisations' own. Bluesky's count, Biology Open's pilot, Perplexity's and ProRata's shares. If you are an expert and would like to be among the first to go on the record on an article here, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The articles on this site are deep and carry their evidence, and that makes them long and hard to consume. The answer tried here is not shorter articles. It is to keep writing the article first, as prose, because writing is how the argument is found, and then to send five readers through it afterwards, each an agent with a defined role. Two build the platform: a Librarian that catalogues every fact, claim, number, question and source with the sentence it came from, and a Cartographer that turns the catalogues into an ontology at three altitudes and draws the maps. Three write for a person: a Historian that says what the article added and where it sits in the arc, an Explainer that says it in two minutes, and a Storyteller that tells it as a deck. We ran it on the five articles about agent behaviour policies published between 7 and 10 October: 662 items catalogued, 32 problems flagged in published articles, 45 concepts, nine maps, five decks, and one new concept in the most recent article. The views are now on those five articles, and the whole run is in a vault you can open.

One article, five readers. The same piece read again after it was written: the Librarian's catalogue, the Cartographer's map, the Historian's place in the arc, the Explainer's two minutes and the Storyteller's deck. The workflow behind the articles on this site has settled into something I am happy with. I record a voice memo, a session turns it into an article with the evidence attached, and another session reviews it. From a technical and a research point of view the articles are where I want them: they argue one thing, they carry their sources and figures, and more and more often there is a vault behind them with the data.

The problem is that they are hard to consume. The five used in this article run from 2,200 to 5,100 words, about 17,100 in all. It is easy to lose the argument in the length, and easy for someone with five minutes never to start. This article is about one way to fix that without making the articles worse, and the simulation that tested it. Keep writing the article first. Writing is how the argument is found. The prose, with its evidence, is the source; everything else is extracted from it afterwards. Then send readers through it. Five agents, each with a role: a Librarian, a Cartographer, a Historian, an Explainer and a Storyteller. None rewrites the article, and none adds a claim it does not make.

Two build the platform, three write for a person. The Librarian and the Cartographer turn the article into a graph: every item anchored to its sentence, and concepts connected at three altitudes. The other three read that graph and the article, and write the short views. We ran it on five articles. 662 items catalogued, every anchor checked verbatim by script; 32 problems flagged in published articles; 45 concepts and 78 edges; nine maps; five decks; five two-minute versions; one arc. The platform readers turned out to be fact-checkers. A total that does not add up, a list of "twelve" that has ten items, a sentence about the military the article never supports. Nobody asked them to check; cataloguing everything with its anchor made the gaps visible. The Historian measured what each article added. New concepts across the five fall 17, 11, 5, 11, 1. The most recent article introduced one concept and reused 25.

The views are live. The five articles now open with a section called Read it another way, and the whole run is in the Article Views vault. In principle you could start the other way round: build the graph, then generate the article from it. I do not think that works, for the reason I gave in Liquid content needs water: "Part of the skill of a journalist is writing the article, because writing it is how they discover the narrative." The same is true of the articles here. The argument is found by writing it, and the evidence is attached as it is found.

That article also said something I did not expect to be testing a few days later. It described the experts a newsroom could rarely afford for one story: "a historian, a librarian, a data scientist, a financial analyst". And it said the other projections of a story "can be produced from the same graph and checked against it". This is that idea, applied to our own articles. It does not change how the writing is done. It maximises what the writing produces. The roles come from the SG/Send agent team, where a Librarian, a Cartographer and a Historian have been working on a code base for months. Each role there has a mission and a sentence that says when it has failed. The Librarian's is the one I keep coming back to: "If a piece of knowledge exists in this repo but cannot be found in under 30 seconds, the Librarian has failed." Here the repo is the article.
