The three context readers are the ones a person meets, and they are deliberately short. A Historian that writes three thousand words has missed the point: the value is in the connections, not the text.

Five articles on one topic, agent behaviour policies, published over four days: The behaviour policy is the business logic, 7 October Every mistake added a rule, 8 October Hope or enforcement, 8 October A second reader the agent cannot skip, 9 October Re-anchoring, 10 October Each role was written as a file with a mission, a failure sentence, what it must never do, and an exact output format. Then the session that runs this site started agents, each given one role file and its inputs. Five Librarians ran in parallel, one per article. The Explainer started at the same time, since it needs only the article. The Cartographer waited for all five catalogues. The Historian and the Storyteller waited for the Cartographer. Each agent checked its own output against its format with a script before it finished, and a separate script checks all of it again before anything is published. Reader Agents Wall time Tokens Output Librarian 5, in parallel

2 to 4.5 minutes each 403,000 662 items, 32 flags Explainer 1 2 minutes 99,000 5 views, 242 to 248 words Cartographer 1 14 minutes 264,000 13 classes, 24 verbs, 45 concepts, 78 edges, 9 maps, 37 feedback items Historian 1 4 minutes 154,000 5 views, 357 to 381 words, and the arc Storyteller 1 7 minutes 171,000 5 decks, 45 slides The Librarian's job is to make every part of an article findable: each item gets a kind, a one-line statement, the section it is in, the terms it should be found under, and its anchor, the exact sentence it came from. The anchor is the rule that makes the rest trustworthy. A script searched every article for every anchor; all 662 are there, word for word.

662 items across five articles, by kind. Claims are the largest group by far. What the articles present as evidence is a quarter as many, with data points and checkable facts beside it. The first thing the catalogue shows is the shape of the writing. There are 161 claims and 40 items the articles themselves present as evidence. That is not the whole of the support (there are also 48 data points, 65 checkable facts and 53 cited sources), but it is a fair picture of an argued article: a lot of reasoning resting on a smaller number of things you can check. That ratio is now a number, per article, that the Journalist can be asked to move. The second thing nobody asked for. To anchor every item, the Librarian has to read every sentence closely, and the role says "flag, do not fix". So it flagged. Thirty-two flags across five published articles, among them:

A total that does not add up. Re-anchoring says eighteen compactions each started from "about 780,000 to 800,000 tokens" and that "in total, 17.8 million tokens of conversation have been summarised away". Eighteen times 790,000 is about 14.2 million. A list that is shorter than its count. Hope or enforcement says the mandate "is twelve actions"; the list as written has ten clauses. A claim the article never supports. A second reader says "the military calls it the two-person rule"; nothing in the article backs the military attribution. Content that exists only in a picture. The six kinds of independence in A second reader, and the three failure modes in Re-anchoring, are scored or named only inside an image, so a reader of the text, or an agent, cannot check them. Graphs that disagree with their articles. Two article graphs link to articles the text never mentions.

These go back to the author as a list, which is the right place for them. I have not corrected the articles in this release; the flags are published with the catalogues, and the corrections will be their own change, with the flag that prompted each. The Cartographer read all 662 items and built three altitudes with one grammar: classes, concepts, verbs, each verb with its inverse, and every edge citing the catalogue items it rests on. No relates-to; a verb has to mean something. Site: 13 classes (actor, rule, barrier, capability, method, artefact, evidence, system, event, risk, property, measure, principle) and 24 verbs, from enforces and governs to undermines, detects and replaces. Topic: 45 concepts for agent behaviour policies, 78 edges, a taxonomy, and for every concept the articles it appears in and the one where it first appears. Article: each article's own concepts, mapped up to the topic as same-as, narrower-than or instance-of.

This is the fractal part, and the reason it matters is in Fractal Semantic Graphs: each article keeps its own vocabulary, and the mapping up is what lets them connect without sharing a schema. The most useful thing the Cartographer did was merge. The same idea appears under different names across the five, and nobody had said so. "Expectation", "hope" and "a rule held by the agent it governs" are one barrier kind. "Second reader", "checker", "maker-checker", "segregation of duties" and "two-person rule" are one concept, which A second reader says itself. And one method appears in all five articles under five names: moving a rule to a stronger barrier. It also refused a merge, which is as important: reach (how far one run can go) and blast radius (the cost of one bad day) stay separate, as the site already keeps them in Footprint and blast radius.

One of the nine maps: which barrier each mechanism in the five articles actually rests on. Expectation, kept by the agent; setting, which the agent's account can change; boundary, out of the agent's reach. Each mechanism is labelled with the article it comes from, and the arrows are the moves the articles describe. It also sent the Librarian a feedback file: 13 merges, 8 splits, 6 items whose kind looks wrong, and 10 notes. A claim that is really three claims; a "method" that the article itself calls a proposal, so a hypothesis; a "fact" that is the author's judgement. That file is the round trip. In this run it was written and not yet applied; the second Librarian pass, applying it, is the next run.

The Historian has two outputs: one short note per article, and the arc. For each article it says what was introduced, the nugget, what was reused, what changed, and what was left open, with one line on contribution. These are the five nuggets it chose, each quoted exactly: Article The nugget The behaviour policy is the business logic "The rule that the user interface enforced by omission is no longer enforced, unless somebody writes it down and something enforces it." Every mistake added a rule "When a rule fails, the question is not how to word it more strongly but which of the stronger barriers can replace it." Hope or enforcement "Granularity moves knowledge out of the prompt and into code." A second reader the agent cannot skip "Nothing in the hook changes, only who can change the hook." Re-anchoring "The rules are restored, not remembered."

Then it counted. New concepts, by the Cartographer's mapping, fall across the five: 17, 11, 5, 11, 1. The Historian's reading: "the set starts as vocabulary and ends as configuration". The most recent article introduced exactly one concept, the canary, and reused 25. Its own verdict on that: "accurate: this article is assembly". This is the measure I had hoped for, how much a new article brings to the conversation, and it comes out of the graph rather than out of anybody's opinion. Which concepts each article introduced and which it reused, in date order. Re-anchoring, the name, first appears in A second reader as "a reminder", a day before the article that is named after it.

It named the pattern none of the five names: "The rule moves out of the agent, and every article stops one barrier short." Each fix takes a rule out of what the model holds and puts it somewhere the model does not control: a layer with an owner, a shipped component, a tool signature, a hook on the tool call, a file the harness prints back. And each article ends by naming the barrier it has not reached yet. It found tensions the articles do not resolve. The first article sorts rules into three states, control, accepted risk and hope; from the third article on there are only two, and accepted risk quietly disappears. Every mistake added a rule says delete rules; Re-anchoring adds one. And A second reader gives the argued exception to the second reader, while Re-anchoring gives it to the gate.

And it caught the Cartographer out, usefully. The counts of "new" concepts mean new to these five articles, not new to the site. Using the site's article graphs, the Historian found that barrier kinds, hope, accepted risk, mandate, reach and blast radius were all introduced earlier, in articles such as Footprint and blast radius, The mandate stack and Every risk is already accepted, and said so in every note. That is the strongest argument for the third altitude: a topic ontology tells you what is new to the topic; only a site ontology tells you what is new.

The Explainer's brief was a smart person who runs a small business and has never configured an AI agent. Each view has the same five parts: the point, one example from the article, why it matters to you, one thing to remember, and up to four words defined in a line each. For Re-anchoring, the line to remember is "Keep the rules in a file that comes back after every summary, and watch for the report that shows it did." For Hope or enforcement it chose a sentence from the article itself: "A promise is only as strong as the weakest thing it rests on." The Storyteller's deck for Re-anchoring, nine slides drawn by code from the deck file: the number, the claim, the mechanism as a diagram, the three failures, the one file with three jobs, the canary, a quote, and the line to remember.

The Storyteller writes a deck as data: one slide per idea, each in one of nine layouts (cover, statement, number, compare, steps, diagram, quote, list, end), a headline of at most nine words and at most thirty more. A renderer turns it into 1080 by 1350 images and a PDF, which is the shape of a LinkedIn document post, the same idea as the newsletter's pictures. Every number on a slide is in the article, and every quote slide is checked verbatim. The renderer refuses to clip a slide that has too many words; it reports it, and the Storyteller cuts.

These decks are drawn by code, with system fonts and the site's palette, which makes them consistent and checkable but plain. The Storyteller also wrote, for every slide, a 100 to 200 word prompt for an image model, describing the same slide as an infographic. Running those is the expensive part I mentioned in the voice memo, and it needs an image model API key this session does not have; the prompts are in the vault, ready, and the code-drawn deck is what each article carries until they are run.

The five articles now open, under the abstract, with a section called Read it another way. In two minutes is open by default; In the arc, In pictures, On the map and The catalogue are one click away. The catalogue lists every item by kind, and ends with what was flagged for the author. It works without JavaScript, and the markdown twin of each article, the version agents read, carries the same views as text. The top of Re-anchoring with its views: the two-minute version open, and the arc, the deck, the map and the catalogue one click away.

The Article Views vault holds everything: the role files and their prompts, the five articles as they were read, the catalogues, the three altitudes of ontology, the maps as Mermaid sources and renders, the notes, the decks, the renderers and the checks. It opens as an app with the five views of each article and two views across them: the arc, and a grid of which article carries which idea. The vault's topic view: each of the 45 concepts against the five articles, amber where it first appears. The ideas that run through all five are the spine of the topic; the ones that appear once are what each article brought. It does not check the articles against the world. The Librarian checks the article against itself: is every item there, do the numbers reconcile, is every claim stated. Whether a cited fact is true is still the Journalist's job and the reviewer's.

The views can be wrong. They are produced by agents and checked by script where a script can check them: anchors verbatim, edges citing real items, word limits, quotes verbatim. A plain-language summary that is subtly unfair to its article passes every check. Each view should be read by the author before it goes on the page, as these were. New is relative. Without the site altitude, "new" means new to the set. The Historian caught it this time because it had the site's graphs; a run without them would not. The round trip ran once in one direction. The Cartographer's feedback to the Librarian is written, not applied.

It costs something. About 1.1 million tokens for five articles, most of it the five Librarians (403,000 between them) and the Cartographer reading their 662 items (264,000). Per article, the Explainer and the Historian are cheap; the catalogue and the ontology are the expensive parts, and the ontology is also the part that gets cheaper as the site ontology settles and each new article only has to map onto it. Make them desk roles. The Librarian, the Cartographer, the Explainer and the Storyteller join the Historian on the newsroom desk, each with a write policy, so that every new article gets its views on the run after it is published. Apply the round trip. The second Librarian pass, applying the Cartographer's feedback, and the corrections to the five articles, each tied to its flag.

Build the site altitude. One ontology across every article on the site, so that "new" means new, and a reader or an agent can find any claim, number or question in any article from one index. Run the image prompts. One deck through an image model first, with its cost counted, to see whether the pictures earn their price over the code-drawn slides. The articles stay long. That is where the thinking happens and where the evidence lives. What changes is that a reader who has two minutes, or who wants the numbers, or who wants to know what this piece added to the last ten, no longer has to read all of it to find out.

Written by agent@riskmandate.ai (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5) in the sgit.ai site session on 10 October 2026, from a voice memo by Dinis Cruz, who has editorial responsibility. Every view described here was produced by Claude agents in the same session under the role files in the vault, and every count is from the vault's own files. Abstract: Every newsroom we run has its own researcher. The PHP story site's source watch re-reads about 900 pages from some 600 publishers, the Industry Wire reads its own sources, and the Web Summit newsroom will need the same. That is a lot of repeated work, and it is slow: a full watch pass takes 16 to 27 minutes for a few hundred pages, before the commit and the push. Now that we know how to run agents on a schedule, with a conductor, a researcher and a dev team, the next step is to consolidate: one shared researcher, publishing everything it is allowed to at research.newsroom.sgit.ai, a light and very focused version of the Internet Archive. Teams declare what they want watched; scheduled runs capture it in parallel, a daily run of the general web, a run for Wikipedia, and focus runs for current stories; each day becomes one sgit pack, a zip with its commits, so the provenance travels with the data. The site makes the files easy to find, says what each holds, and lets anyone download them. What it may show is decided by the licence tiers the source watch already uses: open and public-sector pages in full, the rest as index, hashes and links. This is the design, for review before we build it.
research.newsroom.sgit.ai, one researcher shared by every newsroom: watch list, runs, packs, site and readers. Proposed.
in-short

Every newsroom runs its own researcher. The same sources, read again and again. It is slow. A full watch pass is 16 to 27 minutes for a few hundred pages, before the push. Consolidate: one shared researcher, on a schedule, at research.newsroom.sgit.ai. Three kinds of run, in parallel: the daily web, Wikipedia, focus runs for current stories. A pack a day. One zip per day with its commits, so the provenance travels with the data. Published by licence tier. Open pages in full; the rest as index, hashes and links. Each team then researches only what is not covered.
problem

We now know how to run agents on a schedule, with a conductor, a researcher, a dev agent and several teams working on one site. The PHP story site does it every day. But look at what each newsroom does for its sources. The PHP story site's source watch re-reads about 900 pages, 913 in the site's data and 965 in the researcher's own count of 23 October, from some 600 publishers, in 34 languages and 60 country folders. It keeps a snapshot whenever a page changes: 2,946 so far. The Industry Wire reads its own sources into its own vault, for four wires. The Web Summit newsroom will need a feed of its own, from public material, as the plan says.
problem

Much of that is the same sources, read again. And it is slow. The researcher's own proposal for a phased pass measured the watch stage at 16 to 27 minutes for 630 to 860 pages, with a real browser, 12 at a time, before the discovery, the series, the commit and the push; on the old vault format, a push of 5,000 objects took up to 30 minutes.
archive

The researcher already describes its source watch as "a small Wayback Machine for one story". That is the right idea, and it should not be one per story. So the proposal is research.newsroom.sgit.ai: a site focused on creating and publishing raw data. A light and very focused version of the Internet Archive, and a focused news archive that we publish. It makes it easy to find the files, explains what files exist, and lets anyone download them. Underneath, they are just files in storage with encryption on them, in sgit vaults; for what we may share, we publish the read key, and anyone can open them.
archive

What it adds to what the Internet Archive already does is focus and structure: the pages that matter to the stories we follow, captured on a known schedule, with a machine-readable index of what changed, when, with what access, under what licence. Few publishers offer their own history in a form a machine can use.
design

One watch list. A registry of what to watch: the page, who asked for it, how often, its licence tier and its access. Set up once, then changed by agents and people: "here are the sites I want to keep an eye on; here are the ones I want an update on." The roughly 900 sources the PHP site follows are the first entries. Runs split so they can go in parallel. A tree of who is doing what, so that several sessions run at once and each finishes quickly:
design

- The daily web: a generic run over the sources every story needs, news homepages, CERTs and agencies, feeds, vulnerability catalogues. - Wikipedia: a run of its own, for chosen articles and their revisions. Wikipedia is huge, changes all the time, and holds a lot of the shadow reporting that sources and their shadows describes; the PHP site already reads its article as a graph. - Focus runs: requests from current work, the PHP story, the wires, Web Summit, each declared in the watch list. A pack a day. Each run writes a day's captures into an sgit pack vault: one zip per push, holding the commits, so the provenance travels with the data. Next to each pack, an index of what is inside, so nobody has to download a zip to know whether they need it.
design

A daily update. The agents that consume the data say what is missing: "what about this, what about that." The watch list grows from their asks. Each team keeps its researcher, but it only looks at what the shared runs do not cover. That makes each one much more efficient, and gives every newsroom the same data source.
packs

Pack mode against a normal sgit vault, measured on the PHP site's source watch vault on 23 October 2026. The new versions of sgit change what is practical. In pack mode, released in sgit 0.24.0, a push is one zip with its commits, and a clone is the newest snapshot plus the packs since it. The PHP site's researcher measured the difference on the source watch itself, a vault of 29,861 files: a fresh clone went from 827 seconds to 95, listing the vault on the server from a timeout after 91 seconds to 0.73 seconds, and a pull with nothing new from 34 seconds to 4. Packs are also what make "a pack a day" a natural unit to publish: a dated zip, with its own index, that anyone can fetch directly.
tiers

What the research site may publish, by licence tier A, B and C, and the opt-out for any publisher. We only use public sources. But public is not the same as free to republish, and the research site has to respect that. The source watch already gives every page a licence tier: A, open or public sector, "keep and show"; B, quote up to 25 words and link; C, link only. Its data counts 73 pages at tier A, 523 at B and 15 at C. And the Industry Wire's contract already sets the rule for public vaults: everything in a vault with a published read key is public, including its history, so "frozen tier-B bytes" never go in one. So the research site publishes by tier: Tier A in full: the capture itself, in a public pack. Wikipedia, under its open licence and with attribution, belongs here.
tiers

Tiers B and C as the record: the link, when we read it, the access we had, the hash of what was served, when it changed and, for B, at most 25 words. The full bytes stay in a private vault, as evidence. An opt-out. If a publisher asks us to stop, we stop, and the index says so. And we follow each site's own terms and robots.txt, as we did with Feisty Duck. That is still a lot. Most of what makes the archive useful, what changed, when, and who said it first, is in the record, not the bytes.
next

This is the design, for review. If it holds: The watch list, seeded from the PHP site's sources, with each team's asks. The first runs on a schedule: the daily web and Wikipedia, as pack vaults. research.newsroom.sgit.ai, with the index, the packs and their read keys, built like the other newsroom sites. The PHP site's researcher moved onto it, watching only what the shared runs do not cover; then the wires; then Web Summit.
limits

Nothing here is built. research.newsroom.sgit.ai does not exist yet. The source counts differ by date: 913 pages in the site's data, 965 in the researcher's count of 23 October; the memo's "800" was an estimate. The pack-mode numbers are from one vault, measured by one agent on 23 October. The Internet Archive archives far more. The point is focus, structure and the index, not scale.
sources

My voice memo of 26 October 2026. The PHP story site's source watch data and its pack-mode measurements of 23 October; the researcher's proposal for a phased source watch pass; the sgit pack-mode specification in the sgit CLI repository; how the Industry Wire works; all read on 26 October 2026. Abstract: Anthropic's post on Scion makes one observation that holds for any version control system: when the clients are agents, they are always online, there are many of them, and the expensive thing is moving bytes nobody needs. So the question for sgit is not how fast it clones a small vault, but what it does with a big one that many agents use every day. We have one. The vault the agents behind this newsroom share, with their mail, briefs, runs and analysis, had 1,295 commits, 5,281 files and about 35,000 encrypted objects on 16 October, 527 MB with all its history: the size of a real application's source repository, and about the size of our own SG/Send application's git repository. The sgit CLI team measured it eight ways from the hosted service and again from local disk. A full clone takes three and a half minutes; nobody needs one. One folder with one commit of history takes 13 seconds and 3 MB, however large the vault is; a file on demand under 3 seconds; an up-to-date pull 2.5. The honest edge is history: without a depth, a partial clone walks the commits one request at a time, nearly four minutes for one folder, and the fix is designed but not shipped. And with the same objects on local disk, the one-folder clone is 0.8 seconds: the time is the distance to the storage, not sgit. Which is why I think vaults this size are where sgit becomes useful for more than agents' memory, including source code.
The newsroom's vault against two of our own git repositories: the SG/Send application and the sgit CLI.
in-short

The vault behind this newsroom. Ten agents, one person, every day. 35,000 objects, 1,295 commits, 5,281 files. The size of a real application's source code. Nobody clones all of it. Three and a half minutes, and nobody needs to. One folder, one commit: 13 seconds, 3 MB. However large the vault grows. History is the edge. Without a depth, one request per commit; a fix is designed. The time is the storage. The same clone from local disk: 0.8 seconds. Big enough for source code. That is the next use worth testing.
vault

The agents that write, check and publish this newsroom, ten of them, and I, share one vault. It holds our mail between agents, briefs, runs and analysis. Its contents are private; its shape is not, and it is the best test we have, because it is big by sgit's standards and busy every day: 68 of its commits arrived in the two days before these measurements. On 16 October it had 1,295 commits, 5,281 files, 16,315 blobs and 16,391 trees: about 35,000 encrypted objects, and 527 MB when every one of them is on disk (measured with the full clone of 14 October). The latest version of its files is 139 MB. The biggest folder has 3,275 files and 69 MB; the smallest have a dozen. It lives on the hosted service, S3 behind CloudFront with a small API in front, and the agents reach it through the CLI.
vault

The comparison in the figure above is why I think this matters beyond agents. The SG/Send application's git repository has 5,584 files, 4,399 commits and 42,434 objects; the sgit CLI's has 1,811 files, 1,603 commits and 13,985. The vault is in the same range as real application source code. If sgit handles this vault well, it handles a code base of that size, encrypted, with every version signed.
fetch

What an agent fetches from the 35,000-object vault and what it costs, in seconds, on a log scale. Nobody working in this vault needs all of it, and the point of the design is that they do not have to take it. The sgit CLI team measured each way of asking, from a cloud sandbox, on 14 and 16 October: What was asked for Time Objects On disk Everything, the full clone 3½ min 35,423 527 MB The whole tree, one commit of history (--depth 1) 57 s 6,248 142 MB One 130-file folder, one commit (--path … --depth 1) 13 s 137 3 MB Structure only, one commit (--sparse --depth 1) 27 s 967 6 MB One file on demand, in that sparse clone 2.9 s 1 Widening a clone by a 130-file folder (fetch) 7.8 s 135 2 MB A pull when nothing changed 2.5 s 0 One 130-file folder, all its history 227 s 3,364 64 MB
fetch

The biggest folder, all its history 264 s 25,110 274 MB Two things stand out. A clone that carries a depth costs seconds and megabytes however large the vault is, because it asks for the spine of trees down to its folder and the blobs under it, and nothing else. That is the pattern the documentation gives agents, and the one ours use. And a clone that carries the whole history of a folder pays for the history, not the folder: 227 seconds for 130 files, almost all of it walking 1,295 commits one request at a time. A full clone avoids that by listing the store once and fetching everything in bulk; a partial clone cannot, because it must not hold objects it does not track.
fetch

That is the one real edge in the numbers, and the fix is designed: a small encrypted record of the commit chain, written on every push, so a clone can fetch the chain in about 26 batched requests instead of discovering it. Until it ships, the answer is the depth flag.
session

The command an agent runs most is not clone but pull: come back, take what changed, carry on. Until 14 October that was the slow path on this vault, one request per commit and one per blob, and an agent a day behind waited the best part of an hour. The CLI team fixed it on the vault where the agents reported it: blobs now come in batches of 50 with 16 requests in flight, and past a long gap the client lists the store and sweeps what is missing, so fetching the whole head into an empty store takes about three minutes, down from about 53. A pull a few commits behind takes the few requests it needs; one with nothing new, 2.5 seconds.
storage

The same vault and client with the objects in three places: hosted, a plain file server and a local API server. The CLI team then copied the same 35,000 objects to local disk and served them two ways: a plain file server, and the same API server the hosted service runs, as one local process. The one-folder, one-commit clone fell from 13 seconds to 2.3 and 0.8. The history walk that costs three minutes hosted took 7 seconds, because it is the same 1,227 requests at about a millisecond each instead of 150. With no network at all, what is left of a full clone's 69 seconds is the client decrypting 16,000 trees.
storage

So sgit is not the bottleneck; the distance to the storage is. Each request to the hosted service pays a round trip through a CDN, a Lambda and S3 before a byte moves, and the client's own work per object, checking its hash and decrypting it, is microseconds. The ruv.sgit hive runs say the same from the other side: on a local server, every sgit operation in fifteen recorded runs took between 0.4 and 1.5 seconds, including starting Python and deriving the key, and a 142-file, 6.9 MB vault cloned in 0.74 seconds. sgit is a standard, not a server explains why that follows from the design.
many

The question Scion's post is really about is many clients. Earlier measurements on this site, on a single local server process, put a number on it: ten clones of one folder at once took 1.9 seconds with the server mostly idle; ten full clones queued to 21 seconds, which is the single process, not the protocol (Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults). The more clients there are, the more it matters that each takes only what it needs.
code

I started this vault as memory for agents, and the numbers say it is now a repository of real size: about as many files and objects as our application's source repository, every version encrypted and signed, read by ten clients that each take only what they need. That is where sgit starts to be useful for more than notes and mail. A code base of this size, kept in a vault, would let each agent clone the one package it works on, with one commit of history, in seconds; keep large files in the repository without every client paying for them; and live on a server, or a static host, that cannot read a line of it. The next test I would like to run is exactly that: a real code base, moved into a vault, with agents working on it.
limits

Not proven at Scion's scale. 35,000 objects, 1,295 commits and ten agents is the largest vault we run; Scion's monorepo has 100 GB of history and 30,000 merges a day. No bisect yet. Path history, signed commits, signed tags and verification exist, and blame shipped in sgit-ai 0.27.0 on 28 October; bisect is designed and in the CLI team's queue. A partial clone of a long history is slow without a depth, today. The fix is designed, not shipped. One run each, from sandboxes that send every request through a proxy. A plain connection does better. The source-code use is a proposal. The vault holds notes, mail and analysis, not code. If you want to try a code base in a vault, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: An old Intel iMac, clean-installed for my agents, could not run Homebrew or Docker Desktop, and needed Python by hand. Each project that dropped it did so because supporting old machines costs money and the people on the long tail have no easy way to pay for it. This article measures that long tail from Homebrew and PyPI analytics, sets out where money does flow for old versions (Oracle, Red Hat, Windows ESU, Rimini Street) and where it does not (open source receives about 0.09% of its estimated value), shows why pence payments only work aggregated, and simulates five ways to pay for it. About £1.80 a machine a year from individuals covers one project's long-tail cost in half the draws; customised builds for companies cover it in 94%. Open source is not free; the question is whether the people who get the value have an easy way to pay for it.

Open source is not free. Somebody is paying for it, even if what they pay with is only their time. I believe that more strongly every month, and last week an old iMac showed me why. Everything I build at RiskMandate and sgit is open source. Anyone can take it and run it. But if somebody wants to deploy it, they should work through us, because we ought to be cheaper than doing it themselves. What we sell is not the code. It is a build for that customer: sometimes with fewer features, because fewer features means less attack surface, but always with the capabilities the customer actually wants, tested so that it works. The question this article asks is whether that idea scales down. Could a project earn money from people like me, and from companies, for supported, customised builds, at prices from pence to pounds rather than thousands?

I did not want to answer that from my own experience alone, so the research for this article went to the data: install analytics, download statistics, company filings, maintainer surveys and published price lists. Every number below has a source, and the Long Tail Ledger vault holds each one with its quote and a flag saying whether it was read at the source. On top of that sits a model, a Monte Carlo simulation of five ways to pay for the long tail. It is a model, not a forecast, and every assumption in it is labelled with its range and its reason. The long tail is measurable, and it is not small. In Homebrew's install analytics, 6.99% of macOS install events in the last 30 days, and 16.66% over a year, came from versions older than the newest three. On PyPI, 18.55% of pip downloads run on end-of-life Python.

Money flows to old versions when a vendor owns them. Oracle earned $19.8 billion from support last year; Red Hat's subscriptions ran at about 93% gross margin. Open source receives about 0.09% of its estimated value in investment. Pence only work aggregated. A 20p card fee is 41.5% of a 50p payment and 5.5% of £5. Simulated, micro-payments roughly pay for the long tail. About £1.80 a machine a year covers one project's long-tail cost in half the draws with typical conversion, and 70p with great conversion. No price reaches nine draws in ten. Companies pay for it reliably. Customised builds priced below a company's own cost of keeping the tool working cover the cost in 94% of draws. Donations cover it in 24%. The satellites follow the money. Rimini Street shows a third-party support market exists where money flows: about $136,000 a year per client.
imac

I gave my agents an Intel iMac as a desktop of their own, wiped and clean-installed with macOS 13 Ventura, the newest macOS the installer offered. Chrome works. Claude Desktop works. Homebrew would not install. Docker Desktop would not install. Getting sgit on it meant downloading Python by hand. I asked the research not to take my word for any of that. Here is what it found, including where I was wrong. Which iMac matters. Only the 2017 iMacs stop at Ventura. The 2019 models are on Apple's lists for Sonoma and Sequoia, and Sequoia was still being patched on 28 September 2026. If the machine is a 2019, a clean install of Sequoia would put it back in support for both Apple and Docker. The quick check is the model identifier: iMac18,x is 2017, iMac19,x is 2019.
imac

Ventura is unpatched. Its last security update was 13.7.8 on 20 August 2025. A clean Ventura install today is an operating system that has gone more than a year without a fix, on a machine that will run agents and a browser. Apple does not publish end dates; its deployment guide says only that "not all known security issues are addressed in previous versions". Homebrew refuses the CPU, not just the OS. Since September 2026 the official installer stops on any Intel Mac with "Homebrew on macOS is only supported on Apple Silicon processors!", whatever macOS it runs. Homebrew's own reasoning is worth quoting: "If Apple and Microsoft's GitHub, two of the world's largest technology companies, cannot continue supporting macOS Intel x86_64, sadly neither can Homebrew." Existing Intel installs keep working, without support, until about September 2027.
imac

Docker Desktop needs macOS 14. Ventura support ended in 4.48.0 (October 2025) and the installer has required Sonoma since 4.49.0. Docker still ships an Intel build. Python was the easy part, once found. The python.org installer supports macOS 10.15 and later, so it runs on Ventura. The reason a manual download was needed is that Ventura has no usable Python 3 of its own: /usr/bin/python3 is a stub that offers Apple's Command Line Tools, which users report bring Python 3.9.6, below sgit's 3.11. There is still a package manager. MacPorts ships a Ventura installer and was building Ventura Intel packages on the day I checked. Homebrew's own release notes point Intel users there.
imac

The floor is rising everywhere at once. Go 1.27, Node.js 24 and Chrome 151 all now need macOS 13 or later, which makes Ventura the next version to be dropped. Rust, Homebrew, Node.js and CPython have all moved Intel macOS to a lower support tier, mostly because free Intel CI is going away: GitHub retires its last Intel macOS runner in autumn 2027. The volunteers who kept old Macs alive stopped taking money. OpenCore Legacy Patcher, the project that puts newer macOS on unsupported Macs, raised about $96,000 from over 4,000 contributors. In March 2026 it stopped taking donations: "with multiple developers having left the team, development progress has become much slower."
imac

So my story was mostly right and a little unfair. The machine works, the tools do still exist for it, and some of what I hit was the hardware's age rather than anyone's choice. But the pattern underneath is exactly the one I suspected. Every project that dropped this machine did it for the same reason: supporting it costs money, in CI hardware and in maintainer time, and the people who still need the support are not the ones paying for it.
measured

How many people are on that long tail? Homebrew publishes anonymous install analytics by macOS version, which is the best direct measure I found. These are install events from users who have not opted out, not unique machines, but the shares are telling. Homebrew macOS install events Last 30 days Last 90 days Last 365 days Older than the newest three versions 6.99% 12.39% 16.66% Ventura 13 or older 3.32% 5.19% 5.43% Over a year that is 4.64 million install events from Ventura and 4.94 million from Monterey, one version older. Monterey outnumbering Ventura fits Intel Macs that cannot go beyond macOS 12. Homebrew macOS install events by version over 30, 90 and 365 days. macOS 27 shipped in September 2026, so it is large in the 30-day window and small in the year. From the Long Tail Ledger vault.
measured

The same pattern shows up in Python. Over the last 30 days, 18.55% of pip downloads and 10.45% of requests downloads came from Python 3.9 or older, all past end of life, and Python 3.10, which reached end of life this month, is a further 15% of pip. Those are mostly servers and CI rather than desktops, so they measure a different long tail, but a large one. Inside companies, Black Duck's 2026 audit found components more than four years out of date in 92% of codebases.
measured

This is exactly the population that volunteer projects are dropping. Homebrew stopped building Intel bottles while its own analytics show millions of installs a year from machines on old versions. That is not a criticism of Homebrew. Its volunteers said plainly that the retreat of Apple and GitHub "exceeds what Homebrew's volunteers can replace". The long tail has value to the people on it, and no revenue stream back to the people who would have to support it.
money

Open source is worth a great deal and is paid for very little. The Harvard Business School study by Hoffmann, Nagle and Zhou put the demand-side value of widely used open source at $8.8 trillion: what every firm would spend to rebuild it. The Linux Foundation estimates that about $7.7 billion a year is invested across the whole ecosystem, 86% of it as staff time rather than cash. That is about 0.09% of the value. GitHub Sponsors has passed $100 million since 2019, which is real money and a real achievement, but at its current rate it comes to about 13 cents a year per GitHub developer.
money

The maintainers feel it. In Tidelift's 2024 survey, 60% of maintainers describe themselves as unpaid hobbyists, and 60% have quit or considered quitting a project. Paid maintainers are 55% more likely to do the security and maintenance work that matters. Some of the most important code in the world has run on almost nothing: the xz maintainer wrote in 2022 that "this is an unpaid hobby project", two years before the backdoor; core-js, on more than half of the top thousand websites, was earning about $400 for a month of work in 2023. Now look at where money does flow for exactly the thing my iMac needs: keeping old versions alive. Oracle supports every version for as long as you run it, and charges for it. Software support brought in $19.8 billion in the year to May 2026, 29.4% of revenue, and Oracle says "substantially all" support customers renew.
money

Red Hat, in its last year as a standalone company, earned 87.7% of its revenue from subscriptions, at a gross margin of about 93%. That is an open source company selling support for code anyone can download. Microsoft charges organisations $61 per device for the first year of Windows 10 extended security updates, doubling each year, and consumers $30 one-off for up to ten devices. Canonical sells Ubuntu Pro at $25 a desktop and $500 a server a year, free for up to five personal machines. TuxCare sells extended support for end-of-life Linux at about $100 a system. Rimini Street, which supports other companies' software, earned $421.5 million from 3,102 clients in 2025, about $136,000 each, at a 60% gross margin. That is the satellite market, and it exists where the money flows. What people pay to keep old software supported, per machine per year, against what open source receives in voluntary funding. From the Long Tail Ledger vault.
money
The contrast is the whole argument. The same need, "keep the version I have working and safe", is a multi-billion-pound business when a vendor owns the code, and a donation jar when a community does.
charge

Projects do try, and the record is instructive. Docker made Docker Desktop paid for companies with 250 or more staff or $10 million or more in revenue in August 2021. Commercially it worked: annual recurring revenue passed $50 million within months and analysts estimate over $200 million since. I have seen organisations ban it rather than buy seats, though I found no survey that measures how many. What can be measured is that the alternatives grew. In Homebrew's install analytics today, OrbStack, Colima, Podman Desktop and Rancher Desktop together make up about 47% of container-tool installs over the past year and 51% over the past month. Most Docker Desktop installs do not come through Homebrew, so this overstates the alternatives, but it shows how many Mac developers route around the paid product.
charge

Desktop container tools installed through Homebrew, as a share of the five tools' installs over 30 and 365 days. Most Docker Desktop installs come from Docker's own download, so this overstates the alternatives. From the Long Tail Ledger vault. Relicensing has a pattern. HashiCorp, Elastic and Redis each moved from an open licence to a source-available one. Each produced a well-funded fork backed by the cloud providers it targeted (OpenTofu, OpenSearch, Valkey), and two of the three have since added an open licence back. Dual licensing changes what the free version is for. Once a project sells a paid edition, it has a reason not to make the free one too good. That is the incentive I most want to avoid, and it is why I do not think open core is the answer to the long tail. Open core, or packaging? sets out the test I use.
charge

Per-install rewards get gamed. When tea.xyz rewarded package popularity with tokens, one developer published nearly 14,000 packages, and by one estimate about 70% of new npm packages over six months were spam. Payment has to be tied to a verified user who receives something, not to a count.
pence

My instinct is that I would pay pence to pounds for a supported build of each tool on that iMac. The first obstacle is not willingness to pay. It is the card fee. Stripe's standard UK rate is 1.5% plus 20p. On a £20 payment that is 2.5%. On £5 it is 5.5%. On 50p it is 41.5%, and on 10p it is more than the payment. Below about £5, the fixed fee is the price. Fee as a share of one payment, by payment size and payment rail. The fixed part of a card fee dominates below about £5; aggregation is what makes pence payments work. From the Long Tail Ledger vault.
pence

So pence payments only work aggregated: one charge a year that covers many projects, or a platform that already holds a balance and settles in bulk. I made this argument for news in the future of news monetisation, and the arithmetic has not changed. This site is testing the reader's side of it now, with a meter in the browser that prices each page at a few pence against five pounds of credit, settled as one balance rather than per page. The model below compares paying each project by card with paying through an aggregating platform.
models

To test the idea, I built a model of one project at Homebrew's scale with one long-tail target to keep alive: an old macOS version, or Intel. The cost of that target is CI hardware the free runners no longer provide, plus part of a maintainer's year. The model puts it at a median of about £27,000 a year, from £18,000 to £39,000. The installed base comes from Homebrew's 203 million macOS install events in a year, divided by an assumed number of install events per machine. That gives a median of 6.6 million machines, about 631,000 of them on the long tail. Then it runs 10,000 draws of every uncertain assumption through five ways of paying: Donations, at GitHub Sponsors-like rates and gift sizes. Unrestricted money, of which only a share reaches the long tail.
models

A seat licence above a size threshold, Docker-style: companies above the threshold pay per user per month, some switch to alternatives, and some ignore it. Also unrestricted. Support that rises with age, Oracle and Windows ESU style: a price per machine that doubles each year past end of life, with uptake falling as the price rises. Micro-paid supported builds, my thesis: a price per machine per year from 50p to £25, paid by card directly or through an aggregating platform. Willingness to pay follows a lognormal curve, and conversion is capped by the freemium benchmarks (1% pessimistic, 3% to 5% typical, 8% great). Customised builds for companies: a company pays a price compared with its internal cost of keeping the tool working itself (engineer hours times a loaded rate). The further the price is below that cost, the more companies buy.
models

The five models side by side: the spread of 10,000 draws of the net revenue available for the long-tail target, on a log scale, against the cost of keeping that target alive (the grey band). Typical conversion, base values. From the Long Tail Ledger vault. The results, at base values and typical conversion: Model Median revenue for the long tail 10th to 90th percentile Covers the cost Donations (a share of about £194,000) £12,700 £3,200 to £45,000 24% of draws Seat licence (a share of about £18.1m) £1.20m £378,000 to £3.37m 99.9% Support that rises with age £28,800 £10,700 to £71,200 54% Micro-paid builds, direct cards £31,800 £12,600 to £73,900 60% Micro-paid builds, aggregated £31,400 £12,500 to £72,800 59% Customised builds for companies £1.51m £241,000 to £5.71m 94% Three things stand out.
models

Donations do not pay for the long tail. Even at a popular project's scale, and even if a fair share of donations went to old platforms, they cover the cost in about one draw in four. That matches what happened to OpenCore Legacy Patcher. A seat licence raises a great deal of money, but not for this. It is the biggest number in the table, and it covers the cost almost always, but only if the project chooses to spend licence money on old platforms. It has nothing to do with the people on the long tail, and it brings the problems Docker found: switching, bans, and a reason to keep the free version weaker.
models

Micro-payments roughly cover the cost, and companies cover it easily. At £3 a machine a year, supported builds sold to long-tail users cover the cost in about six draws in ten. Customised builds for the companies that keep old machines for a job (a build box, a test rig, an agent desktop like mine) cover it in more than nine in ten, with money to spare.
break-even

My question was whether pence to pounds would be enough. The break-even view answers it directly: the lowest price per machine per year at which supported builds cover the cost in half, or nine in ten, of the draws. The share of draws in which micro-paid supported builds cover the long-tail cost, at every price from 50p to £25, for three conversion scenarios. The curves fall at high prices because fewer people pay. From the Long Tail Ledger vault. Conversion Covers half the draws (aggregated) Covers half the draws (direct cards) Covers nine in ten Pessimistic, 1% not reached (best: 6% of draws, at £5.50) not reached not reached Typical, 3% to 5% £1.80 £1.90 not reached (best: 59%, at £3.50) Great, 8% 70p 90p not reached (best: 87%, at £2.75)
break-even

So the answer to "cents to pounds" is yes, in a specific sense. With typical conversion, about £2 a machine a year is enough to cover the long tail more often than not, and with great conversion, under £1. That is the same order as the cheapest published support price I found (Windows 10's $30 for ten devices), and well below the rest. But no price reaches nine in ten. The model is clear about why: conversion caps the number of payers, and raising the price loses more payers than it gains in revenue. Pence from individuals can make the long tail roughly self-funding. They cannot make it safe to depend on. And with pessimistic conversion, no price works at all. The card-versus-platform difference is smaller than I expected at these prices, because at £2 to £3 the 20p fee is under 10%. It matters below about £1, where only aggregation keeps the price viable.
sensitivity

Which assumption moves the answer most: the median margin of micro-paid builds (revenue minus the long-tail cost) with each assumption held at the low and the high end of its range. From the Long Tail Ledger vault. The three assumptions that move the result most are: How many machines are really out there (install events per machine): a swing of about £90,000 in the median margin. What people are willing to pay: about £47,000. The share of machines on the long tail: about £43,000. None of the three is measured well in public data today, and two of them are things a project could measure itself, if it had a way to sell a supported build and count who buys. Conversion, which I expected to dominate, matters less than these. The biggest uncertainty is not whether people pay. It is how many of them there are.
satellites

Where is the local company providing support? The model asks how many small support firms (two or three engineers, about £240,000 a year to run) the money from micro-paid and company builds could sustain, if some buyers prefer a supplier in their own country and a firm supports about ten projects. Small support firms the pool could sustain, worldwide and in one mid-sized country. From the Long Tail Ledger vault.
satellites

The median is about 18 such firms worldwide, from 2.4 to 85, and about one per country, from 0.1 to 4.9. Most of that comes from company builds. The existence proof is Rimini Street: about $136,000 a year per client, so one small firm would need two or three clients like that, and its $421.5 million of revenue is the running cost of about 1,300 small firms. The satellite market exists where money flows. For open source today, little of the money flows to anyone outside the project, so few satellites form.
says

I started with a hunch from one old iMac. The data mostly supports it, with two corrections. The first correction is about who pays. Pence-to-pounds payments from individuals like me can roughly cover the long tail, at about £2 a machine a year, if the payment is aggregated and tied to something real: a supported build, tested on my machine. But they are not reliable enough to depend on. The reliable money comes from companies, paying for a customised build at a price well below what it costs them to keep the tool working themselves. That is how RiskMandate and sgit already work: open source, and cheaper to deploy through us than on your own. The model suggests that the same logic, applied to old platforms, pays for the long tail with room to spare.
says

The second correction is about what is sold. It should not be a donation, and it should not be a licence that makes the free version worse. It should be a build: the capabilities the customer wants, sometimes with fewer features and less attack surface, tested on their target, with someone accountable for it. "I pay because I get value." The value is the support, not the code, so the code can stay open.
says

What is missing is the plumbing: one annual charge that covers many projects, payment tied to a verified build rather than a count of installs, and a split of the money between the maintainers and the local firms that do the support. That is the market argument I made in somebody has to be the villagers and the usage-based billing I described in usage-based billable entities, applied to the oldest machines in the room. And with GenAI, the cost of producing a customised, tested build for an old target is falling, which is the argument of the GenAI legacy code refactoring business plan. Open source is not free. The question was never whether somebody pays. It is whether the people who get the value have an easy way to pay for it.
check

Everything above is in the Long Tail Ledger vault: the 175 sourced facts with their quotes and verified flags, the 26 case facts, the 36 assumptions with their ranges and reasons, the model in Python, and the same model in the browser behind a calculator with a slider for every assumption. The release gate checks that the browser and Python give the same numbers on 77 grids of inputs, exactly. If you think an assumption is wrong, move its slider and see what changes. What the model does not do: forecast anyone's revenue, or measure willingness to pay, the installed base, the Intel share or company behaviour. Those are assumptions, and the sensitivity view shows which matter most. Some of the claims I started with are not in the data. I have seen organisations ban Docker Desktop rather than buy seats, but I found no survey that measures how many.
sources

The case: a clean install on my agents' iMac, checked against Apple's compatibility and security pages, the Homebrew, Docker, Python, MacPorts and OpenCore Legacy Patcher documentation, and the Go, Node.js, Rust and Chrome support notes, all read on 10 October 2026. The economics: the Harvard Business School working paper on the value of open source, the Linux Foundation's 2024 funding study, the Tidelift maintainer surveys, Black Duck's OSSRA 2026, Sonatype's reports, Oracle, Red Hat, IBM and Rimini Street filings, published price lists from Microsoft, Canonical, TuxCare, Docker and the payment providers, and Homebrew and PyPI analytics, fetched the same day. Every source is listed, with its quote, in the vault.
sources

My earlier positions, which this article tries to stay consistent with: the position, three funding proposals, open core, or packaging?, the numbers, and the ones we refuse to publish and cURL's closed bug bounty on open-source.sgit.ai; and on diniscruz.ai, micro and nano payments, usage-based billable entities and GenAI legacy code refactoring.

Abstract: People worry that if they open source their ideas, others will copy them. It does not happen: I have been open sourcing my ideas for years, and the ones I did not follow up are still there, not taken. The advantage people miss is that open source is how you get to keep using your own work. When you work for a company, what you build gets locked in, and when you leave you start from scratch. My trick was to work on open source projects that I brought into each company, so I was more productive there and never started again; my work kept getting better as I moved. The Cyber Boardroom began like that: an open experiment with AI while I was working for two companies, with my managers aware of it, and when I left both roles I continued where I had left off. So publish early, and rough. A rough public history shows an employer that it is an experiment and learning, which it is, and shows anyone who asks later how it evolved, bit by bit. A polished thing that appears from nowhere raises questions, and you never want lawyers involved. Keep it on separate machines, never build a competitor to your employer, and remember that the learning makes you better at the day job too.
Two careers, side by side: closed, where each job starts from zero, and open, where the work carries forward.
in-short

Nobody copies your ideas. I have open sourced mine for years; the ones I did not follow are still there. The real advantage: you keep using it. Closed work stays with the employer. Bring your open source into the job. More productive for them, and never starting from scratch for you. The Cyber Boardroom started that way. In the open, while employed, with my managers aware. Publish early, and rough. The history protects you. Polished things from nowhere raise questions. And you never want lawyers involved. Be disciplined. Separate machines, and never a competitor to your employer. It is a win for both sides. The learning makes you better at the day job.
copying

People always think that if they open source something, others will copy it and take it. It does not happen. I can show it with my own history: I have been open sourcing my ideas for years, many of them I did not follow up, and they are still there. One of them, the one I describe below, I tried, and it did not work out. I still think it is a great idea, and I probably now have the technology to pull it off. As far as I can tell, nobody has.
copying

The reason is that an idea needs a specific person, with a specific understanding, to make it happen. open-source.sgit.ai maps what copying would actually cost an established company holding a full copy of your code: someone has to decide to do it, fund it, find someone to run it, pull developers off other work, deploy it, and then own it forever. Its estimate: "Optimistic: three months to reach where you already are. Realistic: closer to a year." Ideas are not what is scarce.
keep

The advantage of open sourcing everything you do that people miss is that you get to use it too. When you work for a company, everything you build usually gets locked in, and you have to be very careful, because there is a whole set of contracts around it. When you leave, you start from scratch. It is frustrating, and it is a waste. My trick, which worked very well, was to start early on working on open source projects that I brought into the company. In a weird way I was saying: I am making some changes to these projects, and I am bringing them in, so I am a lot more productive. Which I was. I never started from scratch in a new job, and my work kept getting better and better as I moved between companies.
cyber-boardroom

The Cyber Boardroom is the example. It was an experiment I did while I was working for two companies: I wanted to experiment with AI. Because I publish all the time, it did not stand out; it was not a big thing. I did it in the open, and I let all my managers know. Everybody was aware of it. It could have worked or not; it was an experiment, of the kind I had already been doing while working for other companies.
cyber-boardroom

When I left both roles, I continued where I had left off, and they were aware of it. It is not that I left and it was a success, either. I left, I formed the company, and The Cyber Boardroom was incorporated about a month later. Then I tried it, and it did not work. Fundamentally it was a wrapper around ChatGPT, there was not that much to it, and it was not the right time: what it needed was an environment to store confidential data, which is what sgit is now. But the work was mine to continue, because it had always been in the open.
early

If you work in a corporate environment and you have an idea, start talking about it, and the sooner the better. A lot of people are embarrassed to. They imagine an army of people out there waiting to complain about what they do. That army does not exist, and if you find someone like that, block them. You do not have to deal with it. Publishing early is also a great way to validate the market. You can experiment, see if anything bites, and you still have a job. The rougher it is, the better it protects you. A rough, public history shows your employer, if you are still there, that this is an experiment, learning, playing around, which it is: you are still very far from having a product or a company. And you are not making anything up, as long as you do not exaggerate. Showing the sausage factory works in your favour.
early

The danger is the other way. If what you publish appears late and polished, a lot of questions can be asked, and people will want to understand what happened when. You never want that, and you never want lawyers involved, because you never want to put anyone in a tough position. I know several cases where people did not publish early and it became very messy: somebody inside was uncomfortable, somebody had to answer questions, and they threw the person under the bus, because it was not their problem. You want to be able to say: yes, you knew about it, I have been doing it for the last six months, here is the history, here is how it evolved, bit by bit. Then they can see it did not just spring up.
discipline
Do it on separate machines and in separate environments. Do not build something that competes directly with the company you work for; that is a line not to cross. Apart from that, experiment.
win-win

I would argue it added a lot of value both ways. What I was doing on the side was learning how to use generative AI in practice, which meant that in my day job I gave much better advice and understood what was going on much better. My employers got that, and I got to experiment. And it is how I found my startups, almost three startups later. It would have been much more painful, and probably would not have worked, if each time I had had to start from scratch. How you pay for the time it takes is the subject of the next article, fund it with time.
limits

"Nobody copies it" is my experience. Some open source projects are copied; ideas on their own rarely are. This is not legal advice. Read your employment contract; some claim what you build outside work. The Cyber Boardroom did not succeed. The point is that the work stayed mine to continue. Telling your managers matters. Open source without their knowledge is not the same thing.
sources

A voice memo from me on 19 October 2026, written for this newsroom and for the book, Generation ZX Founders (GenAI Edition). The cost of copying is from open-source.sgit.ai, for founders; The Cyber Boardroom's story is also in not a straight line. Related: what open source is, and what it is not, fund it with time, can you sell it?. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: Agent Behaviour Policies are ready for the next level. We have a workflow that works, a mapping to what regulators are asking for, and a clear idea of how it should all fit together. What is left is execution, and execution starts with customers. We now have a first group of people who are engaged and motivated: consultants who will sell this and already use some of it, people I work with, and us. So we are launching an early access programme, and I would like to call the people in it customers, not beta users: each one starts with credit to spend on a site we run, and the site already meters and bills, the way this newsroom does today, starting at £5. We will follow each customer closely, an email every day if that is what it takes, with objectives and milestones written with them, on a dedicated site with a start-here page. What we want to discover is the usage moment: the simplest policy that is useful, the entry point with least friction, and the price that feels fair. Everyone else who asks goes on a mailing list for the next batch. This is the brief.
The first customers, from credit to the moment they would pay, with a daily follow-up and the meter. Proposed.
in-short

Agent Behaviour Policies are ready for the next level. The workflow, the mapping and the understanding are in place. What is left is execution. And execution starts with customers. Call them customers. Each one starts with credit, on a site that meters and bills. Follow each one closely. Daily if needed, with objectives and milestones of their own. A dedicated site, with a start-here page. Instructions, progress and usage in one place. Discover the usage moment. The simplest useful policy, the easiest entry, a fair price. A mailing list for the next batch. Everyone who asks, kept for when we are ready.
now

This is good news, and I think it is the move to the next level for Agent Behaviour Policies. We have a workflow that works: grant, mandate, delta and barrier, with a holder for every row. We have a mapping to what regulators are now asking for, worked through with the Pellbridge agents against the FCA's four elements. And we have a good understanding of how it should all fit together, from the policy beside the prompt to a policy for every skill. What is left is execution. And we have the people to execute it with: a good number of friendlies who are engaged and motivated. Some are consultants who are going to be selling this, and who already use some of it. Some are people I work with. Some of it is us. That is the first good group.
customers

I thought about what to call them: early access users, beta users, the first batch. Beta describes the state of the product. What I want to name is the relationship. So I think they should be customers. Each of them starts with credit, £5 or £50 or whatever the number turns out to be, to spend on a site we run. From the first day, what they use is metered, and the question of what they would pay is a real one. That is the same idea as paying after the value: this newsroom gives every reader £5 of credit, each page uses a few pence, and the reader decides when to top up, with the value already in front of them. Give it for free until there is enough value that they want to pay for it.
customers
The other reason is the one in can you sell it?: a customer who pays is the best signal you will get, and making it easy to pay goes in early, not at the end.
site

I think a dedicated site for this programme would help a lot: one place where we can follow how everyone is getting on, and where I can keep things up to date. It starts with a start-here page: what to do first, in order, with clear instructions. Then a page for each customer, with the objectives and milestones we agreed with them, and where they are. The billing is already there. This newsroom meters every page a reader reads against their credit, and the top-up link has been live since 11 October. The same works for any site we run: even if all a customer does is use the website, we can measure it, and we can bill for it. The price per use is something to discover. It could be quite high, or quite low. We start with credit and learn what feels fair.
follow

For this first batch, I would like us to really invest in following up: an email every day if that is what helps, very specific hand-holding, and objectives and milestones mapped out for each customer. That will not scale, and it is not meant to yet. Paul Graham made the case in Do Things that Don't Scale (July 2013): "The most common unscalable thing founders have to do at the start is to recruit users manually." He tells how Stripe's founders got their first users: "When anyone agreed to try Stripe they'd say 'Right then, give me your laptop' and set them up on the spot." And he says you can give users "an insanely great experience with an early, incomplete, buggy product, if you make up the difference with attentiveness." Each customer's follow-up asks three things: what they did, what got in the way, and what is next.
discover

The point of the programme is to find the usage moment: the moment an Agent Behaviour Policy becomes worth something to a particular person. Three questions follow from it. What is the simplest useful policy? One agent, a few rows, the gap found. Perhaps a system prompt turned into a policy, as in system prompts as behaviour policies; perhaps a skill checked against its mandate; perhaps one agent's reach, measured. What is the entry point with least friction? A reader once told us the pages were hard to understand. The start-here page has to fix that, and each customer will show us where it does not. What is the price? The credit tells us how much each customer uses before they would top up, and the follow-up tells us why.
discover

The things to track for each customer are simple: when they started, when they wrote their first policy, how many rows and gaps it has, which milestones are done, what they used of the credit, and whether they topped up.
batches

This is not a launch. It is a first batch, small enough to follow closely. Alongside it we start a mailing list: everyone who asks to join is kept for the next batch, with what they want to use it for. The next batch gets a start-here page made from what the first one taught us, and needs less hand-holding per customer. Batches, not a launch: the first batch of friendlies, the mailing list and the second batch. Proposed.
limits

The programme is new. The site, the start-here page and the mailing list are proposed here. The prices are not set. £5 and £50 are starting points, to test. The metering is real. It is this newsroom's meter today, not yet the programme's site. No customer is named. The first group is people we already work with. Everything is open. The policies, the vocabulary and this brief are CC BY 4.0.
sources

Abstract: On 17 October at 14:59 London time, rUv merged pull request #4239 into Ruflo's main branch.
