Abstract: Bert Kok's essay for The News Stack argues that AI is separating the production of original journalism from the systems that synthesise it and own the interface, and that publishers may fund the most expensive layer and capture the least valuable. I agree with most of it, and we have been building the parts the essay describes. Its "knowledge architecture", where each story keeps which statements are facts and which are claims, where they came from, when they were checked and what has changed, is what the PHP story site does for php2shell, every claim tied to a dated, hashed capture. Its "interface as a sensor" is our feedback loop: one outside collaborator sent three rounds of ideas, and the agents turned them into working features within hours. Two additions. First, agents are not here to replace journalists. What our newsrooms are missing is more journalists, and more readers, because every human in the loop makes the system much better. Second, I disagree that publishers should not own the stack. They should, because the stack is no longer a multi-million investment: I am publishing ours as open source, and others will follow. What publishers must own above all is the reader's trust. That leads to an economic model for local and niche publishers, which I set out in a companion article, and a tour of what we have built, for readers who have not seen it.
What we have built, in twelve pages, from this newsroom's front page to Pulse.
in-short

Bert Kok's essay is right about the shift. Synthesis and the interface are merging, and the platforms see the questions. We have been building the essay's "knowledge architecture". Facts and claims, sources, when checked, what changed. And its "interface as a sensor". Readers' feedback, turned into features within hours. Agents augment journalists; they do not replace them. What we are missing is more journalists, and more readers. I would own the stack. It is no longer a multi-million investment; ours is open source. Above all, own the reader's trust. That is the asset the platforms cannot copy. The economics follow: local trust, certified upwards.
his-argument

Bert Kok's post on LinkedIn, 25 October 2026, sharing the essay for The News Stack. Bert Kok's essay, published in the newsletter The News Stack on 25 October, starts from a new report by the Tow-Knight Center for Journalism Futures at CUNY, The Three-Layer Cake, released on 22 October. The report describes three layers: the products that find out what people want to know, the systems that synthesise answers, and the organisations that produce the underlying reporting.
his-argument

Bert's point is that the top two are converging. ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity "don't just synthesize information. They are also the interface." They see the question, pick the sources and watch what the user does next. Meanwhile, "The most expensive part of journalism is still discovering information that doesn't yet exist in the public record." AI makes processing cheap, not discovery. And scarcity alone does not get you paid: "There is no mature market determining how value moves from platforms that synthesize and deliver information back to the organizations financing its original production." The essay's answer is three capabilities: origination, a knowledge architecture, and, where a publisher can sustain it, a direct relationship with the reader. And it ends with a question I would put to any newsroom too: "If your articles disappeared tomorrow but your verified knowledge and audience relationships remained, would you still have something valuable enough to build products around and negotiate with AI platforms?"
his-argument
I replied under the post that I have been thinking along very similar lines, and building the pieces. This is the longer answer.
agree

Bert's point What we have built "A searchable pile of articles is not a knowledge architecture." Keep which statements are facts and which are claims, where they came from, when they were checked, and what has changed. The PHP story site: every claim points to a source, every source to a dated, hashed capture; a versioned state of affairs; a source watch of 913 pages that keeps a snapshot whenever a page changes, which is how we caught a publisher rewording without a note. The interface is "a sensor for the newsroom": readers' questions show what to report next. This newsroom's search can answer a question only from cited passages, and every article has a Pen for readers' notes; the PHP site has an Ask pane, and an agent, the Sherpa, that answers readers' feedback point by point. Publishers need to know who reads their work: humans, crawlers or agents, and to charge some of them.
agree

The PHP site's private telemetry separates readers, the editor, synthetic readers and crawlers; the source watch records whether each page it reads was open, behind a bot challenge or paywalled. No standard way to measure or price a source's contribution. Sources and their shadows: the licence, access, links and quotes of every reference, and who to pay; signed by the source.
augment

A reply under Bert Kok's post, 25 October 2026, about building MVPs for capturing, linking and monetising story data. I want to be clear about what the agents are for, because it is easy to read this as automation replacing reporters. It is the opposite. The PHP story is covered by 23 agents. A researcher captures every source; a curator turns the captures into evidence; a journalist agent publishes; a correspondent agent reviews the journalist's work, and on its first pass caught nine things the journalist had missed. That pipeline does exactly what Bert says AI does well: processing information that already exists, keeping it structured, current and attributable, at a cost that makes it possible to do continuously.
augment

What it cannot do is what Bert says remains expensive: discovering what is not yet in the public record. Cultivating a source. Attending the meeting nobody else attends. Knowing which caveat matters. So, honestly, what is missing from our PHP newsroom, and from this one, is more journalists. If they were involved, it would be so much better. The agents would be doing the work that buries journalists today, and the journalists would be doing what only they can. And more readers. The feedback loop is real, and it is fast. One outside collaborator sent the PHP site three rounds of comments and ideas. The second, five ideas, turned its risk graph into a working tool within hours. The third said the header took too much of a phone's screen: it went from 233 pixels to one 43-pixel line. One person sending feedback changed the product. Imagine a newsroom with thousands.
augment

On the commodity work, I agree with Bert's caution: do not defend production that a machine can do reliably, but do not cut the routine coverage that keeps readers coming back. With agents, you do not have to choose. The routine coverage can be produced, kept current and sourced by agents, and the time it used to take goes into original reporting.
own-the-stack

Bert writes that "for many, owning the full interface may be unrealistic", and that publishers "are unlikely to outperform the largest technology companies at general-purpose synthesis". On synthesis, Bert is right. On the stack, I disagree. I think publishers should own it.
own-the-stack

The reason they could not in the past is that a stack cost millions to build, and they were stuck with whatever they had paid for. That is no longer true. The stack behind everything on this page, the vaults, the capture, the evidence, the agents, the pages, is open source, and anyone can take it. The reader's half is already packaged: api.newsroom.sgit.ai serves the reading meter, personas, reading lists, the reader's vault, search and the wire reader as Apache-2.0 components, 74 files at release v0.2.5, live on this site and taking money, and a publisher can put the meter on its own pages with a pinned import of about ten lines. This newsroom's repository is public too, to fork. What is not packaged yet is the writing side: the article pipeline and the agents are a pattern to copy, not a kit. Others will do the same, and companies will provide it as a service. Publishers should leverage us, and the others. Owning the stack is now a matter of choosing, not of spending.
own-the-trust

What a publisher must own, more than any stack, is the reader's trust. That is the one thing the platforms cannot copy, and it is where the value is moving. And it is strongest where a publisher is closest to its readers: local, niche, expert, in their language and their culture. That is where the economics change. A local or niche publisher that owns the trust can take everything that has become commodity, including the big outlets' global news, and serve it to its readers from their point of view. And it can certify upwards: when a big outlet runs a story about its patch, the local publisher's journalists are the ones who can say it is right, and should be paid for saying so. I have set that out separately, in local trust, certified upwards.
tour

If you have not seen what we have been building, the collage at the top of this page shows the depth better than a list of links, but here is where to start: PHP October 2026. A live story covered by agents, with every claim tied to its evidence: start with the state of affairs, then the source watch, then Wikipedia, read as a graph. The bridge, followed to the end. A local bridge closure, simulated from the council's first notice to the first car across, kept as a story graph: what one local story is worth when nothing is thrown away. The waiting room knew first. A live local story, and the gap where local information used to be. Story vault underneath, Reader Skills on top. The same conversation with another journalist, Markus Franz, about why local journalism has the most to gain. The future of news is the story vault, not the paywall. The commercial model.
tour
The Industry Wire and World News Day. Feeds and a corpus kept in vaults, read in the browser. The control room. How the agents behind the PHP story are run, and what waits on me.
limits

Bert's essay is quoted from its public page; the summaries of it are mine. The reader's half is packaged; the writing half is not yet. api.newsroom.sgit.ai can be adopted today; the article pipeline and the agents are a pattern to copy, not a kit. Updated on 25 October 2026 to name api.newsroom.sgit.ai, which the first version left out. The agents do not do original reporting. That is the point of the argument. The feedback examples are from the PHP site, with one outside collaborator, not thousands.

Summary: Bert Kok's essay for The News Stack argues that AI is separating the production of original journalism from the systems that synthesise it and own the interface, and that publishers may fund the most expensive layer and capture the least valuable. I agree with most of it, and we have been building the parts he describes. His "knowledge architecture", where each story keeps which statements are facts and which are claims, where they came from, when they were checked and what has changed, is what the PHP story site does for php2shell, every claim tied to a dated, hashed capture. His "interface as a sensor" is our feedback loop: one outside collaborator sent three rounds of ideas, and the agents turned them into working features within hours. Two additions. First, agents are not here to replace journalists. What our newsrooms are missing is more journalists, and more readers, because every human in the loop makes the system much better. Second, I disagree that publishers should not own the stack. They should, because the stack is no longer a multi-million investment: I am publishing ours as open source, and others will follow. What publishers must own above all is the reader's trust. That leads to an economic model for local and niche publishers, which I set out in a companion article, and a tour of what we have built, for readers who have not seen it.

Bert Kok's essay, published in his newsletter The News Stack on 25 October, starts from a new report by the Tow-Knight Center for Journalism Futures at CUNY, The Three-Layer Cake, released on 22 October. The report describes three layers: the products that find out what people want to know, the systems that synthesise answers, and the organisations that produce the underlying reporting.
articles/versions/own-the-stack-and-the-trust/v1.1.0.html
his-argument

His answer is three capabilities: origination, a knowledge architecture, and, where a publisher can sustain it, a direct relationship with the reader. And he ends with a question I would put to any newsroom too: "If your articles disappeared tomorrow but your verified knowledge and audience relationships remained, would you still have something valuable enough to build products around and negotiate with AI platforms?"
articles/versions/own-the-stack-and-the-trust/v1.1.0.html
his-argument
I replied under his post that I have been thinking along very similar lines, and building the pieces. This is the longer answer.
articles/versions/own-the-stack-and-the-trust/v1.1.0.html
augment

What it cannot do is what he says remains expensive: discovering what is not yet in the public record. Cultivating a source. Attending the meeting nobody else attends. Knowing which caveat matters. So, honestly, what is missing from our PHP newsroom, and from this one, is more journalists. If they were involved, it would be so much better. The agents would be doing the work that buries journalists today, and the journalists would be doing what only they can.
articles/versions/own-the-stack-and-the-trust/v1.1.0.html
own-the-stack

Bert writes that "for many, owning the full interface may be unrealistic", and that publishers "are unlikely to outperform the largest technology companies at general-purpose synthesis". On synthesis, he is right. On the stack, I disagree. I think publishers should own it.
articles/versions/own-the-stack-and-the-trust/v1.1.0.html
own-the-stack

The reason they could not in the past is that a stack cost millions to build, and they were stuck with whatever they had paid for. That is no longer true. The stack behind everything on this page, the vaults, the capture, the evidence, the agents, the pages, is being published as open source, and anyone can take it. Others will do the same, and companies will provide it as a service. Publishers should leverage us, and the others. Owning the stack is now a matter of choosing, not of spending.

Abstract: php2shell has done something rare: it has the board's attention, and executives are asking good questions. There is some hype, but the impact is real. Nobody takes a website down lightly, and organisations took real sites down this week because they could not answer one question: are we safe? And you cannot be safe if you cannot deploy a patch. In my experience nobody fails to patch because they do not want to. The teams with the best pipelines patch for breakfast and run out of things to patch, because a patch is a change to a system, and they have the tests and the automation that make a change routine. Without them, patching is surgery: manual testing, people who could deploy long gone, side effects nobody knows. So it gets postponed, and a system that has not been updated in years is a signal of technical debt and of risk that we can measure. The PHP fix itself touched 389 files. The answer is not to patch, bring the site back and move on, because the next flaw will find it in the same state. It is to invest in the pipeline, the tests and paid maintenance, and the money being spent bringing sites back this week says the economics already add up.
A patch is a change to a system: surgery without tests and a pipeline, routine with them.
in-short

Never waste a good crisis. php2shell has the board asking real questions. Sites went dark because nobody could say "we are safe". You cannot be safe if you cannot deploy a patch. Nobody refuses to patch because they want to. The best pipelines patch for breakfast. Without tests and automation, a patch is surgery. So it is postponed, and the debt grows. We can measure it. When was each system last updated, and how long would a change take? Do not do it as a one-off. Invest in the pipeline, the tests and paid maintenance.
the-crisis

php2shell has one advantage over most vulnerabilities: it has board attention. Executives are asking good questions. There is definitely some hype, but the questions are real, and so is the impact. Nobody takes a website down lightly. These were real websites with real users: the PHP story's source watch tracks 295 sites that somebody named as taken offline. Why did they take them down? Because they could not answer a good question: are we safe? And if you cannot deploy a patch, you cannot be safe. So the real question is the next one: why can't they patch?
nobody-refuses

What I have learned over many years is that nobody fails to patch because they do not want to. In fact the best teams patch for breakfast. They run out of things to patch. Not because they are the best engineers, but because they have the best pipelines: they have the tests, they know the side effects, and they have automation that turns a change into a routine.
nobody-refuses

That is the point people miss: a patch is a change to a system. If you have good tests and a healthy pipeline, a change is small and safe. If you do not, patching is like surgery. You go to the operating table. The testing has to be done by hand. The people who could deploy are not there any more. The people who are there may be very capable, but they do not understand the system, they do not know the side effects, and they do not have good documentation. No wonder organisations do not want to patch.
nobody-refuses

The PHP fix shows why this is not about the size of the patch. As the PHP story's journalist found, it touched 389 files, 113 of them outside the tests, changing how the whole engine handles memory errors, and it adds new limits with defaults. Most of the fixes that reached servers did so through someone else's pipeline: a distribution's update, a hosting panel, an extended-support vendor. And for many platforms the fix was "fixed, if you rebuild": nothing already running changes until its owner rebuilds and redeploys it. If your organisation cannot rebuild and redeploy, the fix existing does not help you. As I said in my brief to that team, "if you have a website that's been going for years, updating it is very risky".
a-signal

If you do not patch regularly, that is a massive signal. It is a signal of technical debt, and a signal of risk. When something like php2shell happens, you have to patch anyway, under pressure, on the operating table.
a-signal

And we can measure it, even now, in the middle of the incident. When was this system last updated? How long would a change take, from commit to production? Can we still build it? Who knows its side effects? Two of those are close to what DORA's research measures: deployment frequency, and change lead time, "the amount of time it takes for a change to go from committed to version control to deployed in production". DORA has also found, repeatedly, that speed and stability are not trade-offs: "top performers do well across all five metrics". These are not new ideas. What is new is the moment: this week, every organisation that switched a site off has a list of the systems it could not answer for.
a-signal

I would go further. Show me a system that has not been updated and cannot be touched, and I will show you a system that is probably not serving its users as well as it could, and is not as effective as it could be. There is a direct connection. The ability to patch and the ability to improve are the same ability.
root-causes

A lot of security tools and security actions do not touch the root causes. A scanner can tell you that you are vulnerable; it cannot give you a team that can change the system. What you need is a team, funding, automation, and investment in the non-functional requirements and the whole life cycle of an application: the version control, the tests, the pipeline, the documentation, the ability to rebuild from scratch. I have argued for years that this is a business in its own right, and that whole companies should be built around providing it.
root-causes

It is also more urgent than it was. We are not yet seeing large amounts of AI-driven exploitation, but the tools are arriving: the AI insurance paper I reviewed this week points to a frontier model that can find and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities on its own. The time between a flaw being found and being used will keep shrinking, and so will the time an organisation can afford to spend on the operating table.
not-one-off

So here is the opportunity. Do not answer this crisis by patching PHP, bringing the site back, saying "all good" and moving on. That is the whack-a-mole we have been playing for decades, and the next flaw, next week or next month, will find the same system in the same state. Three ways to answer the crisis: the one-off, the measured and the investment. Instead, invest. Fix the second and third stories, not only the first: the pipeline, the tests, the people who can change the system. And pay for it properly. Somebody should be supporting that work and providing it as a cost-effective service, and the money is there: look at what organisations are spending this week to bring their sites back online, and imagine paying a fraction of that, every month, to keep them maintainable. I would argue the economics add up.
not-one-off

That is also what the signed, supported version in who maintains the PHP you run? is for. When you pay the people who maintain the code to sign off the version you run, and to help you set it up and keep it current, what you are buying is exactly this: the ability to change safely, whenever you need to. Think of a shop or a factory where key pieces of the infrastructure are things nobody knows how they work, nobody knows how to change, and nobody can update, but they are mission critical. We have got away with that in technology for a long time. It is time to move on, and this is a great moment to move the dial.
limits

No cost estimate exists for the shutdowns. "The money is there" is an argument from what organisations are visibly spending, not a measured figure. Some teams cannot patch for other reasons. Vendor contracts, certified configurations and regulated changes are real constraints. A pipeline does not remove judgement. It makes a change cheap to test; someone still decides. AI-driven exploitation is a trend, not yet a measurement of this incident.
sources

Abstract: On 10 October the reading meter on sgit.ai went, in seven releases between 12:09 and 15:49, from an experiment to a working pay-on-demand publication. A reader pays pence for the share of a page they actually read, from a balance that can go below zero without ever blocking them; after reading, they say how useful it was, and that sets the price, from free to double; their reading builds personas and a newsroom of their own, kept in their browser; and they can send it to us, encrypted, for a front page designed for them. Once a Stripe link is set, the only question left is whether people pay. This article introduces each feature, shows how each one grew out of the last, with a Wardley map that adds them one at a time, explains why paying after you see the value is the right way round, and why every decision started from one rule: do not rip off the reader. It ends with an offer to sites with traffic that would like to test it.

On 10 October, between 12:09 and 15:49, what I had been doing with the reading meter on this site stopped being a theoretical exercise. It went from an interesting piece of research to something commercial. As soon as a Stripe link is wired in, sgit.ai is a fully working pay-on-demand publication: every page has a price, readers pay for what they read and what they valued, and the money arrives in one place. The only question left is whether people will pay for it. That is literally the only thing. This article does two things. It introduces what was built, because a lot was added in one afternoon and none of it has been described in one place. And it uses the afternoon as a case study, probably the cleanest one we have, of the way I think innovation should happen when you work with agents: the more you have, the faster you go.

The reading meter at the end of 10 October, as a Wardley map: everything added that afternoon sits on the left, built on components that already existed on the right. The animated version, one release at a time, is in How it grew. Seven releases in 3 hours 40 minutes, alongside seven other pieces of work, with no slowdown: a meter, then paying by depth with no block below zero, then personas, versions, sharing your reading, and finally a rating that sets the price. You pay after you see the value. You read; the meter charges for the share you read; then you say how useful it was, and that sets the price, from free to double. Your reading is yours. It lives in your browser, builds personas and a newsroom for each of them, and reaches us only if you send it, encrypted.

The end state was not planned. Each feature came from using the one before. Designed up front, it would have been a bigger, slower and probably over-engineered project. It is the ILC zigzag at work. Every layer underneath, from sgit in March to the newsrooms in September, matured until it was invisible, and so the next could be built on it. It was fast because of what was already there: the build and its gates, versioned components, git as the history, vaults, append lanes and sealed envelopes, and sessions that release on their own. Every decision started with the reader. Not "money left on the table", but value for money: the reader should always feel the price was fair. What is missing is traffic. If you run a site with readers and little revenue from them, let's test it together.
features

Start with a reader arriving at an article. A price for every page, and you pay for what you read. A new article costs 10p and an older one 5p, read to the end. The meter charges the share you actually scroll through, rounded to 5% and never less than a tenth, once per page per session, topping up as you read further. Bounce off a page and it costs almost nothing. A balance that can go below zero, for ever. Everyone starts with £5.00 of credit. When it runs out, nothing happens: no wall, no bar, no nag, only a small balance in the top bar that turns a warmer colour below zero. Paying is something you do because you want to, not because a page has stopped you.
features

A card at the foot of every article. It shows what the page has cost so far, how much of it you read, and the price to the end. It adds the article to your reading list. And it asks three questions, each on a five-step scale that starts in the middle: How useful was this? This sets the price: 1 is free, 2 is half, 3 is the price, 4 is one and a half times, 5 is double. More like this? This moves the page's topics and tags in your persona, so your picks change. Level of detail. This is kept as your preference, and shown in your newsroom. The reader card at the foot of an article: what it cost, how much was read, the reading list, and the three ratings. Usefulness sets the price; the other two shape the newsroom.
features

Personas, and a newsroom for each. Your default persona is built from everything you read, weighted by how much of each page you read, and named from your top topics until you name it yourself (mine, in the test browser, became "The Fact Finder, with a streak of the Strategist"). You can start from five presets (a founder, a journalist, a security lead, an AI builder, a board member) or add as many of your own as you like, one for each kind of reading you do. Each has a newsroom: a front page of what it would want next, what you kept in it and what you put out of it, and a graph of the topics and pages it has grown. Your newsroom: a front page for one persona at a time, built in your browser from what you read.
features

A reading account that stays with you. The balance, the history, what you spent and your graph, with a top-up, a pause, an export as JSON and a fresh start. All of it is in your browser's storage and nowhere else. The reading account: the balance, what was spent, and the controls. Kept in this browser, and only here. Send us your reading, and get a front page designed for you. This is the one way your reading reaches us. The page shows, word for word, everything that would be sent. You can copy it into an email, or send it encrypted in your browser to our list agent's published key, over a write-only lane, with a consent tick. In return, I reply with what your front page could look like, built from your actual reading. Send us your reading: exactly what would be sent, word for word, then copy it or send it encrypted with your consent.
features

Articles that show their changes. Every article now has versions, read from git, with a page for each showing what changed, paragraph by paragraph. If you pay for writing that keeps improving, you can see what improved. One payment, when you choose. Topping up is one £5 Stripe Payment Link, with no account and nothing that renews. On a standard UK card Stripe's fee is about 27.5p of the £5, so one top-up spreads one card fee over dozens of pages: the aggregation that makes pence payments viable, which the open source economics article argued for earlier the same day.
after

A model I have always liked is Leanpub's. An author sets a minimum price and a suggested price, and the reader chooses what to pay with a slider, from the minimum upwards; Leanpub says readers "will choose to pay you more than your Minimum Price, and even more than your Suggested Price" (Leanpub), and it offers a full refund within 60 days (refunds). The one thing that always felt odd to me is that you choose the price before you have seen the value. The reader card turns that round: you read first, and then say what it was worth. That is a known idea, and the evidence on it is mixed in useful ways.
after

Paying what you want works better than people expect, but not for everyone. In a field experiment with 113,047 people buying souvenir photos, 0.5% bought at a fixed $12.95, while 8.39% bought when they could pay what they wanted, at an average of $0.92 (Gneezy and others, Science, 2010). Across three field studies, prices paid were "significantly greater than zero", and paying what you want "can even lead to an increase in seller revenues" (Kim, Natter and Spann, 2009). In a restaurant run that way for two years, average payments declined slightly and settled "at a positive level" (Riener and Traxler, 2012). The caution is that some people buy less, because they "feel bad when they pay less than the 'appropriate' price" (Gneezy and others, PNAS, 2012). That is why the card starts at the middle, at the price, so a reader who does nothing pays what the page costs and does not have to name a number.
after

Refunds for articles have been tried, and they measure quality. Blendle, the Dutch pay-per-article service, charged tens of cents an article and gave "an instant refund on any article they have purchased within 24 hours" (journalism.co.uk, 2014). Refunds ran at about 3% of articles at first, about 10% on average by 2016, and "as high as 50 percent" for gossip and lists (TechCrunch, 2016). That is the clickbait point in numbers: readers asked for their money back when a page did not deliver.
after

Pay-per-article on its own did not last. Blendle stopped selling single articles in the Netherlands in 2019 to focus on a monthly subscription, saying "We are still not making a profit" (DutchNews), and closed its German and US pay-per-article service in September 2023 because their user bases were "very limited" (journalism.co.uk, 2023). The difference here is not the price per page. It is what the page buys: a persona and a newsroom that get better the more you read, and a balance that never stops you. Elsewhere, refunds come with limits. Steam refunds a game for any reason within 14 days if it was played for under two hours (Steam), and Amazon restricted Kindle returns in 2023 to books less than 10% read (Authors Guild). Charging for the share actually read solves the same problem from the other end: a page you abandon early costs little, so there is little to refund.
after

The context is why this is worth trying. Across 20 countries, 17% of people paid for online news in 2026, and in the UK it is about one in ten (Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026; 2025). The subscription has a ceiling. Paying for what you read, after you read it, is one way past it.
reader-first

Every decision this afternoon was a choice between charging more now and making the reader glad they paid. Looking back at the afternoon, every decision was easy to make, because each one started from the same rule: do not rip off the reader. Make sure they are paying for value, and make sure they are happy with what they paid. That is not how a lot of pricing is done. A common instinct, in management and in sales, is not to leave money on the table: we could charge a bit more, and by not doing so we are letting the customer get away with something. I think that is a bad instinct. You never want to charge a customer the maximum they can pay, because by definition they end up feeling it was expensive, and a customer who feels that is not happy.
reader-first

Think about what "expensive" means. I do not find something expensive when its value for money is high, even if it costs a lot. Something becomes expensive when its value drops below its price. I might still pay for it and I can still afford it, but I now find it expensive, which means I use it less, and I do not recommend it: if something is good but expensive, I am not going to push it on friends and make them carry the cost. The sweet spot is value for money, because that is where people use a thing more and more, which is exactly what a publication wants.
reader-first

So, when the first version had a "Don't charge me" button, it worked, but it felt draconian: a refund you had to ask for, with a reason. The rating that replaced it as the main path says the same thing the other way round: if you saw the value, pay; if you saw more value, pay more; if you did not, do not. "Don't charge me" is still there, as the exception.
reader-first

What about the readers who read and never pay? Those are not readers a publication is losing money on. And a reader who did not value a page is the last one who should pay for it: charging them makes them more jaded, not more loyal. This is also a measure of the journalism. Click on a headline that promised something the article did not deliver, and you feel it: you came for something and did not find it. If you also paid for it, you feel it twice. A rating after reading puts that feeling on the record, page by page, and gives the publication a reason to stop writing pages that cause it.
how

The afternoon from git: seven steps of the reading meter in 3 hours 40 minutes, and seven other pieces of work released in the same four hours. None of the features at the end of the afternoon were where I started. The sequence, from the commits: The experiment, two weeks earlier. The first version of browser-based consumption was on pt.newsroom.sgit.ai, the Portuguese newsroom: a wallet in which "cada página deste site custa um cêntimo a abrir" (every page costs a cent to open), with the record of what you spent on a page of its own, and the balance kept in the reader's browser. 12:09, a meter in the browser (v0.7.24). That wallet brought to sgit.ai: a price for every page, £5 of credit, a history, and picks from it. A simulated top-up with every step except the payment.
how

13:40, the meter goes live (v0.7.26). Using it made the next steps obvious: pay for how far you read, decline a page with a reason, a real £5 Stripe link, and the meter rebuilt as a component, SG Meter, other sites can install. And the step that made it commercial: below zero, with no cut-off. From that moment the offer is simply that readers can pay if they want. 14:23, personas and a newsroom of your own (v0.7.28). Once the history existed, it could become a persona, and a persona could have a front page. 14:29, articles have versions (v0.7.29), read from git. 15:28, send us your reading (v0.7.31). The personalised newsroom raised the obvious question of what readers would actually want, and the way to find out was to ask them to send it, on their terms. 15:49, the reader card (v0.7.34). The last feature, and probably the best: the ratings, with usefulness setting the price.
how

There is a direct line between something working, trying it out, and improving it, and improving it again. Each step was me trying the previous one and saying: now add this. Ironically, if I had designed the end state we arrived at, I think we would have over-engineered it. It would have been the typical big project, with too much attempted at once, months of work, and untested features shaping other untested features. Instead, each feature was shaped by the one before it being in use. The "Don't charge me" button is the best example: it had to exist, and feel wrong, for the rating to be the obvious answer.
how

The Wardley map makes the same point. Every new component sits at the genesis end, on the left, and every one of them is built on components further right that were already there and already boring: browser storage, git, Stripe, the build, vaults, append lanes, the sealed envelope. The afternoon was cheap because the right-hand side of the map was already built. The afternoon as a Wardley map, one release at a time: what already existed, then each feature as it was added and what it was built on, ending with what comes next. Times are UTC, from the commits.
ilc

The same story at a larger scale, built up one layer at a time: each layer matured until it was invisible, and that is what made the next one possible. The map of the afternoon shows one day. The same pattern runs through the whole project, and Simon Wardley has a name for it: ILC, innovate, leverage, commoditise. You "take an existing product that is relatively well defined and commonplace and turn it into an industrialised utility", then "encourage and enable other companies to innovate by building on top of your utility", and "you then repeat this virtuous circle" (Wardley, 2016). His map of it has a platform growing on the right as each component is industrialised, with new things being built on the left. Drawn for this project, it is a zigzag. Here, a thing is commoditised when it becomes invisible: when the layer above can use it without thinking about it.
ilc

sgit, encrypted vaults from a command line. The first release was on 4 March 2026, as sg-send-cli 0.3.0, and after 88 releases it is sgit-ai 0.20.0. Once it just worked, vaults could hold more than files. Vaults that open as apps: HTML in a vault, a read key in the browser. The first on this site was published on 16 August; there are 53 now. Once that was routine, a vault could be an experiment of its own. Claude sessions with a repository and a vault, which is the layer we did not build. Agents with no other access, using a vault as their memory and their shared drive. When that became ordinary, building a website became a conversation. Websites built and released by agents: sgit.ai from v0.1.1 on 11 August to v0.7.39 today, with gates on every release. Once a release was routine, a site could be a product of its own.
ilc

Newsrooms: sgit.newsroom and pt.newsroom, where the one-cent wallet appeared by 27 September. Once the newsroom worked, it could carry an experiment in paying. SG Meter, the reading meter, from v1.0 at 12:09 to v1.3 at 15:49 on 10 October. At the top, the reader: read on demand, pay for use and for value. From the reader's side it already just works: open a page, read it, choose what it was worth. Every layer under it is invisible to them, which is the point. The speed of the afternoon is the zigzag at work. Every time I tried something and it was solid, it became something to stand on: this is working, now do this, now do that. Each step was small because the steps under it had stopped needing attention. The whole zigzag. Solid arrows are a thing maturing, until it is invisible; dashed arrows are what its maturity made possible, one layer up.
fast

I have written several times that small shipped components compound (every mistake added a rule): the more we have, the faster we go. This afternoon is the cleanest case study we have, and the reasons are specific. A build with gates. Every release runs the same build and the same validator, so a feature lands without anyone checking the site by hand, and a broken link, a missing card or a leaked key stops the release. Components on versioned, immutable paths. SG Meter went from v1.0 to v1.3 in an afternoon, each version on a new path with the old ones kept, so nothing that already worked could break. A browser test for the meter (depth, decline, below zero, the return page, personas, restore), added after the second release and run on every one after. git as the history, which is what made article versions a feature rather than a project, and the timeline above a query.
fast

Things already built for something else. The encrypted share reuses the subscribe identity, its published key, its write-only lane and its list agent; the persona graph reuses the site's article graphs. Sessions that release on their own. Several Claude sessions worked on this one repository in parallel, each fetching, rebuilding and releasing in minutes, which is why seven other pieces of work shipped in the same four hours without getting in the way. These are all non-functional requirements: the work that never appears in a feature list. They are why the feature list could grow by one item every half hour.
pieces

I think so, for a first version, and it is worth being exact about what that means. What exists and runs: a price for every page; metering by depth; a balance that never blocks; feedback that sets the price; personalisation through personas and newsrooms; a way for a reader to share their data with consent and encryption; a payment path; documentation for other sites; a security page with nine known gaps, all accepted and costed; and hypotheses with thresholds to check after eight weeks. What does not exist yet: The Stripe link itself. Until it is set, readers see the simulated top-up, and the eight-week clock has not started. Update, 11 October 2026: the link is set and payments are live on newsroom.sgit.ai, so the clock has started.
pieces

Payment verification. A static site cannot receive Stripe's confirmation, so the return page credits without checking it, and says so. That is accepted, because the cost of someone faking a top-up is that they read more of our articles. Your reading on more than one device. Everything lives in one browser; a new device starts again unless you export. The answer is a persona in your own encrypted vault, which follows you and your agent, and which we cannot read. That is the next step, and it is why the vault matters. The accounting side of real money: receipts, and the obligations that come once revenue is material. Readers. This site does not have the traffic to say whether people pay.
pieces

And the real test is not the payment. It is whether a reader prefers the front page personalised for them, or for one of their personas, over the front page everybody gets. The persona that follows you, private by default and readable by us only if you choose, is the value; the payment is what a reader does when they feel it.
others

SG Meter is ready for other sites: five files on versioned paths, a small config, a Stripe Payment Link, and the documentation. How others can commercialise with it, and how we could help as a service, will be a future article, and we will publish it as a fully documented, open model.
others

What I do not have here is traffic: readers who come back every day. This would be far more interesting on a site that has them, and especially on one that is not monetising its readers much today, so it has almost nothing to lose. A blogger with a loyal readership would be a great fit. I am going to reach out to some people I know, and if you run a site like that, let's work together to test it. It will get more interesting still once the persona lives in the reader's own vault, so I would like a couple of sites validating the model before then. Write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Most of what readers are asked to pay for, they pay for because they have to, because they are made to feel they should, or because it is the right thing to do. That works to a degree, and it does not scale. The value proposition we want is the opposite: a reader pays because it helps them, because what they are buying is time, context, focus, the ability to make good decisions and a better experience. On this site that thing now has a name. Your reading builds a persona, with a name and a graph you can watch grow, and you can have several, because a persona is a way to manage focus: one for security, one for AI development, one for everything else. Start from five made from what this site publishes, keep articles in a persona or put them out of it, and switch between them. Today it all lives in one browser, so opening the site on an iPad and then on a laptop gives you two strangers. That is the bad experience worth fixing, and the thing worth paying for: a persona that follows you to your phone, your laptop and your agent, with the privacy intact.

Two ways to ask a reader for money. On the left, the reasons readers are asked to pay today; on the right, the things they would pay for because they help them, and the persona that carries them from device to device. Nobody should pay out of guilt. Paying because you have to, because you feel you should, or because it is the right thing to do works to a degree. It does not scale, and it is not what we want readers to feel. Pay for what it does for you. Time, context, focus, the ability to make good decisions, a streamlined way through, a better experience. That thing is a persona. Your reading builds one, with a name and a graph you can watch grow. Keep articles in it or put them out of it, and it changes.

You are more than one reader. Add personas, one per kind of reading. Five are ready to start from: the founder, the journalist, the security lead, the AI builder, the board member. A persona is a way to manage focus. Today a persona lives in one browser. Open the site on an iPad, then on a laptop, and you are two strangers. That is not a cheat to worry about. It is a bad experience. What people will pay for is a persona that follows them, to their phone, their laptop and their agent, with the privacy intact. There are three common reasons a reader pays for what they read, and most reader-funded publishing uses one of them. Because they have to. The paywall. The Guardian's app, Press Gazette reported in September 2025, "sits within a paywall (free users can only read 20 articles per month)".

Because they feel they have to. The ask, the count of what you have read, the reminder that others pay. The Guardian's middle tier, at £12 a month, buys among other things the right to "avoid intrusive pop-up supporter messages". The feeling of being asked has a price, and the price is paid to make it stop. Because it is the right thing to do. The donation. Wikipedia is the best example there is: the Wikimedia Foundation reports "over 8 million donors giving an average donation of $10.58" in its 2023-24 financial year. That is a remarkable achievement, and it is what one of the most visited sites in the world reaches by asking everybody, every year.

All three work, to a degree. My view, after trying versions of them, is that they do not scale for anyone who is not already enormous, and that they make the reader feel the wrong thing. "We don't want people to pay for content because they have to, because they feel they have to, because you shame them, because they feel they have a moral obligation." The reader should pay because paying helps them. Not the article. The article is free to read here, and it is free to read with the meter below zero. What a reader is buying, on this site and on most good ones, is: time, because they reach the thing worth reading sooner; context, because each piece arrives connected to what they already know; focus, because the site shows them their kind of reading and not everything; the ability to make good decisions, because the evidence comes with the argument;

a streamlined way through, because what they have read, kept and dismissed is remembered; a better experience, because the site knows them back. Each of those depends on the same asset: a record of what the reader read, how much of it, what they kept and what they rejected, organised so that the site can act on it. The reading meter already keeps that record, because a ledger has to. Since today it does something with it that the reader can see.

Your reading builds a persona. It starts empty, and every page you read adds to it, weighted by how far down the page you read. It gets a name from the topics you read most, until you give it one of your own: read mostly about agents and policy and it is The Policy Architect; add graphs and it becomes The Policy Architect, with a streak of the Cartographer. It has a front page, your newsroom, with the articles it would want next. And it has a graph: you in the middle, the topics you read around you, the pages behind each topic, and the citations between those pages. Your newsroom, as one of the five starting personas: who it is, what it would read next, with a Keep and a "Not for this persona" on every pick.

You can steer it. Every pick in your newsroom has Keep and Not for this persona, and every article page has Keep in your persona at its foot. A kept article pulls its topics and tags up; a rejected one pushes them down and disappears from the picks. The graph moves when you do. This is the part that matters most, and it is small: the reader can see the model the site has of them, and change it. A persona as a graph: the persona in the middle, its topics around it sized by weight, the pages behind each topic, and the citations between them. Filled dots were read, green ones kept, hollow ones came with the preset and are still unread.

One persona is not enough, and that is the second thing I learned building The Cyber Boardroom: once users try personalisation, they do not want one persona, they want several. I read about cyber security for one reason and about AI development for another, and the version of me that reads one is not interested in the other's picks. A persona is a way to manage focus. The more a reader can do with it, the more attached they become to it. So you can have as many as you like. Each has its own picks, its own graph, and its own list of articles kept in or put out. What you read while a persona is active counts towards it; your default persona, built from everything you read, keeps counting everything. And so that nobody starts from nothing, there are five ready-made personas built from what this site has published: Persona Starts from For Morgan, the founder

Strategy, pricing, security sized to the startup Building a company: what to build, what to charge, what to secure and when to stop Rowan, the journalist News history, story vaults, local evidence Where news came from, where it could go, and what publishers are owed by the machines that read them Sam, the security lead Insider risk, blast radius, identity, incidents Agents as insiders, and the controls that hold when a model does not Kai, the AI builder Claude Code sessions, hooks, memory, behaviour policies Making agents work day to day Jordan, the board member Business models, due diligence, risk acceptance, governance How AI is changing the business, and how to govern it Each one starts from seven or eight articles and a few topics, and becomes yours as you read and curate. The names are made up and you can change them; your personas is where.

Your personas: the default one built from all your reading, the ones you added, and the five starting points not yet added. I opened the site on my iPad this morning, and it worked well. The balance was in the top bar, the reading account was there, and the front page made sense. Then I thought about opening it on my laptop, and realised I would be a stranger there: a new balance, no history, no persona.

The first article on the meter called that a cheat: open a private window and you start again with £5.00. Who will game the reading meter explained why that does not matter, because the reader who does it was not going to pay anyway. But it is more interesting than that. The more a persona knows, the worse it is to lose it. Two devices, two strangers, is not a security gap; it is a bad user experience, and it gets worse exactly as the product gets better. Today the only fix is manual: export your account as JSON on one device and restore it on the other, from your reading account. It works, and it is clumsy on purpose, because it shows what is missing.

A persona that follows you. To your phone, to your laptop, and to your agent: when I connect to this site through Claude, the agent should read as my security persona when I am working on security, not as a stranger and not as everyone. That is the value proposition, and it is tight: people do not pay because they care about the site, and they should not feel guilty if they don't. They pay because they want to keep their persona, and to have it wherever they read.

The privacy angle does not go away when that happens; it is what makes it possible. The persona lives in the reader's browser today and nowhere else. When it moves, it moves into an encrypted vault whose key only the reader holds, so the site that stores it cannot read it, and the reader can take it elsewhere. The site pays for the storage it cannot read; the reader pays for the persona that lives in it.

If the persona is worth keeping, the next question is whether there is enough worth reading in it. There are about sixty articles on this site today, across six topics, and the five starting personas were chosen so that each has a real starting shelf. The better the graph of each article becomes, the better every persona built on it becomes, which is why the work on extracting more from each article, more facts, more connections, more ways to read it, matters to this as much as to the articles themselves. One article, five readers is the first of it: a librarian, a cartographer, a historian, an explainer and a storyteller sent through each article after it is written, with every item anchored to its sentence.

There is a faster way than waiting for numbers. Use the site as you normally would for a few days, then send us your reading: which pages, how far down each, what you kept, put out or declined. Dinis will reply with what your front page could look like, designed from your actual reading. The page shows you, word for word, everything that would be sent; you can copy it into an email or a message, or send it with your name and email, encrypted in your browser so that only our list agent can open it. It is the tightest feedback loop we have: real reading in, a real front page back.

These are added to the anchors in going live with the reading meter, after its five were written and before the first payment. They cannot be tested until a persona can follow a reader between devices; they are here so that we cannot pretend later that we expected something else. # Hypothesis Proved wrong if H6 When a persona can follow a reader between devices for a price, more readers pay for that than top up the meter for reading alone Fewer pay for the persona than for reading H7 Readers who have more than one persona pay more often than readers who have one No difference, among readers who tell us

You have a persona already; your newsroom shows it. Add one of the five, keep a few articles, put one out, and watch the graph change. Then open the site on another device and see what you have to leave behind, or send us your reading and we will design your front page from it.

Abstract: Almost every time I buy something, I am buying future value. A subscription, a gym membership, a big security product on a good deal, even a one-off purchase: I am betting that I will use it enough for the price of each use to fall to a number I am comfortable with. Often I lose the bet, and the cost of unsubscribing keeps me paying. The research agrees: gym members on a monthly contract paid more than $17 a visit when they could have paid $10. This newsroom is trying the opposite. You start with £5 of credit, each article you read uses a few pence, you can set the price from free to double or refuse it, and the balance can go below zero and stay there. By the time you are asked to pay, you have the value in front of you: what you read, how much, what you liked. The payment is connected to what you received, not what you hope to receive. That only works where the cost of serving is close to zero, which is true of a static site on a CDN, and where the value adds up in a way the reader can see. Wikipedia is the counter-example: £20 a year asked for at a moment with no value in view, even though it is a few pence an article. Add prices fair by country, the Big Mac index for reading, and a view of where the money goes, and payment becomes a choice people are glad to make. The experiment is live, with written hypotheses and a review in December, and I will report back.
Paying for the future, or paying for what you got: a subscription asks first, a meter that can go negative asks last.
in-short

Most purchases are bets on future value. You pay first and hope to use it enough. Often the bet is lost. Gym members paid over $17 a visit when $10 was on offer. Pay after the value instead. Start with credit, use it page by page, let the balance go negative. The payment meets the value. By the time you pay, you can see what you read and what you liked. It works where serving costs almost nothing. A static site on a CDN is the extreme case. Wikipedia shows the other way. A yearly ask with no value in view, for something worth a few pence a page. Fair, visible, chosen. Prices by country, a view of where the money goes, and verified facts as their own product. The experiment is live. Seven hypotheses, a review on 6 December 2026.
future

Almost every time I buy something, I am buying future value. In cyber security this is especially visible: expensive products, and very good deals, where a deal usually means more of the thing for a lower price per unit. A subscription is the same bet in smaller pieces: I will use this enough that the cost of each use falls to a level I accept. A gym membership, a streaming service, a magazine, even a one-off purchase I expect to use for years. The calculation is always the same, and it is always about the future.
future

The research says we are bad at it. Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier's study of three gyms found that "members who choose a contract with a flat monthly fee of over $70 attend on average 4.3 times per month", so "They pay a price per expected visit of more than $17, even though they could pay $10 per visit using a 10-visit pass." Then the cost of leaving does the rest. Subscriptions are easy to start and tiring to stop, which is why regulators keep trying to make cancelling as easy as signing up: the US Federal Trade Commission's click-to-cancel rule was vacated by a court in July 2025 and the process has started again, and the UK's new subscription rules are due in 2027.
psychology

Behavioural economists have a name for part of this: the pain of paying. Drazen Prelec and George Loewenstein wrote in 1998 that "The pain of paying, we argue, plays an important role in consumer self-regulation, but is hedonically costly." Their model also explains why we like paying up front: "consumption that has already been paid for can be enjoyed as if it were free." The same work shows the cost of it. In a study John Gourville and Dilip Soman reported, people who paid in advance for a season of four plays had "a no-show rate of 21.5 percent", against under one percent for people who bought a ticket for a single play: once the payment is in the past, it stops pulling you to use what you bought.
psychology

So paying first feels good at the moment of use and bad at the moment of payment, and it quietly decouples the two. Paying after the value couples them again, on purpose, at the end. The payment comes when the value is in view, and the value is what makes the payment feel fair.
meter

The reading meter experiment: what works now, what is partly built, and what the article proposes, with five hypotheses. This site runs the experiment, and its rules are written down in Pay after you read and Going live with the reading meter. "Everyone starts with £5.00 of credit." Reading uses it: "10p for a new article read to the end, 5p for an older one, less for other pages", and only as far as you read, so the first screen of an article costs a penny. You set the price: a rating moves it from free to double, and you can refuse to pay for a page, with a reason, and the charge comes back. And "Your balance can go below zero and stay there; nothing is blocked and nothing nags." When you want to, you top up with one £5 payment link, which has been live on this site since 11 October, with no account and nothing that renews.
meter

The point of the negative balance is psychological, not financial. By the time you are below zero, you have read dozens of articles, fifty if you read every one of them to the end, you can see which ones, and how far you got. Each one was a small piece of value, and each one, if it was good, felt good. The request to pay arrives after all of that, and it is connected to it. Starting at £5 rather than zero matters too: a reader who tops up again is paying for what they have already consumed, not for what they hope to consume.
wikipedia

Wikipedia is the clearest counter-example, and I say that as someone who values it enormously. Its fundraising raised US$184.5 million in 2024 to 2025, from 7.7 million donors, an average of about US$10. But the ask arrives as a lump sum, at a moment when the value is not in view. Whatever the number, a once-a-year request feels heavy, because the value is thousands of small moments that nobody adds up: the answers found, the time saved, the roads not taken because you knew better. It is the tragedy of the commons applied to your own reading: each benefit is too small to feel, so the total never gets felt either. Imagine the same ask with your year in front of you: the articles you read, how many, which ones you came back to. A penny an article for four hundred articles is £4, and it is easier to give when you can see the four hundred.
where

This model has a condition, and it is worth being plain about it. It only works where there is a very large gap between the cost of serving and what you can charge. Software has always had that gap, and a static website has it in the extreme: this site has no back end, pages are served from a CDN, and the cost of one more reader reading one more article is close to nothing. Even at 10p, the margin is very high. A business with a real cost per unit cannot let balances run negative for ever.
where

It also needs value that adds up in a way the reader can see. That is why I keep wanting the reading history for myself: which pages I read, which I skimmed, which I meant to come back to, which I liked, across every device I use. The billing is a side effect of that tracking, and the tracking is valuable on its own. Pay to keep your persona made it a hypothesis: that readers will pay more for a history that follows them between devices than for reading alone. The reader can always delete it; it is theirs. And it still works for readers who never pay. What they read, and what they rate, tells us which articles are worth writing.
fair

Three more things would make it fairer and, I think, more successful. Fair by country. 10p in the UK is not 10p everywhere. Prices should follow local purchasing power or wages, the way The Economist's Big Mac index is "an informal way of measuring the purchasing power parity" between currencies. Streaming services already do it; reading can too. Visible. A reader should be able to see what the money pays for: better articles, fact checks, follow-ups. There is good evidence that this changes behaviour. In a field experiment at an amusement park, letting people pay what they wanted for a photo meant many bought one but "paid only about 92 cents each"; when half of what they paid went to charity, fewer bought, but they paid an average of $5.33.
fair

Chosen, at more than one level. Verified facts are worth more than unverified ones, and to some readers, especially commercial ones, a lot more. A follow-up on a story they care about, a certified fact, a briefing with every claim checked: those are things people choose to pay for, separately, because they need them.
experiment

The good news is that this is not a thought experiment. The meter is live, real money can move, and the hypotheses were written before the first payment, in Going live with the reading meter: H1, a first real payment within 14 days; H2, at least 10 payers by the review; H3, at least three who pay twice; H4, no disputes; H5, below zero is normal and not a reason to leave. Two more, about a persona that follows the reader between devices, are in Pay to keep your persona. The review is on 6 December 2026. I will come back in a few weeks, and again then, with what happened, including if nobody paid.
limits

No results yet. The meter has no analytics and the review is in December; nothing here says it works. The balance is notional until you top up. No debt is ever collected; a negative balance is a number on your screen. The studies are about other things. Gyms, theatre tickets and photos, not reading; they explain the psychology, not our results. Regional prices, a view of where the money goes and the year-in-reading view are proposals. Not built yet. Wikipedia's figures are its own. From its fundraising report for 2024 to 2025. If you run a site, a product or a service where the cost of serving is close to zero and want to try paying after the value, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Abstract: The second update on php2shell and the newsroom covering it, as of 23:30 UTC on 23 October. The story held: no named organisation has said it was breached through php2shell, CISA still lists neither flaw as exploited, and 109 of 751 affected products in the Dutch NCSC's inventory are fixed. The newsroom changed more. In a day and a half it built tools to see who reads the site and what works on it, private by design, and they found that the front page leaks: 81% of readers who start there read nothing else. An outside collaborator's five ideas turned the risk graph into a tool within hours. Scheduled agents now keep the evidence current, and our biggest data vault went from a 13-minute download to 95 seconds. And 15 of the 20 agents were waiting on a decision from me.
The PHP site's telemetry dashboard on 23 October, filtered to readers in the United Kingdom with phones left out.
in-short

The story held. No named organisation breached through php2shell; neither flaw on CISA's exploited list; 109 of 751 products fixed. The site now watches its own readers, privately. And the first thing it showed is that the front page leaks. A reader's ideas became a tool in hours. The risk graph, rebuilt from a collaborator's five ideas. Readers have a guide. A new agent answers their feedback point by point. Agents on a schedule keep the evidence current. 33 new captures on 23 October. The bottleneck is me. 15 of the 20 agents were waiting on my decisions.
the-story

The journalist agent keeps the state of affairs as a versioned page, so the day can be read as the difference between two versions. Version 1, at 14:11 UTC: Organisations that have said they were breached through php2shell: none. Three cases still open (ČVUT, which stopped an attack it links to worldwide PHP attempts; GMO's FX VPS, with no cause stated; DMM, with PHP not confirmed) and one ruled out (Valtec, which corrected itself). CISA's catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities: neither flaw listed, unchanged since the evening of 22 October. NVD's score: 9.8 out of 10 (CVSS 3.1), beside the 9.2 (CVSS 4.0) the PHP project gave it. Public code repositories mentioning the flaws: 735, up from 586 the evening before. A count of search results, not of working exploits. The Dutch NCSC's inventory of affected software: 109 of 751 products fixed, 389 still under investigation.
the-story

Version 2 followed just after midnight, from 295 sources, with six of the curator's new claims held back and the reason given. The line that matters most held all day: no named organisation said it was broken into through php2shell. That is a time-bounded absence, and the site says so; one statement from one organisation would end it.
telemetry

The biggest change of the day was on the newsroom's side. In a day and a half, the dev desk agent built the tools I had been asking for: a way to see who reads the site and what works on it, without tracking anyone. Private by design. Every page sends one anonymous event: the page, the site that referred the reader, a country and city from a lookup, the language, the kind of screen and a random id that lives in that browser tab. No IP address, no cookie, no name. The event is encrypted in the reader's browser before it leaves, and sent to a write-only lane on a private vault: the lane accepts writes and answers every one the same way, so nobody can read anything back through it. Only the holder of the vault can read the events.
telemetry

Not everyone who opens a page is a reader. The first night looked busy: 356 page views from one session. It was Google's crawler, working through 252 pages. So every session is now in one of five groups: readers, the editor, power users and the team, synthetic visitors (agents and tests, including our own), and crawlers. Of the 1,093 page views by 20:26 UTC, crawlers were 565 and readers 233. Without the groups, every chart would have been mostly Google. All 1,093 page views by group: readers, the editor, power users and the team, synthetic readers and crawlers. Page views per hour from 22 to 23 October, by group, with the crawler working through the night.
telemetry

A public face and a private dashboard. The counts, and only the counts, go into a public vault anyone can open, with a world map of where readers are. The full events stay private, in a dashboard that opens straight from its own vault and works like Kibana: click any bar, country, cell or node to keep only that; shift-click to leave it out; every number follows. Readers by country, on a log scale: eighteen countries, with the United Kingdom first by far.
telemetry

What it found: the front page leaks. The journeys view follows sessions page by page. 113 reader visits started on the front page, and 81% of them read nothing else; the front page is read most and sends the fewest readers on. Of the sites that send readers, kode24.no, a Norwegian developer site, sends ones who stay: more than a third read a second page, against one in five from LinkedIn. That is the kind of finding a newsroom needs on day two, not in month three. How reader sessions move through the PHP site, step by step, from the front page onward. The same moves as a network: each page a node sized by the sessions that saw it, with the front page as the hub. What works, page by page: further right is read more, higher up is where readers go on.
telemetry

How it was built in a day and a half. This is the part I find most powerful. The dev desk did not build a telemetry platform. It assembled one from pieces we had already made into commodities: encrypted vaults that keep their history; write-only append lanes that let a browser send encrypted rows to a vault it cannot read; keys that live inside the vault, so whoever can open it can process it from the browser with no server; and apps that live in a vault of their own, versioned there, and open the data where it sits. No database, no analytics vendor, no server to run. When the pieces are commodities, a capability like this is a day and a half of conversation with an agent, not a project.

One of the workflows I am proudest of is what happens when a collaborator writes in. On 23 October, the same outside collaborator who had sent the first set of ideas wrote back after seeing the risk graph and the redesign mockups. The Sherpa agent turned the message into CI-002: ten numbered items, each with the collaborator's own words, where the site stands today with links, what is missing, what the Sherpa recommends, and who could take it. Five of them went to the dev desk as a brief.

The result, the same day: the risk graph, 713 nodes and 1,418 edges connecting stakeholders, risks, weaknesses, the fix and its tests, became a tool. Every link now says how it is known (read from a capture, read from the fix commit, or inferred by an agent, drawn dashed and hideable). You can start from one thing, a CVE, a risk, a file, a test, and follow it a step at a time. And a gaps page is computed at every build. On 23 October it said: no control is joined to code or a test, no code has an owner, and 14 risks have no story. That is the kind of honest gap list I want every system to have. The dev desk then wrote a before-and-after for the collaborator, every change shown as the old page against the new. There is already a CI-003. readers

A new agent joined: the Sherpa, which walks with the reader. It answers readers' feedback point by point (three pieces on 23 October, with two interface bugs reproduced), keeps a friction log of what gets in readers' way and who can fix each, and sets collaborators' ideas against what the site already does. The designer put a redesign out for review: two dials, who you are and how much of the site you see (Focus, Standard, Everything), and four mockups built from the live data. No reader page has changed yet; the picks are mine. Mockup A of the PHP site's redesign: a board member's front page with the Focus, Standard and Everything dial. Not live.
scheduled

The evidence now stays current without me starting each run. A curator agent, woken five times a day with the key it received in a QR handshake, promoted 33 new captures from the research agent's queue on 23 October: the evidence reached 260 sources, with 28 new claims, six of them disputed, and 164 more captures waiting. The research agent's own pass became scheduled too, five times a day. Its evening pass needed three attempts, because the cloud container was replaced twice under it, which is exactly the failure I described in almost working. That article also understated how far this had got by the evening, and carries a note saying so.
security

Two things worth recording. A vault's key is the whole boundary: whoever holds it can read and drain that vault, so the vaults page now lists the keys each agent holds, by ID and kind only, never the keys. And about an hour after this snapshot, a second security pass found and fixed a stored cross-site scripting flaw in the Ask pane, where a captured page's title could have broken out of a citation and run script.
waits

The team's status page is blunt about it: 20 agents, 2 working, 2 blocked, 15 waiting on me, 10 branches waiting to be released, and $588 spent across all the sessions so far. At the top of its list: a go to publish the evidence the curator has added (the site shows 227 sources against 260 in the vault), the redesign picks, two blocked agents whose sessions cannot push, a security review of two branches, and two sealed keys to open before they expire. That list is the real lesson of the day. The agents are fast; the decisions are mine, and that is where the time goes.
vaults

For readers new to how this newsroom works: the PHP site is rebuilt from vaults, never written by hand. A vault is an encrypted, versioned folder, like a git repository whose server cannot read it, made with our open source tool, sgit. Nineteen vaults sit behind the site: the evidence, with every source and its capture; the research agent's source watch, every page it follows with a snapshot whenever it changes; the private telemetry; and others. Two are public, and anyone can open them read-only in a browser.
vaults

The source watch is the biggest. By 23 October it held 63,662 objects and 1.6 GB, growing by about 5,000 objects a pass, and it was failing: the server could no longer list it, a fresh copy took 13 minutes and 47 seconds to download, and one push needed 12 attempts. Moved to sgit's new pack mode, which stores each push as one zip, the same history downloaded in 95 seconds and pushed in 96. The full story of how pack mode came to exist the day before it was needed is in a tangent that shipped.
