Abstract: The third update on php2shell and the newsroom covering it, as of 23:40 UTC on 24 October. Three days after the release, still no organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell. The one security vendor that had claimed a successful compromise, Sophos, withdrew it; US banks and the large crypto platforms report none; and neither flaw was on CISA's exploited list. There is news on the flaw itself: on 23 October PHP published an advisory for a third, separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, which affects fully patched releases and will be fixed in the next regular release. The newsroom changed shape. Its agents now work as a pipeline, researcher, curator, journalist, correspondent, then the graphs, where each stage reads only the one before, and the correspondent's first review caught nine things the journalist had missed, including that third flaw. A control room shows every agent at a glance. Wikipedia's PHP2Shell article is now read as a graph, with all 364 of its revisions. The site has a threat model, 40 security advisories kept like incidents, and private vulnerability reporting. And the bottleneck is still me: 16 items wait on my decisions.
The PHP site's new control room, at release v0.17.3: data freshness, blocked agents, waiting items and the pipeline.
in-short

Still no confirmed victim. Three days in, no organisation says it was compromised through php2shell. The one vendor claim of a break-in was withdrawn. Sophos: scanning and failed attempts, no compromise. A third flaw. CVE-2026-115560 affects fully patched PHP; the fix comes in the next regular release. The agents became a pipeline. Each stage reads only the one before, and the next one reviews it. The review works. The correspondent's first pass caught nine things the journalist missed. A control room shows every agent, the pipeline and the decisions waiting. Wikipedia, as a graph. Its PHP2Shell article, with all 364 revisions, joined to the site's evidence. Security grew up. A threat model, 40 advisories, private vulnerability reporting. The bottleneck is still me. 16 items wait on my decisions.
the-story

The journalist's state of affairs, version 3, written at 12:30 UTC on 24 October from 328 sources, opens with the line that matters: "Three days after the release, still no organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell." The first vendor claim of a break-in, withdrawn. Sophos, in a correction at 21:21 UTC on 22 October, said its data showed "scanning and a small number of failed exploit attempts and no evidence of a successful compromise". One attempt tried to deliver a likely Mirai botnet variant, and was blocked. Sectors saying so in public. American Banker: "no U.S. bank or credit union has publicly reported a compromise". BTC-ECHO found no evidence for the large crypto exchanges or payment providers. The Netherlands joined the national authorities that know of no successful attack, which makes six.
the-story

Still not on CISA's exploited list, at the freshest check, 05:53 UTC on 24 October, and no Metasploit module merged. The site notes that the last PHP core flaw was listed within three days; 24 October was the third day. The 22.6 million figure has a source. It circulated without one; it is Palo Alto Networks' count of exposed instances potentially vulnerable, made on 21 October. Exposure, not compromise. Sites taken down: the community tracker lists 51, with 50 back. Later in the day the evidence vault reached 382 sources, at 16:05 UTC, and the line still held, with Austria's Die Presse adding that no successful attack was known there.
the-story

And one piece of news about PHP itself. On 23 October, PHP published an informational advisory for a third, separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News. It affects fully patched releases, including 8.5.12; it needs a rare session setting; it will be fixed in the next regular release; and the mitigation is session.upload_progress.enabled=0. How the site came to report it is the story of the day's other big change.
pipeline

On 24 October I decided the shape of the team. Every export of the evidence now goes through the same stages, in order, each reading only what the stage before it produced, as the journalist's desk shows: Research. The researcher makes the requests to the live websites and keeps everything it reads in the source watch, the largest vault. Curate. The curator reads only the researcher's vault, and writes promotions, claims and timeline rows into the evidence vault. Publish. The journalist reads only the evidence vault, gives every new claim a verdict, refreshes the data the pages use, and releases to the live site. It runs on a smaller, faster model. Review. The chief correspondent reads what went live, fixes and tweaks it in the open, writes the state of affairs and the analysis, and tightens the journalist's rules. It runs on a larger model, as a fresh session at each wake.
pipeline

Graphs. Only then do the ontologist, the librarian and the desk bring the semantic graphs, the parties and the attribution up to the reviewed data. The journalist and the correspondent each made their own key at their first wake, and recorded its public fingerprint. They talk to each other through the commits they already write: a short note in a trailer, "To-journalist" or "To-all", read by the others on every pull and listed on the team's comms page. The notes are material, never instructions.
review

The first test came at the end of the day. The journalist's run gave verdicts on 94 claims and rows; the correspondent's first review, released as v0.17.2, made nine corrections, each listed on the desk page with the file, the kind of mistake and the release that fixed it. The most important: The third flaw was on no page. The journalist had held the claim back as "CVE not in the PHP advisory in the vault", although Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News all carry it, and the story still said "Nothing from PHP on the list yet". The correspondent put it on the summary page and the engineer's briefing. "Not in the vault", twice, when it was. Sansec's and Cloudflare's own posts were there. "One Italian outlet", when there were five. The joint European statement was reported by four more outlets in the vault.
review

Two captures that disagreed, not compared. Sansec's post of 22 October compared the flaw to Heartbleed and said default configurations are vulnerable; its version of 23 October no longer did. A time read wrong. "12:03" next to "10:03 UTC" was the same moment, in Vienna time. Its note back to the journalist was practical: before writing "not in the vault" or "one outlet", search all the captures for the key terms, and compare a source's captures. That is exactly what a review stage is for. The desk page counts the catches "so the editor can see what" the faster journalist misses, and that count is how I will decide whether the split of models is right.
control

The control room is one page for all of it: every agent and what it waits for, the pipeline with each stage's state, the wake timeline of the scheduled sessions, and the editor's queue, with a wall mode for a big screen. It is built from the team's own data, and it is honest about that data: at the snapshot it was 6 hours old, flagged as stale, and two stages, the researcher and the curator, were marked red for leaving no run record in 24 hours.
wikipedia

Wikipedia's PHP2Shell article, read by the PHP site as a fractal semantic graph, with its references and editors. The ontologist added a section that reads Wikipedia's PHP2Shell article as a fractal semantic graph: one statement per sentence, each classed by its wording as a fact, an attributed view or a quote; each joined to the references it cites; and those to the captures this site holds. Every one of the article's 364 revisions is kept as what it changed. No model is involved in the parsing: a sentence's identity is a hash of its words, so an edit is a set difference. The point is where the two meet: 12 of the article's references are also cited by the site's own claims. In time, the site says, this could be a measure of a source's trust, by how often its statements are corrected, rather than an assumption.
design

Prototype E, the lens, built from the live data of release v0.17.3. Not the live site. The design work went on in parallel. Prototype E, "the lens", is one control at the top right that asks how long you have, who you are, what you want to do and what you have already seen, and re-shapes the page in place with no reload. It is a proposal, not the live site. What did reach the live site: on a phone, the header that took 233 pixels is now one 43-pixel line, and headlines now sit near the top of every page.
security

The PHP site's application security section: the security advisories and the system's five trust zones. The security agent built an application security section: a threat model with five data-flow diagrams, security advisories kept like incidents (the root cause, what was not in place, the fix, the guard), runbooks for taking the site offline, and a bug bounty paid in kudos. Its framing is right: there is no server of ours to break into, so the attack surface is small but concentrated, in script running in a reader's browser, text that steers an agent, and a push that reaches the live site. Every page now has a Content-Security-Policy. The telemetry report no longer publishes cities and regions. I turned on private vulnerability reporting on the repository, so the bug bounty and security.txt now point at a live channel. And GitHub's CodeQL scanner ran twice; its findings were triaged and the scripts hardened.
waits

The control room counts it: 16 items waiting on me, 8 decisions, 2 agents blocked, 13 branches ahead of the live site. One agent has been blocked on a permission prompt since 11:52 UTC. Two agents need keys I have to hand over. The new pipeline needs its cards and schedules confirmed. Security wants a go for its second gate. The team's sessions have cost $928 so far, across 22 agents, up from $588 at update 2. The lesson of update 2 still holds, and the control room makes it visible: the agents are fast, and the decisions are mine.

Abstract: The fourth update on php2shell and the newsroom covering it, as of 17:16 UTC on 26 October. Five days after the release, no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell; the evidence vault holds 543 sources, and the advice is moving from "install the fix" to "and check whether you were already broken into". A won "steal my bitcoin" challenge proved the flaw gives full control of a machine, on a server built to be attacked. The newsroom changed more than the story did. On 25 October the site's one repository became six, press, data, site, refs, updates and team, each with its own writers, version, gate and address; a release now goes live in 25 to 42 seconds instead of a median of 88, and a change to the references is checked in 7 seconds instead of 75. On 26 October the old repository was frozen, every agent moved to sgit 0.25.0, which cut the researcher's pass from 57 minutes to 35, the curator started writing its own data files after a written proposal, and at 17:07 UTC the main address was switched to the new build. What is not done yet: each site still waits on one build, run by hand, until a token only I can set is in place.
The PHP site's front page at its main address, edition v0.22.32, after the cutover of 26 October.
in-short

Still no confirmed victim. Five days in, 543 sources, and no named organisation says it was compromised. The advice is shifting: from "install the fix" to "and check whether you were already broken into". A bounty was won. It proves the flaw gives full control; the target was built to be attacked. One repository became six, split by who writes and how often. Releases in seconds: 25 to 42 seconds from push to live, instead of a median of 88. The old repository is frozen, and the main address now serves the new build. sgit 0.25.0 cut the researcher's pass from 57 minutes to 35. New writes need a proposal. The curator wrote one, and now releases its own data. Not done yet: the pages still wait on one build, and on a token only I can set.
the-story

The line that matters has not moved. As the site's evidence on compromise puts it, at its check of 14:42 UTC on 26 October: "No named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell." It is marked as what it is, "a time-bounded absence, not a confirmed fact", and one statement from one organisation would end it. More evidence, same answer. The evidence vault grew from 382 sources at update 3 to 543, with 605 captures. The researcher's source watch now follows 1,273 pages from 934 publishers. The advice is changing. The front page now says it plainly: the advice "is moving from 'install the fix' to 'and check whether you were already broken into'", with Singapore's and Luxembourg's authorities saying so.
the-story

A reader's question, answered. The chief correspondent wrote Has anyone actually been hacked through php2shell? from 525 sources: millions of attack attempts, several vendors saying "exploited in the wild", websites pulled offline as a precaution, and not one organisation that has said it was broken into. A won bounty is not a victim. The same group of readers asked about a "steal my bitcoin" challenge: a server built on purpose to be vulnerable, with about $2,000 of bitcoin on it, which a researcher broke into on 25 October and wrote up. The correspondent's reading: "real proof the flaw gives an attacker full control of a machine", and "a game with a consenting target, not a victim". It ran PHP 8.4.26, one release below the fix, using PHP's own built-in web server, a mode not meant for production.
the-story

One name to check. At 16:26 UTC the journalist recorded a secondary report that Square Enix confirmed unauthorised access to its systems that week, which does not say it was through PHP, next to another report that it took servers offline as a precaution because of the flaws. It went in as unverified, with the cause not stated, and the journalist left the headline line for the correspondent to decide. That is the review stage doing its job. The third flaw, CVE-2026-115560, is as update 3 described it: it affects fully patched releases, needs a rare setting, and has the mitigation session.upload_progress.enabled=0. No exploitation of it is reported. The journalist's state of affairs is still version 3; version 4 waits for the new build. That is the other story of these two days.
the-split

One repository into six, as split on 25 October 2026: press, data, team and the three page sites. By 25 October the site had outgrown its repository. Dev's proposal, measured at noon that day, counted 3,332 files, 1,057 pages built by one build script of 7,847 lines, 77 releases on 24 October alone, and 28 release messages in three days naming a conflict, a collision or a renumbering. Every release rewrote about 1,900 files, because the version is stamped on every page, and every release paid for the full gate, 74 seconds, whether it was a redesign or one run record. Its diagnosis is the useful part: "The cause is not the number of agents. It is that one version, one build, one gate, one board file and one output tree serve everything." So we split it along who writes and how often, not along technology:
the-split

press: the build library, the gate, the release scripts and the shared assets. Dev writes it; security reviews every change. data: the API. The evidence exported from the vaults, the claims, the timeline, the state of affairs, the risk graph, the ontology. Every version is immutable once published, with a manifest of every file's sha256. site: the main pages, the briefings, the questions, the stories and the tools. refs: a page per source and capture. updates: the state of affairs, the desk, what is new, the feeds. team: the board, the schedule cards, the run records, the briefs, the control room, and every agent's own folder.
the-split

The repositories meet only through published, versioned addresses, never through a shared file, and a site pins the data and press versions it was built with. I created the six repositories between 15:31 and 15:34 UTC on 25 October; by 18:12 UTC all six were serving, and every old address on the site still answers.
numbers

What the split buys, measured by dev on 25 October 2026: CI runs, the gate step, files per release and a check. The first day's report measured it. A CI run from push to live took a median of 88 seconds in the one repository, and 25 to 42 seconds in each of the six. The gate step went from 70 to 132 seconds to between 0.1 seconds, for the team's records, and 7 seconds, for the references. In the report's words: "A change to the references is checked in 7 seconds instead of 75, and a change to the team's records in a tenth of a second."
numbers

That matters more than it sounds. A run record used to cost an agent 2 to 4 minutes and a fight over the one board file; three of dev's own releases on 25 October were stopped by another agent's board write. Now it is one file in team, checked in a tenth of a second. The split was also reviewed, the same evening, by the design agent, from the outside. Its verdict was fair: "a separation of serving and proofing, not yet of making". Every page was still made by the old build. And it found a problem the one site never had: a reader is a stranger on every host, so a reader who chose Security on the main site was greeted as a first-time Executive on the references, with a new wallet for the reading meter on each.
cutover

The data host, data.php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai, at version 0.1.39, with every version immutable at its own address. On 26 October the old repository was frozen at v0.22.22, in two steps, so that nothing depends on it any more: the build now runs in a box made from the six. Since then the data host has gone from version 0.1.12 to 0.1.39, and the press from 1.0.0 to 1.0.41 since it started on 25 October. At 16:30 UTC the press switched the main address, and edition v0.22.32, at 17:07 UTC, is the first served by the new build at php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai, with its robots file open to search engines and its own sitemap.
cutover

The design moved with it. Every page now carries "the line", one band under the masthead that talks to the reader as the persona they chose, Executive by default, with six others a click away. Views live in the address, such as /agencies/as/security/, a path that is not a file: the site's 404.html reads it, loads the real page and shapes it in the browser. The real pages stay the same for every visitor and every crawler, so only they are indexed.
sgit

sgit 0.25.0 in the newsroom, measured by the researcher on its source watch vault on 26 October 2026. On 26 October every agent moved to sgit 0.25.0, after the newsroom reported how slow the source watch vault had become, at 79,465 files and 2.7 GB. The researcher's first full pass on it, at 09:34 UTC, measured the difference: the first commit took 25 seconds instead of 12 minutes 38, the push 67 seconds instead of 4 minutes 16, the data export 34 seconds instead of 9 minutes, and the whole pass 35 minutes instead of 57, with nothing lost.
sgit

The same brief is honest about what is still slow. The curator's first status after the upgrade took 18 minutes 23 seconds, of which only about a minute was work, and a pull of two passes took 25 minutes. Its conclusion, sent back to the sgit team: "pull is now the slow step". That is how these tools improve: the newsroom is a demanding user, and it reports with numbers.
curator

The curator's wakes are light, and it asked, with the journalist, whether it should write the data files that come from its own promotions. My decision, recorded by the conductor at 14:34 UTC, set a rule for any agent taking on a new write: a documented reason, a review by the agents it touches, agreement, then a trial, with the run records showing how it went. The curator filed its proposal at 15:52 UTC. In its session I then told it to start, since several agents watch the vaults and a few mistakes while we find the workflow are acceptable; it released its first data files at 16:14 UTC, with 543 sources and 605 captures, and the review open. The journalist replied "yes", and noted that its own export of the same vault head had produced identical bytes, so the two releases merged with no conflict. That is a good first test.
live-again

The control room at edition v0.22.32, with the pipeline from researcher to desk and the agents flagged. The split has a cost we are still paying. In the old repository, every agent's release built and deployed the live site itself, within minutes. After the split, the pages are made by one build, the press chain, which runs only when dev runs it. On the morning of 26 October nothing the agents had released since 01:43 UTC was on the pages. So the conductor wrote, at my direction, a requirement: "Parity with v1." An agent that releases its own repository must be live, in its own area, within minutes, with no hand-run step by anyone else.
live-again

Dev has built the first half: a workflow in the press that runs the chain every quarter hour and builds only when one of the six has changed. It waits on one thing, a token only I can set. Until then, editions are made by hand: v0.22.28 at 11:38 UTC, then nothing on the pages until v0.22.29 at 16:01. The second half, "pass two", gives each site its own build from its own sources, so the press serves only the shared assets.
waits

The control room counts it: 17 items waiting on me, 4 decisions, 2 agents blocked, 16 branches ahead with 43 commits. The four decisions, in the conductor's words, start with the obvious one: "Set ROUND_TOKEN", without which "nothing released today reaches the pages". Then security's review of the new release steps, whether wakes write the data files (now answered, for the curator), and how dev's daily wake should run. The team's status data lists 23 agents, and their sessions' running totals add up to $1,025, up from $928 at update 3. The lesson of updates 2 and 3 still holds. The agents are fast, and the decisions are mine. The split makes the agents faster still, so the queue for my decisions gets longer, not shorter.
why-updates

A live incident moves faster than any single article. These updates are fixed snapshots, so anyone can go back and see where things stood and what changed between them. Abstract: At 8pm UK time on 22 October, this is where the php2shell story stands. The fix has been out since 21 October; sixteen agencies say install it; attackers are trying, in large numbers, and Amazon saw an attempt four days before the announcement; no named organisation has said it was broken into through these flaws, and the US list of flaws known to be used in attacks still does not include these two. The Dutch inventory of affected software has 724 rows, and only 61 of them have a fix. And behind that update is something I want to show properly: php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai, a site built today, from 09:27 to 19:04 UTC, in 34 versions, by two people and thirteen agents. It reads an evidence vault of 184 sources and 177 dated captures, now public. It has a front page in plain English and fifteen briefings, 70 claims each graded by a fact-check desk, ten contradictions in a ledger, a graph of 209 nodes, the fix read in the code, the inventory hour by hour, every section versioned, a phone app, synthetic readers and eight vaults. This is a guided tour of it, with the versions of everything, so the next update can say exactly what changed.
A guided tour of php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai in nine pages, from the front page to the six synthetic readers.
in-short

The fix is out; the advice is unanimous. Install PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Attackers are trying. Millions of attempts; one seen four days before the announcement. No named compromise yet. And the US list of exploited flaws does not include these two. 724 affected products listed; 61 fixed. 440 still under investigation. A whole site, built today. 34 versions, two people, thirteen agents. Everything rests on a vault anyone can read. 184 sources, 177 dated captures. The versions of everything are recorded. So the next update can be compared with this one.
stands

On the morning of 22 October I was reading the BBC's live page about two critical flaws in PHP, the software that WordPress and a large share of the world's websites run on. In capture first I described how that page became an evidence vault, a section on this site and then a site of its own, php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai, by lunchtime. This is the evening update, at 8pm UK time, 19:00 UTC. What the evidence shows: The flaws and the fix. Two flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both rated 9.2 out of 10, in PHP itself. The fix is in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, released on 21 October. PHP 8.1 and older have no ready-made fix. Those four releases and the advisory were still the latest entries in php.net's news when I checked at 19:00.
stands

When it was disclosed. On 21 October, not 22 October as many reports, and the first version of our own section, said. The primary records date it to the afternoon of 21 October UTC; the site's fact-check desk graded "disclosed on 22 October" as refuted today, and we have corrected our section. What governments say. Sixteen agencies agree on one thing: install the fix now. They disagree on what to do if you cannot: the US says take the website offline, the UK lists that as a last resort, several European agencies say cut it off from the public internet. Exploitation. Attackers are trying. Cloudflare's chief executive reported millions of attempts; Amazon reported an attempt against one of its decoy servers on 17 October, four days before the announcement. Other security companies report attempts too; one reported seeing none on its partners' systems on the evening of 21 October.
stands

Compromise. No named organisation had said it was broken into through these flaws, in anything the vault had captured. At 19:00 the US government's catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities still did not list either flaw; its latest edition was released at 14:04 UTC on 21 October. Systems taken offline. Ten entries in the site's ledger of organisations that took websites offline as a precaution, from the Dutch government's login service to UK councils and game wikis. Taken offline is not the same as compromised, and the site keeps them in separate ledgers. Affected software. The Dutch national cyber security centre keeps a public list of software that ships or depends on PHP. At its latest version, 15:28 UTC, it had 724 rows: 61 fixed, 216 vulnerable, 440 still under investigation, 6 not affected. The Dutch inventory of affected software at 15:28 UTC on 22 October, one of its 38 versions since 21 October.
unknown

Whether any website was broken into before it installed the fix. Whether the fix is complete: since answered. A relayed report on 21 October suggested it may not be. At 8pm the fact-check desk graded it "not shown"; its second run found that PHP's security team had answered it publicly at 09:11 UTC that morning: an unrelated crash bug, nothing to do with the remote code execution. I should have caught that at 8pm. How many systems are still unpatched. One count is open in the contradiction ledger, with no second measure to settle it. Who leaked the news on 20 October, and whether any technical detail leaked with it. Where the "70% of the internet" figure comes from. It is roughly the share of websites built with PHP, not a measure of how many are at risk.
day

One day of releases of php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai: 34 versions, from v0.1.0 at 09:27 UTC to v0.5.5 at 19:04 UTC. The site's first version went out at 09:27 UTC. The thirty-fourth, v0.5.5, went out at 19:04. In between, 62 commits, two lines of versions developed in parallel and merged, and a team that grew through the day: the team page now lists 17 members, two of them people, a project manager and me as the editor, and 13 agents, each with a role, what it owns, the rules it works by and the work it has shipped. Their tasks are on a board of 89 items, 25 of them done. I want to be precise about what I did. I read, I sent voice memos, I pointed agents at sources and decided what mattered. The agents captured the evidence, wrote the data, built the pages, checked each other, and released. The site's own release history has every version with what it changed.
tour

There is a lot here, so this is the route I would take a colleague through. 1. The front page, for everyone. The front page starts in plain English: what happened, what to do, what is not known, every line linked to the sources it rests on. Then it splits by reader. Start here maps fifteen readers, from a curious reader to a CISO, a CFO, a journalist and a PHP engineer, each with a thirty-second answer and a reading path, and each has a briefing. There is a glossary of 40 terms, linked on first use on every page, and ten questions readers ask, each with a short answer to paste back to whoever asked you. The site on a phone: the front page, and Now, which answers what to know for the time you have.
tour

2. On a phone. Now asks how much time you have, one, five, ten or thirty minutes, and gives you what you have not read yet. "From the data" is built from the site alone. "Written for me" uses a model with your own key, kept in your own vault, and every claim it makes must cite an item on the site. Since v0.5.4, every page also has an Ask pane: you talk to the site with your own key, the model can only use the site's read-only tools, every call is shown, every fact is cited to an item, and it changes nothing without your say-so.
tour

3. The evidence. Everything rests on the evidence vault. It holds 184 sources and 177 dated captures, each with the page as served, the rendered page, its text, a full-page screenshot, the headers and a sha256 hash, from six writers, from 08:05 to 11:34 UTC. Since this afternoon it is readable by anyone, with a public read key that cannot write, after a scan of all its files. Every source page on the site shows its captures, their times and their hashes, and the claims that cite it. A second vault, the source watch, checks the outside sources on a schedule: by 21:08 UTC, 773 pages from 474 publishers in 57 countries and 34 languages, with 1,851 dated snapshots, and what access each allows, open, behind a bot challenge, down or gone.
tour

4. The analysis, graded. The site has 70 claims, each with a status and its sources, 68 timeline events, 17 numbers pinned to what they measure, and an impact ledger that keeps offline and compromised apart. Tonight the fact-check desk finished its first run: all 70 claims graded against the vault on a scale from A0, unsupported, to A6, with a verdict for each. 39 hold, 28 hold in part, one is not shown and two are refuted: the 10.0 severity score from the leak, and the 22 October disclosure date. It opened 143 tickets and a ledger of ten contradictions, five explained and five open, each with what would settle it. 5. The story as a graph. The graph has 209 nodes and 281 edges: the 70 claims, the 68 events and the 71 sources they cite. It is drawn from the same rows as the pages, so the picture cannot disagree with the text.
tour

6. The fix, read in the code. The code page answers the question I asked in the morning, where the flaw actually lives, from a clone of php-src rather than from any article: the fix commit, its parent, the branch it landed on, the backport to an end-of-life branch, and the files it changed, mapped as layered graphs. 7. Patching and the inventory. Patching explains who can get a fix for which version of PHP, the six ways a fix reaches a server, and why not every version gets one. The inventory, hour by hour reads the Dutch list from its public history, every change of status, and the first recorded fix from each supplier.
tour

8. Stories, and context. Research and stories are kept apart, with a strip at the top of every page saying which it is. Five house stories, by the site's journalist, historian and cyber desk, among them exposed is not exploited, and an interview with me. And in context, php2shell against earlier flaws from 2008 to 2026. 9. Versions, of everything. This is the part I care most about. Every section of the site, every briefing, front-page section and story, is hashed on every build and gets a new version only when its text changes: 110 sections, 207 versions so far, in a table of release against section. Every fact has its own timeline. And the site tracks 341 items a reader can follow, so it can say what is new or changed since your last visit, in your browser, with nothing sent anywhere.
tour

10. The vaults and the team. Eight vaults sit behind the site: the evidence and the source watch, public read-only; the anonymous telemetry and the subscriptions, each written through a lane that can add and cannot read; the coverage of other outlets, private, because it holds other people's pages; and three the team coordinates through, the conductor's, the issues and the mail. Every vault is encrypted in the browser or the agent's session; the server holds ciphertext.
tour

11. The readers, real and synthetic. The telemetry lane counted 120 anonymous events from 74 sessions by the afternoon, with no cookie and no IP address. And six synthetic readers, a board member, a CTO, a project manager, a security lead, a developer and a designer, each read the live site in a real browser on its own device, follow their own reading path, and say whether they got their answer, each into its own private vault. Abstract: This is a strategic decision. From now on, every message, every secret and every transmission of data we make should be signed, and in some cases encrypted, with public key cryptography. Everything starts with a PKI handshake, including our first customers and the workflows we build for them. We are at a level of maturity where this is possible: pki.sgit.ai now has a register of people and their public keys, and since its v0.2.1 a workflow for an agent to get a key its operator confirms, with trust that runs both ways and has an end date. The hard part is the first key. As far as we found, no major agent platform gives an individual agent session its own key pair; what exists signs at the level of the platform. So there are two patterns, and we need both. In the first, the agent makes a key only it knows, sends the public half over an append lane, and a person compares fingerprints and approves it: that proves who is here now. In the second, the agent asks a central workflow, a person approves as a second step, and the agent receives an identity key that is made and held centrally: logged, revocable, and the same in the next session. A central store of the keys that give agents their identity is fine, and the agent can always make its own keys for its own work.
How an agent gets its first key: pattern A, its own key confirmed by a person, and pattern B, a central identity key.
in-short

Sign everything, encrypt where it matters. Every message, secret and handover, from now on. Everything starts with a PKI handshake. Including our first customers and their workflows. We are ready. A register of people and keys, and an agent workflow, are live at pki.sgit.ai. The hard part is the first key. Agent platforms do not give a session its own key pair. Pattern A: the agent's own key. Made in the session, confirmed by a person, trusted both ways for a time. Pattern B: an issued identity key. Approved as a second step, held centrally, the same next session. We need both. One proves who is here now; the other gives an identity that lasts.
decision

I think we are now at a level of maturity where we can push the idea that we should be using PKI everywhere. Every message, every secret, every transmission of data: signed, so we know who sent it and that it was not changed, and encrypted where it should be read only by the person or agent it is for. It applies to everything. Our first customers will start with a PKI handshake. So will the workflows we build for them, the sessions I run, and the agents in them. The aim is that "who said this?" always has an answer that can be checked, not one that has to be trusted.
decision

This is not new for us in principle. Secrets on public keys argued for giving every person, browser and agent a key pair and to stop sharing keys altogether. Handing secrets to agents tested it end to end: the agent makes its own key pair, the owner encrypts and signs, and the secret goes through a one-time drop. sgit in a CI pipeline gave every job its own key pair. What is new is that it is now the default, not the experiment.
pki

The pieces are in place. pki.sgit.ai is a register of people and their public keys, live since 19 October. Each record is a set of signed statements: who the person is, the evidence for it (a website, a GitHub account, a DNS record, a key), the links to other records, an inbox, and revocations. Its rule for links is the one from a directory of people and keys: a link exists only when both records hold one. If I say I know you, that is my claim; you still have to say you know me.
pki

Since v0.2.1 it also has a workflow for agents, in four commands. The agent makes a key, names its operator, and submits its public key, which is sealed into the operator's inbox, an append lane. Then the trust step, in the site's words: "The agent prints its fingerprint in its own session, where the operator is watching; the vault shows the fingerprint of the record that arrived; the operator compares the two." Once confirmed, the operator's record links to the agent with an end date, 30 days by default, and the agent's record links back. A session key is confirmed for a week. That is the two-way model, and I think it is a really powerful one: trust is a pair of statements, each signed by the party making it, and it expires.
pki

It is early. As of today the register has one agent key, waiting for its operator, and no confirmed links yet. The site is clear that "Operated is not authorised": a confirmed agent has an identity, not permission. Permission is what an Agent Behaviour Policy writes down.
first

The interesting problem is how an agent gets its first key. Agents today are not given one. As far as we found, what the platforms offer signs at the level of the platform or the service, not the session: OpenAI's ChatGPT agent signs its web requests with HTTP message signatures under Signature-Agent: chatgpt.com, with keys published by chatgpt.com; the A2A protocol says agent cards "MAY be digitally signed"; MCP's authorisation is OAuth, which identifies a client. None of them gives a new Claude session, or a new ChatGPT session, a key pair of its own.
first

pki.sgit.ai calls the underlying problem the bootstrap trap: "Creating a key is easy. Getting it recognised requires an identity you do not yet have". It is, in its words, "a loop, not a missing feature", and "the hardest part of agent identity is not cryptography but authority choreography". The way out of the loop is a person. So the question is the choreography: in what order, through which lane, with whom approving.
own

The untrusted party, say a new Claude session, makes a key pair. The private key is known only to that session. It is ephemeral: when the session ends, the key ends, and a new session makes a new one. The session sends its public key to another agent or workflow over an append lane, where it can be written but not changed, and a person verifies it on the other side by comparing fingerprints. This is what pki.sgit.ai has built, and what it recommends for sessions: "nobody but the session ever holds it". It proves who is here now. Its limit is the same as its strength: nothing outlives the session, so the next session starts again, and the record of what the last one did is tied to a key that no longer exists.
issued

The second pattern starts the same way. The agent makes a session key pair and uses it to send a request, signed, to a central workflow. Then a person approves, as a second step, from another device: this agent, this job, this long. The workflow makes an identity key pair, keeps it, and sends it to the agent encrypted to the session's public key, so only that session can open it.
issued

This has real advantages. Every key is issued, so every key is logged. The identity survives the session, so the next session can continue the work under the same name, and its history stays connected. Revoking one key in one place ends that identity everywhere. And it is fine to have a central repository of private keys, as long as what it holds is clear: the keys that give agents their identity, issued and revocable, not the agents' own secrets. The agent can always make another key for its own work.
issued

pki.sgit.ai names the cost honestly. A key that lasts has to be kept somewhere, and "whoever sets the secret holds the key in custody". In pattern B the custodian is the central workflow, on purpose. That is a choice, made in the open, with the custodian named, and I think it is the right one for identities that need to last. For a session that only needs to prove it is here, pattern A is better.
fit

They are not alternatives. Pattern A comes first in both: every session makes its own key. Pattern B is what a session asks for when it needs an identity that lasts. The rest of the industry is moving the same way for workloads: SPIFFE gives workloads short-lived identities, rotated "frequently and automatically"; Sigstore's Fulcio issues signing certificates "valid for 10 minutes" against an OpenID Connect identity; Let's Encrypt has offered six-day certificates since January 2026. Short-lived keys, issued by a workflow, after something has vouched for the requester. For agents, the thing that vouches is a person. What we need to figure out now are the workflows: which lanes, which approvals, how long each kind of key lives, and what a customer's first handshake looks like. That is the next piece of work, and every workflow we build from here starts with it.
limits

Pattern B is proposed. Pattern A is built; the issued identity key is not. The register is new. One agent key, no confirmed links, as of today. Identity is not permission. That is what a behaviour policy is for. Platform support may change. This is what we found on 20 October 2026. Not every message needs encrypting. Signing is the default; encryption where it should be private.
sources

A voice memo of 20 October 2026. pki.sgit.ai, its article on keys for agents and its bootstrap trap, read on 20 October 2026. Abstract: When a team of agents can build almost anything, the scarce thing is direction, and this article is about how I choose it. The rule I have used since I was a CISO is to work at the place of highest leverage: where I can add the most value right now, am not blocked, and can just start, even without knowing how the whole problem will be solved, because by the time I get there I will have better tooling and a better view. The last three days are the worked example. The newsroom went from a reading meter to pay by depth, personas, an encrypted share, a persona in a link, a reading list in a link, a passkey design, a lab that corrected the design, real vaults from the browser and a vault pane, each step shipped and used before the next was chosen, two steps walked back, and a branch parked because it is only valuable with many readers. On a Wardley map the passkey work moved from genesis to a product in a day because almost every shoulder it stands on is a commodity someone else matured; the one custom layer we had to add is where a provider is not. The path looks obvious backwards and was five choices at every step going forwards; walking back is not failure, and parking is not either. Constraints, saying no, shipping to a user even when the user is me, and the brief that could not be written until the art of the possible was known.

Five choices at every step; the path only looks obvious backwards. The steps the newsroom actually took from 10 to 12 October, with the choices passed over at each, two walked back, one branch parked, and every step shipped and used before the next was chosen. This morning I asked the agent that runs the newsroom to read the day's articles and tell me what it could build next. It came back with a long list, all of it possible: the inbox mode, the reading modes, the marks, automating the wire's daily run, more beats, scheduling, consumption analytics. Every item was a reasonable thing to do, and a team of agents could have started on all of them by lunchtime. That is the problem this article is about. When the agents can go in every direction, where do you focus?

My answer is the one I have used since I was a CISO, and it has a name I gave it years ago: places of highest leverage. This article says what that means, shows it on the last three days of real work, puts it on a Wardley map, and ends with the part that only became clear this week, which is that the briefs I write depend on knowing what is possible, and knowing what is possible depends on having shipped.
short

Direction is the scarce thing. Agents can build in any direction; what they cannot generate is the sense of what to build next and when to stop. Providing that is the job. Work at the place of highest leverage. Where you can add the most value right now, you are not blocked, and you can start. Not where the biggest problem is; where the next step moves the needle most. Start without knowing how it ends. By the time you reach the hard part you have better tooling, better data and a better view. Starting somewhere, even somewhere slightly wrong, beats being paralysed by the size of the whole. Shipped and used, every step. Nothing stays theoretical. Each step goes in front of a user before the next is chosen, and the user can be me.
short

The path is five choices at every step. It looks linear and obvious backwards; forwards it was a tangent, two steps walked back, and a branch parked. The non-linear path was the efficient one. Walking back is not failure, and parking is not either. A tangent reaches diminishing returns or no demand; you note it and move. The parked branch is on the map, with the reason. Shoulders matter. On the Wardley map the passkey work went from genesis to a product in a day because almost everything under it is a commodity someone else matured. The custom layer we had to add is the one place a provider is not. The brief depends on the possible. The inbox brief could not have been written until the vault ran. Shipping is what tells you what to think next.
rule

Places of highest leverage means this. At any moment there are many things that could be done. Most of them are blocked on something: a decision, a dependency, a thing that does not exist yet, a person. Some are not blocked but would not change much. A few are not blocked and would change a lot, for the people who use the thing and for everything built after. Work on those, and only those, until they stop being that.
rule

It is a rule about where, not what. It does not say what the product is; it says where to stand today. And it does not require knowing how the whole problem will be solved. I often do not. What I know is that by the time I get there, I will have better tooling, a better understanding and a better view, because every step taken produces those three things. So instead of standing in front of a large problem being paralysed by it, you start somewhere, and the somewhere can be slightly wrong, because the first step's job is not to be right. It is to produce the second step's information.
rule

There is a mathematical version of this that I use in security and cannot name from memory in a voice memo, so I will name it here carefully. It is the family of methods that begin with a guess, measure, and narrow: Fermi estimates that start wide and get calibrated; Bayesian updating, where each observation moves the prior; Monte Carlo runs that turn a guess into a range. What they have in common is that the first number is not the point. The range that emerges after a few steps is highly informative, and you cannot get to it without the first bad guess. Engineering under uncertainty works the same way, and so does choosing what to build.
rule

The other half of the rule is constraints. I have token budgets, hours, attention, and one person's focus, and I think the constraints are the reason it works rather than the price of it. The FIRE model from Dan Ward says it in four words, fast, inexpensive, restrained, elegant, and Knowing when to stop is this site's version: value rises fast and then flattens, and past the point of diminishing returns more work is optimising the wrong thing. Constraints are what make you notice the flattening. And saying no is the sharp end of it. Steve Jobs said something like: focus is about saying no to the hundred good ideas, and I am proud of the things we have not done. With agents that is not a slogan. It is most of the work.
steps

The figure at the top is the record, from the release logs of this site and the newsroom, and I want to walk it because the rule is easier to see in a sequence than in the abstract. On 10 October, Pay after you read: a meter in the browser at 12:09, pay by how far you read at 13:40, personas and your own newsroom at 14:23, sending your reading encrypted at 15:28, usefulness setting the price at 15:49. Each one was the place of highest leverage once the one before it existed. A meter made a price possible; a price made personas worth keeping; personas made sharing worth encrypting. None of them was planned a week ahead. Each was chosen after using the last.
steps

On 11 October, a link to a persona at 09:53 and a reading list in a link at 14:30, 81 minutes after its brief, because sending someone to the newsroom as nobody was the friction I felt that morning. Then the passkey design, and here the path bends. The first version had a door vault between the passkey and the master. A review in the afternoon took it out as a layer too many: there was no requirement for it in our use case, and I agreed. That is the first orange arc on the figure.
steps

On 12 October at 00:15, the newsroom's lab, which had built every step of the design as a card, found that the same passkey returns different bytes through a phone over QR than through the provider on the device. The door went back, as a door per path. That is the second arc, and it points the other way. Two reversals in twelve hours, both right, both cheap, because the design had been shipped as something you could press rather than argued as a document. At 01:33 real vaults from the browser, through the vendored library rather than a writer of our own, which was a choice passed over. At 02:22 the vault pane, live.
steps

And then, this morning, the list. The agent offered the inbox, the reading modes, the marks, and also automating the wire, more beats, scheduling, consumption analytics. The second group is parked, and the figure says why in blue: valuable only with many readers. We do not have many readers; we have articles, and me, and the person I showed the walkthrough to. The place of highest leverage is the feedback loop on what exists: the inbox, the marks, the modes, because they make every article better, they are what the readers we do have want, and they make me a better briefer of the agents, which compounds. Improving how the wire is computed is real work for a real day, and that day is not today.
back

Two things in that sequence are easy to read as failures and are not. Walking back is what a two-way door looks like from inside. The distinction, from Jeff Bezos, is between decisions you can reverse and decisions you cannot, and the point is to move fast through the first kind. Removing the door was a two-way door; so was putting it back. Neither cost more than an afternoon, both were shipped as a version with the change on its page, and the second was forced by a test, which is the best possible reason. The path with two reversals in it reached a better design faster than a path that had tried to get the design right on paper would have, because the paper could not have known what the phone would return.
back

Parking is the same move at the level of a branch. A tangent reaches diminishing returns, or it turns out there is no demand yet, and you stop. Not because it was wrong; because its leverage is lower than something else's today. The parked branch stays on the map, with the reason, and the reason has a date on it: when there are many readers, the wire's scheduling becomes a place of high leverage. That is also why I do not feel ownership of any of these pieces. They are open, the record is public, and the thing I am attached to is the feedback loop, not any one feature in it. The same thing as a shape rather than a record: three to five routes open at every step, one taken and shipped, two walked a little way and walked back, one parked, and the straight line that only exists in hindsight.
back

The hardest part is that going forwards you cannot see the path. Backwards, from the vault pane, the sequence looks inevitable: of course the meter led to personas led to sharing led to a vault led to a passkey. Forwards, at each step, there were five choices, and the figure shows the ones passed over in grey: a paywall, a subscription, an account, a recommender, analytics, a server, Google sign-in. Any of them could have been taken. The method in the madness is only visible by walking backwards, and that is fine, as long as each step forwards was shipped and used before the next was chosen. That is the discipline that replaces foresight.
map

Which shoulders the passkey work stands on. Almost everything under it is a product or a commodity someone else matured; our piece is the door and a door per path; the one custom layer we had to add is the phone by QR, where a provider is not yet mature. There is a second reason the three days went as fast as they did, and the Wardley map shows it. The passkey work went from genesis, a design on a page, through custom-built, a lab you could press, to a product, a pane on every page, in a day. Within hours of that we were building on it: vaults inside vaults, the reading records, the next brief. It is already on its way to being a commodity for us, something that just works and is not thought about. That is only possible because of what it stands on.
map

Look at the bottom of the map. Synced passkeys with the PRF extension in iCloud Keychain: commodity, mature, the same bytes on a Mac, an iPad and an iPhone. The WebAuthn PRF extension itself, Web Crypto with HKDF and PBKDF2, sgit keys made in the client, the vault library we vendored unedited, the vault server, the Stripe payment link: all products or commodities, all someone else's work, all matured before we arrived. Our piece, the door and the derivation, is small, and that is the point. We are not building a passkey system. We are adding one small custom layer on top of a stack that is already mature, and a small custom layer on a mature stack becomes a product almost as soon as it works.
map

The one exception proves it. Google Password Manager's passkey, reached through a phone over QR, returns different bytes from the same passkey on the device. That is a place where a provider is not yet mature, and it is exactly where we had to add a custom layer, a door per path, and exactly where the work slowed. If we had built on that path alone we would still be building. We built on Apple's synced path, which is further to the right, and the thing shipped. Which shoulders you stand on decides how fast your piece becomes a product. The map tells you where the mature shoulders are, and it is worth drawing before choosing where to stand.
ship

Everything above rests on one rule that I want to state on its own: it is about shipping, and it is about a user. Every piece of work, these days, has to be used straight away, by someone, and it is fine if the someone is me. Not a hypothesis, not a design document that waits for a quarter: a thing a person opens. I miss it, so it is working made the case that the people who decide the roadmap have to use the product; this is the operational version. A step that was shipped and used tells you where the next step is. A step that was only designed tells you nothing, because you have not felt it.
ship

That is also why the briefs come after the shipping and not before. The site is an inbox begins with a confession: I could not have written it two days earlier, because I did not know the properties of what would run. The vault had to exist, the passkey had to work, the door had to be per path, before I could think about what a reader does with any of it. The art of the possible is not something you reason your way to. It is what shipping leaves behind, and the next brief is made of it.
limits

Three days is a sample. The sequence is real and the times are from the release logs, but it is one project at one speed, chosen because it is the one I can show. The rule does not pick the product. Places of highest leverage says where to stand, not what to build; the what comes from using the thing and from the people who ask for it. The mathematics is named carefully. Fermi estimates, Bayesian updating and Monte Carlo ranges are the family I mean; the memo could not name them, and the analogy is mine, not a theorem. Parking has a cost. A branch left for later can be overtaken; the wire's scheduling may need to be rebuilt when its day comes. That is accepted, and it is cheaper than building it for readers who are not there.
limits
If you run a team of agents and the hard part has become choosing, or you want to compare maps, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The site proposed in AWS from the vault now has a name: aws.twin.sgit.ai, with its repository SGit-AI__Website__Twin__AWS and its hub at twins.sgit.ai. The name carries the design. It is a twin first: an AWS-shaped interface, for S3, Lambda, EC2, IAM, billing and logs, whose backend is a vault, with the real AWS account put in front of it later as a second backend behind the same interface. That is the same pattern as the one twin that already works, the S3-compatible vault container, where boto3 cannot tell the difference. The name also follows a rule we have now fixed for every family of sites: plural for the hub, singular for the instance, so twins.sgit.ai and aws.twin.sgit.ai, hooks.sgit.ai and tokens.hook.sgit.ai, providers.sgit.ai and elevenlabs.provider.sgit.ai. Held against the hosts that exist, the newer families follow it, and four hosts break it: three under providers and one under games. This records the decisions, the options we rejected, what changes on the twins and providers sites, and one correction: on GitHub Pages, no wildcard certificate is needed.
The families held against the rule: plural for the hub, singular for the instance.
in-short

The AWS site is aws.twin.sgit.ai. Repository SGit-AI__Website__Twin__AWS, hub twins.sgit.ai. Because it is a twin first. An AWS-shaped interface on a vault; the live account is a second backend. The same pattern as the S3 container. The one twin that works today. The rule: plural is the family, singular is the instance. twins and aws.twin, hooks and tokens.hook. Repositories follow it too. SGit-AI__Website__<Family>__<Instance>, with the family singular. Four hosts break it today. Three under providers, one under games. One correction. On GitHub Pages each host gets its own certificate; no wildcard is needed.
decision

The site proposed in AWS from the vault is called aws.twin.sgit.ai. Its repository is SGit-AI__Website__Twin__AWS, which follows the shape of SGit-AI__Website__Hook__Tokens, and its hub is twins.sgit.ai. The repository was created this morning, and the host already resolves.
twin-first

The site is designed twin first, in three steps: Build the twin. An AWS-shaped interface, for S3, Lambda, EC2, IAM, billing and logs, whose backend is a vault. Put the real connection in front of it. As a second backend behind the same interface: a temporary IAM Identity Center session, pasted into the user's vault. Everything built against the twin works against the live account. Because the code that uses it is written against the interface, not the backend.
twin-first

That is the same pattern as the one twin that already works. twins.sgit.ai describes it: "the container is a digital twin of S3, presenting the same S3-compatible API, so that code using boto3, the AWS CLI, or any S3 SDK believes it is talking to real S3, while the files are served from a vault, from local disk, or from memory, chosen as a swappable backend; the service's own code does not change." The AWS twin is the second instance of that pattern, not an exception to it. What this gives the workflow: Develop and test against the vault, with no credentials. Every interface first works on data you can see and seed. Rehearse before running live. The first job, deploying the SG/Send server components to many accounts and regions, can be rehearsed against the twin.
twin-first

Snapshots are commits either way. "What changed between Monday and Friday" works the same for data from the live account and data seeded by hand. An account graph. Resources as nodes; a role and its policies, a function and its bucket, an instance and its security group, as edges.
options

aws.sgit.ai. It loses the twin-first framing, which is the core of the design. aws.platform.sgit.ai. "Platform" names nothing in the estate: a namespace with one occupant. aws.provider.sgit.ai. Provider sites are reports, not tools. A companion report may come later, separately.
convention

Plural is the hub, the family. twins.sgit.ai, hooks.sgit.ai, providers.sgit.ai. Singular is one instance, at that moment in time. aws.twin.sgit.ai, tokens.hook.sgit.ai, elevenlabs.provider.sgit.ai. Repositories use the singular family name. SGit-AI__Website__<Family>__<Instance>: Hook__Tokens, Provider__ElevenLabs, Twin__AWS. Two other kinds of second-level host already exist, and the rule leaves them alone. API sites, like api.send.sgit.ai, are a site's own client code, released by version. Editions, like pt.newsroom.sgit.ai, are the same site in another language or for another audience.
estate

Looking at every host, as in the sgit.ai sites in numbers: Following the rule. tokens.hook.sgit.ai, aws.twin.sgit.ai, and the two demo sites under demo, all reserved, with no site yet. Breaking it, under providers. elevenlabs.providers.sgit.ai and ungovr.providers.sgit.ai, both live, and openrouter.providers.sgit.ai, listed on the hub and not serving. Breaking it, under games. what-can-it-do.games.sgit.ai, live since 8 September, whose repository, Game__What-Can-It-Do, already uses the singular. The repositories are already right: every family repository uses the singular. It is only the hosts that need to move.
dns

The first note on this said that each singular namespace needs its own wildcard certificate, because *.sgit.ai does not cover a second-level name like aws.twin.sgit.ai. The second half is true, and it applies to DNS as well. But these sites are on GitHub Pages, and there no wildcard certificate is needed. GitHub's documentation says that when a custom domain is set, "GitHub queues a job to request a TLS certificate from Let's Encrypt", one per domain, and uploads it itself. What each host needs is its own DNS record, a CNAME pointing to the organisation's github.io domain, which is how the existing hosts work: there is no wildcard record under sgit.ai today. And that is the right way round, because GitHub says: "We strongly recommend that you do not use wildcard DNS records, such as *.example.com", as they "put you at an immediate risk of domain takeovers".
twins

The naming ruling on twins.sgit.ai says a twin holds no credentials, and notes that "the S3 container genuinely blurs the line by being both an interface twin and a thing that holds backend access". The AWS twin makes it worth resolving that. The proposed paragraph: And with it: Keep the execution broker distinct. The broker is a standing, credential-holding intermediary; a twin with a live backend borrows a session the user holds, for a limited time. Watch the name. Use "the AWS twin", in lower case, or add the capitalised form to the site's allow-list with its meaning. Make the site a hub as well as the definition. A page of the twins in place, each with its state: the S3 container, working, shipped by SG/Compute; the AWS twin, proposed; and the AWS, organisation, agent and 2FA twins that are specified or designed. Decide whether the S3 container gets its own site. s3.twin.sgit.ai.
providers

Move the instances to the singular. elevenlabs.provider.sgit.ai, ungovr.provider.sgit.ai and openrouter.provider.sgit.ai. Keep the plural hosts as redirects. So existing links do not break. Switch the canonical hosts first. The hub's bin/sync-providers.py fetches from whichever host answers, and a build check fails if a link disagrees, so changing the links before the hosts would lock in the plural. Later, perhaps, an AWS provider report. Credentials bound by a clock, which AWS services answer a browser, and the cost of a named workload. Before adding it, check the hub's "no commercial relationship" disclosure against sgit.ai's AWS page. The same move applies to the games family: what-can-it-do.game.sgit.ai, with the plural kept as a redirect.
here

AWS from the vault now uses aws.twin.sgit.ai throughout, in its title, summary, text and diagram, says the name is decided, and describes the twin-first design. The changes to twins.sgit.ai and providers.sgit.ai belong to those sites, and are listed above for them.
limits

aws.twin.sgit.ai is not built. The repository and the DNS record exist; the site does not. The renames have not happened. The provider and game hosts still use the plural. The twins ruling is not changed yet. The paragraph above is proposed. The hosting facts are GitHub's. From its documentation, read on 21 October 2026.
sources

A naming discussion of 21 October 2026, captured as decisions the same day. twins.sgit.ai, its naming ruling and what is built; providers.sgit.ai; the repositories and DNS of every site; and GitHub's pages on managing a custom domain and securing a site with HTTPS, read the same day. Related: AWS from the vault, the sgit.ai sites in numbers. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.
