Abstract: At an event this week a speaker described policy as code as the way to scale governance and AI innovation together, and it clicked. Policy as code is right, and it is where agent governance has to end up. But for agents it answers one question, is this request allowed, and the questions a business, an auditor or an insurer asks are the ones around it, the ones an Agent Behaviour Policy holds. What can this agent reach, measured. What was it asked to do, and why. Where the two differ. Which rules can no engine ever see. And the one that surprised me when I checked: for every rule that is code, who can change that code. A rule the agent can rewrite is a setting, not a control. Because an ABP has those columns, it can be written in both directions. From the policy, generate code: for this article, five rows of a real ABP became a Rego policy that Open Policy Agent ran against seven requests, denying a push to the wrong repository, a commit without a leak scan and a model id in a diff, asking before a pull request, and allowing a sentence no engine can judge. From what exists, reverse engineer the policy: parse the code back, and the gaps show on both sides, a row with no code and a rule nobody wrote a reason for. I did it to this session's own policy: of its eleven rules, eight have some code behind them, and only one has code the agent cannot change. Fractal semantic graphs are what make the round trip work across paper, spreadsheets, regulations and code, because each keeps its own vocabulary and the edges between them carry verbs both ways.
One policy at three altitudes: the business's words, the ABP row for one agent, and the code where decisions are made.
in-short

Policy as code is right, and it answers one question. Is this request allowed. For agents, the governance questions are around it. An ABP holds what the engine does not. The reach, measured; the mandate and its reason; the gap; the rules no engine can see; the owner; and who can change each rule's code. A rule the agent can rewrite is a setting. This session's policy has eleven rules; eight have code behind them; only one has code the agent cannot change. Generate code from the policy. Five ABP rows became a 35-line Rego policy; Open Policy Agent decided seven requests: three denied, one asked, three allowed. Reverse engineer the policy from the code. Parsing the Rego back found a row with no code and a rule with no row, the two gaps that matter.
in-short

The same works from paper and spreadsheets. A control spreadsheet became a graph joined to the law it maps to; a role file becomes both a published table and a check. Fractal semantic graphs make the round trip work. Each altitude keeps its own vocabulary, and every edge reads both ways. The four jobs. Enabler, scaling, enforcer and decision-maker: an ABP does the first and keeps the other three honest.
question

At an event this week, one of the speakers described policy as code as the way to scale governance and AI innovation at the same time. I agree, and I think it is where agent governance has to end up: rules that are versioned, tested, reviewed like code and enforced by something other than the model's good behaviour. The best known engine for it describes the idea well. Open Policy Agent, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation graduated project, lets you "decouple policy from that software service": services "offload policy decisions to OPA by executing queries", policies "are written in a high-level declarative language", and a decision can be "arbitrary structured data", not only allow or deny.
question

That is exactly the right shape for the moment an agent acts. An agent asks to push, to send, to read a table; the engine answers. But it answers one question, is this request allowed, and when something goes wrong with an agent, that is rarely the question anyone asks first.
adds

The questions a board, an auditor or an insurer asks about an agent are the ones around the decision, and they are the columns of an Agent Behaviour Policy, as Footprint and blast radius set them out. The reach, measured. What the agent can actually do, from its connectors and accounts. A policy engine only sees the requests that are routed through it; the reach includes the ones that are not. The mandate, with its reason. What the agent was asked to do, and why each rule exists. Code holds the condition; the reason lives, at best, in a comment. The gap. Reach minus mandate, derived. It is the list of things the agent could do that nobody asked for, which is where the rules should come from.
adds

The rules no engine can see. "Great, not perfect." "The tone is mine." Some rows will always be expectations, kept by a second reader, and an ABP lists them instead of silently leaving them out. The owner. Who answers for each row, which is what The policy draws the liability line argued decides where liability lands. Who can change the code. For every rule that is code, whether the agent's own account could rewrite it. The barrier column types it: "A boundary is enforced above the agent's reach, so it cannot flip it. A setting is a switch the agent's own account could flip." That last one is the column I did not expect to matter so much, until I checked this session.
session

This session's own policy, reverse engineered from its code: eleven rules, the code behind each and the barrier. The agent writing this site works under a written policy, eleven rules, reloaded after every summary, as Re-anchoring describes. So I did the exercise on it: for each rule, find the code that enforces it, in the session's hooks, its leak scan, the site's validators and its git configuration, and then ask who can change that code.
session

Eight of the eleven have some code behind them. The leak scan refuses a staged diff with a key-shaped string, a model id outside the byline, an em-dash in an article or a name on a private list. The validator fails the build on the ladder word and warns on absolutes. A hook prints the policy back after every summary and supplies the status report. Three rules have no code at all: masking keys in output, not using anyone else's credential, and answering when asked for the policy's status.
session

Then the second question, and the honest answer. Nearly all of that code is code the agent can change. The leak scan and the hooks are files in its own home directory; the validators are in the repository it pushes to and in a clone on its own disk. By the policy's own definitions, those rules are settings. Even "never push to sgit.ai", enforced by a push address set to nothing, is a setting on its own, because the agent could set it back. What makes that one rule a boundary is something the agent cannot touch: this session's access to GitHub is scoped to the newsroom's repository by the platform it runs on. One rule in eleven.
session

None of that is a failure; it is the session's real state, and most organisations' agents would look the same if anyone drew the table. It is also why policy as code alone would have scored this session as well governed: most of its rules are code. The ABP is what shows that the code is the agent's own. And reverse engineering finds the reasons where they hide. The validator's rule against em-dashes carries its reason in a comment: readers find them off-putting, "and 2,900 of them do not stay gone without a rule". The rule against absolutes is advisory, and its message says why: "say what was found, not what nobody has". That is the paper policy, scattered through the code. Walking up from the code collects it into rows.
generate

A round trip through Open Policy Agent: five ABP rows generated into Rego, evaluated, then parsed back and compared. The other direction was built for this article. Five rows of the session's policy went into a small JSON file: an id, the rule, why it exists, the decision, a condition where there is one, the barrier, and what enforces it today. A generator of about twenty-five lines turned them into Rego, each rule carrying its row's id and reason as a comment and as the value it returns: # R9: Never push to the sgit.ai repository. Why: sgit.ai is read-only for this session. deny contains "R9" if { input.tool == "git.push" not input.remote in {"github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Newsroom"} }
generate

OPA 1.21.2 checked the policy and evaluated seven requests. A push to sgit.ai: deny, R9. A push to the newsroom: allow. A commit with no leak scan: deny, R2. A commit adding a model id in a code comment: deny, R5. A clean, scanned commit: allow. Opening a pull request: ask, R7b, because the decision is the owner's. And publishing a sentence that says "a perfect result": allow, because the row that forbids it has no condition any engine can check, and the generator wrote that down as a comment instead of pretending.
generate

Then back again. opa parse turned the Rego into its syntax tree, and comparing the rules it found with the ABP's rows gave the two lists that matter. Rows with no code: R6c, the wording rule, which stays an expectation with a second reader. Code with no row: after a second file added a rule against Friday releases, "added in a hurry after an incident", the comparison flagged no-friday-releases as enforcement nobody had written a reason for. That is the rule that will confuse the next person, block the next urgent fix, and have no owner when someone asks why.
paper

Code is not the only thing to reverse engineer, and this site has done the other two. From a spreadsheet: when Jan van Dijke published the AI Baseline Control Framework, twenty controls mapped to the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act, its CSV became, on the day, "a semantic graph with an ontology", "joined to the EU AI Act's own text", and "the six things the graph found that the CSV does not say". Four frameworks, one agent did the same for four frameworks and one agent, as a mapping file with a row for every element and its status.
paper

From paper, in both directions at once: sgit.ai's newsroom roles are written as files, and the check that gates a release reads them. In the words of the check itself, "The policy is the writes and edits lists in admin/content/newsroom/roles/<role>.md, the same files the /newsroom/policies.html table is generated from." One source, rendered as a page people read and as a check a release must pass. That is the pattern I would want for every agent: the ABP is the source, the table and the code are renderings, and neither can drift from the other because neither is edited by hand.
fsg

A round trip like this breaks if every format has to share one schema. A board policy is written in the board's words; a regulation in the legislator's; a control spreadsheet in the auditor's; an ABP in reach, mandate, gap and barrier; Rego in packages, rules and conditions. Asking any of them to adopt the others' vocabulary is why mapping exercises become workshops.
fsg

Fractal semantic graphs are the answer this site has been building: "Zoom into any node and you enter a new world with its own node types, its own verbs, its own taxonomy." Each altitude keeps its own vocabulary; the edges between them are verbs with inverses, so a row answers a policy and the policy is answered by the row; a rule enforces a row and the row is enforced by the rule. Then the questions that matter are walks, not workshops. "A question can cross formats without a join table." Which board policies have no row? Which rows have no code? Which code has no row? Which rows are enforced only by code the agent's own account can change? And when a regulation changes, supersede the node, never delete it, and every row and rule that rested on it becomes the answer to a query.
fsg

That is what makes reverse engineering practical at scale: the code, the spreadsheet and the paper do not need to be converted, only connected. And it is what makes generation safe: the code that comes out carries an edge back to the row it came from, so the next person can ask why.
jobs

The speaker's framing was policy as code as an enabler, a way to scale, an enforcer and a basis for decisions. With an ABP as the source, each one gets sharper. Enabler. A written mandate lets a team ship an agent without a review meeting per agent, because the review was of the policy. The behaviour policy is the business logic: writing it is the work. Scaling. One source, rendered into as many engines and agents as needed, versioned and diffable, with every generated rule traceable to its row. Enforcer. Rows compiled into boundaries, and the barrier column saying, honestly, which ones still are not. Hope or enforcement measured what that is worth: one agent's rules kept only by good behaviour fell from 97% to 23% as they moved into the platform.
jobs

Decision-maker. Every decision returns the row it came from, allow, deny or ask, and every ask goes to a named person, as The human in the loop argued, with the record of decisions moving the line over time.
limits

The round trip is a demonstration. Five rows, a short generator and seven requests, run for this article; it is not a product, and real agents need their requests routed through the engine for any of it to bind. The session table is one agent's. Counted from this session's hooks, scripts, validators and configuration on 14 October 2026; other agents will look different, and I expect most to look similar. The GitHub scope was not tested by trying. It is how this session's access is configured; pushing to sgit.ai to prove it is exactly what the policy forbids. Some rows will never be code. That is a feature of the method, not a gap in it: an ABP says which rows rely on a person. The speaker is not named. I took the idea from a talk and have not checked how they would put it.
limits
If you have policies in code, spreadsheets or paper and want to see the agent behaviour policy they imply, or the code an ABP implies, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: In December 2010, at OWASP's IBWAS conference in Lisbon, I gave a keynote called A 'Web Application Security' Challenge to Portugal. It had 168 slides, five proposed focuses and twelve proposed actions for government and industry, from allowing ethical hacking and publishing security score cards to liability for software, an independent vulnerability-disclosure agency, paying for open-source security and proper SSL for half of all websites. It ended with an argument that Portugal, which had nothing to lose, could become the Switzerland of hacking. Reading it again sixteen years later, more of it came true than I expected, though mostly from Brussels rather than Lisbon: software now falls under strict product liability, Europe has its own vulnerability database, manufacturers must report exploited vulnerabilities, and encrypted connections are the norm. What I got wrong was the mechanism. I thought fear of disasters would move governments; what moved them was regulation built slowly over a decade. And the part about Portugal itself, an open, ethical security industry as a way out of a depressed economy, is still mostly to do. This is the first of a series of articles on the talks I have given about Portugal, ahead of a new edition of Hacking Portugal.
Twelve slides from the IBWAS 2010 keynote in Lisbon: the five focuses, the twelve actions and Portugal as Switzerland.
in-short

December 2010, Lisbon. The IBWAS keynote: 168 slides, five focuses, twelve actions. Software deserves respect. Treat application security as health and safety. Twelve actions. Ethical hacking, score cards, liability, disclosure, paying for open source. Portugal could be the Switzerland of hacking. Because it had nothing to lose. More came true than I expected. Mostly from Brussels, slowly, through regulation. The mechanism was wrong. Fear did not move governments; ten years of law did. The Portugal part is still to do.
talk

On 17 December 2010 I gave the keynote at IBWAS'10, OWASP's Ibero-American web application security conference, at ISCTE in Lisbon. Its title was A 'Web Application Security' Challenge to Portugal, and others that care about application security, and its first slide was a disclaimer: "this is my personal opinion". A few weeks later I wrote that "There are a lot of thought provoking ideas in there, and I don't expect that some of them will become reality any time soon." The press picked up one line: Portugal could be the "Switzerland of hacking". The deck has four movements: a new paradigm, as five focuses and twelve actions; a section on fear, with the disasters that would follow if we kept ignoring software; examples from Portuguese websites; and a challenge to Portugal. This article goes through them with what I think today.
focuses

The five focuses were: treat software and application security "with the respect and care that it deserves"; view application security as business intelligence; view it as competitive advantage; make the application security market "work"; and use OWASP as a resource and enabler. What still stands. All five, and the second one more than I could have known. "Application security as business intelligence" was the idea that understanding how your software really works is valuable in itself, beyond finding bugs. Today that is exactly what I argue for agents and graphs: the value of GenAI is that it can understand, and a security team's job is to understand reality. The fourth, a market that works, is still the weakest: buyers still cannot easily tell secure software from insecure software.
actions

The twelve actions were for government or industry: allow ethical hacking; publish the results of security reviews as score cards; put security requirements in procurement; introduce liability for government and publicly traded companies; create an independent vulnerability-disclosure agency; rewrite computer laws; pay for open-source security; demand that widely used end-of-life applications, like IE6, be open sourced; create an insurance market; reduce the assets held, secrets and private data; improve journalism; and "'Proper' SSL support for 50% of websites". What came true, mostly from Brussels. Liability. From 9 December 2026, the EU's new Product Liability Directive brings software, standalone or embedded, under strict, no-fault liability. My slide said government and listed companies; the law went further.
actions

Disclosure. Europe has its own vulnerability database, run by ENISA since May 2025, and since 11 September 2026 the Cyber Resilience Act requires manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours. Not quite an independent agency, but the same idea: disclosure as a public good. Procurement, and Portugal. Portugal's new cybersecurity law, Decreto-Lei 125/2025, which transposes NIS2, came into force on 3 April 2026, with the national cybersecurity centre as its authority. Proper SSL. Achieved, and then some: Google's transparency report shows most pages loaded in Chrome now use HTTPS, far past my 50%.
actions

What did not. Score cards for software, an insurance market that prices application security well, and paying for open-source security at the scale it needs. On the last one I wrote this month that open source receives a tiny share of its value in investment. Reducing the assets held is the one I would put first today: the best way to protect data is not to have it, or to hold only ciphertext, which is what sgit does.
fear

The middle of the deck was deliberately scary: everything is broken, "Its software everywhere", "How many many people will have to die before we take application security seriously?", and a game, "Bring the internet down for a day", a country-wide fire drill. I compared software to health and safety: we expect a minimum level of quality from water, food, cars and planes, and have laws that regulate them; "But, we have very little (if anything) in software and web applications". What I got wrong. The analogy was right, and the mechanism was wrong. I thought fear, and a big enough incident, would move governments quickly. What moved them was a decade of slow, unglamorous regulation. Health and safety for software is arriving the way health and safety arrived for everything else: through liability and reporting duties, not through a single disaster.
portugal

The last part was personal and blunt. I talked about my frustration with Portugal, a country I described as depressed, "and really needs new ideas", and argued that application security could be one of the solutions, "by showing how an open, vibrant, ethical, multi-cultural industry can work and flourish". Portugal had "nothing to lose (it is already rock-bottom)"; what I was asking for "doesn't cost any money"; "It only takes courage, focus and commitment". And: Portugal could become the "Switzerland of Hacking". What still stands. The core of it: a small country can choose a sector and lead in it. Sixteen years later I made the same argument in Judo for small countries, about AI. Portugal is no longer the depressed country of 2010, and some of the bluntness reads differently now. But Portugal did not become the Switzerland of hacking. That is the thread the next talks pick up: Hacking Portugal in 2016, and GenAI in Portuguese in 2024.
limits

Not that the talk caused any of it. The EU's laws have their own long history. The commentary is mine, now. The slides are from 2010, unchanged. The video seems to be gone. The slides are the record. If you were at IBWAS in 2010 and remember it differently, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: On 11 November 2016 I gave the keynote at BSidesLisbon, Hacking Portugal and making it a global player in software development, 103 slides, and three weeks later published it as a book on Leanpub, 75 pages, which still says 95% complete. The idea was that if to hack means to solve problems, Portugal should hack itself: make its network hostile to insecure code, replace the old military service with a Portuguese Hacking Service for 15 to 21 year olds, create a hackathon league as famous as football, a Code Made in Portugal brand, OpenSource.pt for all government code, a Ministry of Code, a Clear Software Act, and a national bug bounty, because cyber security is a public health problem. Ten years later, the regulation I asked for has mostly arrived from Europe, and Portugal has open-sourced a national AI model, which is the spirit of OpenSource.pt. The Hacking Service, the league and the Ministry of Code have not happened. And the biggest change is one I did not see: with agents, everybody can now build software by talking, which makes the talk's central claim, that a small country can choose to lead in code, more possible than it was. This article goes through the talk and says what a new edition, for Web Summit in Lisbon, needs.
Twelve slides from Hacking Portugal at BSidesLisbon 2016, from the summary to the future of Portugal.
in-short

November 2016, Lisbon. The BSidesLisbon keynote, 103 slides, then a book. The book is still at 95%. Published 1 December 2016, never finished. Hack Portugal. Hostile to insecure code; a Hacking Service; a league like football. Code as a national asset. Made in Portugal, OpenSource.pt, a Ministry of Code. Europe brought the regulation. The Clear Software Act, more or less. The service and the league did not happen. As far as I know. Agents change the bet. Everybody can build now; a small country can choose to lead.
talk

I gave Hacking Portugal as the keynote at BSidesLisbon on 11 November 2016; the video is 49 minutes. Its premise was in the book's first lines: "If the word 'hack' means to solve problems, then 'Hacking Portugal' means to find innovative was to solve existing problems." I wanted Portugal to treat software seriously, "a place where programming, TDD, Open Source, learning how to code, hacking (aka bug-bounty style), and DevOps receive the consideration, investment and respect that they deserve", with application security as the enabler. Three weeks later the talk was a book on Leanpub: 17 chapters, 75 pages, 14,487 words, licensed CC BY 4.0, with a paperback on Amazon. Its page still says 95% complete; it was last updated on 1 December 2016, the day it was published. (Its introduction even gives the wrong date for the talk, 9 November.) It is one of the books I left behind, and the one I most want to come back to.
hostile

The talk opened with a Portuguese network "to be hostile to insecure code": make it hard to create, publish or host insecure apps and devices in Portugal, by regulation, by market pressure and by a community that attacks vulnerable code before criminals do. It used a 2016 scan of the country's exposed systems, open remote desktops, industrial controllers, clear-text protocols and data leaks, to ask "How Secure is Portugal?" The honest answer was insecure, but currently safe: not yet attacked at scale.
hostile

Ten years later. The regulation arrived, from Europe. Since 11 September 2026 the Cyber Resilience Act makes manufacturers report actively exploited vulnerabilities, and its security requirements follow in 2027; Portugal's own cybersecurity law came into force in April 2026. That is close to the Clear Software Act on slide 83, "like the 'Clean Air Act', but focused on code quality and security". The quote I used there still explains the resistance: "It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends upon his not understanding it".
service

The idea people remember was the Portuguese Hacking Service: update the old compulsory military service into a hacking service for 15 to 21 year olds, to "hack everything that is plugged-in to Portugal's network", code-review open-source and strategic code, contribute fixes, and "help SMEs with their digital security and DevOps", paid for by moving a share of the military budget to cyber. Around it: a national hackathon league, teams sponsored to go to DefCon, and hacking taught the way Portugal teaches football, with the kids, the clubs, the pride.
service

Ten years later. As far as I know, none of this happened in that form. I still think the idea is right, and I would change one thing. In 2016 learning to hack meant learning to code first. With agents, a 16-year-old can explore a system by talking to it, which is what I now call explorer coding. A Hacking Service in 2026 would teach young people to direct agents against Portugal's own systems, with a mandate that says what they may and may not touch.
code

The second half was about code as something a country owns. A Code Made in Portugal brand, because "Good software development teams (from developers to management) are one of the most important assets of a company and country." OpenSource.pt: "All code written (and paid) for Government agencies to be released under an Open Source license", and all government documents under Creative Commons. A Ministry of Code, with a government CTO and CISO. A Portugal-wide bug bounty. Cyber security as a public health problem, with specialists trained "using similar techniques to the ones we use to train doctors, nurses".
code

Ten years later. The best news is in the spirit of OpenSource.pt: in 2026 Portugal released Amália, a national language model for European Portuguese, as open source, built on the European EuroLLM model and meant as a platform for public services, companies and researchers. It is exactly the kind of code a country should own and share. The Ministry of Code and the national bug bounty are still ideas. And the public health analogy has only grown more apt: Europe now treats software defects as a liability, from December, under the Product Liability Directive.
why

The talk ended with a choice: Portugal could "be a garden for Europe, a holiday destination", or "a powerhouse that inspires and leads the world in technology and secure coding", working with the Portuguese-speaking countries. The book's last chapter argued it is easier in a small country, "more likely to have fewer agendas and fewer lobby groups wielding influence". What holds. All of it, and I made the same argument this month about AI, in Judo for small countries. What I got wrong is the timescale, and the idea that it would start from security. It did not start from security; it may start from language and AI, where Portugal has just made a real move. And what a book needs that a talk does not: a feedback loop, which is why the next edition will be built from articles like this one, read before they are bound.
next

A new edition of Hacking Portugal, for Web Summit in November, would keep the structure and change the centre of gravity: from application security to agents, language and sovereignty. It needs the 2010 keynote as its origin, this talk as its body, the 2024 talk on GenAI in Portuguese as the turn, the Europe essays as the wider frame, and a new last part on what a small country can do with agents. Most of that is already written; the rest will be published here first.
limits

"As far as I know" means I did not survey it. Some of these ideas may exist in a form I missed. The Clear Software Act is an analogy. The CRA is the EU's law, not mine. The commentary is mine, now. The slides are from 2016, unchanged. If you were at BSidesLisbon in 2016, or want to help with the new edition, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: On 28 June 2024, at OWASP Global AppSec EU in Lisbon, I gave Deterministic GenAI Outputs with Provenance, 132 slides and a live demo of The Cyber Boardroom, the project I had been building for two months: an assistant that explains cyber security to board members, in their language and at their level. The talk opened with a quiz, what is the sixth most powerful programming language in the world, and the answer was Portuguese, because prompts are written in natural languages and 236 million people speak it first. Its core was a set of principles: GenAI matters because it can understand content, not because it creates it; hallucinations are a feature for creativity and a bug for facts; use read-only models, bring your own content, assume every prompt is exposed, and use graphs instead of RAG. And it ended with a challenge to Portugal: the future depends on getting this right, otherwise Portugal becomes just another consumer of global technology. Two years later most of it holds, and some of it is the foundation of what I do now: provenance, graphs and determinism are the core of this newsroom; the board assistant became agents with a mandate; and Portugal has released Amália, an open model for European Portuguese, which is what I asked for. What changed is the word: in 2024 I talked about models and prompts; in 2026 it is agents, and the problem is controlling what they do.
Twelve slides from Deterministic GenAI Outputs with Provenance, OWASP Global AppSec EU, Lisbon, June 2024.
in-short

June 2024, Lisbon. OWASP Global AppSec EU; 132 slides; a live demo. Portuguese is a programming language. The sixth most powerful, by speakers. GenAI understands. That matters more than that it creates. Principles. Read-only models, your own content, prompts exposed, graphs not RAG. The Cyber Boardroom. Explaining security to a board, in its own language. A challenge to Portugal. Lead, or be another consumer of technology. Two years later. Provenance and graphs hold; models became agents.
talk

On Friday 28 June 2024, in the last session before the closing of OWASP Global AppSec EU at the Lisbon Congress Centre, I gave Deterministic GenAI Outputs with Provenance. The page on my site has the slides, the video and a full transcript. I said at the start: "my focus (and this presentation) is on GenAI". The title was the whole argument: deterministic, GenAI, output, with provenance, "Traceability, Source Tracking & Documentation, Lineage, Origin Verification".
language

It began with a quiz for the room: what is the sixth most powerful programming language in the world? "Since data is now code, and GenAI prompts are written in natural languages", the answer was Portuguese: "Portuguese, as English and every other language in the world (dead or alive) can be used to give instructions to LLMs", to "define actions, workflows and create applications". With 236 million first-language speakers, that is a lot of programmers. And I asked for models in our language: "we need Portuguese from Portugal, Portuguese from Angola, Portuguese from Mozambique, Portuguese from Cape Verde". Two years later. It happened, at least for Portugal: Amália, an open model for European Portuguese, built on the European EuroLLM and released as open source in 2026, with a technical report and a benchmark for pt-PT. The other varieties are still waiting. And the idea that language is the programming language is now ordinary: it is what explorer coding is.
understanding

The slides I would keep in any version: GenAI is the next technological revolution "Not because it can CREATE content, But because it can UNDERSTAND content"; hallucinations "Are a FEATURE when creating content and when we want creativity, But are a BUG and PROBLEM when we want facts, evident and trust". Is it secure? No. Is it safe? Maybe, depending on implementation. From an attacker's point of view, GenAI is "Your most vulnerable API", "Your most dangerous Insider Threat" and "A crazy 'Black Box'". Then the principles: "Read-only models", "It's about the Prompts", "Bring your content", "Assume all content and prompts are exposed", "Double down on AppSec and Cyber". And one slide I am proud of now: Use Graphs instead of RAG. In the talk I said: "I think the stuff with graphs is a lot more interesting. I think you take the content, you summarize, you build graphs of it, then you navigate the graph."
understanding

Two years later. This is the part that held best, because it became the work. Provenance is the rule of this newsroom: every claim checked against a source and linked. Graphs became fractal semantic graphs, and every article here has one. Determinism became the principle that the further a thing moves towards commodity, the fewer agents in line. What changed is the threat: in 2024 the insider was a model answering questions; in 2026 it is an agent with tools, and the answer is a behaviour policy and authority outside the model.
boardroom

The middle of the talk was a live demo of The Cyber Boardroom, which I had spent the previous two months building, open source, with every release on PyPI, Docker Hub and AWS. The problem it solved was not specific to security: "how do you communicate with stakeholders using their language, culture, knowledge, state, interests, and level of ownership?" I showed it answering a board member's question in several languages, three board-member personas asking the same question, a fourth model reviewing the other three, and Athena, the cyber security advisor, with the prompt that created her on the screen. And: "Security incidents are a good thing", if you use small ones as training.
boardroom

Two years later. The idea, personalised briefings for people who own the risk, is still at the centre of what I do. The shape changed: one assistant answering questions became teams of agents doing work, each with a role, a mandate and a record, which is what the agentics talk showed last week.
challenge

The talk ended where my Portugal talks always end. To the Portuguese in the room: "the future of Portugal kind of depends on you. I think it can really make a massive difference, but we need to get it right. Otherwise, Portugal just becomes another consumer of global technology, which is not where it should be, because now we actually have the ability to make a difference." What holds. All of it. It is the same challenge as 2010 and 2016, with a better lever: in 2010 the lever was security, in 2016 code, and in 2024 language. Amália suggests Portugal heard some of it. The essays I wrote the next year took it to the scale of Europe.
limits

Not the first time I mentioned The Cyber Boardroom. It was its first live demo in Portugal that I can document. Not that the talk led to Amália. Many people asked for a Portuguese model. The commentary is mine, now. The slides and transcript are from 2024. If you were in the room in Lisbon, or want to talk about agents for boards, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Between February and June 2025 I wrote five essays on diniscruz.ai that took my Portugal talks to the scale of Europe. Portuguese as a programming language in the AI era argued that if language is the new programming, Portugal and the Portuguese-speaking world need their own models and tools. An open-source sovereign cloud for an open Europe proposed a cloud that is 100% open source, compatible with the APIs of the big US clouds so nothing has to be rewritten, and federated across countries, regions and cities. Scaling Europe's regulatory superpower proposed turning flat regulation, NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act, the AI Act, into semantic graphs that answer for a specific context. Europe's strategic opportunity in GenAI named six trends that play to Europe's strengths, from commoditised, deterministic models and AI at the edge to semantic graphs and multilingual AI. And a comparison with the EU's federated cloud initiative asked whether Europe should build the Linux of cloud or a new platform. A year and a half later, two have moved: Portugal released an open model for European Portuguese, and semantic graphs became my daily work. The sovereign cloud has not, and I now think the better route is the one I took since: make the code movable and keep the server dumb, so sovereignty becomes the ability to move.
Sixteen years of talks about Portugal and what happened since, from the IBWAS keynote in 2010 to 2026.
in-short

Five essays, February to June 2025. The Portugal talks, at the scale of Europe. Portuguese is a programming language. So we need our own models. An open-source sovereign cloud. Compatible with the big clouds' APIs, federated. Regulation as graphs. Europe's rules, queryable for each context. Six trends play to Europe. Determinism, the edge, graphs, many languages, openness, people. Two moved, one did not. Amália and graphs, yes; the sovereign cloud, not yet. What I would change. Sovereignty is the ability to move, not a new cloud.
essays

The Europe and learning hub on diniscruz.ai holds them, each with a PDF: Portuguese as a programming language in the AI era, 11 February 2025. An open-source sovereign cloud for an open Europe, 24 February 2025. Scaling Europe's regulatory superpower, 31 March 2025. Europe's strategic opportunity in GenAI, 1 April 2025, with a podcast. Comparing the EU FED Cloud with an open-source federated cloud, 18 June 2025. They continue the line from 2010, 2016 and 2024: a small country, and a continent, can choose where to lead.
language

The first essay took the opening of the Lisbon talk and made it a policy: if natural language is the new programming language, then Portuguese, spoken by more than 260 million people on four continents, needs models, tools and data of its own, built in the open, with the government involved. The cloud essay put it more sharply: digital sovereignty is not just about infrastructure, "it is also about language and culture". A year and a half later. This one moved. Portugal released Amália, an open-source model for European Portuguese, built on the European EuroLLM and funded through the national recovery plan, as a platform for public services. It is close to exactly what the essay asked for. The other varieties of Portuguese are still waiting.
cloud

The second essay proposed a European cloud that is "100% open-source", with "full compatibility with major cloud APIs" so organisations can move "without requiring major code rewrites", and federated, so countries, regions and cities run their own parts. The June essay compared it with the EU's federated cloud initiative, which builds its own platform on open standards rather than cloning the big clouds' APIs: one is an alliance of providers with a jointly designed service, the other "the 'Linux of cloud' that anyone can host or modify".
cloud

A year and a half later. It has not happened, and my thinking moved. The concern is more real than ever: in June 2025 Microsoft France's legal director told the French Senate, asked whether he could guarantee French data would never reach US authorities without consent, "No, I cannot guarantee it". But I no longer think the answer is one new cloud. It is to move the cloud, not the code: keep the code portable, keep the server dumb, and hold the keys yourself, so that sovereignty is the ability to move. sgit is built that way: the server holds ciphertext, and whoever holds the keys holds the line.
graphs

The third essay was about Europe's "regulatory superpower", the Brussels effect, and its weakness: NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act and the AI Act are published as flat documents, the same for everyone. The proposal was to turn them into semantic graphs, so a company can ask what applies to it, in its context, with every answer linked to the article it came from. A year and a half later. This became my work. Fractal semantic graphs, the books on graphs.sgit.ai, and a regulation graph of the AI Act with 1,523 nodes are all descendants of it, and every article on this site carries a graph. Meanwhile the regulation itself got more urgent: the Cyber Resilience Act's reporting duties started on 11 September 2026, and the new product liability rules start in December. A graph of what applies to you is more useful now than when I wrote the essay.
trends

The fourth essay named six trends: commoditised models and deterministic AI, with provenance; AI moving from the cloud to the edge; knowledge moving from text to semantic graphs; multilingual, culturally inclusive AI; open source and decentralisation; and a human-centred vision. Its claim was that each plays to European strengths: openness, many languages, sustainability and regulation. A year and a half later. The direction held, more for some than others. Determinism and provenance are the rules of this newsroom. Graphs, as above. Multilingual AI has its first national example in Amália. Open source is still the foundation of everything we build. The edge moved less than I expected, and the cloud models moved more: most of the agent work I do runs on large models in the cloud, which is one more reason the keys and the code have to stay movable.
next

For the new Hacking Portugal, these essays are the wider frame: the lever is no longer only security or code, but language, graphs and the ability to move. The talks give the story, and the essays give the policy.
limits

Not that the essays caused Amália. Many people asked for a Portuguese model. The sovereign cloud is not dead. I think there is a better route, not that it is wrong. The commentary is mine, now. The essays are from 2025, unchanged. If you work on sovereignty or language models in Portugal or Europe, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The follow-up to "the most important question is whether they miss it". The step after giving something away is to define a product, put a price on it that makes sense to you, find a way to deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time rather than a curve, and then offer it, free, to the people who already know you: early adopters, power users, past customers. What that measures is brutal. The price is a statement of what you think it is worth; the test is whether people take it at zero. If they say it is interesting but they have no time, it does not fit the team, or it is hard to deploy, the problem is not the price, and you go back to the drawing board. The part that is easy to leave out is that free is never free for the other side: engaging costs them attention, thinking and schedule, so the exercise is to measure that cost and cut it, until the service costs you the least and costs them the least. Written as a record of where this came from, and as a brief for the agents who will run it.

The ladder, what each tier costs each side, and the fork. Four tiers already on sale, from the ten-pound pack to the fifteen-hundred-pound reviewed vault, each with a relative cost to us and a cost to the customer. The early access programme gives the five-hundred-pound tier away, free, to people who already run an agent. The question on the right is the whole exercise. Prices as published on 2 October 2026; cost bars are relative, not measured. Price it before you give it away. A price is a statement of what you think the thing is worth. Giving it away at that stated price, to people who know you, is the cleanest test of whether the statement is true.

Deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time. The reason this is possible now is the agentic workflow. Provisioning a vault and a policy for one more customer costs a little more, not a lot more, and that is what lets you give twenty away without flinching. Offer it to the people who already know you. Early adopters, power users, past customers. Not "apply for a chance", which puts work on them before they have anything. "We have twenty; would you like one, or shall I give it to someone else." It is also how you thank them. Free is never free for the other side. They still have to read, think, decide, find a slot, and fit it into a team. A price can even help, because it tells them you are serious. Either way, the cost they bear is the number to measure and the number to cut.

The answer is brutal either way. If they take it, use it and ask for more, you have a product and the question becomes price. If they say it is interesting but they have no time, it does not fit, it is hard to deploy, the problem is not the price and you go back to the board. Count what matters. Policies created per day, customised, used; scenarios run; corrections sent back; and the minutes each one cost the person on the other side. The earlier article ends on a question. Hand the thing to people for free, briefly, then take it away, and ask whether they miss it. If they shrug, you do not have a product yet. If they come back for it, you have something, and the model turns on.

That is the right test and it has a gap in it, which is what happens next. "Something" is not a product until it has a shape, a price and a way of being delivered that does not break you on the tenth customer. So the next step is four moves, in order. Define the product. Not the technology, the thing somebody receives. For RiskMandate the thing is an Agent Behaviour Policy for one agent, as an encrypted vault the customer holds the keys to, with the mandate corrected for their deployment. That sentence took weeks to get to and it is the product.

Price it, at a number that makes sense to you. Not a number from a competitor's page, a number you would be content to be paid. RiskMandate's ladder is four tiers: ten pounds for the pack downloaded, fifty for a working vault, five hundred for the vault corrected for your situation, fifteen hundred for two sessions and a professional's signature. The first two are automated and already on sale. The third is an email thread: we send prompts, the customer runs them, we build the vault and the policy from what comes back. The fourth adds people's time on both sides.

Find a way to deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time. This is the move that was not available a year ago and is the reason to do this now. The agentic workflow means the marginal customer costs a little more, not a lot more. The vault is provisioned by an agent, the policy is drafted by an agent from the customer's prompts, a person corrects it. The cost of serving the twentieth customer is close to the cost of serving the second. That is linear, not exponential, and it is the condition under which you can afford to give twenty away. Then offer it, free, to the people who already know you. Which is what the programme does, and the next section is about why the free part is the hard part.

Here is the thing that is easy to leave out, and the memo was careful about how to say it, because it is easy to say it in a way that sounds like a lecture. When you give something away, or when you say "this is worth five hundred pounds and I would like you to have it", you are not making a zero-cost offer. You are asking the other side to engage. To read the message. To think about whether it applies to them. To consider it against everything else on their list. To find twenty minutes for the prompts and half an hour for a call. To fit a new thing into a team that already has a way of working.

None of that is zero, and all of it is paid by them. The honest version of the offer accounts for it. A price point, oddly, can help here: it says the thing is serious and that you expect it to be used, which is a reason to find the twenty minutes. But whether the price is five hundred or zero, the attrition you place on the other side is real, and the first measurement the programme makes is of that attrition. How long did it take from the message to the first reply. How many people never replied. How many started the prompts and stopped. How many asked a question that the message should have answered.

Then the exercise is to reduce it. The service you want is the one that costs you the least to provide and costs the customer the least to receive. No overhead on them, no overhead on deployment, no second tool to install, no account to create. Those are product decisions, and the programme is where you find out which ones you got wrong, while the people finding out for you are people who like you. Two small rules, both from the memo. Do not make them apply. "Apply for a chance to be considered" asks for work before there is anything in hand, and it inverts the relationship: they are doing you a favour by using the thing, not the other way round. "We have twenty of these in the first round. Would you like one? If not, I will give it to someone else" is honest about scarcity and leaves them nothing to do but say yes or no.

Reward the people who were there early. The early adopters, the power users, the past customers who paid for something before it was finished. They are the ones who should get the first twenty, and the offer should say that is why they are getting it. It is a thank-you that also happens to be the best possible test group, because they know enough to tell you where it is wrong, and they are the ones whose silence means the most.

The early access page went live on 30 September 2026, invite only. Its own words: "A small programme for people who already run an agent with real access: a mailbox, a code host, a workflow tool, a CRM. Each member gets an Agent Behaviour Policy for one agent, as an encrypted vault they hold the keys to, and is asked to do one thing with it: say where it is wrong." The asks of the member: "Run it against the real agent. Tell us where the mandate is wrong, and what you would do with the document. Twenty minutes for the prompts, and a reply; half an hour on a call." The commitments back: "A person confirms your place within a working day, and the vault follows within five." And the caveat that keeps it honest: "Not a security assessment, and not a promise about your agent's behaviour."

That is the five-hundred-pound tier, given away. The programme page does not say the price, and it should not; the price is for the people who come after. What it measures is whether people who already run an agent, and already know us, will spend twenty minutes and half an hour to get a document that describes what their agent can do. If they will not, no price fixes that. It is worth being plain about the two outcomes, because one of them is a bad day and the exercise only works if you are prepared for it.

If people take the offer, run the prompts, read the vault, send corrections and ask what else there is, you have a product. The next question is price, and it is a good question to have: would they buy more, is five hundred too low for what they got, is it too high for the next tier of customer, does the fifteen-hundred tier sell itself once someone has had the five-hundred one free. Those are the questions the earlier article called "can you charge, and can you charge at a profit", and you can only ask them of people who have had the thing.

If people say it is interesting and then do not find the time, or say it does not fit how their team works, or start and stop because the vault was harder to open than the message implied, then you do not have a product yet. You might have a technology, you might have an idea, you might have a document people would read if someone else did the work. But you do not have a commercial product, because a commercial product is one people take when the only cost is their own attention. That is the drawing board, and the sooner you are at it the cheaper it is. Neither outcome is a marketing problem. The earlier article said that about revenue and it is just as true here: if friendlies will not take it free, a bigger audience will not take it either.

The programme runs against numbers that are already defined, and the memo is firm that they are the ones that matter: how many Agent Behaviour Policies get created each day, how many get customised, how many get used, how many scenarios get run. Those are the KPIs. The objectives sit above them and are about the same thing: is anyone building these, is anyone changing them, is anyone running their agent against them. A policy that was created and never customised is a download. A policy that was customised and never used is a document. The commercial value is in the third number. To those four we add the measurement from the section above: the minutes each step cost the person on the other side, and where they stopped. That is the number that tells us what to cut.

This section is the brief. It is written so that an agent picking up the programme in a week, or in a year, knows what to do and why. The list is the early adopters, power users and past customers. It lives in the CRM vault. Nobody outside it gets the first round. The reason is in the section above: they are the best test group and the thank-you is deliberate. The message is short and makes no one apply. It says what the thing is in one sentence, that there are twenty in this round, that they are being offered one because they were early, and asks yes or no. It carries the invitation code. It does not carry the price.

Record the clock. Time from message to first reply. Time from yes to vault delivered, against the five-working-day promise. Time from vault to first correction. Who never replied, who said yes and never ran the prompts, who ran them and stopped. Every one of these is a row in the programme vault, with no message content copied, only the timestamps and the step. Count the four KPIs daily and write them to the same vault: policies created, customised, used, scenarios run. Add corrections received, because a correction is the strongest signal that someone read the thing. Every stop is a finding. When someone stops, the question is not why they did not care; it is what cost them more than it should have. Write it down as a product change to make, not a reason the customer gave.

The stop rule. If, after the first twenty, fewer than a handful have run the prompts and sent a correction, the programme stops and the drawing board starts. That number is for the founders to set before the first message goes out, not after the results are in. This article is part of the record. It says where the programme came from and what it was for. If the shape changes, add a dated note here rather than rewriting it, so the next agent can see the path. Three reasons, and the third is the one the memo was reaching for. The product is a vault. Everything that makes the programme possible, keys the customer holds, a reading app inside, version history, a read key for the person who corrects it, is the machinery this site documents, and the cost structure that makes giving twenty away affordable is the agentic workflow that provisions them.

The method is the one this site runs on. Ship, give away, take away, watch; now define, price, deliver at a flat marginal cost, offer to friendlies, measure both costs. The business plans published here are written to be taken and run the same way. And the site is becoming the memory. An agent that picks this programme up in a year should be able to read, in order, the article that said "do they miss it", the page that published the offer, this article that said why it was shaped this way and what to count, and then the vault that holds the counts. That chain is how the next agent gets context rather than instructions, and it is why a voice memo about a sales campaign became an article rather than a task.

Abstract: The behaviour policy family has policies for agents, decisions, workflows, skills and applications. This one is for a process. It started with sgit and keys: we want sgit to work with PKI keys rather than holding a vault key, so the vault key has to live somewhere else, in a small process acting as a key service or a network broker. That only helps if sgit's own process cannot reach the key, which led to a bigger question. Inside a cloud container, everything runs as root, which is bad practice and no defence in depth. So what is the most locked-down process Linux lets us build there? We built it, in this newsroom's own Claude Code container, and measured it. A policy is derived from one traced run: every file the process reads, every system call it makes, every host it talks to. Then the kernel enforces it with seven walls: a user that exists for one run, an empty read-only root holding only the listed files, its own namespaces, Landlock, a seccomp allowlist, a network broker that only opens tunnels to the policy's hosts, and limits. A probe that, as root, could read /etc/shadow, the agent's home and the internet could do none of it under the policy. The cost was 92 to 187 milliseconds a run. And the size of the policy is a measure of the software: Hello World in C needs 1 file and 12 system calls; sgit needs 1,025 files and 58.
Seven walls around one process, set from its policy and enforced by Linux inside this cloud container.
in-short

A new member of the family. Policies for agents, decisions, workflows, skills and applications; now one for a process. It started with sgit's keys. If sgit should not hold the vault key, its process must not be able to reach it. In a cloud container, everything runs as root. So we built the most locked-down process Linux allows there. The policy is derived, not written. One traced run lists every file, system call and host the process needs. The kernel enforces it. Seven walls, set from the policy; the policy itself executes nothing. It held. A probe that could do 13 of 14 things as root could do none of them under the policy. It is cheap. 92 to 187 milliseconds a run, measured. The policy's size measures the software. 1 file and 12 system calls for Hello World; 1,025 files and 58 for sgit.
why

We already have agent behaviour policies, decision and workflow policies, skill behaviour policies and, since php2shell, application behaviour policies. I want to add one more, for the thing everything else eventually runs as: a process. On Windows and on Linux, it is all processes.
why

This came from a practical question. We want to run sgit with PKI keys rather than vault keys. The logic is that we do not want to give the vault key to the sgit process, but it has to live somewhere. So the idea is a small separate process, an agent of its own, acting like a key management service, or a network broker that adds what is needed to a request on the way out. The key is not the risk made the general point: credential injection is a good pattern, and the first question is still what the process can do. Because if we do this, we need to make sure the sgit process itself cannot reach the key, the broker's memory or its files.
why

And that is where it gets uncomfortable. Inside a cloud container like the one this newsroom's agent runs in, processes run as root. Every process can read every file, signal every other process and talk to anything on the network. That is bad practice, and it is not defence in depth. So why not give sgit a process of its own, and while we are at it, lock it down properly: define everything it may do, and have the operating system refuse everything else?
question

What is the most locked-down process we can create today, with whatever this environment offers? If a process prints "Hello World", or runs a Python program that needs a few files, it should not be able to do anything else. It should have, in effect, an immutable file system. It should run as a user that exists only for that run, with access to a couple of directories, a couple of hosts, and nothing else Linux provides: no other executables, no other processes, no way to look around. And the policy should list every file the process needs, every dependency, all the way down. This is the blast radius idea, the footprint and blast radius of an agent, applied to a process: reverse-engineer what it actually needs, and make that the limit.
container

This newsroom's agent runs in a Claude Code cloud container: Ubuntu 24.04 in a Firecracker microVM, Linux 6.18, as root with nearly every capability. That microVM is already a wall around the whole container. What we wanted was walls inside it, around one process. We checked what was available, and it is a lot: Landlock, at ABI 7. The kernel's own sandbox for a process, which needs no privileges: read, write and execute per path, TCP connect per port, and no signals to processes outside it. seccomp, for an allowlist of system calls. Namespaces: mount, process, IPC, hostname, cgroup and network. cgroups (version 1 here), for process and memory limits. iptables, which can match on the user that owns a connection. useradd, chroot, strace and a C compiler with static libraries. Nothing extra needed installing.
derive

The policy is not written by hand. A script runs the command once under strace -f and reads what it did: every file it opened successfully, every directory it listed, every program it executed, every system call it made, every connection it opened. It adds what the trace cannot see, the ELF interpreter the kernel loads for each binary and the interpreter named on a script's first line, and writes it all down as a policy. The smallest one, for Hello World in C, reads in full: one file, the program itself; no directories; no devices; no network; and twelve system calls, from arch_prctl to write. Nothing else. The policy also records the user (ephemeral, no groups, no capabilities, no new privileges), what the process may see of other processes (nothing), and its limits (64 processes, 512 MB, two minutes).
enforce

A second script takes the policy and builds the process's world, then a small static launcher applies the last walls from inside it and starts the program: An ephemeral user. useradd makes one for this run, and it is removed afterwards. The launcher drops to it, with no groups and no capabilities, and sets no_new_privs, so nothing it runs can gain privileges. An empty, read-only root. A fresh, tiny filesystem in which each file the policy lists is bind-mounted read-only at its own path. Then the whole root is made read-only, and the process is put inside it. For Hello World, the root holds one file. /etc/shadow, /root and /bin/sh are not refused: they do not exist. Its own namespaces. Mount, process, IPC, hostname and cgroup. Inside, the process sees one process: itself. If the policy has no network, it also gets a network namespace with nothing in it.
enforce

Landlock. Read access to the listed files, execute access only to the listed programs, write access only to the listed folders, TCP connect only to the broker's port, and no signals to anything outside. A seccomp allowlist. Only the system calls the traced run made. Everything else returns "not permitted". A network broker. When the policy names hosts, the process's only way out is a small proxy, run outside the sandbox, that opens a tunnel to those hosts and refuses everything else, plus an iptables rule that rejects any other connection from that one user. Limits. A cgroup caps the number of processes and the memory; a timer caps the run. The broker is the shape of the key service. In this test it only decides where a process may go. The next step is for it to hold the credential, so the process never does.
probe

To find out, we wrote a probe: a small program that tries everything a sandboxed process should never do, and reports each result. We ran it three ways. What the probe tried, and what stopped it: as root, under the Hello World policy, and with two walls switched off. As root, today. It could do 13 of its 14 attempts. Only tracing process 1 was refused. Under the policy. It could do none of them. With seccomp and Landlock switched off. The other walls still refused all but two. The files were not there, /tmp was read-only, it saw one process, and there was no network. The two it got through: opening a netlink socket, and signalling process 1, which inside its namespace is the probe itself. That is the point of defence in depth. No single wall has to be right, and switching one off does not open the door.
probe

We also tested the parts that do not show in that table: The broker. Under a policy for a Python script that fetches one page, the script fetched send.sgraph.ai, and the broker refused example.com and api.anthropic.com with a 403. When the probe ran under the same policy and tried to go around the broker, Landlock refused the connection. With Landlock off, the firewall rule for that user refused it. The process limit. A loop of forks stopped at 63 processes. With seccomp on, it could not fork at all, because the traced Hello World never did.
sgit

Then the real target. We traced sgit initialising a vault, committing a file and checking its status, in one working folder, and ran the same thing under the policy. It worked: the vault was created, the file committed. And the trace caught something worth knowing. sgit status talks to the server even when there is nothing to push, so the policy needed its host, dev.send.sgraph.ai, through the broker. A policy derived from a run tells you what the software actually does, not what you assumed.
cost

We expected the setup to be the expensive part, and at first it was: building the root with a shell script, calling mount three times per file, took 1.7 seconds for 169 files. Doing the same with direct system calls from one small program brought it to about 60 milliseconds, whatever the number of files. The size of a policy and what it costs, for four programs from Hello World in C to sgit init, commit and status.
cost

The overhead, the median of five runs, is between 92 and 187 milliseconds: making the user, the firewall rule and the limits, building the root, and cleaning up. The run itself is within noise of the bare run. For sgit, whose clone already takes from seconds to tens of seconds, that is 5% on a three-and-a-half-second job. And most of it can be done in advance: the user, the rules and the root can be prepared before they are needed. Making the user alone is about 20 milliseconds, and a uid that simply is not in use would do without it.
policy-of-policies

This is also a great example of a policy of policies. There is a policy for the operating system, one for the environment, one for Python, one for sgit, and one for this execution. Each narrows the one before it and never widens it, the way decisions at every level may narrow the level above. The process gets only what is left. A policy of policies: operating system, environment, runtime, application and execution, each narrowing the one above. And, as with hooks, the policy executes nothing. It says what is allowed; the runtime enforces it. Hooks are kernel code argued that an agent's rules should move from hope into enforcement. This is the same move, one level down, into the kernel itself.
measure

There is a bonus. Once a process has a policy, you can see how well engineered it is by the size of what it needs. The smallest possible Linux process has a tiny policy: Hello World in C needs one file and twelve system calls. Hello World in Python needs 37 files and 34. A Python script that fetches one page needs 169 files. sgit needs 1,025 files, 66 MB and 58 system calls: 544 files of its own modules, 231 from Python's standard library, 122 from osbot_utils and 85 from cryptography, 15 MB on its own. That is not a criticism; it is a map. It says where the attack surface is, which dependencies carry the weight, and what a smaller, purpose-built sgit for one job could drop. It is all about least privilege, and you cannot have least privilege until you know what the least is.
limits

One run is not every path. A trace sees only what that run did; error paths and rare branches need more runs, ideally the test suite, which is one more reason to have one. seccomp filters by call, not by argument. The netlink socket got through because socket was allowed; filtering on the arguments is the next step. This is a prototype. About 350 lines of Python and C, run in one container, not a hardened tool. The microVM is still the outer wall. This adds walls inside it; it does not replace it. The key service is not built. The broker here decides where a process may go; it does not yet hold a credential. The numbers are this machine's. Four cores, one container; sgit-ai 0.21.0 as installed here.
sources

My voice memo of 24 October 2026. The experiment, run that day in this newsroom's Claude Code cloud container by this site's agent: the code, the four policies and the results are in the data pack. The kernel interfaces are documented in the Linux kernel's Landlock and seccomp pages. Related: application behaviour policies, a skill behaviour policy, allowed is not right, a policy beside the prompt, approve at altitude, hooks are kernel code, the key is not the risk, footprint and blast radius. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: In the book I quote Paul Lockhart's A Mathematician's Lament: if you set out to design a system that destroys a child's curiosity about maths, you could not do better than the one we have. I think we do the same thing with programming. It is usually taught upside down: concepts first, functions and structures that make no sense yet, exercises that build nothing anyone uses. Of course people hate it. What hooks a programmer is something else: the ability to control something, to go from a thought to something that works, in a short loop. I learned that way, on a ZX Spectrum, then an Amiga and an x86, meeting each concept when a problem needed it. The tools that taught people well all had that loop: BASIC at the prompt, Visual Basic, the spreadsheet, Scratch, and the Code Clubs in the UK. And when people were taught programming with nothing useful to build, they went back to Excel, and programmed there. Now explorer coding, by voice, starts at the right end: what you want, and seeing it work. Coding is communication with a computer, and I expect people will end up reading more code, not less, and understanding variables and classes because they already need them.
Programming, taught upside down: how it is usually taught, and how it is learned.
in-short

We teach maths as if to make people hate it. Lockhart said so in 2002; I say it in the book. We teach programming the same way. Concepts first, purpose later, often nothing useful at all. What hooks a programmer is control. Going from a thought to something that works, in a short loop. The tools that taught well had that loop. BASIC, Visual Basic, the spreadsheet, Scratch, Code Club. Taught badly, people went back to Excel. And programmed there anyway. Explorer coding starts at the right end. What you want, by voice, and seeing it work. Coding is communication. People will read more code, not less.
lockhart

One of the books I love is A Mathematician's Lament, by Paul Lockhart, an essay from 2002 and a book in 2009. I quote it in the book, in the chapter Connect the dots backwards. It opens with a musician who "wakes from a terrible nightmare", in which music is taught the way maths is. And it says, of maths: "if I had to design a mechanism for the express purpose of destroying a child's natural curiosity and love of pattern-making, I couldn't possibly do as good a job as is currently being done". For Lockhart, "mathematics is an art", and we teach it as if it were not. (The memo behind this article gave his name wrongly, as it did once before; it is Paul Lockhart.)
programming

I would say we do exactly the same thing with coding. Not every time, but usually, programming is taught upside down. You are introduced to functions, types and structures, capabilities that make no sense yet, before you have anything you want them for. Even at university, when my kids were doing more advanced work and using statistics software like SPSS, they were being introduced to concepts that, from a programming point of view, are important, but were not relevant at that moment. Of course people hate it. It does not make sense, because nothing has made it make sense yet. If we wanted to create a system to make children, and adults, dislike programming and not understand it, we could hardly come up with a better model than the way we usually teach it. That is Lockhart's point, moved from maths to code.
hook

The thing about programming is the ability to control something: to make something work. The hook you get as a developer is the moment you realise that, and it is very exciting, because you can go from a thought to its execution. I was lucky. By the time I was taught any of those concepts, I already knew how to program, on a ZX Spectrum, then on an Amiga, then on an x86. So for me the concepts were interesting, and I met each one because I needed it to solve a particular problem. I learned them by doing, which is the best way, with the feedback loop always there: the REPL, read, evaluate, print, loop. Type something, see what it does, change it. That loop is what makes it addictive, in a good way: you are solving puzzles all the time, little problems, and it is very rewarding, especially when you build tools you use yourself.
loop

The tools that got the loop right, from BASIC on the ZX Spectrum to explorer coding. The places where I have seen programming taught really well all had that short loop: Visual programming for children. Scratch, developed at the MIT Media Lab, is a "block-based visual programming language": you snap blocks together and watch something move. Version 1.0 came out in 2007. Code Club, in the UK. Volunteer-run, after-school coding clubs, planned from April 2012, which joined the Raspberry Pi Foundation in November 2015. I think they did an amazing job, and that is how it should be. Visual Basic. Introduced in 1991, and powerful for the same reason. In Wikipedia's words, "Forms are created using drag-and-drop techniques": you drew the interface, wired it up and ran it. One of the most powerful ways to create user interfaces in a visual and interactive way.
loop
The spreadsheet. Change a cell and see the result. It is programming, even if nobody calls it that.
excel

The irony: people taught programming with nothing to build go back to the spreadsheet and program there anyway. The other problem with teaching programming upside down is that people learn it and then do nothing useful with it, so they do not use it day to day. And guess what? They go back to Excel, where they program anyway. That is the irony. Microsoft's own researchers call Excel "the world's most widely used programming language", and in January 2021, with the LAMBDA function, "Excel has become Turing-complete." The book makes the same point from the other side, in Everyone who can brief an agent is a developer: the persistence of the spreadsheet is evidence that software failed the people using it, because it is the one tool where they control the shape of the thing. And the citizen developer is the spreadsheet grown up. People can program. They program wherever the loop is short and the result is theirs.
explorer

That is why explorer coding, what most people call vibe coding, is so powerful. It starts at the right end: what you want, and seeing it work. People are now coding with their voice, as in omnichannel programming, and the distance from a thought to a running thing is now very short. And here is what I find interesting. I know entrepreneurs who have been explorer coding for a while, and I think they are now ready to understand the concepts the classroom tried to teach first. In fact they are already being exposed to them: a variable, a procedure, a method, a class, a structure. They meet them in the code the agent writes, the way I met them on the Spectrum: because a problem needed them.
communication

Coding is communication: voice and briefs, visual blocks, code and its primitives, and the machine underneath. This is the trick we sometimes miss. Coding is communication: speaking to a computer, through an abstraction layer. Each programming language has its own sweet spot. So I think it is going to be ironic. People will end up reading a lot more code, not less, and reading more of those primitives, because code is still a very efficient way of communicating what a system does. It may become more visual. But the core primitives will still be there, and more people will understand them, because they arrived at them from something they wanted to do.
hope

The visual, conversational way in is still crude, but it is getting better, because the connection between what you do and what happens is now much more real. I hope it means a lot more people come into development and discovery, because it is amazing: solving puzzles, little problems, all the time, and building tools you use yourself. That is the experience the classroom so often took away, and the one the book wants every reader to have.
limits

Not every programming course is like this. Many teachers do it well; the pattern is common, not universal. The experiences are mine. Mine and my children's, not a study. Explorer coding is not a curriculum. It is a way in; the concepts still have to be learned. Lockhart wrote about maths. Applying his argument to programming is mine.
