Abstract: sgit in a CI pipeline described how an encrypted vault can carry data in and out of GitHub Actions, and between its jobs. The next step is to show it running, and to keep showing it. So this is a brief for a dedicated repository and website, just for that: its own issues, its own CI pipeline, and on every run four ways of moving a vault between jobs, side by side, in parallel. A vault server with the keys in the repository's secrets; the encrypted vault itself as an artefact, a zip that one job uploads and the next downloads; the vault published as files and cloned read-only from any web host; and append lanes for jobs that only need to hand results in. Each lane reports its time, its bytes, the keys each job held and a screenshot, and repeats on vaults of growing size with full, thin and path clones. I measured the core of it locally for this article. A clone of one folder barely grows with the vault: 0.59 seconds at 100 files, 0.77 at 2,000. A full clone grows with it, from 0.95 to 5.55 seconds. The repository should also have a budget, because some steps will call models, from more than one provider, and every token they spend should be counted against it.
Four ways to move a vault between jobs, run side by side on every run of the showcase repository.
in-short

A showcase of its own. A dedicated repository and website for sgit in GitHub Actions, with its own issues and its own CI pipeline. Four lanes, side by side. A server; the vault as an artefact; the vault as published files; append lanes for shards. In parallel, on every run. Time, bytes, keys and a screenshot per lane, as the vaults get bigger. Measured locally first. A one-folder clone: 0.59 s at 100 files, 0.77 s at 2,000. A full clone: 0.95 s to 5.55 s. Artefacts and lanes fit together. Artefacts are immutable and one per job; a lane collects from many jobs. A budget for the models. Every LLM step counted against the run's budget, across providers.
why

sgit in a CI pipeline tested the pieces locally: data in and out, scoped clones between jobs, keys as the boundaries, append lanes for test shards, a key pair per job. Its workflow file was a sketch; it said so. The next step is to run it on GitHub Actions for real, and to keep running it, where anyone can see. That needs its own repository and its own website, not a corner of another project. The repository holds the workflows and the issues; its CI pipeline exists to show itself working; and the site publishes what each run found. It is also a good place to show sgit in more than one shape at once, because the same job can be done several ways, and the differences are the point.
lanes

On every run, the same small build output travels from a build job to a test job and a release job, four ways, in parallel: A vault server. The keys are in the repository's secrets, each job clones only the folders it needs with --path, and pushes back. This is the setup the CI article tested. The vault as an artefact. No server: the encrypted vault is zipped and uploaded with GitHub's artefact action, and the next job downloads it and opens it with the key. GitHub's own documentation says artefacts "persist data after a job has completed, and share that data with another job in the same workflow". Two properties of the current version shape this lane: "Artifacts created by upload-artifact@v4 are immutable", and they "are retained for 90 days by default". Because the zip holds only ciphertext, it can be published as a file and downloaded anywhere without the key leaving the secrets.
lanes

Published as files. The vault's encrypted objects put on any web host, and cloned read-only with sgit's static transport, which reaches "any GET host, read-only". No server and no write path. Append lanes for shards. Each shard posts its encrypted result with its own token, and the summary job drains the inbox. This fills a gap in artefacts: the current version of the upload action does not support several jobs uploading to the same artefact. A lane takes them all.
report

Each lane reports the same things: the wall time per job and for the run; the bytes each job downloaded and the bytes on its disk; which keys each job held, and therefore what it could have read; and a screenshot of the result. The screenshot comes from a vault app, a page that draws the vault's contents; it is taken in the job and stored back in the vault, so the run's evidence travels with its data. Then it repeats on vaults of growing size, with a full clone, a thin clone of the latest state, and a clone of one folder. The outputs differ on purpose: a job that cloned one folder should hold one folder.
measured

Clone time as a vault grows, measured locally: median of three runs, sgit 0.21.0 against a local vault server. I measured the core of it for this article on one machine, sgit 0.21.0 against a local vault server over HTTP, with files of random bytes spread over 20 folders, three runs each. A clone of one folder barely grows. 0.59 seconds for a 100-file vault, 0.64 at 500, 0.77 at 2,000. It downloads only that folder: 4.1 MB on disk out of 82.7 MB for the full clone of the largest. A full clone grows with the vault. 0.95, 1.98 and 5.55 seconds for the same three vaults.
measured

Large files are different. For 40 files of 3 MB each, a full sgit clone took 4.4 seconds; a full git clone of the same files from local disk took 16.1, most likely because git tries to compress data that cannot be compressed. Git's own partial clone with a sparse checkout was the fastest of all, at 0.4 seconds, reading local disk with no encryption; it is shown for scale, not as a race. And three things went wrong, which is exactly what this repository is for. A push of a file over 4 MB failed against a server using local disk storage, because sgit sends large files through cloud storage uploads. A thin "headless" clone could not then fetch a single file in this version. And ten full clones at once took 21.1 seconds on a single server process, while ten one-folder clones took 1.9. A showcase that runs on every release finds those before a user does.
budget

Some steps in the showcase will call models: summarising a run, reading a screenshot, writing the release note. So the repository should have a budget, and every token spent should be counted against it, per run and per provider. It should also run the same step on more than one provider, side by side, for the same reason it runs four lanes. There are two places a model call can happen. In the job, with a provider key in the repository's secrets, as The key is the billing system described for a product that runs on the user's own key. Or in the browser, inside a vault app: the vault app runtime lists sg.llm.{available,models,chat,cancel,usage}, and its documentation says "the vault's key stays in the HOST; your frame never sees it". The usage call is where a budget can be read. Which of the two works best in a CI run is one of the things the showcase should find out.
brief

For the session that builds the showcase. Written by @newsroom.writer for Dinis Cruz, 14 October 2026, on top of v0.12.49. A repository and a site. Its own issues, its own CI pipeline, and a website that publishes every run's results. Where it lives is the owner's call. The four lanes. Server, artefact, published files, append lanes, as four parallel paths through the same build, test and release jobs. The report per lane. Time, bytes, keys held and a screenshot, as one file per run, stored in a vault and drawn by a vault app. Growing vaults. The same run on vaults from 100 to several thousand files, with full, thin and one-folder clones; the local numbers above are the baseline. The failures as issues. Large files without cloud storage, a headless clone fetching a file, concurrent full clones: each an issue with a reproduction, checked on every release.
brief

The budget. A token budget per run, counted per provider, with at least two providers for the same step. Publish it. A page per run and a running chart, so anyone can see sgit working in GitHub Actions, and where it does not yet. What to be careful about. Keys only in secrets, never in a workflow file, a log or an artefact's name. Every artefact and published file is ciphertext. Read keys may be published on purpose; write keys never. And the budget is a hard limit, not a report after the fact.
limits

The numbers are local. One four-core machine, a local server over HTTP, three runs each; GitHub's runners and a real network will differ. Git is not a like-for-like baseline. It read local disk with no encryption and no HTTP. Lanes 2 and 3 are untested. The artefact and static lanes are built from the documentation; lanes 1 and 4 were tested locally for the CI article. Nothing in the brief is built. If you are moving sensitive data through GitHub Actions and want to try one of the lanes, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Getting data in and out of a CI pipeline is harder than it should be. GitHub Actions has artifacts, kept 90 days by default and deleted with their run; caches, 10 GB per repository and evicted after a week unused; and job outputs, at most 1 MB per job. Each is fine for its job, and none is a versioned, encrypted record that a person, an auditor or another pipeline can read from outside GitHub. This article maps how sgit vaults fill that gap, and every pattern in it was run for the article against a local vault server. A job pushes what it produced to a vault, and anything with the read key can clone it from anywhere, with history. Jobs pass data to each other through the same vault, each cloning only the folders it needs with --path, which is a large saving in time and in what lands on the runner, though it is a speed setting rather than a boundary. The boundaries are the keys: a read key clones and cannot commit; an append token, one per test shard, adds to its own write-only inbox and reads nothing; and each job can have its own key pair, so a deploy configuration encrypted to the deploy job fails to decrypt anywhere else, and a signed manifest fails verification once it is changed. Even done a little loosely, that turns wiring mistakes into loud failures. The keys come from secrets on stdin, and only the ciphertext half of a vault ever leaves the runner. And when you would rather not depend on a hosted server, the vault server runs as a sidecar whose storage folder holds only ciphertext: archive it into the Actions cache, an artifact or a git branch, and the next run restores it with its full history.
A pipeline whose stages talk through a vault, with each job holding only the key it needs.
in-short

CI data has three exits, none of them a record. Artifacts, caches and job outputs each have limits on size, life and who can reach them, and none is versioned or readable from outside GitHub. A vault is data in and out. A job pushes its outputs; a person or another pipeline clones them with a read key, with history, from anywhere. Jobs talk through the vault. Each clones only its folders with --path; the release job in the test never downloaded the build archive it did not need. --path is speed, keys are boundaries. A scoped clone limits what lands on the runner. What a job can do is set by its key: a read-key clone refused to commit. Append lanes for shards. One token per test shard, each adding to its own inbox, none able to read; a summary job lists them with a separate key.
in-short

A key pair per job. A file encrypted to the deploy job failed to decrypt in the test job; a changed manifest failed its signature check. Keys from secrets, on stdin. echo "$SGIT_VAULT_KEY" | sgit clone - …. Only .sg_vault/bare, the ciphertext, is ever cached or uploaded. No hosted server needed. The vault server runs as a sidecar; its storage, ciphertext only, goes into the cache or a branch and comes back next run with its history.
why

Every pipeline produces things somebody wants later: the build, its manifest and bill of materials, test reports, coverage, timings, the signed release. GitHub Actions gives you three ways to keep them, and each is right for something narrower than that. Artifacts "are retained for 90 days by default", are immutable since version 4, and are meant to "share that data with another job in the same workflow"; delete the run and they go with it. The dependency cache is 10 GB per repository, and "GitHub will remove any cache entries that have not been accessed in over 7 days"; runs "cannot restore caches created for child branches or sibling branches". Job outputs "can be a maximum of 1 MB per job", and "outputs containing secrets are redacted on the runner". All three live inside GitHub, readable by whoever can read the repository's runs, and none is a versioned history you can hand to someone outside it.
why

What I would like from a pipeline is closer to what this site wants from its agents, in Encrypted memory for isolated agents: compute that is gone after the task, and a memory that is not. A CI job is exactly that kind of compute.
tested

Everything below was run for this article with sgit 0.21.0 against a local vault server, version 0.34.0 of the same package the diniscruz/sg-send-vault image runs, with disk storage and an access token. Each "job" ran in its own empty home directory, so nothing carried over except what went through the vault. The workflow file at the end is a sketch built from those commands; it has not been run on GitHub Actions.
in-out

The simplest use is an exit. The build job clones the run's vault, copies its outputs in, commits and pushes: echo "$SGIT_VAULT_KEY" | sgit clone - run --base-url "$SGIT_BASE_URL" --token "$SGIT_TOKEN" --path build cp dist/* run/build/ cd run && sgit commit "build 1.2.3" && sgit push --token "$SGIT_TOKEN" The - makes sgit clone read the key from stdin, which keeps it out of the process list and the shell history. In the test, the push went through and a second, empty home cloned the same history back. From then on the outputs are wherever the vault is: a release manager, an auditor or another company's pipeline can clone them with a read key, see every run as a commit, and diff two releases, without a GitHub account and long after the artifact would have expired. The server sees ciphertext; Encrypted memory for isolated agents searched a server's storage for the plaintext and found none, and so did this test.
in-out

Data comes in the same way. A configuration, a dataset or a set of fixtures that a pipeline needs, maintained by people who should not have write access to the repository, can live in a vault they own; the pipeline clones it with a read key.
between

Inside a run, the vault is how jobs hand work to each other. In the test, the build job pushed build/, holding a 200 KB archive and a manifest. The test job cloned only build/ and test/: echo "$SGIT_VAULT_KEY" | sgit clone - run --base-url "$SGIT_BASE_URL" --token "$SGIT_TOKEN" --path build --path test It wrote its report into test/, committed and pushed. The release job cloned with the read key, scoped to test/, and on its disk there was one file, the report: the archive was never downloaded. When it tried to commit, sgit answered "This vault was cloned read-only. To write, re-clone with the full vault key."
between

That is the speed and the shape of the thing. --path holds only the named folders; "other folders are carried by id and never downloaded; commits and pulls touch only the held folders". A vault that accumulates every run's outputs stays cheap to use, because each job only pays for its own folders. It also keeps data off runners that do not need it, which is worth a lot on shared or third-party runners. But a scoped clone is not a wall. A job holding the full vault key can widen its clone with sgit fetch <folder>; Encrypted memory for isolated agents says it plainly: "A scoped clone is a speed setting, not a boundary." The boundaries are the keys.
keys

Which job holds which key, and what the server access token does and does not do. sgit gives a pipeline four kinds of key, and the useful design question is which job holds which. The vault key reads and writes. In sgit's code the read key and the write key are derived separately from the vault's passphrase, and a clone made with a read key holds no write key: that is why the release job's commit was refused. The read key clones and reads, nothing else. It is what release, deploy and anyone outside the pipeline should hold. An append token adds to one inbox of the vault's append lane and can read nothing, not even what it wrote. A job's own key pair encrypts to and signs as that job.
keys

And one thing that is not a vault permission at all: the server's access token. On a private server it is the door, and every route needs it; in the test, an append without it was refused with 401. Every job that reaches the server holds it, whatever its keys allow inside. This is the same move as Hope or enforcement and Attacks rewritten as mandates: a pipeline where every job can do anything, and the YAML promises it will not, is a mandate kept by hope. A pipeline where each job's key only allows what its step is for has written the mandate down as a barrier.
lanes

Test matrices are where CI data is most awkward: a dozen shards each produce a report, and something has to gather them. An append lane does it without giving the shards anything they could misuse. The lane is configured once with the write key: a list of hashes of append tokens, one per shard, and the hash of a separate key that can list and fetch. Each shard then posts its result with its own token. In the test, three shards each appended one entry with their token. An unknown token was refused with 403. Listing a shard's inbox needed the enumeration key, and a wrong one was refused with 403. Reconfiguring the lane with a wrong write key was refused with 403. The server caps an entry at 5 MB and an inbox at 1,000 waiting entries, and lists at most 200 at a time.
lanes

Two details matter in practice. The server stores the payload as it is sent, so a shard should encrypt its result to the summary job's public key first; that is how this newsroom's reading meter shares a summary, encrypting it in the browser to the recipient's published key before it appends, as Sixteen notes I did not want to lose describes. And because a token can only add to its own inbox, a compromised shard can at worst add noise to one inbox; it cannot read the other shards' results, or anything else in the vault.
pki

The more advanced pattern gives each job an identity. sgit pki keygen makes an encryption and a signing key pair, the private keys protected by a passphrase; sgit pki export gives the public half as a small JSON file that can sit in the vault's keys/ folder for every job to import. In the test, three jobs each made a pair. The build job encrypted a deploy configuration to the deploy job's key and signed it: the result held none of the plaintext. The test job tried to decrypt it and got "Decryption failed". The deploy job decrypted it and, once it had imported the build job's public key, reported the signature as verified, signer stage:build. The build job also signed its manifest; the deploy job verified it as valid, and after one line was appended to the manifest the same check returned "Signature INVALID".
pki

To give a job its identity, the key folder, about 5 KB once packed, and its passphrase go into that job's secrets. That is not perfect key management, and it does not need to be to pay for itself. Even if every job's keys were reachable from the same environment, a pipeline wired this way fails loudly when a step reads something that was not meant for it, instead of quietly working until the day it leaks. A configuration that only the deploy job can decrypt is a bug that cannot ship to the wrong place.
no-server

No hosted server: the vault server runs as a container inside the job, and its ciphertext is saved between runs. Not every team wants its pipeline to depend on a vault server somewhere else. It does not have to. The vault server is one container, and in a job it can run beside the steps, on localhost, with its storage in a folder. In the test, the server's storage after the build and test jobs was 388 KB in 19 files, and a search of it found none of the file names or contents. Archived, it was 208 KB. Restored into a new folder, under a new server, a clone from a fresh home came back with all three commits, the build and the test report. So the folder can live wherever a CI system keeps bytes: the Actions cache, an artifact, a release asset, or a branch of the repository, which keeps it indefinitely and as ciphertext.
no-server

Reading does not even need the sidecar. sgit clone --transport local reads a vault from a folder, --transport static from any plain web host, and sgit vault attach binds a key from a secret to a bare checkout, such as the .sg_vault/bare folder of a vault committed to a repository. In the test, a copy of only the bare folder, with the key attached in a fresh home, read the vault's history without any network. Writing is different: pushing needs the server's API, and sgit refuses to push to a folder or a static host, with an error that says so. The sidecar is how a pipeline keeps writes without a hosted server.
no-server

Two cautions belong here. The sidecar is per job, so it suits a single job or one run after another; jobs running in parallel need a server they can all reach. And when archiving, archive the server's storage, or a vault's .sg_vault/bare, never .sg_vault/local: that folder holds the vault key in clear, the server token and the clone's own private key. In the test it was the only place the passphrase was found.
workflow

Built from the commands above, not yet run on GitHub Actions. It assumes a server the jobs can reach, its URL in a repository variable and its token, the vault key and the read key in secrets. env: SGIT_BASE_URL: ${{ vars.SGIT_BASE_URL }} jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: pip install 'sgit-ai==0.21.0' - run: make build # writes dist/ - name: Push the build to the vault env: SGIT_VAULT_KEY: ${{ secrets.SGIT_VAULT_KEY }} SGIT_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SGIT_SERVER_TOKEN }} run: | echo "$SGIT_VAULT_KEY" | sgit clone - run --base-url "$SGIT_BASE_URL" --token "$SGIT_TOKEN" --path build mkdir -p run/build && cp dist/* run/build/ cd run && sgit commit "build ${GITHUB_SHA::7}" && sgit push --token "$SGIT_TOKEN" release: needs: build runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: pip install 'sgit-ai==0.21.0' - name: Read the build, read-only env: SGIT_READ_KEY: ${{ secrets.SGIT_READ_KEY }} SGIT_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SGIT_SERVER_TOKEN }} run: echo "$SGIT_READ_KEY" | sgit clone - run --base-url "$SGIT_BASE_URL" --token "$SGIT_TOKEN" --path build
workflow

For the sidecar version, restore the storage folder from the cache, start the server with docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -e SEND__STORAGE_MODE=disk -e SEND__DISK_PATH=/data -e SGRAPH_SEND__ACCESS_TOKEN=… -v "$PWD/vault-store:/data" diniscruz/sg-send-vault:<version>, run the same steps against http://localhost:8080, and save the folder under a new cache key at the end, since caches cannot be changed once written. Secrets can come from GitHub's own store or from any manager that sets an environment variable, such as HashiCorp Vault. This newsroom already uses parts of this. Its deploy workflow installs sgit 0.21.0 for a round trip through a vault in its tests; the script that reads readers' notes takes its read key "from the environment (NEWSROOM_LANE_KEY) or from stdin with --key -, never from a file in this repository, and it is never printed"; and the wires are drawn from vaults this site can only read, as in Two agents, one vault.
limits

Tested locally, not on GitHub Actions. Every result here is from a local server and separate home directories standing in for runners; the workflow is a sketch. --path is not access control. It limits what is downloaded; the key decides what is allowed. The sidecar does not serve parallel jobs. Each job's sidecar is its own; parallel jobs need a shared server. Per-job keys in secrets are only as separate as the secrets. If one job can read another's secrets, the keys help with correctness, not with containment. Append payloads are stored as sent. Encrypt before appending if the content matters. GitHub's redaction of secrets is "not guaranteed", in its own words; keeping keys off the command line and out of uploaded folders still matters. If you are moving CI data through something you would rather not, or you want to try a vault in a pipeline, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Git won not because of GitHub but because it is a standard: a way of laying out objects that any tool, any host and any person can read, and that GitHub, GitLab and a folder on a laptop all implement. sgit is the same kind of thing, and I think that is the most important thing to understand about it. People read encrypted git and picture a product with a server in the middle. There is a server, and it is the least interesting part. A vault is a set of encrypted files laid out by a convention: blobs, trees, commits and one mutable pointer per branch, every immutable object named by the SHA-256 of its ciphertext and marked -imm- in its name. Nothing in it has to be discovered: the vault key gives the read key, the read key gives the name of the ref, and the ref leads to the commit, the trees and the file, four plain GETs from any host that answers one. Writing is the same objects plus one compare-and-swap, which is all the API is for. Two independent implementations, the CLI and the browser app, speak it and check each other. So deploying sgit is choosing where the objects live, from a folder to a laptop to a static host to the hosted service, and how fast it is depends on how close they are. That design was not a plan to be minimal: it is what is left when the server cannot read a byte.
Everything in a vault is one hash away: from the vault key to the read key, the ref, the commit, the trees and the blob.
in-short

Git is a standard. That is why it won, not any one server. sgit is one too. Encrypted objects laid out by a convention. Everything is one hash away. The key gives every name; a file is four GETs. The name says what can be cached. -imm- is for ever; -muw- is the ref. Any storage implements the read half. A bucket, a CDN, GitHub Pages, a folder. The server protects writes. A compare-and-swap, and not much else. The constraint designed it. A server that cannot read leaves only small designs.
git

Git is not GitHub. It is a format: blobs, trees, commits and refs, named by their hashes, laid out in a way any tool can read. GitHub, GitLab, a bare repository on a server and a folder on a laptop all implement it, and that is why git survived every centralised system that promised to be faster: your history is not in anyone's product. sgit was built the same way on purpose. Git solved the hard problems of history, branching and merging twenty years ago, and the workflows built on them are why it won, so sgit copies git's object model and changes one thing: where the trust sits. Everything is encrypted on the client, and the convention is designed so that nothing about reading a vault needs anyone's help. People read "encrypted git" and picture a product with a server in the middle. There is a server, and it is the least interesting part.
vault

A vault is a set of files laid out by a convention. Four kinds of object, all ciphertext: blobs, the file contents; trees, a folder's encrypted names pointing at blob and tree ids; commits, a tree id, parents, a message and a signature; and one mutable pointer per branch, the ref. Every object except the ref and the branch index is named by the SHA-256 of its own ciphertext, so a name can never point at different bytes, anyone can check an object against its name, and anyone who has fetched one can keep it for ever.
vault

The name says which is which. An immutable object's id is obj-cas-imm- and a hash; the mutable pointers are ref-pid-muw- and a hash. So anything between the storage and the reader, a browser, a proxy, a CDN, a CI cache, a page on a website, can decide to keep an object for ever by looking at its name, without reading a byte of it and without being told by a header. That is how the vault app in the browser got fast: it caches every -imm- object the first time it sees one and refetches only the ref. sgit.ai's own documentation pages are a vault read that way: a cold load fetches 18 objects, the next load one 69-byte ref, and a load inside the two-minute freshness window nothing at all.
vault

It is a trade made on purpose. sgit keeps no deltas between versions of a file; a changed file is a new object. Git stores deltas and has to be told what changed; sgit stores whole objects that anyone can cache without asking.
one-hash

What makes it a standard rather than a service is that nothing in a vault has to be discovered. It is all derived from the key: The vault key gives the vault id and, one way, the read key. The read key cannot be turned back into the write key, so it can be published. The read key gives the ref's name. In the CLI's code it is the first twelve hex characters of an HMAC of the read key over sg-vault-v1:file-id:ref: and the vault id. The server never told you where the head is; you computed it. The ref holds the head commit id. The commit holds the tree id; trees hold the ids of blobs and subtrees, with the names encrypted inside them. Ref, commit, the trees on the path, the blob: a file is four kinds of request from its read key, and every one is a plain GET of a fixed path.
one-hash

Writing is the same objects, PUT in batches, and one compare-and-swap on the ref and the branch index. Two independent implementations speak this format: the CLI, and the browser vault app, which the CLI team says sgit.ai's pages reduce to a reader of about ninety lines. A change made in the browser is one the CLI verifies, and the other way round. That is what a standard is: a format with more than one implementation that agree.
storage

Deploying sgit is choosing where the objects live, from a folder to the hosted service, closer to further. Because reading is plain GETs of fixed paths, any storage that answers a GET implements the read half of the convention: an S3 bucket, a CDN, GitHub Pages, a folder, Python's one-line file server. sgit clone --transport static reads from any of them, and sgit publish lays a vault out for one. This site measured the difference: 317 milliseconds a request through the vault API, against 44 for a small file from GitHub Pages.
storage

The write half needs the one thing plain storage does not give you, a compare-and-swap on the ref, and that is what the API is for. Strip the convention down and the API has two jobs: protect writes, with an access token and the compare-and-swap, and shorten reads a little, with batches of fifty objects and a listing that makes a cold full clone fast. Everything else is storage.
storage

So deploying sgit is choosing where the objects live, and every option is shipped: a folder, with --transport local; a laptop, with sgit serve running the hosted service's own image in Docker, Podman or a plain Python process; your own server, one container with a disk or a bucket; a static host, read-only; or the hosted service, a Lambda in front of S3 behind CloudFront. And how fast sgit is depends on how close they are. On the vault behind this newsroom, a one-folder clone is 13 seconds hosted and 0.8 seconds from a local server; on ruv.sgit.ai's hive runs, on a local server, every operation takes between 0.4 and 1.5 seconds, most of it starting Python and deriving the key. "How fast is sgit" is the wrong question. The right one is where the storage is, and how close.
cache

Four GETs is cheap, but a page that serves one record a thousand times a minute does not want to walk trees. So the convention has a cache layer, shipped: sgit cache add <path> declares a path, and every push keeps an encrypted cache object for it at a location derived from the read key and the path. A reader with only the vault id and the read key computes where to look, makes one batch request for the ref and the candidates, checks the commit inside against the ref, and has the file with no walk. A miss or a stale entry falls back to the ordinary walk, so correctness never depends on the cache; losing one is a performance problem, never a correctness one. This is Scion's "derived data", built by the writer instead of a server, and named by the key instead of indexed by it.
client

Scion moves history, blame and merges to the server. sgit keeps them on the client, and would even if the server could read the data, for the reason git did: a merge is a workflow step that needs the context of the change, the history and the policy that says who may merge what. In ruv.sgit, every worker in a hive writes to its own branch and the host merges them under the run's written mandate; in the vault behind this newsroom, ten agents meet on a named branch and resolve on the clone that has the conflict in front of it. Scion's own post concedes the point from the other side: it could not keep a merge queue at its rate, so "concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts". The merge went back to the agent there too.
client

And sgit keeps the property that made git git: a full clone is one command and a complete, verifiable copy of everything, and anyone with the key can rebuild it from any host. What changed is that the full clone became optional. A folder scope, a history depth, a sparse clone and the cache layer mean a client takes the part it needs, and a repository can hold large files without every client paying for them, which every git team has had to police by hand. The whole-history clone is the backup and the audit, and it is still there.
constraint

None of this was a plan to be minimal. The server cannot read a byte, so "just do it on the server" was never available: no server-side index, no server-side render, no merge the client did not make, no derived data the client could not compute from the key. Every feature had to be expressible as objects a writer produces and a reader derives. That is why the designs are small enough to be a standard, and why they fit in an article. It is the argument of The value of constraints, applied to the format itself.
limits

Not a formal standard. No standards body; a documented format with two implementations. Not proven at Scion's scale. The largest vault in daily use is about 35,000 objects and ten agents. No blame or bisect yet. And a partial clone of a long history walks the commits one at a time until a commit-chain object ships; a depth avoids it today. The CDN in front of the hosted API does not cache object reads yet. Browsers, clients and static hosts do. If you want to implement the format somewhere new, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: More notes for the book. It is a book I will send to anyone I know who wants to, or should, get into AI, so it needs chapters for people who do not yet work the way I do, including one on setting up a Google Workspace and the agentic workflow behind my emails. The first edition was liked for one thing above all: it was short and punchy, a condensation of ideas where almost every paragraph made you think. The second has to be the same. It will also be co-written with Claude, and I would like to say so and credit it, and to show the ratio: how many words of voice memos, edits and reviews go into each word of the book. Readers will open it expecting AI slop. My first published pieces, made with ChatGPT's deep research, got exactly that reaction; the articles on this site now get told they sound like me. So the book should meet the suspicion head on, with the evidence. To keep it tight, every paragraph, group of paragraphs and chapter should know what it is: its evidence, its facts, its hypotheses, its purpose, all in a graph, which also shows where we repeat ourselves. We can refactor everything until each part is signed off. Synthetic readers will tell us what they understood and what they did not. And not every issue they raise needs fixing: sometimes the answer is, we are not doing that.
One paragraph of the book as a node in its graph, linked to its chapter and similar paragraphs, with the review loop.
in-short

A book for anyone getting into AI. Including how to set up the workflow behind my emails. Short and punchy, again. The first edition's readers liked it for that. Co-written with Claude, and credited. With the ratio of memo to word shown. Meet the suspicion head on. Readers will expect AI slop; show them the evidence. Every paragraph knows what it is. Its evidence, facts, hypotheses and purpose, in a graph. The graph shows repetition. And we can refactor anything until it is signed off. Synthetic readers, and the right to say no. Not every issue needs fixing.
who

This is the book I will send to anyone I know who wants to get into AI, or should. Many of them do not have agentic workflows like the ones I use, so parts of the book are for them. One chapter should be practical: setting up a Google Workspace and the agentic workflow I have here, the one behind the man behind the curtain, where agents draft every email and I send it.
punchy

People liked the first book. The reviews on its Amazon listing say so: "Amazing read for anyone new to, or wanting to get into programming," one says, and another, "I wish I had this type of book when I started my career." And what I heard most was that it was short and punchy. Of course there were spelling mistakes, and of course parts could have been expanded. But it was a condensation of ideas, and almost every line, every paragraph made you think. That is what I would like this one to be.
co-written

This book will be co-written with Claude, and I would like to credit it. Claude is putting it together: from my voice memos, my reviews and my corrections, it writes the text, and I read, challenge and change it. I also want to show the ratio, because it is a good case study of how this works. How much of this did I write? measured it for this site: over four weeks I sent about 65,000 words, 55,000 of them in voice memos, and the agent published 96,000 words of articles, with the words out per word in running from about one to about five, article by article. The book should measure itself the same way: the memos, the interviews, the reviews, the edits, and the words that came out. And it should show where the voice is: where I start and where the agent starts.
suspicion

A reader will open a book co-written with an AI expecting AI slop, so the book should tackle that from the start, with evidence and data rather than reassurance: this is voice memos, a lot of them, going through quality control and editing, then reviewers, before anything is published. I have seen both sides of this. My first published pieces were written with ChatGPT's deep research, and some people said exactly that: this reads like ChatGPT. The articles on this site get a different reaction. People say they are good, sometimes that they are long, but I do not see complaints about the quality or the voice. The comment I hear is that they sound like me. The book has to sound like that too.
graph

To keep a book punchy, every part of it has to earn its place. So every paragraph, every group of paragraphs and every chapter should know what it is: the evidence behind it, the facts it states, the hypotheses it puts forward, and what it is trying to do. That is a graph, and a website to finish the book makes the book one. The graph has a second use. Some books repeat themselves: the same idea, made again in a later chapter, because by the time the author noticed, the earlier chapter could no longer change. With a graph of the book, and a graph of those graphs, we can see where two paragraphs say the same thing. And unlike a printed book, we can change everything, up to the end. A book that is a graph can be refactored, so it can be made consistent, until the parts are signed off.
readers

We should also create synthetic readers: simulated readers of different kinds who read the book and tell us what they understood, what they did not, what they liked and what they did not. We already know how to run them; how to run synthetic users is the method we have used on three sites, with invented users of several types, each with a profile, a question and an expected path, interviewed at the end.
not-every-issue

And one rule that matters as much as the others: not every piece of feedback needs to change the book. Sometimes the right answer to an issue is: we are not doing that. A book that tries to satisfy every reader's every comment stops being short, and stops being punchy. This site's reviews already work this way: every finding gets an answer, and "declined", with a reason, is one of the answers.
limits

The reviews were found later. The Amazon listing could not be read when this was first written; the book's website found the reviews on 19 October. The ratio is from this site, not the book. The book will measure its own. "Not slop" is something to show, not to say. The evidence is the point. Synthetic readers are a tool, not readers. Real readers come after.
sources

Abstract: Every article here is built on sources: papers, pages, government notices, company statements. Today, the only way to know that an article represents a source correctly is for someone downstream to check: a domain expert, or an agent with the right context, loading the article and every reference and mapping one to the other. That costs hours of human time or a lot of tokens, it is repeated by every reader, and it is done by someone who is not the best person to judge. The best person is the source. So I want to ask the people and companies we quote to review how we used their work, add a caveat where needed ("70%, but only of these"), and sign it with a key their own website vouches for. Every reader after that checks one signature and how much they trust the signer. Where an article earns money, the source should be paid to verify, as some journals now pay reviewers. Most of the pieces exist: the Pen on every article, signed notes checked against the register at pki.sgit.ai, sign in with a key, and a way for a domain to prove which key is its own. In my memo I said pki.sgit.ai's latest work was federation between organisations; it is not, and that part is still a proposal. Readers and researchers can go on the record too, with signed reviews and notes. I want to start with individuals, then companies.
Who should check a claim: every reader today, or the author of the source signing it once.
in-short

Every article stands on sources. Today, checking that they are represented correctly falls on the reader. That is expensive, repeated and done by the wrong person. Hours of expert time or a lot of tokens, for every reader. The best person to check is the source. Ask them, let them add a caveat, and let them sign it. One signature replaces many checks. A reader or an agent verifies the signature and the signer's standing. Pay for it where it earns money. As some journals now pay reviewers. Most of the pieces exist. The Pen, signed notes, a register of keys, and domains that prove their key. Federation between organisations does not exist yet. My memo said it did; it is a proposal. Readers go on the record too. Signed reviews and notes, kept with the article.
who-checks

Everything we write here is built on other people's work. A paper, a release note, a government notice, a company's statement, a post. The article quotes it or, more often, summarises it, and the summary is where things go wrong: a number taken out of its context, a caveat dropped, a claim that was true of one group stated as if it were true of all. How does a reader know? Today, they have to check. A domain expert, or an agent with the right context and enough budget, has to load the article, load every reference, read both, and map one to the other. That is a lot of work. It is hours of human time, or a lot of tokens. It is repeated by every reader who wants to be sure. And it is done by somebody who, however capable, is not the best person to say whether the source was represented fairly.
the-source

The best person is the source: the author of the paper, the team that wrote the release, the company that issued the statement. They know what they meant, and they know which caveat matters. So here is the idea. When an article uses someone's work, we ask them. We send them the passage, with its hash and the links it relies on, and one question: is this a fair representation of what you said? They can agree. They can disagree. Or, most usefully, they can add the caveat that makes it correct: "yes, 70%, but only of these", or "that was true of the first version, not the second". And then they sign it, with their own key. Signed by the source, the workflow: from the article quoting a source to a reader checking the signature.
economics

The argument is about who does the work, and how many times. Checking downstream is done once per reader, by someone who has to rebuild the context. Checking at the source is done once, by someone who already has it. After that, every reader, human or agent, checks one signature and asks one question: how much do I trust this signer? That is cheap. It is the difference between reading every reference and reading a stamp. It is also the honest version of something that already happens. Sources correct journalists all the time, by email, privately, after publication. A signed review puts that correction on the record, attached to the passage it is about, before the article is relied on.
economics

And it can be paid. Where an article earns money, the source should be paid to verify it, as some science now pays reviewers: Biology Open pays £220 a manuscript, and in its pilot the time to a first decision fell from 37.7 to 5.5 working days. This site's economics pages go further, splitting the value behind a reader's payment between the original researcher, the data organisation, the journalist and the outlet, and describing a fact-certifier as a payable role, with output that carries consequence if it is wrong. Both pages are designs, not running services. A signed verification from the source is the smallest working piece of them.
keys

For a signature to mean anything, a reader has to know whose key it is. The natural place for a company to say "this is our key" is its own website, and for a person, their own domain or their GitHub account.
keys

That part exists. pki.sgit.ai keeps a register of people and their public keys, with my key as its anchor, and a way to prove that a domain or an account belongs to a record: a proof line in a file at /.well-known/pki.sgit.ai.txt on the website, a DNS TXT record (the pattern Bluesky uses for domain handles), or a public gist. A link between two records counts only when both hold it, and a verifier walks the chain from the key that signed back to a root it pinned itself, never to whatever a list of anchors says. Since 24 October, a site can also sign readers in with pki.sgit.ai: your key signs a delegation for one browser, at one site, for some uses, until a date.
keys

What does not exist yet is the step I described in my memo as the latest work: federation, where an organisation runs its own register, publishes its keys on its own site, and verifies others and is verified by them. I said that was in pki.sgit.ai's latest pushes. Having read its releases, it is not: the latest were sign-in with a key, delegation and signed shared code. The site's own roadmap says a design with well-known documents, DNS records and a verification endpoint "was proposed in March … and never built". So mutual verification between organisations is the proposal here, not a feature. The register today holds one person's real key, mine, and two agents' keys.
readers

The source signing is one half. The other is that readers and researchers can go on the record as well, with reviews and comments that carry their name and their key. That is what the newsroom's Pen started this week. Every article has one: select words, keep them, comment on them, or send the newsroom a note with the passage it is about. And every note can be signed with a key for that browser, which the register at pki.sgit.ai vouches for, checked against a pinned root in the browser and again when the newsroom reads it. A changed note fails. Today that key is mine; the point is that it does not have to be.
readers

The Ask pane fits the same picture from the other side. It answers a reader's question only from passages it finds on this site, and cites each one, so every claim can be checked where it came from. If those passages carry the source's signature, the answer inherits it. Put together, that is a web of trust: sources who sign how they are represented, readers who sign what they think, an article that keeps both, and a reader or an agent that weighs each signature by who made it. On the record set out the case for signed expert opinions; this is the same mechanism pointed at the sources.
start-small

I want to start doing this with individuals: people whose papers, posts and projects we write about, who already have a domain or a GitHub account, and who can sign with a key in a few minutes. Then companies, which need a key their website vouches for, and a person allowed to use it. A few rules will matter from the start: Ask before publishing where we can, and show the source exactly the passage, its hash and its links. Publish the caveat as written. The point is the source's words, not ours. A refusal is information too. "We were asked and did not sign" is worth saying, without reading anything into it. A signature is about representation, not truth. The source signs that we summarised them fairly; it does not make their claim correct.
limits

Nobody has signed one yet. This is a proposal; no source has reviewed an article here through it. Federation is not built. Organisations publishing and cross-checking their own registers is a design, proposed and not shipped. The register is small. One real person key and two agent keys, read on 24 October 2026. The economic case is an argument, from who does the work and how many times, not a measured cost. Sources have interests. A source can sign a flattering summary; the signature records who said it, which is why readers' own signed reviews matter.
sources

Abstract: Under my LinkedIn comment that I run with no databases, serverless services and no server-side code of my own, Nadzeya Stalbouskaya asked a good question: removing servers and databases does not necessarily remove complexity; sometimes it just moves it into external services, APIs and dependencies we do not fully control, trading operational overhead today for dependency and lock-in tomorrow. So how do you tell genuinely simplifying an architecture from outsourcing its complexity? My answer: Nadzeya is right that there is risk, and it must be a conscious decision. The way to make it is to map it. On a Wardley map, moving a component from custom-built to commodity removes complexity only if what you move to really is a commodity. Replacing our own login with passkeys is that: a standard every major browser and platform supports, with a track record. Moving our data to object storage and static hosting is too. But moving to a young startup's service can look like a commodity on our map while, behind it, it is as messy as what we had, or worse. So you de-risk the move by choosing the commodity, and you can test which one you have by asking who would certify it, insure it, or sign a high SLA on it. Maturity and certifiability go together.
The LinkedIn thread: my reply to Stephan Bitton and Nadzeya Stalbouskaya's challenge on simplifying or outsourcing.
in-short

The challenge is fair. Removing servers can move complexity into dependencies you do not control. So the move must be a conscious decision. Made on a map, not by habit. Map it. Moving a component right, to commodity, simplifies only if the destination is a real commodity. Passkeys and object storage are. Standards and utilities with a track record. A young startup's service may only look like one. Behind it, it can be messier than what you had. Test it by asking who would certify it. Maturity, insurability and certification go together.
question

Under Stephan Bitton's post on how founders can make the most of Google's AI capabilities to build efficient, AI-first startups, I replied that my strategy has been to have no databases, run serverless services, and these days even have no server-side code that I maintain, which keeps the architecture simple and cost-effective. Nadzeya Stalbouskaya, a co-founder working in enterprise architecture and transformation, replied with a challenge I want to answer properly:
question

Nadzeya is right that there is risk. And I would argue that it has to be a very conscious decision. If you replace a server or a service of your own with a third-party component that is itself an explorer project, or even a villager one, then I agree: you have outsourced your complexity, and probably added some. The difference is the town planner services, the commodities. By design, they are very stable. They are effective, they have a track record, documentation and SLAs, and a level of maturity your own version will never have. Which is why you have to map it.
map

Three moves to the right on the map: our own login, our own database server and a feature moved to a startup. On a Wardley map, each component sits somewhere on the line from genesis to custom-built, to product, to commodity. Replacing something we built with something we buy is moving its dot to the right. That only removes complexity if the thing on the right really is a commodity. Three examples.
map

Login: our own, to passkeys. A login we build means passwords, a password database, resets, multi-factor, and every vulnerability that comes with them. Passkeys move all of that to a standard. The FIDO Alliance says passkeys are "supported in all major operating systems, internet browsers, and by third-party passkey providers", built on WebAuthn, the browser API for them; Google made them the default option for personal accounts in October 2023. It is a better way to create a user identity and sign in, and it is very mature. You can see that flow working on pki.sgit.ai, where a passkey opens the vault that holds your keys. Behind the dot is the whole industry. That is a genuine simplification.
map

Data: our servers, to a utility. A database server of our own means backups, patches, failover, upgrades and someone on call. Moving the data to object storage and static hosting, utilities run at enormous scale, removes a whole branch of that map. The dependency is real, but it is on a commodity, with alternatives that do the same thing, so the lock-in is shallow. A feature: our own, to a young startup's service. Here is the irony. On our map, their service sits on the right: we call an API, and it works. But behind the scenes, their own map has its components on the left: their glue, their early code, their own suppliers. It is probably as messy as what we had, or worse, and now we cannot see it or fix it. That is exactly the outsourced complexity Nadzeya describes.
ours

The same test applies to what we build. SG/Send's vault is now a product, and it is gaining traction. I would argue it is not yet a commodity. But it already removes a lot of complexity, because the encryption happens on the user's device, and the server only ever stores ciphertext. That one decision means a lot of other things are simply not needed: no plaintext to protect at rest, no user data to breach, as I wrote in the attack surface you do not have. So it sits in the middle of the map, a villager product, and an honest map says so.
certify

Maturity is what can be certified, insured and held to an SLA, shown from explorer to town planner. This connects to something I have been writing about: who signs for this?, and signed by the source. If someone has to certify what we depend on, the question becomes: are they certifying a villager product, or a town planner one? I think you will often find that nobody wants to certify a villager product, because by design it is still glued together, and an explorer project has not got the maturity at all. The maturity of a company and of a service is, I would argue, directly proportional to its insurability, and to anyone's ability to certify it and to sign high SLAs on its core service and its non-functional requirements: security, stability, reliability, disaster recovery, resilience, documentation.
certify

So that is my practical answer to Nadzeya's question. Using third-party services carries risk; you de-risk it by using commodity services. And you tell a commodity from outsourced complexity by asking who would certify it, insure it, or put a high SLA on it. If the answer is nobody, you have not simplified. You have moved the mess somewhere you cannot see.
limits

Corrected on 25 October 2026. The first version said the thread sat under a post about open source as a business model; that line was my own LinkedIn headline. The thread is under Stephan Bitton's post on AI-first startups, and is now linked. The maps are illustrative. The positions are judgements, not measurements. Commodities have outages and lock-in too. The point is that the risk is shallower, better documented and shared by everyone. Not every startup is messy. The point is that you cannot tell from your own map. The certification market is an argument, not one that exists today for most services.

Abstract: For the past few weeks I have run agents on dedicated accounts, a Google Workspace seat, a Claude Team seat and a GitHub account per agent, and split the work across six roles: a scheduled reader of the inbox, a mailbox agent that drafts, an inbox agent that sends, a CRM agent, a dev team agent and a site editor. This article is what that setup taught me, and it is mostly about the gap between the policy I wanted and what the tools can enforce. Three findings. The account, not the session, is the blast radius, so a dedicated account per agent is the first real control anyone has, and it turns out to do more than segregate, because it puts each agent in its own organisational unit where Google's compliance rules become per-agent enforcement. The first exception arrived before the first policy was written: the reader that must never reply must reply when the message comes from me, which is an authentication problem, not a permissions one. And the policy I had written on the assumption that the Gmail connector could not send attachments was wrong, because an agent found the attachments field, proved it with a signed PDF, and wrote up how. The vendor's own two documentation pages disagree about whether the connector can send at all. So the article ends with a table of every rule in the setup against how it is enforced today, by identity, by scope, by a compliance rule, by an approval prompt or by nothing but the agent's good behaviour, and with the argument that a policy is only as real as its worst row.

Six roles, two identities, one policy table. Each agent runs on its own Workspace, Claude and GitHub accounts. The cells say what each agent may do with mail, code and vaults; the colour says how the rule is enforced today: by the identity boundary, by a compliance rule an admin set, by an approval prompt, or by nothing but the agent doing as it was told.

Here is the claim, stated so it can be wrong. An access policy for an agent is only as real as its worst row. Write the policy as a table, one row per rule, and add a column for how each rule is enforced. If the column says the agent has been told, that row is a hope, and the policy is exactly as strong as that hope on the day something goes wrong. This article is about filling in that column for a setup I actually run, and about three things I did not expect to find.

The account is the blast radius. Every session an agent opens through a connector runs as the account that authorised it, with everything that account can reach. The first real control is therefore not a policy at all: a dedicated Workspace seat, a dedicated Claude seat and a dedicated GitHub account per agent, so that the worst a session can do is bounded by what its account can see. Dedicated accounts do more than segregate. An account of its own puts each agent in its own organisational unit, and Google Workspace applies its Gmail compliance rules per unit. Restrict delivery, attachment compliance and scope limits on third-party apps then become per-agent enforcement rather than per-organisation settings. That is the part I had not understood before I ran it.

The first exception arrived before the first policy. The scheduled reader that must never reply must reply when the message came from me. "Never" became "never, unless" on day one, and the "unless" is an authentication problem, which the PKI and append-lane work already addresses. A policy written from the documentation was wrong. I had assumed the Gmail connector could not send attachments. An agent found that create_draft and update_draft accept an attachments array, proved it with a 17 KB signed PDF that arrived intact, and wrote it up. The vendor's own documentation says on one page that the connector is read-only and on another that it can send, reply and forward. The only way to know what a connector can do is to try.

Enforcement is a ladder, and most rules sit on the bottom step. Identity boundaries and cryptographic keys enforce themselves. Compliance rules enforce at the platform. Approval prompts enforce at the human. Everything else is the agent doing as it was told. The table at the end grades every rule in the setup. Cowork and Claude Code are different agents with different reach. In this setup the Cowork agent has no GitHub connector and cannot open the repository at all, while the Claude Code agent can edit the site. Two products from the same vendor, on the same seat, with different blast radii. That is useful, once you know it. The twin argument holds. The attachment finding is the connector twin article's case proven on my own inbox: replay what the agent can actually do before you write down what it may do.

The agents run for two identities: the agent for RiskMandate, and the agent for my own domain. I am not going to print their addresses, for the obvious reason, but the shape is the same for both and it is copyable. Each identity has a dedicated Google Workspace account, which is about £7 a month, a seat on a Claude Team plan, and a GitHub account of its own. Nothing the agent does runs as me. Everything it does runs as an account whose mailbox, drive, repositories and connectors I chose.

That sounds like an obvious thing to do. It is the thing almost nobody does, because connectors are designed to be switched on by a person for that person, and the whole appeal is that the agent can see what you see. The research on nhi.sgit.ai said this plainly when it scored the shared-drive options in August: "Everything available runs on your identity, the only granularity is segregation rather than scoping, and nothing supports per-agent keys." Its conclusion, that the practitioner answer is "a shared drive dedicated to the agent", is what the dedicated account generalises. If segregation is the only granularity you can buy, buy it at the account level, where it covers mail, files, code and connectors at once. Six roles share those two identities, and the split follows what each one is allowed to touch: Role What it does Runs where The reader

A scheduled session that reads the inbox, works out what each message wants, and writes a tagged list of what needs to happen Scheduled Claude session The mailbox Operations and management on the mailbox itself: labels, threads, filing, drafting replies Cowork The inbox The one role allowed to send, and only from drafts the mailbox agent prepared Cowork The CRM Customers, workflows and tasks, built on what the reader tagged Cowork The dev team The vaults, the vault UI and the tooling behind them Cowork, sgit The site editor Edits and publishes the websites Claude Code The point of six roles rather than one is not neatness. It is that each role gets a policy short enough to check, and the policies differ in the one place that matters: who may send.

I expected the dedicated account to bound what an agent could see. What I did not expect was how much it lets an administrator enforce, because Google Workspace's Gmail controls are set per organisational unit, and an account of its own can be a unit of its own. Three settings turned out to matter, all under Apps, Google Workspace, Gmail, Compliance in the Admin console, and all applied to a unit rather than the organisation: Restrict delivery limits a unit to sending and receiving mail only with authorised addresses and domains; anything else "returned to the sender with a bounce message that describes the policy." For the reader, whose only legitimate correspondent is me, a delivery restriction to my own domain means that even if it sends, it can only reach me.

Attachment compliance acts on messages "based on file type, file name, or message size", for outbound mail specifically if you choose, and can reject the message, quarantine it for review, or "remove attachments" and let the text through. For every agent that has no business sending files, an outbound rule that strips attachments turns a policy into a property of the mail system. Scope limits on third-party apps, under Security, API Controls, since December 2024, let an admin "limit third-party app access to specific OAuth 2.0 scopes for Google APIs, like Drive or Gmail." This is the sharpest tool and the one with a catch, which the next finding explains.

None of these is new. What is new is having an account per agent to point them at. On a shared identity you cannot restrict delivery for the agent without restricting it for yourself. On a dedicated one you can, and the rule is enforced by Google, not by the agent. The same move works for code. A dedicated GitHub account is given access to exactly the repositories that agent should touch, either by installing the Claude GitHub App on those repositories alone, or with a fine-grained personal access token, which GitHub describes as able to be "limited to only access specific repositories" with "specific, fine-grained permissions" and an expiry. The site editor's account sees the website repository and nothing else. That is the first time I have been able to say that about an agent with a GitHub connector, and it is worth the price of the seat by itself.

The reader's policy was going to be the simplest: read, classify, write a list, touch nothing else. In particular, never send. It lasted until the first scheduled run. Some of the messages that land in that inbox are from me, and some of what I send it are instructions: do this, file that, reply to them with this. For those, a reader that only writes a list is wasting the one thing a scheduled agent is for. So the rule became: never reply, unless the message came from me, in which case act on it.

Two things follow, and both are bigger than the reader. First, this is how policies actually get written: from the workflow, one exception at a time, not from principles handed down before anyone has run anything. The list of exceptions is the policy, and it is only complete once the workflow has run for a while. Second, "unless it came from me" is not a permissions question. Anyone can put my address in a From header. The exception is only safe if the agent can verify that a message came from me, which is a signature check, and the machinery for that is the one the append-lane messaging work built for agents talking to each other: per-session keys, a pinned registry of who holds which key, a signature over the message. The reader needs the same registry with one more entry in it, mine.

There is also a cheap partial enforcement for this rule, and it comes from finding one. Put the reader in a unit whose delivery is restricted to my domain, and the failure mode of a spoofed instruction is that the reader sends its reply to me, because that is the only place it can send anything. That does not make the policy right. It makes the worst row bounded. When the Gmail policies were first mapped, one assumption was that an agent could not attach files to mail through the Claude connector. There was no "attach a file" call, the documentation did not mention attachments beyond reading their metadata, and so the policy did not bother to forbid what seemed impossible.

On 27 September an agent working in Cowork needed to send a signed letter and found the way. The debrief it wrote is short and worth quoting: "The connector has no 'attach a file from disk' call, but create_draft and update_draft both accept an attachments array. Each item carries the file inline as base64." It shrank a 1.4 MB scanned PDF to 17 KB, base64-encoded it, put it in the draft, verified the MIME structure with get_draft in raw format, and I sent the draft by hand. It arrived intact, with Gmail's "One attachment · Scanned by Gmail" label and a preview. The debrief also records the gotchas an agent would trip over: a later update_draft without the field silently removes the attachments, so attach last; the message and thread ids change on every update but the draft id does not; the bytes pass through the tool call as text, so the practical limit is the size of a call, not Gmail's 25 MB.

I want to be precise about what that finding is and is not. It is not a bypass. The agent used a documented field of a documented call. It is a policy that was written from an assumption about capability, and the assumption was wrong, and the only way it could have been found wrong was by an agent trying to do the thing. That is the connector twin argument exactly: before you write down what an agent may do, replay what it can do.

And the vendor's documentation would not have settled it, because the vendor's documentation disagrees with itself. On 29 September 2026, one Anthropic page says of the Gmail connector: "Claude reads and searches email only; it can't create, send, or modify messages," and lists under limitations "Claude can't create, send, or modify emails." Another says it can "Draft emails with proper formatting and context," "Send, reply to, and forward emails from Gmail," and that "By default, Claude asks for your approval before each of these actions. On Team and Enterprise plans, owners decide whether members can allow these actions to run without asking each time." The debrief proves the second page is closer to the truth, at least for drafts. Neither page mentions the attachments field. I do not say this to criticise the documentation, which is trying to describe a product that changes monthly. I say it because a policy that cites the documentation as its enforcement has cited a moving target.

Here is the catch I promised in finding one. The Gmail API's scopes put drafting and sending in the same grant: gmail.compose is "Manage drafts and send emails," and gmail.modify is "Read, compose, and send emails." There is no scope that allows drafts and forbids sending. So the Workspace admin's scope limit, the sharpest tool in the box, cannot express the one rule the mailbox agent most needs, drafts only. That rule has to be enforced one step down the ladder, by a delivery restriction on the unit, or by an approval prompt, or by the agent doing as it was told. One more thing the setup made visible. The same seat runs two products, and they do not reach the same things.

The Cowork agent, in this setup, has no GitHub connector and cannot open the repository at all, even though the connector is listed in the catalogue and the account has access to the repository on GitHub. The Claude Code agent, on the same seat, opens the repository and edits the site. Whether that is a deliberate boundary or a gap in the product does not matter for the policy; what matters is that it is a real boundary today, and the site editor role is defined around it. The Claude Code agent is the only one that can change the websites, and the only thing its GitHub account can see is the website repositories.

The two products also differ in what an administrator can control. On a Team plan an Owner enables or disables a connector for the whole organisation, and in Cowork there is one further switch, whether members may set "Always allow" for "write-capable connector tools." Per-tool control, where a specific action can be set to "Always allow," "Needs approval," or "Blocked", exists only in the Enterprise plan's role-based permissions. So on a Team plan, never send can be a prompt that a person has to click through, and on Enterprise it can be a block. That difference belongs in the enforcement column too.

Where a rule is enforced, from the top of the ladder down. Identity and keys enforce themselves. Compliance rules enforce at the platform, per organisational unit. Approval prompts enforce at the person. Below that, a rule is the agent doing as it was told. Every rule in the table sits on one of these steps, and the policy is as strong as its lowest. Here is the policy for the setup, one rule per row, with the column that matters. Enforced means the platform or the cryptography prevents the action. Admin rule means a Workspace or GitHub setting an administrator applied to the agent's own account or unit. Approval means a person is asked before the action runs. Told means the agent has been instructed and nothing else stands in the way. Read the last column top to bottom and the shape of the problem is clear. The rows that touch identity, code and vaults are enforced, because accounts, repositories and keys are boundaries the platform or the mathematics maintains. The rows that touch mail are admin rules and approvals, which is good, and better than I expected before I understood organisational units. And two rows are told. One of them, the reply-to-me rule, has a known fix and a bounded failure. The other, acts outside its role, is the row every agent policy in the world shares, and no setting anywhere enforces it. It is the reason the connector twin exists: if you cannot prevent it, you must at least be able to see it afterwards.

Buy the segregation. A Workspace seat per agent is £7 a month. It is the only control that covers mail, files, code and connectors at once, and it is the precondition for every admin rule below. Put each agent in its own organisational unit. Then restrict delivery for every agent that should not correspond with the world, and strip outbound attachments for every agent that should not send files. These are settings, not hopes. Give each agent its own GitHub account and install the app per repository. The site editor sees the site. Nothing else sees anything. Write the policy as a table, with the enforcement column. Fill the column honestly. Anything that says told is where your next incident comes from, and where your next piece of tooling should go. Replay before you write. Have an agent try the things the policy assumes it cannot do. Mine found attachments in an afternoon. The documentation would not have told you.

Expect the exception on day one. Write the policy from the workflow, and treat the growing list of exceptions as the policy maturing rather than failing. Journal everything anyway. For the rows that say told, the twin is the only control there is. The setup described here runs: the accounts, the roles, the scheduled reader, the drafting and sending split, the dedicated GitHub account for the site editor. The Workspace compliance rules exist and are documented, and I have linked the documentation rather than restating it. The attachment finding is proven and written up. The append-lane signature registry exists for agent-to-agent messages.

What does not exist yet: my own key in that registry, so the reader's exception is still enforced by instruction; a broker that would let drafts only be a block rather than a prompt on a Team plan; and any way to enforce acts outside its role. The policy table above is the honest state of a real setup on 29 September 2026, and I would rather publish it with its two told rows than pretend they are something else.
