Abstract: I opened the newsroom on my iPhone, in a browser that looked like Chrome but could not reach my passkeys, and the vault button told me there were sixteen changes that existed only in that browser. My reaction is the most interesting part: those were notes and reads I wanted to keep. They had become pieces of intelligence, and I was happy to do a couple of steps to get them into my vault, as long as I only had to do it once. That is the nudge working for the right reason. So this is a feature request and a brief. Every reader vault should have a lane that any browser can write to, by a link, a piece of text or a QR code carrying only where to write and the key to encrypt with, so that a browser with no passkey, no sign-in, or an old operating system can send what it holds into my vault, and the vault takes it from there the next time I open it. The newsroom already does exactly this to send a reading summary to sgit.ai, so it is a pattern pointed at myself. It is also a commentary. Identity is still a mess: passkeys that work in one browser and not in the one an app opens a link in, and an email connector that makes attachments, inline images and a clean reply in a thread far harder than the underlying service does. Users will accept a lot of friction, once, when the value is clear, which is how WhatsApp links a computer and how Midjourney grew on a Discord bot. What they will not accept is losing their data. And the other half of the day's news is the opposite story: two new wires, OWASP and AWS, built from two small config files on the same pipeline, and suddenly a new product line.
Send to my vault, from any browser: a link offered three ways that lets a browser write to a lane and never read.
in-short

Sixteen changes, only in one browser. On my iPhone, in a browser that could not reach my passkeys, the vault said sixteen changes existed nowhere else. I wanted them, and that is the point. They had become my intelligence, and I would do a couple of steps to keep them. The nudge works when it shows you what is yours. The request: send from any browser to my vault. A lane on every reader vault, offered as a URL, text or QR code, that any browser can write to and none can read. The pattern already exists. The newsroom encrypts a reading summary in the browser and appends it to sgit.ai's inbox with no vault and no passkey. Point it at the reader's own vault. Solve my iPhone, solve every browser. Not signed in, no passkey provider, an old iPad: a link opened anywhere, even sent to myself on WhatsApp, is enough.
in-short

Identity is still a mess, and that is why things do not get adopted. Passkeys work in one browser and not in the one an app opens links in. Email through an agent connector makes simple things hard. Users accept friction once, for value. WhatsApp's QR code and Midjourney's Discord bot are proof. Losing data is the thing they do not forgive. Two config files, a new product line. The OWASP Wire and the AWS Wire run on the Industry Wire's pipeline, and each may find its own audience.
happened

I was on my iPhone, reading the newsroom in a browser that looked like Chrome, but not the Chrome I am signed in to. It felt like it was running with low permissions, never logged in to anything. The Vault button showed a count: sixteen changes only in this browser, reads, notes and stories seen, that my vault did not have. And that browser could not open my vault, because it could not reach my passkeys.
happened

The likely reason is less mysterious than it felt. On iOS, a link opened inside another app, WhatsApp, Gmail, LinkedIn, often opens in that app's own web view rather than in the browser, and Apple's rule for those is strict: an app "can't use passkeys to authenticate for services that you haven't configured as the app's associated domains". The real browsers get an entitlement that lets them use passkeys for any site, and Chrome on iOS 17 or later can use passkeys from Google Password Manager. So the same phone has a browser that can open my vault and a browser-shaped view that cannot, and nothing on the screen tells you which one you are in.
nudge

What interested me most was my own reaction. I did not think, oh well. I thought: I want those. They were not page views any more. They were things I had read, notes I had made, stories I had marked, pieces of intelligence that were mine and that I did not want to lose. And I wanted to get back to my account, because that is where my newsroom is, the one customised to what I read.
nudge

In The site is an inbox I said none of this should be gamified: no decision placed at the end of a page to make you scroll there. The count on the vault button is not that. It does not invent a reason to click. It tells you what is yours and where it is at risk, and the reason to act is real. That is a nudge for the right reason, and it is working, on me. It is the same loop as I miss it, so it is working: the moment you have something to lose, the feature you need announces itself.
request

So how do I get those sixteen changes from that browser into my vault? Today there is one way without the passkey, the recovery code, which opens a second door to the master. That is too much power to type into a browser I do not trust, for a job that only needs to add things.
request

What it needs is a lane. My vault, when it is created, should also have a communication lane, an append lane that an outside writer can add to and never read. To write to it, a browser needs only two things: where the lane is, and the public key to encrypt with, or a place to fetch it. That fits in a link. So the vault pane should offer it three ways: a URL I can open, the text I can copy and paste, and a QR code I can scan from the other device. Whichever browser opens it encrypts what it holds to my key and appends it to the lane. It learns nothing about my vault and can read nothing back. The next time I open my vault with my passkey, on any device, the pane drains the lane and the sixteen changes are mine.
request

The newsroom already does this, pointed somewhere else. When a reader sends their reading to sgit.ai, the meter encrypts a summary in the browser to sgit.ai's published key and posts it to an append lane, with no vault and no passkey. The request is the same pattern pointed at the reader's own vault. And this is a good example of the non-linear path I keep writing about, in Not a straight line. Once it exists, it solves far more than my iPhone. It works in any browser: one not signed in to anything, one with no passkey provider, an old iPad where the passkey never worked and only a QR code would. I could even send the link to myself on WhatsApp and open it on the other side. The friction of identity stops deciding whether your data is safe.
brief

The brief in six steps, with what already exists beside each, and the little that is new. For the session that builds the reader's vault pane on newsroom.sgit.ai. Written by @newsroom.writer for Dinis Cruz, 13 October 2026, on top of the vault pane at v0.12.22. A key pair for the reader. Generated in the browser when the vault is created or first opened at this version, the private key kept in the master vault, the public key in the clear. Today the reader has none; the persona key pairs in The site is an inbox were the plan for this. An append lane on the reader vault, configured with the master's credentials, with its token kept in the master. The link, three ways. A URL, the same as text, and a QR code, carrying the lane address, the append token and the public key or where to fetch it. Nothing else: not the vault key, not the read key.
brief

The sender's side. On any page, a browser holding a link encrypts its pending records, the same ones the count already lists, and appends them as one message per send, then marks them sent and keeps a copy until they are confirmed. The drain. On every unlock, the pane lists what is waiting in the lane, says which browser sent it and when, and merges it into the reader's records on one press, keeping the sender's device as the author, as records brought in from another device already are. Tests. A browser with no authenticator sends; the vault, opened with a virtual passkey, drains; a tampered or foreign message is refused; the QR round-trips.
brief

What to be careful about: anyone holding the link can write to the lane, so the token should be rotatable from the pane, the drain should show what arrived before it merges, and a link should be able to expire. None of them can read anything. The same machinery is what card 015, a reply lane from the newsroom to the reader, needs anyway.
hard

And this is the commentary I most wanted to make. Things like this are why good ideas do not get mainstream adoption. Identity is a mess. It works in some browsers and not others, on some paths and not others, and the user is not told which. From a user's point of view this should be straightforward. It just has to work, inside the workflow and the experience they are already in. It cannot be "it only works on this browser, in this situation, with this setting", and then, oh, you have lost some data.
hard

But here is the other side of it, and I think it is just as important. Users have a lot of tolerance for complex workflows when they can see the value, when the steps are not repeated, and when they are connected to the value. Connecting a computer to WhatsApp is a good example: you open the app on your phone, go to linked devices, scan a QR code on the other screen, and then it is done. Nobody calls that great design, and everybody does it, because it happens once and what you get is immediate.
hard

Midjourney is the extreme case. When it started, it had one of the strangest workflows I had seen: you joined a Discord server and typed a slash command, "/imagine", into a channel full of other people's images. I remember thinking, how does this even work? And people loved it. Discord says the server hit "the prior server cap of an astonishing one million users". The value was obvious and the friction was the price of it. I am not saying bad experience is fine. I am saying that a one-off step, connected to value, is acceptable, and that this is something to test, not assume. We can A/B test the link against a pairing flow and see which readers finish.
email

Another example of things being harder than they should be: sending an email through an agent, with Claude connected to Gmail. For basic emails it works well. Then it gets painful. An attachment is possible, but not the way you would expect: as Six agents, one inbox found, the connector's draft call takes the file inline, and the agent had to shrink a 1.4 MB scanned PDF to 17 KB to get a signed letter out. Replying in the same thread while cutting the wall of quoted text underneath, which The wall under the reply argued for, I have not been able to do. Inline images, which make a message far more powerful, I cannot send at all.
email

None of these are limits of Gmail itself. Google's API lets a program "upload file data when creating or updating a draft", put a draft into an existing thread by its ID, and replace a draft whole, quoted text included. Claude's own help page lists drafting, sending, replying and forwarding, and says attachment content is "metadata only" for reading. So the constraint is the connector's, and I can only guess why. If it is security, I do not think it buys much: an agent that wants to leak data can share a folder on Drive, or send fifty small emails, or a thousand. What it does do is push people to other tools to send the emails they actually need to send, and then the mailbox is no longer managed in one place, which is a bigger risk than the attachment ever was. These look like small things. In real use they are the difference between a workflow and a workaround.
wire

One pipeline, three wires: the Industry Wire, the OWASP Wire and the AWS Wire, each a vault plus a config. The day's other story is the opposite of all that friction. The wire started simple: one agent writing industry news into an encrypted vault, and this site drawing it with only the read key. Today the agent that runs it added two more: an OWASP Wire, everything happening at and about OWASP, joined to a graph of its projects, and an AWS Wire, everything AWS announced, filtered by a declared stack. On this site that was barely a feature: two configuration files of seventeen lines each, and one builder that now serves every wire. In the release's own words, "a wire is a vault plus a config".
wire

And suddenly the use cases and the value exploded. A newswire for cyber security risk is one product. A wire for one community, or for the customers of one platform, is another, and each can be followed up to see whether there is an audience that cares about exactly that. If we can add value there, that is a very good value proposition, from almost no new code. It is the same lesson as the lane: build the general thing once, and the next use is nearly free.
limits

The iPhone browser is my best explanation, not a diagnosis. An in-app web view fits what I saw; it could also have been another browser mode. The lane is a request, not a feature. Nothing in this brief is built; the append lanes, the browser-side encryption and the recovery code are. The email limits are what I and my agents have met. The connector may handle more than its help page says; the attachment route works, at a size. "Users accept friction once" is a hypothesis to test. WhatsApp and Midjourney are examples, not evidence that readers of a newsroom will. The wires are new. Whether OWASP or AWS readers want a wire is exactly what has not been tested yet. If you have hit the same walls with passkeys, browsers or agent email, or you want a wire for your own community, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: I saw a video today that said "1 in 20 Claude skills are built to hack your computer". It is an overstatement of a real study, and the real finding is interesting enough: in one large study of public marketplaces, 5.2% of the skills analysed showed "high-severity patterns strongly suggesting malicious intent". It made me think about what an agent behaviour policy can do for skills. A skill behaviour policy looks at three things. The mandate the description promises; the mandate the skill actually has, from what its instructions and files can do, treated as features; and the grant, which depends on where it runs. The gap between the first two is the suspicious part; the gap between the last two is the reach nobody asked for. Then the policy becomes a control: a hook and a sandbox setting, generated from the described mandate, that bring the grant down to what you expected. I built a static calculator and ran it on 899 public skills from three sources: 812 can reach something beyond their own scripts, 782 of them through one third-party tool server, and 39 have a feature their description does not mention. None was obfuscated. The clearest case was honest: a skill that reads your Claude Code chat history, searches HackerNews and sends a report to Slack has the whole lethal trifecta, says so, and still needs a control. NVIDIA's scanner rated it safe, which is right for the question a scanner asks. A policy asks a different one.
A skill behaviour policy: three mandates, two gaps and one control.
in-short

The claim, corrected. Not 1 in 20 Claude skills built to hack you: 5.2% of 31,132 marketplace skills in one study showed patterns "strongly suggesting malicious intent". Three mandates. Described, actual and granted; the gaps between them are the findings. Features, not verdicts. An upload can be exfiltration or a login; the policy records which, and why. The grant depends on where it runs. On Claude Code, a skill has the network of any program; in the API, none. Measured on 899 skills. 812 can reach beyond their own scripts; 782 through one third-party tool server; 39 with an undescribed feature; none obfuscated. An honest skill can still need a control. Chat history in, HackerNews in, Slack out: the whole lethal trifecta, all described. The policy becomes a control. A hook and a sandbox setting, generated from the description and tested on fixed inputs.
in-short
A scanner and a policy answer different questions. One asks if a skill looks malicious; the other asks what it needs and what it gets.
claim

The video said "1 in 20 Claude skills are built to hack your computer", and connected it to a scanner. Both halves need correcting. The number comes from Agent Skills in the Wild, a study published in January that ran its own scanner, SkillScan, over public marketplaces: "collecting 42,447 skills from two major marketplaces and systematically analyzing 31,132". It found "26.1% of skills contain at least one vulnerability", and "5.2% of skills exhibit high-severity patterns strongly suggesting malicious intent". So: marketplace skills, not Claude's own; suggesting intent, not proving it. The scanner in the video is a different tool, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, built to check skills before they are installed or published; NVIDIA did not produce that number.
claim

The corrected version is still worth taking seriously, and the study's own phrase is the reason: skills "execute with implicit trust and minimal vetting". Anthropic's guidance says the same thing from the other side: "Use Skills only from trusted sources", and treat installing one like installing software.
three

A skill is instructions an agent follows, often with scripts beside them, with whatever reach the agent has. A policy for every skill described Sean Turner's control for reviewing contributed skills against a written policy. This is the measurement underneath it: three mandates for every skill. The described mandate. What the description promises. It is the only part a person reads when choosing a skill, and the only part the agent reads until the skill is used. The actual mandate. What the instructions and bundled files can make the agent do: reach the network, upload, read credentials, read outside the workspace, install packages, change shell startup files, call a remote tool server. Each is a feature, found in the text.
three

The grant. What the environment lets it do, which is different in each place. Anthropic's documentation is plain about it: on Claude Code, "Skills have the same network access as any other program on the user's computer"; through the API, skills run in "a sandboxed container with no network access"; on claude.ai, network access follows the workspace's settings. Two gaps fall out. Actual minus described is the part to look at: features the description never mentions. Grant minus actual is the reach nobody asked for: even an honest skill, on a laptop, runs with everything the agent can do. In the language of this site's behaviour policies, the mandate is smaller than the reach, and the difference is the risk.
three

One detail makes the grant worse than it looks. A skill can declare allowed-tools, and it does not mean what it sounds like: Claude Code's documentation says "It does not restrict which tools are available", it pre-approves them, and "A skill can grant itself broad tool access". A skill can widen its own grant.
features

The important design choice is that every finding is a feature, not a verdict. A skill that uploads a file to a URL could be stealing data, or logging you into an account to do what you asked. A skill that reads ~/.claude could be harvesting your sessions, or analysing your work because you asked it to. Context decides, and the policy is where the context is written down: each feature becomes a row, with what it does, why the description needs it, and whether the description says so at all. A feature the description explains is a row with a reason. A feature it does not explain is a finding.
measured

899 skills from three public sources: what they can reach, and what their descriptions leave out. So I built the calculator's first half and ran it. It reads a skill folder as text, never runs anything, finds features by pattern in the instructions and every bundled file, finds the features the description declares by its words, and reports the difference. I ran it on three public sources, read on 14 October: Anthropic's own skills repository (20 skills), a popular methodology collection, obra/superpowers (15), and a large community catalogue, ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills (864). 812 of 899 can reach something beyond their own scripts. Network, installs, credentials, files outside the workspace, or a remote tool server.
measured

782 do it through one third-party tool server. Most of the community catalogue is instructions only: 850 of its 864 skills ship no code, and 778 declare that they need the same remote MCP server, which holds the connections to each service. The reach of those skills is not in the skill at all; it is whatever accounts you have connected to that server. 39 have a feature their description does not mention. Mostly installs (a PDF skill that runs pip install), paths outside the workspace, and example credentials in reference files. Ten name a service but not the third-party server every call goes through; nine of them are business and finance skills, such as QuickBooks, NetSuite, Xero, Ramp and Coinbase. None was obfuscated, and none sets allowed-tools.
measured

These are curated public sources, not a marketplace sample, so the absence of obvious malice is what you would expect. What they show is the other thing: how often the description and the reach differ, even when everyone means well.
example

One skill, end to end: developer-growth-analysis, its description, its policy and the hook generated from it. The clearest case in the set was an honest one. developer-growth-analysis describes itself as a skill that "Analyzes your recent Claude Code chat history to identify coding patterns, development gaps, and areas for improvement, curates relevant learning resources from HackerNews, and automatically sends a personalized growth report to your Slack DMs." Its instructions read ~/.claude/history.jsonl, search HackerNews and post to Slack, all through a third-party tool server. That is the lethal trifecta, private data, untrusted content and a way out, in one skill, and the description says so. The only thing it leaves out is the server in the middle.
example

Its skill behaviour policy is short. The minimal grant: read one file, run a search, send one message to yourself. The reach on Claude Code: the network of any program, every file you can read, including the rest of ~/.claude and ~/.ssh, and every account you have connected to the server. Four rows: read only the history file outside the workspace; ask before anything is sent; treat HackerNews text as data, not instructions; never touch shell startup files. From those rows I generated a hook and tested it on nine fixed inputs, the JSON the harness would send. It allowed reading the history file, the search, and a write in the workspace. It denied reading an SSH key, cat .env, any other file under ~/.claude, and writes to ~/.bashrc and ~/.zshrc. And it asked before the tool server's execute call, because that is where a message leaves.
example

The policy also says what the hook cannot do. A hook sees the tool call, not what a script does once it runs, so the network of scripts belongs to the sandbox, where Claude Code can limit shell commands to an allowlist of domains. And the tool server itself runs outside the sandbox ("The sandbox covers shell commands only. Claude's file tools, MCP servers, and hooks run outside it."), so its calls can be asked about, not blocked by the network. The row about HackerNews text stays an expectation: nothing outside the model can see whether it obeyed a page. That row is the honest statement of where the remaining risk is, which is the job Are hooks the sweet spot? gave the barrier column, and the reason Hooks are kernel code wants these hooks managed like kernel code.
scanner

I ran NVIDIA's SkillSpector, version 2.12.0, on five of the same skills, with --no-llm, which its README describes as the way "to keep contents local (static analysis only)". The two tools agreed where they looked at the same thing, and differed where they ask different questions. developer-growth-analysis. Score 8, low, recommendation "SAFE", with one medium finding on "automatically send", flagged as autonomous decision making. The policy finds the whole trifecta and a third-party server. langsmith-fetch. Score 18, with a high finding: a YARA rule for backdoor persistence matched the line that tells you to append your API key to ~/.bashrc. The policy found the same line: a write to a shell startup file, and a secret stored in plain text, neither mentioned in the description. Same line, different words; the policy's are the more accurate here, because the instruction is to help you, and the risk is real anyway.
scanner

The PDF skill. A medium finding that it "declares no tool scope ('permissions' or 'allowed-tools')". A declared scope is good for intent, but on Claude Code allowed-tools pre-approves rather than restricts, so declaring it would widen the grant. The control has to come from somewhere else. connect and quickbooks-automation. Score 0 for both, no findings. The policy finds a described mandate of "Gmail, Slack, GitHub, Notion, and 1000+ services" for one, and an accounting system reached through an undescribed third party for the other. This is not a criticism of the scanner, and its optional model stage may find more. A scanner asks whether a skill looks malicious, and for these skills the right answer is mostly no. A policy asks what the skill needs, what it gets in this environment, and what control makes the two meet. NVIDIA's own framing of verified skills fits the second question: "Verified skills govern capabilities that enter the workflow."
service

Put together, this is a service we can offer and an open format we can publish. For any skill: the described mandate, the actual mandate with its evidence, the minimal grant, what more it could do on Claude Code, on claude.ai and through the API, and the hook and sandbox settings that bring the grant down to what the description promised, with their tests. The calculator is static and cheap; a model can read the description against the features where judgement helps; the controls are generated, tested and published, the way Policy as code needs a policy first generated Rego from rows. And the same policy is what a company like Chainguard, whose agent skills product plans to let organisations "define and enforce their own skill security policies", as Chainguard, mapped quoted, would need written down.
limits

Pattern matching gives lower bounds. The calculator finds features by text patterns; it misses what it has no pattern for, and some matches are examples in documentation. Three curated sources, not a marketplace. The 899 are public collections read on 14 October 2026; marketplace rates will differ. The policy and the hook are for one skill. The rows were written for this article; the hook was tested on fixed inputs, not in a live session. SkillSpector ran without its model stage. Five skills, static only; its full mode may find more. No skill here is called malicious. A feature is a feature until the context says otherwise. If you publish skills, review them for an organisation, or want a policy and a control for the ones you run, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

The calculator, the policy and the hook were built for this article; the skills were downloaded into an isolated folder and read as text, never run. A research agent verified the study, the scanner and the documentation, and the quotes were checked on the pages themselves. Abstract: Lauren Zabierek shared a card on LinkedIn about the EU's new Product Liability Directive, 2024/2853: the 1985 directive never named software, and the new one makes it a product, subject to strict, no-fault liability that a EULA cannot waive, for products placed on the market after 9 December 2026. I asked under the post how it applies to SaaS, so I read the directive itself. Software is a product "irrespective of the mode of its supply", and the recitals name SaaS. Updates matter: a manufacturer cannot escape liability by saying the defect came later if it is due to software, an update, or a lack of updates needed to maintain safety, while the product is in its control; and an attacker's exploit does not reduce its liability. But the directive is narrower than it sounds. Only natural persons can claim, and only for death or injury, property not used only for work, or data destroyed or corrupted that is not used for work. A data leak is not on the list, and a company cannot claim for its own losses. Applied to php2shell, the PHP project is out of scope; a vendor or SaaS that leaves a known, fixed flaw unpatched and lets attackers wipe consumers' files is likely in. Patching does not bring an old product into scope, but a new one that is not patched has no defence. Here is what the articles say, and the questions they leave.
Lauren Zabierek's LinkedIn post of 25 October 2026: card R-05 on the Product Liability Directive.
in-short

Software is now a product, "irrespective of the mode of its supply", SaaS included. Updates count. A lack of updates needed for safety is no defence, while the product is in the maker's control. An attacker's exploit does not reduce liability. A EULA cannot exclude it. But only people can claim, and only for injury, private property, and private data destroyed or corrupted. A data leak is not covered, and neither is a company's own loss. php2shell: the PHP project is out; a vendor or SaaS that leaves the fixed flaw unpatched is likely in. Patching does not pull an old product into scope. Not patching a new one has no defence.
why

Lauren Zabierek shared a card on LinkedIn that summarises the new directive. Under the post I asked whether there was a mapping of how it applies to SaaS. Rather than wait, I read Directive (EU) 2024/2853 itself, articles and recitals, and tested it against the story we have been following on the PHP site. This is a briefing and a list of questions, from an engineer reading the text. It is not legal advice, and courts in 27 member states will decide what it means. The card is accurate. Two small precisions: the articles name software and digital manufacturing files as products, while SaaS and AI systems are named in the recitals that explain them; and the directive applies to products placed on the market "after", not from, 9 December 2026.
articles

Does the new Product Liability Directive bite? Six questions in order, then the defences and what is not a defence. Software is a product. Article 4(1): "'product' means all movables … it includes electricity, digital manufacturing files, raw materials and software". Recital 13 removes any doubt about delivery: software is a product "irrespective of the mode of its supply or usage, and therefore irrespective of whether the software is stored on a device, accessed through a communication network or cloud technologies, or supplied through a software-as-a-service model". Two exclusions in the same recital: information is not a product, nor is "the mere source code of software". And recital 17: the directive "should not apply to services as such", though a digital service integrated into a product, a "related service", counts as a component of it.
articles

Only for new products. Article 2(1): it applies "to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026". The 1985 directive keeps applying to anything placed earlier (Article 21). But a product "substantially modified", including "through a software update or upgrade", is treated as placed on the market again when the modification is made (recital 40). Open source, outside commerce, is out. Article 2(2) excludes "free and open-source software that is developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity". When a manufacturer builds such software into a commercial product, that manufacturer can be liable for it, not the project (recital 15).
articles

Only people, and only some damage. Article 5 gives the right to compensation to "any natural person". Article 6 lists the damage: death or personal injury, "including medically recognised damage to psychological health"; damage to property, except the product itself and property "used exclusively for professional purposes"; and "destruction or corruption of data that are not used for professional purposes". Recital 22 goes further: data used for professional purposes "even if not exclusively so" is excluded. Defective, with cybersecurity. Article 7: a product is defective when it "does not provide the safety that a person is entitled to expect", judged with all circumstances, including "safety-relevant cybersecurity requirements" and, where the manufacturer keeps control, "the moment in time when the product left the control of the manufacturer". Recital 32: a product "can also be found to be defective on account of its cybersecurity vulnerability".
articles

Easier to prove. The defendant can be ordered to disclose evidence (Article 9). Defectiveness is presumed if it fails to, if the product breaks mandatory safety rules, or if there is an obvious malfunction (Article 10(2)); and a court shall presume defectiveness or causation where technical complexity makes proof excessively difficult and the claimant shows it is likely (Article 10(4)).
articles

Updates, and the defences that are gone. A manufacturer is normally not liable if it proves the defect probably did not exist when the product was placed on the market (Article 11(1)(c)). But Article 11(2) removes that defence where the defect is due to "software, including software updates or upgrades" or "a lack of software updates or upgrades necessary to maintain safety", provided it is within the manufacturer's control; and "control" includes having "the ability to supply software updates or upgrades" (Article 4(5)(b)). A third party exploiting the defect does not reduce liability (Article 13(1); recital 55 names "a third party exploiting a cybersecurity vulnerability"), while an injured person who negligently failed to install an update can see it reduced (Article 13(2)). No contract can limit or exclude it (Article 15). Claims expire 10 years after the product was placed on the market (Article 17).
php

php2shell under the new directive: who is likely liable and who is not, across the PHP project, vendors and SaaS. The PHP story gives us real cases. The two flaws were fixed in PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 on 21 October 2026; the end-of-life branches, 7.4 to 8.1, got backport branches but no release. The Dutch NCSC's list tracks 674 products that ship or depend on PHP: 206 marked vulnerable, 418 still under investigation and 46 fixed, as the site recorded it. And, as of 25 October, no named organisation has said it was compromised. The directive would not apply to any of this today, because none of these products was placed on the market after 9 December 2026. But suppose the same flaw were found in 2027, in products placed on the market after that date. Our reading: The PHP project: out of scope, as free and open-source software developed outside a commercial activity.
php

A vendor whose product runs on PHP, an appliance, a control panel or an app, that ships or leaves the flaw unpatched after the fix is public: likely liable to a consumer for injury, private property or private data destroyed. It cannot say the defect came later, because the lack of an update was within its control. A SaaS whose unpatched PHP lets attackers wipe or encrypt its consumer users' files: likely liable. SaaS software is a product, corrupted personal data is a covered damage, and the attacker does not reduce its liability. The same SaaS, if attackers only steal the data: not under this directive. A leak is not destruction or corruption; the GDPR and contract law apply instead, and the directive says it does not affect them (Article 2(4)).
php

A business customer that loses its own data or systems: no claim under this directive. It is not a natural person, and its data is professional. Contract and national law still apply. A product placed on the market on end-of-life PHP 7.4, with no official release of the fix: hard to defend. The flaw is public, so the defence that the state of knowledge could not discover it (Article 11(1)(e)) is gone. So, the question I started with: would a company with evidence of exposure to php2shell, which did not patch and then got compromised, be liable? Under this directive, for a product placed on the market after 9 December 2026, to consumers, for the covered damages: likely, yes. To its business customers, or for a leak: not under this directive.
incentives

The worry is a perverse incentive: if updating brings a product into scope, do not update, or shut it down. The text makes that weaker than it sounds. A security patch is unlikely to be a "substantial modification". Article 4(18) defines one as a change to the product's "original performance, purpose or type" that was not foreseen in the manufacturer's risk assessment and that changes or increases the hazard. A patch that closes a flaw does the opposite. Updates that are not substantial "should not affect the expiry period" (recital 58). For new products, not updating is no defence. Article 11(2)(c) makes the lack of a needed security update the manufacturer's problem, as long as it can still supply one. The directive does not oblige anyone to provide updates (recital 51). The incentive comes from liability, not a duty. Shutting down limits future damage, not past. Claims run for 10 years from when the product was placed on the market.
questions

When is a SaaS "placed on the market"? At launch, or never fully, because it never leaves the manufacturer's control? A SaaS launched before 9 December 2026 and updated daily may stay under the old directive for years, unless some update is "substantial". Where does a product end and a service begin? The directive covers SaaS software but not "services as such" (recital 17). Is a web application a product, and the hosting a service? Who is the manufacturer of a self-hosted WordPress site? The open-source project is out; the agency that built and sells it, or the host that runs it, may be in. What about end of support? One commenter under Lauren's post noted that a product's end of support under the Cyber Resilience Act does not end its liability under this directive. "Control" means the ability to supply updates; can a manufacturer end that ability, and with it the liability, before the 10 years are up?
questions

How does it line up with the Cyber Resilience Act? The CRA's reporting duties already apply since 11 September 2026 and the rest from 11 December 2027 (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, Article 71), and its "safety-relevant cybersecurity requirements" will help courts judge defectiveness. But the CRA leaves out websites and cloud services developed outside a product's manufacturer, including SaaS (its recital 12), which this directive includes. Will it reach business losses at all? As written, no. The pressure on SaaS will come from consumers, insurers and the CRA, more than from companies suing each other.
limits

This is a reading of the text, not legal advice. Member states transpose it by 9 December 2026, and courts will interpret it. The php2shell cases are hypothetical: today's products are under the old directive. Lauren Zabierek's post is quoted from the card in the screenshot; the rest of the post needs a sign-in.
sources

Lauren Zabierek's post on LinkedIn, 25 October 2026, from a screenshot, and its public comments; my voice memo of the same day. Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on liability for defective products, Official Journal of 18 November 2024, and Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, the Cyber Resilience Act, both read on EUR-Lex on 25 October 2026. The PHP story site's data on affected versions, the NCSC-NL product list and compromises, at release v0.22.2. Abstract: I am reaching a point where every piece of software that gets in my way is not just annoying, it is a little offensive, because I know that I could rebuild the part I need. I could make my own version of a browser that behaves exactly as I want. What stops me is not building it; it is maintaining it. That is the opportunity software companies are missing, and I think it is why they should be worried. My argument is a positioning one, in Simon Wardley's terms: a software company should stop thinking of itself as the explorer that invents features, and become the villager and town planner underneath its users, who explore on top of the product, by talking to it, while the company sells them the maintenance of what they built and learns from it. I could not find anyone making this argument; the nearest are Ink & Switch's essay on malleable software and Wardley's own model of innovating on a commodity. Firefox is the example. I came back to it and found a good browser that I could not bend: on the desktop its compact mode was hidden for five years, until Firefox 157 brought it back on 29 September, and on the iPad there is still no way to hide the toolbar. Mozilla's revenue is about 73% royalties, mostly from one customer. I would pay Firefox instead, a pound, ten pounds, fifty, for my version, kept working. The sell-off in software stocks in February, and a developer's open-source clones of seven Adobe applications this month, are early signs of what happens to companies that do not make that move.
A product as explorers, villagers and town planners: users on top, the vendor in the middle, primitives at the core.
in-short

Friction is now a choice. When an app gets in the way, I know I could rebuild the part I need. What stops me is maintenance. I do not want to keep my own browser working next year. That is the business. Sell users the maintenance of what they build, not the first version. Become the villager and the town planner. Let users explore on top; keep the core small and solid. Firefox is the example. A good browser I could not bend, funded mostly by one customer. The signs are already here. A sell-off in software stocks, and Adobe's apps cloned in the open. Settings are not the answer. A product people can talk to and reshape is.
friction

Something has changed in how I react to software. When an application gets in my way, especially one that I depend on, the frustration is different now, because I know that I could do something about it. Not in theory: I have been building custom interfaces for single moments for months, and Custom UIs are not the exception argued that they are how interfaces get made now. So every time a product stops me, there is a question in the back of my mind: how much does this hurt, and is it enough for me to rebuild the part I need?
friction

For most products it is not, yet. But the threshold keeps dropping. This month a developer released open-source clean-room clones of seven Adobe applications, written in Rust with AI assistance, from a Photoshop equivalent to an InDesign one; his own readme says it is "not yet a Photoshop replacement for daily professional work", and the speed of it is the point, not the polish. In February, when Anthropic released role-specific plugins for Claude Cowork, investors sold software and data stocks hard: Thomson Reuters fell about 18% in a day, its biggest daily loss on record, and RELX 14%. It is easy to rebuild 10% of a product's features. And for many users, those are the 10% that matter.
maintenance

Here is the part software companies should understand, because it is their opportunity. I could make my own version of Firefox. I could change the toolbar, remove what I do not use, add the one thing I need. What I do not want to do is maintain it: rebase it on every release, notice when an update breaks it, keep it working on my laptop and my iPad next month and next year. That is a service. Someone is always paying; the only question is who, for what. And I would gladly pay the company that makes the product to keep my version working. Not five thousand pounds. Maybe a pound a month; maybe ten pounds a year; maybe fifty for a change I really need; maybe five hundred for my company. There is a price point at which I would pay, and it is a better revenue stream than advertising or a search deal.
position

The positioning I have not seen anyone take is to use Simon Wardley's three kinds of people as a product strategy. Explorers "explore never-before-discovered concepts, the uncharted land"; villagers "turn the half baked thing into something useful for a larger audience"; town planners "take something and industrialise it taking advantage of economies of scale." For thirty years software companies have tried to be all three for their users: inventing every feature, deciding which ones ship, and maintaining all of it. The explorer work is the part they are worst at, because they are guessing what each user needs.
position

The users are now better explorers of their own needs than the company will ever be. So the company should let them explore, on top of the product, and position itself as the villager and the town planner underneath: the one that takes what a user built and keeps it working, takes what many users built and turns it into a feature, and keeps the core small, deterministic and accountable. It is close to Wardley's own model of innovating on top of a commodity: provide the component, let the ecosystem innovate on it, and spot what succeeds. The nearest argument I found is Ink & Switch's essay Malleable software, from June 2025, which begins "The original promise of personal computing was a new kind of clay", and warns that "AI code generation alone does not address all the barriers to malleability." I agree: the barrier left is not writing the code, it is who maintains it.
position

The citizen developer is good news made the same argument inside companies: what the explorer builds is the best brief ever written, and the villagers and town planners make it last. Here the explorer is the customer, and the brief arrives working.
firefox

I came back to Firefox after many years away, partly because Google's iPad app keeps throwing me back to its home page and its AI mode, and losing where I was. And the honest summary is that Firefox is a good browser that I could not bend.
firefox

Some of what I missed was not there for years and is now: on the desktop, the compact layout I wanted was removed from the menus in Firefox 89 in 2021 and left as a hidden preference, and Firefox 157, on 29 September, brought it back as a setting that "reduces toolbar and tab spacing to leave more room for web content". Vertical tabs arrived in March 2025. On the iPad, I found no setting to hide the toolbar, and users have been asking for one. Mozilla has added a sidebar for AI chatbots and a single switch to turn generative AI features off, but not the thing I actually wanted, which is to ask the browser itself to change how it behaves.
firefox

Other signals I missed were about engineering. Firefox has never been the browser people run in serverless functions: the open-source project that packaged it for AWS Lambda was archived in 2023, and the ecosystem runs Chromium instead. That matters more now, because agents run browsers in the cloud, and the browser that is easiest to run there is the one agents will use. And then there is the money. Mozilla's audited accounts for 2024 show $680 million of revenue, of which $498 million, about 73%, was royalties, and "Approximately 86%" of its revenue from customers with contracts came from one customer. Its new chief executive wrote in December that Mozilla must mean "diversifying revenue beyond search". Firefox has 2.8% of browsing across all platforms, by StatCounter, and 6.1% on desktops. Privacy, which I value, has not been enough to move people; it has to be the best product too.
firefox

Mozilla is, to be fair, moving closer. On 12 October it introduced Firefox Enterprise, a separately branded build "built for organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance requirements", with a management console they run themselves; and its paid support for organisations, now called Firefox Professional Support, includes "custom development options". That is the villager offer, sold to institutions. What is missing is the same offer for one person. So here is the offer. Let me tell Firefox what I want, in words. Let an agent make my version, in a sandbox, reversible. And then charge me to keep it working: per version, per change, or a small subscription. Every one of those changes is also a signal of what users want, better than any survey. A custom Firefox of my own works through the plan, and explorer coding is the name I would give the first step.
firefox
Four ways a user would pay the vendor: explore, keep, adopt and own, with a price range for each.
settings

The usual answer to "I want it to behave differently" is a setting, and settings are where a lot of technical debt lives. Every setting is a branch in the code that has to be tested forever, and products accumulate them until nobody can change anything safely. The better answer is engineering: small primitives, clean extension points, design systems that make variation cheap. A good example is dark mode. For years companies announced it as a feature; on the sites we build, five colour schemes are just there, because the design system was built for it. When the product is built that way, a user's change is a small, safe thing to maintain. When it is not, it is a fork nobody wants.
settings

That is why I think this needs real engineering investment from the companies that want to survive it. Being the villager and town planner for millions of explorers means a core designed to be built on, and a pipeline that keeps thousands of personal versions working on every release. Some will not make that move, and their replacements may come from a completely different industry.
limits

Not that products are dead. The clones are early, and most users will not rebuild anything. The positioning is a proposal. I found no vendor selling it to individual users, and no one arguing it in these terms; Mozilla now sells custom development to organisations. The prices are illustrative. Mine, not a market study. Firefox's 157 changes are recent. Some of my complaints were fixed in September; the iPad one was not. The sell-off had many causes. The February moves are reported, not explained, here. If you run a product and want to try selling the maintenance of what your users build, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Abstract: The PHP story is where this newsroom explores, and this newsroom is where the lessons settle: the wires here, the Industry Wire, AWS, OWASP and Portugal, will become more effective with what the PHP agents are learning. One lesson is about references. Every source a story uses comes with a set of primitives worth recording: its licence (Creative Commons, Wikipedia's share-alike, or all rights reserved), its access (open, behind a bot challenge, behind a paywall), its links, its quotes, its quality, and its history. The PHP site's source watch already records the access and keeps the history: of 913 pages it watches, 735 were open, 59 behind a bot challenge and 15 paywalled. The idea I want to explore is the shadow. When we cannot read an article, we can still read what others say about it. Wikipedia's PHP2Shell article rests 8 of its 39 statements on paywalled sources, including a quote from The New York Times, which its editors could read and we can now cite. From enough shadow you can start to see the article. You can also see where the shadow and the source disagree, and, over time, who did the research and who recycled it. And where we use a source's work, there should be a payment funnel back to it, through the micropayments our readers pay us, especially when the source certifies how we used it.
Seeing a paywalled article through its shadow: Wikipedia, other outlets, social posts and our own captures around it.
in-short

The PHP story explores; this newsroom settles. The wires here will learn from the PHP agents. Every reference has primitives. Licence, access, links, quotes, quality, history. Some are already recorded. Of 913 watched pages, 735 open, 59 behind a bot challenge, 15 paywalled. The shadow of an article is evidence. Who cites it, what they quote, what they say it says. Wikipedia shows it well. 8 of 39 statements in its PHP2Shell article rest on paywalled sources. The shadow can disagree with the source. That is worth catching. Over time, a view of who got it right. Who researched, who recycled. And a payment back to every source we use, especially when it certifies us.
explore-settle

This article is for this newsroom, but it comes from the PHP one. Remember that we started experimenting here with the wire: the Industry Wire, then wires for AWS, OWASP and Portugal, each fed from a vault its agents write to. Since then, the PHP story's agents have gone much further in how they find, capture, check and publish sources. That is the explorer work. The plan is to bring what they learn back here, to make this newsroom the villager, and to make our wires a lot more effective. This is one of those lessons.
primitives

What every reference should carry, recorded at each capture: licence, access, links, quotes, quality, history and payee. When a story has a reference, it already comes with a set of primitives that are quite interesting. The licence. What the material is published under. At one end, Wikipedia and the other commons, and bloggers who release their work under Creative Commons, as I do here. At the other, a page that is free to read on a website but whose content is all rights reserved. The licence decides what we may quote, copy and republish. The access. Can we read it? Wikipedia, yes. Most public websites, yes, even the ones full of ads. Some sit behind a bot challenge, some behind a login, and some behind a paywall. Our focus is to use only the access we are entitled to, because what we want, eventually, is to pay every one of them.
primitives

The PHP site's source watch already records the access of every page it watches, every time it looks. Of 913 pages from 597 publishers in 59 countries, 735 served their content to an anonymous browser, 59 served a bot challenge, 61 were down, 8 were gone, 35 were unchecked, and 15 were paywalled: "subscription press we hold no licence for". It also keeps the history: a new snapshot whenever a page changes, 2,946 of them, each with its text, a screenshot and the hashes. What it does not record yet is the licence of each page. That is the first gap. The PHP site's source watch: a vault watching 913 pages from 597 publishers, keeping a snapshot when content changed.
primitives

The links and the quotes. For every page we track, we should also track every link on it and every quote it makes. And, the other way round, every page that links to it and every quote taken from it. Take a BBC story: a whole set of other sites will quote it. We should track the quotes, and what they say about the story. The quality. Of the information, and of the reference. Is it primary, or is it repeating someone else? Did it hold up? Was it corrected, and how?
shadow

Here is the interesting part. Depending on what it is, we might be able to use that information. Say Wikipedia links to an article behind a paywall. The Wikipedia editors could read it, and they quote it. Now we can use that quote ourselves, referenced to them, and see the flow. And from the shadow of an article, we can start to see the real article: if enough references to it say what it says, together they give a good understanding of it.
shadow

The PHP site has just made this measurable. Its ontologist now reads Wikipedia's PHP2Shell article as a graph: one statement per sentence, each joined to the references it cites. At the latest revision it read, 8 of its 39 statements rest on references from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, the Australian Financial Review and The Atlantic, all of them subscription titles. One of those statements is a quote: "Coverage in The New York Times said that PHP was "pervasive" and speculated that "everyday users" could have their personal data put at risk." Another, from the Australian Financial Review: "The Internet Archive briefly shut down to fix the issue." We have not read either article; we can still cite what Wikipedia's editors said they say, and say so. Every reference in Wikipedia's PHP2Shell article as the PHP site reads it: 43 references at revision 1381798757.
shadow

Of the article's 43 references, 16 are pages the site's evidence vault already holds; the rest are requests to the collectors. A reference we hold is evidence we can cite as our own, with the capture's hash. A reference we cannot read, because we have no licence, is still a node in the graph, with its shadow around it.
disagree

The shadow is also where inconsistencies show. Is a comment relevant to what the page actually says? Or is it picking up one specific point, while the article has other, more interesting ones? Does the quote match the source when we can see the source? Has the source changed since it was quoted? That last one is not hypothetical. On 24 October the PHP site's correspondent caught that Sansec's own post had changed between two captures: on 22 October it compared the flaw to Heartbleed and said default configurations were vulnerable; on 23 October, both were gone. Anyone who had quoted the first version was now quoting something the source no longer says. Because we keep a copy of every capture, we can go back, and see historically how it unfolded.
who-got-it-right

Put it all together, and we start to have an informed opinion on the accuracy of a lot of this reporting, and on how it evolved: who got it right, who did not, who did the research, and who was recycling information. That is not a ranking we assign. It is a record that builds up from the captures, the quotes and the corrections. The PHP site's Wikipedia section says the same of its own aim: in time, a source's trust shown by how often its statements are corrected, rather than assumed.
paying

The commercial model follows from the primitives. When we use a source's data for something, and we have the evidence of exactly what we used, there should be a payment funnel back to that source, through the micropayments we charge our own readers. This site's economics pages already argue that the value behind a reader's payment belongs mostly to the people who produced the facts, not to the outlet that distributed them. It works best where the source also certifies how we used it: a source that signs our representation of its work is worth paying more, because that is the check that scales. And for paywalled sources, it gives us a way in that we would choose: not to read around the wall, but to pay through it, per use, for what we actually cite.
here

For this newsroom's wires, the first steps are small: Record the licence and the access of every source each wire uses, on every capture. Keep the links and the quotes of every page, in and out, as a graph the wire's agents can read. Mark the shadow when a source cannot be read: who cites it, what they quote, with the quote's own source. Flag the disagreements between a quote and its source, and between two captures of the same page.
limits

Licences are not recorded yet, on the PHP site or here; access and history are. A shadow is not the article. A quote through Wikipedia is Wikipedia's reading of it, and is cited as such. "Paywalled" is the watch's classification of 15 pages at its last export, on 23 October; it changes. The payment funnel is a design. No source is paid through it today. Who got it right is a record to build, not a verdict anyone has yet.
sources

Abstract: I spent today at a sovereignty event, and what struck me most is how much of Europe's sovereignty conversation is about things we do not control and will not control soon: frontier models, giant data centres, GPUs. That is playing where the ball is, not where it is going, and in padel, which I am learning, that is the difference between having all the time in the world and having none. My view is that technology sovereignty is the ability to move, and that it comes from treating every dot in the stack, commodity, product or custom built, as something you can replace. The test is a Wardley map with one question: take away the dot, what happens? If the answer is that the service stops, that is a board-level risk with a name next to it. The fix is not an alternative that is as good as today, which is why most efforts never start. It is a twin of the thing you do not control, running in your QA environment, good enough for the minimum viable company: the priority customers and the services that must not stop, slower, dearer, tested every week. Can it move is the first question; is it cheap and does it scale is the second, and we keep confusing them. Open source is the only kind of control that survives an acquisition. Europe does not lack startups or talent; it lacks the commercial open source model that would let its many small players add up. And now, with models that can read a map and run a simulation on a twin, this analysis can finally be done at scale.

Take away the dot, in three frames. One service as it runs; object storage removed and the blast radius followed up the edges to the customers; a twin of the storage, tested in QA, putting the service back for the priority customers, degraded but running. Use the controls to stop on each frame.
in-short

Europe's sovereignty conversation is mostly about things it does not control. Frontier models, giant data centres and GPUs are where the ball is today. They take years and capital, and they benefit whoever already has them. Most real work does not need a frontier model. Play where the ball is going. A good padel player always seems to have time, because they read the ball and move to where it will be. If I move after it comes off the glass, there is no hope. Sovereignty is the same game. Sovereignty is the ability to move. Agility, almost liquidity: the ability to move a workload, and an action, from one provider to another, including inside the same cloud. Very few companies can, because everything was hard-coded, clicked into existence, and never deployed twice.
in-short

Take away the dot. Draw the Wardley map, remove one thing you do not control, and follow the edges up. If the service stops, you have found the problem, and it belongs on the risk register, all the way to the top. Do not jump from zero to a hundred. The alternative does not have to be as good as today. It has to work, for the minimum viable company: the priority customers and the services that must never stop. Slower and dearer is fine. Zero is not. Run it in QA, all the time. A twin of every dependency you do not control, running in disposable QA environments, is how this stops being theory. If you only do it in an emergency, you will discover every small problem during the emergency.
in-short

Can it move, then is it cheap. The first question is whether it is possible. Whether it is cost effective and scalable is a second question, and asking it first is how sovereignty conversations end before they start. Open source, or one acquisition away. A European supplier today is one acquisition from not being one. Only open source and Creative Commons give control that survives a change of owner, in either direction.
ball

I am learning to play padel, and the thing that is most striking about watching a good player is how much time they have. They are not faster than me. They read the ball, they know where it will be after it comes off the glass, and they are already there. If I do not read the ball, or I move after it has bounced off the back wall, there is no hope; I am always late, and every shot is a scramble. The same idea is usually told with the line attributed to Wayne Gretzky, about skating to where the puck is going rather than where it has been, and it is the best short description I know of what Europe gets wrong in the sovereignty conversation.
ball

The ball today is the frontier model, the giant data centre and the GPU. Those are real, and they matter, and they are where the ball is now. Building them takes years and a scale of capital that only benefits the players who already have the infrastructure and can leverage it. You cannot compete with that, and trying to is moving after the ball has hit the glass. Judo for small countries, written this afternoon, makes the same point for a single country: the capital race is the wrong end of the map, and most real work does not need a frontier model anyway. The models are becoming a commodity. Very few use cases need the frontier, and for the ones that do not, a frontier model is too expensive, too powerful and more dangerous than the job needs.
ball
Where the ball is going is the ability to move: workloads, data and the actions agents take, from one provider to another, when you decide, and not on the day a supplier decides for you.
move

The way I think about it now is that sovereignty is mostly agility, almost liquidity: the ability to move a workload and keep operating. And the honest test of most organisations is that they cannot do it, not between clouds and often not even within the same hyperscaler. The infrastructure was hard-coded, created by clicks, built up over generations of changes, and never deployed in a second place. That is fragility, whatever the contract says about where the data lives.
move

That is an engineering gap, not a policy gap, in the same way that agentic cost is an engineering problem. And "critical" is a word that gets abused. For a company, a disruption at a supplier, a technology partner or a platform that stops the business is a critical problem whether or not it is national critical infrastructure: you are losing money, losing customers, and not providing what people are paying for. The question for every organisation is the same: can you move the workloads, and are you focusing on what you can control?
dot

The tool for this is the one I keep coming back to, a Wardley map. Put the customer at the top, the service they pay for, your application and your data, and under them the products and commodities you buy. Then ask one question of each dot you do not control: take it away, what happens?
dot

The figure at the top does it in three frames for an illustrative service. Remove the object storage. Follow the edges up: the data has nowhere to live, the application cannot start, the service stops, the customers have nothing. That is the blast radius, the same measure Footprint and blast radius uses for an agent's reach, applied to a dependency. If the blast radius is the whole chain, you know where the problem is, and then you keep asking: what happens when the service stops, and what happens after that. That is the analysis every organisation should be able to do, and the one it should take to the board: by the way, you have a dependency here, and in this scenario you do not have a business.
dot

The important correction to my own first framing is that this applies across the whole stack. It is tempting to say only the products and commodities you buy need an alternative, because custom-built things are yours. But custom-built things stand on commodities, and a custom-built system that only one person can deploy is as much a single point of failure as a supplier. The rule is: you must be able to treat every dot as replaceable, at least to the level of a product, whether you built it or bought it.
zero

A maturity model for every dot you do not control. From 0, it stops, through the data can leave, it runs somewhere once, it runs for the minimum viable company, to 4, it moves when you decide. Each level carries a cost and a population it serves, and each is only real if it was tested. The reason most sovereignty efforts never start is that they set the bar at "an alternative that works just like today, as efficient and as optimised as today". That is a hundred, and nobody gets from zero to a hundred. The bar should be: it works. Unoptimised, maybe not for every customer, maybe not for every feature, but it works.
zero

This is where the minimum viable company comes in, an idea from the resilience and incident-response world: the smallest version of the business that can keep serving customers while the rest recovers. From a disaster recovery and resilience point of view, you should have infrastructure that runs that minimum viable company: the priority customers, the services you must provide, the users who should never go without. Emergency services are the clean example: they should never lose network capability, whatever else fails, so there are backups of backups.
zero

And it is a backup of operations, not only of data. Having the data is necessary and not sufficient. If you do not have the software, the schema and the ability to load and move it, you do not have data mobility; you have an archive. What you need, for every dot you do not control, is the equivalent of a twin: something compatible enough that your application cannot tell, running on infrastructure you can run, perhaps not as efficient, but working. Move the cloud, not the code describes the S3 twin that exists today and why the code must not know it has moved.
zero

Usage and side effects should be a spectrum, not a cliff. When a technology is not available, the service should degrade, not stop. And a point made at the event that I agree with: if customers understood why, understood the disruption and its side effects, many would happily pay for the slower, dearer version that keeps running.
qa

All of this is theoretical until you do it, and if you do it you have to do it all the time. The place to do it is QA and testing. A QA environment should be disposable, created from nothing, and it does not need the scale of production; it needs to work. Run it on the twins: the storage twin, the identity twin, the model you can host yourself. Every time QA is created, you have proved, again, that the business can run without the dots you do not control, for at least a test load. Every time something breaks, you have found it on a Tuesday, not during an outage.
qa

That is also why the alternatives get better. You will discover lots of small problems the first time, and you should solve them when you have time to solve them rather than when there is an emergency. Run it every week and the gap between level 2 and level 3 on the maturity model closes without a migration project anybody had to sign.
possible

When people ask how much technology sovereignty is possible, the question is already loaded, because it mixes two questions. The first is: is it possible? Can this dot be replaced at all, and has anyone tried? The second is: is it cost effective and does it scale? We keep asking the second before the first, and the answer to the second is almost always "not yet", so the conversation ends.
possible

Ask them in order. Possible first, with a cost matrix and a scale matrix written down for each dot: yes, it can run, for this number of customers, this number of users, this set of services, and we tested it last week. Then cost. My expectation is that the engineering benefits of being able to move, deployments that are reproducible, environments that are disposable, dependencies that are understood, end up paying for much of it, even if the main path stays optimised on the incumbent and the alternative runs a little more expensively. And focus on what can move. Do not spend the effort on things you are clearly never going to control, for physical, political, technical or cost reasons. Spend it on the dots where today there is no alternative, or no efficient market, because that is where the ball is going.
open

I have written many times that you cannot have sovereignty unless it is open source, or Creative Commons for content, and the reason is simple. Even if a supplier is European today, you are one acquisition away from losing that. It works both ways: a European company can buy an American one, and the American customers are then in the same position. If you are the underdog, you should be the one playing this game, because you have more to gain and very little to lose. Control that survives a change of owner is the only control that counts, and open source is how you get it: you can read it, run it, fix it and move it. open-source.sgit.ai is my longer argument that open source is a strategy, not a charity.
open

This is also where Europe's real gap is. It is not startups and it is not talent. Prosus and Dealroom's State of AI in Europe, published in March 2026, says "Europe creates as many new AI startups each year as the US", with roughly the same number of AI professionals, "but it converts them into breakout companies at a third of the rate." And the United States is very good at capturing European talent: Stanford's analysis of the founders behind 500 American unicorns, reported by Crunchbase, found that 44% were born outside the US, with the United Kingdom, Germany and France leading the European countries of birth. The gap is positioning, and it is a commercial open source model that Europe never quite developed: many small and medium players that should be connected and aggregated into a bigger play, each leveraging the others and letting the others scale, which is what an open source ecosystem is.
central

It is not realistic to expect every company in a country, or every company in a group or a sector, to build a twin of every dependency on its own. Some of this should be provided centrally, by governments, by industry bodies, by the larger organisations in a supply chain, as infrastructure, in the sense of a road: built once, open, used by everyone, and not a central project that becomes another dependency. Judo for small countries makes the road argument in full, and Move the cloud, not the code describes the business a European infrastructure operator could build by selling the twin layer. The demand, in both cases, comes from the same question asked of every dot.
now

This analysis was always the right one, and it was always too expensive to do properly: drawing a map of every service, removing each dot, following the blast radius, running the simulation, writing it down for the board. That has changed. With today's models the mapping and the simulations can finally be done at scale, and they are much better done on top of twins than in a spreadsheet, because a twin can actually be switched off and the result observed rather than guessed. Map it, take away the dot, run the twin in QA, and put the level-0 dependencies on the register with a name next to them. That is how Europe gets technology sovereignty: by making every part of the stack replaceable, one dot at a time, starting where the ball is going.
limits

The map in the figure is illustrative. It is a typical service, not a measured one; the point is the method. The maturity levels are a proposal. They are how I would score a dependency; they have not been calibrated across organisations. The startup and founder figures are other people's. Prosus and Dealroom report parity in the number of AI startups, not that Europe has more; the Stanford founder study covers unicorns up to 2021 and is not specific to AI. The minimum viable company is not my term. It comes from the resilience and incident-response world; what is mine here is running it on twins in QA. Twins beyond storage are not built. The S3 twin exists; most of the others in this argument are the work to do. If you are running a sovereignty programme and want to take away the dots in your own map, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 12 October 2026, after a day at a sovereignty event, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine.
