Open source as strategy: open-source.sgit.ai.

Abstract: If you are an entrepreneur, start a company, as soon as you have a bit of revenue to put through it. It is more professional, it lets you register for things and keep your work and your intellectual property in one place, and above all it is something a founder has to learn: how companies work, how to read a balance sheet, how shares and the rules between shareholders are set. There is no magic to it. A company is governed by a set of contracts, which today we can read in detail, draw as infographics and make sure are in our favour, and the founder who understands them can bring the rules of the game instead of being played by them. Where you do it matters. In the UK it takes an afternoon: £100 online, model articles by default, and very little to do until you start making real money. In Portugal, forming one is just as quick, but keeping one costs a certified accountant every month, by law, even with no trading, which is why I am closing mine. Lithuania looks as if it has thought this through, and its e-residency is where I would like to look next. I count what I paid in Portugal as the cost of learning. And the first thing to do with the company is the same as before you have one: sell.
Three ways to start a company, side by side: the UK, Portugal and Lithuania.
in-short

Start a company. As soon as there is a bit of revenue to put through it. It is something a founder has to learn. Balance sheets, shares, and who controls what. A company is a set of contracts. Read them, and bring the rules of the game yourself. The UK: an afternoon. About £100 online, and little to do until the money is real. Portugal: the hard way. Quick to form, but a certified accountant every month, by law. Lithuania: next. It looks as if it has thought this through. Count it as the cost of learning. And then do the first thing: sell.
why

If you are an entrepreneur, you should start a company. A lot changes once you have one. It is much more professional. It is the beginning of the journey. You can open accounts and register for things as a business. It keeps things close and connected: the work, the money, and any intellectual property or other assets, managed as the company's and not scattered across your personal life. You will get no credit at first, and that is right: why should anyone give credit to a business with no history and no revenue? What matters is that you are now a company.
why

But the main reason is that it is something you need to learn. As a founder, you need to know how companies work. You need to be able to read a balance sheet. You need to understand how shares are created and given, and what happens to them. And the best way to learn that is to do it, sooner rather than later, and to pay a little for the lesson.
why

My recommendation on timing is simple. As soon as you have a bit of revenue, start the company, because you need somewhere to put the money through. Before that, the alternative every country has is the sole trader: in the UK you register for Self Assessment once your trading income passes the £1,000 trading allowance; in Portugal you open your activity at the tax office, online and free, and in the simplified regime you do not need an accountant. Either way, the point is to start creating revenue and to look as professional as you can. Ask Claude to design you some business cards you can print, and a website, while you are at it.
contracts

There is no magic behind a company. Some readers may not have worked inside large organisations, but I have seen how they work from the inside, and they have far more companies than you would think: financial companies have many, and so do companies you would not expect to. They create them for liability reasons and to reduce risk, to separate what gets sold from what does not, and to segment the business. You can have several companies of your own, for the same reasons.
contracts

The most important thing to understand is that a company is governed by a set of contracts: its articles of association and the agreements between the people who own it. Those contracts are the rules of the game. There are a few things the law does not let you put in them, but for most practical purposes you can put all sorts of clauses there, and you can see both kinds in the tech world: clauses that favour the founders, and clauses that favour the investors or the acquirers. Today we can read those contracts in detail, turn them into infographics, and check that they work in our favour. So I think they should be, first, as simple as possible, and second, on your terms. When the conversation turns to funding and investment, you want to be the one bringing the company and bringing the rules of the game. You want to control them, not be played by them.
contracts

And remember that companies get bought and sold, and so do their shares. I have seen acquisitions done by creating another company. What matters in the end is the share ownership, the allocations, the rights, and who controls what. Part of the founder's journey is learning that, or having someone next to you who knows it. When investment comes, it should come when you are profitable, with product-market fit, and executing; sell, don't issue is how I think that deal should look.
uk

The UK is where this is easy. My first UK company was created when I was still at university. A friend and I had got a project, and the client told us they could not pay us unless we were a company. That sounded complicated. We went to the local business group, they told us to go and create one, we did, and we got paid. How cool is that? And because we were a company, other things became possible. It is still that simple, and the facts as they stand today: It is fast and cheap. Registering online with Companies House costs £100 (it was £50 until 1 February 2026), and "your company is usually registered within 24 hours". Formation companies will do it for you and help with the name and the paperwork; the basic packages cost little more than the fee, and the fuller ones cost a few hundred pounds, which is roughly what I remember paying.
uk

The rules come by default. If you do not write your own articles of association, the model articles for a private company limited by shares apply: a set of shares, the directors, and how decisions are made. You say roughly what you do. You choose a SIC code that identifies what the company does. You prove who you are. Since 18 November 2025, every director has to verify their identity with Companies House. Then very little, until the money is real. Each year you file accounts and a confirmation statement (£50 online), even if the company is dormant. With no revenue and a few costs, an accountant can do it quickly and charge you a little. Miss the date and the first penalty is £150, so do not, but it is nothing dramatic. When there is profit, you pay Corporation Tax on it: 19% on profits up to £50,000.
uk

That is what happened with The Cyber Boardroom, the first of the companies behind my recent work. There was not a lot of trade in its first year, and we submitted the accounts. The UK only starts to care when you start to make serious money, which is how it should be. It is also easy to change. You can dissolve companies, join them, be a director of one. I started a startup with some other people; we worked on it, and eventually I decided to leave. That was fine. It is all pretty straightforward, and that is exactly why it is a good place to learn. If the UK were still in the European Union, I would simply say: start your company in the UK.
portugal

In Portugal, forming a company is not the problem. Empresa na Hora forms one on the spot, at a single counter, for €360. The problem is what it costs to keep it. When I set up a company in Portugal, for MyFeeds, I found that I immediately had a cost of 200 to 300 euros a month for an accountant. I could not believe it. My strategy, probably not the best one, was to go back to my accountant after a couple of months and say: come on, I am not trading, I am not taking any of your time, let us renegotiate. He told me a long story, and I even asked other accountants. Long story short, it is the law.
portugal

The law is two provisions together. The corporate income tax code says companies "são obrigadas a dispor de contabilidade organizada", are obliged to keep organised accounts (CIRC, article 123), with no threshold for companies. And the statute of the certified accountants reserves to them the signing of the accounts and of the tax returns based on them (Estatuto da OCC, article 10). So a company with no trading still needs a certified accountant to sign off its filings: the periodic VAT return, quarterly for a small company, and the annual returns. That means two or three thousand euros a year, before you have sold anything.
portugal

My 200 to 300 euros a month is towards the upper end; published prices for a new small company run from about €150 to €300 a month. But the point stands. In the UK a company with no revenue costs almost nothing to keep; in Portugal it costs thousands a year. So I am closing it, and I have learned my lesson.
lithuania

That is why I am now looking at starting a company in Lithuania. What I like is that they seem to have thought it through and mapped it out. The memo said e-citizenship; the right name is e-residency. Lithuania's e-residency has existed since 2021: it costs €90 for three years, you give your biometrics in person once, and it gives you a Lithuanian digital identity and a qualified electronic signature for the government's e-services. A small partnership, the MB, needs no minimum capital; a private limited company, the UAB, needs €1,000 since May 2023. Every company needs a registered address in Lithuania, and its annual accounts are filed even when it does not trade. I have not found a requirement for a certified accountant.
lithuania

What I do not know yet is how much of the company can be done remotely, end to end, with the e-resident card alone; the sources disagree, and a bank account is its own step. That is what I would like to find out, by doing it, and I will write it up when I have. Estonia is the country that built this road first, and judo for small countries is the case for why every small country should: the plumbing that lets a talented person form a company and sell to the world is an opportunity for a country, and in most of Europe it is still custom built. Ironically, today, the countries that make it easy have a competitive advantage over the ones that do not.
learning

I view all of this as a cost of learning. In the UK the cost was small; in Portugal I lost some money. But we all spend money on all sorts of things, so you might as well spend it on learning. If you look at everything you spend money on, the things where you learned something are the better ones. So my recommendation is: start a company as soon as you can start trading, because the most important thing is not the company. It is to start selling, to start experimenting, and to start being profitable, so that the company pays for itself. That is the other half of this pair: can you sell it?
limits

This is not legal or tax advice. It is my experience, with the rules checked on 19 October 2026. The Portuguese cost is my experience. Published prices are a range; mine was towards the top. The legal requirement is read from two provisions. Neither one says, in those words, that every company must hire a certified accountant; together they mean it. Lithuania is a consideration, not a decision. Nothing is registered, and remote formation with e-residency alone is not confirmed. The UK prices change. The incorporation fee doubled in February 2026.
sources

Abstract: I pay for a lot of subscriptions I do not really use, and I think most people do: a tool with a bit of my data in it, a conferencing service I might need next month, a capability I do not want to switch off because restarting it is painful when the day comes. So I keep paying. This is a proposal for a service that fixes that, run by a helper working for one person, with agents doing most of the work. It starts politely, not with the law: ask the company for a detailed account of how much we used the product, and in parallel do our own analysis from statements, invoices and the account's own dashboards. A few days later, with both sets of numbers side by side, send a friendly request that says what we used, what it was worth, and what we like about the product, and asks for two things: a suspend mode that keeps the data, and a refund for the months we did not use. Either way, stop the bleeding. Only if nobody answers does the right of access come in, and only as a genuine request for our own data. The companies are not obliged to refund, and I want to be honest about that, but the direction of travel is clear, with the UK's new subscription rules arriving in January 2027. Everything we learn, the contacts, the templates and which companies refund, goes into an open register under Creative Commons. The helper is paid 10% of the savings for the next three months and 20% of whatever is recovered, which only works if the agents do the heavy lifting. So the agent drives the browser through Claude in Chrome, and the freelancer only types the passwords and the two-factor codes and sends the drafts; everything else is automated, under a behaviour policy, and the freelancer's interface is a set of vaults: the documentation, the tasks, the map of every subscription and the messages between them. It is a first MVP, and a number of early beta users, me included, are about to run it on their own subscriptions.
One subscription, worked by a helper and an agent for the person who pays: two questions, a letter and an open register.
in-short

Most of us pay for things we keep and do not use. Not because we forgot, but because there is data in there, or we might need it, and restarting is painful. The UK government puts the cost of unwanted subscriptions at £1.6 billion a year. Start with a question, not a demand. Ask the company for a detailed account of our usage, and in parallel do our own analysis. Two sets of numbers are better than one, and the first letter concedes nothing. Then ask for a pause and a refund, nicely. Say what we used and when, what it was worth, and what is good about the product. We want to keep it, in a suspend mode that keeps the data, and we want the unused months back. Stop the bleeding either way. Export the data, then pause or cancel. The payments stop whatever the answer to the refund.
in-short

The law is a floor, not the product. A refund for months you did not use is generally not owed. The right of access is real, and it is for getting your data, never for leverage. The UK's subscription rules come into force in January 2027. Everything goes into an open register. Contacts, templates, which companies offer a pause, which refund and which do not, under Creative Commons, recorded as facts with dates rather than adjectives. A service for helpers, run by agents. 10% of the next three months of savings and 20% of what is recovered. At those rates it only pays if the agent does most of the work. The freelancer types secrets and sends drafts. Everything else is automated. Claude in Chrome drives the browser and stops at a login page; the freelancer enters the password or the code and otherwise watches, without browsing. The Gmail connector writes drafts; the freelancer sends them.
in-short

The vaults are the interface. The documentation, the tasks, the map of every subscription and the messages between the freelancer and the agents all live in vaults, with Issues-FS and Email-FS. A first MVP. A number of early beta users, me included, are about to run it on their own subscriptions, partly to find out which tools do this best.
keep

I have a lot of these. You subscribe to something, you use it for a while, there is a bit of data in it, and then you do not really use it. But you might need the capability. And you do not want to stop the whole thing, because on the day you need it again you will not have the time, and restarting is painful: the account, the settings, the history, the integrations. So it sits there, and you keep paying. It is a conferencing tool, a design tool, a storage plan, a research service, a premium tier of something you once needed for a month.
keep

The numbers say this is not just me. In its consultation on the new subscription regime the UK government estimates that 8% of active subscriptions are unwanted, about 9.7 million contracts, and on 9 August 2026 it put the total at "around 155 million active subscriptions in the UK, with consumers spending an estimated £1.6 billion a year on ones they don't actually want". Citizens Advice found in 2024 that people had spent £688 million in the previous year on subscriptions they did not use. On subscriptions.sgit.ai I put the principle in one sentence: "A subscription is a discount for committing to regular use. It is not rent on something you have the right to ignore." That site is about the standard and the register. This article is about the other half: a practical service that helps one person, today, with the subscriptions on their statement.
ask

The first move is not a legal one. It is a polite email to the company: can you give me a detailed analysis of how much this account has been used? Logins, meetings, storage, seats, documents, by month, for the period I have been paying. It is a reasonable question from a customer, it costs the company little to answer, and it concedes nothing on either side. It is also the question subscriptions.sgit.ai is built on, put slightly differently there: "do you hold a record of my usage?", which every company can answer, even when the answer is no.
ask

In parallel, we do our own analysis, because two sets of numbers are better than one and because we should not depend on the company to know what we did. The statements and invoices say what was paid and when. The account's own dashboards, settings and history pages usually say a lot about what was used: the last meeting, the last upload, the last login, the seats nobody signed into. All of that should be exported now, while we still have access, into a vault that belongs to the person. The workflows page on the subscriptions site describes the pipeline this reuses, which I ran on my own statements in March: the statements go into a vault, an agent works inside it and commits what it finds, and the output, instead of an accountant's pack, is a file per subscription.
ask
Then the two meet. Where the company's numbers and ours agree, the case is simple. Where they disagree, that is the interesting part, and the next question to ask.
request

A couple of days later, with the evidence in hand, we write back. This letter matters, and its tone is the point. It maps exactly what happened: we paid from this month to this month, we last used it on this date, here is our analysis and here is yours. It says what the product was worth to us when we used it. And it says good things about the product, honestly, because there is a reason we chose it, and there is a reason we did not want to cancel it. Then it asks for two things. The first is a suspend mode: we like the product and want to keep using it, but not right now, so please put the account into a state that keeps our data and our settings and does not charge us. The second is a refund for the months we did not use.
request

The first ask is not as unusual as it sounds. Several large services already have a pause button. Netflix pauses a membership "for 1 month", up to three months in total. Zoom lets small monthly Pro accounts pause for up to three months at a time, which is exactly the conferencing case. YouTube Premium, Audible and Hulu have one too, with conditions. Many do not, and the letter is how a company learns that its customers want one.
stop

Whatever the answer to the refund, the payments should stop. If there is a pause, use it. If there is not, export the data and cancel. This is the part that delivers value on day one, whether or not a single penny comes back, and it is the part that most people never get round to, because each subscription is a small decision that is easy to postpone. The order matters: export first, then cancel. The data is the reason the account was kept, so losing it in the cancellation would turn a saving into a loss. And watch the terms: some plans charge for leaving early. Adobe's US subscription terms, for example, charge a fee of half the remaining balance for cancelling an annual plan paid monthly after the first fourteen days. Knowing that before the letter is part of the analysis.
law

I want to be honest here, because the subscriptions site says it plainly and it is true: "'You did not use it' yields nothing on its own." In general, a company does not have to refund months you paid for and did not use. The money comes back as a legal right only in specific cases: inside a cooling-off period, where the trader did not give you the cancellation information it should have (under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 that can extend the cancellation period by up to twelve months), for payments taken after you cancelled, or where the service was not provided with reasonable care and skill. Most of the refunds this service asks for will be goodwill.
law

That is why the request is friendly, and why I think it can work anyway. The direction of travel is clear, and companies will find it harder and harder to justify charging for a period nobody could use. In the UK, the subscription contracts regime in the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 brings reminder notices, an easy exit and a new fourteen-day cooling-off period after a trial or a renewal, and on 9 August 2026 the government said those rules "will now come into force in January 2027", earlier than the spring 2027 date it had given in April. In the EU, a withdrawal button for online contracts applies from 19 June 2026. In California, AB 2863 has required click-to-cancel and annual reminders since July 2025. And in the United States more widely, the FTC's click-to-cancel rule was vacated by the Eighth Circuit in July 2025, and the FTC started again in March 2026. None of these rules says "refund the months I ignored". All of them move the default towards the customer.
access

I would not start with a subject access request, and the reason is the tone: the first letter should be the one a good customer sends. But if the first letter gets no answer, the right of access is the next step, and it is a real one. Under UK GDPR, the ICO's guide says a company "must respond without undue delay, and within one month of receipt of the request", extendable by up to two further months for complex requests, and in most cases cannot charge a fee. The European Data Protection Board's guidelines on the right of access list "activity logs such as access logs, history of website usage" among the data a person can ask for, so the usage record of a personal account is in scope. The ICO also confirms that a third party with the appropriate authority can make the request on someone's behalf, which is the helper's position.
access

One rule, from the subscriptions site, matters more than the mechanics: "Every access request is a genuine request for the person's own data, sent because they want it. It is never sent as leverage, never bundled with a demand." An access request used as a threat is how the mechanism gets refused and how it loses its value for everybody else. So the access request asks for the data, and the refund conversation stays a separate conversation.
register

There are a couple of services in this, but I think we should open source the whole method, under Creative Commons, and publish what we learn as we figure it out. For every company: how to reach the people who can actually decide, the templates that worked, whether a pause exists, how long they took to answer, and what they said.
register

That includes the companies that refund and the companies that do not. I would like to give real kudos to the companies that do it, because they are not obliged to, and that deserves to be said loudly. And I would like to have the data on the companies that say no. The subscriptions site has already worked out how to publish that safely, and I would follow its rules exactly: record, never verdict, with no adjectives anywhere; the reply quoted with the person's details removed; silence recorded as a row, not a blank; "we do not hold that" recorded neutrally; never publish a first refusal, only one given after a second ask; and the good path published as prominently as the bad. A dated row that says "asked on this date, answered on that date, refunded three months" is the kudos. A dated row that says "asked twice, no reply as at this date" needs no adjective. The register publishes a company's behaviour, never a person's case.
helper

This is a service I think a lot of people could provide, and that a lot of people would use: a freelancer, a bookkeeper, a virtual assistant, a student, anybody organised and persistent, working for an individual or a small business. The helper is paid from what they save. My suggestion: 10% of the savings for the next three months, and 20% of any money recovered. Nothing saved, nothing paid.
helper

That is deliberately low. For comparison, Rocket Money's bill negotiation charges "a fee of 35% - 60% of your first year's savings". And it is worth doing the arithmetic, because it explains the rest of this design. The government's figure for the average unwanted subscription is £14 a month. Stopping one earns the helper 10% of three months of that, £4.20. Recovering six months of it, £84, earns 20%, £16.80. Per subscription those are small numbers. They add up only across many subscriptions per client and many clients per helper, which means the helper cannot be doing the analysis, the letters and the follow-ups by hand.
agents

All of this should be done agentically, and the setup is the one I already run, described in Replicating the agentic inbox: an account of the agent's own connected to Claude, a mailbox of its own, vaults for the work, and a behaviour policy written before the first run. Three pieces of tooling do the work.
agents

A browser the agent drives. Claude in Chrome lets Claude read a page and click, type and fill forms in the browser, and since 26 August 2026 it is available on every paid Claude plan. The agent goes to each subscription, finds the usage history, the invoices and the export button, downloads what it needs into the vault, and later pauses or cancels when the decision has been made. The freelancer, the operator, sees all of it happen in the browser, and interacts only when a secret is needed: a password, a two-factor code, a captcha. That is not only my rule, it is the tool's. Anthropic's Claude Code documentation says that "when Claude encounters a login page or CAPTCHA, it pauses and asks you to handle it manually", and its safety guidance lists "Inputting sensitive data" among the things Claude is prohibited from doing. Apart from entering credentials, the freelancer should not be browsing the sites. That matters for the MVP: the point is to learn the best way to use these tools, and which tools are best, and that is only learned if the agent does the work. Anthropic also offers 1Password for Claude, in beta, which fills a login without the password entering Claude's context; that is one of the tools to try. The same guidance recommends a separate browser profile for this kind of work, and The vault crosses Chrome profiles is about how state can follow a person from one profile to another.
agents

Email through a connector. The agent's Gmail is connected to Claude, and the agent writes every letter, the usage request, the refund request, the follow-ups, as a draft. The freelancer reads each one and sends it. Every draft passes a second reader the agent cannot skip first. The freelancer writes on the person's behalf, so the person's authority to act is captured as evidence in their vault before the first letter, which is also what lets the freelancer make an access request for them later.
agents

Vaults as the interface. The freelancer does not work in a dashboard. The vaults are the documentation of what was found, the project management, with tasks as folders in Issues-FS, the map of every subscription with its evidence, and the channel between the freelancer and the agents, with messages as files in Email-FS, as Memory is not a spectator sport describes. The person's statements and evidence sit in a vault of their own; the register's rows sit in a public one. Nothing about a person leaves their vault. So the controls, today, are two, and they are simple to say. Secrets are entered by the freelancer. Drafts are sent by the freelancer. Everything else is automated. And the agent can make the decisions along the way, but, as I argued in Who owns the words, the responsibility stays with the person who sends.
agents

The helper's agent as a behaviour policy: reach, mandate, gap and what stands in the way. A proposal, not measured. The policy is where the hard part stays visible. Once the freelancer has signed in, the session the agent works in has the account's whole reach: the same login that downloads the invoices can delete the data, close the account, upgrade the plan or change the card. And the Gmail connector can send as well as draft; by default Claude asks for approval before sending, and on a Team plan the owner decides whether that can be switched off. So "drafts only" is our policy, held by that approval and by the freelancer, not something the tool makes impossible, and the figure says so. That is fine for a first MVP with beta users who know what they are trying. It is also exactly what the MVP is for: finding which of these rows can be turned into real controls.
agents

There is one more thing to say plainly, because Anthropic says it. Its safety guidance "strongly advise[s] against" using Claude in Chrome for, among other things, "Managing financial accounts or investments" and "Interacting with sites containing personal information of others", and it reminds the user that they remain responsible for every action Claude takes on their behalf. A subscription account is not a bank account, but it has billing pages, and the person whose account it is is not the freelancer. That is why the beta starts with our own subscriptions, why each person's accounts are worked in a browser profile of their own with nothing else signed in, and why a session that reaches anything like a bank or a payment page stops and goes back to the person. Whether this kind of work belongs in a browser-driving agent at all, or in a narrower tool, is one of the things the MVP is meant to answer.
limits

It is a first MVP, not yet run. A number of early beta users, me included, are about to try it on their own subscriptions. The statement pipeline it reuses ran in March on my own statements; the rest is a proposal until they have. Most refunds will be goodwill. Unused months are generally not refundable as of right; the legal levers are narrower, and this is not legal advice. The consumer rules may not cover business accounts. The UK and EU rules quoted protect consumers. A sole trader or small company paying for a business tool may not be one, and the request then rests on goodwill alone. The law is as at 13 October 2026. The UK regime is not in force until January 2027; the EU button depends on national transposition; the US federal rule is being written again.
limits

The fee split is a suggestion. Contingency fees can change how a service looks to a regulator, and the card-issuer route is left out until there is advice on it, as the subscriptions site says. The register has no entries yet. Its rules are written; a solicitor review of the publishing rule is still listed as pending on subscriptions.sgit.ai. The signed-in session is the reach. The freelancer types the secrets, but the session the agent then works in can do far more than the mandate; the red rows in the figure are open. The tool's maker advises caution here. Anthropic advises against using Claude in Chrome for financial accounts and for sites holding other people's personal information; the beta runs on its users' own subscriptions first for that reason.
limits

The person shares access with the freelancer. How a person gives a freelancer the means to sign in, and keeps the ability to take it back, is part of what the MVP has to learn. If you would like to be one of the next beta users, as a helper or as someone helped, or you run a subscription business and want to be in the register for the right reasons, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Summary: I pay for a lot of subscriptions I do not really use, and I think most people do: a tool with a bit of my data in it, a conferencing service I might need next month, a capability I do not want to switch off because restarting it is painful when the day comes. So I keep paying. This is a proposal for a service that fixes that, run by a helper working for one person, with agents doing most of the work. It starts politely, not with the law: ask the company for a detailed account of how much we used the product, and in parallel do our own analysis from statements, invoices and the account's own dashboards. A few days later, with both sets of numbers side by side, send a friendly request that says what we used, what it was worth, and what we like about the product, and asks for two things: a suspend mode that keeps the data, and a refund for the months we did not use. Either way, stop the bleeding. Only if nobody answers does the right of access come in, and only as a genuine request for our own data. The companies are not obliged to refund, and I want to be honest about that, but the direction of travel is clear, with the UK's new subscription rules arriving in January 2027. Everything we learn, the contacts, the templates and which companies refund, goes into an open register under Creative Commons. The helper is paid 10% of the savings for the next three months and 20% of whatever is recovered, which only works if the agents do the heavy lifting, under a behaviour policy, with the one hard problem left in the open: the agent needs to work inside accounts it must never hold the passwords to.

The agent does what agents are good at: reading statements, building the inventory, comparing two sets of numbers, drafting the letters, chasing the replies, keeping the record and preparing the register row. The helper reviews. The person whose money it is approves and sends, from their own address, because the company deals with the account holder, and because, as I argued in Who owns the words, the agent can make decisions but the responsibility stays with the person who signs. This work needs access to a lot of systems: every subscription is an account, with its own login, and the usage history and the export button are behind it. And one row is not solved: the agent must never hold the person's passwords. The direction is right in the products that keep credentials apart from the agent, as I wrote about Meta's design in A personal agent that keeps your secrets, where the agent "has no visibility into people's passwords or payment methods". For this service I think the answer is that the person signs in and the agent works inside that session, with the session's reach written into the policy, but how to do that well, across fifty different login pages, is the thing we need to figure out, and I would rather say so than pretend.

Abstract: Markus Franz published "The Article Is Only the Beginning" on 7 October 2026, proposing Liquid Utility, journalism that helps people understand, follow and act rather than only read, and six Reader Skills to deliver it, with a bridge closure as the example. He then wrote, under my comment, that his idea and the story vault connect at an architectural level: the story vault answers what we know and why it can be trusted, Reader Skills answer what we can reliably help someone do with it. This article draws that connection. Each of his six skills turns out to be an operation the story graph already supports, and each safeguard he asks for is a property the graph already has: versions for Update, supersede edges for corrections, freshness for "could not check", a flag at the node for protected sources. His bridge is drawn as a graph. And his article adds the piece our monetisation had not mapped: locality, where the trust relationship and the brand are strongest. Local contributors feed local journalists, local stories feed national and international ones, and if every use pays back down the chain of claims it rests on, small payments from many people fund the reporting nearest to them.

Where the two ideas meet: each of Markus Franz's six Reader Skills as an operation on the story graph, and the property of the graph that makes it dependable. The skills are his; the mapping is ours. A bridge closes for six weeks. The reporting is clear: what happened, why the repairs are needed, who is responsible. And the parent reading it on Sunday evening still has three questions. Can the children take their usual bus tomorrow? What changes on Monday morning? Will someone tell me if that changes again? That is the opening of The Article Is Only the Beginning, published by Markus Franz on 7 October 2026, and it holds two lines worth keeping: "The article has done its job. You still have a job to do."

His proposal is called Liquid Utility: trusted journalistic knowledge, combined with reusable methods and appropriate tools, to help someone understand, follow or act on what matters to them. He delivers it through six Reader Skills, bounded journalistic capabilities a reader can use directly: Understand, Update, Relate, Compare, Follow and Act. It is careful about what it does not claim. A skill is not a safety guarantee. The case for a publisher over a generic assistant has to rest on original access, maintained data, local reporting and editorial accountability, and even then the service has to be demonstrably better at a particular task. And the business test is kept visible: reach, utility, relationship, reciprocity, measured rather than assumed. I replied under his post that this is close to what I argue in The future of news is the story vault, not the paywall. His answer is the reason this article exists:

He is right, and the connection is tighter than either article said on its own. This is the drawing of it. Read them in order, or start with the one you need: the idea, the connection, the simulation explained, and the working vault. The story vault keeps what was reported as a graph: claims, each tied to evidence that has been fetched, saved and hashed; sources, with how recently each was checked; versions, where a correction supersedes a claim rather than deleting it. The article is one projection of that graph. The figure at the top puts Markus's six skills on top of it, and each one becomes an operation.

Take his own description of Update. He writes that "summarise the latest article" is not enough: the method "would need to establish the previous information state, retrieve current reporting, separate new facts from repetition, flag corrections and show the sources behind each meaningful change." Every clause of that is something a versioned graph gives you directly. The previous information state is the version the reader last saw. New facts are new claim nodes. Corrections are supersede edges, dated. The sources behind each change are the edges from each new claim to its evidence. Over a pile of articles, Update is a summarisation problem. Over a story graph, it is a diff.

Follow is the same diff, run on a schedule for claims the reader chose. Markus adds a line that matters more than it looks: "If it cannot check, it should distinguish that from confirming that nothing changed." That distinction needs freshness, a record of when each source was last checked against what the claim says, and the vault keeps exactly that. Understand is a walk from a claim to its sources and the open questions. Compare sets two claims or two versions side by side, with the typed edges between them, so that "the council says one date and the operator another" is recorded where a reader meets it. Act turns the current claims into a checklist or a reminder, from rules somebody maintains.

Relate is the one that changes the privacy story. Markus writes that "a neighbourhood update should not require an entire personal profile." In the vault model it does not need one at all. The reader's route is held on the reader's side, and joined to the published graph there; the newsroom serves claims and does not learn which bus a family takes.

The same is true of his safeguards. "A correction cannot stop at the article while personalised answers continue repeating the old claim": in a graph, a correction is a supersede edge, so every skill that read the old claim meets the new one. Source protection must survive the move into reader products: an anonymous source is flagged at the node, and every projection, the article, a licensed extract, a skill's answer, redacts it without anybody having to remember. The thing he calls Journalism as a Capability System needs a substrate where the knowledge keeps its qualifications. The story graph is that substrate. Markus Franz's bridge, as a story graph: evidence at the bottom, including a resident's photo; the claims a local journalist wrote from it; the article and three Reader Skills as projections; and the reader's own route, joined on the reader's side. Places, dates and hashes are illustrative.

Here is his example as a graph. The council notice, the operator's diversion plan and a resident's photo of the site notice are evidence, each saved and hashed. The local journalist checked the photo against the notice and wrote three claims from them. The article of 9 October is one projection. When the council moves the reopening date on 21 October, nothing is rewritten: a new claim supersedes the old end date. That single edge is, at once, the Update a returning reader sees, the Follow alert sent to everybody tracking the closure, and the correction. On the reader's side, their route, bus 42 at 08:05 from Elm Street, is joined to the claim about the diversion, and Relate answers: from 13 October, that bus stops at Station Road, with the source and when it was checked.

The reader does not need to see any of this, and Markus is right that they should not have to: "The reader does not need to admire the architecture. The reader needs it to work." The graph is what makes it work, and what makes the working checkable. My story vault article started from the evidence and asked what a newsroom could sell from it. Markus starts from the person and asks what they need done. The second view brings something into focus that I had thought about and not mapped: locality.

Almost everything that touches our day is local. The road we drive, the school run, the high street, the planning application at the end of the street, the bridge. The local paper, or the local reporter, is where a trust relationship and a brand form over years, because they are right about the things we can check ourselves. Journalists save us time, and what they sell is trust. Locally, both are easiest to see: I can tell within a week whether the reporting about my own street was right.

People already pay a little for that, and would pay for more of it if paying were easy and the thing paid for were useful. A pound a month for knowing what changes on my bus route, pence for a check on a planning decision, a small amount each time the reporting saves me an afternoon. Small, from many people, about the things nearest to them, is a large amount in aggregate. Markus is careful here, and so should I be: "Locality alone is not the advantage. Doing that work reliably could be." The vault is how the reliability becomes something a reader, or an agent, can verify rather than assume. The proposal: facts and their evidence travel up from a local contributor to an international wire; every use of them pays back down the same edges. The split is illustrative; the mechanism is the point.

There is a second local element his article opens up, and it is the one I find most interesting commercially. Local journalism has local sources. A resident who photographs the notice. A bus driver who mentions the diversion before it is announced. A parish clerk whose minutes say the repair was deferred twice. In many newsrooms those people are thanked, if they are mentioned at all. In a story graph they are nodes: named, or flagged as anonymous, linked to the claims their evidence supports, and verified by the journalist who checked them.

And stories travel up. The local closure becomes a regional story about every closure on the river this winter, then a national story about ageing bridges, then an international one about infrastructure spending. Each of those cites the level below, or should. Today the money flows the other way and stops at whoever publishes last. In a graph where every claim names who found it, a national story that rests on a local claim can pay for it, per use, in pence, automatically; and a local claim that rests on a resident's photo can pass a share to the resident. The figure shows one illustrative split of one 10p use. The numbers are a proposal. The mechanism is not: a page that cannot name its source cannot pay it.

The same edges carry trust upwards. A national story is more credible when the local source under it is named, verified and current, and the verification API in the story vault design, a paid answer to "did you report this, and is it still current?", is exactly what Markus picked out in his reply as the maintained capability that moves journalism beyond the static article. Asked by a national desk about a local claim, it is how the local newsroom gets paid for being right.

That gives the loop its shape. Trust in a local brand brings use. Use, through skills that solve a local job, brings payment, in small amounts from many people and in larger ones from the outlets that cite the local work. Payment funds the next local story and the contributors behind it. More, better-sourced claims reinforce the trust, at the local level and at every level above it that cites them. It is the opposite of the hollowing out described in how news got here, where the local monopoly went first and the reporting followed. Two honest notes, as before. Nothing on sgit.ai is wired to a payment rail today; the rails exist, and the design names them, but no contributor has been paid through a graph yet. And none of this works unless the service is better than the alternative for a real task, which is Markus's test and the right one.

Markus's advice is to start with "one maintained topic and one tightly scoped service", a local disruption tracker or a "what changed?" service, and to measure it on reach, utility, relationship and reciprocity. I would keep all of that and add three things, one from each layer underneath. Keep the topic as a story vault from day one. Every claim tied to saved evidence, every correction a supersede edge. The Update and Follow skills are then diffs, not summaries, and their answers can be checked. Record the contributors in the graph from day one. Name them, or flag them, and link them to what they supported, so that when payment arrives there is somebody to pay. Publish the ledger. What was used, by whom, and where the money went, so that the reciprocity Markus wants to measure is visible to the readers being asked for it.

One local topic, one vault, one service, one ledger. If it works, the second topic is cheaper, because the methods are reusable, which is his point, and the graph grammar is shared, which is mine. The bridge, the readers, the journalism and the money are now a working simulation: The bridge, followed to the end, with its vault, which since version 0.2 also counts the costs, the two years of long tail, the stories after it and the trust they build. Three readers, three institutions and an agent use one local story kept as a graph, from the first notice to the reopening, and every payment walks back to the people who found the facts. Markus ends his article with this line: "Don't just read our journalism. Use it." I would add one clause. Use it, and pay the people who found it out.

Abstract: A BBC Radio 4 discussion on the cost of food asked for new ideas, and the loudest thing usually said about AI in the food debate is that it is dangerous. This article argues the opposite case, with the evidence it could find. The food chain from a field to a shelf is a series of hops that each keep their own records, mostly in spreadsheets, and share as little as they can; the one party with real systems is the big buyer, and once it holds a large share of a farm's output it names the price, which is the mechanism Giblin and Doctorow call a chokepoint. All of that is logistics, and logistics is what generative AI, used the way this site uses it, is good at: capture everything, structure it, and generate the small, custom tool each piece of the chain needs, then run production without a model in the line. A supply chain of encrypted vaults, one per party, joined by append lanes and a typed graph, is described piece by piece, with what exists today and what is proposed kept apart. The hypothesis that this lowers the price of goods is set against the evidence: two thirds of supply chains on spreadsheets, 13% of food lost before retail, and the gains early adopters of AI planning report. The food pound today. One kilo of supermarket apples at £2.20: the grower spends 76p and keeps 3p. Every hop keeps its own record, mostly in spreadsheets; the big buyer is the one party with real systems, and once it holds a large share of a farm's output it names the price. Figures from Sustain's Unpicking Food Prices and the FAO Food Loss Index. I was listening to The Cost of Food, BBC Radio 4's Food Programme recorded live at the Abergavenny Food Festival, and one line stayed with me: we need new ideas. The tools usually on the table (subsidy, regulation, asking the supermarkets to deal more fairly) matter, and people on that stage have spent years making the case for them. This piece tries to add one more tool, from a direction the food debate rarely looks at.

The one genuinely new thing available to the food debate is generative AI, and the wider debate has largely decided what it thinks about it. It is dangerous, it is a bubble, it is coming for jobs, and anyone who says otherwise is selling something. I think much of that fear is manufactured, a good deal of it by the same investor-driven ecosystem that sells the frontier models, and I think the result is a kind of AI fatigue in which rational people roll their eyes and stop looking. We saw the same cycle with the web. What we are missing, while we roll our eyes, is that generative AI used well is a massive amplifier of the supply chain, and that the supply chain is where the cost of living is actually decided. This article makes that case with whatever evidence I could find, and it says plainly where the evidence stops and my hypothesis starts.

The food chain is a series of hops that each keep their own records and share as little as they can. Surveys put the share of supply chain managers who run on spreadsheets at about two thirds. The FAO estimates that 13% of the world's food is lost between harvest and retail. The one party with real systems is the big buyer, and it uses them. It is the mechanism Rebecca Giblin and Cory Doctorow call a chokepoint, and Sustain's figures show what it leaves the farmer: 3p on a £2.20 kilo of apples. All of that is logistics, and logistics is a data problem. Orders, grades, deliveries, prices and payments are records that today are typed five times and reconciled by email.

A supply chain of vaults changes who holds the data. One encrypted vault per party, joined by append lanes and a typed graph, with no platform in the middle that sees every farm's numbers. Every piece of this exists on sgit today; the chain is the proposal. Use GenAI not to use GenAI. The model is used once, to generate the custom tool each piece of the chain needs from that piece's own brief. Production runs on plain files with no model in the line, kept working by the small companies this site has called villagers and town planners. The hypothesis is that this brings the price of goods down, and the evidence is partial: early adopters of AI planning report large gains, but they are large firms, and nobody has run this for a farm.

Two dogmas are in the way. That falling prices are always bad, which 140 years of data at the BIS does not support for goods prices. And that sharing is giving things away, when the cost we never calculate is the cost of not sharing. Openness is the other half. Open source and Creative Commons for the workflows; open-weight models that run inside your own environment and that you can build on, which is the under-reported advantage the economies using them already have; and sharing the journey rather than the curated success story.

In December 2022 the campaign group Sustain published Unpicking Food Prices, which followed five everyday items from the farm to the till. For a kilo of supermarket apples selling at £2.20, the grower's costs were 76p and their profit 3p, about 1% of the shelf price. For a wrapped sliced loaf at £1.14, the cereal farmer spent 9.03p to grow the wheat in it and kept 0.09p. For a pack of four beefburgers, the processor's profit was ten times the farmer's. The numbers are from 2022, and prices have moved since, but the shape has not: the party that takes the most risk and does the most physical work keeps the least.

Between that farmer and that shelf sit a packer, a haulier, a wholesaler or processor, a distribution centre and a retailer, and each of them keeps its own record of the same consignment. Ask how those records are kept and the answer is spreadsheets. A survey reported by Supply Chain Dive found two thirds of companies treating Excel as a supply chain system; another found spreadsheets to be the primary operational tool for nearly half of supply chain professionals. Both surveys were run by software vendors with an interest in the answer, so treat the exact figures with care. The direction is not in doubt, and anyone who has worked near a farm gate will recognise it. An order, a delivery note, a grade, a price and a payment date are typed in five times, reconciled by email and disputed on the phone.

The loss that produces is not only administrative. The FAO's Food Loss Index puts the share of food lost between harvest and retail, before it reaches a shop, at 13.3% in 2023, slightly worse than when monitoring began in 2015. Some of that is biology. A good deal of it is information: produce graded to the wrong specification, delivered to the wrong window, held because nobody upstream could see demand. There is one party in the chain that does not run on spreadsheets. The big buyer has forecasting systems, contract systems, and the data of every supplier it deals with. That is what lets it do the thing every farmer describes: it buys a large share of a farm's output, and once it holds 20%, 30% or 40% of what a farm produces, it can name the price, because the farm has no other distribution channel and cannot afford to lose the volume.

I want to be careful about how I describe this, because it is not malice. It is ordinary business practice, and it is what any of us would do holding the same cards. Rebecca Giblin and Cory Doctorow gave it a name in Chokepoint Capitalism: a powerful buyer locks in the people who sell to it, makes the market hostile to alternatives, and then uses that position to take more than its share of the value. Their book is about music, publishing and screenwriting, but a farmer will read the chapters on Spotify and Amazon and recognise every move. Doctorow's later book, Enshittification, describes the same cycle from the platform's side: good to users until they are locked in, then good to business customers until they are locked in, then good to nobody but itself. His argument is that none of this is an iron law of economics. It is the result of specific choices, and choices can be changed.

The UK has tried to change them by regulation, and it is worth being honest about how far that goes. The Groceries Code Adjudicator has policed the fourteen largest retailers since 2013, and its 2025 survey found things improving: 30% of suppliers reported a code issue, down from 33%, and perceived compliance averaged 93%, though it ranged from 98% at the best retailer to 66% at Amazon, which the adjudicator opened an investigation into. Under the Agriculture Act 2020 the government has also begun writing fair dealing rules sector by sector, milk in 2024 and pigs in 2025, with eggs and fresh produce reviewed. These are good things. They also share a limit: they regulate the conduct of the party with the systems, and leave the party without them exactly where it was. A code of practice does not give a grower a forecast, a second buyer or a tool that fits their farm. The big buyers can absorb a compliance regime; a compliance regime is, in a sense, a thing only big buyers can afford to follow.

Look at what the chokepoint is actually made of. It is not the buyer's trucks or its shelves. It is that the buyer knows things the grower does not: what demand looks like next month, what every other supplier is charging, which grade will be accepted and which rejected, when the payment will actually land. It is information, held by one party, and the systems that hold it. Everything between the field and the shelf is a workflow, and every workflow is a set of records moving between parties. Orders, grades, deliveries, prices, payments, disputes. That is logistics, and logistics is a data problem before it is a transport problem.

That is precisely the kind of problem that generative AI, used the way this site uses it, is good at. Not answering questions in a chat window, but capturing everything, structuring it, connecting it, and documenting it so completely that a process which used to live in three people's heads and a spreadsheet becomes something a machine can run and a stranger can audit. Every page on this site was made that way, and the Fractal Semantic Graphs work is about exactly the case a supply chain presents: many parties, each with its own vocabulary, nobody willing to adopt anyone else's schema, and a need to connect across the boundaries anyway.

The same chain, as vaults. Every party holds its own encrypted, versioned record and its own key. Orders and answers travel over append lanes; the shopper can follow a read key on the label back to the field. No platform in the middle sees every farm's numbers. Every piece exists on sgit today; joining them into a working chain is the proposal. Here is the shape of it. Every party in the chain, the grower, the packer, the haulier, the wholesaler, the buyer, holds its own vault: an encrypted, versioned record of everything that concerns it, held on any host, readable by nobody who does not hold a key, including the host. The grower's vault holds fields, yields, costs, grades, and every order and payment. The buyer's vault holds forecasts, orders and the contract terms it is now obliged to show its suppliers.

Between the vaults run append lanes: write-only channels through which one party can put a file into another's vault without being able to read anything there. An order is a file the buyer appends to the grower's lane. The delivery note, the grade and the payment are files that answer it. Nothing is retyped. Nothing goes by email. Two agent teams ran exactly this kind of two-way, signed messaging between vaults on 25 and 26 September, without either holding the other's key. Across the vaults runs one graph. Each vault keeps its own vocabulary, because a grower and a wholesaler will never agree a schema and should not have to. Typed edges join them: this delivery fulfils that order, this grade was given to that consignment, this loss happened on that leg. That is what makes waste visible. The 13% the FAO counts is invisible today because it falls between records nobody joins.

Four things change. Records are typed once and read many times. There is nobody in the middle: no platform that sees every farm's numbers and sells them back as a service, because the vaults are encrypted before they leave the party that owns them. Waste, delay and disputed grades become queries on a graph rather than arguments on the phone. And the tools are the grower's own, which brings me to the part that matters most. What this does not do also needs saying. It does not stop a buyer that holds 40% of a farm's output from naming a price. Leverage still needs distribution. What it does is make the grower's costs, the buyer's terms and the alternatives visible, cheaply, to the grower, and make the next buyer reachable at the cost of sharing a read key. That is a smaller claim than "fixing the supply chain", and it is the one I can defend.

Where the model sits, and where it does not. The model is used once, to turn a grower's brief into a working tool. A small company takes the tool and runs it. Production is plain files and plain code, with no prompt in the path and nothing metered per call. The pattern is the one in "The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI" on this site. The phrase I keep using is that I use GenAI not to use GenAI. In production, in the line, there is no model. What the model is for is building the thing that runs in the line.

A grower, or a packer, or a co-op, describes their piece of the chain in their own words: the orders they take, the grades they give, the invoices they chase, the way their particular buyer wants a delivery note laid out. An agent turns that into a working tool, in an afternoon, with the vault as its store. Then a small company takes the finished tool and runs it: hardens it, versions it, secures it, keeps it working, and does the same for a hundred other growers, paid because it keeps working rather than by the seat. I wrote about those companies in the SaaS apocalypse article and called them villagers and town planners, after the roles on wardley-maps.sgit.ai. This is the next phase of vibe coding, and it is the phase that makes it safe: the explorer builds with the model, the villager runs what was built, and the model is nowhere near the order that lands at four in the morning.

That order matters for three reasons. The tool fits, because it was made from that grower's words; fit is the one thing the spreadsheet always had and the big buyer's ERP never will. The tool is cheap to run, because plain files on a small host cost almost nothing, and a cost base that low is what lets prices fall without anyone in the chain losing their margin. And the tool is open by default, because the brief, the tool and the method are published, the way this site publishes its own, so the next grower starts from the last one's work rather than from a blank sheet. Today the only people in the chain with good software, good ERPs and good management structure are the big platforms, and they are the ones making money across the board. That is the asymmetry a custom tool per party removes.

My hypothesis is that a supply chain run this way brings the price of food and goods down. I asked for validation and here is what I found, with its limits. McKinsey reported in 2021 that early adopters of AI-enabled supply chain management had improved logistics costs by 15%, inventory levels by 35% and service levels by 65% against slower competitors. Those are large companies, and the gains are from demand forecasting and planning at a scale a farm does not have; the number tells you what is possible when information is joined, not what a grower would see. The FAO's 13.3% loss before retail is a floor on what better information could recover, and its own estimate of the value lost is about USD 400 billion a year. The spreadsheet surveys tell you how far most of the chain is from the starting line.

What nobody has measured is the effect on a farm, a packer or a wholesaler of tools that fit them, records that are typed once, and a second buyer reachable at the cost of a read key. That is the experiment. It is also, I think, where government money should go. Instead of investing in regulation, which the big buyers can follow and which does nothing for the party without systems, invest in the pieces of the supply chain that are not working: the tooling, the shared vocabularies, the villager companies that will keep a thousand small custom tools running. It is cheaper than a subsidy and, unlike a subsidy, it compounds.

There is a second dogma in the way, and it is the belief that falling prices are bad. I have never understood it. What is wrong with prices being where they were a year ago, or five years ago? In technology we have lived with falling prices for as long as the industry has existed. The ONS found that the price of laptops, PCs and tablets fell 76% between 2005 and 2016, and audio-visual equipment has fallen almost every year since its index began. It did not stop anybody buying a computer.

The standard worry is real and the Bank of England states it plainly: if people expect prices to fall they may delay spending, and debts fixed in money terms get heavier as prices drop. But that is a description of a demand collapse, not of a productivity gain. The BIS looked at 140 years of data across 38 economies and found the link between falling goods prices and lower growth to be weak, and to come largely from the Great Depression; the deflations that hurt were in asset prices, especially property, and especially with private debt attached. In the postwar period, growth in years of goods price deflation was slightly higher than in other years. A cheaper loaf because the chain wasted less is not a Japanese lost decade. It is what technology has done for every other good.

The reason these decisions look uncoordinated is that they are. Nobody has the data joined up well enough to argue from facts, so the argument is made from dogma. That is the thing that changes when the chain is a graph: the effect of a change in the buyer's terms on the grower's margin becomes a query, and the conversation about food prices can finally be had on evidence. The first memo I recorded for this article was about logistics. The second was about the thing I forgot, which is sharing, and it may be the more important half.

Mention open source or Creative Commons in a room full of people who run supply chains and two things happen. First, many of them do not know what the terms mean. Second, somebody steers the conversation to communism, socialism and how that did not work, as though publishing a grading specification were the abolition of property. We showed, over thirty years, that openness works in software. Most of the world's infrastructure runs on it. What we have not yet shown is that it works for the rest of industry, and the supply chain is where to show it.

People do not share for two reasons. The first is that it is not easy. It is easy for me now, because I have an optimised workflow: I record a voice memo, an agent researches it and drafts it, I review it, and it is live on this site the same day, with its sources. This article is that workflow. Before I had it, the cost of sharing an idea was a week, and so most ideas were never shared. The second reason is the belief that an idea is precious and will be copied. Everyone in a startup knows that ideas are cheap and execution is everything, and yet the instinct persists.

What we never calculate is the economic cost of not sharing. The European Commission estimates that about 80% of industrial data is never used, and its own data strategy cites OECD work putting the benefit of more business-to-business data sharing at between 1% and 2.5% of GDP. Those are big, soft numbers, and I do not lean on them for precision. I lean on them because they are the only attempt anybody has made to count the cost of the default, which is silence. In the supply chain that cost is paid every day: every grower who learns the hard way what a buyer will reject learns it alone, and the lesson dies with the season.

And when people do share, they share the curated success story, per medium, in the form that medium rewards. The real stories, the ones with the failures in them, are the ones worth sharing, and they need somewhere to live that is not a slide. That is why the vaults on this site publish the whole journey rather than the result: a plan with its wrong turns, a newsroom with every claim tied to its source, a version log that records what each release got wrong and how it was caught. Imagine every farmer and every supplier able to learn from what the others did, what worked and what did not, at the cost of opening a vault.

The same argument applies to the models, and here is a point that is usually under-reported. China, and the other economies that build on open-weight models, have a large economic advantage that has nothing to do with benchmark scores: their companies can run a near-frontier model inside their own environment and innovate on top of it. The model is one small part of a working solution, a very important part, but a small one; the rest is the workflow, the data, the tooling and the people. When the model is open, all of that can be built and owned locally. The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission's Two Loops paper (March 2026) describes exactly this: most Chinese labs publish weights and charge far less, which "has resulted in the acceleration of global uptake of Chinese AI and created a feedback loop where widespread adoption drives iteration, then further adoption", with Alibaba's Qwen models alone having over 100,000 derivatives on Hugging Face. The paper's own conclusion is that this open ecosystem "enables China to innovate close to the frontier despite significant compute constraints" and that it lets AI be deployed cheaply "across factories, logistics networks, and robotics". That is the supply chain, and it is being done.

I know a good number of startups that have built their products, and their own custom models, on top of open weights, most of them Chinese. Two objections come up every time and both have plain answers. The first is safety: these models run inside the company's own environment, often air-gapped, so there is no call home and no data leaving unless the company sends it, and any attempt to do either is caught by the same cyber security controls that govern every other piece of software the company runs. The second is bias: the harness and the workflow around the model manage it, as they must for every model, because the closed frontier models carry bias too, only less visibly. DeepSeek's technical report says its V3 model needed 2.788 million GPU hours on export-restricted H800 chips for its full training, a run that, as CSIS notes, the company priced at about USD 5.6 million; by one analyst's count, Chinese open-weight models were about 61% of the tokens served through OpenRouter by May 2026. Whatever the exact figures, the consequence in the West, where the conversation is about closed models and the fear around them, is that most companies pay for AI access, per call, to a provider they do not control, when they could have the option not to. The same openness makes it possible to have models per industry, per language and per culture: Switzerland's Apertus, released in September 2025 with its weights, data and method all open, covers more than a thousand languages with 40% of its training data in languages other than English. A model that speaks a grower's language and knows a sector's vocabulary is not a luxury for the supply chain. It is the thing that makes the brief in the first figure possible.

So my point is a simple one. The supply chain needs a much greater degree of openness, open source and Creative Commons are the proven way to get it, and the workflow that makes sharing cheap already exists. We have shown it works for software. Now we can show it works for everything the software was written to manage. Every piece named in the second figure exists on sgit and is published on this site: encrypted vaults with git semantics, read keys that can be handed to a stranger, append lanes and the two-way messaging built on them, typed graphs across vaults, and vault apps that run in the browser with the permissions they ask for declared in a file. The workflow in the third figure, an explorer building with agents and a small company running the result, is how this site itself is made and maintained.

What does not exist is the chain. Nobody has put a grower, a packer and a buyer on vaults and run a season through them. The grading vocabularies are not written. The villager companies for agriculture do not exist yet. The hypothesis about prices is a hypothesis. This article is the brief for the experiment, published in the open so that somebody can run it, and so that when they do, the journey is shared and not only the result.
