Abstract: We tend to explain success by studying the winners: they did this, this and this, so do the same. We rarely count the people who did exactly the same things and failed. My hypothesis is that, when an investor chooses between two founders with the same idea, drive and talent, one of the deciding factors is which one they believe they can control. The investor's relationship with the founder is financial, not emotional; the founder is a means to a return, and replaceable if needed. In Wardley terms, the investor moves the founder towards commodity, the way record labels moved performers once the songs, the producers and the distribution were the real assets. The research gets close to this without testing it directly. Investors prefer coachable founders, even though coachability does not reliably predict success. Venture contracts hand investors control when things go badly, and include clauses that make it expensive for founders to leave. Half of founders were no longer CEO three years in. The investors' answer is that control creates value, and the data partly backs them; but it measures valuations and exits, not the mission, and over the long run founder-led companies have returned more to shareholders. Strong-minded founders with strong ethics are the profile this selection filters out, and I propose how to test whether it does.

Survivorship bias: those who won are studied, while others did the same and failed. Illustrative. One argument in three parts: who investors choose and why, a deal a founder with leverage could offer instead, and what keeps every side honest once control is out of the contract.
in-short

We study survivors. Practices unrelated to success can look like its cause when only winners are sampled. The founder is moved towards commodity. As labels did to performers once the songs were the asset. Investors select on coachability. They prefer it; it does not reliably make the company more successful. Control is in the contract. Investors get full control when performance is poor; vesting and non-competes make leaving expensive. Founders get replaced. Half were gone as CEO by year three; fewer than a quarter led the IPO. The investors have a case. Founder control lowers valuations; replacement can improve exits. The long run says otherwise. Founder-led companies returned about three times more over 25 years. Strong vision reads as a risk. That is the profile this selection screens out, and it can be tested.
survivors

There is a whole genre of business writing that goes: look at these successful companies, here is what they did, do the same and you will succeed. What it almost never does is look for the companies and people who made exactly the same moves and did not make it.
survivors

Jerker Denrell put this on a formal footing in 2003. In Vicarious Learning, Undersampling of Failure, and the Myths of Management, he writes that "The organizations that can be observed at any point in time are the survivors of a selective process that has eliminated a large fraction of the underlying population", and that books and the business press then focus on the winners among them. His sharpest finding is about risk: "risky practices, even if they are unrelated to performance in the full population of organizations, may seem to be positively related to performance in a sample of survivors." Bold bets produce spectacular winners and quiet failures, and we only hear about the winners. Which means the question that matters is not what the winners did. It is why the winner was chosen, funded and backed, when others who did the same were not.
commodity

Who is the commodity: the performer in music and the founder in venture. A sketch of the argument, not measured. One way to say this is with a Wardley map. On the evolution axis, from genesis to commodity, where does the person sit? Record labels behave like investors: someone with capital chooses which artist to put it behind. And some of the most successful pop acts were not the best musicians, singers or performers. What I used to tell musician friends is: look at who is actually the talent. Often it was not the performer. It was the production, the access to venues and radio, and above all the songs.
commodity

The data on songs bears that out. The Pudding found that from 2010 to 2014 the top ten producers were behind about 40% of the songs that reached the top five of the Billboard Hot 100, against about 19% in the late 1980s. In one week of October 2015 only two songs on the Hot 100 were written by a single person, against 51 in 1975. If a label already has the hits packaged, who sings them is, in economic terms, interchangeable. K-pop made it explicit: in 2009 three members of TVXQ challenged a 13-year contract as unjust, a court granted them an injunction, and the country's fair trade watchdog set seven years as the maximum for standard contracts.
commodity

A label that owns the songwriters, the producers and the distribution has moved the performer towards commodity: something to source, standardise and swap. A venture fund can do the same to a founder. There is even a measurement of what investors bring that is not a commodity: when a venture capitalist on a startup's board dies unexpectedly, startups become more likely to fail and less likely to exit, while recruitment, product development and CEO replacement are unaffected; Ewens and Sosyura conclude that "a VC's network and reputation are key irreplaceable assets." My reading, and it is mine, is that in the investor's own map the network is scarce and much of the rest can be sourced.
why

Take two founders with the same opportunity, the same drive, the same idea and the same talent. Sometimes the one who does not get funded even has more advantages. Why does the investor pick the other one? My hypothesis is that one of the deciding factors is control: which founder the investor believes will take direction, accept decisions made in the investor's interest, and step aside if asked. The investor has no emotional connection to the founder. The founder is there to deliver a return, and is, in the end, replaceable.
why

Nobody has tested that directly, as far as I could find. But there is a well-studied trait that sits very close to it: coachability. Investors say it openly; Steve Krein of StartUp Health said that one thing he always looks for in an entrepreneur is the question "Are they coachable?" Research by Mitteness and colleagues showed that coachability influences "whether angel investors recommend moving forward with a company after a pitch", and a study at Babson found that it has an impact regardless of how investors rank the business's fundamentals or the team's competence.
why

The key line comes from the researchers themselves. Reviewing the evidence in 2023, Letwin, Ciuchta, Stevenson and McMahon wrote: "While investors and support organizations such as accelerators prefer coachable entrepreneurs, being coachable doesn't necessarily make your firm more successful." If investors reliably select on a trait that does not reliably predict success, then something other than success is being selected for. Coachability is a polite word for it. Controllability is a less polite one.
contract

Control moves with performance: a schematic of Kaplan and Strömberg's finding, not their data. You do not have to guess whether investors care about control. It is in the paperwork. Kaplan and Strömberg read 213 venture investments in 119 companies. What distinguishes venture deals, they found, is that cash-flow, voting, board and liquidation rights are separated and allocated separately, often contingent on performance: "if the firm performs poorly, the VCs obtain full control. As performance improves, the entrepreneur retains/obtains more control rights. If the firm performs very well, the VCs retain their cash flow rights, but relinquish most of their control and liquidation rights." That last clause is what I call the big stick: once the founder, or the artist, can credibly say "I leave and you cannot replace me", the contract hands power back.
contract

The same study found it "common for VCs to include non-compete and vesting provisions that make it more expensive for the entrepreneur to leave the firm". Read plainly, they make it costly for a founder to walk away before the investor is ready: if they go, they leave unvested equity behind and cannot compete. Replaceability is not an accident of venture capital; it is designed in.
replaced

And the replaceability gets used. Noam Wasserman's study of 212 US startups, reported in The Founder's Dilemma in 2008, found that by year three "50% of founders were no longer the CEO; in year four, only 40% were still in the corner office; and fewer than 25% led their companies' initial public offerings." He also found that most founders are shocked when investors insist they give up control, and that in only about a quarter of replacements did the founder start the change. The Ewens and Marx dataset of 11,929 venture-backed firms is a more conservative count: "Some 15% of the 11,929 firms have at least one founder replacement in our sample period." But the direction is the same. I know many stories of investors with outsized power even at angel, Series A and Series B. The data says those stories are not exceptions.
luck

None of this says talent and hard work do not matter. They do. So do the right people, the right moment, the right technology and the right place, and two of those are measurable. Timing and momentum first. In the MusicLab experiment, Salganik, Dodds and Watts had 14,341 people download unknown songs, some seeing what others had downloaded and some not. Showing popularity made success more unequal and less predictable: "The best songs rarely did poorly, and the worst rarely did well, but any other result was possible." That is why copying the winners' moves does not reliably reproduce their results.
luck

Then place. Innovation comes in geographic bursts, because the same people are talking to each other about the same things at the same moment. Enrico Moretti found that the ten largest clusters in computer science account for 69% of US inventors in the field, that inventors who move into a large cluster produce more, and that when Kodak declined, the productivity of Rochester's other inventors fell too. Being in the room is an advantage the success stories rarely list.
answer

Investors have a serious reply, and the data partly backs it. Wasserman's later study of 6,130 US startups found that "each additional level of founder control (i.e., controlling the board and/or the CEO position) reduces the pre-money valuation of the startup by 17.1–22.0 percent." Ewens and Marx used changes in state non-compete laws to argue that replacing founders improves performance and makes a high-quality exit more likely. On that reading, investors want control because control creates value.
answer

I accept the numbers. What I do not accept is that they settle the question, because both measure value as the investor measures it: the valuation, the exit. Over a longer run the picture changes. Bain found that from 1990 to 2014, founder-led companies in the S&P 500 "performed 3.1 times better" than the others in shareholder returns, and 1.8 times better excluding technology; its update this year puts the gap since 2015 at 2.1 times. And some of the most valuable companies in the world kept their founders in control on purpose: in April 2026 Mark Zuckerberg held 60.8% of Meta's voting power, and Larry Page and Sergey Brin about 53% of Alphabet's, through shares with ten votes each. That is the big stick, written into the share structure.
answer

And there is a selection effect hiding inside the investors' evidence. If investors fund the coachable and replaceable founders in the first place, then the founders in these datasets are already the ones who accepted the terms. The strong-minded founders who walked away, bootstrapped or never got funded are mostly not in the sample. That is Denrell's undersampling again, one level up.
test

The hypothesis can be tested, and I would like to see it done. Three ways: Follow the ratings. Take founders whose coachability investors rated at the pitch, as several studies already did, and follow them for ten years: who was funded, who was replaced, and what happened to the company and its users, not only to the exit. Compare the mission, not the multiple. For founder-replaced and founder-kept companies, measure what users experienced after the change: the product's direction, prices, the ethics commitments made at founding, against what the investors' studies measure. Count the ones who walked away. Survey founders who were offered term sheets and refused them, and compare them with those who signed. If the refusers score higher on independence and lower on coachability, the filter is real.
founders

If the hypothesis holds, a particular profile is at a disadvantage in early-stage funding: the founder with a very strong vision, a very clear direction of travel and, sometimes, very strong ethics. Not because they are worse at building companies, but because an investor reads them, correctly, as someone who will not easily be overruled, and who will not make decisions in the investor's interest against the interest of the mission. That is close to how I would describe many European founders, and it connects to The expert founders: the people who know the problem best are often the hardest to steer, because they know better. Tech is the partial exception: winner-takes-all markets mean investors will sometimes accept a founder they cannot control, because the upside of the rare winner pays for everything. But at angel, seed and Series A, before the big stick exists, the founder is negotiating from the weak end of the contract.
founders

The practical conclusion is not to avoid investors. It is to get to the big stick before you need their money, so that the choice of investor is yours. With agents making execution cheap, that is more possible now than it has ever been. What a founder can do with that leverage is the subject of the next piece, Sell, don't issue; what protects each side once control is out of the contract is the subject of the third, The fork next door.
limits

No study tests "controllability" directly. Coachability is the nearest proxy; the link from one to the other is my argument. The value evidence cuts against me. Wasserman and Ewens and Marx find that less founder control and founder replacement go with higher valuations and better exits. Bain's figures are its own analysis. Not peer-reviewed, and "founder-led" includes founders who stayed on the board. The founder-tenure figures are old. Wasserman's sample covers startups from the late 1990s and early 2000s. The music figures are mostly industry analyses, not peer-reviewed studies. Not that investors are villains. Their incentive is a return; selecting for control follows from that. Not that strong founders always win. Some are hard to work with for reasons that have nothing to do with ethics. I have a stake. I am a founder, and this argument suits founders like me. If you have data that could test this, or a story that contradicts it, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: I wanted one presentation from SlideShare and was offered a 30-day trial and then £10.99 a month. The author of the deck receives nothing from that subscription, under an uploader agreement that grants the platform a royalty-free licence to monetise, charge for, sublicense and train models on the work, and I am one of those authors, with 69 decks uploaded over fifteen years. This article does three things. It says what happened to SlideShare, from a 2006 start through LinkedIn and Scribd to the September 2021 paywall, and why a service with a PDF viewer and a file store has not been replaced: fifteen years of embeds and links, which is inertia in Wardley's sense. It sets out what an author can ask the old platform for today, under the right of access and, in the EU, the copyright transparency duty, including the two questions platforms do not expect, how many downloads and what revenue. And it designs the service the author would have chosen, on the primitives this site already publishes: every author's decks in a vault the host cannot read, access decided by keys rather than settings, a read key for what is free, a receipt turned into a ten-minute key for what is paid once, a revocable grant for what is private, decryption in the browser, an attested enclave for the one step that needs plaintext, seven roles that no single company holds, and a split of 85% to the author on a ledger the author can recompute. The plan is published as a vault with a working mock, the Deck Vault, with its economics worked for one author and its risks as an acceptance register. The marginal cost is storage and bandwidth, which are near zero; the hard row is the fixed part of a card fee, which the plan says so about rather than hides. Somebody should build it. The author will build the first step for their own decks.

The screen that started this, as shown to a reader on 6 October 2026, with the deck and its author left out of the crop. One download offered as a subscription; the author of the deck receives nothing from it. The three complaints, and the one that is not: the licence the author signed allows all of it. One download, one subscription decision. The reader is offered a 30-day trial and then £10.99 a month, $11.99 in the US. There is no one-off option unless the author switched one on, and the setting was reported as off by default when the paywall arrived in September 2021.

The author receives nothing, by agreement. The uploader agreement of August 2024 says it "does not entitle You to any payment, royalties, remuneration, or other compensation", and grants a royalty-free, sublicensable licence to "monetize, charge money for, restrict access to view, restrict access to download, advertise against, create derivative works from, train machine learning, large language, or other statistical or data models" the work. The same company forbids its users from training models on the same content. Why it has not been replaced. Fifteen years of embeds, backlinks and search ranking point at one domain, and about forty million visits a month still arrive, most from search. That is inertia, and it is a stronger moat than the technology.

What an author can ask today. A right-of-access request for the counts and the recipients, with the European Data Protection Board's guidance that derived data counts and the Court of Justice's ruling that recipients must be named; and, in EU states that implemented it without a payment condition, the copyright transparency duty on "all revenues generated". The UK did not implement that duty. The design. Every author's decks in a vault the host cannot read. Keys decide access: a read key for what is free, a receipt turned into a ten-minute key for what is paid once, a revocable grant for what is private. Decryption in the browser. Seven roles, no single owner. The author takes 85%, on a ledger in their own vault.

The economics. Serving one author's whole shelf for a month costs less than the incumbent charges one reader for one download. The hard row is the card fee, 1.5% plus 20p with a 30p minimum, which eats a fifth of a one-pound download; wallets, batching and an open payments protocol are how the plan gets under it. Status. A plan and a mock, published as a vault with a read key. Nothing in the build order beyond the vault exists. The author will build the first step for their own 69 decks.

SlideShare was founded in October 2006 as a place to upload a deck, embed it anywhere and link to it, and it spread because it worked. LinkedIn bought it in May 2012 for about $119 million. Microsoft bought LinkedIn in 2016. In August 2020 LinkedIn announced that Scribd was acquiring SlideShare, with operations moving over on 24 September 2020 and forty million presentations cited. Scribd's own help page from that month said that users would not need a subscription to access or upload, but that "for full access, including the ability to download content directly to your device, a subscription is required" from September 2021. When the paywall arrived, authors found an account-level checkbox, "Allow users to read and download your slideshows without a subscription", which one writer who documented it in October 2021 reported as off by default. The checkbox still exists in Scribd's 2025 help pages, with a per-upload toggle beside it. Scribd's corporate site in 2026 describes SlideShare as twenty-five million presentations, which is fifteen million fewer than the number cited at the sale; the company has not explained the difference publicly.
Twenty years of one service. The owner changed twice and the terms changed once; the links did not change at all. In Wardley's terms this is inertia, and it is also the opening.

Why nothing replaced it. Third-party traffic estimates put slideshare.net at thirty-six to forty-three million visits a month across 2025 and 2026, with seventy to eighty per cent arriving from search and India the largest country. The service persists as a search artefact: every public deck is indexed, embedded on conference pages and blogs, and linked from the decks that cite it. Simon Wardley's observation is the right one: "Past success breeds inertia." For years the balance was good enough that few authors thought about the terms, and a service people feel good about linking to is shared; the sharing built the moat before the terms moved. A replacement needs the authors to move, and the authors' links are the thing the incumbent holds. None of the alternatives I looked at pays authors per download; the only author-payment model among them is a pooled royalty with an unpublished rate.

I want to be precise here because the complaint is easy to overstate. The uploader keeps copyright. The licence is non-exclusive. I uploaded most of my decks under a Creative Commons licence and I am content for them to be shared. What the author grants, in the agreement last updated on 1 August 2024, is "a worldwide, non-exclusive, transferable, assignable, fully paid-up, royalty-free license (with the right to grant and authorize sublicenses)" to, among other things, "monetize, charge money for, restrict access to view, restrict access to download, advertise against, create derivative works from, train machine learning, large language, or other statistical or data models, and otherwise exploit Your Content", and the agreement says it "does not entitle You to any payment, royalties, remuneration, or other compensation in exchange for posting Your Content." The general terms, updated in September 2026, forbid users from using "any content made available through the Services for the purpose of training, fine-tuning, or otherwise developing a large language model". The right the platform reserves for itself it withholds from its users. Whether the right has been exercised, I could not find out; no public report of a licensing deal or of the corpus in a named training set turned up, and the dashboard does not say.

So the three complaints are these. The reader is sold a subscription for one file that the author would have given away or sold for a pound. The author has no say and no share, and cannot change the terms for their own work except by deleting it. And the author does not know where the work went. The licence allows all three, which is why the complaint is not that anyone broke a rule. It is that the service an author would have chosen does not exist, and in 2026 it could. Before designing anything, there is the question of what an author can do with the platform they are already on. Three things. Switch the setting on. Readers can then download without a subscription. It is per account, with a per-upload override, and it is the reason my decks can be downloaded and the deck I wanted could not.

Send a right-of-access request, under GDPR Article 15 or its UK equivalent, asking the ordinary things and two unusual ones. First, the view and download counts recorded against each upload, by month. The platform's likely answer is that these are statistics about content, not personal data. The author's answer is that a count held against a named author's upload, in that author's account, relates to an identifiable person: the European Data Protection Board's guidelines on the right of access say it "includes both inferred and derived data, including personal data created by a service provider", and the Court of Justice has held that information relates to a person where "by reason of its content, purpose or effect, it is linked" to them. Second, the recipients: whether the uploads or text from them have been licensed to third parties, including for training, and to whom. The Court of Justice ruled in January 2023 that a controller must name the actual recipients where it can, not only categories. The deadline is one month, extendable by two with notice. A revenue figure is harder to compel, because the access right discloses data that is processed rather than creating a new statistic, and a subscription platform may not attribute revenue to authors at all; but "we do not compute it" is an answer worth having in writing. The letter is in the vault, as a template.

In the EU, ask under copyright law. Article 19 of the 2019 Copyright Directive gives authors the right to receive, at least once a year, "up to date, relevant and comprehensive information on the exploitation of their works ... in particular as regards modes of exploitation, all revenues generated and remuneration due" from those they licensed. Whether a royalty-free upload licence falls within it is untested: Germany's implementation applies only to licences granted for payment, France's has no such condition, and no case on a user-generated-content platform was found. The UK said in January 2020 it would not implement the Directive, so a UK author has the access right and the terms, and nothing else. I will send the request for my own 69 decks, and the answer goes in the first article the ledger below is built for.

Now the service I would have chosen. It is built from things this site already documents, and the vault at the end of this article is the plan with a working mock. Every author gets a vault the host cannot read. Who may open a deck is decided by which key a device holds: a publishing key for the author, a content key per deck, a read key for what is free, a receipt turned into a ten-minute key for what is paid once, and a revocable grant for what is private. Design sketch; proposal.

Every author gets a vault. An encrypted, versioned store of their own files, on any host, that nobody who does not hold a key can read, including the host. The author's device encrypts a deck before it leaves; the host receives ciphertext and a size. That one decision carries the rest, because a service that cannot read the content cannot sell it, index it for someone else, or change the terms under which it is read. This is the sgit vault model, which the security page describes and which the team in the previous articles runs on.

Keys, not settings. The author's publishing key is bound to a passkey on their device and signs every decision: access rules, grants, revocations, content credentials, licences. Each deck is encrypted under its own content key, wrapped to the publishing key, so re-keying one deck touches nothing else. A read key per deck, derived one way from the content key as vault credentials describes, is published for decks the author marks read-free; it cannot write and cannot be turned back. A grant is the content key wrapped to a recipient's public key with an expiry, signed by the author; revocation is a signed statement and a re-key. And a receipt from the payments service, for a one-off payment, is turned by an attested enclave into the content key wrapped to the reader's device for ten minutes. A setting lives on a server and changes when the server's owner changes. A key lives with the author and is verified by anyone.

Decryption on the client. The reader's browser fetches ciphertext and decrypts it in the tab, as every vault page on this site does today. No account to read what is free. The one bounded exception is the unlock service, an attested enclave that handles one deck's plaintext in memory for one request, to wrap a key, render a preview or build an index, and whose operator cannot read it; the device checks the attestation before trusting it, in the way the personal agent design set out this morning.

The incumbent is one company holding the files, the keys, the payments, the identities and the front page, which is what lets the terms change for everyone at once and what makes it one thing to buy and sell. The plan separates the roles so that no party holds more than one of the content, the keys and the money, and so that each can be provided by several parties the author chooses between. Seven roles: storage host, key service, unlock service, payments, identity and provenance, the front, and add-ons. What each does, what each sees, who could run it, and which exist today. Sovereignty by construction: an archive can hold a nation's authors' ciphertext without reading it.

The storage host stores the vault and serves ciphertext to key-holders; it sees sizes and timings, and it can be any object store, a national archive, a university, or the author's own bucket. The key service publishes public keys and bindings and records grants and revocations as signed statements; it never holds a private key. The unlock service is the enclave. The payments service takes a one-off payment, issues a signed receipt the enclave accepts, settles to the author and publishes a statement the author can recompute. The identity service binds the publishing key to a person in tiers, from key-only through a domain or ORCID binding to a verified identity or an institution's signature, and signs content credentials. The front is the website people see, and because it works from a read key alone, several fronts can list the same vaults; the mock in the vault is one. Add-ons, a semantic graph of a deck, an infographic, question answering, a translation, run inside the enclave on the plaintext, are approved by the author before they are sold, and pay the author the same share.

The sovereignty follows from the separation. Each role can be provided per country, per profession or per company. An archive can hold its authors' ciphertext without being able to read it, which is a role archives already understand. A professional body can verify identities without touching the files. A cooperative of authors can run the payments. An author moves between providers by changing a key binding, not by migrating content, which is the shape the supply chain of vaults argued for one domain over. Pay once and download the original. The payments service sees a payment, the enclave sees a receipt, the host sees a read; none sees all three. The ledger line goes into the author's vault, and the month's statement is computed from lines like it.

Read for free. The reader opens the deck on any front. The browser fetches ciphertext with the deck's read key and decrypts it. The front appends a read to the author's ledger through a write-only lane: a count, not a person.

Pay once and download the original. The reader presses Download original and sees the price the author set, the author's 85% and the platform's 15%. The payments service takes the payment and issues a signed receipt naming the deck's hash, valid for minutes. The enclave checks the receipt and the author's access rule and wraps the content key to the reader's device for ten minutes. The browser downloads the ciphertext and decrypts the original locally. The ledger line names the deck, the amount, the split, the receipt and the hash served. No subscription is offered for a single file; a subscription is allowed for a reader who wants thirty a month, and its revenue is split to authors by downloads on the same statement.

Share privately, and take it back. For a deck marked by grant only, the author wraps the content key to a recipient's public key with an expiry and signs the grant. To revoke, the author signs a revocation; the enclave stops honouring the grant at once and the deck is re-keyed on the next commit. A file already downloaded is the reader's, and the plan says so on every grant rather than pretending otherwise. Publish, and migrate. The author drops a file; the browser hashes and encrypts it and commits the ciphertext; the identity service signs a content credential; the enclave produces a preview and an index. Migration from the incumbent is downloading one's own decks, for authors who switched the setting on, and publishing them with permanent per-deck addresses and an embed that works from a read key, so the links that pointed at the old domain can be updated once.

Serving an author's whole shelf for a month costs less than the incumbent charges one reader for one download. Where a one-off price goes by card, from 50p to the incumbent's subscription for scale: under a pound the rail eats the price. Illustrative figures with list prices as inputs. Take my own case: 69 decks, about 5 MB each, 345 MB in all. Object storage at list price is about $0.015 per gigabyte-month on a provider that charges nothing for egress, and up to $0.09 per gigabyte of egress on one that does. Serving 400 downloads and 9,000 reads a month, with a 1 MB preview per read, costs between nothing and under a pound. Two seconds of enclave time per unlock adds less than a penny. The whole month's infrastructure for an author's shelf costs less than the incumbent charges one reader for one download. For one author, a month Decks 69, about 5 MB each Storage under 1p
Bandwidth 0p to 77p, depending on the host's egress price Enclave time under 1p The incumbent's price for one download £10.99 a month after a 30-day trial

The thing that does not scale down is the payment. A UK card through a mainstream processor costs 1.5% plus 20p with a 30p minimum, so a 50p download loses two fifths of its price to the rail, a £1 download loses about a fifth, and the plan's default of £1.50 loses about fifteen per cent. The plan's answer is to state this rather than hide it. The split is 85% to the author and 15% to the platform, and the platform pays the card fee out of its 15%, which at the default price leaves it almost nothing on a card payment. The platform's margin is in wallet top-ups, where one card fee covers several downloads, in batching settlements, and in add-ons at a 70% author share; it is not in the author's share. An open payments protocol moved to a foundation in 2026 with card networks and processors among its members and is settling machine-to-machine payments at fractions of a cent, so the first readers to pay per download cheaply may be agents; a person still needs a wallet, and the plan's first open question is which rail a UK or EU front can offer a person at under five pence a transaction.

The positive loop the plan bets on: authors who are paid publish more and publish here first; readers who are not sold a subscription for one file come back; fronts compete on discovery and on the share they take, because the content is not theirs to lock.

Strip the storage and payments away and what remains is the thing a reader cannot get anywhere else: assurance that this file, with this hash, was published by this person, who is who they say they are. Every deck already carries a signature over its hash from a key bound to an identity, so the assurance is cheap to produce. A conference wants to know the decks on its page are the speakers'. An employer wants to know a candidate's deck is theirs. A journalist wants a date that cannot move. A reader wants to know the version they are reading is the one that was published and the forty copies elsewhere are copies. On the incumbent, an upload is bound to an account and an account to an email; here it is bound to a key, and the key to a person in tiers the badge names. This is the argument the news articles on this site made about selling provenance and trust, applied to presentations.

The plan is published as a vault, Deck Vault, with a read key on its page. It holds ten plan documents, the data behind them, the right-of-access letter, a register of ten risks written as acceptances with a holder and a date, and a working mock: the shelf of a fictional author with twelve decks, a deck page with pay-once and the split, the author's own view with a statement they can recompute from the ledger, the seven roles, the five flows, the economics and the rights. The app is built as web components in the shape coding.sgit.ai documents, three files per component on one base, bundled into one file for the vault host by a script in the vault; the source stays split so the tool can be reviewed as code, as the review brief asks. Press the pay button on a deck and the ledger line appears on the author's view.

A deck page in the mock, after the pay button: the content credential, the hash, read free in the browser, pay once with the split shown, and the ledger line the payment would write. Click the image to open the vault page ↗ The author's own view: the September statement with the add-ons' share, the ledger as it is written, the keys and grants with a mock revoke, and what each of the seven services knows about the author. Nothing in the last list can read a slide except the enclave for one request and the author's own device. Click the image to open the vault page ↗

Vaults with client-side encryption, one-way read keys, write-only lanes and decryption in the browser exist and are documented with their limits on this site. Confidential compute with attested key release is sold by three cloud vendors. Payment processors issue receipts; identity verifiers charge a few dollars a check; content credentials ship in cameras and phones; the EU's identity wallets are due by the end of 2026. The Agent Behaviour Policy for the platform's agents is written in the vault.

What does not exist: the unlock enclave for decks, the per-task key release, grants and revocation as a service, the receipt that becomes a key, a front that lists a vault from a read key alone, the migration tool, and any payment rail that gets a person under five pence a transaction in the UK. The vault's build order has nine steps, and step zero is one author's shelf as a vault with per-deck read keys and an embed per deck. I will build step zero for my own decks, because I want a home for them that I hold the keys to. The rest is for whoever takes the plan; what they may not do and still call it this is written in the vault's last chapter. The agent team as it runs and A personal agent that keeps your secrets: the vault properties, the three classes of information, and the enclave with per-task key release this plan reuses.

A supply chain of vaults: one vault per party, lanes between them, no platform in the middle. The future of news is the story vault, not the paywall and The reader was always the product: selling provenance rather than access, and what platforms did to the people who made the content. The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI: the same Wardley point, applied to the incumbents of software. Abstract: The review of our strategy has converged, and the next step is not another argument about architecture. It is to deliver one chain, once, for one workflow, well enough that a customer can use it to make a decision and wants us to keep it current: an existing business requirement, an approved delegation to an agent, a control that implements it, an observed result, and evidence that is still valid after something changes. What the customer gets at the end is a delegation record in six parts: the business requirement, the agent delegation, the control mapping, the evidence, the remaining gaps, and the conditions that make it invalid. Two refinements make it work. A rule written for people is not yet a delegation to an agent: it has to be extracted, its ambiguities listed, and the delegation approved by its owner. And the approved baseline is never updated from observed behaviour. The plan runs in three stages, immediate value, maintenance value and repeatability, with a deliberately small first customer. And we start with ourselves: pilot zero is our own inbox, where the rule is that the agent drafts and I send, and where, it turns out, Gmail has no permission that allows drafting without also allowing sending.
The chain to deliver once: requirement, delegation, control, observed result, and evidence that holds after a change.
in-short

Deliver one chain, once. From an existing rule to evidence after a change. The product is the delegation record. Six parts a customer can act on. A rule for people is not yet a delegation. Extract it, list the ambiguities, approve it. The baseline is approved, never learned. Observed behaviour is evaluated, not adopted. Three stages. Immediate value, maintenance value, repeatability. A small first customer. One workflow, one owner, one environment. Pilot zero is our own inbox. Gmail cannot enforce our own rule.
delivery

Over the last two days we have had a public exchange about RiskMandate's strategy: an analyst's blueprint, drift is the mandate moving and approved business mandates, each answering an AI-assisted review written in a ChatGPT session. Its latest round says the discussion has moved from "what are you actually proposing?" to "can you deliver this useful result for a customer?", and recommends completing one chain: existing requirement → approved agent delegation → implemented control → observed result → evidence that remains valid after change. I agree, and I think that is our go-to-market plan. Not a broader architecture, and not more reviews; one workflow, done end to end, with the gaps visible. One caution I want to keep in front of us: three rounds of an AI review agreeing with a refined position is not market validation. Only a customer's decision is.
record

The delegation record in six parts, filled in for pilot zero, our own inbox, as the plan stands. Nothing is tested yet. The answer to a buyer's question, "what exactly will I have at the end?", is a compact record in six parts: Business requirement. The source rule, its version, its owner and its scope. Agent delegation. What the agent is given to do under it, with limits and exceptions. Control mapping. Which existing system keeps each requirement, or that none can. Evidence. What was tested, against which deployment and policy version, and what happened. Remaining gaps. What is unsupported or unverified, and the owner's decision about it. Change conditions. The events that make the record invalid and need a retest, a restriction or a new approval.
record

It is the practical form of the coverage explanation, and it sits naturally on what we already have: the behaviour policy holds the delegation and what keeps each rule; the five states we published in three decisions, mapped, defined, implemented, enforced, observed and verified, become the evidence column, as long as each state says what was tested and where. We will call it the delegation record, make it the thing we sell, and make keeping it true the thing customers pay for.
translate

A rule for people is not yet a delegation to an agent: a refund rule, with the question an agent must also answer. The review adds the refinement that makes approved business mandates workable. A rule the business already approves was written for a person or a role. Handing it to an agent raises new questions. "Staff may refund up to £100": can the agent execute the refund, or only recommend it? What establishes the amount owed? What limits apply across repeated requests and runs that happen at the same time? Who is the approver for an exception, and what exact action does the approval cover? Which record says the customer is eligible? What change requires the whole thing to be approved again?
translate

So the delegation is made in three visible steps: extract the existing requirement; list the ambiguities and conditions that automation introduces; and get the resulting delegation approved by the requirement's owner. Our customer milestones already ask for a mandate "drafted by the agent and corrected by the customer", and add: "The correction is the elicitation." What we add is the approval as an explicit checkpoint. A model can propose an interpretation; it must not quietly inherit the authority of the original policy.
rules

Three rules from the review that I want in the product from the first day: The approved baseline is never learned from behaviour. If repeated behaviour becomes the new normal, the system normalises the drift it was meant to catch; and a new permission is not new authority. A change to authority needs approval; a change in behaviour needs evaluation. That is the line in drift is the mandate moving: drift is the change nobody approved. Obligations, not only permissions. A rule that blocks every refund respects every limit and still fails a process whose purpose is to reimburse eligible customers. The behaviour policy already has "must" beside yes, ask and no; the pilot will measure that the legitimate work still gets done.
rules

One approved case is not a class of cases. Approving an exception once is different from approving future cases that look like it. Before a precedent from case law for agents becomes reusable, it needs its own record: the facts that must match, what prevents reuse, who approved the generalisation, its scope and duration, and how it is withdrawn.
stages

Three stages: immediate value, maintenance value and repeatability, each with what to show. The plan runs in three stages, each testing a different claim: Immediate value. Find one consequential mismatch between how the process should run and the controls it actually has. Fix it. Show a legitimate task completing, and a forbidden effect stopped, confirmed by the protected system's own record. The customer should be able to say why their deployment decision is now better supported. Maintenance value. In the agreed test environment, make a controlled, realistic change: a permission, an approval condition. Show that the affected requirement is identified, the earlier evidence is marked, and the retest or the decision is triggered. This tests the recurring business far more directly than a second version of a document.
stages

Repeatability. A related workflow, or a second customer with a related problem. Measure what was reused and what had to be rebuilt: time to clarify the mandate, time to map and implement controls, tests reused, integration work, and upkeep. Then ask whether the customer will pay to maintain or extend it. Only the third stage tells us what we are building: a valuable service, a software-assisted service, or a software product. Any of the three is a legitimate outcome, and the evidence should decide.
customer

Deliberately small: one workflow, one accountable business owner, one supported environment, a few consequential requirements, one working control change, and a clear account of what remains uncovered. A second enforcement target is a later test of portability, not a condition for learning from the first. The profile: a team with an agent already doing useful work; a concrete concern about one action or decision; existing systems that could enforce the conditions; a business owner willing to define the delegation; and someone able to implement and test the changes. That gives the engagement the best chance of learning about the product, instead of spending it building basic infrastructure. Teams without those controls need a different offer, with a different cost and buyer, and that is fine; it is just not the first one.
pilot-zero

Before the first customer, we start with ourselves, because we have a real workflow, a real owner, and a known gap. In answering a draft, the inbox agent behind agent@riskmandate.ai reads the mail, researches, drafts and labels, and I read and send every email: 178 of them in its first three and a half weeks. The rule that the agent never sends is, in that article's words, "a rule we keep ourselves, not something the mailbox enforces."
pilot-zero

Running the chain on it already found something. Google's documentation lists the Gmail permissions, and creating a draft needs one of three of them; every one also allows sending. gmail.compose is described as "Manage drafts and send emails", and gmail.modify as "Read, compose, and send emails from your Gmail account". So the mailbox itself cannot keep our rule: there is no permission that lets an agent draft without also letting it send. That is exactly the line the record has to be able to write: this target cannot enforce this requirement. So pilot zero has a clear plan: The requirement and the delegation are written: every email is read and sent by me; the agent drafts, labels, and deletes only its own decision drafts.
pilot-zero

The control mapping has to find something other than Gmail: a hook in the agent's harness that refuses send calls, which would be a setting; or drafts kept outside Gmail, in a vault, so the agent never holds a permission that can send. The evidence is a send attempted by the agent, and Gmail's own record that nothing left. The remaining gap, until then, is an expectation, accepted by me, with every send done by hand. The change conditions are a new permission or connector, a new agent on the mailbox, or a change to who sends. Stage 2 is easy to test on it too: add a permission, and see whether the record notices. When it is done, it will be the first public delegation record, and the template for the first customer.
brief

This plan changes what the RiskMandate sites should say, and the agent that maintains them is being briefed. In short: Lead with the delegation record, not with real-time enforcement: one workflow, from an approved business mandate to tested controls and evidence that is kept current. Publish a dated capability table: available artefacts, working demonstrations, piloted integrations, supported capabilities and plans; and name, in every enforcement example, the component that actually stops the action. Add the translation step to the milestones: extract the requirement, list the automation ambiguities, approve the delegation. Add the three stages and the first-customer profile to the customer site, with the six-part record as the template, and pilot zero as the first worked example when it is done.
limits

Nothing here has been delivered yet. The record for pilot zero is a plan; no row is tested. The review is AI-assisted. Written in a ChatGPT session; its agreement is not market validation. The Gmail finding is from documentation. Google's descriptions of its scopes, read on 22 October 2026, not a test. The candidate controls are untested. A hook is a setting; drafts outside Gmail change the workflow. The first customer is a profile, not a name. We are looking for them.
sources

The third round of an AI-assisted review of our strategy, written in a ChatGPT session on 22 October 2026, paraphrased and quoted in short phrases; Google's documentation of the Gmail API scopes and of drafts.create, read the same day; and our own articles. Related: approved business mandates, drift is the mandate moving, answering a draft, three decisions, mapped, case law for agents, our first customers. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: Most of what I tell this newsroom's agent I type into a chat, and most of it is about something I was reading a minute earlier: this sentence is over the top, that figure is too big, this one is fine, ship it. The chat loses where I was. The site already has most of a better channel: a lane I send notes down, an inbox any browser can append to, a vault that carries my reading between devices. What it does not have is an editor's channel, where what I read, what I sign off and what I want changed reaches the agent on its own, and where the agent answers. This proposes one. A browser becomes an editor's when it is given a key, made by the agent or by another editor; without it, the site is the plain reader's site, unchanged. With it, on newsroom pages only, my reads, my sign-offs against the article's version, my fixes with the phrase selected and my tweaks go up to an editor vault, a subset of my reading account and never all of it. Once a day, and whenever I press a button, an agent with a written mandate reads the vault, runs the checks, such as the wording check I asked for today, applies what is cheap to undo, proposes the rest, and writes back. Around it are five audiences, from the plain reader who sends nothing to the editor who sends everything, each with its own lane and its own key: an anonymous append lane behind a checkbox, a named reader's lane, and the two-way editor's vault. The keys are shared secrets today. They should become key pairs, one per person and per agent, and the inbox already uses one. Another agent on this site builds the vault pane; the brief for it is linked at the end.
The editor's channel: how a key turns a browser into an editor's, and the five audiences, each a lane with its own key.
in-short

Editing happens in a chat, away from the page. The chat loses which sentence, which version, which figure. Most of a better channel exists. A lane for notes, an inbox any browser can append to, a vault across devices. What is missing is an editor's channel. Reads, sign-offs and fixes reaching the agent on their own, and answers coming back. A key turns a browser into an editor's. Without it, the plain reader's site, unchanged. An editor vault holds a subset of my account. Newsroom pages only, and only the kinds I choose. A daily pass reads it, and so does a button. Checks, cheap fixes released, the rest proposed, a report back. Five audiences, five lanes. From sending nothing, through an anonymous checkbox, to two-way. Shared keys now, key pairs later. The inbox already seals to a public key; the rest should follow.
chat

Today I asked this site's agent to stop writing sentences like "the clearest example I have seen". It had used one in an article I was reading, and it was the kind of claim that loses a reader's trust. The fix took minutes: the agent found every case in the recent articles, rewrote them, and added a check so the next one fails before it is committed. But look at how the request got there. I was reading on one device, I noticed the phrase, and I went to a chat on another to describe it from memory. The agent then had to search for which article I meant. That is most of my editing: a sentence is wrong, a figure is too big, a section can go, this piece is fine. Each one starts on a page, at a version, with a phrase selected, and each one arrives in the chat stripped of all of that.
chat

The other half is worse. When I read an article and it is fine, nothing happens. The agent never learns that I read it, how far I got, or that I would have signed it off. A sign-off I do not record is one the agent cannot count on, so the gap between what was published and what I have reviewed stays invisible.
exists

This site has built most of the pieces, for readers rather than for editors. The vault pane. Every reader's reading, notes and personas live in their browser, and, if they choose, in a reader vault they own, opened with a passkey and synced between their devices. The newsroom has no key to it. The activity vault is the design. The lane. A note is one tap at a piece: done, read later, follow up, wrong, fix this, idea, with the phrase that was selected. Send to the newsroom puts the notes not yet sent into a vault of their own and hands the newsroom its read key, once. admin/build/lane.py reads it. The feedback loop is the design, and the first lane I sent changed the pane the same day.
exists

The inbox. An append lane on the reader vault that any browser with a link can write to and none can read, with a key pair made in the reader's browser: messages are sealed to the public key, and the private key stays in the reader's master vault. Send to my vault from any browser is the design, and sixteen notes I did not want to lose is why. Two things are missing. The lane only goes one way: the feedback-loop note says it plainly, "What the lane is not: a channel the newsroom can write back on." And nothing reads the lane unless I ask an agent to.
key

I do not want to change the reader's site to get this. The plain reader should see what they see today, send nothing, and never be asked about editors. So the switch is a key. The agent, or another editor, makes an editor key for a browser and hands it over the way the inbox link is handed over, in the fragment of a link that never reaches a server, or as a QR code. The browser keeps it, and from then on, on newsroom pages, it is in editor mode. Without the key, the code that does any of this never runs. There are two ways to build what the key opens, and I think the answer is both, one on top of the other.
key

An editor vault. A vault of its own, shared by the editors and the agent, that holds a subset of my reading account: what I read on this site, and the notes I make here. Not the meter's spend, not my personas, not my other devices' history. The agent gets access to this vault and to nothing of mine beyond it. A mode in the browser. The key is how a browser joins that vault. Once it has it, the newsroom's code syncs the kinds of activity I chose, as I read, without a button: read, how far, signed off, fix this with the phrase, a message, and the tweaks I make to a page with the site's primitives, the ones fix the page yourself argued every site should publish.
key

One new kind of note matters most: Signed off, against the version of the article I read. If the article changes after that, the sign-off is stale, the same way a section summary on this site goes stale when its section changes. The agent can then say, for every article, whether the version that is live is the version I signed off.
pass

The other half is an agent that reads the vault without being asked. Once a day, and whenever I press Process now in the pane, the pass does the same work: Pull the editor vault and group what arrived by article and version. Record the sign-offs. Which live versions are signed off, which are stale, which were never read. Run the checks on the articles I read: the wording check added today, links, mobile widths, quotes against their sources, summaries against their sections. Act on what is cheap to undo. A wording fix, a figure resized, a section removed when I said to: applied, released, and named in the version row by page and kind of note. How cheap is it to undo is the test: an article is a two-way door, so the pass can release; an email is not, so it never sends one.
pass

Propose the rest. Anything that changes an argument, a claim or a title goes back as a proposal, not a change. Write back. A report into the vault's down lane, which the pane shows under the article it is about: what was done, what is proposed, what was refused and why. The pass is an agent with a policy, like every agent on this site: a grant, the editor vault and the newsroom repository; a mandate, act on the editors' notes; and the limits, written down, as three policies for an agent describes. The pass can also be triggered from a chat, which keeps the channel I use today working while this one is built.
audiences

Once there is an editor's channel, the same design answers a question I have had for a while: how much should a browser send, and to whom? I think the answer is five audiences, each with its own lane and its own key, and the reader chooses which one they are in. Audience What leaves the browser Key The plain reader Nothing None A reader with a vault Their records, to their own devices Their vault key Anonymous, by a checkbox Page, kind of note, phrase An append token A named reader The notes they choose to send A read key, handed over An editor Reads, sign-offs, fixes, tweaks Read and write
audiences

The anonymous lane is the new one. A checkbox in the pane, off by default, that says what it sends. When it is on, a tap at a piece appends a small record to the newsroom's lane: the page, the kind of note, the phrase if one was selected. No account, no device id, no reading history, and the browser cannot read anything back, its own records included. The append lanes already work this way; agent workflows on ephemeral vaults measured a hundred writers posting to one at once. More information can be offered as a second box, the persona or the device type, but each extra field is one the reader turns on.
pki

Two kinds of access do almost everything here. Two-way is a vault's read and write keys, held by both sides: the editors and the agent read and write the editor vault. Append-only is a token that can add and nothing else: the anonymous lane and the inbox. Both are shared secrets today. A key given to an agent can be copied, and the only way to take it back is to make a new vault or a new token. That is fine for one editor and one agent. It does not hold for a desk.
pki

The direction is a key pair per person and per agent. A message is signed by whoever wrote it and sealed to whoever should read it. Access to the editor vault is granted to a public key, and revoked by removing it, without changing anyone else's. The inbox already does half of this: every message to it is sealed to a public key made in the reader's browser. What is missing is the signature, so the drain knows who wrote a message rather than only that someone had the link, and the per-person grant on the vault, which is sgit's to provide.
stands

The vault pane, the lane, the inbox and the append lanes are built and in use. The editor key, the editor vault, the Signed off note, the down lane, the anonymous checkbox and the daily pass are not. Another agent on this site, the one that built the vault pane, builds the browser side; the pass is mine. The map between them is a brief: the editor's channel, with what exists, what to build in which order, and the tests that would show it works.
limits

Nothing in the editor's channel is built. The lane, the inbox and the append lanes are; the rest is a design. One editor so far. The design is for a desk; it has been used by one person. Shared keys are not identity. Until there are key pairs, a lane says that someone had the key, not who. The anonymous lane is not anonymous against everything. The server sees when an append arrived and from where; the record carries no identity, but traffic can. The pass acting on its own is limited to what is cheap to undo. A claim, an argument or a title stays a proposal. Editor mode syncs as I read. That is more data than the lane sends, and the reason it is scoped to newsroom pages and to the kinds of note I turn on. If you run a desk and want to try an editor's channel with an agent, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo from me on 18 October 2026, after asking the agent to remove over-the-top phrases and add a check for them. The designs it builds on are this site's notes: the activity vault, the feedback loop, send to my vault from any browser and the vault, opened. The wording check is admin/build/wording.py. Related: sixteen notes I did not want to lose, fix the page yourself, how cheap is it to undo, three policies for an agent, agent workflows on ephemeral vaults.
