Abstract: Four days after php2shell went public, Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of Root Evidence, posted on LinkedIn that the evidence does not support the wave of AI-enabled breaches many were bracing for, that the exploits are environment-specific, that in the same four days over a thousand CVEs were published and almost none were exploited, and that the rule is the old one: patch what adversaries exploit. This is the data behind each claim, re-counted from public sources and from the PHP story site's evidence, with every number traceable to a query or a captured source. Most of it holds. The post's timestamp is the CVE record's to the second; NVD counts 1,394 CVEs in the same window, not 1,448; none references Exploit-DB or Metasploit; VulnCheck published 25 old bugs with 2017 to 2025 IDs on 22 October; CISA had listed one, the Arista flaw. Two things changed after the post: CISA added both php2shell CVEs to its catalogue on 26 October, and their EPSS scores went from 0.06 and 0.12 to above 0.999 the day before. As of 09:43 UTC on 27 October, no named organisation had said it was compromised through php2shell. The yearly numbers are consistent with the post's wider point, but cannot test it: CVE publications more than doubled this year, while additions to CISA's catalogue rose by 30%. Corrected on 27 October after a review by ChatGPT, which the editor asked for; the changes are listed at the end.
Jeremiah Grossman's LinkedIn post on php2shell, four days after it went public, as shared with me on 27 October 2026.
in-short

Jeremiah's post holds up. Most of its numbers reproduce from public data; the rest are marked below. The timestamp is exact. The CVE record was published at 13:48:34 UTC on 21 October. 1,394, not 1,448, by NVD's count for the same window. Close, but not reconciled: we have possible causes, not the two lists compared. Almost none are expected to be exploited. 1,361 of 1,383 have an EPSS below 0.01, a 30-day forecast, not a count; none cites Exploit-DB or Metasploit in NVD. No confirmed victim, as of 09:43 UTC on 27 October. Attempts, honeypot shells and a CISA listing, yes; of eight named organisations, none confirmed as php2shell. The exploits are environment-specific, as the post says: the public ones are tuned, raced, or wrong. Two things changed since. CISA listed php2shell on 26 October; EPSS went above 0.999 the day before.
in-short

The yearly data is consistent with the wider point, but cannot test it. CVEs more than doubled; CISA's catalogue grew by 30%. AI does cut the effort of building exploits, in Wiz's own account. That is a research capability, not evidence of adversaries' use or of victims. Some numbers need data we do not have. We have asked the PHP story site's team for them.
post

Jeremiah Grossman is the CEO of Root Evidence. Four days after the disclosure, Jeremiah wrote that "plenty of people are calling it the arrival of AI-enabled exploitation at scale and bracing for a wave of breaches", and that "the evidence says otherwise". The claims, in the post's order: the exploits that work are built "for specific environments and a generic wide sweeping exploit is unlikely"; honeypots "have caught plenty of attempts"; "nobody has reported mass compromise, some reports of individual breaches, but nothing confirmed"; in the same four days 1,448 more CVEs were published, nobody published exploit code for any of them in Metasploit or Exploit-DB, VulnCheck put 25 of them on its KEV list, 24 of them old bugs given IDs on 22 October, and CISA added just one, the Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator flaw; Censys counts 32 million PHP services on an affected version. Then the opinion: nothing in the record shows AI "driving up how many vulnerabilities adversaries exploit, or how fast", adversaries "keep working a small set of bugs until those stop paying", so patch php2shell, then "patch what adversaries exploit".
post

The PHP story site keeps exactly the record needed to check this, and the rest is public: NVD's API, CISA's catalogue, FIRST's EPSS scores and the CVE records. Every number below comes from one of them, except where marked; the queries and the derived data are in this article's dataset.
claims

The CVEs of the four-day window, re-counted on 27 October 2026, against Jeremiah Grossman's figures. Log scale. Claim in the post What the data says Verdict Public at 13:48:34 UTC on 21 October The CVE record for CVE-2026-109618: published 2026-10-21T13:48:34.845Z Exact 1,448 CVEs in four days NVD: 1,394 in the same window, 12 of them rejected Close; not reconciled No exploit code in Metasploit or Exploit-DB None of the 1,394 NVD records references either Holds, as far as NVD shows VulnCheck: 25 on its KEV, 24 old bugs given IDs on 22 October, years 2017 to 2025 NVD: VulnCheck, as a CNA, published 25 CVEs with 2017 to 2025 IDs, all on 22 October Close, not the same: 25 old-ID CVEs in NVD against the post's 24 old of 25 on the KEV; KEV membership and when the IDs were assigned not checked CISA added one: Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator
claims

CVE-2026-114625, published 22 October, listed 23 October; the other listing that day, a Collabora flaw, was published on 14 October Exact at the time; three now Censys: 32 million PHP services on an affected version Censys's dashboard is quoted at 36.7 million services on 22 October, by Fortinet Not reproduced Honeypots caught plenty of attempts Amazon's MadPot, ELLIO's sensors, Chainguard's honeypots, Cloudflare's "millions" Holds No mass compromise; nothing confirmed No named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell, at 09:43 UTC on 27 October Holds, as a time-bounded absence Exploits built for specific environments The public chains are tuned to one build, raced, or have the wrong mechanism Holds
record
The compromise record on the PHP story site at 09:43 UTC on 27 October, by kind, and what eight organisations said.
record

The PHP story site's evidence on compromise is a list of every statement, each with its captured source. Its line, at 09:43 UTC on 27 October, six days in: "No named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell." Its 53 rows divide as the figure shows. Three kinds of evidence need keeping apart here: attempts, seen by honeypots and sensors; successful exploitation in a lab or honeypot set up for it, such as the 35 shells below; and a confirmed compromise of a production system, of which there is none so far. CISA's listing sits between them: CISA's own assessment, added to both CVE records, marks exploitation as "active", and names no victim. The eight named organisations are the "reports of individual breaches": GMO Internet Group found malicious programs on servers of its trading service and has not stated the cause; Czech Technical University stopped an attack; Valtec first blamed the PHP flaw, then said the attackers used a flaw in its own service; DMM halted services and would not say whether it was PHP; Germany's Interior Ministry said its site "was not hacked"; Anexia confirmed attempts; Ahold Delhaize denied any link; and the Square Enix report is second-hand and does not say how the access happened.
record

Two more data points from the site's claims since Jeremiah posted. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 retracted, on 25 October, its statement of two days earlier that tied an attack on a European government agency to php2shell, having been unable to confirm the initial access (as reported by SC Media). And watchTowr's head of threat intelligence put reliable indiscriminate exploitation at "a firm No".
specific

The record agrees with him, and is specific about why: The CVSS vector itself says attack complexity is high (AC:H) for both CVEs, and CISA's assessment on the CVE record marks it "Automatable: no". The public bounty win needed one exact PHP build and worker setup, succeeded about seven times in ten in its author's own lab, and took about three hours once the target had a PHP page to attack, as we checked yesterday. A honeypot result of 35 working shells came from what the site's sources call a deliberately favourable setup, on a vulnerable build. VulnCheck, as cited by a detection author, found that none of the public proofs of concept it reviewed had the correct mechanism; Fastly says a working exploit needs knowledge of the running binary's layout.
specific

Honeypots did catch plenty: Amazon's MadPot saw an attempt four days before disclosure, ELLIO's sensors logged hits from the first morning, Chainguard's honeypots by 22 October (as reported second-hand), and Cloudflare's CEO counted "millions" of attempts. The site's exploitation timeline lists each with its source.
window

EPSS scores for the 1,383 CVEs in the window, and the daily scores of the two php2shell CVEs. NVD counts 1,394 CVEs published between 13:48:34 UTC on 21 October and the same time on 25 October. The difference from the post's 1,448 is small, and not reconciled. Two possible causes: NVD's publication time is not always the CVE record's, and counts move as records are added, rejected or re-dated. Only comparing the two lists of IDs would settle it, and we do not have the post's list. Of the 1,394, NVD had fully analysed 3 when we counted on the morning of 27 October (30 by 15:44 UTC the same day); 12 were rejected; most were waiting. They came mostly on weekdays: 494 and 497 on 22 and 23 October, 39 on the Sunday.
window

None references Exploit-DB or Metasploit, which says what NVD's references hold, not what exists elsewhere. FIRST's EPSS, which models the probability of exploitation activity in the next 30 days, scored 1,383 of them on 26 October: 1,361 below 0.01, 19 between 0.01 and 0.1, one Brotli decoder flaw at 0.36, and the two php2shell CVEs at 0.99997 and 0.99981. That is a forecast: a low score means the model does not expect exploitation, not that none was seen. VulnCheck, acting as a CVE authority, published 25 CVEs with ID years from 2017 to 2025, all on 22 October, which is close to the post's numbers (it says 25 on VulnCheck's KEV, 24 of them old) and matches the pattern Jeremiah describes. But an ID's year does not show when it was assigned, and we have not read VulnCheck's KEV, so whether these are the 25 on it is not checked.
changed

Two things, both in the direction of "php2shell is exploited", neither in the direction of a wave: CISA listed both CVEs in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 October, version 2026.10.26 released at 22:24 UTC, with a due date for federal agencies of 29 October. A listing requires evidence of exploitation; it names no victim, and the PHP story site's compromise line did not change. So the window's count on CISA's catalogue is now three: the Arista flaw and the php2shell pair. The site's newsroom carried the listing to readers 5 h 21 min later. EPSS jumped first. Both php2shell scores went from about 0.06 and 0.12 on 24 October to 0.99997 and 0.99981 on 25 October, a day before CISA's listing. Meanwhile the Arista flaw, which CISA listed as exploited on 23 October, sits at 0.01. A model of likely exploitation and a catalogue of evidenced exploitation are different instruments, and they disagree in both directions.
attention
News items about php2shell and twelve flaws already on CISA's catalogue, from the PHP site's Pulse agent, 24 October.
attention

The PHP story site has an agent, Pulse, that tracks other vulnerabilities in the news beside php2shell, with two things kept apart: the evidence of exploitation, as eight levels from a public proof of concept to a named victim, and the attention, as counts of news items. On 24 October, with 53 to 55 feeds checked for each row, php2shell had 295 news items and had reached levels 1 and 4: a public proof of concept and attempts reported by a named party. Twelve flaws that CISA had listed as exploited in the same fortnight, or that were old flaws newly listed, had 11 to 48 news items each. Three of them were from 2015 and 2016. Read it as a description of coverage in this collection, not a controlled measure: similar numbers of feeds are not the same feeds, and a named pair of flaws is counted against single CVEs. Even so, it is consistent with the post's closing argument: what is exploited and what is talked about are different lists, and patching should follow the first. A run with the same feeds for every row is in our brief.
ai
CVEs published by NVD and entries added to CISA's KEV catalogue, 1 January to 26 October of each year, 2023 to 2026.
ai

Jeremiah's opinion is that nothing in the record shows AI driving up how many vulnerabilities adversaries exploit, or how fast. The yearly numbers describe the background, but they cannot test that. From 1 January to 26 October, NVD published 89,531 CVEs this year, more than twice the 40,266 of the same period in 2025; CISA's catalogue added 274 entries, 30% more than the 210 of 2025, so additions as a share of publications fell from 0.62% in 2023 to 0.31%. The two numbers count different populations, since CISA's additions include CVEs published in earlier years; the catalogue records what CISA has evidence for, not attack volume or speed; and neither says anything about AI. Testing the claim needs matched cohorts: the CVEs published in a period, each followed for the same time, with the time to the first evidence of exploitation. We have asked for that below.
ai

Three questions need keeping apart. Can AI help build exploits? Yes, by the account of a team that found php2shell: Wiz's researchers wrote that frontier models enabled them "to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours", and that "a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work". Are adversaries using it at scale? Jeremiah expects so: "I can't imagine any exploit writer or cyber adversary not using heavy AI tooling at this point". Has it produced more exploited flaws, faster, or more victims? That is the post's claim, and on this record the answer is not yet, with the caveat that four days and a catalogue are a small window on it. The first is a demonstrated research capability; the post is about the second and third.
exposure

What each published exposure figure for PHP counts, from Censys to Unit 42 and "almost 70% of websites". Log scale. The post's 32 million is Censys's count of services, not servers or organisations. Censys's dashboard was quoted at 36.7 million services on 22 October. If both figures are the same measure, the count went down. That could be patching, but also scan coverage, services going offline, fingerprints or the method changing; and, as Fortinet notes, "version-based estimates may include installations already patched through vendor backports". We could not read the dashboard ourselves, so the trend is a question, not a finding. What the record does show is how far apart the published figures are: from 1.57 million unpatched hosts to "almost 70% of websites", because each counts a different thing, and a version string is not the same as an exploitable server.
asked

Some of the post cannot be checked from public data, and some of it deserves a better dataset than the one we have. We have written a brief for the PHP story site's team asking for: VulnCheck's KEV entries for the window; Censys's exposure count as a series since 21 October, with its definition; the reconciliation of 1,448 and 1,394; a check of Metasploit, Exploit-DB and nuclei for the php2shell pair and the window, which Pulse could not do because its GitHub searches were refused; a Pulse run over all the CVEs CISA and VulnCheck listed in the window, with the same feeds for every row; honeypot and sensor volumes by day, to test whether adversaries "keep working a small set of bugs"; and the time from publication to a KEV listing, by year, to test "how fast".
limits

The post is quoted, not endorsed by its author. This article is ours. NVD's count differs from the post's, and both are snapshots of moving records. VulnCheck's KEV and Censys's dashboard were not read. The table marks them as such. "No reference in NVD" is not "no exploit anywhere". NVD's references are incomplete. The yearly ratio is a rate, not the share of the same set of CVEs. It describes; it does not test AI's effect. EPSS is a forecast. It is used here for what the model expects, not for what was observed. The attention chart is descriptive. The rows do not share the same feeds. The compromise record is a time-bounded absence. The PHP story site has an agent, Pulse, that tracks other vulnerabilities in the news beside php2shell, with two things kept apart: the evidence of exploitation, as eight levels from a public proof of concept to a named victim, and the attention, as counts of news items. On 24 October, in comparable feeds, php2shell had 295 news items and had reached levels 1 and 4: a public proof of concept and attempts reported by a named party. ai

Jeremiah's opinion is that nothing in the record shows AI driving up how many vulnerabilities adversaries exploit, or how fast. The yearly numbers are consistent with it, with one caveat. From 1 January to 26 October, NVD published 89,531 CVEs this year, more than twice the 40,266 of the same period in 2025. CISA's catalogue added 274 entries, 30% more than the 210 of 2025. Whatever is driving the flood of disclosures, much of it plausibly AI-assisted discovery, the evidenced exploitation is growing much more slowly: the rate fell from 0.62% of publications in 2023 to 0.31% this year. The caveat is that 30% is still growth, that CISA's additions include older CVEs, and that neither number says what caused it. "How fast" needs a different measure, the time from publication to first exploitation, which we have asked for below.

Abstract: What is a good exit for a founder? Fundamentally, it is somebody buying the company: buying control of what you created. And control can be sold long before the shares are. A founder can own 50 or 60% and not be calling the shots, because the board and the investors' vetoes decide; another can own 14% and hold 61% of the votes. My argument is that the founder's exit is the day control changes hands, and that is the day to leave. Founders want to create. When the strategy is no longer theirs, and the company moves from explorer to villager and town planner, the founder's energy is no longer what it needs, and staying costs them their health, their sanity and what they could build next, for a couple more zeros. The research agrees that most founders lose the top job early: in Noam Wasserman's study, half were no longer CEO by year three, and four in five were forced to step down. So negotiate the exit at the start, while you have leverage. I call it the Mourinho clause: his exits, whatever caused them, were priced in his contracts before anyone needed them. And write down now the number that would make you happy, so that later you recognise when you have passed it.
The company's path from explorer to villager to town planner, and the founder's exit as the day control is sold.
in-short

The exit is when somebody buys control. Not necessarily all the shares. Control can go long before ownership. A board majority and investor vetoes are enough. That is the day to leave. When the strategy is no longer yours, move on. Founders want to create. The town planner phase needs someone else's energy. Most founders lose the top job early. Half within three years, in Wasserman's study. Negotiate the exit at the start. The Mourinho clause: the exit priced before anyone needs it. Write your number down now. And notice when you have passed it.
exit

A good exit for a founder is somebody buying the company. That is fundamentally what it is: somebody buys what you created, the technology, the service, the team, the customers. The question that follows is whether you sell all your shares or keep some. But I think the shares are the wrong way to look at it. The exit is when somebody buys control.
exit

Control and ownership are not the same thing, and they part company early. A founder can own 50 or 60% of a company and not be calling the shots. Investors who join in later rounds usually take board seats and protective provisions, the right to veto a sale, new shares, new debt or the budget. As a Cooley partner put the investor's position, "thou shall not do anything that will impact my investment… without my blessing". Add a drag-along, which lets a majority force the others to sell on the same terms, and the founder with the most shares may be the one with the least say. It works the other way too. Mark Zuckerberg owns about 13.6% of Meta's shares and holds 61.0% of the votes, because his Class B shares carry ten votes each, according to Meta's 2025 proxy statement. He has sold most of the company and kept control of it.
exit

Owning is not controlling: an illustrative founder with 60%, and Meta's founder with 13.6% of shares and 61% of votes. So the exit is not the day you sell your last share. It is the day you are no longer the one deciding.
leave

My argument is that the founder should move on as soon as they lose control. As soon as they are not calling the shots, as soon as the strategy is not fully in line with what they want to do, that is the time to go. It could be a moment when they still own 50 or 60% or more.
leave

Founders want to found. They want to create, to be in the creative flow for as long as they can, and to be productive. In the terms this site uses, a founder is an explorer. Companies move on from that: they become villagers, with process and a board, and then town planners, run for reliability and for value. That is sometimes exactly what the investors want, and an acquirer who buys a product because they like it and want to extract as much value as they can from it is making a pure town planner play. That can be exactly what the company needs. It is a different game from the founder's.
leave

What worries me is how many brilliant people I know, more intelligent than me, who fall into the trap of staying. They are ridiculously stressed. They may have a couple more zeros in their bank account, but the cost to their personal lives, to what they wanted to do, to their health, to their sanity, and to what they could have created next, was massive. A smaller amount, proportionally, is much better, and for a founder who has sold a company it is still a decent amount of money. Open source makes leaving easier. If the work you care about is open, you take it with you, which is what open source what you build argued: the one way to keep using your own work after you leave.
evidence

Losing the top job early is the norm, not the exception. Noam Wasserman studied 212 American start-ups for the Harvard Business Review in 2008: by the time they were three years old, half of the founders were no longer CEO; in year four, 40% were still in the post; and fewer than a quarter led their companies' initial public offerings. "Four out of five entrepreneurs," he wrote, "are forced to step down from the CEO's post." How long founders stay in charge, from Noam Wasserman's study of 212 American start-ups. His conclusion was that founders choose, knowingly or not, between being rich and being king: they "make 'rich' versus 'king' trade-offs to maximize either their wealth or their control over the company", in the words of the article's abstract. Giving up control tends to build a more valuable company; keeping it tends to mean a smaller one. Neither is wrong. What hurts is not knowing which one you chose.
evidence

Acquisitions follow the same pattern. A study of 4,000 acquisitions of US tech start-ups by J. Daniel Kim of Wharton, reported by MIT Sloan, found that 33% of acquired workers left in the first year, against 12% of ordinary hires. People who built something often do not stay to be managed inside someone else's.
mourinho

I call the answer the Mourinho clause, after José Mourinho, the football manager. My theory about him, and it is a theory, is this. He had great success early, and he realised that what he is very good at is impact: coming into a club, winning something it has not won before, and changing it. So he goes to a club and says: I will come in, I will get you success, I will be here for two years, maybe three, and when my impact wanes and it is time to part, here are the terms. The cynical version is that the friction at the end is part of the plan, so that the club finds it easy to let him go. I do not know that, and nothing I found shows it.
mourinho

What the record does show is that the exits were priced in advance. When he left Real Madrid by mutual agreement in 2013, he gave up, as AFP reported, "the €20 million ($26 million) compensation clause in the event he was sacked", and the club gave up "a clause of the same amount" payable if he left for another club: the exit was priced both ways before either side needed it. Manchester United's dismissal of him in 2018 cost the club £19.6m in compensation to him and his staff. And his contract at Benfica reportedly carried a €15m termination clause, the price at which Real Madrid hired him back this year. His third seasons have been hard often enough that Sky Sports named the pattern "third-season syndrome". Mourinho's clubs since 2004: the length of each spell and how it ended.
mourinho
I think most senior executives do the same these days, once they have enough power and someone who wants them: they negotiate the exit on the way in. Founders should too.
negotiate

The time to agree the exit is at the beginning, when the investors want you, not at the end, when the board does not. Four things are worth writing down. The trigger. What counts as losing control: a new board majority, a change of control, a sale, the strategy no longer yours. The terms. That leaving then makes you a good leaver. In UK shareholder agreements, as Ashfords explains, good leavers are typically "those leaving due to reasons beyond their control", such as illness or redundancy, and keep their vested shares or are paid fair market value; bad leavers, typically "those dismissed for cause", generally forfeit their unvested shares. Leaving because you lost control is not on the usual good-leaver list, which is exactly why it should be written in. Add accelerated vesting, a price for your shares, and a fixed transition period.
negotiate

What you keep. Your name, your reputation, the open source you wrote, and a non-compete narrow enough to let you build again. Your number. See below. This is also leverage in the negotiation. If investors know that asking for too much control means losing the founder, they price that in. Sometimes they will still ask for it, and that may be the right outcome for both sides: the company has matured, it no longer needs that ball of energy, it needs someone to execute, and a new CEO and a new CTO take it from there. That might be the right outcome for everybody, and it is easiest when it was agreed at the start.
number

Write down, today, the amount you would be happy with: the number that would change your life, written while you are broke or close to it. Then, when the alternatives arrive, the next round, the bigger offer, the reason to stay three more years, look back at that number. You will probably find you passed it some time ago. Take a step back, and be happy with what you have. This connects to the previous article. The people who control a company decide how big each slice is and when it is sold. Selling a slice is not an exit; selling control is. A founder who understands the difference can sell slices for years, as sell, don't issue argued, and choose the day they sell the part that matters.
limits

The Mourinho theory is mine. He has not said it; the clauses are documented, the motives are not. Some figures are as reported. The Benfica clause and his later appointment are from press reports. Every company is different. Some founders are the right people to run the company for decades. This is not legal advice. Leaver and control terms need a lawyer, in your jurisdiction. Wasserman's data are from 2008. The pattern is old; the numbers may have moved.

Abstract: For twenty years the winning technology startup was usually built by a clever, ambitious outsider: someone who found a pain point, often through a hundred conversations with people they could reach, raised money on belief, hired the subject-matter experts, and displaced incumbents that had the customers, the knowledge and sometimes the money. It is a very American playbook, many bets for a few large wins, and it changed whole industries. It also has a second act: the disruptors became the incumbents, and much of what they built is now the software everyone complains about. My argument is that generative AI changes who can start. When agents do most of the execution, the people who know the problem can build the product themselves, without the millions that used to come first. The data on experts was always on their side: the fastest-growing US startups are founded at a mean age of 45, and three or more years in the same industry doubles the rate of top-tier success. And this favours Europe: its investors want to see it working, value lower, and ask for more revenue at the raise, which is exactly the discipline an expert founder needs, because money too early is one of the most reliable ways to kill a startup. Three examples: me in security, a knee surgeon in knee health, and a transcriber in legal transcription.
Two playbooks: the outsider who finds a gap, and the expert who lives the problem and builds it with agents.
in-short

The last twenty years belonged to outsiders with capital. Find a gap, raise on belief, hire the experts, displace the incumbents. It worked, and it is not a criticism. Those companies changed industries; sometimes new blood is the only way. Then they became the incumbents. Tools piled up, innovation slowed, and a lot was lost on the way. Execution just got cheap. Agents do most of the building; a third of new US startups now have a single founder. The experts were always the better bet. Mean founding age of the fastest-growing firms is 45; industry experience doubles the odds. Three examples. Me in security, a knee surgeon in knee health, a transcriber in legal transcription. This favours Europe. Investors who want to see it working, and money that comes later, suit founders who can now build first.
playbook

If you look at the technology companies that did well in the last ten or twenty years, and at the many more that got funded, or were bought, a pattern repeats. Someone very clever and very ambitious finds a gap in a market. Often they experienced it personally; often they did the famous hundred calls with stakeholders and asked: what hurts? Which already says something: they were people who could get those calls. Then they raised money, hired the right people, including the subject-matter experts they did not have, and built a company on top of it.
playbook

I have watched this many times in cybersecurity. And it worked because, in execution, these startups displaced a large number of incumbents who had a much better starting position: the customers, the environment, the domain knowledge, sometimes the money, and often they had even done the projects. What the incumbents lacked was the structure, the workflows and, to be fair, the technology culture. The startups competed in markets they did not fully understand and hired their way into them, with better tech, more focused funding and faster feedback loops.
playbook

The money behind it is built for that. It is a portfolio of many bets, of which a few pay for the rest. In Horsley Bridge's data on just over 7,000 venture investments from 1985 to 2014, as Benedict Evans reported it, "Around half of all investments returned less than the original investment", and "6% of deals produced at least a 10x return, and those made up 60% of total returns." That model rewards belief in a founder and speed, because the one winner has to be very large.
not-criticism

These companies built amazing engines, generated a lot of revenue, and changed industries. Sometimes you do need outsiders. Clayton Christensen's study of disk drives found that the firms that led "in every instance of developing and adopting disruptive technologies were entrants to the industry, not its incumbent leaders." The evidence is not that tidy everywhere: when experts reviewed 77 of the cases Christensen and Raynor used, only 7 fitted the theory in full. But the pattern of new entrants beating those with every advantage is real enough that it shaped how a generation of investors thinks.
not-criticism

And the talent was often already inside the incumbents. Adrian Cockcroft, then at Netflix, tells of a Fortune 100 CTO who said to him: "Netflix has a superstar development team, we don't!" His answer, reported in 2014: "Netflix hired them from you, and got out of their way." The people were there. What they lacked was the environment, the motivation and the resources to innovate where they were.
incumbents

The irony is that the same agility that took a company into a market and displaced the incumbents tends to fade, in a very Wardley map way, until the disruptor looks like what it displaced. Simon Wardley wrote in 2016, of the war that follows a wave of change, that "The new entrants are rapidly becoming the new titans", while "The former giants have old models that are dying". There is research behind the fading: older firms produce technology of lower quality, and after a diversifying merger, the novelty of the acquired company's research falls by about 60%. Something is lost when a startup is bought or goes bust; sometimes on purpose: in drug development, 5.3% to 7.4% of the acquisitions studied were killer acquisitions, bought to stop a competing project.
incumbents

It shows in what people live with. Most people will tell you that software is a pain, and while I could not find a clean survey of how satisfied people are with business software, the friction is measured. Workers in three Fortune 500 companies toggled between applications "roughly 1,200 times each day". In security, organisations juggle "an average of 83 different security solutions from 29 vendors", and in Panaseer's latest survey, "84% of CISOs say they have been blindsided by incidents they thought their existing controls and tools should have prevented." Many of those tools were the disruptors once.
cheap

What has changed is who can start. With generative AI, and agents in particular, much of the execution that used to need a funded team can be done by one person who knows exactly what to build. I wrote about the mechanics in Omnichannel programming and The citizen developer is good news: the expert's own application is the best brief ever written, and increasingly, it is the product.
cheap

The data is moving the same way. Carta reports that the share of new US startups with a solo founder rose from 23.7% in 2019 to 36.3% in the first half of 2025. In Stripe's data, the top 100 AI companies on its platform reached $1 million in annualised revenue in a median of 11.5 months. Bessemer puts the fastest AI companies at $1.13 million of recurring revenue per employee, four to five times a typical software company. These are the fastest, not the average, and some of the claims are a promoter's own. But the direction is clear: the millions of pounds that used to be the price of starting are no longer the price of starting.
experts

What the data says about founders with experience in an industry, European startups and premature scaling. The myth of the young outsider was never the whole story. The largest study I know, of 2.7 million US founders, found that "The mean age at founding for the 1-in-1,000 fastest growing new ventures is 45.0", and that "successful entrepreneurs are middle-aged, not young." More to the point: "Prior experience in the specific industry predicts much greater rates of entrepreneurial success." Founders with three or more years in the same industry reached top-tier growth at twice the rate of those with none. What held the experts back was not knowledge. It was access: to capital, to engineers, to the long, expensive build before anything could be shown. That is exactly the part that got cheap.
founders

Three subject-matter experts, building in their own field: what each comes from and what they build for. Me, in security. I come from application security, much of it in OWASP, and from working as a CISO. I tried this before with The Cyber Boardroom, which taught me what personas are worth and paused for want of a place to keep confidential data. sgit.ai and RiskMandate are much better examples of using my security knowledge to build a company: encrypted vaults whose server holds nothing, and behaviour policies for agents that a risk owner can sign. The agents write most of the code, and SG/Send alone has 4,476 commits; the briefs, the buyers and the risk model are mine.
founders

Chim Gupte, in knee health. Chinmay Gupte is a consultant knee surgeon in London, a clinical reader at Imperial College, "an ex professional sportsman who has a PhD in knee ligament research". He is building OmKneeHealth, "a clinically led platform dedicated exclusively to knee health", with My Knee Score, "Ten questions about pain, movement and daily life. One score out of 100." He knows knees, and the patients and clinicians who need the product were his long before there was one. I have been helping him. Kate Curtis-Evans, in legal transcription. Kate is the founder of Audio Genius, which she describes as "the future of Legal Transcription & Workflow Management", "Built by a Transcriber, for Transcription Professionals". It could be used for a lot of things; she knows legal transcription from the inside, so it starts there. Some of the documents I have written were written with her work in mind.
founders

None of these is a hundred-call outsider. Each comes from the field, has the contacts in it, and is focused on one thing. That focus used to be a weakness in front of an investor who wanted a huge market. It is now the advantage, because the build is no longer what stops them.
europe

It is often said that American investors back the founder and the vision and throw money at it, while European investors want to see it working. There is myth and rewriting of history on both sides, but the data has a version of it. In Equidam's data, European companies raise at higher revenue, a median band of $1 million to $5 million against $100,000 to $1 million in the US, at median pre-money valuations of $6.54 million against $14.64 million, with funding targets 46% smaller. The vendor says itself that this does not show cause, and it is aggregated, but it fits what founders say.
europe

I think that scepticism is exactly what this generation needs, because getting money too soon is one of the worst things that can happen to a startup. The Startup Genome study of about 3,200 high-growth internet startups found that "74% of high growth internet startups fail due to premature scaling", and that "Many investors invest 2-3x more capital than necessary in startups in the discovery phase." CB Insights' latest review of failed startups puts it more bluntly, under the heading "Money can't save you". An expert founder who can build the first version with agents, show it working, and then raise for scale rather than discovery is exactly the founder sceptical money is good for. Atomico's 2025 report finds that "European companies are just as capital efficient as their US counterparts"; the gap is in the size of the money, not the skill.
europe

And the values fit. Europe is where open source has a policy behind it: the Commission's technological sovereignty package of June 2026 includes an open source strategy that "will scale up open source alternatives in priority areas", and Mistral released Mistral 3 in December 2025 with the line "All models are released under the Apache 2.0 license." Dealroom found that "Impact took 15% of European VC funding in 2025", about twice North America's share of 7%. A decentralised, open source, humanities-driven way of building, where profit is not the only measure, is closer to how European capital already thinks, and to why open source is about to become the most secure software we have.
europe

The gap is real at the other end, and I do not want to hide it. The Draghi report says "The share of global VC funds raised in the EU is just 5%, compared to 52% in the US", and close to 30% of the unicorns founded in Europe between 2008 and 2021 moved their headquarters abroad. Europe is weak at scaling. My argument is that the first part, the part that now matters most, is where it is strong.
limits

Not that outsiders are finished. New blood still matters; the claim is that experts can now start too. The AI growth figures are the fastest, not the typical. Some, like Y Combinator's, are the promoter's own. The Europe and US comparison is weakly evidenced. One vendor's aggregated data; no clean Series A study was found. No survey of software satisfaction was found. The friction figures stand in for it. Two of the three founders are people I help. What is said about them is from their own public descriptions. Updated on 15 October. Kate's surname, company and her own description were added after publication. I have a stake. sgit.ai and RiskMandate are mine. If you are an expert building in your own field, and want to compare notes, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Abstract: For as long as I have worked in security there has been no clear winner between open source and proprietary software. Open source had the code in view, and fixes that sweep a bug's variants; it also had very few people and almost no budget for the slow, expensive reviews that find the hard bugs. Proprietary software had the budget, and the cover of being hidden, and got away with a lot. That balance just moved. Models can now run deep security reviews over and over, on every project, at a cost that used to buy one consultant for a day. The thing open source lacked was paid attention, and that is the thing that just became abundant. I thought Chainguard had started publishing the projects where its AI found nothing; I could not find that. What I found is better: the maintainer of curl writing about a year in which AI review first drowned his project in noise, then produced hundreds of real fixes, then a frontier scan that found a single low-severity bug, and then, today, deeper tools finding more. That is what a project getting harder to break looks like. Put it next to two things I have argued before, that sovereignty needs open code and open schemas, and that the business is maintaining the version each customer actually runs, and three forces meet at one place: the least amount of code in production.
Open source against proprietary: the balance that moved when model-driven security review became cheap and deep.
in-short

No clear winner, until now. Open source had visibility and few reviewers; proprietary had budget and cover. The eyeballs get cheap. Deep security review by models, repeated on every change, is the attention open source could never pay for. curl shows the shape. Noise, then hundreds of real fixes, then a frontier scan that found one bug, then deeper tools finding more. The scale is real. Over a thousand projects scanned by one lab; thousands of patches by one coalition; maintainers asking for it to slow down. Higher bars, fewer and better projects. Low-hanging fruit disappears; contributions need proof; provenance matters. Three forces meet. Secure, sovereign and paid for, all pointing at the same place. The least code in production. What the maintainer sells, what the customer runs, and what security wants.
balance

The argument for open source security has always been Eric Raymond's, from The Cathedral and the Bazaar: "Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow." The argument against it has always been that the eyeballs were not there. Most open source is understaffed and unpaid; in Tidelift's 2024 survey, as The Register reported, "The portion of respondents who reported they are unpaid hobbyists remains at 60 percent". Projects used by companies with thousands of developers are maintained by a handful of people with almost no revenue. Nobody pays for the slow security review that takes weeks, the kind I have done many times, where finding the bug, proving it and documenting it is work you cannot do in five minutes. The low-hanging fruit was eaten fast; the deep work often never happened.
balance

Proprietary software had the opposite profile. It had budget for security teams and paid reviews. It also had cover: code nobody outside could read, fewer attackers looking, products hidden behind other environments. A lot of software got away with things that would not have survived being public. If the source of some of the major SaaS products were exposed tomorrow, a lot would be found. What open source did have was efficiency. Anyone can read the code, and when a serious bug is reported publicly, the fix rarely stops at the one bug: the variations get hunted down too. We know how to build secure systems; the proof is the number that survive very motivated attackers. The question was always who could afford the attention.
cheap

That is what changed. I now run security reviews with models on the products I work on, and the depth is remarkable: it finds real issues, I can point it at particular areas, we argue about what it found, and we fix it. That used to take a specialist weeks. It now takes an afternoon, and it can run again on the next change. The thing open source lacked was paid attention, and that is the thing that just became abundant. The thing proprietary software had, being hidden, is worth less every month, because the same reviews run on whatever ships, leaks or can be reverse engineered. That is the move: open source on steroids.
cheap

The numbers are already large. Anthropic's update on its Project Glasswing in May reported scanning "more than 1,000 open-source projects" and estimated "6,202 high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities" among the findings; the bottleneck, it said, is now "how quickly we can verify, disclose, and patch", and "some have even asked us to slow down" the rate of disclosures. Chainguard's Athena coalition reported, at its launch in June, "2,000 patches across 500 projects", and its harness, which Chainguard, mapped described, has been run "against over 65 projects and validated over 680 findings". In DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge final in 2025, the systems "discovered 54 unique synthetic vulnerabilities" and also found "18 real, non-synthetic vulnerabilities".
curl

One project, one year of machine eyeballs: curl, from its maintainer's own posts. I went looking for something I thought I had seen, Chainguard publishing the projects where its AI hunting found nothing, with curl among them. I could not find it, from Chainguard or anyone else. What I found tells the story better, in the words of curl's maintainer, Daniel Stenberg. First the noise. curl ended its bug bounty on 31 January 2026. Over its life it had found "87 confirmed vulnerabilities", but by 2025 "Not even one in twenty was real." Low-effort, machine-written reports were swamping a small team. Then the real wave. In the autumn of 2025, AI-assisted reports from careful researchers and tools started landing real bugs, and by May he counted that earlier tools had "triggered somewhere between two and three hundred bugfixes".
curl

Then the quiet scan. In May, a frontier model's scan of curl found one vulnerability, "yes, as in singular one", of low severity, and its report said "Zero memory-safety vulnerabilities found." His conclusion was the right one: "Any project that has not scanned their source code with AI powered tooling will likely find huge number of flaws". And then, today, more. An audit with AI tooling produced "no less than thirty-five published curl vulnerabilities", a high-severity bug was found by Anthropic "using their new OSS Scanner", and curl 8.23.0 shipped with 24 security fixes.
curl

That is not a project failing. It is a project getting harder to break, wave by wave, with each better tool finding what the last one could not, and the fixes sweeping the variants. The cost has moved from paying for attention to judging it: the maintainers' time is now the bottleneck, which is why curl's contribution rules now say that "If you asked an AI tool to find problems in curl, you must make sure to reveal this fact in your report."
changes

So I expect the bar to rise everywhere. More findings, with more proof. Contributions held to a much higher standard, because the small fixes a newcomer used to send can now be done by anyone with a model, and should be. Fewer projects, and better ones. The long tail of tiny packages and single-purpose libraries, the dependency trees with hundreds of entries, will shrink, because a lot of very specific little APIs can now be written in place, better.
changes

What will not go away is security research by people motivated to find what the tools miss, domain experts who understand what a project is for, and maintainers who keep it working. And provenance will matter more: where a piece of code came from, who wrote it, who reviewed it. In Simon Wardley's terms, you do not want mission-critical code written at explorer speed; you want it industrialised. In his words, "Town Planners are brilliant people. They are able to take something and industrialise it". Accountable code, reviewed up to the line, is what makes all of this scale, and it is the same graph from story to line that code review as a fractal semantic graph draws.
forces

Three forces meeting at the least code in production: secure, sovereign and commercially maintained open source. Put this next to two things I have argued before, and they line up. Secure. The eyeballs open source never had, at last, and a higher bar for everything that goes in. Sovereign. You cannot have sovereignty without open source and open schemas. Sovereignty is the ability to move: move the data, the compute and the applications. You can only move what you can read and run elsewhere, and with competition on service rather than lock-in, the bigger companies should win because they serve better, not because the customer cannot leave.
forces

Paid for. The business model I already run in my sgit environments, in vaults and in RiskMandate: the customer gets a private repository with their deployment, their configuration and only the features they actually use, and pays for it to be maintained. They could do it themselves, and then they would have to keep doing it. The SaaS apocalypse made the same point from the other side: what people really bought was never the features, it was that the thing is maintained, and the future is companies that take what was built and run it. This is not a free-for-all; open source is a licence, as What open source is, and is not explained, and Open source is not free measured how little of its value comes back to it. Maintenance as the product is how more of it can.
least-code

Here is the irony where the three meet. The customer wants only the features they use. The maintainer who sells the customised version wants as little as possible to maintain. Security wants as little as possible to review, patch and attack. Everyone ends up aligned on running the least amount of code in production, which is the argument of The minimum code below, where removing what a use case never runs took one real tool from 1,500 files to 428. For the first time, the incentives of the people who write open source, the people who sell it and the people who secure it point the same way. That is the intersection I think we are at: open source that is more secure because the eyeballs finally got cheap, required because sovereignty needs it, and paid for because maintaining exactly what each customer runs is a business.
limits

No list of clean projects. I could not find Chainguard or anyone else publishing the projects where AI hunting found nothing; curl's story is the evidence instead. curl is not clean. It is a well-run project being found harder to break, and still having bugs found, as of today. The counts are the reporters' own. Anthropic's, Chainguard's and DARPA's figures are as they published them. The cost and depth of model review are my experience. On the products I work on; others will see different results. The future part is an argument. Fewer and better projects, a shrinking long tail, and maintenance as the business are predictions. If you maintain an open source project and want help with review at this new scale, or you want your version of one maintained for you, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 14 October 2026, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. A research agent gathered the evidence and the quotes were checked on the primary pages. Daniel Stenberg's blog, including the end of the curl bug bounty, the May scan, a UAF turned RCE and a curl audit by Aisle, and curl's contribution rules; Anthropic, Project Glasswing: an initial update; Chainguard, the first disclosure from its harness; Help Net Security on the Athena coalition; DARPA, AIxCC results; The Register on the Tidelift survey; Eric S. Raymond, The Cathedral and the Bazaar. All read on 14 October 2026.
cheap

What will not go away is security research by people motivated to find what the tools miss, domain experts who understand what a project is for, and maintainers who keep it working. And provenance will matter more: where a piece of code came from, who wrote it, who reviewed it. In Simon Wardley's terms, you do not want mission-critical code written at pioneer speed; you want it industrialised. In his words, "Town Planners are brilliant people. They are able to take something and industrialise it". Accountable code, reviewed up to the line, is what makes all of this scale, and it is the same graph from story to line that code review as a fractal semantic graph draws.

Abstract: On the evening of 22 October, Jeremiah Grossman wrote on LinkedIn that "the false-positives for php2shell from makeshift scanners is what's going to be apocalyptic". I replied that, as of the night before, there was no public record of a company being hit. Both things are true, and the data the PHP story's source watch captured by midday on 23 October shows why they belong together. One scanner maker says most scanners in circulation read the version string, and a version string cannot see a distribution's backported fix: one user has already reported a check script calling Ubuntu's patched PHP vulnerable. One account opened 53 templated "heads up" issues, each saying it may itself be a false positive. A detection guide withdrew its own ModSecurity rule because it never fired. Against that, the compromise map holds millions of attempts and no named organisation saying php2shell was the way in. When the noise is this loud and the confirmed signal this quiet, the false positives are not a side effect: they are what organisations act on, and switching a patched site off because a makeshift scanner said so is an incident of its own.
Jeremiah Grossman's LinkedIn post on php2shell false positives, as captured on 23 October 2026.
in-short

Jeremiah Grossman's warning is right. The evidence a day later already shows the pattern. Most scanners read the version string. That is what one scanner maker says, and a version string cannot see a backported fix. The predicted error has been reported. A community check script called Ubuntu's patched PHP vulnerable. The noise is already in bulk. 53 templated issues from one account, 62 issues for php2shell "false positive". Detection rules fail too, in both directions. One guide withdrew a ModSecurity rule that never fired. The signal is quiet. Millions of attempts, and no named organisation saying php2shell was the way in. Ask how a scanner decides. Then check the package, not the banner, before switching anything off.
the-post

On the evening of 22 October (UTC), Jeremiah Grossman, chief executive of Root Evidence, posted on LinkedIn: "The false-positives for php2shell from makeshift scanners is what's going to be apocalyptic." It is a short, cheeky line, and an important one. I replied under it with a pointer to the PHP story site: as of the night before, there was no public record of a company being hit.
the-post

The two statements are not in tension. They describe the same situation from two sides. When the confirmed damage is small and the fear is large, what organisations act on is whatever their tools tell them. If the tools are wrong, the action is wrong too. So I asked the PHP story's researcher to make it a research angle: how good the scanners and detection rules are, who reports them getting it wrong, and how the noise flows. The brief is public, and by 12:40 UTC on 23 October the source watch (vault oq9gflln) had twelve captured pages in it, each with its snapshot and hash. The twelve pieces of evidence in the scanner-noise angle, captured 12:38 to 12:40 UTC on 23 October 2026.
version-strings

There are two ways a scanner can decide that a server is vulnerable. It can read the version the server advertises, in a banner, a header or the output of php -v, and compare it with the fixed release. Or it can try to produce the fault, harmlessly, and see whether it appears. The first is quick to write and wrong in a predictable way. Linux distributions backport fixes into their own packages without changing the upstream version number. Ubuntu's patched PHP 8.5 package is 8.5.4-0ubuntu1.5, listed as fixed (the Konfirmity advisory collects the distributions' fixed packages and says it plainly: "Distributions often backport the fix without changing the PHP version number"). The upstream number in that package is still 8.5.4, below the fixed upstream release, 8.5.12. A scanner that reads 8.5.4 says vulnerable. The server is fixed. That is not a hypothetical. In the watch:
version-strings

Searchlight Cyber, which released an open-source scanner, is quoted by Help Net Security saying that most of the scanners in circulation "rely on version checks, or do not accurately depict vulnerable conditions for both mod_php and php-fpm". Its own scanner tries to produce the fault first and reads the version only as a last resort. An issue on a community check script, php2shell-check, reports that the script calls Ubuntu's patched 8.5.4-0ubuntu1.5 vulnerable, because the version string is older than the fixed upstream release. Exactly the error the method predicts. Two ways a scanner decides on the same patched Ubuntu server: reading the version string, or trying the fault.
bulk

A false positive in one scanner is a bug. A false positive sent to many people at once is noise, and it scales. 53 templated issues, from one account. Titled "Heads up: this repo pins a PHP version affected by PHP2Shell", at 12:38 UTC. The repositories they landed on include training repositories and an intentionally vulnerable challenge set, which are meant to be vulnerable. To its credit, the template itself says it may be a false positive, or that the image may already carry a distribution backport. Every one of those notices still asks a maintainer, often an unpaid one, to stop and check. 62 GitHub issues match a search for php2shell "false positive", the templated notices among them. 10 issues on nuclei-templates name php2shell, and two merged pull requests are in the watch's series: the scanner templates are being fixed as people report them.
bulk

These are search counts, and they move as GitHub's index updates. The watch tracks them as what the page showed, every pass. The direction matters more than the exact number, and I will report it as it moves.
detection

Scanners look at servers; detection rules look at traffic. They have the same problem from the other side. A rule that never fired. A community detection guide (a GitHub gist) withdrew its own earlier ModSecurity rule: "ModSecurity leaves REQUEST_BODY empty for multipart requests, so that rule never fires." That is a false negative, found and admitted by the author, which is exactly what should happen. How many copies of the first rule are still deployed is a question nobody can answer from the outside. A claim to test. The same guide says its replacement rule "has zero false positives by construction". It may be right. It is a claim, and claims like that are what a lab test is for.
detection

The request alone is not enough. Cloudflare's write-up on its protections says the request does not always separate an exploit from legitimate traffic, and that the origin's response "adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives". Host detections need a baseline. Equixly, citing Huntress, says host detections need a baseline first, "because both can produce false positives". Coverage is still being asked for. The OWASP Core Rule Set has an open request for more PHP2Shell signatures. None of this is a criticism of the people doing the work. It is what the first days of a new class of flaw look like: tools written fast, corrected in public. The problem is that the people downstream act on the first version.
signal

Put the noise next to the PHP story's compromise map, as it stood at 20:50 UTC on 22 October. Millions of attempts against sensors, honeypots and edges. Exploitation reported by three vendors, none naming a victim. One named organisation saying it was attacked, with success not stated. Zero named organisations saying php2shell was the way in. That is a time-bounded absence, not proof that nothing happened, and one statement from one organisation would end it. The compromise map's layers on 22 October next to the scanner noise by 12:38 UTC on 23 October.
signal

This is where Jeremiah Grossman's word, apocalyptic, earns its place. Organisations across Europe switched websites off as a precaution on 21 and 22 October. When nobody can say quickly whether a site is safe, a scanner's red line is the deciding fact. A false positive on a patched Ubuntu server becomes a ticket, then an escalation, then a site taken offline, for real people who needed it. Multiply that by every makeshift scanner and every bulk notice, and the cost of the noise can exceed the cost of the attacks we can see. It is an incident of its own, and it is not in anyone's breach count. It also feeds the problem I wrote about in who maintains the PHP you run?. A site with somebody paid to know it can answer "is this a false positive?" in an hour. A site that was built, launched and left cannot, so it gets switched off.
what-to-do

Ask how the scanner decides. If it reads the version, its "vulnerable" means "an old upstream number", nothing more. Treat it as a question, not a finding. Check the package, not the banner. On a distribution install, look at the package version and its changelog for the CVE numbers (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), and check the PHP that serves web requests, not only the command line. Prefer evidence over inference. A check that produces the fault, in a lab or with permission, beats a version comparison. Cloudflare's point applies to people too: the response tells you more than the request. Before switching off, write down why. "A scanner said so" is a reason to look, not a reason to take a service away from the people who use it. If you make a scanner, say its method. One line on the result, "version check" or "fault reproduced", would remove most of the damage.
lab

The PHP story's board has a lab test on it, owned by its cyber desk and waiting for my go: run the public scanners against a distribution-patched PHP (for example Ubuntu's 8.5.4-0ubuntu1.5) and an unpatched one, in an isolated lab, and record which ones get each right. It tests the tools, never anyone's systems. That would turn this angle from reports into measurements, and I think it is the most useful thing the newsroom can do about this next. The watch, meanwhile, measures the noise every pass: the issue searches, the templated notices, the nuclei-templates issues, and Hacker News comments on php2shell scanners. The places where people complain most about their tools, Reddit, X, Bluesky and LinkedIn, give the watch a sign-in page, so an external collector covers them.
limits

A false-positive report is one person's account. It is recorded as what they said, not as a verdict on the tool. Search counts are rough. They are what the page showed at 12:38 UTC, and they move. No private people are named. Repositories and tools are named as places; the people who opened the issues are not. It maps evidence, not risk. It does not say whether scanners make the internet safer or less safe. The absence of a named victim is time-bounded. True as of the last check; one statement would end it. No cost of the noise has been measured. "Can exceed the cost of the attacks we can see" is my argument, not a number.
sources

Jeremiah Grossman's LinkedIn post of 22 October 2026, and the screenshot I took of it on 23 October; the PHP story's scanner-noise brief and its twelve captured pages in the source watch (vault oq9gflln, index/angles/scanner-noise.json), from Help Net Security, Digital Today, GitHub, a community detection gist, Cloudflare, Equixly, the OWASP Core Rule Set and nuclei-templates; the Konfirmity advisory for Ubuntu's fixed package; and the PHP story's compromise map. Related: who maintains the PHP you run?, the maintenance deficit, with evidence, PHP October 2026, at 8pm. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.
