Abstract: In Sell, don't issue I argued that open source can replace control rights as the investor's insurance: if the founder goes wrong, investors can take the code and back a better service next door. This piece looks at the whole triangle of founders, customers and investors. Each corner is protected from the others by the same thing: anyone can fork. If the founders stop executing, investors can fund a team next door. If the investors or a new owner take the company somewhere the founders will not follow, the founders can leave with the code, as long as no broad non-compete stops them. If either lets the customers down, the customers can move, as long as their data moves with them. The evidence supports the central part of this. Forking is treated as a last resort, few forks merge back, and the famous forks that took hold followed a breakdown: a licence change, a new owner, a governance fight. Where the original kept executing, as MySQL did under Oracle, the fork stayed a hedge. MySQL's own commits have now fallen by about two thirds since 2019, which makes it the case to watch. There are real limits: a bigger player can out-serve you with your own healthy code, the original's brand survives a fork, forks are expensive, and a single copyright holder can still change the terms going forward.

Three corners, one exit each: founders, investors and customers around the open code. Illustrative. One argument in three parts: who investors choose and why, a deal a founder with leverage could offer instead, and what keeps every side honest once control is out of the contract.
in-short

Three corners, one protection. Founders, customers and investors are each protected from the others because anyone can fork. Each exit has a condition. Founders need no broad non-compete; customers need their data to move; investors need to afford a team. Forking is a last resort. In a study of 220 significant forks, only 7 merged back. Forks take hold after breakdowns. LibreOffice, io.js, Nextcloud, OpenTofu and Valkey each followed a new owner, a governance fight or a licence change. Execution is the defence. MySQL kept shipping under Oracle and MariaDB never caught it; MySQL's commits have since fallen by about two thirds. The best investors need it to work. Valkey and OpenTofu were backed by companies whose own businesses ran on the code. Maturity is fine; lock-in is not. A component everyone depends on can move to a neutral home, and the explorers can take the code and carry on.
in-short
The limits are real. A bigger player can out-serve you with your own code, brands survive forks, and forking costs money.
triangle

Start from a healthy position. The founders are focused and executing. The customers are buying. The investors believe in the idea. Everything is open source, so the technology is not the moat; customers stay for the service, the quality and the trust. That is the model I set out at open-source.sgit.ai: we are selling trust, not access to a repository. Now ask what happens when one corner of the triangle goes wrong. In a closed company, the answer is decided by whoever holds control: usually the investors, sometimes the founders, never the customers. In an open source company every corner has an exit, and the exit takes the technology with it. But each exit has a condition, and the protection is only as good as that condition. What goes wrong Who is protected How Only if A real case The founders stop executing Investors and customers Fund a team to run the same code next door
triangle

The investors can pay for that team LibreOffice, from contributors pushing for a faster pace The investors or a new owner change direction, the licence or the mission Founders and customers The founders leave with the code and carry on No broad non-compete stops them Nextcloud The licence changes Everyone who depends on the code They fund the fork under the old licence Enough of them depend on it Valkey, OpenTofu Anyone lets the customers down Customers Move to whoever serves the same code better Their data leaves with them, cheaply Nextcloud's free support for ownCloud customers Everyone keeps executing Nobody needs protecting The fork stays a hedge MySQL and MariaDB The rest of this piece is the evidence for each row, and for the conditions.
breaks

Six forks: what broke, the year each began and what happened next. The theory says anyone can fork at any time. The practice says few do, and usually because something has gone wrong. Robles and González-Barahona studied 220 significant forks in A Comprehensive Study of Software Forks and note that forking "is considered as a last resort", even though it is built into free software. Only 7 of the 220, about 3%, merged back with the original. In 44% both carried on side by side, and in 30% the original was discontinued, often because it was already dying when the fork began. A fork is a serious, expensive and usually permanent decision. The famous forks that took hold all followed a breakdown.
breaks

LibreOffice, after a change of owner. Oracle completed its purchase of Sun on 27 January 2010, and with it OpenOffice.org. The Document Foundation launched LibreOffice on 28 September 2010, led by contributors who had already been pushing for a faster pace of development through Go-oo. By the Foundation's own count, in its open letter to Apache OpenOffice, "In 2019, LibreOffice had over 15,000 code commits, while OpenOffice had only 595." io.js, after a governance fight, and then back again. Core Node.js contributors forked the project in December 2014 over its governance under Joyent. The Node.js Foundation was formed in June 2015, and the two projects came back together in Node.js 4.0 that September. That is the mechanism working as a correction, not a war: the fork fixed the problem, then dissolved.
breaks

OpenTofu, after a licence change. HashiCorp moved Terraform to the Business Source License on 10 August 2023. The companies built on it launched OpenTofu under the Linux Foundation with "a starting commitment of a minimum of 18 full-time developers over at least the next five years". Valkey, after a licence change. Redis moved away from an open source licence on 20 March 2024. Eight days later, on 28 March, the Linux Foundation launched Valkey, backed by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson and Snap. AWS launched ElastiCache for Valkey that October, priced below its Redis equivalent, and Google made Memorystore for Valkey generally available in April 2025. The common thread is not that the original stopped innovating. It is that it stopped doing what its users needed: it changed the terms, slowed down, stopped listening or came under an owner with different priorities.
executing

The reverse case matters just as much. MariaDB was created in 2009 to protect MySQL from its new owners, first Sun and then Oracle. Oracle kept MySQL going, and in October 2026 MySQL is second in the DB-Engines ranking, with MariaDB thirteenth. The fork was a hedge. It never became the default, because the original kept shipping. Commits a year to the trunk branch of mysql/mysql-server, 2019 to 28 September 2026, measured from a clone. That case may now test the argument from the other side. I counted the commits to MySQL's main repository on GitHub, mysql/mysql-server, year by year. They fell from about 8,900 in 2019 to about 2,800 in 2025. Commit counts are a rough measure, and Oracle pushes this mirror in batches, but a fall of two thirds is not noise. If the argument here is right, this is when MariaDB's share should start to grow. That is a prediction, and it can be checked.
executing

So the real defence is not a licence or a patent. It is execution: shipping, focusing on customers, and running an open source commercial model well. And in the generative AI era, it is speed. As I put it on open-source.sgit.ai, the moat is a rate, not a wall: a competitor who forks today gets your position, not your velocity. Agents make it cheaper to fork, but they also make it cheaper for the original team to keep moving. The team that knows the problem and the customers, and uses agents well, stays ahead. The team that stops executing is the one that discovers how quickly a fork can catch up.
executing

There is also a structural reason the incumbent wins while it executes. If you are successful with an open source product, the only credible way to compete with you on the technology is with open source. And if a competitor goes open source, anything good they build, you can adopt. A fork can only pull ahead while the original is not paying attention.
investors

In Sell, don't issue I argued that investors in this model self-select: they are buying the vision, not control. There is a stronger version of that investor, and the forks show it clearly. It is the investor who needs the project to succeed, because their own business depends on it. Valkey's backers were cloud providers whose managed services ran on Redis. OpenTofu's backers were companies whose products ran on Terraform. Neither group needed control of the original company. When it broke, they funded the alternative, and fast.
investors

The research on corporate venture investors, who usually back startups close to their own business, points the same way. Chemmanur, Loutskina and Tian found that startups backed by corporate venture capital produced 26.9% more patents in the three years before their IPO than those backed by independent venture capital, and that those patents received 17.6% more citations. The mechanisms they point to are the corporate investors' "greater industry knowledge due to the technological fit between their parent firms and entrepreneurial firms" and their "greater tolerance for failure". That is the investor this model attracts: committed to the success of the project, not only to the financial return. My guess is that they may well get the better return too, because they are backing something they understand and will not abandon at the first bad quarter. I have no data for that.
founders

The second corner protects the founders. If the investors, or a new owner, take the company somewhere the founders will not follow, the founders do not have to watch their work be locked away. They can leave and continue. Nextcloud is the clearest case. Frank Karlitschek started ownCloud in 2010 and co-founded the company around it. He announced he was leaving ownCloud Inc. in April 2016, and on 2 June Nextcloud launched on a fork of the code. By its own account, Nextcloud "turned profitable by the end of 2016", employee-funded, and it ran for ten years without outside investment before taking a minority investor this month.
founders

That exit depends on a condition I glossed over in the first two pieces. The code is open, so anyone may fork it; but a founder may have signed a promise not to compete. Venture investors usually ask for one. The NVCA's model investors' rights agreement has the company require "[and, to the extent legally permissible, non-competition and non-solicitation agreement]" from key employees, and as I noted in The controllable founder, those clauses exist to make it expensive for a founder to walk away. The law limits them in places: California voids almost all non-competes, and in the UK a non-compete in an employment contract has to be reasonable and protect a legitimate interest, with reform still undecided. But both are more lenient with covenants given as a shareholder or on the sale of a business, which is exactly how a founder gives them.
founders

So the founder's corner of the triangle is only as strong as the founder's contract. A founder who wants the fork to protect them, not only their investors, should refuse a broad non-compete, and offer narrower promises instead: confidentiality, no poaching of staff or customers for a while, no use of the brand. That is now part of the advice in Sell, don't issue.
customers

The customers had a choice in the Nextcloud case too. When ownCloud's US company closed, Nextcloud offered "free support for all current ownCloud customers to simplify a transition". Moving was cheap because the software was the same and the data stayed where it was, on the customers' own servers. That is the condition for the customers' corner. Open code is necessary but not enough. If a customer's data sits in a hosted service in a format only that service reads, the code being open does not help them leave. The customer's real exit is their data, in an open format, that they can take to whoever serves the same code better, at a cost close to zero. A company that means it when it says customers stay for the service should make leaving easy, and say so.
maturity

The third scenario is the one I find most interesting. Not everything that changes is a failure. Companies mature. In Wardley's model of explorers, villagers and town planners, components move from genesis to commodity, and different kinds of people are good at different stages. A company that reaches maturity and focuses on reliable, efficient execution has become a town planner. There is nothing wrong with that. The world needs town planners. The problem is what happens to the explorers, and to the parts of the technology that still need exploring. In a closed company, both stay inside. The founders who wanted to keep inventing leave, but their ideas stay locked in a company that no longer wants to do anything with them. Open source removes that trap in two ways.
maturity

The first is a neutral home. When a component has become something many companies depend on, it can be moved into a foundation, where it is run for everyone and the companies around it compete on service. Google donated Kubernetes to the newly formed Cloud Native Computing Foundation as it reached version 1.0 in July 2015; the foundation took on its intellectual property from 2016, Kubernetes is now a Linux Foundation trade mark, and Google handed over the project's cloud infrastructure in 2018. Google was not being selfless. In my reading, it wanted Kubernetes to become the standard way to run software on any cloud, its rivals' included, and a neutral home was how to get its rivals to adopt it. That is the point: the move served the company and the technology at the same time. Valkey and OpenTofu went the same way, into the Linux Foundation.
maturity

The second is that the explorers can simply take the code and carry on somewhere else. They do not need permission, a licence negotiation or a buyout, as long as they have not signed that freedom away. The technology does not die because the company that started it has moved on to a different stage of life.
care

You can be out-served while you are still executing. Redis and Elastic did not change their licences because they had stopped shipping. They changed them because cloud providers were selling managed versions of their healthy code. Redis said the providers commoditise its investments; Elastic said it was restricting cloud providers from offering its products as a service without contributing back. If customers are locked in by service, whoever serves best wins, and that can be a bigger player with better distribution. Open source protects the corners of the triangle from each other; it does not protect the company from a larger service provider.
care

The original's brand survives. Valkey has AWS and Google behind it, but Redis is still eighth in DB-Engines, with a score far above Valkey's. A fork is a strong check on the original, not a clean replacement. And licence changes can reverse: Elastic added an open source licence again in 2024, and Redis in 2025. That fits the triangle: the credible threat of the fork pushed the original back towards openness. Forks are expensive. OpenTofu started with a pledge of 18 developers for five years. That makes "set up next door" a credible threat for investors who depend on the technology, but not for a small angel. The protection is strongest for the investors who need it most.
care

The copyright structure matters. As I set out in survivability, every catalogued relicensing between 2018 and 2024 was made by a single corporate copyright holder that had gathered contributors' copyright. The fork protects what has already been released; a single holder can still change the terms going forward.
limits

No study tests the triangle as a whole. The cases fit the argument; they are not a controlled comparison. The fork cases are famous ones. Successful forks get written about; failed ones mostly do not, which is survivorship bias in its own right. Higher returns are a guess, not a finding. I found no data showing open source companies return more to investors. The patent figures measure innovation, not financial return. And corporate investors bring their own conflicts. Commit counts are a rough measure. MySQL's fall is real in the repository; whether it means less work, or work done elsewhere, is not something the count can say. Not legal advice. Non-compete law differs by country and state, and by whether the promise is given as an employee or as a shareholder. Not that every component should be moved to a foundation. Some town-planner work belongs inside the company that runs it.

Abstract: Something I have been looking at while reading my book: some of the biggest and most successful companies in the world are graph companies. Google started from a graph of links and built a Knowledge Graph of things, not strings. Facebook is a social graph, LinkedIn calls itself an economic graph, Amazon builds a product graph on top of a supply chain, and Visa and Mastercard are networks that move trillions. Four of the ten most valuable companies today are, at heart, graphs, worth about $12.8 trillion together. Around them are the companies and consultancies that sell ontologies and taxonomies, a digital twin of an organisation, and the old ones too: legal research has been a citation graph since 1873. Even a spreadsheet, a relational database and a language model are graphs. Once a graph has the right connections, and you remove the nodes that do not matter, the answer becomes obvious, like the end of a whodunit. So why did graphs not scale for everyone else? Because building one took a lot of technology, and whoever built it used it to lock the customer in and keep competitors out: no shared schemas, no shared code. Fractal semantic graphs, where nobody has to share a schema, and agents that maintain them, are how they can scale now.
The graph companies: market values on 19 October 2026, with the graph at the heart of each, from Alphabet to Palantir.
in-short

The biggest companies are graph companies. Links, people, products, payments. Four of the top ten. About $12.8 trillion between them. Ontologies are a business too. A digital twin of the organisation, sold and consulted on. Everything is a graph. Spreadsheets, databases, law, contracts, even language models. With the right connections, the answer is obvious. Like the end of a whodunit. Graphs never scaled for everyone else. They were expensive to build, and built to lock in. Now they can. Fractal graphs that need no shared schema, maintained by agents.
companies

Something I have been looking at while reading my book: some of the biggest and most successful companies in the world, especially the ones that do not sell physical resources, are graph companies. Nodes and edges. Connecting A to B to C to D. Look at them: Google began with a graph of links. Its founders' 1998 paper describes a search engine that "makes heavy use of the structure present in hypertext" (Brin and Page). In 2012 it added the Knowledge Graph, which "understands real-world entities and their relationships to one another: things, not strings", starting with more than 500 million objects and 3.5 billion facts (Google, 16 May 2012).
companies

Facebook is a social graph; Mark Zuckerberg used the term when Facebook opened to developers in 2007. Its own researchers measured it in 2011: 721 million active users and 69 billion friendships, with almost everyone in one connected piece (Ugander and others). Meta now counts 3.6 billion people a day across its apps (Meta, July 2026). LinkedIn calls itself the Economic Graph, "a digital representation of the global economy", with more than a billion members (LinkedIn). Microsoft paid $26.2 billion for it in 2016. Amazon is a gigantic graph of products, sellers and supply chain. Its scientists have published how they build a product knowledge graph automatically, across thousands of product types (AutoKnow, 2020). Last year Amazon's sales were $716.9 billion. Visa and Mastercard are networks. Visa processed 257.5 billion transactions in its last financial year, over 4.9 billion payment credentials (Visa 10-K).
companies

By market value on 19 October 2026, Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta are four of the ten most valuable companies in the world, worth about $12.8 trillion together (companiesmarketcap.com). And there is an argument for some of the others: a chip that trains models is a machine for computing graphs.
logistics

Any logistics company is the graph that connects the dots. It is the graph that enables the profitability, that tells you what to do at that moment in time. UPS's route optimisation system, ORION, is a graph problem, and UPS said it would save about 100 million miles and 10 million gallons of fuel a year once fully deployed (UPS, 2015).
ontologies

Then there are the companies that are very successful because of their ontologies and their taxonomies. Palantir is the poster child these days. It describes its Ontology as "an operational layer for the organization" which, "in many settings, ... serves as a digital twin of the organization" (Palantir). Its revenue grew 56% in 2025, to $4.5 billion. It is not alone. LSEG publishes PermID, permanent identifiers for organisations, instruments and people, as open linked data (PermID). Neo4j, a graph database company, passed $200 million of annual recurring revenue in 2024 (Neo4j). ServiceNow agreed to buy data.world in 2025, and described its core as "a semantic layer or a knowledge graph" (TechTarget). And a lot of consulting projects are, at heart, bringing ontologies and taxonomies into an organisation.
everything

A lot of software is just connecting data. A spreadsheet is a graph with a couple of dimensions. A relational database, the model Codd described in 1970, is a graph, probably not in the most efficient way. A language model is a graph: the frameworks that train them record every operation as one (PyTorch). Law is a gigantic graph. Legal research has been a citation graph since Shepard's Citations started in 1873, and researchers have measured the importance of precedents by analysing the network of 26,681 US Supreme Court majority opinions (Fowler and others, 2007). Contracts are graphs. Governments would be a lot more efficient if they thought in graphs and connected one piece of the puzzle to another, and so would most businesses.
obvious

There is a very cool thing in design: once you have the right questions and the right information, the answer is obvious. It is the end of a whodunit. All the clues were there; what changes at the end is that the right connections are made, the irrelevant ones fall away, and only one answer is left. The answer becomes obvious: a full graph, the irrelevant nodes removed, and the short path from question to answer. That is what a graph does once it has the right connections. You remove the nodes that are not relevant, you focus on the ones that are, and the answer becomes obvious. It is why search worked, why a feed knows what to show you, and why a logistics company knows which van goes where.
never-scaled

So you can argue that graphs have already won. But they won for a few. For everyone else, they did not scale, and I think there are three reasons. Why graphs never scaled, and how they can now: before, graphs locked in customers; now, fractal graphs built by agents. First, creating a graph never scaled. It required a lot of technology, and a lot of people to build and maintain it. Second, lock-in. Many of the players were motivated, consciously or not, to lock the customer in. There was no big movement to share schemas, and none to share the code that got created. So whichever company got there first and built the graph gained a competitive advantage, and then used the graph to keep competitors out.
never-scaled

Third, some of the nodes in those graphs were treated as commodities when they should not have been, the customer among them, which is what when the customer becomes the commodity is about. The value in graphs is enormous; it is just not evenly distributed, or not very effectively. The contrast is striking. Analysts put the whole market for knowledge graph software at about a billion dollars in 2024 (MarketsandMarkets, an estimate). The companies built on graphs are worth trillions. The graphs were the moat, not the product.
now

I think that is changing. Fractal semantic graphs are built on the premise that everything connects to everything and nobody has to share a schema: each part keeps its own vocabulary, and the bridges between them are edges somebody declares. Agents are very good at building and maintaining graphs. And open source and open schemas, which already exist for the web in schema.org and for European public services in the EU's core vocabularies, mean a graph does not have to be a moat. So the business case is this. The biggest companies, the most successful ones, and an enormous amount of money are in graphs. What has been missing is a way for everyone else to build them. That is the opportunity for the next generation of founders.
limits

"Graph company" is my lens. These companies also run ads, cloud services, devices and stores. Market values move daily. These are from 19 October 2026. Correlation, not cause. Graphs are at the heart of these companies; they are not the only reason for their value. The market-size figures are estimates. Analysts define the market differently. UPS's savings are its own figures.
sources

Abstract: In August, on graphs.sgit.ai, agents wrote three books from a month of work on fractal semantic graphs, about 100,000 words between them, because I had a long flight the next day and wanted something to read. I read them, printed, and made a lot of notes. They are good, and much of what is in them, and in how they were made, now runs this newsroom. But two months later they are still at v0.3.0, v0.2.0 and v0.1.0, under review or held. This is the story of those books: what each one argues; the experiments around them, from an altitude ladder that compresses a book into one paragraph and lets you climb back down, to a board of workstreams and a book decomposed to the word and rebuilt byte-identical; why the book about making books read far better than the book about graphs; and where it stopped, which is the most useful part. The change-control workflow designed to apply my review notes had seven stages, and the approve stage was me. Nothing ever passed through it. It is a good example of a workflow that moves fast while there is energy and then stops, because the next step is too big, and it is why the next books will be made from articles.
The shelf on graphs.sgit.ai: three books, each with its own version, and v1.0.0 reserved for a final release.
in-short

Three books in a day. Written on 26 August from a month of work, for a long flight. About 100,000 words. 47 chapters, three print PDFs, every claim anchored. Experiments around them. An altitude ladder, a board, the book as a graph. One read far better. The book about making books, written over a real record. They stopped at review. Seven stages, and the approve stage was me. Much of it lives on here. Roles, versions, "where we lose", per-article graphs. The lesson. Small finished pieces beat one big review.
start

graphs.sgit.ai was built in about a month, from 21 August to 20 September 2026, to make one idea concrete: in a fractal semantic graph, a node means nothing on its own, and what it is arrives through its edges, at every level of zoom. A first book, Meaning Through Connectivity, was written in the first days and frozen on 23 August, its files hashed so the build fails if any changes.
start

Then, on 26 August, I sent a memo: "can you write a brief to write three books/pdf created from this repo and the work we have done so far (I have a long flight tomorrow and will use it to read these)". The agent read the flight as the shape of the deadline: each book had to be one self-contained PDF of 60 to 120 pages. Each book got a folder and a README that was its first prompt, and three fresh Claude Code sessions wrote them in parallel, the same day.
books

The shelf gives each book its own version, and keeps v1.0.0 "reserved for a book's actual final release, so a number below it says plainly that the book is still under review." Fractal Semantic Graphs: Meaning Through Connectivity, v0.3.0, is the argument: 15 chapters in five parts, from "A node is just a node" to "Your first graph, tomorrow", 38,824 words and a 119-page PDF. Its opening line is the idea in one sentence: "A node connected to nothing is literally meaningless. This book is what follows from taking that seriously." It says it was "designed to be finished on a flight".
books

Creating a Book Using Agentic Workflows, v0.2.0, is the making-of: twelve chapters, from "The loop" to "The failures, lovingly" and "What it costs, and where it loses", 31,435 words and 92 pages, built from 88 tagged releases over six days. Its subtitle is what this newsroom now does every day: "A voice memo in the morning, a shipped release by the afternoon, and a repository where every claim can be checked." The Universe volume, v0.1.0, held, is an atlas: 90 concepts in eight regions, 168 named verbs, 165 verbatim quotes from 35 sources, and what the atlas found, "6 contradictions · 9 named absences · 23 near-but-nots".
experiments

The first edition at five altitudes, from the book in one paragraph to the book itself, each phrase descending further. What I find most valuable now is not the books but what was tried around them. The altitude ladder. The same book at five altitudes, "where each level is a compression of the level below it, and every highlighted phrase descends into the units it compressed": the book in a paragraph of 135 words, the six parts, the seventeen units, the sections, and the book itself. Its best finding is why this matters: "a compression puts sentences next to each other that the full text keeps forty pages apart", and two of them turned out to contradict each other. And: "Level 3 is where the book becomes readable in one sitting, level 2 is where it becomes quotable, and level 1 is where it becomes a claim you either accept or reject."
experiments

The book as a graph. Decomposed all the way to the word, book, chapter, section, block, sentence, word, "and provably put back together": "Every chapter below rebuilt byte-identical on this build." The point was to make a big edit a transformation on the graph, checked by a gate, instead of an edit in a word processor. Worked examples and vaults. Graphs with real numbers, from a two-factor authentication finding traced up to the board and the regulator, to Article 26(5) of the AI Act, where five of nine questions are unanswered and the brief calls those five "the actual output of the exercise". The team. Seven roles, one folder each, librarian, researcher, writer, editor, developer, QA and publisher, each with its briefs and debriefs, and my memos kept verbatim, because "the founder's voice is source material and is not edited."
better

The book Creating a Book Using Agentic Workflows as a graph, from book and chapter down to sentence and word. When I read them, the difference was striking. In my memo after the flight I said the alignment of the making-of was "way stronger, like by orders of magnitude" than the book about graphs; reading it, "there was actually not that much stuff I felt wanted to change." The site's release notes give the reason, and it is the most important lesson in the whole estate: "the same agent, the same day, the difference being that book C was written over 41 narrated release rows, 38 verbatim briefs and a repository it could interrogate, while book B was written over an argument."
better

That is what these articles are now: a record. Every article here starts from a voice memo, is checked against sources, and lands in a repository the next article can read. That is why I think books can be made from them.
stopped

The project board for the making-of book: queued, up next and in progress, with nothing done. This is the part worth learning from. After the flight I asked for review as change control: "we start by planning, mapping, defining, reviewing, approving, and then implementing, and then approving the implementation". The agents built it, with care: a board of eight workstreams, 40 tasks and seven stages per change. And the board tells the story itself: "The two change-control workstreams are both blocked at the same stage, on the same person." The state map says it more plainly: the approved stage "has two items waiting and nothing has ever passed through it".
stopped

The last release was on 20 September. My energy had moved on, to the next place of highest leverage, and the books stayed where they were. I said in another memo why my Leanpub books never finished, and it is the same story: "I got to that sort of 60 70% of the content, and then the overhead of making changes." The workflow was well designed for quality and badly designed for momentum: every step was big, and the biggest one waited on me.
lives-on

A lot of it moved into this newsroom, which is why I do not think of the books as wasted: Seven roles, one folder each, the team here, whose shape, its page says, is borrowed from graphs.sgit.ai. "Where we lose", the participant disclosure, and what ships against what is argued, both here as pages. Versions you can read, a release history, and versions per article instead of per book. A graph per document: every article here has one, with its nodes, edges and quotes, the small descendant of the book as a graph. llms.txt and a markdown twin for every page. Memos as source material, kept and quoted, never edited. And the state map went the other way: graphs.sgit.ai borrowed it from this newsroom's brief. That is how it should work; ideas move between the sites as they prove themselves.
limits

The books are not finished. Two are under review, one is held, one is frozen. The flight notes are not on the site. It records "a bunch of notes", not each one. Not that the workflow was wrong. It was right for quality; it needed smaller steps. The comparison is one case. Two books, one agent, one day. If you want to try writing a book this way, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The homepage of this site has to be fresh every day, and today it changes only when someone releases the site. I would like a job that runs every morning at about 05:45, reads the latest articles, the wires and what is happening in the industry, and writes a new edition of the homepage. And that homepage should be a vault. Every edition a commit with a signed tag and its own version line; every edition carrying the links it showed and why, a screenshot of itself and the release note that explains it; any past homepage one commit id away; variants side by side for A/B tests; and anyone who wants their own homepage, in another language or for another audience, forks the vault. The encrypted objects can be served as plain files from S3, a CDN or GitHub Pages, read in the browser with a published read key. I had two facts wrong: this site is not served by a Lambda, it is on GitHub Pages; the Lambda is the vault API the wire reads through, and that is where the time goes, at 317 milliseconds a request against 44 for a static file. This site's agent built the homepage vault locally: three editions, three signed tags, a static export, and a browser that rendered today's edition in four requests, yesterday's in three, and nothing at all inside two minutes. A stats lane took 300 page-load beacons. This is the design, the measurements, and the brief.
The homepage as a vault: the morning job, static hosting, the GitHub Pages shell and the browser reading the edition.
in-short

Fresh every morning. A scheduled job writes a new homepage edition at about 05:45, or every hour if we want. The homepage is a vault. Every edition a commit, a signed tag and a version of its own. Every past homepage, one commit away. With its links, its screenshot and its release note. Plain files, not a function. The encrypted objects can sit on S3, a CDN or GitHub Pages. Where the time goes. 317 ms a request through the vault API, 44 ms from GitHub Pages. Measured locally. Today's edition in 4 requests, yesterday's in 3, nothing at all inside two minutes. Variants, stats and synthetic users. A/B variants in one commit, a stats lane for page loads, a daily run of readers who do not exist. Fork it. A homepage for another language, culture or publisher is a fork of the vault.
why

The homepage is the page that most needs to be fresh and the one that changes least. Today it is generated when the site is released, so it moves when I publish and stands still when I do not. What I have in mind is an edition: every morning, a job that looks at the latest articles, the wires, and what is happening in the industry we write about, and decides what leads, what follows and what rotates out. The structure, the highlights and the selections are the edition. Parts of the page can stay dynamic: the wire and the full list of articles load live, from their own sources, as they do now.
correction

I had two facts wrong. This site is not served by a Lambda function: newsroom.sgit.ai is on GitHub Pages, whose responses say server: GitHub.com. The Lambda is the vault API, behind CloudFront, that the Industry Wire reads its vaults through. And the wire is half of what I described: it does read encrypted vaults in the browser with a published read key, as Two agents, one vault explained, but through that API, not from plain files.
correction

That is where the time goes. On one cold load of the wire from this sandbox, the browser made eight requests to the API, one after the other, each taking between 360 and 810 milliseconds, and the last one ended 3.9 seconds after the page itself had loaded. On a warm connection, one request to the vault API took a median of 317 milliseconds; one request to GitHub Pages for a small file took 44. The API also sent no cache header for an immutable object, which sgit.ai's own measurements noted in September: "the read endpoint returned no Cache-Control header at all for an immutable object".
static

The good news is that sgit already reads from plain files. sgit.ai's update Take the API out of the path cloned the same vault in 65.4 seconds through the serverless API and in 2.63 seconds from plain GETs: "Twenty five times faster, with nothing about the vault changed." It was honest that the static host was on the same machine, so a real CDN adds its own latency. Its conclusion is the one that matters: the API is "a convenience over a store, not a requirement of it".
static

The browser side is documented in Static hosting: the same reader runs against the API or a folder of files laid out as api/vault/read/<vault id>/bare/, where content-addressed objects can be cached for ever and the one ref, the pointer to the latest commit, must never be. It also names the limit: "Read-only and frozen." A static copy changes only when it is exported again, which is not a problem for a homepage that is released once a day. It is exactly the model.
demo

Three editions of the demo homepage vault, each a commit with a signed tag. This site's agent built the homepage vault on a local vault server with sgit 0.21.0. A small script, the edition job, reads the articles and their graphs and writes one edition: index.html with the structure, edition.json with the lead, the picks, the topics and every link shown with the reason it was chosen, variants/a.html and variants/b.html, a release note in releases/, and a screenshot in shots/. It ran three times, for 13 October, the morning of 14 October and the evening of 14 October, and each run was committed, pushed and tagged: home-v0.1.0, home-v0.1.1, home-v0.1.2, each "signed by this clone". The homepage now has its own version line, separate from the site's.
demo

Then the agent exported the vault as plain files with sgit publish, put the objects in the documented layout, and served them from a plain static server with the cache headers S3 or a CDN would send. A reader cloned it with --transport static in 0.38 seconds, against 0.33 through the local API: on one machine, the network costs nothing either way. In a browser, using the same reader the wire uses, the results were these. Today's edition, cold. 4 requests and 4.7 KB: the ref, the commit, the tree and the page. The same reader inside two minutes. No requests at all: the ref is reused for 120 seconds and the objects come from the browser's cache. Yesterday's edition. 3 requests, by commit id; no ref is needed, because history is just another object. The other variant. 2 requests, for the variants folder and the page.
demo

Those are counts, not network times. With 44 milliseconds a request, four chained requests are about 0.2 seconds from static files; at 317, about 1.3 seconds through the API. The live vault docs on sgit.ai found the same shape in production: a cold load of 18 objects, then "one 69-byte request per reader per two minutes".
sequence

One page load: the shell from GitHub Pages, four chained requests to the static host, and a beacon to the stats lane. The order matters because each step needs the one before it. The shell comes from GitHub Pages, with the read key and the reader. The ref says which commit is today's edition; the commit names the tree; the tree names the page. Only the ref can change, so it is never cached; everything else is named by its own hash and can be cached by every layer in between for ever. The browser decrypts with the read key, renders, and records which variant it showed. The read key is public on purpose: sgit.ai's credentials page says it is "derived from the vault key by a one-way function, so a read key can never be turned back into write access."
history

Version control of the homepage is the feature I like most. Every edition is a commit, so any day's homepage can be opened again exactly as it was, with the links it showed, the screenshot of how it looked, and the release note that says why it changed. That also means we can rotate: the job can see every link that has led the page and give the rest a turn. Variants sit in the same commit, so an A/B test is a choice the page makes, not a second deployment. And a fork is a whole homepage: another language, another culture, another publisher, or one reader who wants their own front page, takes the vault, changes the edition rules and publishes their own.
stats
The measurements: live numbers from this sandbox to newsroom.sgit.ai, and vault numbers from local servers.
stats

For the test to mean anything, we need to know what happened. An append lane is "A write-only channel attached to a vault, gated by a token the writer holds and nothing else", and sgit.ai already has a brief for telemetry through one. The agent configured a lane on the homepage vault and sent it 300 synthetic page-load beacons, each with the edition, the variant, a load time and whether a link was clicked: 2.6 milliseconds each on the local server, and all 300 read back with the enum key. The click rates in that test were invented by the script, so they show the plumbing, not a result. Two limits apply. A static host cannot take writes, so the beacons still go to the API; and the cap is "1000 pending files per token → 507", so the morning job has to collect and clear the lane every day, writing the totals into a stats vault.
stats

The other daily input is the synthetic readers. How to run synthetic users describes five to ten invented readers who drive a real browser and report what they saw; run every morning against the live page, with their findings and timings in their own vault, they tell us when something has broken or slowed down before a reader does.
handled

Search engines. sgit.ai's case study is plain about it: "Search engines and agents see an empty shell." The shell on GitHub Pages should therefore carry a plain snapshot of today's edition, generated from the same commit and naming it. Surfaces gives the rule for that: "What must never be duplicated is the content itself"; the snapshot is a projection of the edition, not a second copy to edit. Revocation. sgit publish warns that bytes deployed into a git repository "stay in its history after any later deletion, so rotation cannot revoke access to what you publish now", and suggests object storage when that matters. For a public homepage it does not, but it is a reason to put the static objects on S3 rather than in this repository.
handled

A mirror needs a reader. sgit.ai learnt this the hard way when it removed its own vault mirror: "give a mirror a reader before giving it a remote". The homepage vault has a reader from the first day: the homepage.
brief

Start on a separate page. Build /front/ from the homepage vault and leave the homepage alone until the numbers say it is better. The edition job. Every morning at 05:45 UK time, read the articles, the wires and the stats, write one edition, commit it, tag it home-vX.Y.Z and add its screenshot and release note. Plain files. Export each edition to S3 behind a CDN, with immutable objects cached for a year and the ref never cached; keep the vault API as the writer's path only. A shell with a snapshot. A small page on GitHub Pages with the read key, the reader, and a plain snapshot of the edition for search engines, naming its commit. Every edition reachable. A "this page on another day" link that opens any tag by its commit id.
brief

Variants and stats. Two variants per edition, assigned in the browser; a beacon per load to a stats lane; the morning job collects, totals and clears it, and writes the totals to a stats vault. Synthetic users daily. Five readers against /front/ and the homepage, findings and timings in their own vault. Prove it. Time the live cold and warm loads of /front/ against the current homepage, every day for two weeks, and report; move the homepage only if /front/ is at least as fast and the variants show which works better. Move the wire too. The same export for the wire's vaults would take its eight API requests off the reader's path.
limits

The demo is local. A local vault server and a local static server; the vault numbers count requests and bytes, not network time. The live timings are from this sandbox. One location, medians of ten requests; readers elsewhere will see other numbers. The beacons and clicks were synthetic. They show the lane works, not which variant is better. Nothing is scheduled yet. The morning job, the S3 export and /front/ are proposed. A/B tests need readers. With this site's traffic, a difference between variants may take weeks to show. If you want your own homepage to be a vault, or want to fork ours, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 14 October 2026, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The demo and the timings were run by this site's agent on 14 October 2026; a research agent read sgit.ai's documentation, and the quotes were checked against it. From sgit.ai: Take the API out of the path, Static hosting, Live vault docs, Fractal graphs performance, Surfaces, Credentials, Append lanes, Vault telemetry through append lanes and The mirror is gone.

Summary: The homepage of this site has to be fresh every day, and today it changes only when someone releases the site. I want a job that runs every morning at about 05:45, reads the latest articles, the wires and what is happening in the industry, and writes a new edition of the homepage. And I want that homepage to be a vault. Every edition a commit with a signed tag and its own version line; every edition carrying the links it showed and why, a screenshot of itself and the release note that explains it; any past homepage one commit id away; variants side by side for A/B tests; and anyone who wants their own homepage, in another language or for another audience, forks the vault. The encrypted objects can be served as plain files from S3, a CDN or GitHub Pages, read in the browser with a published read key. I had two facts wrong: this site is not served by a Lambda, it is on GitHub Pages; the Lambda is the vault API the wire reads through, and that is where the time goes, at 317 milliseconds a request against 44 for a static file. This site's agent built the homepage vault locally: three editions, three signed tags, a static export, and a browser that rendered today's edition in four requests, yesterday's in three, and nothing at all inside two minutes. A stats lane took 300 page-load beacons. This is the design, the measurements, and the brief.

why

The homepage is the page that most needs to be fresh and the one that changes least. Today it is generated when the site is released, so it moves when I publish and stands still when I do not. What I want is an edition: every morning, a job that looks at the latest articles, the wires, and what is happening in the industry we write about, and decides what leads, what follows and what rotates out. The structure, the highlights and the selections are the edition. Parts of the page can stay dynamic: the wire and the full list of articles load live, from their own sources, as they do now.

Abstract: Someone shaping a roundtable in London asked me this week for my thoughts on a question that keeps coming up: is the human in the loop a safety net or a bottleneck? Plenty of companies have agent pilots that look great, and very few trust an agent to make a real decision without someone checking every output. My answer is that a person checking every output is both, and is mostly neither: it is a bottleneck because it does not scale, and it is a weak safety net because people approve almost everything they are shown, which Anthropic measured at 93% of permission prompts. The question is not whether there is a human in the loop. It is which outputs need one, what that person is given to decide with, and what moves the line over time. Put the person where an output cannot be undone and the blast radius is large, sending an email in my name, typing a password, spending money. Everywhere else, replace the human check with controls that do not get tired: a validator, a second reader the agent cannot skip, a policy whose rows are enforced outside the model, and a record read afterwards. Make the review a quality step that fixes the source, not a sign-off. And let the record move the line: trust is built from drafts nobody had to change. This is how far I have got in production. On the day I am writing this, the newsroom shipped fourteen releases, every commit made by an agent, with nobody approving each one before it went live, while the agents that run my correspondence draft every email and send none of them: I do.
Where the person belongs: two questions place every output an agent produces, can it be undone, and what it would cost.
in-short

Checking every output is both, and mostly neither. It is a bottleneck because it does not scale, and a weak safety net because people approve almost everything: Anthropic measured 93% of permission prompts approved. The question is where, not whether. Which outputs need a person, what that person is given to decide with, and what moves the line. Put the person where it cannot be undone and the blast radius is large. Sending in my name, typing a secret, spending money, deleting what has no backup. Replace the other human checks with controls that do not get tired. Validators, a second reader the agent cannot skip, policy rows enforced outside the model, and a record read afterwards. A review should fix the source, not sign the output. A correction that becomes a rule is worth more than a hundred approvals.
in-short

The record moves the line. Trust is built from drafts nobody had to change, and the record is what lets a business give the agent more. How far I have got. Fourteen releases of this site in one day, every commit made by an agent, none approved one by one; and an agent team that drafts all my email and sends none of it.
question

Someone who is shaping a roundtable in London sent me a message this week. The topic that keeps coming up in their conversations is the human in the loop: safety net or bottleneck? Their observation, paraphrased, is that plenty of companies have AI pilots that look great, and very few trust an agent to make a real decision without someone checking every output. They asked what I thought, and how far I had got with AI in production. I said I had a lot of thoughts on this, and that I would put them in an article. This is it.
both

A person checking every output is a bottleneck, obviously. The whole point of an agent is that it does more work than a person can, and if every piece of that work waits for a person, the agent runs at the speed of the person. That is the pilot that looks great and never scales. The less obvious part is that it is also a weak safety net. People approve almost everything they are asked to approve. Anthropic, writing about its own coding agent in March 2026, opened with the number: "Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts". In October 2025 it had already named the effect, "approval fatigue", where people "might not pay close attention to what they're approving", and reported that sandboxing "safely reduces permission prompts by 84%". The fix the vendor reached for was fewer prompts, not more attentive people, and I think that is right.
both

I wrote about the deeper problem in Agency is not a yes. Most human-in-the-loop designs ask the person for a yes or a no, with little context, no time and no authority over the system that produced the request. Below a certain level on that scale, the person is not a safety net at all. They are where the liability lands for a decision the system made, and the accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point. Where is the why? is the same argument about one permission prompt that asked me to decide and kept the reason. So the honest answer to the roundtable's question is: checking every output gives you the cost of a bottleneck and the protection of a rubber stamp.
where

The useful question is not whether there is a human in the loop. It is which outputs need one. Two questions place every output an agent produces: can it be undone, and how much would it cost if it were wrong? That second one is what Footprint and blast radius calls the blast radius, what it would cost the business if a row of the agent's reach were used in full, today.
where

Where the output cannot be undone and the blast radius is large, put a person there, and make it a real decision. In my own setup, as Replicating the agentic inbox describes, that is sending: the agents write drafts, and I read, change and press send, because an email in my name cannot be recalled and, as I argued in Who owns the words, the responsibility for it is mine. In the subscriptions service it is two things: the freelancer types every secret, and sends every draft. Spending money and deleting what has no backup belong in the same place. Everywhere else, the person is the wrong control.
controls

How far I have got in production, as it ran on 13 October 2026, with who or what checks each kind of output. An article on this site is a good example, because it can be undone: a correction is a new version, with a page that shows what changed. So nobody approves an article before it goes live. What stands in the way instead is a set of controls that never get tired: a validator that fails the build on a broken link, a quote that is not word for word in its source, a banned word or a missing figure; browser tests; a leak scan on every commit that refuses a key or a name on the private list. I read every article, but I read it after it is live, and what I find becomes a new version and, if it is about wording, a rule.
controls

For outputs that matter more, the control can be another reader. After two emails went out in my voice that should not have, the fix was a second reader the agent cannot skip: every draft passes a separate model call that sees only the rules, the sources and the draft, and anything but an explicit pass stops it. Banks call that maker-checker. It is a check on every output, and it is not a person.
controls

And the strongest control is the one that makes the bad output impossible. Hope or enforcement took one customer service agent and redesigned it three times; the share of its policy kept only by the model's good behaviour fell from 97% to 23%, and the reach of one run fell from 38,000 customer records to one customer. Every row moved from hope to a boundary is a row nobody has to check by hand. That is also the argument of A policy beside the prompt: write the rules down, and get the platform to enforce as many of them as it can see.
source

When a person does review, the review should be worth more than a yes. In Agency is not a yes the higher levels of the scale are where a review stops being a sign-off and becomes a quality step: each draft is a chance to fix whatever produced it, the rule, the prompt, the data, rather than the draft itself. That is how I review this site. When a word jars, it becomes a rule in the session's behaviour policy, and I never see it again; How the voice works counted the effect, with almost all of my corrections now about content and direction rather than words. A human in the loop who fixes the source makes the loop need them less every week. A human who approves outputs makes it need them exactly as much forever.
record

The last piece is what lets a business give an agent more room over time. Trust in my email agents is not a feeling; it is a record of drafts I did not have to change, the draft's hash beside the email that went out, read whenever I want. When that record says a kind of message has gone out unchanged for long enough, that kind of message is a candidate to leave the human step, by a decision written into the policy, with an owner and a date. The agent team has exactly one such exception today: a security agent may send one email, to one address, to put the team on hold. Everything else is still a draft.
record

The same record catches what the person would have missed. Reading the footprint afterwards against the mandate finds the near misses, the times the agent went somewhere it was not asked to go and nothing stopped it, which no approval prompt would have shown.
production

So, to the second half of the question. On 13 October 2026, the day I am writing this, the newsroom shipped fourteen releases, v0.12.5 to v0.12.18. Every commit in them was made by an agent session: one writes the articles, one works on the reading experience, one runs the wire. Five articles were written and published in this repository. The four written by this session were each researched, checked against their sources, given their figures and graph, built, validated, tested and leak-scanned by an agent, and none was approved by a person before it went live. I read them afterwards, and corrected them, as new versions.
production

At the same time, the twelve agents that run my correspondence, the agent team as it runs, draft every email and send none; the one exception in their policy is a security agent allowed one email, to one address, to put the team on hold. That is not a contradiction. It is the same rule applied to two different blast radii. An article can be corrected tomorrow. An email cannot.
roundtable

If I were in the room, these are the questions I would bring: Which of your agent's outputs can be undone, and which cannot? Is the person only on the second kind? What is the person shown when they approve? Could they say no, and would anybody notice if they did? What share of your approvals are yes? If it is above ninety per cent, what is the check for? Which of your human checks could be a validator, a second model or a boundary in the platform instead? When a reviewer corrects an output, does the correction change the source, or only that output? What record would let you remove a human check next quarter, and who decides?
limits

The 93% is one vendor's figure for one product. It is about permission prompts in a coding agent; other approval flows may differ. My production is small. One person, one newsroom, one agent team. The pattern is what I would defend, not the scale. Some outputs need a person by law or by their nature. Medicine, law and money moved on someone else's behalf have rules of their own; this is not an argument for removing those. "Nobody approved each release" is not "nobody was responsible". I own what the agents publish, and the controls are mine; I chose where to put myself. The roundtable question is paraphrased. It came in a private message, and its author is not named. If you are running agent pilots and want to work out where your people belong, or you are in the roundtable and want to compare notes, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Abstract: This afternoon I ran one of those experiments that starts as a small question and ends somewhere much more interesting. Can two AI sessions that share nothing, no memory, no network link, no files, send each other data through QR codes that I screenshot in one browser tab and paste into another? In about three hours the answer went from maybe to yes, all the way to the format's limit. One session generated the codes; the other decoded and verified them. Text, then signed JSON, then public keys and an X.509 certificate, then images, then a real key exchange: one session published an encryption key as a QR code, the other encrypted and signed a message to it and returned it as a QR code, and the first decrypted it. The densest code, 2,953 bytes, the most one QR code can hold, decoded from a screenshot at about 1.3 pixels per square, and every screenshot payload was byte-identical to the original. The failures are as useful as the results: the AI cannot read a QR code by looking at it, the decoder mattered more than the resolution, and a lost key turned the experiment into a lesson in why fingerprints matter. For me the result is simple: QR codes are a far friendlier way to move keys and encrypted messages than the blobs of text we have been pasting.
Six QR codes passed between two Claude sessions by screenshot and paste, from plain text to a certificate.
in-short

Two sessions, no shared anything. The only link between them was me, with screenshots and paste. It worked up to the format's limit. 2,953 bytes in one code, decoded from a screenshot. Nothing was lost. Every screenshot payload matched the original, byte for byte. Keys, a certificate and images fit. A whole infographic took 539 bytes. The finale was encryption. A public key out as a QR code, an encrypted message back. The failures taught the most. No reading by eye; the decoder mattered; a key was lost. QR codes are friendlier than blobs of text. That is the part I want to build on.
question

This was, as I said in my voice memo afterwards, "one of those super interesting sort of serendipity things that happens when you're doing a bunch of experiments." I asked a Claude session whether it could create QR codes and read them, and whether that could beat copy and paste for moving data between sessions. So I set it up properly. Two independent Claude sessions, in two browser tabs, with no shared memory, network link or files. Session A generated the codes. Session B decoded and verified them. The only connection between them was me: a screenshot on my Mac, a paste into the other tab, and later a ZIP file. Both sessions wrote up what they did, and this article is built from their two debriefs and the data they produced.
layers

The experiment went up a layer every time the previous one worked: Text. "hello from session A", 53 bytes, a small code. Trivial. Signed JSON. A key offer signed with Ed25519. After the trip by screenshot, the signature still verified. Keys and a certificate. Ed25519, P-256, RSA-2048 and RSA-4096 public keys, and a self-signed X.509 certificate. Session B parsed each key and checked the certificate's signature. Binary and images. A compressed vector infographic, and photo-like images in AVIF, WebP, JPEG and palette PNG, each rebuilt from its decoded bytes. Encryption. A real exchange of keys and an encrypted, signed message, below. Session A built a graded test set of eleven codes, each carrying its own length and hash, from 53 bytes to the 2,953-byte maximum. Session B decoded all eleven and checked every hash against a separate manifest.
screenshot

The screenshot that carried four QR codes from one session to the other, as Session A showed them in its chat. This was the moment the experiment became interesting. Session A showed four of the codes in its chat. I took one screenshot of the row, with the rounded frames of the chat around them, and pasted it into Session B. That is a browser's rendering and scaling, a Retina screenshot and a clipboard, with nobody trying to keep the image clean. All four decoded. The largest, a version 40 code with 177 by 177 squares, had been squeezed into about 230 pixels: about 1.3 pixels for each square. It decoded on the first attempt. And when the original files arrived later, Session B compared them: every payload from the screenshot was identical, byte for byte, to the one from the original image. The error correction built into QR codes absorbed everything the screenshot did to the image.
capacity

Left: the bytes in each code of the graded test set. Right: what a version 40 code holds in raw, base45 and base64. The numbers that matter: 2,953 bytes is the ceiling. One QR code, version 40, with the lowest error correction. Reached, and decoded. Elliptic-curve keys are tiny. An Ed25519 public key is 43 characters. RSA-4096 still fits, at 800. Compression did not help certificates. A certificate compressed with zlib came out larger than an RSA-4096 key, because signed data is close to random and base64 adds back a third. How the bytes are written matters. Raw bytes hold the most, but many decoders hand them back as text and corrupt them. Base45, which packs bytes into the characters QR codes store most efficiently, cost about 3 % and survived everywhere.
images

Two images inside single QR codes, each next to the image rebuilt from its decoded bytes. This is the part I did not expect to work as well as it did. The whole infographic, as compressed SVG, took 539 bytes, about a fifth of one code, and came back exact and sharp at any size. A 480 by 320 photo-like image, generated for the test rather than a real photograph, fitted as AVIF in 2,083 bytes. The same infographic as a raster image needed between 1,881 and 2,810 bytes, and lost detail. For anything drawn, vector wins by a long way.
exchange

The key exchange by screenshot: Session B publishes a key as a QR code, Session A answers with an encrypted message. Then the finale. Session B made an X25519 key pair and published the public half as a QR code, and wrote a small format for encrypted frames, which it called QRE1. Session A decoded the key and confirmed its fingerprint, aab8 bef5 da4f aa76 096b fea0 85f5 ef26. It then encrypted a message to that key, with a fresh key of its own for this one message, signed the result with Ed25519, and returned it as a single QR code of 1,329 bytes. Session B decrypted it: "Hello session B. If you can read this…"
exchange

As I said in the memo, "it worked really well." And notice what I carried between the two tabs: a public key in one direction and ciphertext in the other. Nothing I relayed could be read by anyone else, so it would not have mattered if the same images had gone by email or a chat message.
failures

These are the best part of the debriefs, and I want to keep them: The AI cannot read a QR code by looking at it. Session A could see that an image was a QR code, but could not decode it by eye, and said so instead of pretending, especially as it already knew what the code contained. Every decode was done by code, with a decoding library. The decoder mattered more than the resolution. OpenCV's detector failed on the dense codes even in clean, high-resolution images; the ZXing library read all of them, down to 1.3 pixels a square. Session B had first blamed the resolution, and corrected itself when the evidence came in.
failures

The lost key. Session B asked Session A to sign with the key from the test set. That private key had only ever existed in memory, and it was gone. Session A did not fake it: it made a new signing key, signed with that, and said so inside the encrypted message, with the new key's fingerprint, 7e45 70bf 5e8c d3fa 2bc1 ebce 1347 169c, for me to confirm. Integrity is not authenticity. Both sessions kept saying this, and they are right. A signature proves the bytes did not change; a key that travels inside its own message proves nothing about who sent it. That needs a person comparing fingerprints, or pinning a key the first time it is seen.
why

Session B's reply to the first QR code: it verified the signed key offer and noted what that proves. For me the advantage is practical. In my words from the memo: "QR codes are way more user friendly than what we were using to share the vault keys and the encrypted messages." When I have tried to send a big blob of text, "it's just unusable. It's not practical. It looks messy." A QR code is something a person can see, move and hand over, and it carries a decent amount of data, including images.
why

And it points at something bigger: a data channel that runs entirely on the client side, with no server in the middle, on top of public keys. We have been heading there for a while: the QR code in send to my vault, the ways a secret moves in secrets.sgit.ai on public keys, and the keys in a directory of people and their keys. Today we measured the channel. The workflow it makes possible, and who else is already doing this, is the next article.
limits

No reading by vision. A decoding library reads the codes, not the model. No proof of who sent it. That needs a fingerprint checked out of band, or a key pinned on first use. The new signing key is not yet accepted. Its fingerprint was still waiting for my check when the debriefs were written. Not forward-secret. Session B's key is long-lived; if it leaked, past messages could be read. An experiment, not a product. The private keys lived in cloud sessions, which is fine for a test and not for production. About 2.9 KB a code. Anything bigger needs several codes.
sources

The experiment of 21 October 2026, about 14:20 to 17:30 BST: Session A's debrief pack, with its results, manifest, scripts and images, and Session B's own briefing, including the QRE1 format it wrote; and my voice memo afterwards, quoted above. The images were all made in the experiment; the photo-like image was generated, not photographed. Related: sixteen notes I did not want to lose, secrets.sgit.ai on public keys, handing secrets to agents, a directory of people and their keys. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.
