Abstract: Dion Wiggins has written the piece I wish I had written about php2shell. Dion puts a number on something I have been arguing for months: Germany spends about €27 million a year on its federal website platform, built on PHP, and contributed about €112,000 a year to PHP's security, a maintenance deficit ratio of 241 to 1. Then Dion walks the same gap through the rest of the stack governments are migrating onto. This is a follow-up with our evidence. I checked the main figures against their primary sources: the order of magnitude holds under every cut, from 179 to 263 to 1, and a few details differ, which I list. I add what our evidence vault and the PHP story's site show two days on: 751 downstream products in the Dutch inventory, only 109 of them fixed; no named organisation saying it was compromised through these flaws, and the US catalogue of exploited flaws still not listing them; and an independent assessment of the incident, built in a day by a team of agents. Then the argument: this is not a story about generosity. Open source's business model pays the integrator, the host and the platform, and almost never the maintainer or the packager, and AI has just made the discoverers richer than the people who have to fix what they find. The money exists; what is missing is a model that pays for maintenance as the product.
Dion Wiggins' illustration of a building labelled Digital Sovereignty resting on a cracked column of volunteer software.
in-short

Dion Wiggins measured the gap. A maintenance deficit ratio: 241 to 1, for Germany and PHP. The number holds. Every cut of the sources gives two orders of magnitude. Two days on, most downstream software is not fixed. 109 of 751 rows in the Dutch inventory. No named compromise yet. The shutdowns were decisions under uncertainty. An independent assessment took a day. Built by agents, from an evidence vault anyone can read. The business model pays the wrong layer. Integrators and hosts, not maintainers and packagers. AI made finding cheap and fixing scarce. The discoverer now has more resources than the maintainer.
piece

Dion Wiggins published a post and a long-form article on 23 October that I think everyone working on digital sovereignty should read. The metric is simple: divide what a government spends migrating onto open source by what it contributes to maintaining that open source. For Germany and PHP that gives €27 million a year against €112,000 a year: 241 to 1. Dion's line for it: "Any government whose ratio exceeds 10:1 does not have a sovereignty strategy. It has a procurement preference with no supply chain behind it."
piece

Dion then walks the rest of the stack: LibreOffice, Nextcloud, FFmpeg, curl, OpenSSL, Kubernetes Ingress-NGINX, pgBackRest, libxml2, core-js, each with a funding gap, a staffing gap, or both. And Dion points at a post the PHP Foundation published seven weeks before php2shell, "Digital Sovereignty Is Written in PHP", whose author, Sebastian Bergmann, named the problem in advance: "the institutions most dependent on PHP have no established mechanism" to turn that dependency into maintenance funding. This is very much what we have been talking about here, with numbers attached. So this is a follow-up, with the evidence we have.
checked

The maintenance deficit ratio, checked three ways: Dion Wiggins' figures, the whole contract and the migration share. I checked the main figures against their primary sources on 23 October: The contract. €108 million over four years, from Bergmann's post. Of that, €73.2 million is migration and relaunch, €26.88 million product development and support, and €8 million operations. So €27 million a year is the whole contract, and the migration alone is about €18.3 million a year. The investment in PHP. The Sovereign Tech Agency's own page for PHP lists €205,000, for 2023 and 2024: an extension distribution overhaul, a security audit, documentation and a testing tool. Dion's €112,000 a year comes from a figure of about €223,000 for 2025 and 2026. Either way, about €100,000 a year. The ratio. 241 to 1 on Dion's figures, 263 to 1 on the agency's page, 179 to 1 on the migration share alone. Two orders of magnitude, however you cut it.
checked

The PHP Foundation. Its report for 2025: $730,534 donated by 536 organisations and individuals, expenses of $784,376, a deficit of about $139,000 taken on purpose, and "11 contracted developers who worked part- and full-time". Bergmann's post gives thirteen by September. The shutdowns. The PHP story's impact ledger records them on 21 October, as Dion says. Two details are narrower than that summary: Finland's Valtori restricted incoming public traffic from 12:45 local time, as a precaution, with internal networks unaffected; and the UK figure is a minister saying that 32 central government services were unavailable and four partially, at one moment, which the site's fact-check desk keeps as an open question. UK councils. Bergmann counts "over 58 councils" sharing LocalGov Drupal; Dion has Drupal at 100 councils. Possibly different measures; I could not reconcile them. Not checked. The 50,000 warnings, DigiD's 17 million users, Datadog's 3.10 seconds, and Sansec's update of 22 October, which I could not find.
checked
None of that changes the argument. It sharpens it: the migration share alone is nearly 180 times the investment in the language underneath it.
two-days

The Dutch NCSC's inventory of software that ships or depends on PHP, as of 22 and 23 October. Dion writes that "every government in every country waited for the same patch from the same" small team. The patch itself came fast: PHP's four fixed releases were all out by 21 October. What followed is the part Dion's article calls the packaging and distribution layer, and our data shows how slow that layer is. The Dutch national cyber security centre keeps a public inventory of software that ships or depends on PHP. Read from its history, at 12:50 UTC today, about two days after the fix, it has 751 rows: 109 fixed, 222 vulnerable, 389 still under investigation, 30 not affected. That is 15% fixed. The patch was the easy part. Getting it through every vendor, distribution and appliance is where the time goes, and that work belongs to nobody in particular.
two-days

And the risk itself? The PHP story's compromise map, as of 20:50 UTC on 22 October, lays out 33 statements behind one claim: no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell. Millions of attempts; three vendors reporting exploitation without naming a victim; one university saying an attack was stopped. At 14:41 UTC today, the US catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities still did not list either flaw. As I wrote in application behaviour policies, that silence lowers the likelihood; it does nothing to the blast radius. The shutdowns were decisions under uncertainty, made without a map of what each site could reach.
assessment

Dion makes a point I want to take one step further: no government had "the independent capability" to assess the flaw before shutting down its services. That was true on 21 October. It no longer needs to be. The PHP story's own site, as I described in PHP October 2026, at 8pm, was built in one day by two people and a team of agents, from an evidence vault anyone can read: 184 sources and 177 dated captures, 70 claims graded by a fact-check desk, the fix read in PHP's own code, the inventory hour by hour, the compromise map. None of it needed the PHP Foundation's time. That is the kind of independent assessment a government could commission, or run itself, in the first hours of the next incident. The capacity to understand an incident has become cheap. The capacity to fix the code has not.
model

Where the money flows: the contracts and revenues on one side, against the PHP Foundation's donations and engineers. I want to be careful about the framing. This is not a story about governments or companies being mean. It is a business model that pays the wrong layer. Look at where the money in Dion's article goes. The integrator wins a €108 million contract to build on TYPO3. The platform company is sold for a billion. The host charges every month. All of them sell something a customer can buy: a project, a product, a service with a contract and a phone number. The maintainer of the language underneath, and the person who packages it for most Debian and Ubuntu servers, sell nothing a procurement process can buy. They take donations. That is not a funding gap; it is a missing product.
model

And AI has just made the imbalance worse. In the eyeballs get cheap I argued that models make deep security review abundant for open source, which is good news. php2shell shows the other side. As Dion describes it, the flaws had been glimpsed by two audits that could not exploit them; two teams with frontier models turned them into working exploits within days. Dion's line for FFmpeg applies to all of it: "The discoverer had more resources than the maintainer." Finding is now cheap and well funded; deciding, fixing, back-porting and packaging are not. In the Foundation's own words after the incident, quoted by Dion, the delay was "a structural failure" of its decision process and its resources.
work

Three ideas, which fit together. Pay for maintenance as the product. In the code you do not ship I argued that the specialist who knows a component best should be paid to maintain the version their customers actually run: the smallest one that does the job, with its behaviour, decision and workflow policies. That is something a procurement process can buy, because it has a scope, an owner and a service level. Tiffany Farriss's proposal, which Dion cites, of a maintainer line item in public contracts is the obvious way to buy it: 1% of the German contract is more than the PHP Foundation's whole year.
work

Pay at the source. In free to copy, paid at the source I argued that open code can be free to copy and still paid for where it is trusted: the official source, reviewed and signed. A patched PHP build from the people who maintain it, signed and on time, is worth paying for, per server or per use, even though anyone may rebuild it. Measure it, everywhere. Dion's ratio should be on every sovereignty plan, and the same idea works inside companies: what you spend on what you build on top, against what you spend on what you build on. And with the method in application behaviour policies, every organisation can know, before the next incident, what each of its sites can reach and what it would lose, so the next shutdown is a decision with a map rather than a reflex.
work
The money exists, as Dion shows. What is missing is a product that lets it reach the people doing the maintenance.
limits

The ratios are illustrative. Contracts and grants cover different periods and scopes. Some of Dion's figures I have not checked. Listed above; they are Dion's, with Dion's sources. The inventory counts rows, not servers. And "under investigation" means nobody has said. The compromise map is a time-bounded absence. As of 20:50 UTC on 22 October; one statement would end it. The proposals are mine. Not Dion's, though Dion's article points the same way.

Abstract: Some of the people who get emails from my agents have assumed they were talking to a chatbot, and, because most of us have learned that chatbots are not very clever, read them that way. They are not talking to a chatbot. They are talking to me. The agents draft, follow up, map the thread and collect the evidence; I read every draft, use it to think, change it, and send it. It is the Wizard of Oz in reverse. In 1984 an IBM researcher named the method where a hidden person makes a half-built program look clever; here the program is the visible part and the person is the one hidden. And there is a second thing behind the curtain: an article. When I answer an email, there should almost always be an article behind the answer, with the evidence and the explanation, and if there is not one ready, that is a sign it is worth writing. That is why a short email to me can get a long answer, and why it scales: I write the article once and link it many times. The voice memo for this article also changed my mind about how the first email to someone should look. Every part of an email buys the next: the subject buys the first line, the first line buys the paragraph, the paragraph buys the email. So the first email should open with plain text, a short paragraph that says it all, and put the banner and the detail below. This page is also meant to be the link at the bottom of those emails.
In front of the curtain, one email in my name; behind it, the agents that draft and track, and me.
in-short

Some people think my agents' emails come from a chatbot. And read them the way we have learned to read chatbots. They come from me. The agents draft; I read, think, change and send every one. It is the Wizard of Oz, in reverse. The program is visible; the person is behind the curtain. There is an article behind almost every answer. If there is not one ready, it is worth writing. That is how it scales. A short email can get a long answer, because the answer is written once and linked many times. Every part of an email buys the next. Subject, first line, first paragraph, the email, the article. So the first email should start like an email. Plain text, the short answer first, the detail below.
chatbot

A few of the people I have emailed through my agents have gone the opposite way from what I expected. They assumed the email came from a chatbot: an automated reply, a model behind a form, with nobody reading. And I understand why. Most of us have been trained, by years of customer-service bots and support widgets, that a chatbot is not very clever. The few that are, ChatGPT, Claude and the other labs' models, we use in a chat window, not in our inbox. So when an email arrives that is clearly written with an agent's help, the easy reading is: another bot.
chatbot

That reading is wrong, and it matters that it is wrong. How you read an email depends on who you think wrote it: what you forgive, what you trust, whether you bother to answer. Who is speaking made the same point about this site, and proposed a line on every email saying who drafted it and who sent it. This article is the fuller answer, and I would like it to be the link at the bottom of those emails.
oz

The analogy I keep coming back to is the Wizard of Oz: the voice and the machinery in front, and a man behind the curtain. In this case the man is me. It is also, almost exactly, a research method. In 1984 J. F. Kelley, at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center, described how he built a natural-language calendar program using what he called the OZ paradigm, "in which experimental participants are given the impression that they are interacting with a program that understands English as well as another human would." In the early stages, a hidden experimenter supplied the answers the program could not; as the program improved, the hidden person did less and less (Kelley, ACM Transactions on Office Information Systems, March 1984). It is now usually called the Wizard of Oz method.
oz

My emails reverse it in two ways. First, nobody is being given an impression: I am telling you, here and in the email, that I am behind it. Second, the hidden person is not being phased out. For emails, the person stays, on purpose. An article can be corrected tomorrow; an email cannot be unsent. That is the line the human in the loop drew: put the person where the output cannot be undone, and an email in my name is exactly that.
behind

The agents that run my correspondence, the agent team as it runs, do a lot. They draft the reply. They follow up the thread. They map what was said into a CRM, one folder per person, with where each fact came from. They collect the evidence and the data. They keep track of what is owed to whom. And they send nothing to the people I write to: every email waits in drafts. Then it is my turn. I read every draft. More than that, I use the drafts as a way to think: a draft is a first answer, and reading it tells me what I actually want to say. Often I change it a lot. And often, as I was doing earlier today, I decide the answer needs more than an email can carry, and I ask for an article instead, so that the email can be short and point to it.
article

These days my rule is: if I am sending an email that answers a real question, there should almost always be an article behind it, or a set of articles, with the evidence, the explanation and what can actually be done. And if there is not one ready, that is the signal that it is worth writing one. Some of the articles on this site started exactly like that. What can your agent reach? answers a reader who spent real time on RiskMandate and came back with four fair points. The human in the loop answers a question from someone shaping a roundtable. Research, delivered as a vault came out of a meeting.
article

Someone pointed out to me that they had sent me an email of about two hundred words and got back something closer to two thousand. Fair. But it works, because I only have to write it once. The next person who asks the same question gets a link. The article can be read later, forwarded to a colleague, checked against its sources, and corrected as a new version when I learn more, none of which an email can do. Each answer makes the next one cheaper. One article, many emails: questions arriving, the test of whether an article answers them, and the article itself.
buys

Recording the memo for this article changed my mind about how the first email to someone should look. Each part of an email buys the next. The subject, a few seconds of attention, buys the first line. The first line buys the rest of the paragraph. The first paragraph buys the decision to read the email. By the end of the email the reader is more committed, and the email buys the article. Nothing further down gets read if something higher up did not earn it. This matters more than it sounds, because of what the inbox shows. Next to the subject, most mail clients show a preview, which is normally "pulled from the first text in your email", and they show up to about 140 characters of it, often fewer, by Customer.io's estimate. So the first sentence of the email is, in practice, part of the subject line.
buys

Today, when my agents send a first email to someone, it starts with an HTML banner that explains who we are. That spends the most valuable space on the least useful thing. I think the first email should start like a normal email: plain text, one short paragraph that is the whole answer, the TL;DR, so that someone who reads only that has what they need. Then the detail, the banner and the links below. The US Army has a rule for this: its correspondence regulation asks for "putting the main point at the beginning of the correspondence (bottom line up front)" (AR 25-50, 2013, paragraph 1-36). So the changes for the agents that draft my emails are: Open with plain text. One short paragraph that answers the question or says why I am writing. The detail and the banner go below. For the reader who has decided to keep going.
buys

Say who is speaking. A line saying the email was drafted with my agents and sent by me. Link this article at the bottom. For anyone who wonders who is behind the curtain. We are starting to try variations of the first email, and I will report what we learn. Every part of an email buys the next, and the same first email two ways: a banner, or a plain paragraph.
memo

This article is also an example of why I write by voice memo. I started recording with one idea, that people misread my agents' emails, and by the end I had three: the curtain, the article behind every email, and how each part of an email buys the next. The memo zooms in as I talk. Then the agent that writes with me checks it against the record and the sources, and what I thought I remembered becomes something I can link. That is the method in your own newsroom. And there is a bigger point I will write next: people who can work this way, with agents behind them and an article behind every answer, are highly employable. It is a real opportunity, and I would like to say so clearly in its own article.
from-an-email

Then yes: the email was drafted with my agents and sent by me. I read it before it went. If it was long, it is because I wanted you to have the full answer, and the article behind it is where the full answer lives. If you only read one paragraph, the first one should have been enough; if it was not, tell me, and I will fix how the next one starts.
limits

The chatbot reading is anecdotal. A few people, not a measured result. The new email layout is a proposal. The current first emails start with a banner; the plain-text-first version is what we are starting to try. The preview length varies. About 140 characters is an estimate; many clients show fewer. Not every email gets an article. Short replies stay short; the rule is for answers to real questions. The analogy is loose. Kelley's participants were not told; my correspondents are. If you have read one of these emails and want to say how it read to you, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

This article is the fuller answer, and I want it to be the link at the bottom of those emails.

Abstract: RiskMandate runs its business with about fifteen agents and one person, four times a day on a schedule and whenever the person sits down with them, with the person's name on every message that leaves. The agent that runs its CRM wrote the briefing this article is built from. The system is described in eight layers, from rented compute and channels, through encrypted vaults as shared memory, domain vaults, semantic graphs over people and policies, a scheduled conductor and written behaviour policies, to a human who holds the one step that cannot be undone. The article follows an input from the outside world through the layers to the person who sends; explains why the vault is an app platform rather than storage, and the loop in which a friction becomes a tool in the same session and the tools compound; names the feedback loop that makes the setup hold, the draft as a release candidate with the recipient closing the loop; and draws two Wardley maps with Mermaid, from the outside and from the inside, showing what the team is turning into a commodity and what it is turning into a product. Every layer is linked to the article or document on this site where it was worked out. The published record of agent projects that stall is kept for the end, each reason mapped to the mechanism that answers it. Everything described is in use.

The Mandate Stack as it runs on 6 October 2026, read from the bottom: compute and channels rented from vendors, then the team's own files, graphs, schedule and policies, then one person above a line of their own. The right column says what each layer gives the team. Infographic from the CRM agent's briefing; everything shown is in use. This runs. About fifteen agents and one person run RiskMandate's relationships, research, writing and events, four times a day on a schedule and whenever Dinis sits down with them, in production, today. Eight layers. Compute and channels are rented. Everything above them is the team's own: encrypted vaults as shared memory, a vault per domain, semantic graphs over people, teams and policies, a conductor, written mandates, and one human at the top. One line. Many small agents, one written mandate each, everything connected as a graph, one human who sends.

The world writes in from the left; nothing leaves without the person on the right. Email, a web form, other teams' agents and an event extension all enter as data. The only exit is a send by the person whose name is on the message. The vault is an app platform, not storage. A model that writes good HTML and a vault that serves it give one person a loop: hit a friction, build the tool in the same session, deploy it into the vault, use it, repeat. The tools compound, down to an interface for one person. Without that loop, this would be another project that stalled.

The loop is the design. The agents automate the hard part, capturing, connecting and remembering. The draft the person sees is a release candidate for the whole pipeline. The recipient's reply comes back through the same capture path. Mistakes are traced to captured data, a graph edge or the model, and fixed at the source. Two maps. Shared memory and the sgit tooling are being pushed toward commodity, on encrypted storage that already is one. The behaviour policies and the graphs are being pulled toward product. That is the team's strategy, drawn. The record, last. The published record of agent projects that stall is real, and it is kept for the end, each reason mapped to the mechanism here that answers it.

RiskMandate.ai runs its own business with a team of agents and one human, Dinis Cruz. Each agent has a narrow, written mandate, an Agent Behaviour Policy. All shared state lives in encrypted, versioned vaults driven by sgit. Everything the team knows about people, organisations and its own work is connected as semantic graphs. The human holds the one step that cannot be undone: nothing goes to the outside world unless Dinis sends it. The briefing counts about fifteen agents. The agent team as it runs, written from the briefs role's field notes in the same week, names twelve roles. Both are the agents' own counts; this article keeps the briefing's and notes the difference. The collaboration vault, by the briefing's count, holds over 620 commits and 9,000 files, and every change any agent has made is in its history.

What the briefing calls the Mandate Stack is this arrangement, described as layers. The layers are not an architecture diagram drawn before the fact. They are the shape the setup had when an agent in it was asked to describe what was running. Left to right: the outside world writes in by email, by the subscribe form, through other teams' agents and an event extension; the input passes through the layers as data; the person enters from the right through Claude and Gmail, and is the only exit. From the briefing of 6 October 2026; fictional senders.

Follow one message. A person emails the agents' address. The inbox role, which can read but cannot draft or send, captures it word for word into that person's folder with a hash. It lands in the relationships vault, or in the mission vault it belongs to. Edges are added to the person's graph: who they are, what they care about, which of the team's materials meets it, which does not. On the next scheduled run the drafts role, which never reads raw mail, turns a row in the email register into a Gmail draft. Each step happens inside a written mandate, with the security role checking first and last. The draft waits in Gmail for Dinis.

Other inputs take the same shape. A reader fills in the subscribe form on this site, and the message goes into a vault the form cannot read, encrypted in the browser to the agent's key, through a write-only lane. The newsroom's agent, in another environment, writes through a signed and encrypted lane. The Web Summit browser extension feeds the mission vault. LinkedIn is reached through its own agent and a shared vault channel.

From the right, Dinis enters three ways: in a Claude session with the vault, for research, writing, design and analysis; by email to the agents' address, with a note the next run picks up; and by answering a decision draft in the thread, lettered options and an answer box. Anyone else on the team enters by the same three paths, and a new agent joins in two chat messages. What leaves is what Dinis sends, plus the SG/Send links the roles share, Slack status posts and Drive exports into the agents' own folder. The one exception is the security role's single hold email, to Dinis.

The agents are Claude sessions. Most run as Cowork sessions in a Claude Teams account, each with its own role and connectors. Some run as Claude Code cloud sessions on a separate account, with access to the vault and nothing else: no email, no calendar, no CRM write. The second kind still joins the team, takes work, reports and leaves a trail. The vault is the interface, not the account.

Why the sessions run in the cloud rather than on a laptop is the subject of Why my agents do not run on my laptop: an operating system has two hard walls, the kernel and the user account, and an agent on a laptop runs inside the one marked you. Why Cowork and Claude Code are treated as different agents with different reach is in Six agents, one inbox. What a Claude Code cloud session needs from an administrator before it can reach a vault at all is in the Team and Enterprise egress how-to, and the agent-facing surface of sgit itself, the session pattern of clone, work, commit, push, is in Working with AI agents. One Workspace identity, cut into roles. The reader of raw inbound mail has the least power; the roles with more power never read raw mail; the send row has no agent in it. From the briefing of 6 October 2026; agents named by role.

The channels belong to one Google Workspace identity, the agents' published address, reached through connectors. Each channel is split by role rather than given whole to one agent. The inbox role reads, triages, labels and captures every message to or from a known contact word for word into that person's folder. The drafts role creates Gmail drafts only from a row in the email register, formatting only, never content. Decision drafts are how a question reaches Dinis: a draft in the thread with lettered options and an answer box, read back on the next run. Drive holds exports of vault data in one agent-owned folder. Slack carries status. LinkedIn is reached through a separate agent and a shared vault channel. SG/Send provides encrypted, revocable links for sharing. Zapier is a second connector route, tested against Gmail drafts.

The row for sending has no agent in it. One exception exists: on a critical finding the security role sends a single "SECURITY HOLD" email to Dinis. The rule behind the split, that the account is the blast radius and no agent should hold a whole channel, is worked out in Six agents, one inbox, down to what a Workspace administrator can lock per organisational unit. What Gmail and Calendar can and cannot undo, and why a connector should be given a twin before an agent is given the connector, is in Before you give an agent a connector, give the connector a twin. The attempt to give each agent its own Workspace identity, and the line in Google's terms that stopped it, is in The identity we wanted to give the agents.

The vaults are the team's shared brain. A vault is a folder of plain files, JSON, Markdown and JSONL, encrypted on the client with AES-256-GCM, versioned like git, and synced through a server that does not see plaintext. Every agent session clones the vault, works, commits and pushes. Git for things you cannot put on GitHub is the introduction; Vault credentials explains the key classes, and why a read key can be published while a vault key travels only in chat; the security model says what the server can and cannot see.

Agents talk to each other through Email-FS, a mail protocol made of files. A message is an .eml file with headers for kind, priority and references. Sending writes it to the recipient's mailroom and to the sender's outbox. Moving it from mailroom to inbox is the read receipt; moving it to a done folder is completion. Each agent owns its folders and no other agent writes there. Any agent, model or person with the key can read the whole conversation with ls and cat. The convention and its history are in The agent team as it runs and Replicating the agentic inbox; why a message in that system carries its own graph and is rendered by its own interface is Custom UIs are not the exception.

Append lanes let the outside world write in without a key. A sender gets a write-only slot on a vault: it can add files but cannot list or read anything, including what it wrote. Messages are encrypted to the recipient's public key and signed by the sender. This is how the newsroom agent, in another environment, and the Web Summit browser extension feed vaults they cannot read, and how this site's subscribe form reaches the team. The mechanism is documented in append-lane messaging, sending messages between vaults and the append lanes API; the site-to-site version, where each site's agent publishes its keys and lane token, is Agent Contact. That memory lives in files rather than in a model's context, and why that is the right place for it, is the argument of Memory is not a spectator sport.

Context is scoped the way tools are. The relationships vault holds one folder per person. The collaboration vault links read-only to it and to the LinkedIn channel vault. A focused project gets its own mission vault with its own owner, policy and key holders: for Web Summit Lisbon 2026 there is a data vault, a discovery inbox and an extension vault, and the set can be shared with a partner without exposing the team vault. The briefing's phrase is least privilege applied to context, not just to tools.

The publishing method behind many vaults from one source, and the near-miss that taught the team to escrow write keys before publishing, is in Seven vaults, one method. The branch discipline that lets many sessions share one vault is the two-branch model. How vaults owned by different parties join through lanes and a typed graph, which is what a mission vault shared with a partner is, is in A supply chain of vaults. Which classes of information the team's vaults hold and which they refuse, public, private-ish and personal, is in the privacy section of The agent team as it runs. One person's subgraph in the relationships vault, with a fictional person, organisation and interests. An interest met by one of the team's materials is a reason to send it; an interest with no edge is a gap. Contexts are further graphs laid over the same people. The folder behind the picture is in the lower panel.

The team thinks in graphs, and the vaults are built that way. A record is not a row in a table. It is a node with typed edges to other nodes, and its meaning comes from those connections. The principles carry over from the published work on fractal semantic graphs and from graphs.sgit.ai: meaning is found in relationships rather than declared in a schema; confidence comes from how well connected an assertion is; unknowns are drawn as explicit nodes rather than hidden. The risk register as "a graph of graphs" on risks.sgit.ai is the same idea in another domain.

The CRM is a graph of people, organisations, interests and materials. As of 3 October the relationships vault held 71 people, 24 organisations, 281 timeline events and 12 campaigns, by the briefing's count. Each person's folder is a small subgraph: the contact record is the node; a graph file holds nodes of kind person, their work, interest and our material, with edges such as wants and met-by; a ledger holds the timeline as an append-only edge list, each line linking the person to a message, meeting, call, task or stage change, with the last line for an id winning; every message is kept word for word with who captured it, how, and a SHA-256 hash; a materials file records every link and vault sent, by whom, when, on which channel; a sources folder, a research file and a case file hold where each fact came from and the story so far; and a README is generated, never hand-written, from all of it. Around the folders sit organisations, campaigns, a shared vocabulary with stages S0 to S7, and an index the interface reads first. Agents and websites are entities in the same graph, so the graph can answer who an external agent's human is and what the team last told it.

Contexts are layers of graphs over the same people. The Web Summit crowd, the RiskMandate crowd, early adopters, design partners, friendlies: each is a graph over the same contact nodes with its own campaign, targets and next steps. One person can sit in several. Contexts can be layered on contexts, a sub-group of the Web Summit crowd for investors, because each is another graph over shared nodes rather than a copy of the data. A context can be parked and picked up later without losing anything, because the people, their timelines and their graphs carry on underneath. This is the fractal idea at work: the same structure at every scale. The same move, graphs per bounded context over a shared grammar, is what If somebody built a company on code review proposes for code, and Code review as a fractal semantic graph shows on a real repository.

What the graph is used for. Who gets what: an interest with a met-by edge to one of the team's materials is a reason to send it; an interest with no edge is a gap, either something to make or a reason not to email. Article nudges and campaign membership come from these edges, not from a list. Meeting preparation writes itself: a person's subgraph is the brief. "Here is what we know about you": Dinis can show a person their own graph as an honest, correctable picture; the first was sent on 3 October, rendered as a card from that person's graph file, and it is a natural reason to reply. Who has the ball: the ledger gives days since last contact, open tasks by owner and the next step. Stage as a path: known, replied, understands, using is movement along recorded edges, not a field somebody overwrites.

The rest of the system is graphs too. The team is a graph: every open Email-FS message is an edge from the agent asking to the agent holding it, and each session's snapshot records the picture before and after. An ABP is a capability graph: each row links an agent to a capability, a verb, object and reach drawn from a vocabulary of 23 primitives, and an instance; edges are marked granted, mandated or both, and the gap and the barrier are properties of those edges. The data-governance register is a graph of custody: each dataset links to who can read it, who has seen it, where it is stored and why it is held. Because all of it is plain files with typed edges in a versioned vault, any agent can traverse it with ordinary tools, and every edge has a history: when a relationship was added, by whom, from what source. The articles on this site are kept the same way, and the articles as graphs is that graph, this article included.

One conductor run: open and lock, security, drafts, inbox, briefs, CRM, the event mission, research, dev, security again, a card to Dinis, stop. The order is a design decision. Beside the schedule: emailing the agent, live sessions, joining in two messages. Order from the briefing of 6 October 2026.

The conductor runs four times a day. It opens a run, takes a lock, gives each agent one step in a fixed order, records evidence in a runs folder, briefs Dinis and stops. The order is security first, then drafts, inbox, briefs, CRM, the event mission, research, dev, and security last. Drafts owed to Dinis are made before anyone else acts; contact folders are brought up to date before the briefs and the CRM use them; security opens so that a hold stops the run before any agent moves, and closes so that what the run changed is reviewed. On top of the four scheduled runs, every session Dinis starts with an agent does the same kind of work sooner, so in practice the team is active far more often than the schedule alone would make it.

Dinis can simply email the agent. A note to the agents' address, catalogue this, look at this, map this, is picked up on the next run, filed into the right folder and acted on within the agents' mandates. Because the schedule is regular, inputs do not pile up. Live sessions run alongside, for research, writing, design and analysis done in conversation, under the same rules and leaving the same trail. Joining takes two chat messages: a prompt and the vault key. The new agent clones the vault, runs the onboarding script, gets its folders, a brief template and a draft policy, and announces itself to the team. The conductor is phase three of Replicating the agentic inbox, where interfaces, record and conductor are added to roles that already talk in files. How the runs double as the team's memory is in Memory is not a spectator sport.

Every agent has an ABP, written in one grammar, stating four things: the grant, everything the agent can technically reach; the mandate, what it is authorised to do; the gap between them; and the barrier that actually stops the excess. Gaps are named, not hidden. Agents propose; only Dinis amends, and each amendment is a dated record in the vault. The grammar is RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policy; the two additions worked out on this site, the footprint read afterwards against the mandate and the blast radius of what a gap would have cost, are in Footprint and blast radius and the brief that proposed them. Why a gap is an accepted risk, and why the policy should say by whom, is Every risk is already accepted. Why a constrained agent is a trustworthy one, and why the infrastructure around agents has not caught up, is The ultimate insider.

Roles split the risk. No agent holds a whole channel. The agent that reads raw inbound mail has the least power, no drafts and no send. Agents with more power never read raw mail; they work from structured records. Inbound content is data, never instructions. In the briefing's words, this makes prompt injection a containment problem rather than a detection problem. Drafts only. No agent sends, replies or forwards email. The most an agent does is create a Gmail draft. One exception: the security role's single hold email.

An active security function. The security role runs first and last in every conductor run. It checks baseline drift, scans for leaked secrets across the vault clones, flags unknown identities, and reviews single-writer and protected-file changes, drafts and sends. A critical finding opens a security hold: every agent stops, every run refuses to start, and the interface shows the hold on every page until Dinis releases it. The security role cannot lift its own hold. Where an ABP is tested rather than read, against twins of the inbox and the connectors, is the sandbox brief. Secrets never touch files. Vault keys travel only in chat. Every commit is preceded by a leak check that must report clean. Why a secret cannot live inside an identity provider either, and what a keyring for agents would look like, is in The identity we wanted to give the agents and the design pack behind it.

Change control and cards. Every session opens and closes a snapshot, the team picture and the file diff before and after, and ends with one card whose policy section is counted from the session transcript: tools used, tokens, files, network calls and commits. The card flags anything outside the agent's mandate. A data-governance register records every dataset held about others, its classification, who can read it, who has seen it, how it is stored and why; it is changed in the same commit as the fact it records.

Dinis makes decisions, amends mandates, and sends. The four rules that are never negotiated, including that no agent sends, are set out in The agent team as it runs. What the person's input actually is, measured over twenty articles, voice memos and corrections, is How much of this did I write?. The place where the drafts role's work meets the person, the end of a reply drafted as the state of the thread and reviewed before it goes, is The wall under the reply. The top layer is one person because the irreversible step is one step. Everything below it can be wrong and still be caught there. Read, eval, print, loop, applied to a business: a friction, a request in the session, a tool as HTML, deployed into the vault, used and corrected. The loop stops when a piece of work no longer calls for a tool. Below: apps already deployed into vaults on this site.

The layers above could be read as a storage architecture with a CRM on top. That is not what makes them work. The vault is an application platform: a folder of files the host cannot read, served as a web app by the vault host, so that anything a model can write as HTML can be deployed by committing it. Building vault apps is the contract, and three surfaces is the choice between a page inside the vault, a vault app and a page on a site.

Put that beside a model that writes good interfaces, and one person gets a loop. Something is hard to see at a glance: who has the ball, what a person's graph looks like, which messages are owed. Ask for a view of it, in the same session, from the same files. The model builds the tool as HTML, sized to the one use case. It is committed and pushed, and the next session, on any account, has it. It is used on real work, and what it gets wrong goes back to the start. Read, eval, print, loop, applied to a business rather than to a line of code.

Three things follow. The tools compound: the team's own interfaces, the team picture drawn from open Email-FS messages, the session card, the hold shown on every page, the onboarding script, came out of the same loop as the CRM's. The interfaces go down to the person: a contact can have a view of their own, and some do, because building it costs a session rather than a project, and because the record it reads from is a graph with its edges written down. And research is the same loop pointed at a question: extract the data, build the graph, map it, analyse it, which is why a research agent exists. A data-science agent would join the same way; there is not one today.

The loop has a natural stop. A piece of work is mature when it no longer calls for a tool. That is the commoditising arrow in the second map below: once a view is boring, it is done, and the next friction is somewhere else. Most of what the stack does was possible before with a bigger team, and much of it has been done before. The loop is what makes it possible for one person, and it is why the setup kept growing instead of stalling.

The pattern is already on this site in other clothes. Custom UIs are not the exception makes the argument for the inbox, where every message gets the interface for its moment. The vaults in the business plans section each carry an app built this way: the Deck Vault, eight web components bundled into one page; the evidence vault behind How much of this did I write?; the connector twin with its replay; the risk graph explorer; Kit Bag, a browser extension shipped in a vault. The code review navigator in the review-folder brief is the same move for repositories. Twenty sites in fifteen days is what the loop did to a network of websites.

Nine steps, six of them the agents' on the schedule: capture, graph, research, write, register, format. The draft in Gmail is the release candidate. The send is the person's. The recipient's reply comes back through step one. Below: the three causes a mistake is traced to, and the two levels of error correction. From the briefing of 6 October 2026. What the agents automate is the hard part, not the send. The scarce work was never pressing send. It was capturing, reading, tagging, connecting and remembering everything about every relationship. The agents do that, inbound processing, capture into contact folders, graph building, research and writing, on a regular schedule. Dinis keeps the step with the lowest volume and the richest feedback.

The draft is a release candidate. When a message arrives in Gmail for Dinis, the whole pipeline has already run: capture, graph, research, writing, register and formatting. Reviewing it is QA on the full system, like checking pre-production before it goes live. It is also where the thinking happens. People often find out what they want to say halfway through saying it. Seeing the message as it would land is when Dinis sharpens the point, changes the ask or rethinks the next step.

Every mistake is traced to its cause. A wrong detail in a message leads back to wrong captured data, a wrong or missing graph edge, or a model error. Because every fact carries its source, capture method and hash, the cause is fixed at the source, not patched in the email. The briefing's observation is that model error is now the rarest of the three causes, because the data the agents work from is solid. That matches what How much of this did I write? found on this site's own corrections, traced memo by memo.

The world closes the loop. Every sent email is tested against reality. If it is wrong, the recipient says so quickly, and the reply comes back through the same capture path into their timeline. The system has error correction at two levels: Dinis before sending, the recipient after. The same two-level shape, a replay of what an agent would have done before it is allowed to do it, and a record of what it did read afterwards, is what the connector twin and Footprint and blast radius describe separately. The result is control and throughput together. Nothing on the schedule is missed, every follow-up is known, and every outgoing message has been seen by the person whose name is on it.

Map one, from the outside. The anchor is a person who writes to the team. What they see, a reply with Dinis's name on it, is custom. What they do not see, the vaults, the sessions, Workspace and encrypted storage, is product or commodity. Rendered with Mermaid wardley-beta from the source below; every placement is a claim. A Wardley map places each component by how visible it is to the user, vertically, and by how evolved it is, horizontally, from genesis through custom-built and product to commodity. The maps here are drawn in the spirit of wardley-maps.sgit.ai: a map is a claim, not a picture, and the source is published next to the render so the claim can be argued with. The placements are this article's, made from the briefing, and a reader who would put a component elsewhere is probably right about something.

The first map takes the point of view of a person outside the team. What they can see is a reply with Dinis's name on it, the agents' address and the subscribe form. Everything that produces the reply sits below their line of sight: the drafts and inbox roles, the person's folder and graph, the behaviour policies, the conductor and Email-FS, all custom-built. Below those, the vaults, the Claude sessions, Google Workspace and encrypted storage are product or commodity. The shape says what the stack is: a thin custom layer where the relationship is, resting on rented parts.

Map two, from the inside. The anchor is Dinis. The dashed arrows are the movement the team is making: shared memory and the sgit CLI toward commodity, the behaviour policies, the graphs and the custom interfaces from genesis toward product. Everything rests on encrypted storage, which is already a commodity. Rendered with Mermaid wardley-beta from the source below.

The second map takes Dinis's point of view and adds movement. What he sees is a CRM that is current without typing, drafts to review, decision drafts in the thread, and the custom interfaces the tool loop produces. The arrows say what the team is doing to its own components. Shared memory runs on sgit, and sgit runs on encrypted object storage, S3. Each of those is being pushed to the right on purpose, so that a vault is a folder, a push is a command, the host sees ciphertext and sizes, and nothing above them has to know how any of it works. Two notes on reading them, both borrowed from the mapping site. Coordinates are visibility first, evolution second, and transposing them renders without an error and asserts something else. And a component cannot be more evolved than the least evolved thing it depends on, which is why the custom middle of these maps cannot move right until the policies do. The briefing gives five reasons the setup holds. Each of them answers something in the record kept for the end of this article. The control surface is small, explicit and versioned. Trust grows one mandate at a time, and every change to a mandate is visible: a written policy per agent, in one grammar, amended only by the human, with each amendment dated.

The human holds the irreversible step. Everything else can be wrong and still be caught at the draft. This is the pattern the email products shipped and the guides from the model vendors ask for, applied here as a rule rather than a default. Shared state is files, not context windows. Agents do not need to remember; they read. Any session, on any account, can pick up where another left off. A fixed schedule, one step per agent, and a card per session that counts tools, tokens, files and network calls mean the cost is read rather than guessed. The graph puts meaning on the read path. Agents do not query raw data and guess. They traverse records whose relationships, sources and vocabulary are written down and shared. A wrong detail is traced to a captured fact, an edge or the model, and fixed where it came from.

Everything leaves a trail. Commits, ledgers, snapshots, cards, run evidence. The system can be audited by the same tools that run it. Roles split the risk, inbound content is data, a security role runs first and last and can stop the team, and secrets never touch files. None of this makes the setup immune. It says where a failure would have to get through.

The briefing calls the pattern the Mandate Stack. The name has to carry three things. The mandate, because the unit of the design is a written policy per agent, not a model or a framework. The stack, because the layers are real and the lower ones are rented while the upper ones are owned. And the human who sends, which the name does not say and the one-line version does: many small agents, one written mandate each, everything connected as a graph, one human who sends. A better name may come. The description is what matters, and it is the description of something that runs.

Every component named above is in use on the date of writing; that was the briefing's rule and it is this article's. What is not in it is the list of things the team knows it lacks. The things The agent team as it runs lists as not working yet still apply: commit authorship is not signed, so an agent's identity inside a shared vault is its branch rather than a signature; a vault key cannot be revoked, only replaced by a new vault; most barriers are policy-only, enforced by the process they constrain, and a separate permission authority that holds the credentials and decides each action does not exist in this setup. The three wishes in Why my agents do not run on my laptop, an identity, a secret store and a key pair per agent, are the platform-side half of the same list.

And the question underneath stays open: who gives the mandate over a piece of information, and whether the recipient of an email has the authority to hand it to an agent at all. The setup's answer so far is to hold less and to say what it holds. The question gets a document of its own. The reasons the record gives for agent projects failing, each with who said it and when, beside the mechanism in the stack that answers it. The dark panel is the fair reading: the record is of pilots that stall, and the pattern that shipped stops at the draft. Sources in the Sources section. The complaint is familiar: agents do not behave, agentic workflows do not work, projects are cancelled or never pushed to production. The record supports the complaint, and it is worth being exact about what it says and when. When Who What was reported 25 Jun 2025 Gartner, prediction

More than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, for "escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls". About 130 real agentic vendors among thousands; the rest "agent washing". Mar 2025 S&P Global, survey of more than 1,000 42% of companies abandoned most of their AI initiatives, up from 17% the year before. The average organisation scrapped 46% of proofs of concept before production. Aug 2025 MIT NANDA, report 95% of organisations "getting zero return" from generative AI. The report's own funnel, read by its critics, puts the success rate of actual pilots nearer a quarter; the figure is the report's word "directional". 30 Sep 2025 Gartner, survey of 360 IT leaders 15% considering, piloting or deploying fully autonomous agents. 19% trust vendors' hallucination protection. 74% see agents as a new attack vector. 13% strongly agree they have the governance in place. Nov 2025 McKinsey, survey of 1,993

23% scaling an agentic system somewhere, 39% experimenting; in any one business function, at most 10% scaling. Inaccuracy the most common harm, reported by 30%. Jan 2026 Deloitte, survey of 3,235 25% have moved 40% or more of their AI experiments to production; pilots stretch "to 18 months or more"; 21% report a mature governance model for autonomous agents. Jun 2026 Forrester, report 75% say they have adopted agentic AI; "only a small minority" run production deployments beyond "agentish" chatbots. ROI uncertainty, "trapped in pilot mode", governance gaps, a "trust tax". Jul 2026 KPMG, survey of 2,145 49% scaled back or paused agent rollouts because operating costs outran returns. 7% report established ROI. 26% have real-time visibility of what agents cost to run. Sep 2025 Carnegie Mellon, benchmark The best agent completes 30% of 175 simulated office tasks end to end.

The same period has its reversals: Klarna hiring human support staff again in May 2025 after calling its AI support "lower quality"; Taco Bell slowing its drive-through voice AI in August 2025 and keeping people in the loop at busy sites; Commonwealth Bank of Australia reversing 45 redundancies it had attributed to a voice bot; Ford rehiring about 350 quality inspectors in June 2026 after AI inspection missed defects. In each case the company kept the AI and put a person back at the step that mattered.

A fair reading has two more lines. First, agents do reach production: Google Cloud's September 2025 survey of organisations already using generative AI found 52% with agents in production, and LangChain's developer survey, fielded in late 2025, found 57%. The record is of pilots that stall, not of a technology that cannot ship. Second, the pattern that shipped in email is the same everywhere: Gmail's Gemini drafts (May 2025), Outlook's Copilot and its agent mode (April 2026), Superhuman's auto-drafts (July 2026) and Shortwave's triggered drafts (January 2026) all stop at the draft and leave the send to the person. OpenAI's April 2025 guide to building agents tells builders to escalate "high-risk, sensitive, or irreversible actions" to a human; Anthropic's December 2024 note on effective agents says to pause for human feedback at checkpoints and to add complexity only when it demonstrably helps.

The MIT report's own explanation of failure, tools that do not learn from or adapt to workflows, and McKinsey's finding that the organisations seeing value were three times likelier to have redesigned their workflows, are the closest the record comes to describing the setup above from the outside. Append lanes let the outside world write in without a key. A sender gets a write-only slot on a vault: it can add files but cannot list or read anything, including what it wrote. Messages are encrypted to the recipient's public key and signed by the sender. This is how the newsroom agent, in another environment, and the Web Summit browser extension feed vaults they cannot read. The mechanism is documented in append-lane messaging, sending messages between vaults and the append lanes API; the site-to-site version, where each site's agent publishes its keys and lane token, is Agent Contact.

Abstract: A conversation at Chainguard's event today sharpened something I have thought for a while. Chainguard does security from the bottom up, and does it very well: it rebuilds the operating system and the libraries from source, keeps the images minimal and manages the whole process. But even the most locked-down image still holds a great deal of code the application never runs, the assurance still depends on testing, and the loop that caused the problem in the first place is still there: when something breaks, you give it more. As soon as the work reaches the application, it stops. My proposal is to come from the other end. Start from the user story and, at every layer down, ask one question: what is the minimum code below this that the layer above needs? Keep that, remove everything else, and draw the immutable line as high as the evidence allows. It did not scale before; with models and fractal semantic graphs, it can. I measured it for this article on a real tool, sgit and its dependencies, running a CI-style use case under coverage and then running it again from a tree holding only the files that ran. Of 1,500 files, 428 were kept, and the use case passed; commands outside it failed because their code was not there. It also showed the limits: one compiled binary held three quarters of the bytes and no coverage tool can see inside it, and coverage missed a compiled module the tests then caught. Tools that minimise containers at run time already exist, so the new part is the direction: from what the application is for, through a graph, down to a build that can be certified. Chainguard is unusually well placed to offer it, and someone will build it.

Top down, one question at every layer: what is the minimum code below this that the layer above needs? Code is a liability: remove what each use case does not call, apply it to the browser, and build on small blocks you did not have to write.
in-short

Chainguard secures from the bottom up. Rebuilt from source, minimal images, a managed process, and it stops where the application starts. Three gaps remain. Code the application never runs, assurance that depends on testing, and the loop of granting more when something breaks. Come from the top. At every layer, ask for the minimum code below that the layer above needs, and remove the rest. Measured on one tool. sgit and its dependencies, one use case: 1,500 files down to 428, the use case passing, other commands failing because their code was gone. And its limits. One compiled binary was three quarters of the bytes; coverage missed a compiled module; only 38% of the statements in the kept files ran. Others minimise at run time already. SlimToolkit and RapidFort watch what a container touches. The new part is starting from the use case, through a graph.
in-short
The prize is assurance. If the code with a vulnerability is not there, there is nothing to patch, and a build traced to its use case can be certified.
bottom-up

I have a lot of time for what Chainguard does. In Attacks rewritten as mandates its public ledger of supply-chain attacks was the example, and the controls it sells, packages rebuilt from source, no install-time scripts, actions pinned to a commit, would by my reading have held in most of them. Its images come in minimal variants without shells or package managers. That is security built from the bottom up: take the operating system, take the libraries, rebuild them, keep them current, and give the customer something they can trust more than the public registry. But bottom up has three gaps, and the conversation today made them clearer.
bottom-up

First, even the most locked-down image holds code the application never runs. My estimate is that in most images it is the large majority; the one case measured below found about 70% of the files in the dependency tree never ran. Every one of those files is attack surface and a source of vulnerability reports. Second, the assurance still depends on testing. A hardened base says the parts are trustworthy; whether the application still works on them, and does only what it should, is the customer's problem.
bottom-up

Third, the loop that caused the problem in the first place is still there. When something breaks, the reflex is to give it more: another package, another permission, a shell back in the image. Chainguard's own tool for tailoring images, Custom Assembly, is built in that direction. Its documentation says it "only allows you to add packages into a given container image" and that "you cannot remove the packages included in the source application image by default." And the application itself, where the code is hardest to change, is where the bottom-up model stops. When I asked about virtual patching and similar fixes at the application layer, I did not hear that it is something they do, and I could not find it on their public pages.
top-down

My proposal is to come from the other end, and ask one question at every layer: what is the minimum code below this that the layer above needs? Start from the user story. What is the code needed to run this use case? Then the workflow: which commands does it call? Then the modules those commands load, the functions in them that actually run, the files in each dependency those functions touch, the parts of the language runtime the code imports, and the binaries and libraries in the operating system the runtime calls. At each layer, keep what the layer above needs and remove everything else. The higher you can draw the line below which nothing changes, the immutable line, the more of the system is fixed, exact and small.
top-down

This is the same shape as the review model in If somebody built a company on code review: a graph projected from the top, from objectives and stories down to the commands they will touch, joined to a graph derived from the code. In that article's words, a node the code has and no story asked for is "derived, not projected". In a code review that is a question for the author. In an image, it is code to remove.
top-down

What it kills is living off the land. An attacker who gets into a process uses what is already there: a shell, an interpreter's standard library, a network tool, a module that can write files. If the only code on the box is the code the use case runs, there is very little to live off. It is what a good linker does when it pulls in only the functions a program references, applied to the whole stack, from the story to the operating system.
measured

One use case, measured: sgit 0.21.0 and its dependencies before and after keeping only the files that ran. Years ago I did a version of this by hand. I had a Python application with close to full code coverage, ran the coverage across the dependencies as well as my own code, took every file the coverage had touched, built a new package from only those, and deployed it. It worked. I used it to shrink Python deployments for Lambda functions, and the cut, as I remember it, was close to 90% of the dependency code.
measured

So I did it again for this article, on a real tool. The tool was sgit 0.21.0, installed in a fresh virtual environment with its four dependencies: cryptography, osbot-utils, cffi and pycparser. The use case was the one from sgit in a CI pipeline, run against a local vault server: create a vault, commit a build manifest, push it, clone only the build folder in a fresh home, make a key pair, encrypt a file and decrypt it. I ran it under coverage, measuring every file in the dependency tree, not only sgit's own. Then I copied only the files that had run, plus the compiled modules and data files beside them, into a new tree, and ran the same use case again from that tree with the original packages out of reach. It worked. The use case passed from the minimal tree: the manifest came back from the scoped clone and the decrypted file read "secret".
measured

The tree was much smaller. 1,500 files became 428. Of 1,416 Python files, 418 had run, and the Python source went from 4.72 MB to 1.98 MB. Two of the four dependencies, cffi and pycparser, ran no Python code at all. What was not needed was not there. Commands outside the use case failed: sgit history log and sgit vault backup both stopped with ModuleNotFoundError, because the code they needed had been removed.
limits-measured

Three results matter as much as the cut. The compiled code did not move. 14.78 MB of the dependencies is compiled, three quarters of the whole, and almost all of it is one file: the 14.4 MB Rust binary inside cryptography. Coverage sees Python; it cannot see which functions inside a compiled library ran, so file-level minimisation keeps all of it. Going further means building that binary with only what is used, which is a build-time decision, made by whoever builds from source. Coverage was not enough. cffi ran no Python code, so a pure coverage cut would drop it. When I removed its compiled backend, the use case failed with No module named '_cffi_backend': something in the stack loads it without running any of cffi's Python. The tests caught what the coverage missed, which is the point of the method. The evidence for what is needed is the test suite passing, not the coverage report.
limits-measured

Files are a coarse unit. sgit publish, which was not in the use case, still worked, because the module it lives in was loaded by commands that were. Inside the 418 files that ran, only 38% of the statements executed. Function-level removal would cut much more than file-level, and that is where a semantic graph of the code, function by function, earns its place.
scale

None of this is new as an idea. Doing it for one application, by hand, with coverage and a script, works and is too much effort to do for every service and every release. What changed is that the expensive part, understanding what each layer is for and what it calls, is now the part models are good at, and the result can be held as a fractal semantic graph: the story, its workflows, the modules, the functions, the dependencies and the files of the operating system, each in its own vocabulary, with named edges between them. Then "what is the minimum below this?" is a walk, and "why is this file here?" has an answer, the path up to the story that needs it.
scale

And it is deterministic where it matters. The graph says what should be kept; the build keeps exactly that; the tests prove the use case still works. Change the use case, and the build is regenerated.
landscape

Three ways to get to less code: bottom up and hardened, runtime minimisation, and top down by use case. I said it never scaled before, and that needs a correction: minimising containers is a real field already. SlimToolkit, formerly DockerSlim and now a CNCF Sandbox project, runs a container, watches what it touches and builds a smaller image, by up to 30 times in its own words. RapidFort profiles applications at run time and removes the components that never run, and reports large reductions in attack surface and in vulnerabilities; those are its own figures. Both work from what a container did. What I am proposing starts from what the application is for: the use case defines what must run, the graph traces every layer, the unit of removal goes down to the function and the build, and the tests are the evidence. Runtime observation is one input to that, not the whole of it.
certify

Here is the question that turns this into a business. A package has a vulnerability. If the vulnerable code is never called by the use case, why care? And more to the point, why is that code there at all? In a build that keeps only the code a use case needs, a vulnerability in removed code is not a patch to apply; it is a line in the record saying the code is absent.
certify

That is something that can be certified. A build traced from the story to the operating system, with the graph saying why every remaining line is there and the tests proving the use case, is a high-assurance artefact: a third party can check that the code with each known vulnerability is not present, and say so. That is the next product for a company like Chainguard, which already builds every layer from source and is trusted to say what is in it. It is also the product that, built by someone else on top of a platform like theirs, could eventually deploy without needing the base images at all, which is why I think they should build it, or partner with whoever does.
limits

One tool, one use case. sgit and four dependencies, measured once; other applications will differ, and the bottom two layers, the Python runtime and the operating system, were not measured here. The 70% to 90% figures are estimates and memory. My Lambda result is from memory; the 70% is this measurement's share of files that never ran. Chainguard's plans are not public to me. That they do not do this is from their public pages and one conversation; they may be working on it. Runtime minimisation tools exist. SlimToolkit's and RapidFort's figures are their own; I have not tested them here. A use case is only as complete as its tests. Anything the tests do not exercise is removed, so the test suite becomes the definition of the application. If you are running hardened images and wondering how much of what is in them your application needs, or you want to build the top-down version, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
