Abstract: This is a blueprint, for founders and for the agents that work with them, of a kind of product that a lot of what I have written here adds up to. Phase one has no server and no database of its own. The product is a folder of HTML, CSS and JavaScript, built from native web components with the few libraries it needs vendored inside it, so it runs offline and anywhere a web page can be served, from a laptop to GitHub Pages to a customer's isolated network. The user brings the expensive parts: their own AI key, capped and paid by them, called straight from the browser; their own storage, in the browser, in an encrypted vault or in their own cloud drive; and their own passkey, which can give the browser a secret that only their device can produce. You are not in the line of any request, so the product scales with its users, not with your servers. The pieces mostly exist today, OpenRouter's OAuth among them, which bills each user's requests to their own credit. The gaps are on the providers' side: a user's own key with a cap, and paying the app that brought them the customer, which none of the providers I checked offers. Then how to build it, with agent sessions, a dev and a main site and an explorer as the first hire; how to charge for it; a checklist an agent can work through; and an MVP of it, an infographic studio, mostly simulated, in a vault, with a business plan for somebody to build.

The usual SaaS beside the no-server product: the company in the line of every request, against a folder of files. A blueprint for products with no server and no database of their own, a tour of an MVP built to it, and the MVP itself, in a vault, with its business plan.
in-short

No server and no database of yours. Phase one is a folder of HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Native web components, few libraries, all vendored. It runs offline, and anywhere a page can be served. The user brings the expensive parts. Their AI key, their storage, their passkey. You are not in the line. No request passes through you, so it scales with users. The pieces mostly exist. The gaps are capped per-user keys and paying the app that brings the customer. Build it with agents. A dev and a main site, synthetic users, an explorer as the first hire. Charge for the build, the users and the keys. Even when they bring their own. A checklist for agents. Each step can be marked done. An MVP and a business plan, in a vault. For somebody to build.
what

A lot of what I have written here over the last weeks is one idea in pieces: the passkey that opens the vault, free models with your own key, the code you do not ship, Cloudflare as Lego blocks, explorer coding, your own newsroom, paying after the value. This puts the pieces in one place, as principles, a worked example and next steps. It is written for two readers. For a founder, it is the shape of a product that costs almost nothing to run and that nobody needs permission to deploy. For the agents a founder works with, it is a set of requirements and a checklist: what to build, what not to build, and what to mark done.
what

It needs a name. I would call it a no-server product, and a company built that way a no-server startup. Serverless is taken, and it means something else: there are servers, you just do not manage them. Here, in phase one, there are none of yours at all.
principles

No server and no database of yours. There is a CRM and an email list somewhere, but the product itself has no backend. Everything it does, it does in the user's browser. HTML, CSS and JavaScript, as native web components. No JavaScript framework for components, no build step. The browser is the runtime. The conventions are written down at coding.sgit.ai: a component is three files, behaviour, markup and styles, with one URL per version. What the code must also be, version controlled, reliable, resilient, secure, backed up, consistent, explainable and documented, is at nfrs.sgit.ai, the non-functional requirements. Do not reinvent the wheel; vendor it. If you need Mermaid for diagrams, or a library for charts, use it, at a pinned version, copied into the product's vendor/ folder. Nothing is fetched from a CDN at run time.
principles

It runs offline, and anywhere. From a file on a laptop, a simple local server, a container, a Lambda or Cloud Function that returns files, Cloudflare, any cloud, or a customer's isolated network. If something can serve a web page, it can run the product. The user brings the compute. The expensive part, the AI model, is paid for by the user, through a key that is theirs, ideally capped, and called from their browser. The user's data stays with the user. In the browser's storage, in an encrypted vault, or in their own cloud drive. You never hold it, so you never have to protect it. The passkey is the identity. A passkey can give the browser a secret that only the user's device can produce, and from it the keys to their data, with nothing to remember and nothing to sign up for.
principles

You are not in the line. No request passes through you. The product scales with its users, not with your servers, and an outage of yours does not stop anyone. Everything is in version control, and agents maintain it. A dev site and a main site, every change a commit, every release a note, held to the non-functional requirements from the first release. Charge for value, not for servers. For building it, for its users, and for the keys, even when the user brings their own. One folder, served from anywhere: a laptop, a simple server, a container, GitHub Pages, any cloud, a customer's network.
example

Take a product that turns a document into infographics. Today it would be built as a SaaS: an account, a server that calls an image model with the company's key, a database of every user's images, and a margin on top of the model's price. As a no-server product, it looks like this.
example

The user opens the studio, which is a folder of static files, served from anywhere. They sign in with a passkey, and the browser gets a secret only their device can produce, from which it derives the keys to their storage. They connect an AI provider. With OpenRouter's OAuth flow, "Each user signs in to OpenRouter and authorizes your app, and your app receives an API key tied to their account. Their requests are billed to their own OpenRouter credits." If they have no credit, they buy it there, from the provider, and come back. The studio calls the image model from the browser, with their key, and keeps the results in the browser, in an encrypted vault, or in the user's own Google Drive, in the application data folder, which "is only accessible by your app and its contents are hidden from the user and from other Google Drive apps."
example

Nothing in that loop passes through the company that built the studio. It did the work once, in the product, and a sale can happen without anyone at the company doing anything. The infographic studio as eight steps, none through the company that built it: six work today, one has a catch. Every AI feature should also work without a key, in a simulation mode that returns example results. It is how a prospect tries the product before paying anyone, how the synthetic users test it, and how a demo survives a bad network.
gaps

The pieces mostly exist. The gaps are on the providers' side, as their documentation reads on 20 October 2026. A cap on the user's own key. OpenRouter can create keys with a credit limit through its provisioning API, but those keys belong to your account, so you pay, and you are back in the business of reselling. Its OAuth page documents no spending limit for a key a user grants an app. OpenAI has project hard spend limits, and a key the user creates in their own project could carry one, but that is a setting the user has to make.
gaps

Keys in the browser. OpenAI's API reference says "Don't share it with others or expose it in any client-side code such as browsers or apps", and Google's Gemini guidance says "Never expose keys client-side in production". Both are about a developer's key shipped to every user, and both are right about that. A user's own key, held in their own browser, is a different case, and OpenRouter is the provider built for it. The user's own plan. OpenAI's Sign in with ChatGPT lets "Eligible ChatGPT Plus and Pro users" use their plan for AI requests in participating apps. It is "currently available to selected commercial partners through a limited trial", and for a website the app's backend exchanges the code, so it does not fit phase one yet. It is the right direction.
gaps

Paying the app that brought the customer. OpenRouter's app attribution gives an app rankings and analytics. I could not find a revenue share from OpenRouter, or from OpenAI, Google or Anthropic. This is the biggest gap and the biggest opportunity: a provider that gives the app a share of the credit its users buy, say a fifth, would turn every no-server product into a sales channel for that provider, with no work on either side. Hosting when you sell. GitHub Pages is the right place to start, but its own rules say it is not for a site "primarily directed at either facilitating commercial transactions or providing commercial software as a service (SaaS)". Build and demo there; when the product sells, move the same folder to a host that allows it, such as Cloudflare or any cloud's static hosting.
stack

The product: HTML, CSS and JavaScript; native web components; vendored libraries; no build step. Hosting: GitHub Pages to build and demo; Cloudflare or any static host to sell; or the folder, shipped to the customer. Identity: a passkey, with the WebAuthn PRF extension giving the browser a per-user secret, as in the passkey opens the vault. Storage: the browser's own storage for what is small and can be lost; an encrypted sgit vault for what must last and move between devices, as the vault crosses Chrome profiles showed; or the user's own Google Drive, in an app folder only this product can see. AI: the user's own key, capped, called from the browser. Payments: ideally the provider's; otherwise a payment link, with the credit kept in the browser or the vault, as this newsroom does with pay after you read.
build

Start on GitHub Pages, with a repository, two branches, and a site per branch, and move hosts when it starts to sell. Dev is where things change, and main is what customers use. An agent session, such as Claude Code wired to the repository, maintains it, and every change is a commit with a release note. This newsroom is built exactly that way, and your own newsroom describes how. Add synthetic users early: personas that use every page on every release, and tell you when something stops working for them. Add more agents as the product grows, each with a role and a written behaviour policy.
build

The team grows in Simon Wardley's order, in the names this site uses: explorers, villagers, town planners. The founder's first hire is an explorer, one person who works with the agents in explorer coding mode, from a chat or the command line, and changes the dev site fast. Villagers come next, to turn what works into a product: tests, versions, releases that do not break. Town planners come last, when it has to be a utility. How a founder builds it: agent sessions and synthetic users around one repository, and the team hired in order.
model

The costs are almost nothing, so the price is about value, not about covering servers. For building it. A new site for a customer, their segment, their workflow, their brand, is a project with a price. For its users. Per user, per month or per use. For the keys. Even when users bring their own key, they pay you for the product that uses it: a share of what they buy, when providers allow it, or a fee for the credit you manage for them. For running it where they are. The same folder, installed inside a customer's own network, is a licence. This newsroom uses the same model on itself: you start with credit, you pay for what you read, and the price falls as you read more. The product is the same set of files for everyone; what changes is who brings what.
mvp

The worked example is now a working one. The no-server studio is that infographic studio, built to this blueprint and published the way this site publishes its demos: in an sgit vault you can open. It is one HTML file of seven native web components, with no framework, no build step and no server. Pick a document or paste your own, choose a layout and a theme, and the browser draws the infographic.
mvp

Most of it is simulated, on purpose, which is why a vault is the right place for it. With no model connected, a deterministic extractor stands in for the model, so every feature works, offline, and replays exactly. Inside the vault, the studio asks the vault host for a model: the host holds the AI key, caps the spend per session and asks the user before the first call, and the studio never sees the key. That is the capped key the providers are missing, at the vault layer. The flow walks all eight steps with invented money, and three synthetic users walked the studio before it was published. The tour says what is real and what is simulated. The no-server studio in its vault: an invented bakery's quarter as a poster, drawn in the browser, in simulation mode.
business

I think this should be a business, and possibly three, and the studio's vault holds the plan, for somebody else to run or to run with us. The first is the studio itself: a no-server product for one segment, infographics for small businesses from their own reports and plans, where the user brings the key and the studio charges for the product. The second is a no-server product studio: a company that builds these for founders and for teams inside companies, a new product in weeks, handed over as a folder they own, with agents that maintain it. The third is the credit layer the providers are missing: capped keys for each user, and a share of the credit they buy paid to the app that brought them, which a provider, or a broker in front of providers, could build.
business

The plan in the vault has who it is for, packages and prices as hypotheses, go-to-market, the first ninety days, a calculator, the risks as acceptances, and the open questions. It sits with the other business plans published for founders. The pitch is one line long: infographics from your own documents, in your browser, with your own AI credit, and nothing kept by us. The business plan in the vault: three businesses in one blueprint, with packages, prices, ninety days and risks.
next

Each step is a checkbox an agent can mark, with the evidence that it is done. [ ] NS-01 Repository. One repository, a dev and a main branch, a site per branch, a version file and a release note per release. [ ] NS-02 No backend. No server code, no database, no secret in the repository. A scan in the release script proves it. [ ] NS-03 Components. Every UI element is a native web component, three files, versioned path. No framework. [ ] NS-04 Vendored. Every library is in vendor/, pinned, with its licence. The site loads nothing from another origin except the AI provider and the storage the user chose. [ ] NS-05 Offline. The product opens from a file and from a local server with the network off, and says clearly what needs the network. [ ] NS-06 Anywhere. The same folder is served from GitHub Pages and from one other host, with no change.
next

[ ] NS-07 Passkey. Sign-in with a passkey; the PRF secret derives the user's storage keys; nothing to remember. [ ] NS-08 Storage. Local storage first; then an encrypted vault; then, optionally, the user's own drive. [ ] NS-09 The user's key. Connect the user's AI provider, store the key only where the user's data is stored, show the cap and the spend. [ ] NS-10 Simulation mode. Every AI feature works without a key, with simulated results, for demos and tests. [ ] NS-11 Synthetic users. Personas that walk through every page on every release, in the release script. [ ] NS-12 Pricing. A price page, and a payment path that never requires a server of yours.
limits

Phase one only. Some products will need a server later; the point is not to start with one. The name is a proposal. No-server, as distinct from serverless. Provider terms change. What each provider allows is as of 20 October 2026. Not every product fits. Anything that must hold shared state between users needs more than this. The MVP is mostly simulated. The studio's own key path is written, not yet run against a live key.

A dev site and a main site, every change a commit, every release a note. 10. Charge for value, not for servers. For building it, for its users, and for the keys, even when the user brings their own.

Summary: This is a blueprint, for founders and for the agents that work with them, of a kind of product that a lot of what I have written here adds up to. Phase one has no server and no database of its own. The product is a folder of HTML, CSS and JavaScript, built from native web components with the few libraries it needs vendored inside it, so it runs offline and anywhere a web page can be served, from a laptop to GitHub Pages to a customer's isolated network. The user brings the expensive parts: their own AI key, capped and paid by them, called straight from the browser; their own storage, in the browser, in an encrypted vault or in their own cloud drive; and their own passkey, which can give the browser a secret that only their device can produce. You are not in the line of any request, so the product scales with its users, not with your servers. The pieces mostly exist today, OpenRouter's OAuth among them, which bills each user's requests to their own credit. The gaps are on the providers' side: a user's own key with a cap, and paying the app that brought them the customer, which none of the providers I checked offers. Then how to build it, with agent sessions, a dev and a main site and an explorer as the first hire; how to charge for it; and a checklist an agent can work through.

Abstract: The Open Security Summit is something I started a long time ago, out of the OWASP Summits of 2008, 2011 and 2017. What made the in-person summits work was that every participant was treated as a presenter: working sessions, collaboration, outcomes. In 2018 the website was part of that: 180 different people committed to it that year, editing their own pages and sessions, 434 commits on the first day alone. Then the summit went online, became monthly mini-summits, and kept going until the end of 2024. But each year's site was a copy of the last, with more exceptions added and no time to refactor. The template code grew from about 5,200 lines to 9,600 and then froze in 2022, while the content kept coming; the number of people committing fell from 180 to 14. The technical debt ground it to a halt, and the follow-up, the personal path for each participant that the in-person summits had, never scaled. It holds a lot of very good material on security, 194 recorded sessions among it. I kept it alive at a cost to me. Now, with agents to map it, follow up and personalise, it is time to restart it: in person in London, online, and as a home for open source projects. It needs someone to fund it.
Left: commits a quarter across the four summit websites. Right: people committing each year, 2018 to 2025.
in-short

Every participant was a presenter. That was the model, from the OWASP Summits to the Open Security Summit. The website was part of it. In 2018, 180 people committed to it, 434 commits on the first day. Then the debt grew. Each year's site was a copy of the last, with more exceptions and no refactoring. The code froze in 2022. About 9,600 lines of templates, while the content kept coming. The people went. From 180 committing in 2018 to 14 in 2024. The follow-up never scaled. And that was what made the in-person summits work. It is time to restart it. With agents, in London, online, and as a home for projects. It needs funding.
history

The Open Security Summit grew out of the OWASP Summits I helped organise: the Algarve in 2008, Lisbon in 2011, and Woburn in 2017, which I wrote up in a history of the in-person summits. After 2017 it carried on as the Open Security Summit: in person at Woburn Forest, 4 to 8 June 2018, and again in England, 3 to 7 June 2019; fully online, 15 to 19 June 2020; and then as monthly online mini-summits, from October 2020 to September 2024. Since 9 April 2019 it has been a UK community interest company, Open Security Summit CIC, and this week we proposed it as the home of Agent Behaviour Policies. What made the in-person summits powerful was simple to say and hard to do: every participant was treated as a presenter. It was never a conference of talks. It was working sessions, collaboration, people preparing before and producing outcomes after. That is even more needed today.
website

The website was not a brochure. It was a Hugo site in a public repository, and participants edited it: their own pages, their sessions, the outcomes. In 2018, 180 different people committed to it. On 4 June 2018, the first day of the summit, the site took 434 commits; on 2 and 3 June 2019, nearly 600. I was the one doing a lot of the programming, and in a couple of those summits we really nailed the structure: participants, sessions, tracks, schedules and outcomes, all as files, all linked.
code

Left: lines of Hugo template code, 2018 to now. Right: content files in the current site, 2020 to 2024. I went back to the repositories. The OpenSecuritySummit organisation on GitHub has 24 of them; four are the summit websites, oss2018, oss2019, oss2020 and oss-website, with 19,045 commits between them. Read as a record, they show the debt growing: Each year was a copy of the last. 171 of the 2019 site's 186 template files had the same paths as 2018's, and 272 of the current site's 315 came from 2020. The templates kept growing. About 5,200 lines in 2018, 5,700 in 2019, 8,500 in 2020 and 9,600 in the current site; the if and with conditions in them went from 255 to 408, and the partials from 110 files to 218.
code

Then the code stopped changing. From 2022 the template code barely moved, about 9,600 lines from mid-2022 to today, while the content files went from 140 to 998. Nobody had the time to change the structure, so everything new went into a structure that could not change. Exceptions accumulated. 39 template files have a year written into them, and 37 of the 218 partials are never called by name, among them pages for 2017, 2018 and 2019 that stayed in. Leftovers were copied forward. The 2019 venue page still says year: 2018; the 2022 sessions page still carries a note to add content "from the next 2021 main Summit event"; the current repository's README still welcomes you to the Open Security Summit 2021.
code

The platform kept moving underneath. The build went from Hugo 0.55 on AWS CodeBuild in 2019 to GitHub Actions, and the Hugo version was pinned and re-pinned: 0.75 in 2020, four different versions in January 2023, 0.139 in December 2024. The theme is a third-party Hugo theme, kept as a submodule. None of that is unusual. It is what happens to any site that is built in bursts, around an event, by someone who is also organising the event. It was a salad of code, and whenever we had a new summit and wanted to change something, there was never the time to refactor first. So the debt just kept growing, until it stalled.
people

The clearest number is the one on the right of the first chart. 180 people committed to the summit's website in 2018, 121 in 2019, 50 in 2020, 24 in 2021, and 14 in 2024. Commits stayed high through 2022 and 2023, but they came from fewer and fewer people. The site stopped being something participants could change, and became something a few of us maintained. And the live site shows where it stopped. Its home page still says "Open Security Summits in 2024", with "Next Summit: 9th - 13th Dec 2024". The last session page is from 2025, the last real work from December 2024.
follow-up

Sessions on the current site by year, and how many link a recording, from 2020 to 2024. The sad part is what is in there. The summit holds a lot of very good material on security: working sessions on application security, threat modelling, DevSecOps, governance, and, when this whole AI wave started, some very good sessions on it. The current site alone has 409 session pages from 2020 to 2024, and 194 recordings. Some of my own history, and a lot of knowledge I shared in those sessions, is in those videos, and it got lost.
follow-up

What never scaled was the follow-up. In person, the summit worked because of what happened before and after the sessions: preparation, outcomes, people connected to the next thing. Online, we could run the sessions, but we could not afford to create a personal path for each participant, to follow up, to connect what was said to who should hear it. That is the same pattern as the jobs that never scaled: the value is in the before and the after, and they cost too much. I kept funding it, at some cost to me, and it still did not fulfil its potential.
now

How the debt grew, as a loop of copying, exceptions and slower changes, and the restart that follows. The difference now is the workflow I have. I am not going to start by rebuilding the website. I am going to put an agent on the case: to understand everything that is there, map the data, connect the dots, analyse the videos and what was said in them, and create much better personal pages for everybody. Then follow up with people, which is the part we could never afford. From there, the plans: In person, in London. Real events again, working sessions, prepared and followed up. Online sessions. Shorter and more condensed, with more people bringing their work, and some of what I have been working on. Hosted open source projects. An independent home for projects that want one, as we described for Agent Behaviour Policies, the first of them.
now

And I still think we should go back and capture what was said at the in-person summits too. If we organised one now, with the capability we have to capture the information and follow up, I think it would be remarkable. We just need somebody to fund it.
lesson

The Open Security Summit is my clearest example of what technical debt does when there is no development team to pay it down. Nothing broke all at once. Each summit added a little, each exception made sense at the time, and the cost arrived as friction: changes that took longer, people who stopped contributing, follow-up that never happened. The potential was there the whole time. The debt, and the cost of the follow-up, stopped it being reached.
limits

The counts are from the public repositories. Read on 21 October 2026, all branches. People committing are counted by email address. One person with two addresses counts twice. Partials "never called by name" may be called another way. The count is a sign, not proof. Hosting projects is a proposal. As described in the Agent Behaviour Policies article. The plans are plans. The London events and online sessions are being organised; they need funding.
sources

The git history and files of oss2018, oss2019, oss2020 and oss-website, and the OpenSecuritySummit organisation on GitHub; the live site, open-security-summit.org, read the same day. Abstract: The missing piece of the client-side puzzle is a user who can open their own vaults on any device, in a few seconds, with nothing to remember and nothing to sign up for. This is the design, in its third version, and this one has been tested. A passkey, through the WebAuthn PRF extension, gives the browser 32 bytes that only your authenticator can produce for this site, and from those bytes the browser computes the key and the address of a small door vault, which holds the key of your master vault, which holds the keys of everything else: your reading vault, the read keys you have been given, your access key, and your key pairs, which are generated at random and never derived from the passkey. A review on 11 October took the door out of the design as a layer too many; a test on newsroom.sgit.ai on 11 and 12 October put it back, for a reason the review could not have known. One Google Password Manager passkey gave the same bytes on a Mac and an iPhone through the provider on each device, and the derivation agreed with sgit's Python byte for byte; the same passkey, answering a QR code from an iPad and from that same Mac, gave a different set of bytes, consistently, with the same credential id. Apple's forums report the same for iCloud Keychain since late 2024. So the claim is narrower than I wrote: the same passkey gives the same bytes through the same kind of path. The unit of the design is the path, not the passkey: a door per set of bytes, each recording where it came from, added in a normal first-week step that moves no key through a person, with the recovery code as the way in where no door opens yet, and an unknown door address meaning no door here yet, never an error. The platform path, which an iCloud Keychain passkey gave identically across a Mac, an iPad and an iPhone in Safari and Chrome, is the common case and works.

The key chain, after the test. The passkey's PRF output, by one path, computes a door; the door holds the master vault's key and a record of where it came from; the master holds the keys of everything else and the list of its doors. A different path to the same passkey can give different bytes, and gets a door of its own. This is the missing piece of the puzzle. In I miss it, so it is working I described the feature I miss: the newsroom on every device, in sync, through my own encrypted vault. In No server, by design I listed identity as one of the last things that still seemed to need a server. This article joins the two, in detail.

It is the third version, and the first with a test behind it. The first version had a door vault between the passkey and the master. A review on 11 October asked where the requirement for that layer was, found none in our use case, and took it out. On 11 and 12 October the newsroom built a lab with every step of the design as a card you can press, ran it on a Mac, an iPhone and an iPad, and found the requirement: the same passkey, reached two different ways, gives two different sets of bytes. The door is back, and it is now the unit of the design. What changed is listed at the end, and the lab's own note has the runs.

The experience I want is unchanged. I open newsroom.sgit.ai in a new browser. I am asked to touch my passkey. And my reading account opens, the same as on every other device, because it is now in a vault only I can open. Two steps, one of them a gesture, no server of ours anywhere, and nothing to sign up for.
short

You are already signed in, somewhere else. On a Mac you are signed in to Apple, in Chrome to Google, on Windows to Microsoft, and that is where your passkeys live. The site does not need you to sign in to it. It asks the passkey store you already use, and the vault goes wherever that store goes. The passkey is what opens the vault, through a path. With the WebAuthn PRF extension, a passkey returns 32 bytes that only your authenticator can produce for this site. The same passkey gives the same bytes on every device it syncs to, through the same kind of path. A different path, a phone answering a QR code instead of the provider on the device, can give different bytes, and in our test it did.
short

Where is the door key stored? Nowhere. sgit vault keys are made in the client, a passphrase and a vault id. So the browser computes the door's key and address from the PRF bytes, opens it, and finds the master vault's key inside. No chicken and egg, no new storage, only vault APIs. The lab did this against a real vault server and opened the door again. A door per set of bytes. Every door holds the master's key and records its provider, its path, its credential id, the device and the date. The master lists its doors with their keys, so any door can be retired from any other.
short

Adding a door is a normal first-week step, and no key passes through a person. While unlocked on a device where both paths run, a Mac with Chrome, ask for the bytes by the other path and the page writes the new door from memory. Where no device has both paths, the recovery code opens the recovery door and the new door is written from there. "No door here yet" is not an error. A device that derives an address and finds nothing is on a path that has no door. The page says so and offers the two ways in.
short

The master is the keyring, and the passkey is a lock, not an identity. The master holds the keys of your reading vault and your notes vault, the read keys you have been given, your access key, and your key pairs, which are generated at random and never derived from the passkey. Change a lock and the identity is untouched. Several passkeys for several roles are several masters. An admin passkey on a hardware key and a reader passkey in the cloud open different masters, chosen in the provider's own picker. Keys move between masters by copying; a door is retired by deleting its one file, never by destroying its address.
short

Support is good enough to build on, and where the passkey lives decides what the reader gets. PRF works in Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello and Firefox. The platform path is the common case: an iCloud Keychain passkey gave the same bytes on a Mac, an iPad and an iPhone, in Safari and in Chrome. A clean browser with no store gives one device, and Chrome's own store returns no PRF bytes, so the page checks at creation and offers a ladder. One rule the design depends on: the whole origin loads no third-party scripts, on any page, because browser storage is per origin and a script on one page can read what another page kept. The vault code is vendored into the reader repository, not loaded from anywhere else.
short
It is not just for the newsroom. Every site we build needs the same thing: an account with no server, data nobody else can read, on every device. This is that, as a pattern.
test

The lab has seven cards: what the browser can do; make a passkey for this site with PRF; touch it and show a fingerprint of the bytes; derive the door; make a recovery code; compare the derivation with sgit's Python, value by value; and create the door on a vault server, open it again as a new device would, and delete its file. On 11 and 12 October it was run with one Google Password Manager passkey, made on the Mac and synced, and with one iCloud Keychain passkey. What held: The platform path. The Google passkey gave the same bytes in Chrome on the Mac, answered by Google Password Manager with Touch ID, and in Safari on the iPhone, answered by the same provider with Face ID. The iCloud Keychain passkey gave the same bytes on the Mac, the iPad and the iPhone, in Safari and in Chrome.
test

The derivation. From the bytes to a door address and passphrase, and from those to sgit's read and write keys, the browser and sgit's own Python agreed on every value, from a fixed test vector and from the live bytes. The door. With an access key, the page created the door at its derived address on the vault server, wrote its one file, the master's key encrypted under the door's read key, opened it again the way a new device would, and deleted the file. What did not hold: Run Client How the passkey answered Bytes 1 Chrome on a Mac Google Password Manager on the Mac, Touch ID A 2 Safari on an iPhone Google Password Manager on the phone, Face ID A 3 Safari on an iPad A QR code, scanned by the iPhone; the phone's provider answered B 4 Chrome on the same Mac, "use a phone, tablet or security key"
test

A QR code, scanned by the same iPhone; the same provider answered B Same credential id, same user handle, same input, same flags. Runs 1 and 2 share the platform path and share a result; runs 3 and 4 share the hybrid path and share the other. Run 1 and run 4 are the same browser on the same machine, minutes apart, differing only in which way the phone's provider was reached. Each path was deterministic; the two paths disagreed.
test

This is a known class of bug. Apple's developer forums carry the same symptom for iCloud Keychain passkeys since late 2024: one PRF value when the passkey is used on the device, another when an iPhone or iPad scans a QR code shown by a Mac, for the same credential and the same salt. An Apple engineer called it a bug, pointed at the extension's two seeds, one for when the user was verified and one for when not, and said a fix was in the iOS 18.4 and macOS 15.4 betas; a later tester reported it persisting. Our passkey was Google's, served to the QR flow through iOS's cross-device role for third-party providers, so either the bridge or the provider behaves differently on that path, and the lab cannot tell which. What it can tell, now, is which path a result came from, because the browser reports whether the authenticator was platform or cross-platform, and the card shows it.
test

The thing to notice is how long this has sat. A defect in the one property that makes PRF useful for encryption, visible to anyone who tries two paths, would not survive long under real load. The reasonable inference is that few people derive encryption keys from passkeys across the hybrid path in production. That is not a reason to avoid the technique. It is a reason to design as if the bytes are a key a provider lends for one path, and to keep every door replaceable.
pieces

It helps to separate the pieces, because they are easy to blur. Piece What it gives the page What it does not give The account you are already signed in to (Apple, Google, Microsoft) Nothing, directly. It is what syncs your passkey store between your devices, so the passkey you make on one device is on the others Anything to the site: not your name, not your email, not that you have an account A passkey for this site A gesture (touch, face, PIN), a signature, and with PRF, 32 bytes computed from a secret the authenticator keeps for this site and this passkey The bytes to anyone but the page on this site that asked, after the gesture; and not, in 2026, the same bytes by every path The path How the passkey was reached: the provider on this device, a phone over the hybrid link, a hardware key A guarantee that two paths compute the same bytes
pieces

The passkey store Where the passkey lives: Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello, a hardware key, or the browser's own profile Anything about what the bytes are for sgit Vault keys made in the client (a 24-character passphrase and an 8-character vault id), read and write keys derived from them, ciphertext on the server, files that can be deleted, and vaults that can be destroyed A way to find a vault you have no key for; a way to reuse a destroyed id The access key The right to create vaults and write to them on the vault server, the thing people will buy Any way to read a vault
pieces

One clarification that matters. What people call "the Google passkey" is a passkey for this site, registered by this page under this site's name, which your store keeps and syncs. It is not the passkey you use to sign in to Google, and a website cannot get PRF bytes from that one. There is no sign-in to the site at all: the page registers a discoverable credential with a user handle it chose, and the only login involved is the one you already have with your platform, which syncs the store. The site learns a credential id, a public key and, after your gesture, 32 bytes. Not your email, not your name, not which account syncs it.
pieces

That is also why the vault travels. If you are signed in to Apple on your iPhone, your iPad and your Mac, the passkey you make on one is on the others, and so is the door it opens, as long as each device reaches it the same way. The choice of store is the choice of where the vault goes, and the reader made it long before they met this site.
where

The places the key could live, and how you would find each before you could open it. Deriving the door from the passkey needs nothing to be found; the stored options become backups. Every option for storing an encrypted vault key has the same problem: you have to find the encrypted key before you can open it, so it has to live somewhere you can reach with only what you have at that moment, which is your passkey. Inside the vault itself: you need the key to read the vault. The chicken and the egg. An SG/Send transfer: if the transfer id is assigned on upload, you need to have stored the id somewhere first.
where

A cloud folder in the user's own account, such as Google Drive's app-data folder: it works from the browser, with the user present for each token, and it needs a sign-in to that account, which this design does not have. If it is ever used, it is an availability backup of an encrypted copy, not the main path. A bucket keyed by the account id: the design secrets.sgit.ai has, with Identity Platform and Cloud Storage. It works, and it is a cloud project per environment. Inside the passkey (largeBlob): support is too uneven to depend on.
where

And then the option that needs none of it. sgit vault keys are generated in the client: a random passphrase and a random vault id, and sgit init accepts a key it is given. So instead of generating the door's key at random and storing it, the browser computes it from the PRF bytes: the passphrase, and the vault id, with HKDF. On any device where the passkey is reached by the same path, the same gesture gives the same bytes, the same address and the same key. The browser knows where to look and how to open it before it has fetched anything. The door holds the master vault's key, which is random and made once. The master holds everything else.
where

The review on 11 October asked why the master's key was not computed from the bytes directly, with no door. In our use case there was no requirement for it, and I agreed. The test is the requirement. If the master's key were derived from the bytes directly, a path that gives other bytes would derive another master, and nothing could join the two. With the door in between, a second path is one more small vault holding the same master key, written once. The layer costs one vault per path and one derivation on unlock, and buys independence from how any provider computes its bytes on any day.
derive

For the newsroom, with the relying party ID newsroom.sgit.ai, as the lab runs it: The PRF input is a fixed, public value: SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai/door/v1"). An input is not a secret; only the authenticator can turn it into the 32 bytes. The door seed is HKDF-SHA256(ikm = PRF bytes, salt = SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai"), info = "sgit/door/v1"). The door's passphrase and vault id are two more HKDF outputs from the seed. sgit accepts any printable ASCII passphrase up to 256 characters, so the passphrase is the hex of 32 bytes (info = ".../passphrase"), keeping all 256 bits. The vault id has to be lowercase letters and digits, 4 to 24 of them, so 8 characters are drawn from a third output (info = ".../id") with rejection sampling, so that no character is favoured. The id is the door's address.
derive

The door vault key is the sgit vault key made of those two, and from there, sgit's own derivation gives the read and write keys, exactly as the command line does: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations, once for the read key and once for the write key. That is the cost of this design. Door, master and reading vault need up to six derivations; measured in headless Chromium on a four-core machine, one takes about 105 ms and six run together about 640 ms, and a phone is several times slower, so a cold unlock can spend two to four seconds deriving keys before it fetches anything. The page derives each vault's keys once per session, runs them in a worker, and derives a write key only when there is something to write.
derive

The recovery door is the same, with the recovery code in place of the PRF bytes: 26 characters of base32, 128 bits, made by the page and shown once. It is long so that it needs no password stretching, as in the secrets.sgit.ai keyring design. Collisions are not a practical worry with 36⁸ possible ids, but the page checks: a derived address that already holds something it cannot open is skipped, with a counter in the HKDF info. The browser and the command line agree byte for byte: the lab's test vectors run the same derivation from a fixed, fake PRF output through the browser code and through sgit in Python, and compare every value when the page opens.
layout

A door: one file. The master vault's key, encrypted under the door's read key, and a small record: the kind of door (a passkey, or the recovery code), the provider as the browser named it, the path (platform or cross-platform), the credential id, which is public, a device label the reader typed, and the date.
layout

The master vault: the keyring. The keys of the vaults below it, by site and purpose: the reading vault first, then the notes-to-the-agent vault, then whatever an agent creates for the reader. Read keys the reader has been given. The access key: a read-only clone needs no token, so after the unlock the browser finds the access key here, and the reader pastes it once, on the first device. The key pairs for this site: a signing pair and an encryption pair, as RFC 0001 separates them, and plausibly one per persona, each with a label, a purpose, a date and a status. And the list of doors, each with its own vault key, so that from any open door the page can read, rewrite or delete every other door.
layout

The reading vault: one log per device, appended, never edited: pages read and how far, ratings, personas, the reading list, notes, receipts by payment reference. Every device computes the same state from all the logs, as described in I miss it.
layout

The key pairs are generated at random and stored. They are never derived from the passkey, and after the test that is more obviously right than it was: a key pair derived from bytes that depend on the path would be a different identity on the iPad than on the Mac. The passkey is a lock, not an identity. It opens a door and does nothing else. Everything that represents the person survives any change of lock, a new passkey, a second path, a hardware key, a recovery, a provider's fix. The trade-off against a non-extractable Web Crypto key is real: a non-extractable key is stronger on one device, but it is one device, and an identity that has to be the same on the phone, the iPad and the iMac has to travel. The private keys exist in browser memory only while the master is open.
path

The unit of the design is the path. Whatever produced a distinct set of bytes gets a distinct door: a passkey through its provider on the device, the same passkey through a phone over the hybrid link, a hardware key, a second passkey for the same role, the recovery code. Every door points at the same master and says where it came from.
path

Adding a door moves no key through a person. The page is unlocked, so the master's key is in its memory. The reader asks for the PRF bytes again by the other path. The page derives the new door from those bytes, encrypts the master's key under the new door's read key, writes the door's one file with the access key, and adds the door to the master's list. The provider that answered sees a PRF request and returns bytes; it never sees the master's key, a vault key or a passphrase. Nothing is typed, nothing is pasted, nothing public carries a key. A Mac with Chrome is where both paths run in one session, as run 4 showed: the provider on the Mac answers locally, and "use a phone, tablet or security key" reaches the same passkey over the hybrid link. So the setup for the phone-by-QR path is two gestures on the Mac, in the first week: open the door you have, then add the QR path as a door. Afterwards the iPad, or any browser that reaches the phone by QR, derives that door and finds the master.
path

Where no device has both paths, the recovery code is the way in. A new tablet whose only route is the QR path, before that path has a door, derives an address and finds nothing. The page says "no door here for this path yet" and offers two ways in: add the door from a device that is already open, or type the recovery code. The code derives the recovery door, which holds the master's key; the page is now unlocked; the new path's door is written as above. The recovery code is the one secret a person ever types, and only on a device where no door opens.
path

An unknown address is not an error. A derived address with nothing at it means a path with no door yet. The page never treats it as a failure, because a provider's fix can move a path's bytes at any time: if Apple or Google changes one path so that its bytes match the other, the door for the path that moved stops opening and the door for the other path takes over, with no loss. If a change moves a path's bytes to something new, that path finds no door, says so, and the reader adds one. The design never has to guess which output was correct. It only has to keep every door replaceable.
path

Providers without PRF hold the recovery code, and are not doors. A provider that returns no PRF bytes, Chrome's own store today and any password manager whose passkeys do not support the extension, cannot be a door, because there are no bytes to derive one from. It can hold the recovery code as a secure note. That makes it a holder of a door's passphrase, which is a weaker thing: whoever can read the note can open the recovery door. It is a fair place for the code for a reader who already trusts that manager with their passwords, and the page describes it as what it is.
path

A lost device. From any open door, delete the lost device's door, its file on the server and its entry in the list. That stops that path from finding the master from the next unlock on. It does not undo a copy of the master's key the lost device may have had in memory; the full answer is to rotate the master's key and rewrite the doors that are kept, which is designed and not built.
several

Doors are paths to one master. A second passkey for a different role is a second master, with its own doors. The facts that make this work, and the one that trips people up: The store dedupes by user handle. When a passkey is created, the site gives it a user id and a display name. iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager treat a new passkey with the same user id for the same site as a replacement for the old one. So two passkeys that must coexist get two user ids and two names, "Dinis · admin" and "Dinis · reader".
several

The picker is the switch. When the page asks for an assertion without naming a credential, the store shows its own sheet listing the passkeys it holds for this site, and the person picks one. If the page remembers a credential id and a label in local storage, which are not secret, it can offer "Unlock admin" and ask for that passkey by id, with the sheet as the fallback. Two stores in one browser. In Chrome on a Mac the sheet offers both iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager, plus a phone by QR and a hardware key, so one person can have a reader passkey in one store and an admin passkey in the other, on the same site in the same browser. Safari offers iCloud Keychain, hardware keys and a phone, not Google's store.
several

An admin master holds what the desk needs: access keys, the write side of the newsroom's vaults, the publishing key pair. A reader master holds the reading vault, the notes vault and the persona key pairs. The admin passkey lives on a hardware key in a drawer, or in a different store from the reader one, so that the keys that can publish are not available every time the keys that can read are. The page shows which master is open, with a lock button that clears memory.
several

Moving keys between masters. A master is a small file of entries, so a move is: unlock A, copy the entry into B, delete it from A. The catch is history. Vaults keep their versions, so an entry deleted from A is still in A's past for anyone who can open A. The rule: keys that move for security reasons get rotated, which for a vault key means sgit rekey, a new vault with a new id and the content re-pushed, and the references in every master updated; keys that move for tidiness do not.
several

Retiring, and the one thing never to destroy. sgit can delete a file from a vault, and it can destroy a vault, sgit vault delete-on-remote, with the write key and a typed confirmation. A destroyed vault id can never be used again. That is the right tool for a master or a reading vault being retired for good, because their ids are random. It is the wrong tool for a door, because a door's address is derived from the passkey and the path: destroy it and that passkey can never open a door by that path again. So a door is retired by deleting its one file, and the address is left free for the day a door is wanted there again. Retiring a master is: move or rotate what it held, delete its doors' files, destroy the master and the vaults below it that are not kept, delete the saved recovery code, then delete the passkey in the store's own settings, because a site cannot delete a passkey, only the person can.
flows

The first device, a new device on a path that has a door, adding a door while unlocked, a new device on a path with no door yet, and a lost device. Every step runs in the browser, against the passkey store for the gesture and the vault server for ciphertext. First device. Make a passkey, named for its role. Get its bytes. Derive the door. Paste the access key. Make the master's key, the reading vault's key and the key pairs at random, and a recovery code. Create the door, the master, the reading vault and the recovery door. Move the reading account from this browser's storage into the reading vault. Show the recovery code once. The master records one passkey door and the recovery door.
flows

Second path, same device, in the first week. Unlocked on the Mac. Ask for the bytes by the other path, the phone by QR. Derive. Write a second door with the same master key. The master now records three doors. A new device that reaches an existing door. Ask for the bytes, derive, open the door, read the master, read the reading vault. Reading needs no access key; the access key comes out of the master, so this device can write too. Merge this browser's reading into its own log. Nothing to set up. A new device that reaches only a path with no door. The page derives an address, finds nothing, and says "no door here for this path yet". Type the recovery code. The recovery door opens the master. Add this path as a door. From now on this device opens without the code.
flows

A lost device. From any open door, delete the lost door from the master's list and the server. Rotate the master's key when that is built. Signing out and locking. Keys exist only in the page's memory: cleared on lock, after a period of inactivity, and when the page is closed. The browser's own copy of the reading account stays as it is today.
security

What each party sees. The vault server: ciphertext, sizes, times and ids that look random. Your platform account: that a passkey exists for this site, under the name you gave it, and a secret it never sees used. The provider that answers a PRF request: the request, and that it answered. Not which key pairs exist, not what they signed, not which personas they belong to. Only this page, in your browser, after your gesture, holds the PRF bytes and the keys. Whoever can use the passkey by a path that has a door can reach everything below the master. That is exactly the passkey's protection, the biometric, the device and the store, and nothing in our stack adds to it or weakens it. A second passkey for the admin master is how the reach is split.
security

A path's bytes are a key a provider lends. The test showed that two paths can compute different bytes from one credential, and that a provider's fix could change either. The door layer is what makes that survivable: no door is the only way in, and every door can be replaced from any other or from the recovery code. The origin loads no third-party scripts, on any page. Storage is per origin, so a script on any page of the site could read what the account page keeps. The newsroom's pages load only code from the reader repository, with the vault code vendored into it rather than loaded from the vault web app or tools.sgraph.ai. The lab lists every call it makes to a vault server as it happens.
security

The relying party ID is a trust boundary. A passkey for sgit.ai would work on every *.sgit.ai site, and any of those sites could ask it for PRF bytes, so every one of them would have to be as strict as the strictest. The lab uses newsroom.sgit.ai exactly, as secrets.sgit.ai uses its own host. Sharing across sites is part two. Passkeys cannot be phished across sites. They are bound to the site's name; a look-alike domain gets nothing. Losing everything is final. Every door's passkey and the recovery code gone means no one can open the vaults. That is the property that makes the design worth having, and the first run says so before it shows the code. Availability is not secrecy. The vault server could delete or roll back ciphertext. It cannot read it. The local copy covers the first; nothing is needed for the second.
security
Agents do not have passkeys. An agent that should read part of a user's data gets a read key for one vault, given by the user from the master, never the master itself.
support

enables

Once these dots are connected, we have something we did not have before: an end-to-end path from a gesture to a vault, entirely in the browser, on commodity pieces, and now tested against a real vault server. And just about every site and project we build needs exactly that. Accounts with no server, and no identity. A static site gets a user who can open their own data on any device, and keep it private from the site's operator. No account database, no password, no email, no back end. Data the operator cannot read. Not as a promise in a privacy policy, but as a property: the vault server holds ciphertext, and the keys are on the user's devices. One master, many vaults. The reading vault is the first. The same master can hold the key to secrets.sgit.ai's keyring, a RiskMandate customer's policies, the memory of an agent the user runs, or the notes a reader sends to the newsroom.
enables

Sharing without shared secrets. The key pairs in the master are what RFC 0001 needs: give someone a vault key by encrypting it to their public key, with no secret sent in a chat. One account across sites. Two ways, later. A key hub, such as secrets.sgit.ai, holds the master and hands a site only the key to its own vault, after the user approves it in a pop-up, the way a wallet connects to a site. Or, across different domains, WebAuthn's Related Origin Requests let one passkey work on a list of related sites, in Chrome and Safari today. For anyone else. None of this is specific to us. Any static site, on any host, could use a passkey with PRF and a vault, and give its users the same thing. I would like it to become a small, open component, the way SG Meter is for reading, and the lab is the start of it.
enables

If a site ever needs a stronger statement of who the user is, for a purchase that must be refunded to a person or a support case that must find them, a sign-in with Google or Apple can be added on an origin of its own, handing back an account id and nothing else. With no back end to hold that id, I am not sure we will ever need it, and the design does not depend on it. This is why I think it matters more than a login feature. It is the moment the client-side pattern stops needing anyone's server for identity and storage, and becomes something other sites can use.
limits

The lab is a lab. It shows each step as a card, and it created, opened and deleted one door on a real vault server. The master vault, its door list, adding a door, the reading vault and the move are not built. The support table is a snapshot, and so is the test. The vendor rows are from documentation and published tests in 2026. Our own rows are two passkeys, three devices and two days. A provider's fix could change the QR path's bytes tomorrow, which is why the design treats an unknown address as "no door here yet". The lab cannot say which path is right. Both outputs need the credential's secret to check against the specification. It can say that each path was deterministic and that the two disagreed.
limits

Computing the door is a choice with a cost. A door is lost with its passkey, or with its path; the other doors and the recovery code are what cover it. What changed in this version. The door is back, as a door per path rather than per passkey, and each door records where it came from. The claim about synced passkeys is narrowed to the same kind of path. Adding a door is a first-week step with no key typed; an unknown address means no door yet. The recovery door is back, and providers without PRF hold the code rather than being doors. A door is retired by deleting its file, never by destroying its derived address. The key pairs stay random, sign-in stays out, and several passkeys for several roles are several masters.

# The passkey opens the vault: sign in with Google, touch a passkey, and a master vault for every user, with no server of ours
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.1.0.html

Summary: The missing piece of the client-side puzzle is a user who can open their own vaults on any device, in a few seconds, with nothing to remember. This is the design. Sign in with Google says who you are. A passkey, through the WebAuthn PRF extension, gives the browser 32 bytes that only your authenticator can produce for this site, and from those bytes the browser computes the key of a small door vault, which holds the key of your master vault, which holds the keys of everything else, starting with your newsroom vault. The question I could not answer, where the encrypted vault key is stored, has a simple answer: nowhere. sgit vault keys are made in the client, so the door's key and its id can be computed from the passkey on any device, before anything is fetched, and there is no chicken and egg. A recovery code makes a second door to the same master. Google holds no key; its Drive app-data folder can keep a backup. PRF is now supported by Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello and Firefox. The first part is the technical design and the brief for the MVP on newsroom.sgit.ai, end to end; the second is what it enables: accounts with no server, for this site and for any other.

design

One clarification that matters. When I say "the Google passkey", what the page uses is a passkey for this site, registered by this page under this site's name, which your provider stores and syncs. If you use Chrome, that provider is Google Password Manager. It is not the passkey you use to sign in to Google itself, and a website cannot get PRF bytes from that one. Sign in with Google and the passkey are two separate steps, for two separate jobs: who you are, and what you can open.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.1.0.html
design

1. The PRF input is a fixed, public value: SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai/door/v1"). An input is not a secret; only the authenticator can turn it into the 32 bytes. 2. The door seed is HKDF-SHA256(ikm = PRF bytes, salt = SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai"), info = "sgit/door/v1"). 3. The door's passphrase and vault id are two more HKDF outputs from the seed (info = ".../passphrase" and ".../id"), mapped to sgit's alphabet of lowercase letters and digits with rejection sampling so no character is favoured: 24 characters and 8. 4. The door vault key is the sgit vault key made of those two, and from there, sgit's own derivation gives the read and write keys, exactly as the command line does. 5. The recovery door is the same, with the recovery code in place of the PRF bytes: 26 characters of base32, 128 bits, made by the page and shown once. It is long so that it needs no password stretching, as in the secrets.sgit.ai keyring design. 6. Collisions are not a practical worry with 36⁸ possible ids, but the page checks: a derived id that already holds something it cannot open is skipped, with a counter in the HKDF info.

1. The PRF input is a fixed, public value: SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai/door/v1"). An input is not a secret; only the authenticator can turn it into the 32 bytes. 2. The door seed is HKDF-SHA256(ikm = PRF bytes, salt = SHA-256("newsroom.sgit.ai"), info = "sgit/door/v1"). 3. The door's passphrase and vault id are two more HKDF outputs from the seed. sgit accepts any printable ASCII passphrase up to 256 characters, so the passphrase is the hex of 32 bytes (info = ".../passphrase"), keeping all 256 bits. The vault id has to be lowercase letters and digits, 4 to 24 of them, so 8 characters are drawn from a third output (info = ".../id") with rejection sampling, so that no character is favoured. 4. The door vault key is the sgit vault key made of those two, and from there, sgit's own derivation gives the read and write keys, exactly as the command line does: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations, once for the read key and once for the write key. That is the cost of this design. Door, master and newsroom vault need up to six derivations; measured in headless Chromium on a four-core machine, one takes about 105 ms and six run together about 640 ms, and a phone is several times slower, so a cold unlock can spend two to four seconds deriving keys before it fetches anything. The brief measures it on a phone, derives each vault's keys once per session, runs them in a worker, and derives a write key only when there is something to write. 5. The recovery door is the same, with the recovery code in place of the PRF bytes: 26 characters of base32, 128 bits, made by the page and shown once. It is long so that it needs no password stretching, as in the secrets.sgit.ai keyring design. 6. Collisions are not a practical worry with 36⁸ possible ids, but the page checks: a derived id that already holds something it cannot open is skipped, with a counter in the HKDF info.

articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design
The browser and the command line must agree byte for byte, so the brief includes test vectors: the same inputs through the browser code and through sgit in Python, with the same keys out.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design
### What is in the top vault {#layout}
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

The top is a keyring: one small file of named entries, rarely written, and nothing else. The pattern is the one we already use everywhere, vaults that hold the keys of other vaults, so the only new thing here is where the top key comes from.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

The key pairs are generated at random and stored. They are never derived from the passkey, and this is a decision, not an omission. A derived key pair cannot be rotated without changing the passkey, and you want several of them. More important, the passkey is a lock, not an identity: it opens the top and does nothing else. Everything that represents the person survives any change of lock, a new passkey, a second one, a hardware key, a recovery, a derivation bump. Rotate a lock and the identity is untouched; rotate an identity and the locks do not care. The trade-off against a non-extractable Web Crypto key is real and worth stating: a non-extractable key is stronger on one device, but it is one device, and an identity that has to be the same on the phone, the iPad and the iMac has to travel. An encrypted vault that only the passkey opens is the right vehicle for it. The private keys exist in browser memory only while the top is open.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

Below the top, the reading vault holds one log per device, appended, never edited: pages read and how far, ratings, personas, the reading list, notes, receipts by payment reference. Every device computes the same state from all the logs, as described in I miss it.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

A site can hold any number of passkeys for one person. Each passkey has its own PRF secret, so each computes its own top, and two passkeys are two independent trees. The facts that make this work, and the one that trips people up:
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

The scenario this is for is separation of authority. An admin top holds what the desk needs: access keys, the write side of the newsroom's vaults, the publishing key pair. A reader top holds the reading vault, the notes vault and the persona key pairs. The admin passkey lives on a hardware key in a drawer, or in a different store from the reader one, so that the keys that can publish are not available every time the keys that can read are. The page shows which top is open, with a lock button that clears memory, and opens one top per tab by default.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

Moving keys between tops. A top is a small file of entries, so a move is: unlock A, copy the entry into B, delete it from A. The catch is history. Vaults keep their versions, so an entry deleted from A is still in A's past for anyone who can open A. The rule: keys that move for security reasons get rotated, which for a vault key means sgit rekey, a new vault with a new id and the content re-pushed, and the references in every top updated; keys that move for tidiness do not; and a top being deleted takes its history with it.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

Retiring a top. sgit can delete a vault from the server, sgit vault delete-on-remote, which needs the write key and a typed confirmation, and the vault's own files are gone. So the order is: move or rotate what the top held; delete the top's vault with its write key; delete the saved copy of its key from the password manager; then delete the passkey in the store's own settings, because a site cannot delete a passkey, only the person can. The coupling runs both ways and is worth noticing. Once the vault is deleted, the passkey still computes the same key, and the key opens nothing: a passkey whose vault is gone is inert. And once the passkey is deleted, the vault's ciphertext, if any survived, has no key. Deleting either side retires the pair. That is another reason to compute the top from the passkey rather than store its key: the lifecycle of the key is the lifecycle of the vault.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

Changing the derivation is the same operation as adding a passkey: a new input gives a new top from the same passkey, the entries are copied across, the old top is retired. Nothing below the top moves.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

First run. Create a passkey for the site with prf enabled, named for its role; if the authenticator cannot do PRF, the page says which kinds can and offers another. Touch it: the PRF bytes give the top. Paste the access key. Generate the reading vault's key and the key pairs. Create the top and the reading vault. Move the reading account from the browser's storage into the reading vault. Show the top vault key once, behind "I have saved it in my password manager".
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

A new device. Touch the passkey, synced to this device or used from a phone by QR. The PRF bytes give the same top, the top gives the reading vault. Reading needs no access key; the access key comes out of the top, so this device can write as well. Merge this browser's reading into its own log.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design
A second passkey. Create it with a different user handle and name, in another store or on a hardware key. It computes its own top. Copy into it the entries it should hold, and nothing else.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design
Lost a passkey. Paste the saved top vault key; the top opens; create a new passkey, which computes a new top; copy the entries across; retire the old top in the order above.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html

As of October 2026, from vendor documentation and published tests (see the sources):

design

| Passkey provider | PRF | |---|---| | Google Password Manager (Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet; Android) | Yes, by default; desktop Chrome from version 136 | | iCloud Keychain (Safari 18, macOS 15) | Yes | | Windows Hello | Yes, since the February 2026 update to Windows 11 | | Firefox | Yes, on macOS from version 139 and Windows from version 148 | | Hardware security keys | Yes through hmac-secret, but not with YubiKeys in Safari | | Chrome's own profile authenticator | No |

The table above is about browsers. The question that matters to a reader is about devices: will the newsroom I opened on my laptop be the same one on my phone? That depends on where the passkey lives, which is a choice the reader made long before they met this site, usually without noticing.
articles/versions/the-passkey-opens-the-vault/v1.4.0.html
design

| Where the passkey lives | Needs | Travels? | PRF | What the reader gets | |---|---|---|---|---| | Google Password Manager (Chrome signed in, Android) | A Google account | Yes, to every device signed in to it | Yes | The same newsroom everywhere | | iCloud Keychain (Safari, iPhone, iPad, Mac) | An Apple ID | Yes, across Apple devices | Yes, Safari 18 and macOS 15 | The same newsroom on every Apple device | | Windows Hello (Windows 11) | The device; a Microsoft account to sync | Device-bound, unless synced | Yes, since February 2026 | This PC, or every PC on the account | | A hardware key (YubiKey and others) | The key, and its PIN | Yes, wherever the key is plugged in | Yes, through hmac-secret; not with YubiKeys in Safari | No account anywhere; a few dozen passkeys per key | | Your phone, by QR (the hybrid flow) | A passkey on the phone, in its own store | Yes, one scan at a time | Where the phone's store does | A clean laptop opens with the phone beside it | | Chrome's own profile store (a clean Chrome, no store signed in) | Nothing | No: this browser, on this computer | No, in 2026 tests | Signs, returns no bytes: the top cannot be derived |

design

So the rule, in one line: the same newsroom on every device needs a synced store or a hardware key in your pocket. A clean browser with neither gives you this device, plus the saved key. A passkey made there still works, as a passkey; it is stored by the device, tied to that browser profile on that computer, and deleted with it. The catch for this design is the last row: Chrome's own store, used when there is no provider (a clean Chrome on Linux, or on a Mac with iCloud Keychain off), signs but returns no PRF bytes in 2026 tests, so the top cannot be derived there at all.

That is a real limitation of PRF today, not of the design, and the article would be dishonest without it.
