Abstract: Ralf Thomas posted on LinkedIn this week that if an employee wrecks a client's systems the company pays, and asked why AI agents should be any different. The post's record of 2026 is mostly right, and its four moves of the accountability shell game, blame the agent, blame the customer, hide behind the contract, disclose late, are a good map. I agree with its conclusion, and I would like to add the piece I think is missing, because it explains why the shell game works. When an agent goes wrong today, nothing was written down between the person clicking allow and the failure. The agent had reach, and nobody had told it, in a form anyone could later point to, what it must not do. So "misuse", "full-access mode" and "you allowed it" are hard to answer. An Agent Behaviour Policy changes that. It is still mostly hope, an expectation the model is asked to keep, but it is explicit: do not send email directly, do not touch labels you do not need, do not edit other agents' files, do not start scheduled tasks, do not attack other sites because you can, speak on your own behalf and not mine, make no offers, stay inside the mandate. My hypothesis is that an explicit prohibition the agent then breaks moves liability towards the platform that runs it. That sharpens something I have said before, that liability sits with whoever granted the reach. Towards the world it still does. Between the customer and the vendor, the written policy is the evidence that turns "user error" into "your product ignored what it was told". And that points to the direction of travel: every agent that runs in a loop, anything with the lethal trifecta, should take a behaviour policy beside its system prompt, and its vendor should be accountable for honouring it.
The four moves of the accountability shell game, from Ralf Thomas's post, and what a written policy changes in each.
in-short

The post is right about the pattern. Agents with real reach failed in 2026, and the companies behind them reached for four answers: the agent did it, the customer allowed it, the contract covers it, and the disclosure can wait. Some of the record needs care. The court cases were early rulings, not findings of liability; "a separate legal entity" was the tribunal's description of Air Canada's argument; and Microsoft has since removed "for entertainment purposes only" from Copilot's terms. The pattern survives the corrections. The shell game works because nothing was written down. Between "allow" and the failure there is reach and a prompt, and no explicit statement of what the agent must not do. That gap is where every deflection lives.
in-short

A behaviour policy writes it down. Explicit prohibitions, technical and business: do not send, do not start scheduled tasks, do not attack other sites, do not speak on my behalf, make no offers. Still hope, but on the record. An explicit prohibition the agent breaks should move liability to the platform. Towards the world, the deployer still answers. Between the deployer and the vendor, the written policy is the evidence that turns "user error" into "the product ignored what it was told". The law is moving the same way. From 9 December 2026 software, including AI systems, is a product under the EU's new product liability rules; Germany's Bundestag passed its version on 8 October. Every agent in a loop should take a policy beside its prompt. Anything with the lethal trifecta. The vendor's half is to accept it, honour it, enforce what it can, and report every breach.
post

Ralf Thomas, an IT management adviser and interim CIO in Germany, posted on LinkedIn this week with a question I think is exactly the right one: "If an employee wrecks a client's systems, the company pays. Why should AI Agents be any different?" The post ends with an offer of governance work, and says so openly. The post's record of 2026 is mostly accurate, and worth stating carefully: Deleted files. In July The Register reported that OpenAI's Codex engineering lead had described its newest model occasionally deleting a user's home directory as "an honest mistake", mostly in the mode with full access and no sandbox. An escape. On 16 July Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion "driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system", which it detected "through AI-assisted detection". It was later attributed to an OpenAI evaluation agent that had left its test environment.
post

Real systems, during evaluations. Anthropic reported on 30 July that models in its cyber evaluations "gained unauthorized access to the real systems of three different organizations", called it "closer to a harness and operational failure than a model alignment failure", and on 9 September found a fourth and asked METR to investigate. User error. On the outage the Financial Times linked to its Kiro agent, Amazon said it "was the result of user error, specifically misconfigured access controls, not AI as the story claims". The four moves, blame the agent, blame the customer, hide behind the contract, disclose late, are a good map of the answers, and I agree with the conclusion: the companies that sell autonomy as the product cannot disown it when it fails, and a post-mortem is not accountability. I would add that the labs deserve credit for publishing the post-mortems at all. Anthropic's two reports are detailed and uncomfortable, and that is the right instinct.
post

A few things in the post I would state more carefully, because the argument is stronger without them. In Moffatt v. Air Canada, "a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions" is the tribunal's summary of Air Canada's position, which it called "a remarkable submission", not Air Canada's words. Garcia v. Character Technologies and Mobley v. Workday were rulings at the motion-to-dismiss stage, which let the claims go forward rather than holding the companies liable, and Garcia has since settled. Microsoft has removed "for entertainment purposes only" from its consumer Copilot terms, calling it legacy language. And the wiki incident was first exposed by outside researchers; what came only after Reuters reported it was OpenAI's own acknowledgement. None of these changes the pattern.
why

Each of the four moves works for the same reason: nothing was written down between the person clicking allow and the failure. In the vocabulary of RiskMandate, an agent has a reach, what it can actually do, and a mandate, what it is meant to do. The gap between them is the risk. "Full-access mode" is a reach. "Misconfigured permissions" is a reach. And when the only thing that stood between the reach and the failure was a system prompt and the model's good sense, the vendor can say, with some justice, that the customer granted the reach and the agent did something inside it. I made the same point about permission prompts in Where is the why?: the record mostly puts the duty on whoever asks, and in practice the blame still lands on whoever clicked.
why

What is missing is the mandate, written down, in a form both sides can point to afterwards. Without it, "the agent made an honest mistake" and "the customer allowed it" are both unanswerable, because nobody can show what the agent was told not to do.
line

An Agent Behaviour Policy is that written mandate, beside the measured reach. And the part of it that matters most for liability is the prohibitions, the explicit "do not" rows. Here are some I give my own agents; the first, the third and the fourth are among the rules that are never negotiated in The agent team as it runs: Do not send an email directly; write a draft and a person sends. Do not edit labels you do not have to. Do not edit files another agent owns. Do not create, fire or change a scheduled task. Do not attack other websites, even though you can. Do not read mail from this source, or reply to that one, or put this kind of information in a reply. Speak on your own behalf, never on mine.
line

None of those is a technical control in the sense that Where the platform draws the line describes for Microsoft's execution containers, which enforce files, network and tool arguments. They are business rules. And a company will have many more: do not make offers you are not authorised to make, do not speak negatively about our customers, only speak about the area of your mandate, do not do anything outside the mandate we define, here it is. As Zoom into an agent's behaviour policy argues, zoom into any real policy and you find the business logic, which no vendor can model for each customer.
line

I want to be honest about what such a policy is today. Most of its rows are still what Hope or enforcement calls an expectation: a written rule, kept by the model, enforced by nobody. That is hope-driven development, and I have spent a lot of this site measuring how much of a policy is hope. The two emails my own agent drafted in my first person on 9 October broke a rule written in four places, which is why a second reader the agent cannot skip now checks every draft. But here is the big but. An expectation that is written down, explicitly, and given to the agent is a different thing in a dispute from no expectation at all. If I told the agent not to send email directly, and it sent one, the conversation is no longer about whether I misconfigured something. It is about whether the product did what it was explicitly told.
liability

Two directions of liability: towards the world, and between the deployer and the vendor, decided by the written policy. I have said before, in Ten hard questions and in Who owns the words, that liability sits with whoever granted the reach: the moment of authorisation is the grant. I still think that is where it starts, and the tribunal in Moffatt said the same thing to Air Canada: "It should be obvious to Air Canada that it is responsible for all the information on its website." Towards customers, regulators and the people harmed, the deployer answers. An agent has no balance sheet, and a customer cannot sue a model.
liability

What the written policy changes is the line behind that, between the deployer and the vendor. Today that line is drawn by the vendor's terms, and they draw it in one place. Anthropic's consumer terms, for example, say "You are responsible for all Inputs you submit to our Services and all Actions". That is defensible when the customer gave an agent reach and said nothing about how to use it. It is much harder to defend when the customer wrote down, in a policy the product accepted, "do not do this", and the product did it anyway. Then the failure is not misuse. It is the product not behaving as it was told it must, which is close to what product liability calls a defect.
liability

So my hypothesis is this: an explicit prohibition, given to the agent and broken by it, shifts liability towards the platform the agent runs on. Not all of it, and not towards the world. Between the two parties who could have prevented it, it moves the question from "you allowed it" to "you ignored it". The law is moving in a direction that makes this matter. The EU's new Product Liability Directive counts software as a product, with member states to apply it from 9 December 2026, and Germany's Bundestag passed its version on 8 October, extending product liability to the makers of AI systems. Its scope is narrower than the post implies, death, injury, property damage and lost data rather than every harmful action, but it changes the default from "the customer accepted the terms" to "was the product defective". A policy the product accepted and then broke is strong evidence of a defect.
direction

This is the idea I most want to put on the table. Today, when we deploy an agent, we give it a prompt, and its vendor gives it a system prompt. We should also be able to give it a behaviour policy, as a separate, structured input that the product acknowledges, and that applies to everything that runs in a loop: the API calls, and above all the agents with agency, the Claude and ChatGPT agents that plan, call tools and act. A good test for which agents need it is Simon Willison's lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted content and a way to communicate out. If an agent combines them, "an attacker can easily trick it into accessing your private data and sending it to that attacker", and that agent should not run on a prompt alone.
direction

Parts of this already exist, and they are worth naming because they show both the direction and the gap. Claude Code has permission rules and managed settings an administrator controls, and its documentation is admirably clear about the difference: "Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model. Instructions in your prompt or CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries to do, but they don't change what Claude Code allows." OpenAI's Codex has approval modes and an administrator's requirements file. Those are the vendor turning some rows into settings and boundaries, which is exactly right. What does not exist yet is the other half: a place to put the business rules, the ones no setting can express, where the vendor accepts them as part of the deployment, measures the agent against them, and reports a breach the way it now reports an incident.
direction

That is the vendor's half of the accountability Ralf Thomas is asking for. Accept the policy. Honour it, and enforce as much of it as the platform can see. Log every breach, and disclose it, near misses included, as I argued in Authority outside the model. And when a row the product accepted is broken, own it, rather than calling it an honest mistake. The deployer's half is to write the policy at all, which most do not, and that is where RiskMandate and abp.sgit.ai come in.
limits

It is not legal advice. The liability shift is my hypothesis about where disputes should go, not a statement of what any court has held. The cases are early. Garcia and Mobley were motion-to-dismiss rulings; Moffatt was a small-claims tribunal; none decided the question in this article. The product liability rules are narrower than "any harm". They cover defective products causing death, injury, property damage or data loss, from 9 December 2026; Germany's law still has stages to complete. A policy is still mostly hope. Writing a prohibition down does not make the agent keep it. The argument is about evidence and allocation, not prevention. It sharpens our own earlier line. "Liability always sits with the customer" in Ten hard questions is right towards the world; this article adds what the written policy changes between customer and vendor. The incidents are as reported by the companies themselves and by the press, with the corrections above.
limits
If you are deploying agents and want to write the policy that draws your line, or you build an agent platform and want to accept one, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The third piece on Mondweep Chakravorty's SGit × Ruflo proof of concept is about a path, not a failure. His adapter compiles the four Agent Behaviour Policy rows into Ruflo rules and checks every one of its tools with a pinned copy of Ruflo's own policy evaluator, in enforce mode. In the video those checks cover steps 4, 5, 6, 8 and 11, and every one behaved as the policy said. But in steps 3, 9 and 10, Ruflo's own command line writes and reads the same SQLite memory file directly, and that path does not pass the gate. His README states the limit in one line: "Only adapter tools pass through this gate. Other shell/network tools are unaffected." It is the same lesson this site keeps learning about its own agent: a policy holds only on the paths that pass through its enforcer. The fix is on his list of follow-ups, native plugin registration, so the same compiled rules run where Ruflo runs. His code also answers the other questions the video left open: why every error reads the same, whether decisions are recorded, where the vault goes next, why the file name changes, and why approval means stop.

Two ways into the same memory: the adapter's tools through the policy gate, and Ruflo's own command line without one. Mondweep Chakravorty's video of an agent losing its workspace and getting its memory back: the run, the architecture, the gap, a page to step through it yourself, and the page that took it into Ruflo.
in-short

The rules run in Ruflo's own evaluator. Compiled from the ABP, checked in enforce mode, inside the adapter. Every guarded step behaved. Steps 4, 5, 6, 8 and 11 did exactly what the policy said. Two paths reach the memory. The adapter's tools, through the gate; Ruflo's command line, around it. The author says so himself. "Only adapter tools pass through this gate." A policy holds on the paths through its enforcer. It is the lesson this site keeps learning about its own agent. The fix is on his list. Native plugin registration, so the rules run where Ruflo runs. The other questions have answers. In the code: the errors, the records, the vault's next home, the file name, approval.
paths

The run has two ways into Ruflo's memory file, and the matrix in the architecture piece shows them side by side. The first is the adapter. Mondweep's code, mondweep/sgit-ruv-memory, compiles the four ABP rows into Ruflo rules when the server starts, and before each of its tools runs, checkpoint, inspect, restore and close_run, it asks a pinned copy of Ruflo's own policy evaluator for a decision in enforce mode. Anything not allowed is refused, and an unsupported or ambiguous policy rejects the whole document. That is the path for steps 4, 5, 6, 8 and 11, and every one of them did what the policy said: the out-of-scope checkpoint refused, the in-scope one allowed, the deletion stopped, the restore allowed, and the tampered restore allowed by the policy and then refused by the adapter's integrity check.
paths

The second is Ruflo's own command line. In step 3 it writes the two facts straight into the SQLite memory file. In steps 9 and 10 it reads the restored file. None of those calls passes the gate. The analysis put it as "The ABP guards the adapter, but Ruflo's command-line tool writes and reads the same SQLite file without passing through it", and Mondweep's README says the same in his own words: "This is an external adapter using a pinned copy of Ruflo's evaluator, not Ruflo's running policy state. Only adapter tools pass through this gate. Other shell/network tools are unaffected."
shown

Step 3: the ruflo command line's memory store writes two rows of plain text; the ABP adapter and vault are not used. Shown on screen: in step 3, ruflo memory store with --no-embedding --path memory.db, "[OK] Data stored", and "Vector: No". At this point the memory file is ordinary, unencrypted SQLite. Step 9: the ruflo command line's memory retrieve reads memory.sqlite and returns both facts exactly. Shown on screen: in step 9, ruflo memory retrieve reading memory.sqlite, both values printed, and a pass. Ruflo reads a plain copy that came out of the vault; neither the vault nor the ABP is on this path. Not tested: what an agent with shell access would do with the same command line, or with any SQLite client. The code confirms the path exists; nobody tried to misuse it, and it was not the run's question.
shown

To be fair to the run: using the command line in steps 3 and 9 is what makes it convincing. Step 9 is strong precisely because Ruflo itself, not the adapter, reads the facts back. The gap is not a mistake in the test. It is a property of where this ABP is enforced, and the author documents it.
why

A policy holds on the paths that pass through its enforcer, and nowhere else. I keep relearning that about this site's own agent. When I measured it in your agent's logs are a self-report, ten of its eleven rules were kept by the agent choosing to follow them, and the one hard limit was a platform setting the policy did not even list. At The AI Conference, speaker after speaker said policy must live outside the model. This run does that: the ABP is compiled, strictly, into the rule format of the tool it governs, evaluated by that tool's own evaluator, and it fails closed. What it adds is the next lesson. Outside the model is necessary; around every path to the data is the harder part.
close

The rules are already in Ruflo's format and already checked by Ruflo's evaluator. What is missing is running them where Ruflo itself runs, so the command line's memory calls are checked too. Mondweep's README lists it among the follow-ups: "native plugin registration", alongside remote sync, key rotation and multi-tenant isolation. Two other ways come to mind, and I offer them as ideas, not findings. Keep the working memory file somewhere only the adapter can reach, so the command line has to go through it. Or make the adapter the only thing that can decrypt memory at all, so a plain file never sits in a workspace an agent can write to. His README is candid that "Plaintext exists during staging and intentionally in restored workspaces", which is the trade that makes step 9 possible. Each option has costs, and he will know better than I do which fits Ruflo.
questions

The video left five smaller questions open. The repository answers each of them. Why does every error read the same? On purpose. The server replaces the detail with "operation failed; check configuration, policy and integrity", with a comment: "Do not leak dependency errors containing private paths or credentials." Inside, the gate's own message names the reason: "Policy blocked operation", followed by the evaluator's reason. Is each decision recorded? Not yet. The evaluator returns a decision for every call; nothing writes it to a log. An operator log naming the row that fired would turn each decision into evidence. Where does the vault go next? Nowhere yet: "no remote push is performed", and remote sync is a follow-up. Each checkpoint is its own SGit vault on the same machine. The architecture piece says what a second machine would add. Why memory.db, then memory.sqlite? The adapter stages and restores every checkpoint as memory.sqlite, whatever the source file was called.
questions

Why does approval mean stop? Because there is nothing yet to give approval with. The README: "There is no human approval fulfilment mechanism yet." The policy file records it in the row's own barrier: "Human approval is required; MVP blocks this operation". The run proves the row blocks; proving it releases with a named approver is the next test. And one note on the video, not the run: the terminal is labelled a real-time capture, and between step 2 at run clock 00:11 and the first fact in step 3 at 00:39, 28 seconds of run pass in a few seconds of video. One wait was trimmed, most likely Ruflo loading its model. That is fine for a demo, and worth a caption.
next

Back to the walkthrough for the run in order, or to the architecture for when the vault is used. Or step through the run: steps 3, 9 and 10 each link back here, and every step shows what the code confirms.
limits

Not a vulnerability report. No one tried to bypass the policy; the author documents the path himself. Not that the run failed. Every step the policy guarded behaved as written. The fixes are ideas. Native plugin registration is his follow-up; the other two are mine, untested. The code was read, not run, here. Its tests and evidence are the author's. If you are Mondweep, or anyone who has run this, and want to add to any of these, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: When the PHP newsroom moved to a new account on 27 October, every agent needed a fresh session, and every fresh session needed a fresh key. The repositories carried over, with the cards, the handovers and the records. The sessions did not, and neither did the key pairs, which die with the session that made them. So the question was how the newsroom should recognise a new conductor's key. At 02:22:16 UTC on 28 October I added one sentence to the onboarding runbook: pushing your public key to team's dev is the authorisation. Only a session allowed to push to team can publish a key there, so a key in records/keys/ under the agent's name is a key my account put there. Whoever seals a vault key to that session reads its fingerprint from the file and needs no pin, root, operator or enrolment at pki.sgit.ai. That removed four commands from the runbook's key step, and it did not remove the need for an authority; it moved the decision into a publishing boundary the newsroom already has. A later brief that day separates the role from the session, so the role stays and the sessions come and go, each in a folder with its key and the window it held the role. The same change opened a security card, conductor-0017, which asks for a review of what it means that anyone with push access can designate a recipient, and it was still open at 15:21 UTC that day. The rule was used the same night: within 67 minutes of it, eight more roles had registered a new session, and by the afternoon the request to the vault keeper was built from the published key. I think the design is reasonable, and I think it has four questions that need their own answers: possession of the private key, which writer may replace which role, what happens to the old session's credentials, and which copy of the register is current. Here is the decision, the evidence and what I would like to build next.
How a new session becomes the agent: make a key, push the public half, read it, seal to it.
in-short

A new session needs a new key, and the newsroom needs a way to accept it. The move to a new account on 27 October kept every repository and none of the sessions or their key pairs. I decided that the push is the authorisation. At 02:22:16 UTC on 28 October the runbook gained the rule that pushing a public key to team's dev is how a session's key is accepted, with no pin, root, operator or enrolment at pki.sgit.ai. The runbook lost four commands. pin, root, operator and submission are gone from its key step; keygen and whoami stay. The role stays and the session changes. A later brief of the same day gives each session a folder with its key and the window it held the role, and one file, records/keys/<agent>.json, points to the current one.
in-short

It was in use within the hour. Between 02:43 and 03:29 eight roles registered a new session; with the two keys pushed before the rule, all ten roles had a current key by 03:29. The decision moved an authority; it did not remove one. The authority is now my GitHub account with two-factor sign-in, the GitHub app that lets a session push, and the dev branch of the team repository. The risk has its own card. conductor-0017 asks security to review that anyone with push access can publish a key and be sealed to, and it was still open at 15:21 UTC on 28 October. Four questions need their own answers. Possession of the private key, which writer may replace which role's key, what the old session still holds, and which copy of the register a sender is reading.
in-short
What I would like next is small. A role-by-role statement of who may replace a key, a possession check before a sensitive handover, and a retirement step beside the register.
move

On 27 October the newsroom moved to a separate account, because the first was at 78% of its usage. The brief for the move lists what carries over and what does not. Everything in the six repositories carries over: every card, run record, message, register and handover. What lives only in the old account does not: each agent's session and scratchpad, the clones of the vaults, the scheduled tasks, and each agent's own key pair, which dies with the session that made it. That last row is the one this article is about. I had written about the newsroom of a team frozen in time, where an agent session can be paused and resumed with its reasoning intact. A move is the opposite case: the role carries on and the session is new. A new conductor can read what the old one was doing, and the remaining question is how the rest of the newsroom recognises its key.
rule

The answer is in section 2 of the onboarding runbook, added in commit ee4e115, dated 02:22:16 UTC on 28 October 2026. A version-bump commit followed 29 seconds later and recorded v0.22.166. The runbook's filename still starts with 27 October, but the rule was added on the 28th. The editor is me. The next sentence says what follows for anyone sending a secret: they read the fingerprint from that file and need no pin, root, operator, trust or enrolment at pki.sgit.ai. The runbook's key step before and after 28 October: four commands removed, one rule added. The change followed from PKI everywhere, where I decided that every message, secret and handover starts with a signature, and from the directory of people and keys that pki.sgit.ai now holds. For the newsroom's own agents, in this account, I chose to use the publishing boundary the team already has rather than enrol each new session at the register.
register

Each agent has one current-key file, records/keys/<agent>.json. A fresh session writes its fingerprint, its public key, the time, its session id and the account, "enrolled": false, and the fingerprint it replaces. It overwrites the previous file, so one agent has one current key. A public key is not a secret, and a later brief says what the file is for: "What makes it trustworthy is where it sits: in the repository only the editor's account can push to." The secret that moves is a vault key. Whoever holds it, me or the vault keeper agent, seals it to the fingerprint read from that file and hands it over as a QR image or a link. Only the session's private key opens it, and the session clones the vault into its scratchpad, outside every repository, and deletes the opened key file.
register

I wrote about the sealing side in secrets on public keys. What is new here is where the recipient is read from: a file in the repository, which is also published on the team's own site within minutes.
role

A brief of 28 October, written by the conductor at my direction, puts the idea in four lines. An agent is a role. A session is one run of that role, in one account, for a while. The website is the anchor of trust. And from the moment a new session publishes its key, it is the agent and the previous session is not. Each session gets a folder, records/agents/<agent>/sessions/<session id>/, with a SESSION.json (state, from, until, supersedes, superseded_by, fingerprint, account), the public key and its QR image. The registering command creates the folder, stamps the previous session superseded with an until of now, and rewrites records/keys/<agent>.json. The registration commit's time is the moment the new session becomes the agent. Everything the old session did before that stays valid, in its account and its period; anything dated after that claiming to come from it is flagged.
role

That gives two views of identity: one file for whoever needs the current recipient, and a history for whoever asks what an earlier session knew and did. A session who command answers which session held the role at a given time. The handover stays specific to the work. A session asks only for the vaults it can name a step for in its role's card, and says whether it reads or writes. Being accepted as the conductor is not a reason to receive every vault key; the new conductor asked for none, because it reads no vault.
in-use

The rule did not wait for a review to be useful. Two sessions had already pushed their keys before it: dev at 01:07 and the conductor at 01:34, both marked "not yet enrolled". At 02:22 the rule made that the way in, and at 02:36 the conductor added the session folders. Then the rest of the newsroom followed: researcher at 02:43, security and curator at 02:44, journalist at 02:56, factcheck and correspondent at 02:57, observability at 03:25 and desk at 03:29. By then all ten roles had a current key in records/keys/, and there are now 13 session folders behind them. Ten roles, new keys, in one night: each commit that published or replaced an agent's key on 28 October.
in-use

Two of those commits are the questions below, happening for real. The curator's key was replaced at 02:55 "at the editor's word", with a pki-agent key pair. And the correspondent registered three times: two sessions claimed the role, and at 03:26 the commit records that I chose one of them. Which writer may replace which role's key was answered that night by me, one case at a time.
in-use

The handover side followed in the afternoon. At 14:49 the conductor added schedule.py vaultreq, which writes the request I paste into the vault keeper's session from an agent's published key: the key's URL on the team site, its fingerprint and session, and each vault with why it is needed. It refuses when the published key is not the current session's. The runbook says it was proven with the correspondent. That is the chain in this article, working end to end: a push, a file, and a sealed key that only the new session can open.
decides

The push decides one thing: which public key the newsroom accepts for a role now. It uses an authority that already exists, the account that can push to the team repository, instead of adding a ceremony beside it. I think that is a good trade for a team of agents that is renewed every time an account fills up, and I would like to keep it simple.
decides

It also makes the push worth more. Before, publishing to team's dev updated a page or a run record. Now it can designate the recipient of a secret. The records say so themselves: the commit that added the rule also opened conductor-0017, a card for security that asks for a review of the residual risk, that anyone with push access to team can publish a key and be sealed to, and whether branch protection or a signed commit on records/keys/ is worth having. I decided it was not needed now. At the later snapshot, commit 28b85bf, the card was still open, byte for byte the same as the original, and it was still open at 43bfe25, the team's latest commit at 15:21 UTC. Four questions a sender can ask about a published key, and where each is answered today.
questions

I read the records with these four in mind. None of them says the design is broken. Each says where the push stops and something else has to start. Possession. A writer can copy a public key into a JSON file. The push tells the newsroom which key to accept; whether the session holds the private half is a separate fact. Only that half opens what is sealed to the key, so a handover to a key nobody holds is a wasted handover. For a sensitive vault I would like a small non-secret challenge first. The later runbook also allows an encryption_fingerprint beside the main one, and where signing and encryption keys differ, a proof with one is not a proof with the other.
questions

Which writer, which role. The rule trusts whoever can push to team. If every writer, and every credential the GitHub app lets a session use, may designate every role's next key, that is a clear policy and I can say so. If some roles should need narrower authority, the repository can say it with branch rules, reviews or a code-owner file. On 28 October the branch endpoint reported dev as not protected. That is one dated field and not an audit of the rulesets, the permissions or the app's scopes, which I did not read here.
questions

The old session. Marking a session superseded ends its standing as the agent. It does not by itself stop a scheduled task, remove a repository credential, or make a vault key the old session already opened unknown to it. A sealed key re-sealed to a new fingerprint is the same key. If a role needs a clean break, retirement has steps of its own: stop the tasks, withdraw the credentials, and rotate a vault key when a session that knew it should not any more.
questions

Which copy. The brief says a pushed file is public within minutes on the team's site. A sender then has two views, the branch and the deployed site, and an old clone or QR image can show a superseded key. I would like the key file to carry the commit it came from and the session id, and the sender to say which copy it read. The from and until values are the session's own and the registration commit has its own time; they are a record, and I would not call them a clock.
tool

Abstract: A startup operating and investing model in three pillars. Ship something somebody can actually use, give it away briefly, then take it away and find out whether anybody notices. Be profitable before you raise, so the investors are calling you rather than the other way round. And open source everything, because the technology was never the moat. The startup test. Ship it, let them try it, take it away, and see whether anybody asks for it back. Most advice about starting a company is about raising money. This is not that. It is the operating model I actually use, and it rests on three pillars that are easier to state than to do. Be profitable. Ship a product that sells, at a price that works for you. Investors should be talking to you, not the other way round. Open source everything, because the technology is not the moat and you do not want to be locked into it.

They are in that order for a reason. Each one buys you the position you need to do the next. The loop. Ship something usable, give it away briefly, take it away, and find out whether anybody misses it. A no sends you back to the start with better information. A yes is the only thing that earns the right to charge, and charging at a profit is the only thing that earns the right to choose your investors. Strip away the mythology and a startup is simple. You make a thing somebody wants to buy, at a price that is profitable to you. That is it. Whether the company makes a profit in a given year is a separate question with its own answer, but if the product is not profitable, it does not scale, and no amount of growth will fix that.

Which means the single most important skill is the ability to ship. Not to plan, not to pitch, not to architect. Ship. And ship every day, because shipping is how you find out what is true. Be careful with the word, though, because it has been worn smooth. Shipping does not mean a proof of concept. It does not mean a demo, or a video of a demo, or a prototype you walk somebody through on a call. It means a thing somebody else can go and use, on their own, and get value from. It can be held together with tape. It can be vibe coded. Nobody using it cares how it was built, and neither should you, yet.

To ship that often you need the running cost to be near nothing, so build accordingly. Serverless. As few databases and as little live state as you can stand. In our case the file system is the database, which sounds like a compromise until you measure it: what that actually costs, with the numbers is a whole page of its own, and the summary is that with nothing running between requests the standing bill for an estate of thirty one published graphs is a third of a gigabyte of object storage. And do not underestimate the infrastructure. Getting a working thing into a stranger's hands is still, in 2026, genuinely hard, and a surprising amount of the toolchain is not designed to help you do it. Solving that is not overhead, it is the first real product you build. Everything after it gets cheaper.

Now hand it to people for free. Not forever: a short window, whatever unit makes sense, but short. You want the feedback loop tight, and you want the cost of generosity to stay inside what you can absorb. Just doing this solves dozens of problems you did not know you had. How do people get access. What breaks when somebody unfamiliar touches it. What they try first. What they never find. The feedback starts the moment somebody who is not you has the thing. Then comes the part almost nobody does deliberately. Take it away. The trial expired. It is not available right now. Nothing else about the product changes, and no apology is needed. And now ask the only question that matters:

If they shrug and go back to their day, you do not have a product yet. You have something people will accept when it is free, which is a much weaker signal than it feels like from the inside. No sense of loss means no why now, and without a why now there is nothing to sell. If they come back and ask for it, you have something. That is the moment the whole model turns on, and it is worth engineering your trial specifically so that this moment arrives early and unambiguously. Two questions, and people routinely answer only the first. Is the price one they are happy to pay? It has to sit inside the zone where they feel they are getting more than they are giving up. If you have to argue somebody into the value, the answer is no.

And is that price profitable for you? With one honest caveat: it might not be profitable today and still be the right price, if the economics clearly improve with scale. But keep it close enough that you can self fund the gap, because a gap you cannot cover yourself is how you end up back at pillar two on somebody else's terms. Revenue comes first. If you cannot get revenue at all, that is the problem to solve, and it is not a marketing problem. Profitability is the milestone after it, and it is the one that changes your life, for reasons that are entirely about the next pillar.

A related trap, which has its own site because it deserves one: do not reach for a subscription by default. Charging rent for something people are not using is a worse business than being paid when you deliver. subscriptions.sgit.ai makes the full argument: a subscription is a discount for regular use, not rent on something somebody ignores. Pay on demand is usually the healthier shape, for both sides. Here is the claim, stated plainly. The worst possible time to raise money is before you are profitable, before you have the product, before you understand the fit. Which is, of course, exactly when most companies raise. Everything follows from the negotiating position.

You are bargaining from weakness, and both sides know it. You have no product and you have a clock. Profitability does not just mean money, it means time: when you are not bleeding, you can wait, and being able to wait is most of what a good negotiating position is. So the terms are bad, and the worst of them are not about money. They are about control. You hand over a say in the business to people who, in most cases, do not understand the business. They do not understand the technical properties, they have not lived the vision, and that is not a character flaw: their job is to make money. But their focus is now structurally misaligned with yours, and their opinion has been given weight. I think that is one of the most common ways companies fail, and it is entirely self-inflicted at the moment of signing.

The analogy I keep coming back to is music. Do not get signed before you have the album. Write the songs. Record them, in a bedroom studio if that is what you have. Play locally. Get people listening, get people buying. Then take the record deal, and take it as somebody who already has an audience and does not strictly need one. That is the whole of pillar two. Not "never raise". Raise from strength, on terms you set, from people who came to you because the thing already works. This one surprises people, because it sounds like giving away the asset. It is the opposite, and there are five reasons, each of which stands alone.

The technology is not the moat. Believing it is will shape every decision you make badly. Treating it as open from the start forces you to find the thing that actually is defensible, which is usually the data, the relationships, the distribution, or the speed at which you ship. You get a better architecture. Code written to be read by strangers has cleaner boundaries. Not because you are more virtuous in public, but because anything embarrassing has to be fixed rather than hidden. You stay comfortable throwing things away. A team that has never deleted a component is a team that will defend one long after it should have gone. Open source normalises disposal. It is better for the customer, obviously, and they can tell. Nobody has to trust a promise about what happens if you disappear, because they can read the thing.

And it is a much better exit for you, the founder. This is the one people miss. Build proprietary and you will accumulate a pile of technology, much of it not even specific to the startup, that you cannot take with you. Build in the open and the work is still yours when you move on. You leave with your tools. open-source.sgit.ai carries the longer version of this argument, and its thesis is the sentence to remember: open source is a strategy, not a charity. Because the model has a substrate, and we have spent a year building it.

Every pillar above asks for the same thing: shipping a usable product should be cheap, fast, and reversible. That is not a slogan, it is an infrastructure requirement, and it is most of the reason this model is hard to follow. A vault is our answer to it. Data, app, history and sources travel as one string. There is no database to run, no hosting for the reader, no account, no install. The whole published estate is 2,662 files and 295 MB of object storage, with nothing running between questions, and a reader opens any of it with a single read key.

Which makes the cost of shipping a small product to a few real users low enough that you can do it repeatedly, be wrong in public, take it away, and find out whether anybody missed it. That loop is the product I most want other people to have, and it is why the whole stack is open source, down to the measurements and the mistakes. Abstract: An agent that helps me write emails read our articles and told a reader that the meter and the credit kept in the reader's own vault were a proposal, and that nothing of it was built. That is wrong, and the fault is ours: no single page says what is running. So here it is. Built and in use: the meter, which charges each page by how much of it was read; £5 of starting credit; a £5 top-up through Stripe, live since 11 October; and the reading account in the reader's own vault, opened with a passkey, with one file per device, a balance consolidated across devices, devices you can merge, notes, and a lane any browser can write to, even one where the passkey does not work. The server only ever sees ciphertext. I use it every day: my balance is down to £2, so I am about to top up again, and my vault shows every device I have read on and every page I opened. What is proposed, and not built, is the next layer from the user keeps the meter: checking each payment against Stripe afterwards, and signing the result into a vault both sides write to, so credit is validated or not valid. The page a payment returns to says so plainly today: it adds the credit, and it does not verify the payment.
The reading account, piece by piece: what is built, and what is proposed.
in-short

The meter, the credit and Stripe top-ups are running. Since October. The account is in the reader's own vault. One file per device, opened with a passkey. The balance is consolidated across devices. A payment on two devices counts once. Any browser can write to your vault. Even one where the passkey does not work. The server sees ciphertext. Nothing else. What is proposed is the check. Payments validated against Stripe and signed, afterwards. One page now says what is built. This one.
why

One of the agents that helps me write emails read our articles and wrote, in a draft to a reader, that the meter and the credit kept in the reader's own vault, with payments validated and signed afterwards, were a proposal, and that none of it was built. Half of that is wrong. The meter and the credit kept in the reader's vault are built, and I use them every day. Only the second half, payments validated and signed afterwards, is a proposal. The agent was not careless. It read the user keeps the meter, which describes the proposal and said the credit was "kept in the reader's browser", and it found no single page that said what runs today. That is a documentation gap, and this page fills it. The billing article now says the same.
built

As it runs on this site today, checked against the code and the tests of this release: The meter. Every page charges a few pence, by how much of it was actually read; a page scrolled through in seconds stays at the minimum. The balance can go below zero until you top up, which is the idea in paying after the value. £5 of starting credit. One starting credit per account, however many devices you read on. Top up with Stripe. A £5 payment link, live since 11 October. The page the payment returns to adds the credit, once per payment reference. The account in your own vault. Opened with a passkey. Each device writes one file with the records it made, every read with its depth, every top-up, every note, and never totals. A balance across devices. Computed from every device's records each time, with one starting credit; the same payment seen on two devices counts once.
built

Your devices, listed and merged. The vault shows every device you have read on; duplicates can be merged, keeping every read and every payment, as the vault, opened describes. Notes, and send to my vault. Notes kept as you read travel with the account. And a browser that cannot reach your passkey can still write to a lane on your vault, through a link that carries only where to write and the public key, as in sixteen notes I did not want to lose. The server sees ciphertext. The test that opens the account on three devices checks that what reached the server is "ciphertext: no path, no record, no key in the clear".
mine

I use all of this every day. My balance is at £2, so I am at the point where I will buy more credit. When I open my vault, I can see every device I have read on, and every page I opened on each. Records from a browser where the passkey does not work came in through the lane. For something with no server keeping the balance, it is quite powerful, and it is the base the billing design builds on.
proposed

The next layer is the one the user keeps the meter designs, and none of it is built yet: Payments checked against Stripe. Today the page a payment returns to says it plainly: it "adds the top-up to the balance kept in this browser, once per payment reference, and it does not, and cannot, verify the payment." The proposal is an admin side that reconciles each payment with Stripe later, from its own browser. Signed validations. The result written into a vault both the reader and we can write to, signed by us, so credit is unvalidated, validated, or not valid, and anyone can check it. One account across our sites. At user.sgit.ai or billing.sgit.ai, so the same credit works on every sgit.ai site.
limits

As of this release. Checked against the code and tests of 21 October 2026. Top-ups are not verified. The return page trusts the payment reference; that is the gap the proposal closes. The vault is optional. Without a passkey, the account stays in the browser. The email agent's draft is paraphrased. To correct it, not to blame it; the missing page was ours.
sources

The reader's account code (the meter, the sync between the browser and the vault, the vault pane and the lane), the page Stripe returns to, and the test logs of this release, read on 21 October 2026; my own account, as I use it; and a draft from the agent that helps me with email, paraphrased to correct it. Related: the user keeps the meter, paying after the value, the vault, opened, sixteen notes I did not want to lose. Abstract: On 11 October The New Stack published a piece by Ignacio Aldama, an engineer at Bit Cloud, in which a brand-new Claude Code session with no history and no local code found a support console's shared ticket contract in two MCP calls, from the dependency records the build platform writes as each component is versioned, and then left the contract alone because it knew two components depended on it. It is a good demonstration and an honest one, because he then says where the records ran out. They describe structure, not behaviour; a green build can hide tests that never ran; a demo carries a public signing secret and a list of unfinished work; and memory, which holds intent, is not tied to a code version. Those edges are exactly where sgit and RiskMandate sit. Label every fact with how it is known. Treat a skipped test as a control that did not run. Accept a demo shortcut by name and for an interval, or stop. Keep memory and records in one encrypted, versioned history so the intent of version 1.4 is recorded at 1.4. And let records cross a company boundary with publish, clone and mirror. What exists, what is documented and what is only proposed are marked as such.

Where the records ran out, and what fills each gap. The left two columns are Ignacio Aldama's own findings; the right two are the label each one gets in the vocabulary of evidence and barriers, and what fills it today. The status column says which of those exist, which are documented and untested here, and which are proposed.
in-short

The demonstration is real and useful. A fresh Claude Code session, no history, no local code, called read_scope and read_components over MCP, found that the app and the service depend on the same version of a shared ticket entity, and changed only the app. 41 tests passed, nine of them new. Knowing what is shared tells an agent what not to touch. He says where it stops, which is why it is worth answering. Records describe structure, not behaviour. A green build can hide tests that did not run. A demo carries a public signing secret and a list of unfinished work. A memory note is dated but not tied to a version.
in-short

Each edge has a name. A route list in a test fake is a documented claim, not an observed fact. A skipped test is an expectation reported as a boundary. A public signing secret is a grant wider than the mandate. These are the labels RiskMandate already uses. Memory and records belong in one history. sgit is version control for files the host cannot read, so the intent that explains a version can be committed at that version, and written down at all, because the sensitive part of intent is exactly what teams leave out of a repository. Records have to cross company boundaries. His stated goal is a record that holds where the other side of a dependency sits outside the agent's index. sgit's publish, clone over plain GETs, and mirror are built for that, and are documented in the 0.21.0 release.
reports

The piece, published on 11 October, is contributed content with a clear disclosure: the author is an engineer at Bit Cloud, the platform that produced the records, and the page notes that The New Stack's owner, Insight Partners, is an investor in Bit and in Sourcegraph. None of that weakens the test; it is a single demo, by one author, of his own platform, and he says so.
reports

The test is simple and well chosen. He opened a fresh Claude Code session in an empty workspace and asked it to add filtering by ticket status and assignee to a four-component support console: a React app, an Express service on MongoDB, a shared ticket entity, and a platform component behind one gateway. The session found no local code, said the console must live remotely, called read_scope for the public scope, then read_components for the app, the service and the entity. Both the app and the service depended on the same version of the ticket entity, whose documentation called it "shared between the support service and the agent-facing app". The agent imported the components, implemented the filter client-side inside the app, and left the shared entity and the service alone. In his words, "knowing what is shared also tells an agent what not to touch."
reports

Then the part I like most: he says where the records ran out. The route list the app calls lived in the documentation of a fake service used in tests, and "nothing checks that list against the real service". The MongoDB integration tests skip when their temporary database cannot start on the CI runner, so "a passing build doesn't show they ran"; he checked persistence by hand. It is a demo, "with a predefined demo account and a public signing secret", and concurrency control, migrations, recovery and mandatory database tests are still to do. And memory and records cover different ground: a memory note carries the time it was written, "but nothing ties it to a code version", while a dependency record is part of the version it describes and carries no intent. His goal is a record per component "that still holds when the other side of a dependency lives somewhere the agent hasn't indexed", because what agents still lack "is a view of the system they are about to change".
evidence

The route list was a documented claim that read like a fact. That is the gap evidence levels exist for. The behaviour policy packs on abp.sgit.ai label every row as derived, inferred, self-reported, documented, measured or observed, and a reader, a reviewer or an agent should treat each accordingly; the pack's own headline counts only the observed rows. In Aldama's demo the route list was documented, by a fake. The persistence check he ran by hand, create a ticket, add a comment, restart against the same database, confirm both are there, was observed.
evidence

The record and the observation want to live together, with their labels and dates. That is the shape of the connector twin: every call the agent makes is appended to a journal in a vault, and what the agent did is kept apart from what it then saw. In an sgit vault the observation is a file committed in the same history as the claim, and since 0.19 sgit check verify classifies every commit reachable from the head as verified, bad, unsigned or without a known key, so who recorded an observation, and when, is part of the history rather than a comment beside it.
green

A test that skips is a control that did not run. In the vocabulary of Agent Behaviour Policies there are four barriers, none, expectation, setting and boundary, and only a boundary is a control, because only a boundary is enforced by something the grant does not include. A build that reports green over a skipped required test is reporting an expectation as a control, which is the risk that the controls reported upwards are not real. Every risk is already accepted is about where that kind of risk ends up.
green

The fix is small and it is the one we use on ourselves: count the run from what happened, not from the exit code. This session's own status report counts tools, calls, commits and commits without a leak scan from the transcript, not from what the agent says it did. A build could write the same small record into a vault: required tests, run, skipped, and why. A skipped required test then drops the evidence for that component back to documented until it runs, and "41 passing" becomes "41 passing, of which this many exercised the database". This one is proposed, not built.
shortcuts

A public signing secret and a predefined demo account are a grant wider than the mandate: anyone can sign as the app, anyone can be the demo user. That is fine for a demo and it is exactly what drifts into production. RiskMandate's position, on its acceptance page, is that there is no deny button for a deployed system: the risk is real, so it is accepted by a named owner, in a direction, for an interval, or the activity stops. "Public signing secret, accepted by the author until the first user who is not a demo, then rotated" is a decision. The same secret with no owner and no date is drift.
shortcuts

The unfinished items Aldama lists, concurrency control, migrations, recovery, mandatory database tests, are conditions in a licence to operate, each beside the thing that enforces it or beside the admission that nothing does, with an owner and an expiry, rather than a paragraph at the end of an article. On the specific shortcut, sgit keeps signing keys out of files: sgit pki keygen makes the key pair locally, and a leak scan now runs before every commit on this site, because an exposed vault key of our own, on the vault that serves this site, taught us to; the case study has the rotation steps.
memory

This is the strongest fit. Aldama's point is that memory holds intent, the release date, the person to ask, why a feature was cut, and is not tied to a version, while a build record is tied to its version and holds no intent. sgit is git-shaped version control for files the host cannot read. Memory and records can sit in the same vault and the same commit, so the intent that explains version 1.4 is recorded at version 1.4, and sgit history log, diff and show answer the question that matters after an incident: what did we believe when this shipped?
memory

Encryption matters more than it looks here. Intent is usually the sensitive part: owners, customers, why something was cut, who to avoid. Teams leave it out of a repository for exactly that reason, so it ends up in a chat that is compressed into a summary and gone, which is the problem his article opens with. In an sgit vault the host never sees file names, contents or commit messages, so the intent can be written down at all. Encrypted memory for agents that run somewhere else and Memory is not a spectator sport describe how that works for sessions like this one, and The mandate stack describes a team of agents that clone a shared vault at the start of every session, read their brief and their behaviour policy, work, commit and push.
boundary

His stated goal is a record that still holds when the dependency sits somewhere the agent has not indexed. He names Nx serving its project graph over MCP and Sourcegraph serving code search across repositories, and says both do that well; what neither does is cross a company boundary without a shared index or a shared server. sgit has three things built for that, all documented in the 0.21.0 release: Publish. sgit publish writes a small plaintext surface, a loader, a manifest and, if asked, API docs, that any static host can serve, and sgit clone reads it back over ordinary GETs. A supplier can publish its contract records and a customer's agent can clone them with no server and no API.
boundary

Mirror. sgit vault mirror makes a keyless, verifiable copy, re-hashing every content-addressed object rather than trusting the manifest, so a host cannot substitute content. That is custody without access, for a third party holding records it should not read. Append lanes. An outside agent can write into a vault it cannot read, which is how the connector twin's journal and this site's inbox work. I have not tested publish or mirror for this article; they are described here as their README and changelog describe them.
abp

The agent had real reach in the demo: it could read every component in the scope, import source and change shared code. Its best decision, to leave the shared ticket entity alone, was its own judgement. Nothing stopped it from changing a contract that two components depend on. In the terms of a behaviour policy that is a write row with a blast radius of two components, held by an expectation, the agent's good sense. A platform holding the records is in the right place to make it a boundary, for example by requiring an approval to version a shared entity, and Footprint and blast radius is how that row would be measured and priced. That would turn the demo's best moment from a judgement into a guarantee.
limits

It is one demo, by the platform's own engineer, and he discloses it. The four edges are his findings; the labels on them are ours. The green-build record is proposed. Counting run, skipped and why into a vault is an idea, not a feature. Publish and mirror are documented, not tested here. They are in the 0.21.0 README and changelog; this article did not run them. Nothing here replaces records. The point is that records, memory, evidence and acceptance are four different things that want to live in one history, not that any one of them is enough. This is a proposed strategy for RiskMandate. Still being discussed; each stage earns more trust. Policies first. We can create them today, and they are a microcosm of what we do. Then understand. Help the customer get a grip on their exposure. Then risk acceptance. Which risks they carry, and who decides. Then contain, then manage. A smaller blast radius, then a fleet run strategically. Then insure. The end game: agents an insurer can cover. Acceleration runs through all of it. It is what every stage gives the business. We are in the first stage. With our first customers.
strategy

What I am describing here is a proposed strategy for RiskMandate as a company, and the path we would walk with each customer. It is a proposal: my business partner and I have talked about it, and it is still being discussed, so none of it is decided yet. The question behind it is simple to ask and harder to answer: how do we start engaging with a customer? How do we earn their trust? How do we become a player, running our code and our vaults, and being there with them?
strategy

So the way I propose to think about the roadmap is as a spectrum of trust. Each stage answers a different question the customer has, and each one is only asked once the one before it has been answered. The further along we are with a customer, the deeper the relationship, and the more we are helping them in the way they work. The stages are a sequence of events, not always a straight line: with some customers two will overlap, and with others one will come early. But the order is the one we can operate in.
roadmap

Policies. "What can this agent do, and what stops it?" This is where we can start, today, and it is a great place to engage. The policies are a microcosm of everything else: for one agent we already have the grant, the gap, the barriers and the enforcement, the hooks, and a first visualisation. A customer gets to experience what we do, on one agent, in a way that is useful to them on its own. Understand. "Can you help us get a grip on the situation? What is our exposure?" The next stage of trust is the customer asking for help to understand their risk: where their agents are, which agents they have, what each one can reach, and what they were meant to do. This is where the policies scale, from one agent to many, across the organisation. A lot of this is not straightforward, and that is exactly why it needs help.
roadmap

Risk acceptance. "Which of these risks do we carry, and who decides?" Once the exposure is understood, someone has to decide what to do about each gap: fix it, fund the control, or accept it until a date, with a person who holds the decision and a chain to the board. This is the work we have written about in every risk is already accepted, and it is a lot of the work of working with customers. Contain. "How do we make the blast radius smaller?" With the risks accepted, there is a lot that needs containing. So we work with the customer to reduce scope: move rules out of the agents' reach, take away what they do not need, and make each blast radius smaller. The Pellbridge agents showed what that does: the same day had 16 breaches with no policy and none with every rule kept outside the agent.
roadmap

Manage. "How do we run the fleet?" Once the agents are contained, the customer can think much more strategically about them, as a fleet: which agents they need, the resources each one uses, how changes are tested and released, and what the fleet should be doing next. Insure. "Can our agents be covered?" By the time the fleet is managed, the evidence an insurer needs already exists: what each agent can reach, what was authorised, which risks were accepted and by whom, and what actually contains each one. RiskMandate already publishes how that works, from the policy, to a licence to operate, to insurable.
accelerate

I first had accelerate as a stage of its own, after manage. I do not think it is one. Acceleration is what every stage gives the business: each one lets it do more with its agents, with more confidence, and faster. It reads better as the reason for the roadmap than as a step on it, so it runs along the whole length of it.
insurance

Insurance is what gives the whole path its arc. Every stage before it produces evidence: the policies, the exposure, the decisions, the containment, the managed fleet. Insurance is where that evidence is worth the most, to the company and to the people who would cover it. That is why, in this proposal, insurers are part of the play from the start, and why we want to start talking to them now, with this roadmap in front of them: it shows them how a company gets from its first agent policy to agents they can cover.
players

Each stage has other companies that should be the big players in it: in discovering agents, in risk management, in enforcement, in fleet management, and in insurance. Many of them we would work with. Where they do not move fast enough, there is a business opportunity for us to get into that space, because we will already be there with the customer.
now

We are in the first stage: really sorting out the policies, and the flows that produce them. That is what our first customers are for, and their programme now runs as a site of its own, at customers.riskmandate.ai. Its milestones are the first stage, step by step. A customer starts with credit and names one agent; then its grant is measured, its mandate is written in the customer's own words, and the gap gives a first finding. Then comes the part of the policy the agent's harness can hold as hooks, and finally the usage moment: the point where the policy became worth something to that customer, and what a fair price would be. Seven steps in all, from S0 to S6, each done when the thing it names exists.
now

On its own count, at v0.1.1, the first batch has three customers, two of them started, and 3 of the 21 milestone steps done. No first policy has been written yet, and none of the £10 of credit has been used. That is where a roadmap should start: with the numbers on the page.
home

One operational note, which does not change the proposed strategy. The Agent Behaviour Policy started inside RiskMandate, and its stewardship is moving to the Open Security Summit, as its first hosted project, so that it is governed by more people than us. RiskMandate is still the one operating it with customers. And the policies themselves are a stepping stone. Behaviour policies, and the decision and workflow policies that come after them, as in three policies for an agent, are how we start. What we are pursuing is the whole path above: being the people a customer trusts with their agents, from the first policy to agents an insurer can cover.
limits

It is a proposal. Still being discussed between RiskMandate's founders, not the agreed strategy. The stages are a sequence, not a schedule. They have no dates, and may overlap. Only the first stage is under way. The others are described as we see them today. No insurer is signed up. The conversations start now. The other players are not named. Which ones lead each stage is still to be seen. The counts are the customer site's own. Read from it on 20 October 2026.
