Abstract: The agents that build this site can change the pipeline that checks them. In the last eleven days, 62 of 227 commits touched the workflow, the validator, the tests or the build scripts, from six agents, and 17 changed the workflow itself, one of them a speed-up this session made. That is useful work, and it is also the hole: an agent that can change the check can pass any release. So we wrote the rules of the game down as a policy, in five zones: content an agent changes freely; the gates, which need a second key; identity, which only the owner changes; vendored code, refreshed only from its source; and the rules themselves, which no agent touches. Then we mapped what GitHub can enforce on a public repository today, with no new tool. The answer is less than I expected, but enough. A hook in the agent's harness and a guard job in CI mean an agent has to make two deliberate changes to get round them, which is no longer a mistake. One setting by the owner, a token that cannot change workflow files, turns the guard into a boundary. GitHub's path rules for pushes exist, but only for private repositories; and there is a known gap we describe. The next article puts the last step in a repository the agent cannot touch.
The rules of the game in five zones: content, the gates, identity, vendored code and the rules themselves.
in-short

Agents change the pipeline. 62 of 227 commits in eleven days; 17 to the workflow. So we wrote the rules down. Five zones, from free to never. A gate needs a second key, not a ban. The changes are often good ones. Two deliberate changes to get round it. A hook, then the CI guard. One owner setting makes it a boundary. A token that cannot change workflows. GitHub's path rules are for private repositories. Not for this one. There is a known gap. Closed properly by the sidecar.
hole

This site is built and released by agents. Every push to dev is a release: the workflow validates the site, runs the reader's tests in a browser, tags the release and deploys it. In where a check runs I argued that moving checks out of the agent's environment and into that pipeline turns them from settings into gates. But a gate is only as strong as the agent's inability to open it. And today the agents can open it. Between 11 and 22 October, 62 of the 227 commits to this repository touched a file that checks the work: the workflow, the validator, the test files, the build scripts. They came from six agents and from commits with no agent label. 17 of them changed the workflow itself, including one from this session, v0.13.7, which cached the browser the tests use and made every release faster. So the credential this session pushes with can change the pipeline that gates it.
hole

None of those changes was malicious; most were improvements. That matters for the design. A rule that says "never change the pipeline" would have blocked good work 62 times. The rule we want is that the agent can propose a change to what checks it, and someone else has to agree. Commits that touched the checks, by agent, from 11 to 22 October 2026: 62 of 227 in all.
policy

So the first step is the one I asked for in the memo: write the rules of the game down, so that whatever enforces them, now or later, has something to enforce. The policy is published with this article. Its principle is one sentence: an agent may change content freely; it may change what checks its work only with a second key; it may never change its own rules. It has five zones: Content, free. The articles, the newsletter, the release notes, the notes, and every page the builders generate. The version file only to the next version, which CI already checks. The gates, a second key. The workflow, the validator, the test runner and the test files, the wording and summaries checks, the publish and sync scripts, .gitignore, and the code that runs in the reader's browser, which is not content even though it ships with it.
policy

Identity, the owner only. Who the agents are, the published vault keys, the domain the site is served on, and the agents' own settings. Vendored, from upstream only. Code copied from another project and pinned by hash. The rules, never by an agent. The policy itself, and whatever enforces it. The copy published here is for reading. The copy that counts has to live somewhere the agent cannot write, or the last zone means nothing; that is the subject of the sidecar repository.
github

What GitHub offers a public repository today without a new tool, and what needs a paid plan or an organisation. Then the research: what can GitHub itself enforce, on this repository, today? This site's repository is public, owned by an organisation, and its release branch had no protection when we checked on 22 October. From GitHub's documentation: Path rules for pushes exist, but not here. A push ruleset can "prevent commits that include changes in specified file paths from being pushed", and GitHub's own example is the workflow files. But push rulesets are available "in internal and private repositories" on the Team plan and above. For a public repository, the one rule that does exactly what we want is not on offer.
github

Required workflows are for pull requests. A ruleset can require a workflow from another repository to pass, but it is set at the organisation level, and the documentation says it "will block direct pushes" and belongs on branches "where all changes to the branch are performed by pull requests". Our releases are direct pushes. Code owners need pull requests too. A CODEOWNERS file with a required review means "any pull request that modifies content with a code owner must be approved by that code owner", and the file can own itself. But it applies to pull requests; a branch rule requiring them applies to the whole branch, content and all. Branch rules that are not about paths are available. Rulesets and protected branches work on public repositories on the free plan: block force pushes, block deletion, restrict who can create branches.
github

Deployments can require a person. Environments with required reviewers work on public repositories on every current plan, and "users who initiate a deployment cannot approve the deployment job". A token can lack the right to change workflows. A classic token needs the workflow scope, and a GitHub App the Workflows permission, to change files in .github/workflows. A token without it cannot push a change there. So, on a public repository where agents push straight to the release branch, GitHub has one boundary that is about paths, and it covers only the workflow files. Everything else is either about the whole branch or needs a private repository. That is the starting point.
minimal

The controls in order, and what it takes to get round each, from the policy to the sidecar repository. Here is the smallest set that works, in the order of the barriers in an Agent Behaviour Policy: The policy. An expectation. It catches nothing on its own; it is what the rest enforce. A hook in the agent's harness. A setting. Claude Code can deny edits to paths with permission rules, such as Edit(/.github/workflows/**), and a PreToolUse hook "can block" a tool call before it runs. This catches mistakes at the moment they are made. Its documented limit: the rules do not apply to "a Python or Node script" that writes the file. So it is a guard against accidents, not against intent.
minimal

A guard job in CI. A setting. In the validation job, before anything else: compare the files changed since the last release with the policy's paths, and if any gate, identity or rules path changed, fail, unless the commit arrived as a pull request approved by an account the agent does not act as. Validation failing stops the tag and the deploy, as it does today. A token that cannot change workflows. A boundary, and the owner's step. The sidecar repository. A boundary even under full compromise, in the next article.
minimal

With only the first three, getting a change to the validator into a release takes two deliberate acts: getting round the hook, by writing the file some other way or by changing the agent's settings, which are themselves in the identity zone; and editing the guard out of the workflow. An agent does not do both by accident. If it does both, it is, as I put it in the memo, borderline malicious, and both acts are in the history for anyone to see.
minimal

Step 4 changes the picture more than its size suggests. If the agent's token cannot change workflow files, it cannot edit the guard either, and the guard lives in the workflow. So the guard becomes a boundary, not just for the workflow but for every path the policy lists: one owner setting turns the whole gates zone into a second-key zone. The guard's path list has to be written in the workflow file itself, not read from a script the agent could change. And whether the integration this session pushes through can be given a token without that permission is something I have not been able to check; v0.13.7 shows it can change workflows today.
gaps

Assuming the agent tries, here is what the first four steps leave open: An old workflow can come back. GitHub's documentation for the classic scope says a workflow file "can be committed without this scope" if an identical file exists on another branch. So an agent that can create a branch at an old commit, from before the guard, may be able to bring the old workflow back. Blocking branch creation for the agent with a ruleset closes the obvious route; the sidecar closes it properly, because it compares the workflow with an approved copy. Rewriting history. A force push to dev could replace the history the guard compares against. Blocking force pushes on dev and main is available today on the free plan. Manual runs on other branches. The workflow can be run by hand on a branch. The deployment environment already restricts which branches can deploy, and that restriction is a setting only the owner can change.
gaps

Approving itself. If the agent acts as the owner's account, the owner's approval is not a second key. The approver has to be an account, and a person, the agent does not act as. Content is still free. An agent can still publish a bad article, or leak something into one. The validator's tripwires and the leak scan catch some of that; the private lists belong in the sidecar, where the agent cannot read them.
second-key

The point of the design is not to stop agents improving the pipeline. They have improved it, many times, and some of those changes, like the browser cache, made every later release faster. The point is that a change to what checks an agent's work is a different kind of change from an article, and it should be seen and agreed by someone other than the agent. That is the same rule, at a smaller scale, as in the delegation record: a change to authority needs approval; a change in behaviour needs evaluation. And even if all we have done today is write the policy, that is worth something: it is the specification that somebody else, a hook, a CI job, an owner, a second repository, can now enforce.
limits

Nothing here is enforced yet. The policy is proposed; no hook, guard or token change is in place. The GitHub findings are from documentation. Read on 22 October 2026, not tested on this repository. The token step is untested. I do not know yet whether this session's integration can be given a token without the workflow permission. The old-workflow gap is documented for the classic scope. Whether an App token behaves the same is not stated. The commit counts are by path. A commit touching a gate file is counted, whatever it changed.
sources

My voice memo of 22 October 2026; this repository's history from 11 to 22 October, counted by path and by the agent label in each commit's subject; the workflow file as it is at v0.13.38; and GitHub's documentation, read that day, on rulesets and the rules they offer, push rulesets, protected branches, code owners, deployment environments, OAuth scopes and GitHub App permissions, and Claude Code's documentation on permission rules and hooks. The research was done by a background agent and checked against the documentation's source. Related: where a check runs, behaviour policies from the checks, the checks, measured, the sidecar repository. Written up and checked by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: On 10 October Satya Nadella published "Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era", a short post arguing that because we can no longer trace what a model does back to a code path, we should treat models the way we treat any powerful insider, and keep the authority over them outside them. Reading it, I kept translating. His lost code path is what I have been calling software was the law. His insider that need not be malicious is the ultimate insider. His split between the supply of intelligence and the authority over it is RiskMandate's founding line, the grant is not the mandate. His controls outside the model are the enforcer test. And his last line, that the most trustworthy system is the one that needs to trust the model least, is the irony The ultimate insider ended on: the more you can constrain an agent, the more autonomy you can afford to give it. This article puts the two vocabularies side by side, idea by idea, shows where ours came from, and names the two places where they differ: his unit is the model and ours is one agent in one deployment, and his frame is observation where ours is authority, accepted by a named person for a stated interval. A companion article takes his seven principles one at a time.

His words and ours. Each idea in Satya Nadella's post, paraphrased, beside the word this network has been using for it, and the page where that word is defined and worked through. On 10 October Satya Nadella published Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era. It is short and careful, and as I read it I kept doing the same thing: translating it, line by line, into the words we have been using on this site and on RiskMandate for the last few weeks, and in some cases for much longer.

This is a big deal, and not for the reason you might think. It is not about who said it first. When the CEO of one of the largest AI vendors arrives at the same conclusions from the other side of the market, from the side that builds the models rather than the side that has to live with them, that is evidence the conclusions are right. Two very different starting points, one set of answers. So this is not a rebuttal. It is a translation, because the most useful thing I can do with his post is show how the two vocabularies map onto each other, and where they do not.

This is the first of two articles. The second, Authority outside the model, takes his seven principles one at a time and says, for each, what we run, what we have only designed, and what we have only argued. His post is worth reading in full first. I paraphrase it here, and quote it once. We are describing the same thing. He starts from what we lost when models replaced code; I called it software was the law. He treats models as insiders that need not be malicious; I called that the ultimate insider. He separates the supply of intelligence from the authority over it; RiskMandate's first line is that the grant is not the mandate.

His most important idea is our enforcer test. Controls have to sit outside the thing they control. In the ABP's words, a control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include. Everything else in his post follows from that, and so does everything in ours. We got here from risk, not from models. Twenty-five years of security work, much of it in application security and as a CISO, taught me that most damage is not malice, that every risk is already accepted by somebody, and that the interesting number is the gap between what a credential allows and what its holder was meant to do. Agents made that gap the whole problem.

Two differences are worth naming. His unit is the model; ours is one agent in one deployment, because the same model is harmless in one setup and serious in another. His frame is observation; ours is authority: a mandate written before the agent runs, and the risk that is left accepted by a named person for a stated interval. The ending is the same sentence, read from opposite ends. His: the most trustworthy system is the one that needs to trust the model least. Ours: the more you can constrain an agent, the more you can trust it, and the more autonomy you can afford to give it.
lineage

It helps to say where our vocabulary comes from, because it was not built for models. It was built for risk. Most of the worst damage I have seen in twenty-five years of security work was not an attack. It was a bug, a misconfiguration, a script run against the wrong environment, a person doing something that was allowed and should not have been. So when I say threat, I mean anything that causes business impact, malicious or not. And underneath the damage, the same thing kept turning up: what somebody could do was much larger than what they were meant to do, the difference was rarely written down, and so it was rarely accepted by anyone.
lineage

That became the research behind risks.sgit.ai, which starts from an inversion: you cannot deny a risk, you can only say how long you accept it. A risk with a real exposure under it exists whether or not anyone signs for it. Take away the deny button, ask a named person to underwrite the exposure for a stated interval, and risk management stops being a gate and becomes a forcing function, because whoever has to sign starts asking for evidence.
lineage

Then agents arrived, and every part of that problem got worse at once. An agent is given a credential whose reach has rarely been measured, a job that is usually clear but rarely written down, and a set of rules it is asked to keep itself. RiskMandate exists to answer one narrow question about that arrangement: what can this agent we just connected actually do, and who said it could? The answer is a document, the Agent Behaviour Policy, and its four words are the vocabulary the rest of this article translates into: Reach: what the agent can do, measured. Mandate: what the business authorised, written down. Gap: reach minus mandate, derived, never written by hand. Barriers: what stands in the way of each row of the gap: nothing, an expectation, a setting, or a boundary.
lineage

How the vocabulary was built, in dated public work. Most of it was written in the three weeks before Nadella's post, on top of risk and identity research going back to 2025. The convergence is the point: two very different starting places, one set of conclusions.
law

He opens with a loss. For decades, when software did something, we could follow the behaviour back to a code path. With frontier models we cannot, and yet these are the systems we are connecting to sensitive data and letting act for us. I described the same loss from the business side, in Zoom into an agent's behaviour policy and you find the business logic. For decades, the rules of a business lived in its systems. A clerk could not send an unapproved invoice, because the finance system had no button for it until the approval was recorded. Those rules were enforced by omission, by the screen that did not show the button. An agent works through APIs, not screens: it can call the endpoint the button would have called. So the rule is no longer enforced, unless somebody writes it down and something outside the agent enforces it.
law

The translation adds one thing to his version. What we lost was not only traceability. It was the place where the business kept its rules. Many organisations have never written those rules down, because their software was the law. The behaviour policy is where they get written down, and that is why, a few layers in, an agent's policy stops being about security and starts being about how the company actually works.
insider

His frame is insider risk: treat a frontier model, closed or open, as an insider, not because it means harm, but because anything capable with access to important systems can make mistakes or be compromised. That is the argument of The ultimate insider, from 30 September. Insider threat was always real and always hard to scale, because the insider was either a person, bounded by hours, skills and conscience, or code, which did exactly what it was written to do. An agent is neither. It is a reasoning engine in a loop with tools, fluent in every language and every schema, able to write the connector it lacks and try again. Three of the five public incidents in that article were not attacks at all, just agents being agents. The way I put it then: the distance between the benign case and the hostile one is a prompt.
insider

Knowing when to stop adds the part that is easy to miss. The variability that makes an agent dangerous is also what makes it useful; in a person, we would call it creativity. You cannot engineer it away without losing the point of the agent. A model that can go in every direction needs someone with a direction, and something that stops it.
accepted

He is clear that responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf stays with us, and that a model provider's assurances do not move it. In our words: every risk is already accepted. The day an agent is connected, the exposure exists, and somebody is carrying it, signed for or not. There is no deny button, only the question of who holds it and until when. A risk that nobody accepted has not gone away. It has come to rest on whoever is nearest, and it rolls upward to the board without anyone choosing to escalate it.
accepted

The vendor point has a sharper edge in our vocabulary. On nhi.sgit.ai we separate agents you run from agents you rent. Almost every agent a business can name today is rented: it runs on somebody else's infrastructure, and the only thing the business controls is the credential it hands over. For those, the honest current workflow is to hand over a broad credential and hope. Hope is not a control, and it does not change who is accountable.
supply

This is the centre of his post, and of ours. In his words, we need to "separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it." RiskMandate's first page says the same thing in five words: the grant is not the mandate. A grant is what the credential technically permits. A mandate is what the holder is authorised and expected to do. In practice the first is much larger than the second, and the difference is where the exposure lives. The supply of intelligence arrives with a grant attached. The authority is the mandate, and it only exists if somebody writes it down.
supply

Our vocabulary is stricter about what counts as authority. A mandate has an issuer, a subject, a scope, an interval and a way to revoke it; an instruction in a chat has none of these. And a mandate with no clock is just a grant. That last line is the one I would most like to see in an industry standard, because an authority that never expires is not separated from the supply. It has quietly become part of it. Supply and authority, in RiskMandate's terms. The supply arrives with a grant; the authority is a mandate with an issuer, a scope and a clock. The gap between them is derived, and each row of it has a barrier. Only one kind of barrier is a control.
enforcer

He grounds the separation in an old security principle: a program must not be able to bypass or tamper with whatever enforces its permissions. So the controls over what a model can reach and do have to sit outside it, which means pulling apart the model, the harness that drives it, and the space of actions it can take. The ABP turns that principle into a test you can run on any rule: a control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include. Four kinds of barrier follow from it: Nothing. An expectation: a rule in prose, enforced by nobody. A setting: a switch the agent's own account could flip. A boundary: enforced above the grant, out of the agent's reach. Only the last one is a control. RiskMandate's home page says it shorter: a prompt asks, a policy enforces.
enforcer

His worry about models checking models, an opaque system watched by another opaque system, is the same test applied to verification. A second reader the agent cannot skip starts from the line that a rule kept by the agent it governs is hope, and ends on this: the same checking code is a setting when the agent's own account installed it, and a boundary when somebody else did. Same code, different owner. Independence is not a property of the checker. It is a property of who controls it.
code

He asks for engineering before alignment: wrap the non-deterministic model in deterministic system design, human controls and dependable procedure. Hope or enforcement measured what that does. One customer service agent, built three ways, with the same rules each time. With one model and broad connectors, 97% of the policy was hope. Behind a harness of business tools, 73%. As a team of narrow agents behind a deterministic gateway, with tools that take no customer argument and limits written into the tools, 23%, and one run could reach one customer instead of 38,000. The phrase that came out of it is my translation of his: granularity moves knowledge out of the prompt and into code. And there is a finding he does not mention: as the reach falls, the policy gets shorter, because it no longer has to forbid what the agent has no way to do.
calibrator

He wants every meaningful action to leave evidence that cannot be tampered with and that a person can read, so that an outcome can be reconstructed without relying on the model's account of it. We arrived at the same rule by being wrong. I wrote a policy for an agent from the vendor's documentation, which said the connector could not send attachments. The agent found a way, proved it with a signed PDF, and wrote it up; that story is in Six agents, one inbox. Since then the rule has been that the grant is measured on the thing itself, and calibrated against what the logs show it did: the footprint. Reality is the calibrator. The connector twin is the same idea for actions: journal every call, replay it as the agent saw it, and turn "can we undo this?" into a list.
calibrator

Our version adds two conditions. First, the evidence should not be held by whoever is being observed, which is why ours lives in vaults whose host stores ciphertext and never holds a key. Second, observation needs something to compare against. A footprint read against a written mandate produces findings: a near miss, where the agent went somewhere it was not asked and nothing stopped it, or a dormant mandate, where something you relied on never ran. A footprint read against nothing produces logs. That is why RiskMandate's order is to instrument before you enforce: the measurement is what tells you where enforcement is worth its cost.
brake

He asks us to assume the model is compromised from the start, and to make sure an authorised person can always pause or stop it mid-task. Our first containment rule came from running agents, not from theory: the account is the blast radius. Every session an agent opens runs as the account that authorised it, so the first real control is a dedicated account per agent. The brake, in RiskMandate's language, is the question a board asks in one sentence: who can pull the plug? The plug always exists. What is missing is its profile: who holds it, how fast it works from the decision, what breaks when it is pulled, and what can never be undone. The last of those matters most, because a brake stops the next action and does nothing for the ones already taken.
disclosure

He asks for timely disclosure to the people affected, and for the industry to share what failed and how to prevent it. The ultimate insider argued that the main reason we do not see more agent incidents is that almost nobody is required to report them, and pointed at aviation, where confidential near-miss reporting, about 100,000 reports a year, helped make a complex system safe. Our own practice is to write up our incidents the day they happen: the second reader article opens with two emails that went out wrongly in my voice. And our vocabulary gives disclosure something precise to count. A near miss is footprint in the gap: the agent went somewhere it was not asked to go, and nothing stopped it. It happens long before anything breaks.
brakes

His last line is that the most trustworthy system will not be the one with the most trusted model, but the one that needs to trust the model least. Ours, from the end of The ultimate insider: the more you can constrain an agent, the more you can trust it, and the more autonomy you can afford to give it. Once you know the universe of what an agent can do, and that universe fits inside your risk appetite, you can let it act freely within it, and every human decision becomes an exception worth making rather than one alarm among thousands. We put brakes on cars so that we can go faster. They are the same sentence. His is written from the point of view of the system that has to be trusted. Ours is written from the point of view of the business that wants to use it.
differ

A translation is most useful where it is not one to one. There are two differences, and both matter. The unit. His post is about models. Ours is about one agent in one deployment. The same model, connected to a mailbox with the broadest scope and a read-write database, can reach 38,000 customers; behind a gateway with bound tools, one. RiskMandate's home page says it in a heading: not a model property, a property of this deployment. Standards written for models will miss most of the risk if they do not describe deployments.
differ

The frame. His principles are mostly about seeing: observability, verification, audit, disclosure. Ours start one step earlier, with deciding. A mandate written before the agent runs. A gap derived from it. And the risk that is left, accepted by a named person for a stated interval, where the interval is the decision: accepting for four hours is declaring an incident, for a month is funding the work, for six months is a named decision to wait. Observation tells you what happened. Authority tells you whether it was allowed, and acceptance tells you who carries it if it was not. Neither difference is a disagreement. They are the two halves a business needs: the vendor's half, which makes the system observable and containable, and the deployer's half, which says what it is for and who answers for it.
next

For me, the most useful thing about his post is that it names principles at the level where an industry can agree on them. The next step is a vocabulary precise enough to write them down for a real agent, and to test them. Ours is open. The ABP model, its four objects, its barrier kinds and the enforcer test are published under CC BY 4.0, with sixteen example policies anyone can read. It is not the only possible language, but it is a working one, and it already says, row by row, how much of a given agent's policy is a control and how much is hope. If you are working on agent standards, or deploying agents and want to try writing the mandate down, let's compare notes: agent@riskmandate.ai.
next

For the detail, Authority outside the model takes his seven principles one at a time, says what we run, what is published as design and what is only argued, and lists the five things I think the principles need in order to work.
sources

Satya Nadella's post, Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, sn scratchpad, 10 October 2026, read in full; it is paraphrased throughout and quoted once. I asked an agent in a separate Claude session to read it alongside the articles, vaults and sites of this network, check every claim against the page that owns it, and draft this answer with its figures; this site's agent then rewrote it in the voice of this site. The argument is mine, and so is the editorial responsibility. The pages it translates into: on this site, The ultimate insider, the business logic, Every risk is already accepted, Knowing when to stop, Six agents, one inbox, Hope or enforcement, A second reader the agent cannot skip, Footprint and blast radius and the connector twin; on RiskMandate, the grant is not the mandate, Who can pull the plug? and the home page; the model and vocabulary at abp.sgit.ai and the barrier and the enforcer test; and the research sites risks.sgit.ai and nhi.sgit.ai.

Abstract: I usually give a talk by reading it, with the slides behind me. For a short slot tonight I would like to try something else: a talk that is completely scripted, where the slides, the builds, the animations and even the demo play on a clock, and I speak to them instead of reading from them. This grows out of two talks already published as vaults on sgit.ai. The Black Hat Europe 2025 keynote made the slides data: 26 slides in one JSON file that the app reads at load time, with ten versions of the slide system beside it. The VoiceDebrief pitch added a presenter with per-slide timings, a countdown and speaker notes, built from a template by a script. The next step is to make the whole talk a timeline. This site's agent built a first version: one HTML file that plays a file of beats, each with a start, a duration, a slide and the words to say, with builds, a terminal that types a command and prints its recorded output, tables that reveal row by row, video, and a presenter view with the words, the seconds left and what comes next. A rehearsal mode records planned against actual times. The first timeline is the five-minute demo for ruv.sgit.ai, the newest site in the sgit family, built for tonight's Agentic Engineering Live with rUv in London. And Claude Motion, which Anthropic released in beta on 8 October, makes the animations the same way: as code, exported as MP4.
A scripted talk, from the memo to the room: a file of beats, a player on a clock, a speaker view and a rehearsal record.
in-short

A talk as a timeline. Slides, builds, animations and the demo play on a clock; the speaker speaks to them. It grows out of two vaults. Black Hat made the slides data; the VoiceDebrief pitch added timings and a presenter. A player, built and tested. One HTML file, a file of beats, a presenter view and a rehearsal mode. The demo is recorded truth. The terminal types the command and prints the output the real run produced. Animations as code. Claude Motion, Manim or Remotion: editable, versioned, exported as MP4. First use, tonight. The five-minute demo for ruv.sgit.ai, at Agentic Engineering Live with rUv in London.
why

I usually read my presentations, with the slides behind me as a backdrop. It works, but it splits the attention: the audience reads the slide while I read the script, and the two drift apart. For a short slot, where every second counts, I would like to try the opposite: a talk that is completely scripted. The slides, the builds, the animations and the demo are written down as a timeline and play on a clock, and I speak to them. The pace is set before I walk on, the demo cannot fail live, and the whole thing can be rehearsed, measured and changed like code.
lineage

Three talks, one direction: Black Hat Europe 2025, the VoiceDebrief pitch, and tonight's player, all living in vaults. This is the third step of something I have done twice before, and both are published as vaults on sgit.ai. The first was AI vs. AI, my keynote at the AI Security Summit at Black Hat Europe on 9 December 2025. The deck was fully generated from scripts. Its 26 slides, in seven layouts, are one JSON file: "The app reads it through the vault bridge at load time, so a content change needs no rebuild." The vault also carries the slide system itself at ten versions, six PDF exports, and the eight research papers the talk was built from. The lesson I took from it is the one that matters here: content is data, the renderer is code, and they change separately.
lineage

The second was the VoiceDebrief pitch to Founder Institute on 2 September 2026: a presenter app with per-slide target timings, a three-minute countdown and speaker notes, built from a template by a script in the vault, with the spoken script extracted from the notes and the PDF and PPTX regenerated on every release. That added time to the slides: each one knew when it should be on screen. The next step is to let the clock drive. Instead of a deck with timings beside it, a timeline with slides on it.
player

The prototype's presenter view at 2:58 of the five-minute demo: the slide, the words, the time left and a progress bar. This site's agent built a first version, and it is deliberately small: one HTML file and one JSON file, no build. It is a page made for one moment, which Custom UIs are not the exception argued is normal now: "A custom interface per message or moment is not an exception". The talk is a list of beats. Each beat has a start in seconds, a duration, a title, the words to say, and a slide with a layout: statement: a line of text, with builds that appear at set seconds; terminal: a command typed out character by character, then the output the real run produced; table: rows revealed every few seconds; bullets, video, for example an MP4 exported from Claude Motion, and iframe, for a live page.
player

A clock drives everything. Press Space and it plays; the beat at the current second is on screen, its builds appear at their offsets, and the next beat starts on time without a click. The arrow keys jump between beats if the room needs a moment. P opens the presenter view: the words for this beat, the seconds left, highlighted in the last five, and what comes next. R starts a rehearsal, which records when each beat actually began; when it stops, it saves a file of planned against actual times, the evidence of whether the script fits the slot.
player

It was tested in Chromium: every beat came on at its second, the builds and rows appeared on schedule, the terminal finished typing and then printed, the arrows jumped forward and back, it stopped at 5:00, and the page raised no errors. A version with the talk inlined opens straight from a file, with no server and no network, which is the version to carry into a room with bad wifi.
demo

The part I like most is the terminal. A live demo is where talks go wrong: the network, the package cache, the one command that behaves differently on stage. In a scripted talk, the command is typed on the timeline and the output is the one the real run produced, captured beforehand and kept with the talk. That is not faking the demo. It is the same principle as every vault on sgit.ai: the evidence is recorded, versioned and inspectable, and anyone can run the command again from the vault and compare.
motion

The memo's transcription garbled two names. The first is clearly Claude Motion, which Anthropic released in beta on 8 October 2026 for Team and Enterprise plans: "Claude writes code that animates your text, charts, shapes, and images, so you can change any word, number, or timing." It "doesn't use a video generation model", and the result downloads as an MP4. I could not make out the second word with confidence; the code-based animation tools it most likely refers to are Manim, the Python library for mathematical animation, and Remotion, which makes video from React components, and both are already used with Claude Code through community skills.
motion

They all fit the timeline the same way. An animation made as code can be edited a word or a number at a time, versioned beside the talk, exported as an MP4, and placed on a beat. The talk stays data from end to end: the words, the slides, the animations and the recorded output, each in a file, each with a history.
ruv

The first timeline is a real one. ruv.sgit.ai is the newest site in the sgit family, built on 14 October for Agentic Engineering Live with Reuven Cohen, rUv, in London on 15 October. It shows sgit vaults and agent behaviour policies running inside his stack, Ruflo, RuVector, RVM and MetaHarness, as six proofs of concept, and it already has a five-minute demo written in five beats. The agent turned those beats into the first talk.json: the claim, Ruflo's default saying yes to sending email, the same eleven actions with and without the behaviour policy, read from the site's own data, memory with history across runners, and the ask. A ten-minute version is the same file with more beats.
brief

The talk vault. talk.json, the player, the assets and every rehearsal file in one vault, with a published read key once the talk is given. Recorded demos. A script that runs each demo command and saves its output beside the beat that shows it. Motion on beats. Animations made in Claude Motion, Manim or Remotion, exported as MP4 and referenced by path. Rehearsal as a test. A rehearsal file committed after each run-through, and a check that fails if any beat runs more than ten seconds over. Exports. The same timeline rendered to a PDF, one page a beat, and to one MP4 of the whole talk. A vault app. The player served from the vault itself, as the Black Hat deck is, so the talk and its evidence travel as one object.
limits

It has not been given yet. The player was tested in a browser, not in a room. Scripted is not read. The words are in the presenter view; whether to read them is the speaker's choice. The second animation tool is a guess. The transcription was unclear. Claude Motion was not used here. Its details are from Anthropic's pages; it is in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. The exports and the talk vault are proposed. The player, the timeline and the tests exist. If you give talks and want yours to be a timeline with its evidence attached, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Summary: I usually give a talk by reading it, with the slides behind me. For a short slot tonight I want to try something else: a talk that is completely scripted, where the slides, the builds, the animations and even the demo play on a clock, and I speak to them instead of reading from them. This grows out of two talks already published as vaults on sgit.ai. The Black Hat Europe 2025 keynote made the slides data: 26 slides in one JSON file that the app reads at load time, with ten versions of the slide system beside it. The VoiceDebrief pitch added a presenter with per-slide timings, a countdown and speaker notes, built from a template by a script. The next step is to make the whole talk a timeline. This site's agent built a first version: one HTML file that plays a file of beats, each with a start, a duration, a slide and the words to say, with builds, a terminal that types a command and prints its recorded output, tables that reveal row by row, video, and a presenter view with the words, the seconds left and what comes next. A rehearsal mode records planned against actual times. The first timeline is the five-minute demo for ruv.sgit.ai, the newest site in the sgit family, built for tonight's Agentic Engineering Live with rUv in London. And Claude Motion, which Anthropic released in beta on 8 October, makes the animations the same way: as code, exported as MP4.
articles/versions/the-scripted-talk/v1.1.0.html
why

I usually read my presentations, with the slides behind me as a backdrop. It works, but it splits the attention: the audience reads the slide while I read the script, and the two drift apart. For a short slot, where every second counts, I want to try the opposite: a talk that is completely scripted. The slides, the builds, the animations and the demo are written down as a timeline and play on a clock, and I speak to them. The pace is set before I walk on, the demo cannot fail live, and the whole thing can be rehearsed, measured and changed like code.

Abstract: It is worth taking a step back and looking at all the sgit.ai sites together. On 21 October 2026 there were 53 website repositories under SGit-AI, the first started on 11 August. 45 of them answer as live sites, one is built and not yet serving, and seven are placeholders, two of them created this morning for the AWS twin and the user site. Between them they hold 1,679 commits, 33,541 files and 5,419 pages listed in their sitemaps. The estate grew in bursts of about ten new sites a week, and the busiest week for commits was the one of 12 October, with 331. The shape is a long tail: four repositories, sgit.ai, the newsroom, graphs and PKI, hold 62% of the commits, while the median site has seven, because most sites were built in a session or two and then left to do their job. Families are appearing, hubs with instances under them, which is why the naming now needs a rule. This is the data, with the charts, and what I read from it.
Fifty-three repositories in eleven weeks: new site repositories each week, and commits across all of them.
in-short

53 repositories, 45 live sites. One built and not serving yet, seven placeholders. 1,679 commits in eleven weeks. The first repository started on 11 August 2026. 5,419 pages in the sitemaps. And 33,541 files across the repositories. It grew in bursts. About ten new sites in each of five weeks. A long tail. Four repositories hold 62% of the commits; the median site has seven. Families are appearing. Hubs with instances under them, which is why naming needs a rule.
counted

On 21 October 2026 there were 53 repositories under SGit-AI whose names start with SGit-AI__Website, each one a website. I fetched the history of every one of them, all branches, without the file contents, counted the files at the head of each, and asked every host whether it answers, how many pages its sitemap lists, and which version it says it is. 45 answer as live sites. Every one of them on GitHub Pages, under sgit.ai. 1 is built and not serving. ux.sgit.ai has a repository of 209 files and a domain set, and returns 404. 7 are placeholders. A README and little else: hooks, tokens.hook, demos and two demo sites, all made on 14 October, and aws.twin and user, made this morning.
counted

Together they hold 1,679 commits, 1,416 of them with a version number in the subject, which is how these sites mark a release. At their heads there are 33,541 files: 9,317 HTML pages, 9,602 markdown files and 5,995 images. And the live sites list 5,419 pages in their sitemaps. Most of them can be read by an agent as well as a person: 35 of the 46 repositories with content publish an llms.txt, 41 of the 45 live sites serve a sitemap, and 33 publish their version at the usual path.
growth

The first repository, sgit.ai itself, started on 11 August 2026. Then the estate grew in bursts. Nine new sites in the week of 17 August and ten in the week of 24 August, as the first ideas each got a site of their own: NHI, PKI, graphs, the newsroom, risks, standards, twins and others. Ten more in the week of 7 September, with the games, the providers family and the store. A quieter stretch through September and early October, with the Portuguese and sgit editions of the newsroom, MyFeeds, vCISO and secrets. Then ten in the week of 12 October, with the newsroom's API, Ruv, the hooks and demos placeholders, UX, NotebookLM and the Gen Z Developers book; and eight in the week of 19 October: the CLI, storyboards and its API, send and its API, startups, and, this morning, the AWS twin and the user site.
growth

Commits follow a different rhythm. The busiest week was the one of 12 October, with 331 commits across all repositories, more than any other week by far; the quietest the week of 28 September, with 60.
work

Commits per repository, the fourteen busiest, with sgit.ai, the newsroom, graphs and PKI at the top. The shape is a long tail. Four repositories, sgit.ai, the newsroom, graphs and PKI, hold 62% of all the commits. The median site, among the 46 with content, has seven. And 22 of those 46 have their whole history inside a single day. That is not a sign of neglect. It is how these sites are made: an idea gets a site in one session, the site does its job, and it is left alone until the idea needs it again. 22 repositories were touched in the last week; 12 have not changed since the end of August. The ones that keep growing are the ones that are used every day: the hub, the newsroom, and the two that hold primitives the others rest on, graphs and PKI.
pages

Pages listed in each live site's sitemap, the fourteen largest, led by the newsroom and its Portuguese edition. Pages tell a slightly different story from commits. The newsroom lists 1,282 pages, and its Portuguese edition, pt.newsroom.sgit.ai, 929, built in 74 commits. The Gen Z Developers book site lists 496 pages from 70 commits in three days. A site that renders a book or a corpus can be large and young at the same time.
families

The site families held against the naming convention agreed on 21 October. The newest thing in the data is families: a hub site, and instance sites under it. There are three kinds of second-level host today: API sites. api.newsroom, api.send and api.storyboards: a site's client code, released by version. Editions. pt.newsroom and sgit.newsroom: the same newsroom, in another language or for another audience. Family instances. elevenlabs and ungovr under providers, what-can-it-do under games, and, reserved, tokens under hook, two demos under demo and aws under twin. The last kind is where the naming was inconsistent, so on 21 October we fixed a rule: plural for the hub, singular for the instance. Plural for the family, singular for the site sets it out, with the decisions behind it. Held against the hosts that exist, four live or listed hosts break it, the three provider instances and the game, and the newer families already follow it.
reading

A site is cheap. Most were built in one or two sessions. That is why there are 53. Attention concentrates. Four repositories carry most of the work; the rest are finished, or waiting for their idea to come back. Hubs make families. Once there are several sites of one kind, they need a hub and a naming rule. The loose ends are few, and visible. One site not serving, four without a sitemap, seven placeholders, four hosts to rename.
limits

The counts are of 21 October 2026. They change with every release. Commits are across all branches. Including working branches that were later merged. A version in the subject is how release commits are counted. Not every site marks releases that way. Sitemaps list what a site chooses to list. Not every file it serves. The version check looked at the usual paths. A site may publish its version elsewhere.
sources

The git history of the 53 SGit-AI__Website repositories on GitHub, all branches, and the files at the head of each, fetched on 21 October 2026; each site's home page, sitemap.xml and version file, and the DNS of each host, checked the same day. Related: plural for the family, singular for the site, v0.12 in numbers, how a memo becomes a release. Abstract: The PHP story site now holds enough data to go back in time and see how php2shell evolved, and that opens up stories beyond the headline. Provenance, which almost nobody does except Wikipedia. Building features against a real problem: 179 releases in three and a half days, each answering a need, none good enough the first time, and all of it a template for the next incident and for this newsroom. Who corrects their reporting: twelve correction requests are drafted, and one publisher, Amazon, changed "broadly exploited" to "broad exploitation attempts" without a note. A crisis with no named victim, which raises three questions at once: nobody has to disclose, nobody was hit, or sites were taken down for a danger that did not come. Detection: if an attack can be counted, it can be blocked, so why so few shared rules? The 17 entries in the ledger of sites that went dark, and what that cost. Who is being paid, when nobody is exploiting it. The flaws nobody watched: Zimbra's remote code execution is on CISA's exploited list with a national CERT reporting compromises, and got 16 news items to php2shell's 175. And how much of this was AI: AI helped find the flaws, but none of the public proofs of concept VulnCheck reviewed works the way the flaw does. If AI could do what people say it can now, where is the exploitation?
The side stories of php2shell, from the data the PHP site keeps, from provenance to how much of it was AI.
in-short

We now have data that lets us go back in time. The evolution of the story, not only its latest state. Provenance is rare. Wikipedia is the other place I have seen it done well. Features built against a real problem. 179 releases in three and a half days, none good enough the first time. Who corrects? Twelve correction requests drafted; one publisher changed its words without a note. No named victim. Nobody has to disclose, nobody was hit, or sites went dark for nothing? Detection is immature. If you can count attacks, you can block them. The sites that went dark, and what that cost. Follow the money. Who is being paid, when nobody is exploiting it? The flaws nobody watched. Real exploitation, a fraction of the coverage. How much was AI? It helped find the flaws; where is the AI-driven exploitation?
data

The PHP story site now keeps a lot: 418 sources in its evidence vault, each with its captures; a source watch of 913 pages that keeps a new snapshot whenever a page changes; and versioned views of the state of affairs. Because nothing is thrown away, we can go back in time and see the evolution, and that lets us ask questions beyond the headline. These are the ones I want to explore. Some we can answer now; most need the record to keep growing.
provenance

The first is provenance itself. It is very rare for a site to show where each of its claims comes from. The only site I have seen do it well is Wikipedia, and even there you cannot easily see what a reference said or whether it changed. The PHP site goes further: every claim points to a source, every source to a dated capture with its hash. That is what makes the rest of this article possible.
features

This project is also a case study in how features should be built. If you develop features in a vacuum, you are predicting the problem. Here, every feature is built to solve a specific problem we have, right now, and we zoom in and iterate. The PHP site went from its first commit on the morning of 22 October to 179 releases by the afternoon of 25 October. Some of those features would normally take a week, or a month. The key point is what happens when you use them: they are not good enough. The observability, the workflows, the UI: each one works, and each one immediately shows what it is missing. There is a lot of data to show, and the only way to understand how to show it is to see it and iterate. I wrote about one example, why agent loops are hard.
features

When this stabilises, we will have two things. A template for the next major incident, or the next major story. And a set of features to bring back to this newsroom: the observability is the first, and we are already finding its limits, its scalability, what works and what does not.
corrections

Once we know which parts of a story were wrong, the next question is who goes back and corrects them. How many publishers revisit what they wrote, change it, and say "we did not get this right"? And does anyone correct without acknowledging it? The PHP site's corrections liaison has twelve correction requests drafted, each quoting the publisher only from a capture. They are about two kinds of mistake. The first is the 70%: Wiz's headline said the flaws affect 70% of the internet, when its own post says PHP powers 70% of websites, and the BBC, CNN, Fortune and Clarín carried a version of it. The second is "exploited": headlines from WIRED and BankInfoSecurity said hackers exploited the flaws, when their own sources described attempts. None has been sent yet; I send each one myself.
corrections

And one publisher has already corrected without a note. Amazon's security blog said on 22 October that PHP2Shell "is now being broadly exploited in the wild". At 21:25 UTC that day it revised the sentence, as the PHP site's fact-check desk recorded, "without a note", to "now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild". That is a better sentence, and it is what the evidence supports. But anyone who quoted the first version is now quoting words that are no longer there, with nothing to tell them it changed. We only know because we kept both captures.
no-victim

The most interesting arc of the story is that, four days in, no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell. That touches two important points at once. First, organisations do not have to disclose this kind of exploitation, so the absence of a named victim is not proof of no victims. Second, if organisations have not been hit, then many of them probably took sites offline that did not need to be. You take a site offline when there is a clear and present danger. Unless a lot of applications are being compromised, which the evidence does not show, this looks like an overreaction, and that is worth measuring.
no-victim

Not to blame anyone. Somebody has to be accountable, in the sense of making the right decision. As a CISO I was always aware that you have a limited number of credits with the business, unless you are adding a lot of value. Taking a site offline spends a lot of them. If you do it because of a clear and present danger, and the danger is not there, you have a problem the next time you need to ask.
detection

Detection does not seem mature yet, both of whether a site is vulnerable and exploitable, and of intrusions, with WAF rules. There are two sides to that. Some say they will not share detection details because it would help attackers. But if you do not share them, you do not help the defenders, and defenders who do not know what to block cannot block it. And there is an inconsistency in the numbers. We have seen lots of figures about exploitation attempts. But if you can detect that an attack is happening, you should be able to put a rule on the WAF that blocks it. Cloudflare says its rules blocked the traffic it saw, and that attackers mutated their payloads to get past them; Switzerland's national cyber security centre says "even a web application firewall alone is not sufficient". We need good data on this, because we need good protections.
offline

This is the area I want to research most. Which sites went offline, what did that cost, which are still offline, why were they taken down, when are they coming back, and how much of it was acknowledged? The PHP site's ledger has 17 entries, from the Dutch national cyber security centre's own site, taken down "as a precaution", to Finland's and Latvia's government services, the Wikimedia Foundation, city councils in the UK, banks in Japan and Morocco, and, on 25 October, government portals in Nepal. Two are confirmed by the organisation; the rest come from the press. The community tracker lists 51 sites, with 50 back.
offline

Some of the most striking cases are security products themselves. The Dutch NCSC's inventory, at its last change on 23 October, listed 10 products from security and network vendors as vulnerable, 26 as not, and 16 under investigation. How many of their users knew that the products protecting them ran PHP? And then there is the economic question we have already written about: who pays for the fix.
money

Over time, I want to see whether money is flowing into this, and to whom. If there is little exploitation, it is not criminals making money, or not much. But a lot of teams are spending a lot of time on it: vendors, consultants, incident responders, extended-support providers, and every organisation that patched, tested, took something down and brought it back. Following the money means mapping who is being paid, and for what. Then we can do the calculation. If that money had instead gone into the model I described, paying maintainers to sign off versions, paying for the tests and the pipeline that make a patch routine, and paying for certification, would we not be in a much better place? I think so, but I want the numbers.
coverage

How fast the coverage faded: sources in the PHP site's evidence vault by publication day, 20 to 24 October. We also need to track the coverage over time. If you just follow the news, it is not sustainable: the energy goes, everyone moves on, and nothing changes. The evidence vault shows the curve: 117 of its sources were published on 21 October, the day of the release, 94 the next day, 34 the day after, and 8 on 24 October, though the latest days are partly the time it takes to capture them. So the real question is whether the conversation moved. Are we now talking about the sustainability of open source, or about who maintains the software everything runs on? That is a story the data can answer, given time.
nobody-watched

Attention against evidence, from the Pulse data: news items over 30 days against the furthest step of exploitation. The other big story is all the other vulnerabilities released at the same time, which got a fraction of the attention and, in some cases, have real exploitation behind them. We know the number of vulnerabilities is going to rise. The site has quietly started monitoring this, in a section called Pulse, which keeps, for 26 flaws, the evidence of exploitation as eight dated steps, and beside it the attention each one gets, never combined.
nobody-watched

The contrast is stark. php2shell had 175 English-language news items in the like-for-like count, a public proof of concept and exploitation attempts reported by a named party, and it is not on CISA's list of known exploited vulnerabilities. Zimbra's remote code execution flaw is on that list, and a national CERT reports compromises through it: 16 items. A SharePoint remote code execution flaw, on the list, with exploitation attempts reported: 1 item.
ai

The last question is the one I most want answered. We talk about AI discovering vulnerabilities and about mass exploitation by AI. But we have always had this. We have always had big vulnerabilities, some with brands and logos; we have had Metasploit; we have had automatic scanners for decades; and we have had mass exploitation before. AI did help find these flaws: the discovery came out of an AI-assisted research project, and the discoverers used AI models, as the reporting says. But on the other side, the evidence is thin. AhnLab, as reported, examined 100 related GitHub repositories and classed 27 as proofs of concept. Sophos, as reported, found working exploitation difficult even with AI support. And the PHP site records that none of the public proofs of concept reviewed by VulnCheck had the correct mechanism. Neither flaw is on CISA's exploited list.
ai

So, if AI can do now what people say it can do, and I am not saying it will not in the future, where is the exploitation? I think the answer is a mix of three things. Orchestrating this is hard. Someone needs a business model or an agenda to do it at scale. And, for many of these assets, the value of exploiting them, beyond making some noise, is probably not that significant. If there were a lot of value on the other side, people would be doing it. I could be wrong. That is why I want to answer it from the data we have, rather than from the headlines.
limits

These are questions, not findings. Most need more time and more data. No named victim is time-bounded. One statement would change it, and disclosure is not required. The ledger of sites taken offline is incomplete, and most of its entries come from the press. Attention counts are hard to compare. The like-for-like English-language count is used here; the PHP site warns that its wider counts, over different numbers of feeds, should not be compared row with row. The coverage curve includes capture lag for the latest days. The correction requests are drafted, not sent. The publishers have not yet been asked. The AI evidence on exploitation is as reported by AhnLab, Sophos and VulnCheck, through the press and the PHP site.
sources

My voice memo of 25 October 2026. The PHP story site at release v0.21.4, read on 25 October: its sources (data/sources.json, 418 sources), its state of affairs (data/state.json, version 3), its corrections requests (data/outreach.json) and fact-check record of Amazon's revision (data/factcheck.json), its ledger of systems taken offline (data/impact.json), its defence claims (data/claims.json, Cloudflare and the Swiss BACS on WAFs), its Pulse section (data/pulse.json), and its git history (179 releases since 22 October). Related: who maintains the PHP you run?, patch for breakfast, who signs for this?, sources and their shadows, why agent loops are hard, PHP October 2026, update 3. Abstract: In the rules of the game we wrote down which files an agent may change and found that, on a public repository, GitHub can enforce only part of it. This is the other part. A sidecar repository, which no agent can write to, holds the Agent Behaviour Policies, the policy for this repository, the approved hashes of every file that checks the agent's work, the public keys, and the private lists. At the end of each release it reads the release commit; checks the changed paths against the policy; compares the workflow and the tests with their approved copies; verifies GitHub's signed attestation that the approved tests passed on that exact commit, instead of running them again; runs its own checks, which the agent can neither see nor change; and only then deploys the site, which moves to the sidecar. We designed it assuming the worst: an agent that removes its hooks, rewrites the workflow, fakes statuses and adds workflows of its own. Each of those either does nothing or stops the deploy until the owner looks. It uses only what we already have: GitHub Actions, GitHub's attestations and its command-line tool, and our own signing. It is a design, not yet built, and it has residual risks we say plainly.
The sidecar end to end, from the agent's release push to the site's deployment.
in-short

A second repository the agent cannot write to. It holds the policy and the keys. It is the only thing that deploys. The site moves there. It treats the site's repository as data. It never runs that code with secrets. It trusts a signed check, not a status. Only from the approved workflow. Changed gates wait for the owner. Everything else goes straight out. Designed for full compromise. Each attack does nothing, or stops the deploy. No new tools. Actions, attestations, and our own signing.
why

In the rules of the game we set out five zones and found the limit of what GitHub enforces on this public repository: a hook and a guard job make getting round the rules a deliberate act, and a token without the right to change workflows turns the guard into a boundary. But the last zone, the rules themselves, cannot live in the same repository as the agent. Anything an agent can write, a compromised agent can rewrite. And there is a known gap: an older workflow, without the guard, may be able to come back.
why

So the memo's second idea: a sidecar. A separate repository, with its own CI, which the agents have no access to. It holds what the agents must not change, and it decides what goes live. The site's own pipeline still runs, still gives the agent fast feedback, and still does the expensive work. The sidecar checks that work, and adds the checks the agent should never see.
holds

The Agent Behaviour Policies and the repository's policy. The copy of the policy that counts. The lock. The approved hash of every file in the gates zone: the workflow, the validator, the test files, the build scripts and the reader's code. It changes only when the owner approves a change. Its own checks. Its own copy of the validator's rules and the voice, summaries and graph checks, pinned in the sidecar. The private lists, as secrets. The names that must never appear, the local key fragments the leak scan looks for. The agent cannot read them, so it cannot write around them. The public keys. Of each agent, from their key pairs, and of the owner. The site. The domain and the Pages deployment move here, so nothing else can publish. The record. A signed line for every release it deployed, or refused.
does

At the end of each release, in order: Read the release commit. The site's repository is public, so the sidecar can read dev and check out the commit with no credential at all. It deploys only commits that follow on from the last one it deployed. Check the paths. Compare the files changed since the last deployed release with the policy's zones. Content goes on. Identity and rules paths stop the run. Check the lock. Hash every gate file in the commit and compare with the lock. If they all match, the pipeline that tested this commit is the approved one. Verify the signed result. The site's CI attests a small results file: the commit, the hashes of the test files, and each test's outcome. The sidecar verifies the attestation with GitHub's own tool, requiring that it was signed by the site's repository, by the deploy workflow, for this exact commit.
does

Run its own checks. The cheap ones, on the files as committed: the voice, the summaries, the version, the private lists. Seconds, as we measured in where a check runs. Ask the owner when the gates changed. If any hash differs from the lock, the deploy job waits on an environment with the owner as required reviewer, showing the diff. On approval, the lock is updated with the new hashes. Deploy, and sign the outcome. Publish the site, and add a signed line to the record: the commit, the policy version, the checks run, the checks trusted, and the result. Nothing in it needs a new tool. GitHub Actions runs it. Artifact attestations are built into Actions; for a public repository they are recorded in a public transparency log, and GitHub's hosted runners already have the command-line tool that verifies them. Our own key pairs, the kind described in a secret is a QR code, sign the record.
trust

When the sidecar trusts a check and when it runs it again, depending on the lock and the attestation. The efficiency in the memo comes from here. The reader's tests are the slowest part of a release: 227 seconds in the last run, against 19 for validation and 44 for the deploy. The sidecar should not run them again if it can know they ran honestly. What makes that possible is what an attestation records. It is signed with a short-lived certificate tied to the identity of the workflow run, and it records the repository, the commit and the workflow that produced it. So the sidecar can ask a precise question: did the deploy workflow, on this commit, produce this result? And the lock answers the rest: was that workflow, and were those tests, the approved ones? If both answers are yes, the result is as good as one the sidecar produced itself, and it does not re-run anything.
trust

A commit status, or a green tick on a check, is not the same. Anything with the right token can post a status. An agent that can write to the repository may well be able to post one. The sidecar ignores them. The agents' own signatures fit here too, with a clear label. When the agents have their key pairs, they can sign their local test runs, and the sidecar can verify them against their public keys. That proves which agent claims to have run what. Under full compromise, the agent's key is compromised with it, so the sidecar treats an agent's signature as attribution, never as a reason to skip a check.
compromise

What a fully compromised agent can try, and what the sidecar does about each attempt. The memo asked for the analysis to assume the agent is fully compromised: it can do anything its credentials allow. So, attack by attack: It removes its hooks. Nothing in the sidecar relies on them. They were there to catch mistakes early. It rewrites the workflow, the validator or a test. The lock differs. The deploy waits for the owner, who sees exactly which gate changed. It brings back an old workflow without the guard. The lock differs, so the same thing happens. This closes the gap left in the first article. It fakes a status or a check. The sidecar reads neither. It forges a signed result. It cannot get a certificate for the deploy workflow without running the deploy workflow; and if it changes the deploy workflow to sign a false result, the lock differs.
compromise

It adds a workflow to steal secrets. The site's repository holds no secrets today: its workflow uses none. The Pages deployment, the private lists and the owner's approval all live in the sidecar. The design depends on keeping it that way. It rewrites the history. The sidecar deploys only a commit that follows on from the last one it deployed. Anything else waits for the owner. It plants code that runs during the tests. When the sidecar has to run the tests itself, it runs them in a job with no secrets and no write permission, and keeps only the result.
compromise

It rings the doorbell, or never rings it. If the site's CI triggers the sidecar, the token for that lives in the site's repository, where the agent can find it. So it is only a doorbell: the sidecar ignores what the message says and reads the commit itself, and it also runs on a schedule, so silence does not stop a release check. It leaks a key, or a name, in an article. Content is free in the policy, but the sidecar's leak scan uses the private lists the agent has never seen.
residual

Total compromise of the agent is covered; other things are not: The owner's approval is the last line. A compromised agent can ask for it with a plausible reason. The approval page shows the diff, and that is what has to be read. The sidecar's own owner and GitHub itself. If either is compromised, so is the sidecar. That is outside this design. Content within the rules. An agent can still publish a bad but valid article. The sidecar checks rules, not judgement; the editor's review does that. The reader's code in the free zone, until the lock covers it. The policy now lists it as a gate; the lock has to hash it from the first day. It is a design. None of it is built. The first version will find gaps this one missed.
cost

Two repositories instead of one, and a few changes to the site's pipeline: attest the test results; remove the deploy job and the domain, which move to the sidecar; keep validation and the tests for fast feedback. A release that changes only content would cost the sidecar its own checks, a few seconds, plus verification and the deploy, instead of running the tests a second time. A release that changes a gate costs the owner a look at the diff. Over the last eleven days that would have been a look at 62 of 227 commits, which is too many; the answer is to batch machinery changes, not to drop the rule.
next

For the owner to decide, in order: Create the sidecar repository, with no agent given access to it. Put the policy, the lock and the private lists there. Add the attestation to the site's test job. Build the sidecar workflow, with the owner as required reviewer on its deployment. Run it alongside the current deploy for a week, comparing what each would have published. Move the domain, and remove the deploy from the site's repository.
limits

Nothing here is built. It is a design, and a proposal to the owner. The timings are from one run. The jobs of v0.13.38, on 22 October 2026. The GitHub features are from documentation. Attestations, environments and their availability, read on 22 October 2026, not yet tested here. The agents' key pairs are not yet in use. Their signatures are planned, and are attribution only. The secrets claim is about today's workflow. It uses none; a later change could add one.
sources

My voice memo of 22 October 2026; this repository's workflow at v0.13.38 and the job timings of its last run; GitHub's documentation, read that day, on artifact attestations, the verify command, OpenID Connect claims, deployment environments, the events that trigger workflows, and rulesets; and the research and policy in the rules of the game. Related: where a check runs, behaviour policies from the checks, the delegation record, a secret is a QR code.
