Abstract: With the reader's vault live on newsroom.sgit.ai, the next brief is about what a reader does with it, and it starts from one image: the site is an inbox that starts empty. Every piece that arrives, an article this site wrote or a story the wire aggregated, is something I have not decided about yet, and the first thing I do with it is decide, in a second, with nothing loaded: read now, read later, not for me, more of this, less of this, comment, move it to another persona. That is the inbox mode, and it is thinking fast. Reading is the slow mode, and it is where the marks live: highlights of different kinds, not one or two as Medium has but interesting, great phrase, not sure, fact, evidence, question, each a node in a graph the reader owns and that connects to the graphs this site already publishes for every article; the pane on the right becomes about the piece in front of you; the piece can be shown with every term a link, or classified sentence by sentence. The signals that come free, scroll depth, time while awake, where you came from and went to, are kept the way the meter keeps them: in the browser, in the vault when you ask, shown to an agent only by your read key. Comments for the newsroom go down the write-only lane, signed by the persona's key, with a copy kept. None of it is gamified: a decision is offered where you would take it, never at the end of a page to make you scroll there. The brief is the second part. The first part is why I could not have written it two days ago: the properties of what runs are the constraints I think with, and the constraints are what let me think.

Two modes. The inbox mode decides what happens to a piece with nothing loaded; the reading mode is where the marks and the signals live. Everything stays in the reader's browser and vault, and the reader chooses what an agent sees. The vault is live, and I have a brief for what to do with it. But the brief is the second half of this article, because the first half is about why I have it at all.
short

I could not have written this brief two days ago. Not for lack of time or ideas. For lack of constraints. Until the passkey worked and the sign-in was not needed, until a door was per path, until the sync was one file per device, I did not know the properties of the thing I would be writing for. The properties are what let me think. The site is an inbox, and it starts empty. Every piece that arrives, an article this site wrote or a story the wire brought in, is something the reader has not decided about. Deciding is the work; reading is one of the decisions. Two modes. The inbox mode decides, fast, with nothing loaded: read now, read later, not for me, more like this, less like this, comment, move to a persona. The reading mode does, slowly, with the piece open and its context loaded.
short

No gamification. A decision is offered where the reader would take it, never at the end of a page so that they scroll there. A signal the site engineered is not a signal. Marks build the reader's own graph. Not one highlight but kinds: interesting, great phrase, not sure, fact, evidence, question. Each is a node, connected to the graphs this site already publishes for every article. Meaning comes from connectivity, and the reader's graph is worth more the more it is used. The signals come free and stay yours. Scroll depth, time while awake, where you came from and went to. Kept as the meter keeps everything: in the browser, in the vault when you press Update, seen by an agent only through a read key you gave it.
short

Personas have keys. Each persona is disposable and has its own key pair, so a comment to the newsroom is signed by the persona that made it, goes down the write-only lane, and leaves a copy in your vault. The reply is a new version of the article. The test is simple. It works if reading here, with a graph that grows, is better than reading without one.
constraints

The vault is live ends with a sentence I want to start from, because this article is the proof of it. The brief below did not exist on 10 October. I had the ideas; some of them are years old. What I did not have was the shape of the thing they would run on, and without the shape I could not hold them.
constraints

This is not the usual point about agents making things cheap to build, true as that is, and I made it in Pay after you read: the more you have, the faster you go. It is a point about thinking. When the vault did not exist, "a reader's marks on an article" was an open question in every direction: where would they live, who could read them, what would it cost, would the reader have to sign in, could a mark be sent to us and by whom. Each of those questions is big enough to stop a brief. Now each has an answer, and the answers are not mine, they are the properties of what runs. Marks live in the reader vault, in a file per device. Nobody can read them but the reader, and an agent the reader gives a read key to. Writing them costs one commit when the reader presses a button. There is no sign-in. A persona can have a key pair in the master, so a mark can be signed. Those five facts close off most of the design space, and what is left is small enough to think about in a morning.
constraints

I did not expect this, and I think it is the more important half of the feedback loop. I had it as: use it, miss it, build it, use it again. It is also: build it, learn its properties, and only then have the next idea, because the next idea is made of the properties. The constraints limit what I can write, and without that limit I would write everything and finish nothing. So the order matters. Ship first, think second, and do not pretend the thinking could have come first.
brief
For the session that runs newsroom.sgit.ai. Written by the sgit.ai site session for Dinis Cruz, 12 October 2026, on top of the vault pane at v0.11.0. Dinis decides what ships, and is the first user.
inbox

Start from this image and most of the rest follows. The site has two kinds of content now: the articles it writes, and the wire it reads from a vault that other agents keep, which will grow into sources the reader chooses to follow. For a reader, both arrive the same way: as pieces they have not decided about. So the site, for that reader, is an inbox. It starts empty, cleared, nothing to see. As pieces arrive, each one waits for a decision. When the decision is made, the piece leaves the inbox and the decision becomes a record. The state the site should always be able to return to is empty. This is a different thing from a front page, and it is why the front page can stay the Editor's: the inbox is the reader's view of the same pieces, and it is personal because the decisions are.
modes

Kahneman's distinction between thinking fast and thinking slow is the right frame, and I would build the two modes to match it. The inbox mode is fast. The reader meets a headline, a line, and where it came from, and nothing is loaded: not the article, not its graph, not the reader's context for it. The only thing to do is decide what happens next, and the decision should take a second: read now; read later; not for me; more like this; less like this; comment; move it to another persona. Each is one tap, offered at the piece, and each clears the piece from the inbox. For the wire especially, "not for me" is the most important button, and the most useful signal: it says which concern the join got wrong.
modes

The reading mode is slow. The piece is open, its context is loaded, and the pane on the right, which today holds the vault and the meter, becomes about this piece: its graph beside the text, the reader's marks on it, the decisions already taken, and what it cost. This is where the reader does something with the piece, and it is where the next three sections happen.
modes

The split matters because today the newsroom asks for the reader's judgment at the end of the article, where the meter's card is. That was the right place for a rating that sets a price, and it is the wrong place for a decision, because a decision at the end is a reason to scroll to the end, and that is gamification: a signal we engineered, which is then not a signal. The rule for both modes is that a decision is offered at the moment the reader would take it, and nothing is placed to make them go somewhere.
marks

The reader's graph is made of marks, each with a kind; the marks land on the public graphs this site already publishes; a chosen slice goes to the newsroom, signed; a new version comes back. Medium lets you highlight, and I used it, and what I did not like is that it had one or two kinds of highlight and I have six. When I read, I mark things for different reasons: this is interesting; this is a great phrase; I am not sure about this; this is a fact; this is evidence; this is a question. Each of those is a different kind of node, and the moment the site lets me say which, I am not highlighting any more. I am building my graph.
marks

A mark is a node. It carries the phrase, the article and its version, the persona that made it, the kind, and the time. A comment is a node with an edge to the phrase it is about. An inbox decision is an edge from the persona to the piece. Marks land on the public graphs. Every article here already has a graph as JSON beside it, and every wire story has entities, claims and a quote. A mark on a phrase links to the node that phrase belongs to, so "not sure" on a claim is an edge to that claim, and a reader who marks the same claim in two articles has connected them without naming anything.
marks

Meaning comes from connectivity. A phrase marked three times, from three articles, is a topic the reader did not have to declare. That is what Fractal Semantic Graphs are for, and what Obsidian users already know: the graph is a by-product of use, and it is the most valuable thing the reader makes. The vocabulary view, on demand. Not always on, because it is noisy. But a switch that turns every term in the piece into a link into the vocabulary, the facts, the connections, the way some of our vaults already do, so that the reader can walk from a word to everything it touches, including their own marks.
marks

The piece, classified. Another switch: the same text shown by what its sentences are, facts, observations, evidence, claims, questions, and by tone or confidence. The site's agents already read its articles this way, as five readers; the reader should see that view and be able to disagree with it, sentence by sentence, and the disagreement is a mark.
marks

This is where the economics of the whole thing sit, and I want to say it plainly. The more a reader marks, the more they use the site; the more they use it, the more they pay, by the meter; and the more they pay, the more their own graph is worth to them, because it is theirs and it is connected. That loop only closes if one thing is true: reading here, with a graph that grows, is a better experience than reading without one. Every feature in this brief is a bet on that sentence, and the vault is what makes the graph the reader's rather than ours.
signals

The reading mode can record four things without asking, and it should, because they are useful to the reader first. How far. The scroll depth, which the meter already charges by. The bottom of the page means read; a little means glanced. Shown to the reader as a simple "you read this" or "you read a third of this", which is the information I most often want about my own past reading. How long, awake. Time on the piece counted only while there is movement, scroll or pointer or key, so that a tab left open for an hour is not an hour of reading. This is an experiment: whether movement is a good enough proxy for attention is something to measure, not assume.
signals

From and to. The page the reader came from and the page they went to. The site already knows the latter; the former is what lets it answer "how did I get here", and give the reader back and forward through their own reading, which will matter more once search works. The decisions. Every inbox decision and every mark, with the persona and the time. All of it is kept the way the meter keeps everything today: in local storage as it happens, in the reader vault when they press Update, as records and never totals, and shown to any agent only through a read key the reader gave it. The reader can see every record, which is the other half of not gamifying: the signals are the reader's, and they can watch what they produce.
lane

The reason this brief needs the vault and not just local storage is in two places. The first is personas. I will have several, and one of them is the newsroom's editor: I read every article, I see what works, I review it, and I need to comment on everything. That is a different lens from my CISO persona or my founder persona or my general-interest one, and the inbox mode's "move to a persona" is how a piece gets to the right one. Personas should be disposable, and each should have a key pair of its own, kept in the master vault as the passkey design describes: one to sign, one to receive. What the editor persona signs is not what the CISO persona signs, and a persona can be handed to an agent as a read key to its slice of the graph, and only its slice.
lane

The second is the lane. A mark or a comment the reader addresses to the newsroom, "not sure" on a claim, a wrong flag on a wire story, a comment on a sentence, goes the way sending your reading already goes: encrypted in the browser to the newsroom's published key, into a write-only lane only the newsroom's agent reads. Two things are new. It is signed by the persona's key, so the newsroom knows which of my personas said it and that it was me. And a copy stays in the reader's vault, so the reader always knows what was sent, which is the privacy property: the user controls what goes, and can see it afterwards. The reply, as with the brief in I miss it, is a new version of the article, and the version page shows it.
lane

In my own case I will go further and give the agent that edits the site a read key to my editor persona's vault, so that it sees every mark I make as the editor, not only the ones I send. That is my choice, as a reader, and it is the point: the same mechanism serves a reader who sends nothing and a reader who shares everything.
order

The inbox mode on the front page and the wire: the seven decisions as one tap at each piece, clearing it, recorded as an edge in local storage. Test with the wire first, where "not for me" is the signal the join needs. The pane about the piece. On an article, the right-hand pane shows the article's graph, the reader's marks and decisions on it, and what it cost. The vault and the meter move to a tab of the same pane. Marks with kinds. Select a phrase, choose a kind, see it in the pane and in the graph. Six kinds to start; the reader can add one. The free signals: depth as "you read this", awake time, from and to, in the reader's records, visible to the reader on the account page. The persona key pairs in the master, as the passkey design specifies, generated at random on first use, one pair per persona.
order

The signed lane: a mark addressed to the newsroom, signed, sent, copied to the vault; and the reply as a version. The views: vocabulary on demand, and the piece classified, starting from the five readers' output where it exists. An experiment per feature. Each of these is small enough to ship in two versions and compare, and that is how they should be built: a synthetic reader, two variants, a measurement, and the one that holds. The inbox decisions, the kinds of mark and the awake-time proxy are the first three to test.
not

No decision placed at the end of a page to make the reader reach it. No signal sent anywhere without the reader pressing something. No mark the reader cannot see in their own records. No server of ours.
limits

None of the brief is built. The vault, the meter, the personas, the share lane, the article graphs and the five readers' views exist; the inbox mode, the marks, the signals and the signed lane are a design. The science is a frame, not a finding. Thinking fast and slow is a useful way to split the two modes; whether readers behave that way on this site is what the experiments are for. Awake time is a guess. Movement as a proxy for attention is an assumption to measure. The economics are a bet. The loop closes only if reading with a graph is better than reading without one, and one reader's experience, mine, is where that will first be tested. If you build reading tools, or you want to be a reader whose marks build a graph you own, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on the morning of 12 October 2026, recorded after the newsroom's overnight releases and before I had tested the vault pane myself, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The brief builds on what runs: the vault pane and the activity vault design at newsroom.sgit.ai v0.11.0, the meter, the personas, the share lane and the article graphs, as described in The vault is live, Pay after you read and Two agents, one vault. The two figures were drawn for this article. Related: The passkey opens the vault, I miss it, so it is working, Fractal Semantic Graphs and One article, five readers.

Abstract: It is easy to spend a lot of money on model calls without seeing where it goes, and the user is the person who sees least. So I asked for a small, focused agent behaviour policy about tokens: in observe mode first, it should show the user, in a box of ASCII under each answer, how many tokens the session has read, how many came from the cache, how many it wrote, how big the context is and roughly what it has cost. This site's agent built it as a Claude Code hook of 132 lines with a policy file, and tested it. A prompt cannot do this job: asked to report its own usage, the model said twice, correctly, that it could not see the numbers. The hook gave it the exact figures, one turn behind, in about a millisecond. Building it found a bug in our own session report, which had been counting every response two or three times, because the transcript repeats a response's usage on each of its content blocks. It also found that, in this version of Claude Code, the transcript a hook can read carries the system prompt and every tool definition, though the documentation does not say so. This session has read 99% of its input from the cache, which at list prices is the difference between about $170 and about $1,950. The other tools vary: Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor have hooks and usage commands, the chat apps show only limits. And this is the brief for tokens.hook.sgit.ai, a small site for a small, mission-critical piece of code.
The tokens hook: a policy file, a hook that counts and prices each response, and where its output goes.
in-short

A behaviour policy about tokens. Observe first: show the user what the session reads, caches, writes and costs. A prompt cannot do it. The model cannot see its own usage, and said so twice. A hook can. Exact figures, one turn behind, in about a millisecond a call. It found a bug in our own report. Usage repeats on every content block; counting lines counted responses two or three times. The transcript holds more than the docs say. In this version, the system prompt and every tool definition. Caching is most of the bill. This session read 99% of its input from the cache. Other tools differ. Hooks and usage commands in Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor; only limit bars in the chat apps. A site for one small hook. tokens.hook.sgit.ai: the code, the policy, the graph, the tests, the releases.
why

Models are paid for by the token, and an agent spends tokens in ways nobody sees: every call re-sends the system prompt, the tool definitions and the whole conversation, and the only thing that makes that affordable is the prompt cache. Anthropic's Claude Code team put it plainly in Prompt caching is everything: "we run alerts on our prompt cache hit rate and declare SEVs if they're too low", because "A few percentage points of cache miss rate can dramatically affect cost and latency." That is a reason to treat tokens as one more thing an agent behaviour policy governs, with its own small policy: what to count, what to show, what limits to set, and what to do when one is crossed. The first mode is to observe. Before anything is limited, the user should be able to see what is happening.
prompt

The same two-turn conversation in headless Claude Code, once with a system prompt and once with the tokens hook. The obvious first attempt is a line in the system prompt or in a project's instructions: report your token usage and cost at the end of every answer. This site's agent tried it, with a two-turn conversation in headless Claude Code. The model was honest both times: "I can't give you these figures… Any split or dollar amount from me would be invented." The numbers existed, 37,019 tokens of input in the first turn, $0.05 and then $0.09, but not anywhere the model could read them.
prompt

Then the same conversation with the tokens hook. Before each prompt, the hook added the running totals as context; after each answer, it showed the box to the user. In the second turn, the model reported a context of 37,087 tokens, 353 output tokens and about $0.05, which were exactly the first turn's figures. They are one turn behind, because a hook that runs before the answer cannot count it. A prompt can ask for behaviour; only a hook can supply data, which is why hooks are the sweet spot for anything that has to be true rather than hoped for.
see

Every hook receives a small JSON object; the hooks reference lists its common fields, among them the session id and transcript_path. No event carries token usage in general: the only token fields are on a resumed or forked session's start, context_tokens and estimated_cache_write_usd. Everything else has to come from the transcript, a JSON file with one line per event. Two findings came out of reading it.
see

Each response is written several times. One API response with text, thinking and a tool call becomes several lines, and each one repeats the response's full usage. In this session's transcript, 2,621 lines carried usage, for 1,165 responses; 849 responses appeared more than once, always with identical figures. Counting lines gave 1.06 billion cache-read tokens; counting responses gave 459 million. This session's own status report, the ABP block at the end of each answer, had been counting lines since it was written: it said "2.9M out · 1.0B cached" when the truth was 1.1 million and 460 million. It now counts each message id once.
see

The transcript carries the request, not only the conversation. The documentation does not say whether a hook can see what is sent to the model. In this version of Claude Code, 2.1.300, it can: the transcript has prompt_snapshot records holding the system prompt, in 13 parts, and all 49 tool definitions, about 34,000 and 198,000 characters. A marker added to the system prompt for a test appeared there too. Two consequences follow. A token hook can see the fixed cost of every call; at about four characters a token, the tool definitions alone are around 50,000 tokens, six times the system prompt. And anything that can read the transcript can read everything the model was told, so a token hook should handle numbers only and never send text anywhere. This is an undocumented internal format, and it may change.
hook

The hook is one Python file of 132 lines and a policy file. Every time it runs, it seeks to where it stopped last time, reads only the new lines, counts each response once, prices it by its model, and saves the totals. The first run on this session's 66 MB transcript took 252 milliseconds; every run after it took about one millisecond inside the hook, and about 31 milliseconds including starting Python. If the file gets shorter, as it can after a compaction or a restore, it starts again.
hook

The policy carries the version, the mode, the limits and the prices, with their source. Prices are per model, from Anthropic's pricing page: a five-minute cache write is 1.25 times the base input price, a one-hour write twice, a read a tenth, and "Cache hits and refreshes on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are priced at 0.05x the base input price." The modes are the ones I would like for every policy: observe shows and logs; warn also warns when a limit is crossed; enforce blocks the next prompt once the session's budget is spent. Where the output goes decides who sees it. A systemMessage on Stop is shown to the user under the answer. Additional context on UserPromptSubmit goes to the model, so it can be frugal. A log line per event stays on the machine. Here is the box for this session, as the hook drew it while this article was written:
hook

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ tokens · observe · policy 0.1.0 │ │ calls 1,193 responses │ │ input 474.0M: 467.6M cache read, 6.4M written, 2.4K fresh │ │ cache ██████████ 99% read from cache │ │ context ████░░░░░░ 361.4K of 1.0M │ │ output 1.1M (253.0K thinking) │ │ cost ~$171.68 at policy prices · cache saved ~$1,784.03 │ │ ! over the session budget of $25.00 │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Claude Code's own estimate for the session, which it writes into the transcript from time to time, was about $175, including the helper model and the agents. At list prices, reading those 467 million tokens fresh instead of from the cache would have cost about $1,780 more. The cost is at list prices; on a subscription the bill is different, but the cache share matters just as much to the limits.
elsewhere

Claude Code already shows a lot without any hook. The status line receives the session's cost, the context window's size and use, and the latest call's cache reads and writes, and it updates as messages arrive; /usage and /context show the same from inside the session. For a team, the OpenTelemetry export sends a claude_code.token.usage metric with types for input, output, cache reads and cache writes, and an event per API request with its tokens and cost; prompt text is only included if OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS is set. That is the central telemetry collector, already built.
elsewhere

The hook still earns its place, because it is a policy: it carries limits and modes, it can tell the model, it can block, and it is the same small file wherever it runs. For a collector without OpenTelemetry, it can also send numbers, never text, to an sgit append lane, which a sender can write to but not read. Locally, that took the hook from about 31 to about 96 milliseconds a call; all 20 test events arrived, with nine fields each and no text.
tools
Where the token numbers are, tool by tool: what a hook can see and what the user is shown.
tools

The coding agents are converging on the same shape. OpenAI's Codex CLI has hooks for prompts, tools and stops, a /status command that shows "token usage" and "remaining context capacity", and OpenTelemetry. Google's Gemini CLI has hooks before and after each model call, and its /stats command shows "token usage and cached token savings". Cursor added hooks in version 1.7 on 29 September 2025, "to observe, control, and extend the Agent loop"; its documented hooks carry context tokens only before a compaction, and its admin API reports cache writes, cache reads and cost. GitHub Copilot moved to usage-based billing on 1 June 2026, where the cost "depends on … the model and the number of tokens consumed". Cline shows prompt tokens, completion tokens, cache writes, cache reads and cost on every task. The chat apps show least: Claude.ai has bars for the five-hour session and the week, and I found no token count per conversation in Claude.ai or ChatGPT.
tools

Caching works differently in each. OpenAI's is on by default and discounts reused tokens "up to 95%"; Gemini's implicit caching is on by default for its recent models, with savings passed on automatically. The policy file is where those differences belong: one hook, one price table per provider.
site

I would like this to live at tokens.hook.sgit.ai, as an example of how a mission-critical hook should be run: a small code base, mapped completely, measured, and released like any other software. Hooks are kernel code made the argument; this is the first hook to get the treatment. The code and the policy. The hook, the policy file and its schema, under version control, with releases signed and tagged. The graph. Every input field, every output, every mode and every limit, as a graph that links to the line of code that handles it. The tests. Fixtures of real transcripts with known totals, including the repeated usage lines, a rewritten file and a missing model price, run on every change. The numbers. Time per call cold and warm, on transcripts from 1 MB to 100 MB, published with each release.
site

Install and distribute. For one user, a few lines of settings; for an organisation, managed settings, which Claude Code applies "above every other level", or a plugin; for sgit users, a vault with the hook, its policy and its releases, and an append lane beside it. Other tools. The same policy file read by a Codex hook and a Gemini CLI hook, once their payloads are mapped.
limits

One tool, one version. The hook ran in Claude Code 2.1.300; the transcript format is internal and may change. The prompt test was small. Two turns each, one model; other models may guess where this one refused. Costs are at list prices. Subscriptions, discounts and regional pricing change the bill. The token estimate for tool definitions is rough. Characters divided by four. The other tools are from their documentation. Not run for this article. tokens.hook.sgit.ai does not exist yet. It is the proposal. If you are trying to see where your agents' tokens go, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Billing is usually a server problem: a server, a database, a balance every action has to update, race conditions, and either a bottleneck or a scheduler to keep it all in step. This is an exploration of doing it the other way round, on the client, with vaults. Each user gets a billing vault that both they and I can write to. The user's browser meters its own activity and appends it there, signed with the user's key, the way this newsroom's meter already works. When the user pays, their browser adds the credit straight away, so they can carry on. My admin vault, which can be offline for a while, later reconciles payments with Stripe, from my browser, and commits a validation back into the user's vault, signed with the admin key, so anyone can check it. Credit is then unvalidated, validated, or not valid, and the product keeps working on unvalidated credit, because on the client it costs us nothing. Since the vault's first commit is pinned and every commit is signed, we always know who wrote what. The one server left, the sgit upload server, does a light check only: is the key valid, and is there credit, read from a cached, signed value through a small credits API. Four parties, each with its own key: the admin vault, the user, the upload server and the API. And because the user's data lives in their vault, it travels with them across our sites. It is all PKI from here. Where it lives is open: user.sgit.ai, or billing.sgit.ai, so others can use it too. This is a proposal, with the open questions written down.
The proposed design: a user's billing vault, the admin vault, Stripe, the credits API and the upload server.
in-short

Billing is usually a server problem. A database, a balance every action updates, and races. This proposal does it on the client. Each user has a billing vault; their browser keeps the meter. Two writers, two keys. The user signs activity; the admin signs the validation of credit. Credit now, validated later. The user carries on straight away; the admin side catches up. Stripe is reconciled from the admin's browser. Payments are read, matched and validated. One server, one light check. The upload server asks: is the key valid, and is there credit? The user's data travels with them. Across every site, because it lives in their vault. It is a proposal, on parts that run. The billing vault is not built yet; the meter and the account in the reader's vault are.
problem

Every time I have built billing, it has been the same shape. You need a server and a database. Every action a user takes has to update something central, a balance, a usage count, and the moment two actions arrive at once you have a race condition on that balance. You can try to make a file the single source of truth, but keeping one file in sync across many writers is hard. The usual way out is to append first and update later: write every event to a log, and work out the balance from it. But then either every action goes through the thing that updates the balance, and it becomes the bottleneck, or the update runs on a schedule, a cron job or a set of Lambda functions, which works, and is messy, and is one more thing to run, watch and pay for.
have

What made me look at this again is that most of the pieces already exist on our sites. A meter, and an account in the reader's own vault. This newsroom already charges per use, without a server keeping the balance: every reader starts with £5 of credit, each page draws a few pence from it, and the balance can go below zero until they top up with a £5 payment link, live since 11 October. I wrote about why in paying after the value. The account is kept in the browser and, when the reader opens their vault with a passkey, carried into it: one file per device, a balance consolidated across devices, and a lane that browsers without the passkey can write to. What is not built is the check: the page a payment returns to adds the credit, and does not verify it. The reading account, as built lists every piece.
have

Append lanes. A vault can have a lane that others write to and only its owner reads. On this site that is already in use: in the editor's channel, "An append lane on the reader vault that any browser with a link can write to and none can read, with a key pair made in the reader's browser". And from secrets on public keys: "Append lanes are already write-only inboxes, read with an enum key, and this site has measured a hundred writers on one." Version control. A vault is versioned. Every change is a commit, and two writers' changes can be seen, ordered and merged, which is exactly what a balance kept in a file was missing. Keys. PKI everywhere set the direction: every message, secret and handover starts with a signature, and the public keys live in a register, at pki.sgit.ai, that anyone can check.
idea

So the idea is to do user management, activity tracking and billing on the client, with vaults. Where it lives is a question in itself. It could be user.sgit.ai, with api.user.sgit.ai for its client code. Or, because we want it to be easy for others to use, our other sites and other people's, the billing part could stand on its own: billing.sgit.ai, with api.billing.sgit.ai. Either way, the API sites would be released the same way as our others. The insight that makes it work is a simple one. A user very rarely runs several clients at the same time. The race condition that hurts a central server, many writers on one balance, mostly does not exist for one person's own activity. And for the cases where it does, two tabs or a laptop and a phone, the vault's version control already does the merging.
idea

So each user has a vault that tracks their own activity. Their browser collects what they do, at intervals, and appends it to a lane in that vault. That is the same model as this newsroom's meter, use first, then buy or top up, but with the record kept in a vault rather than only in one browser, so it can be backed up, synced, checked and billed.
writers

The design settles on one billing vault per user, which two parties can write to. The user writes activity. Their browser commits what they used, signed with the user's key. That record belongs to them: they can read it, keep it and take it elsewhere. The admin validates credit. When the user comes back from paying, their browser adds the credit straight away, with a signed claim. Later, the admin side checks that claim against Stripe and commits a validation into the same vault, signed with the admin key. Because it is signed, anyone can verify it against the admin's public key, and nobody else, the user included, can write a validation that verifies. A validation record could be as small as this. The field names are a sketch, not a format:
writers

{ "billing_vault": "the vault's id", "claims": [ { "claim": "the user's claim commit", "stripe_event": "the event's id", "pence": 500, "status": "validated" } ], "validated_balance_pence": 4210, "covers_activity_to": "the last activity commit counted", "as_of": "2026-10-21T10:00:00Z", "valid_until": "2026-10-28T10:00:00Z", "signed_by": "the admin key's fingerprint", "signature": "over everything above" } Each side signs only what it is responsible for. The user can add credit their browser believes in, but cannot make it validated, and the admin cannot invent activity the user did not sign.
stripe

The other half is a central admin vault, which I control. Usage data flows into it from the users' vaults: close to anonymised, but tied to the user, so it can be billed. And it is where payments are reconciled with Stripe, from the admin's browser. How that reconciliation should work needs some care, because of how Stripe works: Webhooks need a server. Stripe's documentation says "Registered webhook endpoints must be publicly accessible HTTPS URLs", and its webhooks are signed with a shared secret, an HMAC with SHA-256, not with a public key. That does not fit a design with no server to receive them. So the admin side reads instead. Stripe's API can "List events, going back up to 30 days", so the admin's browser can pull recent payments when it runs, rather than wait for a push.
stripe

The key that reads Stripe stays on the admin's machine. Stripe is plain that "Only publishable keys are safe to expose outside your application's backend". The admin's browser, on my machine, plays the role of that backend, with a restricted key that can only read. A payment can say which vault it is for. A payment link can carry a client_reference_id, which Stripe describes as "a unique string of your choice", and returns with the completed payment. It should be the billing vault's id, never anything secret.
stripe

So the flow is: the user is sent to Stripe with a payment link tagged with their billing vault; Stripe sends them back to a page that gives them the credit, and their browser adds it straight away and appends a signed claim, "I paid"; later, the admin's browser lists recent payments, matches each claim to a payment, and commits a signed validation. Two-way sync between the two vaults, with each side writing only its own records. A top-up, step by step: the payment link, the signed claim, the admin's signed validation and the upload server's check.
when

When should a payment count? The user should be able to use what they paid for straight away. That has to be immediate. So the credit goes into their browser the moment they come back from Stripe, and they carry on. The check comes afterwards, as a layer on top. The admin side does not need to be online when the user pays; it can catch up hours later. When it does, it adds a note to the user's vault, signed by us as the commercial authority: payment validated, or payment not accepted. Nothing central sits in the path of the user's work. The product keeps working, and the credit simply moves from unvalidated to validated. So credit can be in one of three states: Credit not yet validated. The user paid, or says they did, and the admin side has not checked yet. Normal, and short-lived.
when

Credit validated. The admin side matched it to a payment in Stripe, and signed it. Credit not valid. No matching payment. In our case this is unlikely: it means an attack, or a bug. That is why the product should carry on with the credit the user has, validated or not. Most of what it meters runs on the client, so letting a user carry on with unvalidated credit costs us nothing. And Stripe's own guidance fits this order: "You can't rely on triggering fulfillment only from your checkout landing page, because your customers aren't guaranteed to visit that page." The admin side reads Stripe directly, so a payment whose user never came back can still be credited, and one that is slow to confirm, like a bank debit, which "can take 2-14 days to confirm the payment", simply stays unvalidated for longer.
threat

The question that sizes this design is the one in who are you protecting against?. Here, the party that could cheat is the user, by gaming the client: adding credit they did not pay for, or leaving out activity. In the short term that is unlikely, and it is also very easy to detect. Every claim has to match a payment in Stripe, every commit is signed, and a claim with no payment behind it shows up as not valid the next time the admin side runs. So the design does not try to make cheating impossible on the client. It makes it visible, and it puts the hard check where a mistake would cost us money: at the server.
shared

There is a more general idea underneath this. The billing vault is shared by an untrusted party, the user, and a trusted one, us. Once the vault exists, we pin its first commit. From then on, every later commit can be checked for consistency against it: that it descends from that first commit, and that it is signed by a key we know. That gives a two-way channel between the two parties, through the vault, where we always know who did what. The user writes activity and claims; we write validations; and because of PKI, neither can pass off their writing as the other's. Billing is the first use, and the same pattern fits any place where a user and a service need to keep a shared record that both can trust.
server

Most of our sites already run with no server of their own. The one that remains in this picture is the sgit upload server, which stores vaults, and it is also where usage costs us money, in storage and transfer. So that is where the check belongs, and it should stay light: Is the key valid? A PKI check, against the register. Is there credit? A read of the user's latest signed validation record, verified against the admin's public key. The upload server should not compute a balance or keep a database of its own. It reads a cached, signed value, through a small credits API with its own simple definition, separate from the rest. A cached value can be slightly out of date, so the record carries a valid_until, and the upload server can also count what it serves, so the units that cost real money are measured where they happen, not reported by the client.
server
Today, the access key gates use of the upload server, but it does not meter it: vault creation, for example, is not tracked per user. That is the gap this design fills.
parties

Put together, there are four parties, each with its own role and its own key: The admin vault. Writes the licensing and validation records, collects the usage, and reconciles with Stripe. The user. Commits their own activity, and owns the record of it. The upload server. The inline billing unit: checks the key and the credit before it does the work. The credits API. A simple read of the signed credit, so the server's check stays small and cacheable.
benefits

This is not only a billing design. Once a user is logged in, their data lives in their vault, and it travels with them across all of our sites: what they read, what they set, what they bought, their keys and their preferences. A logged-in user gets a better experience on every site, without each site keeping a copy of them on a server.
trust

Activity reported by the browser is on trust. The same as this newsroom's meter, where the reader can set the price of a page. That is fine where the cost to us is small. What costs us real money is counted at the server. Storage and transfer are measured where they happen. Validated credit cannot be forged by the user. It needs the admin's signature. Unvalidated credit could be, and it would show up as not valid. A cached record can be a little stale. So it carries an end date. The admin key matters most. It should live where PKI everywhere says keys should: made on the device, never exported.
open

Where does it live? user.sgit.ai and api.user.sgit.ai, or billing.sgit.ai and api.billing.sgit.ai, so others can use it easily. Should the upload server accept unvalidated credit? Where usage costs us real money, it may want only validated credit, or a small amount on top. Who creates the first vault? Maybe we create a user's first vault for them, when they first log in. For now the design assumes the vault already exists. How does login work? It should start with a PKI handshake, as everything now does. How anonymous is the usage? The admin vault needs enough to bill, and should get no more. How often does the browser sync? Often enough to bill, not so often it slows the user down. How are refunds and disputes written? Probably as signed validation records too, with their own status.
versioning

api.user.sgit.ai, or api.billing.sgit.ai, would follow the rule our other API sites already use, written down on api.send.sgit.ai: every release is a complete, independent copy at its own versioned path, never edited after it is published, with a manifest of hashes. A site pins the version it uses, so a change to the API is a new version, not an edit to an old one. This newsroom has not written about that rule yet; it should, and it is now on the list.
limits

The billing vault is not built. Neither user.sgit.ai nor billing.sgit.ai exists yet, and payments are not yet checked or signed; the meter and the reading account in the reader's vault are, as the reading account, as built lists. The record formats are sketches. The field names will change. The Stripe flow is not tested. Its constraints are from Stripe's documentation, read on 21 October 2026. Client-reported activity is not proof. The design says where it is trusted and where it is counted. The pieces it builds on exist. The meter, the append lanes, the versioning and the key register are in use today.

Abstract: The value I get from two of sgit's design choices is not the obvious one. sgit is encrypted on the client, and we often lead with that, but I made that mistake myself: nobody will buy sgit for its encryption. If it succeeds, it will be because it has better features and better workflows, and many of those came from the encryption, as a constraint. Encryption on the client moves the security problem from protecting all the data to protecting the keys, and moves the sovereignty line from where the data is stored to who holds the keys; the European Data Protection Board treats that as an effective measure for transfers. It does not take you out of GDPR, which my memo said it did: the data is still personal data for whoever holds the keys, but a breach of the ciphertext alone need not be notified to the people in it. The biggest benefit, though, is engineering. A server that cannot read the data removes the temptation to process anything on it, so there is no server code to write, deploy and secure, and the features that make sgit good, like scoped clones, came from working within that. Open source is the same kind of constraint: no private code removes the temptation to lock customers in, makes the code easy to deploy anywhere, and ends the startup curse of building every customer's integration. That is why it has to be all of it; open core is an evaluation version. The business model that follows is selling customisation.
Two constraints and what they take away: client-side encryption and open source, all of it.
in-short

Encryption is not the selling point. Better features and workflows are; many came from the constraint. Protect the keys, not all the data. And the sovereignty line moves to whoever holds them. It does not remove GDPR. It reduces the exposure; my memo overstated it. No server code is the biggest gain. A server that cannot read has nothing to compute. Open source removes temptations too. Lock-in, the evaluation edition, every customer's integration. It has to be all of it. Open core is an evaluation version. Take away until it hurts. Not more than that.
mistake

When we describe sgit, we usually start with the encryption: an encrypted, version-controlled store, where the server holds ciphertext and nothing else. Agents do it when they write about it, and I did it at the beginning. But I do not think anyone will buy sgit because it is encrypted. Encryption is an important property, not a reason to choose a tool. If sgit succeeds, it will be because it has better features, better workflows and a better solution, as the comparison with Scion showed this week.
mistake

What took me a while to see is where those features came from. Innovation needs constraints and the loop of trying, failing and shipping, and the constraint that shaped sgit most was the encryption. Research on this is more careful than the slogan: a review by Acar, Tarakci and van Knippenberg found "an inverted U-shaped effect of constraints on creativity and innovation", which is to say some constraint helps, and too much hurts. These two have been on the right side of that curve for us.
keys

Encryption on the client moves the problem from the data to the keys, and the sovereignty line with it. The security benefit is the one everyone expects, and it is real. When the server can read what it stores, all of it has to be protected: every copy, backup, log and replica, and every person and process with access. When the server holds ciphertext, named by the hash of that ciphertext, the problem moves to protecting the keys, which is a much smaller problem.
keys

The sovereignty benefit is less obvious. The sovereignty line stops being where the data is stored and becomes who holds the keys. So the data can sit with a provider, or in a country, that has sovereignty gaps, and you can still be sovereign over it, and keep the ability to move it. That is not only my view. The European Data Protection Board's recommendations on transfers take exactly this case, storage that does not need the data in the clear, and conclude that with strong encryption, and keys "retained solely under the control of the data exporter", "the EDPB considers that the encryption performed provides an effective supplementary measure." It is the same idea as sovereignty as the ability to move.
gdpr

My memo said that with the data encrypted you do not have to worry about GDPR. That is too strong, and the article should say so. For whoever holds the keys, encrypted personal data is still personal data: the UK regulator's encryption guidance says not to "think the encrypted data is not subject to the UK GDPR", and that storing it is still processing. The controller's duties stay.
gdpr

What encryption does is reduce the exposure, and the law recognises it. The GDPR lists encryption as a security measure in Article 32, and under Article 34(3)(a) a breach need not be communicated to the people affected if the data was made "unintelligible to any person who is not authorised to access it, such as encryption", provided the key was not lost with it. The European Court of Justice held in September 2025 that pseudonymised data is not personal data "in all cases and for every person", which may help a store that never has the keys; but that store still processes data on someone's behalf, under a contract. So: much less to worry about, not nothing.
server

The benefit that matters most to me is engineering. A server that cannot read the data cannot do anything with it, so the constraint removes both the possibility and the temptation of processing on the server. That sounds small. It is not, because once nothing can run on the server, there is no server code: no complexity there, no deployment, nothing to patch. sgit's server is, in the words of the first brief, "a dumb key-value blob store", and the deployment is the client. I know the temptation well, because I have fallen for it. Any developer makes a change in the cheapest place with the fewest moving parts, and for a lot of changes that looks like the server, until you have to maintain it. Even with a fast CI pipeline that let me ship quickly, the server was always a lot of moving parts.
server

And here is the part I find most interesting: some of sgit's most powerful features exist because we had to solve the problems the constraint created. The usual reason for a server is to serve just the files a client needs; the web vaults already do that, by fetching only the objects a page needs. sgit could not do it on the server, so it does it in version control: clone --path holds only the folders you ask for, and every other folder is carried by its id and never downloaded. With the objects immutable and encrypted, a read is a plain GET, so any static host can serve a vault. Each of those is a better engineering decision than the server-side one would have been.
open

Open source is the second constraint, and for me its biggest value has also little to do with what people usually say. The constraint is that there is no private code. What it gives, from an engineering point of view, is that the code is available everywhere, which makes it very easy to deploy, to run and to change, including by the customer, which solves a lot of sovereignty problems on its own.
open

And, like the encryption, it removes temptations. The first is to lock the customer in, and to think of the technology as something bigger than it is; without lock-in, the only reason anyone uses the product is that they want to. The best product is not the one you use because you have to; it is the one that hurts when you stop. The same is true of design, by the way: take things away until it hurts, and stop there, because past that point it gets worse. Sometimes that is one button and sometimes fifty; what matters is what that use needs, in that context.
open

The second temptation is what I think is the curse of most startups. They win customers, and the customers get them to build all sorts of features and integrations that only they need, until the roadmap belongs to everyone but the startup. With open source, the answer is: here is the code; integrate it yourself, or pay us to do that specific thing.
all

That is why you cannot open source half of it. A community edition that turns proprietary as soon as you use it for real is an evaluation version with a better name. It brings back every dependency open source was meant to remove, and the companies that closed it later learned what it costs: Elastic, HashiCorp and Redis each moved to a licence that is not open source, and each produced a well-funded fork: OpenSearch, OpenTofu and Valkey; Elastic and Redis have since added an open licence back. The Open Source Initiative's verdict on one of those licences was that it was not an open source licence at all.
all

I also think this is part of how very small teams can now build and maintain software that companies with millions or billions in budget cannot. Working in the open, with no private code to protect and no lock-in to defend, is simply more efficient; and if more companies worked this way inside, there would be far more reuse of what each team builds. It is what I meant when I wrote that the SaaS shake-out should bring an explosion of small and mid-sized companies.
business

The two constraints also remove the opportunity to make a lot of bad business decisions, and that leaves the good one. If the code is open and the server holds nothing, you cannot sell access to the code or rent the data back. What you can sell is what the previous articles argued for: customisation, and keeping it working. Somebody is always paying; with these constraints, they pay for the part that is actually worth paying for.
limits

Not that encryption removes GDPR. It reduces exposure; the controller's duties remain. Not that constraints always help. The research says a moderate amount does. Not that small teams always win. It is my view, from what I see, not a study. sgit's success is not shown here. The features are real; the market will decide. I have a stake. sgit is ours. If you want to talk about building on these two constraints, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: In the newsroom workflow we just found something I did not plan. I keep separate Google accounts in separate Chrome profiles, and moving anything between them has always been awkward. The newsroom's reader vault fixed that without a line of new code. It got there by a path that was not a straight line: first we tracked what a reader does, in local storage; then the activity was worth keeping, so we persisted it, driven by what the reader valued; then we opened sgit vaults in the browser, which we already knew how to do; then the marks arrived, read later, not for me, more like this, and I started to have a stake in my own newsroom, with the usage and the payment travelling with it. Across devices was the feature I asked for. Across Chrome profiles is the one I found, and I suspect it is the more common case, because people switch between browser profiles far more often than between computers. What it really is, is memory and state between sessions, the same thing sgit already does for agents in different Claude accounts, now done through the interface of a website. This is how it works, what each profile needs to get in, and why the best features are sometimes the ones you discover by using what you built.
Two Chrome profiles on one computer, each signed in to a different Google account, sharing the reader's vault.
in-short

I use separate Chrome profiles for separate Google accounts, and moving anything between them has always been awkward: copy, paste, email it to myself. The reader's vault crossed that line without new code. The newsroom on one profile now shows what I read, marked and paid for on the other, the same way it does across devices. It got here by a path that was not a straight line. Activity tracked in local storage; persisted because it was worth keeping; vaults opened in the browser, which we already had; marks that gave me a stake in my own newsroom; then devices; then profiles. Profiles are probably the more common case. People switch browser profiles during the day far more often than they switch computers. I think this matters more than the feature I asked for.
in-short

What it really is: memory and state between sessions. sgit already carries state between agents in different Claude accounts. Here the same thing happens through the interface of a website, for a person. Each profile gets in by its own path. Where the passkey lives decides it: a Mac's iCloud Keychain answers both profiles alike; a passkey in one Google account does not follow into the other, and the phone or the recovery code adds a door once. Found, not built. Nothing in the code mentions Chrome profiles. The property was there because each piece was built to be general, and I found it by using it.
problem

I have several Google accounts, and each lives in its own Chrome profile: mine, and the accounts my agents use, which Replicating the agentic inbox explains, because the agent's mailbox, calendar and Claude account must never be mine. A Chrome profile is, for most purposes, a separate browser. It has its own history, its own passwords, its own extensions, and its own storage for every website. That separation is exactly what I want for the accounts, and exactly what makes it hard to get anything from one to the other. The usual answer is to copy and paste, or to email it to yourself, which, for the agent's account, means sending something into a mailbox I am trying to keep clean.
path

Six steps over three days, from the release histories of sgit.ai and the newsroom. None of this was designed as a way to cross profiles, and the path is worth telling, because I wrote yesterday that progress is not a straight line and this is a small, clean example of it. Track what the reader does. On 10 October the reading meter started recording every page read and every penny spent, in the browser's local storage, with no account and no server. Personas, ratings and declines followed the same afternoon, all in the same local state. Keep it, because it was worth keeping. The next day I noticed my iPhone, iPad, laptops and iMac did not agree: four balances, four reading histories. I miss it, so it is working was the moment the activity became something I wanted to keep, and the reason to persist it came from the value to the reader, not from a plan.
path

Open vaults in the browser, which we already knew how to do. The passkey opens the vault, and by two in the morning on 12 October the vault was live: a pane on every page, three real sgit vaults, the vault library that already ran elsewhere, vendored unedited. It was an extension of things we had built, not a new system. Marks, and a stake in it. The same day the newsroom added notes as you read, read later, not for me, more like this, liked, wrong, fix this, and an idea, and the next day the wire became an inbox whose seen stories travel in the device's file. This is the part of The site is an inbox that is now real. Once I was marking which stories I want and which I do not, I had a vested interest in keeping my newsroom, and the usage and the payment went with it.
path
Across devices, as asked: one file per device in the reader vault, every device's activity brought into the browser you are holding, one balance. Across Chrome profiles, as found.
found

The moment was simple. I was in the Chrome profile of another account, opened the newsroom, and wanted my newsroom there: my marks, what I had read, my balance. Not the empty one a fresh profile shows. And it was there, by the same steps as on a second device, because to the vault a second Chrome profile is a second device. It has a device id of its own, it writes its own file, and it reads the files of every other device, including the profile next door.
found

Nothing in the newsroom's code mentions Chrome profiles, and no test covers them. The tests treat a device as a browser whose storage has been cleared, which is exactly what a new profile is. The property was there because each piece was built to be general: the reader's state is records, not totals; each device writes only its own file, so there is nothing to merge; the view is computed when the vault opens. A design that works for an iPad and an iMac works for two profiles on one iMac, without anybody deciding that it should.
door

The honest detail is in how a profile opens the vault, because a passkey lives in a store, and the store decides. The passkey article has the table; for profiles it comes down to three cases. A passkey in iCloud Keychain, on a Mac. The store belongs to the Mac, not to the Chrome profile, and the lab found an iCloud Keychain passkey gave the same bytes in Safari and in Chrome. Both profiles reach the same door. A passkey in Google Password Manager. Google says such passkeys are "synced to your Google Account", so they follow the account signed in to the profile, so a profile signed in to a different account does not have it. That profile gets in by the phone over QR, which gives different bytes and therefore its own door, or by the recovery code, once. After that, it opens without the code.
door

Chrome's own profile store, in a clean profile with no provider, returns no bytes for a door at all; the recovery code is the way in. So "it just worked" needs one sentence of care: it just worked once each profile had a door, and with a Mac's keychain the first door is the only one needed.
common

Here is the angle I think matters most. I asked for the newsroom across devices because that was the pain I felt first. But how often does anyone move to another computer in a day? A few times. How often do people switch between browser profiles, between work and personal, between clients, between a person's account and an agent's? Many times, every day, on the same machine. My hypothesis is that state across profiles is the more common need, and the less served one, because every website treats each profile as a stranger.
common

I looked for numbers and found none: neither Google nor the Chromium project publishes how many people use more than one profile. What Google's own help says is what profiles are for: "Keep your different accounts, like work and personal, separate". Chromium's documentation is explicit that each profile is its own directory, with its own history, bookmarks and cookies, and a site's local storage lives in the profile too, which is why a fresh profile opens the newsroom empty. And agents are about to make profiles more common, not less: Anthropic's own advice for Claude in Chrome is to consider "a separate browser profile without access to sensitive accounts". Every person who follows it will have one more profile, and one more place their state does not reach.
memory

Step back and this is not really about Chrome. It is a way to give a person memory and state between sessions, in whatever browser and whatever account they happen to be in, without a server that holds it and without signing in to anything. We already do this for agents. My agents run as separate Claude sessions on separate accounts, and the only memory they share is encrypted vaults: each clones what it needs, works, commits and pushes, and they talk through files, an inbox and a done folder per agent in Email-FS, issues as folders in Issues-FS, as Memory is not a spectator sport describes. The reader's vault is the same idea with a different interface. The sessions are browser profiles, and the interface is a website.
memory

That opens more than it looks. A browser session can now hand state to another browser session through a site's own interface: a reading list, a set of marks, a half-finished task. It also fits the service in Stop the bleeding, then ask for it back, where an operator works in one browser while an agent drives another, and the vaults are the place they meet. I do not want to overstate it: today the newsroom carries the newsroom's state, and only when the reader presses Update. But the pattern is general, and that is the point.
discovered

The last point is the one I keep relearning. This feature needed no new development. It needed the earlier features to be built well enough to be general, and then it needed somebody to use them in a way nobody had planned. That is the loop in I miss it, running one more time: use it, notice what it does, and only then decide what it is for. If I had set out to build "state across Chrome profiles" I would have designed something specific, and probably something worse. Instead it fell out of records that are never totals and files that have one author. The next step is to treat it as a feature: test it with two real profiles, make the pane say which profile is which, and see what else a person wants to carry from one browser session to another.
limits

No test covers Chrome profiles yet. The tests treat a device as a cleared browser, which is what a new profile is; a run with two real profiles, each signed in to a different account, is the next experiment. The sync is by hand. Each profile updates the vault when its reader presses the button; automatic sync is still open work. The way in depends on the passkey's store. The iCloud Keychain result is from the lab's runs on a Mac; a Google Password Manager passkey does not follow into another account's profile, and that profile needs its own door. "More common than devices" is a hypothesis. I looked for figures on how many people use several browser profiles and found none published by Google or Chromium; the claim rests on how profiles are meant to be used, and on mine.
limits

The state is the newsroom's. What crosses today is the reader's newsroom: reading, marks, notes, balance. Anything wider is the pattern, not a feature. If you switch between browser profiles all day and want to try carrying something across, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
