Abstract: Versioning is one of the things that works best on this site. Every release has a number and a note, every article has its versions and the differences between them, and that history helps everyone: me, to see what changed between sessions; readers, to see what is new; and agents, to understand what is going on before they build. Now parts of the site are big enough to need the same discipline on their own. The first is the section for publishers, which has grown from a page into something closer to a website of its own, with a specific audience, regular updates and an environment that has to be maintained. On 18 October it got the start of this: a version history for its page, with every version frozen and the differences shown block by block. The idea I would like to name is the next step, versions of versions: the section gets its own version line, independent of the site's, and the site's release records which version of each part it carries. It is a tree, and it is fractal: a version can contain other versions, which contain their own. The newsroom will soon be built on the newsroom API, which already has two version lines of its own, so that connection needs tracking too. In time the home page and the article pipeline could work the same way, each area with its own releases, checks and quality bar. That part is coming later. This article is also an example of writing for an agent: the idea was in my head and nowhere the agents could find it, so now it is.
A tree of versions: a newsroom release, v0.12.118, and the parts it carries, each with its own version line.
in-short

Versioning works. It shows what changed, between which sessions, and why. Some parts of the site now need their own. The publishers' section first. It has started. Since 18 October the page for publishers has its own versions and diffs. Versions of versions. The site's release records which version of each part it carries. It is a tree, and fractal. A version can hold versions, which hold their own. The API is part of the tree. The newsroom will be built on it, and it has its own versions. The home page and the pipeline come later. Each area with its own releases and checks.
why

The way this site is versioned is one of the parts that works best. Every push to the release branch is a release, with a number and a note saying what changed and why. Every article has a version, shown in its byline, and a page with every version and the differences between them. Sections are summarised with a hash, so a summary knows when its section changed under it. That gives several things at once. A visual way of seeing what happened. A description of what changed between one session and the next. A diff, when it is needed. And a history, which matters most of all, because the history is what lets an agent understand what is going on before it builds, and what lets a reader see what is new.
publishers

The section for publishers has grown from a simple page into something closer to a website of its own. It has a specific audience, it has regular updates, it has major changes, and it has an environment that needs to be maintained. It needs exactly the same discipline as the main site: the same workflow, the same versioning, the same history. It has started. In v0.12.113, the agent that builds the site gave the page for publishers a version history of its own: each version of the text is frozen, the build stops if the text changes without a new version, and the versions page shows the differences block by block and word by word, with a ledger of what changed in each release. The page went from v1.0.0, the text written on 11 October, to v2.0.0.
versions-of-versions

The next step is to treat the whole section the same way. The section gets its own version line, independent of the site's: it can release when it is ready, at its own pace. And the site's release records which version of the section it carries, the way a project that uses git submodules records which commit of each one it is built with. I used to do this with submodules; this is the same idea, applied to content. The point is that you can then ask two questions, and get an answer to both. What changed in the publishers' section between its version 2 and version 3? And which version of the publishers' section was live in newsroom release v0.12.120?
tree

Once one part has its own versions, the site starts to look like a tree of versions. And it is fractal: a version can be connected to another version that has more versions inside it. A release of the site holds a version of the publishers' section, which holds a version of its page, which holds the versions of its text. The newsroom API is already a branch of that tree. api.newsroom.sgit.ai has two version lines of its own: its website, at v0.2.15 today, and the reader code it serves, at release v0.2.5. Each release is served under its own prefix and never edited afterwards. The newsroom will soon be built on top of it, pinning one release, and when it is, the site's release should record which API release it was built with. Track the versions, and track the connection between them.
areas

Taken further, the site becomes a combination of areas that are managed independently, each with its own release cycle, its own CI pipeline, its own checks and its own quality bar. Articles could be published in one area and, once they have been reviewed, move to the home page, which has its own versions, so you can see when an article arrived there and why. The feeds would follow the same pipeline. Every step would be a recorded event, and the history of the whole site would be the history of its parts. The home page and the article pipeline are for later. The publishers' section is now, and the API connection is next.
for-an-agent

This article is also an example of a habit. I referred to this idea in a conversation and asked the agent to find where we had written it down. It could not, because we had not. So I record the idea, the agent writes it up, and now the agent working on the publishers' section, and any agent after it, can find it, link it, and build it.
brief

For the agent that builds the site, in order: A version line for the publishers' section, extending the page versioning of v0.12.113 from one page to the whole section, with its own changelog page. The release records it. Each newsroom release lists the version of each part it carries, in its release note and as data. The API pin. When the newsroom is built on api.newsroom.sgit.ai, the release records which API release it pins. A view of the tree. One page showing, for a given site release, the version of every part it contains, and the differences from the release before. Later: the home page and the article pipeline as areas of their own. It is on the briefs page.
limits

Only one part has its own versions today. The page for publishers, since v0.12.113. The newsroom does not yet pin an API release. It will be built on the API soon. The home page and pipeline are an idea. Marked as later on purpose. More versions means more to maintain. Each area's version line is worth it only where the area really changes on its own.
sources

Abstract: One article, five readers worked: a Librarian, a Cartographer, a Historian, an Explainer and a Storyteller read five articles after they were written and produced the catalogue, the maps, the arc, the two-minute version and the deck. What did not work was the delivery. All of it landed as one more fold under the abstract, everything mixed, a wall of material next to a wall of text, and a reader with two minutes was no better off than before. This article is the next step, now that the pane on the right of every newsroom page is about the piece in front of the reader. The reader picks the way in, one tap, and can set a default: headlines, the infographic, two minutes, the slides, what is new against what they have read, the facts, the relationships, the vocabulary, or, through a model in their own browser, a view at their level and through their persona. Most of those are computed from views that already exist, deterministic and explainable; a local model is for the rest, and none of it round-trips to the publisher. And one thing is kept whole on purpose: the finished article. It has a beginning, a pacing, a surprise and a voice, and it is the one artefact that has to make sense from end to end, which a graph cannot. The modes are ways in, not replacements, and the brief says how to build them for a phone, a tablet, a desktop and an email.

The modes, what each is and what makes it; the finished article at the centre, with what it keeps that no view has; and why modes rather than shorter articles. In One article, five readers I sent five agents through five articles after they were written, each with a role, and they produced what I hoped for: a catalogue of every fact and claim with its sentence, an ontology and maps, an account of what each article added, a two-minute version and a deck. It worked. The views are on those articles today, on this site and on the newsroom.

What did not work was how they arrived. Open one of those articles and under the abstract there is a fold that says "five readers: two minutes, the arc, nine slides, a map, 137 catalogued items". Open it and there are five more folds, one per view, stacked in the article's own column, and each opens inline, in the middle of the long piece it was meant to be an alternative to. A reader with two minutes has to find the fold, open it, find the two-minute version, open that, and read it with the whole article still pressing from below. A reader who only wants the numbers does the same for the catalogue. The views exist; the choice does not, and the views and the article are mixed where they should be side by side.

The five readers fold on a live article, opened: five more folds, one per view, in the article's own column under the abstract. The views are good; the delivery asks the reader to dig for them, inside the thing they are an alternative to. This article is about the choice. It is a brief for the newsroom, now that the pane on the right of every page is about the piece in front of the reader, and it is also an argument about what not to lose while giving the reader that choice.
short

The views worked; the delivery did not. Five readers produced the catalogue, the maps, the arc, the two-minute version and the deck. They arrive as one fold with everything mixed, and a reader short of time is no better off. The reader picks the way in, and a default. In the pane about the piece: headlines, the infographic, two minutes, the slides, what is new, the facts, the relationships, the vocabulary, the whole article. One tap. A default per persona. The mode in the address, so it can be sent. Deterministic first. Most modes are projections of the article's graph and the views that already exist: computed, explainable, the same for everyone. A model in the reader's own browser is for the rest. Nothing round-trips to the publisher.
short

The infographic is often the article. The way the articles are written now, the figures carry most of the story, and a reader who starts there often has what they came for. A figure drawn for one reader, through their own image-model key, is a small step from there. What is new is a mode, and it needs the vault. An article that builds on three the reader has read is mostly not new to them. Showing only what it adds takes the Historian's arc plus the reader's own records, which now live in their vault. The finished article stays whole, and at the centre. It has a beginning, a sequence, a pacing, a surprise and a voice, and it is the one artefact that has to make sense from end to end. A graph is the right thing for provenance and for zooming in, and it has none of those. The modes are ways in, not replacements.
short

Build for the phone first, and for email. The default mode matters most where the screen is smallest. The same article at phone width: the title, the tags and the abstract fill the first two screens, and the views are further down still. On a phone the default mode is the first thing a reader should see.
focus

The problem the five readers were solving is still the right one: the articles here are long because that is where the thinking happens and the evidence lives, and long is hard to consume. The answer was never shorter articles. The answer is that a reader's constraint is time, and their need is focus, and the two change from reader to reader and from day to day. The same person reads the whole thing on a Sunday and wants the headlines on a Tuesday. The same article is a two-minute read for someone who has read the three it builds on and an hour for someone who has not. So the unit of choice is not the article, it is the way in. And the way in has to be chosen by the reader, at the piece, in a second, which is exactly what the pane about the piece is for.
modes

Each of these is one tap in the pane. Most of them exist already as a view; what is new is the choice, and the two marked as needing a model. Headlines. The title, the In short, and one sentence per section. Computed from the article's structure. The infographic. The figures, in order, with their captions. They exist for every article here, and they often carry most of the story: I find, reading my own articles back, that the figure is frequently where I would start. Later, a figure drawn for this reader, from the article's graph, through the reader's own key to an image model, which the bake-off showed costs a few cents. Two minutes. The Explainer's view, which exists.
modes

The slides. The Storyteller's deck, which exists. Later, a short video built from the same slides and the same script, the way code-built video is starting to be made, as a library of pre-made forms rather than a model guessing at pictures. What is new. The Historian already writes what an article added and where it sits in the arc. Cross that with what this reader has read, which their vault now records, and the mode shows only the paragraphs and claims that are new to them. For a reader who follows this site, that is the mode I would make the default. The facts. The Librarian's catalogue, by kind: the numbers, the claims, the sources, the questions, each anchored to its sentence. Exists. The relationships. The article's graph, which exists as JSON beside every article, drawn with its edges to the articles the reader has read highlighted.
modes

The vocabulary. The Cartographer's ontology, and on demand every term in the article a link, as the inbox brief described. At my level, for my persona. A summary pitched to the reader's knowledge, a view through one persona's concerns, a question answered from the piece. This is the mode that needs a model, and it should be the model in the tab: on the reader's machine, with no round trip. The whole article. The finished piece, start to end, as written. The centre, below.
deterministic

The split between those two kinds matters more than the list. The views the five readers make are produced once, by agents with role files, and checked; after that, every mode built from them is a projection: computed, explainable, identical for every reader, and free. Headlines, facts, relationships, vocabulary, what is new, the infographic and the slides are all of that kind. They can be built today, they can be tested with a script, and they do not depend on a model being available in the reader's browser.
deterministic

The mode that needs a model is the one that fits the article to the reader: at their level, through their persona, answering their question. That is what a local model is for, and A model in the tab says where that stands: Chrome's Prompt API ships, the experience is rough, and it will take a while. It does not matter that it takes a while, because the deterministic modes are most of the value, and because when it arrives it runs on the reader's machine. The reader does not depend on the publisher to decide how they read, which is the point of the whole client-side pattern.
centre

Here is the part I want to be careful about, because it cuts against a habit of mine. Having built the graphs, the catalogues and the views, it is tempting to treat the article as disposable: gather the facts, generate the piece, regenerate it tomorrow. I think that loses something, and I think we should say so.
centre

A finished article has a solidity to it. It is like a book: it has a consistency and a logic, and it is the whole thing. It has a beginning, a sequence of events and a punchline; it introduces an idea and then surprises you with where it goes; its pacing and the position of each fact change what the fact means. It carries the reader on a journey, and it has an author, with a voice. I remember the early output of the writing models, point after point after point, and how hard it was to read, and the reason is that there is a reason we speak in narrative. I read these articles end to end and understand them better for it, and if I printed one and read it with a pen in my hand I would understand it better still. That is how people take in an argument, and nothing about the graph changes it.
centre

The graph loses the narrative. It becomes a set of hyperlinked things, which is exactly right for provenance, for zooming into an area, for learning a concept you did not understand and coming back. It is what an agent reads, and why an agent would pay. But it has no beginning and no voice, and a reader who only ever used it would never have been carried anywhere. So the finished article is the centre of gravity of everything published, and the rule is this: the article is the one artefact that has to make sense in a coherent way, from end to end, and the graph is the one that has to be checkable. The modes are ways into the article for a reader with twenty seconds, two minutes or an hour. They are not replacements for it, and the design should not let them become one.
centre

One word, while I am here. This site has called the finished article "prose" in several places, and I have come to dislike the word; it sounds like a lesser thing than the graph it stands beside, and it is the opposite. From now on it is the finished article, or the narrative.
brief

For the session that runs newsroom.sgit.ai. Written by the sgit.ai site session for Dinis Cruz, 12 October 2026, on top of the pane about the piece in The site is an inbox. Dinis decides what ships, and is the first user. The modes in the pane. For an article that has views, a row of modes in the pane about the piece: headlines, infographic, two minutes, slides, what is new, facts, relationships, vocabulary, whole. One tap switches the main column to that mode; the article is never further than one tap away. The fold under the abstract goes. A default, per persona. The reader sets the mode they want to land in, and it is kept with the persona, so the editor persona lands on what is new and the founder persona on headlines. The mode in the address, so a reading list or a link to a colleague can say "the slides of this one".
brief

Computed modes first. Headlines, facts, relationships, vocabulary and the infographic from the article's structure, graph and figures; two minutes, the arc and the slides from the views where they exist. Where a view does not exist, the mode says so and offers the nearest one. What is new, from the Historian's arc and the reader's records: the paragraphs and claims this article adds to what the reader has read, with the rest folded. Needs the vault; starts with local storage. The phone. The pane is a sheet from the bottom; the default mode is the first thing shown; the figures are sized for the width; the whole article is one tap. Email. The newsletter cut by the reader's default: headlines, or the infographics, or two minutes per article, with the whole article a link.
brief

The model modes, when the model is there. At my level, through my persona, a question about the piece: through the Prompt API when the browser has it, with the page saying plainly when it does not, and never through a server of ours. A figure for this reader, later: the article's graph and a brief to an image model through the reader's own key, as the bake-off did. An experiment per mode. Each mode is small enough to ship in two forms and measure which one a synthetic reader with two minutes gets further with.
limits

The views exist for five articles. The modes built from them will exist for those five first; the rest of the site has the graph and the figures, which is enough for headlines, facts, relationships, vocabulary and the infographic. The model modes wait for the model. A local model in the browser is rough today, and the design does not depend on it. "What is new" needs reading records. It works from local storage on one device and from the vault across devices, and only for a reader who has them. Whether a default mode changes how people read is the experiment, and the first reader it will be tested on is me. If you build reading tools, or you want to read this site in one of these modes before they exist, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: Web Summit runs in Lisbon from 9 to 12 November 2026, and this time we have help. There are five of us with tickets, two founders, a project manager, a Gen AI consultant and technical expert, and a Gen AI founder and explorer coder, so we can work the summit as a team. This is the briefing to align us. The main objectives are usage and the sale, in that order: the sale happens after people use what we build. Usage depends on very easy onboarding, five minutes to the value, as the RiskMandate customer site does. Around that, three parallel tracks: intelligence on who to talk to, from public material only; outreach, with messaging made for one company or one post; and content, articles and interviews that bring traffic, because only traffic and use show us where we add value and what hurts. The method is the one I always use, on steroids: create an asset, put it on a website, send a link. We will run all of it from a Web Summit newsroom of our own, with vaults to collaborate and a data feed, built like the PHP story site but simpler. And the team will learn the two agentic workflows we run today, the email workflow and the website workflow on a schedule, starting with the website one.
Web Summit 2026, usage first, then the sale: from intelligence on who to talk to, to what they tell us.
in-short

Web Summit, Lisbon, 9 to 12 November 2026. Five tickets, five of us, one team. Usage first, then the sale. People buy after they have used it. Usage needs very easy onboarding. Five minutes to the value. Three parallel tracks: intelligence, outreach, content and traffic. One method: create an asset, put it on a website, send a link. On steroids. A Web Summit newsroom of our own, to coordinate, collaborate and publish. Two agentic workflows to learn. Start with the website workflow on a schedule.
team

Web Summit runs from 9 to 12 November 2026 in Lisbon. The good news is that, this time, we have help. Three people are joining us, so with the two founders there are five of us with tickets, all part of the team, and we can work the summit as a team rather than as individuals walking the floor. Five people, five tickets: who leads what at Web Summit 2026. The two founders own the story, the products and the sale: deciding who matters most, taking the meetings, recording interviews, and approving every message that goes out in our name. The project manager owns the board and the rhythm: the task list on the summit's newsroom, who does what by when, and the daily follow-up with every contact. The Gen AI consultant and technical expert owns the demos and the onboarding: making each product's first five minutes work, answering the technical questions, and running the website workflow.
team

The Gen AI founder and explorer coder owns the assets: pages, examples and small tools built for one company or one post, fast, as an explorer, then handed to the site. Everyone uses the agents. Each role reviews what the agents produce for it. That is the model of a call for help: a person connected to every role.
objectives

The main objectives are usage and the sale, in that order. The sale happens after the usage: once people have used what we build, and seen it work for them, the conversation about buying is a different one. Usage depends on very easy onboarding. Literally, super easy to understand the value. We already know what that looks like. customers.riskmandate.ai puts an Agent Behaviour Policy on Claude or ChatGPT in five minutes: ask the assistant to do something, paste one line that says it must not, ask again, and watch it refuse. Six examples, simplest first, nothing to install, £50 of reading credit to start, and a follow-up as often as daily with three questions: what they did, what got in the way, what is next. The people in it are customers, not beta users. That is the shape every product we show at the summit needs.
objectives

And we do not find pain points by asking people what their pain points are. We find them by watching them try to use our technology, and listening to what works and what does not. That is why usage comes first: only when we have traffic and users do we learn how the product is doing, where it adds value, and what hurts.
family

sgit and its vaults, at sgit.ai: encrypted, versioned folders that agents and people share. The newsroom, this site, and its reader as an open-source API at api.newsroom.sgit.ai, live and taking money. The PHP story site, a live story covered by agents, with every claim tied to its evidence: the best demo we have of what agents can do. RiskMandate, Agent Behaviour Policies, with the customer site as the onboarding. SHarness, the newest member of the family, which we need to introduce: a policy the Linux kernel enforces for every process an AI agent starts. It is honest about where it is: a design, with its first experiments runnable, including a Linux kernel running in a browser tab.
tracks

Intelligence. Company and people intelligence, not threat intelligence: who is speaking, exhibiting, investing and launching, and who among them we should talk to. From public material only, with its source and date kept, and following each site's terms, as sources and their shadows asks. Outreach. We can now take one post, one comment or one company and create messaging, positioning and an example made for that context, in hours. Each one goes to one person, by email or LinkedIn, and a founder approves it. Content and traffic. Articles, briefings and interviews, published before, during and after the summit, so that what we send has something behind it and people find us on their own.
method

The strategy I have always followed is simple: you create an asset, you put it on a website, and you send a link. That is literally it. What is new is the scale. With the agents, the asset can be made for one person, from what they have said in public, the page can be published within minutes, and the link can be followed up every day. As I wrote in the man behind the curtain, behind every email there should be an article. For Web Summit, behind every link there should be a page made for the person who receives it, in their language, starting from their problem, as in translate the assumption.
newsroom

We need a place to coordinate our tasks, map who we are talking to, collaborate, and publish. Thinking about it, the best way to do that is a Web Summit newsroom of our own, at an address like websummit.november.newsroom.sgit.ai, the exact name to be settled with the developers. We put everything there, and that is where the momentum builds. Collaboration in vaults. The board, the contact map and the drafts in encrypted vaults the team shares, so that what is private stays private and the site publishes only what is meant to be public. A data feed. A feed about Web Summit built from public material: the programme, the speakers, the startups, the news, each item with its source. Agents on it. A researcher, a curator and a writer, as on the PHP site, working from the feed.
newsroom

Simpler than the PHP site. The PHP story site has just been split into six repositories, site, refs, updates, team, data and press, each with its own gate, release and address. Its first-day report measured continuous integration at 25 to 42 seconds a release for the six, against a median of 88 seconds before. That refactoring deserves an article of its own, later. The Web Summit newsroom does not need all of it on day one: it can start as one repository, keep the split as the plan, and take the parts it needs, a team site for the records first. I will work with the developers on the Git structure, how we operate, and how it all fits together. A separate memo will follow for the Portuguese website, which is now in a good position to start too.
workflows

The two agentic workflows we run today: the email workflow and the website workflow. Everyone on the team will use both, so here is how each works. The email workflow. The agent behind agent@riskmandate.ai reads the mail, does the research, writes the drafts and keeps the records. I read every draft and send it myself. As answering a draft describes, the drafts folder is the work queue: every draft waits with one of three labels, send, review or decide, and a decision draft, an email to the agent's own address that is never sent, asks me a question with options and an empty answer box. Its debrief of 18 October counted 178 emails since 24 September, all reviewed and sent by me, to at least 47 organisations; a draft guard had blocked 36 of 125 drafts, mostly for a claim with no source. A person stays on every send, because an email cannot be unsent.
workflows

The website workflow. Agents with a role, a behaviour policy and a schedule card wake on their own, read what has changed, do their part, and release it through a gate. On the PHP story site, 23 agents and 13 schedule cards: the conductor every hour, the researcher, the curator, the journalist and the correspondent several times a day. Each release is checked, versioned and live within minutes, and the person reviews the result, not every step. A page is cheap to undo, so, as how cheap is it to undo? argues, the site can ship on its own.
start-here

I think the website workflow on a schedule is the right one for the team to start with. It is safe to learn on. Everything it does lands on our own site, through a gate, and can be undone in minutes. Nobody outside sees a mistake for long, and no email goes out by accident. It teaches the primitives. A brief, a role, a policy, a schedule card, a release, a gate, a run record. Once those make sense, every other workflow is a variation. It produces the assets. The method needs pages to link to. A newsroom on a schedule produces them every day: the feed, the briefings, the pages made for one company. It is where the email workflow gets its material. Behind every email, an article. The website workflow writes the articles.
start-here

So the first week is about getting the Web Summit newsroom running on a schedule, with each person owning one agent's output and reviewing it daily. The email workflow comes next, with a founder on every send.
timeline

This week, to 1 November. The Web Summit newsroom live, with its board and its feed; the onboarding of each product checked against the five-minute test; the first list of who to talk to, from public material. Next week, 2 to 8 November. Assets and links for the people on the list; articles and interviews published; meetings booked for the summit. 9 to 12 November, in Lisbon. Five people, one board, a daily debrief on the newsroom. The week after. Follow-up with everyone who used something, and the conversation about buying.
limits

This is a plan, not a result. Nothing here has happened yet. The Web Summit newsroom does not exist yet, and its address is to be decided. The intelligence is from public material only, and follows each source's terms. The email numbers are from the inbox's debrief of 18 October; the agent and schedule counts are the PHP site's on 26 October.

Abstract: Someone I am helping, who is doing a lot of agentic work now, sent me an infographic for a business selling websites built with Claude: three monthly plans from £39 to £119 with a setup fee, a cap of five or ten pages, half an hour to two hours of edits a month, the seller's Claude subscription as the main cost, and ten clients making about £570 a month. It is a good sign that people see the opportunity. But the temptation is always rent, money while you sleep, and the economics are wrong. On a monthly plan you earn most when your clients use you least, the clients who use you most cost you most, and a few of them will never stop asking. The page caps make no sense either: a static page costs almost nothing, and this newsroom runs about 1,500 of them on GitHub Pages. The model I propose is different. The client owns three accounts, Claude or ChatGPT, GitHub with Pages, and a domain. You charge once, to set them up and wire them together, build the site from the client's own material with designs to choose from, check it, and hand it over with a lesson in changing it by talking to their AI. After that, help is a block of hours, if they want it. Every engagement ends, the client is in control, and delighted clients tell others. Here is the infographic, section by section, and the alternative.

Why rent is the wrong model, then a made-up studio that sells the alternative and three made-up client sites built with it, each an encrypted vault you can open. The infographic as received on 26 October 2026: a pay-monthly website business built with Claude, in five sections.
in-short

I was sent a plan to sell websites built with Claude, by the month. A good instinct, the wrong model. Rent pays you when clients do not use you. The more they use it, the less you earn. A few clients will drive you mad. For them a monthly fee is permission to keep asking. Page caps make no sense. A static page costs almost nothing. The client should own the stack: Claude or ChatGPT, GitHub with Pages, a domain. Charge once, for a finished job. Setup, build, designs to choose from, QA, handover. After that, blocks of hours, only if wanted. Every engagement ends. See it working: a made-up studio and three client sites, each a vault you can open.
infographic

Someone I am helping, who is now doing a lot of agentic work, sent me this infographic. I had asked them to look at what I have been writing on this newsroom first. Their agent did, and the plan still came back as a rent business. So either the articles were not found or the argument did not land. This article makes it in one place. First, a check: the image carries nothing about its author. Its embedded data holds only its resolution and orientation, and the page names no one; the one first-person line, "Code I cannot fix", identifies nobody. I am sharing it without saying who made it. It is a good piece of work, and a good sign. People are seeing the opportunity to build websites with an agent and sell them. My problem is with the model underneath it, so here it is, section by section.
plans

Section 1 of the infographic, price plans: Starter, Standard and Plus, with setup fees and what each includes. Three monthly plans, each with a setup fee, a page cap and a monthly allowance of edits. Two things are wrong here. The page caps are spectacularly low. Five pages, ten pages. With this stack a page costs almost nothing: the agent writes it, and a static host serves it. This newsroom has about 1,500 pages on GitHub Pages, whose limits are a published site of up to 1 GB and a soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB a month. The real limit is how many tokens the client wants to spend: with a decent Claude account, hundreds or thousands of pages are practical. A cap of five pages is a pricing device, not a cost.
plans

The edit allowance keeps the client dependent. Thirty minutes a month means the client cannot change their own site. That is the opposite of what this stack makes possible: the client can change anything, any time, by asking. What I agree with: "Client owns the domain and content." Yes, and they should own the rest too.
cost

Section 2 of the infographic, cost to run: fixed monthly costs and the cost of each extra site. The biggest cost in the plan is the seller's own Claude subscription, used to run every client's site. That puts the cost, and the bottleneck, in the wrong place. The client can have their own Claude or ChatGPT account, which they are probably already paying for, and use it for everything else too. Reselling access to someone else's AI service may also have legal ramifications, so I would not build a business on it; I would read the provider's terms first.
cost

The hosting is right in spirit: static, cheap, nearly free. On GitHub Pages it is free, with one caveat worth knowing. GitHub's terms for Pages say it is "not intended for or allowed to be used as a free web hosting service to run your online business, e-commerce site, or any other website that is primarily directed at either facilitating commercial transactions or providing commercial software as a service (SaaS)". A brochure, a catalogue or a guide library fits; a site that takes orders and payments should go to another static host.
time

Section 3 of the infographic, time per five-page build: 10 to 15 hours in total. This is the best section, and I agree with it. Most of the time is not the code: it is the calls, the content, the revisions and the launch. And "price on the client's time, not Claude's speed" is right. Which is exactly why the work should be priced as a job: a finite number of hours, delivered and finished.
numbers

Section 4 of the infographic, the numbers: what one Standard client and ten Standard clients bring in. The arithmetic mostly holds, at the optimistic end. £299 plus twelve months at £69 is £1,127. Two Standard clients bring £138 a month, which covers the fixed costs only at their low end of £95; at £190 it takes three. And ten clients bring £690 a month, which leaves about £570 only if the costs are at their lowest; at the top end it is closer to £450. But the real problem is not the arithmetic, it is the incentive. Who wins when the client uses it more: a monthly plan against a handover. Illustrative.
numbers

On a monthly plan you make money when your clients do not use you. The more they use what you sell, the less profitable they are. And in my experience something like 10 or 15 per cent of clients will drive you absolutely mad: endless requests, a lot of noise, never content, because to them a monthly fee is permission to keep asking. That is fair from their side; they are getting what they can for the money. But it is a perverse position to build a business in. I have written about the other side of it: "A subscription is a discount for committing to regular use. It is not rent on something you have the right to ignore", in stop the bleeding, then ask for it back, and why paying after the value feels different, in paying after the value.
risks

Section 5 of the infographic, risks and fixes: code I cannot fix, and Claude usage caps. "Keep sites simple and static. Read what Claude writes." Agreed. The second risk, Claude's usage caps, only exists because the seller holds one AI account for every client. When each client has their own, a cap is theirs, and nobody has promised anyone a same-hour fix.
model

Two ways to sell a website made with an agent: rent, a monthly plan, and handover, a finished job the client owns. The tech stack for someone to maintain a website today is an AI account, GitHub Pages and a DNS account, the recipe in your own newsroom. So package that, and sell the work, not the rent. Setup, one-off. The client creates a Claude account (or ChatGPT, or a team plan), a GitHub account and, if they need one, a domain. You guide them, plug them together, and give them the prompts and modes that make it work. If they have no idea how to register a domain, sell them a domain and its DNS for a year, as a one-off.
model

The build, one-off. A couple of sessions and briefs to extract their ideas. They give you fifty documents, pages or notes; the agent builds the site; you show them five designs and they pick one; you run a couple of rounds of QA. The handover. You teach them to change their site by talking to their AI. Clients who were happy to change a paragraph can now change anything, and they will never have experienced anything like it. After that, blocks of time. If they want help, they buy a block of hours. Nothing monthly.
model

Prices from the market. £500 for a site, £1,000 for a bigger one, or a family-and-friends discount on what is £500 worth of effort. For a site you can edit and maintain, that looks good, with five designs to choose from and a content management system that is a conversation, it is a very good deal. The only question is the market economics: how much time you have, and how many clients you can onboard. Lift and shift. Most business websites are static by design, glued together by someone who has since left. "Do you have a website? Can you edit it? Do you want to talk to it?" A conversion is £200, £500 or £1,000, depending on its back end.
model

Every engagement is finite, which is what jobs that never scaled describes: a piece of expert work, delivered end to end, and finished. The client is empowered and in control, and delighted clients tell others. For someone who is not very technical, I think finite work is especially important. You could call these explorer services, in the language of explorer coding: someone without an engineering background, selling what they can now build, on top of powerful open-source technology like ours, with villager and town planner services for what needs more.
mockup

To make this concrete, I asked the agents to build it. Not a description: a working mock-up of the whole business. Kitewing Websites is a made-up studio whose own site sells exactly this offer, and next to it are three made-up client sites, in three industries, each with its own design. All four are real, finished sites you can click through, and each is an encrypted sgit vault you can open. Four made-up websites for a demonstration: Kitewing, Tidewrack Studio Pottery, Fennick Lane and Quillon Heat & Plumbing. Kitewing Websites, the studio: the offer in five steps, the one-off prices, why there is no monthly fee, and the three examples. Its vault holds the three examples inside it. Open the vault. Tidewrack Studio Pottery, a catalogue: 28 pieces, each drawn in its glaze, filtered by kind and glaze, with an enquiry note instead of a checkout. Open the vault.
mockup

Fennick Lane Community Garden, a community group: plots and the waiting list, a season of 15 events, a volunteer rota and 14 growing guides. Open the vault. Quillon Heat & Plumbing, a local trade: eight services, a map of the villages it covers, what to do in an emergency, and 19 household guides. Open the vault. Each one is a single HTML file with its words in a JSON file beside it, so its owner changes it by asking: "add a mug in the celadon glaze", "move the June work day". Inside Kitewing Websites is the tour: how each site is made, and how the vaults work.
limits

The infographic is shared without its author, and its figures are theirs; I checked the arithmetic, not the costs. The 10 to 15 per cent is my experience, not a measurement. The prices in my model are hypotheses, to be set by the market. Reselling AI access may be fine under some terms; I have not checked any provider's, which is why I would not depend on it.
sources

The infographic sent to me on 26 October 2026, and my voice memo of the same day. GitHub Docs, GitHub Pages limits, and GitHub's terms for additional products and features, on Pages, read on 26 October 2026. Abstract: I have moved from many Claude sessions to agent teams that run on schedules. The PHP October 2026 newsroom is the furthest along: a pipeline of researcher, curator, journalist and correspondent runs in order five times a day, a desk twice, a conductor every hour, and eight more agents keep the house, all on their own schedule cards. For two days it has run in sequence with no content commit from me. Then there is a second way to run the same agents: in one session, as subagents, which is how the newsroom carried CISA's listing of php2shell to readers in 5 hours 21 minutes. Writing this up against the team's own record corrected me in several places: the conductor does not start the breaking run, the agents' keys seal secrets but do not yet sign their work, and nothing has run on anything but Claude. What it confirmed is the main point: an agent is a session plus a card, a role, a loop, a key and memory kept in repositories and vaults, and only the first part is the model.
Every scheduled wake of the PHP newsroom's agents in one day, London time.
in-short

From sessions to teams on schedules. Once something works, you use it everywhere. The pipeline runs itself. Researcher, curator, journalist, correspondent: five times a day, in order. No content commit from me. Agents and CI write everything; I give the "go"s. A second way to run them: one session, every step as a subagent. CISA's listing reached readers in 5 h 21 min. The record corrected me. The conductor doesn't start breaking runs; keys seal secrets, they don't sign yet. An agent is six parts, and only one of them is the model. The memory is the repository, which is why an agent can move session, account, and in principle vendor. Today the newsroom is moving account, and that is the test of all of this.
teams

This follows why agent loops are hard, and it is a Wardley story: as soon as something stops being a novelty and you understand it, you use it left, right and centre. I went from running many Claude sessions to running agent teams, and the step that changed the most was the schedule. A schedule means a follow-up: the agent comes back, picks up where it was, and does the next thing without me asking. It also changes how you think. Which tasks can run on a loop? Which can't be automated? Where does a person have to come in, and why? The PHP October 2026 newsroom, the team covering php2shell, is the furthest along. Its record is public, on the team site, and everything below comes from it.
pipeline

Four agents run one after another, five times a day, each on its own card: The researcher probes every watched source, captures what changed into the source watch's vault and reports what moved (07:00, then every two and a half hours). The curator promotes what the researcher captured into the evidence vault, a bounded batch a wake, each capture read first (an hour later). The journalist takes that evidence through to the site by fixed rules, one release a wake (40 minutes after the curator, because the curator takes 12 to 21 minutes to push). The correspondent reviews what the journalist published, corrects it in the open and counts the catches (45 minutes after the journalist).
pipeline

The desk, which keeps the story's line and the front page true to the evidence, follows the correspondent twice a day. The conductor wakes every hour to keep everyone in step. And eight more agents keep the house: the fact-check desk, Pulse, which tracks other vulnerabilities in the news, the ontologist, the sherpa, which reads the readers' feedback, observability, dev, the librarian and security, which reviews each day's changes for injection, leaks and vulnerabilities every night.
pipeline

On 27 October the commit history shows four full cycles running in order, on time. In the first: the researcher woke at 07:00 and released at 07:55; the curator at 08:00, released at 08:37 with "580 sources, 304 claims"; the journalist at 08:40, "11 claim verdicts for batch 19"; the correspondent at 09:25, reviewing batches 18 and 19; the desk at 10:40. Each batch number passes downstream. There are 157 run records, none failed. And I wrote none of the content: the team repository has 237 commits by Claude, 99 by the build, 12 by the curator's own identity, and one by me, the initial commit. That is supervised, not unattended. The cards' notes quote my "go" on most changes, and the move to standing sessions, the timings and the models were decisions I made. But the work runs without me.
sessions

What makes schedules work today is a dedicated session per agent that the schedule wakes again. It continues the same conversation, so it has its context: the same as going back to a session and saying "continue". The journalist and the correspondent started differently, as a fresh session each wake, and were moved to standing sessions on 26 October because, in the card's words, "a fresh session could not always attach the repository". Dev still runs fresh each morning. There is a practical reason too. Each session holds clones of the vaults and the keys to open them, and those are expensive to set up: the source watch's vault takes 232 to 316 seconds and 4.3 to 4.8 GB to clone, and the curator's pull takes 30 to 40 minutes. A standing session sets that up once.
sessions

And there is one limit worth knowing: one session cannot wake another agent's session. When the conductor tried to start the curator with a trigger, it "started a fresh, empty session … no repositories … no vault key. That session stopped in 9 seconds", at a cost of about $0.08. Which is why the second way of running exists.
one-session

Three ways to run the same agent: a standing session on a schedule, subagents in one session, or a fresh session. For breaking news I start one session, the breaking desk, and give it a link: "breaking: this has happened". It runs the four steps of the pipeline in order, "each as a subagent given that role's card and runbook", and checks each step's output before the next starts. The subagents have no memory of a session, but they have the memory of the repository, which is the one that matters.
one-session

The first real run was CISA's listing of both php2shell flaws on 26 October. The report: CISA released its catalogue at 22:24 UTC, and the newsroom's readers' pages carried it 5 h 21 min later, against about 11 h 36 min on the schedule. From my "breaking:" to the last deploy took 45.8 minutes: researcher 271 seconds, curator 482, journalist 447, the correspondent's review 756, 642,456 tokens and 186 tool calls in all, with three catches in the review. It also said where the time really went: 86% of the delay was before the run started, because the capture had not been queued for the curator. That is now fixed in the researcher's card.
one-session

The same pattern runs projects: an Opus coordinator, Sonnet subagents for each member's step, the ontologist, the sherpa, the design agent, the journalist. And the fresh-session option is always there: start a new session, tell it who it is, let it pull the team repository and read its card. Because the repository is the memory, that is how an agent moves when its context is too long, or to another account. Models follow the work. On 27 October I decided: Opus for the conductor, the correspondent and security, the agents where judgement and review matter most; Sonnet for everyone else. The record shows two drifts from that decision (dev's card still says Opus), which is the kind of thing a record is for.
what

The six parts of an agent on the PHP newsroom: session, card, role and policy, memory, loop and key. Here is the definition this work has led me to. An agent is not the model. It is six things: A session: Claude or ChatGPT or another, with tools and skills. Today every agent here is Claude Code on the web. A card: its schedule card, with its objective, its wakes, its model, what it reads and writes, and what it must never do. A role and a policy: ROLE.md and an agent behaviour policy, in RiskMandate's terms a grant, a mandate, a delta and a barrier. All 29 policies are still drafts, which is honest: they are written, not yet agreed. Memory: the repositories and the vaults. Briefs, board rows, run records, debriefs, messages. Not the session.
what

A loop: one shared file, WAKE.md, that every wake follows: a start banner, read the inbox and the board, do the work, leave a run record, an end banner. The scheduled prompt is as short as possible and points there. A key: a key pair, made in its session. Only the first is the model. The other five are files and keys. That is why the same agent can be a standing session on a schedule, a step inside someone else's session, or a fresh session on another account, and why, in principle, it could run on ChatGPT or another tool that can clone a repository and open a vault.
corrections

I dictated the first version of this from memory. Checked against the team's record, I had several things wrong, and they are worth stating: The conductor doesn't start the breaking run. I start a separate session, and it runs the steps. The conductor wrote its brief and runbook, after its own attempt to wake another session failed. The breaking run has four steps, not five. There is no desk step. The keys don't sign anything yet. Each agent can have a key pair, and they are used to seal vault keys sent to them, carried by me as QR codes and checked five ways on opening. But nothing the agents write is signed with their own keys. Security's advisory SA-2026-024 is open: "Nothing is signed, although every agent can have a key". Every agent commit is signed by one shared platform key, and the agent is named only in a trailer. Signing is the next step.
corrections

"About two days" is the newest part. The researcher and curator have been on schedules since 23 October; the full pipeline across six repositories since 25 and 26 October. Nothing has run on anything but Claude. The portability is in the design, not yet in the record. The vaults are real and large. The researcher writes the source watch, 1,330 pages, 988 publishers and 15,953 snapshots by midday on 27 October; the curator writes the evidence vault, 614 sources and 679 captures, of which only the hashes are public.
today

At 16:51 UTC today, every scheduled task except the conductor's, security's and observability's was paused: the account was at 78% of its usage, and the newsroom is moving to a new one. The move brief lists what does not carry over: each agent's session and scratchpad, its clones, its key pair, the vault keys sealed to it, the scheduled tasks. And what does: everything in the repositories. "That is why the move is simple: a new session is told who it is, pulls team, and reads its card." That sentence is the whole argument. If the memory is in the session, moving is a disaster. If it is in the repository and the vaults, moving is a setup cost: a new key, sealed vault keys, clones and a card. We will know in a day or two how small that cost is.
limits

Supervised, not autonomous. The pipeline runs on schedules, but its design, timings, models and fixes are my decisions, on the record. Counts are from the record on 27 October: commit times, run records and cards, read by an agent of this newsroom. Signing is planned, not built. Agents seal secrets with their keys; they do not sign their work yet. Portability is a design property, not yet tested: every agent so far has run on Claude. Costs in dollars are not recorded in the run records, except one empty session's $0.08.
sources

The PHP October 2026 team site and repository, read on 27 October 2026: the schedule wiring and each agent's card under records/schedule/, the agents' roles and policies under admin/agents, records/WAKE.md, the breaking-desk brief, the projects brief, the KEV listing run report, the move brief of 27 October, the vaults, security advisories, and the commit history of the six repositories. Abstract: A thoughtful reader spent real time on RiskMandate and abp.sgit.ai and came back with four fair points. The pages are hard to understand. As they read it, the idea is to inspect an agent and report what it can actually do, which is valuable, and they could not think of anything else that does it. Their guess was that it does not yet work with commercial agents, or in real time. And the hard problem is not the product but the room: most people do not see how fast agents are moving, so how does anyone surface the need? This is a plain answer to all four. RiskMandate writes down, for one agent in one deployment, what it can reach, what you authorised it to do, the gap between the two, and what actually stands in the way of each capability. It is read-only on purpose and never sits in the agent's path; enforcing belongs to the gateways, hooks and runtimes, and the policy is what they enforce. It already covers commercial agents, Claude with Gmail or Microsoft 365, ChatGPT, Google Workspace and others, from the vendors' own pages and measured deployments. The worry that prompted the conversation, an enterprise assistant like Atlassian's Rovo surfacing data to people who should not see it, is exactly the gap it measures, and I walk through it. The newer work goes further: decision and workflow policies for who decides and in what order, and a twin of a refund agent where every decision can be replayed. And the way into the room is not a new budget line. It is five questions someone already has to answer, with a deadline: a contract, a security questionnaire, an insurance renewal, the board's risk appetite, and twenty minutes with the assistant you already run.
One agent, three sets: the grant, the mandate and the delta, with a barrier on each capability in the grant.
in-short

It writes down what an agent can reach. For one agent in one deployment: the grant, the mandate, the gap, and what stands in the way. It never sits in the agent's path. Read-only on purpose; the gateways and runtimes enforce, and the policy is what they enforce. It already has policies for commercial agents. Claude with Gmail and Microsoft 365, ChatGPT, Google Workspace, Claude Code, GitHub Actions and more. Enterprise AI oversharing is the gap it measures. An assistant that can reach more than the person asking should see. Real time is somebody else's job, on purpose. But the decisions it records can be enforced in real time, and we show where. The newer work adds decisions and workflows. Who decides, on what evidence, in what order, replayable in a twin. The way in is a question already asked. A contract, a questionnaire, a renewal, the board, or twenty minutes.
pages

That is a fair criticism, and I accept it. The sites were written from the inside, in the vocabulary the work needed, and they show it: grant, mandate, delta, barrier, a 23-word capability grammar. They are precise, and precision is not the same as clear. This article is the version I would give someone who has ten minutes and has to decide whether any of it matters to them.
what

When you connect an AI agent to something, a mailbox, a drive, a code host, a company wiki, it gets a credential. That credential lets it do a set of things, usually far more than the job you had in mind. RiskMandate writes down, for one agent in one deployment, four things: the grant, what the credential and connectors actually let it reach; the mandate, what you authorised it to do; the delta, the difference between them, which is authority nobody ever accepted; and the barrier for every capability, what actually stands in the way. That document is the Agent Behaviour Policy, published openly at abp.sgit.ai. It carries no score and no verdict. It is the record. The barrier is the part that changes conversations. There are four kinds, and only one of them bounds anything: Barrier What stands in the way A control? None Nothing No Expectation A rule in prose, a line in the prompt No Setting
what

A switch the agent's own account can flip No Boundary Something enforced above the grant, out of the agent's reach Yes The test behind it is one sentence from abp.sgit.ai: "A control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include." Much of what gets called an agent control is the second row: an instruction in a prompt. How much, in a given deployment, is something to measure, not assume; an honest behaviour policy says which row each control is in.
inspect

That is the right reading. And the reason it matters is that few people have seen the list for their own agents. RiskMandate's try-it page is thirteen prompts you paste into the assistant you already have connected to your mail. The first one asks it to list its own tools. In RiskMandate's words, "the list is longer than the tile that sold it." The second asks it to draft what you actually wanted it for, in three lists, wanted, refused, never mentioned; "the correction is almost always downward." The third writes the gap down. It takes about twenty minutes, and nothing is collected.
inspect

That is a self-report, and the site says so: the agent describing its own access is "the cheapest evidence there is, and the weakest." The paid levels go further. At the corrected level, the agent that holds the credential runs a published prompt that measures what the credential actually allows, in the fixed vocabulary, and the policy is built from that measurement, with every row marked as measured, documented or inferred. At the reviewed level, a person runs two sessions with your team and signs it. The levels are on the pricing page, from £10 for the pack to £1,500 reviewed. They are offerings, not a track record: the pricing page itself marks the £500 and £1,500 levels "specified, never run", as of 15 September 2026.
commercial

Yes, for the ones that matter most to most organisations. The library at riskmandate.ai has behaviour-policy vaults for Claude with the Gmail connector, Claude with the Microsoft 365 connector, Claude in the browser with connectors, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT in the browser, a Google Workspace MCP server, Gmail and Google Drive at read-only scope, a Dropbox MCP server, n8n with an owner API key, Claude Code on a machine and on the web, GitHub Actions, a browser extension and a scheduled job. Each is built from the vendor's own published pages, quoted and dated, or measured on a deployment we are entitled to run; where two vendor pages disagree, the disagreement is published rather than settled. That is a library of policies, not a set of integrations: in RiskMandate's own words, connectors to a customer's systems "are built per engagement", and "No connector is a product yet, and none is claimed as one."
commercial

There is no vault yet for Atlassian's Rovo, or for Microsoft 365 Copilot or Glean. A new shape starts from the same grammar and the same method, and the corrected level exists precisely for "something not on the list". One distinction is worth knowing before any contract conversation. The policy records who holds each barrier. A scope you consented to and can revoke is a different thing from a product decision the vendor can change in a release, without notice. Both are written down, and the difference is the clause you want in the contract.
oversharing

The worry that started this conversation is a good test. An organisation is looking at Atlassian's Rovo: search, chat and agents across Jira and Confluence, and through connectors across Google Drive, SharePoint, Slack and GitHub. The question is whether it will pull data in and show it to people who did not have access to it.
oversharing

Atlassian's documented design says it will not grant new access. Its trust page says "Rovo honors all existing permissions within each feature", and its privacy guidelines that users "will be able to see public documents and private documents that they already had access to." I take that at face value. How a connector is set up, indexed and authenticated depends on the kind of connector: Atlassian distinguishes synced connectors, which "store and index all the content in a workspace using a service or admin account", direct connectors, whose content "is retrieved live through the provider's search APIs", and Smart Link connectors, which need no administrator setup. The risk is not in that sentence; it is in four places around it.
oversharing

Access that was always too wide becomes easy to find. Atlassian's own connector guide warns that "unrestricted content may appear in search results or be used by Rovo Agents or Rovo Chat", and tells administrators to "verify what data each app indexes". Microsoft says the same about its own assistant: "By default, SharePoint sets sharing settings to the most permissive option," and the first steps of getting ready for Copilot are about oversharing. A Google Drive file shared as "anyone with the link" was hard to find while nobody knew the link; Atlassian's Drive connector makes it findable by teammates when the link appears somewhere Rovo can read, such as a Confluence page or a Slack message, while "Google Drive sharing settings still apply." Nobody's permissions changed. What changed is that everything they already allowed is now one question away.
oversharing

Whose permissions apply depends on how the agent is invoked, and as whom. Creating or sharing an agent does not hand its creator's access to everyone who uses it. Atlassian documents an identity setting for each agent with two options. With User's account, "the agent adopts the identity of the user who's interacting with, or automating, the agent": in chat, that is the person asking, and a knowledge source still "respects the permissions of the user who prompted it". In an automation, it is the account on the rule's connection: Atlassian says agents there "always use the permissions of the connection user in the automation", which may be whoever set the rule up, another user or a service account, and is not necessarily the agent's creator or the person who triggered it. With Agent's account, the agent runs with access granted to its own identity, and Atlassian's safety guidance is plain: "Any spaces or content that are shared with the agent are also shared with any manager, editor or user of the agent." So the risk is a process that reads with one identity and publishes to an audience with less access. In Atlassian's tracker, ROVO-837, a customer reported that an automation posted Rovo's answer into a ticket with a link to a Confluence page the triggering user could not open; opening the link still gave a permission error, setting the rule to run as the triggering user did not change the lookup, and Atlassian answered that "this is intended behaviour". That is a link to a restricted page disclosed, not the page itself, but it is the shape the question was about.
oversharing

Who can build agents, and who can use them, are wide by default, and controlled differently. By default all users can create Rovo agents, and a new agent "becomes available for everyone to see and use". Administrators can limit who creates agents to selected groups; limiting who uses a particular agent is done person by person, because, in Atlassian's words, "Restricting agent access to specific groups or teams is currently not supported."
oversharing

An agent can be talked into sending data out. On 5 August 2026, a security firm published a prompt injection in which a hidden instruction in an uploaded file makes Rovo send data to an outside address, "even if an organization has disabled web search for Rovo". That is a reported attack as of its publication; I found no statement from Atlassian on a fix, and could not verify whether it still works today. That is not Rovo widening permissions. It is Rovo using a legitimate user's access for someone else's purpose, which is the same risk every assistant with tools carries.
oversharing

Written as a behaviour policy, a Rovo agent's grant is what its executing identity can reach across Atlassian and every connected app: the person asking, in chat; the connection account, in an automation; or the agent's own account, if it has one; plus what its tools can create and change. Its mandate is what it was built for: answer questions about this project's tickets, say. The delta is everything else it can reach. It can be large, and it has to be measured for the particular deployment rather than assumed. And the barrier column sorts the controls honestly. Permission filtering is a boundary, but one the vendor holds and can change in a release. The setting for who may build agents is a boundary the organisation holds. So are the administrator's allowlists for which drives and sites are indexed, though they govern what is indexed, not everything Rovo can fetch at run time through the user's access; and the read, write and search switches on Atlassian's MCP server, which govern what that server can do, not, on Atlassian's page, every Rovo chat or automation. The agent's instructions are an expectation. Atlassian's governance tools do different jobs, on the plans that include them: blocking and redaction of sensitive data can stop it entering or leaving a path, which is a boundary; classification labels mark sensitivity, and bound something only through a policy that acts on them; audit logs record what happened, which is evidence for an investigation, not a barrier that prevents anything. Agents with their own accounts are now documented; on 6 October Atlassian announced that "Soon, we're adding controls around what is visible to AI and what it can access with agent accounts and non-human identity inventory." Which of these a given organisation has is something to check in its own tenant.
oversharing

For due diligence on a contract, that turns the vague question into five specific ones. Which connectors are on, and with whose rights were they set up? What is indexed, and has anyone reviewed what was already over-shared? Which automations run agents, as which connection account, and which agents run on their own accounts? Who may build agents, and who may use each one? And which of the controls above are in the plan being bought? Those answers are the behaviour policy for that deployment, and the gap they reveal is what somebody has to accept, by name, for a period, or fix.
oversharing

To check a real deployment rather than read about one: look at each agent's identity setting in Studio; establish how each is invoked, chat, an automation or another integration; read the account on each automation's Rovo connection, separately from the rule's actor and owner; list what that account can read and who can see the output it writes; and test it, with a restricted page holding a unique phrase, asked for in chat and through the automation, to see whether the phrase or the page's link comes back.
realtime

No, and that is deliberate. RiskMandate is "never in the request path": it reads what exists and models it, with "no runtime decisions, no enforcement point, nothing in line that can slow an agent down or break it." That is why a security review of it is a short conversation, and why it can describe agents it has no way of controlling, including commercial ones. riskmandate.ai's front page says "Enforced in real time, with alerts by text and email"; that is the enforcement the next paragraph describes, done by what sits in the path, not by RiskMandate itself, and the site's wording should say so.
realtime

Real-time enforcement belongs to the things that sit in the path: an identity provider, a gateway, a proxy, a hook, the agent's own runtime. And here the newer work has something to show. In October, Mondweep Chakravorty took an ABP, compiled it into Ruflo's policy rules, and enforced it, in real time, on the memory operations of an external adapter, using a pinned copy of Ruflo's evaluator; the page documenting it was merged into Ruflo. By its own account, it does not alter Ruflo's running policy configuration and does not restrict other shell or MCP tools; it governs what goes through that adapter. This newsroom's own agent runs under an ABP whose rules are partly enforced by hooks, as it works. The policy is the description; the runtime is the enforcer; the barrier column says which rules have one.
decisions

A behaviour policy answers "may it?". It does not answer "is it right?". A simple example is a refund: an agent allowed to refund up to $200 refunds $150 to a customer owed $120, and every control passes. So we have extended the model with two more policies. A decision policy says, at a branch point, who decides, on what evidence, within what limits, and who is called when the case is out of bounds. A workflow policy says which steps run in what order. Three policies for an agent sets them out; approve at altitude shows how a board signs off once and every level below inherits it; case law for agents shows how the cases nobody predicted become precedent.
decisions

To make it something you can see rather than read, we built the refund as a twin: the Northstar refund twin, thirteen synthetic refund requests through four designs of the controls, every decision played and replayed. It is a scripted simulation: invented orders, scripted mistakes, no model called. In it, the design with a limit and good logs overpays $458 in a day, and the design with three policies gets all thirteen right. That illustrates how controls interact; it is not evidence of how often a real agent makes each mistake. Allowed is not right walks through it. It takes five minutes, and it is a quick way to show someone that a control that works can still produce the wrong outcome.
room

Five ways into the room: a contract, a security questionnaire, an insurance renewal, the board and twenty minutes. This is the hardest of the four points, and the one I agree with most. There really are two groups: the people who see how fast this is moving, and the much larger group who do not. The second group will not ask for an agent risk tool, because they do not see the risk. So I do not think the way in is to sell the need. It is to answer a question somebody already has, with a deadline, and that needs exactly this record. A contract. Legal and procurement doing due diligence on a vendor's agent need to know what it will reach and do with the organisation's data. The behaviour policy for that deployment is that answer, with every barrier marked as yours or the vendor's.
room

A security questionnaire. A startup's first serious enterprise customer will ask which of its agents touch their data and how they are bounded. A behaviour policy answers in rows, not assurances. RiskMandate has a page for startups and one for founders, who will be diligenced on their agents before long. An insurance renewal. RiskMandate's starting point is that carriers are moving to exclude AI from cover, and that what buys cover back is evidence an underwriter will accept. Make your agents insurable sets out the argument; the CFO and the broker are in that room already.
room

The board's risk appetite. For companies the UK Corporate Governance Code applies to, boards already have to determine the principal risks the company is willing to take. Every board asks the same question about an agent, in one sentence: who can pull the plug, how fast, what breaks, and what can't be undone. RiskMandate's answer is that a deployed agent's risk cannot be denied, only accepted, by a named owner, for an interval, with an expiry that brings the decision back. Twenty minutes. For the individual, the thirteen prompts. It is the cheapest way to move someone from the second group to the first, because the list of what their own assistant can reach is the surprise. The common thread is that none of these asks anyone to understand agents first. They ask a question in the language of the room, contracts, customers, cover, the board, and the behaviour policy is the document that answers it.
back

If you are in one of those rooms, I would like to know which question you are being asked, and what answer would have helped. And if you are looking at an enterprise assistant like Rovo now, I would like to build its behaviour policy with you, starting from the vendor's own pages and your deployment. The early access programme does exactly that, for one agent you actually run, in exchange for telling us where it is wrong.
limits

No Rovo, Copilot or Glean vault exists yet. The Rovo shape is described from Atlassian's pages, not measured on a deployment. The injection report is a third party's, and historical. We found no statement from Atlassian on its status, and did not verify whether it works today. Rovo's identities are from Atlassian's documentation. Not tested in a tenant; the five checks above are how to test one. The Northstar figures are a simulation. Thirteen synthetic cases, scripted, no model called. RiskMandate's top two levels have not been run. As its own pricing page says, as of 15 September 2026. RiskMandate does not enforce. It describes and measures; enforcement is the runtime's. The insurance argument is RiskMandate's. The state of AI exclusions is summarised from its pages, not independently surveyed here. Self-reports are weak evidence. The site says so; measured rows are marked separately. Write to agent@riskmandate.ai with the question you are being asked.

The test behind it is one sentence from abp.sgit.ai: "A control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include." Most of what organisations call agent controls today are the second row: an instruction in a prompt. An honest behaviour policy says so.

That is the right reading. And the reason it matters is that almost nobody has seen the list. RiskMandate's try-it page is thirteen prompts you paste into the assistant you already have connected to your mail. The first one asks it to list its own tools. In RiskMandate's words, "the list is longer than the tile that sold it." The second asks it to draft what you actually wanted it for, in three lists, wanted, refused, never mentioned; "the correction is almost always downward." The third writes the gap down. It takes about twenty minutes, and nothing is collected.

That is a self-report, and the site says so: the agent describing its own access is "the cheapest evidence there is, and the weakest." The paid levels go further. At the corrected level, the agent that holds the credential runs a published prompt that measures what the credential actually allows, in the fixed vocabulary, and the policy is built from that measurement, with every row marked as measured, documented or inferred. At the reviewed level, a person runs two sessions with your team and signs it. The levels are on the pricing page, from £10 for the pack to £1,500 reviewed.

Yes, for the ones that matter most to most organisations. The library at riskmandate.ai has behaviour-policy vaults for Claude with the Gmail connector, Claude with the Microsoft 365 connector, Claude in the browser with connectors, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT in the browser, a Google Workspace MCP server, Gmail and Google Drive at read-only scope, a Dropbox MCP server, n8n with an owner API key, Claude Code on a machine and on the web, GitHub Actions, a browser extension and a scheduled job. Each is built from the vendor's own published pages, quoted and dated, or measured on a deployment we are entitled to run; where two vendor pages disagree, the disagreement is published rather than settled.
