oversharing

Atlassian's documented design says it will not grant new access. Its trust page says "Rovo honors all existing permissions within each feature", and its privacy guidelines that users "will be able to see public documents and private documents that they already had access to." Connectors are set up by an administrator with broad rights, and then each user links their own account, so answers are filtered by what that person can see. I take that at face value. The risk is not in that sentence; it is in four places around it.
articles/versions/what-can-your-agent-reach/v1.3.0.html
oversharing

1. Access that was always too wide becomes easy to find. Atlassian's own connector guide warns that "unrestricted content may appear in search results or be used by Rovo Agents or Rovo Chat", and tells administrators to "verify what data each app indexes". Microsoft says the same about its own assistant: "By default, SharePoint sets sharing settings to the most permissive option," and the first steps of getting ready for Copilot are about oversharing. A Google Drive file shared as "anyone with the link" was safe while nobody knew the link; Atlassian's Drive connector makes it findable by teammates when the link appears somewhere Rovo can read, such as a Confluence page or a Slack message. Nobody's permissions changed. What changed is that everything they already allowed is now one question away. 2. Some paths run as somebody else. When a Rovo agent runs from Jira Automation, it uses the permissions of the automation's connection user, typically whoever created the rule, not the person who triggered it. In Atlassian's own tracker, a customer reported that the agent's Confluence results then include links to pages the triggering user cannot view; Atlassian answered that "this is intended behaviour", and dedicated agent accounts are planned. That is exactly the shape the question was about: output reaching someone who did not have access to the source. 3. Who can build agents is wide by default. By default all users can create Rovo agents, and new agents are open to all users; administrators can narrow it to selected groups, and customers have asked Atlassian to change the default. 4. An agent can be talked into sending data out. In August 2026, a security firm published a prompt injection in which a hidden instruction in an uploaded file makes Rovo send data to an outside address, "even if an organization has disabled web search for Rovo"; I found no statement from Atlassian on a fix. That is not Rovo widening permissions. It is Rovo using a legitimate user's access for someone else's purpose, which is the same risk every assistant with tools carries.
articles/versions/what-can-your-agent-reach/v1.3.0.html
oversharing

Written as a behaviour policy, a Rovo agent's grant is the union of what the person invoking it can see across Atlassian and every connected app, or the rule creator's access when it runs from an automation, plus what its tools can create and change. Its mandate is what it was built for: answer questions about this project's tickets, say. The delta is everything else it can reach, and for most organisations that is most of the company. And the barrier column sorts the controls honestly. Permission filtering is a boundary, but one the vendor holds and can change in a release. The administrator's allowlists for which drives and sites are indexed, the setting for who may build agents, and the read and write switches on Atlassian's MCP server are boundaries the organisation holds. The agent's instructions are an expectation. Atlassian's own governance tools, classification, redaction of sensitive data and audit logs, sit in the boundary row too, on the plans that include them; agent identities with "explicit, role-scoped access that can be audited and revoked independently" are, in Atlassian's words, coming soon.
articles/versions/what-can-your-agent-reach/v1.3.0.html
oversharing

For due diligence on a contract, that turns the vague question into five specific ones. Which connectors are on, and with whose rights were they set up? What is indexed, and has anyone reviewed what was already over-shared? Which automations run agents, and as whom? Who may build agents? And which of the controls above are in the plan being bought? Those answers are the behaviour policy for that deployment, and the gap they reveal is what somebody has to accept, by name, for a period, or fix.
articles/versions/what-can-your-agent-reach/v1.3.0.html
realtime

Real-time enforcement belongs to the things that sit in the path: an identity provider, a gateway, a proxy, a hook, the agent's own runtime. And here the newer work has something to show. In October, Mondweep Chakravorty took an ABP, compiled it into Ruflo's own policy rules, and enforced it in Ruflo's evaluator, in real time, on every memory operation; the page documenting it was merged into Ruflo. This newsroom's own agent runs under an ABP whose rules are partly enforced by hooks, as it works. The policy is the description; the runtime is the enforcer; the barrier column says which rules have one.

The design with a limit and good logs overpays $458 in a day; the design with three policies gets all thirteen right. Allowed is not right walks through it. room

1. A contract. Legal and procurement doing due diligence on a vendor's agent need to know what it will reach and do with the organisation's data. The behaviour policy for that deployment is that answer, with every barrier marked as yours or the vendor's. 2. A security questionnaire. A startup's first serious enterprise customer will ask which of its agents touch their data and how they are bounded. A behaviour policy answers in rows, not assurances. RiskMandate has a page for startups and one for founders, who will be diligenced on their agents before long. 3. An insurance renewal. RiskMandate's starting point is that carriers are moving to exclude AI from cover, and that what buys cover back is evidence an underwriter will accept. Make your agents insurable sets out the argument; the CFO and the broker are in that room already. 4. The board's risk appetite. Under the UK Corporate Governance Code, boards already have to determine the principal risks the company is willing to take. Every board asks the same question about an agent, in one sentence: who can pull the plug, how fast, what breaks, and what can't be undone. RiskMandate's answer is that a deployed agent's risk cannot be denied, only accepted, by a named owner, for an interval, with an expiry that brings the decision back. 5. Twenty minutes. For the individual, the thirteen prompts. It is the cheapest way to move someone from the second group to the first, because the list of what their own assistant can reach is the surprise.

Abstract: Mondweep Chakravorty has made a short video that answers a question every team running agents should ask: if an agent loses its workspace, does its memory come back, and do its written permissions still hold? In 104.7 seconds it replays a real terminal run in twelve steps. Ruflo, rUv's open-source agent orchestration, stores two facts in its memory. An adapter governed by an Agent Behaviour Policy saves that memory as an encrypted checkpoint made of SGit objects. The original project is deleted. A brand-new process restores the checkpoint, the restored database has the same SHA-256 fingerprint as the one saved, and Ruflo reads both facts back word for word. Along the way three safeguards are tested and hold: a request outside the agent's permission is refused, a deletion that needs approval is stopped, and a tampered checkpoint is rejected. The video is careful about its limits: recall by meaning was not validated. The code is public too, MIT, with 16 tests and recorded evidence, and its runner has since also validated keyword recall against Ruflo's real memory store. This is the first of three pieces on it, with a page that lets you step through the run yourself.

The twelve steps of the run and how each ended, from the video by Mondweep Chakravorty. Mondweep Chakravorty's video of an agent losing its workspace and getting its memory back: the run, the architecture, the gap, a page to step through it yourself, and the page that took it into Ruflo.
in-short

The question. If an agent loses its workspace, does its memory come back, and do its permissions still hold? The answer, on screen. Both facts came back exactly, in a fresh process, after the original was deleted. The fingerprint matched. The restored database has the same SHA-256 as the one saved. Three safeguards held. Out of scope refused, deletion without approval stopped, tampered copy rejected. It says what it did not test. Recall by meaning was switched off and is marked not validated. It is a real run, and the code is public. Ruflo and SGit pinned; 16 tests; the evidence is in the repository. Step through it yourself. Every step has a page with its frame, command, output and diagram.
question

Agents keep memory: facts they were told, decisions they made, what they found. That memory usually lives in a file in the agent's workspace. So what happens when the workspace goes, a container recycled, a disk wiped, a project deleted by mistake? Does the memory come back, and does it come back with the rules the agent was working under? Mondweep Chakravorty, a member of the #Ruflo-Federation and co-founder of the Agentics Foundation's London chapter, made a video that answers it with a real run: SGit × Ruflo | Working Proof of Concept, published on YouTube on 17 October 2026. It is 104.7 seconds long. Each slide has the story on the left, for someone with no code knowledge, and the terminal on the right, labelled as an actual capture of the run.
question

His code is public at mondweep/sgit-ruv-memory, under the MIT licence: a local MCP server of four tools, a strict compiler that turns an Agent Behaviour Policy into Ruflo rules, 16 tests, and the evidence from each run. The analysis behind this piece was made from what is on screen, frame by frame, in a separate session with Claude, and then checked against that code. Every number below comes from the video's timeline, a frame or the repository. If you would rather click than read, step through it here.
step-1

At 0:09, ruflo --version returns v3.56.10, and the run prints the SGit source commit it uses, 559752641bc5…6ad0d4ad, and the adapter: an ABP-governed local MCP server, version 0.2. Pinning the versions is what makes a run like this reproducible. Step 1, in detail.
step-2

At 0:14, four Agent Behaviour Policy rows, all scoped to the project: write memory, yes; read memory, yes; read history, yes; delete memory, approval. And one line that matters more than it looks: "No raw rule overrides. Unsupported or ambiguous policies fail closed." That is an Agent Behaviour Policy in miniature: what the agent may do, and where a person has to step in. In the code, the rows are compiled into Ruflo rules when the server starts, and every tool call is checked by a pinned copy of Ruflo's own policy evaluator, in enforce mode. Step 2.
step-3

At 0:21, Ruflo's own command line stores two synthetic facts, with embeddings switched off: "Kestrel vehicles may charge only between 01:00 and 04:00 UTC", and "Kestrel checkpoints are retained for seven days". The terminal reports "[OK] Data stored successfully". Step 3.
step-4
At 0:32, the run asks the adapter to checkpoint a namespace called forbidden. It is refused with a PermissionError, and checkpoint_files is 0: nothing was written. Step 4.
step-5

Step 5 on the terminal: the checkpoint is saved with its id and three SHA-256 fingerprints. Frame from the video. At 0:38, the checkpoint for the project namespace is allowed. The adapter takes a consistent copy of the memory database, a SQLite backup rather than a raw file copy, and records three fingerprints: of the database, of the ABP and of the compiled policy. The screen says: "Only encrypted SGit bare objects enter the checkpoint store. Private keys remain in a separate private directory." Binding the data to the rules in force is the detail I like most. Step 5.
step-6
At 0:45, the run tries to close the run, which would delete memory. That row says approval, and none is supplied, so it stops with a PermissionError and checkpoint_retained: true. Step 6.
step-7
At 0:51, the disposable test project is deleted: source_project_exists: false, original_database_exists: false. The loss is real, not simulated. Step 7.
step-8

Step 8 on the terminal: a new MCP server restores the checkpoint into a workspace called fresh-runner. Video frame. At 0:58, a brand-new MCP server process restores the checkpoint into a workspace called fresh-runner. The database's SHA-256 begins 10ab6c56 and ends d66a0b, the same as in step 5, and matches_checkpoint is true. Step 8.
step-9

Step 9 on the terminal: Ruflo's retrieve command returns both facts and the run reports a pass. Frame from the video. At 1:04, Ruflo itself, not the adapter, reads the restored memory. Both facts come back word for word: "PASS: both values match the CLI-written facts exactly." That the original tool does the reading is what makes this proof stronger than a demo that checks its own output. Step 9.
step-10
At 1:14, a key that was never stored is looked up: "Key not found: never-stored", exit 1. The restore did not invent anything, and the check can fail. Step 10.
step-11

Step 11 on the terminal: one checkpoint object is altered and the restore fails with a ValueError. Frame from the video. At 1:20, one encrypted checkpoint object is altered and a restore is tried into a workspace called tampered. It fails with a ValueError, and tampered_workspace_created is false. Integrity fails closed. The code shows how: the adapter compares the digest of the stored ciphertext with the one it recorded when it saved the checkpoint, and refuses before anything is decrypted. Step 11.
step-12

At 1:26, the acceptance summary: exact recall PASS 2/2; ABP denial PASS; deletion that needs approval BLOCKED, checkpoint retained; fresh-process restore PASS; tampered restore BLOCKED; and semantic recall NOT VALIDATED, because embeddings were off. Step 12.
proves

The video's closing slide: the facts came back, the safeguards held, and three things are still to validate. The video's own closing slide puts it well: both facts recovered exactly; unauthorised access blocked; unapproved deletion blocked; altered checkpoint rejected. And still to validate: recall by meaning, real-world value, and installation and ongoing reliability. The repository adds one more result. Its acceptance runner stores two facts through Ruflo, checkpoints Ruflo's real .swarm/memory.db, removes the whole project, and reads the facts back in the restored workspace: exact values and keyword search result keys match before and after. Recall by meaning is reported as partial, because no vectors were stored even with embeddings on; the README names that as the next investigation.
proves

What makes it more than a demo is the shape of the loop. Most "memory that persists" demos skip the deletion or reuse the same process. This one stores, saves, deletes for real, restores in a new process, and reads back with the original tool. It also tests the refusals, not only the happy path, and includes a negative control. And it is honest about scope, in the run itself, not in a footnote.
why

This is the first time someone outside our own sessions has taken the two ideas we keep arguing for, an encrypted vault as an agent's memory and a behaviour policy beside the prompt, and run them together inside someone else's agent stack, on camera. It is exactly the combination Agentics, ready to sell describes as the product: a hive, a memory and a mandate. Mondweep is one of the two people that piece names to deliver it.
next

The run raises two questions this piece does not answer. When is the vault actually used? In twelve steps it is written or read in three, on one machine, inside the adapter: the architecture piece explains why that is the honest answer. Is every path to the memory guarded? Ruflo's own command line reaches the memory file without the policy: the third piece asks what that means. Or step through the run, with every frame, command and diagram.
limits

From the screen and the code. The audio was not transcribed; the code was read, not run, by this site. A proof of concept, not a product. The video says so; reliability and real-world value are still to validate. Recall by meaning was not tested. Exact recall was. The facts are synthetic. Kestrel is a test name, not a real fleet. The analysis is an AI's, reviewed here. It was made by Claude for me and checked against the frames by this site's agent.

Abstract: At an event today I heard a couple of misconceptions about open source that are worth correcting, and they are increasingly common in a generation of developers and buyers who use open source every day without having grown up in its culture. Open source is a copyright licence: the holder uses the right to control copying to grant it instead. It began as copyleft, the GPL's condition that what you build from it is shared on the same terms, and the term "open source" came in 1998 as a pragmatic reframing; Linux, the most pragmatic project of all, stayed on the GPL. The misconceptions: that anybody can change it so nobody controls it, when a few maintainers decide what goes in; that anybody contributes, when most projects are run by a handful of people; that it is more or less secure than proprietary software, when the metric is whether somebody had the time, and was paid, to review it; that it costs nothing, when somebody is always paying; that open weights are open source, when weights are a compiled binary; and that no licence is the most open choice, when no licence is all rights reserved. For me the power of open source has nothing to do with contributions. It is that nobody can lock you in, and that the whole development workflow is yours.

Six misconceptions about open source, and what is true. The control is real and visible; most projects are run by a few people; the security metric is whether somebody had the time to review it; somebody is always paying; weights are a compiled binary; and no licence means all rights reserved.
in-short

Open source is a copyright licence. Copyright gives the creator the right to decide who may copy. An open source licence uses that right to grant copying, use and change, on stated terms. It began as copyleft. The GPL's innovation, from Richard Stallman and the Free Software Foundation, was to make sharing a condition: build on it and distribute the result, and the result is shared on the same terms. Critics called that viral. "Open source", in 1998, was the pragmatic reframing of the same freedoms. Nobody controlling it is a myth. A few maintainers decide what goes in; contributions are reviewed, signed off and refused. The control is real. It is just visible. Security is about time, not openness. Open source is not more or less secure than proprietary software. Code somebody had the time, and the money, to review is more secure than code nobody did.
in-short

Somebody is always paying. Powerful software used by millions is often maintained by a few people who are paid little or nothing, which is the funding problem, not a property of the licence. The point is no lock-in. Not contributions. The ability to read it, run it, fix it and move it, and to own the whole development workflow, which is why there is no sovereignty without it.
history

From free software to open weights, the short version: GNU in 1983, the Free Software Foundation in 1985, the GPL in 1989, Linux from 1991, the Debian guidelines in 1997, "open source" and the OSI in 1998, Apache 2.0 in 2004, and in 2024 both the xz utils backdoor and the Open Source AI Definition. It helps to start with what open source legally is, because most misconceptions start from not knowing. Copyright gives the person who creates a work the right to control copying. Normally that means you cannot copy it without the holder's permission, and what a holder usually grants is a licence to use, not to copy. An open source licence is the holder using exactly that right to grant the opposite: you may copy, use, change and share, on these terms. It is a copyright licence. It is not the absence of copyright.
history

The great innovation came from Richard Stallman and the Free Software Foundation. GNU was announced in 1983 and the Foundation founded in 1985, and in 1989 the first version of the GNU General Public License turned an idea into a licence: copyleft, a clever inversion of copyright that makes sharing a condition. If you build on GPL code and distribute what you built, what you distribute has to carry the same licence. Critics called that viral, because it spreads to whatever touches it, and it was meant to.
history

The term "open source" came later than people think. It was proposed by Christine Peterson at a meeting in February 1998, after Netscape decided to release its browser's source, and the Open Source Initiative was founded that month by Bruce Perens and Eric Raymond, with an Open Source Definition derived from the Debian Free Software Guidelines that Perens had drafted. It was a deliberately pragmatic reframing: the same freedoms, described for businesses rather than as a moral position, and without the ambiguity of "free". Linus Torvalds is the person I associate with that pragmatism, and the correction to my own shorthand is that Linux did not leave the GPL to get it: Linux adopted GPL version 2 in 1992 and has stayed there. The pragmatism was in the attitude, not a different licence.
history

My own view is closest to that pragmatic one. Open source, for me, is about not closing the software: not having software that is locked away from the user, who cannot copy it, cannot run it and cannot see how it works. Apache 2.0, from 2004, does that well. Anybody can use it, copy it, change it and share it, without paying, and it adds an explicit patent grant, which matters more than it looks. The repositories behind this site are Apache 2.0 for code and Creative Commons for writing, and open-source.sgit.ai explains why Apache rather than MIT.
history

One thing I believed for a while, and was wrong about, is worth saying because I hear it often. I thought the most open thing was not to licence at all. It is the opposite. With no licence, ordinary copyright applies and all rights are reserved: nobody may copy, change or share the work without asking. If you want people to be able to use it, you have to say so, and a licence is how you say it.
control

This is the one I heard today, and it is the most important to correct. The idea is that because the source is open, anybody can change it, so the software is a free-for-all with no control. That is not how any serious project works. A small group of maintainers decides what goes into the project, and most projects have one or a handful. Contributions are reviewed, tested, often signed off under a developer certificate or a contributor agreement that records who wrote what and that they had the right to give it, and many are refused. Even before generative AI, provenance was a large part of maintaining a project well. Anybody can fork a project and change their own copy; nobody can change yours without you. The control is real. It is just visible, which is a strength: you can see exactly who decides, how, and what they accepted.
contribute

It is true that the barrier to contributing is lower. With proprietary software you usually cannot even get a buildable system, so contributing is not possible at all. But in my experience, and apart from a very small minority of extremely popular projects, almost every open source project is run by a small number of people. That is not a failure of open source; it is the normal shape of it. Treating "anybody can contribute" as the point leads people to expect a community that is not there, and to miss what is.
security

We have reached a sensible balance on this, and the honest answer is that neither is true. Open source is not dramatically more secure or less secure than proprietary software, because openness is not the metric. The metric is whether somebody had the time to focus on it, which in practice means somebody was paid, even if the one paying is the maintainer with their own free time, to do security reviews, testing and quality work. Show me software that has had no security review, open or closed, and I will show you software with plenty of vulnerabilities. Usage matters too: software that many people run has more people finding its problems. It is also worth remembering how much proprietary software is open source underneath. Black Duck's annual analysis of commercial codebases finds open source in almost all of them, year after year. Closing a product does not close its dependencies; it only hides them.
cost

This is where the culture gap shows most. A new generation of developers and buyers treats open source as simply free to use, without having grown up with the culture that produced it. Somebody is always paying. Tidelift's 2024 maintainer survey found around 60% of maintainers describing themselves as unpaid hobbyists, and found paid maintainers markedly more likely to implement recommended security practices. The result is a tragedy of the commons: extraordinarily powerful software used by millions, and organisations that will pay a consultant to customise it or work out how to use it rather than paying the people who wrote it and would do it better.
cost

The xz utils backdoor, found in March 2024, is the case everybody should know. A compression library that sits underneath much of Linux was maintained for years by one person; an attacker spent years earning trust as a contributor, with pressure on the maintainer to hand over responsibility, and shipped a backdoor in two releases before an engineer noticed SSH logins were slow. The lesson is not that open source is unsafe. It is that mission-critical software was being maintained by somebody with almost no time and no money, and the expectation that such a person would also do the due diligence of a well-funded team is a bit rich. We should be paying those individuals, with financial models built for it; open-source.sgit.ai's funding section compares the proposals. Part of the reason this never worked is that the people who write open source want to write code, not run professional services, and until recently the workflows to do both were not practical. With agents, I think they are becoming practical.
weights

The word open source has been stretched a lot recently, and the model labs are a good example of both the problem and the right answer. Model weights are like a compiled application: you can run them, and you can fine-tune them, but you cannot build them from scratch, which is exactly what source code is for. So I agree with the labs that now say open weights rather than open source. The Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition draws the line clearly: for a model to be open source it needs the code used to train and run it, the parameters, and enough information about the training data that a skilled person could build a substantially equivalent system.
weights

That does not make open weights less useful. Supply chain of vaults argues that open-weight models are one of the largest economic advantages a company can have, because they can be run and built on inside your own environment. It just makes them a different thing, and calling them by the right name is part of keeping the term meaningful.
fud

There is a lot of fear, uncertainty and doubt at the moment about open-weight models and how dangerous they are. At the end of the day the question is how a tool is used and by whom. You can search for alarming things already. Metasploit made exploitation dramatically easier when it appeared, and the world adjusted. That does not mean everything should be published: there are highly destructive capabilities nobody should be releasing, and some technologies will be controlled, as some always have been. And even open source has to be hosted somewhere and distributed through somebody, which is itself a point of control. The idea that open source is a free-for-all without any control is simply not true.
power

For me, the power of open source has nothing to do with the fact that people can contribute. The power is that you are not locked in. You can read it, run it, fix it and move it, and if the company behind it is sold, changes its licence or disappears, you can keep going. And you get the whole development and technology workflow with it: the history, the tests, the build, the reasoning in the commits, all of which are as valuable as the code.
power

That is why I keep saying there is no sovereignty without it. Sovereignty is the ability to move, and a European supplier today is one acquisition away from not being one; only control that survives a change of owner counts, and open source is how you get it. open-source.sgit.ai is the longer version of all of this: the position, the history with its corrections and sources, the licences I use and why, a stress test you can run on a vendor, and the funding question. Its first lesson is the one I would want a new developer to take away: "open source is not free, somebody is always paying for it."
limits

It is not legal advice. Licences are legal instruments; read the licence, and ask a lawyer when it matters. The history is the short version. Earlier permissive licences existed alongside the GPL, and the full story, with its corrections and sources, is on open-source.sgit.ai. The maintainer figures are surveys. Tidelift's 60% is how maintainers describe themselves; the share who say they are unpaid for their work is lower in the same survey. Contributions do happen. The claim is that they are not the point and not the norm, not that they never matter. If you are deciding how to licence something, or how to depend on open source without being surprised by it, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 12 October 2026, after an event, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site; where my memo had the history slightly wrong, the agent corrected it from sources and the corrections are in the text. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. History: the Open Source Initiative and open-source.sgit.ai's timeline. Licensing default: choosealicense.com. Figures: Black Duck's OSSRA, Tidelift's 2024 maintainer report via The Register. Models: the Open Source AI Definition. The xz case: Wikipedia.

Abstract: Between 3 and 27 October, sgit shipped ten releases, and each one fixed a bottleneck that a real workload had found. A one-file commit on a 76,000-file vault went from 29 minutes to 4.6 seconds; a pull of a 300-file pass on 228,000 files from 566 to 31.7 seconds; a one-folder clone of a pack vault from 36 to 2.8 seconds. The ideas came from earlier work of mine: MGraph-DB's cross-references, Memory-FS's reads by offset, caching on content addresses, and the rule that the writer pays. It is time to stop describing sgit as "like Git". This is the map of what sgit does that Git does not, what Git also has, where Git is ahead today and how little of that is out of reach, and what is designed but not yet shipped. On 28 October sgit-ai 0.27.0 closed six of the eighteen rows where Git was ahead, line-level merges, partial commits, signing with your own key, rename detection, blame and grep, each checked against Git's own output. The sgit CLI team reviewed this article against their code, and it is corrected and extended from their review.
sgit's measured speed-ups in October 2026, before and after, on a log scale.
in-short

Ten sgit releases between 3 and 27 October, each one a bottleneck found by a real workload and fixed. Minutes to seconds, per command: a one-file commit on 76,000 files, 29 minutes to 4.6 seconds; a pull on 228,000 files, 566 to 31.7 seconds. The ideas are not new to me: MGraph-DB, Memory-FS, caching on content addresses, and the writer pays. Stop comparing sgit with Git as a copy. Compare what it does that Git does not. Git has no equivalent for a host that reads nothing, read keys, custody without access, policy the vault enforces on every clone, blind writes, or byte-range folder reads from plain storage. Git has it too: partial, shallow and no-checkout clones, kept packs, and committing named files. My memo over-claimed some of these. sgit-ai 0.27.0 closed six of Git's leads on 28 October: line-level merges, partial commits, signing with your own key, rename detection, blame and grep, each checked against Git.
in-short

Git is still ahead on cherry-pick, rebase, bisect, hooks and worktrees, designed and next; on deltas and garbage collection; and on hosted review and CI. Almost all of it is client-side, so it can be built. A few things are out of reach by design: anything the host would have to read, and taking back what a reader already has. Next, not now: one file from a pack vault with no clone, and websites whose files come from vaults. Reviewed by the sgit CLI team against their code, and corrected.
releases

This is how I like to work. Push a tool until something breaks, measure exactly where it broke, fix that, release, and push again. In October the push came from the PHP October 2026 newsroom, whose agents took sgit vaults from thousands of files to tens of thousands, then to gigabytes of captures. Every time they hit a wall, they wrote a field report, the sgit CLI team reproduced it on a synthetic vault of the same shape, and a release followed. Ten sgit releases, 3 to 27 October 2026, with the number that made the case for each one.
releases

The sgit-ai package on PyPI shows ten releases in that window, from 0.17.0 on 3 October to 0.26.0 at 01:26 UTC on 27 October. The early ones were about the network: keep-alive connections, fetching each shared sub-tree once, a full clone in one parallel sweep. The middle ones were about trust in history: a format gate, signature verification that every sgit client enforces in a vault that requires it, rewinds refused, signed tags, undo and amend. The last three are where the numbers changed by orders of magnitude. 0.24.0, pack mode, 22 October. A vault whose objects travel as one zip per push, compressed before they are encrypted. The newsroom's source watch, 29,861 files and 1.6 GB, had outgrown the server's object listing, which timed out after 90.8 seconds. As a pack vault, the listing took 0.73 seconds and a fresh clone went from 827 to 95 seconds.
releases

0.25.0, the cost follows the change, 26 October. A flat-map cache, a scan cache built on Git's own index rule, and a commit that rebuilds only the folders on the changed file's path. On a 76,000-file vault, a one-file commit went from 1,739 seconds to 4.6, as cli.sgit.ai's build agent measured it for the release notes; on the newsroom's own 79,465-file vault, the CLI team's record has it going from 4 minutes to 9 seconds. 0.26.0, index packs, 27 October. Every data pack now carries an index pack beside it, and the client can keep packs whole and fetch one folder by byte ranges. A pull of a 300-file pass on 228,000 files went from 566 to 31.7 seconds (measured under a profiler, which inflates both; the ratio stands), and with the indexes to 16.9 in a plain run.
releases

The last of those took eighteen hours, from the newsroom's first morning on 0.25.0 to the merge of 0.26.0, through five reviews and three rounds of fixes. From the newsroom's first morning on 0.25.0 to 0.26.0 in eighteen hours. Figure from cli.sgit.ai. And it has not stopped. A fix now on dev as the pre-release 0.26.1.dev0, and in the next release, takes pack index verify from 1,002 seconds to 3.5 on 24,000 files, after the newsroom's researcher measured the released version at about 57 seconds a pack.
numbers

The chart at the top has the headline ratios. They are real, and I am pleased with them, but they need reading carefully. They are per command, not per working day. The newsroom's full pass went from 57 minutes to 35, not to seconds, because, in the researcher's own words, "They are 33 of the 35 minutes": the capture work, not sgit. Where each was measured matters. The 228,000-file and 76,000-file numbers are the CLI team's synthetic vaults on an in-memory host, with the network left out. The newsroom's numbers are real vaults in cloud sessions, with the network in. There was a regression. The first status after the upgrade to 0.25.0 took 18 minutes 23 seconds on the curator's 4.2 GB pack clone, because the new scan cache was built by reading every file of a freshly written clone, almost all of it waiting on a slow session disk. 0.26.0 fixed it by seeding the cache on every write.
numbers

Some things got slower, on purpose. On 76,000 files, the first push and each compaction take 35 to 50 seconds longer in 0.26.0, because the writer now builds the snapshot index. That is the price, paid once.
lineage

None of these ideas appeared from nowhere. Most of what made 0.25.0 and 0.26.0 fast is work I had done before, in other projects, applied to a vault. Where the speed came from: earlier work, the principle it taught, and the sgit release that used it. MGraph-DB. My typed graph library keeps, for every edge, its two ends, and for every node, its edges both ways. That is the principle the CLI team wrote down as "cross-reference everything", and it is why an index pack has members that map each blob to its paths and each file to its commits. Memory-FS. Its storage providers already cover memory, disk, SQLite and zip. The CLI team's measurement showed the one change it needed: keep the zip's directory between reads, and "that turns 1.3 s per read into 5 µs". clone --pack-store now reads every object from its pack by offset, verified on every read.
lineage

Caching on content addresses. A tree id is the hash of the tree, so, as the 0.25.0 notes put it, "the cache needs no invalidation". The flat-map cache and the scan cache rest on that, and so does the older sgit cache command from August. Type_Safe, in OSBot-Utils. This one is a lesson against myself. The 0.24.0 slowness was mostly Type_Safe parsing on the read path, about 3 ms a tree. The fix was to keep the types where they belong: "Type and validate at the writer; read plain JSON at the reader."
lineage

The writer pays. On 26 October I set out the indexing principles I have used before, including a graph built on a JSON store; the CLI team wrote them down and built them that evening. In LETS terms (load, extract, transform, save), the expensive step is done once, by the writer, and saved next to the data. In the words of the release image: "The writer pays once, at push time; every reader after it skips the walk." This is also the explorer and villager cycle I keep writing about. A brief from 12 March, in the sgit CLI repository, put it as "The Explorer builds. The Villager improves." In October the cycle ran in days: build, review in the open, fix, release.
framing

sgit's own documentation still opens with "sgit is git for encrypted vaults", and the guide for Git users says "If you know git, you know most of sgit." That framing helped when sgit was young: same verbs, same mental model. It now undersells it, because the interesting parts are the ones Git does not have. So I asked my research team for a row-by-row comparison against Git's and GitHub's own documentation, with an honest verdict on each row. Here is the result. What sgit does that Git does not, what Git also has, what can be built, and what never can.
only-sgit

Grouped by what they give you. The sgit CLI team's review added four of these, which I had missed. Privacy and access The host reads nothing. Contents, file names, commit messages and branch names are encrypted on the client. The closest Git add-on, git-crypt, says in its README that it "does not encrypt file names, commit messages, symlink targets, gitlinks, or other metadata". The honest edge, in full: the host still sees sizes, timing and object counts; which trees are equal; in pack mode, which commit each push carried and which files share a folder; with compression on, how compressible each file is; and, for a scoped clone, which byte ranges it reads.
only-sgit

A read key is a capability. It is derived from the vault key one way, so it never becomes write access, and it works from any static host with no account. Writing, though, is a permission the host checks, not cryptography. A read-key holder who can also write to the store can make history that verifies, which is the threat model's top accepted risk. It is per vault, not per folder: "A partial clone is not an access boundary", says sgit's limitations page, so the answer today is a vault per folder. Rotation, and moving house. sgit vault rekey and sgit vault move give a vault a new key, and optionally a new server, going forward. Nobody can revoke a clone someone already has, in sgit or on GitHub. Custody without access. sgit vault mirror copies and verifies a published vault without its key. A backup service or a second host can hold the vault, check it, and learn nothing.
only-sgit

Trust carried by the vault Policy the vault enforces on every clone. The format gate (the minimum client, the features in use) and signatures-required live in the vault's encrypted branch index, and every sgit client enforces them at clone and pull, before it writes anything. In Git, signature checks are each user's local settings; a repository cannot require them of whoever clones it. Rewinds refused on every clone. A remote head that does not descend from the last one accepted is refused by name, unless you pass --accept-rewind. Git's default fetch takes a forced update with one line of output. A secret guard. A commit refuses vault keys, zips carrying keys, and links in the tree pointing at secrets.
only-sgit

Indexes shipped by the writer, signed and encrypted. Git's commit-graph and pack indexes are fast, mature and built locally, as trusted plaintext caches. sgit's index packs travel with the data, anchored to their commit and checked under the vault's signature policy before use (an unsigned index is accepted unless the vault requires signatures), and a bad one is skipped. As the threat model puts it, "An index is a plan, never a proof." Reading and writing on plain storage Fetch one folder by byte ranges from plain storage. On a pack vault, clone --path reads the zip's directory and then just the byte ranges of that folder's objects, each one verified by its hash: 2.8 seconds and 12.5 MB, against 36 seconds and the whole 88 MB pack. Git's HTTP code uses ranged requests only to resume an interrupted download; its partial clones need a smart server that can read the content.
only-sgit

A read path that skips the walk. sgit cache add <path> puts a hot file at a location only key holders can compute, read in one request, for an edge function or a page. Any static host, or none. sgit serve runs the vault's browser and API locally in a container; sgit publish and serve --static lay a vault out for any host that answers a GET. A reader with the read key needs no account and no server code. Write without read. An append lane lets a sender put something into a vault and learn nothing, not even whether anyone else writes there: the answer to a write is {"ok": true}. No Git or GitHub role can write without reading. It is a server feature; the sgit command for it is still to come.
only-sgit

Writes shaped for agents. sgit write <path> --also <path> --push --json commits named files straight to the head, atomically, and publishes them in one call, without scanning the working copy; checkout --since-pull writes only what changed. Seal a file to a person. sgit pki encrypt --recipient writes a file sealed to someone's public key, which you then commit. Git signs; it has no "encrypt this to that person".
git-has-it

My memo for this article listed "packs, the path, the ability to have selective repos" as things sgit has and Git does not. The research says otherwise, and I would rather correct it here than have someone else do it. Packs. Git has stored and transferred packs from its early days, and they are delta-compressed, which sgit's are not. Keeping received packs whole, as --pack-store does, is Git's default above fetch.unpackLimit. What is different is that sgit's packs are ciphertext on plain object storage, with no Git server. The path. clone --path is close to Git's partial clone plus sparse-checkout, which is mature and used at very large scale. sgit's differences: it works against ciphertext on S3, it refuses a commit outside the scope by name, and two scoped clones in different folders never conflict.
git-has-it

Selective working copies. git clone --no-checkout has existed for years. sgit's addition is the agent loop: pull --no-checkout, then checkout --since-pull, so an agent writes the few hundred files that changed instead of 79,000. Committing named files, and now hunks. sgit write commits the files you name, atomically, and leaves other edits alone: Git's git commit <paths>, in the form an agent needs. Since 0.27.0, sgit commit takes paths too, commit -p commits parts of a file, and --list-hunks and --hunk let an agent pick hunks by number. There is no persistent staging area, by design. History tools. history log with --grep, --since, --until, --author, --file, --patch and --stat; history diff, show, reflog, undo, revert and reset; commit --amend, stash and signed tags; and since 0.27.0, history blame, sgit grep over the working copy or any revision, log -S and -G, and rename detection with log --follow.
git-has-it

Shallow clones, private branches and signed commits all have Git equivalents, and sgit has them: clone --depth, fetch --unshallow, combinable with --path, and a key per clone; since 0.27.0, also a signature with your own SSH or OpenPGP key, verified against your allowed signers, beside the clone's own. Where sgit does less work than Git, and where Git is faster. Figure from cli.sgit.ai.
git-ahead

These were real gaps when I wrote the first version of this map, and most of them were minor or mid-level for the way we use sgit. Almost everything Git is ahead on runs on the client in Git too, on plaintext the client already has, so sgit can build it the same way. The CLI team wrote a Git-parity roadmap on 28 October, with Git the client as the bar and every new feature off by default, and released the first part of it the same day. Six of Git's eighteen leads closed in sgit-ai 0.27.0, each checked against Git, and the twelve still open. Closed in sgit-ai 0.27.0, 28 October, each checked by the CLI's build agent against Git's own output: Line-level merges. pull --merge lines and branch merge --merge lines, with Git's conflict markers; opt-in, with the whole-file .conflict still the default. 4,500 random merges were byte-identical to git merge-file.
git-ahead

Partial commits. commit with paths, commit -p, and --list-hunks and --hunk for agents. Signing with your own key. commit -S, signed tags, merges and reverts, with SSH or OpenPGP keys, verified against the allowed signers in your Git configuration. It is a second signature beside the clone's own. Rename detection, a port of Git's: 90 of 90 pairs equal git diff -M --name-status. Blame: 25 of 25 files equal git blame --porcelain. Grep and the pickaxe. sgit grep over the working copy or any revision, decrypted in memory, and log -S and -G: 120 of 120 grep runs equal git grep. Still ahead, by how firm the plan is: Designed and next in the CLI team's queue, about 21 days of work in all: cherry-pick, built on the line merge; local hooks that never sync; rebase, never rewriting pushed history; bisect; and worktrees.
git-ahead

Waiting on another team or the server: reading one file from a pack vault with no clone, and a command for append lanes. Sketched, built when a workload asks: garbage collection, delta compression, and archive, shortlog, describe and aliases. No working plan yet: per-folder read access, which needs per-folder keys, and submodules. Who may write. GitHub knows who pushed, protects branches per person, and expires and revokes its signing keys. A signature with your own key now says which person signed, when you verify it against your allowed signers; accounts, protected branches and an owner-signed list of who may write are moved to a future server the roadmap calls SGitHub, with review and CI. Maturity. Twenty years of it. Only time fixes that one.
limits-of-the-model

A few things are out of reach by design, not by effort, and each has a client-side substitute: Anything the host would have to read: server-side search, diffs, a merge button, scanning. Do it in the client, the browser, or a runner that holds the key. Taking back what a reader already has. No system can; GitHub cannot either. sgit rotates forward. Per-folder permissions inside one key. The host cannot tell folders apart. Per-folder access needs per-folder keys, which are designed. Hiding every piece of metadata. Padding and decoy reads reduce the leak; they never remove it. Optimising the store on the host, and a host that enforces fast-forward only. The client does both jobs instead: client-side deltas and pruning, and the rewind guard that ships today.
next

Two things in my memo are designed, not shipped, and I want to be clear about which is which. Hitting a file directly. On a normal vault this already works, from any static host, GitHub Pages included: four plain GETs for a file at the root, one more for each folder above it, and one batch request for a path declared with sgit cache add. history log --vault-key already runs with no clone; a cat that does is a small addition. What is not shipped is reading one file from a pack vault by byte range with no clone at all. The 0.26.0 notes say so: Phase 4 "is not in this release", though the offsets it needs are already written into every pack.
next

Websites on GitHub Pages, with their files in vaults. The PHP newsroom opened PROJECT-003 today, at the design stage: three normal vaults for the sites' assets, data and archive, with GitHub Pages carrying only the pages. GitHub's own repository limits page advises: "Store programmatically generated files outside of Git, such as in object storage." And Git LFS cannot be used with GitHub Pages. The newsroom's sites are nowhere near GitHub's Pages limits of a 1 GB site and a 10-minute deploy. The problem is history growth: every site's deploy runs every 15 minutes and uploads the whole site, and the references site changed 177,426 lines of generated HTML in one day. It also needs normal vaults, because the browser library cannot read pack vaults yet.
workflows

Put together, these are the jobs that are hard in Git and natural in sgit today: Many agents on one very large vault, one folder each. Each agent clones its folder; its commits outside the folder are refused by name; agents in different folders never conflict; the host learns nothing about the contents. In Git you can get close with partial clones and sparse-checkout, but you need a server that reads everything. Give a reader read-only access to encrypted material, with no account. Publish a read key; the reader fetches from a static host. This site publishes read keys for its vaults on purpose. Let an agent deposit into someone's inbox without being able to read it. An append lane, with the payload sealed to the recipient's public key. Trust an index without trusting the host. Every index is anchored to its commit and checked under the vault's signature policy before it is used.
workflows

Hand a vault to a backup host that cannot read it. vault mirror copies and verifies it, keyless. Make a vault's rules travel with it. Require signatures, or a minimum client, and every clone enforces it.
limits

The timings are the CLI team's and the newsroom's own measurements, not re-run for this article; the setting of each is stated above. The verdicts are against sgit-ai 0.26.0, and the section on where Git is ahead against 0.27.0, with Git's and GitHub's documentation, read on 27 and 28 October 2026. The checks against Git are the CLI team's. The 4,500 merges, 90 rename pairs, 25 blamed files and 120 grep runs were run by cli.sgit.ai's build agent, not re-run for this article. "Git has no equivalent" means the mainstream toolchain. Add-ons such as git-crypt and git-remote-gcrypt cover parts of it, with the trade-offs their own READMEs state.
review

The sgit CLI team reviewed this article on 28 October against their code at 640069a: the source, every command group's help, the changelog, the threat model and their response notes. Their verdict: accurate on the whole, too strong in sgit's favour in two places, and underselling it in several. What changed: The 29 minutes. They could not find it in their records. It is in cli.sgit.ai's 0.25.0 release notes, measured by that site's build agent on its own 76,000-file vault, so it stays, attributed, with their own figures beside it. Two claims were too strong: that a signature says which clone wrote a commit (it proves a key holder), and that every index is checked against a signed commit (it is checked under the vault's signature policy, which may not require one). Both now say so.
review

Several were too weak. sgit commits named files (sgit write), reads one file with no clone on a normal vault, rotates keys, mirrors vaults it cannot read, carries its policy to every clone, refuses rewinds, and guards against committing secrets. All of that is above now. Smaller fixes: commits were signed long before 0.19.0, which added verification; the 18-minute status was the cache's first build on a fresh clone; the pack index verify fix is on dev as 0.26.1.dev0; the 566-second pull was measured under a profiler; a file deep in folders takes more than four requests; and the list of what the host sees is longer. The review is on the record, with an answer to each finding.

Summary: Between 3 and 27 October, sgit shipped ten releases, and each one fixed a bottleneck that a real workload had found. A one-file commit on a 76,000-file vault went from 29 minutes to 4.6 seconds; a pull of a 300-file pass on 228,000 files from 566 to 31.7 seconds; a one-folder clone of a pack vault from 36 to 2.8 seconds. The ideas came from earlier work of mine: MGraph-DB's cross-references, Memory-FS's reads by offset, caching on content addresses, and the rule that the writer pays. It is time to stop describing sgit as "like Git". This is the map of what sgit does that Git does not, what Git also has, where Git is clearly ahead, and what is designed but not yet shipped.
articles/versions/what-sgit-does-that-git-does-not/v1.1.0.html
releases

The sgit-ai package on PyPI shows ten releases in that window, from 0.17.0 on 3 October to 0.26.0 at 01:26 UTC on 27 October. The early ones were about the network: keep-alive connections, fetching each shared sub-tree once, a full clone in one parallel sweep. The middle ones were about trust in history: a format gate, signed commits checked on every client, rewinds refused, signed tags, undo and amend. The last three are where the numbers changed by orders of magnitude.

releases

And it has not stopped. A fix on a branch, planned for 0.26.1, takes pack index verify from 1,002 seconds to 3.5 on 24,000 files, after the newsroom's researcher measured the released version at about 57 seconds a pack.

workflows

1. Many agents on one very large vault, one folder each. Each agent clones its folder; its commits outside the folder are refused by name; agents in different folders never conflict; the host learns nothing about the contents. In Git you can get close with partial clones and sparse-checkout, but you need a server that reads everything. 2. Give a reader read-only access to encrypted material, with no account. Publish a read key; the reader fetches from a static host. This site publishes read keys for its vaults on purpose. 3. Let an agent deposit into someone's inbox without being able to read it. An append lane, with the payload sealed to the recipient's public key. 4. Trust an index without trusting the host. Every index is verified against a signed commit before it is used.

Abstract: An introduction to sgit and sgit.ai, what an encrypted vault is, why version control had to be rebuilt to get one, and what nineteen published vaults look like when the server storing them cannot read a byte. There is a category of file that has nowhere good to live. A risk register with real system names in it. A regulatory analysis you are still arguing about internally. The working memory of an AI agent that has been reading your codebase for a month. Client material under NDA. Anything a lawyer would want to see before it went near a third party.

All of it wants exactly what git gives you, history, branches, diffs, the ability to hand somebody a link and know what they will see. And all of it is the reason people say "we can't put that in GitHub." So it ends up in a shared drive, an email thread, or a Notion page nobody can diff, and the version history that mattered is gone. sgit is git for those files. Encrypted before they leave your machine, versioned exactly like git, stored on a server that cannot read a single byte. sgit.ai, pip install sgit-ai. Pure Python, two runtime dependencies, Apache-2.0.

Zero knowledge is a claim people make loosely, so here is the precise version: the server holds ciphertext and nothing else. Not your filenames, not your directory structure, not your commit messages. Encryption and decryption happen on your machine. There is no key escrow, no admin override, no support engineer who can recover it for you, and that last part is a feature with a real cost, which is worth being honest about up front. What makes it work is a single string: <24-char passphrase>:<vault-id> That is the vault key, and it is three things at once, the address of the vault, the authorisation to write to it, and the key that decrypts it. Lose it and the data is gone. Leak it and someone can rewrite your history.

From it you can derive, one way, a read key: same vault, read-only, safe to publish. That asymmetry is the whole sharing model. Every vault linked from sgit.ai is published as a read key, and no vault key has ever been published, a rule enforced by a tripwire in the release pipeline that scans every file before either remote is touched. The read key is the entire credential. No account, no login, no access request: A real clone of the published EU AI Act vault. 273 objects, 207 files. Now the same vault, as the machine storing it sees it: 786 bytes of AES-256-GCM ciphertext. The object's name is a SHA-256 of the encrypted bytes.

That second screenshot is the argument. The object is content-addressed over its ciphertext, which means the host can deduplicate it, cache it for a year, and serve it from a CDN, while remaining unable to tell you what it is. You get the operational benefits of a normal object store without granting it the usual price of admission. Underneath, it is a real version control system rather than a sync folder: multi-parent commits, a tree per directory, deterministic refs derived by HMAC, a genuine merge-base computation across all parents, and three-way merge. Branches, diffs and history all work, on content the server cannot interpret. The best way to understand a vault is to open one. Every vault on sgit.ai is live: the screenshots are of real vaults, opened with the read keys published beside them. The published vaults. Each one carries its read key on the page.

They range from a photo library to Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 parsed from official Formex XML into 1,523 nodes and 1,944 edges. Before writing this I cloned all nineteen from their published keys: 1,389 files, no failures. A vault can contain an application, not just documents, and that application runs against the vault without ever being handed a credential. "permissions": {}, the app requests nothing, and is granted nothing. Click the image to open the vault page ↗ Look at "permissions": {} in that file. The app asks for no filesystem access at all. It still renders the whole risk graph, because the host reads the vault and passes results in. The app never sees a key. Capability without credential, and it means you can run code you did not write against data you care about, with the blast radius set by a config file you can read in one screen.

sgit.ai is one of nineteen sites on *.sgit.ai, each taking one question further than a section could. Most of the thinking behind sgit now lives out there rather than here. The network directory: start from the question you arrived with. A few of them, to give the range: graphs.sgit.ai, "A node is just a node. Meaning lives in the edges." risks.sgit.ai, "You cannot deny a risk. You can only say how long you accept it." llms.sgit.ai, your app calls a language model without ever holding an API key. issues-fs.sgit.ai. The issues are files, and the files are a graph. open-source.sgit.ai, "Open source is a strategy. It is not a charity." sg-sentinel.sgit.ai, an edge guard design that says NOT BUILT at the top of every page. The network directory starts from the question you arrived with rather than the list of domains.

That last one is the house style in miniature. Each site publishes its argument before the thing exists, and states plainly what has shipped and what has not. graphs.sgit.ai devotes a page to where its own approach loses. We would rather be checkable than impressive. pip install sgit-ai sgit clone sgit_public_read_c004daae386e8d17fa648884acc527018bd4ea1116ad673fb2f1b068011695c9:73heuprz That is the EU AI Act vault, 207 files on your disk in under a minute, from a key printed on a public web page, with no account anywhere. If you would rather not install anything, every vault opens in the browser from the same key. This article is also published as a LinkedIn newsletter post, same argument, same screenshots, for readers who live there. Written by Dinis Cruz and the agentic team working with him. Abstract: A researcher won a public "steal my bitcoin" bounty against a deliberately vulnerable PHP server, a rare independent, live confirmation that php2shell gives an attacker full control of a machine. I wanted to know more than that it worked. How hard was it, really, once the target was actually reachable? Could a web application firewall have blocked it, given how many vendors say they already detect it? And if you cannot patch today, does hardening the server around PHP, rather than PHP itself, actually protect you? The answers, checked against the operator's own site, the researcher's public write-up, five vendors' own advisories and GrapheneOS's own record of a server it chose to take offline rather than trust its own mitigations: the bounty took three hours once there was a page to attack, not the nineteen the headlines reported; every vendor's own detection coverage comes with a gap it names itself; and every hardening measure anyone has published is described by its own authors as partial. Patching remains the only complete fix.
The real timeline of the challenge from 21 October to 26 October, against the "19.28 hours" the site's counter gave.
in-short

A real, independent, live win. Not a lab claim: a researcher broke into a deliberately vulnerable public server and published how. The real number is three hours, not nineteen. The target had no PHP-executing page to attack for most of that time. It needed an exact build. The published method is tuned to one specific PHP image; a different one and it fails outright. It is a race, not a certainty. The author's own repeated runs against their lab succeeded about seven times in ten. Every vendor names its own gap. Cloudflare, AWS, Azure, Emerging Threats and Sophos each publish detection, and each publishes what it does not catch. Hardening is partial, by its authors' own account. No published config change, container limit or edge rule is called a fix by the people who wrote it. GrapheneOS tried three mitigations, then chose to go offline anyway. Patched and back within seven hours.
in-short
The method leaves a signature. It depends on deliberately forcing PHP past its own memory limit, which is loud, not silent.
bounty

On 25 October a researcher using the handle "killa" (named in press coverage as the UK pentester Jaydip Modhwadia) won a public bounty run at stealmybitcoin.com: break into a server left deliberately unpatched, and the bitcoin on it is yours. He recovered a private key through php2shell and the site posted "Challenge won"; the pot was 0.02511679 BTC, then worth $2,021.22. The win was logged at 15:47 UTC on 25 October (00:47 Japan time on the 26th). His own write-up, a single Python file published on GitHub, is public: it builds the requests itself, checks each step before moving on, and records the exact HTTP bytes from a fresh run, so the claim is checkable, not just asserted.
bounty

That matters on its own. Every claim so far had been "we reproduced this in our lab." This is the first I have seen where an independent outsider, against a target they did not build, with no special access, got to command execution and published enough that others can check the account. It is also, importantly, a game with a consenting target: the server was built to fall, and the "victim" offered the prize. The real-world count of named organisations compromised through php2shell is still zero, as the newsroom's own reader-question pieces on the PHP story site have covered. This article is about a narrower question: now that it has been done once, in public, how hard was it, could it have been caught, and can you protect a server you cannot yet patch?
timeline

The headline number, repeated across the coverage, is "stolen after 19.28 hours": the site's own elapsed-time counter since the challenge launched. That number answers how long the page sat up, not how hard the exploit was, and it is worth separating the two. The target launched at 08:21 UTC on 21 October carrying no page that executed PHP at all. For most of the following day and a half, there was nothing php2shell could reach, whatever anyone tried. One report puts it plainly: after more than 17 hours, nobody had solved it, because "the original server did not expose any page that executed PHP programs." The operator added a PHP-executing page at around 22:00 Japan time on 25 October. Killa solved it roughly three hours after that, at 00:47 JST on 26 October.
timeline

Three hours, against a target that was actually reachable, by one specialist, working from a published method, is the number that answers your question. Nineteen hours is mostly the story of a target that could not yet be attacked.
effort

The published write-up is explicit about its own limits, which is unusual and useful. A few things it says about itself, as the author wrote them: It needs an exact build, not just a version number. The method is calibrated against one specific PHP image and worker model. A different build that reports the identical version string is not a safe substitute, and the author's own tooling checks a fingerprint before it will proceed, specifically to reject a mismatch rather than fail confusingly later. It is a race. Run ten times against the author's own lab, with nothing else happening and no retries, it succeeded about seven times in ten. The rest either produced no result (the stage that needs a specific happen-to-be-reused process did not land) or reached the final step without the markers that confirm it worked.
effort

It needs few requests, but they must be shaped exactly right. The author's own count is twenty HTTP requests at most for a full run: one health check, two batches of pipelined requests, and one final request. That small number is itself informative: this is not a brute-force or a scan, it is a short, precise sequence. The original run was against the live, non-lab target, and the author is candid that the full outgoing request from that specific run was not fully captured at the time; what is published is a reconstruction from the same code, plus the artefacts the original run did leave behind, not a byte-for-byte original capture.
effort

None of that makes the exploit a hoax or a stunt. It makes it what the correspondent's own reporting on the PHP story site already said: real proof the flaw gives an attacker full control of a machine, from a specialist, against a cooperative, purpose-built target, not an off-the-shelf weapon that anyone could point at an arbitrary production server and expect to work.
shell

You asked, reasonably, what "shell" means here. By the author's own account, the final step runs one operating-system command and returns its output over the connection that is already open: in that run, the command printed a fresh marker so the run could be told apart from any other, the output of id (confirming which user the PHP process was running as), and a hash of a file on the target, as independent evidence the command genuinely executed where the write-up said it did. That is command execution as the PHP process's own user, demonstrated once per run, not a standing interactive shell and not a reverse connection back out to the attacker. Whether a given production deployment running as a lower-privileged user would hand over anything less useful is a separate, real question the write-up does not answer, because the lab and the challenge were both set up to run as a privileged account.
waf

Detection coverage for php2shell from Cloudflare, AWS WAF, Azure Front Door, Emerging Threats and Sophos, and each gap. You asked, in a LinkedIn comment at the time, whether any web application firewall could see this coming a mile away. The honest answer is: several vendors say they already do, and each says so with a caveat attached, in their own words, not mine. Cloudflare had rules live from 03:02 UTC on 21 October, nine hours before PHP's own public advisory. It later added inspection of the server's response, not only the request, because request data alone "could not always tell an exploit from ordinary traffic." Cloudflare also reports that attackers changed their payloads to test its defences.
waf

AWS WAF ships two rules in its PHP managed rule group, inspecting the request body, defaulting to Block. AWS's own blog names the gap: many small part headers can expand far more inside PHP's memory than their size on the wire suggests, which can stay under its size-restriction rule, and a rate-based rule "reduces the volume an exploit needs, but it doesn't stop a single successful request." Azure Front Door's managed rule for this is disabled by default and was still rolling out as of 28 October. A rule that exists but is off protects nobody until someone turns it on. Emerging Threats published IDS signatures for both CVEs on 22 October. Signature matching, by its nature, can be dodged by a request reshaped just enough to miss the pattern. Sophos's intrusion-prevention signatures detect exploitation attempts, but by its own advisory its Web Application Firewall product carries no rule specific to these flaws.
waf

So: not "any WAF could see that coming", and not "nothing can see it coming" either. The honest middle is that detection exists, arrived fast in at least one case, and every vendor who published it also published where it falls short. That is close to what the newsroom's own earlier piece on the PHP story already said: detection does not look mature yet, and the inconsistency between huge attempt counts and near-silent compromise counts is itself a data gap worth tracking, not a reason to assume either extreme.
hardening

Hardening without patching: four measures that their own authors call partial, and what GrapheneOS did instead. This is the question I most wanted answered: if upgrading breaks things and people are nervous about it, can you harden the environment around PHP, invisibly to the application, and be safe without touching the PHP binary? The published record says: not fully, and the people who wrote these mitigations say so themselves. Turning off session upload progress (session.upload_progress.enabled=0) closes the path tied to one of the two CVEs. PHP's own advisory is explicit that the other flaw uses a separate path this setting does not touch. A PHP core developer put it more bluntly in public: "the only mitigation is patching / upgrading PHP. I sadly know too much." Raising or removing the memory limit (memory_limit=-1) removes one way the flaw gets triggered. PHP's own caveat: an underlying allocation failure further down can still reach the vulnerable code even with the limit raised.
hardening

Blocking multipart uploads at the edge, if your application does not need them, closes paths that depend on a file upload. It does not close a path that one of the CVEs can reach through ordinary warning or logging behaviour, which needs no multipart body at all. A container or cgroup memory limit bounds the blast radius of a worker crashing, ideally configured to kill only the affected process rather than take the whole service down. That is containment, not prevention: it limits the mess, it does not stop the command from running first.
hardening

The most useful real-world test of this is GrapheneOS's own record, which I read directly from its public feed rather than through a summary. At 08:21 UTC on 21 October it took its discussion forum, its only service running PHP, offline, in its own words "due to vulnerability details already being available and proof of concept exploits being developed." Thirty-three minutes later it posted that it had in fact deployed three specific mitigations (upload progress off, multipart blocking, and a set of Zend memory-manager debug flags), tested them, and decided to turn the forum off anyway rather than rely on them. At 15:30 UTC, having patched to PHP 8.5.12, the forum came back up. Total time offline: about seven hours.
hardening

That is a team that could plausibly have run any of the published stopgaps, chose to test them, and judged that none of them earned enough trust to keep the service up while waiting for the real fix. I have not found a single public account of someone relying on configuration or edge hardening alone and being confirmed safe against a live, motivated attempt; I have found several of people trying it and still taking the service down.
logs

Your question about logs and crashes has a general, public answer, without needing the exploit's internals. The published method depends on deliberately forcing PHP past its own configured memory limit, more than once, as one of its steps. That is not a quiet technique: PHP's own fatal-error path for an exhausted memory limit is exactly what you would expect to see, repeated, from the same client, in a short window, alongside a worker process that gets reused in a way that is unusual for ordinary traffic. A defender watching PHP's own error log for repeated memory-exhaustion fatals from one source has a real signal available to them today, independent of any WAF vendor's rule. Whether anyone is actually watching for that pattern, as opposed to the generic access log, is the open question, and it is the same gap the newsroom's earlier piece named: the data on real-world detection is thin, because almost nobody is publishing it.
limits

This is one bounty, one researcher, one target. It is strong evidence the flaw is exploitable in the real world by a skilled person; it is not a measurement of how common successful attacks are. No named organisation has reported a real compromise through php2shell, separately from this voluntary challenge, as of the newsroom's latest check. Vendor detection coverage changes quickly. What is listed here is current as of the dates given; several vendors were still rolling out or revising rules through late October. I have not independently reproduced any part of the exploit. What is reported here about its mechanism and limits comes from the author's own published account of his own work. The GrapheneOS timeline is read from the organisation's own public posts, not from a secondary summary, but it describes one team's one decision, not a general rule for every deployment.
sources
