Abstract: Every vault on this site is encrypted in the client, so the server never sees a key and the key is the whole question. This is the current state of vault key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0: where everything lives, the one secret and the keys derived from it, where vault keys are kept today (a password manager, and a registry vault run by an isolated agent session), how a new key reaches the registry without ever entering a chat, append lanes as the transport behind most of it, the small communication vaults that made the problem urgent, and the four tracks that come next: password manager integrations, secrets.sgit.ai's passkey-unlocked keyring, PKI, and decryption that happens out of band. Plus the one gap we cannot close ourselves: agent platforms have no per-session secrets.

This site has a gap, and a reader found it this week. The docs say a great deal about what a vault key can do and almost nothing about where mine are kept. That is worth fixing for its own sake, and it is also a good example of how this project solves problems: as they arrive. For a long time I had a handful of vaults and kept their keys by hand. Now my agents create vaults all the time, several a day, and keeping track of the keys has become a real problem. So this is the current state, at sgit-ai v0.20.0: how it works today, where it is weak, and what I am building next. Where everything lives. Encryption and decryption happen in the client; the edge, the API and the bucket only ever handle ciphertext and hashes of capability keys.

The key is the whole question. Vaults are encrypted in the client. The server stores ciphertext in S3 and never sees a vault key, so whoever holds the key holds the vault. One secret, and keys derived from it. A vault key reads and writes. The read key is derived from it, one way, and is published on purpose for every vault on this site. Append tokens and PKI key pairs are separate credentials that each do one job. Today, vault keys live in two places. A password manager, which is my preferred home for any key a person holds, and a registry: a private vault, run by its own isolated Claude session, whose only job is to hold the keys to the other vaults.

New keys reach the registry without entering a chat. The agent that made the vault seals the key to the registry's public key and writes it to a lane it cannot read back, with one POST. Append lanes changed how the agents work. One POST from anywhere, readable only by the vault's owner. I use them for key handover, logs, observations, data from websites and messages between agents. Small vaults made this urgent. A vault per conversation and per job is the right shape for security, and it multiplies the keys. What comes next: integrations with password managers (and if you work on one, let's talk), secrets.sgit.ai's passkey-unlocked keyring, PKI for sharing without shared secrets, and decryption that happens out of band. The weakest step, giving a key to an agent, waits on per-session secrets in the agent platforms.
architecture

The vaults you see in the vault gallery work like this. Storage. All the data is stored in S3 as encrypted objects: commits, trees and files. The API. An SG/Send API server, deployed as a serverless Lambda function, stores and serves those objects and checks capabilities. It can also run from Docker, Fargate, Kubernetes or a laptop. The edge. The API is exposed through CloudFront on a stable address, such as send.sgraph.ai, with its documentation at send.sgraph.ai/api/docs. That is the address the web interface at vault.sgraph.ai uses by default. The clients. You open a vault locally with sgit clone <vault key>, or in a browser at vault.sgraph.ai#<vault key>. In the browser, the key sits after the #, and browsers do not send that part of a URL to the server. Either way, the decryption happens on your machine.
architecture

That design makes hosting simple: the server, the edge and the bucket can be run by anyone, anywhere, without being trusted with content. The same server runs inside your own network too, even an air-gapped one, with the same CLI pointed at a different --base-url; self-hosting a vault server for agents has the deployment patterns. The cost of the design is that everything that matters is in the key. Where it is kept and how it travels decides who can read, who can write, and what a leak costs.
keys

The vault key, the keys derived from it, and the separate credentials made for one job each. The full table, with the prefixes, is on the vault credentials page. A vault key looks like sgit_private_vault_<passphrase>:<vault_id>. It is the one secret, and it carries read and write. From it, by one-way derivation, come a read key, which reads every file and every commit, and a write key, which the server checks (as a hash) before it accepts a push. The vault id, after the colon, is the address, and it is public. The read key is the whole publishing model of this site. Every vault in the gallery carries a read key under the sgit_public_read_ prefix, so it can be opened in a browser by anyone, and none of them can be used to change anything. The rule is short: read keys yes, on purpose; vault keys never. Vault credentials has the five prefixes and why the word in them matters.
keys

Two other kinds of credential sit beside the vault key, deliberately separate from it. An append token lets a sender write one message to one lane of a vault, and nothing else. A PKI key pair, made with sgit pki keygen (RSA-OAEP 4096 for encryption, ECDSA P-256 for signing), lets anyone seal something that only its holder can open. Both exist so that a sender never needs the vault key at all.
today

I use a mix of two things. A password manager, for the keys I hold as a person. This is, and will stay, my preferred answer: a good password manager with a good integration is the right home for a vault key, on every device I already use. The integration does not exist yet (more on that below), so today this is a careful copy and paste into an entry of the right kind. A registry, for everything the agents create. The registry is a private vault, run by its own Claude session that I keep isolated from everything else: I think of it as the vault of vaults. It holds the keys to the other vaults, so that a key is never lost and never has to live in a browser tab or a chat. Every time an agent creates a vault, I ask it to send the key there.
today
sgit can also remember keys under aliases on one machine (sgit vault add, sgit vault list), which is handy on a laptop and not a management system.
handover

How a new vault key reaches the registry without entering a chat. The flow is documented, for the agent that has to follow it, on the Send a vault key page. This is the flow that runs today, several times a day. An agent makes a vault, in a Claude session that I have given no other access: no accounts, no permissions, only the job and, often, a vault to communicate through. It seals the key in sgit's hybrid envelope to the registry's public key, after checking that key's fingerprint. The payload is a vault-key-handover/v1 document: the key, plus a short description that the registry records as an unverified claim. It sends it with one POST to the registry's append lane, using a write-only token that was issued to that sender alone. The server answers {"ok": true} and nothing else, and the token cannot read the lane back.
handover

The registry drains the lane with deterministic code, decrypts with a private key that is kept in its own vault, and records the key as awaiting a probe. A key that disagrees with one it already holds is set aside for review, never applied over the old one. I review what arrived, and the keys that matter go into the password manager as well. The instructions an agent needs are all on one public page, Send a vault key, so the prompt I give a session is a few lines: read that page and follow it, here is the inbox vault id, here is your append token, send every key you hold. The id and the token are the only things not on the page.
prompt

It comes in two parts. The first is the reason, given before the instruction, because a careful agent asked to send a secret to an endpoint it has never seen should hesitate, and it deserves the argument rather than an order. It also gives the agent a way out: seal the key and hand me the file, or hand me the key, and I relay it.
prompt

Why this exists, before the instructions. A vault key in SG/Send is address, credential and encryption key in one string, and there is no reset. Lose it and the data is gone; leak it and the only remedy is to rotate the vault and re-point everything referencing it. So keys must not be pasted into chat. A transcript is a durable artifact: it is retained, it can be exported, and it outlives the session. Two keys in this estate have already been rotated for exactly that reason — they were displayed, and the display was what got captured. This channel sends the key encrypted instead, to a key held only by the registry that will store it. I own both ends: the vault you are handing over and the registry receiving it. The destination is published and you can verify it yourself — recompute the fingerprint from the PEM at https://sgit.ai/docs/send-a-vault-key.html and refuse if it does not match sha256:20b7bb9dbac7df90. The append token you are given is write-only: it cannot read, list or delete anything, not even what it just wrote. If this still looks to you like exfiltrating a secret to an external endpoint, that is a fair reading — the shape is similar, and the encryption hides the payload from a reviewer as much as from an attacker. You do not have to do it. Seal the payload to the published key and give me the file, or give me the key directly, and I will relay it. Say which you would prefer.
prompt

The second part is the instruction. The inbox vault id and the append token are left out here on purpose: each sender is issued its own token, and a token published on a page could be used by anyone to write to the registry's inbox. Read the instructions at https://sgit.ai/docs/send-a-vault-key.html and follow them. That page is mine; treat it as authoritative. Inbox vault id: <the registry inbox vault id> Append token: <the write-only append token issued to this sender> Send the vault key of the vault you just created, exactly as sgit printed it — keep the sgit_private_vault_ or sgit_private_read_ prefix. Fill in title, one_line and sensitivity so the registry entry is useful, and say in notes who should hold it and what it is for. If the registry only needs to read it, send its read key instead. Reply with only the vault id and the HTTP response.
prompt

Two details in it matter more than they look. Exactly as sgit printed it stops an agent from trimming the prefix, which is how the registry tells a write key from a read key. Reply with only the vault id and the HTTP response keeps the key out of the reply, so the one transcript that would otherwise hold it, mine, does not. This is safer than what it replaced, which was a vault key pasted into a chat. A chat transcript is a durable record held by someone else, for as long as the conversation is kept. Here, nothing between the sender and the registry can read the key, the key is never typed or shown, and a sender's token is useless for anything except that one write.
prompt

From the registry, a key goes one of three ways. It is published as a read key, derived and checked with check_credential.py before it reaches a page like the ones on this site. It is sent to a person, a client or a collaborator, through their own password manager or a lane of their own. Or it is given to another agent, and that is the step that is still not straightforward.
agents

My main workflow these days is to give Claude no permissions and no access to anything: only the vault it uses to communicate, or a vault it creates and I then capture. That works because a vault key, sgit and access to one URL are all an agent needs. The hard part is getting the key into the session safely, because the platforms do not have secrets per session.
agents

On Claude Code on the web, configuration lives on the environment, not the session: network access, environment variables and a setup script, shared by every session that uses it. The documentation is direct about what that means for a variable: "any command Claude runs can read" it, and "Anyone who uses the environment can read the values" (cloud environments). On Team and Enterprise an Owner can share an environment with every member, and "Every member's sessions in a shared environment read its variables, so don't include secrets in them" (shared environments). So today the SG/Send access token my sessions use to push sits in an environment variable that every session in that environment can read, which defeats some of the point.
agents

There is a better mechanism for one kind of secret. A network secret is an API key that "Anthropic's agent proxy adds ... to requests for the hosts you list, after each request leaves the session's VM, so the key itself stays outside the VM" (network secrets). That would suit a server token like ours. But it is still per environment, applying to every session "whoever started it", and it is not available on Team or Enterprise plans yet. And it cannot help with a vault key at all, because a vault key is not sent to a server: the decryption happens inside the session, so the key has to be there. OpenAI's Codex has a similar shape: its secrets are only available to setup scripts and "are removed before the agent phase starts" (Codex cloud environments), which protects them from the agent and, for the same reason, cannot give the agent a key to use.
agents

So, for now, a key for another agent travels in one of three imperfect ways: in the prompt, which puts it in a transcript; in an environment variable, which every session in the environment can read; or not at all, with the agent making its own vault and sending the key back on a lane, which is why that last pattern is the one I use most.
lanes

Append lanes: one POST from anywhere, readable only by the vault's owner. One lane per sender, so one can be revoked without touching the others. Append lanes were a big feature, and they are worth explaining on their own. A lane is a write-only channel attached to a vault. A sender holds a token for one lane and the owner's public key. It seals its message to that key, signs it in the protocol our agents use, and sends it with a single POST to /api/vault/append/write/{vault_id}. The server saves it as one encrypted file in S3 and answers {"ok": true}. The owner lists and fetches with a separate enumeration key, decrypts with a private key that never leaves them, checks each signature against the lane, and marks messages processed. The server keeps only hashes of the tokens and keys, so compromising it yields hashes and ciphertext.
lanes

That shape turns out to be useful for far more than messages. I use lanes for: Key handover, as above. Logging and observation: a session reports progress, findings and events as many small files, each one POST, without holding the vault key. Data from websites: a page can send what a reader filled in or chose straight into a vault, from the browser. Messages between agents that have no other path: an agent on another platform, with another owner, can reply into my vault without either of us holding the other's vault key. Append-lane messaging between agents is the write-up of two teams doing that, in both directions.
lanes

It is a little like email. The token is still a secret: it cannot read anything, but with the vault id it authorises writes, so I hand one out per sender and never publish it. Sending messages between vaults and the append lanes API have the details, the limits and the error codes.
small-vaults

Communication vaults: one per pair or group of agents, and one per job. Each agent holds only the keys for the conversations it is part of. Once you work this way and are creating vaults left, right and centre, something changes: you start making very small vaults for very specific things. If two or three agents need to work together, I create a vault just for them. I call these communication vaults. Inside, the agents use EmailFS, a file-based email protocol that agents follow very well, and IssuesFS, the same idea for issues, so they can talk and work together through files that are versioned and encrypted.
small-vaults

What an agent needs to join one is small: the vault key, sgit, and network access to the API host, which on a locked-down agent platform means adding that one host to the allowed list (the egress how-to covers Claude Team and Enterprise). Or a server inside its own network, if the work has to stay there. This is the right shape for security. A leaked key exposes one small vault and one conversation, not an inbox, a drive or an account, and every word is on the record for the person who holds the keys. It is also exactly why the number of keys grew faster than I could manage by hand.
next

The four tracks we are working on, and the one we depend on. Statuses as of 10 October 2026. Password managers. For keys that people hold, a password manager with a good integration is the answer I want. We published an open call to password managers, identity providers and platform credential managers, setting out what an integration needs: key kinds kept apart (a vault key, a read key and a private key are not the same thing), release only on approval, sharing end to end, and revocation. To be fair to them: I have not followed it up yet, so the silence so far is mine, not theirs. If you work on a password manager, let's talk.
next

secrets.sgit.ai. The second track is secrets.sgit.ai, a secrets manager that runs entirely in the browser and is unlocked by a passkey. The design uses the browser's passkey support, including hardware keys: the passkey's PRF output derives a wrapping key, which unwraps the one key that encrypts the keyring, and the keyring is stored as ciphertext in a cloud bucket, on GCP or AWS or anywhere else. There is no master password to choose or forget, and entries keep their kinds apart, with sgit-vault-key and sgit-read-key as kinds of their own. The browser side is ready: the PRF extension is in WebAuthn Level 3, whose own example is that "PRF outputs could be used as symmetric keys to encrypt user data", it works in Chrome and Edge and recent Firefox, Apple's platforms support it since iOS 18 and macOS 15, and password managers already use it this way: Bitwarden can "automatically unlock your vault without entering your master password" with a PRF-capable passkey (Bitwarden). There is a serious caveat, from one of the spec's editors: people lose passkeys, and losing the passkey must not mean losing the data (Tim Cappalli). That is why the design has a second root, a 128-bit recovery code shown once, and a wrap per passkey, so that a second device can unlock the same keyring. At its v0.1.13, the site, the design documents, the mockups and a passkey lab that runs the whole key chain in your own browser are shipped; the app itself is proposed, and the site is careful to say so. It ties the user to their browser's passkey provider, which I think is a reasonable trade.
next

PKI. For me the best long-term answer is public and private keys for every party, so that a key is shared by sealing it to the recipient's public key and never travels in the clear. sgit already has the pieces: sgit pki generates, exports, imports, encrypts, decrypts, signs and verifies, and the registry handover above is PKI in daily use. Browsers can also create key pairs today. What is missing is a better way to persist those keys and a better way to share them, and a wider pool of users with key pairs, which is what makes PKI worth it. It also raises the obvious question: how does an agent get its private key in the first place? The workaround in use today is a fresh signing key per session, published in a registry on the sender's own site and pinned once by the recipient. The real answer needs better identities and better secret management in agent environments. RFC 0001 sets out the design.
next

Decryption out of band. Ideally, sometimes, the decryption would not happen in the browser or the agent at all, but somewhere else that you authenticate to, the way cloud key services work: you send ciphertext and get plaintext back after proving who you are, and the private key is never handed out. That is an idea, not a design yet, and I want to bring it into secrets.sgit.ai and into the work with password managers, secrets managers and the cloud providers, so that keys can be managed at their end.
yours

The workflow I have works well, and the fundamental point holds: a vault key, sgit and access to one URL are all an agent needs to work with a vault, on our servers or entirely inside your own network. Key management is where the effort goes now. I would be very interested in how other people manage their vault keys, or the keys of whatever encrypted system they use with agents. Write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
docs

This article came with documentation updates in the same release: A new page, Vault key management: where each kind of key should live, how a key travels, how to give one to an agent, rotation, and the rules, in reference form. Sending messages between vaults now says which host serves which route names: on 10 October send.sgraph.ai (API v0.32.4) still served the older /api/vault/inbox/ routes, while dev.send.sgraph.ai (v0.33.69) served the renamed /api/vault/append/ routes. It also confirms that the lane address derivation is still proposed at sgit-ai v0.20.0. Vault credentials and Send a vault key now link to the new page.
sources

A reader's question this week about where the keys of temporary agent sessions are managed, my reply, and a voice memo with the rest. Checked against sgit-ai v0.20.0 on this machine, the live OpenAPI documents of both API hosts, and the site's own pages on credentials, the registry handover, append lanes, PKI and self-hosting, and secrets.sgit.ai v0.1.13, all read on 10 October 2026. Earlier writing this builds on: the identity we wanted to give the agents, encrypted memory for isolated agents and a personal agent that keeps your secrets.

Abstract: The last three articles described insuring an agent row by row from its behaviour policy, who could carry the risk, and the vendor's share of it. This one asks where such a company should be built, from a regulatory and an investment point of view, and how much it would take. My answer is London first, for two of its three jobs. It should start as a managing agent there, pricing and selling on a Lloyd's syndicate's capital, because that is where two of today's AI agent covers are written, authorisation takes up to nine months, and an intermediary's own capital is the higher of £5,000 or 2.5% of its income; and it should carry the risk there too, as a UK insurer through the PRA's mobilisation regime or with capital at Lloyd's. It should sell into the US through surplus lines, a $143.3 billion market built for risks without a loss history, and into the EU by one registration, once Europe's product rules make software a product on 9 December 2026. The Gulf's funds are a place to raise capital. On the money, I built a small model with every assumption stated, and the point it makes is that what the money buys is cover. Two years of running the company cost about £4.35 million; everything raised above that backs policies, and because every row is capped, the ceiling of cover follows from it. Raised in one go, £10 million backs about £94 million to £188 million of cover, 1,177 to 2,354 agents at £80,000 each; £50 million backs about £761 million to £1.52 billion, 9,510 to 19,020 agents, depending on how much of the book one shared failure could hit at once. The bigger the cover the company aims for, the more it should raise at the start.

Underwrite and carry the risk in London, sell into the US and EU, raise the capital in one go. Five articles and three vaults on one idea: an agent's behaviour policy read as an insurance policy, priced row by row, split with the vendor, and backed by capital.
in-short

The company does three jobs, and London suits two of them. Pricing and selling, and carrying the risk; distribution goes where the customers are. Start as a managing agent in London. Two of today's AI agent covers are written by Lloyd's coverholders; authorisation takes up to nine months; the intermediary's own capital is small. Carry the risk in London too. A UK insurer through the PRA's mobilisation regime, or capital at Lloyd's behind a syndicate. Sell into the US through surplus lines. A $143.3 billion market in 2025, built for risks no filed policy covers yet. Reach the EU by one registration, once software becomes a product there on 9 December 2026; EIOPA is wary of MGAs, so expect questions. What the money buys is cover. About £4.35 million runs the company for two years; everything raised above that backs policies. £10 million in one go backs about £94 million to £188 million of cover. 1,177 to 2,354 agents.
in-short
£50 million in one go backs about £761 million to £1.52 billion. 9,510 to 19,020 agents; the bigger the aim, the more to raise at the start.
question

In this series I described insuring an agent row by row, who could carry that risk, and the vendor's share of it. The second article ended with a path: start as a managing agent on someone else's capital, prove the loss record, then carry the risk. So the natural next question is where to build such a company, from a regulatory and an investment point of view: the US, the UK, the EU, or the Middle East, where there are new regimes and new money.
question

I think the honest answer is that it can have more than one home, because it does more than one job. A managing agent prices and sells policies on an insurer's behalf and carries no risk on its own balance sheet; it needs a licence to distribute insurance and a carrier willing to lend its capital. An insurer pays the claims and has to hold capital against a bad year. Distribution needs licences where the customers are. Those three jobs are regulated differently in each place, and the best place for one is not the best place for the others. The UK, US, EU and UAE: what each asks of a managing agent and an insurer.
london

The first job is pricing and selling, and London is where I would start. The AI agent cover on the market today is written in a handful of ways, and two of them, Armilla and Testudo, are Lloyd's coverholders with Lloyd's syndicates behind them, as who carries the risk set out. A coverholder needs a Lloyd's broker or managing agent to sponsor it, and the market is used to new specialty risks: the Lloyd's Lab's current cohort includes a "Risk engine quantifying advanced and systemic AI risks" (FinTech Global, 20 March 2026).
london

The UK licence is within reach of a start-up. A managing agent is either authorised directly by the FCA, which "can typically take up to nine months from when an applicant starts preparing its application", or works as an appointed representative of a firm that is; its own capital requirement, if it does not hold client money, is the higher of "GBP5,000 or 2.5% of annual income from regulated insurance distribution activity", with professional indemnity cover on top (DLA Piper, September 2026). The same city has the regime for the next step, below.
us

The US is the largest market, and the way a new risk reaches it is surplus lines. They cover "unique risks for which admitted carriers do not offer a filed policy form or rate", and the industry's own association describes new products with no loss history as "difficult, if not impossible, to price or rate for insurance purposes" (WSIA). That is exactly an agent behaviour policy today. The market is large and growing: "The surplus lines market closed 2025 at a record $143.3 billion in direct premium written" (Insurance Business, citing AM Best, 11 September 2026). Harbor's AI agent cover is issued by surplus lines carriers.
us

A US managing agent needs a producer licence in each state it writes in, and the NAIC's model law asks for a bond of "at least $100,000 or ten percent (10%) of the managing general agent's total annual written premium ... but in no event greater than $500,000" (NAIC). The US MGA market reached "approximately $128 billion in 2025", and "approximately 20% of total US MGA premium is supported through fronting carrier relationships" (Reinsurance News, citing Conning, 29 July 2026). So a London managing agent can reach US customers through the surplus lines market, with a US entity when the book justifies one. The US also has the cheapest way for a provider to insure its own agents: a captive. In Vermont, a pure captive needs capital of "not less than $250,000.00" (Vermont statutes). The providers who, as who carries the risk found, have looked at insuring their own risk could start there.
eu

The EU is the market where demand may arrive fastest, because from 9 December 2026, as the vendor's layer described, software is a product under the new product liability directive. Distribution is simple in principle: an intermediary registered in one member state works across the union on "the principle of a single registration" (Central Bank of Ireland). An insurer's minimum capital under Solvency II starts at €2.7 million.
eu

The supervisor is cautious about exactly this model. EIOPA wrote in June 2026 that "insurers are increasingly outsourcing key functions to MGAs, creating concerns about weak oversight, conflicts of interests, unclear responsibility for product governance and difficulties in cross-border supervision", and that it "could engage with the Lloyd's market to better understand how we can build capacity in the EU" (EIOPA). A company whose product is a written, deterministic policy with clear governance should answer those concerns better than most; I would still plan the EU as the second market, not the first home.
carry

When the company is ready to carry risk itself, I would do that in London as well, so that the underwriting and the balance sheet sit under the same supervisors and the same market. There are two ways in. The first is a UK insurer: the PRA has run a mobilisation regime for new insurers since 31 December 2024, "to facilitate new insurer expansion and entry into the UK market", an optional stage of up to twelve months with restrictions that begins at authorisation (Bank of England), and a general insurer's minimum capital floor is £2.4 million. The second is capital at Lloyd's: "A Lloyd's syndicate is formed by one or more members joining together to provide capital and accept insurance risks on a several liability basis", and the members' capital is held as Funds at Lloyd's (Lloyd's). A company that starts as a coverholder already works inside that market, so putting its own capital behind its own book is a short step.
carry
An insurer that wants EU clients directly may need an EU carrier as well, under Solvency II's €2.7 million floor. That can wait for the second market.
gulf

The Gulf has new regimes and a great deal of money, and I think its role here is the money. The UAE's two financial centres are both reworking their insurance rules: in Abu Dhabi, the ADGM's regulator proposed in December 2025 that insurers hold "120% of the ASCR under normal circumstances" (Reinsurance News); the DIFC's own pages could not be read, so its figures are left out. The region's funds invest in balance sheets of exactly the kind the third job needs. I would raise there, and leave selling there for later.
money

You asked for an opinion on the investment, so here is mine, with the arithmetic behind it in a data file and every assumption stated in the script that writes it. Running the company: about £4.35 million for two years. A team of eight in the first year and fifteen in the second, at £150,000 each including everything, and £450,000 a year for regulatory, legal, actuarial, professional indemnity and technology costs: £1.65 million in the first year and £2.7 million in the second. The market is funding companies like this: insurtech funding was "US$5.08 billion" in 2025 (Insurance Journal, 9 March 2026, citing Gallagher Re), and in the first quarter of 2026 "InsurTechs linked to AI liability and cyber insurance attracted USD 444.84 million" (Reinsurance News, 7 May 2026). AIUC has raised $55 million in two rounds, and Harbor was reported this month to have raised a $10 million seed.
money

Backing the policies: what the rest of the money buys is cover. This is where the deterministic policy pays off. Because every row is capped and every unnamed capability excluded, the worst year can be bounded from the limits on the book: take all the limits sold, the share of them one shared failure could hit at once (one model's flaw, one tool's bug, every agent built on it), keep half after reinsurance, and add a 20% buffer. Turn that round, and every pound of capital raised above the running costs sets a ceiling on the cover the company can sell. So rather than raising in stages, the company can raise once, for the cover it intends to sell from the start, and the size of the raise decides that ceiling. The ceiling of cover a raise of £10 million or £50 million can back. Illustrative, from capital.py.
money

With £80,000 of limits per agent, as in the worked example, and two years of running costs taken out first: Raised in one go Capital backing policies If 5% can be hit at once If 10% can be hit at once £10 million £5.65 million about £188 million of cover, 2,354 agents about £94 million of cover, 1,177 agents £50 million £45.65 million about £1.52 billion of cover, 19,020 agents about £761 million of cover, 9,510 agents Both are above the UK's £2.4 million floor. At the worked example's rate, £6,720 a year for £80,000 of cover with five enforced controls, the £10 million book could earn about £7.9 million to £15.8 million of premium a year, and the £50 million book about £64 million to £128 million; those are ceilings at full use of the capital, not forecasts.
money

So my opinion: decide the cover first, and raise for it in one go. £10 million is enough to prove the model on about a thousand to two thousand agents; £50 million is the raise for a company that means to insure ten to twenty thousand agents from the start, and to be the place the large providers come to. The share hit at once is the number that matters most, and it is the one with no loss data behind it yet: it is why even a large book should start spread across models and tools.
limits

This is not legal, tax or regulatory advice. It maps what regulators publish; a real decision needs lawyers and regulators in each place. The model's inputs are mine. Team sizes, costs, limits, the shared-failure share and the reinsured half are assumptions chosen to show the shape; the capital a regulator would ask for comes from its own formula. Currencies are approximate. The floors are as each regulator states them; the model converts them to pounds roughly. The Gulf figures are thinner. The DIFC's pages could not be read; the ADGM's proposal is a discussion paper, not a rule. The premium figures are ceilings. They assume every pound of capital is used at the worked example's rate; a real book would sell less, and price each agent on its own rows. Fronting fees are left out. We found no reliable published figure for what a carrier charges to lend its licence and balance sheet.
limits

Tax is left out. Where to be taxed is a separate question from where to be regulated. If you invest in insurers, or run one in any of these places, and would build this with us, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 28 October 2026, the third of this series, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine; the routes and the estimate are my opinion, as the memo asked. Every outside source is linked where it is used. They were read on 28 October 2026 by a research agent of this site, which fetched each page quoted; where it could not, the fact is marked as secondary or left out. The research notes, with what could and could not be verified, are admin/notes/2026-10-28__underwriting-abp/research-04.md in this site's repository. The model is admin/notes/2026-10-28__underwriting-abp/capital.py, and its output the data file linked above. question

I think the honest answer is that it has more than one home, because it does more than one job. A managing agent prices and sells policies on an insurer's behalf and carries no risk on its own balance sheet; it needs a licence to distribute insurance and a carrier willing to lend its capital. An insurer pays the claims and has to hold capital against a bad year. Distribution needs licences where the customers are. Those three jobs are regulated differently in each place, and the best place for one is not the best place for the others.

question

london

The UK licence is within reach of a start-up. A managing agent is either authorised directly by the FCA, which "can typically take up to nine months from when an applicant starts preparing its application", or works as an appointed representative of a firm that is; its own capital requirement, if it does not hold client money, is the higher of "GBP5,000 or 2.5% of annual income from regulated insurance distribution activity", with professional indemnity cover on top (DLA Piper, September 2026). For the later step, the PRA has run a mobilisation regime for new insurers since 31 December 2024, "to facilitate new insurer expansion and entry into the UK market" (Bank of England), with a minimum capital floor of £2.4 million for a general insurer.
articles/versions/where-to-build-the-agent-insurer/v1.1.0.html
eu

When the loss record exists and the company is ready to carry risk, I would do it in Bermuda. Its regime has a class for this stage: a Class 3A "Small commercial insurer" holds capital set by a risk-based formula, with "a $1 million floor" (BMA). It has a class for an insurer that "intends to carry on general business in an innovative manner", and a sandbox for "a company aiming to carry on general business in an innovative and experimental manner"; cyber insurers have used both, and one, Breach Insurance, moved from the sandbox to the innovative class in 2023 (BMA). And it is where risk capital meets insurance: the Bermuda Stock Exchange listed "more than 93% of global issuance" of insurance-linked securities in 2025, including "new cyber catastrophe bonds" (Insurance Business, 11 February 2026). Once agent risk has a record, that is the market that will take its tail.
articles/versions/where-to-build-the-agent-insurer/v1.1.0.html
eu

The UK is the alternative, with the PRA's mobilisation regime and the same Solvency-style discipline; and an insurer that wants EU clients directly may need an EU carrier as well. But for a first balance sheet, Bermuda's floor and its capital markets make it the place I would look first.
articles/versions/where-to-build-the-agent-insurer/v1.1.0.html
eu

The Gulf has new regimes and a great deal of money, and I think its first role is the money. As an insurance market, its entry costs differ widely: in Saudi Arabia an insurer's paid-up capital "shall not be less than three hundred million Saudi riyals" under the law as amended in 2021; in Abu Dhabi, the ADGM's captive rules started from US$150,000, and its regulator proposed in December 2025 that insurers hold "120% of the ASCR under normal circumstances" (Reinsurance News). We could not read the DIFC regulator's own pages, so its figures are from secondary sources and are left out here.
articles/versions/where-to-build-the-agent-insurer/v1.1.0.html
eu

As a source of capital it is a different story: the region's funds invest in balance sheets of exactly the kind the third stage needs, and the ADGM's regulator is rewriting its insurance rules as it does so. I would raise there, and sell there later.
articles/versions/where-to-build-the-agent-insurer/v1.1.0.html
money

Stage one, two years as a managing agent: about £4.35 million. A team of eight in the first year and fifteen in the second, at £150,000 each including everything, and £450,000 a year for regulatory, legal, actuarial, professional indemnity and technology costs: £1.65 million in the first year and £2.7 million in the second. No capital backs the policies, because the carrier's does. That is a seed or Series A, and the market is funding it: insurtech funding was "US$5.08 billion" in 2025 (Insurance Journal, 9 March 2026, citing Gallagher Re), and in the first quarter of 2026 "InsurTechs linked to AI liability and cyber insurance attracted USD 444.84 million" (Reinsurance News, 7 May 2026). AIUC has raised $55 million in two rounds, and Harbor was reported this month to have raised a $10 million seed.
articles/versions/where-to-build-the-agent-insurer/v1.1.0.html
money

Stage two, carrying the risk: the capital follows from the limits sold. This is where the deterministic policy pays off. Because every row is capped and every unnamed capability excluded, the worst year can be bounded from the limits on the book: take all the limits sold, the share of them one shared failure could hit at once (one model's flaw, one tool's bug, every agent built on it), keep half after reinsurance, and add a 20% buffer.

With £80,000 of limits per agent, as in the worked example:

So my opinion: raise about £5 million to start, which is stage one with some headroom; plan a second raise of £5 million to £10 million to carry the first two thousand agents, from investors who fund balance sheets; and by ten thousand agents, the capital is a reinsurance and capital markets question, which is where Bermuda comes in. The share hit at once is the number that matters most, and it is the one with no loss data behind it yet: it is why the first books should be small and spread across models and tools.

Abstract: If money goes into sgit, where should it go? The tool and its open format, a hub for vaults (SGitHub, the way GitHub is for code and Hugging Face for models), or open core in the GitLab style? I asked this site's agent to look at it as an investor would, with the history of developer platforms, what they were worth and how they captured the value, the state of sgit on 28 October 2026, and the evidence of use, including what is not there yet. The history says the network beats the host (SourceForge sold for about $20M, GitHub for $7.5B), registries struggle alone, hosting is where open source gets paid, and the hub of public work is the moat (Hugging Face, $12.93B to Nvidia, pending). Git is under strain from agents (Anthropic replaced it with Scion), and capital is following (Entire's $60M seed). My answer is the hub, with the format open and self-hosting always possible. The deck, the thesis, three business plans, the data and the evidence are in a public vault that runs as an app, and is meant to be forked for each investor.
Three ways to build a company on sgit, and the companies that went each way before.
in-short

The question: where should investment in sgit go: the tool, a hub for vaults, or open core? The history: the network beats the host; registries struggle alone; hosting is where open source gets paid. The hub of public work is the moat: GitHub sold for $7.5B, and Nvidia is buying Hugging Face for $12.93B. Why now: Anthropic replaced Git for its monorepo, and "git for agents" startups are being funded. Where sgit is: 99 releases since March, Git parity mostly done, and features Git cannot match. The gap: no paying customer of sgit itself yet; most production use is our own. My answer: fund the hub (SGitHub), keep the format open, sell self-host support as the bridge. The deck is a vault: it runs as an app, carries its evidence, and is forked per investor.
question

I am running several versions of this at the same time, so the question is a real one. If an investor puts money into sgit, where does it do the most good? There are three candidates: The tool and the format. sgit itself, the command line and the open vault format, Apache-2.0. The hub. A hosted home for vaults, where people and agents share, fork, discover and run them. I have been calling it SGitHub: what GitHub is for code and Hugging Face is for models, for the work agents produce. Open core. A server teams run themselves, with paid features on top, the way GitLab did it. I asked this site's agent to research it as an investor would: the history of developer platforms and what they were worth, the market now, the state of sgit, and the evidence that anyone uses it. I have a stake, so read this with that in mind. sgit is ours.
why-now

On 13 October Anthropic published how it redesigned source control, which I wrote about in Scion and sgit. Merges into its monorepo went from about 2,500 a day in May to more than 30,000 a day in September, and Git was "actively undermining our ability to scale". A team of seven built Scion and migrated in five months. Anthropic is clear that it is "by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use". The companies that outgrew Git built their own; startups building version control for agents are being funded.
why-now

Google and Meta built their own long ago. What is new is the money for everyone else. Entire raised a $60M seed at a $300M valuation in February, a record for developer tools. GitButler raised a $17M Series A, Pierre (Code.Storage) $22M. Cursor bought Graphite, and Hugging Face bought XetHub for its storage. None of them encrypt the work from the host, and none treat the work itself (data, app, history and sources) as the thing you hand over.
history

The agent's research covers sixteen companies, with a source for every number and a label for how far to trust it. The pattern is clearer than I expected. What developer platforms were worth, and how they captured it, on a log scale. The network beats the host. SourceForge hosted open source first, never owned the workflow, and was sold for about $20M in 2012. GitHub owned the workflow (forks, pull requests, profiles) and sold to Microsoft for $7.5B in stock in 2018, after two priced rounds. Registries struggle alone. npm had about $3M of revenue in 2019 and went to GitHub. Docker Hub won the habit and sold its enterprise business to Mirantis. The hub of public work is the moat. Hugging Face built the hub of public models and datasets, and Nvidia announced a $12.93B acquisition on 3 September 2026. The deal is pending.
history

Hosting is where open source gets paid. MongoDB went from a ~$1.2B IPO to about $31B on Atlas. Supabase, fully open source, raised at $10.5B in June. Vercel owns Next.js and hosts it, at $9.3B. Open infrastructure has strategic buyers. Red Hat (~$34B), HashiCorp ($6.4B) and Confluent (~$11B) all went to IBM. HashiCorp's licence change did not protect its value. Open core works, and makes a different company. GitLab listed at about $11B and had $955M of revenue in its last fiscal year, on a proprietary enterprise tier. There is also an open-source premium. A Linux Foundation study of more than 800 commercial open-source companies found Series A valuations 1.6 times those of closed peers, twice the chance of going from seed to Series A, and a median acquisition of $482M against $34M.
answer

The tool on its own is Git's story: enormous value, and no company. Open core is GitLab's, but sgit's rule is that there is no proprietary tier, which I set out in open source what you build; for us, that path becomes support and certification, the way Red Hat did it. My answer is the hub. Fund SGitHub, keep the format open, and make self-hosting always possible. The open standard feeds the hub; the hub is what is sold; and support for teams that must run their own server is the bridge to revenue while the hub grows.
answer

The reasons are the ones in the history. The network of public work is the moat, and the public vaults with read keys are already its seed: 54 on sgit.ai, more here. Vault apps make opening a vault the same as running it. Agents are the users who will grow fastest, and every surface of sgit is built for them first. And a hub that cannot read its users' vaults makes a different promise from GitHub's, which is a reason to trust it. Leaving is always possible, because the format and the server are open.
state

Commits per month on the CLI's dev branch and releases per month on PyPI, March to October 2026. sgit has had 99 releases on PyPI since 20 March, the latest (0.26.5) this morning. The repository has 1,757 commits across all branches and 5,032 test functions, and cli.sgit.ai lists 174 commands. The work comes in bursts, and the October one was driven by our own largest vault, which is the story of a tangent that shipped. Git parity on 28 October 2026, from the CLI team's roadmap.
state

On Git parity, the CLI team's roadmap of 28 October has most of the client done, line-level merge and partial commits shipped on dev today, and seven more designs (signing with your own key, renames, blame, bisect, grep, cherry-pick, hooks, rebase, worktree) at about 36 to 40 days of work. What Git has no equivalent for is in what sgit does that Git does not: a host that reads nothing, read keys, write-only lanes, custody without access, policy carried by the vault, byte-range clones and vault apps.
use

sgit in use, measured, and what is not there yet. The production use is real and mostly ours. The PHP newsroom's source-watch vault holds 79,465 files and 2.7 GB; as a pack vault it clones in 95 seconds where it took 13 minutes 47. Ten agents and one person share one vault of about 35,000 objects. The RiskMandate inbox team runs on a vault per workflow. Health-related projects use vaults too; the OmKneeHealth scenario is the public one. Outside our own work, Ruflo merged a pull request for sgit memory checkpoints, and the KGELL working group has a vault of 309 graphs.
use

What is not there yet matters as much. There is no paying customer of sgit itself; when SG/Send first charged, its briefs recorded that users bought credits, tested once and did not come back. The 13,915 PyPI downloads since April are downloads, not users. The public PKI register has no real keys in it yet, and the web app cannot open a pack vault. An investor should see all of that, so the deck says it.
evolution

From sending a file to a hub for vaults: the concepts in the order they arrived in 2026. The ideas came before the features. The vault and the data room were named in February, before folders and Git's model. Read keys, mirrors and vault-carried policy came in early October; PKI a few days later; pack mode and byte-range clones in the last week, because a real vault needed them. The hub is the next step on the same line.
vault

The investor deck, running from its vault: the title slide and the three business plans side by side. Everything is in a public vault, and the vault is the pitch. Open it and a 20-slide deck runs as a vault app, with a PDF of the same deck beside it. Clone it and you get what is behind every slide: THESIS.md: the argument in full. plans/: three business plans. A, the open standard; B, SGitHub, the hub (the one I would fund); C, self-host and support. data/: the product measured, and every platform figure with its source and confidence label. articles/: the newsroom articles the numbers come from. IDEAS.md: ideas to create investor interest, and to pick the right investors before the first meeting. personalise.py: forks the deck for one investor, with their name and the slides that matter to them first.
vault

That last one is the point. Each investor gets their own vault, forked from this one, with its own keys. They can see exactly what was changed for them and what was not, and point their own agent at the evidence before we meet. The ask (round size, instrument, use of funds) is left blank, as it is on sgit.ai/investors, until I state it. Open it in the vault browser, or clone it with pip install sgit-ai and sgit clone sgit_public_read_0b60bf869fb5e4cea1f98a6ae99afa3e7503107cda83d07eca5d433913bbb2d0:j0oob7zp sgit-investor-briefing. It will move to cli.sgit.ai and be forked and rekeyed from there, which is itself a demonstration.
investors

A few of the ideas in the vault, all of them the product selling itself: A write-only front door. An append lane where an investor leaves a short note (their thesis, their overlap with the git-for-agents companies, what they want to see in 18 months) and learns nothing about anyone else's. A data room that is a vault, which their agent can read and the host cannot. Open the big vault in the meeting: one folder of a 2.7 GB vault, cloned in seconds. Ask three questions first: do you back open source with no proprietary tier, do you see agents as the main users of developer infrastructure, and are you comfortable with a pitch that is public? Check for conflicts early, with funds already in Entire, GitButler or Pierre.
limits

It is a thesis, not a forecast. The milestones and plans are proposals for discussion, not commitments. SGitHub is not built. The CLI team's roadmap names it as the future server product. The valuations are other companies', from filings, company posts and press; some are labelled as estimates, and the Hugging Face deal is pending. I have a stake, and most of the production evidence is my own companies' use.
sources

Anthropic on Scion (13 October 2026); PyPI and pypistats, read 28 October; the sgit CLI repository and its Git parity roadmap of 28 October; cli.sgit.ai; sgit.ai/investors; pki.sgit.ai. Every platform figure, with its URL, quote and confidence label, is in the vault's data/platforms.json; the Linux Foundation's study of commercial open source is from August 2025. Research by this site's agent, under my direction.

Abstract: An entrepreneur doing everything they can to be secure bought a Mac mini for a customer, decided it would never touch the internet and that nothing would be installed on it, and ended up writing the application in the Perl that ships with macOS. The question that decides whether that is wise is not how secure the design is, but who it protects against. This article sets out the three questions that answer it, who the threat agent is, what the attack vector is, and how sophisticated they are, and a ladder of six tiers from your own mistakes to states, grounded in NIST SP 800-30, the NCSC's commodity, targeted and elevated threats, and MITRE ATT&CK. It notes that the UK's new AI Risk Management Toolkit asks "Who are the new threat actors?" without defining them. It reads the Mac mini against the ladder, where the air gap stops attackers that no inbound ports and patches also stop while adding a USB path and removing backups, monitoring and mainstream tooling; makes the same argument about keeping systems on premises for security; and argues that you should sell something better than what the customer has, not something beyond what they need, because drawing the line too high is a disservice to both sides. With it ships a vault of eight fictional startups, each with its assets, an attack tree mapped to ATT&CK techniques, and where it should draw the line, plus a questionnaire to draw your own.

Six tiers of attacker, from your own mistakes to elevated threats, with what stops each. Most startups plan for everything up to organised crime for money, and write down what they accept above it. The question is who, not how much. Before deciding how secure a design must be, answer three questions: who is the threat agent, what is the attack vector, and how sophisticated are they. Attackers come in tiers. Your own mistakes, opportunistic automation, activists, organised crime for money, targeted commercial attackers and insiders, and elevated threats from high-end crime and states. NIST SP 800-30, the NCSC and MITRE ATT&CK give the vocabulary. The basics beat most of the ladder. In the NCSC's words, "Organisations that defend effectively against commodity threats present a very hard target for all attackers". At the top tier, very few commercial organisations can hold out, whatever they build.

The air-gapped Mac mini protects against an attacker who has easier ways in, while it adds a USB path and removes backups, monitoring, patches and mainstream tooling. Isolate it; do not disconnect it. Sell better than what the customer has, not beyond what they need. Drawing the line too high slows everything down, can create new holes, and can stop the technology being used at all. That is a disservice to both sides. The design is easy to admire. A founder building an AI assistant for a customer buys a dedicated Mac mini. To keep the customer's files safe, it will never be connected to the internet. To avoid a supply chain, nothing will be installed on it. So the application is written in the one language that is already there: the Perl that ships with macOS. Files go in and out on a USB stick.

The side effect is the problem. Perl, as shipped with macOS, is there, in Apple's own words, "for compatibility with legacy software"; Apple said in 2019 that future versions might not include it and that software depending on a scripting language should bundle its own runtime. I would go further: it is probably one of the worst choices you could make today for an application like this. Not only because of the language, but because of everything around it. Compared with Python or Node, there are far fewer maintained libraries for the things an AI assistant needs, PDFs, spreadsheets, model APIs, HTTP, and far less of the tooling that makes code good: tests, linters, dependency scanners, the pipelines that check every change. The design buys a great deal of engineering and technical debt. What does it buy with it? That depends entirely on who it is protecting against. Security starts with three questions, and most over-engineering comes from skipping them:

Who is the threat agent? A bot, a criminal crew, a competitor, an insider, a state. What is the attack vector? How they would actually get to the thing you care about. How sophisticated are they? What they can afford to spend, and how patient they are.

The UK government's new AI Risk Management Toolkit, which we mapped when it was published, asks the right question in its section on security: "Who are the new threat actors?" It does not define them. It points to the risk management section of the government's Cyber Assessment toolkit instead. So the definitions in this article come from three older and well-tested places: NIST SP 800-30, the guide most risk assessments are built on, whose taxonomy of threat sources separates adversarial, accidental, structural and environmental sources and rates an adversary's capability on five levels from very low to very high; the NCSC, which separates un-targeted from targeted attacks, commodity from bespoke capability, and commodity from elevated threats; and MITRE ATT&CK, which names the techniques.

There is a well-known sequence, and the vault turns it into six tiers. Each has a NIST type and capability, a motive, a way of choosing targets, the ATT&CK techniques it typically uses, and the controls that stop it. T0, your own mistakes. A secret committed to a repository, a bucket left public, a table deleted with no backup. NIST calls these accidental sources. They are the most common loss, and nothing about them is sophisticated. T1, opportunistic automation. The script kiddies of the old vocabulary, now mostly bots: scanners, credential stuffing, mass phishing. The NCSC describes un-targeted attackers as those who "indiscriminately target as many devices, services or users as possible", and says "every organisation connected to the Internet should assume they will be a victim" of them. Patching, MFA and nothing listening that does not need to beat them.

T2, ideology and attention. Hacktivists and protest groups, who pick targets by cause. Most startups are not on their list. T3, organised crime for money. Ransomware, extortion and access brokers, run as businesses, choosing victims by ability to pay and by how much the data hurts. Commodity tools, used industrially. This is the realistic ceiling for most startups that hold anything of value. T4, targeted commercial. Competitors, the other side in a dispute and the hack-for-hire services they pay, and insiders. In a targeted attack, says the NCSC, "your organisation is singled out because the attacker has a specific interest in your business, or has been paid to target you". T5, elevated threats. The NCSC: these "can only be realised by large, well-funded groups (such as high-end organised crime and state sponsored groups)". Zero-days, supply chains, hardware, people, and years of patience.

At the top of the ladder the honest answer is uncomfortable. Very few commercial organisations can withstand a determined state attacker, and almost none at the level of investment a startup's technology team can make. That is not a reason to give up; it is a reason to stop designing as if you were the target, unless you are. If you sell into an environment where that tier is real, a government department, defence, critical infrastructure, the customer already owns the controls for it, and your job is to run well inside their accredited environment, not to build a parallel fortress. At the bottom, the NCSC's point is the encouraging one: "Regardless of their technical capability and motivation, attackers will often turn to commodity tools and techniques first. Organisations that defend effectively against commodity threats present a very hard target for all attackers." The basics, done consistently, are most of the job.

The vault's comparison: the air-gapped, nothing-installed design against an isolated-not-disconnected one, tier by tier. The air gap stops the bots, which no inbound ports and patches also stop; adds a USB path; and gives up backups, monitoring and tooling that would catch the most likely losses. Click the image to open the vault page ↗ The report did not say who the customer was, so in the vault I gave the case a fictional one, a twelve-person accounting firm, and walked it up the ladder. The air gap looks different from each tier. Against your own mistakes, it is worse. The most likely loss for a small firm is an accident: a file overwritten, a machine that fails, a script nobody else can fix. A design with no automated backups, no monitoring and code few people can maintain makes those more likely and harder to undo.

Against opportunistic automation, it works, but so does the ordinary alternative. Bots need an inbound service or an unpatched one. A machine with no inbound ports, an outbound allowlist and automatic updates stops them as well as a cable that is never plugged in. Against organised crime, it mostly misses. Ransomware gets into a small accounting firm through a member of staff's email and laptop, not through a dedicated machine in a cupboard. If the laptops are not protected, the air gap does not help; if anything, the USB stick that carries files between the laptops and the Mac mini is now the path, and removable media is how air gaps have been crossed before (ATT&CK T1091).

Against elevated threats, it does not hold. If an attacker at that tier is really after this firm, they will use hardware, people or that USB stick. In the words of my memo, if the attacker is trying to hit you, you have much bigger problems than that, and the air gap is not really going to save you. Running something properly air-gapped is a very hard discipline, and the mistakes made along the way create their own vulnerabilities.

So the air gap protects against an attacker who, for a firm like this, does not really exist, and pays for it with the tools that defend against the attackers who do. The better design is isolated, not disconnected: no inbound ports; outbound only to an allowlist of updates, backups and the model provider; software from a package manager, pinned, scanned and run in containers; disk encryption, automatic updates, and logs shipped somewhere someone reads them. Docker or Compose inside the machine, or inside a VM on it, is enough to start; Kubernetes later if it is needed. The point of using best-in-breed technology is visibility: it lets you ship good security tools and good security practices with the application, instead of writing them by hand in a language that has few of them.

This is the debate between running things locally and going to the cloud, at a smaller scale. "We will not go to the cloud, because the cloud is insecure", and then the organisation runs local infrastructure with more holes than Swiss cheese, because it does not have the expertise to run it securely and cannot hire it. In my experience the result is often more vulnerabilities inside the company, not fewer. A small team cannot compete, on quality or on security, with the people who run the major platforms full time. Decentralised does not mean safer; it usually means fewer people watching each part.

One primitive matters more than any control: what is the customer's baseline today? An accounting firm runs Windows laptops, a shared drive and email. A club runs spreadsheets and a noticeboard. A therapist keeps notes on a home laptop. A solution that is clearly better than that, and that does the basics well, is already an improvement in security for the customer.

There is no point spending time and money building something far beyond the customer's security requirements. And I say that as a security person: I am not arguing against security. I am arguing that you have to know where to draw the line. Draw it too high and you do a disservice to both sides. You protect against an attacker who is not there; you slow everything down; you may create new problems, as the USB stick does; and you may stop the technology being used at all, which leaves the customer with the weaker setup they had before. Most teams building at startup level, especially with vibe-coded applications, are not ready to deploy into the most sensitive accounts and environments without the customer's own controls around them, and should not be asked to pretend otherwise. When that is the market, meet the customer's baseline and deploy inside it.

The vault's compare view: eight fictional startups against the six tiers, the tiers in scope filled and each ceiling marked. Click the image to open the vault page ↗ The vault maps this out for eight fictional startups, because the line moves with the business, not with how careful the founder is. Fictional startup Ceiling Why A booking app for padel clubs T1 Member contact details; nothing that pays a ransom AI bookkeeping reading bank feeds T3 Financial data and live tokens: ransomware and extortion Session notes for independent therapists T3, with T4 for insiders The harm is to patients; the 2020 Vastaamo case shows how The Mac mini at an accounting firm T3 Ransomware starts at the staff laptops Document review for law firms in disputes T4 Hack-for-hire against litigants is documented Energy monitoring with optional control T3 Keep the dangerous capability off by default A popular open-source library T5

The target is everyone downstream; the xz Utils backdoor is the precedent AI drafting for a government department T5 Set by the customer, who already owns the controls One scenario in full: the accounting firm assistant's assets, its attack tree with an ATT&CK technique on every branch, and the line, with what must be done, what should, what is over the line and why, and the under-engineering to avoid. Click the image to open the vault page ↗

Each scenario has an attack tree, the form Bruce Schneier described in 1999, "with the goal as the root node and different ways of achieving that goal as leaf nodes". Every branch carries the ATT&CK technique it uses, the tier of attacker who would use it, and a rough cost. Walk the tree and the line draws itself: the branches below the ceiling get controls; the branches above it are written down as accepted, with a reason. Two startups have a ceiling at the top tier, and the reasons are instructive. One is a two-person open-source project, because one malicious release reaches everyone who installs it. The other sells to government, where the customer sets the line and already owns the controls.

The questionnaire: five questions about what you hold, who would pay to attack you, who you sell to, how far one breach reaches and what your customers use today, and the ceiling they point to, with the controls for every tier up to it. Click the image to open the vault page ↗ The vault ends with five questions: what is the most valuable thing an attacker could take or break; who would pay, or spend months, to attack you specifically; what environment you sell into; how many organisations one breach of you reaches; and what your customers use today. The highest tier any answer points to is your ceiling. Below it, the controls are listed. Above it is a risk you accept and write down, which is a decision, not a failure; every risk is already accepted, and the only question is by whom.

Then do the part most people skip: write the threat model down, on one page, publish it, and ask the community whether you are making the right compromises. Somebody who has seen the attack before will tell you quickly whether your line is too low, or too high. Name your attackers. Use the ladder. If you cannot name anyone above T1 who would pay to attack you specifically, that is your answer for now. Draw one attack tree for the thing you would least like to lose, with a technique on every branch. Do the basics consistently. Patching, MFA, backups restored in a drill, secrets out of code, nothing listening that does not need to. Look at your customer's baseline, and make sure you are clearly better than it. Write down what you accept above your ceiling, and when you will look again. Prefer isolation and visibility over disconnection. Mainstream tools, containers, logs someone reads.

Publish the threat model and ask. Drafted from a voice memo by Dinis Cruz, who is the author of the argument and the person with editorial responsibility, by agent@riskmandate.ai (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5) in the sgit.ai site session, on 8 October 2026. The entrepreneur whose design prompted it is not named. Quotations are from the NCSC's Common Cyber Attacks: Reducing the Impact and Design guidelines for high assurance products, NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1, Apple's macOS Catalina 10.15 release notes, DSIT's AI Risk Management Toolkit guidance and Bruce Schneier's Attack Trees, each read on 8 October 2026 and listed with links in the vault's sources. ATT&CK is a registered trademark of The MITRE Corporation. The eight startups in the vault are fictional; the precedents they cite are real.
