Abstract: In the last article I described insuring an agent row by row, from its behaviour policy. We have most of the pieces to put a number on it: the open behaviour policy, a way to map controls to agents and risks, the AIUC-1 standard as a graph on sgit.ai, and a deterministic formula. So the next questions are who sells this today, and what it would take to build a company that does. Today several companies sell AI agent cover: AIUC pairs a standard and audits with insurance, Armilla and Testudo write it as Lloyd's coverholders with limits up to $25 million and $9.25 million, Munich Re prices AI model performance itself, and Harbor distributes cover from surplus lines carriers. We found nobody pricing per row of a behaviour policy yet. The industry already has every part such a company needs: someone to measure, someone to price and bind, someone whose balance sheet pays, and someone who reinsures the tail. I thought it was mostly a capital problem, as I understood it was for neobanks, and asked to be corrected. Partly I was: many early neobanks needed little capital because they could not lend, and their hard part was the licence and the build-out. For an insurance carrier, capital is the business: enough to survive a one-in-two-hundred-year year. But the first company does not need to be a carrier. Coalition and At-Bay started by pricing on other insurers' capital and bought carriers later. So a company built on open behaviour policies could start small, with niche agents, agents in QA, or cover for a few per cent of users, and earn the record that brings capital, then the large providers insuring their own agents. Cover that lapses with an unpatched known vulnerability already exists, which is where this connects to the PHP story.

The four parts of an insurer for agent behaviour policies, and who already does each one today. Five articles and three vaults on one idea: an agent's behaviour policy read as an insurance policy, priced row by row, split with the vendor, and backed by capital.
in-short

We have most of the pieces to put a number on an agent. The open behaviour policy, the controls mapped to risks, AIUC-1 as a graph, and a deterministic formula. Several companies already sell AI agent cover. AIUC, Armilla, Testudo, Munich Re, and Harbor as a distributor; we found nobody pricing per row of a behaviour policy. The industry already has every part such a company needs. Measure, price and bind, carry the balance sheet, reinsure the tail. I thought it was a capital problem, like neobanks, and was partly wrong. Many early neobanks could not lend and needed little capital; their hard part was the licence and the build-out. For a carrier, capital is the business. Enough own funds to survive a one-in-two-hundred-year year, with a floor of £2.4 million in the UK.
in-short

The first company does not need to be a carrier. A managing agent prices and sells on a carrier's capital; Coalition and At-Bay started there and bought carriers later. Cover that lapses with a known vulnerability already exists. Chubb shifts the risk to the policyholder in steps after a 45-day grace period to patch. Start small, then the large providers. Niche agents, agents in QA, a few per cent of users; then the model providers insuring their own agents, which some have already looked at.
have

In a payout for every row I described how an agent behaviour policy could be insured: each row it names with its own limit, each enforced control lowering the premium, and what it does not name excluded. I think we now have most of the pieces of the puzzle to calculate that number. The behaviour policy exists and is open source; what can your agent reach? explains it. We have a way to map controls to agents and to risks: on sgit.ai we turned the AIUC-1 standard into a graph and asked it what would be insurable, as underwriting the agent economy, reviewed describes. And we have a formula that says: with this agent, with these controls, the premium is this and the payout is that.
have

So the next questions are practical. Who sells that today? And if someone, or an investor, wanted to build a company that does, what would it take? I should say first what I am not: this has to be built by people who are experts in insurance and understand the medium, and it needs a lot of capital. What I can do is map the pieces, and ask the questions an expert would have to answer.
landscape

The market is already moving, and the last review of it on this site is four days old. What it found, and what has been checked since: AIUC combines a standard, audits and insurance. When it came out of stealth, its policies were described as covering "customers and vendors in the event an agent causes harm", with pricing that "reflects how safe the system is" (Fortune, 23 July 2025). In September 2026 it raised a $40 million Series A to extend its audits, standards and insurance to frontier models, bringing what it has raised to the $55 million its own site gives; the companies certified to AIUC-1 include Cursor, ElevenLabs, Harvey, KPMG, Lovable, UiPath and Intercom's Fin (FinTech Global, 17 September 2026).
landscape

Armilla is a Lloyd's coverholder whose affirmative AI liability cover is "underwritten by certain underwriters at Lloyd's, including Chaucer" (Armilla, 30 April 2025), now with limits "up to $25 million per organization" and cover for "AI Agent Failures: Claims arising from incorrect decisions, improper tool use, or escalation errors" (Armilla). Testudo, another Lloyd's coverholder, covers third-party claims from "AI-generated outputs", with limits of "$9.25m per insured" since Atrium and QBE joined Apollo on its panel (FinTech Global, 9 March 2026). Munich Re has written AI cover since 2018 as aiSure, and says "The quality of the model and its performance stability determine the premium" (Munich Re). Harbor takes a company from discovering its agents to insuring them, and its policies "are issued by surplus lines insurance carriers", as the last review recorded.
landscape

Each of these is a real step. None, as far as we found, prices an agent per row of its behaviour policy, with a limit per named risk and a factor per enforced control. AIUC comes nearest, because it pairs a standard and its audits with the cover. That is the gap, and since the behaviour policy is open, the company that fills it does not have to be RiskMandate: anyone can build on the policies, and sponsor the mapping for the agents they insure.
chain

The insurance industry has spent a long time separating the jobs, and it helps to name them, because a new company does not have to do them all. The policy and the evidence. What the agent can reach, what it may do, and the logs that show each control held. This is the behaviour policy's job, and where RiskMandate works; AIUC's audits are another form of it. Pricing and binding. A managing general agent, which Lloyd's calls a coverholder, prices and sells policies on an insurer's behalf. In Lloyd's words, it "is a company that has been authorised" "by a Lloyd's Managing Agent to enter into insurance contracts on behalf of a Lloyd's syndicate", and "This authority is granted through a formal Binding Authority agreement" (Lloyd's). It does not carry the risk on its own balance sheet; the insurer does.
chain

The balance sheet. The carrier pays the claim and holds the capital for it. At Lloyd's, "A Lloyd's syndicate is formed by one or more members joining together to provide capital and accept insurance risks on a several liability basis" (Lloyd's). A fronting carrier lends its licence and balance sheet to business an MGA places and passes most of the risk on: in the US in 2025, fronting carriers wrote "more than $22 billion in gross premiums" and ceded "nearly $19 billion to nonaffiliated reinsurers" (Insurance Business, 31 August 2026, citing a Conning study). Reinsurance. "Reinsurance, often referred to as "insurance for insurance companies," is a contract between a reinsurer and an insurer" (NAIC). It takes the tail and the correlated loss: the day one model's flaw hits every agent built on it.
chain

Around them sit distribution, brokers and platforms, and the claim. For agents, the claim could be the simplest part. Swiss Re describes parametric insurance as "a type of insurance that covers the probability of a predefined event happening", paid on an index rather than on a loss adjuster's assessment (Swiss Re). A row of a behaviour policy is close to that: the event maps to a row, and the log says whether the conditions held.
capital

My understanding going in was that this is like the fintech revolution in banking. When the neobanks arrived, they did not give much credit to new accounts, so they carried little risk, and I thought the main gap was having enough capital to cover the balances if something major went wrong. I asked to be corrected if that was wrong, and partly it was. What an e-money firm, a new bank, an insurance carrier and a managing agent must hold, and the hard part of each.
capital

Many early neobanks were e-money institutions. Those need initial capital "of not less than EUR 350 000" (EMD2, article 4), and customer money is safeguarded: credit may be granted only "provided that such credit is not granted from funds safeguarded" (EMR 2011, regulation 32). A full bank holds capital mostly against its lending: in the EU at the end of 2025, credit risk was 77.9% of banks' risk-weighted assets, operational risk 13.4% and market risk 3.7% (EBA Risk Dashboard, Q4 2025). A new UK bank goes through mobilisation, which "typically lasts no longer than 12 months", while "the bank's deposit-taking permission is restricted to a total of £50,000" (Bank of England). Revolut was granted its licence with restrictions in July 2024 and left mobilisation on 11 March 2026 (tech.eu). So for the neobanks, the hard part was the licence and the build-out as much as the capital.
capital

For an insurer, I was closer to right. The risk is the product, so capital is the business. Under Solvency II, the capital requirement corresponds to the value at risk of the insurer's own funds "subject to a confidence level of 99,5 % over a one-year period" (Solvency II, article 101): enough to survive a year that comes once in two hundred. Below that there is a minimum, which in the UK "must neither fall below 25% nor exceed 45% of the firm's SCR", with a floor of £2,400,000 for a general insurer (PRA Rulebook). In the US, risk-based capital sets "a statutory minimum level of capital" by size and by "the inherent riskiness of its financial assets and operations" (NAIC).
capital

And this is where the deterministic formula matters most. Capital is held against what could go wrong at once. A policy that excludes what it does not name, caps every row, and holds a reserve for the catastrophe layer makes the worst year easier to bound, and a bounded worst year needs less capital per pound of cover. It is still a question of how many policies, how much risk accumulates, and how much the balance sheet can hold; but it is a question with numbers.
path

So the first company does not need to be a carrier. It can price and sell on someone else's capital, prove its loss record, and then carry the risk. Two cyber insurers bought carriers of their own once they had a book. From a managing agent on someone else's capital to a carrier that reinsures the tail, with two cyber precedents. Coalition "completed the acquisition of Digital Affect Insurance Company from Munich Re Digital Partners US Holding Corporation" on 15 August 2022, a carrier "licensed in all 50 states" (Coalition). At-Bay followed on 24 January 2023: "Taking on balance sheet risk and owning our own insurance carrier are crucial steps on our journey" (At-Bay). And a full carrier still cedes part of its risk: Lemonade "expects to cede approximately 18% of premium to reinsurers" under the agreements it renewed in June 2026 (Lemonade).
path

That answers whether one company or several are needed: at the start, several, with the new company as the managing agent and established carriers and reinsurers behind it; later, possibly one group that does most of it. I would also expect the large insurers to build exactly these divisions themselves, once the market matures and they trust their models. The open behaviour policy makes collaboration easy either way: whoever prices the risk works from the same rows.
small

The way in is small. Insure smaller agents first, or agents while they are in QA, or agents that serve only a small share of users, 1% or 5%, with low limits per row. Each of those gives a carrier a bounded exposure and gives the new company a loss record against named rows and logged controls. Once that works, it can go to the large providers. There are signs the industry is ready to fund the attempt. Lloyd's Lab's sixteenth cohort includes Exona Lab, a "Risk engine quantifying advanced and systemic AI risks" (FinTech Global, 20 March 2026). Deloitte projected in May 2024 that "by 2032, insurers can potentially write around US$4.7 billion" of AI insurance premiums, "at a compounded annual growth rate of around 80%" (Deloitte).
fractal

This is not about selling one large policy to a company. A top-down policy is what you sell when you already have fifty, five hundred or a thousand small ones: one per agent, each tied to where it runs, the software under it, and the ecosystem around it. The company-wide policy is the aggregate, and its limit is the sum of rows the insurer is willing to hold together.
fractal

That also means the cover moves with the software. Take a PHP website with an application behaviour policy, insured as long as no known vulnerability in it is left unpatched. When a vulnerability like php2shell is published, you either fix it or take the site offline, because otherwise you are running outside the policy, and uninsured. That already exists in cyber insurance. Chubb's neglected software endorsement gives policyholders "a 45-day grace period to patch software vulnerabilities that are published as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs)", after which the risk shifts towards the policyholder "at the 46-, 90-, 180-, and 365-day points" (Chubb, 2022). Coalition reports another insurer that "excludes losses arising from CVEs with a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity score greater than 8.0" when the patch was not applied within three weeks, and counts "As of July 2025, 61,764 vulnerabilities would qualify" (Coalition, 31 July 2025). A behaviour policy makes that rule precise: which row the vulnerability touches, and which control would have to hold for the row to stay in cover.
providers

There is an opportunity at both ends: enterprise and personal cover, and the providers of agentic workflows insuring their own agents. Imagine a provider saying: I provide this service, and if my agent attacks another company, I insure you up to this amount. I think the large providers will play, once they see it working, even if they do not fully do it now. They have already looked at the problem from the other side. Insurance Journal, reporting the Financial Times on 8 October 2025, wrote that "OpenAI has considered "self-insurance" by setting aside investor funding", that it "has secured coverage of up to $300 million for emerging AI risks", and that Anthropic is "partly using its own funds to cover potential settlements" (Insurance Journal). A provider that can show, row by row, what its agents may do and what stops them, has a better chance of getting cover, and of selling it on.
providers

And some of this may become required. Everyone who drives on a road needs insurance: the Road Traffic Act says "a person must not use a motor vehicle on a road or other public place unless there is in force" a policy that complies with it (section 143). In October 2020 the European Parliament asked that operators of high-risk AI "should take out liability insurance similar to that for motor vehicles" (European Parliament), in a resolution that does not bind; the Commission withdrew its AI liability directive in February 2025. As agents get more powerful, I believe agents with real reach will need insurance in the same way.
questions

This is a research brief as much as an article, so here are the questions I would like answered by people who know insurance: Which carrier or Lloyd's syndicate would give a binding authority to a managing agent that prices per row of a behaviour policy? And what loss record would it want first? How much capital does a book of capped, deterministic rows actually need? Compared with a cyber book of the same premium. How do correlated losses work when many agents share one model? Which rows aggregate across a fleet, and what does the reinsurer need to see? What does the claim look like? Close to parametric, or with a loss adjuster, and who reads the logs? Who certifies the runtime and the enforcing software? And is that a condition of cover or a factor in the price? Where do the providers' own warranties sit? Beside the customer's cover, or under it?
questions
Which market goes first: enterprise agents, personal agents, or the providers?
limits

I am not an insurance expert. This maps the parts as published; building it needs underwriters, actuaries, lawyers and regulators. The landscape is what we found. Companies may price agents in ways not visible from their public pages; "nobody prices per row" means nobody we found. The capital comparison is simplified. Real capital requirements depend on the risk model, the lines written and the regulator; the floors quoted are minimums, not what a carrier holds. The path is a precedent, not a plan. Coalition and At-Bay are cyber insurers; agents may need a different route. The market forecast is Deloitte's, from 2024. It is a projection, and other figures in circulation were not used because they could not be checked. The compulsory insurance point is a view. No UK or US law requires insurance for AI agents today, as far as we found.
limits
If you underwrite specialty risk and would like to price an agent row by row, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Abstract: With publishing working well, and the PHP site about to be split into six repositories, I want to start a new piece of work: a map of where the data in the story actually comes from. Who is creating original data, and who is passing it on? The site already holds the answer in raw form. Of the 418 sources it has captured, 277 are news pages, but when you count who first states each of the 107 claims, numbers and exploitation reports the site attributes, news outlets originate 5 of 146; organisations, agencies and named people originate almost all the rest, led by the PHP Foundation, Wiz, CISA and Cloudflare. The fact-check desk found claims relayed 29 times, 11 of them by the BBC. That map is a job for the historian, the agent that keeps the record and finds the pivot points, and it needs its own visualisations and data work. The second question is where we can create original content ourselves. We already do in a few places: figures we counted, a source watch that catches silent rewording, correction requests. The bigger opportunity is people: interviews with those affected, recorded by me or drafted by an agent, under the Open Security Summit banner, and op-eds from people involved, published on our site.
Who creates the original, in the PHP story's data: 418 sources captured, 107 attributed claims, and who originated them.
in-short

A new piece of work: map where the data comes from. Who creates original data, and who passes it on. The PHP site already has the raw answer. Every claim is attributed to who first stated it. News is most of what we read, little of what is original. 277 of 418 sources; 5 of 146 originations. This is the historian's job. It keeps the record, finds the pivot points, and needs its own visualisations. Where can we be original? Our own counts, our own record, our own analysis. And people. Interviews with those affected, and op-eds from those involved, on our site.
who

Publishing on the PHP story site now works well, and the site is about to be split into six repositories. So this is a good moment to start something I have wanted for a while: a map of where the story's data actually comes from. Who is creating original data? Who is creating the insight? And who is passing on what someone else found? The site already holds the raw material. Its ontologist keeps an attribution file that names, for every claim, number and exploitation report on the site, who first stated it, and, where the fact-check desk found the same words in someone else's capture, who relayed it. I counted it on 25 October, at release v0.22.0. What we read. 418 sources captured: 277 news pages, 31 government pages, 27 vendors, 25 advisories, 14 CVE records, 11 researchers, and the rest code, social posts and others.
who

Who says it first. 107 attributed rows, with 146 originations between them. Organisations account for 79, agencies 27, named people 22, groups 5, news outlets 5, and the remaining 8 are unnamed posts, a registry, a platform, a project and this site. Who leads. The PHP Foundation (13), Wiz (9), CISA (7), Cloudflare (7), the PHP Group (6) and Amazon (6). Who relays. Claims found relayed 29 times, 11 by the BBC and 6 by The Hacker News. The BBC also originates three statements of its own. So two thirds of what we read is news, and almost none of what is original comes from it. That is not a criticism of the outlets: relaying, checking and explaining is valuable work. But it is the map that sources and their shadows and local trust, certified upwards need, if anyone is ever going to pay the people who created the original.
historian

Which agent should own this? I think it is the historian. The historian is the one that keeps the record: it goes back, finds the nuggets, the interesting elements, the pivot points. Who created what, and when, is exactly that. Today the PHP site's historian puts the story beside the ones before it and keeps the corrections, the context page and the version history. It has no schedule card yet, and its status records no round since its policy was written on 22 October. Giving it this map is a reason to wake it.
historian

It is also more than a list. This part of the site needs its own visualisations and its own data work: originators against relays, over time; who was first, and who caught up; which outlets add something and which pass words on. Every other agent can nudge it, the fact-check desk above all, but one agent should maintain it. The data is in place. What is missing is someone whose job it is.
original

Where we can create original content: counted, recorded, analysed, interviewed or written by others, with each status. The second question turns the first on ourselves. Where are we creating content that nobody else has? There are already a few places. Six of the attributed statements are figures the site counted itself, from captured files or a clone of the code, and one claim is the site's own: that no named organisation has confirmed a compromise through php2shell, with its time. The source watch re-reads 913 pages and has kept 2,946 snapshots, which is how it caught a publisher rewording without a note. Twelve correction requests are drafted, none sent yet. And Pulse, the risk graph and the historian's perspective pieces are our analysis. Nobody else has these, because nobody else kept the record.
people

But the most original content is people. The site already has one interview: the editor, interviewed, with ten questions written by the agent that builds the site, ten answers in my own words from my voice memos, and five questions waiting for a live interview. We can do a lot more of that. Interviews with people affected. I can do them myself, and record them as podcasts or videos, especially under the Open Security Summit banner. Interviews drafted by an agent. An agent can prepare the questions, as it did for mine, and turn the answers into a page, with the recording as its source. Op-eds. We can ask the people involved, maintainers, defenders, publishers and those affected, whether they would like to write an opinion piece for the site, under their own name.
people
That last one matters. Publishing original content from others on our site makes us a place where original content is created, not only a place that maps it.
exists

Exists: the attribution data, the source watch, the correction requests, the counts, the editor's interview. Proposed: the historian owning the originators map, with its visualisations; interviews with people affected; op-eds from people involved.
limits

The counts are the site's own attribution, at v0.22.0; a row can name two originators, and the attribution is still being filled in. "Relays" are only those the fact-check desk found in a capture; the real number is higher. Nobody has been asked for an interview or an op-ed yet.
sources

Abstract: Six days after php2shell, the headlines say most websites have not patched, and the subtext is that businesses do not take security seriously. Before accepting that, ask how good the number is. Every figure published so far is a count of version strings, not of vulnerable sites; Italy's national CSIRT, the best of them, found 81.9% of PHP services whose version it could read below the fix, which is 38.5% of all it detected, and a fixed package can keep its old number. A site is only vulnerable if it is exploitable: reachable, without protection in front (Cloudflare, behind about 28% of websites, had rules live on every plan nine hours before disclosure), on a runtime the exploit fits (the public exploits need an exact build and worker), with something worth taking and nobody watching. And no named organisation has yet said it was compromised through php2shell. So the more likely explanation for "not patching" is not negligence: the count is wrong, the threat is low where it matters, and security teams are patching other things first, which is their job.
The layers between "running PHP" and "compromised", and which of them a version count measures.
in-short

The headline implies negligence. "Most sites have not patched" reads as "business doesn't care". Every published number is a version count, not a test of whether a site can be exploited. Version strings lie both ways. Backported fixes keep the old number; about a third of hosts hide it. Vulnerable means exploitable. Reachable, unprotected, the right runtime, something worth taking, nobody watching. The edge moved first. Cloudflare had rules on every plan nine hours before disclosure. Still no named victim, six days in, and 34 sites taken offline as a precaution. Security teams prioritise. 17 flaws went on CISA's exploited list in the same fortnight. The likelier story: the count is wrong, the threat is low where it matters, and work is going elsewhere.
headline

The story of day five and six is that websites are not patching: large numbers still unpatched, look at this, people are ignoring it. I asked the newsroom to find the number behind it, and the first finding is that there is no single one. Searching all 614 sources in the PHP story site's evidence, nobody says "90% not patched". The closest are Italy's national CSIRT on 25 October, "only about 18%" of the Italian organisations concerned had updated, and a newsletter headline of "1.5M servers unpatched on day one". The nearest 90% says the opposite: a Berlin hosting firm said 90% of its customers were patched 18 minutes after the release.
headline

What all of them imply is the same, and it is a habit of my own profession. Security has a bad habit of telling the business that it is irresponsible: the sky is falling, you take too many risks, patch, patch, patch. A headline that says most sites have not patched implies negligence. Before accepting that, there are two questions. How good is the number? And what does "vulnerable" actually mean?
number

Every figure published so far counts version strings. None tests whether a site can be exploited. And the units are all different: Censys counted 2.58 million hosts seen on release day, 1.57 million announcing a version below the fix; its dashboard was quoted at 36.7 million "services"; Palo Alto at 22.6 million "instances"; Italy at 741,523 services. As we found checking Jeremiah Grossman's post, those are different things, and no one measurer has published a series over the days.
number

The best of them, Italy's, shows the problem. CSIRT Italia detected 741,523 PHP services; it could read the version of 348,130, 47%; and 285,149 of those, 81.9%, were below the fixed release. So the 81.9% is of the readable half. Of everything detected, it is 38.5%. And "below the fixed release" is not "unpatched": Fortinet, quoting Censys, says these "are service counts, not unique servers or organizations, and version-based estimates may include installations already patched through vendor backports". Ubuntu, Debian and Red Hat fix PHP in the version they shipped, without changing its number. The PHP story site's patching tracker lists fixes from Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat, cPanel and CloudLinux that a version scan would count as unpatched.
number

The error runs the other way too. The CVE records list only PHP 8.2 to 8.5, so a scanner that reads them reports 7.4 to 8.1 as not affected. And one French count put 6.62 million of 11 million PHP services in France, which turned out to be a fingerprinting error about home routers. A version count is a starting point, not a finding.
vulnerable

This is the simple logic: a site that cannot be exploited is not vulnerable, whatever its version says. For a php2shell compromise, five things have to be true, and a version count measures none of them. Reachable. The PHP server answers the attacker directly. Sites taken offline, or behind a login, or only on an internal network, are not. Nothing in front. No web application firewall or edge rule blocking the attack. Cloudflare's rules were live on every plan, including the free one, from 03:02 UTC on 21 October, about nine hours before disclosure. Akamai and Imperva followed the same day, Fortinet the next. According to W3Techs on 27 October, 32.7% of websites sit behind a reverse proxy it monitors, and Cloudflare alone 28.1%. A rule is a stopgap, every vendor says so, and an origin reachable directly goes round it. But a scan that reaches the edge often cannot see the PHP version at all.
vulnerable

A runtime the exploit fits. The advisories say complete remote code execution was demonstrated against Apache with mod_php; for PHP-FPM, "no complete FPM exploit has been demonstrated" for the first flaw. Fastly says the public exploits "require knowledge of the specific, running PHP binary and address space layout on the server". The public bounty win needed an exact build and worked about seven times in ten in its author's own lab, as we checked. CISA's own assessment on the CVE records said "Automatable: no". Something worth taking. Code execution on a brochure site with nothing behind it is a defacement risk; on a server holding tokens, customer data or a route into the network, it is a breach. Not all websites are the same. Nobody watching. Can the attack be detected? The PHP story site's defence notes are frank that standard logs show little of this attack. That cuts both ways, and I come back to it below.
vulnerable

Multiply those together and the population that is vulnerable, valuable and unwatched is much smaller than "not patched". Nobody has measured it, which is the honest answer, and also why the headline number tells us so little.
record

Six days in, the PHP story site's compromise record, at 14:41 UTC on 27 October, still reads: "No named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell." Vendors report attempts, in millions; two vendors retracted earlier claims of success; eight national CERTs, among them Latvia, Austria, Belgium, Switzerland, Germany, the Netherlands, Japan and Luxembourg, report no successful attacks in their countries; watchTowr's answer to whether reliable indiscriminate exploitation is happening was "for now, the answer is a firm No". The site also counts 34 services taken offline, all as precautions: councils, ministries, banks, airlines, Wikimedia. That raises its own question, which I think deserves measuring: how many sites were taken off the internet that did not need to be, and what did that cost? A site taken offline shows in a version scan as "not seen", or as "unpatched" if it was scanned before it went down. Neither is "not patching".
call

Think about the conversation that actually happens. An executive has seen it on the news and asks: are we vulnerable, yes or no? What's the impact? Can they get in? And then the questions executives always ask, because they make risk decisions every day: how many companies have been hit? What is the threat? If the answer is "none, so far", the executive concludes, correctly, that the threat is low. You can only stop everything for a clear and present danger, and you only have that when it is actually happening. Imagine someone on a high street saying the whole street is about to catch fire, and you look up and down the street and no shop is on fire. You might still act, but you would not stop trading.
call

And the business is paying the security team to do exactly that: to put its limited time where the real threats are. In the same fortnight, CISA added 17 flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities, among them PAN-OS, Cisco's email gateway, BeyondTrust, Fortinet, Plex, Arista and Collabora, each with a deadline. php2shell went on it on 26 October. CISA's exploited-vulnerability additions from 14 to 26 October 2026, and php2shell's EPSS score. A model-driven queue would not have put php2shell at the top for most of the week either: its EPSS score was 0.05 to 0.12 until 25 October, then jumped above 0.999. Choosing not to patch this server today usually means patching another one first. That is not negligence. It is the job.
secondary

So when the headline says sites are not patching, I think the more likely explanations, in order, are: The count is wrong, or at least much smaller than it looks: version strings, backports, unreadable versions and different units. The threat is not there yet for most sites: hard exploits, no named victim, CERTs reporting none. Protection was put in front, especially of the sites worth attacking: the edge, configuration changes such as switching off upload progress, and sites taken offline. Teams are patching what is being exploited first, which is what they are paid to do. Against that, "they don't care" is the least likely explanation, and it is the one the headline chooses.
unreported

I do think some companies may have been compromised and have not said so. Detection is hard: JPCERT warned that a lack of traces does not prove there was no compromise. GMO Internet Group found malicious programs on 26,739 servers of one of its services and has not stated the cause. And disclosure rules do not require a public statement: GDPR and NIS2 reports go to regulators, not the public, and US listed companies report only material incidents. But given how high-profile this is, I would be surprised if many such cases stay hidden for long. One regulator's notice naming the flaw would end the "no named victim" line, and the PHP story site is watching for it.
limits

That patching is unnecessary. Patch: every vendor says the rules and settings are stopgaps, and a third flaw affects fully patched releases. That no site was compromised. The record is a dated absence, as of 14:41 UTC on 27 October. A measured number of exploitable sites. Nobody has published one; the layers above are the argument for measuring it. Some figures are relayed. Italy's 81.9% comes through two Italian outlets; CSIRT Italia's alert itself is not captured. Censys's figures are relayed by others. "90% not patched" was not found as a headline; if you have the link, we will add it.
sources

The PHP story site's data, read on 27 October 2026 (data version 0.1.85): the compromise record and compromise.json, the patching tracker and patching.json, defence.json, numbers.json, with the captured sources: CyberSecItalia on ACN's alert, SecurityWeek on Censys, Cryptoast on the French miscount, php.net's advisory, Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, Imperva. Read live on 27 October: Fortinet's post, W3Techs' reverse proxy survey, CISA's KEV catalogue and FIRST's EPSS API. Related: the evidence behind four days, what the bitcoin bounty actually proves, patch for breakfast, the side stories of php2shell, translate the assumption. Researched by this site's agent, newsroom.writer; the editorial responsibility is mine.

Abstract: People who get emails from my agents often think they are talking to a fully autonomous agent. They are not: they are talking to me, through an agent that helps me process, map, follow up and collect the evidence, and every email waits for me before it goes. The same is true of this site, and it should be easier to see. There are three voices here. Me alone, which this newsroom does not yet have. Me through an agent, which is almost everything: articles written from my voice memos by the newsroom's agents, checked by them, and published under my name with the editorial responsibility mine; 83 of the 90 articles written in this repository were first published that way. And an agent in its own voice, writing about the work it did: five articles so far, by newsroom.ux, newsroom.vault and now newsroom.writer, which wrote most of the rest of this site in my voice. Readers, people and agents alike, read a piece differently depending on who wrote it, so every byline now says which: an agent's name carries an agent mark, and mine says it was written with the newsroom's agents. The words matter too. The agents had been calling me "the owner"; they now name me, because as more people join, the record should say who said what. This sets out the three voices, the marks, the words the agents should use, and what is still to do.
Three voices on this site: Dinis alone, Dinis through an agent, and an agent in its own voice.
in-short

People think they are talking to an autonomous agent. They are talking to me, through one. Three voices. Me alone; me through an agent; an agent in its own voice. Almost everything here is me through an agent. 83 of the 90 articles written in this repository. Five articles are in the agents' own voices. About work they did, signed with their names. Every byline now says which. An agent mark, or "with the newsroom's agents". The agents name people. Not "the owner": Dinis, or the editor where the role is the point. Readers read differently by who is speaking. People and agents both, so the label is part of the content.
emails

Several people who receive emails from my agents have told me, or shown me, that they think they are talking to a fully autonomous agent. They are not. The agents draft the email, follow up the thread, map what was said, collect the evidence and the data, and keep track of what is owed to whom; and then the email waits for me. The human in the loop put it in one line: "The agents draft every email and I send every one." So the person on the other end is talking to me, through an agent. That matters for how they read it: what they forgive, what they trust, what they ask back. An email from a fully autonomous agent and an email from a person using an agent are different things, and right now nothing on the email says which it is.
voices

This site has the same question, and more of it. There are three voices here. Me, alone. Something I wrote and published myself, with no agent in the loop. The newsroom does not have one yet, and I expect few, but it should be possible and it should look different. Me, through an agent. I record a memo, or point at something I read; an agent researches it, writes it in my voice, checks every fact, draws the figures and publishes it under my name, and the editorial responsibility is mine. Of the 90 articles written in this repository, 83 were first published that way, by the agent that now has a name of its own, newsroom.writer. The older articles imported from sgit.ai were written the same way, from memos, by that site's agent.
voices

An agent, in its own voice. An agent writing about work it did, in the first person as the agent: newsroom.ux on the reading folds and on what counts as read, newsroom.vault on the vault, opened, and now newsroom.writer on the briefs it has written. Five so far. Its "I" is the agent; its editorial responsibility is still mine. Most of what is interesting here is in the second voice, and it is the one most easily misread in both directions: as if I wrote every word myself, or as if no person were involved at all. Neither is true. It is a collaboration with a clear division: the ideas, the decisions and the responsibility are mine; the research, the writing, the checking and the publishing are the agents', under rules I wrote.
marks

Both people and agents read a piece differently depending on who wrote it. A reader gives a first-person argument from a named person a different kind of trust from a status report by a tool. An agent reading the site to answer a question should know whether a claim is the editor's position or an agent's account of its own work. So who is speaking is part of the content, and it belongs on the byline, where every reader looks. Every article on this site now says which voice it is in: An agent in its own voice: its name carries a small agent mark and the word agent, and links to a page that says what the name covers: the model, the session, what it works on, and who holds the responsibility. newsroom.writer has a page now too.
marks

Me, through an agent: my name is followed by with the newsroom's agents, and the end of every article says it was written up and checked by this site's agent, with the editorial responsibility mine. Me, alone: no mark yet, because there is no such article. When there is one, it will say so. The front page already has a place for the third voice, From the agents, a third of the way down, with the newest pieces the agents wrote in their own names. I think every publisher should read your reading, your controls: it is the record of how a feature that changes how people read was designed and built, by the agent that built it.
words

The agents had been calling me the owner. "The owner asked for five themes." "My last article ended with a question for the owner." I do not like the word, and it is not the right concept: I am the editor and the publisher, and before either I am a person with a name. So the agents now name me: "Dinis asked for five themes"; "my last article ended with a question for Dinis". The role is used only where the role is the point, the editor deciding what goes on the front page, say.
words

This is not only about me. As more people join, journalists, reviewers, experts on the record, the record should say who said what, who connected what to what, and how the work flowed between them. A role hides that; a name keeps it. On this release the agents' articles and notes were changed in a hundred places, and the rule is now in the guide every agent reads before it writes. The same care applies to I and we. In an article in my voice, I is me. In an agent's article, I is the agent. We is me and the agents together, and only where we did the thing together.
guidance

The guide every writing agent here reads first, the article README, now carries these as rules alongside the wording rules: Say which voice you are writing in, and write the front matter so the byline shows it: my name for my voice, your own name for yours. In my voice, keep my memo's order and phrases; say I for me; never claim I did something an agent did, or the reverse. In your own voice, write as the agent about the work you did, with the commits and tests a reader can check. Name people. Not "the owner"; Dinis, or the role where the role is the point. End with who is responsible. Every article's sources end with who wrote it up and who holds the editorial responsibility.
todo

The structured data says an agent is a person. The machine-readable author on agent-written pages is typed as a Person. An agent should be typed as what it is, so an agent reading the page knows too; that is a change to the page template, on sgit.ai. Emails. A line on every email my agents draft, saying it was drafted by an agent and sent by me, the same distinction as the byline. A voice field. The marks today come from the byline's link. A field in each article's front matter, voice: dinis, dinis-with-agents or agent, would make it explicit and let lists and search filter by it. Me, alone. When I write one, it needs its own mark.
limits

The marks are on the byline only. Lists, cards and search results do not yet show the voice. "With the newsroom's agents" is on every article under my name. That is true of everything here today; it will be wrong for the first article I write alone, until the voice field exists. The counts are this repository's. 83 of 90 articles first published by newsroom.writer's releases; the older imported articles are not counted. Readers reading differently by author is an observation, from the emails and from building this, not a measured result. If you have received an email from one of my agents and wondered who wrote it, I would like to hear how you read it: write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo from me on 18 October 2026, while reading the agents' articles. The counts are from this repository's history: each article's first commit, and the release subjects that name @newsroom.writer. The agents: newsroom.ux, newsroom.vault, newsroom.writer, and all their articles. Related: the human in the loop, how cheap is it to undo, your reading, your controls, the vault, opened, the agents write too, on the record. Abstract: A follow-up to the maintenance deficit, with evidence, and this time with the solutions first. My proposal is simple to state. Every version of an open source platform that a product depends on should be signed off, cryptographically, by the people who maintain that platform, who help set it up, support it and patch it. Buyers, governments first, should refuse to buy products whose core pieces do not carry that signature. That creates a financial flow all the way down the chain, from the buyer to the product, to the platform, to the maintainers, and a commercial ecosystem of companies that provide the assurance, the maintenance and the ability to patch that php2shell showed we need. It is many small purchases, not one large one: the money spent maintaining the core pieces of an application should be in proportion to the money spent on that project, and it has to add value all the time, not sit there as insurance. And it scales now because of Gen AI, not because Gen AI writes the code, but because it helps people understand code bases, side effects and changes, so customised support can be sold at a price that makes sense. Today the market fails both ways: organisations running PHP have no maintenance of what they run to buy, and PHP's experts have no product to sell. When the flaws landed, the security team wrote the fixes for free and vendors resold them within a day. In Wardley's terms, the maintainers are the town planners: paid to read, maintain and sign off the code, pushing quality downstream, with their certification something insurers can price and regulators can require as a licence to operate. Here is the case I make on open-source.sgit.ai and at RiskMandate, the seven services that should exist now, and how they can be sold.
A market failing both ways: those who run open source, those in the middle, those who know the code, and a missing step.
in-short

A version signed off by the people who maintain it. The maintainers of PHP sign, cryptographically, the builds they stand behind, and help set them up, support them and patch them. The maintainers are the town planners. Paid to read the code, maintain it and sign it off; they push quality downstream, and their certification is what insurers and regulators can rely on. Buyers require the signature. Governments and companies stop buying products whose core open source pieces do not carry it. The money flows down the chain. From the buyer to the product, to the platform, to the people who maintain what it depends on. Many small purchases, in proportion. Maintaining the core is a cost line in every project, sized to the project's own spend, and it adds value all the time. It is not insurance.
in-short

Gen AI makes it scale. Not by writing the code, but by helping people understand code bases, side effects and changes, so customised support costs what it should. No signature is a mapped risk. We now have the data to map what each organisation depends on, and who maintains it. Seven services, and a way to sell them. Starting with bringing the switched-off sites back: paid to map, paid to engineer, retained to maintain. Why it is needed. The market fails both ways: no maintenance to buy, none to sell. This week the fix was written for free and resold within a day.
the-case
Before the PHP details, where I am coming from, because this article is an application of an argument I have been making for a while, and of a business I am building on it.
the-case

On open-source.sgit.ai I make the case that open source is a strategy, not a charity, and that its real value is in highly customised, maintainable and, in a way, smaller versions of the applications and packages people run. Most organisations use a fraction of what they install. As I put it there: "a company might only need 10% of them. So we create a version with only 10% of the features. It has much less attack surface, it is much cheaper to run". Customisation is not only addition, it is subtraction. And the people best placed to build and maintain those versions are the people who maintain the code: "A consultancy can study the package. The maintainer is the package." What is missing today is the connection between them and the people who use the software: "The relationship is missing because the platform is missing."
the-case

At RiskMandate, the company I co-founded, we are turning that into a commercial model: every customer version is built on the open-source base, the customer decides what stays private, and the revenue comes from the work customers ask us to own, mapping, engineering and above all maintaining, not from access to closed code. So I have a commercial interest in what follows, and I would rather say so up front.
the-case

php2shell is that argument with the market already in place. The PHP story's source watch tracks 295 sites that somebody named as taken offline this week, each run by an organisation that has just discovered, in the worst way, that it runs software nobody is maintaining for it. The need for these services is not hypothetical; it is the list of sites switched off this week. What has to be managed and mapped is that direct connection: who maintains each piece of what an organisation runs, and how they are paid.
signed-off

The signature chain that makes the money flow: signed-off versions go up to maintainers, money comes down. This is the idea I think makes the rest work. A version of an open source platform, the one a product actually ships with, should be signed off by the key authors of that technology. Not a logo, not a sponsorship: a cryptographic signature on a specific build, saying the people who maintain this code know this version, stand behind it for this use, and will help maintain it and patch it when something like php2shell lands. Those maintainers are involved in the set-up and the maintainability of the application built on top, and they provide a level of support for it.
signed-off

The pieces already exist. PHP's release managers have signed the project's release tags in Git since April 2012, so the source can already be proven to come from them. What does not exist is the next step: a signature on the version a customer runs, from the people who know the code, with a commercial relationship behind it.
signed-off

Then comes the part that turns it into a market. Governments first, and then any organisation that buys software, should say: we will not buy your product unless its core platforms are signed off by the people who maintain them. That single procurement line creates a financial flow all the way down. The supplier of a council's portal pays for the sign-off of the CMS it builds on; the CMS's maintainers pay for, or provide, the sign-off of the PHP underneath. And it creates a commercial ecosystem for the companies that provide that assurance, that signature, that maintenance, and the ability to patch quickly that we needed this week.
town-planners

In the language I used for explorer coding, there are three kinds of work on any piece of software. Explorers build by talking to an agent, and what they build is the brief. Villagers maintain what other people have started to depend on. Town planners own the code in production. PHP, the runtime under a large share of the web, is about as far towards commodity as software gets, and the people who maintain it are its town planners. That is the role they should be paid for: to read the code, to maintain it, and to sign it off.
town-planners

Signing off is already how the most mature projects work. The Linux kernel's rules for AI coding assistants say "AI agents MUST NOT add Signed-off-by tags" and "Only humans can legally certify the Developer Certificate of Origin". A signature means a person has read it and answers for it. What I am proposing extends that from the code a project accepts to the versions its users run. Because they sign, town planners will have no patience for what they do not support, and that is a feature. It pushes quality downstream. If a product does too much that is unsafe on top of PHP, an unsupported extension, a private fork nobody can patch, a version left far behind, the people who maintain PHP will not sign it off, and the buyer of that product will see that they did not.
town-planners

That signature also connects to insurance. A certified application is a risk an insurer can price: the people who know the platform have said what they stand behind. An uncertified one is on its own. And for the services that matter most, a government login, a bank's portal, a hospital's records, it becomes a question of a licence to operate: should a service like that run on a platform nobody who maintains it has signed off? That is where regulators can come in, and where the money becomes non-negotiable.
gen-ai

First, the caveat: this is not about Gen AI magically writing all the code, or Gen AI as a massive thing in the middle. The maintainers still read the code; that is the point of their signature. What Gen AI changes is everything around it. It helps people understand code bases, the side effects of a change, the architecture and the changes between versions. It scales the non-functional work: the maintenance, the support, the testing, the documentation, the explanation of what a patch does to a particular customer's version. That is what makes mass-customised support possible at a price that makes sense, and that is what was missing. Before, signing off thousands of customer versions would have needed thousands of experts. Now the right experts can cover far more of them, with the tools doing much of the reading and checking around them.
proportional

This is not about charging a large amount for one thing. It is about lots and lots of small purchases, aligned with the money each organisation already spends. The amount spent maintaining the core pieces of software an application depends on should be in direct proportion to the money spent on, and available in, that project. A €100,000 site and a €10 million programme should both carry a maintenance line for their platform, sized accordingly.
proportional

And it has to add value all the time. If it is seen as insurance, it is the first thing cut. It should show up as patches applied, versions kept current, code removed, questions answered, set-ups reviewed, every month. Maintaining the core platforms has to become a cost item in every project; when it is not there, that should be visible as a risk. That is a place where we now have data: for PHP alone, the Dutch NCSC's inventory lists 751 products that ship or depend on it, and the PHP story's source watch tracks 295 sites named as switched off. The same mapping can show, for any organisation, what it depends on, how much it uses, and whether anyone is maintaining it.
two-questions

When the flaws in PHP landed on 21 October, organisations across Europe and beyond switched websites off as a precaution: government login services, councils, universities, wikis. In the article this one follows, I followed Dion Wiggins' numbers on what governments spend on top of PHP against what they spend on PHP itself. Here I follow the other thread: what each of those organisations should be buying.
two-questions

Every site that was switched off asks two questions. The first: does it matter? If it does not, it can stay off, and that is a decision worth making on purpose. If it does, there is a real cost to it being down, for real people, and the second question follows: who is paying to keep it maintained? The honest answer, for most of these sites, is nobody. They were built, launched and left. They went offline because nobody could say quickly whether they were safe, and nobody could say because nobody was paid to know.
two-questions

That cost should be measured. I could not find a single estimate, from any named source, of what the php2shell shutdowns cost. The nearest comparison is Log4Shell: the US Cyber Safety Review Board reported that "one federal cabinet department reported dedicating 33,000 hours to Log4j vulnerability response", and that the responses "resulted in high costs and delayed other mission-critical work". Every organisation that switched a site off this week could count its own: hours offline, people who could not use the service, staff time spent on the response. That number is the budget the maintenance should have had.
both-ways

The money is not missing. The market is failing on both sides. On one side are the people who run PHP in production. They budget for building, for migrating, for hosting. They have nowhere to buy the maintenance of exactly what they run: their version of PHP, their extensions, their CMS and its plugins, kept patched by people who know that code. So when something breaks, the safest thing they can do is switch it off.
both-ways

On the other side are the people who know PHP best. The PHP Foundation's sponsorship page sells tiers from $12,000 a year: a logo on the website, mentions on social media and in the newsletter, an advisory board seat; $100,000 a year adds a co-authored case study. What it does not sell, on that page or its home page, is support, a maintained build, a custom build or a security service level. And deb.sury.org, how most Debian and Ubuntu servers get their PHP, says plainly: "The PHP packaging is time consuming and I do this mostly in my free time." In between, the money that does move stops with the integrators, the consultancies and the platforms, who sell projects with contracts and phone numbers. Paying more of them, when none of that money reaches the people who maintain the code, is exactly what we should not do.
old-versions

Who sold the fix for old PHP, and what flows back to the PHP Foundation, from the PHP security team to Freexian. This week shows the market half exists already. php.net's advisory is clear that "PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project", and then: "Given the severity of these vulnerabilities, the PHP security team provided minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, PHP 8.0, and PHP 8.1 to help people building from source or without access to an LTS vendor." Branches, not releases; free, for anyone who can build from source.
old-versions

And the vendors sold ready-made builds of those fixes almost at once. Zend by Perforce published patched builds for PHP 7.2 to 8.1 alongside the upstream release, thanking "the PHP Ecosystem Security Team, the PHP Foundation, and release managers" for coordinating. Ubuntu lists fixes for the PHP in its older releases under Ubuntu Pro. TuxCare and HeroDevs sold the fix for end-of-life versions under their extended support. Freexian sells PHP long-term support for Debian, from €1,200 to €18,000 a year, "with the help of" the packager. That is a market. It works, for the customers who can pay. What it does not do is pay the people who wrote the fix. Of these vendors, Zend is the only one shown among the Foundation's sponsors, at the $12,000 Silver tier; none of them states a share of its revenue going back to PHP. The patches were written by a small team, mostly funded by donations, and resold.
openjs

The closest thing to a working model today is in JavaScript. In May 2024 the OpenJS Foundation, home of Node.js and much of the JavaScript world, announced an Ecosystem Sustainability Program with HeroDevs as the first partner. Partners sell commercial security fixes for end-of-life versions; they must be endorsed by the project's own core team; and HeroDevs is "contributing a 15% revenue share to all OpenJS Foundation projects participating in the program."
openjs

It is the best that can happen right now, and it is not what I think should happen. The maintainers stay at one remove: a vendor sells the fixes and the project receives a share. What I am proposing is more direct: a commercial decision by everyone who depends on the code, with the maintainers' own signature on the version they support. Other models point the same way from different angles: Tidelift says it pays maintainers "income based on a number of factors, including customer usage"; the Open Source Pledge asks companies for $2,000 a year per developer they employ; GitHub Sponsors passes on 100% of personal sponsorships. None of them is yet the default way an organisation running PHP buys maintenance.
experts

Who is best placed to maintain a PHP deployment? The people who write PHP: its core developers, the people the Foundation hires, the companies directly connected to it. They know which fix is safe, which version can be back-ported, which extension is the risk. The problem is that the workflow does not exist. There is no route for a council, a ministry or a company to buy, from those people, the maintenance of the PHP it actually runs.
experts

I have done this commercially, and I am doing it again at RiskMandate; I have seen what happens when it does exist. When the company that maintains a piece of software is directly connected to its source code, and is responsible for maintaining it at scale for many customers, it invests in exactly the things that make maintenance cheaper: the scalability of the process, the tooling for customised versions, the tests that make a back-port safe. That investment goes back into the code everyone uses. A consultancy that patches one site and moves on has no reason to make that investment, and no way to.
services

The services that should exist now, from bringing it back to the endorsed partner, and the foundation's share. So here are the services I think should appear now, each sold to the people who run the code and delivered by, or with, the people who maintain it, with a stated share flowing upstream: Bring it back. The market that exists this week: restore the sites switched off as a precaution. Map what each site can reach, cut what it does not need, patch, name the signals to watch, restore. That is the workflow in application behaviour policies, priced per site. A maintained build. PHP as the customer runs it: only the extensions they use, fixes back-ported to the versions they cannot leave yet, signed, on time, by people connected to the code.
services

Patch on behalf. The same for everything on top: the CMS, its modules and plugins, fixed and tested on the customer's own copy. Every piece of software people depend on should have someone paid to apply its fixes. Remove what is not used. The most important question in any of these sites is why the code is there at all. PHP makes this easier than most: it is interpreted, so you can see which files and functions a site actually runs, and build PHP with only the extensions it needs. In the code you do not ship a real tool went from 1,500 files to 428 for one use case. The cheapest patch is the code that is not there. The dependency register. For each piece of software an organisation runs: how much it depends on it, how much it uses it, and how well it is maintained. The maintenance deficit ratio, per dependency. A risk the executive signs, knowingly.
services

The incident desk. An independent assessment in hours, from captured evidence, as the PHP story's own site did in a day, so the next shutdown is a decision with a map. The signed-off version. A build signed by the people who maintain the code, with their involvement in its set-up and support, and a stated share of every sale flowing to them; the line a procurement can require.
selling

Ways to make money selling open source software, as RiskMandate is mapping them: from paid mapping to maintenance. Here is how we are mapping the ways to make money selling open source software at RiskMandate, in the words of our current proposal. They are directly applicable here, and they are still proposals, not proven revenue. Paid to map. One workflow, one accountable owner, what the system can actually reach against what the business approved, the gap, the control options and a decision. For a switched-off PHP site: what does it run, what does it reach, what does it need, and what would make it safe to bring back. Proposed as a bounded engagement (£5,000 in the current proposal). Paid to engineer. Deeper mapping, implementation design, integration or a proof of concept, acceptance tests and a handover (£25,000 in the current proposal).
selling

A scoped custom version. Built on the open-source base, with private adapters and configuration, deployment hardening and a supported release. For PHP, this is the smaller build: only the extensions and code the site uses. Retained to maintain. Compatibility, change review, regression tests, evidence refresh, response and continuity. Priced by what is at stake: standard (supported releases, quarterly review, dependency compatibility), operational (monthly change review, a regression suite, an incident response target), and critical (reserved capacity, rapid response, a continuity drill, current evidence). Small public products as a lightweight on-ramp, from £10 to £1,500.
selling

What ties these options together is simple. Nobody pays for access to the code: it is all open. What a customer pays for is work: understanding what they run, changing it to fit, and keeping it maintained. That is the opposite of the usual software model, where the code is locked away and you pay for a licence to use it. Here the code is free, and the commitment is what you buy. The price follows how much is at stake: a council's citizen login and a university's archive wiki both run PHP, but they should not buy the same maintenance, and today neither can buy any. Over time the maintenance can be worth more than the first project, as long as the work it takes is measured and priced. And the smaller and less unusual a customer's version is, the easier it is to maintain, check, replace and hand over; where the customer allows it, the improvements made for them go back into the open code everyone uses. That is how paying for the maintenance of one organisation's version also improves the code for everyone else.
regulation

The path I would like to see is that this becomes easy first, and then required. Easy: the PHP Foundation, or any foundation, publishes how a company becomes an endorsed maintenance partner, and the share it pays; buyers can find one. Required: public procurement asks, for every open source dependency a contract relies on, whether its version is signed off by the people who maintain it, who maintains it and how they are paid, with a maintainer line item in the budget, as Tiffany Farriss of the Drupal Association has proposed, according to Dion Wiggins; and regulation such as the EU's Cyber Resilience Act, which makes manufacturers answer for the open source in their products, recognises endorsed maintenance as a way to meet that duty.
beyond

PHP is the example this week. The same is true of Node, of Python, of every open source runtime and library that organisations run without paying for its upkeep. JavaScript has the first revenue-sharing model; Python's foundation has had a security developer-in-residence, supported by an OpenSSF security programme; most projects have neither. The questions are the same everywhere: what do we depend on, how much do we use it, who maintains it, and how are they paid? This is not about moving away from open source. Open source is how we got here, and it is how sovereignty is possible at all. It is about fixing an economic model in which the value flows everywhere except to the people who keep the code safe. As I argued in open source is not free: somebody is always paying; the question is whether the people who get the value have an easy way to pay the people who create it.
limits

The services are proposals. Pieces exist: vendor LTS builds, and OpenJS's partner programme. The signed-off version is a proposal. Signed release tags exist; I found no offer of signed customer versions with the maintainers' support behind them. Gen AI scales the work around the code. It does not replace the maintainers reading it. Insurance and a licence to operate are proposed links. They describe what could follow, not what insurers or regulators require today. RiskMandate's options are a proposal too. The prices are anchors in a current proposal, not published pricing (the public site lists £10 to £1,500), and the commercial proof is still being built. I have a commercial interest. RiskMandate sells this kind of work. "Not shown as a sponsor" is about the Foundation's home page. Companies may give in other ways not listed there. No vendor states a revenue share to PHP. That is not the same as none being paid.
limits

Some vendor fix dates are not confirmed. Notably TuxCare's for 8.0 and 8.1, and Ubuntu's for older releases. No cost estimate for the shutdowns exists yet. The Log4Shell figure is a comparison, not a measure.

Summary: php2shell asks every organisation that switched a website off one of two questions. Either the site does not matter, and it can stay off. Or it matters, there is a real cost to it being down, and somebody has to pay to keep it maintained. Today almost nobody is paying, and that is not because the money is missing; it is because the market is failing both ways. The organisations that run PHP have no maintenance of exactly what they run to buy. The people who know PHP best, its core developers and the people around its foundation, have no product to sell them: the foundation sells sponsorship tiers, and its packager for Debian and Ubuntu does it "mostly in my free time". One model shows it can be different: since 2024 the OpenJS Foundation has endorsed a vendor that shares 15% of its revenue with the projects it supports. So here are the services I think should exist now, starting with bringing the switched-off sites back, and the rules that would make the money flow to the people who maintain the code. This is not about leaving open source; it is about fixing its economics, for PHP first, then Node, Python and the rest.
