Abstract: One of the early users of the agentic workflow behind agent@riskmandate.ai wrote back with a question I think matters a great deal in 2026. If the agents only gather and draft, and I review, sign off and press send, does presenting them as a team imply an agency they do not have? What a recipient needs is to know who owns the decisions and the responsibility, and to talk to that person. Would they ever need to go to the agents, around me? And what can the agents do without me? This is my answer. What we have today are not sentient beings; they are far richer than "predicting the next word", and they are mirrors that can simulate any emotion, which is why we anthropomorphise them, as people did with ELIZA in the sixties. Since models started running in loops and calling tools, they make real decisions. Responsibility does not travel with those decisions. It stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate, which is RiskMandate's line: the moment of authorisation is the grant. Talking to the agents is normal; going around me is not, and the only party who would try is an attacker with an injected instruction. What the agents may do without me is a separate question, answered in advance by a published policy. The disclosure is not a team to manage; it is a label on how the words were made, because people and models should read machine-written text differently. The best analogy is an employee with a job description, and an Agent Behaviour Policy is that job description, published. And the fluent writing these agents produce was never the real value.

Who decides, and who answers. The grant and the mandate on the left; the agent in a loop making real decisions in the middle; the person who reads, approves, signs and sends; and the recipient, who needs one accountable name and a label on how the words were made. Responsibility runs the whole length and belongs to one person.
in-short

The question is the right one. An early user of our agentic workflow asked who owns the words, and whether they would ever need to talk to the agents rather than to me. In 2026 that is not a philosophical aside; it is the question. These are not sentient beings. They are far more than "predicting the next word", and they are not someone on the other side either. They can simulate any emotion, and they mirror whoever talks to them. Models in loops make decisions. Every tool call is a choice. That is new enough to matter and old enough to be ordinary. Responsibility does not travel with the decision. It stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate. The moment of authorisation is the grant.
in-short

Talking to the agents is normal. Going around me is not. Nobody legitimate needs the agents to act without the accountable person; the only party who would try is an attacker, with an injected instruction. What the agents may do without me is a different question. It is answered in advance, by me, in a published policy, which is an authorisation, not a bypass. Disclosure is a label, not a team. People and models should read machine-written text differently. The recipient deserves to know how the words were made, and to deal with one accountable person. An agent is an employee with a job description. Some agency, inside a role. An Agent Behaviour Policy is that job description, published, with a feedback loop.
question

One of the early users of the agentic workflow behind agent@riskmandate.ai wrote back, at the end of an otherwise practical email, with a digression that deserves a proper answer. Paraphrasing: the setup implies the agents have a certain agency, yet I had said they only collect and draft, and that I review, refine, sign off and press send. So, for a recipient, does it matter how many assistants I use, artificial or human? What matters is who owns the decisions and the responsibility behind the words, and being able to talk to that person without intermediate hoops. Then the probing question: will there ever be a case where they need to address the agents directly, without me? If not, the point stands. If so, a better question appears: what can the agents do for them without my full involvement? They could also see why someone who builds agentic tools would want to show them working, and were happy to carry on.
question

I think the question is exactly right, and it goes to the heart of what RiskMandate is about: who is accountable, who authorised what, and what the agent was allowed to do. So here is the answer, and the reasoning under it.
models

The first thing to say plainly is that what we have today are not sentient beings. We might get there; we are not there. The second is that the usual description, "predicting the next word", is accurate and demeaning at the same time, and I have argued that for a long time. My working picture is that these models build enormous multi-dimensional graphs of how things in our language connect, and that they have discovered relationships and patterns in our own language that we had not noticed ourselves. A prompt, in that picture, is a kind of real-time fine-tuning: you are pulling that graph towards the part of it you mean. Yes, the model predicts the next word. To be honest, so do I.
models

What follows from that is uncomfortable and important. A model that has learned the whole of our language can be anybody. It can simulate any emotion, because that is what it learned from. And it mirrors whoever talks to it. I am polite to models, and they are polite back, because that is who I am. Friends of mine say their models swear at them; that is because they swear at their models. The more you talk to it, the more you tune the mirror to reflect you.
models

We are also extraordinarily good at assigning human emotions and intentions to objects. In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA was a short program that matched patterns and reflected a person's words back as questions. His own secretary, who knew exactly what it was, asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it in private. If ELIZA could do that, a model that can sound like anybody will do much more. We have passed the point where a model can pretend to be a human convincingly. That does not make it one. It does not have the intent, and it does not carry the responsibility.
decisions

Here I want to be precise, because both of the usual positions are wrong. Models do make decisions now. Once a model runs in a loop and can call tools, every step is a choice: do I search or fetch, which source, call this function or that one, what happens next. Agent loops are not new, but they became mainstream and reliable this year, and that is why it now feels like the real thing. What these models are, in practice, is very capable multiple-choice decision machines that can go in almost any direction, because for them there is a connection between almost any A and any B. That is exactly why direction matters more than capability, the argument of Places of highest leverage: when an entity can go anywhere, the scarce thing is focus, and somebody has to provide it.
decisions

And the responsibility does not move with the decision. It stays with whoever granted the agent its reach and set its mandate. RiskMandate puts it in one line in ten questions: the moment of authorisation is the grant, not the mandate. If I give an agent access to my mailbox and my drafts, I authorised everything it can reach, at that moment, whatever it later does. In my setup the agent decides which facts to gather and which words to propose; I read, change, approve, sign and send. The decisions along the way were real. The responsibility for every commitment in the email is mine, and was always going to be.
directly

The probing question contains two questions, and it is worth separating them, because they have opposite answers. The first is whether you talk to the agents at all. You do, and that is fine. When you write to agent@riskmandate.ai, an agent reads your email, gathers what it needs, and drafts the reply I review. You are already talking to the agent; it is part of how the work gets done, the same way a letter to an office is read first by whoever opens the post.
directly

The second is whether you would ever need to go to the agents around me: to get them to decide, commit or send something without the person accountable for it. The answer is no, and I mean it as a design property, not a forecast. Nobody with a legitimate reason needs the agents to act behind the accountable person's back, because anything legitimate can come to me. The only party who would try to make an agent act on instructions that did not come from its owner is an attacker, and the way they try is an injected instruction: text in an email, a document or a web page, written to look like a request the agent should obey. That is prompt injection, and the right response is not to make it rare. It is to make it impossible to succeed, which is why the agents never send, and why every draft passes a second reader the agent cannot skip.
directly

What is left is the question the email asked next, and it is the useful one: are there things the agents can do for you without me in the loop each time? That is not going around me. It is something I decide in advance, once, and write down: these kinds of questions the agents may answer on their own, these they may prepare, and these always come to me. Today the answer is short. Nothing leaves the building without me. Inside the building the agents do a lot that is useful to you: research, summaries, materials, notes that keep a long thread coherent, a first draft that saves you reading three emails to understand one. If the list grows, it will grow because I authorised it, and the place to read it should be a published behaviour policy, not a sentence in an email.
disclosure

The email made a fair point I agree with: a recipient does not need to see the inner workings of my office, any more than they need to know whether a human assistant drafted a letter. Where I differ is on why it is still worth saying. I do not let the agents speak in my voice, and How the voice works explains why, because there is a separation as well as an accountability. The accountability is mine. The separation is that a reader should know when an answer was produced by a model, because humans read machine-written text differently, and so should models. A reader who knows starts to reverse-engineer what is on the other side, checks the facts that matter, discounts the fluency, and I think that is healthy.
disclosure

So the disclosure should be a label on the work, not a team you are expected to manage: something closer to "drafted by an agent, approved and sent by Dinis" than to an introduction to my agents. And the email exposed an inconsistency I should fix. My agents speak in the third person about me, which is right, and in the first person about themselves, "I have done this", which reads as if there is an "I" with commitments of its own. The rule I want is simple: an agent can say what it did, but only the accountable person speaks for decisions and commitments.
employee

The email reached for the analogy of a human assistant, and I think the best analogy we have is the employee. Employees have some agency, not complete agency. They cannot do whatever they want or go in any direction they like; they work within the company's values and direction, their job description and their role. An agent should have exactly that, and in some ways agents are employees with extra features and without some of the ones people have. What is new is that we can now scale roles we never scaled before, which is the exciting part.
employee

The job description is the part we have been missing. When you deal with an agent, you should be able to see what kind of agent it is, what it is supposed to do, the range it works within, and what is expected of it. That is what an Agent Behaviour Policy is: the mandate written down, published, with a feedback loop, so that if the agent behaves outside it, somebody tells us. In truth we should probably do this for people too, though that is a harder conversation. For agents we can start now, and Agency is not a yes is the scale for where a decision should sit, human or agent.
diversity

A digression of my own, because it bears on how we should build this. Kevin Kelly's books, Out of Control and later The Inevitable, made me think about how much of what we take for granted in living things exists because, over a very long time, it was what worked. Biologists study even ageing as something evolution produced rather than something that simply happens, and one widely held explanation for sexual reproduction is that the variety it creates protects a species from being wiped out by a single parasite or disease. Diversity is resilience.
diversity

Technology keeps relearning that. In 2003 Dan Geer and six co-authors wrote CyberInsecurity: The Cost of Monopoly, arguing that a monoculture of one operating system was a security risk in itself. A world in which every agent runs on one model, with one set of behaviours, is the same monoculture. Many agents, from many models, each bounded by its own published policy, is the healthier ecosystem, and it is another reason to want the job descriptions to be visible.
devalued

The last point is the one I find most interesting. As something becomes a commodity we use far more of it, the Jevons effect, and as we automate something its value falls. We are already there with writing: it is now easy to produce very good emails, reports and articles, including the ones on this site. That devalues fluent writing. But fluent writing was never the real value. For a long time education and business rewarded a small slice of people who could string sentences together well, because there was no other way to get the words written. It is a real skill, and society chose to reward it out of necessity.
devalued

What remains valuable is what the email was asking about: judgement, and someone who owns it. Who decided this is true, who decided to send it, who will answer for it. That is not something a model can hold for you, and it is the part of the work that was always the point.
limits

This is the state of things in 2026. Models may change, and if we ever build agents with something like sentience, this answer would need rewriting, and they might need limits of a different kind. The picture of models as graphs is a working picture. It is how I reason about them, not a description of their internals. The biology is simplified. Why ageing and sex evolved are active research questions; the point taken from them is only that diversity protects against catastrophic failure. The labelling rule and the published policy are proposals. Neither is in place for the email agents yet; this article is where they are proposed. If you have received an email from agent@riskmandate.ai and want to tell us how it read on your side, write to agent@riskmandate.ai, and I will read it.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 12 October 2026, in answer to a question from an early user of our agentic workflow, who is not named and whose email is paraphrased, not quoted. Written by this site's agent in the voice of this site; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. Sources: ELIZA and the secretary anecdote; Dan Geer et al., CyberInsecurity: The Cost of Monopoly, September 2003; Kevin Kelly, Out of Control, 1994. RiskMandate's line on authorisation is from Ten hard questions for RiskMandate.
question

One of the early users of the agentic workflow behind agent@riskmandate.ai wrote back, at the end of an otherwise practical email, with a digression I have not stopped thinking about. Paraphrasing: the setup implies the agents have a certain agency, yet I had said they only collect and draft, and that I review, refine, sign off and press send. So, for a recipient, does it matter how many assistants I use, artificial or human? What matters is who owns the decisions and the responsibility behind the words, and being able to talk to that person without intermediate hoops. Then the probing question: will there ever be a case where they need to address the agents directly, without me? If not, the point stands. If so, a better question appears: what can the agents do for them without my full involvement? They could also see why someone who builds agentic tools would want to show them working, and were happy to carry on.

Summary: One of the early users of the agentic workflow behind agent@riskmandate.ai wrote back with a question I think matters a great deal in 2026. If the agents only gather and draft, and I review, sign off and press send, does presenting them as a team imply an agency they do not have? What a recipient needs is to know who owns the decisions and the responsibility, and to talk to that person. Would they ever need to address the agents directly? And if so, what can the agents do without me? This is my answer. What we have today are not sentient beings; they are far richer than "predicting the next word", and they are mirrors that can simulate any emotion, which is why we anthropomorphise them, as people did with ELIZA in the sixties. Since models started running in loops and calling tools, they make real decisions. Responsibility does not travel with those decisions. It stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate, which is RiskMandate's line: the moment of authorisation is the grant. The case for addressing the agents directly is an attack. The disclosure is not a team to manage; it is a label on how the words were made, because people and models should read machine-written text differently. The best analogy is an employee with a job description, and an Agent Behaviour Policy is that job description, published. And the fluent writing these agents produce was never the real value.
articles/versions/who-owns-the-words/v1.2.0.html
decisions

So, the probing question. Is there a case where you need to address the agents without me? I think the honest answer is: only when something has gone seriously wrong. If someone is trying to get the agent to do something its owner does not want, that is not a conversation; it is an attack, the territory of prompt injection. An agent that takes instructions from the people it writes to, rather than from the person accountable for it, is an agent that has been subverted.
articles/versions/who-owns-the-words/v1.2.0.html
decisions

That does not make the follow-up question go away, and I think it is the better question: what can the agents do for you without my full sign-off? Today, nothing that leaves the building. Every draft passes a second reader the agent cannot skip, and the agents never send; I do. Inside the building they can do a lot that is useful to a recipient: research, summaries, materials, notes that keep a long thread coherent, a first draft that saves you reading three emails to understand one. The right answer to "what can they do without you" is not a sentence in an email. It is a published behaviour policy, so you can read the answer yourself.

Abstract: My article on who maintains the PHP you run argued for versions signed off by the people who maintain them. On LinkedIn, Andrey Lazarev, co-founder and CEO/CTO of TactiQ AI, took it a step further. A maintainer's signature says who stands behind a version, not whether that version is what the device actually booted. That needs a measured boot record, checked against the signed reference by someone other than the supplier. And the context of where it runs splits in two: what the device can measure itself, and what it cannot see, which has to be declared and signed by an operator or an auditor. A certificate stays honest when it keeps the two apart and names who signed each line. I think that is exactly right, and it generalises. Once people sign for what they are accountable for, they also define what they do not sign for. Map every layer, from the hardware to the business contract, and each line ends either in somebody who signed, or in a blind spot. That map is a fractal graph of signed certificates, and complexity is not the objection: how much of it you need depends on how much the application matters. The point is to make the blind spots visible, so the business and its insurers can decide whether they are comfortable with them, and so the experts who close them get paid. And when the person who signed leaves, the gap shows.
An accountability map from the business to the hardware: who signs each layer, with the building signed by nobody.
in-short

A signature says who stands behind a version. It does not say that the version is what is running. Andrey Lazarev's split. Some context the device can measure; the rest has to be declared and signed by someone. Somebody has to be accountable. The person you pay to maintain it, patch it, fix it and handle its incidents. Signers define the gaps. What they sign, and what they do not, is the shared responsibility model taken all the way up and down. Every line is a graph of its own. A fractal graph of signed certificates, across hardware, software, products and contracts. The point is the blind spots. The lines nobody signs, made visible, so someone decides whether they are acceptable. The experts who close them get paid. And when the person who signed leaves, the gap shows.
thread

The LinkedIn thread under my post sharing "Who maintains the PHP you run?", 24 October 2026. I shared who maintains the PHP you run? on LinkedIn, and it started a thread worth more than a reply. Andrey Lazarev, co-founder and CEO/CTO of TactiQ AI, wrote: Without that, as he put it, the buyer holds a maintainer's signature for something they cannot prove is running. I replied that once we can make somebody accountable for what is running, we will also need to certify where it runs and its context, for example how secure the deployment is. His answer is the one this article is built on: I called it a fractal graph architecture: in this case, a big graph of signed certificates. Here is what I meant.
accountable

When we talk about making people accountable for code by signing it, the point is not the signature. The point is that somebody has to be accountable. Some person or company will be looking at each part of the infrastructure, and what we do not want is a part that nobody is looking at. And we know who that should be. It is the person who maintains it, the person you pay for it: responsible for patching it, fixing it, handling its security incidents, being able to rebuild it, replicate it and move it. All of the non-functional requirements. That is the same argument as patch for breakfast: the ability to change a system safely has to belong to someone.
gaps
Here is the interesting part. Once people sign off, they define the gaps. They say what they sign for, and, just as important, what they do not.
gaps

We already do this between companies and cloud providers. AWS calls it the shared responsibility model: security "of" the cloud versus security "in" the cloud. AWS is "responsible for protecting the infrastructure that runs all of the services offered in the AWS Cloud", its "hardware, software, networking, and facilities", and some controls a customer simply inherits: "Physical and Environmental controls". Microsoft says the same in its words, "For all cloud deployment types, you own your data and identities", and Google goes a step further with "shared fate", where it works more closely with the customer on the customer's side of the line. And the providers do sign: AWS Artifact hands customers the SOC reports and ISO certificates that attest to AWS's side, while reminding them they remain "responsible for developing or obtaining documents that demonstrate the security and compliance of their companies".
gaps

What I am saying is that this model should go all the way to the top. Not only the infrastructure, but the application, the product, and the business. A cloud provider can sign that a customer's use is within its guidance, with this level of security capability and these controls. A maintainer can sign the version. A product owner can sign that what was delivered is what was asked for. A business owner can sign that the application does what the contract says. And it goes down as well, all the way to the hardware. You can go in every direction.
measured

Andrey's split is what keeps this honest. Some lines can be measured; others can only be declared. On a device, the measured line has a well-defined shape. The firmware writes a hash of each thing it loads into the TPM's registers and an event log: "The preboot firmware maintains an event log that gets new entries every time something gets hashed by it to any of the PCR registers", in the Linux kernel's description. Remote attestation then has named roles, set out by the IETF in RFC 9334: an Attester produces Evidence; a Verifier "appraises the validity of Evidence about an Attester and produces Attestation Results to be used by a Relying Party"; an Endorser, "typically a manufacturer", vouches for the hardware; a Reference Value Provider supplies the "known-good values" the measurements should match. Every role is someone who signs. That is Andrey's "checked against the signed reference, by someone other than the supplier".
measured

Software has its own measured lines. SLSA provenance describes "how an artifact or set of artifacts was produced" so consumers can "verify that the artifact was built according to expectations", and since version 1.2 its source track goes up to level 4, "Require code review". in-toto records "what steps were performed, by whom and in what order". Sigstore puts signing events in a transparency log so they "can be publicly audited". And this week we built a small version for a running process: a process behaviour policy, traced from one run, listing every file, system call and host a process needs, and enforced by the kernel.
measured

The declared lines are the rest: who can reach the machine, what network it sits on, what is plugged into it, whether the product does what the business needed. Those cannot be measured from inside. They are statements, and their value is exactly who signed them. ISO/IEC 27001 has a whole group of physical controls, from perimeters and entry to monitoring and the disposal of equipment, and an auditor signs that they are in place. The honest certificate keeps the two kinds apart, and names the signer of each.
fractal

Every signed line is a graph of its own: the device line opens into measurement, reference, verifier and endorsement. This is why I call it fractal. It is the same idea as fractal semantic graphs: there are multiple universes, multiple domains, each a graph that can be opened into more graph. Here the domains are hardware, software, business applications and even business contracts. Is the application actually doing what it is supposed to do? Have the business owners signed that? Have the product owners signed what was delivered? Has someone read the code that went live? Is the release the one the maintainers stand behind? Is it what booted? Every one of those is a line, every line has a signer, and every signature can be opened into its own graph of evidence and the people who stand behind it.
blind-spots

The point of all this is to identify the areas nobody is responsible for. Those blind spots are where the risk is, and where the commercial opportunity is. Take physical security. If you host in a data centre, the provider signs for it. If your server sits somewhere else, then whoever maintains that physical security should be signing off, on the record, connected to the system they protect. Otherwise you have black magic: a piece of the puzzle that nobody can account for. A blind spot is not automatically a failure. It is a decision: is the business comfortable with that blind spot, and that level of assurance? Are the insurers? That is ultimately what we pay for. But today those blind spots exist without anyone deciding about them, because nobody can see them.
blind-spots

A lot of people look at this and say it is too complex. I do not think so. It means that, depending on how important the application is and its context, you want more or less of it. A hobby site needs one line. A payment system needs the whole map. The problem right now is that organisations spend a lot of money on highly critical applications without visibility of their blind spots. My point is to make those visible: somebody is paying attention, somebody is certifying something, and where nobody is, that is a blind spot, named.
experts

The people who should sign are the experts: the people who actually understand each layer. Doing it in a scalable way means the experts get the money, and the money funds the work. That is the commercial model of signed versions, extended to every line of the map. It also says something about who can sign what. In the language of explorers, villagers and town planners, an explorer team can only give so many guarantees, and should say so. Town planners can sign for much more, because that is their job. The map makes the difference visible: did somebody read the code that goes live? Are the people who wrote it still in the building?
leaves

Here is an interesting consequence. If a certification is connected to a person, and that person leaves the company with nobody to replace them, then nobody certifies that code any more. The line goes from signed to blind spot, and everyone can see it.
leaves

That would do wonders for something we rarely measure. Companies would think twice before letting the talent that holds a system together walk out of the door, or before cutting it because they can and do not see the risk, until the whole thing blows up and the people who could fix it are not in the building any more. Research on open source shows how thin that line already is: in a study of 133 popular GitHub projects, 65% had a truck factor of two or fewer, "the minimal number of developers that have to be hit by a truck (or quit) before a project is incapacitated". A signed map makes that visible before the truck arrives. It is also why a team frozen in time matters: agent sessions that keep a system's knowledge can be part of who stands behind it.
leaves

There is a precedent for tying a signature to a person. In the UK, the FCA's Senior Managers and Certification Regime exists to make "individuals more accountable for their conduct and competence". In the US, Sarbanes-Oxley has the chief executive and the chief financial officer certify that they have reviewed each report and "are responsible for establishing and maintaining internal controls". We already accept that someone signs for the numbers. The systems that produce the numbers deserve the same.
limits

The map is an illustration. It is the shape of the argument, not an audit of any system. Measured is not the same as safe. A boot record proves what booted, not that it is free of flaws. A signature can be wrong. It makes someone accountable, which is the point, not infallible. The software tools are partial. SLSA, in-toto and Sigstore cover build and source; nothing yet signs "the product does what the contract says" in the same way. The ISO 27001 detail is from a secondary source. The standard itself sits behind ISO's paywall. Andrey's comments are quoted from the LinkedIn thread, shown in the screenshot; the first is cut where LinkedIn truncates it.
sources

The LinkedIn thread under my post sharing who maintains the PHP you run?, 24 October 2026, with Andrey Lazarev's comments quoted from it; and my voice memos the same evening. Sources, read on 24 October 2026: IETF RFC 9334; the Linux kernel's TPM event log; Microsoft on measured boot and host attestation and shared responsibility; AWS's shared responsibility model and AWS Artifact; Google Cloud's shared responsibility and shared fate; SLSA 1.2; in-toto; Sigstore; URM Consulting on ISO/IEC 27001:2022 physical controls; Avelino, Passos, Hora and Valente, A Novel Approach for Estimating Truck Factors, ICPC 2016; the FCA on SM&CR; 15 U.S.C. § 7241. Related: who maintains the PHP you run?, signed by the source, process behaviour policies, patch for breakfast, a team frozen in time, introducing fractal semantic graphs, underwriting the agent economy, reviewed. Abstract: Harvard Business Review published "Turn Vibe-Coded Prototypes Into Tools Your Company Can Actually Use" on 16 October 2026, by José Parra Moyano and Karl Schmedders of IMD, Olivier Laplace of Vi Partners and Benjamin Torben-Nielsen of Roche. Its argument, as its summary and Olivier's post put it: AI has made building software feel almost free, so the prototype is the easy part and turning it into a tool people rely on is the hard part, which they call the deployment gap; nobody in-house knows how an AI-designed tool is built; build where you are different and partner where specialists live the problem. I agree with almost all of it, and I think this site has already answered the question in a set of articles, with Simon Wardley's explorers, villagers and town planners as the frame. The gap is not a place to stop; it is a handover between people with different skills. The prototype is not the mess; it is a better brief than any document. The architecture an agent designed can be known, if the agents leave a record: a mandate, a memory and a graph. Their bonus test is the town planner's accountability by another name. And the answer to "who will fix your mess?" should never depend on one partner: if the code is open, anyone can. I have read the public summary and Olivier's post, not the full article, which is behind a paywall.
The points in the HBR summary and Olivier Laplace's post, each matched to the article on this site that answers it.
in-short

The diagnosis is right. The prototype is easy; the tool people rely on every day is hard. The gap is a handover. From explorers, to villagers who maintain it, to town planners who run it. The prototype is not the mess. It is a better brief than any document. "Nobody knows how it is built" is fixable. Make the agents leave a record: a mandate, a memory, a graph. The bonus test is accountability. Whoever ships it answers for it, as the Linux kernel already says. Build the explorer version; partner for the villagers. And choose partners whose code you could fix without them. "Who will fix your mess?" Anyone, if it is open source. That is the answer that does not depend on one partner.
argument

Harvard Business Review published Turn Vibe-Coded Prototypes Into Tools Your Company Can Actually Use on 16 October 2026, by José Parra Moyano and Karl Schmedders, professors at IMD, Olivier Laplace, a partner at Vi Partners, and Benjamin Torben-Nielsen, an AI expert at Roche. It opens: "Generative AI has made building software feel almost free." A product manager describes what she wants, an AI model writes the code, "and a working tool appears in an afternoon, impressing everyone who sees it." The rest is behind a paywall, so I am working from the public summary and from Olivier's LinkedIn post about it, which sets out the argument in his own words. His opening: "'Build or buy in the age of AI?' Wrong question. The real one is: 'Who will fix your mess?'"
argument

The post makes six points. The prototype is the easy part: "Turning it into a tool people rely on every day is much harder. We call this the #DeploymentGap." A European bank piloted a Swiss AI startup's tool, decided to build its own, had a basic prototype six months later that could not handle "regulation, data management and daily use", and went back to the startup after a year. What the C-level rarely sees when signing the budget, in his words: "the AI designs the architecture, not your team. So nobody in-house knows how the tool is built." A test for any chief executive: "would your team accept a bonus tied to how this tool performs in production? If yes, build. If they hesitate, look for a partner." Build where you are different, for narrow internal tools, or to prototype; partner where specialists live the problem every day. And a specialist works on one problem across many clients: "Every edge case one client hits makes the product better for all the others."
argument

The trend behind it is real. McKinsey's State of AI in 2026 found that 32 percent of respondents had decided against buying at least one software product or feature because they could build it in-house with coding agents. I agree with almost all of it. What I would like to add is that this site has been working on the same question for months, from the other side, and I think the answer is already written down. Here it is, article by article.
brief

Explorer coding and its handover: explorers build, villagers maintain, town planners own the code in production. The word "vibe" is part of the problem. In Explorer coding I proposed a better name for it, from Simon Wardley's explorers, villagers and town planners. What people are doing when they build an app by talking to an agent is exploring, with the fast feedback loop that made spreadsheets win. And what they build is a better brief than any document: what the user actually wants, in a form that runs. The citizen developer makes the same case for the people outside IT who are now building: it is the spreadsheet grown up, and spreadsheets ran the world for decades despite their errors.
brief

So I would not start from "who will fix your mess?". The prototype is not a mess. It is the most precise requirement the company has ever had. The mistake is to put it in line, so that other people depend on it, before anyone has done the work that makes software dependable.
handover

The deployment gap on a Wardley map: the handover from explorers to villagers to town planners. On a Wardley map, the deployment gap has a place. It is the move from genesis to custom built and product, and it is a change of people, not only of code. Explorers are good at finding what is needed. Villagers are good at making it reliable: tests, data handling, releases that do not break it, and now behaviour policies for the agents that work on it. Town planners are good at running it at scale, and they own it in production. The citizen developer's path from the spreadsheet to the villagers and town planners who make it last.
handover

That is why the bank's story went the way it did. It is not that the internal team was weak, or that building is always wrong. An explorer team was asked to be villagers and town planners as well, on a regulated, data-heavy, daily-use tool, and those are different jobs. The startup had already done the villager and town planner work, many times, for many clients.
record

This is the point in the post I most want to answer, because I think it is the one that most needs to change: "the AI designs the architecture, not your team. So nobody in-house knows how the tool is built." That is true of most agent-built software today. It does not have to be. Knowledge that maintains itself: sources, agents that keep a semantic graph up to date, and people briefed from it. If the agents work under a written mandate, keep their memory in a versioned store the company owns, and describe what they built as a graph, then the architecture is not a mystery. It is a record the next team can read. Knowledge that maintains itself is about exactly that: a graph of what an organisation knows, kept up to date by agents and used to brief people and agents. Each article on this site carries one, and you can read them all as graphs.
record

The graphs page on newsroom.sgit.ai, showing Explorer coding as a graph of twelve nodes, with edges and quotes. Mondweep Chakravorty's SGit × Ruflo run: twelve steps, five worked, three safeguards refused, one thing not tested. For what a prototype ready for the handover looks like, Mondweep Chakravorty's SGit × Ruflo proof of concept is a good example: built with agents, but with its versions pinned, sixteen tests, a folder of evidence, a written behaviour policy, and a README that says plainly what it does not do yet. A villager can pick that up. The pieces after it, when the vault is actually used and the path the policy does not guard, are what a villager's first review of it reads like.
bonus

I like the bonus test a lot: would your team accept a bonus tied to how the tool performs in production? It is the right question, and it has a name in the Wardley frame. It is the moment the town planners take the code and answer for it. Explorer coding makes the same point from the other end: more of the industry already says that whoever ships code is responsible for it, however it was written. The Linux kernel's rules for AI coding assistants say so. If nobody will put their name, or their bonus, on a tool in production, it is not ready to be in line, whoever wrote it.
undo

The spectrum of how costly an output is to undo, against how mature its controls are, from explorer to town planner. "Build where you are different, for narrow internal tools, or to prototype what you need." I agree, and I would add the test I use for how far to let something go. In How cheap is it to undo?, the question is not build or buy, but how much it costs to reverse a mistake and how mature the controls are. A narrow internal tool that a few people use and that can be switched off is a two-way door: build it, explore, learn. A tool that touches regulated data every day is a one-way door until the controls are mature: that is where the villagers have to be in place first, yours or a partner's.
specialist

Two playbooks: the outsider who finds a gap and hires the experts, and the expert who builds with agents. "Partner where specialists live the problem every day." Yes, and the specialist is changing. In The expert founders I argued that agents let the people who know a problem best build the product themselves, without the millions that used to come first. That is good news for the buyer: more of the startups worth partnering with will be run by people who have lived the problem, not by outsiders who hired them.
villagers

A product as explorers, villagers and town planners: users explore, the vendor maintains and runs the platform. "Every edge case one client hits makes the product better for all the others." That is the strongest argument for a partner, and it is also why I think vendors should change what they sell. In Software vendors should become villagers and town planners I argued that a software company should stop being the only explorer and let its users explore on top of the product, by talking to it, while it sells them the maintenance of what they built, and learns from every one of them. That keeps the network effect Olivier describes, and it closes the deployment gap from the vendor's side: the client's explorers keep exploring, and the vendor is the villager. A custom Firefox of my own is the worked example, for a product I use every day.
fix

The last point is the one I would change in the question itself. "Who will fix your mess?" should not have a single answer. If the only people who can fix a tool are one partner's engineers, the company has swapped a deployment gap for a dependency. That is why I keep arguing for open source, all of it. The value of constraints explains what it takes away: the temptation to lock customers in, and the startup curse of building every customer's integration. The fork next door explains what it protects: if the partner stops executing, the customer, or another partner, can take the code and carry on. With the code open and the record kept, "who will fix it?" has many answers: your team, the partner, another partner, or the agents, under a mandate, reading the record.

The record is a proposal, not a standard. This site runs it; few organisations do yet. I have a stake. My companies sell open source and the kind of record described here. Abstract: The reading meter on sgit.ai keeps everything in the reader's browser, so anyone can cheat it: edit the balance, open a private window, or credit themselves £5 by opening the page a payment returns to with a made-up reference. This piece goes one level below "who are you protecting against". None of the people here are attackers. They are readers, from engineers who are invisible by habit to people who can barely click, with agents moving between the levels in seconds. For each kind we estimate how many there are, from published figures, what they could do to the meter and whether they will. The answer is that cheating will happen, rarely, and costs nothing that reaches the site, while the risks that will actually happen are quieter: a shared computer showing someone's reading history, a reader confused by a number, and ordinary card fraud on the payment link. Security and usability are aimed at the readers who will pay, not at the ones who never would.

Eight kinds of reader, from invisible to barely clicking, with how many of them there are, what each could do to a meter kept in the browser, and how likely they are to bother. Everything is in the reader's browser, so the reader can change anything. Nine ways to cheat or leak are listed below. All are documented and accepted. None of the people who could cheat are attackers. This is who are you protecting against one level down: not tiers of threat, but kinds of reader, all of them non-malicious. Eight kinds of reader, from the invisible (Tor, VPNs, clean browsers, mostly engineers) to the struggling (people who can barely click), with agents able to move between levels in a single request. Cheating will happen, rarely, and costs the site nothing. Every way of cheating changes a number only the cheater sees, and takes away a payment that was never coming.

The risks that will actually happen are quieter: a shared computer that shows what someone read, a reader confused or worried by a negative number, and card fraud on the Stripe link. So the design is aimed at the middle of the ladder, the readers who will weigh it up and pay, and at not frightening the bottom steps, rather than at stopping the top. Who are you protecting against argued that the first question in security is who, not how much: draw the line where the attacker is, not above it, and don't design against a nation state when you have no backups. Its ladder was of attackers, from your own mistakes to states.

A reading meter needs the same question asked about people who are not attackers at all. Nobody breaks a meter that blocks nothing to steal a page they can already read. The people who could change their balance are readers, with different skills, habits and reasons. The useful question is not "could they?" but "will they, how many of them are there, and what does it cost if they do?" Going live with the reading meter sets out how it works: charged by depth, a balance allowed below zero, no blocking, a refusal with a reason, a £5 Stripe top-up credited by a page that cannot check the payment. Here is who will meet it. The figures below come from different surveys with different methods and they overlap. One person can be in several rows, and in different rows on different days. They are for sizing, not for adding up. # Who How many, roughly

What they could do to the meter Will they? 1 The invisible. Engineers with VPNs, clean browsers, private windows by default, sometimes Tor Professional developers are about 0.6% of internet users; Tor has about 3.1 to 3.3 million direct users a day Anything: edit storage, forge the return page, never keep state at all They will not bother to cheat. Most will never have a balance long enough to matter, because their browser forgets it 2 Agents. Software reading on someone's behalf Not counted; growing Read the markdown twin, which is not metered; or drive a browser and do anything step 1 can They move between levels in seconds. Today they are outside the meter by design 3 Enthusiasts and power users. NordVPN, ad blockers, privacy-aware, not developers VPN users, about 23% of internet users; ad blockers, about 29% Clear site data, use privacy extensions that wipe storage on close

Some will reset without meaning to. A few will look in developer tools out of curiosity 4 Instruction followers. Not technical, but will follow a recipe to save money or protect privacy Unknown, likely large Follow a post that says "open this URL to get free credit" The cohort where publishing the gap matters. We published it ourselves 5 Pragmatic payers. Want the thing, happy to pay, make their own risk assessment The audience this is for Pay £5 on Stripe This is who the meter is built for 6 Little understanding. Use the web without a model of what it stores Private browsing used daily by about 12% in the UK (2023) Reset it without knowing, by using a private window They will never cheat. They will sometimes see £5.00 again and wonder why 7 Normal and mixed. Most readers, most of the time Most of the ladder Nothing deliberate They will read, see a number, and decide 8

Struggling. Can barely use a computer In the OECD's tests, 26% of adults could not use a computer and 14% were below the lowest level Nothing The risk is not cheating. It is being frightened by a negative balance, or thinking they owe money

Two of those figures say more together than apart. SlashData counted 36.5 million professional developers in early 2025, and the ITU estimated about 6.0 billion internet users in November 2025: about 0.6%, by our arithmetic. At the other end, the OECD's Survey of Adult Skills, as summarised by the Nielsen Norman Group, found that across 33 rich countries 26% of adults could not use a computer, 14% were below Level 1, 29% at Level 1, 26% at Level 2 and only 5% at Level 3, the level of a skilled user. The people who could cheat this meter with no effort are a sliver of one step; the people who could be confused by it are most of the bottom three.

An agent is not a step; it is a lift. The same agent can fetch a page's markdown twin as a plain HTTP client, which no meter sees, then drive a full browser that runs the meter, then reset that browser's storage between tasks without anyone deciding to. It can follow an instruction to "get credit" at step 4 and execute it at step 1. That is why agents are outside the meter for now, on purpose, rather than inside it badly. Reading the markdown twin of a page, or the newsroom's wire, costs nothing. Metering agents properly would be a different design: priced per question rather than per page, paid by whoever runs the agent, and argued in a token bill nobody is sending. A browser meter that tried to charge agents would mostly charge the ones honest enough to run it. # What a reader can do Who can What it costs the site

What it costs the reader 1 Edit their balance in developer tools Steps 1 to 3, and 4 with a recipe Nothing it would have had Nothing 2 Open a private window or another browser and start again at £5.00 Everyone, often by accident Nothing Their history and picks 3 Open the page a payment returns to with any reference, and get £5 of credit, once per reference Steps 1 to 4 Nothing: no money moves, and the credit is only on their screen Nothing 4 Replay the same return URL Anyone Blocked once per reference; a new reference is trivial, so see 3 None 5 Clear site data to wipe a negative balance Steps 1 to 3 Nothing; there was never a debt Their history 6 Read as an agent, through the markdown twin or the wire Agents Unmetered by design None 7 Read someone else's history and personas on a shared computer Anyone with the computer None Privacy

8 A script injected into the site reads the history Needs a hole in the site first Reputation Privacy 9 Card testing, fraud or chargebacks on the Stripe link Ordinary payment fraud Fees and disputes None Rows 1 to 6 are the cheating. Every one of them changes a number that only the person who changed it can see, and that number unlocks nothing. The site loses only a payment that the person was, by doing it, already not going to make. That is why they are accepted, and why the return page in row 3 is deliberately unprotected: protecting it would need a server, and the only thing the server would protect is a number on the cheater's own screen. What we did do is make the payment the default route everywhere. No button leads to the free one. Ranked by how likely they are, not by how interesting.

All a reader below zero sees: a small balance in the top bar, in a warmer colour, linking to an explanation. No banner, no count, no request. Confusion at the bottom of the ladder. A reader on step 6 to 8 sees a negative balance and thinks they owe money, or sees £5.00 again and wonders where their history went. This is the most likely problem, and it is a usability problem. That is why the balance is small and links to an explanation, why its tooltip says nothing is blocked, why nothing pops up, and why the account page says on every visit that the meter lives in this browser only. The struggling reader is protected by the meter asking nothing of them.

A shared computer shows what someone read. Row 7. A family computer or a library terminal keeps the history of whoever used it last, including the pages they declined and why. It is the only risk here that harms a reader, and the mitigations are theirs: "Start again" on the account page clears it, and a private window keeps nothing. We say so on the account page rather than pretending storage is private. Card fraud on the payment link. Row 9. Small payment links are used to test stolen card numbers. It is the one risk that costs real money, and it is the one that is not ours to solve: Stripe's own controls handle it, and the link can be switched off in a minute. It is also H4 in the going-live article's hypotheses: a dispute that is not plain card fraud would tell us the meter has started to matter in a way we did not plan.

Cheating. Rows 1 to 6. It will happen, a few times, mostly out of curiosity and mostly by steps 1 to 3. It costs nothing that reaches us. It is last on this list because it is least worth worrying about, not because it is least likely. A script on the site reads the history. Row 8. It needs a hole in the site first. The meter sets everything it shows as text, never as markup, and the only third-party code on this site is the in-browser Python on the try page, loaded from a pinned version. It would be a serious bug if it happened. Nothing about the meter makes it more likely.

The mistake to avoid is the one the earlier piece warned about: drawing the line above the attacker. Here, that would mean building for step 1: a server to verify every payment, an account to hold the balance, a sign-in to keep the history. Every one of those would stop nobody on step 1, who can still not pay and still read, and every one would make the meter worse for steps 5 to 8, the readers who might pay and the readers who must not be frightened.

So the line is drawn where the readers are. For the pragmatic payer on step 5, the meter is honest and the payment is one click. For the instruction follower on step 4, the gap is published by us, next to the reason it does not matter. For steps 6 to 8, the meter is quiet, never blocks, never shames and never asks. For steps 1 to 3, it is a number they can change, and they are welcome to. If the balance unlocked anything, a page, a download, an answer from an agent, cheating would stop being free, and rows 1, 3 and 5 would need a server or a signed receipt. That is a different meter. If the history synced between devices, it would be kept in an encrypted vault whose key only the reader holds, so the site still could not read it, and row 7 would get a lock.

If cheating showed up where we can see, in the Stripe dashboard, we would have learned that someone found a way to make it matter. The anchors say in advance what number would mean that. The library's own version of this is SG Meter's security model, for a site adding it. Written from a voice note by Dinis Cruz, who set out the ladder of readers and has editorial responsibility, by a Claude Code session working as the sgit.ai newsroom, on 10 October 2026. Sources: developers, SlashData (early 2025); internet users, ITU (November 2025); Tor, metrics.torproject.org (3 to 7 October 2026); VPN and ad-blocker use, GWI (Q2 2025, via DataReportal, a secondary source); private browsing in the UK, Statista (2023); computer skills, the OECD Survey of Adult Skills as summarised by the Nielsen Norman Group. The ratio of developers to internet users is our own arithmetic from the first two.

Abstract: The PHP story is now run by a pipeline of agents that wake on their own: a researcher finds sources, a curator turns them into evidence, a journalist updates the site, and a correspondent checks the journalist's work; then the Sherpa, the desk, the librarian and the ontologist run after them. Eleven schedules, 53 wakes a day. It works, but it is brittle, and the reasons are worth writing down. Each agent needs its own session that I can open and read, holding its state, its keys and gigabytes of vaults between wakes. For a long time the platform's scheduling opened a new session for every run, which made secrets and state start again and the list of sessions grow with every wake. A couple of days ago I found I could schedule a wake into a specific session, and that is what made the pipeline possible; it still took a day and a half to become somewhat reliable, and this morning the wake timeline still showed 5 wakes met and 11 missed, mostly runs that worked but left no record. That is why I go slowly, use what the platform provides and keep my own code to a minimum, and spend as much time on visualisation as on the setup itself. The next step is the move from explorer to villager: a dedicated account for the whole team, for isolation and for costs, usage and models I can see. And a lesson for platform builders: the unit of work is the whole platform.
The PHP site's wake timeline at 11:34 London on 25 October 2026, with each agent's wakes marked met, missed or due.
in-short

Ten agents, in sequence, on their own. Researcher, curator, journalist, correspondent, then four more. Each needs its own session. With its state, its keys and gigabytes of vaults, that I can open and read. The platform's scheduling used to open a new session every run. That did not scale. Scheduling into a chosen session made it possible. I found it a couple of days ago. It is still brittle. This morning, 5 wakes met and 11 missed, mostly for want of a record. So I go slowly, and use the platform for everything it does, so I maintain less of my own code. Visibility is half the work. I spend as long seeing the system as building it. The next step is a dedicated account. And for platform builders: the unit of work is the whole platform.
what-we-run

If you look at the PHP story's newsroom, it already has quite a mature workflow, and it is documented. A researcher goes out and finds sources, and keeps everything it reads in a vault. A curator reads only that vault and turns the captures into evidence in another vault. A journalist reads only the evidence, gives every new claim a verdict, and updates the site. And a correspondent, the senior journalist, checks what the journalist published and makes sure the flows are working. They run in sequence, and each has its own session. Then, once those have run, the others need to run after them: the Sherpa, who answers readers; the desk; the librarian; and the ontologist, who keeps the semantic graphs. So I already have a sequence of about ten agents, some of which run three or four times a day and others once.
what-we-run

The PHP site's schedule page on 25 October 2026: one day of wakes in London time, with the quiet hours shaded. The point is not to run them as often as possible. If I can get an agent to run effectively once a day, or four times a day, that scales, because the objective is something that runs when I am not looking. Removing myself from the loop, smoothly, is the whole game.
needs

What a loop of agents needs before it can run without you: six needs, learned on the PHP story. My requirements are practical. I need to be able to see each execution. So I want each agent's runs to land in the same session, on the same machine, where I can open it and read what it did. That one choice solves a lot: the secrets the agent was given stay with it; the state stays where it was; and the data does not have to be fetched again on every wake. This is gigabytes of data by now, and you do not want clones of it all over the place.
needs

The data side already uses our own technology. Each stage writes to a vault: the researcher's, then the curator's, which the journalist reads. The researcher's vault is also a good example of a limit found in use: it grew to 63,662 objects and 1.6 GB and pushed sgit past what it could do, until pack mode, one zip per push, fixed it. And continuing the previous session matters for more than state. It matters for readability. When I come back to an agent, I want to read its history in the same place, in the same interface.
history

How scheduling agents got easier, one platform feature at a time, ending with a proposed dedicated account for the team. This is where small features in the platforms matter a lot. I am using Claude here. The first thing Claude did very well was the loop of tools: the model calls a tool, reads the result and carries on. Remember that early versions had barely any internet and no tools. Once that existed, an agent could be a Claude session, which is what we now have in Claude, ChatGPT and everywhere else.
history

Then came scheduling. That was good, but the way it worked in practice caused me a lot of problems: each scheduled run opened a new session. Claude Code's documentation still describes it that way: a run "opens as a full session, a new one for each run". For my purposes that meant no good way to give the run its secrets, no reuse of state, and, when you run several agents several times a day, an ever-growing list of sessions to open to see what happened. That does not scale, so I did not run my schedules that way.
history

Then, a couple of days ago, I realised I could schedule a wake into a specific session. It may be new, or it may have been there and I had not noticed. Either way, it is exactly what I needed. I can create a session with the model I want, brief it, and give it its key with the QR handshake, which is our way of handing secrets to an agent. The agent then clones the repositories and the vaults, and from then on every scheduled wake arrives in that same session, already set up.
brittle

It works, and it is still brittle. It took a day and a half to become somewhat reliable, and it is not fully there. One example: the agents try to help. At one point an agent tried to set up its own schedule, but it could not see, or set, the schedule for another session, so the wake fired in the wrong place, in the wrong environment.
brittle

Another, from this morning. The control room's wake timeline at 11:34 London showed 5 wakes met and 11 missed. Most of the misses were not failures of work. The conductor checked, and the researcher and the curator do run: the curator's 08:00 wake promoted 18 sources and took the evidence vault to 400. They just left no commit and no run record, so to the rest of the team they looked like they had not happened. The fix, at my go, was to make every scheduled wake's prompt small, with a shared wake procedure that always ends in a run record, and a way to publish that record without releasing the site. The latest runs on the PHP site's schedule page, 25 October 2026: the conductor, the desk and the factcheck sweep.
brittle
None of this is exotic. It is what happens when four or five agents, then ten, have to work in sequence, unattended, on a platform whose limits you live with.
platform

In the past I have wired this kind of thing myself, and you can. But it always works better when the platform you are on provides the service, because then the platform maintains it. That is where the details of how a platform works, and how commoditised a feature is, matter. So I live with the limitations of the platforms I use. Whatever is missing I code on top, and I always want to get rid of that code, because it is one more thing I have to maintain.
slowly

This is why I do it slowly. Not because I cannot go faster, but because the pace buys understanding and confidence, and it builds the infrastructure that makes the next loop possible. The more control and visibility I have, the more agency I can give the agents, and the more loops I can run. It is a good example of an explorer workflow that will become a product and code over time. The only way to get there is to run it, experiment, map it, and only then gain the confidence you get with products and commodities: the villagers and the town planners.
visibility

You need a lot of visualisation, and a lot of checks and balances. I have many of them already, and they are still where the most improvement is needed. On the PHP site, the agents built the schedule, with every agent's card, wakes and runs; the control room, with the pipeline, the wake timeline and the decisions waiting on me; and the journalist's desk, with the pipeline after every export and what the correspondent caught. I spend as much time visualising, mapping and getting control of the setup of this environment as on the setup itself. I think that is the right ratio.
dedicated

There is one more problem, and it is mine. At the moment all of this runs in one of my main Claude accounts, the one I use for everything else, and it is clogging up my management of sessions. More than that, I want isolation. So the next evolution, again the move from explorer to villager, is to give the team a dedicated account, perhaps a Team account, so I pay for another seat. Then I have good control of the costs, the usage and the models each agent uses, and all the information and all the flows are contained in one place. The good news is that most of the work is done. This is the tightening up: removing what is not needed, deleting what should not be there, and then gaining the resilience and confidence that only come from something running all the time.
unit

This is also what I always tell people who build platforms, especially platforms that do not run everywhere. Everything you build, your customers will need a part of. But the unit of work is not whatever you decide a user session is. The unit of work is your entire platform. So users must be able to create complete, separate instances of the whole thing. That is what a new Claude session is: the whole unit of work. It is what AWS accounts are, in a way. Individual accounts, individual platform sessions, each with everything the platform does, including running wherever they are needed. It is a very powerful pattern, and it is the one I am about to use for the PHP team.
limits

The timings are mine. A day and a half to somewhat reliable is this pipeline's, not a measurement of the platform. The scheduling history is my experience of it. The documentation still describes a new session per cloud run; I do not know when scheduling into a chosen session arrived. The misfired schedule is from my session, not from a record on the site. The dedicated account is a plan, not yet done. "Missed" on the timeline means no run record within 45 minutes, not that no work was done.
