The flagship MVP, and the only one with a date attached. A bilingual daily publication mapping one country's generative-AI ecosystem — companies, funding, policy, academia, diaspora — on a knowledge-graph backbone, produced by an eleven-role agentic newsroom on a daily clock. A trip supplied the deadline. Designed 12 May 2026 across two briefs; never launched.

Update, 13 September 2026 — a first instance is running, and it is much smaller than this. Portugal Startups is live on this site. It takes this design's scoping sentence and its ontology, and it takes almost nothing else: one beat rather than a country, one event rather than a daily clock, seven agent roles rather than eleven, and no personalisation layer at all. The design below is still a design and is still unlaunched — the ≥200-entity graph, the daily rhythm, the fifteen departments and the bilingual publication have none of them been built. What the instance does have is the thing this design never got to: the sources are primary, frozen and hashed, so a claim walks back to bytes rather than to a URL. That is the step The Governance Wire specifies and cannot run. And question 5 below is answered. See the note against it.
why

The scoping argument is the most transferable thing in the whole document, and it is one sentence: That is the actual MVP criterion. Not “a smaller version of a news site” but a beat whose entity graph can be closed — where you can plausibly name every company, every funder, every institution, every relevant researcher, and then keep that map current. A publication that has mapped its whole domain can answer questions no general outlet can, and that completeness is reachable in a small market and unreachable in a large one. Three secondary reasons are given, and they are honest about self-interest: the coverage gap (most reporting on the market happens in English, from outside it), the relationship value (people written about seriously tend to talk to you), and the platform demonstration (bilingual publishing shown rather than asserted).
surface

Eight sections define what the publication covers. Each item becomes one or more articles, an entry in the knowledge graph, and a node in the ecosystem map — so the section list doubles as the graph's top-level schema. Section What it holds The companies Startups, their funding, their teams, their products The players Founders, researchers, investors, advisors The institutions Government bodies, universities, accelerators, foundations The policies EU AI Act implementation nationally, strategies, public funding The use cases Real deployments in companies and the public sector The open source National contributions to open-source AI projects The diaspora Talent abroad and the work they are doing The events Conferences, meetups, hackathons, public consultations
graph

Each article sits in a graph of entities, relationships and sources rather than standing alone. The graph captures every company, person, funding round, product launch, policy document, event and open-source contribution mentioned — and then earns its keep by powering things an article list cannot: This company, this person — every piece of coverage in one place, assembled rather than authored. Who invested in whom; who works with whom. The relationships are the story as often as the events are. How funding evolved; how policy changed. Queryable, because the dates are structured rather than prose. Read about a company in one language, click through to the coverage in the other. Entities carry labels in both. Every article mentioning a given entity — by identity, not by string match.
graph

The design note is that the graph is language-agnostic: entities have labels in both languages and cross-language entity resolution happens at the graph layer, not the article layer. That is what makes the bilingual property structural rather than a translation pipeline bolted on the end.
bilingual

The brief is explicit that this is not “English with translations”: content is created with both audiences in mind, sometimes from the same source material with different angles per language. Storage is one markdown file per language per article; routing is by URL or an explicit reader choice; each version cross-links to its counterpart; and a reviewer fluent in the second language reviews that version specifically rather than trusting the generation. That last point is the one that costs real money and is the easiest to quietly drop, which is presumably why it is written into the acceptance criteria as a named human review pass rather than left as an aspiration.
newsroom

The companion brief of the same date specifies the operating model. It opens by asking what a modern editorial operation would look like if built from scratch with agents in mind, and answers with a mapping from traditional roles rather than an invention: Function Traditional role Agentic equivalent Editorial direction Editor-in-chief, managing editor Conductor — sets daily priorities, allocates stories Story sourcing Reporters with beats Researcher agents — continuous monitoring of named sources Investigation Investigative reporter Deep-research agent — multi-day stories, evidence accumulation Fact-checking Fact-checking desk Verifier agents — cross-reference sources, flag uncertainty Writing Reporters, feature writers Writer agents — multiple voices, tunable per story Copy editing Sub-editors Editor agent — style, tone, length, clarity Localisation Multilingual desk Translator agents Visual production Photo desk, graphics Visual agent — infographics, headers Personalisation Did not exist traditionally Briefing agent — tailored views per reader Publication Production team Publishing pipeline — vault to website, social, briefings Audience engagement Community team
newsroom
Community agent — responses, follow-ups, reader signal The line the brief draws under that table is the doctrinal one, and it is the same commitment the newsroom section of this site is built on:
clock

06:00Researcher agents finish overnight scans of national news sources, official feeds and social signals; candidate stories surface with summaries written to the newsroom's shared vault. 07:00The conductor reviews the overnight surfacing, picks the day's priority stories, and allocates each to a writer and a verifier. 08:00Writer and verifier work in parallel, not in sequence — the verifier builds the evidence set while the writer drafts against it, citing as they go. 10:00The editor agent returns notes on clarity, tone, length and missing context; the writer revises. 11:00The visual agent produces headers and infographics from the story's own graph. 12:00Final review, with a human spot-check. Publication. Personalisation agents fan out to generate the sector- and audience-specific versions. 13:00Distribution: social posts, briefing emails. 14:00 onwardThe community agent monitors response and surfaces follow-up signals; researchers begin scanning for tomorrow; investigative agents continue multi-day pieces.
clock

The parallelism at 08:00 is the structural claim worth noticing. In a conventional newsroom fact-checking follows writing, which is why it is the step that gets cut under deadline pressure. Here the evidence set is built alongside the draft and the draft cites into it, so a story that skipped verification would be visibly missing its evidence rather than merely unchecked.
story-vault

Every story that moves from “watched” to “active” gets its own vault. The layout is the data model: story-{date}-{slug}/ ├── brief.md what this story is, why it matters ├── sources/ │ ├── primary/ original documents, statements, releases │ ├── coverage/ how other outlets reported it │ └── interviews/ ├── evidence/ │ ├── facts.json verified facts, with source attribution │ ├── disputed.json claims under dispute, with both sides │ └── contradictions.md where sources disagree ├── drafts/ v1 research → v2 writer → v3 edited → v4 published ├── personalisation/ general, business-leader, per-sector, regional ├── graph/ │ ├── entities.json people, companies, places mentioned │ ├── relationships.json what connects to what │ └── semantic.json the knowledge graph for this story └── _page.json how this story renders
story-vault

Two folders in that tree are the ones a conventional CMS has no place for. evidence/disputed.json and evidence/contradictions.md mean disagreement between sources is stored rather than resolved away — the published article makes a call, but the record of what did not reconcile survives it. That is the same commitment the agenda-is-context argument makes, arriving here as two filenames.
personalisation

The personalisation layer generates per-audience projections from the same source material after publication: a general version, a business-executive version, a technology-leader version, per-sector versions, an investor version, a version tailored to a named subscriber's declared interests, and a version translated and contextualised for readers outside the country. Each is generated by a personalisation agent from the same evidence, which is what stops them from drifting into seven differently-wrong stories.
personalisation

This generalises a pattern from an earlier personalised-briefing product built by the same team for a security audience: take a domain's news, project it for a specific reader based on their role and concerns, deliver it as a briefing. The newsroom brief's claim is that the pattern is domain-independent — that if it works for general news it works for any structured-information-projection product. The brief also notes the reader can supply their own model key and generate a projection nobody designed for them, which is the part that makes it a graph being sold rather than an article.
launch

Three phases, each with an explicit decision point — the detail that separates this from a wish-list: One story per day. Human conductor. Low-stakes subject matter. The question being answered is whether the vault structure holds, the personalisation generates sensibly and the pipeline ships — not whether the journalism is good yet. Two or three stories per day. A community agent joins to monitor response. Traction tracking starts, per story and per personalisation. Five or more stories per day. The conductor role passes to an agent under human oversight. Personalised briefings go to a small pilot subscriber set.
launch

The publication brief adds a separate and more demanding set of ten acceptance criteria, of which two are worth quoting because they are the ones a demo would fail: at least three articles reviewed and approved by a fluent human reader in the second language, and the publication surviving the trip ending — a cadence that continues without the project lead running it manually. The second is the real test. An intensive burst of content around a trip proves nothing about a publication; what it proves is that a person was available for two weeks.
replication

The publication brief closes by naming the generalisation: Spain, Brazil, Italy, Germany — each with its own publication on the same infrastructure, same workflow, different domain, different language pair. The stated strategic value is that a platform visibly running several national AI publications has a presence in each of those markets that a publishing tool cannot buy. The source labels this speculative, and so does this page. The brief's own words are that the pattern is revisited only “if this works as a publication and as a case study” — the first instance is the precondition, and the first instance did not launch. Reproduced here because the replication argument is the reason the first instance was scoped the way it was, not as a roadmap.
open

The newsroom brief ends with six questions it declines to answer, and they are published here in the same state. Three are ordinary product questions; three are the ones that make this a news organisation rather than a content pipeline. # Question Why it is not a detail 1 Editorial voice — bold or restrained, opinionated or neutral, analytical or narrative Named as needing to be decided before the agents are tuned. House style is a configuration input here, not a culture that emerges. 2 Primary language only, or bilingual from day one Determines whether translation is a parallel output or a second-tier feature. The companion brief assumes bilingual; this one leaves it open. The two briefs of the same date disagree. 3 Funding model — free with paid personalisation tiers, sponsor-funded, or no revenue model initially The rest of this site argues a specific answer to this. The launch plan does not adopt it. 4
open

Distribution — own site only, or also third-party platforms Effort allocation, and a dependency question for a publication whose whole point is owning its chain. 5 Editorial accountability — who is the editor of record, and who carries legal responsibility for published content The unanswered question that matters most. An agentic newsroom publishing daily in a jurisdiction needs a named human who is legally answerable. No candidate is named. 6 Pace — is daily too ambitious to start The brief asks whether twice-weekly is the sensible opening. The phased plan assumes daily anyway. Question 5 is the one this site should be most uncomfortable about. A publication built to make provenance walkable, that has not decided who is accountable for what it publishes, has an unclosed chain at exactly the point where the chain has to terminate in a person. It is recorded as open in the source and it stays open there.
open

Answered on 13 September 2026, four months after it was asked. Dinis Cruz is the named editor of record for the running instance, and reads every page before it publishes. The answer arrived with a constraint the design did not anticipate: the journalistic route is not available. Article 24(3) of Portugal's Lei 58/2019 conditions processing for journalistic purposes on the national rules governing access to and exercise of the profession, which an unaccredited publication does not satisfy. So the instance runs on legitimate interests instead, with a published notice, a written balancing test and an unconditional removal route. That is an answer, not a clearance. No lawyer has reviewed it, and the statutory article was returned truncated to the research that found it. It is recorded here because the alternative — leaving the question open while publishing the names of 64 people — is worse.

The last MVP in the family is not a publication at all — it is the business idea itself, given away. Seven fully-formed, Creative Commons-licensed company descriptions, published so that somebody else can pick one up and build it. One of the seven is an evidence-research company aimed squarely at journalists and investigators, which is why this page is on a news site. Designed 17 May 2026; none of the seven was ever published.
what

The source brief spends its first section on getting the category right, and the distinction it lands on is load-bearing: The brief records that it tried “fake company” first and rejected it, on the grounds that the phrase implies deception. What it settles on is a genuinely unusual artefact defined by three properties held at once: fully-formed (market analysis, product, pricing, operating model, technology stack, investment ask — not a paragraph), Creative Commons-licensed (so it can be taken and built without asking), and platform-aware (the economics assume a specific substrate, which is what makes it viable at small scale).
what

Each of those exists on its own — business plans get written, CC licensing is ordinary, platform-dependent businesses are everywhere. The combination is the thing. And the brief insists on a fourth property that is really an editorial standard: open about its own status, so a reader is never in any doubt they are looking at a proposal rather than a going concern.
seven

# Seed What the company would do 1 CV / job search Vault-grounded CV, portfolio and application workflow; agents tailor per application; the candidate owns and controls the artefact. 2 Pitch creation A firm helping founders build investor pitches — human pitch coaches using the platform as their working substrate rather than documents and slides. 3 Health score Individual health data held in the person's own vault; the company sells the analysis layer, the user keeps the data. Named as the most validated seed, with the most prior material behind it. 4 Evidence researchthe one that belongs to this site Gathering and presenting evidence on a specific question, for people who are not a large institution — journalists running investigations, expert witnesses, researchers, advocacy groups. Detail ↓ 5 Accountant workflow A small accountancy delivering strategic-partner service at SME prices via platform-grounded workflows. Empower the existing small firms rather than displace them. 6 Lawyer workflow
seven

The same shape applied to law — client communication, documents, case tracking, evidence handling. Encrypted storage and a free audit trail map unusually well onto privilege requirements. 7 Local AI enablement Connecting local small businesses with local people who can teach them to use these tools well. Short engagements, per-task pricing. Community-rooted rather than platform-rooted, and flagged in the source as the odd one out.
evidence

This is the seed that belongs to this site, and it is the commercial form of the argument the rest of the site makes abstractly. The company sells the evidence work rather than the article: the vault as an evidence locker, agents doing source-checking, citation management and document analysis, cross-document linking as the deliverable. The economic claim is the interesting part, and it is a claim about who gets served rather than about margin: That is the same argument as paying the fact creator approached from the buying side. This site argues that near-zero-cost settlement makes it possible to pay for a single fact; the evidence-research seed argues that near-zero-cost evidence assembly makes it possible to commission an investigation that no newsroom would fund and no law firm would quote for. Local accountability reporting, a single-issue campaign group, an expert witness working alone — these are the buyers that currently fall below the floor.
evidence

The brief also names, in one line, the relationship between this seed and the one property in the family that actually runs: myfeeds.ai is the live instance of the evidence-research seed. The seed is the generalised business; the property is one person's version of it, already operating. What that property charges and who it serves is deliberately not published here — see the note on the MVP index.
why

Six reasons are given. Five are ordinary strategy — it demonstrates capability without a sales pitch, it seeds an ecosystem, it is cheap to produce relative to building each one, it generates publishable content, it forces the authors to articulate what the platform actually enables. The sixth is the one with an edge on it: For a news site there is a sharper version of that, and it is the reason this page is not merely adjacent to the argument. This site's whole thesis is that the value is in the graph rather than the paragraph — that the assembled, evidenced, structured thing is what is worth paying for, and the readable projection on top of it is nearly free. A publisher who believes that should be entirely comfortable publishing their business plan, because the plan is a paragraph and the operation is a graph. Giving away the seven seeds is the thesis being tested on its authors.
structure

Each seed is one vault with a consistent layout — the investor-pack template filled in, plus the working detail a builder would need: seed-{name}/ ├── pack.md the investor pack, against the shared template ├── operating-model.md how the company runs day to day ├── product.md what it builds ├── financials/ projections · unit economics · assumptions ├── go-to-market/ strategy · pricing · partnerships ├── technology/ architecture · platform leverage · build vs buy ├── examples/ sample customer flow, sample output ├── license.md Creative Commons └── readme.md front matter; how to use this vault
structure

Underneath the seven sits a reusable investor-pack template — the same thirteen sections any company would present, held as a vault rather than a slide deck. The brief argues the vault form buys four things a PDF cannot: the reader can change the financial assumptions and see the model move, every market claim links to the source behind it, each reader can annotate their own copy without affecting anyone else's, and when the pack is updated the reader sees what changed rather than receiving a new file. That last one is supersede-never-delete applied to fundraising.
risks

A seed that is obviously hype rather than a real model damages the thing it is meant to demonstrate. The stated mitigation is to write each one as if genuinely pitching it, with financials validated against real market data rather than chosen to look good. Creative Commons means no control over who picks a seed up or what they ship under it. The mitigation is framing rather than enforcement: these are templates, not endorsements, and no builder is presented as a partner without review. Open-sourcing a business you may later want to build yourself is awkward. The stated resolution is deliberate: publish only the seeds you are confident you will not build, and say which ones are being held back.
risks

Risk 3 has a consequence the brief accepts explicitly — a numbered task requiring a documented decision per seed: published, internal-only, or deferred. Whether the evidence-research seed would have survived that filter, given that myfeeds.ai already occupies exactly that space, is not recorded. A cluster of the source material's strongest documents — the evidence-economy briefs, credibility calibration, the fact-creator payment mechanism — were originally written for a corporate risk-management product, framing news as the evidence supply for risk graphs. risks

A client-side-assembled vault page, served the way sgit.ai serves one, can be invisible to a crawler. Measured and documented as a known limitation of the delivery substrate this site cites rather than re-explains. For most sites that is a nice-to-have fix. For a news site it is close to existential — almost all of a news site's reach depends on being findable by search and by other agents, and a site that argues for provenance while being unreadable by the tools that would check it has undermined its own case before a reader ever arrives. Decide rendering before content; this is flagged here rather than left implicit.

Following the house convention every sibling site uses: a question this material cannot yet answer is stated and numbered, not smoothed into confident prose. # Question Where the material gets closest Q1 Who pays for contextual validation, and what stops it becoming a toll on inconvenient facts? "In companies that's okay… but in the real world at the moment we don't have that." The commons has no maintenance budget Q2 What is the unit that actually gets paid — the claim, the paragraph, the evidence pack, or the graph? What happens when the author refuses to be the oracle, or is dead? The Ericsson case in the claim that would not die is exactly this, and it is not resolved Q6 Can a newsroom that publishes its own costs survive competitors that do not? The brief asserts the legal stick; no legal review exists anywhere in the material
tensions

Provenance is the product — and provenance is expensive. The £8.40 story cost is the argument and the objection in the same number. Corrections propagating is a feature until it is a liability. A graph that can answer "what rests on claims since corrected" can also be subpoenaed for the answer. "More humans, not fewer" is a design principle, not an economic result. Nothing in this material tests whether it actually holds once real budgets are involved. Selling trust makes the seller a target. A warranted fact-certifier has created a liability surface the material notes but does not size — see trust as a service. This site inherits sgit.ai's crawler-invisibility problem — see above. For a news site, existential rather than cosmetic. Two licences over one thread. docs.diniscruz.ai is CC0; *.sgit.ai is CC BY 4.0. The resolution this site argues for, stated on the disclosure page.

Written. A contributor or the Journalist adds admin/content/articles/<slug>.md, its graph, figures and card. The build makes it a page. Live. For a desk of agents working in one repository, the reach is every file and the mandate is a short list of paths. never

Editor never: rewrite another agent's article (a correction is proposed to its author, or recorded as a correction note); hold an article back from Latest because it is not placed; place an article that is not published; edit the homepage outside the articles band. Journalist never: write front.json or a collection; edit another role's note; publish a number that was remembered rather than counted. Historian never: edit an article; write front.json; editorialise past what the articles say, a note quotes and connects, it does not add claims the articles do not make. Designer never: decide what leads (the Editor), change copy (the Journalist), or add an external font, script or image host. Developer never: change content to make a check pass; weaken a check without a log entry saying why. Contributor never: write front.json, a collection, a desk note, the desk board or the log; edit another agent's article.
principles

Create anywhere, edit your own. Any role adds files; only a file's author edits it. The one exception is a pitch's status line, which is how the Editor answers. One owner for each shared surface. The front is the Editor's, collections are the Historian's, the build is the Developer's. Ownership is what stops two agents rewriting the same thing in turn. Flag, do not fix. A problem in another role's file becomes a pitch, a board card or a correction note. From the SG/Send Librarian.

A lab: the passkey opens the vault Each step of the design, as a thing you can press in your own browser: a passkey, its PRF bytes, the door derived from them, a recovery code, and the door created on a vault server. The design is in The passkey opens the vault: a passkey, through the WebAuthn PRF extension, gives the browser 32 bytes that only your authenticator can produce for this site; from those bytes the browser computes the key and the address of a small door vault, so nothing has to be stored to be found; the door holds the master vault’s key. Each card below is one step of that, as a thing you can press.
poc0
WebAuthn, the platform authenticator, and whether the browser says it supports the PRF extension. Nothing to press: it is read when the page opens.
poc1

navigator.credentials.create() with rp.id set to this host, a resident key, user verification required, and the prf extension. The passkey is stored by your provider (Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello, a hardware key, or the browser’s own store); the page learns a credential id, a public key and whether PRF is on. It never learns who you are.
poc1-ladder

Sign in to a passkey provider (Google Password Manager in Chrome, iCloud Keychain in Safari), so the passkey syncs and PRF is available. Use your phone by QR: a passkey on the phone, one scan at a time. Plug in a hardware key. Stay on this device: the browser’s own copy of the reading account keeps working, and the recovery code (4) is the way back.
poc2

navigator.credentials.get() with the fixed input, the SHA-256 of a public string. The authenticator returns 32 bytes computed from a secret it keeps for this site and this passkey. The same passkey gives the same bytes on every device it syncs to, through the same kind of path; that is the whole trick. Through a different path (a phone over QR, instead of the provider on the device) the same passkey can give different bytes, which a test here found on 12 October 2026; the result shows which path answered, and the design gives each path its own door: one door per passkey path.
poc3

The article’s derivation, made exact: HKDF to a seed, a passphrase and an 8-character vault id; then sgit’s own derivation of the read key and the write key, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations each, timed on this device. The door’s key is not stored anywhere: it comes out the same every time.
poc4
26 characters of base32, 128 bits, made by the page and in the real flow shown once. In place of the PRF bytes it derives a second door to the same master, for the day every passkey is gone.
poc5

The same derivation from a fixed, fake PRF output, compared value by value with what sgit’s own Python produced (vectors.json, from admin/build/passkey_vectors.py). Runs when the page opens. If any line is wrong, the browser and the command line would open different vaults.
poc6

With the door from 3 (or the recovery code from 4, or the test vector), the vault library that runs dev.vault.sgraph.ai, vendored here and loaded from this origin, creates and opens real sgit vaults: the door at its derived address, holding the master’s key and a record of where it came from (kind, provider, path, credential id, device, date); the master, made at random, holding the reader vault’s key and the list of doors; the reader vault, where a note is written and read back. Every vault made here is one sgit clone opens, with write access, from the key shown behind each reveal. Writing needs an access key for the server, which is the thing a reader will buy; opening and reading need nothing.
poc6

An address with no door says so; it is not an error. A vault id is never destroyed, because a destroyed id can never be used again and a door’s is derived. The test vector’s door has the same address for everyone, so on the real server only the first person can create it. Moving the reading account into the reader vault is the next step and is not built.
notes

The relying party id is this host. On newsroom.sgit.ai a passkey made here is for newsroom.sgit.ai exactly, as the article’s trust boundary asks; it does not work on sgit.ai or on any other site. The derivation’s constants name newsroom.sgit.ai whichever host runs the page, so the test vectors are the same everywhere. Where the passkey lives decides what you get. Card 1 shows whether the passkey is backup-eligible, which is the browser’s word for synced. A clean browser with no provider may make a passkey that signs and returns no PRF bytes; card 2 says so if it happens, and card 1 shows the ladder.
notes

A door per path, not per passkey. On 12 October 2026 one Google Password Manager passkey gave one set of bytes through the provider on a Mac and on an iPhone, and a different set, consistently, when a phone answered a QR code from a Mac or an iPad: same credential id, same user handle, same input. Apple’s developer forums carry the same symptom for iCloud Keychain passkeys since late 2024, with a fix announced and a tester reporting it persisting. A second passkey in iCloud Keychain gave the same bytes on a Mac, a current iPad and a current iPhone, in Safari and in Chrome, which is the common case; an older iPad that could not use it locally offered only the QR path. The design therefore treats every distinct set of bytes as its own door to the same master, adds a door while unlocked on a device where both paths run (a Mac with Chrome runs both in one session), and uses the recovery code to bring a new path in where no door opens. The finding, the bug and the revised design are written out in one door per passkey path.
notes

Not built here: the master vault, the newsroom vault, moving the reading account into it, adding a second path or passkey as a door, retiring a door, and anything that signs the reader in. The brief’s phase five is where those land, after the move. The door record this lab writes is one sgit object (obj-cas-imm-…, content-addressed), encrypted the way sgit encrypts, so sgit’s own code can decrypt it; it is not yet a commit in a tree, so sgit clone of the door would show an empty history. The real door will be a vault with one committed file. Tests: admin/build/test_passkey.mjs drives the page in Chromium with a virtual authenticator that has PRF, checks the derivation against the vectors, and runs the server flow against a stand-in server; the real server is tried by a person with an access key.

The captures are third-party pages, so they are not republished here. This page links to the originals and quotes them briefly, and the sources page lists every capture with its hashes. Anyone the vault is later opened to can check that the bytes are the ones we saw, on the day we saw them.

what

A publication mapping the Portuguese startup ecosystem, beginning with one event. It originates no facts. Everything it carries was published by somebody else; what it adds is a typed graph over that material, a path back to it, and a hashed copy of what it said on the day we read it.
limits

88 frozen files: the event’s own pages, and 7 pages by other publishers about the event. That is enough to report what the event says about itself and what the press says about it, and to notice where they differ. It is nowhere near enough to report on an ecosystem: there is no company registry, no funding record and no institutional source, and every third-party page here is about the event rather than about anything the event does not itself describe. The original brief scoped a country. This is a conference. The scoping argument holds — a closeable graph — but a publication that stops when the doors close on 2026-09-18 has proved nothing except that somebody was available for a week. The real test is whether this is still running in October.
limits

The original brief asked for both languages, and its two source briefs disagreed with each other about whether that was a day-one property. Nothing here is published in Portuguese. Section labels carry a pt alongside the en in the generator, so the second language is a projection to switch on rather than a retrofit — but the switch has not been thrown, and a structural capability is not a translation. There is a named editor of record, which is a person taking responsibility. It is not a legal opinion. The publication therefore does not assess, rank or characterise any named person or company, and the editor role refuses it structurally rather than case by case. It is one organiser’s selection for one event. Several of the organisations are not Portuguese and several are not startups. Treating it as a map of the ecosystem would be the most obvious mistake available here.
disclaimer

Not advice of any kind. Nothing here is investment, business, travel or professional advice, and no reader should act on it. Agent-produced. Research, extraction and drafting are done by software agents. Dinis Cruz reviews every page before publication, which catches what a person catches and not more. Errors of fact and emphasis should be assumed present rather than exceptional. Ticket prices, dates and venues change. Everything here is as published on the frozen copy named beside it. Check the event’s own site before buying anything or travelling anywhere. We do not explain absences. Where a name has left a published list, that is recorded without a reason. Do not read one in.
where

Inside newsroom.sgit.ai as a self-contained folder that can be lifted out whole — its own data, frozen sources, generator and gate. It is built from the 12 May 2026 briefs, which are the documents to read for why any of this is shaped the way it is, and which this section is the first attempt to actually run. The commissioning brief for what comes next — a natively Portuguese newsroom at pt.newsroom.sgit.ai, written for the agent that will build it — is here. The next three things, in order: a second publisher in the register so something can be corroborated; session-to-speaker joins so the graph answers “who is on which stage”; and a post-event snapshot, because the most valuable copy of this list will be the one taken the day after it stops being updated.

What the queries stand on. Each speaker’s own page on the event site is frozen and hashed like every other source. Two things are read from it and nothing is reproduced: the event’s own Topics list for that speaker, verbatim (60 of 64 pages carry one; 23 distinct topics, led by Leadership (37), Founder journey (33), Future of work (19), AI (18), Fundraising (16), European startups (15), Go-to-market (15), Scaling (15)), and the words on the page that match a published lexicon of industries, technologies, ideas, services and products (63 pages match at least one entry; Idea 180 · Service 97 · Industry 78 · Technology 46 · Product 16). A derived tag says the page contains those words. It carries the matched words on the edge and nothing else, and gate 17 re-runs every pattern against the frozen bytes on every build, so a tag cannot be typed in by hand or left out by hand.

Why organisations and not people. The data-protection notice refuses any characterisation of a named person, and “X should talk to Y” is one. So the unit here is the organisation a speaker is listed under; the person-level join is one query away in the SQL console for a reader who wants it, and this page does not make it.

WITH ground AS ( SELECT DISTINCT p.org AS org, t.type AS kind, t.tag AS what FROM person_tags t JOIN people p ON p.id = t.person WHERE t.type IN ('Industry', 'Technology', 'Idea') AND p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) UNION SELECT DISTINCT p.org, 'Topic', pt.topic FROM person_topics pt JOIN people p ON p.id = pt.person WHERE p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ), offers AS ( SELECT DISTINCT p.org AS org, t.tag AS service FROM person_tags t JOIN people p ON p.id = t.person WHERE t.type = 'Service' AND p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ), founder_led AS ( SELECT DISTINCT n.org AS org FROM nodes n WHERE n.type = 'Person' AND n.role_class = 'founder' AND n.org IS NOT NULL AND n.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ) SELECT a.org AS org_a, b.org AS org_b, COUNT(*) AS shared, GROUP_CONCAT(a.kind || ':' || a.what, ' · ') AS on_what FROM ground a JOIN ground b ON a.kind = b.kind AND a.what = b.what AND a.org < b.org GROUP BY a.org, b.org HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ORDER BY shared DESC, org_a, org_b LIMIT 40;

WITH ground AS ( SELECT DISTINCT p.org AS org, t.type AS kind, t.tag AS what FROM person_tags t JOIN people p ON p.id = t.person WHERE t.type IN ('Industry', 'Technology', 'Idea') AND p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) UNION SELECT DISTINCT p.org, 'Topic', pt.topic FROM person_topics pt JOIN people p ON p.id = pt.person WHERE p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ), offers AS ( SELECT DISTINCT p.org AS org, t.tag AS service FROM person_tags t JOIN people p ON p.id = t.person WHERE t.type = 'Service' AND p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ), founder_led AS ( SELECT DISTINCT n.org AS org FROM nodes n WHERE n.type = 'Person' AND n.role_class = 'founder' AND n.org IS NOT NULL AND n.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ) SELECT o.org AS provider, o.service AS offer, f.org AS founder_led, COUNT(g2.what) AS shared, GROUP_CONCAT(g2.kind || ':' || g2.what, ' · ') AS on_what FROM offers o JOIN founder_led f ON f.org <> o.org JOIN ground g1 ON g1.org = o.org JOIN ground g2 ON g2.org = f.org AND g2.kind = g1.kind AND g2.what = g1.what WHERE o.service IN ('investment', 'incubation', 'compute-support', 'advisory', 'coaching') GROUP BY o.org, o.service, f.org HAVING COUNT(g2.what) >= 2 ORDER BY shared DESC, provider, founder_led LIMIT 40;

path

Every page of the source site, pulled into sources/frozen/<date>/. Not one page — all of them, so a claim made from one page can be checked against what the others said on the same day. The copy is committed to this repository. It is what the extractor reads and what a reader can download. The live site is never read at publish time. Every frozen file is hashed and the hash is published. Two runs that produce different hashes mean the source moved, and on this beat that is a story rather than a nuisance. Speakers and organisations are parsed out of the frozen HTML. Organisations are derived from speaker cards rather than typed by hand, so the graph cannot contain an organisation no source mentions. Added, removed, edited — with the hash of both sides. This is the whole reason to keep more than one copy, and it is what turns a directory into a record.
notreproduce

Speaker biographies are not stored as data and not published. They are the speakers’ and the organisers’ own writing, and this publication adds structure over other people’s material rather than republishing it. We hold the frozen page for verification; the reader gets the pointer. Since v0.3.4 each speaker’s own page is frozen too, and two things are read from it: the event’s own Topics list for that speaker, verbatim, and the words that match a published lexicon. The matched words travel on the edge; no sentence of the biography does, and gate 10 fails the build if one ever did. The same rule governs session descriptions and sponsor copy.

why

The basis is legitimate interests, and the journalistic route is deliberately not claimed. The journalistic derogation is not claimed. Article 24(3) of Lei 58/2019 conditions processing for journalistic purposes on the national legislation governing access to and exercise of the profession. This publication is not accredited under it and does not meet that condition, so it does not rely on it. Reporting what a public event has published about itself, and demonstrating a verification method on it. Both are matters of public interest and neither is commercial — the section carries no price, no advertising and no tracking. The reporting cannot be done without the names, because the subject IS who is speaking. The data held is the minimum: the four published professional fields and nothing else. No biography is stored, no contact detail is stored, and no inference about anybody is made or published.
why

Every datum was published by the event itself for the express purpose of announcing these people as speakers, in their professional capacity, and carries no private-life content. Against that: being listed on a third-party site is not something anybody consented to, which is why the objection route below is unconditional rather than assessed. We also record that data having been made public does not by itself mean it may be processed on this basis — it is a factor in the balance, not an answer to it.
notice

Where personal data is not obtained from the person it concerns, Article 14 of the GDPR requires that they be told. Article 14(5)(b) exempts a controller where individual notification would involve disproportionate effort — but that exemption is conditional, and one of the measures it expressly requires is making the information publicly available. This page is that measure. It exists so the exemption is earned rather than assumed, and it was published before this section's first update following the discovery that it was missing. And the part that reflects badly on us. It should have been published at the same time as the pages naming these people, not after. It was not. That is recorded here rather than quietly fixed, and the release note says the same.
rights

Ask what is held about you, and get a copy Have anything inaccurate corrected Object to being included, and be removed Have the removal propagate to every page on the next build, which runs on request rather than on a schedule Complain to the Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados, or to the supervisory authority where you live
object

How. Email the controller above. Say who you are and that you want your entry removed. No reason is required and none will be asked for. Removal is not assessed, argued with or delayed pending a balancing exercise. What happens. The entry is removed from the derived data, the section is rebuilt, and the person's name no longer appears on any page. Because removal changes what the snapshot diff would otherwise show, the changes page records that an entry was removed at the subject's request, with no name — which is the only way to keep the diff honest without re-publishing the name it was asked to remove.
object

We also never say why you left somebody else’s list. Where a name has left the event's own published list between two of our snapshots, this publication records the change and states no reason. Withdrawal, a scheduling clash, a duplicate record and an editing error are indistinguishable from outside, and attaching a motive to a named person on that evidence is the most harmful thing this section could do.
retention

The frozen source snapshots are permanent, because they are the evidence that makes every claim checkable and deleting them would break the method. The derived entity data is rebuilt from them on every run. If a person objects, their entry is removed from the derived data and from every rendered page; the frozen snapshot is not altered, because it is a copy of what somebody else published on a date, not our record of them.

what-the-press-says-is-happening-on-wednesday

On 29 July 2026 two Portuguese outlets published the same story on the same day. AICEP Portugal Global, the state trade and investment agency, and Portugal Business News both reported that Startup Summit Lisbon would host a 48-hour non-stop startup pitch marathon as an official attempt on a Guinness World Records title, with almost a thousand founders taking part, remotely or in person at Unicorn Factory Lisboa's Beato Innovation District, on 16–17 September 2026. Both pages are frozen in this repository with their hashes. Neither is quoted here; the links are in the table at the foot of this page and the wording is theirs.
what-the-event-s-own-agenda-says

The event's agenda page, frozen on 13 September, lists a Welcome Drinks on the evening of the 16th, a Morning Run at 07:30 on the 17th, an Opening Keynote at 09:30, four named sessions across two stages, lunch, investor office hours and a Founder Social. It does not list a pitch marathon. It does not mention a record attempt. The word Guinness does not appear on it. So the honest description is not "the agenda contradicts the press". It is: the two pieces of coverage describe a headline event, and the event's own published programme, as of four days before it, does not carry it. Those are compatible. A summarised agenda can omit things. A record attempt run alongside the summit rather than inside it might live on a different page. This publication does not know which, and says so.
one-page-two-dates

There is a smaller wrinkle inside one of the two reports. Portugal Business News' summary line dates the marathon to 17 September; the body of the same article dates it to 16–17 September. Both are on one page, frozen with one hash. AICEP says 16–17 throughout. That is the kind of thing a reader never notices, because nobody reads a summary line and a body paragraph against each other. A graph layer notices, because it extracts a date from each and finds two.
why-this-is-the-third-story-and-not-the-first

The first story on this site was about a list that changed. The second was about two names for the same three stages. This one is about the gap between what the press says will happen and what the programme says will happen. All three have the same shape, and it is deliberate: publish the record, never the verdict, and no adjective about a named party. None of them says the event is disorganised. what-the-two-copies-say

On 8 September 2026 at 00:43 UTC this publication fetched the Startup Summit Lisbon 2026 speakers page and kept the bytes. the-addition-is-not-a-finding

An event adding five speakers nine days before it opens is an event working exactly as advertised. The speakers page says so itself: more are "announced weekly". Nothing in the growth is surprising, and nobody should read this as a correction to anything. What is worth noticing is smaller and duller. The number in the prose moved with the list — 60 with 60 cards, 64 with 64 cards. A page whose stated count tracks its own contents is a maintained page, and that is more than can be said for most.
so-what-is-the-story

The story is that five days ago this list said something else, and by the time the doors open nothing on the open web will remember what. The earlier version is not archived anywhere the reader can reach. It is not in the page's history, because the page has no history. Search engines will show the current one. An assistant asked "who is speaking at Startup Summit Lisbon" will answer from whatever is live at the moment it is asked, with no sense that the answer had a different shape last week.
so-what-is-the-story

This is the ordinary condition of nearly everything published on the open web, and it is invisible precisely because it is ordinary. A conference speaker list is a harmless example. The same property holds for a company's pricing page, a regulator's guidance, a government consultation and a hospital's waiting-time figure — and it is the reason this network keeps arguing that a link is not evidence, because the thing on the other end of a link is free to change and usually does.
what-it-cost-to-be-able-to-say-this

The expensive part is having done it before you needed it, which means doing it on a cadence when nothing is happening, which is why almost nobody does. the-same-three-rooms-named-twice

Startup Summit Lisbon 2026 has three stages. Every page of its site agrees on that, and every page agrees that one of them is called Workshop Rooms. The other two depend on which page you open. The agenda schedules sessions on the Unicorn Stage and the Impact Stage — AI or Die and The LP Perspective on one, The Fundraising Meta-Game on the other. The what-to-expect page and the speakers page use those names too. The AI-summary page lists "3 stages (Main Stage, Startup Stage, Workshop Rooms)". The sponsors page sells "naming rights for one of the three stages (Main Stage, Startup Stage, or Workshop Rooms)". Two disjoint sets, split cleanly by page, published simultaneously by the same event on the same site, in copies frozen and hashed on 13 September 2026.
a-likely-explanation-which-is-not-a-finding

The venue is Unicorn Factory Lisboa, in the Beato Innovation District. That is stated in the event's own llms.txt and nowhere else on the site — the human-facing pages name only the district. A stage called the Unicorn Stage in a venue called the Unicorn Factory is not a coincidence, and the obvious reading is that Main Stage and Startup Stage are the earlier, generic names and the venue-specific ones came later. The pages carrying the older names would then be the ones nobody has revisited. That reading is an inference and this publication is not publishing it as a fact. The event has not said which set is current. The opposite explanation — that the agenda is a draft and the formal names are the generic ones — fits the same evidence. Both are recorded; neither is resolved. If the event states which is correct, that statement becomes the source and this note gets a correction.
why-a-naming-wobble-is-worth-a-page

On its own it is worth almost nothing. Nobody will fail to find a room. The two sets are not contradictory in any way that matters to somebody standing in Beato with a lanyard on. It is worth a page for two reasons that have nothing to do with this event. First, it is the cheapest possible demonstration of what a graph layer does that reading does not. No human reads a conference website end to end holding all of it in their head. A reader opens the agenda, or opens the sponsors page, and each is internally consistent. The inconsistency only exists between pages, which is exactly the place where nobody is looking. Extracting typed entities from every page of a site and comparing them is a five-line diff, and it surfaces the class of problem that human proof-reading is structurally bad at.
why-a-naming-wobble-is-worth-a-page

Second, it is a rehearsal on something harmless. The same technique pointed at a regulator's guidance, where one page defines a term one way and another page defines it differently, finds something with consequences. This site's sibling publication has a whole section about regulatory texts where exactly that matters — and cannot currently do this, because its ingestion path was specified and never built. Here it runs. Running it first against a conference's stage names is how you find out whether it works before you point it at something where being wrong is expensive.
what-this-note-does-not-say

It does not say the event is disorganised, careless, or misleading anybody. An event mid-way through naming its rooms, with two of its pages not yet updated, is an event in the perfectly ordinary condition of every website that has more than three pages and more than one person editing them. It says: there are two published answers to the same question, both live right now, and nothing on the open web was checking.

Stage Cost Research £3.20 Reporting £2.80 Fact-checking £0.90 Translation (EN ↔ PT) £1.10 Graphics £0.40 Total £8.40
process

Zero human hours is stated plainly, not smoothed over — this is a design for an agent-produced story, and the ledger says so rather than implying a journalist's byline did work an agent actually did. Twelve sources were consulted; two received expert validation rather than being taken at face value. Three separate reader contributions were incorporated during production, and the story went through four draft versions, each recorded with a change log rather than overwritten.
why-persuasive

Every other page in this section argues that transparency is possible in principle. This page is what that principle looks like as a real ledger for one specific story, with a currency symbol and a line-item breakdown instead of an adjective. The economics section is the argument for why a ledger this granular also makes per-source payment computable — the £3.20 research line is not an abstraction, it is a number that could, in principle, be split among the sources that made the research possible.
tension

Provenance is the product — and provenance is expensive. £8.40 and 6h 23m for one story is the argument and, simultaneously, the objection: a wire-service rewrite costs a fraction of that and ships in minutes. Whether a reader, or an advertiser, or a subscription market will pay the premium for the itemised version is an open question this site does not resolve.

Under this design, each article is not a single HTML file with metadata bolted on. It is a vault: the published text, the evidence it cites, the story graph it belongs to, the source list, the translations, and every prompt and decision that produced it, held together as one addressable unit.
what-a-vault-holds

The published article is one projection out of a vault that also contains the research notes, the fact-check log, the draft history with a change log between versions, the source citations with their own provenance, and — distinctively — every prompt and decision that produced it. That last piece is what makes the design's transparency claim structural rather than aspirational: the provenance is not a report written after the fact about how the story was made, it is a by-product of how the story was actually made, captured as it happened.
delivery

How a vault is actually served as a website — static shells, read-only vault content, mini-site deployment, vault CI — belongs to sgit.ai, not to this site. This section covers what a vault holds and why holding it that way makes provenance-as-product structural; the delivery substrate is cited, not re-explained. One documented failure mode carries over from the delivery substrate and is worth naming here rather than only on the network page: a client-side-assembled vault page can be invisible to a crawler. For a news site, that is not a minor UX concern — it is close to existential, since most of a news site's reach comes from being findable by search and by other agents. See the network page.

Traditional newsrooms have an editorial process readers never see — who tipped the story, who reported it, who checked it, what it cost, what changed between drafts. A newsroom that shows its work earns trust that a black-box newsroom cannot. The differentiator is not the byline; it is the walkable chain. every-claim-links

Most articles do not provide evidence, they provide a link. The link is never followed, and it could go to a site that no longer exists. There is no reference of what references what. Provenance-as-product means every claim carries a citation the reader can actually follow, and the review process that produced the article is itself a public, walkable artefact — a decision graph with named ownership at every step, not a black box that emits a byline.

Traditional newsrooms have an editorial process readers never see. A newsroom that shows its work earns trust that a black-box newsroom cannot. The design makes the newsroom's own departments public pages, not an internal org chart.
departments

Rather than a single opaque "editorial" function, the newsroom design splits into fifteen departments — assignment, research, reporting, translation, fact-checking, graphics, community, and others through to the corrections desk — and each one is specified as a page a reader can visit, not a role that only shows up in a byline. A reader can see who tipped a story, who was assigned to it, what it bounced back for, and what it cost before it ever reached them.
corrections-desk

Not a form buried three clicks deep. Under this design, corrections have the same standing as reporting or fact-checking — a department with its own public page, its own record of what was corrected, when, and why. That is the site's own most distinctive argument given an organisational home rather than left as an abstract principle.
not-yes-no

"A decision should never be a yes or no. A decision should always be a graph that collects a bunch of evidence." Editorial review under this design is not a single approve/reject gate — it is a sequence of named, owned steps, each contributing evidence to the final decision rather than replacing it. The decision graph, in full.
"A decision should never be a yes or no. A decision should always be a graph that collects a bunch of evidence." Editorial review, redesigned as a chain of owned steps rather than a single gate.
ownership

Under this design, every stage of a story's production — research, drafting, fact-checking, translation, graphics, publish — is owned by a specific role, human or agent, whose decision at that stage is itself recorded as part of the story's graph. "The question becomes who takes ownership." A story is not "approved" by an undifferentiated editorial function; it accumulates a trail of specific, attributable decisions.
spectrum

Not every step needs the same human involvement, and the design does not pretend otherwise. Some steps — a first-pass source scan, a translation draft — are specified to run near-entirely by agent, with human review as a spot-check. Others — a legal risk judgement, a decision to run a story naming a real person — are specified to require full human ownership. The point is not to maximise automation everywhere; it is to place human attention where it actually changes the outcome. "There is no point having humans in the loop who just approve without context, that is not human in the loop." A human rubber-stamping a decision they were not given the evidence to actually evaluate is not oversight. It is a compliance ritual wearing oversight's name. The decision graph exists specifically so the human step in any given decision has the same evidence trail everyone downstream will see — not a summary, the actual graph.
relation

The £8.40 worked story is what this decision graph produces when it runs end to end on one real story. The newsroom section covers the roles that own each step and the daily operational clock that sequences them.

For publishers, journalists and anyone thinking about the future of news

For the last two months I have been writing about where publishing could go: readers who pay for what they actually read, after they have read it; personas instead of profiles; stories kept as evidence; agents as readers, and as part of the newsroom. On 11 October it stopped being a set of articles, and I wrote the first version of this page to say so. In the week since, this site shipped more than in the month before: the meter now charges for what you read rather than how far you scroll, an article remembers what you have read and folds it away when you come back, every article can be reviewed on the record, and your reading follows you between devices in a vault only you can open. So this page is now built with every release, from the same register of features the rest of the site uses, and it keeps its own version history. It is a first version of a newsroom: parts are rough, and the workflow changes most days. But the mechanism is live, end to end, and I would rather you try it than read about it.

This page: v2.0.0, 18 Oct 2026, every version and what changed. Built with newsroom.sgit.ai v0.13.131: 323 articles, 20 features a publisher can use today, the newest article 29 Oct. Open newsroom.sgit.ai →. No sign-up. You start with £5.00 of free credit, kept in your own browser.
what-it-is-in-one-paragraph

A news site where every page has a price of a few pence, and you pay for the share of it you actually read, after you read it, from a balance kept in your own browser. Read is measured as time spent on each section against its words, not as how far you scrolled: a page flicked through in seconds costs a tenth of its price, a page read costs its price. You never hit a wall: the balance can go below zero and nothing is blocked. At the foot of each article you say how useful it was, and that sets what you pay, from nothing to double. Come back to an article and the sections you have already read fold away, so you see what is new to you. What you read builds personas, several per reader, and a front page for each. Nothing about your reading leaves your browser unless you choose to send it, and then only encrypted; if you want it on your other devices, it travels in an encrypted vault opened with your passkey. When you want to pay, it is one £5 payment on Stripe's page: no account, no subscription, nothing renews. The articles are written by agents from my voice notes, reviewed on the record by other models and by me, and every article keeps its full version history.
try-it-in-five-minutes

Open the front page and read one article, as far as it deserves. Watch the chip at the foot of the page: it says how much of each section you have read and what the page will cost, never more than its price (a new article is 10p, an older one 5p). I just want to buy the article is a good first one, because it is the argument for this model written for publishers. At the foot of the article, rate it. How useful was it (1 is free, 5 is double), do you want more like it, and was the level of detail right. If something was wrong with the page, say so and you are not charged.
try-it-in-five-minutes

Come back to it. Open the same article tomorrow, or scroll back up: the sections you read can show as a line in the margin, faded, folded to a paragraph or a line, or hidden. You choose in the chip's Settings, for every article or for one. You are only charged for what you read beyond last time; pause the meter, or reset a page, whenever you like. Open Your account. What you opened, what it cost, and the balance, all from your browser's own storage. Export it as JSON if you like: it is yours. Read as someone else. Open the newsroom as Rowan, the journalist, or as a founder, a security lead, an AI builder or a board member. Each one is a link you can send to someone. Or make a reading list for a colleague: a link that opens the newsroom as the articles you chose for them, with your note.
try-it-in-five-minutes

Optional, and real: top up £5 on the top-up page. It is a real card payment on Stripe's page, live since 11 October. Optional: open your vault with a passkey, and the same reading account, notes and personas are on your phone and your laptop. The newsroom holds no key to it. From the same pane you can send the newsroom a note about any sentence you select.

Each of these ideas exists somewhere else on its own. Micropayments have been tried; recommendation engines are everywhere; privacy-first sites exist. What I have not seen is all of them together, working, in one publication: paying for what you read, after you read it, with no wall; the reader keeping their own data and their own personas; agents treated as readers with their own door; and a newsroom whose own rules, reviews and decisions are public. You may have seen it somewhere, and if you have, I would genuinely like to know. The reader comes first, on purpose. Every decision started from one rule: do not rip off the reader. No wall, no nag, no subscription to forget, no charge for a page that was not worth it, and since last week, no charge for a page that was only scrolled.

Personalisation without surveillance. The site knows what you read only inside your browser and your own vault. The value is a front page made for you, not a profile of you sold to someone else. The reading meter is a library any site can add, the reader's side is published at api.newsroom.sgit.ai, and the newsroom publishes how to replicate it. Quality control you can see. Every article has its versions, its sources and its reviews on the page, and every finding gets an answer. A correction is a new version, dated and linkable, not a silent edit. Reviews · criteria v1.2

Criteria v1.2, 27 October 2026. (v1.2 adds what the first scheduled review, ChatGPT's of The evidence behind four days, showed a fact check needs: each finding says how it failed (verification), with the source's own words and the calculation or query behind it, and the record lists the claims checked and found sound and those not checked. It adds the review queue, which says what to review next, and the review lane, which takes a review from anyone with its link. v1.1 answered the questions the first reviewer raised: which text is canonical, what each verdict means, product names, conversions with nothing to convert, the severity of a weak link, and where the files are.) For any reviewer: an agent from any vendor, an open-weight model, the editor, a journalist on the desk, and later a reader who signs what they write. Read all of this before the first review, and again when the version above changes.
what-a-review-is

A review is a record. It is about one article, at one version of its text, by one reviewer, against these criteria. It is kept beside the article for good, shown on the article's page, and answered by the newsroom, finding by finding. It is not a comment thread and it is not a rewrite: it says what is wrong, where, why, and what would fix it, and it says what was checked and found sound. Three rules make it scale: One reviewer, one article, one text: one review. If you have reviewed an article and its text has not changed, do not review it again. The status file below says what you have done. Batches, newest first. Take the next five articles you have not reviewed at their current text, not the whole site.
what-a-review-is

Read your own past reviews first. They are in the status file and in the records. Do not repeat a finding the newsroom has already answered; if you disagree with its answer, say so in a new finding that cites it.
before-you-start

Know your reviewer id. The registered reviewers are in status.json under reviewers (the source is admin/content/reviews/reviewers.json; status.json is rebuilt from it at every release). If you are not there, use <vendor>-<product> in lower case (for example openai-chatgpt) and say which model you are in the record's model field; the newsroom registers you when your first review arrives. Find your batch. The newsroom keeps a queue for each scheduled reviewer at https://newsroom.sgit.ai/reviews/queue/<your id>.json (and .md, and the page queue/): today's articles, in the editor's order, each with its hash, why it was chosen and the findings to recheck. Take today's batch from it. With no queue for your id, in status.json, each article has its current hash and the reviews it has. Your batch is the five newest articles with no review by your id at the current hash. Articles you reviewed at an older hash come after every article you have never reviewed. With repository access, the same list is:
before-you-start

`` python3 admin/build/reviews.py --next <your id> --batch 5 `` Read the article as written. The source is https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/<slug>.md (in the repository, admin/content/articles/<slug>.md), the page is https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/<slug>.html, and the graph is /articles/graphs/<slug>.json. The page's text is canonical: it is what the hash is made from and what quotes are checked against, so copy a quote as a reader sees it, without link brackets or URLs. Read the articles it says it builds on where a claim depends on them, and open the sources it links.
the-questions
Answer each one for each article: pass, issues, or not-checked. Say not-checked rather than guess; a review that checked three things well is worth more than one that skimmed six.
1-facts

Every number, name, date and version: is it what the linked source says, on the date given? Every quote: is it word for word, and is it attributed to the right person or document? Every link: does it make the point it is cited for? A link to a page that does not support the sentence is a finding even if the sentence is true. Every count: does the article say what counted it, and does the count hold if you count again? Is anything stated as built that is only proposed, or as documented that is only reported? Has anything changed since the article was published that makes a statement wrong today? Say so, with the date of the change; that is a finding about the article's health, not an error at the time.
2-voice

Most articles are written by an agent in Dinis Cruz's voice, from his voice memos. The question is whether he would say it. What his articles do: First person, and honest about where he stands: "I think", "my hypothesis", "I could not find who said it". The memo's order, including the turn that looks like a tangent and turns out to be the connection. Plain words for concrete things: the file, the commit, the button, the vault, the lane. Say what the other side gets right, then add what is missing; turn the question round; name the test and where it comes from; then where things actually stand, with the counts. Public sources named and dated; private people never named. What he would not say, each one a finding:
2-voice

Superlative self-claims. "The clearest example I have seen", "the best case study I can think of", "one of the clearest statements", "the best brief ever written". They claim more than an article can show. Praise and hype. For the work, for us, or for a vendor: "groundbreaking", "game-changing", "incredible". "Great" is the strongest word, and it is for a thing. Absolutes without a count. "Nobody has", "the first to", "never scaled", "everyone knows". Overstated feelings or events. A small thing described as a turning point; a disagreement described as a fight. Certainty the evidence does not carry. A forecast stated as a fact; a vendor's claim stated as the article's own.
2-voice

The house wording rules: no em-dashes; British spelling; "great", not "perfect"; not "massively"; not "prose" for the article; never the word for a step of a ladder; no "obviously"; and no naming of the model that wrote the article. Products are named when the article is about them (an agent product, a vault for it, the tool that did a setup); that is not a finding.
3-claims-and-limits

Is what exists, what is documented and what is proposed marked as such? Does What this does not claim cover the real weaknesses, or only safe ones? Where the article corrects the voice memo, does it say so?
4-conversions-and-translations

Currency, units, percentages and dates: is each conversion right, with the rate or the basis and its date? A percentage from two numbers: does the arithmetic hold? A quote translated from another language: is it marked as a translation, with the original linked? The same number in the summary, In short, the body, a figure, a caption and the graph: is it the same everywhere? Nothing to convert is a pass, with a note saying so and that the same-number check was done.
5-health

Links that no longer resolve, or that now point somewhere else. Figures whose captions do not match the text, or that a reader cannot read on a phone. In short and the summary: do they say what the body says? The section summaries (shown when a reader folds a section): stale or wrong? The graph: do its quotes appear in the article, and do its links point at articles that make the point? Anything the newsroom said it would do in the article that has not happened since.
6-people-and-safety
A private person named, or a private message quoted. A key, a token, a password, or anything that looks like one. A claim about a named person or company that the sources do not support.
severity

high: a wrong fact, a misquote, a misattribution, a link that says the opposite, a private person named, anything that looks like a secret. medium: an overstated claim, a missing caveat, a voice slip a reader would notice, a stale statement, a number that differs between two places. low: wording, spelling, a better link, a figure that could be clearer. A link that does not support its sentence is medium when the sentence carries a quote or a number attributed to the source, and low otherwise. A link that now redirects somewhere else is medium if the content is gone, low if it only moved.
the-record

One file per article reviewed, in the article's folder: admin/content/articles/reviews/<slug>/<YYYY-MM-DD>__<reviewer id>.json If a second review by you of the same article is due on the same day (the text changed), add __2.

the-record

verdict is one of: approve: no findings, or only low ones you would accept as they are; approve-with-changes: findings to fix, none high; changes-needed: any high finding, or a medium one that changes what the article claims; comment: a note on the record rather than a verdict (the editor's later notes, an expert's opinion). kind is agent, editor, journalist or reader. section is the section's anchor, from the {#...} after its heading; top for the part before the first heading. quote is copied from the article's current text, exactly, so the finding can be found. Keep it short: the words that are wrong, not the paragraph. article_hash is the hash for the article in status.json when you started. With the repository, leave it out and run python3 admin/build/reviews.py --stamp straight after writing the record. verification (v1.2) says how the claim failed, so findings can be counted across reviews: contradicted: a source says otherwise;
the-record

unsupported: the cited source does not say it, and none found does; inconsistent: the article says two different things (a number in two places, a date that cannot be both); overstated: the source supports a weaker claim than the article makes (a forecast stated as observed, a correlation stated as a cause); unverifiable: the source could not be reached or read (a paywall, a dead link), so the claim is not checked; stale: true when published, wrong today, with the date of the change; style: voice and wording, not fact. It is optional for voice findings and expected for every facts, claims and conversions finding. source_passage is the source's own words that show the problem, copied; method is the arithmetic, the query or the steps, so the newsroom can repeat the check. A conversion or a count without its method is a weak finding.
the-record

verified and not_checked (v1.2) are short lists: the material claims you checked and found sound, with their source, and the ones you did not check, with why. A clean bill of health is a finding too: the next reviewer starts from it. When a source may change (a count, a catalogue, a live page), say in the finding's evidence when you read it; the newsroom rechecks it, and the queue asks the next reviewer to recheck it. A finding without a quote is allowed only for something missing ("the limits do not mention…"). Write nothing else in the file. No markdown, no commentary outside the JSON.
sending-it

The review lane (v1.2): open the send link the editor gave you (https://newsroom.sgit.ai/reviews/send.html#rv1…, also as a QR code), paste everything you wrote, records and all, and press Check: the page finds the records, checks each one against these criteria and the article's current text, and says what is wrong before anything is sent. Send seals them in the browser to the newsroom's key and appends them to the lane, which the newsroom drains on a schedule. Anyone with the link can add to the lane; nobody with it can read it. A reviewer that runs on a schedule and cannot open pages writes its records in its answer, and whoever reads the answer pastes it there. A pull request to the dev branch of the newsroom's repository, touching only files under admin/content/articles/reviews/. One pull request per batch. Title: review: <reviewer id>, <n> articles.
