- Consolidating two devices the vault already has into one row (merge files, retire the id). The alias machinery is most of it; the ask was "we might need to", so it waits for the need. Nothing is deleted meanwhile, which is the rule the ask set for payment records. - Automatic sync on a timer or on leaving a page (card 029); the inbound side now runs on an explicit open, the outbound side is still a press. - A choice of device on the sending side. The link would have to carry the devices; it stays minimal. - The table's pennies. Each device's spend is rounded to a tenth of a penny before it is shown at two decimals, so the column can add to a penny less than the total. Top-ups now show a dash in the total when there are none, as the rows do.
tests

admin/build/testsync.mjs: inbound() before and after a merge; a cleared browser taking a device as its own; refile(); a write combined with the file as it is. testpane.mjs: nothing to name before opening; device B asked which device it is, choosing a new one, and the vault's records coming in on their own with the account's balance; device C opening with the recovery code and taking device B as its own: B's read is its own there, A's is tagged A, the id and label are B's, the balance is the account's, nothing left to bring in. testinbox.mjs: the File under choice before anything is brought in, B's batch filed under A itself, A's own notes and one row across the devices, the choice remembered in the master. testnotes.mjs: device B through the chooser.

13 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.7; Ask in v0.12.9. Status: running, on every page through the Search link in the nav. The cards are 031 (search), 032 (a test made robust on the way) and 033 (asking the site). The page is /search/.
in-short

- Dinis's guess was right: most of a search engine was already published. Every page has clean HTML with anchored headings and a .md twin; every article has a teaser, topics, tags and a graph whose nodes name its ideas; every article keeps its earlier versions; the wire keeps a snapshot of its headlines. What was missing was an index and a ranking, and both fit in a static site. - The index is built at release. admin/build/searchindex.py reads every page in the sitemap and writes two files: search/docs.json (one entry per page: title, kind, number, date, teaser, topics, tags, the graph's core idea and node labels, headings with anchors; about 290 KB) and search/text.json (the text in paragraphs, each with its anchor; about 4 MB, served compressed). - The ranking runs in the reader's browser. assets/search/search.js fetches the two files from this site and ranks with BM25 over fields and paragraphs. Searching sends nothing anywhere. - It finds what changed. For each article, the paragraphs of its earlier versions that are no longer in it are indexed with the version they read that way in, so a sentence that has since been corrected is still found, and the result links to the version page that shows the change. - Ask: a model that answers from the same index (v0.12.9, card 033): Chrome's built-in model where the browser has it, or the reader's own OpenRouter key, with the passages it was given shown under the answer and cited by number.
what-is-searched-and-how-much-each-part-counts

A page's score is its fields plus its best paragraph plus a third of the next two, multiplied by the square of the share of the query's words it contains at all, so a page with every word beats a page with one word many times; then by its kind (an article counts a little more than a page, the archive less). Pages of every kind are in it: 97 articles, the newsletter, collections, the desk, the decks, the wire's 40 stories (from its snapshot), the engineering cards, this site's notes and the other pages, 375 documents and about 5,600 paragraphs at the time of writing.
the-query

- Words are folded (case, accents) and lightly stemmed, so agents finds agent and thinking finds think. Common words are dropped unless they are all there is. - "Quotes" require the exact phrase, in the page or in an earlier version of it. - A number alone is that article: 97 opens Who owns the words. - The last word is also a prefix, so results come as you type. - Soft phrases: the whole query, and anything typed as one token that is really several, such as agent@riskmandate.ai, count for more where they appear together, without being required. - Filters: everything, articles, the wire, engineering, pages, the archive; and, with the reader's records, hide what I marked done. A result the reader has read says so, and how far; one they decided about says how. The address keeps the query (/search/?q=…&f=articles), so a search can be linked to.
why-not-a-bigger-engine

A search service would need a server and would see every query. A prebuilt inverted index would be larger than the text it indexes at this size. Lunr or a similar library would add a dependency for what is a few hundred lines. The two JSON files are regenerated with the site, cached by the browser like any file, and readable by an agent that wants to rank them its own way.
what-is-not-built

- The live wire. The index holds the wire's snapshot, taken at release; stories added to the vault since are on the wire page, not in search, until the next release. - Search inside the vault pane, over the reader's own notes and reading. - Synonyms and spelling: a misspelt word finds nothing; the prefix helps only from the start of a word.
asking-the-site-card-033-v0-12-9

The search page has an Ask button beside Search. The question is searched with the same index; passagesFor (in assets/search/ask.js) takes the best paragraph of each of the top pages, two from the very best, up to eight, each cut to about 700 characters, current wording only (text that is only in an earlier version is left out, so an answer is never built on a sentence the site has since corrected). They are numbered and given to a model with one instruction: answer only from them, cite them by number, and say so when they do not hold the answer. The answer is shown with the passages under it, each linked to its page and section; a citation is a link to its passage, and a number with no passage behind it stays plain text. What the model is given shows the instruction, the question and the passages, exactly as sent. Which model answers, in order:
asking-the-site-card-033-v0-12-9

1. Chrome's built-in model (the Prompt API: LanguageModel, or the older window.ai.languageModel), when the browser has it. It runs on the reader's machine: no key, nothing sent. The first use may download the model, once; the page shows the progress. 2. The reader's own OpenRouter key, pasted under How questions are answered, with a model (by default openrouter/auto). The key is kept in the tab's session storage, and in local storage only when the reader ticks Keep the key in this browser; Forget the key takes it out of both. It is sent to openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions in the Authorization header, with the question and the passages in the body, and nowhere else: this site has no server to send it to. The page says which model answered and how many characters and tokens were sent. When the built-in model is there but cannot answer, the key is used and the page says why. 3. Neither: the page says so, and Ask shows the passages alone.
asking-the-site-card-033-v0-12-9
?q=…&ask=1 in the address asks on arrival, so a question can be a link.
what-is-not-built

- The key in the master vault, typed once for every device, like the access key. - A conversation: each question is asked fresh, with its own passages. - Tools: the model cannot search again or open a page; sgit.ai's site chat (assets/site-chat.js on sgit.ai) has that, and is the next step if one round of passages is not enough. - Answers kept as notes, sent to the newsroom through the lane like any other note.

13 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.26. Card 049. The request and the brief are the article Sixteen notes I did not want to lose (No. 105). The sending page is /vault/send.html; the link is made in the vault pane's Vault tab.
in-short

- The problem. The vault opens with a passkey, and some browsers cannot reach one: a web view an app opens a link in, a browser signed in to nothing, an old iPad. What they hold stayed there, counted on the Vault button as changes only in this browser. The only way in without the passkey was the recovery code, which opens the master: too much power for a job that only needs to add. - The answer is a lane. Every account can have an inbox: an append lane on the reader vault that any browser can write to and none can read, and a key pair made in the reader's browser whose private half is in the master. The link carries where to write and the key to encrypt to, nothing else. - A browser with the link sends its own device file, the same file the vault already holds for every device, sealed to the key. The vault takes it in the next time it is opened with the passkey: the pane lists what is waiting, opens it, shows it, and on one press writes it into the reader vault as that browser's file, so the merge that already exists brings it in, with that browser as the author. - Nothing new on the server. The append routes (/api/vault/append/ on dev.send.sgraph.ai), the envelope (sgit's hybrid v2) and the device files existed; the pieces new here are the reader's key pair, the link, the sending page and the drain.
the-four-capabilities

The append-lanes API splits what a lane can do into four, and the design puts each where it belongs: The link is https://newsroom.sgit.ai/vault/send.html#sgi1.<reader vault id.<append token.<public key, SPKI, base64url, about 650 characters. The fragment never reaches a server, and the sending page takes it out of the address once it has kept it, so a copied address or a screenshot does not carry it.
the-flow

1. Make the link (the Vault tab, unlocked): a key pair in this browser; a random append token (16 bytes) and enum key (32 bytes); configure on the reader vault with appendanchors: [sha256(token)] and enumkeyhash, with the reader vault's write key and the access key from the master; the record inbox.json written into the master. 2. Send (any browser, vault/send.html, or Send to my vault in the strip above the pane once a link is kept): extract() this browser's own records into one device file, wrap it as {kind: "sgit-newsroom-inbox/v1", to: <key fingerprint, sentat, file}, seal it (a fresh AES-256-GCM key wrapped with RSA-OAEP, the envelope {v: 2, w, i, c}, base64 twice as the API documents), and POST /append/write with the token. The answer is {"ok": true} and nothing else. The browser keeps every record; the time of the send becomes its last update, so the count goes to zero. 3. Drain (the Vault tab, every time it is drawn, and on Look in the lane): list with the enum key, fetch each lane's pending files, open each with the private key, check it. Valid messages are listed by the name the browser gave itself, the time and what they carry; refused ones with the reason. 4. Bring them in: each browser's files combined (combine(): every record of either, the one that knows more where both have it), combined again with the file already in the vault for that browser, written, one publish; mark-processed; then the merge every device already uses, which reloads the page and says what arrived. 5. A new link: a new token, the same key; configure replaces the anchors, so the old token is refused (404). It waits until the lane is empty, so nothing is stranded in a lane no anchor names.
what-is-refused

A message that does not open with the key (sealed to another one), one whose ciphertext was changed (AES-GCM's tag fails), one that opens but is not a newsroom inbox message, is addressed to another key's fingerprint, carries a browser id that is not a plain file name, or has notes that claim another browser. They are listed and can be discarded; nothing in them is merged. What is not refused: a well-formed message from whoever holds the link. That is the brief's model: the link writes, it does not prove who wrote. The drain shows the browser's name, its platform, the time and the counts before anything is brought in, and a new link stops the old one.
choices-and-why

- RSA-OAEP 3072, not 4096. The sgit CLI makes 4096-bit keys. 3072 is 128-bit security, and it keeps the link at about 650 characters and the QR code at 89 modules, which a phone camera reads off a laptop screen; at 4096 the link is about 820 characters and the code 97 modules. - The device file as the message. Inventing a second format for the same records would have needed a second merge. A browser that sends through the inbox is a device like any other: it gets a row across the devices, and its records keep it as their author. - The lane on the reader vault, not a new vault. The brief asks for it there; it keeps the account at four vaults (door, master, reader, the newsroom lane) and the inbox's files out of every commit tree (bare/append/…). - The sending page loads no vault library. It reads local storage, encrypts with Web Crypto and makes one POST, so it works where nothing else of the vault does.
not-built

- Expiry. The append routes have no expiry on a token; a date in the link would be honoured by this page and by nobody else. A new link is the revocation the server enforces. - Signatures. A sender holds no key; the link is the credential, as for the subscribe form. - Purge of processed files (write key and access key; a later release). - The reply lane (card 015): the newsroom answering under a message. The same machinery, pointed the other way. - An A/B test of the link against a pairing flow, which the article proposes.
tests

admin/build/testinbox.mjs: in Node, the link, the envelope, the refusals and combine(); in Chromium, against the mock of the vault API (now with the append routes), browser A with a virtual passkey makes the account and the link (the QR code decoded back with jsQR), browser B with no passkey at all reads, keeps notes and sends twice, three bad messages are appended beside them, A brings B's in and refuses the three, discards them, makes a new link, and the old one can no longer write.

13 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.6. Status: a beta with one named reader. It applies The site is an inbox to the Industry Wire, on the pieces of the feedback loop and the activity vault. The cards are on the engineering board, 023 to 030.
in-short

- The wire is read as an inbox. Every story the reader has not decided about is in it; a decision takes the story out. The state to return to is empty. - New means first seen in this visit. Every story drawn is recorded as seen; a story nobody had drawn for this reader before, on any of their devices, carries a New flag until the visit ends. A reload keeps the visit. - For me and not for me come from the lens the reader reads as, which is now remembered, and from the join the wire's vault records. The bar says how many new stories are for the reader and how many are not, and the not-for-me ones can be checked and corrected. - What changed comes from the vault. When the wire's agent publishes a release note (the release file, below), the bar shows the releases since the last visit; until it does, it shows the head commit's message and says the vault publishes no release notes yet. - Local first, update explicitly, and see what you would lose. Decisions and seen stories are kept in the browser as they happen and reach the reader vault only on Update the vault. Until then the Vault button carries a count, the pane a strip, and the wire a line with Update the vault one press away.
the-workflow

1. The desk updates the vault. Dinis asks the wire's agent for a new edition, and for a description of what changed, written as a release (the release file). That is a commit to the wire's vault; this site needs no release to show it. 2. Open the wire. The bar at the top says: since your last visit, N new stories, X for you and Y not for you; what the desk says changed, release by release, with the stories added and updated; and the counts per filter. 3. Work the inbox. At each story, one tap: Done (processed), Read later, Follow up (act on it, or write about it), Not for me, More like this, Wrong. Each is a note with the story's id and takes the story out of the inbox, with undo. Under a lens, the stories withheld from you are listed per beat with the join's reason; on those, Should reach me says the join missed you, and Done clears them. 4. Look back by filter. Inbox, New, Read later, Follow up, Done, Everything. In Everything and Done a decided story folds to its headline. 5. Update the vault. Explicitly, from the wire's bar, the pane's strip or the Vault tab. One file per device, rewritten whole, one commit, as before; it now also carries the stories seen, so another device does not show them as new. 6. Send to the newsroom, when the decisions should reach the desk: the notes go down the reader's own lane (the feedback loop), and the desk reads them with the lane's read key.
the-records

Kinds: done, read-later, follow-up, not-for-me, more-like-this, wrong. A story with any note is decided; the latest note is its state. Notes brought in from another device count as decisions here, and say which device made them.
what-new-means

A visit starts when the wire is opened in a tab that has not opened it before; it lasts as long as the tab. When the edition is drawn, every story not yet in seen is recorded with the time. A story is New when it was recorded in this visit, here. So: the first visit to the wire in a browser shows every story as new; a reload keeps them new; the next visit shows only stories that arrived since. When another device's activity is brought in through the vault, its seen stories come too, tagged with that device, and are not new here.
for-me-and-not-for-me

The lens is the persona the reader reads as. It is taken from the address (#lens=), else the lens chosen last time, else the active persona of the meter when it maps to one of the wire's. Under a lens, the wire's own join (data/deliveries.json, written by the vault's code, not by this page) says which stories reached the reader and which were withheld, with the reason. The bar splits the new stories by it, and every beat lists what was withheld. Without a lens, every story is in the inbox and the bar suggests choosing one.
the-release-file

For the agent that keeps the wire's vault. This is what Dinis asks for when they ask you to "describe what changed on the release". On every publish of an edition or a change to one, add an entry at the top of data/releases.json in the vault, in the same commit as the change:
the-release-file

- One entry per publish, newest first, never edited afterwards; a correction is a new entry. - at is the time of the commit, in UTC, ISO 8601. The page shows the entries newer than the reader's last visit, or the latest one when none is newer. - added, updated, withdrawn are story ids from data/bundle.json. The page links each to its story and marks updated stories with an Updated flag. - summary is plain text, a few sentences, written for the named reader: what changed and what deserves attention. No markup; the page draws it as text. - The commit message starts with the release id, so the history and the file agree. Until the file exists, the page shows the head commit's message and says the vault publishes no release notes yet. Nothing else in the vault's contract with this site changes (how the wire works).
local-first-update-explicitly-and-see-what-you-would-lose

Everything here is kept in this browser first, and nothing is sent until the reader presses something. The cost of that rule is that until the reader updates the vault, what they did exists in one browser only, and clearing it loses it. So the site counts what the vault does not have yet (assets/vault-pane/pending.js): reads started, rated or declined, top-ups, notes kept, given words or sent, after this device's last update; and, separately, stories seen. The count of things done is on the Vault button, with an amber dot; the pane has a strip above its tabs that names them, with Update the vault; the wire's bar has the same line. Updating is still an explicit press: automatic or regular sync is a later decision (card 029).
what-is-not-built

- The release file in the wire's vault (card 026): this site reads it; the wire's agent writes it. Until then the head commit's message stands in. - Automatic or regular sync (029), on purpose: explicit first. - The desk reading the decisions (030): a Not for me or a Should reach me is the signal the join needs, and today it reaches the desk only if the reader sends it down their lane and the wire's agent reads that lane. The morning read in the vault's own workflows writes to a feedback file in the vault, which a reader with a read key cannot do; the lane is how it gets there without a write key. - Editions as history. The page reads the vault's current bundle; a story that left the bundle is gone from the page, though the reader's decision about it remains. - The front page (017): it is imported, so the decisions are on the wire and on article pages only.
the-experiments

1. A week of morning reads by the named reader: how long the inbox takes to empty, which decisions are used, how often a Should reach me appears. 2. Two devices: decide on the phone, update, open the wire on the laptop: nothing the phone saw is new, the decisions are there. 3. The first release file from the wire's agent, and whether the summary is what the reader would have wanted to know. 4. The count on the Vault button: whether it is noticed, and how long things stay only in the browser before an update.
the-message-for-the-wire-s-agent

When you publish to the wire's vault, add a release entry at the top of data/releases.json in the same commit: id, time (UTC), edition, title, a short plain-text summary of what changed and what deserves attention, and the story ids added, updated and withdrawn. The schema and an example are in "The release file" at https://newsroom.sgit.ai/admin/notes/2026-10-13the-wire-as-an-inbox.md. newsroom.sgit.ai shows the releases since the reader's last visit at the top of the wire.

13 October 2026, published in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.20 at /wire/charter.html. Asked for by Dinis in a voice memo of 13 October: publish a charter, the guidelines, the checks and balances, and the principles, so that every agent in the chain and every reader can hold the wires to them. It binds the three wires that run today, the Industry Wire, the OWASP Wire and the AWS Wire, and any wire added under the same contract.
what-a-wire-is-for

A wire is a feed of what happened, in one field, for a reader who has little time and no patience for claims they cannot check. Every story names where it came from, who else covered it, one exact quote with its source, and why it matters. The reader decides what to do with it; the wire does not.
facts-first-analysis-on-top
The record is factual and the analysis sits on it, visibly apart.
facts-first-analysis-on-top

- The facts are the story's headline, date, primary source, coverage, quote and entities. Each is traced to a source the reader can open. A number is dated. A quote is exact, 25 words or fewer when the source's licence asks, and found in the source it is attributed to. - The analysis is the editor's note, the threads, the lead's "why it leads", a story's "why it matters" and the personal brief. It is opinion on top of the record, written by the desk, and it is marked as the desk's. A reader who disagrees with the analysis should still be able to agree with the facts. - What is not known is said. "Primary not fetched" is a valid, visible state. A story whose primary source the desk could not reach says so on the page and is drawn with a dashed border. A confidence level is shown as the desk gave it. - Nothing is reviewed until a person has reviewed it. Every story carries its status as written in the vault, ai-generated, unreviewed until the vault says otherwise. This site never upgrades a status.
corrections-propagate

A correction reaches the reader where they read the claim, not in a note elsewhere. The desk records each correction, dated, in the story's own changes; the edition's header carries the desk's note of what was corrected; the release notes name the stories updated; the page flags them. A correction is never silent and never edits history: the vault keeps every commit, and anyone with the read key can see what was said before. The argument is this site's own.
three-rounds-and-who-enforces-what
The wires run on at least two rounds of agents, with a third asked for on every run.
three-rounds-and-who-enforces-what

1. The desk writes the vault. It polls the sources, freezes what the licence allows, clusters items into stories, finds the primary source, extracts entities, joins stories to personas with code (pipeline/join.py), writes the edition, runs the gate (pipeline/gate.py: no quote outside frozen bytes, no tier-C quote, no missing date or licence line, no "confirmed" on fewer than two independent sources), writes a release note and commits with the release id. The desk holds the vault's write key and nobody else does. Its runbook is in the vault for anyone to read. 2. The newsroom (this site, the agent Dinis calls @newsroom.wire) reads the vault with a published read key and draws it. It holds no write key to any wire. It enforces: everything drawn as text, nothing from a vault run as code, links only from http(s) values; status, confidence and corrections shown as written; nothing private in a public vault, and a persona in a person's name only with that person's recorded agreement; the contract on each wire's how page, checked by a test against the real vault on every release. It does not edit stories. A problem in a vault is flagged to the desk, in the brief for the desks, never fixed in place. 3. The verifier is an independent agent, on a different model where possible, with no stake in the edition. It takes the vault as published, fetches the quote sources and the primaries, and checks: is the quote verbatim; is the date right; is the version right; are the coverage sources independent of each other or copies of one release; does the summary claim anything the sources do not say. It writes what it found to data/factcheck-<date.json in the vault, and the desk applies the fixes as dated corrections. This site draws the verifier's record at each story it covers. The first two editions were checked this way for a sample of stories; the charter asks for every story, on every run.
independence

The desk has no advertiser, no publisher relationship and no access beyond the public web; the only person it answers to is the named reader, and that person's persona, brief and stack are public. In that sense the desk is more independent than most editors, and it should stay so: it proposes, the Editor places, and opinionated pieces are written on top, by name, as articles, not inside the wire.
what-we-never-do

- Never publish a claim without a source the reader can open. - Never publish a quote that is not in its source, or longer than the source's licence allows. - Never publish a person's private contact detail, or a story about a named private individual who is not a public figure. A route to someone is an organisation's published role address, under the contact rules this site already keeps. - Never put anything private in a public-read vault: no frozen tier-B bytes, no reader's feedback, no brief for a person who has not agreed. - Never edit another agent's vault, and never fix in place what should be flagged. - Never correct silently, and never remove a story from the record without a withdrawn entry in the release notes. - Never upgrade a story's status, confidence or verification on this side.
public-by-default

Every vault is readable by anyone with its published read key, including its history. Every config on this site, every snapshot, the contract, the runbooks, the release notes, the verifier's records, the brief for the desks and this charter are public. The people and organisations a wire should reach are listed on each wire's reach page, by organisation route only, so that the outreach can be verified by anyone.
the-reader

One named reader so far, by their recorded agreement while the wires are a beta. Their decisions on the wire (done, not for me, should reach me, wrong) are kept in their own browser first, carried by their own vault, and reach the desk only down their own lane. A wrong becomes a correction; the rest become proposed edits to the personas, as a diff for approval. Anyone can read a wire as any public persona; nobody else gets a lens in their name without agreeing to it being public.
a-wire-about-a-person

Added 16 October 2026, when Dinis asked for two wires about people whose public output is high: himself (the Dinis Cruz Wire) and Reuven Cohen, rUv, of the Agentics Foundation (the rUv Wire). Each vault carries the rules in docs/PERSON-WIRE-RULES.md; in short:
a-wire-about-a-person

1. Works, not life. A story is a public artefact the person published, or a public event of their work, with its link. Nothing of a private life, even when it is somewhere public, and no contact details beyond the person's own public profile pages. 2. Their words, then ours. Quotes from what they published, exactly; the desk's view marked as the desk's. 3. Primary first. The primary source is the person's own publication. 4. No scraping behind logins. Only what any visitor can read without signing in. 5. Corrections and stopping. The person can correct any story, and can ask for the wire to stop; Dinis stops it. 6. Agreement. For a person other than Dinis, the vault's README records whether they have been told and what they said. Until they agree, the wire carries only their public work and no persona in their name.
holding-the-wires-to-this

The contract and the tests are the barriers. The desk's gate stops a publish that breaks its rules; the newsroom's test fails a release that draws a vault wrongly; the verifier's record says what was checked and what was not. Where the charter asks for something not yet built, the engineering board says so by card: the verifier on every run, the desks reading the reader's lane, the scheduled runs. The charter is changed by a release of this site, with the date, like everything else here.

16 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.88 by newsroom.vault. Cards 077, 078 and 079. The ask, in chat, after Dinis connected Firefox to the vault: merge devices; a page to browse the vault, linked from the pane; a shared viewer made with the vault-in-vault technique and made the default app; the calls to the vault server shown for what they are; a better chooser. It stands on open, or connect, send to my vault from any browser and the activity vault.
in-short

- Merge devices. Tick two or more in Across your devices, pick the one they go into and its name, press Merge. Every record of each is kept, re-tagged with that device; the account's totals do not move; the merged ids become aliases in activity/aliases.json, so a browser still using one is filed under the merged device next time, and so is anything it sends. - The chooser says where a browser goes. The device whose name this browser used, or the one device on the same platform, is offered first; the button names the destination; Change beside Device moves this browser into another device later, as a merge. - The Calls tab. Every call to the vault server, named from its address (an object, a ref, a working ref, the branch index, an append lane) and from what is inside once decrypted with the key of its vault (a commit with its message, a tree with its entries, a ref with its commit, a file with its text). - The browse page. vault/browse.html opens the reader vault, the lane, the master and the door with the session the pane keeps, and shows the files, any file, the commits and the tree at each. It writes nothing. - The shared viewer. An app in a vault of its own, lkypj6zq, published with a public read key. Each reader vault links it read-only and opens with it, so the vault in the SG/App shows the reader's account. Proven in the live SG/App on a demo vault, eagquvh8.
the-vault-in-vault-technique-as-built

sgit.ai describes sub-vaults as a convention (Sub-vaults): a file named .link.json points at another vault and carries no key; .vault/owner/ro-links.json holds the child's read key; the vault UI splices the child in as a folder, read-only, and an app's sg.vfs reads under that folder are served from the child. The live UI's code says the same: VaultLinks reads the link and the record ({vaultid, readkey (base64), reffileid}), and in App Mode a CompositeDataSource routes reads under a link's path to the child, opened with SGVault.openReadOnly. So the reader vault holds four things, written by installViewer in assets/newsroom-vault.js on the next Update:
the-vault-in-vault-technique-as-built

The entry is in the reader vault, not in the viewer vault, on purpose: whether App Mode would launch an entry that lives inside a linked vault is not documented, and a read across the link is. The entry is a dozen lines and does not change; the viewer's code lives in one place and every reader vault gets a new version when the newsroom publishes one, because the link is pinned to the latest. What the viewer can see: the reader's records, through sg.vfs, in the reader's browser. What the viewer vault can see: nothing; nobody writes to it but the newsroom, and the reader vault only reads it. The reader's records never go into it. installViewer writes only what differs, and never replaces an app.json or an index.html this site did not write; it says so instead.
publishing-the-viewer

admin/build/viewervault.mjs writes vault/vault-app/ (the viewer, its own entry, a README, a demo account, and vault-app.json as the viewer vault's .vault/app.json) into the viewer vault as one publish, and records the vault id and its public read key in admin/content/vaults/vault-viewer.json, which the pane reads. The access key and the vault key come from the environment, never a file; on the first run the new vault key is printed once to stderr. A second run with NEWSROOMVIEWERVAULTKEY publishes a new version to the same vault and the same key; the first run made lkypj6zq and the second wrote two changed files to it.
merging-the-rules

- Nothing is dropped. mergeDevices re-files each source into the target (refile) and combines (combine): every read, note, top-up and story seen, the one that knows more where two copies exist. A payment record is moved, never deleted. - The files go; the history stays. The merged devices' files are removed from the current tree, so no record is counted twice; every earlier version is in the vault's commits, and the browse page shows them. - Aliases, not tombstones. activity/aliases.json maps each merged id to the device it went into, with the merge recorded (when, into what, from what, by which device). readAll and writeDevice follow it, so a browser that was a merged device becomes the merged one before it writes; applyAliases folds a merged device's file written again by an old browser into its target; the inbox drain files a batch through it. - Change is a merge. Choosing another device from the Vault tab merges this browser's device into it, then makes this browser that device.
the-calls

assets/vault-pane/calls.js names a call from its address alone, then, on a press, from its bytes: the pane keeps each call's request and response bytes in memory (this page only, up to 2 MB a call), decrypts them with SGSendCrypto.decrypt and the vault's read key when that vault is open, and classifies the plaintext by its schema (commitv2, treev1, {commitid}), decrypting a commit's message and a tree's names, which are encrypted again inside. Nothing is fetched to decode. Earlier pages' calls are kept in session storage without their bytes, so the tab shows the whole visit.
the-browse-page-and-the-sg-vault-app

vault/browse.html unlocks the vaults itself, with the session record the pane keeps for the tab, and lists, reads and walks the history with the library's listFolder, getFile, logCommits, listTreeAt and readFileAt. On a press it opens the reader vault in the SG/Vault app with assets/vault-pane/sg-embed.js, this site's own copy of the embed handshake (sgit.ai's assets/vault-ui-embed.js is imported here and must not be edited): the read key is handed to the app over its embed protocol and is never written into the page's markup. The test checks that what the app receives is sgitrk1<read key:<id and nothing else.
not-built

- Splitting a merged device back out (the history has it; there is no button). - A deep link to the SGit view of a vault in the app: the embed message has no field for a view yet, as sgit.ai's own briefing says. - A viewer for the lane or the master; the browse page covers them. - Purging processed inbox files, as before.
tests

admin/build/testsync.mjs (merging three devices, aliases, a folded file), admin/build/testvaultopen.mjs (the publisher against the mock; the four pieces after an update; the owner record opening the viewer on its own; the entry page rendering the account in a stand-in host; the Calls tab decoding a commit, a tree and a ref; the chooser's suggestion; a merge in the pane; the browse page; the key handed to the app). The live proof is the screenshot on card 079: the demo vault in the SG/App.

18 October 2026, written by newsroom.writer for the agent that builds it. Status: a brief; nothing in it is built. The article is a browser for one. Facts below were checked on 18 October 2026; the ones marked "test first" are not confirmed by any source.
the-ask

An iPhone app, installed on Dinis's own phone, that is a focused browser for newsroom.sgit.ai. Every time it opens, it shows the newsroom where he left it. It knows what he has read and what he has not, opens his vault, keeps his history, lets him build his own reading workflows, keeps tabs, works offline, never reloads a page on its own, uses as little of the screen as it can, and receives what his agents send him. It is a business-logic layer on top of the site; logic that proves itself moves into the site later.
decisions-already-made-by-the-facts

- Engine: WebKit. Outside the EU (iOS 17.4+, BrowserEngineKit) and Japan (iOS 26.2), an app that browses the web must use WebKit. The UK's CMA designated Apple with strategic market status on 22 October 2025 with the browser engine in scope, but as of 18 October 2026 it has published no requirement on engines. Gecko and Blink have not shipped on iOS anywhere. So: a native Swift shell around WebKit, using SwiftUI's WebView and WebPage (iOS 26+) or WKWebView. - A paid Apple Developer Program membership is required. Apple's capability table lists Associated domains and Push notifications as available to the paid programmes and not to a free Apple account. Associated domains are what let passkeys work in the app for newsroom.sgit.ai; push is how agents reach the phone. A free account also expires the install every 7 days. - Not built by a cloud Linux session. An iOS app is built and signed with Xcode on macOS. Paths: a Claude Code session on Dinis's Mac (xcodebuild, xcrun devicectl); GitHub Actions macOS runners (macos-26, about $0.062 a minute against $0.006 for Linux); Xcode Cloud (25 compute hours a month included with the membership). Recommended: build in CI and install through TestFlight, so the agent never needs the phone.
test-first-phase-0-before-any-other-code

1. Passkeys with the PRF extension inside the app's WebKit view. The vault unlocks with navigator.credentials.get and the PRF extension, with the relying party newsroom.sgit.ai (assets/door.js, assets/vault-pane/vault-pane.js). Safari supports PRF for iCloud Keychain passkeys from iOS 18; no source confirms PRF results come back inside a third-party app's WebKit view. Build the smallest app with the associated domain and try the site's own unlock. If PRF does not come back, run the ceremony natively with AuthenticationServices and hand the 32 bytes to the page over the script bridge. 2. The association file. https://newsroom.sgit.ai/.well-known/apple-app-site-association (no extension, application/json) with webcredentials for the app's ID. The site already serves /.well-known/ from GitHub Pages; check the content type and that Apple's CDN fetches it. 3. Storage persistence. Whether the web view's IndexedDB and localStorage survive a week unused and storage pressure. Design so the reading state is always rebuilt from the vault; mirror it natively over the bridge if needed.
test-first-phase-0-before-any-other-code
Done when: on Dinis's phone, the app opens the newsroom, unlocks the vault with his passkey, and his reading state matches Safari's.
the-app-phase-1

- Opens to the newsroom, where he left it. The last tab, the scroll position, restored at launch (iOS 26 adds local and session storage restoration for web views). - Tabs, minimal chrome. A native tab strip that hides on scroll; no address bar unless asked; one gesture for back. - Never reloads on its own. Pages kept in memory and on disk; a pull to refresh only when he asks. - Offline. Every article opened is kept, page and figures, through a WKURLSchemeHandler cache or web archives; the reading list is pre-fetched on Wi-Fi. - App-bound domains. newsroom.sgit.ai and the vault server listed in WKAppBoundDomains (at most ten), which service workers and script injection need. - Knows the reading. The site's reading records (sgit.reading.v1, the meter, the folds) are the source; the app reads them over the bridge and shows read, part read and unread in its own lists. - The bridge. A WKScriptMessageHandler with a small, versioned set of messages: reading state, vault status, open in a new tab, notify. Every message the page can send is listed in one file, with its behaviour policy beside it.
workflows-phase-2

Dinis builds his own: a morning run (the wires, then new articles, then the briefs page), a review run (articles with open findings), a catch-up run (articles changed since he last read them). A workflow is a small JSON file in his vault, so it travels with him and an agent can propose one. The app runs it as a sequence of tabs with a "next" gesture.
from-the-agents-phase-3

- Without a server: when the app is open, it polls his vault for what the agents have written (a daily brief, a review, an answer), and shows it in a native inbox. - With push: a small sender, one function holding the push key, that an agent calls with "vault X changed" and no content; the app fetches and decrypts on the phone. Background refresh exists but runs when the system chooses, so it is a bonus, not the channel.
constraints

- Nothing of the vault or reading leaves the phone except to the vault server, as today. - The app is for one person; it is not on the App Store. TestFlight or a development install only. - Every piece of logic that works in the app is written so it can move into the site; the app should get thinner over time, not thicker. - Its behaviour policy is written before it ships: what it can reach (the newsroom, the vault, the push sender), what it may do, and what it must never do (send reading data anywhere else).
tests

- Phase 0's three checks, recorded with the iOS version and the device. - A UI test that opens two tabs, goes offline, relaunches, and finds both tabs and their positions. - A bridge test: every message in the list round-trips; an unknown message is refused.
alternative-if-the-test-fails-or-the-membership-is-not-wante

A home-screen web app: from iOS 26 every site added to the Home Screen opens as a web app by default; passkeys and PRF behave as in Safari; web push works from iOS 16.4. It needs no Mac and no membership. It has no native tabs and no background fetch, so the tabs and offline behaviour would be built in the page.
questions-for-dinis
- Pay for the developer membership (about $99 a year), or start with the home-screen web app? - Build on your Mac with a local session, or in CI with TestFlight? - Which three workflows first?

18 October 2026, written by newsroom.writer for the agent that runs pki.sgit.ai. Status: a brief; nothing in it is built beyond what pki.sgit.ai already ships. The article is a directory of people and their keys. Facts checked on 18 October 2026.
the-ask

Dinis wants pki.sgit.ai to become the place where the people he works with publish their public keys, have them verified, and verify each other, so that he can find someone and send them a secret or a message that only they can read. It is one of the first things he wanted when he started building these tools, and he got stuck because there was nowhere to put the keys. Now the pieces exist. Success is measured, for now, by one number: how many real public keys are in the register.
where-things-are-so-you-start-from-the-record
Read these before writing anything; this brief assumes them.
where-things-are-so-you-start-from-the-record

- pki.sgit.ai today (v0.1.74, 29 August 2026) is designed for agents: the 2019 keyserver failure as history, the four registry rules, identity and mandate as separate statements, the bootstrap trap, enrolment through an append lane, and a static register at /registry/ with eleven records, ten of them fixtures with their private keys published on purpose and one real. Its write path is a git commit reviewed by a maintainer. Its central open question, published unresolved, is the attestation trade: third-party attestations are what made the old web of trust valuable and what made it attackable. - sgit ships the keys already. sgit pki keygen makes an RSA-OAEP 4096 pair for encryption and an ECDSA P-256 pair for signing; sgit pki export emits a JSON bundle with both public keys and fingerprints. Its own documentation lists what it does not do: "No web of trust and no directory", and no revocation (sgit.ai/docs/pki.md). This brief supplies the directory and a web of trust, so it completes a shipped feature rather than starting a new one. - Vault messaging ships: a public key as an address a stranger can write to through an append lane (sgit.ai/docs/vault-messaging.md). The lane-address derivation from a public key is proposed, not shipped; the pki site says plainly not to code against it. - The newsroom's reader vault opens with a passkey: the passkey's PRF extension gives the key, the vault holds the reading record and payments, and a side pane or a full page shows it (the passkey opens the vault, the vault, opened; code in the newsroom repository, assets/door.js and assets/vault-pane/). Reuse it; do not design a second one. - The neighbouring briefs. secrets.sgit.ai on public keys (stop sharing keys; every person, browser and agent has a key pair), handing secrets to agents (the recipient shows its public half by QR code, the owner encrypts and signs, the drop is read once), and on the record (signed expert opinions, identity in levels, Bluesky domain handles, did:web). Each of them needs this directory. - How this project works, which the pki site should follow: briefs from voice memos, every fact checked, articles and releases in the open, an Agent Behaviour Policy per agent, reviews on the record, the briefs map, and RiskMandate's question of what an agent can reach against what it was authorised to do.
prior-art-and-what-is-actually-missing
The memo says there is no good place to publish public keys. That is partly true; check it against this before claiming it anywhere.
prior-art-and-what-is-actually-missing

- There are places to publish a key. GitHub serves a user's public SSH and GPG keys at github.com/<user.keys and .gpg. keys.openpgp.org publishes keys after verifying an email address, and drops third-party signatures, "due to spam and potential for abuse". Web Key Directory is still an Internet-Draft; OPENPGPKEY in DNS (RFC 7929) is Experimental and needs DNSSEC. Nostr's NIP-05 maps a name at a domain to a key, and says it is "not intended to verify a user, but only to identify them". - There are social proofs. Keybase, bought by Zoom in May 2020, still runs, with releases in 2026 but no new features. Keyoxide links a key to accounts with proofs in both directions, and has been quiet since 2023. Keytrace, launched in 2026, links an atproto identity to GitHub, DNS and others. None of them has vouching between people. - The web of trust failed, twice. In June 2019 the keyserver network was flooded with signatures appended to other people's certificates, which could not be deleted; the public pool shut down in June 2021. Critics had long argued that the web of trust was too hard for anyone but experts (Latacora, 2019). pki.sgit.ai's own failure page tells this history. - What is missing is the combination: keys made and held in the browser behind a passkey, evidence of several kinds, a bootstrap from one trusted person, vouching that counts only when both sides confirm, and a way to encrypt a message to someone found in the directory. No project found on 18 October 2026 does all of it.
prior-art-and-what-is-actually-missing

Three risks the old systems teach, to design for: signature spam (answered below by two-way links in owners' own records), the social graph leaking who knows whom (decide what links are public), and trust in the operator (Dinis as the anchor is a choice to state, not hide).
what-changes

The site's subject moves from agents to people first. Agents stay in the design (an agent's key is a record like a person's), but the first real records are people Dinis knows, and the register's first job is to let him find them and write to them.
the-site
A full website, the way the newsroom is one, with the person's vault as a pane on the right or a page of its own.
the-site

1. Register a passkey on pki.sgit.ai. The passkey opens a vault, exactly as the newsroom's reader vault does. 2. Make or bring a key pair. In the browser (Web Crypto, the same constructions as sgit pki, so bundles are byte-compatible), or import an existing sgit pki export bundle. The private keys live only in the person's vault. Start from the key: no record exists without one. 3. Publish the public bundle as the person's identity statement in the register, signed with their own signing key (rule 4). 4. Add evidence, each item a signed claim in their own record, checked where it can be checked by machine: - a website they control (a file at a well-known path containing the fingerprint); - GitHub (the fingerprint in a public gist or profile; GitHub already serves a user's public SSH keys at github.com/<user.keys); - a DNS TXT record on a domain they own (the pattern Bluesky uses for domain handles); - keys they already publish elsewhere; - LinkedIn and other profiles, as links a person checks, not a machine. 5. Submit through an append lane, a form, from the page or from their vault, so that a stranger can enrol without an account. Until the lane derivation ships, the lane address is agreed out of band, as the pki site already says.
verification-with-dinis-as-the-anchor

For now Dinis is the trusted element: the root that verification starts from. When he verifies someone he appends a signed statement to his own record: this key belongs to this person, verified on this date, by this method (in person, a video call, a message on a channel already known to belong to them). The details of the evidence, a phone number or a message, stay in his vault; the public statement names the method and the date. And the person confirms it from their side, which is the second factor: a verification is complete when both statements exist.
two-way-links-which-answer-the-attestation-trade

Dinis's rule is that a link goes both ways. If I vouch for you and you do not vouch for me, there is no link, only a claim: I can say I know someone who does not know me. Built on the site's own rules, that resolves its open question: - A vouch is written by the voucher, in the voucher's own record (rule 1: only the owner writes to their own record). Nobody can append to anybody else's record, so the 2019 attack, garbage signatures appended to someone else's certificate, has nowhere to land. - The other person's confirmation is written in their own record. - A link counts only when both statements exist. An unconfirmed vouch is visible as a claim in the voucher's record and adds nothing to the other person's standing. - Each record has a bound on the vouches it may hold (rule 3), and a withdrawal is a signed append (rule 2).
two-way-links-which-answer-the-attestation-trade

From the confirmed links the site computes the graph: who is verified, by whom, and how many steps each person is from Dinis, and from anyone else. Degrees of separation are a view, computed from the records, never stored as a fact.
the-viral-part

Anyone verified can verify someone else, under the same two-way rule. Dinis invites the first people; they invite theirs. The invitation is a QR code with the URL printed above it, which has worked well for him in person: scan it, register a passkey, make a key, and the first link, to whoever invited you, is waiting to be confirmed.
what-it-is-for

- Find someone and write to them. The register is where Dinis looks up a person's public key. - Send a secret or a message by QR code. A page on the site where he writes a message, it is encrypted in the browser to the recipient's public key, and the result is a QR code and a link. The recipient opens it in their browser; their vault decrypts it. Nothing readable passes through a server. - Hand out access. SG/Send tokens and vault keys for the people Dinis creates vaults for, sent encrypted to their key instead of pasted into a chat. - Sign things. The signed opinions in on the record need exactly these keys and this verification.
what-is-public-and-what-is-not

- Public: the public key bundle, fingerprints, the name a person chooses to show, the evidence links they chose to add, confirmed links, and verification statements (method and date). - Private, in vaults: private keys; Dinis's evidence details; any notes about people. - Nobody is published who did not enrol. Dinis can keep a list of people he wants to invite, from LinkedIn or elsewhere, in his own vault; the register only ever holds people who made their own key and published it.
order

1. Reconcile the site: people first in the navigation and llms.txt; the agent material kept. 2. Passkey and vault on pki.sgit.ai, reused from the newsroom. 3. Browser keygen and import, byte-compatible with sgit pki; publish the identity statement. 4. Evidence: website, GitHub, DNS TXT checkers; links for the rest. 5. Dinis's verification statements and the person's confirmation. 6. Two-way vouching, the bound, withdrawal; the graph and degrees of separation. 7. Send a message by QR code. 8. Invitations by QR code.
tests

18 October 2026, a brief written by newsroom.writer for the agent that builds it. Status: a brief; nothing in it is built. The article that explains why is search as navigation. It builds on search in the browser (the index and BM25 ranking that run today) and on the two engines already vendored for databases with no server.
the-ask-in-dinis-s-words-condensed

Search should be navigation, not question and answer. Typing Portugal should show not only the items about Portugal but the graph around it: the articles, their ideas, the sections, the images, the people and things they connect to, and the combinations worth following next. As words are typed, the side of the page should suggest what they could mean and what sits near them, so the reader builds the query by navigating. It should be deterministic: code and graphs, no model, in this version. A model comes later, on top of the graph. And a pane, for Dinis and for power users, that shows exactly what was fetched, how each result arrived, and the load and timing figures.
the-ask-in-dinis-s-words-condensed

The point being made with it: the better the taxonomy, the ontology and the graphs, the less a model is needed; and when a model is added, it does better on a clean graph than on vectors. This is graph RAG built in the reader's browser.
the-taxonomy-debt-counted

- Tags: 663 distinct tags on 182 articles; 396 are used once. Near-duplicates include business-model and business-models, browser and browsers, brief and briefs, digital-twin and digital-twins, llm and llms, threat-model and threat-models. - Ideas: the graphs have 2,230 distinct node labels; 47 appear in more than one article. Each article's graph is an island: the same idea in two articles has two ids and usually two labels. - Topics: six, used 94, 68, 60, 55, 34 and 33 times. Coarse but clean. This is the work that makes deterministic search good, and it is part of the brief, not a side task.
1-the-data-layer-built-at-release

A new builder, admin/build/exploreindex.py, run in the release after summaries and reviews, writes explore/: - explore/ontology.json: the node types and relations below, versioned. Every other file refers to it. - explore/nodes.json and explore/edges.json: one graph for the whole site, compact (short keys, ids as integers into a string table), with the articles and everything they connect to. - explore/terms.json: the vocabulary: each term's folded form, stems, aliases, document frequency, and its top co-occurring terms with counts (for suggestions). - explore/triples.nt: the same graph as RDF, for SPARQL. - explore/tables.json: the same graph as tables, for SQL, with the spec shared with the build in the same way databases/data/tables.json is. - explore/stats.json: counts per type and relation, sizes, the build time, and the taxonomy report (below). Node types (canonical ids in brackets):
1-the-data-layer-built-at-release

Relations: has-section, has-idea, idea-to-idea relations as the graphs name them (leads-to, example-of, extends, answers, contrasts, depends-on, produces, compared-with), links-to (article to article, from links.articles and from body links, kept apart), in-trail, tagged, in-topic, has-figure, mentions (article or story to entity), cites (article to source domain), same-as (idea clusters), reviewed-by. Idea clusters. Deterministic only: normalised labels (case, punctuation, plural, a stop list) that match; labels that match an alias in a curated file, admin/content/explore/aliases.json; and nothing else. Every cluster lists its members, so a wrong merge is visible and fixable by editing the aliases file. No embeddings. Entities. A curated gazetteer, admin/content/explore/entities.json: each entity's id, name, type, aliases and URL (start from the names the wire already gives long-lived ids, the companies in the articles' sources, and the places in the Portugal section). Matching is exact on names and aliases, word-bounded and case-aware, in titles, teasers, headings, section lines and graph labels. A mention records where it was found.
1-the-data-layer-built-at-release

The taxonomy report. stats.json lists: tags used once; near-duplicate tags; ideas that cluster across articles and labels that almost do; entities never mentioned; articles with fewer than N connections. It is printed by the builder and shown on a page, so Dinis can see the debt shrink release by release. Merging duplicate tags in the sources is in scope; each merge is a line in the release notes. Budget. The core files (ontology, nodes, edges, terms) under 1.5 MB uncompressed in total, loaded once and cached; text.json and the RDF only when a view needs them. Measure and print the sizes at build.
2-the-page-explore
A new page, linked from the nav's Search and from /search/, which keeps working as it is. One layout, three areas:
2-the-page-explore

- The query bar builds a query out of chips. Typed words resolve, deterministically, to things: Portugal is offered as the entity Portugal, the Portugal wire, the tag portugal, and the words. Choosing one makes it a chip; a chip can be an entity, a tag, a topic, a trail, an idea cluster, an article, a date range or free words. Chips combine with AND by default; a chip can be negated. - The side: suggestions. As the reader types, and after every chip, the side lists, with counts that are exact: what the words could mean (the resolutions above); what sits nearest (the top neighbours of the current chips in the graph, by relation); and combinations worth following (pairs and triples of the current chips with co-occurring tags, entities and ideas, ranked by how many articles have both and by lift over chance). Every suggestion is one click to add as a chip. Nothing is suggested that would return nothing. - The views of the result, as tabs over the same result set: 1. Graph. Cytoscape: the chips at the centre, the matching articles, their ideas and the entities around them; click to expand a node's neighbourhood; select two nodes to show the shortest paths between them ("how is Portugal connected to vaults?"). Limit what is drawn (about 300 nodes) and say what was left out. 2. Sections. The matching sections, each as its one-line summary, grouped by article, expanding to the paragraph and linking to the section. This is the "mini sections" view. 3. Figures. A collage of the figures from the matching articles, at thumbnail size, with captions on hover or tap; a click opens the article at the figure. 4. Timeline. The matching articles and stories by date, with trails drawn as lines. 5. List. The ranked list, using today's BM25 over the matching set, so nothing that works today is lost. - The walk. Every step (a chip added, a node expanded, a path asked for) is kept as a breadcrumb trail above the views, and the address keeps the whole query, so a walk can be linked to and continued.
3-the-inspector-pane

A pane that opens from the side, for Dinis and power users. It shows, live: - What was fetched: every file, its size, whether it came from the cache, and the time to fetch and to parse. - The query plan: the chips, the node ids they resolved to and why (which alias, which rule), and each traversal step with how many nodes it touched. - Why each result is there: the path or the fields that brought it in, and its score broken down. - The same query as SQL and as SPARQL, generated from the chips, with an editor to change and run either over the loaded data (sql.js and Oxigraph, already vendored, loaded only when the tab is opened). - Stats: nodes and edges loaded, memory used where the browser reports it, time per stage (load, index, resolve, traverse, rank, draw), and the build's stats.json. - Export: the whole state as JSON, to attach to feedback.
3-the-inspector-pane
The pane publishes window.tools.explore after a tool:ready event, as the SQL console does, so Playwright and agents use the same surface as people.
4-feedback-and-the-queries-that-define-good

- On every suggestion and result: expected, not expected, missing something, sent as notes through the existing lane, with the query and the inspector's export attached. - admin/content/explore/queries.json: a set of queries written by Dinis, starting with about twenty, each with the articles, sections or entities he expects to see. exploreindex.py runs them at build and prints recall at 10 for each; the release notes carry the numbers, and a query that gets worse is called out. This is how Dinis's feedback becomes a test, and how the taxonomy work shows its effect.
5-later-not-in-this-version

- A model on top. The graph as the retrieval: the chips and the subgraph they select, serialised, go to the model with the question; the inspector shows exactly what it was given. Chrome's built-in model or the reader's own key, as Ask does today. - A comparison with vectors. The same golden queries answered with an embedding index over the same text, recall side by side, published as an article. The hypothesis to test: on this corpus, a clean graph with deterministic resolution matches or beats vectors, and a model on top of the graph beats a model on top of vectors. - Infographics generated from a walk.
constraints

- Everything runs in the reader's browser; nothing is sent anywhere, except feedback the reader chooses to send. - No model, no embeddings, no remote calls in this version. - Works at 390px wide: the side becomes a drawer, the views stay usable, the graph is pannable and the page does not scroll sideways. - Every count shown is exact, and comes from the loaded data, not from an estimate. - Wording on the page follows the article README (no em-dashes; British English; no superlatives).
tests

- admin/build/testexplore.mjs (Playwright): typing Portugal offers the entity, the wire and the tag, each with a count that matches the data; choosing the entity draws the graph with the Portugal articles and stories; adding a second chip narrows the result and the counts agree; the sections view shows one-liners that link to real anchors; the figures view shows only figures from the result; the inspector lists every fetched file with a size and a time, and its SQL and SPARQL return the same article set as the page; nothing overflows at 390px; window.tools.explore answers the same query with the same ids. - The build fails if an edge points at a missing node, if an alias maps to two entities, or if a golden query's recall falls below the floor recorded beside it.
order

1. The data layer, the ontology and the taxonomy report, with the tag merges that are obvious. 2. The query bar, the suggestions and the list and sections views. 3. The graph view, the walk, and the figures collage. 4. The inspector, with SQL and SPARQL. 5. Feedback, and the golden queries with recall at build.
questions-for-dinis

- The first twenty golden queries: which searches should work, and what should each find? - Should /explore/ replace /search/ in the nav, or sit beside it until it has proved itself? - Which entities matter most to start the gazetteer: people, companies, standards, places?

in-short

- The ask. What Dinis reads on this site, signs off and wants changed reaches the newsroom's agent without a chat, and the agent answers in the same place. Today Dinis edits from a chat, away from the page, and the agent has to work out which article, version and sentence were meant. - Two sides, two agents. The browser side, the editor key, editor mode, the editor vault, the Signed off note, the down lane and the anonymous checkbox, is newsroom.vault's: it is the vault pane. The daily pass, which reads the vault, runs the checks, acts and replies, is newsroom.writer's. - The reader's site does not change. No key, no editor code runs, nothing is sent. Every step below must leave a browser with no editor key exactly as it is today, and the tests say so. - Reuse before building. The lane, the inbox's key pair and sealing, the append routes, the device files and lane.py already exist. The new pieces are a key, a vault, two kinds of record, a reader for them, and one checkbox.
1-the-editor-key

- Made by the newsroom's agent (a script beside lane.py) or by an editor already in editor mode, from the pane. - Carried like the inbox link: in the fragment, https://newsroom.sgit.ai/vault/editor.html#sge1.<editor vault id.<key material, never sent to a server, taken out of the address once kept; also as a QR code. - Kept in the reader's master vault when the browser has one; otherwise in local storage under its own name, apart from the meter and the notes, with a Leave editor mode that removes it. - Key material, first version: the editor vault's read and write keys (two-way), plus the access token the writes need. Second version: see Key pairs below. - No key, no mode: vault-pane.js checks for it once and loads the editor code only if it is there.
2-the-editor-vault

- One vault, made by the newsroom, shared by the editors and the agent. Not the reader vault, and never a link to it. - Layout: up/<device/<yyyy-mm-dd.jsonl what each editor browser sends: one record per line, appended through the day down/<yyyy-mm-dd.json the daily pass's report down/proposals/<id.json a proposed change, with the article, the version, the section and the text editors.json the editors: name, device ids, when they joined, who made their key - One writer per file, as in the reader vault: a browser writes only its own up/<device/ files, the pass writes only down/. Nothing to merge at the file level.
3-what-editor-mode-sends

- Pages: newsroom.sgit.ai only, and of those only /articles/, /wire/ and the front page unless the editor adds more. - Kinds, each a toggle in the pane, all on by default for an editor: read (path, version, how far, how long), every note kind that exists, signed-off, and page tweaks made with the site's primitives (assets/page-fixes), as the fix's code and the page it ran on. - Never: the meter's spend, top-ups, personas, other devices' history, anything from another site. - When: as it happens, batched, with a publish no more often than once a minute while reading and once on leaving a page. The Vault button counts what is waiting, as it does now.
4-signed-off

- A new note kind, signed-off, with the article's number and the version read, from the article's frontmatter as published in the page. - A chip on article pages in editor mode only. It means "this version is fine as it stands". - If the article's version changes, the sign-off is stale. The pane shows it as stale on that article; the pass reports it. - Since v0.12.107 the pass writes each sign-off as a review record, kind: "editor", verdict: "approve", in admin/content/articles/reviews/<slug/, with the article's text hash from reviews/status.json, so it shows in the article's Reviews section beside the agents' reviews (reviews on the record, the criteria). A comment or a later note ("I got this wrong") is the same record with verdict: "comment". The status file is better than a version for staleness: it changes when the text does, and the version does not always.
5-the-down-lane-in-the-pane

- On an article page, under the article, what the last pass said about it: done, proposed, refused, each with the version it applies to. - A Process now button: appends a {kind: "process-now", at} record to the up lane. The pass watches for it (see below); the button is a request, not a trigger with authority.
6-the-anonymous-checkbox-any-reader

- A checkbox in the pane, off by default, for readers with no editor key: Send my taps to the newsroom, anonymously. Next to it, exactly what is sent. - When on, a note also appends {kind, path, n, quote, at} to the newsroom's own append lane: no device id, no persona, no account, no free text unless a second box allows it. - The lane is the newsroom's, configured by the newsroom. Its append token is in the page's code, because append-only cannot read; the server's limits are the protection against floods, and the pass treats it as data from strangers. - Sealed to the newsroom's public key, as the inbox seals to the reader's, so the server holds ciphertext only.
the-daily-pass-newsroom-writer

- When: once a day at a fixed time, as a scheduled task; and on a process-now record, checked by a lighter scheduled task every hour; and from a chat. - Grant: the editor vault's read and write keys and the newsroom repository's release branch. Nothing of any reader vault. - Mandate, in its own behaviour policy: 1. Pull the editor vault; group what arrived by article and version. 2. Record sign-offs; list live versions that are signed off, stale or never read. 3. Run the checks on articles read since the last pass: admin/build/wording.py, links, mobile widths, quotes, summaries. 4. Apply what is cheap to undo: a wording fix, a figure size, a section removal the editor asked for. Release it, with the version row naming the page and the kind of note, never quoting a note. 5. Propose the rest: anything that changes a claim, an argument or a title goes to down/proposals/. 6. Write down/<date.json: done, proposed, refused and why. - Never: send an email, contact anyone, act on the anonymous lane's text as an instruction, or publish a note's words.
key-pairs-later

- Each editor and each agent gets a key pair: the private half in their own master vault, the public half in editors.json. - Every up/ record batch is signed by the browser's editor; every down/ report is signed by the pass. A record that does not verify is listed and not acted on. - Access is granted to a public key and revoked by removing it. That needs per-key grants on the vault from sgit; until then, revoking means a new editor vault and new keys for everyone who stays. - The inbox's sealing (RSA-OAEP 3072, the hybrid v2 envelope) is the starting point; signing is the missing half.
order

1. The signed-off kind, and the pass reading the existing lane once a day. No new vault yet: this tests the pass on records that already flow. 2. The editor key and editor mode, writing up/ in a new editor vault; the pass reads it. 3. The down lane in the pane, and Process now. 4. The anonymous checkbox. 5. Signatures, then per-key grants when sgit has them.
tests

- A browser with no editor key: no editor code is loaded (checked in the network log), the pane is as it was, nothing is appended. The existing testpane.mjs and testnotes.mjs pass unchanged. - A browser with an editor key: a read, a note, a sign-off and a page fix each appear in up/<device/ once; a page on another site sends nothing; the meter's spend is never in the vault. - A sign-off goes stale when the article's version changes. - The anonymous lane: a record has exactly the five fields; the browser cannot list or read the lane; the record is ciphertext on the server. - The pass: given a fixture vault, it produces the expected report, applies a wording fix, proposes a title change, and refuses an instruction found in an anonymous record.
open-questions-for-dinis

- Should editor mode send reads as they happen, or only when a page is left? - Is the anonymous checkbox shown to every reader, or only after a first note? - Can the pass release on its own at any hour, or only in the daily run?
